units.la: VAM necessaria sit VIRI amplissimi, ac prudentissimi, ad beatam illam immortalitatem, vitam, ac salutem æternam consequendam, Iesu Christi, Domini, Redemptoris, ac Saluatoris nostri, & beneficiorum spiritualium, nobis per ipsum partorum, notitia & cognitio, non quidem otiosa & sterilis, quæ frigida speculatione, & nuda atque eua-
units.tr: How necessary is the knowledge and recognition of Jesus Christ, our Lord, Redeemer and Saviour, and of the spiritual benefits obtained for us through him, for attaining that blessed immortality, life and eternal salvation, most distinguished and prudent sir? I do not mean an idle and barren knowledge, which ends in cold speculation and the bare, empty contemplation of truth,

units.la: 2 nida veritatis contemplatione terminatur ; sed viua illa, quæ bonis operibus ceu fructibus fœcunda,atque virtutumChri-stianarum splendore & ornamentis conspicua, cum serio ac sincero pietatis erga Deum,& charitatis erga proximum stu-dio coniuncta est, & quæ non aliunde, quam ex saluti-feræ doctrinæ Christi purissimis fontibus hauritur: vel ex eo liquet euidentissimè, quòd Iesus Christus in scientia sui multos iustificaturus esse dicitur, & ipsemet vitam æternam, id est, salutis æternæ in vnius veri Dei & sui cognitione si-tam esse testatur ; nec vllus etiam vere Christianus ignorat. Quàm perfectam vero fidei morumque regulam nobis præ-scribat,sanæta ipsius,ex cuius penu prædicta illa cognitio de-promitur,doctrina,quantaque autoritate, maiestate, digni-tate & potestate, eadem apud omnes pollere, & nos ad fi-dem,&obedientiæ ex fide obsequia obstringere debeat,ma-nifestum est, tum ex voce testimonioque & mandato ipsius Dei,ex nube lucida,Hic est Filius meus dilectus,in quo mihi bene placitum est,hunc audite, dicentis : quibus verbis Deus pater nos, quotquot ad cœlestem ac æternam beatitatem as-piramus,ad Christum tanquam vnicum Ecclesiæ Doctorem ac præceptorem,penes quem omnis magisterij præsideat au-toritas,reuocat,& ab omnibus omnium hominum doctrinis abductos, huic vni sistit, ab hoc vno omnem salutis doctri-nam, cunctaque sapientiæ cœlestis documenta petere, ab v-nius ore pendere, in vno hærere, & vnius voci auscultare iu-bet:tum etiam quòd Apostolus Paulus in Epistola ad Colo-senses, omnes illas pseudoapostolorum corruptelas & impo-sturas sophisticásque argutias, & quidquid sophismatum in humani ingenij cerebro fabricari potest, ad simplicitatis & puritatis Euangelicæ fontem lympidissimum turbandum, vnico hoc generali argumento,ceu ariete,subruit,prosternit, & funditus euertit, quod nimirum non sint secundum Christum, nec doctrinæ ac veritati ipsius consentanea, sed nos ab eo seducant, & vitam ac salutem æternam alibi quàm in ipso solo quærendam esse docceant. Et certè cùm Apostolus Petrus, in solo Christo salutis vitæque æternæ, ac benedictionum spiritualium omnium fontem & scaturiginem residere, nec aliud nomen, seu causam & medium sub cœlo inter homines datum esse palam affirmet, in quo nos oporteat salvos fieri; & alibi testetur ipsum verba vitæ æternæ, id est, doctrinam salutarem ac viuificam habere, per quam videlicet Deus suam in nobis salvandis virtutem & potentiam exerat; liquidò constat, salsissimam ac perniciosissimam esse doctrinâ aliam omnem, quàtumuis specioso rationis & sapientiæ humanæ fuco & titulo inducatur, pulchrisque & plausibilibus argumentis, &specioso rationis prætextu sese insinuet in animos hominum, quæ perfectam integramque salutem, non in solo Christo statuit, sed illius quærendæ & consequendæ alias rationes & alia adminicula confingit.
units.tr: but that living knowledge, which bears good works as its fruit, is conspicuous for the splendour and ornament of Christian virtues, and is joined with a serious and sincere zeal for piety toward God and charity toward our neighbour. Such knowledge is drawn from no other source than the purest springs of Christ's saving doctrine. This is most clearly shown by the fact that Jesus Christ says he will justify many by his own knowledge, and he himself testifies that eternal life, that is, eternal salvation, lies in the knowledge of the one true God and of himself. No truly Christian person is ignorant of this. How perfect a rule of faith and morals the wholesome doctrine of Christ, from whose store that knowledge is drawn, prescribes for us, and with what authority, majesty, dignity and power it ought to hold sway over all and bind us to faith and to obedience that springs from faith, is plain. It is plain both from the voice, testimony and command of God himself, out of the bright cloud, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him," and from the words by which God the Father calls us back, as many as aspire to heavenly and eternal blessedness, to Christ as the one Teacher and master of the Church, in whom resides the whole authority of teaching. Having led us away from all human doctrines, God bids us set ourselves before him alone, to seek from him alone every doctrine of salvation and every lesson of heavenly wisdom, to hang upon his lips, to cling to him alone and to listen to his voice alone. It is plain also from the fact that the Apostle Paul, in his Epistle to the Colossians, overthrows, levels and utterly destroys all those corruptions and impostures of false apostles, their sophistical subtleties, and whatever sophisms can be fashioned in the brain of human wit to trouble the most limpid spring of Evangelical simplicity and purity, with this one general argument, as with a battering-ram: namely, that they are not according to Christ and do not agree with his doctrine and truth, but lead us away from him and teach that life and eternal salvation are to be sought anywhere other than in him alone. And indeed, since the Apostle Peter plainly affirms that salvation, eternal life and all spiritual blessings reside in Christ alone, and that no other name, cause or means has been given under heaven among men by which we must be saved; and since he elsewhere testifies that he has the words of eternal life, that is, a saving and life-giving doctrine, through which God puts forth his power and might in saving us; it is clearly established that every other doctrine is most salty and most pernicious, however much it is introduced under the specious colour and title of human reason and wisdom, and however much it insinuates itself into men's minds with pleasing and plausible arguments and the specious pretext of reason, when it sets up a complete and whole salvation not in Christ alone but devises other methods and other aids for seeking and attaining it.

units.la: Quum deinde Christus character personæ, & splendor gloriæ paternæ sit, in quo inuisibilis illa Dei gloria ac maiestas velut in lucidissimo speculo refulget, nobisque quodammodo conspicienda præbetur, & perfecta imago Dei inconspicui, in qua operum diuinorum virtus, splendor, maiestas, & excellentia ita elucet, vt in ipso Christo mediatore ac χαρακτὴρ, tanquam expressa effigie, patris cœlestis gloriosa potentia, paterna voluntas, summa misericordia ac φιλανθρωπία, denique ineffabilis & πολυποίκιλος illa σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ nobis contemplanda proponatur: in ipso denique, qui in sinu Patris requiescens, solus omnium consiliorum ac secretorum ipsius conscius est, omnes sapientiæ ac scientiæ Dei thesauri repositi sint, totaque proinde iustitiæ, sanctitatis, virtutis, bonorumque omnium plenitudo inhabitet,&ex ipso ceu inexhausto,perenni & affluentissimo viuarum aquarum fonte,omnes benedictiones spirituales,omniaque beneficia ac dona Dei ad hoc vt sempiterna beatitate,omniumque bonorum Dei ineffabili torrente, & glorificata diuinitatis cömunione ( quæ in hac vita supra omnem captum est humanarum mentium) in æternum perfruamur,in nos redundent: quis non videt grauissimi ac perniciosissimi erroris, & summæ stultitiæ damnādam esse doctrinam illam, quæ sapientiæ, iustitiæ ac scientiæ perfectissimo colophone isto,nimirū Christo,non contenta,animos humanarū traditionū figmētis & deliriis imbuit · aliamq; vitæ ac salutis æternæ extra Christum consequedæ via ac rationem profitetur? Quum denique Christus non tantum summus noster Propheta sit,qui arcanum Dei consilium,decretum, ac voluntatem,de redemtione generis humani, & reconciliatione cum Deo,omnémque doctrinam, veritatem,ac scientiam, ad salutem ac vitam æternam consequendam necessariam, nobis fidelissimè patefecit,tum prædicatione Euangelii externa, quā ex Scripturæ Veteris Testamenti authoritate,& omnis generis argumentis ac signis, quibus doctrinæ alicuius diuina veritas,& infallibilis certitudo , demonstrari potest , confirmauit: tum illuminatione per Spiritum Sanctum interna , qua pulsis ac dissipatis cœlesti luce,natiuæ cæcitatis & ignorantiæ tenebris,mentes nostras sic illustrat, vt diuinam veritatem in verbo,& potentiam in operibus,agnoscere,& ad salutem nostram amplecti valeamus: verùm etiam fidelissimus Sacerdos & summus Pontifex, qui personæ, ac naturæ sanctitate,& vitæ summa integritate perfectissimus , seipsum hominem inculpatum , per Spiritum æternum , in sacrificium proprie ac veré propitiatorium , peccatis nimirum nostris in se vt sponsorem ac vadem nostrum deriuatis , in cruce , Deo obtulit,& sic extinctis peccatis, & morte, ac deleto, quod aduersum nos erat, chirographo, sedauit iram Dei, gratiámque eius amissam recuperauit, atque vnica pro peccatis oblata sui victima, remissionem peccatorum, æternam redemptionem, & Spiritum gratiæ, nobis impetrauit, maledictionem abstulit, iustitiam seculorum ac vitam æternam, quin & Ecclesiam, cui ista bona omnia communicantur, summámque super omnia in cœlo & in terra potestatem acquisiuit,& totum ius in vitam æternam,& quæcunque ad illam tum dandam,tum accipiendam sunt necessaria,adeptus,pro nobis apud Patrem indesinenter intercedit, & simul aduersus omnes accusationes, quas nobis & conscientiæ nostræ intentat aduersarius, potenter defendit: Denique Rex, ac Dominus noster,qui salutis, iustitiæ ac vitæ æternæ prophetia sua demonstratæ & sacerdotio partæ, electos reddit participes,ex statu videlicet peccati & miseriæ, ad fœderis æterni & gratiosi, proprio suo sanguine confirmati, participationem verbo & Spiritu illos vocando:Deinde etiam omnia bona, tum ad hac animalem, tum ad spiritualem vitam necessaria fidelibus communicat, Ecclesiam suam potenter tuetur, hostésque eius reprimit & coercet: Denique tanquam vniuersorum à Deo constitutus Iudex, sententiam iustificationis Electis suis pronuntiaturus, eosque in vitæ æternæ possessionem introducturus, aduersus reprobos verò sententia damnationis prolata, eos pœnis æternis affecturus est. Hoc est quum Christus sit via, veritas ac vita,& principium, medium atque finis salutis nostræ: ideo manifestum est, fraudulentos impostores agere omnes illos, quicunque præter aut contra doctrinam Christi in Euangelio comprehensam, traditionibus, ac legibus aliis, tanquam ad verum Dei cultum,& vitam æternam consequendam necessariis, conscientias onerant atque obstringunt,& ex obser uatione illarum, peccatorum remissionem, iustitiam ac salu-tem quærendam esse docent, totámque religionis ac pietatis summam in eis constituunt: ac proinde Paulum inanem il-lam ματαιολογίαν ac vniuersam traditionum humanarum colluuiem, firmissimo illo argumento simul ac semel conuellere atque euertere, quod nimirum non sint secundum Christum, & vitam ac salutem æternam alibi quam in solo Christo quæ-rendam esse doceant.
units.tr: Next, since Christ is the express image of the person and the brightness of the Father's glory, in whom that invisible glory and majesty of God shines as in the clearest mirror, and is in some measure set before us to behold; and since he is the perfect image of the unseen God, in whom the power, splendour, majesty and excellence of God's works so shine forth that in Christ the Mediator himself, as the character [χαρακτήρ], as an exact likeness, the glorious power of the heavenly Father, his fatherly will, his supreme mercy and loving-kindness [φιλανθρωπία], and finally the ineffable and manifold [πολυποίκιλος] wisdom of God [σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ] are proposed for us to contemplate; and since in him, who rests in the bosom of the Father and alone is conscious of all his counsels and secrets, all the treasures of God's wisdom and knowledge are stored up, and therefore the whole fullness of righteousness, holiness, virtue and of all good things dwells, and from him, as from an inexhaustible, perpetual and most abundant fountain of living waters, all spiritual blessings, all the benefits and gifts of God flow into us, so that we may enjoy in eternity the everlasting blessedness, the ineffable stream of all the good things of God and the glorified fellowship of the Godhead (which in this life surpasses all the grasp of human minds): who does not see that the doctrine which, not content with this most perfect capstone of wisdom, righteousness and knowledge, namely Christ, imbues men's minds with the fabrications and delusions of human traditions, and professes another way and method of attaining life and eternal salvation outside Christ, is to be condemned as a most grave and pernicious error and the height of folly? Finally, since Christ is not only our chief Prophet, who has most faithfully revealed to us the secret counsel, decree and will of God concerning the redemption of mankind and reconciliation with God, and all the doctrine, truth and knowledge necessary for attaining salvation and eternal life, confirming it both by the external preaching of the Gospel, from the authority of the Old Testament Scripture and by all kinds of arguments and signs by which the divine truth and infallible certainty of any doctrine can be demonstrated, and by the internal illumination of the Holy Spirit, by which, the darkness of our native blindness and ignorance having been driven off and dispelled by heavenly light, he so enlightens our minds that we may recognise the divine truth in the word and the power in the works, and embrace them for our salvation; but also he is the most faithful Priest and high Priest, who, most perfect in the holiness of his person and nature and in the highest integrity of his life, offered himself, a blameless man, through the eternal Spirit, on the cross to God as a sacrifice truly and properly propitiatory, since our sins had been imputed to him as our surety and bail; and so, with sins and death put to death and the handwriting that stood against us blotted out, he appeased the wrath of God and recovered his lost favour, and, having offered himself as the one victim for sins, he obtained for us the forgiveness of sins, eternal redemption and the Spirit of grace; he took away the curse, acquired everlasting righteousness and eternal life, and indeed the Church, to which all these good things are communicated, and supreme power over all things in heaven and on earth, and having obtained every right to eternal life and everything necessary both for giving and for receiving it, he ceaselessly intercedes for us with the Father, and at the same time powerfully defends us against all the accusations which the adversary brings against us and against our conscience. Finally, he is our King and Lord, who, through his prophetic office, which has demonstrated salvation, righteousness and eternal life, and through the priesthood obtained by his own sacrifice, makes the elect partakers, calling them by the word and the Spirit from the state of sin and misery into participation in the eternal and gracious covenant, confirmed by his own blood. Then too he imparts to the faithful all the good things necessary both for their animal and for their spiritual life, powerfully protects his Church, and restrains and checks its enemies. Finally, as the Judge appointed by God over all, he is to pronounce the sentence of justification on his elect and to bring them into possession of eternal life, but against the reprobate, after pronouncing the sentence of condemnation, he is to inflict eternal punishments. Therefore, since Christ is the way, the truth and the life, and the beginning, means and end of our salvation, it is plain that those are fraudulent impostors who, beyond or against the doctrine of Christ contained in the Gospel, burden and bind consciences with traditions and other laws as if they were necessary for the true worship of God and for attaining eternal life, and teach that forgiveness of sins, righteousness and salvation are to be sought from their observance, and place the whole sum of religion and piety in them. Accordingly, with that most firm argument, Paul at once and in a single stroke overthrows and destroys that vain babbling [ματαιολογία] and the whole sewer of human traditions, namely that they are not according to Christ, and teach that life and eternal salvation are to be sought anywhere other than in Christ alone.

units.la: Vt autem hæc personæ & officii Christi notitia ad salu-tem summè necessaria est, & ipsius doctrina integram fidei ac salutis nostræ summam & fundamentum in se complecti-tur perfectissimè: ita etiam cœlesti ipsius luci, grauissimorum ac perniciofissimorum errorum & hæresium pestilentissimarū præstigiis, maximæ tenebræ, seculis ac temporibus omnibus sunt offusæ. Acerrimè enim iam à multis seculorum periodis clarissimam eius veritatem impugnauerunt non tantum Iu-dæi, qui reiectis Noui Testamenti Scripturis, Messiam quidem promissum fatentur, sed exhibitum esse negant: Iesum Christum autem ex Maria Virgine natum execrantur, & hor-ribili odio prosequuntur, atque omnis generis nefandis blas-phemiis, indomita ac ineluctabili cum pertinacia proscin-dunt: Et Mahumetistæ (quæ mundi lues anno duodecimo Heraclij Imperatoris, sub extremo Pontificatu Bonifacij V. circa annum à Christo passo quingentesimum octuagesi-mum nonum, nata esse perhibetur) qui Christum magnum quidem & sanctum Prophetam, sed natura ac essentia me-ram ac nudam creaturam, nec reuera Dei filium, quippe quē Deus sine vxore gignere non potuerit, denique nec passum nec crucifixum esse, sed phantasma quoddam suppositum, & Iudæis oblatum fuisse, quod illi sic delusi ac decepti, pro Christo cruci affixerint, aliaque horrenda errorum monstra, ex omnium quasi turpissimarum haereseon lacunis & sordibus conflata & hausta, nefanda cum impietate profitentur: verum etiam Monarchici, Sabelliani, ac Noëtiani, qui statuêtes Patrem, Filium, ac Spiritum Sanctum unam eandemque hypostasin esse, quae variis nominibus, prout necessitas & usus exigit, appelletur, personas in S.S. Trinitate non tantum confundunt, sed omnia tollunt. Samosateniani deinde à Paulo Samosateno Ecclesiae Antiochenae Episcopo, Pauliani, & Paulianistae, atque ab haereseos illorum instauratore & propagatore, Photino, Photiniani appellati, qui docuerunt Christum Iesum natura esse <bl>φλον ἀνθρωπον</bl>, gratia divina tamen insigniter ornatum, eumque tum demum esse coepisse, cum in utero Virginis Mariae conciperetur, ac proinde verbum Dei vel Deum, non aliter in ipso, quam in aliis Prophetis habitasse, nec ipsi <bl>σημαντικῶς</bl> aut <bl>ὑποστατικῶς</bl> vnitum fuisse, sed tantum gratia & efficacia ipsi adsedisse: ipsum denique esse <bl>λόγον σαρκ</bl>, sed <bl>ωφελικὸν</bl> & <bl>ἀνυπόστατον</bl>, non autem <bl>διδακτικὸν</bl>, ut loquuntur, ex qua infelici haeresi postmodum Mahumetismus ortus esse perhibetur. Denique Arriani cum tota & amplissima sua prole ac propagine, qui Christum non verum atque aeternum Deum, sed creaturam, excellentem quidem, & caeteris dignitate praestantiorem, in tempore tamen <bl>ὡς ἐν ὑπο</bl> ante reliquas, creatam & conditam esse, ac proinde Deum appellari, non origine, sed operatione & gratia, quo Pater tanquam instrumento in rebus caeteris creandis sit usus, eundemque corpus tantum humanum, non vero animam etiam, quippe cuius partes & actiones diuinitas in eo expleuerit, assumpsisse, mordicus contenderunt. Ut nihil dicam de Ebionitis, Valentinianis, Apollinaristis, Marcionitis, Cerdonianis, Manichaeis, Nestorianis, Iacobitis, Eutychianis, Schwenckfeldianis, & Anabaptistis, quorum alij conceptionem Christi ex Spiritu Sancto, alij natiui-
units.tr: Just as the knowledge of this person and office of Christ is most necessary for salvation, and his doctrine perfectly comprehends the whole sum and foundation of our faith and salvation, so too his heavenly light has been surrounded by the deepest darkness in every age and time, through the deceptions of the most grave and pernicious errors and the most pestilential heresies. For from many periods of the centuries, not only the Jews have attacked his clearest truth most bitterly. They reject the Scriptures of the New Testament and confess that the Messiah was promised, but deny that he has been revealed. They curse Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, pursue him with horrible hatred, and tear him apart with every kind of impious blasphemy, with an untameable and inescapable obstinacy. The Mohammedans (a plague of the world, said to have arisen in the twelfth year of the Emperor Heraclius, under the last pontificate of Boniface V, about the 589th year after Christ's passion) profess with impious wickedness that Christ was indeed a great and holy prophet, but by nature and essence a mere, bare creature, not truly the Son of God, since God could not beget him without a wife. They also hold that he was neither suffered nor crucified, but that a certain phantasm was substituted and offered to the Jews, who, deceived and misled, nailed it to the cross in place of Christ, and other horrible monsters of error, compounded and drawn from the dregs and filth of almost all the most shameful heresies. Moreover, the Monarchians, Sabellians and Noetians, who hold that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and the same hypostasis, called by various names as need and usage require, not only confuse the persons in the Holy Trinity but abolish them altogether. Then the Samosatenians, called Paulians and Paulianists after Paul of Samosata, bishop of the Church of Antioch, and Photinians after Photinus, the restorer and propagator of their heresy, who taught that Christ Jesus by nature is a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον], but richly adorned with divine grace, and that he began to be only when he was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary. Therefore the Word of God, or God, dwelt in him no otherwise than in the other prophets, was not united to him significantly or hypostatically, but merely sat with him by grace and efficacy. Finally, they taught that he is the Word made flesh [λόγον σαρκ...], but useful and without hypostasis, not, as they say, didactic. From this unhappy heresy Mohammedanism is said to have arisen afterwards. Finally, the Arians, with their whole and very wide offspring and progeny, who stubbornly contended that Christ is not the true and eternal God but a creature, excellent indeed and more eminent than others in dignity, yet created and made in time before the rest [ὡς ἐν ὑπο...]. Therefore he is called God not by origin but by operation and grace, the Father having used him as an instrument in creating other things; and he assumed only a human body, not also a soul, since the divinity supplied its parts and actions in him. I say nothing of the Ebionites, Valentinians, Apollinarians, Marcionites, Cerdonians, Manichaeans, Nestorians, Jacobites, Eutychians, Schwenckfeldians and Anabaptists, some of whom deny the conception of Christ from the Holy Spirit, others his birth from Mary, others the truth of his human nature and essence, others his passion and death, others the union of the two natures in one person, and others finally their distinction.

units.la: * * tatem ex Maria, alij veritatem naturæ & essentiæ humanæ,alij passionem ac mortem: alij duarum naturarum in eadem persona vnionem, alij denique distinctionem earundem tollunt atque negant. Nihil deinde de impura Pelagianorum caterua, qui facto quasi agmine & impetu, scelerata manu in gratiam Dei irruunt & irrumpunt, aliisque infinitis errorum autoribus (quis enim omnia illa monstra sigillatim recenseat?) nihil denique de Pontificiis integra officii Christi vim ac naturam labefactantibus,ac beneficiorum spiritualium,veritatis ac gratiæ diuinæ fontem limpidissimum, non turbantibus modo,sed penitus obturatibus & occludentibus: Quorum omnium erroribus pestilentissimis ceu fluctibus, quàm grauiter salutifera doctrinæ Christi veritas exagitata, & quàm miserè Ecclesia Christi iisdem turbata ac vexata fuerit, cum experientia quotidiana, historiæ Ecclesiasticæ luculenter & abundè testantur. Et quamuis ad Arrij, Macedonij, Apollinaris,Sabellij,Nestorij,Eutychetis & aliorum impostorum atque Hereliarcharum in Ecclesiis grassantium, petulantiam refrænandam & compescendam, errores illorum nocentissimos profligandos, & ex agro Domini euellendos, celeberrima orthodoxa & Oecumenica, virisq; pietatis,eruditionis & virtutum excellentissimarum laudibus clarissimis,frequentissima concilia conuocata, & maximo cum fructu habita ac celebrata fuerint: nunquam tamen hæreses illas ita potuerunt eliminari, quin à patrono & fautore aliquo denuò instaurarentur, & quasi postliminio in Ecclesias reducerentur, nec vnquam radicitus funditusque extirpari (tam altas nimirum radices agit, & tam patulis sese diffundit ramis,vbi semel Ecclesiæ fundum ingreditur herefeos malum) quin femina aliqua, radices & surculi remanerent, qui postmodum repullascerent, & noua germina emitterent, sic vt ex turbidis illis errorum fontibus, impuri quidam torrentes, per tot seculorum interuallu, ad hanc vsque aetatem nostram perruperint, & nouo quasi impetu Ecclesias nostri temporis infestauerint, & hodie adhuc diuexent. Nam Michaelem Seruetum Hispanum, qui ex teterrimis haeresibus, totus compositus & confutus, Matthaeum Gribaldum Fargiarum Dominum, fautorem, Valentinum autem Gentilem, Georgium Blandratam & Francifcum Dauidis, collegas & asseclas habuit, Sabellij, Arrij, Marcionis & Eutychetis perniciofissimas haereses, & nefanda enthymemata, ex orco reuocasse, & dicteria atque blasphemias tam horrendas in S.S. Trinitatem ex venenato impuri pectoris fui gurgustio exhalasse, ad quas pius animus penitus contremiscat, & ipsi etiam intimi hominis pij sensus constipentur, notius est quam vt probatione vlla indigeat.
units.tr: Nor shall I say anything of the impure band of Pelagians, who rush and burst upon the grace of God in a body, as it were, with a scelerate hand and onslaught, nor of the infinite other authors of error (for who could list all those monsters one by one?). Finally, I say nothing of the Papists, who weaken the whole power and nature of Christ's office, and who not only trouble but utterly block and close up the most clear fountain of spiritual benefits, of truth and of divine grace. How gravely the saving doctrine of Christ's truth has been shaken by the most pestilential errors of all these, like waves, and how wretchedly the Church of Christ has been disturbed and harassed by them, daily experience and ecclesiastical history bear witness clearly and abundantly. And although, to curb and check the insolence of Arius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Sabellius, Nestorius, Eutyches and the other impostors and heresiarchs raging in the Churches, to crush their most harmful errors and root them out of the Lord's field, very famous orthodox and ecumenical councils, convened from men of piety, learning and most excellent virtue, have been held and celebrated with the greatest fruit; yet those heresies could never be so eliminated that they were not renewed again by some patron and supporter and, as it were by right of return, brought back into the Churches. Nor could they ever be uprooted entirely and from the foundations (for once the evil of heresy enters the soil of the Church, it strikes such deep roots and spreads its branches so widely) but some seed, roots and shoots always remained, which afterwards sprouted again and put forth new germs. Thus from those troubled fountains of error impure torrents broke through, over so many intervals of centuries, down to this age of ours, and with a new kind of onslaught have infested the Churches of our time and still harass them today. For Michael Servetus of Spain, who was wholly made up and compounded of the most hideous heresies, and who had as his supporters and associates Matthaeus Gribaldus, lord of Farges, Valentinus Gentilis, Georgius Blandrata and Franciscus David, revived the most pernicious heresies and abominable enthymemes of Sabellius, Arius, Marcion and Eutyches, and breathed out from the foul gullet of his impure breast such horrible sayings and blasphemies against the Holy Trinity that a pious mind shudders at them completely and even the inmost pious feelings of the heart are struck cold. This is too well known to need any proof.

units.la: Laelium vero Socinum Senensem, quis ignorat, Pauli Samosateni dogmata postliminio in Ecclesiam reduxisse, & filium paternae haereseos, deteriorem haeredem, nempe Faustum Socinum post se reliquisse, qui cum Georgio Eniedino, prisca Samosatenianorum dogmata, sub incudem reuocauit, & interpolauit, multisque doctrinae capitibus, ex impuris Pelagianorum & aliorum haereticorum lacunis, haustis, locuplectauit: Atque, sicuti scripta ipsius testantur, ipsum fidei orthodoxae fundamentum subuertere, omniaque ipsi superstructa dogmata diruere conatus est? Atqui ex huius officina & schola prodiit ille, cum quo nos in arenam descendimus, & in litem abimus, CHRISTOPHORVS OSTORRODIVS GOSLARIENSIS, qui ex Socini, Eniedini, aliorumque Samosatenianorum & Arianorū libris, illas quas modò refutauimus, institutiones catecheticas compilauit, & Germanico idiomate conscriptas, typis publicis promulgandas curauit.
units.tr: Who does not know that Laelius Socinus of Siena brought the doctrines of Paul of Samosata back into the Church by right of return, and left behind as his successor in the paternal heresy a worse heir, namely Faustus Socinus, who with Georgius Enyedinus summoned the ancient doctrines of the Samosatenians back to the anvil and reworked them, and enriched many heads of doctrine from the impure dregs of the Pelagians and other heretics? And as his writings attest, did he not strive to overthrow the very foundation of the orthodox faith and to tear down all the doctrines built upon it? Yet from this workshop and school came forth that man with whom we descend into the arena and go to law, CHRISTOPHORUS OSTORRODIUS of Goslar, who compiled from the books of Socinus, Enyedinus and other Samosatenians and Arians the catechetical institutes which we have just refuted, and saw to it that they were written in German and published in print.

units.la: Quum autem viri quidam doctissimi ac pientissimi, in
units.tr: Since certain very learned and most devout men in

units.la: Belgio, vbi & ego ante quadriennium studiorum gratia versatus sum, animaduerterent, illum Oftorrodij librum, vt & alia Samofatenianorum scripta auidissime à plurimis legi, & vndique conquiri, multósque illius doctrinæ fermeto infici, nostrorum Theologorum orthodoxa & excellétissima quæque scripta, paulatim vilescere, & in contemptum adduci, incertos etiam ac dubios quamplurimorum animos, quippe quos nemo aduersus clandestinam illam impressionem muniret, reddi, non paucos vero diuturnum illud Ecclesiarum nostrarum silentium perinde interpretari, ac si illæ Aduersariorum sententiam ac doctrinam tam firmis ac solidis argumentis, quæ refutari à nemine possent, suffultam esse, se vero causam malam defendendam suscepisse, tacitè confiterentur: cœperunt illi mecum agere, méque multis & grauissimis argumentis ac rationibus vehementer vrgere atque hortari, vt Institutionum illarum catechèticarum refutationem suscipe-rem, quorum tamen petitioni & votis multum sum reluctatus. Deterruit enim me ab initio vehementer, tum rei tractandæ amplitudo & dignitas, & quòd viderem, multa incidere enucleanda, quæ hactenus explicata non sint, ac proinde quanta eruditionis adminicula, ad vniuersæ fidei orthodoxæ, quam Aduersarij labefactare & conuellere conantur, defensionem adornandam requirantur: tum etiam propria tenuitatis, & quàm mihi curta, ad tanti momèti opus inchoandum ac perficiendum, esset supellex, conscientia: tum denique & potissimum quidem, effera, crudelis, ac sæua illa præsentis nostri seculi malignitas, præcoctorum iudiciorum iniquitas, & linguarum, quæ hodie inualuit, tam effrenis ac tanta petulantia, vt in arenam publicè cum Aduersarius prodeunti, non tam hostium veritatis inimica tela, quàm venenata inuidorum zoilorum rostra sint metuenda ac pertimescenda. fcenda. Tantas hodie, proh dolor! inter Christianos vires acquisiuit morosa illa inuidia, & arrogans ac superba αἰσχροκέρδεια, vt fraterna charitate in exilium eiecta & explosa plurimi, qui tamen pietatis, eruditionis, & virtutum Christianarum laudibus prae aliis omnibus conspicui videri volunt, neglectis aliis, quos & donis Dei indignos iudicat, & omnibus quibus possunt modis opprimunt, illorumque famae, existimationi, & fortunis, nullis non confutis dolis insidiatur, seipsos solos diligunt, amant, atque admirantur; oderunt autem, detestantur, ac fastidiunt quidquid ab aliis proficiscitur: quin etiam eo vsque impietatis nonnullos, pruriens illa qua sibi ceu idolo applaudiuntur, φιλαυτία prouexit, vt non personae tantum, & gratiae ipsi collatae, sed etiam successui & profectui Ecclesiae, aut Scholae, qui fit personae ministerio, inuideant. Atque licet optimi inter illos (modo vel bonus quisquam talis dici possit) suum Ecclesiae Dei & Scholae optent successum: tamen per se id fieri vellent, vt in ipsos quoque aliqua gloriae pars redundet, tam videlicet studiosi sui ipsorum sunt, & in proximum iniqui, vt non possint oculo simplici Dei gloriam intueri, ac pati, Deum quibus velit instrumentis, in opere suo perficiendo, vti, tam versipelles deinde & astuti, vt ad latentem in pectore nequitiam, & animum excruciantem ac adurentem inuidiam tegendam, speciosus nunquam deest praetextus. Et quamuis has & alias grauissimas iustissimae excusationis causas, ob quas publicam iudiciorum aleam subire detrectarem, illis, qui huius defensionis conscribendae primi authores mihi extitere, exposuissem, & addidissem, me quoque, si quid operis in luce emitterem, haud dubie quamplurimos huiusmodi crabrones, zoilosque, & otiosos ardeliones in me concitaturum esse, qui omnes pectoris sui aestus & motus in me effusuri, & nihil non molituri sint, quo opus a me cóscriptum in contemptum adducere possint:fortasse etiam non defuturos, qui contra omne fas & ius, contráque non Christianam charitatem tantùm, sed vel gentile etiam æqui-tatem(qua in re an plane hallucinatus sim, penes Deum καρδιο-γνώστην & quorundam conscientiam, atque bonos quosdam viros,seo iudicium) operi meo, priusquam etiam prælo excederet, adeoque illud legi & examinari ab illis penitius pos-set, nequissimarum suspicionum, & odiosissimorum conui-tiorum laqueum iniecturi, & illud vel sub prælo, & in ipso quasi partu suffocare conaturi essent: nihil tamen apud illos proficere potui. Horum igitur authoritate, qua iure apud me pollent maxima,& veritatis defendendæ ac propagandæ gloriæque diuinæ illustrandæ studio motus atque compul-sus,spretis illis conuitiatorum latratibus,in nomine Domini, hanc Fidei Orthodoxae Defensionem auspicatus sim,& postmodum à viris optimis ac doctissimis,tum in hac nostra patria,tum in vicinis locis degentibus, quibus pagel-las aliquot operis inchoati legendas ac ventilandas exhibue-ram,& qui per crebras literas me, vt telam exorsam pertexe-rem, hortati sunt,confirmatus,illam tandem, horis ab occu-pationibus grauissimis & laboribus ordinariis, residuis opera isti impensis, sed innumeris obstaculis ac impedimentis (sola enim amplißimi nostri Magistratus Bernensis, postquam primas tres libri pagellas conscripsissem, interueniens mei, ex Belgio, in hanc ipsorum Academiam euocatio, per integrum fere annum incepti operis cursum remorata est) supe-ratis,ad finem per Dei gratiam, licet non sine ingenti labore, perduxi.
units.tr: In Belgium, where I too spent four years ago for the sake of study, they noticed that this book of Ostorodius, like other writings of the Samosatenians, was most eagerly read by very many and sought out everywhere, and that many were almost infected with its teaching. They saw that the orthodox and most excellent writings of our theologians were gradually becoming cheap and falling into contempt, and that the uncertain and doubtful minds of very many were being unsettled, since no one was guarding them against that secret infection. They saw too that not a few interpreted the long silence of our Churches as a tacit admission that the opponents' view and doctrine rested on such firm and solid arguments that no one could refute them, and that we had taken up a bad cause to defend. These men began to deal with me and pressed me vehemently with many weighty arguments and reasons, urging me to take up the refutation of those Catechetical Institutes. I struggled much, however, against their request and wishes. At the start I was strongly deterred, partly by the magnitude and dignity of the task, and because I saw that many matters would arise which had not hitherto been explained, and so how great an apparatus of learning is needed to prepare a defence of the whole orthodox faith, which the opponents try to shake and overthrow. I was also deterred by my awareness of my own slenderness, and of how meagre my stock of resources was for beginning and finishing a work of such importance. Finally, and chiefly, I was deterred by the savage, cruel and fierce malice of our present age, by the unfairness of hasty judgments, and by the tongues, now so widely prevalent and so unbridled and wanton, that when one comes forward publicly into the arena against an opponent, the venomous beaks of envious Zoiluses are to be feared and dreaded more than the hostile weapons of the enemies of truth. Alas, today that peevish envy and that arrogant and proud greed (αἰσχροκέρδεια) have gained such strength among Christians that many, cast out and driven away from brotherly love, yet wishing to appear conspicuous above all others for the praises of piety, learning and Christian virtues, neglect the others, whom they judge unworthy of God's gifts, and oppress them by every means they can. They lie in wait for their reputation, standing and fortunes with every sort of deceit. They love, cherish and admire only themselves, but hate, detest and loathe whatever comes from others. Indeed, the itching self-love (φιλαυτία), by which they applaud themselves as if they were an idol, has carried some to such impiety that they envy not only the person and the grace bestowed on him, but also the success and progress of the Church or school that comes through that person's ministry. And although the best of them (if indeed anyone of that sort can be called good) wish the Church of God and the school success, they would want it to happen in such a way that some part of the glory spills over onto themselves too. They are so self-interested and so unfair to their neighbour that they cannot look upon God's glory with a single eye, nor bear that God uses whatever instruments he wills to perfect his work. And they are so shifty and crafty that, to hide the wickedness lurking in the breast and the envy tormenting and burning the mind, a specious pretext is never lacking. I had explained these and other most weighty and most just reasons for excusing myself, for which I would decline to submit to the public lottery of judgments, to those who were the first authors of this defence. I had added that if I published anything of this work, without doubt very many hornets of this kind, Zoiluses and idle busybodies, would be stirred up against me; all of them would pour out the heat of their breasts upon me and attempt everything to bring my written work into contempt. Perhaps, I said, there would not be lacking those who, against all right and law, and against not only Christian charity but even common fairness (whether I am utterly mistaken in this, God, who knows the hearts, and the conscience of certain men and of some good men must judge), would cast the noose of most wicked suspicions and most hateful insults over my work before it even left the press, so that they could read and examine it more thoroughly, and would try to suffocate it under the press and in its very birth. Nevertheless I could achieve nothing with them. Therefore, moved and driven by their authority, which rightly carries the greatest weight with me, and by zeal for defending and spreading the truth and making the divine glory shine, I undertook this Defence of the Orthodox Faith in the name of the Lord, scorning the barking of those who insult. Afterwards, encouraged by the best and most learned men, both in this our homeland and in neighbouring places, to whom I had shown a few sheets of the work begun for reading and discussion, and who by frequent letters urged me to finish the web I had started, I at last brought it to completion by God's grace, though not without great labour. I gave to this work the hours left over from very heavy occupations and ordinary duties, but I overcame countless obstacles and impediments. (For after I had written the first three pages of the book, my call from Belgium into this their Academy, which intervened, delayed the course of the begun work for almost a whole year, and that was the doing of the most illustrious Magistrate of Bern alone.)

units.la: Quantum verò ipsum ordinem ac methodum(nam er-rorum & capitum summa in ipsa Defensione nostra extat) concernit Institutionum illarum, quas Aduersarius in qua-draginta draginta duo capita distinxit: ad duas illas partes, omnia quæ ibi tractantur, non incommodè reuocari possunt, quarum prima, de Scriptura & verbo Dei, veluti certo salutis ac salutaris doctrinæ instrumento, eiúsque perfectione, authoritate, certitudine ac perspicuitate, & incidenter de naturali Dei in homine notitia agit, capite primo, quæ à nobis tribus primis capitibus Defensionis nostræ sunt examinata: parte verò secunda doctrinam de fide & obiecto eius exponit. Sententiam suam de fide capite secundo proponit, nos controversiam illam, quippe quæ ad Iustificationis, cuius materiam illam statuit Aduersarius, negotium pertinet, capite trigesimo & trigesimoprimo tractauimus. Obiectum verò fidei duplex statuere videtur, Deum nimirum, & Christum: illud tractat capite tertio, quarto (in quo etiam de Spiritu sancto agit, eiusque personam impugnat, quam nos capite decimo nono defendimus) & quinto, & tum de Essentia diuina, atque attributis eius quibusdam, tum de personis diuinis, tum denique de voluntate diuina disserit, de quibus omnibus videntur caput quartum & quintum Defensionis nostræ: hoc verò exponit toto reliquo Institutionum corpore, atque in notitia tū personæ, tum officii Christi distinguit. De illa agit capite sexto, & sequentibus capitibus decem, à sexto nimirum usque ad decimum septimum, <bl>ἀπόδειξιν</bl> instituit argumentorum quorundam, quibus Ecclesiarum orthodoxarum doctores æternam Christi deitatem demonstrant, capite autem decimo septimo, decimo octauo & decimo nono, doctrinam & argumenta de Incarnatione Filij Dei impugnat, de quibus in defensione veritatis, à capite quinto usque ad caput vigesimum tertium, à nobis actum est. Officium Christi capite vigesimo describit, illúdque in Propheticum ac Regium, seu duas illas actiones, nempe voluntatis diuinæ tum reuelatio-
units.tr: As for the order and method (for the sum of the chapters and errors is set out in our Defence itself), the Institutes which the opponent divided into forty-two chapters can conveniently be reduced to two parts. The first, on Scripture and the Word of God as the certain instrument of salvation and saving doctrine, and on its perfection, authority, certainty and clarity, and incidentally on the natural knowledge of God in man, is treated in chapter one, which we examined in the first three chapters of our Defence. The second part sets out the doctrine of faith and its object. The opponent proposes his view of faith in chapter two. We treated that controversy in chapters thirty and thirty-one, since it belongs to the matter of justification, which the opponent holds to be its subject. The object of faith seems to be twofold, namely God and Christ. He treats God in chapters three, four and five (in chapter four he also discusses the Holy Spirit and attacks his person, which we defend in chapter nineteen). He then discusses the divine essence and certain of its attributes, the divine persons, and finally the divine will, all of which seem to be covered by chapters four and five of our Defence. The knowledge of Christ he sets out through the whole rest of the body of the Institutes, distinguishing his person from his office. He deals with the person in chapter six and the following chapters, from six to sixteen, where he sets out a demonstration of certain arguments by which the teachers of the orthodox Churches prove the eternal deity of Christ. In chapters seventeen, eighteen and nineteen he attacks the doctrine and arguments concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God, and on these matters, in defence of the truth, we have written from chapter five to chapter twenty-three. He describes the office of Christ in chapter twenty and divides it into the Prophetic and the Kingly, that is, into the two actions of the revelation of the divine will

units.la: {ἀπόδειξιν} Greek word printed in the text, transcribed as printed in Greek. nem, tum administrationem distinguit, de qua descriptione ac distinctione videatur caput Defensionis nostræ vigesimū tertium. Officium Propheticum seu muneris illius functionem primam, pro duplici voluntatis diuinæ, quatenus nimirum illa salutis ac vitæ æternæ consequendæ viam respicit, obiecto ; tum in promissorum,tum in mandatorum diuinorum expositionem diuidit, illáque capite vigesimo primo recenset & explicat, hæc vero in moralia & ceremonialia distinguit, & illa nempe moralia decem sequentibus capitibus exponit, & horū occasione capite trigesimo tertio,de Libero hominis Arbitrio, & incidenter de primi hominis statu & conditione, tam ante, quàm post lapsum, de imagine item Dei in homine, & peccato Originali, capite deinde trigesimo quarto de Liberi Arbitrij viribus, capite vero trigesimo quinto de Prædestinatione Diuina, denique capite trigesimo sexto & trigesimo septimo de. Iustificatione hominis coram Deo, & de satisfactione Christi, ipsiusque in hunc mundum aduentus, causis,prolixè disputat. Nos veritatem orthodoxam de promissionibus diuinis capite vigesimo quarto, de mandatis diuinis capite vigesimo qninto, de Libero Arbitrio capite vigesimo sexto & vigesimo septimo, de Liberi Arbitrij viribus capite vigesimo octauo, de æterna Dei Prædestinatione capite vigesimo nono, de iustificatione autem hominis coram Deo, & satisfactione Christi pro peccatis nostris, capite trigesimo secundo, trigesimo tertio, trigesimo quarto,trigesimo quinto, trigesimo sexto explicamus ac defendimus. Leges autem cæremoniales cum dicit, doctrinam de Sacramentis, Cœna Domini videlicet & Baptismo intelligit, eáque capite trigesimo octauo, trigesimo nono explicat, quam doctrinæ partem, vtpote passim à nostris tractatam, præteriimus. Officium vero Christi Regium capite quadragesimo describit, & hac occasione capite quadragesimo primo, qualenam corpus habeat Christus, ab eo tempore quo Deus ipsum Regem constituit, ac proinde qualia etiam fideles post resurrectionem corpora sint habituri? exponit, de quibus videantur caput trigesimum septimum, & trigesimum octavum Defensionis nostrae. Tandem vero tractatu de Ecclesia, cuius Rex Christus est, capite quadragesimo secundo, suas Institutiones claudit. Et quia hoc ultimo capite, contra Pontificios & Anabaptistas directe disputat, animadversione ac censura supersedendum, & meis quoque defensionibus finem imponendum esse iudicavi.
units.tr: demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν] revelation and administration. For the description and distinction of these, see the twenty-third chapter of our Defence. The prophetic office, or the first function of that office, he divides, with respect to the twofold will of God insofar as it looks to the way of obtaining salvation and eternal life, into the exposition of God's promises and of God's commands. He sets out and explains these in the twenty-first chapter. He then divides the commands into moral and ceremonial. He expounds the moral commands in the ten following chapters, and on the occasion of these, in the thirty-third chapter he discourses at length on man's free will, and incidentally on the state and condition of the first man both before and after the fall, on the image of God in man, and on original sin. Then in the thirty-fourth chapter he treats of the powers of free will, in the thirty-fifth of God's predestination, and finally in the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh of the justification of man before God and the satisfaction of Christ, and the causes of Christ's coming into this world. We set forth and defend the orthodox truth concerning God's promises in the twenty-fourth chapter, concerning God's commands in the twenty-fifth, concerning free will in the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh, concerning the powers of free will in the twenty-eighth, concerning God's eternal predestination in the twenty-ninth, and concerning the justification of man before God and the satisfaction of Christ for our sins in the thirty-second, thirty-third, thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth. When he speaks of the ceremonial laws, he means the doctrine of the sacraments, namely the Lord's Supper and Baptism, and he explains this in the thirty-eighth and thirty-ninth chapters. Since this part of doctrine has been treated throughout by our own writers, I pass it over. The kingly office of Christ he describes in the fortieth chapter, and on this occasion, in the forty-first chapter, he sets out what kind of body Christ has from the time when God made him King, and consequently what kind of bodies the faithful are also to have after the resurrection. On these matters see the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth chapters of our Defence. Finally, in his treatise on the Church, of which Christ is King, he closes his Institutes with the forty-second chapter. And because in this last chapter he disputes directly against the Papists and the Anabaptists, I have judged that I should refrain from further comment and criticism, and also put an end to my own defences.

units.la: In horum autem capitum omnium animadversione ac refutatione, & veritatis ipsius explicatione ac defensione universa sic versatus sum, ut verba Adversarij germanica, vel saltem summam illorum, quibus sententia & argumenta ipsius comprehenduntur, fideliter & quantum fieri potuit, simpliciter ac dilucide in Latinam linguam, huius etiam puritatis ratione superstitiose non habita, transtulerim: (Nam si mens Adversarij alicubi non dextre, quod tamen ignoro, a me est proposita, illud inde profectum est, quod illam non assequutus sim, non autem quod quidquam studio malitiose ac veteratorie peruertere voluerim) rationes & argumenta deinde utriusque partis, ut plurimum syllogistice, quo videlicet pondus & momentum illorum, veritasque ipsa, eo evidentius elucesceret, propositurum: tam diversa etiam religionis ac fidei capita, totque controversas quaestiones (quarum varietas, praesertim cum hasce Defensiones nostras non nisi per varia temporis intervalla conscribere potuerim, alicubi etiam ituli aliquam diversitatem forte peperit) interdum diversa methodo, quam libertatem nec eripi mihi, nec etiam iuste culpari posse, autumo, tractauerim: ab omnibus insuper
units.tr: In the examination and refutation of all these chapters, and in the explanation and defence of the truth itself, I have proceeded in this way. I have translated the Adversary's words, whether German or at least the summary in which his opinions and arguments are contained, faithfully and as far as possible simply and clearly into Latin, without anxious concern for the elegance of the style. (If I have somewhere stated the Adversary's meaning inaccurately, which I do not know, this came about because I did not grasp it, not because I wished to distort anything through malice or trickery.) I have then set out the reasons and arguments of each side, mostly in syllogistic form, so that their weight and force, and the truth itself, might stand out more clearly. I have also treated the many different heads of religion and faith, and the many controverted questions, sometimes by different methods. The variety of these, especially since I could write these Defences only over various intervals of time, has perhaps produced some diversity here and there. I think no one can rightly take this freedom from me or blame me for it. Moreover, I have abstained from all slander, abuse and insult, which tend to defile and pollute the truth rather than defend and illustrate it. If anything too harsh has slipped from me, I wish it to be struck out and erased, and I want it attributed to the heat of debate rather than to a desire to revile. Finally, lest I seem to have acted on my own opinion, to have rushed rashly into this arena and to have intruded into the treatment of so great a matter, I have followed the example of that most learned and renowned man, Lord William Bucanus, once Professor of Holy Theology in this Academy of blessed and famous memory, and of the reverend, distinguished man of most exquisite judgment, Lord Simon Goulart, most faithful minister of the Church of Geneva. As frequent letters written to me attest, these Defences of mine were approved by the judgments and votes of him and of others teaching in that famous Genevan Church and illustrious school. So I handed my works over to be examined with rigour, and thus I have diligently directed everything to the glory of the one God, the defence of the truth, and the building up of the Church.

units.la: * * * .calumniis, conuitiis atque dicteriis, quibus veritas confpur- catur potius, ac polluitur, quam defenditur ac illustratur, ab- stinuerim, ita vt si quid mihi acerbius excideriẗ, id expungi & obliterari velim, ac disputationis feruori potius, quam stu- dio conuiciandi imputari cupiam: Denique ne proprio meo sensu siti velle, ac temere in arenam hanc prodiisse, & in tă- tæ rei tractationem [illegible, ~3 letters] inuolasse videar, omnes illas lucu- brationes meas, sequutus nimirum exemplum, Doctissimi ac nominatissimi viri, Domini Gvlielmi Bvcani, SS. Theo- logiæ olim, in hac Academia beatæ ac celebris memoriæ, Professoris, reuerendo, clarissimo, & exquisitissimi iudicij viro Da. Simoni Govlartio, Ecclesiæ Geneuensis Pastori fi- delissimo, cuius vt & aliorum in celebri illa Geneuensium Ec- clesia & illustri schola docentium, calculis & suffragiis, com- probatas suisse hæsce Defensiones meas, crebræ ad me exara- tæ literæ testantur, rigidè examinandas tradiderim, & sic o- mnia ad vnius Dei gloriam, veritatis defensionem, & Eccle- siæ ædificationem studiose direxerim.
units.tr: * * * .I have abstained from calumnies, reproaches and sneers, with which truth is rather soiled and polluted than defended and illustrated. So if anything too bitter has slipped out of me, I wish it struck out and blotted out, and I want it imputed to the fervour of debate rather than to a desire to abuse. Finally, so that I may not seem to have acted on my own opinion, to have rashly come out into this arena and to have meddled in the treatment of so great a matter, I have followed the example of the most learned and renowned man, Lord William Bucanus, once Professor of Holy Theology in this Academy, of blessed and famous memory, and of the reverend, most distinguished man of most exquisite judgment, Lord Simon Goulart, most faithful minister of the Church of Geneva. I have handed all these my laborious writings over to be examined rigorously, as frequent letters written to me testify that they were approved by the calculations and votes of him and of others teaching in that famous Genevan Church and illustrious school. And so I have studiously directed everything to the glory of the one God alone, the defence of the truth, and the edification of the Church.

units.la: Vt vero sub Magnifici ac celeberrimi vestri Nominis pa- trocinio Viri Amplissimi ac prudentissimi, hanc ipsam Re- ligionis Christianæ & fidei orthodoxæ Defensionē nostram in lucem emitterem, & iuris facerem publici, impulit me sin- gularis illa vestra ac rara (vt nihil de Inclytæ vestræ Vrbis splendore & magnificentia, ac politicis & polemicis rebus præclarè & feliciter gestis, nihil de aliis plurimis ac maximis Ecclesiæ ac Reipublicæ præsidiis & ornamentis, quibus Deus illam benignissimè instruxit: nihil denique de laudatissimo & liberalibus artibus ac studiis, virisque doctissimis illustri Gymnasio literario, Ecclesiæ ac Reipublicæ seminario ferti- lissimo ac fœcundissimo, dicã, cuius Vos liberalissimi ac be- nignißimi fundatores & conseruatores extitistis, quibus vt & aliis omnibus laudibus vestris decantandis ac praedicandis me imparem agnosco) humanitas, gloriaeque diuinae & salutis ciuium vestrorum promouendae studium summum, cui ab optimis & clarissimis quibusque viris testimonium perhibetur amplissimum: tum etiam quod licet cura tuendae Ecclesiae & fidei ac veritatis defendendae, omnibus piis & Christianis Regibus, Principibus ac Magistratibus, qui illam profitentur atque amplectuntur, sit communis, Vobis tamen hoc ipsum negotium quod tractamus, quodammodo peculiariter incumbit curandum, eo quod Institutionum illarum catecheticarum Autor Christophorus nimirum Oftorrodius, qui hactenus non procul a laudatissimae Vrbis vestrae pomeriis habitauit, vestrae Ecclesiae potissimum, cuius tutandae & ab hostium veritatis insultibus vindicandae, curam, auctoritatem ac potestatem, Deus Vobis commisit, cum aliis sociis & assectis suis, insidias struxit, & ex ouili illo vestro, quascunque potuit oues abegit, quo nomine etiam Amplitudini Vestrae hanc Defensionem nostram gratam futuram esse, spes maxima ac indubitata affulget.
units.tr: But I have sent forth this Defence of ours of the Christian religion and the orthodox faith into the light under the patronage of your magnificent and most famous name, most distinguished and prudent men, and have made it public property. What impelled me was your singular and rare humanity, and your zeal for the glory of God and the salvation of your citizens, to which the highest testimony is given by the best and most distinguished men. I shall say nothing of the splendour and magnificence of your renowned city, nor of its brilliant and successful political and polemical achievements, nor of the many other great defences and ornaments of Church and State with which God has most kindly furnished it. Finally, I shall say nothing of its most praiseworthy illustrious literary Gymnasium, the most fertile and fruitful seminary of the Church and State, with its liberal arts and studies and its most learned men, whose most generous and kindly founders and preservers you have been. I acknowledge that I am unequal to proclaiming and celebrating these and all your other praises. Still, although the care of protecting the Church and of defending the faith and truth belongs in common to all pious and Christian kings, princes and magistrates who profess and embrace it, the very matter we are treating falls in some way especially upon you to attend to. The author of those catechetical Institutes, Christoph Ostorrodius, who until now has lived not far from the boundaries of your most praiseworthy city, has laid snares against your Church above all, whose care, authority and power over protecting it and defending it against the assaults of the enemies of truth God has committed to you. Together with his companions and followers, he has driven off from that fold of yours whatever sheep he could. For this reason, there shines the greatest and undoubted hope that this our Defence will also be welcome to your Magnificence.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint, obnixe, & ea qua par est obseruantia, magnificam Amplitudinem Vestram oro atque obtestor, ut celeberrimi nominis vestri titulum, huic meo operi, velut lucidissimam facem quandam praelucere, haud graviter, aut indignabundi patiamini, hancve meam ἀσφάλειαν, & in Vobis compellandis, παρρησίαν in meliorem partem, pro solita vestra benignitate; interpretemini, & Defensionem hanc Fidei Orthodoxae, quam syncero animo & veritatis propugnandae ac illustrandae studio Vobis offero, sereno ac benigno vultu a me accipiatis. Deus Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi florentissimum celeberrimae vestrae Reipublicae statum potenti sua dextra, tueri, vobisque Proconsul Magnifice CONSULES ac SENATORES amplissimi ac prudentissimi, clementiam, iudicium, iustitiam, ac pacem, ad nominis sui gloriam, vestramque & civium vestrorum tranquillitatem, ac salutem, largiri, clementissimè pergat. Ex illustris ac praepotentis REIPVBLICAE BERNENSIS Academia. Lausannae Helvetiorum, pridie Idus Februarij, Anno Domini sesquimillesimo centesimo decimo tertio.
units.tr: Since these things are so, I earnestly and with the respect that is fitting beseech and entreat your magnificent Excellency not to be displeased or indignant that the title of your most renowned name should shine forth upon this work of mine, like a bright torch. Please interpret in the better sense, in keeping with your customary kindness, my security [ἀσφάλεια] and my frankness [παρρησία] in addressing you, and accept from me with a calm and kindly countenance this Defence of the Orthodox Faith, which I offer you with a sincere heart and with zeal for defending and illustrating the truth. May God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, with His mighty right hand, continue most graciously to protect the most flourishing state of your most famous Commonwealth, and to grant to you, Proconsul Magnificent, Consuls and most distinguished and prudent Senators, clemency, judgment, justice and peace, for the glory of His name and for the tranquillity and salvation of you and your citizens. From the illustrious and most powerful Academy of the Commonwealth of Berne, at Lausanne in Helvetia, the day before the Ides of February, in the year of the Lord 1613.

units.la: D. IACOBO AD PORTVM, Theologo in Academia Lausannensi clarissimo: OSTORRODII DOCTRINAE ET κακωσισς ad XXXVIII. Religionis titulos & capita censori ac confutatori doctissimo, AETERNITATIS AC DIVINITATIS CHRISTI, DEO PATRE AGONOTHETA, Filio Epistata, Spiritu S. Xystarcha, ASSERTORI AC PROPVGNATORI IVSTISSIMO, M. V. H. A. P.
units.tr: To James à Port, the most distinguished theologian of the Academy of Lausanne: to the most learned critic and refuter of Ostorodius's doctrine and of the thirty-eight titles and chapters of religion, whose rebuttal is a handling [κακώσις]: the eternity and divinity of Christ, God the Father as the judge of the contest, the Son as overseer, the Holy Spirit as the leader of the games, the most just asserter and champion, M. V. H. A. P.

units.la: Νὶ δοξῆπος ἑνὸς Γ' ἀπάπτε σωὴ πλέσα βέβηκε Καὶ πλέον ἡ ἀρχὴ παντὸς ἐφρετο καλή. Μὴ κ' ἃ ἀμβῶν πάνας ἡ πλίων ὁρμα δὴν ἃκ δῶ Τῷξ ἀρχῆς, ἐξ ἃ πᾶν συνεφελκομον Τίς μαθη αυτὸ τὸ ὃν, χ' ὑπόσαπον, ἵν τε ἡ ἕν τε, Τὰς τεσὴν αἰδιον τᾶμαν ὑποσάσεσι. Ὃ μεχὶ παν απίφνε θεὸς, μάκορ ἃ ἂ, νοῦμον Γισιν, ἡμιερτης ἴδιον ἐξ λόγον. Δηλονοῦ ἡ βίβλῳ πὴν πορθμὸν σωΐπομε, πορθμόν Εὔπορθμον πορθμεῖ πὼ δ' ἀπῆκε χαεν.
units.tr: Whoever sails the sea of this book, having been carried along by the first breeze, finds that every beginning is good and fair. Do not let the wave of the sea drive you away from the beginning, which draws everything along with it. Let whoever reads learn what the being is and how it subsists, and that the eternal God is one and also subsists in three; he who was God from the beginning, his Son, is not a mere part of the Word. Clearly the book is a passage, a ferry, a harbour; a good crossing has been made. [Greek verse, acrostic on the word for harbour, in garbled form]

units.la: AD ADVERSARIVM.
units.tr: To the Adversary.

units.la: HEu male multiplici & pleno subis ostia velo Errorum: illæ pios mentibus horror inest:
units.tr: Alas, you enter the gates of error wrapped in a many-folded and heavy veil; a horror dwells in pious minds.

units.la: Huc flecte, OSTORRODI, cursus, huc vela: Salutis Namq; tibi porta hic & tibi PORTVS inest.
units.tr: Turn here, Ostorodius, turn your course, turn your sails here: for here lies a gate of salvation for you, and here inside is a HARBOUR for you.

units.la: STEPH. A CASTRO BELLO Verbi Dei Minister.
units.tr: Stephanus à Castro Bello, Minister of the Word of God.

units.la: IN REFVTATIONEM OSTORRODII A Reuerendo & Clarissimo viro DN. IACOBO AD PORTVM compositam.
units.tr: AGAINST OSTORRODIUS, composed by the Reverend and most Distinguished Mr. JAMES AD PORTUM.

units.la: TItanum soboles superis indicere bellum Nititur, & Christum summa detrudere sede OSTERRODIDES sacri mysteria verbi Rodit, in æthereum vomicas eructat olympum. O parilis diuina Patris clementia nati: Quæ SAMOSATENICVM potis est tolerare piaclum! Suiphureos non ille globos, non feruidus ira, In caput vltrices Lernæum fulminat ignes. AD PORTVM reuocat placidus, non gurgite vasto In pelagum ductas voluit submergere puppes. Eripit è Scylla, clariq; tridente IACOBI In vada transmittit reduces, & littore ponit.
units.tr: The Titan's brood seeks to declare war on the gods above and to hurl Christ down from the highest throne. OSTERRODIDES gnaws at the sacred mysteries of the Word and belches his sores up into the heavenly Olympus. O divine clemency of the Father, equal to the Son! Who could endure the Samosatene sacrilege? He does not hurl sulphurous balls or fiery wrath, nor does he launch avenging Lernaean fire upon the head. Calmly he calls him back to PORTUS. He did not want to sink the ships, led out into the deep, in the vast whirlpool. He snatches them from Scylla and, with JAMES's bright trident, sends them across the shallows back home and sets them down on the shore.

units.la: IOH. STEKIVS BASIL. I.V.D. In Academia Lausannensi Professor.
units.tr: JOH. STEKIVS, Basel, Doctor of Both Laws, Professor at the Academy of Lausanne.

units.la: CLARISSIMO, SPECTATISSIMOQVE viro D. Domino IACOBO AD PORTVM, S.S. Theologiæ in Academia Lausannensi Professore doctissimo, sapientiss. Aduersus OSTOKRODII Samosateniani blasphemias scribenti.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and most illustrious man, Lord James à Port, most learned Professor of Sacred Theology at the Academy of Lausanne, a man of great wisdom, who is writing against the blasphemies of Ostorodius the Samosatenian.

units.la: INclyta Martis opus nostri Germania: cedis Terra nulli aliy manibus studissq; Minerue. Musarum domus es: Summum & quod culmen honoris, Religio horrendis seclorum vera tenebris Eripitur per te: per te lux ipsa salutis, Impietas quam dira suis includerat autris, Redditur in Christo. Fœlix, tua si bona nosses.
units.tr: Glorious Germany, work of Mars, you yield to no land in the skill of your hands and in the studies of Minerva. You are the home of the Muses. Your highest crown of honour is this: true religion is snatched from the horrid darkness of the ages through you, and through you the very light of salvation, which dire impiety had shut up in its caves, is restored in Christ. Happy would you be, if you knew your blessings.

units.la: Ast heu iam infœlix, variis erroribus acta Christiadum scindis studia in contraria vulgus. In te blasphemus Stygio quid percitus æstro Christum sic rodit? sacri quid sanguinis unda, Ille eius turbans purgatos fascinat agnos? Non tamen impune hoc, infert Helvetia bellum. Arma ciet contra generosi filius Vrsi AD PORTVM: vincit: tecum Rex Christe triumphat.
units.tr: Alas, now unhappy, driven by various errors, you split the studies of the Christians into opposing camps. Against you, what blasphemer, goaded by a Stygian gadfly, gnaws thus at Christ? What wave of holy blood, what troubler, bewitches the purified lambs? Yet not with impunity does Helvetia make war on you. Against him arms are raised by the son of the noble Bear, à Port: he conquers, and with you, Christ the King, he triumphs.

units.la: ΠΡΌΣ ΑΥΤΌΝ.
units.tr: TO HIM.

units.la: Ὢν ἢ ὁ Ἰὼν, ἢ ὁ ἑαυτὸν Ϛ᾽ ὁ Χεισὸς ἀνάοτει Κρεισ̈ τῶν ὑπαπης, ἢ κυεῖ ꝏ κωεί ων. Κεῖνον τί βλάπλεις· δάκνεις ἀσιζέσατε κεῖνον; Τίσόμα καὶ κεἰνω ἠρυχλοιδορέον; Ἀθλιέρομφαί· ὀξέίη χόλιός σε πατύζει. Τοιῶδ᾽ τ᾽ ἁ φεγνέων παύεο κερτομίης. Μῶνον ὁρᾶς κεῖνα τὴν Πεισ-λιμεὶν; ὡς ἐπαίοντες Οὐ δὲωη ὁρώ ꝏ τῷ γε βίλω ἐμέμῳ. Σ᾽ ἐρύοτας κρατερῶς ἄρχει ἀυμαλχῇ δισμῶ. Ἐλπὶς τίς λοιπή; παύεο κερτομίης. Σὺ ὃ ἀρισδυσας ὠεσμαχ κλέ ꝏ ἄαπτον αἴρης, Πεισ-λιμεὶν᾽, α φτύρτῳ τῇ σεφαίῳ σεφανεῖ.
units.tr: Whether you are Ion, or whoever calls himself Christ, you tear the peoples' minds apart with your varied errors. Why do you harm him? Why do you bite him so savagely? Why do you rage at him so, and what is the wound you bring on him? Wretched man, bitter anger drives you on. Cease your mocking. Do you see only what lies before Peislimen's eyes? Lord, you have been strong in rousing fresh battles. What hope remains? Cease your mocking. You, who have raised your weapon against Christ, Peislimen, will be crowned with the victor's garland.

units.la: Ὅλως(ἐφῳ) ὃπισαμένῳ, ἢ ὅλως πηπαρδυμένῳ Ιακώξῳ τῇ Πεισ-λιμένα φιλ ꝏ πισο᾽ς
units.tr: To Jacob Peislimen, friend of the Christian faith, wholly ... and wholly ... (?).

units.la: ΣΑΜΣΩΝ ΓΕΝΙΑΛΙΩΑ Τυμπ. Λαυσ. 12. Febr. 1613.
units.tr: SAMSON GENIALIS. Tymp. Lausanne, 12 February 1613.

units.la: Τῷ Ιακώξῳ Πεισ-Λιμέν α ὃπισημονικατότῳ τε ἢ ὅλως πηπαρδυμένῳ αἰ δοί, ἀξιωτάτῳ Σκολό᾽ γῳ τῇ ἐν τῇ Λαυσαινῇ Θεολογικῶν ἀ διδασκάλων φρεστύουντι τῷ τῆς τῆς Οσορρόδις αἱρετικῶν δεγμάτων ἐν διδόντι Ανασκθυλιῶ.
units.tr: To Jacob Peislimen, most distinguished and most learned, and wholly ... , most worthy scholarch and professor of theology in the Lausanne academy, who has undertaken the refutation [Ἀνασκευή] of the heretical doctrines of Christoph Ostorodt.

units.la: ΕΠΙΝΙΚΙΟΝ.
units.tr: Epinikion.

units.la: Ατρεκίλῳ μὴ κνει φιλεῖν ἢ σώφεγα ἡμᾶς Μὴ φεγνέειν δόξαι μεςπων φρασπίλλη διώκειν, Ρῆμα Θεῦ πιντῶς μὴ δῆς χ᾽ ἡμῖν ἐρθυναν. Εὖ ἀφαρματοπεῖς, οἱ λοὺς, φς σίνορας αἴδρας, φέῖγες δηθεῖης ἐχπιυκίοι δόγμασ᾽ ἀείρειν Βελομένοις βίβλοις δ᾽ ἰωδίοι, ποικιλομόρφυς. Νιπακοις δεῖλῶς θαναπφόρα βρώματα πάοτιν.
units.tr: Let no one who loves truth, nor any sober man among us, be eager to pursue the vain glory of the ill-fated tongue, but let him hold to the word of God alone. You, dear friends, who wish to set up the wicked doctrines of the Socinians, I know you by these many-shaped books, and they are food that brings death.

units.la: Τοῖ᾽ ἐΐω Ὀσορρόδιος μεμαὼς κακὰ βάλλειν
units.tr: Ostorodius, eager to hurl evils,

units.la: Δόγματα αὐτ᾽ ἀγαθῶν, ἐπιφθὴς δ᾽ ἡ ὁ ζῳος λόγον ἀρεῖν.
units.tr: Sets up his own doctrines of good, and it is hateful to the living to raise a word against them.

units.la: Καὶ τῆς ἀτρεκέος λαμπρὸν φάος ἐξολοθρεῦσαι.
units.tr: And he seeks to destroy the bright light of the truth.

units.la: Αὐτὰρ ὁ Ἀτρεκέης ἐκφάανσης Θεὸς ἡμῶν
units.tr: But our God, who reveals the truth,

units.la: Ἀνδρας πεπνυμένας, θεοδέγμονας, ἠμιάζεις τε
units.tr: Brings forth men of wisdom, God-taught, and half-divine,

units.la: Ἠδὲ θεοπνεύστως ΘΕΟΦΡΩΝ, μὴν ἀμωμήτον ἡ κατὰ.
units.tr: And Theophron, inspired by God, the blameless one, as his guide.

units.la: Ὥς δ᾽ ἀὸ Ἡρακλῆς, διὸς τέκος, ὄλβιος, ἥρως
units.tr: As the son of Zeus, blessed Heracles, the hero,

units.la: φῶτας ἢ φῶτας βλαβερὰς κτὰς, τεύξ᾽ ὀνομαζθείς,
units.tr: Destroyed the harmful beasts of men and was named for it,

units.la: Οὕτως σὺ βλαβερεῖν λύσας καὶ δόγματα φωτὸς
units.tr: So you, having loosed the harmful and corrupt doctrines,

units.la: Εἴ τε ἡμῶν θεῖον, μάκαρ, ἥρως, ἡ μάλα κείνῳ,
units.tr: Are a divine and blessed hero, and the very man for that task,

units.la: Καὶ γὰρ δηλῆσαι δίζημενον ἰσὺ ἰδήσειν,
units.tr: For you will know how to search out and destroy the enemy,

units.la: Τὸν δ᾽ Ὀσορρόδιον, Λογίοις Θεῖσ ἐφιαίρειν.
units.tr: And to drive out Ostorodius from the oracles of God.

units.la: Ψευδαλέως σκεδάσας ἀνοφερὲν σκότος, ὄλβιος ἐστι,
units.tr: Having scattered the deceitful, murky darkness, you are blessed,

units.la: Τοῦξεο ὁ κῦδος, σωτηρίας ἠματ᾽ ἀμωμάς.
units.tr: And you have won glory, the blameless day of salvation.

units.la: Λάμπεις ὡς ἥρως σφέρας σκοτομηδέα φῶτα,
units.tr: You shine like a hero, bringing light to the darkened man,

units.la: φῶς γὰρ, φωτὶ δίδος φῶς, φαίνεις φάτα καὶ καλκιτάς.
units.tr: For light, giving light to the one who is in the light, you show forth.

units.la: Σχίζει ὃν Ὀσορρόδιος, Λιμέν᾽ ἐν δὲ κοχήσας
units.tr: Ostorodius splits and rends his Limen, but being in it,

units.la: Εἰν ὠ οἱ συγκρεσὶς, θάνατος, ἡ ταρταρεὸς ὄξη.
units.tr: There is a fight, death, and the infernal Tartarean abyss.

units.la: Ἔσῃ δ᾽ ἐν Λιμέν᾽ ὄνδ᾽ ὁ Λιμὼ λικμήσατο πάμπαν.
units.tr: Yet in Limen he will be utterly swept away by famine.

units.la: Εὑρ᾽ ἀρα αἱρεσικὸς Λιμέν᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἀπώλετ᾽ ἐν ἀυτῷ.
units.tr: The heretic who found Limen perished in it.

units.la: Οὐχὶ Λιμὼ λιμέν᾽ οἱ πέρεν ἡχ ὅτ᾽ ἐφεῦρε
units.tr: Famine did not find Limen, but he (Ostorodius) found Limen,

units.la: Κίνδυνον εἰν ἀκόσμοις ἐν ζωῇ κῆρα μέλαιναν.
units.tr: A danger in the disordered life, a black doom.

units.la: Ἐκπὸς δῆος πέλαγος, πηλὸν θελέων, βέλος ὀξύ.
units.tr: Like a swift arrow he falls into the sea, wishing for mud.

units.la: Ὡς ὄφελον πάντας θεομιτέας αὐτόθι ὀλέσθαι.
units.tr: Would that all the enemies of God had perished there!

units.la: Χαῖρε δ᾽ ἀχαλλόμενον, τεραπικτοντε, ὅ ποτ᾽ ὀλεῖταί,
units.tr: Rejoice, then, exulting, for the one who will perish

units.la: Σὸν κλέος, ἀραναὶ ἐσπείξεν μακρὰ κάρλωα.
units.tr: Shall have your glory, and he has been long withered.

units.la: Σπῦδε δ᾽ δηλῆσαι τοῖς αὐλαλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν,
units.tr: Hasten to refute those who speak against you,

units.la: Τὰξεω οὐνόματος, πολυκλεῖτου, οὐραομήκεις,
units.tr: Bearing the name of the far-famed one, the long-stretched spear,

units.la: Οὗτος δηλῆσης θεόμαχος κρατερὸς τ᾽ αἰχμητής.
units.tr: Which will refute the God-opposing, mighty warrior.

units.la: Περσεφώνη
units.tr: Persephone

units.la: Franciscus Blondetus Phys. & Mathem. Profess. Lausannæ.
units.tr: Franciscus Blondetus, Professor of Physics and Mathematics, Lausanne.

units.la: ADVERSVS CHRISTOPHORI OSTORRODII SAMOSATENIANI INSTITVTIONES RELIGIONIS (vt vocat) CHRISTIANAE
units.tr: AGAINST CHRISTOPHORUS OSTORRODIUS THE SAMOSATENIAN, HIS INSTITUTES OF (AS HE CALLS IT) CHRISTIAN RELIGION

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Scripturæ sacræ perspicuitate.
units.tr: On the perspicuity of Holy Scripture.

units.la: QVVM de Scripturæ sacræ autoritate, necesitate, origine, & perfectione, nihil inter nos, & Aduersarium, quod sciam, controuertatur; ideò illis capitibus omnibus omissis, nos rectà ad ipsam Quæstionem controuersam, quæ est de Scripturæ diuinæ perspicuitate, conferemus. Ne autem propositæ disputationis cursus incertus, ac vagus existat, Scripturæ sacræ perspicuitatem dupliciter à nobis considerari, indicamus, in se videlicet, ac respectu nostri. In se, Scripturam si consideremus, dicimus eam totam in se, & per se, esse clarissimam, & apertissimam siue materiam, siue formam, hoc est, siue verba, siue sensus, & res verbis significatas, respiciamus. Respectu vero nostri, dum de Scripturæ perspicuitate agimus, consideramus, qualia illa sint, quæ in Scripturis nobis proponuntur, & pro illorum diuerso respectu, aliter, atque aliter de perspicuitate earundem, pronuntiamus. Quæ enim ad salutem necessaria non sunt, ea quoque non omnia perspicua esse confitemur, sed nonnulla ita obscura, ac difficilia, vt ne ab ingeniosissimis, ac perspicacissimis in hac vita perfectè intelligi queant. Quæ verò simpliciter ad salutem scitu sunt necessaria, ea dicimus, ita abundè, ac perspicuè in sacris litteris esse tradita, vt quiuis electus Dei filius, qui alta mente, ferióque studio legem Dei diésque noctésque, piè ac reuerenter reuoluit, ad salutem sufficienter, non tamen sine speciali, & singulari Spiritus sancti gratia, & illuminatione, illa percipere queat. Secus autem sentit Osiorrodius, qui omnem Scripturarum intelligentiam, sublato Spiritus diuini lumine, & subsidio, humani intellectus viribus ascribit. Vt enim Pontificii in defectu, dum Scripturas omni ferè perspicuitatis luce orbatas, nimiis obscuritatis tenebris inuoluunt, grauiter peccant; ita Sociniani in excessu delinquunt, omni difficultate eas exutas, hominis etiam non regeniti, & lumine supernaturalis gratiæ destituti, ingenio, captuique subiicientes.
units.tr: Since, as far as I know, there is no dispute between us and our opponent about the authority, necessity, origin and perfection of holy Scripture, we will omit all those chapters and go straight to the question in dispute, which concerns the perspicuity of divine Scripture. So that the course of the proposed disputation may not be uncertain or wandering, I point out that the perspicuity of Holy Scripture is to be considered by us in two ways: in itself and with respect to us. If we consider Scripture in itself, we say that it is altogether and of itself most clear and most open, whether we look at its matter or its form, that is, whether at its words or at its meanings and the things signified by the words. But with respect to us, when we deal with the perspicuity of Scripture, we consider what sorts of things are set before us in the Scriptures, and we pronounce differently about their perspicuity according to their different relation to us. For we confess that not all things which are unnecessary for salvation are perspicuous, but some are so obscure and difficult that they cannot be fully understood in this life even by the most gifted and sharp-sighted. But those things which are simply necessary to know for salvation, we say are so abundantly and clearly delivered in the sacred letters that any chosen son of God who, with a lofty mind and diligent study, reverently and piously turns over the law of God day and night, can grasp them sufficiently for salvation, yet not without a special and singular grace and illumination of the Holy Spirit. Ostorrodius thinks otherwise, ascribing all understanding of the Scriptures, with the light and help of the divine Spirit removed, to the powers of the human intellect. For just as the Papists, in defect, while they wrap the Scriptures, deprived almost of all the light of perspicuity, in excessive darkness of obscurity, sin grievously, so the Socinians err in excess, stripping the Scriptures of all difficulty and subjecting them to the wit and grasp of man, even of one who is not regenerate and is destitute of the light of supernatural grace.

units.la: Quæritur igitur inter nos, & Osiorrodium: Vtrum sacra Scriptura ita sit perspicua, vt à nobis eam legentibus, vel audientibus, solius intellectus auxilio intelligi queat: an verò speciali, & interna Spiritus sancti illuminatio requiratur? Seu; Vtrum sint tanta vires intellectus humani, vt homo illius ductu, Scripturam sacram intelligere queat: an verò ita debilitata, & tanta caligine obscurata, vt singulari Spiritus sancti illuminatione ad illam in se lucidissimam, & clarissimam intelligendam, nobis opus sit. Aduersarius negata sententia posteriore, prioris patrocinium suscipit: nos contrà repudiata priore vt falsa, & absurda, posterioris veritatem declarabimus.
