Et quamuis Scriptura sacra in se sit perspicua, luce clarissima per totum eius corpus diffusa: hominibus tamen Spiritus S. gratia destitutis, etiam ea, quæ in se clarissima sunt, ita difficilia & obscura esse, vt absque interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione, veritatem eorum nec percipere, nec intelligere queant, ex sequentibus, opinor, rationibus, Osiorrodius, modò & illi Spiritus sancti virtute animus, à tenebris nativis, ad degustandam veritatem Dei, purgatus fit, cuiusdam agnoscet.
units.tr: The question between us and Ostorrodius is this: Is holy Scripture so perspicuous that it can be understood by us who read or hear it with the help of the intellect alone, or is a special and inward illumination of the Holy Spirit required? Or again: Are the powers of the human intellect so great that a man can understand holy Scripture under its guidance, or are they so weakened and obscured by such a mist that we need a singular illumination of the Holy Spirit to understand it, though it is in itself most bright and clear? The opponent, denying the latter view, takes up the defence of the former; we, rejecting the former as false and absurd, will set forth the truth of the latter. And although holy Scripture is in itself perspicuous, its light most clear and diffused through its whole body, yet for men destitute of the grace of the Holy Spirit, even those things which are in themselves most clear are so difficult and obscure that without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit they can neither perceive nor understand their truth. I think Ostorrodius will in some measure acknowledge this from the following reasons, provided that his mind too is purged, by the power of that Spirit, from its native darkness, so that it can taste the truth of God.

units.la: Iohannes enim cap. 1. verf. 5. lucem, ait, in tenebris lucere, & à tenebris non comprehendi: vbi omnem intelligentiam nostram, priusquam Spiritus Christi eam illuminet, nihil nisi meram cæcitatem, ac tenebras esse docet, nosque semel spoliat omnis spiritualis intelligentiæ facultate, dum videlicet causam, cur homines clarissima illa ma illa luce,qua diuinitus irradiatur mundus,in cognitionemDei viuentis, perduci non potuerit, à diuinitate, & maiestate Christi remotam,in natiuam mentis nostræ caliginem transfert. Vt enim cæcum aliquem ad solem meridianum si producas,quærasque ecquid videat,nihil sibi misero, nisi meras tenebras obiectas esse respondebit:ita quoque lucem verbi Dei clarissimam,mentis nostrę oculis percipi non posse, docere hic vult Euangelista, quia videlicet natiuæ cæcitatis tenebris penitus sint oppressi. Vnde etiam fideles qui Christum amplectuntur, non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, aut viri, sed ex Deo natos asserit Iohan.1.vers.13.haud secus, ac si diceret, non esse tam sublimis sapientiæ capacem carnem,vt Deum,& veritatem eius suscipiat, nisi Dei Spiritu illuminetur,sicuti Christus speciali Patris illuminationi tribuit, quòd à Petro agnosceretur, Matth.16.17. Et quanta mentis nostræ ad illam veritatis lucem sit hebetudo, manifestè sub exemplo nos docet Nicodemus Iohan.3.vers.4.& 9.vir alioquin magnus, & in lege diuina tam bene institutus, vt Doctor haberetur in Israel, quàm miserè enim ille,licet discendi esset cupidissimus,ac doctrinam Christi de spirituali hominis πνευματικῶν cæcutiuit,dum ea,quæ à Christo spiritualia dicebantur,ille animalis & carnalis,crasso, & carnali modo,de refectione,& regeneratione physica intelligeret, nec illam toties à Mose, ac Prophetis inculcatam cordis circumcisionem animaduerteret, rationis videlicet suæ acie, acduƈtu, ad tantam mysteriorum Dei altitudinem pertingere non valens, nec aliud quicquam, nisi terrenum & carnale sapiens? Sed quemadmodum testa recens,quo semel est imbuta odorem seruat, ac postea etiam in alium infusum liquorem transmittit:ita etiam ratio nostra,quia ab ipsa natiuitatis origine carnali odore & affeƈtu imbuitur,inficitúrque, quicquid postea audiuerit, pro veteri suo sapore, hoc est, carnaliter intelligit. Si deinde voluntatis humanæ nemo testis esse potest,nisi Spiritus,qui est in homine,1.Cor.2.11.diuinæ voluntatis, dic nobis, quæso, Ostorrodi, qui certus esse potest homo,nisi Spiritus sanctus, qui solus omnia, etiam profunda Dei scrutatur,internæ illuminationis suppetias ferat? Quid?annon Deum huius mundi opificem esse multis in locis clarissimè docent Scripturæ? at eum per verbum Dei construƈtum esse, non nisi per fidem à nobis intelligi disertè asserit Paulus Hebr.11.3. Fidem autem nonnisi per internam Spiritus sanƈti lucem in nobis accendi, suo loco demonstrabimus. Sic Moses Deut. 29. 2. dum affirmat, populum ideo veritatem vsúmque beneficiorum Dei ignorare, quantum-uis oculis suis magna & ingentia portenta viderint, quia Dominus nec cor ad intelligendum, nec aures ad audiendum, nec oculos ad videndum dederit, manifeste nos in rebus diuinis caecos, & surdos esse docet, vitiositate naturali, nec posse nos in Dei mysterio aliter sapere, nisi eius beneficio: Vnde Dominus per Ieremiam cap. 24. 7. singularis gratiae loco pollicetur, se Israelitis daturum cor, vt ab illis agnoscatur, docens hoc modo tantum in rebus spiritualibus sapere mentem, quantum à Deo fuerit illustrata. Sic Lydia, tum demum ea, quae à Paulo dicebantur, intellexisse dicitur Act. 16. 14. cum Deus vi Spiritus sui cor lapideum adaperuisset, cuius aures externa verbi praedicatione frustra verberaturus fuisset. Et certe intellectum hominis tum demum vere, ea, quae ad regnum Dei pertinent gustare, incipere, vbi Spiritus sancti lumine irradiatus fuerit, suo nos exemplo docent duo Christi discipuli, apud quos Christus regni sui mysteria praeclare edisserens, nihil tamen profecit, donec sensum illis aperit, vt Scripturas intelligant; Luc. 24. 27. 43. Si ita facile absque Spiritus sancti illuminatione, verum Scripturae sensum assequi quiuis ingenii sui viribus potest, quare Apostolis ipso Christi ore edoctis, Spiritus tamen veritatis mittendus erat, qui inforum mentibus eandem doctrinam instillaret, quam auribus surpauerant? Iohan. 16. 13. Et verissimum est illud, Scripturam Θεόπνευστον, vt omnino tradi, & inueniri non potuisset, nisi Spiritu S. inspirante, & reuelante: sic etiam à nobis percipi, aut intelligi non posse, nisi eodem demonstrante, & mentes nostras illuminante, ob summam nempe illam ἀσυμμετρίαν, quae est inter captum nostrum, & mysteriorum Dei profunditatem. Vnde enim, quaeso, existunt assiduae illae, & ardentissimae sanctissimorum hominum preces, ad Deum effusae, vt velit aperire oculos mentis ipsorum, ad hoc, vt videant lucem illam Scripturarum, in se alioqui clarissimam, nisi ex sensu hebetudinis, & veritatis, quae ex natiua illa corruptione in ipsis est reliqua? Sed manifestissime refutat Oftorrodium Paulus 1. Cor. 2. & 14. dum palam asserit hominem animalem, qui a Spiritu sancto nondum renouatus naturae suae lumine nititur, non posse intelligere mysteria Spiritus, quia videlicet humanae perspicaciae penitus abscondita, per solam Spiritus reuelationem patefiunt, adeo, vt etiam pro stultitia ducantur, vsque dum illius lumen coelitus illutus illuxerit. Hominem itaque animalem sacras Scripturas absque interno Spiritus adminiculo intelligere posse, quæ efficiente, materia, forma, ac fine spirituales sunt, ac diuinæ: & tamen eundem non posse percipere ea, quę sunt Spiritus Dei, si ex verbo Dei me docuerit Oflorrodius, erit mihi, crede, magnus Apollo: Docebit autem tum, cùm contradicentia simul vera esse, & propositionem diuinitus enuntiatam, à se vere negari posse demonstrauerit.
units.tr: For John (ch. 1, v. 5) says that the light shines in darkness and the darkness does not comprehend it. There he teaches that all our understanding, before the Spirit of Christ illumines it, is nothing but mere blindness and darkness, and he strips us once for all of every faculty of spiritual understanding. For while he traces the cause why men could not be led to the knowledge of the living God by that most clear light with which the world is divinely irradiated, he refers it to the native darkness of our mind, which is remote from the divinity and majesty of Christ. For just as, if you bring some blind man out into the midday sun and ask whether he sees anything, he will answer that nothing is set before his wretched eyes but mere darkness, so the Evangelist here wishes us to understand that the most clear light of the word of God cannot be perceived by the eyes of our mind, because they are utterly oppressed by the darkness of native blindness. Hence also he asserts (John 1:13) that the faithful who embrace Christ are born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of man, but of God, just as if he were saying that flesh is not capable of so sublime a wisdom that it could receive God and his truth unless it were illumined by the Spirit of God, just as Christ attributed to the special illumination of the Father the fact that he was recognised by Peter (Matt. 16:17). And how great the dullness of our mind is with respect to that light of truth, Nicodemus clearly shows us as an example (John 3:4 and 9): a man otherwise great and so well instructed in the divine law that he was regarded as a teacher in Israel. How wretchedly, though most eager to learn, he was blinded regarding Christ's doctrine of the spiritual [πνευματικῶν] man! For he, being natural and carnal, understood in a crude and fleshly way, as physical refreshing and regeneration, the things that Christ called spiritual, and he did not notice the circumcision of the heart so often impressed by Moses and the prophets. His reason, with its own edge and guidance, could not reach such a height of God's mysteries, and he was wise in nothing but earthly and carnal things. But just as a new jar keeps the smell with which it was first imbued, and afterwards passes it on to whatever liquid is poured into it, so too our reason, since from the very origin of its birth it is imbued and tainted with a carnal odour and disposition, understands whatever it hears afterwards according to its old flavour, that is, carnally. Next, if no one can be a witness of the human will "except the spirit that is in man" (1 Cor. 2:11), of the divine will, tell us, I beg you, Ostorrodius: who can be certain of it, unless the Holy Spirit, "who alone searches all things, even the depths of God", brings the help of inward illumination? Do not the Scriptures teach in many places, most clearly, that God is the maker of this world? Yet Paul expressly asserts (Heb. 11:3) that it was framed by the word of God, and this we cannot understand except through faith. That faith is kindled in us only by the inward light of the Holy Spirit I will demonstrate in its place. So Moses (Deut. 29:2) affirms that the people did not know the truth and the benefits of God, however greatly they had seen the great and wondrous portents with their eyes, because the Lord had given them neither a heart to understand, nor ears to hear, nor eyes to see. He clearly teaches that we are blind and deaf in divine things through natural corruption, and cannot be wise in God's mystery except by his gift. Hence the Lord, through Jeremiah (Jer. 24:7), promises the Israelites, as a pledge of singular grace, that he will give them a heart so that they may know him, teaching in this way that the mind is wise in spiritual things only as far as it has been enlightened by God. So Lydia is said to have understood the things that were said by Paul (Acts 16:14) only when God, by the power of his Spirit, had opened her stony heart, whose ears Paul would have beaten in vain with the external preaching of the word. And indeed the two disciples of Christ teach us by their own example that the human intellect truly begins to taste the things that belong to the kingdom of God only when it is irradiated by the light of the Holy Spirit. Christ, expounding the mysteries of his kingdom most clearly to them, made no progress until he opened their sense so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:27, 43). If anyone can so easily grasp the true sense of Scripture by the powers of his own wit, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, why was the Spirit of truth to be sent to the Apostles, who had been taught by Christ's own mouth, to instil into their minds the same doctrine which they had taken in with their ears (John 16:13)? And that saying is most true: Scripture, God-breathed [θεόπνευστον], could not have been delivered and found at all unless by the inspiring and revealing Holy Spirit. So likewise it cannot be perceived or understood by us unless the same Spirit demonstrates it and illumines our minds, on account of that supreme incommensurability [ἀσυμμετρίαν] which lies between our capacity and the depth of God's mysteries. For whence, I ask, come those constant and most fervent prayers of the holiest men, poured out to God, that he would deign to open the eyes of their minds, so that they might see that light of the Scriptures which is otherwise most clear in itself, unless from the dullness and the lack of truth which remains in them from that native corruption? But Paul, in 1 Cor. 2 and 14, most manifestly refutes Ostorrodius, while he openly asserts that the natural man, who has not yet been renewed by the Spirit and relies on the light of his own nature, cannot understand the mysteries of the Spirit. These are hidden utterly from human acuteness and are disclosed only by the revelation of the Spirit, so that they are even counted as foolishness until the light of that revelation shines down from heaven. Therefore, if Ostorrodius teaches me from the word of God that the natural man can understand the holy Scriptures without the inward aid of the Spirit, though they are spiritual and divine in their efficient cause, matter, form and end, and yet that the same man cannot perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, he will be, believe me, a great Apollo to me. He will teach this, however, only when he has shown that contradictory things can be true at the same time, and that a proposition divinely uttered can truly be denied by him.

units.la: Ex hisce autem omnibus luce meridiana clarius cuadit, id quod supra diximus, Verbum quidem Dei instar solis esse clarissimum, sed intellectus nostri cęcitatem à natura tantam, vt, nisi Spiritus S. sua nos luce illustret, illius splendorem contemplari non valeamus: & legendo, audiendóque nihil vnquam nos proficere queamus, nisi Θεοδιδακτοι simus, & ad externum verbum interior ille Doctor, Spiritus nempe Dei accedat, qui illuminet mentes nostras, & aperiat corda nostra, doceat, ac subministret animis nostris interioribus, quæ ipse auribus inculcat.
units.tr: From all these things it follows more clearly than midday light what we said above: the Word of God is indeed like the sun, most bright, but the blindness of our intellect by nature is so great that, unless the Holy Spirit illumines us with his own light, we cannot contemplate its splendour; and by reading and hearing we can make no progress at all, unless we are taught by God [θεοδίδακτοι], and that inner Teacher, namely the Spirit of God, comes to the external word, to enlighten our minds, open our hearts, teach, and supply to our inner souls what he himself impresses on our ears.

units.la: CAPVT II. In quo sententia Aduersarij proponitur, ac refellitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. In which the opponent's view is set out and refuted.

units.la: OSTORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite primo, tres potissimum quæstiones controuersas tractat: primam de Scriptura perfectione: alteram, de eiusdem interpretatione aduersus Pontificios: tertiam, de Scripturarum perspicuitate aduersus receptam in Ecclesiis nostris sententiam. Nos relictis duabus prioribus, argumenta Aduersarii, quæ contra nostram adfert sententiam, breuiter diluemus.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in the first chapter of his Institutes, treats three main controversial questions: the first on the perfection of Scripture; the second on its interpretation, against the Papists; the third on the perspicuity of the Scriptures, against the view received in our churches. Setting aside the first two, we will briefly dissolve the arguments that the opponent brings against our position.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM PRIMVM
units.tr: FIRST ARGUMENT

units.la: Si singulari Dei consilio res diuinæ ideo scriptæ sunt, vt quilibet eas legere, & intelligere possit: tum sequitur Scripturam à nobis absque interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione intelligi posse: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo, &c. Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam, quum subordinata minime pugnent, & posito fine, non remouenda, sed adhibenda sunt media, & adminicula omnia, quæ nos ad illum finem perducunt, & sine quibus eum assequi non possumus. Scriptura, inquit, ideo inspirata esse, vt a nobis percipiantur, & intelligantur: Quid inde? An ergo sequitur viribus nostris sine illuminatione Spiritus S. illud a nobis præstari posse? Totum Euangelium scriptum est, vt credamus Iesum esse Christum filium illum Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeamus per nomen eius, Iohan. 20, 31. quis tamen sanæ mentis inde concluserit, nos viribus nostris, aut in Christum credere, aut in cælum euolare posse, mediis illis, quibus Deus Electos suos subuehit, destitutos?
units.tr: If by God's singular counsel the divine matters were written so that anyone might read and understand them, then it follows that we can understand Scripture without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit. But the first is true; therefore, etc. Reply: the consequence is false, since subordinate things do not conflict. Once an end is posited, the means and all the aids that lead us to that end are not to be removed but applied, and without them we cannot reach it. Scripture, he says, was inspired so that it might be perceived and understood. What follows from this? Does it follow that we can accomplish this by our own powers, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit? The whole Gospel was written so that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing we may have life through his name (John 20:31). Yet who of sound mind would conclude from this that we, deprived of those means by which God carries his Elect aloft, can believe in Christ or fly up to heaven by our own powers?

units.la: ARGVMENTVM SECVNDVM.
units.tr: SECOND ARGUMENT.

units.la: Si homo absque interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione non posset illa omnia in Scripturis intelligere, quæ ipsi ad salutem scitu sunt necessaria, tum hoc fieret, vel vitio hominis, vel vitio ipsius Scripturæ: Atqui vtrumque consequens falsum est: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: If a man, without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, could not understand in the Scriptures all those things that are necessary for him to know for salvation, then this would happen either through the fault of the man or through the fault of Scripture itself. But both consequents are false; therefore the antecedent is too.

units.la: Primę partis in assumptione, quod videlicet hoc non fiat vitio hominis, καθολικὴ talis est.
units.tr: That the first part, in the minor premise, namely that this does not happen through the fault of man, is universally true, is as follows.

units.la: Si hoc fieret vitio hominis, tum vel Deus hominem talem condidisset, vt natura suares diuinas, etiam cum docentur, intelligere non possit: aut eius natura ita corrupta esset, ac depravata, vtres spirituales, absque interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione, intelligere amplius non posset:
units.tr: If this happened through the fault of man, then either God would have made man such that his nature could not understand divine things even when they are taught, or his nature would be so corrupted and depraved that, without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, he could no longer understand spiritual things.

units.la: Consequens autem connexi vtrumque falsum est:
units.tr: But both parts of this connected consequent are false.

units.la: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Primæ iterum partis in assumptione ἐπιλογισμῷ sumit a testimonio nostrorum Theologorum, qui statuunt, Deum tanta scientia, ac sapientia hominem primum instruxisse, vt non physicarum tantum, ac terrestrium, sed etiam diuinarum rerum scientia polleret. Alterius vero partis demonstrationem in loco de Libero arbitrio cap. 33. & 34. pollicetur. Absoluta hoc modo καθολικὴ primæ partis in propositione minore, sy llogismi principalis, quod videlicet hominis natura non sit imputandum quod absque Spiritus sancti illuminatione interna Scripturam sacram intelligere non possit, ad partis alterius in eadem propositione, quod nempe Scripturæ sacræ culpa idem non fiat, demonstrationem progreditur.
units.tr: As to the first part of the minor premise, he takes it by inference from the testimony of our theologians, who maintain that God endowed the first man with such great knowledge and wisdom that he excelled not only in the knowledge of physical and earthly things but also of divine things. He promises a demonstration of the other part in the place on Free will, chapters 33 and 34. Having thus completed the universal of the first part in the minor premise of the principal syllogism, namely that it is not to be imputed to human nature that without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit it cannot understand Holy Scripture, he goes on to demonstrate the other part of the same minor premise, namely that this does not happen through the fault of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Resp. Mirum est profecto, si montes non crepuerint, cum Ostorrodius hæc oracula ex tripode Sociniano ederet, tantúmque sapientiæ thesaurum proferret. Quum enim omnes communi consensu doceamus, sacram Scripturam in se esse clarissimam, totámque splendore lucidissimo perfusam, a nobis tamen sine interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione, intelligi non posse, tum quia intellectus noster, priusquam ex huius naturæ ambitu, & circumferentia ad rerum cœlestium centrum euehatur diuinitus, natiuæ cæcitatis caligine totus opprimatur, tum etiam, quia homines arrogantes, superbi, & peruersi, clarissimæ Dei veritati, & cœlesti Scripturarum luci, nocentissimorum errorum præsigiis tenebras offundant: ideo frustra Ostorrodius, saltem aduersus nos, Scripturæ sacræ perspicuitatem defendendam suscipit, hoc est, Andabatarum more aerem clausis oculis verberat, cum nullum ex nostris hac in parte sibi aduersantem habeat. Quum deinde creationis opus, non in huius naturæ pollutionis, & corruptionis contagione, sordibus & squalore, sed integræ naturæ splendore, ac magnificentia contemplantes, maxima animi cum certitudine asseueremus, hominem primum ante functam illam apostasiam, non modo notitia vera, & integra, de Deo, ciusque voluntate, tanta, quanta ipsi ad salutem obtinendam, si in primæva integritate perstitisset, necessaria fuisset, sed insuper etiam omnium virtutum choro, & cumulo a Deo instructum fuisse: quum denique ingenuè vel sexcentis in locis fateamur, vitio natiuæ cæcitatis nostræ fieri, quod res diuinæ tam perspicuè nobis in Scripturis traditæ, a nobis non percipiantur: ideo frustra Ostorrodius hanc syllogismorum telam nectit, nec tota hac disputationis serie quicquam agit contra nos, nisi quod dies promisisse, hominem peccato non esse corruptum, se capite Institutionum suarum trigesimo tertio, & trigesimo quarto, demonstraturum esse pollicetur, quod recta illis ambagibus, de quibus nulla est controversia, relictis, præstare, aut hanc de qua agimus, controversiam ad eam quoque classem referre, debuisset.
units.tr: Reply: It is truly remarkable that the mountains did not quake when Ostorrodius delivered these oracles from a Socinian tripod and produced such a treasure of wisdom. For since we all teach with one voice that Holy Scripture is in itself most clear and wholly bathed in the most brilliant light, yet that it cannot be understood by us without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, both because our understanding, before it is divinely lifted from the circle and circumference of this nature to the centre of heavenly things, is wholly oppressed by the darkness of its innate blindness, and also because arrogant, proud and perverse men cast the darkness of most harmful errors over the clearest truth of God and the heavenly light of the Scriptures: therefore Ostorrodius vainly undertakes to defend the perspicuity of Holy Scripture, at least against us, beating the air like the Andabatae with eyes closed, since he has no one among us who opposes him in this respect. Then, since we, contemplating the work of creation not in the contagion, filth and squalor of this nature's pollution and corruption but in the splendour and magnificence of its integrity, affirm with the greatest certainty that man, before that apostasy, had not only a true and complete knowledge of God and his will, as much as would have been necessary for obtaining salvation had he persisted in his primeval integrity, but was also furnished by God with a whole chorus and abundance of all virtues; and since finally we frankly admit in countless places that it is through the fault of our innate blindness that the divine matters so plainly delivered to us in the Scriptures are not perceived by us: therefore Ostorrodius vainly weaves this web of syllogisms, and by this whole series of argument he achieves nothing against us, except that he promises to demonstrate, in chapters 33 and 34 of his Institutes, that man is not corrupted by sin. He should have done this directly, leaving aside those circumlocutions about which there is no controversy, or referred the present controversy to that class.

units.la: Ne autem Ostorrodius hanc controversiam plane relinquat intactam, dicit, nos ipsos in hac sententia, qua statuimus, naturam humanam peccati originalis labe miserè pollutam, & corruptam esse, non esse constantes. 1 quia homini post lapsum eam tribuamus facultatem, ut viribus naturæ ex nuda creaturarum contemplatione, præsertim autem cæli, terræque intuitu cognoscere queat, non modo Deum esse, verùm etiam eum generis humani curam gerere. 2. quia nonnulli affir- mare audeant, ex rerum creatarum contemplatione, & huius mundi consideratione, quicquid ad veram religionem, verùmque Dei cultum scitu sit necessarium, cognosci posse. Hinc concludit posito illis necessario sequi naturam humanam minime corruptam esse, culpmque cur Scriptura sacra à nobis intelligi nequeat, non homini, sed Scripturae, imo potius ipsi Deo imputandum esse, qui noluerit quosdam ad agnitionem suae voluntatis peruenire: quam sententiam dicit tueri illos, qui docent, Deum ab aeterno quosdam, imò maximam partem humani generis ad interminam damnationem, & omnia damnationis media praedestinasse: qua de re polliceatur se capite trigesimo quinto acturum esse.
units.tr: Yet, so that Ostorrodius may not leave this controversy entirely untouched, he says that we ourselves are not consistent in this view, by which we hold that human nature is miserably polluted and corrupted by the stain of original sin: (1) because we grant man, after the fall, the faculty by which, by the powers of nature alone, from the bare contemplation of creatures, and especially from the sight of heaven and earth, he can know not only that God exists but also that he cares for the human race; (2) because some dare to affirm that from the contemplation of created things and the consideration of this world, whatever is necessary to know for true religion and the true worship of God can be known. From this he concludes that, given these premises, it necessarily follows that human nature is not corrupted at all, and that the blame for why Holy Scripture cannot be understood by us is to be imputed not to man but to Scripture, or rather to God himself, who was unwilling for some to attain to the knowledge of his will. He says that those who teach that God from eternity predestined some, or indeed the greatest part of the human race, to endless damnation and to all the means of damnation defend this view; and he promises to deal with this matter in chapter 35.

units.la: Nos conditionem amplectimur, sed nunquam à nobis discedet Oftorrodius, quin haec tria capita breuiter perstringamus: primò, an ex sententia nostra sequatur humanam naturam non esse corruptam. 2. an illud unquam à nobis fuerit affirmatum, quod ille secundo loco praesupponit. 3. an illa sententia de praedestinatione merito nobis impingatur.
units.tr: We accept the condition, but Ostorrodius shall never get away from us without our briefly touching on these three points: first, whether it follows from our view that human nature is not corrupted; second, whether that was ever affirmed by us, which he presupposes in the second place; third, whether that doctrine of predestination is fairly charged against us.

units.la: Primum igitur quod attinet, quum discrimen non obseruet, quod est inter generales illas, & confusas θεολογίας, ac notitias in homine post lapsum reliquas, atque solidam illam, veramque Dei scientiam, qua iustificaturus dicitur Christus electos suos, quámve ex sola scriptura sacra lumine Spiritus sancti nobis praelucente haurimus, mirum non est, eum ab vna ad alteram, tam absurdam ducere consequentiam.
units.tr: As to the first, since he does not observe the difference between those general and confused notions of God, and the other knowledge left in man after the fall, and that solid and true knowledge of God by which Christ is said to justify his elect, which we draw from Scripture alone with the light of the Holy Spirit shining upon us, it is no wonder that he draws so absurd a consequence from the one to the other.

units.la: Secundum, si impingat Theologis nostris Oftorrodius, non disputatorem candidum, sed conuitiatorem malitiosum agit. Producat enim vnum ex nostris, qui tanti erroris patrocinium suscipiat, doceatque hominem ex sola creationis contemplatione, cognoscere posse, quaecunque ad veram religionem, ac sacrum Dei cultum sunt necessaria, aut se insignem hanc calumniam commentum esse, fateatur, sciatque si quis tantas liberi arbitrii vires homini in statu corruptionis constituto, tribuat, eum non ex orthodoxo nostro coetu, sed ex Pelagianorum impuro grege oriundum, à nobis censeri. Non enim obscurum est, quàm studiosè Ecclesiarum nostrarum Doctores in vniuersum omnes, stupidas ac caecas nostrae naturae imbecillitatem, aduersus ebrios illos vana opinione perspicaciae nostrae, inculcent, eam si Oftorrodius nobiscum agnosceret, & abiecto collapsae naturae studio, gratiaeque diuinae odio dio, veram humiliationis gloriam Deo tribueret, certum est, cum in tam foedos, ac blasphemos errores nunquam prolapsurum fuisse.
units.tr: As to the second: if Ostorrodius attacks our theologians, he acts not as a candid disputant but as a malicious reviler. Let him produce one of ours who undertakes the defence of so great an error, and who teaches that man can know from the contemplation of creation alone whatever is necessary for true religion and the sacred worship of God; or let him admit that this notorious calumny is his own invention, and let him know that if anyone ascribes such great powers of free will to man in a state of corruption, we count him not of our orthodox body but as sprung from the impure flock of the Pelagians. For it is not hidden how earnestly the teachers of our churches, almost all of them, inculcate the dull and blind weakness of our nature against those drunkards with their vain opinion of our own perspicacity. If Ostorrodius agreed with us on this, and, abandoning zeal for fallen nature and hatred of divine grace, ascribed to God the true glory of humility, it is certain that he would never have fallen into such foul and blasphemous errors.

units.la: Tertium æque ac secundum falsum, conuitium est, quod dicit, à nobis doceri, Deum ab æterno quosdam, imo maximam partem hominum, non modò ad damnationem, sed omnia damnationis media prædestinasse, quod & falsum est, vt infra in loco de Prædestinatione ostendemus, & falso nobis tribuitur. Dum enim cum Scriptura multos vocatos esse, paucos electos dicimus, interim vnanimi consensu docemus, credimus, ac confitemur, electionem quidem causam esse, & eius, quæ expectatur in futura vita, gloriæ, & eius, quæ percipitur in præsente, gratiæ: Reprobationem autem non esse eius, quæ est in hac vita culpæ, sed eius, quæ in futuro iusto Dei iudicio redditur, poenæ: hoc est, dari electis, vt boni sint, & bonum assequantur, reprobis præstari, non vt mali sint, sed vt malum assequantur, quod est bonum iustumque iudicium Dei. Atque hinc liquidò Christiano, & æquo lectori constat, quo æquitatis titulo quibusque argumentis motus Ostorrodius illam conclusionem inferat, culpam, cur Scriptura à nobis intelligi nequeat, necessario in Scripturam, aut Deum ipsum deriuandam nobis esse, aut si blasphemiam hanc euitare velimus, confitendum, Scripturas sacras absque interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione percipi, & intelligi posse.
units.tr: The third charge, like the second, is false: that he says we teach that God from eternity predestined not only some, indeed the greater part of men, to damnation, but also all the means of damnation. This is false, as we will show below in the place on Predestination, and it is wrongly attributed to us. For while we say with Scripture that many are called but few chosen, we at the same time teach, believe and confess with one united consent that election is indeed the cause both of the glory expected in the future life and of the grace received in the present; but reprobation is not the cause of the guilt that exists in this life, but of the punishment that is inflicted in the future by the just judgment of God. That is, the elect are given grace so that they may be good and attain the good, while the reprobate are left to themselves, not so that they may be evil, but so that they may attain the evil, which is the good and just judgment of God. From this it is clear to the Christian and fair-minded reader, under what pretext of fairness and by what arguments Ostorodius was moved to draw that conclusion: that the fault, "why Scripture cannot be understood by us," must necessarily be traced back to Scripture or to God himself; or else, if we wish to avoid this blasphemy, we must confess that the holy Scriptures can be perceived and understood without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: In quo de naturali cognitione Dei in homine disceptatur.
units.tr: In which the natural knowledge of God in man is debated.

units.la: DISPVTATIONI, de Scriptura sacra per speculitate, aliam quæstionem interserit Aduersarius de naturali cognitione Dei in homine: An videlicet homo ante lapsum potuerit, & possit etiamnum post lapsum ex mera, & nuda creationis contemplatione, & consideratione, naturali facultate, absque speciali & diuina revelatione, Deum, & eius voluntatem cognoscere. Si de Deo, & eius voluntate, siue eam à nobis, siue de nobis fieri, voluisse existimet, simul quærat, libenter cum Orthodoxio per negationem respondemus, cum voluntatis diuinae cognitio, ex creationis intuitu, principioque naturali vllo, hauriri neutiquam possit, sed ex fonte supernaturali fluat. Verum quia Aduersarius simpliciter etiam negat, ex illa operum diuinorum contemplatione Deum esse, vel quicquam de Deo sciri posse, libenter etiam rationum, & argumentorum momenta cum ipso conferemus. Quum autem ipsum quaestionis subiectum, non fit vnum quid, & simplex, atque iisdem qualitatibus vestitum, sed eiusmodi circumstantiis diuersum, quibus praesupponuntur causae, quae statum hominis integri, & in sanctitate primaeua constituti, ac hominis corrupti, & lapsi, ita distinguunt, vt idem hic de vtroque enuntiari nequeat: ideo iis, quae primi hominis conditionem attinguunt, disputationi de Libero arbitrio, quo etiam Aduersarius eam reiicit, reseruatis, hic tantum de notitia hominis post lapsum reliqua, disputiciemus.
units.tr: Into the dispute about Holy Scripture by speculation, the opponent inserts another question, about the natural knowledge of God in man: namely, whether man before the fall could, and even now after the fall can, know God and his will from the mere and bare contemplation and consideration of creation, by natural faculty, without special and divine revelation. If he thinks we have wished to say that God and his will are made known either by us or from us, let him ask at the same time. We answer, with Orthodoxius, by denial: the knowledge of the divine will can by no means be drawn from the sight of creation or from any natural principle, but flows from a supernatural source. But since the opponent also flatly denies that God's existence, or anything about God, can be known from the contemplation of his works, we will gladly weigh the force of reasons and arguments with him as well. Yet the subject of the question itself is not one simple thing, clothed in the same qualities. It differs according to circumstances, which presuppose causes that distinguish the state of man in his integrity, established in original holiness, from the state of man corrupted and fallen, so that the same thing cannot be asserted of both. Therefore, reserving those matters that concern the condition of the first man, on which the opponent also rejects free will for the disputation on that subject, we will discuss here only the knowledge of man remaining after the fall.

units.la: Atque vt rectius intelligatur disceptatio nostra, notitiam Dei naturalem duplicem esse dicimus, vnam obiectiuam, qua videlicet toti naturae vestigia diuinitatis sic sunt impressa, vt amplissimam, & vberrimam cognitionis Dei materiam nobis exhibeat: alteram subiectiuam in mentibus nostris, quibus diuinitatis sensum naturae sic insitum haerere dicimus, vt in omnibus sit non modo Deum noscendi naturalis vis ac facultas, sed nulla etiam sit natio tam barbara, nulla gens tam efferata, cui non insideat ex naturali lumine haec persuasio, Deum esse. Tria itaque haec ordine affirmamus ac demonstrabimus: Primo, sensum diuinitatis, ac notitiam, Deum esse, omnibus naturaliter esse insitum. Secundo, mundum hunc vniuersum sufficiente m praebere materiam cognoscendae diuinitatis. Tertio, in homine etiam post lapsum, esse facultatem ex operibus creationis diuinitatem cognoscendi, & notitiam alteram primam augendi & confirmandi.
units.tr: So that our dispute may be understood more correctly, we say that the natural knowledge of God is twofold: one objective, by which the traces of divinity are so impressed upon the whole of nature that they present to us a very ample and abundant matter for knowing God; the other subjective, which we say cleaves to our minds, implanted in them by nature, so that in all men there is not only a natural power and faculty of knowing God, but no nation is so barbarous, no people so savage, that this persuasion, that God exists, does not dwell in it from the natural light. Accordingly, we affirm and will demonstrate these three things in order: First, that the sense of divinity and the notion that God exists are naturally implanted in all men. Second, that this whole world provides sufficient matter for knowing the divinity. Third, that in man, even after the fall, there is the faculty of knowing the divinity from the works of creation, and the ability to increase and confirm the first notion.

units.la: Argumentum primum pro thesi prima, omnium videlicet animorum medullis insculptam esse hanc persuasionem, Deum esse, deducitur ab vniuersali, & perpetuo omnium populorum & gentium consensu, quarum nulla vnquam, teste Cicerone libr. 1. de natura Deorum, tam efferata aut barbara fuit, quin aliquod numen agnouerit. Et qui in aliis vitae partibus minimum videntur a belluis differre, quoddam tamen perpetuo religionis semen retinent, vt pulchre docet Lactant. lib. 3. diuinarum institutionum cap .10.adeo tenaciter videlicet omnium visceribus inhæret communis illa præsumptio.Ex eo igitur sic concludimus:
units.tr: The first argument for the first thesis, namely that this persuasion, that God exists, is engraved in the marrow of all souls, is drawn from the universal and perpetual consent of all peoples and nations. As Cicero says in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods, none has ever been so savage or barbarous that it did not acknowledge some divinity. And those who seem to differ least from beasts in other parts of life nevertheless retain some perpetual seed of religion, as Lactantius teaches well in the third book of the Divine Institutes, chapter 10. So tenaciously does that common presumption cling to the inmost parts of all. From this we therefore conclude thus:

units.la: Quod vniuersis cuiusque nationis hominibus commune est, id non ex disciplina aut traditione,sed a natura ipsis insitum est.
units.tr: What is common to all men of every nation is implanted in them by nature, not derived from teaching or tradition.

units.la: Atqui sensus diuinitatis omnibus,quantumuis barbaris,&ab humanitate alienis remotisque communis est: Ergo,&c.
units.tr: But the sense of divinity is common to all, however barbarous and remote from civilised life: therefore, etc.

units.la: Maiorem propositionem verissimam fatetur Aduersarius,dum affirmat,si hæc notitia naturalis esset, omnibus hominibus eam insitam fore. Verùm assumptionem syllogismi nostri, & consequens connexi sui,falsum esse,exemplorum aliquot inductione demonstrare conatur,& dicit, 1.Indos de Deo vllo ne cogitare quidem.2.non tantùm ex idiotis indoctis,sed etiam ex Philosophis, extitisse quosdam, qui Deum aliquem esse negauerint.
units.tr: The opponent grants the major premise as entirely true, when he affirms that if this knowledge were natural, it would be implanted in all men. But he tries to show by the induction of several examples that our minor premise, and the consequence of our syllogism, are false, and says: (1) that the Indians do not even think of any God; (2) that not only uneducated laymen but also philosophers have existed who denied that any God exists.

units.la: Resp. Indos quod attinet, tantùm abest vt diuinitatis sensu & notitia omni careant,vt potius Solem, Lunam, aliòsque Deos fictitios, variis figuris & simulachris depictos, Zemes etiam suos, Corocottos,Epilguanitas,& idolum bombycinum,ipsos denique dæmones colere & adorare malint, quàm vt putentur nullum se habere Deum.Quin etiam ipsis Brasiliěsibus,hominibus licet obcæcatissimis, & ab omni penè religionis studio alienissimis, aliquod tamen religionis semen inesse,ex animarum, quam credunt immortalitate,& virtutum, quæ expectant, præmiis, aliisque documentis,historici demonstrant.
units.tr: Answer. As for the Indians, far from lacking all sense and knowledge of divinity, they would rather worship the Sun, the Moon, and other fictitious gods depicted in various forms and images, their Zemes too, Corocottos, Epilguanitas, and a silk idol, and finally even demons themselves, than be thought to have no God at all. Indeed, historians demonstrate that even the Brazilians, men most blinded and most alien to nearly every pursuit of religion, nevertheless have some seed of religion within them, from their belief in the immortality of souls, the rewards of virtues they look for, and other such teachings.

units.la: Philosophi autem quidam Deum esse negarunt, quò ad conatum,nefariúmque studium, omnem Dei notitiā & memoriam ex illorum mentibus delendi & obliterandi,licet illud effectum dare nunquam potuerint. Dum itaque Dei sensum ex animis summo conatu extirpare cupiunt,& id, non quod sentiunt, verùm quod sentire cupiūt,palā absq; pudore profitentur,rectè Deū negare dicuntur.Deū igitur illi negant vita,non conscientia:negant quoad prouidentiam,non quod ad essentiam:negant professione oris,nō cordis,quod mordet intus conscientiæ vermis omnibus cauteriis acrior.Nā si revera nullo diuini numinis sensu afficeretur,Deúmque ex animo negarent, ipsis etiam bestiis hac in re stupidiores essent, quippe quæ aliquomodo Deū agnoscunt, nobisque indicāt, Iob.12.v.7.8.9. Interroga bestias, & docebunt te,ac volucres cæli indicabunt tibi:vel terram alloquere,illa docebit te,&pisces maris enarra-bunt tibi.Quis ignorat Deum hæc omnia fecisse? Argumentum secundum ducitur ab effectu mirabili, videlicet Idololatria, quę huius vniuersalis conceptionis, videlicet esse Deum, amplissimum est documentum. Notum enim est omnibus,quàm non libenter se deiiciat homo,vt alias præ se creaturas suspiciat,miretur,& reuereatur.Quum igitur gentes,quę veraDei notitia haftenus caruerunt, lapides etiam, & ligna colere,atque ita infra vilissimas creaturas se abiicere maluerint, & quid vis potius Deum esse,quàm nullumDeum esse persuasæ fuerint,constat inde vehementissimam esse illam in homine impressionem, quæ adeo ex hominis mente obliterari nequeat, vt facilius fit naturæ effectum frangi, quemadmodum vere frangitur, dum homo ex naturali illa inflatione ad infima quæque sponte se demittit, quò Deum reuereatur,vnde iterum sic concludimus:
units.tr: Some philosophers, however, denied that God exists, in so far as they made the attempt, and pursued the wicked aim, of wiping out and obliterating every knowledge and memory of God from their minds; yet they could never bring that about. So while they desire with the greatest effort to root out the sense of God from their souls, and openly profess without shame not what they feel but what they wish to feel, they are rightly said to deny God. They therefore deny God in life, not in conscience; they deny him as to providence, not as to essence; they deny him by the profession of the mouth, not of the heart, while the worm of conscience gnaws within them, sharper than any cautery. For if they were truly affected by no sense of the divine power, and denied God from the heart, they would be more stupid even than the beasts in this matter, since beasts in some way acknowledge God and point him out to us: Job 12:7–9, Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; and the birds of the air will tell you. Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; and the fishes of the sea will declare to you. Who does not know that the Lord has done all this? The second argument is drawn from a remarkable effect, namely idolatry, which is a very ample proof of this universal conception, that God exists. For it is known to all how unwillingly man humbles himself, so as to look up to, admire and revere other creatures above himself. Since therefore the nations, which until now have lacked the true knowledge of God, have preferred to worship stones and wood, and so cast themselves down beneath the vilest creatures, and have been persuaded that anything whatever is God rather than that there is no God, it is clear that this impression in man is most vehement, and cannot be so wiped out of the human mind that the effect of nature is more easily broken. It is indeed broken, when man of his own accord, from that natural self-inflation, lowers himself to the basest things, so that he may revere God. Hence we again conclude thus:

units.la: Quod hominis superbiam, φιλαυτίαν, atque ambitionem frangit, ipsumque ad rerum vilissimarum, & longe infra humanam conditionem positarum, venerationem prosternit, id homini est naturale:
units.tr: What breaks man's pride, self-love [φιλαυτία], and ambition, and prostrates him in veneration of the vilest things, placed far below the human condition, is natural to man.

units.la: Atqui sensus diuinitatis hominem eo deiicit, vt vilissima quaeque colat, & coram iis se prosternat:
units.tr: But the sense of divinity brings man down so that he worships the vilest things and prostrates himself before them.

units.la: Sensus igitur diuinitatis homini est naturalis.
units.tr: Therefore the sense of divinity is natural to man.

units.la: Argumentum tertium desumitur à conscientia, quæ post admissa peccata, licet nulli hominum cognita, non cessat tamen hominem accusare,ac cæcis tormentis vellicare, & excruciare: contra autem in negotio bene gesto,etiam aduersus aliorum calumnias, & mendacia nos excusare, & gaudio quodam perfundere solet, Rom. 2. 15. Qui ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis vna testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. Has compunctiones,hoc iudicium,& hoc tribunal,quod Deus exercet, & erigit in cuiusque cōscietia,illos denique terrores,ac morsus ob malefacta,ac clādestina scelera,tumultuatis animi,vsq; adeo subterfugere nemo potest, vt vereretur potius ne ipsæ volucres clàm patrata flagitia reuelarent, quàm vt nullo eorum sensu afficeretur conscientia:quemadmodum cestè præclarum exemplum de quodam Beffo recenset Plutarchus, cuius parricidium postquam diu clàm fuisset,confessionem metus ab hirundinibus iniectus extorsit,quarum ille nido hasta præteriens deiecto,pullos interfecit, eò quod sceleris commissi ipsum arguere, patremque ab ipso trucidatum datum esse, vociferari misero ipsi viderentur, ad iusum posca supplicium rapto. Et certè, ut primùm quis improbè egit (sicut optimè ait idem Plutarchus) iam obstrictus poenæ tenetur, & suavitate flagitii veluti esca illico devorata, conscientiam intus urgentem, plectentemque habens,
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from conscience, which, after sins have been committed, though known to no man, does not cease to accuse man, and to torment and rack him with hidden torments. On the other hand, in a well-done deed it is wont to excuse us even against the calumnies and lies of others, and to fill us with a certain joy. Romans 2:15: who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another. No one can escape these pangs, this judgement and this tribunal, which God exercises and sets up in each one's conscience, nor the terrors and bites of the soul in turmoil over evil deeds and secret crimes, to such a degree that a man fears rather that the very birds might reveal the crimes committed in secret than that his conscience should feel nothing of them. Plutarch records a notable example of this concerning a certain Beffus: after his parricide had long been kept secret, fear, struck into him by the swallows, forced a confession from him. When he passed by, he struck down a swallow's nest with his spear and killed the young, because the birds seemed to him to cry out that they accused him of the crime and that he had slain his father, and so he was dragged off to the punishment of the vinegar and the rack. And indeed, as soon as anyone has acted wickedly (as the same Plutarch rightly says), he is already bound to punishment, and, having devoured the sweetness of the crime as if it were bait, he has within him a conscience that urges and lashes him,

units.la: Vt thynnus rapidus percurrens æquora sæuit.
units.tr: Like a swift tuna, racing through the waves, it rages.

units.la: Hoc autem conscientia nostra non præstaret nisi aliquem superiorem iudicem agnosceret, qui, ut scelératis poenas, ita probis præmia constituit, præsertim cùm improborum animos etiam inuitos compungat, Esai. 57.21. Impijs non est pax. Atque hinc denuò concludimus:
units.tr: Our conscience would not do this unless it recognised some higher judge, who appoints punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good, especially since it pricks the minds of the wicked even against their will: Isaiah 57:21, There is no peace for the wicked. From this we conclude again:

units.la: Quod excitat in omnibus hominibus conscientiam, quæ ipsos ob admissa peccata accusat, cacisque excruciat tormentis: e contra vero in negotio bene gesto, etiam aduersus aliorum calumnias & mendacia nos excusat, id homini est naturale.
units.tr: What stirs up in all men a conscience which accuses them for sins committed and tortures them with a hidden torment, and on the other hand, in a well-performed deed, even against the slanders and lies of others, excuses us, that is natural to man.

units.la: Atqui sensus diuinitatis hoc facit, Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But the sense of divinity does this. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Argumentum quartum ducitur à lege naturæ, quam Gentes lege Moßis scripta carentes, animis ac mentibus suis impressam, atque insculptam habuisse, Apostolus Paulus Rom. 2. 14. ab effectu ostendit, quia videlicet naturæ rationis instinctu compulsæ, interdum ea, quæ Legis sunt, opera præstiterint. Sed qui legem mentibus inscriptam diuinitus habuerunt, qui legislatoris, ac numinis diuini, cuius sensu reverentia, ac metu ad legum obseruantiam, & vitæ externam honestatem instigentur, cognitione caruissent? Hinc igitur sic concludimus.
units.tr: The fourth argument is drawn from the law of nature. The Apostle Paul, Romans 2:14, shows from its effect that the Gentles, who have no written law of Moses, had the law impressed and engraved on their souls and minds: namely, that moved by the impulse of natural reason they sometimes performed the works that belong to the Law. But how could those who had the law divinely written on their minds lack knowledge of the lawgiver and the divine power, by whose awareness, reverence and fear they are urged to keep the laws and to live outwardly honourably? Hence we conclude as follows.

units.la: Qui legem naturæ habent animis inscriptam, illi sensum quoque ac notitiam legislatoris mentibus naturaliter insculptam habent. Atqui omnes homines legem naturæ animis insculptam habent, Ergo & notitiam legislatoris.
units.tr: Those who have the law of nature written on their souls also have the sense and notion of the lawgiver naturally engraved on their minds. But all men have the law of nature engraved on their souls. Therefore they also have the notion of the lawgiver.

units.la: Argumentum quintum, & vltimum sumitur à stabilitate huius impressionis, quod videlicet homines extremæ quoque & desperatæ impietatis, numinis diuini sensum, ac timorem ne summo quidem conatu excutere ex animis vnquam potuerunt. Testantur hoc animorum trepidationes miserrimæ, etiam in illis, qui tamen propter summam potentiam nihil, quod humanum est, sibi metuendum autumant. Nullus enim vnquam in audaciorem, & effrænatiorem numinis contemptum prorupisse, legitur, quàm Caligula,nec miserius quoque trepidasse,quam primum aliquod iræ diuinæ iudicium se proferebat, quàm idem ille, qui micantibus fulguribus,oculos, & caput linteis obvoluit, existente autem tonitru sermone supremi,quod contemnebat, numinis,se ipsum ex lecto proripuit: ita videlicet Deum, quem studebat ex professo contemnere, inuitus exhorrescebat. Vnde denique sic concludimus.
units.tr: The fifth and last argument is taken from the permanence of this impression: namely, that men of extreme and desperate impiety have never been able, even by their greatest effort, to shake from their souls the sense and fear of the divine power. The most wretched trembling of their spirits bears witness to this, even in those who, on account of their great power, claim that nothing human is to be feared by them. For no one is read to have broken out into a more audacious and unbridled contempt of the divine power than Caligula; nor did anyone tremble more wretchedly when some judgment of divine wrath showed itself, than the same man who, when the lightning flashed, wrapped his eyes and head in linen cloths, and when thunder sounded, which was the voice of the supreme power he despised, dashed himself out of bed. So unwillingly did he shudder before the God whom he had made it his business to despise. Hence finally we conclude thus.

units.la: Quod homines impii,ac profani nullo vnquam conatu, & studio ex animis potuerunt euellere, id firmiter ac naturaliter illis inhæret.
units.tr: What impious and profane men could never by any effort or zeal tear from their souls, that is firmly and naturally fixed in them.

units.la: At homines etiam scelestissimi, ac profanissimi numinis diuini sensum, ac timorem nullo studio & conatu ex animis euellere potuerunt.
units.tr: But even the most wicked and profane men could never by any zeal or effort tear the sense and fear of the divine power from their souls.

units.la: Sensus igitur diuinitatis naturaliter ipsis inhæret.
units.tr: Therefore the sense of divinity is naturally fixed in them.

units.la: Hæc argumenta si aduersarius æquo,ac veritatis studioso animo nobiscum perpendat,facile animaduertet, non ex disciplina, aut traditione, sed naturali impressione fluere persuasionem illam, Deum esse. Sed thecseos secundæ demonstrationem aggrediemur.
units.tr: If the opponent weighs these arguments with us in a fair and truth-loving spirit, he will easily perceive that that persuasion, that God exists, flows not from teaching or tradition but from natural impression. But we shall now take up the demonstration of the second thesis.

units.la: In hoc igitur mundi opificio ceu speculo aliquo tatum diuinæ maiestatis fulgorem, ac splendorem relucere, vt ex eo præstantissimam Deum cognoscendi materiam habeamus, tot argumenta euidentissima, & documenta illustrissima, tota hæc rerum vniuersitas, nobis exhibet, quot in se opera diuina continet, quibus singuliis, certas gloriæ suæ notas insculpsit, vt quaqua versum oculos coniicias, scintillas aliquas gloriæ diuinæ emicare videas. Atque hinc est, quod Psalmista cælestibus creaturis linguam, & idioma attribuit, Psal. 19. vers. 1. Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum eius annuntiat firmamentum; Dies diei eloquitur sermonem, & nox noctи indicat scientiam. Sic Iob. 12. vers. 7.8.9. Interroga bestias, ac docebunt te, ac volucres cœli indicabunt tibi: vel terram alloquere, illa docebit te, & pisces maris enarrabunt tibi; Quis ignorat Deum hæc omnia fecisse? quia videlicet euidentior ibi exstet diuinitatis testificatio, quàm vt nationem vllam vel obtusissimam latere queat. Quum enim mundus hic vniuersus omnia naturæ opera, summa præstantia conuestita, & mirabiliter, si vtilitatem spectes, instructa, si specie, ornata esse videantur, sic vt miro modo vtilitas consentiat tiat cum decore, suauitas, & concinnitas cum necessitate,nonne hæc ipsa rerum excellentia clamitat, ea omnia ab autore quodam optimo, & principio perfectissimo esse profecta, siquidem ipsa natura talis est causa, qualem illa effectum producit, & quidem gradu præstantiore? Vnde & Psalmista dicit: Qui au-rem condidit,num ille non audiret? Et qui fecit oculum, num ille non videret? Psal. 94. vers.9. Vt rectissime Antonius Eremita in Ae-gypto, philosopho, quomodo res sublimes contemplaretur omnilibrorum chartaceorum suppellectile destitutus, percon-tanti, respondisse existimandus sit, Vniuersum dicendo hunc mundum sibi librorum & instructa bibliotheca vice esse, hanc omni tempore, & vbiuis locorum præsto extare, in eadem se res diuinas, & cœlestes lectitare. Quin & euidentissimum diuinitatis documen-tum est diuina beneficentia, quam omnes mortales sentiunt, ex infinitis commodis, cum ex cœlo desuper, tum ex tellure inferne prouenientibus, sic vt nulla creatura extet, in quam non ef-fusa sit eximia Dei bonitas, quæ tam illustre diuinitatis signum est, vt etiam gentibus, quas tamen Deus sinit suis ipsorum viis incedere, nulla videlicet religionis, & cultus ratione ipsis præ-scripta, omnem ignorantiæ prætextum ademerit, Act.17.13.14. Illa denique operum diuinorum amplissima maiestas, infinita multitudo,admirabilis varietas, constantissimus ordo,pulcherri-ma harmonia, indefinens perpetuitas, iucundissima rerum alter-nantium vicissitudo, ordinata rerum omnium dispositio, & sa-pientissima ad finem suum directio,satis superque indicant esse a-liquem summum rectorem, & gubernatorem, qui totius mundi clauum teneat, qui astrorum cursum, & slationes, temporum mutationes, rerum omnium vicissitudines, ordinésque conseruet, qui terram & maria contemplans hominum commoda tueatur,adeoque totam vniuersitatem suo nutu, & arbitratu gu-bernet,ac moderetur, qui denique extremus rerum omnium finis existit.Sed vt nihil dicam de rarissimo illo bonitatis, & sapientiæ Dei specimine, homine videlicet, nihil de connexione, sym-metria, pulchritudine, & vsu in humani corporis structura, nihil de admiranda huius mundi gubernatione, nihil de perpetua omnium temporum historia, nihil denique de infi-nitis penè miraculis apud alias etiam gentes extra Dei popu-lum notissimis, quæ tamen omnia diuinitatis tanta documenta in fe continent, vt ne plebeii quidem,ac rudiffimi,qui externi, & communis sensus adminiculo suffulti sunt,ignorare queant diuinæ maiestatis excellentiam : illa in nobis existens diuina particula auræ , illa mens cælo ducens originem , nos Dei progeniem esse . euidentissime docet, vt Apostolus ex Arato disserit, Act. 17. verf. 29. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissime colligimus id quod fecundo loco affirmauimus , totam videlicet hunc mundum,in cuius opificio ita fe Deus quotidie offert: vt aperire oculos nequeamus, quin eum aspicere cogamur,vberrimam , & amplissimam esse Deum cognoscendi materiam.
units.tr: In this workmanship of the world, as if in some mirror the whole splendour and brightness of the divine majesty shines back, so that we may have from it the most excellent matter for knowing God, this whole universe of things sets before us as many most evident arguments and most illustrious proofs as the divine works contain in themselves, each of which has engraved certain marks of his glory, so that wherever you cast your eyes you see sparks of divine glory flashing forth. Hence it is that the Psalmist gives to the heavenly creatures a tongue and a language, Psalm 19:1, The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows his handiwork; day to day pours forth speech, and night to night declares knowledge. So Job 12:7–9, Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; and the birds of the heaven will tell you; or speak to the earth, and it will teach you, and the fishes of the sea will declare to you. Who does not know that God made all these things? For there the testimony to the divinity stands out more clearly than any nation, however dull, could fail to notice. For since this whole world appears to have all the works of nature clothed in the highest excellence, and wonderfully equipped, if you look to their usefulness, and adorned, if you look to their beauty, so that in a marvellous way usefulness agrees with comeliness, and pleasantness and harmony with necessity, does not this very excellence of things cry out that all of them have proceeded from some best author and most perfect principle, since nature itself is a cause of the kind that produces its effect, and indeed of a more excellent degree? Hence the Psalmist also says, Psalm 94:9, "He who formed the ear, shall he not hear? And he who made the eye, shall he not see?" Just as Antony the Hermit in Egypt, rightly so, when a philosopher asked him how he contemplated sublime things, being without any furniture of paper books, is thought to have answered, that the whole world, so to speak, served him as a book and a well-stocked library, that it was always and everywhere at hand, and that he read the divine and heavenly things in it. Indeed the divine goodness, which all mortals feel, is also a most evident proof of divinity, from the infinite benefits that come both from heaven above and from the earth below, so that there is no creature in which the exceptional goodness of God is not poured out. This is so clear a sign of divinity that even the nations, whom God nevertheless allows to walk in their own ways, without any rule of religion or worship prescribed to them, have been deprived of every pretext of ignorance, Acts 17:13–14. Finally, that most ample majesty of the divine works, their infinite multitude, admirable variety, most constant order, beautiful harmony, unfailing perpetuity, most pleasing alternating change of things, orderly arrangement of all things, and most wise direction to their end, sufficiently and more than sufficiently indicate that there is some supreme ruler and governor who holds the helm of the whole world, who preserves the course and stations of the stars, the changes of seasons, and the alternations and orders of all things, who, surveying the land and seas, watches over the good of men, and who thus governs and directs the whole universe by his nod and will, and who finally is the ultimate end of all things. But to say nothing of that most rare specimen of God's goodness and wisdom, namely man; nothing of the connection, symmetry, beauty and use in the structure of the human body; nothing of the wonderful government of this world; nothing of the continuous history of all times; nothing finally of the almost infinite miracles, most well known even among other nations outside the people of God, which nevertheless contain in themselves such great proofs of divinity that not even the common folk and the most unlearned, supported by the aid of external and common sense, can fail to know the excellence of the divine majesty: that divine particle of the breath which exists in us, that mind which derives its origin from heaven, clearly teaches us that we are God's offspring, as the Apostle argues from Aratus, Acts 17:29. From all these things we most manifestly gather what we affirmed in the second place, namely that this whole world, in whose workmanship God so offers himself every day that we cannot open our eyes without being compelled to behold him, is a most abundant and ample matter for knowing God.

units.la: Restat vt thefeos tertiẹ,qua asseruimus, inesse homini etiam post lapsum naturaliter facultatem ex operibus creationis diuinitatem cognoscendi,& notitiam innitam nobis,augendi & confirmandi, apodixin , & probationem subiungamus, cuius quidem tam euidens est veritas,vt eam facultatem,quicunque hominibus adimit , sensum quoque communem , & rationem humanam omnem ; eiusque vsum tollere cum,ac negare, fit necessarium. Quum enim sensus noster,motum esse in mundo animaduertat,rationi autem noftrę ex lumine naturali constet,quicquid mouetur,ab alio moueri , ex illa mouentium,& rerum nostrarum nexu ac serie , quia illa in infinitum progredi non potest , tandem aliquando ad primum omnium motorem deuenien dum esse concludit , qui primus motor, fit immobilis,hoc est,qui semper actu fit,nūquam potentia,& in illo primo motore consistendum:in quo viuimus , mouemur , ac fumus: Act. 17. v. 27.28. Quin etiam idem sensus euidenter nos docet,naturaliter ex nihilo nihil fieri,& tamen quotidie multa noua fieri , quorum vtrumque perpetua rerum generatio , & corruptio aperte testatur:nihil autem fieri cum possit à fe ipso,nihil fiquidē potest simul esse , & non esse,simul esse prius , & posterius seipso , denique simul esse causa , & effectus fui ipsius, ratio nostra verifime inde concludit , ab aliqua causa, & ea quidem plane necessaria , i.necessario præexiftente,illa omnia fieri,cum sequeretur aliquin nihil aliquando fuisse , ac proinde ne nunc quidem aliquid esse, & in eiusmodi causarum fubordinatione non dari progressum in infinitum. Vnde efficitur esse aliquam causam primam à qua reliquæ omnes,vel mediatè, vel immediatè dependeant,quæque necessitatis fuę principium à fe ipsa habeat. Videt igitur Offorrodius dum spoliare conatur humanam naturam facultate illa,omnem se rationem,omnem intellectus vim, proprietates ess‐entiales, ac ipsam naturam,imprudenter destruere. Quum denique Aduersarius tantum acumen ingenio hominis tribuat, ut ex libro Scripturę solius rationis ductu, absque omni Spiritus sancti illuminatione interna, percipere,& intelligere queat, non modo Deum esse, verum etiam quicquid ad totius religionis Christianæ mysterium pertinet,hoc est,quicquid ad verâ fidem,solidámque Dei cognitionem, sanctam etiam,ac Deo placentem vitam scitu, factúque est necessarium: qua fronte quæso librum naturę, & operum Dei ita nobis claudet, ut ne suspicione quidem vllam de Deo ex illo concipere queamus? Atque vt infinita pene argumenta alia euidentissima omittamus, duas nostras enuntiationes posteriores diserte confirmat ipse Paulus Rom.1.20.21. Id quod de Deo cognoscipotest, inquiens,manifestum est in ipsis, Deus enim illis patefecit,quia quæ sunt inuisibilia illius,ex creatione mundi dum per opera intelliguntur, peruidentur, ipsáque æterna eius potentia, & diuinitas,in hoc vt sint inexcusabiles.
units.tr: It remains that we add, for the third thesis, which we asserted, that man has, even after the fall, a natural faculty of knowing God from the works of creation, and a notion innate in us, to be increased and confirmed, the proof and demonstration. Its truth is so evident that whoever takes away that faculty from men must also take away and deny common sense and all human reason and its use. For since our sense perceives that there is motion in the world, and our reason, from the natural light, holds that whatever is moved is moved by another, our reason concludes from the chain and series of movers and things, which cannot go on to infinity, that we must at last arrive at a first mover of all, who is immovable, that is, who is always in act and never in potency, and that we must rest in that first mover: in whom we live, move and have our being, Acts 17:27–28. Moreover the same sense clearly teaches us that by nature nothing comes from nothing, and yet many new things come into being every day, both of which the perpetual generation and corruption of things plainly attest. But since nothing can make itself, for nothing can at the same time be and not be, nor be both before and after itself, nor finally be at the same time the cause and effect of itself, our reason rightly concludes that all these things come into being from some cause, and indeed a wholly necessary one, that is, one that necessarily pre-exists; otherwise it would follow that nothing has ever existed, and therefore that nothing exists even now; and that in such a subordination of causes there is no progress to infinity. From this it follows that there is some first cause on which all the others depend, either mediately or immediately, and which has the principle of its necessity from itself. Ostorodius, therefore, while he tries to strip human nature of that faculty, imprudently destroys all reason, every power of the intellect, the essential properties and nature itself. Finally, since the opponent attributes to the human mind such keenness that he can, from the book of Scripture by the guidance of reason alone, without any inner illumination of the Holy Spirit, perceive and understand not only that God exists, but also whatever pertains to the mystery of the whole Christian religion, that is, whatever is necessary to know and do for true faith, solid knowledge of God, and a holy life pleasing to God; with what face, I ask, does he close to us the book of nature and of God's works, so that we cannot form from it even the slightest suspicion of God? And, to omit almost countless other most evident arguments, the Apostle Paul himself expressly confirms our two latter propositions, Romans 1:20–21, What can be known of God, he says, is manifest in them; for God has shown it to them. For his invisible things, namely his eternal power and divinity, are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through his works, so that they are without excuse.

units.la: Ad hunc Pauli Apostoli locum respondet Osiorrodius ex suo præceptore Fausto Socino, non agi ibi de operibus prima creationis, sed de gloriosis Christi, & Apostolorum factis, quibus Euangelij doctrinam confirmarunt, sic vt sensus sit, Deum impios & infideles, qui doctrinæ Euangelij reluctantur,iustissime puniturum esse, quoniam quicquid de ipso sciri potest,vel potius scitur,illis patefecit: sempiternam enim virtutem,ac diuinitatem,hoc est,voluntatem Dei tam in promissionibus,quam mandatis,quæ post quam mundus creatus erat,conspecta non fuerant,per miracula ad Euangelij prædicationem confirmandam a Deo per Christum & Apostolos patrata,intellectas, & intelligendo conspectas esse. Atque hunc verum& genuinum sensum esse verborum Pauli, ex antecedentibus satis patere affirmat.
units.tr: Ostorodius replies to this passage of the Apostle Paul, following his teacher Faustus Socinus: the passage does not speak of the works of the first creation, but of the glorious deeds of Christ and the Apostles, by which they confirmed the doctrine of the Gospel, so that the sense is: God will most justly punish the impious and unbelieving, who resist the doctrine of the Gospel, since whatever can be known about him, or rather is known, has been made manifest to them; for his everlasting power and divinity, that is, his will as set out in both promises and commands, which had not been seen after the world was created, were perceived through the miracles performed by God through Christ and the Apostles to confirm the preaching of the Gospel, and having been perceived, were seen by understanding. He affirms that this is the true and genuine sense of Paul's words, and that it is sufficiently clear from what precedes.

units.la: Resp. Si tam euidenter ex ipso Paulo suam interpretationem stabiliret Osiorrodius, quàm temerè ac confidenter eam ex antecedentibus confirmari posse affirmat, gratissimo, & æquissimo animo eam amplectęremur,sed falsam illam esse ibíque de operibus creationis,non miraculis Christi, & Apostolorum, agi, ex descriptione gentium,de quibus eo in loco disputatur ex eo quod Apostolus ex operibus legis iustificari non posse, verbis citatis,vult demonstrare,adeóque tota disputationis serie,& ipso denique textu manifestissimè liquet. Agit enim ibi Apostolus non de toto genere humano,sed gentibus profanis, & idololatricis, verbo Dei carentibus,& extra Rempublicam Ifraeliticam constitutis, nec ad societatem populi Dei vocatis,vt tum ex sequentibus, vbi scelerum ac flagitiorum ab ipsis perpetratorum prolixũ recenset catalogum:tum etiam cap. 2 v.12.&14.liquet manifestissime, vbi Paulus dicit eas ne legis quidem,puta per Mosen latas,doctrinam habuisse. Si igitur gentes,de quibus ibi agit Apostolus, solum ius naturale,ac ne legem quidem Mosis habuerunt, qua fronte quaeso integram illis doctrinam de voluntate, hoc est, promissionibus, & praeceptis, eamque Christi, & Apostolorum mirandis operibus confirmatam,intelle&tam, ac propositam fuisse,Oftorrodius affirmabit? Quin etiam omnes circunftantiae, quibus gentes illae describuntur,fatis indicant de illis gentibus ibi agi,quas Deus a Paulo,& Barnaba Act.14.16. fuisse dicitur, suis ipsorum viis incedere, hoc est,idololatras esse, ac creaturis honorem foli Deo debitum exhibere,nulla religionis, aut cultus ratione ipsis praescripta, nec tamen fine testimonio fui reliquerit. Quin & textus ipse Oftorrodianam explicationem luculenter refutat,dum potentia, & diuinitas Dei ex operibus diuinis, statim a condito mundo,seu ab origine mundi perspecta fuisse dicitur,quod miraculis Christi, & Apostolorum,tempore Noui Testamenti demum praestitis, conuenire non potest. Verus igitur Apostoli sensus est, quamuis gentes lege Dei scripta caruerint,nihilominus tamen iustificari illas non posse,nec quicquam habere, quod excusandae idololatriae praetexere possint, quia homines statim ab origine mundi potentiam ac diuinitatem, maiestatem, gloriamque ex operibus creationis viderint, quam veritatem gentes profanae in iniuftia detinuerint, idololatria videlicet, & aliis nefandis sceleribus, ac flagitiis sese contaminantes:sed veritatem facile animaduerterent Aduersarii, fi glaucoma,quod oculis eorum contradicendi studium offundit, ferio abstergerent.
units.tr: Reply. If Ostorodius established his interpretation from Paul himself as clearly as he rashly and confidently claims it can be confirmed from what precedes, we would embrace it with the greatest gratitude and fairness. But that interpretation is false, and the passage does not speak of the works of creation rather than the miracles of Christ and the Apostles. This is clear from the description of the Gentiles, of whom the Apostle is discussing in that place, since he wants to show, with the words cited, that people cannot be justified by the works of the law. It is also clear from the whole course of the argument and from the text itself. The Apostle is speaking there not of the whole human race, but of profane and idolatrous Gentiles, who lacked the Word of God and were outside the commonwealth of Israel, not called into the fellowship of the people of God. This is evident from what follows, where he gives a lengthy catalogue of the crimes and shameful deeds they committed, and also most manifestly from chapter 2, verses 12 and 14, where Paul says that they did not even have the law, that is, the law given through Moses, as their teaching. If, then, the Gentiles of whom the Apostle speaks had only the natural law and not even the law of Moses, with what face, I ask, will Ostorodius affirm that a complete teaching about the will of God, that is, about promises and precepts, and confirmed by the wonderful works of Christ and the Apostles, was understood and set before them? Indeed, all the circumstances by which those Gentiles are described sufficiently indicate that the passage is about those nations which, as Acts 14:16 says, Paul and Barnabas said God allowed to walk in their own ways, that is, to be idolaters, giving to creatures the honour due to God alone, with no religious or worshipful order prescribed for them, yet not leaving himself without witness. Moreover, the text itself plainly refutes the Ostorodian explanation, since it says that the power and divinity of God were perceived from the divine works from the moment the world was made, or from the beginning of the world. This cannot apply to miracles of Christ and the Apostles, performed only in the time of the New Testament. The true sense of the Apostle is therefore this: although the Gentiles lacked the written law of God, they nevertheless cannot be justified, and they have nothing with which to excuse their idolatry, because from the very beginning of the world men saw the power, divinity, majesty and glory of God in the works of creation. The profane Gentiles held this truth captive in unrighteousness, namely by idolatry and other unspeakable crimes and shameful deeds by which they defiled themselves. But the opponents could easily perceive the truth if they would wipe away with a serious effort the film which the desire to contradict casts over their eyes.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De personis diuinis.
units.tr: On the divine persons.

units.la: ABSOLVTA illa disputatione de Scriptura sacra, Ostorrodius capite secundo de fide in Deum, & capite tertio de Essentia diuina disserit: quia tamen infra ex professo de fide nobis erit agendum, & ea quae in capite tertio de Essentia diuina attributis nonnullis disputat, non sint inter nos controversa, licet aequiuocationibus quibusdam ludat: animaduersionibus in caput secundum suo loco reseruatis, ad quartum de personis diuinis progrediemur.
units.tr: Having finished that disputation on Holy Scripture, Ostorodius treats of faith in God in the second chapter, and of the divine essence in the third. Since, however, we shall have to deal with faith expressly later on, and since the things he disputes in the third chapter concerning the attributes of the divine essence are not controverted between us, although he toys with them through certain equivocations, we shall reserve our remarks on the second chapter for their proper place and proceed to the fourth, on the divine persons.

units.la: Deum igitur illum Israelis, Iehouam exercituum, coeli terraeque conditorem, ac moderatorem tantum unum esse essentia, non autem plures Deos, inter nos, & gentem Socinianam extra controuersiae, & dubitationis aleam est constitutum. Sed quaeritur, Vtrum in illa essentia Dei, plures, & inter se non tantum nominibus, sed certis, & incommunicabilibus proprietatibus distinctae personae subsistant; an vero, sicut una tantum, eaque simplex est, ac indiuisa essentia Dei, sic etiam una tantum sit persona?
