Ostorrodius prius negat, posterius affirmat, nos contra prioris sententiae veritatem, posterioris blasphemam falsitatem demonstrabimus, non quidem omnib. illis argumentis, quae ad sententiae nostrae κατασκευὴν adduci possent, sed iis ac tot tantum, quae ad thesin Aduersarii euertendam, & nostram stabiliendam, sufficient.
units.tr: That God, the God of Israel, Jehovah of hosts, the creator and governor of heaven and earth, is only one in essence, and not several gods, has been settled between us and the Socinian people beyond the hazard of controversy and doubt. But the question is this: Do several persons subsist in that one divine essence, distinct not merely by names but by definite and incommunicable properties; or rather, just as the divine essence is one only and simple and undivided, so is there also only one person? Ostorodius denies the former and affirms the latter. We shall demonstrate the truth of the former and the blasphemous falsehood of the latter, not indeed with all those arguments which could be brought forward to establish our position, but with those and only so many as are sufficient to overthrow the opponent's thesis and to establish ours.

units.la: Argumentum primum. Gen.1. v. 26.27. Faciamus hominem (inquit Deus ille mundi totius conditor) ad imaginem nostram secundum similitudinem nostram. Verba haec sunt alicuius personae diuinae, aut alloquentis alias sibi aequales, & in creatione socias, eiusdemque potentiae, maiestatis, & essentiae: aut ad alios, qui non sunt eiusdem cum loquente essentiae, maiestatis, & potentiae directa, aut denique honoris tantum caussa in plurali numero. prolata: Atqui ad alios, qui non sint eiusdem cum loquente essentiae, maiestatis, ac gloriae haec verba non sunt prolata, tum quia non faciatis, sed faciamus, inquit, ἰσότιμον demonstrans, tum etiam, quia ad nullius alterius, quàm ipsius Dei creatoris imaginem conditi sumus, nec denique quisquam Deo in creatione socius fuit. Multò minus autem verba haec sunt honoris causa in plurali numero prolata, cùm hoc inauditum sit in sacris litteris, quenquam apud Hebraeos de se loquentem plurali numero uti, eiusque rei nullu exemplum potest produci in homine licet ambitiosissimo. Sequitur ergo, verum esse primum, videlicet verba illa esse personae alicuius diuinae alias sibi potestate, gloria, ac maiestate aequales, & in creatione socias alloquentis. Patris nempe Filium, ac Spiritum sanctum compellantis, ac proinde plures esse unà diuinas personas, & quidem eiusdem potentiae, essentiae, & gloriae, ac in creatione socias.
units.tr: First argument. Gen. 1:26–27. "Let us make man," says God, the creator of the whole world, "in our image, after our likeness." These words are spoken either by some divine person addressing others who are equal to him, and co-workers in creation, of the same power, majesty and essence; or they are addressed to others who are not of the same essence, majesty and power as the speaker; or, finally, they are uttered in the plural number only out of respect. But these words were not spoken to others who are not of the same essence, majesty and glory as the speaker. This is shown both because it says not "make ye" but "let us make," thereby signifying equal honour, and because we were created in the image of no one other than God the Creator himself, and finally because no one was a partner with God in creation. Still less are these words uttered in the plural in honour of anyone, since this is unheard of in the sacred writings: no one among the Hebrews speaks of himself in the plural, and no example of such a thing can be produced even in the most ambitious of men. It follows, therefore, that the first alternative is true, namely that these words are spoken by a divine person, equal to the others in power, glory and majesty, and co-worker in creation, addressing the Father's Son and Holy Spirit. Consequently there are several divine persons together, and indeed of the same power, essence and glory, and co-workers in creation.

units.la: Argumentum secundum.
units.tr: Second argument.

units.la: Vbicunque Angelus Iehouae, ab ipso Iehouah distinguitur, & tamen verus Iehouah, Deus Israelis, Iehouah exercituum dicitur, ibi plures diuinitatis personae esse docentur. Atqui prius (ut ex plurimis pauca recensemus) verissimum esse loca sequentia manifestè testantur. Sic enim Angelus Dei in somnio alloquutus Iacobum Gen. 31. v. 11. dicitur Deus Beth-el, cui Iacob votum vouerit, v. 13. Deus Abram, & Deus Isaac, Gen. 28. 13. & 32. 9. & Gen. 19. 24. Iehouah super Sodomum, & super Hamoram demisit dicitur pluuia sulphuris, & ignis à Iehouah in caelis. Christus videlicet, qui est potentia Dei, 1. Cor. 1. v. 24. à Deo Patre qui Filio omne iudicium dedit, Ioh. 5. 22. Hic ergo cum unus Iehouah, ab altero, id est, persona agens, à persona agente diuina distinguatur quis nisi caecus, non videat plures esse vna in essentia illa diuina, & alterna personas? Sic Angelus, qui Zach. 1. 12. Angelus Iehouae dicitur, & à Iehouah exercitum mittente eum, distinguitur cap. 2. v. 12. Iehouah exercituum appellatur cap. 2. v. 13. & 15. Hunc locum etiamsi miris modis eum tractet, & in omnes formas torqueat Socinus, pro defensione confessionis nostrae, Samosateniani nunquam excutient.
units.tr: Wherever the Angel of Jehovah is distinguished from Jehovah himself, and yet is called true Jehovah, God of Israel, Jehovah of hosts, there it is taught that there are several persons of the divinity. Now the first point (to list a few out of many) is manifestly attested as most true by the following passages. For thus the Angel of God, speaking to Jacob in a dream, Gen. 31:11, is called "God of Bethel," to whom Jacob made a vow, v. 13; "God of Abraham" and "God of Isaac," Gen. 28:13 and 32:9; and Gen. 19:24: "Jehovah rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from Jehovah out of heaven." This is Christ, who is the power of God, 1 Cor. 1:24, to whom the Father, who has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22, belongs. Here, then, since one Jehovah is distinguished from another, that is, the acting person from the divine acting person, who that is not blind would fail to see that there are several persons in that one divine essence, and that they alternate? Likewise the Angel who is called "the Angel of Jehovah" in Zech. 1:12, and is distinguished from Jehovah who sent him, cap. 2:12, is called "Jehovah of hosts" in cap. 2:13 and 15. Even though Socinus handles this passage in marvellous ways and twists it into every shape, the Samosatenians will never shake it in defence of our confession.

units.la: Argumentum tertium. Matth. 28. 19.
units.tr: Third argument. Matt. 28:19.

units.la: Profecti docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eas in nomine Patris, Filij, ac Spiritus sancti. In cuius autem nomen baptizamur, ille est verus Deus, & creator noster, nostraeque consciencie Iudex ac Dominus: Primò, quia in cuius nomen baptizamur, in eius familiam externo, videlicet illo ablutionis symbolo adhibito, ascribimur, id est, in illius Ecclesiam recipimur, eius priuilegiis donamur, & in eiusdem filios adoptamur: unde Paulus ex eo probat nos filios Dei esse, quia videlicet in Baptismo Christum induerimus. Gal. 3.17. Deinde in cuius nomen baptizamur, ad eius obedientiam & cultum obstringimur, sic vt illius imperio simus addicti, ab eiusque nutu ac mandatis toti pendeamus, Matth. 28. 20. 1. Cor. 1. 13. Deus autem solus est in cuius Ecclesiam ac Rempublicam adscribimur, in cuius filios adoptamur, Eph. 1.5. ei denique soli in obedientiam & cultum obligamur: Dominum enim Deum adorabis, & ei soli seruies, Deut. 6.13. Et is solus potest nostram conscientiam ad fidem & obedientiam obligare, qui eius est creator ac Dominus. Secundo, quia Paulus haec tria sic connectit, fidem, Deum, ac baptismum, vt ab vno ad alterum ratiocinetur: vt quia vna est fides, ex eo vnum esse Deum demonstret: quia vnus est baptismus, inde quoque vnā esse fidem ostendat, Ephes. 4. v. 5. Vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma: v. 6. Vnus Deus & Pater omnium, qui est super omnia, & per omnia, & in omnibus vobis. Fides enim in vnum Deum spectare & conferri debet, ac in eo haerere, vnde conficitur, quod si varia sint fidei genera, plures etiā Deos esse oporteat. Iam quia sacramentum fidei est baptismus, ipsius vnitatem nobis confirmat ex eo, quod vnus est. Hinc etiam conficitur, vt non nisi in verum eundemque vnum Deum baptizare liceat, quia eius amplectimur fidem, in cuius nomen baptizamur. Atqui tres sunt inter se distinctae personae, in quarum nomine baptizamur. Matth. 3. 16. 17. & 28.19. Vnde necessario sequitur, tres esse inter se proprietate incommunicabili distinctas personas diuinas, quarum vna quaeque sit verus Deus.
units.tr: "Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Now he in whose name we are baptized is the true God and our creator, and the judge and lord of our conscience. First, because into the name of him in whose name we are baptized we are enrolled in his family, by the external sign of the washing of ablution, that is, we are received into his Church, endowed with his privileges, and adopted as his sons. Hence Paul proves from this that we are sons of God, because we have put on Christ in baptism, Gal. 3:27. Next, into the name of him in whose name we are baptized we are bound to his obedience and worship, so that we are devoted to his command and wholly depend upon his nod and precepts, Matt. 28:20; 1 Cor. 1:13. But God alone is he into whose Church and commonwealth we are enrolled, into whose sons we are adopted, Eph. 1:5; and finally to him alone we are bound in obedience and worship: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve," Deut. 6:13. And he alone can bind our conscience to faith and obedience who is its creator and lord. Secondly, because Paul connects these three, faith, God and baptism, in such a way that he reasons from one to the other: since faith is one, he shows from this that God is one; since baptism is one, he shows likewise that faith is one, Eph. 4:5, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism"; v. 6, "One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." For faith ought to look to and be directed toward one God, and cling to him; hence it follows that if there were various kinds of faith, there would have to be several gods as well. Now, since baptism is the sacrament of faith, it confirms for us the unity of God himself from the fact that he is one. Hence it also follows that it is lawful to baptize only into the one true and same God, because we embrace the faith of him in whose name we are baptized. But there are three persons, distinct from one another, in whose name we are baptized, Matt. 3:16–17 and 28:19. Whence it necessarily follows that there are three divine persons, distinct from one another by incommunicable property, each of whom is the true God.

units.la: Argumentum quartum.
units.tr: The fourth argument.

units.la: 1. Ioh. 5.7. Tres sunt, qui testificantur in coelo, Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres vnum sunt. At quorum testimonia citatur vt diuina, eos personas eiusdem naturae ac maiestatis esse necesse est: Filij autem, & Spiritus sancti testimonia hic aeque citantur vt diuina, ac ipsius Patris, vnde tres illas personas eiusdem naturae ac maiestatis esse sequitur. Quum insuper Pater, Filius, ac Spiritus sanctus vt tria distincta ὑποστάσεις inducantur, Patérque ac Spiritus sanctus de Filio tanquam de persona diuersa testimonium perhibeant, manifestissimè colligitur id quod affirmamus, plures vna esse personas diuinas. Argumentum quintum & efficacissimum desumitur ex illis argumentis, quibus demonstratur nō solum Patrem, sed etiam Filium ac Spiritum sanctum cum Patre vnum illum,& æternum Deum, cœli,terræque conditorem esse, cum tamen certum sit, & extra controuersiam inter nos positum, Patrem & Filium personas esse proprietatibus incommunicabilibus distinctas. Argumentum autem pro æterna Filii ac Spiritus sancti deitate infrà suo loco adducemus, vbi prius rationes Aduersarii refutabimus.
units.tr: 1. 1 John 5:7. There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. But those whose testimonies are cited as divine must necessarily be persons of the same nature and majesty. The testimonies of the Son and of the Holy Spirit are here cited as divine just as much as that of the Father is; hence it follows that those three persons are of the same nature and majesty. Moreover, since the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are introduced as three distinct hypostases, and the Father and the Holy Spirit bear witness concerning the Son as concerning a different person, the very thing we affirm is most clearly inferred: that there are several divine persons in one. A fifth and most effective argument is drawn from those arguments by which it is demonstrated that not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit together with the Father are that one and eternal God, the creator of heaven and earth, although it is certain, and beyond controversy between us, that the Father and the Son are persons distinguished by incommunicable properties. But we will bring forward the argument for the eternal deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit later in its proper place, when first we have refuted the reasons of the Adversary.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CAPUT V.

units.la: In quo Obiectiones Aduersarii diluuntur.
units.tr: In quo objectiones adversarii diluuntur.

units.la: HANC autem doctrinam orthodoxam, & ex ipsis Scripturarum fontibus haustam,de tribus inter se distinctis,ac in vna æternaque essentia, ac natura diuina subsistentibus personis, ad salutem scitu minimè necessariam esse,Oftorrodius Institutionum suarum capite quarto,duobus argumentis ostendere conatur,quæ ordine refutabimus.
units.tr: This orthodox doctrine, drawn from the very sources of Scripture, that there are three persons distinct from one another, subsisting in one eternal essence and divine nature, is by no means necessary to know for salvation, Ostorrodius attempts to show in chapter four of his Institutes, by two arguments. We shall refute them in order.

units.la: Primum igitur inquit, doctrinam hanc ideo ad salutem scitu necessariam non esse, quia Deus ea de re nihil nobis patefecerit, cum in sacris literis nihil de eadem doceatur, contineaturque. Et quamuis Theologi nostri plurimùm in hoc elaborent, ac desudent,vt variis collectionibus, consequentijs, & syllogismis, dogmatis illius veritatem demonstrent: quia tamen hoc ipsum primarium fidei ac religionis caput à nostris aßimetur,& sine cuius notitia salutem ac vitam æternam consequi nemo possit, ac proinde non illis consequentiis, ac syllogismis, sed euidentibus,apertis, & manifestis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis niti debeat, in sacris autem literis nunquam legatur, tres personas distinctas, quarum vna quaeque verus sit Deus, Patrem, nempe,Filium, ac Spiritum sanctum in vno illo Deo subsistere, illáque ipsas denique consequentias nullius momenti ac ponderis esse: ex plurimis ipsorum, puta Samosatenianorum scriptis luculenter appareat, ideo omnem illorum, nempe Theologorum nostrorum laborem frustraneum, & inanem esse.
units.tr: First, he says, this doctrine is not necessary to know for salvation because God has revealed nothing to us about it, since nothing about it is taught or contained in the Holy Scriptures. And although our theologians labour and sweat greatly to prove the truth of this dogma by various collections, consequences and syllogisms, yet since this very point is taken by our side as the chief head of faith and religion, without knowledge of which no one can obtain salvation and eternal life, it must therefore rest not on those consequences and syllogisms but on clear, open and manifest testimonies of Holy Scripture. Yet nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is it read that three persons, each of whom is true God, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, subsist in that one God. And finally, those consequences are of no weight or moment at all; this clearly appears from many writings of their own, namely of the Samosatenians, so that all the labour of those theologians of ours is useless and empty.

units.la: Resp. Audax certè asseueratio, & thrasonica plane de triumpho ante victoriam partam gloriatio, cuius veritatem tot doctissimorum Ecclesiarum nostrarum luminum eruditissima monumenta luculeter euincunt, quorum solida, & inuictissima argumenta allatrare annlib. suis subtilitatibus, euertere verò gens SocFiniana nunquam poterit. Sed vt Oftorrodianæ quoque temeritatis fœditas detegatur, sic breuiter habeto. Dogma, inquit, illud plures personas inter se distinctas, quarum vna quaque sit verus Deus, Patrem nempe, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum in vna essentia subsistere, in Scripturis sacris neutiquam docetur. Si verba docendique & interpretandi modum specites, verissimum effatum illud: sin verò sensum, & res ipsas significatas respicias, impium, blasphemum, & à veritate diuina alienissimum, Tres personas diuinas esse, quæ vnam eandemque numero essentiam diuinam communem habeant, hisce ipsis verbis in sacris literis non legitur, fateor, at leguntur æquipollentia, & ὁμοούσια, nempe Patrem esse Deum verum Israelis, naturæ item viuentis, intelligentis, potentis, volentis, & agentis; Filium esse Deum naturæ viuentis, intelligentis, potentis, volentis, & agentis: Spiritum sanctum denique esse Deum naturæ viuentis, intelligentis, potentis, volentis, & agentis: quæ certè attributa non nisi veris ὑφισταμένοις competere, vel pueri ipsi norunt. Extra controuersiam deinde est, Patrem nec Filium esse, nec Spiritum sanctum, sed Patrem duntaxat: Filium deinde nec Patrem, nec Spiritum sanctum esse, sed Filium duntaxat: Spiritum sanctum denique nec Patrem, nec Filium esse, sed Spiritum sanctum duntaxat: & vnum tantum esse verum Deum Israelis. Si igitur tres sunt naturæ diuinæ viuentis, intelligentis, potentis, volentis, & angelis, nonne tria quaque sunt ὑφιστάμενα inter se distincta, sic vt nullum de altero prædicari possit? Si tria insuper sunt ὑφιστάμενα diuina, Deus autem essentia, & natura vnus, nonne tres personas diuinas, essentiam, & naturam illam vnicam communem habentes esse, luce meridiana clarius elucescit? Antecedens probauimus capite superiore, & in sequentibus demonstrabimus amplius, illud, si absque dolo, & fraude nobiscum agnosceret, ac pie profiteretur Oftorrodius, de verbis non magnopere laboraturi, eiusdem doctrinae ac religionis Christianae socium libenter cum agnoscceremus, nec in hereseos vllius suspicione raperemus. Quamuis enim in significatione ὁμοουσίας habeant, & æquipollentiam, cum iis quae in Scripturis leguntur, adeoque non nouationem, sed fidam ac planam scripturae interpretationem contineant, non tamen affectato aliquo magistero illas phrases adhibemus ab haereticorum importunitate, inconstantia, & fraudulentia extortas: nec illis innitimur tanquam firmis argumentis, quibus aduersarios constringamus, sed tanquam adiumentis, & discretionis notis vtimur.
units.tr: Reply. This is certainly a bold assertion, and a boast of triumph quite like a braggart's before the victory is won. The truth of the matter is clearly demonstrated by the most learned monuments of the most learned lights of our Churches, whose solid and invincible arguments he may bark at with his subtleties, but the Socinian tribe can never overthrow them. But so that the foulness of Ostorrodius's rashness may also be exposed, take this briefly. The dogma, he says, that several persons distinct from one another, each of whom is the true God, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, subsist in one essence, is in no way taught in the Holy Scriptures. If you look at the words and the manner of teaching and interpreting, I grant that the statement "three divine persons who have one and the same numerically common divine essence" is not read in these very words in the Holy Scriptures. But what is read are equivalent statements and [ὁμοούσια]: namely that the Father is the true God of Israel, and likewise of a living, intelligent, powerful, willing and acting nature; that the Son is God of a living, intelligent, powerful, willing and acting nature; and finally that the Holy Spirit is God of a living, intelligent, powerful, willing and acting nature. Even children know that these attributes belong only to true [ὑφισταμένοις] subsistences. Further, it is beyond controversy that the Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit, but the Father only; that the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son only; and that the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Holy Spirit only; and that there is only one true God of Israel. If therefore there are three natures of the divine living, intelligent, powerful, willing and acting [being], are not three subsistences distinct from one another, each of which is so that nothing can be predicated of another? And if there are three divine [ὑφιστάμενα] subsistences, while God is one in essence and nature, does it not shine forth more clearly than the noonday light that there are three divine persons having that one common essence and nature? We proved the antecedent in the preceding chapter, and in what follows we shall demonstrate it further. If Ostorrodius would acknowledge this with us without deceit or fraud, and would piously profess it, we would gladly acknowledge him as a partner in the same doctrine and the Christian religion, not troubling much over words, and we would not snatch him into any suspicion of heresy. For although the terms homoousios have an equivalence in meaning with what is read in the Scriptures, and so contain not a novelty but a faithful and plain interpretation of Scripture, nevertheless we do not use those phrases with any affected mastery, wrung from the importunity, inconstancy and deceitfulness of heretics. Nor do we rest on them as firm arguments by which to bind our adversaries; we use them as aids and marks of discernment.

units.la: Hinc euanescit alterum Oftorrodii effatum, meris nimirum consequentiis, collectionibus, & syllogismis hoc dogma inniti. Si enim rem ipsam speetes, eam & manifestis Scripturae locis, & indubitatis certisque consequentiis à nobis demonstrari, ex superioribus patet, & ex sequentibus magis elucescet. Verùm si dogma aliquod ex manifestis Scripturae locis necessaria consequentia eliciamus, an ideo illud minus verum esse arbitraberis, Oftorrodi? Quid magis ad salutem necessarium fide? Hanc tu Institutionum tuarum capite secundo definis, Fiduciam esse in Deum, & obedientiam eius præceptis præstitam, eámque ex Psalmo 78. verf. 21.22. vbi Deus Israelitis offensus fuisse dicitur, eo quod in ipsum non crediderint: exemplis etiam Danielis, & Niniuitarum demonstrare conaris. Detur tibi falsam tuam definitionem veram esse, illam tamen ex particularium illorum exemplorum inductione absque consequentiae, & syllogismi beneficio tum euinces, vbi enuntiationem singularem, propriam, aut particularem in vniuersalem, ac communem, noua & inaudita metamorphosi, nouus & inauditus Logicus commutare, hoc est, hunc ipsum naturae ordinem inuertere, naturae rationis lumen extinguere, & nouum aliquod, nouus Prometheus cœlo deductum humanis mentibus inspirare poteris.
units.tr: Hence his other saying vanishes, namely that this dogma rests on mere consequences, collections and syllogisms. For if you look at the matter itself, that it is demonstrated by us from clear passages of Scripture and from indubitable and certain consequences, is plain from what has gone before, and will become clearer from what follows. But if we deduce some dogma from clear passages of Scripture by a necessary consequence, do you think, Ostorrodius, that it is therefore less true? What is more necessary to salvation than faith? You define this in chapter two of your Institutes as trust in God and obedience rendered to his commands, and you try to prove it from Psalm 78, verses 21 and 22, where God is said to have been offended with the Israelites because they did not believe in him, and also from the examples of Daniel and the Ninevites. Grant that your definition is true; yet you will prove it from the induction of those particular examples only without the aid of consequence and syllogism when you change a singular, proper or particular proposition into a universal and common one by a new and unheard-of metamorphosis, a new and unheard-of logician. That is, you will be able to invert this very order of nature, extinguish the light of reason, and breathe into human minds some new thing, a new Prometheus brought down from heaven.

units.la: Sed pergit Aduersarius, & has ipsas consequentias vanas, nulliusque roboris, ac ponderis esse, à societate Sociniana luculenter demonstratum esse, audacius, quàm verius affirmat. Quae enim quaesto sunt doctissima illa scripta quibus aciem argumentorum nostrorum tam misera strage fuderunt, vt tam confidenter triumphum ante victoriam canere audeat Oftorrodius, à nostris non doctissimè refutata? Præter alios eruditissimos Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctores, non priscos illos, sed recentiores tantum, grauissimus, & luculentissimus testis est clarissimum illud Christiani orbis lumē Franciscus Iunius, Socinianæ turbæ haud dubiè optimè notus, qui in defensionibus suis totam illam astutissimarum fraudum, & sophismatum copiam, ita in cineres, & sauillas redegit, vt ex tota illa Samosatenianorum turba refutationem publico scripto concinnandam aggrediaufus nullus fuerit. Nihil ergo hactenus contra doctrinam catholicam, & orthodoxam de personarum Trinitate, præter vanas iactationum ampullas attulit.
units.tr: But the adversary goes on, and asserts more boldly than truly that these very consequences are empty and of no strength or weight, as the Socinian society has clearly demonstrated. For what are those most learned writings with which they have scattered the edge of our arguments in such wretched rout, that Ostorrodius dares so confidently to sing triumph before victory, and have not been learnedly refuted by our side? Besides other most learned teachers of our Churches, the most weighty and most lucid witness is not the ancient but only the more recent, that most famous light of the Christian world, Franciscus Junius, certainly well known to the Socinian rabble, who in his defences reduced that whole abundance of most cunning frauds and sophisms to ashes and dust, so that no one from the whole Samosatenian crowd has undertaken to compose a refutation in a public writing. So far, therefore, he has brought nothing against the catholic and orthodox doctrine of the Trinity of persons except empty bombast of boasts.

units.la: Secundò inquit Aduersarius, hanc eandem doctrinam non modò ad salutem scitu necessariam non esse, verùm etiam sine periculo credi à nobis non posse, quia contradictionem implicet, adeoque seipsam destruat, cùm Deus vnus esse dicatur, contra autem tres affirmentur, quorum vnusquisque verus sit Deus. Fieri enim non posse, vt tres sint, vbi vnus tantùm est, aut vnus tantum vbi tres esse dicuntur.
units.tr: Secondly, says the adversary, this same doctrine is not only not necessary to know for salvation, but also cannot be believed by us without danger, because it implies a contradiction and so destroys itself, since God is said to be one, while on the contrary three are affirmed, each of whom is true God. For it cannot be that there are three where there is only one, or only one where three are said to be.

units.la: Verùm vt huius argumenti, cui plurimum tribuit Ostorrodius, futilitas eo magis patefiat, nec ille sub ambiguitatum involucris vllis latere possit, ipsius argumentum ad formam redigemus, quæ talis est:
units.tr: But so that the futility of this argument, on which Ostorrodius relies greatly, may be made all the more plain, and so that it cannot lie hidden under any veils of ambiguity, we shall reduce his argument to form, which is as follows:

units.la: Si Deus vnus esse dicitur, contrà autem tres esse affirmantur, quorum vnusquisque sit verus Deus, tùm manifesta implicatur contradictio, & alterum altero tollitur.
units.tr: If God is said to be one, but on the contrary three are affirmed, each of whom is true God, then a manifest contradiction is implied, and the one is cancelled by the other.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Atqui prius est verum; ergo et posterius.

units.la: Connexum sic probatur.
units.tr: The connection is proved thus.

units.la: Si cùm Deus vnus est, tres esse non possunt, & cùm tres sunt vnus esse nequit, tùm, quicunque affirmat, Deum vnum esse, & simul asserit tres existere, quorum vnusquisque verus sit Deus, ille contradictionem implicat, & alterum altero tollit.
units.tr: If, since God is one, three cannot be, and since there are three, one cannot be, then whoever affirms that God is one and at the same time asserts that three exist, each of whom is true God, implies a contradiction and destroys the one by the other.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum; Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp. Si Deus vnus esse affirmetur, non tantum essentia, sed etiam subsistendi modo: contrà autem tres dicantur esse, quorum vnusquisque sit verus Deus non modo proprio subsistendi modo, sed etiam peculiari essentia prædirus, tum manifestè implicatur contradictio,& alterum altero necessario tollitur,adeóque verif- simū erit connexum vtrumque cum assumptione posteriore tam enim certum est,si vnus sit Deus,tres Deos esse nō posse,quàm verum est vnū non esse tria,aut bis duo esse quatuor: sed assumptio principalis falsa est , & falsò nobis , nullóque titulo æquitatis tribuitur.Vnum enim verum Iehouâ, Deum Israelis,& tres diui- nas personas,Patrem , Filium,ac Spiritum sanctum religiose cre- dimus,& adoramus,& tamen non tres Deos cū Tritheitis,sed vnū Deum ⁠s&c, seu tribus personis subsistentem profitemur.Sin vero Deus vnus affirmetur essentia, & tres personæ dicantur esse diuinæ,quarum vnaquęque sit verus Deus,Pater nempe,Filius,ac Spiritus sanctus, tum assumptio prior verissima, consequętia autē cum assumptione profyllogismi salsissima fuerit. Cūm enim vnū & trinum,siue multa contraria quidem sint,si eidem subiecto se- cundū idem,& ad idem,& eodem tempore tribuantur; Deus autē vnus dicatur,& trinus,non secundum idē,sed vnus essentia,trinus personis,seu vnus & tres non de eodē dicantur, sed vnus de essen- tia,tres non de essentia,sed personis,& hypostasibus:inde manifestè liquet præcipuas iustæ contradictionis cōditiones omitti, ac pro- inde verā contradictionē,seu oppositionē nullam esse.Nam quod essentia vnū est,id absque contradictione,ratione multa,aut mul- tiplex dici posse,nemo inficias ibit , nisi qui totum naturæ ordinē negare voluerit,nihil siquidē est,quod à lege,illa eximi queat.Nā ens creatum,quod per se,& simpliciter vnum est, secundùm quid nō est vnū,sed multiplex,vel causavel effecto,vel subiecto,vel ad- iuncto:quod toto vnum est siue per se,siue per accidens illud vnū dicas,secundùm partes in multa diuiditur:quę vnum sunt genere, formis distinguuntur,quæ vnum sunt specie , differunt numero: quæ vnum sunt causa, vel principio, differunt processionibus. Sic anima cuiusque hominis ἑνὰ vna tantum est numero , ac plane ἀδιαίρετος,& tamen intelligendi,sentiendi,& vegetandi facultatibus triplex,τῷ ἔξ quidem , hoc est , realiter,vtpote definitione diuersa differentibus , & tamen minimè disiunctis , sic vt,licet ab ipsa a- nimæ essentia ratione distinguantur , reipsa tamen nihil aliud sint quàm ipsa anima intelligens , sentiens , ac viuens, animáque vt totum essentiale de singulis facultatibus prædicetur , & hæ vi- cissim de illa enuntientur. Vtcumque igitur Deus simplicissimus sit, & vnus vnitate indiuisa secundum essentiam, processionis tamen, & personarum ratione sine ulla contradictione trinus dicitur, sic ut nihil per illam processionem, seu personarum Trinitatem de sua simplicitate, aut unitate deperdat. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissime liquet Ostorrodium vanis, & fraudulentis ambiguitatibus ludere in adorando hoc mysterio, & grauissimum oppositorum elenchum committere.
units.tr: Answer: If God is affirmed to be one not only in essence but also in the mode of subsisting, while on the contrary three are said to be, each of whom is the true God not only in his own mode of subsisting but also distinct in his own peculiar essence, then a contradiction is plainly implied and one is necessarily destroyed by the other. So the connection, taken together with the latter assumption, will be entirely true. For it is as certain that if there is one God there cannot be three Gods as it is true that one is not three, or that twice two is not five. But the principal assumption is false, and is wrongly and without any ground of fairness attributed to us. For we religiously believe in and worship the one true Jehovah, the God of Israel, and the three divine persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and yet we do not profess three Gods with the Tritheists, but one God subsisting in three persons. But if God is affirmed to be one in essence, and three persons are said to be divine, each of whom is true God, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, then the first assumption is most true, but the consequence, together with the assumption of the prosyllogism, is most false. For although one and many are indeed contraries when they are attributed to the same subject in the same respect, in the same relation and at the same time, God is not said to be one and three in the same respect: he is one in essence and three in persons. Or, to put it another way, one and three are not said of the same thing: one is said of the essence, three not of the essence but of persons and hypostases. From this it is manifestly clear that the chief conditions of a genuine contradiction are omitted, and therefore there is no true contradiction or opposition. For that what is one in essence can, without contradiction and by reason of a plurality, be called many or multiple, no one will deny, unless he wishes to deny the whole order of nature, for nothing can escape that law. A created being which is one in itself and simply, is not one in every respect but is multiple, either in its cause or effect, its subject or its adjuncts. What is one as a whole, whether you call it one in itself or one by accident, is divided into many parts. Things that are one in genus are distinguished by forms; things that are one in species differ in number; things that are one in cause or principle differ in their processions. Thus the soul of each man is one in number and altogether indivisible [ἀδιαίρετος], and yet threefold in its faculties of understanding, feeling and vegetating, [τῷ ἔξ] that is, really, as things differing in definition yet by no means separated, so that although they are distinguished from the essence of the soul by reason, in fact they are nothing other than the soul itself understanding, feeling and living; and the soul as a whole essential being is predicated of each faculty, and the faculties in turn are predicated of the soul. Therefore, although God is most simple and one with an undivided unity according to essence, yet by reason of procession and of the persons he is called triune without any contradiction, so that by that procession, or the Trinity of persons, he loses nothing of his simplicity or unity. From all these things it is most manifestly clear that Ostorodius is playing with vain and deceptive ambiguities in dealing with this mystery, and commits the most serious fallacy of opposites.

units.la: Hanc autem distinctionis nostrae inter unitatem essentiae, & trinitatem personarum, summam nihil ad sententiouis obiecta intentatum nobis crimen amoliendum conducere, affirmat Aduersarius. Quum enim essentia intellectu praedita, qualis est essentia Dei, idem sit quod persona, ita ut ubicunque tres sint personae, tres quoque essentiae esse necessarium sit, ideo cum in Deo una tantum sit essentia, necessario sequi non tres, sed unam tantum personam diuinam existere.
units.tr: Our opponent affirms that this distinction of ours between the unity of essence and the Trinity of persons is of no use at all in removing the charge of heresy which has been levelled at us. For since an essence endowed with understanding, such as the essence of God, is the same as the person, so that wherever there are three persons there must also be three essences, therefore, since in God there is only one essence, it follows necessarily that there exists not three but only one divine person.

units.la: Argumentum tale est;
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Si essentia intellectu praedita unum ac idem est cum persona, ita ut ubicunque tres sunt personae, tres quoque necessario sint essentiae: sequitur, ut una tantum essentia, ita quoque unam tantum diuinam esse personam.
units.tr: If an essence endowed with understanding is one and the same as the person, so that wherever there are three persons there must necessarily also be three essences, it follows that, just as there is only one essence, so there is only one divine person.

units.la: At qui prius est verum, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp. Si essentia intellectu praedita ita unum esse dicatur cum persona, ut tamen ratione certa, secundum quam unum, & idem cum ipsa esse nequeat, tum minor quidem de personis creatis, & finitis vera, tum quia quantitate ipsorum essentia finitur: tum etiam quia ex materia constant, & composita sunt, unde necessario unius personae ab altera non modo distinctio, sed etiam separatio necessario consequitur. At in diuinis falsa est utraque praemissa, quia diuina essentia ob simplicitatem, & immensitatem perfectissimam pluribus personis integra absque ulla diuisione esse potest: neque contrarium absque ullo Aduersariorum hactenus est demonstratum. Si autem essentia, & persona ita unum & idem esse intelligantur, ut nulla ratione inter se distinguantur, tum assumptio est absurdissima, & salsissima. Absurdissima est: Sic enim sequeretur Pontificem Romanum & Aedituum Venetum, Patrem, matrem ac liberos unum, idemque esse, nec ulla ratione distingui posse: sequeretur etiam Oftorrodium, qui gente eft Germanus, doctrina Syrus, & me,qui natione fum Heluetius, doctrina Chriftianus : fequeretur denique, omnes hominess, qui funt,fuerunt,& nafcentur adhuc, omnes inquam, qui in cœlis, & in terra, ac apud inferos funt, v-nam, eandémque perfonam effe, quia omnibus, & fingulis ef-fentia intellectu prædita ex æquo competit, quæ fi ita, vnum & idem eft cum perfona, vt nulla ratione ab ea differat, nihil amplius reftabit, quo vnus homo ab altero,vna perfona ab altera diftinguatur. Falfiffima eft, quia omnium hominum eft effentia vna, perfonæ autem pene numero infinitæ. Deinde, quorum eft definitio diuerfa,ea faltem ratione tali diftinguuntur, fecundum quam vnum idémque dici nequeunt. At effentiæ intellectu prædita, & perfonæ intelligentis diuerfa eft definitio : quia effentiæ definitio complectitur ea quæ funt communia effentiæ, perfonæ autem definitio, quæ funt propria,& characteriftica, feu indiuidualia in eadem effentia ratione diftingui iubet. Atque hæc eft illa ratio, fecundum quam ita diftinguuntur, vt effentia, & perfona ratione prædicationis non fint ἀντίστροφα. Quum deinde propriæ fpeciei cuique fuæ indiuiduis quoque fingulares fuæ fint differentiæ, & vocabulum effentiæ, vtpote pluribus indiuiduis commune,latius pateat, & de perfonis numero differentibus prædicetur:perfonæ autem feu hypoftafeos vocabulum, vt pote rem fingularem & incommunicabilem denotās,vnámque numero,fit anguftius, fequitur veriffimum effe id, quod illis Samofatcnianis multoties inculcarunt noftri, nec effentiam videlicet effe hypoftafin, nec vnam effentiam effe vnam hypoftafin, nec vnum effentia,effe vnum hypoftafi,proprie, folùm,femper,atque fimpliciter,fed tum demum effentiam effe hypoftafin,quam circumfcribunt, ac determinant fuæ differentiæ, non fpecificæ,fed idiomaticæ, quas proprietates characteriftcas, & in iis, quæ ratione in-ftructa funt,perfonales,appellamus, adeóqj inter perfonam, & effentiam præfertim in creaturis tale effe difcrimen, quale eft inter entis,& effentiam entis,inter fubftantiam, & effentiam fubftantiæ, inter concretum,& abftractum, inter communicabile, & incommunicabile,inter fubfiftens,& non fubfiftens, feu inter ὑπόστασιν & οὐσίαν. Quod autem perfona humana vnaquæque extra alteram fubfiftit, fic vt, quot fint numero effentiæ, totidem fint numero perfonæ, & viciffim (quamuis hoc ipfum arguargumentum Aduersarii nulla necessitate inferat, quot sunt numero personæ, tot etiam sint numero essentiæ, id ipsum rationi diuinæ hypostaseos nihil præiudicat, nisi cùm essentiæ, tum personæ diuinæ eandem rationem esse, cum humanis, demonstretur, quum communis illa ratio, qua essentiam à persona distinguimus, nec eádem rationem rerum per omnia, inferat, nec singularem earundem veritatem tollat. Inter naturam igitur creatam, finitam, & compositam, ac essentiam infinitam, & simplicissimam, purúmque actum, ac personam in illa essentia subsistentem, nulla cum sit proportio, sed genere toto disserant, ideò ab vna ad alteram nulla datur consequentia.
units.tr: Answer: If an essence endowed with understanding is said to be one with the person in such a way that, by a certain reason according to which the one and the same cannot be the same with it, then the minor premise is true of created and finite persons, both because their essence is limited by quantity and because they consist of matter and are composite, whence the distinction, and indeed the separation, of one person from another necessarily follows. But in divine things both premises are false, because the divine essence, by reason of its most perfect simplicity and immensity, can be entire in several persons without any division; and the contrary has not so far been demonstrated by any of our opponents. But if essence and person are understood to be one and the same in such a way that they are not distinguished from one another by any reason, then the assumption is most absurd and most false. It is absurd: for it would follow that the Roman Pontiff and a Venetian sexton, a father, a mother and children, are one and the same person, and cannot be distinguished by any reason; it would follow also that Ostorodius, who is German by race and Syrian by learning, and I, who am a Swiss by nation and a Christian by learning, are one and the same; and it would follow finally that all men who are, have been and will yet be born, all, I say, who are in heaven, on earth and in the underworld, are one and the same person, because the essence endowed with understanding belongs equally to all and to each one. If this is so, and one is the same as the person so that it differs from it in no way, nothing would remain by which one man could be distinguished from another, or one person from another. It is most false, because all men have one essence, but persons almost infinite in number. Further, those things whose definitions are different are distinguished at least by a reason such that they cannot be called one and the same. But the definition of an essence endowed with understanding and of an intelligent person is different: for the definition of the essence comprises what is common to the essence, while the definition of the person states what is proper, characteristic, or individual, and bids us distinguish them in the same essence by reason. And this is that reason by which they are distinguished in such a way that essence and person are not convertible in predication [ἀντίστροφα]. Then, since each proper species has also its own singular differences in its individuals, and since the word essence, being common to many individuals, has a wider range and is predicated of persons differing in number, while the word person or hypostasis, denoting a singular and incommunicable thing and one in number, is narrower, it follows that what our side has often urged against the Samosatenians is most true: that essence is not hypostasis, that one essence is not one hypostasis, and that one thing in essence is not one thing in hypostasis, in the proper, sole, always and simple sense; but essence becomes hypostasis only when it is circumscribed and determined by its differences, which are not specific but idiomatic, which we call characteristic properties, and in those things endowed with reason, personal properties. And so between person and essence, especially in creatures, there is such a difference as there is between being and the essence of a being, between substance and the essence of a substance, between concrete and abstract, between communicable and incommunicable, between subsisting and non-subsisting, or between hypostasin and ousian. As for the fact that each human person subsists apart from the others, so that as many essences as there are in number, so many persons there are in number, and conversely (although our opponent's argument does not necessarily infer that as many persons as there are in number, so many essences there are in number), this does not in itself prejudice the divine account of hypostasis, unless it is shown that both the divine essence and the divine person have the same account as the human ones. For that common principle by which we distinguish essence from person does not infer that the account of things is the same in every respect, nor does it remove the peculiar truth of each. Therefore, since there is no proportion between the created, finite and composite nature and the infinite, most simple essence, which is pure act, and the person subsisting in that essence, but they differ wholly in genus, no consequence can be drawn from the one to the other.

units.la: Ad hanc nostram responsionem nihil excipit Aduersarius, nec ad paradoxum illud absurdissimum stabiliendum quicquam afferre conatur, sed eiusmodi monstrosis axiomatis, ceu indubitatis principiis, & rescriptis regiis nobis obtrusis, astutè ad illius argumenti refutationem se per occupationem confert, quod à nostris ad astruendam veritatem trium personarum in vna essentia subsistetium, verissimè assertur, quod videlicet in sacris literis ea de Filio Dei, & Spiritu sancto affirmentur, ex quibus necessario sequatur, aut vnam essentiam diuinam esse in tribus personis subsistentem: aut non vnum tantum, sed tres Deos esse. Assertio verissima, & inuictissimis argumentis à nostris munita. Sed bellam quæso Ofl orrodii attendite resposionem. Quum ipsa ratio hominis, inquit, expresse dicet, Trinitatem personarum diuinarum esse falsam, neminem sana mente præditum affirmare posse illud ipsum verum esse, aut ex scripturis sacris demonstrari posse.
units.tr: The adversary makes no answer to this reply, and he does not try to establish his absurd paradox by any argument. Instead, he thrusts monstrous axioms at us, as if they were indubitable principles and royal decrees, and cleverly evades the refutation of that argument, which our side rightly puts forward to establish the truth of the three persons subsisting in one essence. The argument is: that the things said in Holy Scripture about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit necessarily lead to one of two conclusions, either that there is one divine essence subsisting in three persons, or that there are not one God but three. This is a most true assertion, fortified by most unconquerable arguments. But please, look at Ostorodius's fine answer: Since human reason itself, he says, plainly declares the Trinity of divine persons to be false, no one endowed with a sound mind can affirm that this same doctrine is true, or that it can be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Si ipsa ratio, aut intellectus hominis expresse ostendit trinitatem personarum falsam esse, cum illa non potest simul esse vera, aut ex Scripturis demonstrari: Ratio consequentia est, quia nihil verum ac falsum simul esse potest.
units.tr: If reason itself, or the human intellect, plainly shows that the Trinity of persons is false, then it cannot at the same time be true or be demonstrated from the Scriptures. The consequence is valid, because nothing can be both true and false at once.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Si per rationem intelligat Aduersarius reliquias illas, & particulam sapientiæ, ac imaginis diuinæ, quam principio in nobis effinxerat Deus, & cuius lucidissimū speculum, & effigies perfectissima est sanior Philosophia intra metam, & terminos suos se continens, Deo & cœlesti doctrinæ non repugnans, sed tanquam subordinata inseruiens, tum de maiore sobrie & modeste iudican-dum, minorem simpliciter falsam esse dicimus. Quum enim res Physicæ, seu naturales, & diuinæ, ac Theologicæ toto genere differant, & hæ omnia principia modum, ac rationem rerum non modo physicarum, sed etiam metaphysicarum omnibus numeris, ac infinite superent: ideo harum neque veritas neque falsitas in rationis iudicium, vt primum iudicandi principium, ac regulam cadit. Certissimum enim est illud propter mysteriorum Dei altitudinem, & rationis humanę ἀναμμτεἰα ex illis superioribus hanc, non ex hac illa iudicari. Atque hoc vnum licet ad debilem falsámque Oftorrodii assumptionem profligandam abunde sufficeret, tamen quo anilis istius argumenti vaniffima faifitas, & refponfionis nostræ solida veritas eo magis elucescat, amplius hanc confirmabimus, & illustrabimus, præsertim cum eandem crambem sæpius nobis reponat Oftorrodius.
units.tr: Answer. If by reason the adversary means those remnants and that small spark of wisdom and of the divine image, which God at the beginning impressed on us, and whose clearest mirror and most perfect image is a sounder philosophy, keeping within its own boundaries and limits, not opposed to God and to heavenly doctrine but serving it as subordinate to it, then we must judge soberly and modestly about the major premise, and we say the minor is simply false. For since physical or natural things and divine and theological things differ in their whole kind, and those principles surpass in every respect, and infinitely, the manner and reason of things, not only physical but also metaphysical, therefore neither the truth nor the falsity of theological matters falls under the judgment of reason as the first principle and rule of judging. It is most certain that, on account of the depth of God's mysteries and the lack of proportion [ἀναλογία] of human reason, the former must be judged by the higher things and not the latter by the former. And although this one point would be quite sufficient to overthrow Ostorodius's weak and false assumption, nevertheless, so that the utter falsity of this old-wives' argument and the solid truth of our answer may shine out the more, we will confirm and illustrate it further, especially since Ostorodius serves up the same hash to us again and again.

units.la: Quod igitur non est subiectum Philosophiæ, id proprie non potest dici falsum in Philosophia, quia posito adiuncto necesse est poni subiectum, & negato subiecto negari adiunctum: & quod à toto alienum est, non potest proprie, & fine contradictione in illa aliquam affectionem, vel naturam subire à sua contrariam, &cum ea pugnantem: Atqui res Theologicæ non sunt subiectum rationis naturalis, aut philosophiæ, eiusque præcepta in huius constitutione sunt heterogenea, cum Theologia, & Philosophia, scientiæ sint, non quidem aduersę, sed diuersæ, ac toto genere differentes. Ac proinde res Theologicæ in philosophia non possunt primo ac proprie dici falsæ. Sic etiam, quę non sunt de subiecto Theologiæ, in ipsa falsæ dici non possunt: ex nihilo enim nihil fieri, & virginem nullam parere, quatenus intelligitur hoc de ordine naturæ communi, & consueto, ac virtute causarum fecundarum, quia non est pars documentorum Theologiæ, in hac falsum dici nequit: at quatenus hoc intelligitur, de vi infinita, potentia supernaturali, & virtute causæ primę, quia subiectum Philosophiæ transcendit, in Philosophia non rectefalsum dicitur. Veritas igitur simplex est, nec verum vero contrarium, modo principia, ac termini scientiarum non confundantur, nec mysteria Theologica contra rationem aut Philosophiam, sed supra eam, non antiphyfica, sed hyperphyfica est censenda. Tres itaque esse in vna essentia diuina personas inter se distinctas, licet nullum exemplum in toto naturæ ordine reperiatur, non tamen illico falsum est in Philosophia, aut secundum rationem, sed superat eam, ac subiectum eius, ac proinde normam ac regulam ipsius excedit. Si autem hoc non supra captum intellectus humani, sed contra rationem suam existimet Aduersarius, tum morbo grauissimo animi se laborare, & vulnus ab Adami lapsu toti naturæ inflictum, ac mentem humanam notitia vera, & integra de Deo, eiusque voluntate spoliatam, è contra vero multis ac densis caecitatis tenebris obrutam agnoscat, connexi sic intellecti blasphemam impietatem tollat, & mysteriorum Dei altitudinem infra mentis nostræ glaucoma, caecitatem ac suffusionem, delirium, & vertiginem nefario facto deiicere non pergat.
units.tr: What is not the subject of philosophy cannot properly be called false in philosophy, because when the adjunct is posited the subject must be posited, and when the subject is denied the adjunct is denied; and what is wholly foreign to a thing cannot properly, and without contradiction, take on in that thing some affection or nature contrary to and at war with its own. But theological matters are not the subject of natural reason or philosophy, and their precepts in its constitution are heterogeneous, since theology and philosophy are sciences that are not indeed opposed but different and differing in their whole kind. Accordingly, theological matters cannot be called false in philosophy, primarily and properly. Likewise, things that do not belong to the subject of theology cannot be called false within it. For that nothing comes from nothing, and that no virgin bears a child, understood of the common and customary order of nature and the power of secondary causes, is not part of the teachings of theology, and so cannot be called false in it; but understood of infinite power, supernatural might and the power of the first cause, since it transcends the subject of philosophy, it is not rightly called false in philosophy. Truth is therefore simple, and no truth is contrary to another truth, provided that the principles and limits of the sciences are not confused, and theological mysteries are judged to be not contrary to reason or philosophy but above it, not antiphysical but hyperphysical. Thus, that there are three distinct persons in the one divine essence, although no example of it is found in the whole order of nature, is not at once false in philosophy or according to reason; it surpasses reason, and its subject, and therefore exceeds its norm and rule. But if the adversary thinks this is not above the grasp of the human intellect but against its own reason, then let him acknowledge that he is suffering from a very grave sickness of the mind, and that the wound inflicted on all nature by the fall of Adam has despoiled the human mind of true and whole knowledge of God and of his will, and has rather overwhelmed it with many thick shadows of blindness. Let him then give up his blasphemous impiety in so understanding these connections, and stop thrusting the depth of God's mysteries down beneath the cataract, blindness and suffusion, the delirium and vertigo of our mind, by a wicked deed.

units.la: Sed alio nos cornu petit Aduersarius, ac dicit, Etiamsi discrimen illud essentiæ, ac personæ ad euitandam Deorum pluralitatem a nobis confictum sit, nihil tamen impedire, quo minus ex eodem discrimine concludatur vnam quidem personam, sed tres essentias diuinas esse: siquidem demonstratum sit ab ipso essentiam, ac personam idem esse, ac proinde trinitatem personarum æquè, ac essentiarum, plures Deos introducere.
units.tr: But the adversary attacks us from another horn and says: Even if that distinction between essence and person has been invented by us to avoid a plurality of Gods, nothing nevertheless prevents it from being concluded from that same distinction that there is indeed one person but three divine essences, since it has been shown by him that essence and person are the same thing, and therefore that the Trinity of persons introduces as many Gods as the Trinity of essences would.

units.la: Argumentum tale est;
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Si idem, ac vnum est essentia ac persona, ac proinde tam personarum, quàm essentiarum trinitas, Deos plures introducit, tum discrimen illud essentiæ, ac personæ confictum nihil impedit, quo minus ex eo concludatur, vnam quidem personam, sed tres diuinas essentias existere.
units.tr: If essence and person are the same thing, and therefore a Trinity of persons no less than a Trinity of essences introduces several Gods, then the supposed distinction between essence and person does not prevent it from being concluded that there is one person but three divine essences.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter too.

units.la: Resp. Vix iurato alicui credidissem, tantam esse Ostorrodii impudentiam, vt quiduis pro lubitu, nullis adhibitis argumentis, aut rationibus affirmare, & negare auderet, dicenti, nisi scripta eius palàm hoc testarentur. Sed argumentationis singulas partes excutiemus: Primum igitur quod attinet, paulo ante affirmauit, essentiam intellectu præditam, & personam plané vnum, ac idem esse, sed ne quidem cùm attulerit, quo vel conaretur probare, illam enuntiationem suam, quæ fronte igitur hic affirmat idem à se demonstratum esse? Si affirmasse ipsum sufficiat, & Pythagoricum illud αὐτὸς ἔφα nobis obtrudat, blasphemia item sua, ineptissima deliria pro oraculis diuinis à nobis haberi vel-lit: iustas certè & æquas disputandi partes ac conditiones nobis nō relinquit. Falsum igitur quum hoc esse supra fusius ostenderimus, falsò inde colligitur & concluditur secundum ex illo, numpe tam personarum, quàm essentiarum trinitatem plures Deos constitue-re. Sed quibus argumentis demonstrabit Oftorrodius, discrimen illud essentiæ & personæ à nobis confictum esse, aut, quod quarto loco considerandum venit, nihil impedire, quo minus ex illo discrimine sequatur vnam tantùm personam, tres autem essentias diuinas existere? Essentiam omnem communiter, dicimus differre à persona, quia illa absolutum quid est, & communicabile, hæc autè relatiuum quid, & incommunicabile, quod idem de essentia, ac personis diuinis, licet modo singulari enùtiamus. Essentia diui-na differt à personis diuinis, quia essentia est absolutū quid, indeterminatū, & licet vna sit numero, omnibus tamē tribus personis eadem communis, quia infinita est, & ἀμέρης, vnde non reipsa, sed ratione differunt: non realiter, cum inter nomina naturæ, & nomina personarū, mutata fit prædicatio, & Deus verus dicatur Pater, Filius, ac Spiritus sanctus, & rursus Pater, Filius, ac Spiritus sanctus verus Deus, nec tamen aliud & aliud in Deo, sed alius & alius statuatur. Ratio autem illa, qua differunt essentia, ac persona diuina est relatio, vel modus subsistendi, & proprietas in ipsis personis, quæ discrimen facit, non quidem essentiale, sed tamen tale & eiusmodi, quod prædicationem vnius de altero fieri non permit-tit. Quum igitur essentiam illam numero vnam doceamus, id est, principium vnum, æternum, infinitum, immensum, simplicissimum, omnisciū, optimum, sapientissimum, causam & originem reliquorum entium omnium, quæ attributa non sunt idiomatica, & personalia, sed essentialia. Quum insuper demonstretur, Pa-trem esse verum Deum, Filium esse verum Deum, Spiritum san-ctum esse verum Deum: Quum denique has tres personas docea-mus differre ratione ab essentia, à se invicem autem numero, quia vna non est altera: proprietate deinde incommunicabili, & actu ad intra, Pater videlicet à Filio, ac Spiritu sancto ἀρχή, & generatione Filii, Filius à Patre ac Spiritu sancto, quod genitus sit à Patre, Spiritus sanctus à Patre & Filio, quia ab vtroq; emanauit pro-cessione arcana, denique agendi modo, & ordine: ideo libentissimè ab mè ab Ostorrodio audiam, quod affirmat confidentissimè, quomodo ex illo essentiæ & personæ discrimine à nobis tradito, & multoties ipsis inculcato, demonstraturus sit, vnam tantùm personam, tres autem essentias diuinas existere: audiam vero sine dubio tunc, cùm ipsum ceruos in æthere pascentem videro.
units.tr: I could scarcely have believed, had anyone sworn to it, that Ostorodius would be so shameless as to dare to affirm and deny whatever he pleases, with no arguments or reasons brought forward, were his writings not plainly witness to it. But let us examine the separate parts of the argument. First, then, as to the claim he made a little earlier, that an intelligent essence and a person are plainly one and the same: he has not even tried to prove it, so how does he now say, as though it were settled, that this has been demonstrated by him? If it is enough for him simply to have asserted it, and he wants us to accept his Pythagorean dictum [αὐτὸς ἔφα], and to regard his blasphemy and most absurd nonsense as divine oracles, then he leaves us no fair and equal terms of debate. Since we have shown above at greater length that this claim is false, the second claim, that a Trinity of persons no less than of essences makes several Gods, is falsely inferred and concluded from it. But by what arguments will Ostorodius demonstrate that the distinction between essence and person has been invented by us, or, what we must consider in the fourth place, that it does not prevent it from following from that distinction that there is only one person but three divine essences? We say that every essence differs in general from a person, because the one is something absolute and communicable, while the other is something relative and incommunicable; and we say the same of the divine essence and the divine persons, although we speak in the singular. The divine essence differs from the divine persons because the essence is something absolute and undetermined, and although it is one in number, it is common to all three persons, since it is infinite and without parts; hence they differ not in reality but in concept. They do not differ really, since the predication changes between the names of the nature and the names of the persons: the true God is called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and again the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the true God, yet in God there is not one thing and another thing, but one person and another person. The reason why the divine essence and the divine person differ is relation, or the mode of subsisting, and the property in the persons themselves, which makes a distinction that is not essential but nevertheless of such a kind that it does not allow one thing to be predicated of another. Since, then, we teach that this essence is one in number, that is, one principle, eternal, infinite, immense, most simple, all-knowing, best, most wise, the cause and origin of all other beings, which attributes are not idiomatic and personal but essential; and since it is further shown that the Father is the true God, the Son is the true God, and the Holy Spirit is the true God; and since, finally, we teach that these three persons differ from the essence in concept, but from one another in number, because one is not the other; then by an incommunicable property and by acts ad intra, namely the Father's being the principle [ἀρχή] of the Son and the Spirit, the generation of the Son, the Son's being from the Father and the Spirit in that he was begotten of the Father, and the Spirit's being from the Father and the Son because he proceeds from both by a hidden procession; and finally by mode of operation and order: I will most gladly hear from Ostorodius, who asserts so boldly, how he will demonstrate from that distinction between essence and person which we have delivered and repeatedly impressed upon them, that there is only one person but three divine essences. I will hear him, however, without doubt, only when I see him grazing stags in the sky.

units.la: Sed ne diutius eiusmodi recessus ac subterfugia quærere videatur Aduersarius, pollicetur se omnia illa argumenta, quibus nostri demonstrare conantur, tam Filium, quàm Spiritum sanctum, vnum illum verum, ac æternum Deum esse, paulò post refutaturum esse: nos conditionem oblatam amplectimur: & quamuis ea quæ Spiritum S. concernunt in hoc ipso capite obiter, ἡ ὡς ἁ παρό- σῳ tractet & percurrat, vberius tamen à nobis post locum de persona Filii Dei explicabuntur, cætera, quibus Aduersarius caput illud de personis diuinis claudit, quia ipsam controuersiam non spectant, hic studio præterevntibus.
units.tr: But lest the adversary seem to seek further such retreats and escapes for longer, he promises that shortly he will refute all those arguments by which we try to demonstrate that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are that one true and eternal God. We accept the offered condition. And although in this very chapter he touches on and runs through, in passing [ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ], the matters that concern the Holy Spirit, these will be explained more fully by us after the place on the person of the Son of God. The rest, with which the adversary closes that chapter on the divine persons, since they do not bear on the controversy itself, we here pass over deliberately.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CAPVT VI.

units.la: De persona Iesu Christi Filij Dei, & duabus in ipso naturis.
units.tr: Concerning the person of Jesus Christ the Son of God, and the two natures in him.

units.la: STORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite quinto, absoluta videlicet disputatione de personis diuinis, capite antecedente, docet, quid de voluntate diuina ad salutem scitu & creditu sit necessarium: verùm quia nihil ferè ibi tractatur, quod inter nos & ipsos sit controuersum, nisi quod Patres, qui sub veteri Testamento eiusdem fœderis nobiscum socios, eorundémque bonorum spiritualium consortes fuisse negat, adeóque à promissionibus rerum cælestium & spiritualium excludit: de hac autem ipsa quæstione infrà capite vigesimo quarto in loco de Officio Christi fusius agendum erit: ideo illis omissis, & hisce in locum suum reseruatis, ad caput sextum, quod est de natura & persona Christi, progrediemur.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter five of his Institutes, after finishing his discussion of the divine persons in the preceding chapter, teaches what must be known and believed about the divine will for salvation. But since almost nothing is treated there that is in dispute between us and them, except that he denies that the Fathers who lived under the Old Testament were partners with us in the same covenant and sharers in its spiritual goods, and so excludes them from the promises of heavenly and spiritual things, and since this very question will be discussed more fully below in chapter twenty-four, in the place on the office of Christ, we will set those matters aside, reserve them for their proper place, and proceed to chapter six, which concerns the nature and person of Christ.

units.la: Verùm vt maxima hæc, & tot seculorum disputationibus celebris disputatio eo illustrior, & clarior fiat,primo omnium, quid vtraque pars Ecclesiae videlicet tum Orthodoxae tum Samosatenianae,de natura & persona Christi sentiant,explicabimus: deinde sententiae nostrae veritatem,ex Scripturarum fontibus demonstrabimus. Denique argumenta Aduersariorum, quibus veritatem impugnant,placidè diluemus.
units.tr: But so that this greatest of disputes, which has been debated for so many centuries, may become more illustrious and clear, we will first explain what each part of the Church, namely both the Orthodox and the Samosatenians, thinks about the nature and person of Christ. Then we will demonstrate the truth of our view from the sources of Scripture. Finally, we will calmly refute the arguments by which our opponents attack the truth.

units.la: Quid nos de natura,& persona Iesu Christi sentiamus.
units.tr: What we think about the nature and person of Jesus Christ.

units.la: NOS credimus & confitemur Filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum ab aeterno praedestinatum, vel praeordinatum esse a Patre Saluatorem mundi,credimusq; hunc esse genitum non tantum,quum ex virgine Maria carnem assumplit, nec tantum ante iacta fundamenta mundi,sed ante omne aeternitatem,& quidem a Patre ineffabiliter. Ac proinde agnoscimus in vno atque eodem Domino nostro Iesu Christo, duas naturas, diuinam & humanam, & has ita coniunctas, vel vnitas esse, vt absorptae, aut confusae, aut immixtae non sint,sed saluis potius,& permanentibus naturarum proprietatibus,in vna persona,vnitae vel coniunctae:ita vt vnum Christum Dominum nostrum,non duos veneremur, vnum, inquam, verum Deum, & hominem iuxta diuinam naturam Patri, iuxta humanam vero nobis hominibus consubstantialem,& per omnia similem,peccato excepto.
units.tr: WE believe and confess that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was predestined or foreordained from eternity by the Father to be the Saviour of the world. We believe that he was begotten not only when he took flesh from the Virgin Mary, nor only before the foundations of the world were laid, but before all eternity, and indeed by the Father in an ineffable manner. Accordingly, we acknowledge in the one and the same Lord our Jesus Christ two natures, divine and human, and these so joined and united that they are not absorbed, confused, or mixed, but rather, with the properties of the natures remaining intact and abiding, they are united or joined in one person. Thus we worship one Christ our Lord, not two: one, I say, true God and man, who according to the divine nature is consubstantial with the Father, and according to the human nature is consubstantial with us men and like us in all things, sin excepted.

units.la: Quid Socinian,& Samosatenian moderni de natura, & persona Christi sentiant.
units.tr: What the modern Socinians and Samosatenians think about the nature and person of Christ.

units.la: Faustus Socinus in praefatione libri, quem scripsit aduersus Iacobum VVieckum Iesuitam,pag. 8.
units.tr: Faustus Socinus, in the preface of the book he wrote against James Wieck the Jesuit, page 8.

units.la: NOS de Iesu Christo sentimus, eū esse illum hominem,qui in Mariae virginis vtero,ex Spiritu sancto,conceptus est,& ex ea natus, & hunc ipsum hominem illum vnigenitum Dei Filium esse affirmamus,quem diuina testimonia nobis commendant,nec alium extra, aut ante ipsum. Cuihomini ea potestatem, atque imperium a Deo ipsius Patre datum, donatum esse asserimus, vt merito, ac necessario illi ipsi per se,& Dei nomen,& diuinus cultus tribuatur.
units.tr: WE think of Jesus Christ as that man who was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit and born of her, and we affirm that this very man is that only-begotten Son of God whom the divine testimonies commend to us, and no other outside or before him. We assert that power and authority were given and granted to this man by God his Father, so that by right and of necessity divine honour and the name of God itself are rightly ascribed to him in his own person.

units.la: Apologia,ad decretum illustrium Ordinum Prouinciarum foedera-tarum Belgij,editum contra Christophorum Ofiorrodium,& Andream Vuidouium,die 3.Sept.1598.scripta ab eis-dem duobus & edita:pag.21.22.
units.tr: Apology, written by the same two men against the decree of the illustrious Orders of the United Provinces of Belgium, issued against Christophorus Ostorrodius and Andreas Vuidovius, on 3 September 1598: pages 21 and 22.

units.la: Credimus,& confitemur, hominem illũ Iesum Nazarenũ, qui dicitur Christus,Abrahamo ciúsque posteris aliquan-do promissum, ex Spiritu sancto vero postmodum concep-tum,& ex virgine Maria natum,Dei vnigenitũ Filium esse. Hunc autem ipsum Iesum,hominem(inquam)illum, & non alium, postquam natus ex virgine esset,cœlitus à Deo mis-sum fuisse,vt nobis Dei voluntatem patefaceret, eandémque stupendis,& plane diuinis operibus comprobaret, & sic no-uum,æternumque fœdus nobis cum Dei nomine pangeret, quod & fecit, idq; proprio suo sanguine sanciuit,& cõfirma-uit:vnde quoque Deus illũ à mortuis excitatũ omnium hæ-redem costituit, eiq; omnem potestatem in cœlo,& in terra dedit,gloriáque eum & honore coronauit adeo,vt nõ solùm omnium hominum,sed & Angelorum Dominus factus fue-rit:vnde omnes,qui in ipsum credunt,perfectè seruare,& Ec-clesiæ Dei,quæ etiam eius Ecclesia est, omnia bona, potissi-mũ vero spiritualia,perpetuò largiri potest,& deniq;(vt vno verbo dicamus)ipsum suum solium illi Deus impertiuit: idq; totum in eũ fine,vt eum omnes sicut & Patrem honorent,in eius nomine omne genu flectatur, ad ipsum tanquam ad re-gem nostrum perpetuũ venerabundi confugiamus,eúmque in precibus nostris inuocare audeamus, ei ex animo seruia-mus,& obediamus,vnde fiet,vt eius gratia, & præsidio ab o-mnibus peccatorum pœnis, & sic ab ipsa morte tuti simus, ac tandem ex eius manibus vitam æternam accipiamus.
units.tr: We believe and confess that the man Jesus of Nazareth, who is called Christ, promised at one time to Abraham and his posterity, was afterwards truly conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, and is the only-begotten Son of God. This same Jesus, that man (I say) and no other, after he had been born of the virgin, was sent from heaven by God, to reveal the will of God to us and to confirm it by stupendous and plainly divine works, and thus to make with us a new and eternal covenant in the name of God. This he did, and he sealed and confirmed it with his own blood. Hence also God, raising him from the dead, made him heir of all things and gave him all power in heaven and on earth, and crowned him with glory and honour, so that he became Lord not only of all men but also of the angels. Hence he is able to keep perfectly all who believe in him, and to bestow perpetually on the Church of God, which is also his Church, all good things, especially spiritual ones. And finally, to put it in one word, God has bestowed on him his own throne. And all this with this end: that all should honour him as they honour the Father, that every knee should bow in his name, that we should come with reverence to him as our perpetual king, and dare to call upon him in our prayers, and serve and obey him from the heart. Hence it will come about that by his grace and protection we are safe from all the penalties of sins, and thus from death itself, and at last receive eternal life from his hands.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus manifestissimè liquet, hanc esse quæstionem inter nos controuersam: An videlicet Iesus Christus, si eius naturam, & essentiam spectes, non tantum sit verus homo, nobis per omnia, excepto peccato, similis: sed etiam verus, & æternus Deus, adeóque non tum demum esse incœperit, cum in utero virginis conciperetur, & ex ea nasceretur, sed ab æterno ineffabili modo sit genitus: Nos sanctè hoc & religiosè credimus: Ostorrodius cum suis confidenter negat.
units.tr: From all of these things it is most plainly clear that the question in controversy between us is this: whether Jesus Christ, if you look at his nature and essence, is not only a true man, like us in all things except sin, but also a true and eternal God; and so he did not begin to be only when he was conceived in the womb of the virgin and born of her, but was begotten from eternity in an ineffable manner. We hold this devoutly and religiously; Ostorrodius and his followers confidently deny it.

units.la: Nos ad confirmandam veritatem sententiæ nostræ duo ordine demonstrabimus. PRIMO videlicet in Christo praeter humanam naturam, de qua non est inter nos controuersia, aliam quoque esse, sic vt persona Christi, ex duabus inter se distinctis naturis constet. DEINDE Christum secundum alteram naturam verum, æternum, ac vnum illum cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto, Deum Israelis esse.
units.tr: To confirm the truth of our view, we will demonstrate two things in order. FIRST, that in Christ, besides the human nature, about which there is no controversy between us, there is another nature as well, so that the person of Christ consists of two natures distinct from each other. SECOND, that Christ according to the other nature is true, eternal, and one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the God of Israel.

units.la: Argumenta pro thesi nostra prima.
units.tr: Arguments for our first thesis.

units.la: Argumentum I. ex 1.Tim.3.16. Sine controuersia magnum est pietatis mysterium, Deus conspicuus factus est in carne, iustificatus est in Spiritu, conspectus est ab Angelis, prædicatus est Gentibus, fides illi habita est in mundo, receptus est in gloriam. Et frustra Aduersarii desudant vt hunc locum de Deo Patre intelligendum esse ostendant, cum Deus Pater nec manifestatus sit in carne, id est, caro factus, assumendo videlicet humanam naturam, nec in gloriam receptus dici possit. De persona igitur Iesu Christi hoc est intelligendum, cui & diuinam & humanam naturam hic tribuit Apostolus in qua ipse Deus natura sua inaspectabilis conspicuus hominibus est factus.
units.tr: Argument I. From 1 Tim. 3:16: Without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up in glory. The opponents labour in vain to show that this passage refers to God the Father, since God the Father was neither manifested in the flesh, that is, made flesh by assuming human nature, nor can he be said to have been received up in glory. It must therefore be understood of the person of Jesus Christ, to whom the Apostle here ascribes both the divine and the human nature, and in whom God, invisible in his own nature, was made visible to men.

units.la: Argumentum II. Hebr.2.19. Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps est factus eorundem. Et ver.16. Non enim vtique Angelos assumpsit. Quum igitur alia sit natura assumens, alia assumpta, alia natura sanguinis & carnis expers, alia verò carnis & sanguinis, quæ assumitur, & per Abrahami semen veram & integram naturam humanam ex Abrahami stirpe propagatam, intelligi ex ipso textu manifestum sit: ideo hinc euidenter liquet duas naturas in persona Christi vnitas esse.
units.tr: Argument II. Heb. 2:14, Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise also took part of the same, and v. 16, For verily he took not on him the nature of angels. Since one nature is the assuming nature and another the assumed, and since the nature that is free from flesh and blood is one thing, while the nature of flesh and blood that is assumed, the true and complete human nature propagated from the stock of Abraham through the seed of Abraham, is another, it is clear from the text itself that there are two natures in the person of Christ. Hence it is evident that two natures are united in the person of Christ.

units.la: Argumentum III. De vna eádemque natura contradicentia, & contraria prædicari non possunt, vt ab æterno fuisse, & in tempore natum esse, aliquid ignorare, & omnia scire, filium alicuius & Dominum simul esse, & quæ sunt eiusmodi alia. Atqui Christum ab æterno fuisse, capite octauo luculenter demonstrabimus: at eundem in tempore ex Maria virgine natum esse, extra controuersiam est. Sic Mar.13.verf.32. diem vltimi iudicij ignorare, & contra Ioh. 16. ver.30. omnia scire à discipulis dicitur. Dominus,ac filius Dauidis appellatur. Sic etiam,qui in cœlo,& in terra simul est, quod de Christo affirmatur.
