Ioh.3.13. eum non ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ εsse necesse est, siquidem corpus finitum & circumscriptum pluribus in locis simul esse nequit. Sic denique Heb.7.3. sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, nec initium dierum habere dicitur. Aut falsum igitur dixit Apostolus, quod cogitare blasphemum esset, aut concedendum præter humanam Christi naturam etiam aliam esse, cuius respectu ille sine matre, & initio dierum fuisse dicatur, cum secundum humanam naturam Mariam matrem ipsum habuisse constet.
units.tr: Argument III. Contradictory and contrary things cannot be predicated of one and the same nature: that it has existed from eternity and has been born in time, that it is ignorant of something and knows all things, that it is at once the son and the Lord of someone, and other things of this kind. But that Christ existed from eternity we shall demonstrate clearly in chapter eight, while that the same Christ was born in time of the virgin Mary is beyond dispute. Thus in Mark 13:32 he is said to be ignorant of the day of the last judgment, while in John 16:30 he is said by the disciples to know all things. He is called Lord and the son of David. Likewise he is said to be in heaven and on earth at the same time, which is affirmed of Christ. In John 3:13 it must be that he who is [ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, being in heaven] is necessarily not in heaven, since a finite and circumscribed body cannot be in several places at once. Finally, Heb. 7:3 says that he was without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days. Either the Apostle has said something false, which it would be blasphemous even to think, or we must concede that, besides the human nature of Christ, there is another nature, with respect to which he is said to be without mother and without beginning of days, since it is established that according to his human nature he had Mary as his mother.

units.la: Argumentum IV. Actor. 20.28. Deus sanguine suo Ecclesiam redemisse dicitur, quem autem non Pater, sed Filius pro salute Ecclesiæ passus,& mortuus sit, manifestissimè hoc loco personæ Christi duæ diuersæ naturæ tribuuntur, diuina, cum Deus dicitur, humana, cum sanguine suo Ecclesiam redemisse dicitur. Argumentum V. Phil.2.v.6.7. Christo duplex forma Dei nempe, & hominis tribuitur: Atqui per vocabulum μορφῆ non intelligendam esse formam accidentariam, figuram ac speciem diuinitatis, & humanæ infirmitatis, sed essentialem, id est, ipsam naturam, & essentiam veri Dei, & veri hominis, infra demonstrabimus. Sequitur igitur Christi personam duabus naturis inter se distinctis diuina nempe, & humana constare. Argumentum VI. Duas etiam in Christo naturas esse, manifestissimè docet Scriptura, illis loquendi formulis, quibus personæ Christi communiter, sed κατὰ δύο ἐν δύο, addens videlicet particulas distinctiuas & restrictiuas, quibus illa attributa toti quidem personæ, at certo alterius naturæ respectu inesse declarat: cuiusmodi sunt hæc, Roman.1.3. Filius factus ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem, declaratus Filius Dei potenter secundum Spiritum sanctificationis. Et cap.9.5. Ex quibus est Christus secundum carnem: Deus benedictus in secula. Mar.2.8. Cognovit cogitationes Pharisæorum Spiritu. 1.Petr. 3.18. Mortificatus carne, viuificatus Spiritu.
units.tr: Argument IV. Acts 20:28 says that God redeemed the Church with his own blood. But that it was not the Father but the Son who suffered and died for the salvation of the Church is most plainly shown here: two distinct natures are ascribed to the person of Christ, the divine, since he is called God, and the human, since he is said to have redeemed the Church with his own blood. Argument V. Phil. 2:6-7 ascribes to Christ a twofold form, namely of God and of man. But that the word μορφῆ [form] is not to be understood as an accidental form, the figure and appearance of divinity and of human weakness, but as essential, that is, the very nature and essence of true God and true man, we shall show below. It follows, therefore, that the person of Christ consists of two natures distinct from each other, namely the divine and the human. Argument VI. Scripture most plainly teaches that there are two natures in Christ by those modes of speech in which things are said of the person of Christ in general, but κατὰ δύο [according to two] and ἐν δύο [in two], that is, by adding distinguishing and restricting particles which declare that those attributes belong to the whole person, yet with respect to one nature in particular. Such are these: Rom. 1:3-4, Made of the seed of David according to the flesh, declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of holiness; and Rom. 9:5, Of whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever; Mark 2:8, He perceived in his spirit their reasonings; 1 Pet. 3:18, Being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit.

units.la: Argum. vltimum & efficacissimum inde desumitur, quod Christus sit verus Deus, à Patre ab æterno genitus, Iehoua ille Israelis, Patri coæternus, & coæqualis, vt cap.8.& seqq. abundè ostendemus.
units.tr: The last and most effective argument is drawn from the fact that Christ is the true God, begotten of the Father from eternity, that Jehovah, the God of Israel, co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, as we shall abundantly show in chapter eight and those that follow.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: In quo argumenta Aduersarii diluuntur.
units.tr: In which the adversary's arguments are refuted.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM primum, quo demonstrare conatur Christum, si eius naturam, & esse entiam spectes φλον ἀνθρωπον esse, illud est, quod videlicet ex sacris literis ne χῤ quidem adferri possit, quo doctrina illa de duabus naturis in Christo hypostaticè vnitis confirmetur.
units.tr: The first argument, by which he tries to show that Christ, if you look at his nature and essence, is merely a man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον], is this: not even one passage of Holy Scripture can be cited to confirm the doctrine of two natures hypostatically united in Christ.

units.la: Resp. At falsam esse hanc Aduersarii asseverationem ex antecedentibus sufficienter, & ex capite octauo & sequentibus apparebit amplius, ac proinde hoc ipsius argumentum prolixiore responsione non indiget.
units.tr: Reply: that this assertion of the adversary is false is sufficiently clear from what has gone before, and will appear more fully from chapter eight and what follows. Therefore his argument needs no lengthy answer.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM II. Si duae essent in persona Christi essentiae, vel naturae, diuina nempe & humana, quatum vnaquaq; de persona praedicari possset, tum sequeretur non diuersa modo, sed etiam contraria de vna eademque persona praedicari, Christumque immortalem simul, & suo tempore vere mortuum dici posse.
units.tr: Argument II. If there were two essences or natures in the person of Christ, the divine and the human, then whatever could be predicated of each of them would be predicated of the one person. It would follow that not merely different but contrary things are predicated of one and the same person, and that Christ could be called at once immortal and, at his appointed time, truly dead.

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum & impossibile.
units.tr: But the consequent is false and impossible.

units.la: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is too.

units.la: Assumptio probatur.
units.tr: The assumption is proved.

units.la: Si Filius Dei mortuus est, & vnus tantum est Filius Dei, sequitur aut, Filium illum Dei, cum mortuus esset, simul viuere non potuisse, aut duas personas cum Nestorio (qui animaduertit positis duabus in Christo naturis, duas etiam personas affirmandas esse) contra veritatem, & ipsum rationis lumen statuendas.
units.tr: If the Son of God died, and there is only one Son of God, it follows either that this Son of God, while he was dead, could not also have been living, or that, with Nestorius (who observed that if two natures are posited in Christ, two persons must also be affirmed), we must posit two persons, contrary to the truth and to reason itself.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo ex consequentibus alterutrum, ac proinde, cum manifestum sit non duas personas esse in Christo, sequitur vnam quoque naturam ipsum habuisse: & cum extra controuersiam sit, eum verum hominem esse, necesse est humanam tantum, & nullam aliam naturam in ipso esse.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore one of the consequences follows, and since it is plain that there are not two persons in Christ, it follows that he also had only one nature. And since it is beyond controversy that he is a true man, it is necessary that in him there is only a human nature and no other.

units.la: Resp. Perpetua elenchi ignoratione fallit Aduersarius, quę fraus & fallacia, quò magis detegatur, hoc sciendum est, Deum nempe & hominem, licet naturaliter sint opposita ac disparata, in Christo tamen minimè opposita, aut disparata esse, cùm non illico ea, quæ physicè sunt opposita, hyperphysicè quoque, & in subiecto totius naturæ limites transcendente, opposita ac disparata esse censeri possint. Vt enim se habet æternum ad non æternum, ita se habet Deus ad hominem: æternus autem, & non æternus φυσικῶς, sunt opposita, ὑπερφυσικῶς in Christo non sunt opposita. Ergo etiam Deus & homo φυσικῶς sunt opposita, hyperphysicè in Christo non sunt opposita. Vt se habet virgo ad matrem, sic se habet Deus ad hominem, sed naturaliter virgo & mater sunt opposita, supernaturaliter verò, & speciali miraculo in Maria non sunt opposita, quia virgo est, quo virum non cognouit, & incorrupta mansit: mater autem quà peperit, quod ex sua ipsius substantia virtute Spiritus sancti concepit: Ergo etiam Deus, & homo naturaliter sunt opposita ac repugnantia: supernaturaliter autem in Christo nec opposita sunt, nec repugnantia. Propter subiectæ enim rei, vel respectus diuersitatem, notionumque quoque Logicarum, seu argumentorum affectionem mutari est frequentissimum. Vt autem duo illa subiecta, Deus, & homo in Christo non repugnant, ita nec proprietates vtriusque naturæ, siue illa naturam vtramque per se, & definitionem, vt loquuntur, siue statum & conditionem tum personæ διαδοχῆς, tum naturæ humanæ consequantur, oppofitionis rationem nullam habent. Vt enim proprietates diuinæ ex natura diuina, humanæ ex humana fluunt: ita quoque illæ de natura diuina, hæ de humana, proprie, primo, ac per se, de tota autem persona per ἀλλοίωσιν quasi synecdochicam, seu κατ' ἄλλο, ἢ ἄλλο prædicantur sine repugnantia aut oppositione vlla. Atque hinc facilis est ad argumentum propositum responsio. Si enim duæ sint, vt sunt in Christo naturæ, diuina nempe, & humana, sequitur quidem ea, quæ alioquin etiam e diametro inter se pugnant, de vna eademque persona Christi prædicari posse, sed diuersarum naturarum respectu, ac proinde citra contradictionem vllam, vt ex iustæ oppositionis legibus patet. Hoc igitur sensu intellecta minor, nempe Christū diuerso naturarū respectu, immortalem fmul, & in tepore mortuū dici non posse, falsa est, vt exempla tum ex rebus naturalibus, tum etiam sacris literis petita,luculen ter demonstrant. Homo enim mortalis est & immortalis,sed illud respectu corporis,hoc respectu animæ: & quis eum sapere existimet, qui ipsum mortalem propter immortalitatem animæ,aut immortalem propter mortalitatem corporis,neget?Et vt se habet vita ad mortem, sicut se habet mortalitas ad immortalitatem, seu mortuum simul, & immortalem esse : Atqui viduam,inquit Paulus, 1. Tim.5.6. quæ in luxu vivit,viuentem mortuam esse sine vlla contradictione: Imperite ergo Oftorrodius negat, Christum ideo immortalem non esse,quia videlicet in tempore vere mortuus fuerit. Si exemplum Paulinum dispar esse dixerit, quia alia ibi vita, nempe essentialis homini, ac naturalis,alia vero mors, nempe spiritualis, & quasi θάνατος, intelligatur,tū iustæ oppositionis leges æquè violari meminerit, si idem confequeus de subiecto affirmetur,& negetur,sed diuer so respectu ὡς κατ' ἀνθρ. ac non secundum idem : quàm si diuersa prædicata, de eodem antecedente enuntientur, ac respondeat quomodo Christus sine patre,& sine matre extitisse, & tamen Deum Patrem, virginem Mariam matrem habuisse sine contradictione manifesta dicatur,nisi duæ naturæ in ipso esse statuantur ? Atque hinc quoque ad prosyllogisDnum,quo ille assumptionem suam astruere nititur, respondetur neutrum videlicet consequentium ex illo antecedente sequi:non primum, quia manifesta est fallacia ex ignoratione elenchi,qua videlicet negatur id de persona, quod est persona secundum naturam vnam, sumpto ex naturæ alterius ratione argumento: quamuis igitur Christus sit verus Dei Filius, & vnus tantùm:duplici tamen respectu,naturę videlicet diuinæ,& humanæ Filius Dei dicitur, vt Deus, naturâ Dei Patris filius , vt homo idem filius,sed gratia vnionis hypostaticæ: affirmatis autem vnius naturæ proprietatibus,alterius imperite tolluntur. Non secundum, quia numerando duas naturas in Christo ,& proprietates, vtriusque distinguendo , non tamen duas personas cum Nestorio à nobis induci vel sexcenties in locis à nostris est demonstratum, nec ab vllo Aduersariorum hactenus refutatum. Ad personæ enim constitutionem non modò natura intelligens, eiusque partium essentialium vnio, sed separata ab omnibus aliis subsistentia requiritur. Quum igitur humanam Christi naturam à primo conceptionis momento, non à λόγῳ separatim , sed in λόγῳ vnitam sustentari asseramus, falsum illum esse liquet, quod subnectit Aduersarius, rius,nullam naturam intelligentem absque peculiari persona, id est, fe-parato subsistendi modo,existere posse. Huius tamen argumenti propositi difficultate,ac pondere,ita nos argui,ac premi gloriarurAduersarius, vt omni responsione destituti eo nos refugio tueri cogamur, quo alia etiam absurda, & impossibilia religionis nostrae capita defendere soleamus : nempe quamuis secundùm rationis humanae iudicium res ita,vt illi volunt,sese habere videatur,aliam tamen rationem esse rerum diuinarum , vt pote quas intellectus noster sua acie complecti minime possit.
units.tr: Reply. The adversary deceives by a continual ignoratio elenchi. To expose this trick more clearly, it must be understood that God and man, although they are naturally opposed and disparate, are by no means opposed or disparate in Christ. Things that are physically opposed cannot straightaway be regarded as also opposed hyperphysically, in a subject that transcends the limits of all nature. For as the eternal stands to the non-eternal, so God stands to man. But the eternal and the non-eternal are opposed [φυσικῶς], naturally; in Christ they are not opposed [ὑπερφυσικῶς], supernaturally. Therefore God and man are naturally opposed, but in Christ they are not opposed hyperphysically. As the virgin stands to the mother, so God stands to man. Yet naturally a virgin and a mother are opposed, while supernaturally, and by a special miracle, they are not opposed in Mary: she is a virgin because she did not know a man and remained uncorrupted, and a mother because she conceived and bore from her own substance by the power of the Holy Spirit. Therefore God and man are naturally opposed and incompatible, but supernaturally in Christ they are neither opposed nor incompatible. For it is very common for the nature of the subject or of the relation to vary, and with it the logical notions and the character of the arguments. Just as those two subjects, God and man, do not conflict in Christ, so the properties of each nature, whether they belong to each nature in itself and by definition, as they say, or to the state and condition of the person or of the human nature, have no ground of opposition. For as the divine properties flow from the divine nature and the human from the human, so the former are predicated of the divine nature and the latter of the human, properly, primarily and in themselves, but of the whole person by a kind of synecdochic alloiosis [ἀλλοίωσις], or by "according to the one, not the other" [κατ' ἄλλο, ἢ ἄλλο], without any conflict or opposition. From this the answer to the proposed argument is easy. If there are two natures in Christ, the divine and the human, then it does indeed follow that things which otherwise are mutually contrary may be predicated of one and the same person of Christ, but with respect to the different natures, and therefore without any contradiction, as the laws of proper opposition show. So understood, the minor premise, that Christ cannot be called at once immortal and at his time dead with respect to different natures, is false, as examples drawn both from natural things and from Holy Scripture clearly demonstrate. A man is mortal and immortal, but the former with respect to the body, the latter with respect to the soul. And who would think him sane who denied that he is mortal because of the immortality of the soul, or immortal because of the mortality of the body? And just as life stands to death, so mortality stands to immortality, or to be dead and immortal at once. Paul says, 1 Tim. 5:6, that a widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives, without any contradiction. Therefore Ostorrodius foolishly denies that Christ is immortal on the ground that he truly died in time. If he says the Pauline example is unlike, because there the life is essential and natural to man, while the death is spiritual and, as it were, thanatos [θάνατος], let him remember that the laws of proper opposition are equally violated if the same consequent is affirmed and denied of a subject, but with a different respect, as regards the man [ὡς κατ' ἄνθρωπον], and not according to the same thing. Is it not much more so when different predicates are asserted of the same antecedent? Let him explain how Christ existed without a father and without a mother, and yet is said to have had God the Father and the Virgin Mary as mother, without manifest contradiction, unless two natures are posited in him. And so, against the prosyllogism by which he tries to establish his assumption, the reply is that neither of the consequents follows from that antecedent. Not the first, because it is a manifest fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, namely that what is said of the person according to one nature is denied of the person on the ground of an argument taken from the other nature. Therefore, although Christ is the true Son of God and only one, he is called Son of God with a twofold respect: as God, the Son by nature of God the Father; as man, the same Son, but by the grace of the hypostatic union. When the properties of one nature are affirmed, the properties of the other are foolishly removed. Not the second, because it has been demonstrated by us in many places, a thousand times over, that we do not introduce two persons with Nestorius by numbering two natures in Christ and distinguishing the properties of each; and none of the adversaries has refuted this so far. For the constitution of a person requires not only an intelligent nature and the union of its essential parts, but also a subsistence separate from all others. Since we assert that the human nature of Christ from the first moment of conception was sustained not separately from the Word but united in the Word, it is clear that the statement the adversary adds is false: that no intelligent nature can exist without a peculiar person, that is, without a separate mode of subsisting. Yet, as to the difficulty and weight of the proposed argument, by which he boasts that we are so pressed and hemmed in that, lacking all reply, we are forced to take refuge in that shelter to which we usually resort in defending other absurd and impossible articles of our religion: namely, that although, by the judgment of human reason, the matter seems to be as they wish, there is nevertheless another reasoning for divine things, since our intellect can by no means grasp them with its keen sight.

units.la: Verum an Ostorrodius suis rationum acuminibus nos in illas angustias compegerit,illamque confessionem nobis extorserit, vt rationis humanae iudicium illis patrocinari concedamus,ex rationum vtrinque allatarū mometis,Christianus,&æquus lector iudicet.Miranda haud dubie misero suo popello persuadebit Ostorrodius,qui palam scripto publico , vanas illas gloriationum ampullas proiicere tam impudenter audet. Quicquid enim hactenus ab Aduersariis allatum est , vt orthodoxæ doctrinæ nostræ hærefin Nestorianam impingerent, tam solide ac docte à nostris est refutatum , vt puduerit sine dubio Ostorrodium vllum ex illis argumentis in medium producere. Atque hæ pueriles nugæ,hæ aniles fabulæ,hæc indocti,& rerum etiam naturalium ignari ingenii deliria,sunt illi horrendi arietes quibus illa Samosatenianorum turba totius orbis Christiani Ecclesiæ nescio ex quibus Poloniæ, aut Transyluaniæ cauernulis impetere non veretur.
units.tr: Whether Ostorrodius, by the sharpness of his arguments, has driven us into those straits and extorted from us the confession that we concede the judgment of human reason to be on his side, let the Christian and fair reader judge from the arguments adduced on both sides. Undoubtedly Ostorrodius will persuade his wretched little people of wonders, he who in a public writing openly dares so shamelessly to fling out those empty boasts of his. For whatever the adversaries have so far brought forward to fix the Nestorian heresy on our orthodox doctrine has been refuted by our men so solidly and learnedly that Ostorrodius would doubtless be ashamed to bring forward any of those arguments. These puerile trifles, these old wives' tales, these deliriums of unlearned men, ignorant even of natural things, are the dreadful battering rams with which that Samosatenian crowd does not hesitate to assault the whole Church of Christ, from I know not what dens in Poland or Transylvania.

units.la: Sed videamus tamen,quomodo hanc ipsam responsionem allatam refellere conetur.
units.tr: But let us see how he tries to refute this answer as we have given it.

units.la: Primo igitur dicit,Nos fumere hoc pro concessō,quod tamen inter nos controuertatur, duas illas nempe naturas in persona Christi ex ipsis Scripturis sacris demonstrari posse.Sed doctrinam illam de duabus Christi naturis ex ipsis sacrarum Literarum fontibus haustam esse, ex capite antecedente satis liquet, & in sequentibus fusius demonstrabitur.
units.tr: First, then, he says: We assume as granted what is nevertheless disputed between us, namely that those two natures in the person of Christ can be demonstrated from the Holy Scriptures themselves. But that the doctrine of the two natures of Christ is drawn from the very sources of the sacred Letters is clear enough from the preceding chapter, and it will be demonstrated more fully in what follows.

units.la: Secundo,ait,ipsam etiam rationem humanam luce meridiana clarius ostendere, falsum esse illud, duas nempe in persona Christi naturas esse diuersas:quamuis enim multa sint credenda, quae intellectus humani vires exuperent, neminem tamen obligari ad credendum id quod ipsum rationis iudicium falsum esse dicet. Argumentum eius tale est;
units.tr: Second, he says: Human reason itself shows, clearer than the noonday sun, that it is false that there are two different natures in the person of Christ. For although many things are to be believed that exceed the powers of the human intellect, no one is bound to believe what the judgment of reason itself will declare to be false. His argument runs as follows:

units.la: F
units.tr: F

units.la: Si ipsa ratio humana luce meridiana clarius ostendit falsum esse quod duae sint in Christi persona naturae, tum illud etiam non est credendum:
units.tr: If human reason itself shows, clearer than the noonday sun, that it is false that there are two natures in the person of Christ, then that also is not to be believed:

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp. Quid de utraque praemissa fit sentiendum, capite quarto prolixe ostendimus. Duas naturas in Christi persona esse, diuinam nempe & humanam, creatam, & increatam, non contra, sed supra naturam est, quia ratio eius, vt pote diuina, & de subiecto non physico, sed hyperphysico, à ratione rerum naturalium, ac physicarum toto genere differt; ac proinde, nec ipsius iudicio subiicitur, nec primo, ac per se vera aut falsa dicitur, cum eius modi in tota rerum natura nullum existat. Si vnionis harum naturarum, & in vnam hypostasin coniunctionis modum non vsque adeo exacte, & perfecte complecti, nostri ingenii modulo possumus, non tamen illico rei ipsius veritatem negare, aut in dubium vocare debemus, cum ab ignoratione modi, quem Scriptura Ecclesiam nunquam docuit, ad negationem ipsius rei non nisi salsissima detur consequentia. Qua ratione, aut quo modo fieri posset, vt virgo, quae virum non cognouerat, pareret, quum Maria ipsa Christi mater Angelum percontaretur, nihil aliud illi respondit, quam promissum illum saluatorem non ex virili semine, sed Spiritus sancti virtute conceptum esse, Luc. 1. 35. Aut igitur verum est, quod iam diximus, nempe ab ignoratione modi ad negationem rei in rebus diuinis praecipue, non dari semper consequentiam: aut certe statuendum Christum ex Maria virgine natum non esse, quod vel cogitare blasphemum esset. Sic Christus Iohan. cap. 3. verf. 8. Nicodemo regenerationis beneficium fide amplectendum proponit, de modo autem quo illa fieret sollicitum ad exemplum ventorum ablegat, qui e qua regione terrae prodeant, & ad quam ferantur ignoremus. Et Paulus dementiam vocat hanc, non credere resurrectionem corporum, etiamsi modus eius ignoretur, praesertim cum ex putrefacto, & mortuo grano spica oriri conspiciatur, cuius tamen ortus ratio & modus nescia-tur. 1. Corinth. 15. 36. 37. Et certe, cum inuestigari non possit quo-modo consueto naturae cursu de femine viri concipiatur, viuifi-cetur.
units.tr: Answer. We have shown at length in the fourth chapter what should be thought of both premises. That there are two natures in the person of Christ, the divine and the human, the created and the uncreated, is not contrary to nature but above nature. Its reasoning, being divine and concerning a subject not physical but hyperphysical, differs in its whole kind from the reasoning of natural and physical things. Therefore it is neither subject to the judgment of reason, nor is it said to be true or false in the first and proper sense, since nothing of this kind exists in the whole of nature. If we cannot grasp, with the measure of our own wit, the manner of the union of these natures and of their conjunction in one hypostasis with full exactness and perfection, we ought nonetheless not to deny or call into doubt the truth of the thing itself. From ignorance of the manner, which Scripture never taught the Church, the denial of the thing itself follows only by the most false inference. By what reasoning, or in what manner, could a virgin who had not known a man bear a child? When Mary, the mother of Christ, asked the angel, he answered her only that the promised Saviour would be conceived not of male seed but by the power of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35). Either, therefore, it is true, as we have said, that in divine matters especially a consequence does not always hold from ignorance of the manner to denial of the thing; or else we must hold that Christ was not born of the virgin Mary, which it would be blasphemous even to think. So too Christ, in John 3:8, sets before Nicodemus the benefit of regeneration to be embraced by faith, and as for the manner in which it happens, he sends him off to the example of the winds, whose region of origin and destination we do not know. And Paul calls it madness not to believe in the resurrection of bodies, even though the manner of it is unknown, especially since we see an ear of corn spring from a rotted and dead grain, whose way and manner of arising is nonetheless unknown (1 Cor. 15:36, 37). And indeed, since it cannot be investigated in what manner, by the usual course of nature, a child is conceived from the seed of a man, nourished, and grows in the mother's womb,

units.la: Cap. 4. cetur,alatur, & crescat puer in utero matris, qui facta fit illa Incarnatio tam stupenda, cuius ingenii humani acies indagando assequi valeret? Idcirco quod olim Bernhardus de Trinuno, id ipsum nos de Θεοπάτωρ affirmare non dubitamus: Sacramentum hoc magnum est, venerandum, non scrutandum, quomodo pluralitas sit in unitate, & unitas in pluralitate: Scrutari hoc temeritas est: credere pietas: nosse vero, vita aeterna.
units.tr: ...is quickened, nourished and grows in the mother's womb, how could the keenness of the human wit, by inquiring, attain to that stupendous Incarnation? Therefore what Bernhard of Trino once said, we too do not hesitate to affirm of Theopator [Θεοπάτωρ]: This is a great sacrament, to be venerated, not to be searched into, how there is plurality in unity and unity in plurality. To search into this is rashness, to believe is piety, to know it is eternal life.

units.la: Assumptionem igitur syllogismi propositi negamus, non propositionem, quemadmodum falso, & temere nobis affingit Aduersarius. Falsissimum enim est nos statuere, credenda esse quaedam, quae tamen cum ipsa ratione humana manifeste pugnent: falsum etiam, nos salsissimam illam thesin eo argumento confirmare velle, quod videlicet multa sint in Scripturis quae ingenii humani captum superent, quae sententia in se alioquin est verissima, ut etiam agnoscit Aduersarius. Sic igitur, non nobiscum, sed cum idolo & figmento imprudentis sui cerebri pugnat, dum videlicet, & falsas theses, & falsas responsiones pro lubitu nobis affingit, quo liberius in nos debacchari, nostramque doctrinam apud miserum suum popellum in contemptum adducere facilius queat. Quo igitur candore, & quam iustis legibus nobiscum contendat Osiorrodius, in his & similibus locis animaduertatur.
units.tr: We therefore deny the minor premise of the proposed syllogism, not the major, as our adversary falsely and rashly attributes to us. For it is most false that we hold that some things are to be believed which nonetheless plainly conflict with human reason itself; and false also that we wish to confirm that most false thesis by the argument that there are many things in the Scriptures that exceed the grasp of the human wit. That view in itself is most true, as the adversary also admits. So he is not fighting with us, but with an idol and a fiction of his own imprudent brain, while he freely invents for us both false theses and false answers, so that he may rage more freely against us and more easily bring our doctrine into contempt among his wretched little people. Let it be noted, then, in these and similar passages, with what candour and by what just rules Ostorodius contends with us.

units.la: Tertio loco proponit Aduersarius illud Argumentum, quo verissime demonstratur, personam Christi duabus naturis, diuina nempe, & humana, constare, quia videlicet in sacris literis talia de ipso praedicantur, quae de humana ipsius natura enuntiari non possint. De hoc autem argumento pollicetur se deinceps acturum esse, ac manifeste demonstraturum, omnia illa, quae de Christo dicuntur, de ipsius natura humana intelligi, & posse & debere, & in praesentiarum ad alteram causam progressurum, ob quam nec credant nec credere possint, in persona Christi praeter humanam naturam, etiam diuinam naturam esse. Nos conditionem amplectimur, & aequo pede in hoc certamine libenter progrediemur.
units.tr: Third, the adversary puts forward an argument by which it is most truly demonstrated that the person of Christ consists of two natures, the divine and the human, namely because such things are predicated of him in the sacred letters as cannot be said of his human nature. Concerning this argument he promises that he will afterwards deal with it and clearly demonstrate that all those things which are said of Christ can and must be understood of his human nature, and that for the present he will proceed to the other cause, on account of which they neither believe nor can believe that in the person of Christ there is, besides the human nature, also a divine nature. We accept the condition, and we shall gladly advance on an equal footing in this contest.

units.la: Quarto igitur loco dicit Aduersarius, ideo illos duas illas in Christo naturas credere non posse, quia videlicet illa doctrina pugnet cum illis Scripturae locis, quae affirmant ipsum Christum a Patre iudicem, Regem, ac Dominum constitutum, omniaque ipsi subiecta esse, & similia.
units.tr: Fourth, then, the adversary says that they cannot believe those two natures in Christ because that doctrine conflicts with those passages of Scripture which affirm that Christ himself has been appointed by the Father as judge, king and lord, and that all things are subject to him, and suchlike.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Quod pugnat cum illis Scriptura locis in quibus Deus Pater dicitur Christum iudicem, Dominum ac regem constituisse, ipsique omnem potestatem in coelo, ac in terra dedisse, & omnibus eij subiectis, nomen ei donasse, quod est supra omne nomen, ut videlicet ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat, coelestium ac terrestrium, & subterraneorum: illud sine dubio falsum est, nec credi potest.
units.tr: What conflicts with those passages of Scripture in which God the Father is said to have appointed Christ judge, Lord and king, and to have given him all power in heaven and on earth, and to have subjected all things to him, and to have bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth: that is undoubtedly false and cannot be believed.

units.la: Atqui doctrina illa, quae persona Christi statuitur, non humana tantum, sed insuper etiam divina natura constare, cum praedictis Scripturae locis pugnat. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But that doctrine which holds that the person of Christ consists not only of a human nature but also, moreover, of a divine nature, conflicts with the aforesaid passages of Scripture. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Minorem propositionem syllogismi propositi in hunc modum confirmare nititur.
units.tr: He attempts to confirm the minor premise of the proposed syllogism in this way.

units.la: Qui iam ante omnia habet, ac possidet, ei nihil dari, ac donari potuit.
units.tr: To whom something already has and possesses everything, nothing can be given or granted.

units.la: Atqui Christus, si eius persona, non humana tantum, sed etiam divina natura constat, iam antea omnia habuit.
units.tr: But Christ, if his person consists not only of a human nature but also of a divine nature, already had everything before.

units.la: Ergo Christo nihil dari, aut donari potuit, & per consequens illa doctrina, quae statuit personam illam etiam divina natura constare, cum locis praedictis pugnat, in quibus tam multa ipsi donata esse, affirmatur.
units.tr: Therefore nothing could be given or granted to Christ, and consequently that doctrine which holds that this person also consists of a divine nature conflicts with the aforesaid places, in which so many things are affirmed to have been granted to him.

units.la: Resp. Negamus syllogismi principalis assumptionem, & quo euidentior fit ad prosyllogismum responsio nostra, primo ipsius subiecti, nempe Christi, deinde attributorum, quae de ipso enuntiantur, distinctiones quaedam nobis sunt praemittendae. Vt enim Christus a nobis consideratur, vel ut est natura Deus aeternus, infinitus, & eiusdem essentiae, maiestatis, ac gloriae cum Deo Patre particeps, vel quatenus homo est in tempore ex Maria virgine natus, nobis per omnia, excepto peccato, similis. Vel denique secundum oeconomiam, ac dispensationem voluntariam, ut est Mediator inter Deum & homines: ita etiam quaecunque de Christo enuntiantur, aut divina sunt simpliciter, adeoque ad eius naturam divinam pertinentia: aut humana, humiliaque ad naturam humanam: aut denique communia, mediaque ad totam personam in utraque ipsius naturae pertinentia. Sic gloria, potentia, maiestas, & similia, quum de Christo enuntiantur, his tribus modis distinguenda sunt. dis consideranda est, vt diuina, vt humana, vt media, seu mediatoria. Vt diuina essentialis, ac propria est Dei vnius, solius, & semper, nec cum re vlla creata communicabilis: Ergo & Christi, sed duntaxat quâ Deus absolutè. Vt humana solum, propria fuit Christi, dum hîc in terris ambularet in forma serui, & carnis infirmitate: vt Media denique ac mediatoria, propria est personæ Christi in vtraque natura simul, atque communiter, tum per gratiam vnionis, quæ in solo Christo est ad opus mediationis perficiendum, tum per exaltationem illam supra omne nomen, quæ perpessiones eius sequuta est. Hisce igitur ita præmissis, ad argumentum respondemus: Qui omnia habet, illi nihil dari potest, illo videlicet respectu, & secundum illam naturam, secundùm quam omnia habet. Sic Christo nihil dari potest, aut potuit vnquam, si consideretur secundum naturam diuinam absolutè, quia nihil ei addi, nihil etiam subtrahi vnquam potest. Hoc tamen minimè impedit, quò minus ei dari & conferri plurima potuerint, si eius natura humana, si deinde voluntaria illa dispensatio, & œconomia, si denique officium eius mediationis spectetur. Sic enim potestatem omnem habet, ac iudicium, vt rerum omnium est Dominus. At Dominus est ratione triplici, primo secundum naturam diuinam, Dominus est, iure ac dominatu essentiali, qui ipsi cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto communis est. Secundo ratione officii vt est Σταυρώσεως, & Dominus, vt loquuntur, dispensatiuus, proprio ac personali dominatu Rex, & Dominus Ecclesiæ in tempore datus: tertio secundum humanam naturam Dominus est, non quidem priore illo dominatu, quia ille Deitatis proprius est, & incommunicabilis, sed posteriore, Dominus nimirum à Patre factus & constitutus per gratiam vnionis in vnitate personæ. Quò ergo loca Scripturæ in assumptione syllogismi principalis allegata non agât de gloria illa aut potestate pure diuina & essentiali, quæ personæ Christi quidem competit, sed secundùm naturam ipsius diuinam, verum de media illa, ac mediatoria, adeoque de Christo Σταυρώτῳ ac Mediatore, manifestè liquet Ostorrodium grauissimum oppositorum elenchum committere, dum videlicet naturam in Christum diuinam tollit, sumpta ab officio eiusdem ratione. Vt enim officium Christi Σταυρώτῳ cum eius natura diuina minimè pugnat, ita etiam ab iis attributis, quæ de Christo ratione ossi cii ipsius, & certi finis causa prædicantur, ad eandem illam naturam diuinam tollendam, nonnisi vitiossima,& plane imperita nectitur, & ad nauseam vsque lectori doctrina Logica vel leuiter tincto , à Socinianis obtruditur , consequentia.
units.tr: Answer: We deny the assumption of the principal syllogism. And so that our answer to the prosyllogism may be clearer, we must first set down some distinctions, first concerning the subject itself, namely Christ, and then concerning the attributes that are predicated of him. For Christ is considered by us either as eternal, infinite God by nature, sharing the same essence, majesty and glory with God the Father; or as man, born in time of the Virgin Mary, like us in all things except sin; or finally according to the economy and voluntary dispensation, as Mediator between God and men. So too, whatever is predicated of Christ is either simply divine, and so pertains to his divine nature; or human and lowly, pertaining to his human nature; or finally common and intermediate, pertaining to the whole person in both natures. Thus glory, power, majesty and the like, when they are predicated of Christ, must be distinguished in these three ways: they must be considered as divine, as human, and as intermediate or mediatorial. As divine they are essential and proper to the one God alone, always, and are not communicable to any created thing; therefore they belong to Christ too, but only as God absolutely. As human they belonged to Christ alone while he walked here on earth in the form of a servant and the weakness of the flesh. As intermediate and mediatorial they belong properly to the person of Christ in both natures together and in common, both through the grace of union, which is found in Christ alone for the work of mediation to be accomplished, and through that exaltation above every name which followed his sufferings. Having premised these things, we answer the argument thus: He who has all things can be given nothing, in that respect and according to that nature by which he has all things. So nothing can be given to Christ, or ever could have been, if he is considered absolutely according to the divine nature, because nothing can ever be added to him or taken from him. Yet this in no way prevents many things from having been given and conferred on him, if his human nature is regarded, and then that voluntary dispensation and economy, and finally the office of his mediation. For thus he has all power and judgment, as the Lord of all things. But he is Lord in a threefold way. First, according to the divine nature he is Lord by an essential right and dominion, which is common to him with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Second, by reason of his office as crucified [Σταυρώτῳ], and as Lord in what they call the dispensational sense, he was given, by a proper and personal dominion, to be King and Lord of the Church in time. Third, according to his human nature he is Lord, not indeed by the former dominion, since that belongs to the Deity alone and is incommunicable, but by the latter: namely, as Lord made and appointed by the Father through the grace of union in the unity of the person. Therefore, since the passages of Scripture cited in the assumption of the principal syllogism do not speak of that glory or power which is purely divine and essential, which belongs to the person of Christ indeed, but according to his divine nature, but of that intermediate and mediatorial glory, and so of Christ as crucified and Mediator, it is clear that Ostorodius commits the most serious fallacy of opposites, when he removes the divine nature from Christ on the ground taken from his office. For just as the office of Christ as crucified does not in the least conflict with his divine nature, so too the inference drawn from those attributes which are predicated of Christ by reason of his office and for a certain end, to remove that same divine nature, is most faulty and utterly unskilled, and is thrust upon the reader by the Socinians, even to nausea, by someone only lightly tinged with logic.

units.la: Hoc argumento sic proposito, Aduersarius per θεολογίαν refutat quandam responsionem, quam contra ipsius argumentum afferri dicit, Quâ videlicet illa omnia humana Christi natura data esse dicantur.
units.tr: With this argument so set forth, the opponent refutes by a theological argument [θεολογίαν] a certain answer which he says is brought against his argument by our side: namely, that all those things are said to have been given to the human nature of Christ.

units.la: Respondet igitur, ne hanc quidem responsionem consistere posse, quoniam illi, nempe, qui hoc respondent, statuant, humanam illam Christi naturam, statim ab initio in vtero virginis Mariae per unionem hypostaticam, illorum omnium participem factam esse. Verbum autem Dei tefletur Christum illa omnia tum demum habuisse, postquam Deo ad mortem vsque crucis obediens fuisset, cum propter illam obedientiam Deus ipsum ita extulerit, & honore ac gloria coronauerit. Philip. 2. 9. Hebr. 2. 9. Si igitur vera esset, inquit, illa responsio falsitatis coarguendam esse Scripturam: quod quia absurdum sit, iure, meritoque illam sententiam falsam iudicandam esse.
units.tr: He therefore replies that this answer cannot even stand, since those who give it hold that the human nature of Christ, from the very beginning in the womb of the Virgin Mary, through the hypostatic union, was made a partaker of all those things. But the Word of God testifies that Christ then had all those things only after he had been obedient to God unto the death of the cross, when God, because of that obedience, exalted him in this way and crowned him with honour and glory. Phil. 2. 9. Heb. 2. 9. If therefore that answer were true, he says, Scripture would have to be convicted of falsehood; and since that is absurd, that opinion must rightly and justly be judged false.

units.la: Resp. Tria igitur hic breuiter nobis sunt discutienda, primo videlicet ipsa responsio, quam à nostris ad argumentum propositum afferri dicit: secundo illa quam inter illam responsionem, & alteram sententiam nostram extruit, & qua illam responsionem refutat: tertio denique ratio illa, & Scripturae loca, quae ad refutationem posterioris sententiae adducit. Ad primum igitur quod attinet, gloria illa, potestas, iudicium, & reliqua, aut intelliguntur per exaltationem Christo homini ita collata esse, vt Christus secundum humanam naturam tantum illa acceperit, non autem secundum vtramque, diuinam nempe & humanam: aut dicuntur toti personae donata esse secundum vtramque naturam, etiam humanam, sed non solam. Si priore modo intelligat Aduersarius responsionem nostram, falsitate manifesta ludit, & responsionem falsam nobis affingit. Quaecunque enim exaltatione Christi, obedientiam eius consequuta, Christo data sunt, partim ad diuinam naturam, sed secundum oeconomiam illam, ac dispensationem voluntariam, consideratam: partim vero ad totam personam secundum vtramque naturam, partim denique ad naturam humanam,sed in personae vnitate omnia referenda esse, ex superiori responsione liquet, & nostri vel sexcentis in locis docuerunt. Si posteriore sensu intelligit Aduersarius, vera est illa responsio,nec quicquam adducitur,quod illam euertat, vt ex sequentibus apparebit. Ad sententiam igitur alteram quod attinet,quam ille responsioni illi vt contradicentem opponit, cum ista per exaltationem, haec autem in utero Mariae per vnionem hypostaticam illam gloriam, ac dominatum acceptisse statuat,ambiguitate ludit. Intelligit enim per gloriam, ac dominatum illum, aut proprietates essentiales, ac diuinas, totique Trinitati communes:aut illa dona, quae totipersonae Christi per exaltationem sunt collata. Si priora intelligat idiomata, fatemur quidem proprietates diuinas communicatas esse humanae Christi naturae per vnionem hypostaticam, sed vna cum subiecti eiusdem communicatione,quae sine omni tum naturarum, tum proprietatum effusione, confusione, ac diffusione in personali vnione fundata,ab aliis communicationis speciebus, toto genere differat. Sed hoc sensu illa sententia,nec responsionem priorem tollit,nec ratione tertio loco adducta tollitur: hanc enim sive cum responsione,sive cum ratione Aduersarii & locis Scripturae quae in illa allegantur,contuleris,nulla ἀντίφασις apparebit: quia genus praedicationis mutatur,cum ista de idiomatibus aeternis, & naturae diuinae essentialibus,humanae autem naturae modo peculiari in vnitate personae communicatis: Illa autem, & haec de illis attributis, quae non vnionem per se, aut definitionem eius,sed statum personae, & exaltationem, in vnione quidem naturarum, sed non per illam primo, ac proprie sunt consequuta. Si autem posteriori sensu illa intelligantur, tum denuo falsam nobis sententiam impingit Aduersarius. Nostri enim,vt vnionem naturarum ab exaltatione etiam definitione ab illa differente, ita quoque vtriusque effecta inter se perpetuo & accurate distinxerunt. Si autem de alterutro, aut utroque capite alii senserunt, & docuerunt aliter, qui tamen orthodoxam de Trinitate doctrinam nobiscum tuentur, id falso & non sine fraude omnibus communiter & promiscue ab Aduersario imputatur.
units.tr: Answer. Three things must therefore be briefly discussed here: first, the answer itself which he says is brought by our side against the proposed argument; second, the distinction which he constructs between that answer and our other view, and by which he refutes that answer; third, finally, the reasoning and the passages of Scripture which he adduces to refute the latter view. As to the first, then: either that glory, power, judgment and the rest are understood to have been conferred on Christ the man by exaltation, so that Christ received them according to the human nature only, and not according to both, the divine and the human; or they are said to have been given to the whole person according to both natures, including the human, but not to that alone. If the opponent understands our answer in the former sense, he plays with manifest falsehood and attributes a false answer to us. For whatever was given to Christ by the exaltation which followed his obedience, is to be referred partly to the divine nature, considered according to that economy and voluntary dispensation; partly to the whole person according to both natures; and partly to the human nature, but all of them in the unity of the person. This is clear from our previous answer, and our writers have taught it in six hundred places. If the opponent understands it in the latter sense, that answer is true, and nothing is brought forward that overturns it, as will appear from what follows. As to the other view, which he sets against that answer as contradicting it, namely that the one holds that glory and dominion were received through exaltation, while the other holds that they were received in the womb of Mary through the hypostatic union, he plays with ambiguity. For by that glory and dominion he understands either the essential and divine properties, common to the whole Trinity, or those gifts which were conferred on the whole person of Christ through exaltation. If he means the former, the properties, we indeed confess that the divine properties were communicated to the human nature of Christ through the hypostatic union; but together with the communication of the subject itself, which, being founded in the personal union without any outpouring, confusion or diffusion of either the natures or the properties, differs entirely in kind from other species of communication. But in this sense that view neither overturns the former answer nor is overturned by the reasoning adduced in the third place. For if you compare it either with that answer or with the opponent's reasoning and the passages of Scripture cited in it, no contradiction [ἀντίφασις] will appear; because the kind of predication differs, since the one speaks of the eternal idioms and the essential properties of the divine nature, communicated to the human nature in the unity of the person in a peculiar mode, while the other speaks of those attributes which followed not the union itself, nor its definition, but the state of the person and his exaltation, in the union of the natures indeed, but not primarily and properly through that union. If, however, those things are understood in the latter sense, then again the opponent foists a false view upon us. For our writers have consistently and carefully distinguished the union of the natures from the exaltation, which differs from it in definition, and likewise the effects of each. And if others, on either or both of these heads, have thought and taught otherwise, while nevertheless maintaining with us the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, this is falsely, and not without deceit, imputed by the opponent to all alike and indiscriminately.

units.la: HANC autem contradictionem, nempe, & argumenti propositi difficultatem, inquit Aduersarius, cum animaduerti ssent nonnulli, ad aliam quandam mirabilem responsionem confugerunt, affirmantes, exaltationem Christi nihil aliud significare, quam maiestatis, hoc est, diuinae potentiae & gloriae Christi, a Deo factam manifestationem. Quam responsionem postea sectione quinta, & sexta refutat.
units.tr: "This contradiction, namely the difficulty of the proposed argument," says the Adversary, "when some men had noticed it, took refuge in another marvellous answer, asserting that the exaltation of Christ signifies nothing other than a manifestation, made by God, of his majesty, that is, of the divine power and glory of Christ." He refutes this answer afterwards in the fifth and sixth sections.

units.la: Resp.Sed nonne perpetuos falsitatum,& fraudum nodos, Aduersarius nobis nectit,dum videlicet pro lubitu sibi hostem fingit, quem postea magno cum applausu apud suos iugulet, atque confodiat? Falsissimum enim est,quenquam ex nostris docere, exaltationem, seu glorificationem Christi nihil aliud esse,aut significare,quam maiestatis,gloriae, ac potentiae diuinae declarationem, ac manifestationem. Nos enim exaltatum quidem esse Christum etiam secundum ipsius naturam diuinam,sed illa sola totam glorificationem non definimus, sed multa quoque tum naturae humanae ipsius, tum toti personae ratione officii mediatorii per exaltationem illam collata esse docemus, adeoque exaltationem consideramus primo respectu diuinitatis, quam dicimus exaltatam esse, non quod ipsi quicquam datum, aut concessum fuerit, quod antea non habuerit, sed quod depositam humilitate, potentiam, & gloriam suam, quam ante iacta fundamenta mundi apud Patrem habuerat,tempore autem humiliationis quasi occultauerat, exeruerit,ac manifestauerit. Sicut enim diuinitas illa se humiliauit, ita etiam rursus exaltata & glorificata est, atque illa humiliatio facta est:non quod natura illa diuina fuerit mutata, quae in se omnis mutationis, corruptiouis, & alteratiomis expers est;sed quod assumpta forma serui, per opera nec semper,nec multis nec vbique,nec omnib.quibus potuit modis suam patefecerit gloriam. Hanc exinanitionem eleganter expoluit Ambrosius de fide contra Arianos,Exinanitus,inquit,semetipsum formam serui suscipiendo,non vt aliud, quam quod erat,fieret, id est, non vt mutaretur ab eo quod erat, sed vt sepositio interim maiestatis suae honore, humanum corpus induceret, quo susceptio salus gentium fieret. Vt enim sol cum nube tegitur,claritas eius comprimitur,non caecatur: at lumen illud quod tota orbe dispersum claro splendore cuncta perfundit, paruo obstaculo nobis includitur: Sic homo ille quem Deus induit, Deum in homine non intercepit, sed abscondit. Haec ille. Hinc sequitur, etiam glorificationem, & exaltationem diuinitatis nihil aliud esse quàm illius potentiæ,maiestatis,& gloriæ diuinæ exsertione,manifestationémq;,humilitatis verò depositione, ac plenæ,& liberæ vsurpationis ius,quo'sc in assumptione humanæ naturæ quasi abdicauerat. Atque hoc ipsum nos docet Christus Ioh. 17. verf.5. dum videlicet glorificari cupit, & gloria, quam habuit iâ apud ipsum Patrem ante iacta mūdi fundamenta. Glorificare enim frequentissimè ipsam gloriæ declarationem, & manifestationem significare,plurima scripturæ loca euidenter demonstrant. Atq; hæc non est tota illa exaltatio, quasi hac circumscriberetur, & terminaretur, tota Christi, quam nos profitemur glorificatio, vt falsò affirmat de nobis Osiorrodius,sed tantum eius pars,& primus quasi gradus.Secundò,respectu humanæ naturæ, cuius exaltatio est gloriosa eius à mortuis resurrectio,ascensio in cœlum,& donorum, nempe sapientiæ, potentiæ,fulgoris,gloriæ completæ, aliorúmque longè maiorum, ac plurium, quàm vlli vel Angeli, vel homines acceperint,excellentia,& realis communicatio.Tertiò,respectu totius personæ,cuius exaltatio est ipsa excellentia,& perfectio officii mediatorii honoris,reuerētiæ, & cultus,de hostibus gloriosa victoria, potestas, & regnum in omnia. Hac aperta fraude Aduersarii detecta, non opus esset vt cætera, quibus fictam hanc responsionem refutat,diluceremus:sed quò futilitas plusquam puerilis, argumentorum, quibus orthodoxam impugnat veritatem, eò magis detegatur, etiam illa examinabimus.
units.tr: Reply. Does the Adversary not weave for us knots of falsehoods and deceptions, when he invents for himself an enemy at will, whom he then cuts down and stabs with great applause before his own people? For it is most false that anyone among us teaches that the exaltation or glorification of Christ is nothing other than a declaration and manifestation of divine majesty, glory and power. We indeed teach that Christ was exalted even according to his divine nature, but we do not define the whole glorification as consisting in that alone. We teach that much was also conferred through that exaltation, both on his human nature itself and on the whole person in respect of the office of mediator. We therefore consider the exaltation (first) with respect to the divinity, which we say was exalted, not because anything was given or granted to it that it did not have before, but because it laid aside the humility it had taken on, and brought forth and manifested its power and glory, which it had with the Father before the foundations of the world were laid, and had as it were hidden during the time of humiliation. For just as that divinity humbled itself, so again it was exalted and glorified, and that humiliation came to pass, not because that divine nature was changed (it is free of every change, corruption and alteration in itself), but because, having taken on the form of a servant, it did not always, nor by many means, nor everywhere, nor by all the means it could, reveal its glory. Ambrose neatly expounded this emptying in his work On the Faith against the Arians: "Emptied," he says, "by taking on the form of a servant, not so as to become something other than what he was, that is, not so as to be changed from what he was, but so that, meanwhile, by setting aside the honour of his majesty, he might take on a human body, through which the assumption would become the salvation of the nations. For just as, when the sun is covered by a cloud, its brightness is checked but not blinded, yet that light which spreads over the whole world and bathes everything in clear splendour is enclosed for us by a small obstacle, so that man whom God put on did not cut off God in the man, but hid him." Thus far Ambrose. From this it follows that the glorification and exaltation of the divinity is nothing other than the putting forth and manifestation of its power, majesty and divine glory, while its humility is a laying aside, and a recovery of the full and free use of the right which it had as it were renounced in assuming human nature. Christ himself teaches us this very thing in John 17:5, where he desires to be glorified with the glory which he had with the Father himself before the foundation of the world. For that the word "glorify" very often signifies the declaration and manifestation of the glory itself, the many passages of Scripture clearly demonstrate. And this is not the whole exaltation, as though the whole glorification of Christ, which we profess, were circumscribed and bounded by this, as Osiander falsely asserts about us, but only a part of it and its first, as it were, step. Secondly, with respect to the human nature, whose exaltation is his glorious resurrection from the dead, his ascension into heaven, and the real communication of gifts, namely of wisdom, power, splendour and complete glory, and of other far greater and more numerous things than either angels or men have ever received, and the excellence of these. Thirdly, with respect to the whole person, whose exaltation is the very excellence and perfection of the office of mediator, of honour, reverence and worship, of a glorious victory over enemies, and of power and dominion over all things. With this open fraud of the Adversary exposed, there would be no need for us to clear up the rest, with which he refutes this invented answer; but so that the more the utterly childish futility of the arguments, with which he attacks the orthodox truth, is laid bare, we shall examine these too.

units.la: Quatuor itaque adducit argumenta,quibus illam responsionem fallam esse conatur euincere. Primò videlicet, quia nullo Scripturæ fundamento,ac testimonio nitatur.Secundò, quia Scriptura sacra non tantum Christi illam exaltationem tum demum factam esse testetur, postquam ille munus mediationis hic in terris executus esset: verum etiam affirmet, Christum illa exaltatione, propter ebedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam,donatum esse.Tertiò, quia solidam nostram consolationem, quam ex illa glorificatione haurimus, nobis eripiat.Quartò,& vltimò,quia etiam Deum suo honore & gloria spoliet.Quæ argumenta nos ordine disponemus,& refutabimus.
units.tr: He therefore brings forward four arguments by which he tries to prove that this answer is false. First, because it rests on no foundation or testimony of Scripture. Second, because Holy Scripture does not merely testify that that exaltation of Christ took place only after he had executed the office of mediation here on earth, but also affirms that Christ was granted that exaltation on account of the obedience he rendered unto death, even the death of the cross. Third, because it takes from us the solid consolation which we draw from that glorification. Fourth and last, because it also strips God of his honour and glory. We shall set out these arguments in order and refute them.

units.la: Primum igitur tale est:
units.tr: The first therefore runs thus:

units.la: Omnis responsio, quæ nullo Scripturæ testimonio,ac fundamento nititur,falsa est.
units.tr: Every answer which rests on no testimony or foundation of Scripture is false.

units.la: Atqui responsio illa, quod videlicet exaltatio Christi nihil aliud, quàm potentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis diuinæ manifestationem, & declarationem significet, nullo Scripturæ sacræ testimonio, ac fundamento nititur.
units.tr: But that answer, namely that the exaltation of Christ signifies nothing other than a manifestation and declaration of divine power, glory and majesty, rests on no testimony or foundation of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Ergo falsa est.
units.tr: Therefore it is false.

units.la: Resp. Quia iam supra ostendimus, illam responsionem nobis falsò affingi, cùm illam exaltationem non sola gloriæ, ac potentiæ diuinæ manifestatione contineri, ac definiri, docuerimus, ideò totum argumentum concedere possumus. Sic enim illa responsio, non modò Scripturæ fundamento nullo niteretur, sed etiam manifestissimis eiusdem testimoniis contradiceret. Verùm quia Osiorrodius simul etiam illis argumentis cuincere conatur, illa exaltatione, nullam plane gloriæ, ac potentiæ diuinæ declarationem significari, ideò assumptionem syllogisminiverisimè negamus. Secundùm quam naturam enim scriptura Christum se exinaniuisse, & humiliasse affirmat, secundùm eandem etiam ipsum exaltatum esse testatur. Atqui exinaniuit ille, & humiliauit se, non tantùm secundùm naturam humanam, sed etiam secundùm diuinam, vt ex Phil. 2. verf. 7. manifestissimè liquet, vbi Christus ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ verus & æternus cum Patre & Spiritu sancto, Deus, hoc ipso se exinaniuisse dicitur, quod formam serui assumpserit, hoc est, vnita sibi humana natura, gloriáque, maiestate, ac potentia diuina occultata, ex Domino seruus, & diuite pauper, aliisque naturæ humanæ adiacentibus infirmitatibus obnoxius factus fuerit: formam enim Dei in illo loco non accidentariam speciem, figuram, & similitudinem deitatis, sed ipsam essentiam diuinam omnibus suis qualitatibus vestitam significare in sequentibus demonstrauimus. Vnde necessariò sequitur, ipsam exaltationem Christi, inter cæteram gloriæ, maiestatis, ac potentiæ diuinæ manifestationem, & declarationem denotare. Adde quod ipse Christus Ioh. 17. 5. glorificari petit illa gloria, quam apud Patrem ab æterno habuit, quod certè non nisi de gloriæ, ac maiestatis æternæ, per assumptam autem carnem ad tempus occultatæ, manifestatione, intelligi potest. Nec insuetum esse Spiritui sancto ita loqui, vt glorificare aliquem dicatur is, qui gloriam ipsius deprædicat, & patefacit exxs Scriptura constat. Sic Ioh. 17. v. 4. Ego glorificaui te Pater: sed quo-modo, hoc ipse exponit verf. 6. dum inquit, Manifestaui nomen tuum. tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi, hoc est, qualis fis Pater declaraui & prædicaui, tuámque immensam erga illos charitatem patefeci & illustraui. Eat igitur Ostorrodius, & illam responsionem nostram nullis Scripturæ testimoniis niti clamitet.
units.tr: Reply. Since we have already shown above that this answer is falsely imputed to us, because we have taught that the exaltation is not contained and defined by the manifestation of divine glory and power alone, we can grant the whole argument. For in that case the answer would not only rest on no foundation of Scripture, but would even contradict its most manifest testimonies. But because Ostorodius at the same time tries to prove by these arguments that the exaltation signifies no declaration of divine glory and power at all, we deny the assumption of the syllogism most emphatically. For according to the nature in which Scripture affirms that Christ emptied and humbled himself, according to the same nature it also testifies that he was exalted. But he emptied and humbled himself not only according to his human nature, but also according to his divine nature, as is most plainly evident from Philippians 2:7, where Christ, being in the form of God [ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ], true and eternal God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is said to have emptied himself by this very thing, that he took the form of a servant; that is, by uniting human nature to himself and hiding the divine glory, majesty and power, he became from Lord a servant, and from rich a poor man, and subject to the other infirmities that cling to human nature. For in the following passages we have shown that the form of God in that place does not mean an accidental species, figure or likeness of deity, but the divine essence itself clothed with all its qualities. Hence it necessarily follows that the exaltation itself of Christ denotes, among the other things, a manifestation and declaration of divine glory, majesty and power. Add that Christ himself in John 17:5 asks to be glorified with that glory which he had with the Father from eternity, which certainly can only be understood of a manifestation of eternal glory and majesty, which was hidden for a time by the assumed flesh. Nor is it unusual for the Holy Spirit to speak in such a way that he is said to glorify someone who proclaims and reveals his glory, as is clear from Scripture. Thus John 17:4: "I have glorified you, Father"; but how this is done he himself explains in verse 6, when he says, "I have manifested your name" to the men whom you gave me; that is, I have declared and proclaimed what sort of Father you are, and I have revealed and made clear your immense love towards them. Let Ostorodius therefore go and cry out that our answer rests on no testimony of Scripture.

units.la: Argumentum secundum.
units.tr: Second argument.

units.la: Si Scriptura sacra non tantum testatur, illam exaltationem Christi tum demum factam esse post quàm ille munus mediationis hic in terris exequutus est, verùm etiam affirmat, Christum, propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, exaltatum esse: tum exaltatio Christi, potentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis diuinæ declarationem, & manifestationem significare non potest: quia ille, qui reuera Deus est, nec obedire vlli, nec pati, moriqúe, nec vllare donari potest:
units.tr: If Holy Scripture not only testifies that the exaltation of Christ took place only after he had discharged the office of mediation here on earth, but also affirms that Christ was exalted on account of the obedience he rendered unto the death of the cross, then the exaltation of Christ cannot signify a declaration and manifestation of his power, glory and divine majesty. For he who is truly God can neither obey anyone, nor suffer, nor die, nor be given anything.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. In hoc argumento duo nobis sunt discutienda: ipsa nempe consequentia, & ratio, qua illa fulcitur. Consequentiam ipsam quod attinet, nullius illam ponderis, sed salsissimam esse, luce meridiana est clarius. Quia enim propter totius humiliationis obedientiam Christus ad tantam euectus est sublimitatem, eam verò obedientiam non alterutra tantum natura, sed tota persona secundum vtramque naturam (vnaquaque videlicet illarum agente quod suum est) etiam diuinam, ratione tamen voluntariæ illius, & liberæ dispensationis, consideratam, præstitit, ideò neutra etiam natura ab illius exaltationis fructu & præmii participatione excludi potest. Ratio autem consequentiæ duplex affertur, sed infirma vtraque: Prior, quia Deus nec pati, nec mori possit. Ambiguitatem mitto, ad rem respondeo: Si Christus secundùm naturam diuinam nec pati, nec mori potuit, nihil ne propterea ad passionem, mortemque contulit, quod certè Aduersario ad stabiliendam suam hac ratione consequentiam, necessario probandum esset? Falsum: Seipsum enim per Spiritum æternum obtulit Dominus inculpatum Deo Patri, & idem emundat conscientiam nostram à mortuis operibus ad seruiendum Deo viuo, Hebr. capite nono, versiculo nono. Nec solum secundum hanc nostram naturam,sed etiam secundum di-uinam illam perficit tum quæ apud Deum postulat mediatio, sacrificium puta,tum, quæ apud nos, puta efficacitatem ex merito illius. Posterior,quia videlicet ille,qui verus est Deus, nec obedire vlli, nec quicquam ipsi dari, aut donari potest. Verum est, sed ad stabiliendam vel consequentiam, vel ipsam Aduersarii sententiam nihil conducit,Christum enim Mediatorem dicimus humiliatum, & exaltatum,non qua Deus est simpliciter,& absolutè,sed quatenus secundum voluntariam dispensationem factus est. A voluntaria autem dispensatione, & œconomia, ad conditionem naturæ, & contrà, salsissimam Ostorrodius nectit consequentiam.
units.tr: Answer. Two things must be examined in this argument: the consequence itself, and the reasoning on which it rests. As for the consequence itself, that it has no weight but is utterly foolish is clearer than the noonday sun. For Christ was raised to such great exaltation because of the obedience of his whole humiliation, and he rendered that obedience not by one nature alone but by the whole person according to both natures (each acting what is proper to it), and the divine nature too, considered however in view of that voluntary and free dispensation. Therefore neither nature can be excluded from the fruit of that exaltation and from sharing in its reward. The reason for the consequence is given in two forms, but both are weak. The first is that God cannot suffer or die. I set aside the ambiguity and answer the point: if Christ according to the divine nature could neither suffer nor die, did he therefore contribute nothing to his passion and death? That is surely what our opponent would have to prove necessarily, if he wished to establish his consequence by this reasoning. It is false: "For Christ through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God the Father, and the same cleanses our conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Heb. ch. 9, v. 9). Not only according to our nature but also according to that divine nature he accomplishes both what mediation requires before God, namely the sacrifice, and what is effected among us, namely the efficacy that flows from his merit. The second reason is that he who is truly God can neither obey anyone, nor can anything be given or granted to him. This is true, but it contributes nothing to establishing either the consequence or the opponent's own position. For we say that Christ is humbled and exalted as Mediator, not as God simply and absolutely, but insofar as he was made so by voluntary dispensation. Yet Ostorrodius foolishly links a consequence from voluntary dispensation and economy to the condition of nature, and conversely.

units.la: Argumentum tertium tale est.
units.tr: The third argument runs as follows.

units.la: Quæ responsio veram nobis tollit consolationem, quæ ex Christi exaltatione in nos redundat,illa falsa est.
units.tr: That answer which takes away from us the true consolation that flows to us from the exaltation of Christ is false.

units.la: Atqui illa responsio, quòd videlicet per Christi exaltationem etiam gloria, potentia, & maiestatis diuina manifestatio, & declaratio sit intelligenda, aufert nobis veram illam consolationem, quæ ex Christi exaltatione in nos redundat.
units.tr: But that answer, namely that the manifestation and declaration of divine glory, power and majesty is to be understood through the exaltation of Christ, takes away from us that true consolation which flows to us from the exaltation of Christ.

units.la: Ergo, falsa est.
units.tr: Therefore it is false.

units.la: Minor probatur.
units.tr: The minor is proved.

units.la: Si Petrus 1. Pet. 1. vers. 21. affirmat, Deum, Christum ex mortuis resuscitasse, vt nostra fides, ac spes in Deum esset, illi autem, qui ipse talis Deus ac Dominus est, qui omnia in sua potestate habeat, nemo quicquam dare, aut donare potest, tum certè illa responsio quæ affirmatur exaltatione Christi etiam secundùm diuinam naturam aliquid datum esse, illam consolationem nobis aufert.
units.tr: If Peter (1 Pet. 1, v. 21) affirms that God raised Christ from the dead so that our faith and hope might be in God, and no one can give or grant anything to him who is such a God and Lord, who has all things in his power, then certainly that answer which asserts that something was given through the exaltation of Christ even according to the divine nature takes that consolation away from us.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Quàm perperam in alienû sefum, citatum diui Petri locû, ad negadam satisfactionem,& meritum Christi,& Socinianâ illâ hærefin, de exemplari mediatione ac redemptione, Ostorrodius detorqueat, ad hanc præsentem disputationem, non pertinet ostendere. Consequentiam ipsam iustissimè negamus. Christum enim in hoc negotio non considerabamus secundùm ius & conditionem naturalem, vel vt Deus est absolutè, vt sæpius iam dictum est, sed quatequatenus secundum voluntaria dispensatione est ϑεολογικῶς. Gloriam deinde Christi duplicem esse docemus, unam naturae diuinae essentialem, aeternam & infinitam: voluntatis secundum quam dispensauit Christus abiectionem suam, alteram. Christum vero secundum naturam diuinam ipsius, per exaltationem nullam gloriam, quam ante non habuerit, accepisse docemus, sed quia vsu & demonstratione illius gloriae ac maiestatis diuinae cessDerat per dispensationem voluntariam, exinaniens se, ea glorificatum ipsum de integro esse cum Scriptura affirmamus, quum videlicet, & diuinum vsum recepit illius, quem sustinuerat, & inhibuerat quodammodo in forma serui, & humanitatem suam euexit in tantam gloriam, quantam natura humana potest obtinere. Haec vero doctrina tantum abest vt animabus nostris illum auferat solatium, vt omnium beneficiorum coelitus in nos redundantium fontem ostendens, salutiferae consolationis solidissimae basis & fundamentum validissimum exstat. Si totum exaltationis beneficium illa gloriae, ac maiestatis diuinae manifestatione definiremus, merito falsitatis coarguenda esset responsio nostra, sed quum illud a nullo nostrum fieri constet Ostorrodio, mirum est illum Ecclesias Christianas tam impudentibus calumniis proscindere, & vanis sophismatum praestigiis, oculos mentesque sui populi fascinare audere.
units.tr: Answer. It is not relevant to the present dispute to show how wrongly Ostorrodius twists the cited passage of the blessed Peter into a foreign sense, in order to deny the satisfaction and merit of Christ and to support that Socinian heresy of a mediation and redemption by example. We deny the consequence itself most justly. For in this matter we were not considering Christ according to his natural right and condition, or as God absolutely, as has been said often enough, but insofar as he was made so by voluntary dispensation, theologically [θεολογικῶς]. Next, we teach that the glory of Christ is twofold: one essential to the divine nature, eternal and infinite; the other of the will, by which Christ dispensed his abasement. But we teach that Christ did not receive, through his exaltation according to the divine nature, any glory he had not had before. Rather, because the use and display of that divine glory and majesty had ceased through the voluntary dispensation by which he emptied himself, we affirm with Scripture that he was glorified by it anew, when he took back the divine use of what he had borne and in a sense restrained in the form of a servant, and lifted his humanity up to the greatest glory that human nature can attain. This doctrine is so far from robbing our souls of comfort that, by showing the fountain of all the benefits poured down on us from heaven, it stands as the most solid basis and very firm foundation of saving consolation. If we defined the whole benefit of exaltation by the manifestation of divine glory and majesty, our answer would rightly be convicted of falsehood. But since it is clear that none of us has done this, it is remarkable that he dares to tear the churches of Christ apart with such shameless calumnies, and to bewitch the eyes and minds of his people with the empty conjuring tricks of sophisms.

units.la: Argumentum quartum & vltimum tale est.
units.tr: The fourth and last argument runs as follows.

units.la: Quae responsio Deum suo honore & gloria, propter quam illam exaltationem factam esse, Paulus docet, Phil. 2. verf. 9. spoliat, illa falsa est.
units.tr: That response which deprives God of his honour and glory, on account of which Paul teaches that exaltation was made (Phil. 2, verse 9), is false.

units.la: Atqui illa responsio, quod videlicet exaltatio Christi etiam gloriae, potentiae, ac maiestatis ipsius manifestationem, & declarationem significet, Deum suo honore spoliat.
units.tr: But that response, namely that the exaltation of Christ signifies also a manifestation and declaration of his glory, power and majesty, deprives God of his honour.

units.la: Ergo falsa est.
units.tr: Therefore it is false.

units.la: Minor probatur.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved.

units.la: Quomodo enim, inquit, Deo honori, & gloriae hoc cedere potest, si dicatur, illi aliquid donasse, qui nulla re indiget? illum Regem, ludicem, ac Dominum constituisse qui iam ab aeterno regnauerit? hoc enim, quid aliud est, quam falsis & puerilibus interpretationibus Deo illudere? E cutrà vero, si Deus dicatur, & credatur Christo homini, qui antea pauper erat, aliquid donasse, illum Iudicem, Dominum, ac Regem constituisse, qui antea a principibus huius mundi iudicatus, & condemnatus, & vile mancipium ac servus fuerit, illum qui vere passus, & mortuus sit, resuscitasse, & in aeternum salvum fecisse, hoc non tantum nobis magno est solatio, sed gloriam, & honorem Dei commendat.
units.tr: "For how," he says, "can this redound to the honour and glory of God, if it is said that he bestowed something on one who needs nothing, that he appointed as King, Judge and Lord one who had already reigned from eternity? For what else is this than to mock God with false and childish interpretations? On the other hand, if it is said and believed that God bestowed something on Christ, a man who was previously poor, that he appointed as Judge, Lord and King one who had previously been judged and condemned by the princes of this world and had been a vile slave and servant, that he raised up and saved for ever him who truly suffered and died, this is not only a great comfort to us but also commends the glory and honour of God."

units.la: Resp.
