Assumptio prosyllogismi est falsa, nec ratione subiuncta ab Aduersario demonstratur, tum quia a persona Σαντηρίας, ac voluntaria dispensatione, ut iam ante dictum est, ad ipsam conditionem naturę, quippe quę imperitissimè inter se opponantur, futilis sit consequentia: tum etiam, quia tum demum aliquid contra nos concludere posset argumentum illud, si totam exaltationem Christi illius potentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis diuinæ declaratione definiremus. Et quia illa de re in antecedentibus responsionibus prolixè egimus, longiore repetitione hic supersedemus.
units.tr: Reply. The assumption of the prosyllogism is false, and the Adversary does not demonstrate it by any reasoning added. For the consequence is trifling, since the person of salvation [σωτηρίας] and the voluntary dispensation (as was said before) are set in the most inept opposition to the very condition of nature. Moreover, that argument could conclude anything against us only if we defined the whole exaltation of Christ as a declaration of his power, glory and divine majesty. And since we have dealt with that matter at length in the earlier replies, we shall not go over it again here at such length.

units.la: Hisce sic tractatis, Ostorrodius cofessionis suę, de persona Christi, compendio repetito, de quo nos ab initio huius capitis egimus, ad refutationem illorum argumentorum, quibus nostri diuinam Christi naturam afruunt, pergit, ad cuius etiam examen progrediemur, licet argumenta non eodem ordine quo ab ipso in aciem producuntur, prosequuturi sumus.
units.tr: Having treated these matters thus, Ostorrodius, repeating in brief his confession concerning the person of Christ, which we discussed at the beginning of this chapter, proceeds to refute those arguments by which our people assert the divine nature of Christ. We too shall proceed to examine these, although we shall take up the arguments not in the same order in which he brings them into the field.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: In quo primum argumentum pro vera, & æterna Deitate Iesu Christi Σωτῆρος adducitur.
units.tr: In which the first argument for the true and eternal Deity of Jesus Christ, the Savior [Σωτήρ], is adduced.

units.la: FACTENVS priorem nostram thesin, qua affirmamus personam Christi, duabus inter se distinctis naturis constare, ex Scripturarum sacrarum fontibus demonstrauimus: & ab Aduersarii cauillationibus vindicauimus: restat igitur ut ad thesfeos secundæ, qua docemus, Iesum Christum, non tantum verum hominem, sed etiam verum, ac æternum Deum esse, a Patre ante omnem æternitatem genitum, Θεὸν, ac demonstrationem progrediamur.
units.tr: Having demonstrated from the sources of the sacred Scriptures our first thesis, by which we affirm that the person of Christ consists of two natures distinct from each other, and having defended it against the Adversary's cavils, it remains that we proceed to the demonstration of the second thesis, by which we teach that Jesus Christ is not only a true man but also a true and eternal God, begotten of the Father before all eternity, God [Θεός].

units.la: Argumentum primum.
units.tr: First argument.

units.la: DE quo in novo Testamento a Christo ipso & Apostolis ea exponuntur, quæ in veteri Testamento, de solo vero Iehouah, & Deo Israelis enuntiannuntiantur: ille non tantum ratione officii, sed natura & essentia Deus est, Patri consubstantialis, coaeternus & coaequalis, eiusdemque cum ipso essentia, maiestatis, & gloriae particeps: quia unum tantum verum Deum esse ex Scripturis inter nos & Adversarios constat.
units.tr: Concerning whom, in the New Testament, Christ himself and the Apostles set forth those things which in the Old Testament are proclaimed of the one true Jehovah alone, and the God of Israel: he is God not merely in respect of office but by nature and essence, consubstantial with the Father, coeternal and coequal, and a partaker with him of the same essence, majesty and glory; because it is agreed between us and our Adversaries from the Scriptures that there is only one true God.

units.la: Atqui de Christo Iesu in nouo Testamento ea exponuntur, ab ipsemet Christo, & Apostolis, quae in veteri Testamento, de solo vero Iehouah, & Deo Israelis dicta sunt.
units.tr: But concerning Jesus Christ in the New Testament, those things are set forth by Christ himself and the Apostles which in the Old Testament were said of the one true Jehovah alone, and the God of Israel.

units.la: Ergo Christus Iesus non ratione tantum officii, sed natura, & essentia Deus est, Patri consubstantialis, coaeternus, & coaequalis, eiusdemque cum ipso essentia, gloria, ac maiestatis particeps.
units.tr: Therefore Christ Jesus is God not merely in respect of office but by nature and essence, consubstantial with the Father, coeternal and coequal, and a partaker with him of the same essence, glory and majesty.

units.la: Minor demonstrari potest ex collatione plurimorum utriusque Testamenti locorum, ex quibus nos pauca tantum seligemus.
units.tr: The minor premise can be demonstrated from the comparison of many passages of both Testaments, of which we shall select only a few.

units.la: LOCVS I. Numer. 21. vers. 5. 6.
units.tr: Passage I. Numbers 21, verses 5, 6.

units.la: Locutus est populus contra Deum & contra Mosen, quare fecistis ut ascenderemus ex Aegypto, ad morien dum in hoc deserto? non est enim panis, neque est aqua, & animam nostram taedet huius panis vilissimi: Tum in misit Iehouah in populum illum serpentes ignitos, qui mordebant populum ipsum, itaque moriebatur populus multus ex Israel. Hoc vero ipsum 1. Cor. 10. 9 de Christo exponitur a Paulo, dum inquit, Ne tentemus Christum, sicuti quidam tentarunt ipsum, & a serpentibus perierunt. Tentarunt enim veteres eundem, quem nos, alioquin non aeque peccaremus ac ipsi, imo ne peccaremus quidem, cum non creaturam, sed Deum creatorem tentare fit vetitum, Deut. 6. 16. nec similis nobis metuenda poena. Etsi aliusab illis, quam a nobis fuisset tentatus, sine dubio Apostolus id dixisset, nec tentatio creaturae tentationi creatoris aequaretur. Nec adversarios illud iuvat figmentum, quasi Veteres Christum tetrauerint in figura, nos autem reipsa. Etiasi enim populus ille Ecclesiae typum gessit, nihilominus tamen non figurate, sed reipsa peccavit, Christumque tentavit. Nam ut filii Israel dicuntur fornicati, & idola coluisse, ac propterea variis modis a Deo puniti, proprie tamen fornicati sunt, idola coluerunt, & poenas tulerunt, licet in his omnibus figuram gesserint populi Christiani, quem Deus similiter puniturus sit, si eadem peccata committat: ita quoque hic vere peccavit, & tentavit Iehouam, qui non fuit figura, aut typus Christi, sicuti petra, sed Christus ipse. Ex hoc igitur loco tale extruimus argumentum.
units.tr: "The people spoke against God and against Moses: why have you made us go up out of Egypt to die in this wilderness? For there is no bread, nor is there water, and our soul loathes this most worthless bread." Then Jehovah sent fiery serpents among that people, which bit the people, and so many of the people of Israel died. Now this very passage is applied to Christ by Paul, when he says: "Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by the serpents" (1 Cor. 10:9). For those of old tempted the same one whom we do; otherwise they would not have sinned in the same way as we, indeed we would not even sin, since it is forbidden to tempt not a creature but God the Creator (Deut. 6:16), nor is a punishment like ours to be feared. Even if the Apostle had said that he was tempted by others than by us, he would undoubtedly have said it, and the temptation of a creature would not equal the temptation of the Creator. Nor does the adversaries' fiction help them, as if the ancients tempted Christ in a figure, but we in reality. For although that people bore the type of the Church, nevertheless they sinned and tempted Christ not figuratively but in reality. For just as the sons of Israel are said to have committed fornication and to have worshipped idols, and were therefore punished by God in various ways, yet they truly committed fornication, worshipped idols, and bore the penalties, even though in all these things they bore the figure of the Christian people, whom God will likewise punish if he commits the same sins: so too here they truly sinned and tempted Jehovah, who was not a figure or type of Christ, as the rock was, but Christ himself. From this passage, therefore, we construct the following argument.

units.la: Qui ab Israelitis in deserto, una cum Mose tentatus fuit, ille est verus Deus Israelis, & Iehouah excelsus: Ps. 78. 56. & 106. 14. Num. 21. v. 5. 6. Atqui Christus is est, qui vna cum Mose in deserto ab Israelitis fuit tentatus, 1. Cor. 10. 9.
units.tr: "He who was tempted by the Israelites in the wilderness, together with Moses, is the true God of Israel and the most high Jehovah" (Ps. 78:56; 106:14; Num. 21:5, 6). "But Christ is he who, together with Moses, was tempted by the Israelites in the wilderness" (1 Cor. 10:9).

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus Deus Israelis, & Iehova excelsus.
units.tr: "Therefore Christ is the true God of Israel and the most high Jehovah."

units.la: LOCVS II.
units.tr: Locus II.

units.la: Exod. 20. 2. Ego Iehouah Deus tuus, qui eduxi te e terra Aegypti, e domo seruorum: Et Deut. 32. 12. Iehouah solus duxit eum, nec fuit cum eo fortis alienigena. Hanc autem liberationem ex seruitute Aegyptiaca Iudas Apostolus ipsi Christo tribuit, verf. 5, vbi inquit, Volo autem vos isthorum commonefacere, vt qui semel hoc sciatis, Dominum, quum populum ex Aegypto liberasset, rursum eos, qui non crediderant perdidisse. Quem Dominum verf. 4. solum illum verum herum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum esse affirmat.
units.tr: Exod. 20. 2. "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." And Deut. 32. 12: "The LORD alone led him, and there was no foreign god with him." Moreover, Jude the Apostle attributes this deliverance from Egyptian bondage to Christ himself, at verse 5, where he says: "I wish therefore to remind you, though you once fully knew this, that the Lord, having saved the people out of Egypt, afterwards destroyed those who did not believe." And at verse 4 he affirms that this Lord is "the only true Master and our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: Vnde denuo sic concludimus:
units.tr: Hence we conclude again as follows:

units.la: Qui populum Israeliticum ex Aegypto liberauit, ille verus, & aeternus ille Deus Israelis: Exod. 20. 2. Deut. 32. 12.
units.tr: Whoever delivered the Israelite people out of Egypt is the true and eternal God of Israel: Exod. 20. 2; Deut. 32. 12.

units.la: Atqui Christus populum Israeliticum ex Aegypto liberauit, Iud. v. 4. 5.
units.tr: But Christ delivered the Israelite people out of Egypt: Jude vv. 4, 5.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus, & aeternus ille Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: LOCVS III.
units.tr: Locus III.

units.la: Mal. 3. 1. Ecce mittam Angelum meum, qui paret viam ante me, inquit Iehouah. Esa. 40. 3. Vox clamantis in deserto, parate viam Domino. Hunc autem Angelum Christus interpretatur fuisse Iohannem Baptistam antecursorem suum, Matth. 11. verf. 10. Marc. 1. 2. Luc. 7. v. 27. Et haec vox clamantis in deserto de eodem Iohanne dicitur Matth. 3. 3. Marc. 1. 3. Luc. 3. 4. Ioh. 1. 23. Ex quorum locorum collatione tale exurgit argumentum.
units.tr: Mal. 3. 1. Behold, I will send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before me, saith the LORD. Isa. 40. 3. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord. Christ explains that this messenger was John the Baptist, his forerunner: Matt. 11. 10; Mark 1. 2; Luke 7. 27. And this voice crying in the wilderness is said of the same John: Matt. 3. 3; Mark 1. 3; Luke 3. 4; John 1. 23. From the comparison of these passages the following argument arises.

units.la: Qui missurus erat Angelum ad parandas sibi vias, & cuius semitas planandas esse Angelus clamauit, ille est verus, & aeternus Deus Israelis, Mal. 3. 1. Esa. 40. 3.
units.tr: He who was to send a messenger to prepare his ways, and whose paths the messenger cried out should be made straight, is the true and eternal God of Israel: Mal. 3. 1; Isa. 40. 3.

units.la: Atqui Christus missurus erat, & misit etiam postea Angelum, ad parandas sibi vias, & ipsi planandas esse semitas, clamauit Angelus, Matth. 11. verf. 10. Mar. 1. verf. 2. Luc. 7. verf. 27. Matth. 3. verf. 3. Mar. 1. 3. Luc. 3. 9. Ioh. 1. 23.
units.tr: But Christ was to send a messenger, and afterwards did send one, to prepare his ways, and the messenger cried out that his paths were to be made straight: Matt. 11. 10; Mark 1. 2; Luke 7. 27; Matt. 3. 3; Mark 1. 3; Luke 3. 4; John 1. 23.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus, & aeternus ille Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: LOCVS IIII.
units.tr: LOCUS IV.

units.la: Psal. 68. 18. 19. Currum Dei dua myriades, millia multiplicia. Dominus cum illis est (Dominus) Sina in sanctuario (habitans) Ascendens in sublime captiuam fecisti captiuorum multitudinem, accipiens (dedisti) dona hominibus, etiam rebelles habitando (captiuos facis) Iah Deus. Hoc ipsum autem disertis verbis ipsi Christo à Paulo tribuitur Ephes. 4. 8. Quum ascendisset, inquit, in altum, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dona dedit hominibus. Vnde sic denuò concludimus.
units.tr: Ps. 68:18-19. "The chariot of God is twenty thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them, Sinai is in the sanctuary. Ascending on high, thou hast led captive a multitude of captives; thou hast received gifts for men, yea, for the rebellious also, that the LORD God might dwell among them." And Paul attributes this very thing to Christ himself in plain words, Eph. 4:8: "When he ascended on high, he says, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." Whence we conclude again in this way.

units.la: Qui ascendens in altum captiuam duxit captiuitatem, ille est verus, & æternus Deus Israelis,Psal.68.18.
units.tr: He who, ascending on high, led captivity captive, is the true and eternal God of Israel: Ps. 68:18.

units.la: Atqui Christus ascendens in altum captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dona dedit hominibus.Eph. 4.8.
units.tr: But Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men: Eph. 4:8.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus, & æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: LOCVS V.
units.tr: Passage V.

units.la: Ef.8. verf.14. & 15. Et erit (Iehoua exercituum) sanctificationi, in lapidem autem allisionis, & in rupem offensionis ambabus domibus Israelis, in laqueum & tendiculum habitatori Ieruschalaimorum, in quæ offendant multi, & cadentes confringantur, aut irretiti capiantur.Hoc idem autem de Christo exponitur Luc. 2. 34. Ecce positus est iste in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel, & in signum cui contradicatur:quemadmodum scriptum est, Ecce pono in Sion lapidem, ad quem impingirur, & petram offendiculi, Rom. 9 v.33. & 1.Pet.2. 6. Vnde iterum sic concludimus.
units.tr: Isaiah 8:14–15: "And he shall be for a sanctuary (says the LORD of hosts); but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a snare and a trap to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared and taken." This same thing is applied to Christ in Luke 2:34: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against," as it is written: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone to which men shall stumble, and a rock of offence," Romans 9:33; also 1 Peter 2:6. Whence we again conclude thus:

units.la: Qui est lapis ille allisionis, & rupes offendiculi, ille est Deus exercituum, i. verus Iehouah, & Deus Israelis, Esa. 8. verf.19.15.
units.tr: He who is that stone of stumbling and rock of offence is the God of hosts, that is, the true Jehovah and the God of Israel: Isaiah 8:19, 15.

units.la: Atqui Christus est lapis ille allisionis, & rupes offendiculi, Luc. 2. 34. Rom. 9.33. 1.Pet.2.6.
units.tr: But Christ is that stone of stumbling and rock of offence: Luke 2:34; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6.

units.la: Ergo Christus est Deus exercituum, verus Iehouah, & Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of hosts, the true Jehovah, and the God of Israel.

units.la: LOCVS VI.
units.tr: Passage VI.

units.la: Zach.12.verf.10. Respicient ad me, quem transfixerunt, clangentque super hoc tanquam planctu de vnigenito, & amarè plangent de eo, vt amarè quis plangit de vnigenito. Quod ipsum de Christo quoque dicitur, Ioh.19.verf. 27. Vnde tale argumentum conficitur.
units.tr: Zech. 12, verse 10: They shall look on me whom they have pierced, and they shall lament over this as one laments an only son, and they shall mourn bitterly over him, as one mourns bitterly for an only son. The same thing is said of Christ too, Ioh. 19, verse 27. From this the following argument is constructed.

units.la: Ille quem transfixisse, & super quem plancturi dicuntur, ille est verus Iehouah, & Deus Israelis, Math.12. & 10.
units.tr: That one whom they are said to have pierced, and over whom they are to lament, is the true Jehovah and God of Israel, Matth. 12 & 10.

units.la: Atqui Christum transfixisse, & super eum planxisse dicuntur Iudæi.
units.tr: But the Jews are said to have pierced Christ and to have lamented over him.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus Iehouah, & Deus Israelis, Iohan.19. & 27.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true Jehovah and God of Israel, Ioh. 19 & 27.

units.la: LOCVS VII. & vltimus.
units.tr: Passage VII, the last.

units.la: Psal.102.verf.26. Tu Domine, initiò terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli, ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes. Et Psal. 92. verf.2. Adorate eum omnes Angeli eius. Hæc verò omnia de Christo totidem penè syllabis enuntiantur, Heb.1.v.6.& 10. Vnde sic concludimus.
units.tr: Ps. 102:26: "You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the works of your hands are the heavens; they will perish, but you remain." And Ps. 97:7 (Vulgate 96): "Worship him, all his angels." Yet all these things are said of Christ in almost the same words, Heb. 1:6 and 10.

units.la: Qui initio terram fundauit, & cuius manuum opera sunt cali, qui denique ab Angelis est adorandus, ille est verus & æternus Deus Israelis, Psal.102.26.& 97.vers.2.
units.tr: "He who in the beginning founded the earth, and whose works of hands are the heavens, and who finally is to be worshipped by the angels, is the true and eternal God of Israel," Ps. 102:26; 97:7.

units.la: Atqui Christus initio terram fundauit, & opera manuum eius sunt cœli, atque ab Angelis adoratur, Hebr.1.vers.6.10.
units.tr: "But Christ in the beginning founded the earth, and the works of his hands are the heavens, and he is worshipped by the angels," Heb. 1:6, 10.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus, & æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: "Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel."

units.la: Hic autem mihi monendus est Ostorrodius, me ex hisce vlti-mis locis non simpliciter ab adoratione, aut rerum omnium creatione (de quo validissimo argumento posteà capite decimo agemus) argumentari : sed quia Christus is est, qui ex sententia Dauidis est adorandus, cælúmque ac terram creauit, nempe Ieho-uah Zebaoth, & Deus Israelis.Quod vero Socinus ait, Authorem Epistolæ ad Hebræos, non de filio, sed de Deo Patre agere, inane est Samosateniani cerebri figmentum, vt ex scopo illius loci ma-nifestissimè liquet. Vult enim Apostolus ibi docere, Christum esse maiorem Angelis, quod vt probet, inter cætera argumenta, e-tiam hæc duo adfert, quod videlicet iuxta Psalmos & adorandus sit, & cœlum, terràmque creauerit. Quum igitur quæstio, quæ ibi tractatur, non sit de Patre, sed de filio, nempe Christo, necessariò inde sequitur etiam argumenta, ad quæstionis confirmationem adducta, non de Patre, sed de filio intelligenda esse.
units.tr: Here, however, I must warn Socinus that I do not argue from these last passages simply from the worship or from the creation of all things (on which most weighty argument we shall speak later, in chapter ten), but because Christ is he who, according to David's words, is to be worshipped, and who created heaven and earth, namely Jehovah Sabaoth, and the God of Israel. As for Socinus's claim that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews is speaking not of the Son but of God the Father, it is an empty fancy of the Samosatene brain, as is plain enough from the purpose of that passage. For the Apostle there wishes to teach that Christ is greater than the angels, and to prove this he brings forward, among other arguments, these two: that he is to be worshipped according to the Psalms, and that he created heaven and earth. Since, therefore, the question treated there concerns not the Father but the Son, namely Christ, it necessarily follows that the arguments brought forward to confirm the question must also be understood of the Son and not of the Father.

units.la: Itaque, quum ex illa locorum vtriusque Testamenti collatio-ne, manifestissimè liqueat, ea in Nouo Testamento de Christo exponi, quæ in Veteri Testamento, de vero illo, & æterno Deo Israelis enunciantur, necessariò inde sequitur, id quod tota Ca-tholica Ecclesia, docet, credit, & confitetur, Christum nempe na-tura & essentia, non hominem tantùm, sed etiam verum Deum esse, Patri consubstantialem, & coæternum, eiusdémque cum ip-so essentię, gloriæ ac maiestatis participem: præsertim cum illa etiam Christo, tanquam præterita, aut præsentia applicentur, quę tamen ipsius ex virgine natiuitatem multis seculis antecesse-runt. Atque hoc argumentum euidentissimum, & grauissimum, quia Ostorrodius planè non attingit, sed callidè præterit, ideò ad sequentia progrediemur.
units.tr: Therefore, since the comparison of these passages of both Testaments makes it most clearly evident that what the Old Testament says of the true and eternal God of Israel is set forth in the New Testament concerning Christ, it necessarily follows what the whole Catholic Church teaches, believes and confesses: that Christ, by nature and essence, is not only man but also true God, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, and a partaker of the same essence, glory and majesty with him; especially since those things are applied to Christ as past or present, though they preceded his birth from the virgin by many ages. And since Socinus altogether fails to touch this argument, which is most evident and weighty, but craftily passes it by, we shall proceed to what follows.

units.la: CAPVT TVM
units.tr: CHAPTER IX

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quo argumentum secundum pro æterna Deitate Filii proponitur & defenditur.
units.tr: In which the second argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is set forth and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum fecundum inde desumitur, quod Christus in Scripturis peculiari modo Filius Dei appellatur, vnde duplex, & quidem firmissimum aduersus Oftorrodium cōcludēdi nobis suppeditatur medium, & prius quidem inde, quod Christus in Scripturis sacris filius Dei,& quidem vnigenitus, ac proprius dicitur, Iohan.1.verf.18. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, vnigenitus ille Filius,qui est in sinu Patris,nobis exposuit. 1.Ioh.5.verf.5. Quis est,qui vincit mundum,nisi qui credit Iesum esse Filium Dei? Et v.20. Scimus Filium Dei venisse, & dedisse nobis mentem, vt cognoscamus illum qui verax est, & sumus in verace illo, in Filio eius Iesu Christo : hic est verus Deus, & vita aeterna. Rom. 8.verf.31.3. Si Deus, qui proprio Filio non pepercit,sed pro nobis in mortem tradidit, est pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quod autem Christus vnigenitus ac proprius filius,adeóque Deus ipse appellatur, tantundem valet, ac si naturalis Dei filius diceretur : Vnde tale argumentum extruimus.
units.tr: Our second argument is drawn from the fact that Christ is called, in the Scriptures, Son of God in a special way. This gives us a twofold and very firm means of concluding against Ostorrodius. The first is this: in the holy Scriptures Christ is called the Son of God, and indeed the only-begotten and proper Son. John 1.18: No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known. 1 John 5.5: Who is it that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? And v. 20: We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life. Rom. 8.31, 32: If God, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, is for us, who is against us? That Christ is the only-begotten and proper Son, and so is called God himself, amounts to the same as if he were called the natural Son of God. Hence we construct the following argument.

units.la: Qui non ex gratia,aut adoptionis beneficio, nec tantùm natus ,sed natura ipsa Dei filius est,ille etiam ab aeterno à Deo Patre genitus est, adeóque vetus Deus, Patri consubstantialis,& coaeternus, ac eiusdem cum ipso maiestatis,gloriaque particeps.
units.tr: Whoever is the Son of God not by grace or by the benefit of adoption, nor merely by birth, but by nature itself, is also begotten by God the Father from eternity, and so is true God, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, and a partaker of the same majesty and glory with him.

units.la: Atqui Christus,non ex gratia ,aut beneficio adoptionis , nec natus tantùm,sed natura ipsa Dei Filius est.
units.tr: But Christ is the Son of God not by grace or by the benefit of adoption, nor merely by birth, but by nature itself.

units.la: Ergo Christus ab aeterno à Deo Patre est genitus , adeóque verus Deus, Patri consubstantialis,& eiusdem cum ipso essentia,maiestatis,ac gloria particeps.
units.tr: Therefore Christ was begotten by God the Father from eternity, and so is true God, consubstantial with the Father, and a partaker of the same essence, majesty and glory with him.

units.la: Minor sic probatur.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved thus.

units.la: Christus non est ex gratia , aut beneficio adoptionis Dei filius, tum quia nos per ipsum in filios adoptamur, Ioh.1. verf.12. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem, ut filii Dei fierent: tum, quia alias filius Dei unigenitus non esset. Nec enim natus tantum, id est, quia statim a natiuitate ex virgine, filius fuit, quia corrueret argumentum Pauli, quo demonstrat Christum Angelis esse praestantiorem. Hebr.1. verf.4.5. Tanto praestantior factus Angelis, quanto excellentius prae illis sortitus est nomen. Nam cui unquam dixit Angelorum, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Ac rursum, Ego ero ei Pater, & ipse erit mihi Filius. Hoc autem argumentum nihil concluderet, nisi ab ipsa excellentia essentiae Christi desumptum, quum ipsi quoque Angeli creationis beneficio filii Dei censeantur.
units.tr: Christ is not the Son of God by grace or by the benefit of adoption: first, because we are adopted as sons through him. John 1.12: But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God. Second, because otherwise he would not be the only-begotten Son of God. For he is not Son merely by birth, that is, because he was the Son from the moment he was born of the virgin; otherwise Paul's argument, by which he shows that Christ is superior to the angels, would collapse. Heb. 1.4, 5: Having become as much better than the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say, You are my Son, today I have begotten you? And again: I will be his Father, and he will be my Son. This argument, however, would prove nothing unless it were drawn from the very excellence of Christ's essence, since the angels too are reckoned sons of God by the benefit of creation.

units.la: Oftorrodius autem ineptarum suarum Institutionum cap. 7. hoc argumentum duabus rationibus ex profesto impugnat, Priorem exceptionem quod attinet, licet ille multa, quae ipsum argumenti neruum complectuntur, mala fide omittat, tamen illud prout ab ipso adducitur, proponemus, & ab eius sophisticis exceptionibus vindicabimus.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter 7 of his worthless Institutes, attacks this argument with two objections, the first of which is of the kind he has set out. Although he dishonestly omits many points that make up the very sinew of the argument, we will nevertheless set out the argument as he presents it and defend it against his sophistical objections.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is as follows.

units.la: Omnis filius naturam habet sui Patris:
units.tr: Every son has the nature of his father:

units.la: Atqui Christus est Filius Dei:
units.tr: But Christ is the Son of God:

units.la: Ergo aut diuinam naturam habet, aut non revera est Dei Filius.
units.tr: Therefore he either has the divine nature, or else he is not truly the Son of God.

units.la: Vbi denuo videt Christianus Lector, quam subdole & fraudulenter ille Samosatenianus agat, dum neruum argumenti nostri, quem videt se extorquere nobis non posse, aliute omittit. Non enim dicimus Christum ideo eiusdem cum Deo Patre, naturae, & essentiae esse, quia simpliciter Filius Dei nuncupetur: sed quia Filius Dei proprius, unigenitus, & Filius Dei, ac Deus a Iohanne, & Paulo appellatur, ac proinde ab aeterno a Patre genitus sit. Sed videamus tamen quomodo hoc ipsum argumentum impugnet.
units.tr: Here again the Christian reader sees how craftily and fraudulently that Samosatenian acts, in that he leaves out another part of our argument, the sinew which he sees he cannot wrest from us. For we do not say that Christ is of the same nature and essence as God the Father merely because he is simply called the Son of God; we say it because he is called by John and Paul the proper, only-begotten Son of God, and God, and therefore has been begotten by the Father from eternity. But let us see nonetheless how he assails this very argument.

units.la: Responsio igitur ipsius talis est.
units.tr: His response, then, is as follows.

units.la: Si haec Trinitariorum ratio vera, ac bona est, quod videlicet Christus eiusdem cum Deo Patre sit particeps essentiae, tum sequitur Deum eodem modo, ac ratione genuisse Filium suum, quo gignunt homines, & animantia cetera.
units.tr: If this reasoning of the Trinitarians is true and sound, namely that Christ partakes of the same essence as God the Father, then it follows that God begot his Son in the same manner and way as men and the other living creatures beget.

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum, Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is false. Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Ratio consequentiæ est.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is this.

units.la: Q uia hoc connexo non concesso, necessario quatuor in argumento erunt termini, & de genitura naturali maior, de alia autem minor intelligenda.
units.tr: B ecause, if this connection is not granted, there will necessarily be four terms in the argument: the major must be understood of natural begetting, and the minor of the other, divine begetting.

units.la: Ratio assumptionis.
units.tr: The reason for the assumption.

units.la: Si enim Deus naturaliter gigneret, tum missis aliis plurimis inde sequentibus absurdis, necessario sequeretur Deum esse mortalem, siquidem naturalis generatio est ad conseruandam speciem, percunte individuo. Illi autem, qui immortales sunt, ac illa ad conseruandam speciem generatione, non indigent, naturali modo liberos non gignunt, unde etiam nec uxores ducunt, nec nuptum dantur, quemadmodum Christus dixit de illis, qui digni habiti fuerint, ut eauum illud futurum, & resurrectionem ex mortuis consequantur. Luc.20.35. cuius rei nullam aliam reddit causam, quam quod illi post resurrectionem Angelis similes, & Filij Dei futuri, mori amplius non possint. Unde mira superbia, petulantia sibi ipsi applaudens, hoc argumentum in nos retorqueri, nólque proprio nostro gladio iugulari posse, gloriatur in hunc modum:
units.tr: For if God begot naturally, then, leaving aside the many other absurdities that would follow, it would necessarily follow that God is mortal, since natural generation serves to preserve the species while the individual perishes. Those, however, who are immortal, and who have no need of generation to preserve the species, do not beget children in the natural way. Hence they neither take wives nor are given in marriage, just as Christ said of those who were deemed worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead. Luke 20.35. And he gives no other reason for this than that after the resurrection they, being like the angels and sons of God, cannot die any more. Whence, with wondrous arrogance, and applauding himself for his petulance, he boasts that this argument can be turned back against us, and that we cannot be slain with our own sword, in this fashion:

units.la: Omnis Pater talem habet naturam, qualem habent eius liberi:
units.tr: Every father has such a nature as his children have:

units.la: Atqui Filij Dei, qui nempe modo perfecto tales sunt, eiusmodi habent naturam, ut liberos gignere non possint.
units.tr: But the sons of God, who in the perfect mode are indeed such, have a nature such that they cannot beget children:

units.la: Ergo etiam Deus Pater, eiusmodi habet naturam, ut liberos parere aut gignere non possit, ac proinde etiam Filium suum non genuerit.
units.tr: Therefore God the Father too has such a nature that he cannot bear or beget children, and so he has not begotten his Son.

units.la: Resp. Quid quæso turpius, aut etiam insulsius est, quàm de Deo simplicissimo & sanctissimo illo Spiritu disputantem, documenta suę disputationis, nonnisi à crassioribus illis corporibus desumere, & illū horū naturæ legibus, ac modulo subiicere? Sed quò rei huius turpitudo, ac fœditas eò magis elucescat, argumentum ipsū excutiamus. Consequetia igitur est salsissima, vtpote quæ res diuinas, spirituales, ac simplicissimas, hyperphysicas deinde cum crassis corporibus & rebus physicis imperitissimè confundit. Vt enim tria sunt subiectorū genera, physica, metaphysica, & diuina, ac transcendentia, modò hæc subiecta appellari liceat, ita quoq; triplex genitura cōsideratur, physica, seu logica vna: metaphysica, seu mentalis altera: diuina, & transcendens tertia, quarum vnaquæq; naturę sui subiecti respondet exactissimè. Generatio physica, quæ & prædicamētalis dicitur, est rerū corporearum, quę per fe, ac de fe gignunt extra fe, sicut à parentibus liberi, ab homini-bus homines, & leonibus leones producuntur. Hæc generatio transit, & fecundùm hanc genituram qui gignit, is potentia actiua gignit, & qui gignitur, potentia passiua gignitur, quorum nullum de genitura transcendente dici potest. Generatio enim transcendens, seu metaphysica, est Spirituum, quæ propterea mentalis dicitur, quia mens, vt subiecto simplex gignit non de se, sed per se in seipsa, sicut à mente gignitur λόγος seu ratio, quam non potest non gignere, quia partus vel genimen est naturale mentis, & quidem τῷ νοῒ σωαίδιον, id est, menti coæternum. Generatio suprema, seu diuina est, qua Deus Pater gignit filium suum, persona personam, de se & in se, in vnitate essentiæ: Quæ cùm ita sint, quæ est illa quæso consequentia. Si Filius Dei, Christus habet eandem naturam cum Deo Patre, tum Deus genuit eodem modo, quo gignunt homines, & animantia catera? Vel, Si Deus de sua essentia genuit Filium suum, tum genuit ipsum, quemadmodum homines & animantia catera gignunt? Apage; Tu viuis Ostorrodi, secus enim veritatem personæ, καὶ πρῶτος tot cauillis minimè impugnares: Ergo aut viuere te vitam rudentis alicuius & stupidi asini, aut plane non viuere, tam certò concludam, quàm tu ex eo, quod Deus filium suum de essentia, & in vnitate essentiæ genuisse dicitur, eundem eodem modo, quo homines, & animalia gignunt, genuisse vere demostraueris. Vtrobiq; enim posito genere ibi Logico, hic analogico ad speciem determinatam imperitè concluditur, & remota vna specie, non modò species altera tollitur, sed etiam talis conclusio infertur, quasi propterea totum genus auferretur. Si igitur cùm Ostorrodius res metaphysicas ac diuinas cum physicis & corporeis, & si toto genere differant, inter se, confundat tamen, & ad harum modum illas iudicet, salsissimum esse connexum eius liquidò constat, & non à veritate tantùm, sed etiam pietate, & diuini numinis reuerentia alienum. At vero si consequentia hæc negetur, tum quatuor in ipsorum argumento, inquit, sunt termini, cùm de genitura naturali maior, de genitura autem diuina, minor loquatur.
units.tr: What, I ask, is more shameful or even more inept than to dispute about God, that most simple and most holy Spirit, drawing the proofs of one's argument only from those grosser bodies and subjecting him to the laws and measure of their nature? But so that the shamefulness and foulness of this matter may stand out all the more, let us examine the argument itself. The inference is therefore utterly absurd, since it recklessly confuses divine, spiritual and most simple things, which are hyperphysical, with gross bodies and physical things. For just as there are three kinds of subjects, physical, metaphysical and divine (or transcendent, if these may be called subjects), so too there are three kinds of begetting: the physical, or logical, the first; the metaphysical, or mental, the second; and the divine and transcendent, the third. Each of these corresponds most exactly to the nature of its subject. Physical generation, which is also called predicamental, belongs to corporeal things, which beget from themselves and of themselves outside themselves, as children are produced from parents, men from men, and lions from lions. This generation passes away. In this begetting, he who begets does so by active power, and he who is begotten is begotten by passive power; neither of these can be said of transcendent begetting. For transcendent or metaphysical generation belongs to spirits, and is therefore called mental, because the mind, being simple in its subject, begets not from itself but through itself, in itself, as the word or reason (logos [λόγος]) is begotten by the mind, which it cannot but beget, since its offspring is the natural product of the mind, and indeed coeternal with the mind (syn-aidion [σύναιδιον]). Supreme or divine generation is that by which God the Father begets his Son, person from person, from himself and in himself, in unity of essence. These things being so, what consequence, I ask, is this: If the Son of God, Christ, has the same nature as God the Father, then God begot him in the same way that men and the other living creatures beget? Or: If God begot his Son from his own essence, then he begot him just as men and the other living creatures beget? Away with such nonsense! You are alive, Ostorrodius, for otherwise you would not assail the truth of the person with so many quibbles. Therefore either you live the life of some braying and stupid donkey, or you do not live at all. I shall conclude this as certainly as you would truly demonstrate that, because God is said to have begotten his Son from his essence and in unity of essence, he begot him in the same way as men and animals beget. For in both cases, when a logical genus is posited there and an analogical one here, the inference is unskilfully drawn to a determinate species. When one species is removed, not only is the other species taken away, but such a conclusion is drawn as if the whole genus were thereby removed. Therefore, since Ostorrodius confuses metaphysical and divine things with physical and corporeal ones, although they differ in their whole genus, and judges the former by the manner of the latter, it is clear that his connection is utterly false, and alien not only to the truth but also to piety and to reverence for the divine majesty. But if this consequence is denied, then, he says, there are four terms in their argument, since the major speaks of natural begetting, but the minor of divine begetting.

units.la: <bl>Resp.</bl> Minimè verò, quia maior, nec de Physica, nec metaphysica, nec diuina generatione determinatè, ac simpliciter, sed de generatione quauis communiter, seruata tamè analogicæ veritate, loquitur, & de subiecto hocattributum verissimè enuntiat, quod omnis filius salem habeat naturam, qualem Pater, seu quod filius omnis eiusdem cum patre suo sit naturæ: Vel, quòd ille genitus sit ex aliquo eiusdem cum illo naturæ, quod attributum non de vna tâtum specie, sed de omni generatione communiter prædicatur. In minore autem de Patre prædicatur, quod filium genuerit: de filio, quòd à Patre genitus sit, rectissimè infertur conclusio, quod Christus filius Dei, eiusdem sit cum Deo Patre naturæ, quæ est syllogisticæ consequentiæ necessaria veritas: quam si miser ille Logicus Oftorrodius teneret, nec toto ἀσυλλογίστως imperitè necteret, nec argumentum verissimum, & legitimè dispositum, vitii quatuor terminorum temerè accusaret.
units.tr: Resp. Not at all. The major premise speaks neither determinately nor simply of physical, metaphysical or divine generation, but of generation in general, while preserving the analogical truth. It rightly predicates of this subject the attribute that every son has a nature like his father's, or that every son is of the same nature as his father. Or, to put it another way, that the one begotten is from something of the same nature as himself. This attribute is predicated not of one kind of generation only, but of all generation in general. In the minor premise, however, it is predicated of the Father that he begat a son, and of the Son that he was begotten by the Father. From this the conclusion rightly follows that Christ, the Son of God, is of the same nature as God the Father. This is a truth necessary by the necessity of syllogistic consequence. If that wretched logician Ostorrodius understood this, he would not tie the argument together so unsyllogistically [ἀσυλλογίστως] and so ignorantly, nor rashly accuse a most true and legitimately arranged argument of the fault of four terms.

units.la: Atque falsitate consequentiæ hic demonstrata, non opus esset, vt de assumptione, in qua effatum impium negatur verissimè, quicquam ageretur, cùm destructa propositione tota corruat argumentatio, obseruari tamen cupimus callidissimam Aduersarii fraudem, qua silentio praeterita ipsa connexi consequentia, quæ inter nos controuersa est, eiusdem partem consequentem prolixè refutat, quasi verò quisquam è nobis extitisset vnquam, qui blasphemiæ illius patrocinium suscepisset, & Deum creatorem de suo solio deturbatum in huius naturæ circunferentiam coniicere voluisset. Vnde illo, quem stringit, gladio, non nostrum iugulum, vt ille gloriatur, sed aerem ferit, & simul tamen maximam fallaciam committit, cùm nos agamus de filiis propriis, & naturalibus: Argumentum verò illud, quod in nos retorquet, de adoptiuis loquatur, à natura autem vnius, ad conditionem alterius, nulla sit consequentia: quam fallaciam, etiam in exceptione sequente committit.
units.tr: Even if the falsity of the consequence has been shown here, there would be no need to deal with the assumption, in which the impious statement is most truly denied. Once the proposition is destroyed, the whole argument collapses. Still, we wish to point out the very cunning trick of our opponent. He passes over in silence the connection of the consequence itself, which is the matter in dispute between us, and instead refutes at length its consequent part, as if any of us had ever existed who defended that blasphemy and wished to hurl God the Creator from his throne into the circumference of this nature. So he strikes with a sword that does not reach our throat, as he boasts, but beats the air. At the same time he commits a very great fallacy, since we are speaking of proper and natural sons, whereas the argument he turns against us speaks of adopted sons. From the nature of one to the condition of another there is no consequence. He commits this same fallacy also in the exception that follows.

units.la: Secundò igitur inquit Aduersarius, non de solo Christo in Scripturis sacris dici quod Filius Dei sit, & quod Deus ipsum genuerit; verum etiam de aliis Christianis hominibus omnibus, & tamen neminem inde concludere audere, Deum illos naturaliter genuisse, illósque eandem cum ipso Deo naturam habere.
units.tr: Secondly, then, says the opponent, it is said in the holy Scriptures not of Christ alone that he is the Son of God and that God begat him, but also of all other Christian men. Yet no one dares to conclude from this that God begat them naturally, or that they have the same nature as God himself.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si Christus ideò eiusdem cum Deo Patre naturæ, ac essentiæ particeps est, quia Filius Dei, & Deus ipsum genuisse dicitur in Scriptura sacra, tum sequitur omnes homines Christianos eiusdem cum Deo Patre essentiæ, & naturæ esse, quia & illi Filii Dei, & à Deo geniti esse dicuntur. Atqui consequens est absurdum: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: If Christ is a partaker of the same nature and essence as God the Father because he is called the Son of God, and because God is said in Holy Scripture to have begotten him, then it follows that all Christian men are of the same essence and nature as God the Father, since they too are called sons of God and begotten of God. But the consequent is absurd. Therefore the antecedent is too.

units.la: Resp. Mala fide assumit, ac proponit Oftorrodius argumentum nostrum: non enim dicimus hanc tantum ob causam Christum eiusdem cum Deo Patre naturae & essentiae esse, quia Filius Dei dicitur in Scripturis, sed quia filius vnigenitus, proprius, & Deus, & quidem ab aeterno a Patre genitus, ab eadem Scriptura perhibetur, quorum prius iam ostendimus, posterius autem mox demonstrabimus. Consequentia igitur est falsa, quia tum demum illud consequens ex antecedente sequeretur, si videlicet homines regeniti, & Christiani eodem modo, ac ratione Filii Dei, & ab ipso geniti esse dicerentur, quod est, vel ipsa Aduersariorum cofessione, salsissimum. Christus enim Filius Dei est naturalis, nos omnes adoptiui. Deus Christū genuit natura, nec potuit no gignere, nos regenuit ex gratia, & potuisset non generare denuo, sed in natiua corruptione relinquere, Christus vt ab aeterno fuit, ita ab aeterno filius Dei fuit: Christiani autem existunt aliquando, & tamen non sunt filii Dei, sed filii irae, quamdiu in statu dominatis peccati sunt constituti. Quid? quod nequidem ex illo Aduersarii argumento de humana Christi natura quicquam concludi potest, quia etiam secundum hanc non est factus filius ex non filio, sed eo ipso momento, quo coepit esse, coepit etiam filius esse, nos autem ex non filiis regni coelestis, & mancipiis Diaboli, & peccati, per gratiam propter mortem Christi, adoptamur in filios. Vnde videre est, quibus argumentis Oftorrodius veritatem orthodoxam impugnet.
units.tr: Resp. Ostorrodius assumes and sets forth our argument in bad faith. We do not say that Christ is of the same nature and essence as God the Father for this reason alone, that he is called the Son of God in the Scriptures. We say it because the Scripture also affirms that he is the only-begotten, proper Son and God, and indeed begotten of the Father from eternity. The first of these we have already shown, and the second we shall now demonstrate. The consequence is therefore false, because the consequent would follow from the antecedent only if the regenerate, the Christians, were said to be sons of God and begotten of him in the same way and by the same reasoning as Christ. Even by the admission of the opponents themselves, that is most false. Christ is the natural Son of God; we are all adopted. God begat Christ by nature, and could not not beget him; he regenerated us by grace, and could have not regenerated us, leaving us in our native corruption. Christ, as he was from eternity, so from eternity was the Son of God. Christians, however, begin to exist at some time, and yet they are not sons of God but sons of wrath, as long as they remain under the dominion of sin. Moreover, not even from Ostorrodius's argument about Christ's human nature can anything be concluded, since according to that nature too he was not made a son out of one who was not a son. Rather, at the very moment he began to exist, he also began to be a son. We, however, from not being sons of the heavenly kingdom, and being slaves of the Devil and of sin, are adopted as sons through grace, on account of the death of Christ. From this one may see with what arguments Ostorrodius attacks orthodox truth.

units.la: Videns autem Aduersarius ipse, aut futile esse argumentū fuū, aut certe ex ipso sequi, aequales a se, Christo omnes Christianos constitui, hanc ipsam blasphemiam studiose conatur euitare, & sequentia subiicit axiomata. I. non eo fine a fe dici, etiam Christianos caeteros Dei filios esse, quasi illos Christo pares constitueret, sed vt liqueat quam anile, & infirmum sit Aduersariorum argumentum. II. se credere & confiteri Christum longe excellentiore modo Dei filium esse, quam nos, quum nullus nostrum ex Sp. S. sit conceptus. III. veros Christianos in illa Christi diuina ὁμοούσια cum ipso Christo multa habere communia, vnde non puduerit ipsum eos fratres appellare. Hebr. 2. v.11. vnde sequi, inquit, tam Christum, quam Christianos Deum habere patrem, quod verum nulla ratione esse possest, nisi etiam Christiani magna ex parte ita etiam Filii Dei essent, quemadmodum ipse Christus.
units.tr: But the opponent himself sees that either his argument is worthless, or else it follows from it that all Christians are made equal to Christ. So he tries eagerly to avoid this very blasphemy, and he adds the following axioms. First, that he does not say this in order to make the other Christians sons of God as if he were making them equal to Christ, but so that it may be clear how old-womanish and feeble the argument of our opponents is. Second, that he believes and confesses that Christ is the Son of God in a far more excellent way than we are, since none of us was conceived of the Holy Spirit. Third, that true Christians have much in common with Christ himself in that divine homoousia, so that he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb. 2:11). From this, he says, it follows that both Christ and Christians have God as Father, which cannot be true in any way unless Christians, for the most part, are also sons of God in the same way as Christ himself.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum:quo fine illæ blasphemiæ euomantur, non dis- ceptabimus, hoc saltem manet certissimum, Ostorrodium aut omnes Christianos æquales facere Christo, quoad ψιοτοκία illam diuinam, aut certè argumentum nostrum neutiquam ab ipso labe- factari. Nos enim dicimus Christum esse Deum æternum, ab æter- no à Deo Patre genitum, quia videlicet Dei Filius (quamuis hoc argumentum non ita nude proponatur) dicatur. Hanc conse- quentiam Ostorrodius negat ratione negationis à pari desumpta, quod videlicet omnes Christiani Dei filii sint, nec tamen affir- mare quisquam audeat, illos à Deo genitos, ciusdémque naturæ, & essentiæ cum ipso participes esse. Hinc ita concludo : Aut est eadem, & æqualis ratio ψιοτοκίας Christi, & Christianorum omnium, aut non est æqualis : Si æqualis est, tum falsa fuerit quidem consequentia nostra, at blasphemiam frustra excusauerit Ostorrodius. Si non est æqualis, sed dispar, tum firmum, & incon- cussum manebit argumentum nostrum, manifesto comparatorum elencho ab aduersario comissa. Si enim alia ratione Christus sit Filius Dei, quam nos Christiani, tum nō sequitur, si Christus propte- rea æternus est Deus ciusdémque naturæ, & essentiæ cum Deo Patre particeps, quia Filius Dei Patris esse & Deus Pater ipsum genuisse dicitur, tum etiam omnes Christiani à Deo geniti, ciusdémque naturæ, & essentiæ cum ipso participes erunt, quia & illi filii Dei dicuntur : cum ratio ψιοτοκίας sit plane diuersa. Aut igitur blasphemiam confiteatur ac deprecetur Ostorrodius, aut robur ac veritatem nostri argumenti candide agnoscat. Ad secundum: Vt- cumque Ostorrodius confiteatur Christum longe excellentiore modo, quam cæteros Christianos Dei Filium esse, reipsa tamen non essentiale, sed accidentale discrimen inter nostram, & Christi ψιοτοκίας facit à causa efficiente desumptum, quia videlicet ille solus à spiritu sancto sit conceptus. Ad tertium,quàm exiguum ille discrimen inter Christum & Christianos statuat, apertis ille prodit verbis : quæ omnia, quum cum ipsa thesi, & quæstione controuer- sa concidant, non tam refutare, quàm simpliciter recen sere volui.
units.tr: Resp. To the first point: we shall not dispute with what purpose those blasphemies are spewed out. This much remains most certain, that Ostorrodius either makes all Christians equal to Christ with respect to that divine generation [ὁμοτοκία], or else our argument is in no way damaged by him. For we say that Christ is the eternal God, begotten from eternity by God the Father, because he is called the Son of God. (Although this argument is not put forward so bare.) Ostorrodius denies this consequence by the method of denial drawn from a parallel case, namely that all Christians are sons of God, and yet no one dares to affirm that they are begotten of God and are partakers of his nature and essence. So I reason thus: either the reason for the generation of Christ and of all Christians is the same and equal, or it is not equal. If it is equal, then our consequence is indeed false, but Ostorrodius has excused his blasphemy in vain. If it is not equal but different, then our argument remains firm and unshaken, exposed by the opponent's own manifest comparison. For if Christ is the Son of God by a different reason from ours as Christians, then it does not follow, if Christ is therefore eternal God and a partaker of the same nature and essence with God the Father because he is called the Son of God the Father and because God the Father is said to have begotten him, that all Christians who are begotten of God will also be partakers of the same nature and essence with him, because they too are called sons of God. For the reason for the generation is plainly different. Therefore Ostorrodius must either confess and deprecate his blasphemy, or candidly acknowledge the strength and truth of our argument. To the second point: Although Ostorrodius confesses that Christ is the Son of God in a far more excellent way than the other Christians, in fact he makes the distinction between our generation and Christ's not essential but accidental, drawn from the efficient cause, namely that he alone was conceived by the Holy Spirit. To the third point: How small a distinction he sets between Christ and Christians he reveals in plain words. Since all these points fall apart together with the thesis itself and the disputed question, I have wished not so much to refute them as simply to set them out.

units.la: Quæstionē porrò illam, quomodo videlicet Deus Christū genuerit, & quā ob causam Christus sit Dei Filius, pollicetur se in loco de officio Christi prolixè, & sufficiēter explicaturū, unde & nos eo illam reii- ciemus. Atque sic hactenus fuit medium prius: posterius tale est:
units.tr: Moreover, the question of how God the Father begat Christ, and for what reason Christ is the Son of God, he promises to explain at length and sufficiently in the place on the office of Christ. We too will therefore set it aside here. So far the first premise. The second is as follows:

units.la: Quia ab æterno in vnitate essentia diuina à Deo Patre est genitus, ille etiam est verus & aeternus Deus, eiufdemque cum Deo Patre effentia ac natura particeps.
units.tr: Because he was begotten by God the Father from eternity in the unity of the divine essence, he is also true and eternal God, and a partaker of the same essence and nature as God the Father.

units.la: Atqui Christus ab aeterno a Patre in unitate effentia diuina genitus est: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But Christ was begotten by the Father from eternity in the unity of the divine essence. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Minorem propositionê nostri demôftrant, tum scripturæ locis, & rationibus iam supra explicatis, tum duobus illis sequentibus scripturæ testimoniis, nonnulli eandem confirmant Pf.2.v.7. Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Mich.5.v.2. At tu Bethlehem Ephrata, minima vt fis in ducibus Iehuda, ex te mihi prodibit futurus dominator in Israele, cuius exortus inde a principio, a diebus seculi. Et quamuis de horum locorum interpretatione genuina, non idem sentiant Theologi nostri, neque etiam argumenti nostri robur in hisce duobus tantum testimoniis, sed maximè in illis, quę iam ab initio capitis a nobis explicata sunt, consistat, experiemur tamen, quibus rationibus Oftorrodius etiam hæc nobis eripere conetur.
units.tr: Our people prove the minor premise both from passages of Scripture and from the arguments already set out above, and also from the two following testimonies of Scripture. Some confirm it with Ps. 2:7: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you." And Mic. 5:2: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." Although our theologians do not all agree on the genuine interpretation of these passages, and although the strength of our argument rests not on these two testimonies alone but chiefly on those things already explained at the beginning of this chapter, we shall nevertheless see by what arguments Ostorodius tries to wrest these from us.

units.la: Priorem locum quantum concernit, respondet Oftorrodius, nullius ibi aeternitatis mentionem fieri, sed certi diei tempus nominari, quod ipsi aeternitati manifeste repugnet. Quam responsionem suam testimonio Caluini confirmat, non de generatione aeterna, sed de resurrectione Christi verba illa cum Apostolo Paulo, Actor. 13. v. 33 intelligentis: unde manifestum sit in illo loco Prophetiam contineri, quæ necessario ad tempus futurum sit referenda. Ac proinde concludit, Ex illo Dauidis loco manifestum esse, quod Deus filium suum ab aeterno non genuerit.
units.tr: As far as the former passage is concerned, Ostorodius replies that no mention of eternity is made there, but a certain day and time is named, which plainly contradicts eternity itself. He confirms this answer by the testimony of Calvin, who understood those words, with the Apostle Paul at Acts 13:33, of the resurrection of Christ and not of eternal generation. From this, he says, it is plain that the passage contains a prophecy which must necessarily be referred to a future time. And so he concludes: "From that passage of David it is manifest that God did not beget his Son from eternity."

units.la: Resp. Nos primò loci genuini sensum eliciemus: deinde argumentum nostrum inde extruemus: & tertiò Oftorrodio respondebimus. Sensum quod attinet, in illa Prophetica narratione duarum naturarum in persona Christi veritas proponitur: diuinæ, quum ait, Filius meus es tu: humanæ vero in qua Deus est factus conspicuus, cùm ait, Ego hodie genui te: in vtroque dicto autem veritas personæ demonstratur, quæ de fe prædicat, Dixit mihi. Hæc igitur duo membra ita distinguimus, vt vnam eandemq; personâ secundùm naturam diuinâ, quæ humanâ assumpsit, dicamus filium esse Dei: secundùm illam vero quę assumpta est, dicamus personâ certo dicto fuisse genitam, i. Deum fuisse conspicuum in carne factum, vt loquitur Paulus 1.Tim.3.16. siue vt Iohan. sermone fuisse factum carnem, Ioh.1.14. Hunc autem genuinum loci citati esse sensum, docet Apostoli imitatio: Epist.ad Heb.c.1.v.4.5.6. argumetum ex hoc loco deductum, in quo etiam ... etiam vis argumenti nostri consistit. Postquā enim v. 4. dixit, Christum tantò præstătiorem esse Angelis factum, quantò excellentius quàm illi sortitus est nomen, id postea confirmat argumentis à natura, vocatione, administratione, gloriáque sumptis. Primum argumetum probat autoritate scripturę, nomen Christi cum nomine Angelorum comparando. Nam, inquit Apostolus, Christus solus est is, cui dixit Pater, Filius meus es: de Angelis verò dicit, Adoret eum omnes Angeli Dei. Itaque sic argumentatur Apostolus,
units.tr: Reply. First we shall draw out the genuine sense of the passage, then build our argument from it, and thirdly answer Ostorodius. As to the sense, this prophetic narrative sets forth the truth of the two natures in the person of Christ: the divine, when it says "You are my Son," and the human, in which God was made visible, when it says "Today I have begotten you." In both sayings the truth of the person is shown, which speaks of itself, "He said to me." We therefore distinguish these two clauses so that we say that one and the same person is the Son of God according to the divine nature, which assumed the human, and that according to the nature which was assumed he was begotten at a certain day, that is, that God was made visible in the flesh, as Paul says at 1 Tim. 3:16, or as John says, that the Word was made flesh, John 1:14. That this is the genuine sense of the cited passage is shown by the imitation of it by the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 1:4-6, where the argument drawn from this passage, in which also the force of our argument consists, is set out. For after saying in v. 4 that Christ has become much better than the angels, as much as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs, he afterwards confirms this by arguments taken from his nature, calling, administration and glory. The first argument he proves by the authority of Scripture, comparing the name of Christ with the names of the angels. For, says the Apostle, Christ alone is the one to whom the Father said, "You are my Son," whereas of the angels he says, "Let all the angels of God worship him." So the Apostle argues thus:

units.la: Quodcunque nomen est à Deo ipso in Scripturis sacris inditum, id veritati coniunctum est.
units.tr: Whatever name is given by God himself in the holy Scriptures, that name is joined to truth.

units.la: Atqui Christo inditum est peculiare nomen, nempe Filius Dei.
units.tr: But Christ has been given a peculiar name, namely Son of God.

units.la: Ergo Christus singulariter & verè Dei Filius est.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is singularly and truly the Son of God.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus manifestè liquet, Christum, nō vt Angelos ac fideles in Ecclesia Dei versantes filii nomen ϑεόπνευστος, sed à natura habere, non adoptione, sed genitura, nec gratia, sed natura Dei filium, ac proinde ab æterno à Patre genitum esse. Vbi videt Aduersarius vim argumenti nostri, non in posteriore, sed priore dicti parte positam esse, ac proinde non labefactari argumetum nostrum, etiamsi illud hodie ad certum diē ac tempus referatur, cùm hoc de persona Christi secundùm humanam naturam intelligendum esse statuamus. Quòd verò illam accommodationem Pauli Act. 13. v. 33. concernit, etiamsi concedatur locum illum Dauidis à Paulo ad resurrectionē referri, quod tamen disputatio Pauli nulla necessitate infert, tamen illud nostrum argumentum nullo modo infringit, siue posterior pars de diuina, siue de humana Christi natura intelligatur. Per resurrectionem enim manifestum fuit Christum esse filium Dei, Rom. 1. v. 4. Declarato filio Dei potenter, secundùm Spiritum sanctificationis per resurrectionem à mortuis, nempe Iesu Christo Domino nostro: non quod tum filius Dei esse cœperit, qui ab æterno fuerat, sed quia tunc res aliqua fieri dicitur, quando talis agnoscitur, seu tum dicitur facta γεγένηται, cùm fuit facta γεγονώς. Quinimò ne quidem de persona Christi secundùm eius humanam naram, si ad illā posterior illa dicti Dauidis pars, vt debet, restringatur, quicquā inferre potest accōmodatio illa Pauli, cùm Christus etiam secundùm humanam naturam ante mortem eius, filius Dei fuerit, & secundùm illam quoque naturam filius Dei declaratus.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear that Christ does not have the name of Son as the angels and the faithful dwelling in the Church have it, but from nature; not by adoption but by begetting, not by grace but by nature he is the Son of God, and accordingly was begotten by the Father from eternity. Here our opponent sees that the force of our argument lies not in the latter but in the former part of the saying, and so our argument is not weakened even if that "today" is referred to a certain day and time, since we hold that this must be understood of the person of Christ according to his human nature. As for Paul's application at Acts 13:33, even if it be granted that Paul refers that passage of David to the resurrection, which nevertheless Paul's argument does not require, that application in no way undermines our argument, whether the latter part is understood of the divine or of the human nature of Christ. For by the resurrection it was made manifest that Christ is the Son of God, Rom. 1:4: "Declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, namely Jesus Christ our Lord." This does not mean that he who had been from eternity then began to be the Son of God, but that a thing is said to be made when it is recognised as such; it is said to have been made [gegenētai] when it has been made [gegonōs]. Indeed, even as regards the person of Christ according to his human nature, if that latter part of David's saying is confined to it, as it ought to be, Paul's application can prove nothing, since Christ also according to his human nature was the Son of God before his death, and was declared the Son of God according to that nature too.

units.la: Ad locum posteriorem ex Michea, duo respondet Aduersarius: Primùm per concessionem, quòd videlicet etiamsi illa versio Lutheri probaretur, nihil tamen locus ille causæ nostræ esset patrocinaturu, cuibi nullius generationis fiat mentio, nec aliud quicquam inde sequeretur, licet non necessario, quàm Christum ab æterno fuisse. Aliud autem esse, ab æterno extitisse, & aliud ab æterno genitum esse. Secundò ait, Lutherum perperam locum prædictum transtulisse, cum sensus sit, ipsius exortum esse à multis diebus seculi, nempe ex tribu, & prosapia Iuda, ac Dauidis, & nomen שלום sicuti etiam nomen seculum, non semper æternitatem, sed frequenter longum temporis spatium, seu tempus finitum, & secularia tempora significare. Atque hanc suam interpretationem autoritate Iohannis Tossarii Aquilouicani, Doctoris Theologi, confirmat.
units.tr: To the latter passage from Micah the opponent makes two replies. First, by way of concession: even if Luther's version were approved, that passage would nevertheless not support our cause, since no generation is mentioned there, and nothing else would follow from it, though not necessarily, than that Christ existed from eternity. But to have existed from eternity is one thing, and to have been begotten from eternity is another. Secondly, he says that Luther translated the passage wrongly, since the sense is that his origin is from the many days of the age, namely from the tribe and lineage of Judah and David; and that the word שלום, like the word seculum, signifies not always eternity but frequently a long span of time, or a finite time, and the ages of time. He confirms this interpretation by the authority of Johannes Tossanus of Aquila, a learned doctor of theology.

units.la: Resp. Primum quod attinet, si concedatur Filii Dei egressum ab æterno fuisse, tum necessariò sequitur, aut ab æterno ipsum à Patre per generationem æternam egressum esse, aut modum illius egressus generatione fuisse posteriorem, unde iterum generationis stabilietur æternitas: aut certè alius æterni illius egressus erit monstrandus modus, quem Samosateniani confingere non potuerunt, nisi Filium Deo Patri collateralem statuere velint. Quod autem versionem Lutheri attinet, etiamsi nomen שלום seculum, modò finitum, modò infinitum significet, vt Gen. 17. 8. Exod. 22. 6. 1. Sam. 1. 22. & 13. v. 13. 2. Sam. 12. 10. non tamen infringitur argumentum nostrum, cùm non sequatur שלום aliis in locis interdum significat seculum finitum, ergo etiam hic idem significare, præsertim cùm alii Scripturæ loci eidem Filio æternitatem tribuant, vt in sequentibus videbimus. Iohannis Tossarii Aquilouicani, viri aliouin eruditissimi, cuius paraphrasin citat Oiorrodius, autoritati tantùm tribuimus, quantùm interpreti humano, ac priuato, in explicandis Scripturis tribui fas est, quàde re non opus est, vt contendamus. Inuicta igitur ac immota persistunt argumenta nostra, quibus demonstramus Christum vnigenitum, proprium, ac naturalem esse Dei Filium, ab æterno à Deo Patre genitum, ac proinde eiusdem cum illo essentiæ, ac naturæ participem, verumque ac æternum Israelis Deum.
units.tr: Reply. First, as to this: if it is granted that the going forth of the Son of God was from eternity, then it necessarily follows either that he went forth from the Father from eternity by eternal generation, or that the mode of that going forth was posterior to the generation, whereby again the eternity of the generation is established; or else another mode of that eternal going forth must be shown, which the Samosatenians could not devise unless they wished to make the Son a collateral of God the Father. As for Luther's version, even if the word שלום signifies age, now finite, now infinite, as at Gen. 17:8, Exod. 22:6, 1 Sam. 1:22, 13:13 and 2 Sam. 12:10, our argument is nevertheless not overturned. For it does not follow that because שלום sometimes signifies a finite age in other places, it therefore signifies the same here, especially since other passages of Scripture ascribe eternity to the same Son, as we shall see in what follows. We attribute to the authority of Johannes Tossanus of Aquila, a man otherwise most learned, whose paraphrase Ostorodius cites, only so much as is right to attribute to a human and private interpreter in explaining the Scriptures; and on that matter we need not contend. Our arguments therefore stand unconquered and unshaken, by which we demonstrate that Christ is the only-begotten, proper and natural Son of God, begotten by God the Father from eternity, and accordingly a partaker of the same essence and nature with him, and the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: CAPVT X. In quo argumentum tertium pro æterna Filii Deitate, proponitur ac defenditur.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. In which the third argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is set forth and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum tertium inde desumitur, quod Christo in Scripturis sacris illa tribuuntur opera, quæ non nisi à Deo ipso præstari possunt. Hæc autem opera sunt triplicia: primum est creatio mundi ex nihilo, & perpetua eius conseruatio. Secundo opera illa, quæ fiunt contra naturæ ordinem, & miracula dicuntur. Tertiò, mundi reparatio, ac restauratio, de quibus singulis nos ordine videbimus.
units.tr: OUR third argument is drawn from the fact that the holy Scriptures ascribe to Christ works that can be performed only by God himself. These works are of three kinds. The first is the creation of the world out of nothing and its continual preservation. The second is those works which happen contrary to the order of nature and are called miracles. The third is the repair and restoration of the world. We shall examine each of these in turn.

units.la: Argumentum à creatione, & conseruatione rerum omnium tale est.
units.tr: The argument from the creation and preservation of all things runs as follows.

units.la: Qui creauit cœlum, terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt, & simul etiam omnia sua vi, & potentia sustentat, ac gubernat: ille non tantum ratione officii, sed natura, & essentia Deus est, Patri consubstantialis, coæternus, & coæqualis, eiusdemque cum ipso essentia, gloria ac maiestatis particeps.
units.tr: He who created heaven, earth, and all that is in them, and at the same time sustains and governs all things by his power and might, is God not only by office but by nature and essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with the Father, and a partaker with him of the same essence, glory, and majesty.

units.la: Atqui Christus creauit cœlum, terramque & omnia quæ in eis sunt, & simul omnia sua vi, ac potentia sustentat, & gubernat:
units.tr: But Christ created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and at the same time sustains and governs all things by his power and might.

units.la: Ergo Christus non tantum ratione officij, sed natura & essentia Deus est, Patri consubstantialis, coæternus, & coæqualis, eiusdemque cum ipso essentia, maiestatis, & gloriæ particeps.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is God not only by office but by nature and essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with the Father, and a partaker with him of the same essence, majesty, and glory.

units.la: Propositio maior extra controuersiæ, ac dubitationis aleam est constituta. Dñ enim, inquit Ierem. cap. 10. ver. 11. qui cœlum ac terram non fecerunt, eliminentur de terra, & vers. 12. qui fecit terram virtute sua, stabiliit orbem habitabilem sapientia sua, & prudëtia sua extendit cœlos. Es. 44. v. 10. Sic ait Iehouah creator cælorum, ille ipse Deus formator terræ, & opifex eius idem stabiliens eam, non ad inanitatem creauit eam, sed ad inhabitandum creauit eam, ego sum Iehouah, & nullus praeterea. Psalm. 96.5. Omnes dii populorum sunt idola, Iehoua autem coelos fecit. Ex quibus omnibus euidentissimè liquet id quod in propositione, diximus, nempe, creatorem coeli ac terrae, verum ac aeternum illum Deum Israelis esse.
units.tr: The major premise is established beyond any risk of controversy or doubt. For the Lord says in Jeremiah 10:11, "The gods that did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth," and in verse 12, "He made the earth by his power, he established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding he stretched out the heavens." Isaiah 44:10: "Thus says the LORD, the Creator of the heavens, the very God who formed the earth and made it; he established it, he did not create it in vain, but formed it to be inhabited. I am the LORD, and there is none besides me." Psalm 96:5: "All the gods of the peoples are idols, but the LORD made the heavens." From all these passages it is most evidently clear what we said in the proposition, namely that the creator of heaven and earth is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Assumptionis partem primam (vt de illa primò agamus) quod videlicet Christus coelum, ac terram condiderit, clarissimè docet scriptura, Ioh. 1. v. 3. Omnia per hunc sermonem facta sunt, & sine eo nihil factum est quod factum est. & v.10. In mundo erat, & mundus per eum factus est, sed mundus eum non agnouit: & cap. 5. v. 19. Quaecunque Pater facit, haec etiam Filius pariter facit. Atqui Pater fecit coelum, & terram, & omnia quae in eis sunt. Ergo filius quoque eadem fecit pariter, h.e. eadem authoritate, potentia, & voluntate. Col. 1. 16. Nam per eum condita sunt omnia quae in coelis sunt, & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, sive throni, sive dominia, sive imperia, sive potestates, omnia per eum, & eius respectu condita sunt. 1. Cor. 8. 6. Nobis tamen unus Deus Pater ille a quo omnia, & nos in ipso, & unus Dominus Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Heb. 1. v. 2. Quem constituit haeredem omnium, per quem etiam mundum condidit: & v. 10. Et tu in initio Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt coeli. Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius elucescit, nihil esse in totius mundi huius ambitu, cuius Christus, nō creator extiterit. Quin & ipsi Aduersarii, qui Christum nomine Dei indigitandum censent, hoc idem fateantur necesse est. Si enim Christus Deus est, tum aut coelum ac terram creauit, aut certè de terra eliminandus est: quorum posterius cum saltem verbis dereliquentur Aduersarii, Christumque Deum colendum & adorandum profiteantur, ipsum etiam coeli terraeque opificem & conditorem esse, concedant necesse est.
units.tr: As for the first part of the assumption (to deal with it first), that Christ founded heaven and earth, Scripture teaches this most clearly. John 1:3: "All things were made through this Word, and without him nothing was made that was made." Verse 10: "He was in the world, and the world was made through him, but the world did not know him." And John 5:19: "Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does." But the Father made heaven and earth and all that is in them. Therefore the Son too made the same things likewise, that is, by the same authority, power, and will. Colossians 1:16: "For through him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him." 1 Corinthians 8:6: "Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist." Hebrews 1:2: "whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds." And verse 10: "You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands." From all these passages it shines forth clearer than midday that there is nothing within the whole compass of this world of which Christ is not the creator. Indeed, the very opponents who think Christ should be named as God must necessarily confess the same thing. For if Christ is God, then either he created heaven and earth, or else he must be removed from the earth. Since the opponents, at least in words, reject the latter, and profess that Christ is to be worshipped and adored as God, they must necessarily concede that he is also the maker and founder of heaven and earth.

units.la: Oftorrodius Institutionum suarum cap. 11. statum quaestionis subdole format: nō enim quaerit, An ex eo quod Christus in Scriptura omnia creasse dicitur, coelumque ac terram condidisse, sequatur ipsum, verum & aeternum Deum esse? vel: An ex operibus Christi eiusdem aeterna deitas demonstrari possit? Verum, An ex eo quod per Christum omnia creata esse dicantur, sequatur Christum, verum & aeternum Deum esse? quò & totam disputationem illo capite dirigit, quasi omnibus testimoniis, quibus Christo creatio absolutè tribuatur, destituere-mur. Verum quia & illam quaestionem quoque prout ab ipso proponitur, affirmamus, argumenta ipsius, quibus illam negat, examinabimus. nabimus. Ad argumetum igitur nostrum prædicto capite respon- det primò, Ex eo, quod Deus omnia per Christum condidisse dicitur, ne- cessariò sequi Christum minimè verum Deum esse, cùm ille hac ratione tantùm secunda, non autem prima creationis causa constituatur.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in chapter 11 of his Institutes, cunningly frames the question. For he does not ask whether it follows from the fact that Christ is said in Scripture to have made all things and founded heaven and earth that he is the true and eternal God; nor whether the eternal deity of the same can be demonstrated from the works of Christ. Instead he asks whether, from the fact that all things are said to have been created through Christ, it follows that Christ is the true and eternal God. To this question he directs his whole discussion in that chapter, as if we were left without any testimonies by which creation is absolutely ascribed to Christ. But since we also affirm that question as he proposes it, we will examine the arguments by which he denies it.
