In the aforementioned chapter he first replies to our argument as follows: "From the fact that God is said to have made all things through Christ, it does not necessarily follow that Christ is not the true God, since he is constituted in this way only as the secondary, and not the primary, cause of creation."

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Verus & æternus Deus mundi, & creationis prima est causa.
units.tr: The true and eternal God is the primary cause of the world and of creation.

units.la: Atqui Christus non est prima, sed secunda tantùm creationis causa.
units.tr: But Christ is not the primary, but only the secondary, cause of creation.

units.la: Ergo Christus non est verus ac æternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not the true and eternal God.

units.la: Minorem sic probat:
units.tr: He proves the minor premise thus:

units.la: Si Christus in Scripturis S. nusquam creator appellatur, sed tantùm omnia per ipsum facta & creata esse dicūtur: sequitur Christū eorū omnium, quæ creata sunt, non primam, sed secundam causam esse.
units.tr: If Christ is nowhere called creator in the holy Scriptures, but it is only said that all things were made and created through him, it follows that Christ is not the primary but the secondary cause of all the things that have been created.

units.la: Atqui Christus in Scripturis S. nusquā creator dicitur, & in Symbolo, vt vocant, Apostolico, solus Pater creator appellatur, per Filium autem omnia facta, & creata esse perhibentur.
units.tr: But Christ is nowhere called creator in the holy Scriptures, and in the so-called Apostles' Creed only the Father is called creator, while all things are said to have been made and created through the Son.

units.la: Ergo Christus rerum creatarum non prima, sed secunda est causa.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not the primary but the secondary cause of created things.

units.la: Resp. Argumentum syllogismi principalis cum scriptura sacra verissimè negamus, quæ etiam illo prosyllogismo minimè proba- tur, cum eius cõsequentia, vnà cum assumptione. Quia autem du- plici medio constat syllogismus, ad singula ordine respõdebimus.
units.tr: Reply. We most truly deny the argument of the principal syllogism together with the holy Scripture, which is not proved at all by that prosyllogism, with its consequence along with the assumption. Since the syllogism rests on a double middle term, we shall answer each part in order.

units.la: Quantum igitur illud concernit, quod affirmat Christū nusquam in scripturis S. creatorem dici: Resp. primò ex eo nihil contra nos sequi, Christus creator nō dicitur, ergo creator non est, aut creator dici nō debet? Cum enim ille cœlum & terram creasse, disertis scripturæ verbis perhibeatur, quo iure, aut quam sequutus Logicam nomine creatoris ipsum spoliabis? Si quicquā valet Qstorrodi argumentū, ab huius mundi opificio, & creatione, ipse quoque Pater excludetur, qui hoc ipso nomine disertè in scripturis nusquam appellatur.
units.tr: As to what he asserts, that Christ is nowhere called creator in the holy Scriptures, we reply first that nothing against us follows from this: "Christ is not called creator, therefore he is not creator, or ought not to be called creator"? For since he is expressly said in the words of Scripture to have created heaven and earth, by what right, or by what logic, will you strip him of the name of creator? If Ostorodius' argument holds at all, then the Father himself will also be excluded from the making and creation of this world, since he too is nowhere expressly called by this very name in the Scriptures.

units.la: Deinde assumptionem esse falsam, vt liquet ex Es.45.v.12. Sic ait Iehouah creator cœlorum, ille ipse Deus formator terræ & opifex, idem sta- biliens eam, qui non ad inanitatē creauit eam, sed ad inhabitādum for- mauit eā, ego sum Iehouah, & nullus præterea. Christū autem Iehouā illū esse, qui verba allegata de se dixerit, hoc modo demõstramus.
units.tr: Next, the assumption is false, as is clear from Isaiah 45:12: "Thus says the LORD, the Creator of the heavens, the very God who formed the earth and made it, he established it, who did not create it in vain but formed it to be inhabited; I am the LORD, and there is none besides me." We show that Christ is the LORD who spoke the words quoted above about himself in the following way.

units.la: Qui per Esaiā dixit, Certè mihi sese fleƈtet omne genu, & omnis lingua palā agnoscet Deū. Esa. 45. v. 23. ille etiā superius allegata verba de se dixit: Atqui Christus de se verba illa dixit per Esaiam, Certè mihi sese fleƈtet omne genu, & omnis lingua palam agnoscet Deū, vt patet ex Rom.1.v.10.11. Omnes sistentur apud tribunal Christi: scriptū est enim, Certè mihi sese fleƈtet omne genu, & omnis lingua palā agnoscet Deum. Ergo Christus etiam seipsum in antecedentibus creatorem appellauit. Quòd verò solus Pater in Symbolo, re & nomine Apostolico, non autem Filius, aut spiritus sanctus nomine creatoris indigitatur, eo ipso nec Filius, nec spiritus sanctus à creationis opere excluditur. Symbolum enim illud vt essentiam diuinam, quæ omnium actionum & operationum diuinarum ad extra, vt loquuntur, commune est principium, sic & operationes, ac ipsam quoque creationem omnibus tribus personis communem, & indiuisam tradit. Cum autem singulis personis peculiaris sit vt subsistendi, ita & agendi, atque operandi, modus, adeoque, Pater, vt est à se, ita agat, & creet à se, Filius vt est à Patre, ita agat à Patre, & Pater per ipsum: spiritus sanctus, vt est à Patre ac Filio, ita agat à Patre & Filio, & Pater ac Filius per ipsum: ideo propter hunc agendi modum, & ordinem in Symbolo Patri, vt diuinarum actionum & operationum fonti creationem tribuit, quæ prædicatio, non inæqualitatem dignitatis, essentiæ, aut potentiæ, sed agendi ordinem, & modum innuit. Hactenus igitur non sequitur Christum rerum creatarum, non primam, sed secundam tantum causam extitisse.
units.tr: He who spoke through Isaiah, "Surely to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall openly acknowledge God," Isaiah 45:23, also spoke the words quoted above about himself. But Christ spoke those words about himself through Isaiah, "Surely to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall openly acknowledge God," as is clear from Romans 14:10–11: "We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ; for it is written, 'Surely to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall openly acknowledge God.'" Therefore Christ also called himself creator in the preceding verses. As for the fact that only the Father is designated creator in the Creed, in reality and by name the Apostles', and not the Son or the Holy Spirit, by this very fact neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is excluded from the work of creation. For that Creed hands down the divine essence, which is the common principle of all the divine actions and operations toward the outside, as they say, and so it hands down the operations and creation itself as common to and undivided among all three persons. But since each person has a peculiar mode of subsisting and therefore of acting and operating, the Father acts and creates from himself, as he is from himself; the Son acts from the Father, as he is from the Father, and the Father acts through him; the Holy Spirit, as he is from the Father and the Son, acts from the Father and the Son, and the Father and the Son act through him. Therefore, because of this mode and order of acting, the Creed attributes creation to the Father as the fountain of the divine actions and operations, and this statement indicates the order and mode of acting, not any inequality of dignity, essence, or power. Thus far it does not follow that Christ was only the secondary, and not the primary, cause of created things.

units.la: Ad hoc autem ipsum probandum medium secundum, quod videlicet Deus Pater per Christum omnia creasse dicitur, nihilo plus momenti aut ponderis habet. Per illas enim particulas non semper diuersas causarum species, aut causam administram, vel etiam inæqualitatem aliquam in Scriptura sacra denotari, cum illa actiones, aut operationes aliquas tribus illis personis tribuit, inde liquet, quod illæ particulæ ... tum Patri, tum Filio, tum spiritui sancto tribuuntur, Rom. 11.33. & 36. O altitudo diuitiarum, sapientiæ, ac scientiæ Dei, quoniam ex ipso, per ipsum, & in ipsum sunt omnia. 1 Cor. 1 v. 9. Fidelis est Deus per quem vocati estis in communionem Filij ipsius Iesu Christi Domini nostri. Vide etiam Ephes. 4 v. 16. Col. 2 v. 19. Hæ igitur particulæ ad denotandas personarum proprietates, & significandum agendi modum, & ordinem, non autem propterea, quod vna persona instrumentum sit alterius, adhibentur.
units.tr: Now for the second medium, meant to prove this very point, namely that God the Father is said to have created all things through Christ, the argument carries no more weight or force. For from those little particles it is plain that Scripture does not always denote different kinds of causes, or a subordinate cause, or indeed some inequality, when it ascribes certain actions or operations to those three persons. The particles are attributed to the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit alike: Rom. 11:33 and 36, "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! For of him, and through him, and to him are all things." 1 Cor. 1:9, "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord." See also Eph. 4:16 and Col. 2:19. These particles, therefore, are used to denote the properties of the persons and to signify the mode and order of acting, and not because one person is the instrument of another.

units.la: Ad illud autem quod illæ particulæ etiam de Patre prædicari dicantur, excipit Oftorrodius, & ait, Quamuis illæ particulæ etiam de Deo Patre enuntientur, aliter tamen de Deo, quam de Christo intelligendas esse, cum nemo per Deum quicquam fecisse, aut creasse legatur, quod etiam fit impossibile, quia ipso nemo alius superior exstat, per Christum Christum vero à Deo omnia, & ipsa secula facta esse perhibeantur.
units.tr: As for the objection that these particles are also said of the Father, Ostorrodius takes exception and says: "Although those particles are also pronounced of God the Father, they must be understood differently of God than of Christ, since no one is read to have made or created anything through God, which is in fact impossible, because there is no one superior to him; whereas all things and the very ages are said to have been made through Christ, and by God through Christ."

units.la: Resp. Particulas illas non de solo filio, sed etiam de Patre praedicari, ideò à nobis allegatur, quia inde certò concluditur ex illis particulis ad statuendas causarum species, aut operandi inaequalitatem, stabiliri minimè posse. Sed cùm per Deum Patrem nemo superior ( quis enim ipsius diuinitatis fonte superior, aut subsistendi, ac proinde agendi quoque ordine primo prior alius ? ) per filium, autem Pater operatus esse dicatur, filiũ propterea ut causam tantùm administram, seu instrumentalem operatum esse, iustis legibus concludi posse autumas? Minimè verò, operatus enim est per ipsum, non tanquam instrumentum, sed tanquam principalem efficientem, & cooperatorem, aequalem tempore, aequalem dignitate, essentia unum, verùm persona secundum. Nam sicuti filius est subsistentia sua posterior, & secundus ordine, prius siquidem subsistit Pater, deinde subsistit filius à Patre ab aeterno genitus: sic etiam ordine agendi posterior est, & secundus. Praecedit enim voluntas Patris, comitatur voluntas filii in omnibus rebus agendis. Inde haec loquendi formula existit, quod Pater per filium omnia fecerit, nempe à Patre secundum, non tempore, non dignitate, sed agendi ordine. Atque haec de Ostorrodii exceptione. Rem ipsam quod attinet, Christum, non vt instrumentum, seu causam secundam, & administram, hunc mundum creasse liquet, Primò, quod Apostolus ipsum alloquens Hebr. 1. vers. 10. Tu Domine, inquit, ab initio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt coeli: quod de causa instrumentali, administra, aut secunda intelligi non potest, quia Dauid hoc idem de Deo aeterno Israelis enuntiat, Psal. 102. vers. 26. quem, ipso etiam Ostorrodio teste, creationis causam non secundam, aut instrumentalem, sed primam, ac principalem fuisse est certissimum. Secundò, qui omnia facit pariter, quaecunque facit Pater, is nō tantum vt instrumentum operatur. Atqui Christus omnia pariter facit, quaecunque Pater facit. Ergo causa instrumentalis, administra, aut secundaria esse non potest. Atque haec de Profyllogismi connexo. Assumptio autem eiusdem falsa est, duabus de causis: primò, quia innuit Patrem in symbolo Apostolico ita creatorem appellari, vt filius à creationis opere excludatur; cùm tamen vna persona diuinitatis nominata, caeterę non remoueantur, sed tantùm existendi, vel operandi ordo notetur. Secundò, quia temerè in illa affirmatur in Scriptura, quantum ad hoc negotium creationis, nihil aliud de Christo affirmari, quàm Patrem omnia per ipsum condidisse, cùm tamen aperta protulerimus testimonia, in quibus omnibus, illis omissis articulis, creatio cœli ac terræ, ipsi Christo tanquam Deo Israelis absolutè, & simpliciter adscribitur: de qua re iam egimus.
units.tr: Reply: We cited those particles as applying not to the Son alone but also to the Father, because from them it cannot be firmly concluded that different kinds of causes, or an inequality in operation, are established. But since no one is superior to God the Father (for who is superior to the fountain of the divinity itself, or who is prior in the first order of subsisting, and therefore of acting?), and since the Father is said to have worked through the Son, can it be justly concluded that the Son worked only as a subordinate or instrumental cause? By no means. For the Father worked through him not as an instrument but as the principal efficient and co-worker, equal in time, equal in dignity, one in essence, but second in person. For just as the Son is posterior and second in order of subsistence (the Father indeed subsists first, and then the Son, begotten from the Father from eternity, subsists from the Father), so also he is posterior and second in order of acting. For the will of the Father goes before, and the will of the Son accompanies him in all things to be done. Hence this form of speech arises, that the Father made all things through the Son: that is, the Son is second to the Father not in time, not in dignity, but in the order of acting. So much for Ostorrodius' exception. As to the matter itself, it is clear that Christ created this world not as an instrument or a secondary and subordinate cause. First, because the Apostle, addressing him, says in Heb. 1:10, "You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands"; this cannot be understood of an instrumental, subordinate or secondary cause, because David says the same of the eternal God of Israel in Ps. 102:26, who, as Ostorrodius himself bears witness, was certainly the cause of creation not secondary or instrumental but primary and principal. Second, whoever does all things equally, whatever the Father does, does not work merely as an instrument. But Christ does all things equally, whatever the Father does. Therefore he cannot be an instrumental, subordinate or secondary cause. So much for the connected form of this prosyllogism. The assumption, however, is false, for two reasons. First, because it implies that the Father is called Creator in the Apostles' Creed in such a way that the Son is excluded from the work of creation; yet when one person of the divinity is named, the others are not removed, but only the order of existing or of acting is noted. Second, because it is rashly asserted that Scripture, as far as this business of creation goes, affirms nothing about Christ except that the Father made all things through him; yet we have brought forward clear testimonies in which, leaving aside those articles, the creation of heaven and earth is ascribed to Christ himself absolutely and simply, as God of Israel. We have already dealt with this matter.

units.la: Secundò, respondet Aduersarius, neminem tam imperitum esse, quin videat Christum, eo ipso, quod Pater omnia per ipsum condidisse dicitur, à Patre manifestè distingui.
units.tr: Second, the adversary replies that no one is so unlearned as not to see that Christ, by the very fact that the Father is said to have made all things through him, is clearly distinguished from the Father.

units.la: Resp. Quid tum? An igitur sequitur, vel Christum vnum, & æternum, verùmque Deum Israelis cum Patre & Spiritu sancto non esse, aut in creationis opere Patri tantùm vt causam administram, secundariam, & instrumentalem adstitisse? Minimè vero: non primum, quod tamen inferre conatur Aduersarius, quia omnes tres personas salua vnitate essentiæ, indiuisæ inter se differre numero, proprietatibus, adeóque nominibus, & agendi modo ac ordine, manifestissimè est demonstratum, & supra capite quinto, sufficienter à nobis declaratum. Sed hoc effugium de personarum diuinarum discrimine nihil nos iuuare, ait Osiorrodius, quia plures vna diuinas personas esse, nondum à nobis sit demonstratum.
units.tr: Reply: What then? Does it follow either that Christ is not the one, eternal and true God of Israel together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, or that in the work of creation he stood by the Father only as a subordinate, secondary and instrumental cause? By no means. The first does not follow, although the adversary tries to infer it, because it has been most clearly demonstrated that all three persons, while the unity of essence is preserved and they are undivided, differ from one another in number, in properties, and therefore in names, and in mode and order of acting, and we have sufficiently declared this above in chapter five. "But," says Ostorrodius, "this escape by the distinction of the divine persons does not help you, because it has not yet been demonstrated by us that there are more than one divine persons."

units.la: Resp. Tres esse diuinas personas in vnitate essentiæ subsistentes, euidentius à nobis est confirmatum, quàm vt tu, aut tui similes in æternum labefactare doctrinæ illius veritatem queatis. Tu certè, Osiorrodi, institutionum tuarum capite quarto ad refutandam doctrinam illam nihil nisi puerilES eiusmodi nugas attulisti, quæ vix dignæ sunt, vt illis diluendis vel puræ chartæ, vel bonæ horæ insumantur. De qua re vide refutationum nostrarum caput quintum.
units.tr: Reply: That there are three divine persons subsisting in the unity of essence has been confirmed by us more evidently than you, or men like you, could ever overturn the truth of that doctrine. You, Ostorrodius, in chapter four of your Institutions, to refute that doctrine, have brought forward nothing but trifles of this sort, which are scarcely worth wasting either pure paper or a good hour in refuting. On this matter see chapter five of our refutations.

units.la: Tertiò addit Aduersarius, quum in Scripturis sacris nusquam cœli ac terræ mentio fiat, quasi Christus illa creasset, sed tantum earum rerum quæ in cœlo, ac super terram sint, aut fateri nos volentes nolentes oportere, Spiritum S. illis in locis non de creatione prima, verum secunda verba facere: aut in castra Arianorum transeundum nobis esse, qui statuunt, Deum per Christum tanquam causam secundam, & instrumentalem, cœlum atque terram creasse.
units.tr: Thirdly, the adversary adds: since in the Holy Scriptures there is nowhere any mention of heaven and earth as if Christ had made them, but only of those things which are in heaven and upon the earth; and since we, whether willing or unwilling, must admit that the Holy Spirit in those places speaks not of the first creation but of the second; or else we must pass over into the camp of the Arians, who hold that God created heaven and earth through Christ as a secondary and instrumental cause.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si in Scriptura [sacra Christus nullibi cœlum ac terram creasse dicitur, sed tantum ea quæ in cœlo ac terra sunt, condidisse: tum aut concedendum est, illis in locis,non de prima, verùm secunda creatione agi: aut cum Arianis statuendum, Deum per Christum,tanquam causam secundam, & instrumentalem omnia creasse.
units.tr: If Christ is nowhere said in Holy Scripture to have created heaven and earth, but only to have founded the things that are in heaven and on earth, then either it must be conceded that those passages speak of the second creation, not the first, or with the Arians it must be held that God created all things through Christ as a secondary and instrumental cause.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo etiam ex posterioribus alterutrum.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore one of the latter must also follow.

units.la: Resp. Vtramque præmissam esse falsam. Connexum, quia neutrum consequens ex illo antecedente etiam dato, non tamen concessso, confici potest. Si enim omnia quæ in cælis, & quæ in terra sunt, per Christum creata esse dicantur, tum neutiquam inde sequitur, vel de creatione secunda, & restauratione illa intelligenda esse, quia posito genere ad speciem determinatam male concluditur: Vel, Si illa de restauratione intelligantur, Christum propterea à creatione eorundem excludendum esse, quasi creatio, & gratiosa restauratio ita inter se opponerentur, vt vni eidémque causæ efficienti tribui non possent: Vel denique cum Arianis statuendum, Deum per Christum, tanquam causam secundariam & instrumentalem omnia illa condidisse, quasi posito effecto cuius plures causæ efficientes & sunt, & esse possunt, cooperatrices,& æquales ad modum aliquem vel certum,vel inferiorem,vlla concedatur consequentia. Nònne hasce tuas summas ineptias,vel balbutientes pueri,atque Batti deprehenderent, & tu tamen illis Christo creatori tuo, honorem creationis eripere infelici ausu conaris, & scipioni illi vix arundineo innixus, totius veritatis diuinæ, & Ecclesiæ vniuersæ impetum sustinere? Demonstrabimus autem deinceps ordine omnes illos locos,quos nos afferendam Christo creationis gloriam, allegauimus, de creatione prima intelligendos esse. Nunc superest, vt falsitatem assumptionis etiam detegamus. Huic enim diserte contradicit Christus. Iohan. 5. verf. 19. quum se pariter facere omnia illa profitetur, quæcunque Pater facit. Huic contradicit verissimus & luculentissimus Christi testis Iohannes cap. 1. verf. 3. & 10. quum vniuersale nomen signo vniuersali coniungens, & mundum,& cætera vsque adeò omnia per ipsum facta esse, vt nihil facti, vel factum sine ipso,existat,palam testetur. Huic contradicit grauissimus ille honoris, & nominis Christi assertor,nempe autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos c.1. v. 2.&10 qui Deum ita per Christum creasse mundum affirmat, vt tamen coelum, terramque ab ipso creatam esse, diserte testetur. Cui igitur plus fidei habendum existimabit Oftorrodius, Christone ipsi, Paulo, & Iohanni in ipsius Christi sinu iacenti, an vero Ario alicui inter sua viscera & intestina sese volutanti? Sed pergo ad sequentia.
units.tr: Response: both premises are false, and so is the connection, since neither consequent can be drawn from that antecedent even if it be granted, which it is not. For if all things that are in heaven and on earth are said to have been created through Christ, it by no means follows either that they must be understood of a second creation and restoration (since concluding from a genus to a determinate species is a faulty inference), or, if they are understood of restoration, that Christ must for that reason be excluded from their creation, as though creation and gracious restoration were so opposed that they could not be ascribed to one and the same efficient cause. Nor finally does it follow that with the Arians we must hold that God made all those things through Christ as a secondary and instrumental cause, as though, given an effect with several efficient causes, co-operating and equal in some definite or lesser degree, any consequence could be conceded. Would not even stammering boys and Battus detect these utter absurdities of yours? And yet you, in your unhappy daring, try to snatch from Christ, your Creator, the honour of creation, and, leaning on a staff scarcely stronger than a reed, to withstand the assault of all divine truth and of the whole Church. I shall demonstrate in order, hereafter, that all those passages which I cited to assert for Christ the glory of creation are to be understood of the first creation. Now it remains to expose the falsity of the assumption too. Christ himself directly contradicts it, John 5:19, where he declares that he does in like manner all the things that the Father does. The most true and most luminous witness of Christ, John, contradicts it, ch. 1 vv. 3 and 10, where, joining a universal term to a universal sign, he openly testifies that all things were so made through him that nothing exists as made without him. The most serious champion of Christ's honour and name, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 1 vv. 2 and 10, contradicts it too, affirming that God created the world through Christ and expressly testifying that heaven and earth were created by him. Whom then will Ostorrodius think more worthy of trust: Christ himself, Paul, and John who lay in Christ's bosom, or Arius, who wallows among his own bowels and entrails? But I proceed to what follows.

units.la: Quarto, inquit Oftorrodius, In illis locis, in quibus omnia per Christum facta esse dicuntur, nihil de terra, aut coeli creatione agi, illámque vocem OMNIA necessario restringendam esse ad illa, quae per Euangelij praedicationem, sint à Deo condita: quia nihil ipsorum sine Christo sit factum. Vocem enim illam OMNIA ad rem de qua agitur, restringendam esse, praeter alia plurima Scripturae dicta, locum illum Pauli 2. Cor. 5. v. 17. manifeste testari. Si quis, inquit, in Christo nova creatura est, vetera praeterierunt, ecce nova facta sunt omnia. Vbi tamen non omnia in vniuersum, sed tantum ea, quae per Christum sunt renouata, intelliguntur.
units.tr: Fourthly, says Ostorrodius, in those passages in which all things are said to have been made through Christ, nothing is said about the creation of earth or heaven, and that word ALL must necessarily be restricted to those things which were founded by God through the preaching of the Gospel, since nothing of them is made without Christ. For that word ALL must be restricted to the matter in hand; apart from many other sayings of Scripture, the passage of Paul, 2 Cor. 5 v. 17, clearly shows this. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." Where, however, not all things in general are understood, but only those that have been renewed through Christ.

units.la: Resp. Vocem Omnis, & Omnia ad materiam subiectam de qua agitur restringendam esse, & modo collectiue, modo distributiue intelligendam, testantur loca Scripturae quamplurima: sed hoc Aduersarium non iuuat: quia enim in locis illis, quorum auctoritate freti, Christo coeli, terraeque creationem tribuimus, non de secunda, sed de prima creatione agitur, omnino sequetur illam vocem omnia ad materiam subiectam creationis, id est, ea, quae per Christum creata sunt, restringendam esse. Nos veritatem antecedentis in vno saltem, aut altero loco (omnium enim analysin instituere, nimis foret prolixum) demonstrabimus. Locum igitur illum Iohannis cap. 1. verf. 3. quem de renouatione, & restauratione intelligendam arbitratur Aduersarius, & in quo omnia per sermonem illum facta dicuntur, restringens illud Aduersariorum glossema non admittere, tum ex natura ipsius enunciationis, tum etiam ex falsitate absurdissima, quae ex illa restrictione sequeretur, manifeste demonstramus. Prius quod attinet, genus illud loquutionis, non ad restrictionem, sed ad enunciationem vniuersalitatis pertinere, omnium literarum, & literatorum consensus testatur: quum enim sermoni illi, nihil quod factum est, aequipolleat hic, nihil factum, vel nihil facti, ac proinde nomen facti vniuersale fit, & nomen nihil vniuersale signum, sequitur enunciationem hanc vniuersalem, in qua nomen vniuersale, cum signo vniuersali, coniungitur, restringi non posse, nisi quis & vocum & enunciationum naturam, mutare velit. Sed & falsitas, quę illam restrictionem comitatur, eandem refellit. Quę enim Iohannes vers. 3. per Christum facta esse affirmat, ea vers. 10. mundi nomine, quem per eundem conditum esse testatur, indigitat. Quoscunque autem Christus creatione secunda refingit, ac renouat, illorum intellectus noua luce spirituali illustratur, voluntásque renouatur, sic vt vocem Christi audiant, eum Seruatorem ipsorum agnoscant, Deo reconcilientur, iustificentur, atque saluentur. Quum autem eodem versu testetur Iohannes, mundum illum, qui per Christum conditus dicitur, Christum non agnouisse, necessario inde sequitur, aut ibi non de secunda, sed prima creatione agi: aut aliquos regenitos Christum non agnoscere, contra id quod affirmat Christus Ioh. 10. vers. 27. Vbi oues meæ, inquit, vocem meam audiunt, & ego eas agnosco, & sequuntur me, aut denique mundum ipsum Christum agnoscere & falsum de mundo à Iohanne cap. 1. vers. 10. vbi negat Christum à mundo cognosci, testimonium perhiberi. Vnde cognoscit Ostorrodius, quàm impiæ falsitatis laqueis absurda illa & violenta restrictio ipsum constringat. Sed & Paulum Col. 1. vers. 16. non de secunda, sed prima creatione agere, ex argumentorum serie, quibus quæstionem sibi propositam demonstrat, & ipsa subiectorum, de quibus ibi agitur, natura liquidò constat. Dignitatem enim personæ Christi commendaturus Apostolus, summatim colligit ipsius epitheta, & elogia, quę nostra scire interfuit: ac primò quidem ipsum Christum imaginem Dei inconspicui, & primogenitum vniuersæ creaturæ appellat: deinde huius nominis, quare videlicet Christus sit primogenitus omnis rei creatæ, rationem reddit, tum ab operibus creationis, & conseruationis, quod videlicet per illum & eius respectu non tantùm creata sint omnia, quæ in cœlis sunt, & quæ in terra, siue throni, siue dominationes, siue principatus, siue potestates, verùm etiam per illum omnia consistant: tùm ab operibus redemptionis, quòd ille sit caput corporis Ecclesiæ, primogenitus ex mortuis, & quæ amplius de ipso prædicantur. Alium igitur hic sermonem esse Apostoli, quum agit de creatione, & alium quum agit de redemptione, seu restauratione, & creatione secunda, inde patet, quod illa cœlestia solia, dominatus, principatus, potestates, quæ in sua perstiterunt origine incorrupta, & integra, nulla restauratione, aut renouatione opus habuerunt vnquam. Atque hæc sufficiunt ad demonstrandam Ostorrodii temerariam in Scripturis interpolandis,& obtorto collo ad suas imposturas stabiliendas, rapiendis.
units.tr: Response: that the words "all" and "all things" must be restricted to the subject matter under discussion, and understood now collectively and now distributively, very many passages of Scripture attest. But this does not help the adversary. For in those passages, on whose authority we ascribe the creation of heaven and earth to Christ, it is the first creation, not the second, that is under discussion; it will altogether follow that the word "all things" must be restricted to the subject matter of creation, that is, to those things which were created through Christ. We shall demonstrate the truth of the antecedent in at least one passage, or another (for to analyse all of them would be too lengthy). Therefore we shall clearly show, from the nature of the statement itself and from the most absurd falsity that would follow from such a restriction, that the passage of John, ch. 1 v. 3, which the adversary thinks should be understood of renewal and restoration, and in which all things are said to have been made through that Word, does not admit that gloss of the Adversary's. As to the first point, the agreement of all writers and scholars attests that this kind of expression pertains not to restriction but to the assertion of universality. For since that phrase "nothing that was made" is equivalent to "nothing made" or "nothing of what is made", the noun "made" becomes universal and the noun "nothing" a universal sign; it follows that this universal statement, in which a universal noun is joined with a universal sign, cannot be restricted unless someone wishes to change the nature both of words and of statements. But the falsity that accompanies that restriction refutes it equally. For what John in v. 3 affirms to have been made through Christ, that he designates in v. 10 by the name "world", which he testifies was made through the same Christ. Moreover, whomever Christ re-forms and renews by the second creation, their understanding is illuminated with a new spiritual light and their will is renewed, so that they hear Christ's voice, acknowledge him as their Saviour, are reconciled to God, justified and saved. Since, however, in the same verse John testifies that this "world", which is said to have been made through Christ, did not know him, it necessarily follows either that there it is not the second but the first creation that is in question; or that some of the regenerate do not know Christ, contrary to what Christ affirms, John 10 v. 27: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me"; or finally that the world itself acknowledges Christ, and the testimony of John, ch. 1 v. 10, where he denies that Christ is known by the world, is false. Hence Ostorrodius may see into what snares of impious falsity that absurd and violent restriction binds him. But also that Paul, in Col. 1 v. 16, treats not of the second but of the first creation is plain from the sequence of arguments by which he sets out the question put to him, and from the very nature of the subjects of which he speaks there. For the Apostle, about to commend the dignity of Christ's person, briefly gathers together the epithets and eulogies of him that it concerns us to know. First he calls Christ the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of every creature; then he gives the reason for this name, why Christ is the firstborn of every created thing: both from the works of creation and preservation, namely that through him and with respect to him not only "were all things created that are in heaven and that are on earth, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers", but also "all things consist in him"; and from the works of redemption, that "he is the head of the body, the Church, the firstborn from the dead", and whatever else is predicated of him. It is therefore plain from this that the Apostle's discourse is one thing when he treats of creation, and another when he treats of redemption, or restoration and second creation. For those heavenly thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, which persisted in their original state, uncorrupted and whole, never had any need of restoration or renewal. These points suffice to demonstrate Ostorrodius's rash handling of Scripture, and his wrenching of it by force to establish his impostures.

units.la: Quintò, & vltimò, inquit Aduersarius, per mundū & secula, quæ per Christū condita esse dicuntur, nihil aliud quàm vitam æternam, & nouum mundum intelligendum esse (qui Heb. 2. v. 5. ideò futurus dicatur, quod licet ipsi Christo præsens, nobis tamen futurus sit, & expectandus) què Deus per Christum fecerit, hoc est, quod per Filium suum æternam & beatissimam vitæ rationem, & statum hominibus concesserit, & illius beatitatis ipsum autorem, & principem constituerit, quam ipsum ob causam, idem Pater æternitatis, vel futuri seculi appelletur, Ef. 9. 6.
units.tr: Fifthly and lastly, says my opponent, by the world and the ages, which are said to have been created through Christ, nothing else is to be understood than eternal life and the new world (which is called "future" (Heb. 2:5) because, although it is present to Christ himself, it is still future for us and something to be awaited); and what God made through Christ is this, that through his Son he granted men an eternal and most blessed way and state of life, and constituted him the author and prince of that blessedness, for which reason the same Father is called "the Father of eternity" or "of the future age" (Isa. 9:6).

units.la: Resp. Vana sunt quæcunque adferuntur, omnia. De hoc enim non quæritur, An Christus sit Pater futuri seculi, & autor restaurationis, secundæque creationis, quam sanctè credimus, ac docemus: sed an inde sequatur, aut omnia citata loca de hac secunda creatione intelligenda esse, aut propterea Christo primam rerum creationem tribui non posse? Quæ autem quæso est consequentia illa, Christus est Pater futuri seculi, vel æternitatis, & per Christum restaurantur omnia: Ergo loci citati non de prima creatione, sed secunda sunt intelligendi? Vel: Christus est autor futuræ vitæ: Ergo non creauit cælum, ac terram? Nulla plane. Quum enim actus Christi non sit vnicus, sed multiplex, & vtrumque opus creationis, nempe & renouationis, Christo in Scripturis tribuatur, pessimè & imperitè opus renouationis operi creationis ita opponitur, vt alterum altero euertatur, nec vtrumque eidem causæ efficienti tribui possit. Non solùm igitur propterea clenchi ignoratione hic ludit Ostorrodius, sed etiam locum illum Hebr. 1. vers. 10. vbi creatio cœli, ac terræ Christo disertis verbis tribuitur, alto silentio pro sua calliditate prætərit, ac proinde irrita sunt omnia ipsius argumentationum tela: quibus euidentissimum æternæ Deitatis testimonium, creationem nempe aspectabilis huius mundi, nefario ausu nobis conatur eripere. Tibi Domine qui in initio terram fundasti, & cuius manuum opera sunt cœli, sit laus & honor in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Reply. Everything that is brought forward here is empty. For the question is not whether Christ is the Father of the future age and the author of restoration and of the second creation, which we devoutly believe and teach. The question is whether it follows from this that all the passages cited must be understood of this second creation, or that for this reason the first creation of things cannot be ascribed to Christ. And what kind of inference, I ask, is this: Christ is the Father of the future age or of eternity, and through Christ all things are restored; therefore the passages cited must be understood not of the first creation but of the second? Or this: Christ is the author of future life; therefore he did not create heaven and earth? It is plainly no inference at all. For the work of Christ is not single but manifold, and both work of creation and work of renewal are ascribed to Christ in the Scriptures. Foolishly and ignorantly, Ostorrodius sets the work of renewal against the work of creation in such a way that one overthrows the other, and cannot ascribe both to the same efficient cause. Therefore Ostorrodius is not only playing here with a sophistical trick based on ignorance of the point, but he also passes over in deep silence, with his usual cunning, the passage Heb. 1:10, where the creation of heaven and earth is expressly ascribed to Christ. Accordingly all the arrows of his arguments are useless, by which he wickedly dares to snatch from us the most evident testimony to eternal Deity, namely the creation of this visible world. "To you, O Lord, who in the beginning founded the earth, and whose hands' works are the heavens, be praise and honour for ever and ever. Amen."

units.la: Atque sic hactenus fuit prima assumptionis nostræ pars, quod nempe Christus cœlum, terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt creauerit: rit:sequitur iam secunda,quod idem omnia sua vi,ac virtute cum Patre conseruet,ac moderetur quod confirmant sequentia Scripturæ testimonia: Ioh.5.verf.17. Pater meus adhuc operatur,& ego operor:quod non de creatione, sed de conseruatione est intelligendum, vt omnes loci circunstantiæ cuincunt. Col. 1. verf.17. Per eum omnia consistunt. Hoc est ille omnia illa opera creationis, quę prius per species ordine recensuit, per suam vim, gubernat, vegetat,moderatur,agitat,& conseruat, sic vt præsideat tam Angelis, quàm hominibus,cogátque in ordinem omnes creaturas in cœlo & in terra. Hebr.1.v.3. Qui cùm sit splendor gloriæ, & character personæ illius,sustinéatque omnia verbo illo potente suo, &c. quibus verbis Christo rerum omnium conseruatio, & sustentatio diserté tribuitur. Atque de hac prouidentia, & conseruationis operibus cùm nihil agat Aduersarius, hisce sic breuiter propositis, ad sequentia progrediemur.
units.tr: And so far the first part of our assumption has been dealt with, namely that Christ created heaven, earth, and all that is in them. There follows the second part, that the same Christ, with the Father, preserves and governs all things by his power and virtue. This is confirmed by the following testimonies of Scripture: John 5:17, "My Father is still working, and I am working," which must be understood of preservation and not of creation, as all the circumstances of the passage make clear. Col. 1:17, "In him all things consist." That is, he governs, quickens, directs, moves, and preserves by his power all those works of creation which he earlier listed in order by kinds, so that he presides over angels as well as men, and brings all creatures in heaven and on earth into order. Heb. 1:3, "who, being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person, upholds all things by the word of his power," etc. In these words the preservation and sustaining of all things is expressly ascribed to Christ. Since my opponent says nothing about this providence and these works of preservation, and since these points have now been briefly set out, we shall proceed to what follows.

units.la: CAPVT XI. In quo argumentum secundum,ab operibus diuinis, nempe miraculis,proponitur,ac deferditur, & simul de potentia, ac potestate Christi agitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. In which the second argument, from the divine works, namely miracles, is proposed and defended, and at the same time the power and authority of Christ are discussed.

units.la: VIA capite superiore actum est de operibus creationis,& conseruationis rerum omnium,sequitur vt hoc capite opera Christi miraculosa subiiciamus: & quia Osiorriodius vno eodemque capite, de persona ac potestate Christi agit,vtramque nos quoque considerabimus.
units.tr: In the previous chapter we dealt with the works of creation and preservation of all things. It follows that in this chapter we set out the miraculous works of Christ. And because Ostorrodius, in one and the same chapter, treats of the person and power of Christ, we too shall consider both.

units.la: Argumentum igitur à miraculis talè est.
units.tr: The argument from miracles, then, runs as follows.

units.la: Qui propria virtute,non tantùm potest miracula,id est,opera contra naturam, & causarum secundarum ordinem,seu effectus naturæ cursum,&aciem humani ingenii superantes,edere,vcrùm etiam aliis miracula autoritate ipsius dispensandi facultatem committere:ille est omnipotens,ac proinde verus & æternus Deus,
units.tr: He who by his own power can perform not merely miracles, that is, works which are beyond nature and the order of secondary causes, or which surpass the course of nature and the reach of human understanding, but can also commit to others the faculty of working miracles by his authority, is omnipotent, and therefore the true and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui Christus propria virtute non tantum miracula plurima, id est, opera contra naturam, & causarum secundarum ordinem, seu effectus natura currum, & aciem humani ingenii superantes, edidit, verum etiam aliis, nempe discipulis suis, facultatem commisit, autoritate ipsius, eiusmodi miracula dispensandi.
units.tr: But Christ by his own power performed not merely very many miracles, that is, works beyond nature and the order of secondary causes, or which surpass the course of nature and the reach of human understanding, but also committed to others, namely his disciples, the faculty of working such miracles by his authority.

units.la: Ergo Christus est omnipotens, ac proinde verus & aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is omnipotent, and therefore the true and eternal God.

units.la: Maior probatur.
units.tr: The major premise is proved.

units.la: Quia videlicet nulla est omnium creatura quae possit ordinem inuertere potentia finita, non homo, non Diabolus, non Angeli, sed solus Deus id praestare potest, qui autor, Dominus, & gubernator est naturae, ac potentia sua naturae totius limites infinite superat, Psal. 72. 18. Benedictus Iehoua Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Psal. 136. 4. Eum, scilicet, laudate, qui facit mirabilia magna solus.
units.tr: For clearly there is no creature at all which can overturn the order of things by finite power: neither man, nor the devil, nor angels; only God, who is the author, Lord, and governor of nature, can do this, and whose power infinitely surpasses all the limits of nature. Psalm 72:18, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things." Psalm 136:4, "To him who alone does great wonders, praise him."

units.la: Christum autem eiusmodi miracula sua sibi insita virtute patrasse, ex historia Euangelica liquet. Sic aegri grauissimis liberantur morbis, modo verbo Christi nudo tum praesentes, vt paralyticus, Matth. 9. verf. 6. 7. tum absentes, vt Centurionis famulus, Matth. 8. verf. 13. modo per contactum, vt socrus Petri, Matth. 8. 15 duo caeci, Matth. 9. verf. 28. 29. & mulier, Matth. 9. verf. 22. Sic imperat ventis, & mari, daemones eius agnoscunt imperium, & trepidi fugiunt, mors ipsa ad nutum eius reddit mortuos viuis, morbi deploratissimi quiquam diffugiunt, & sanitati locum credunt, fames etiam insolito more ab eo sedatur. Vide Ioh. 9. verf. 11. Matth. 8. verf. 3. & 32. Matth. 9. verf. 25. & 12. verf. 13. & 14. verf. 19. & 15. verf. 36. Mar. 4. 38. & 9. 23. Luc. 4. 35. & 6. 19. ac passim alibi.
units.tr: That Christ performed such miracles by a power inherent in himself is clear from the evangelical history. Thus the sick are freed from the gravest diseases, sometimes by his bare word, both when present, as the paralytic (Matt. 9:6, 7), and when absent, as the centurion's servant (Matt. 8:13); sometimes by touch, as Peter's mother-in-law (Matt. 8:15), the two blind men (Matt. 9:28, 29), and the woman (Matt. 9:22). So he commands the winds and the sea; the demons acknowledge his authority and flee in terror; death itself at his nod gives back the dead to the living; the most desperate diseases flee away and yield their place to health; even hunger is quelled by him in an unusual manner. See John 9:11; Matt. 8:3, 32; Matt. 9:25; Matt. 12:13; Matt. 14:19; Matt. 15:36; Mark 4:38; Mark 9:23; Luke 4:35; Luke 6:19, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: Non solum autem ipse, propria vi ac virtute, quam in se ipso habuit eiusmodi stupenda edidit miracula, verum etiam aliis, nempe discipulis suis, in nomine ac virtute ipsius, eiusmodi miracula dispensandi, vim ac facultatem concessit: Matth. 10. 1. Tunc vocatis duodecim discipulis, dedit eis potestatem aduersus Spiritus impuros, vt eiicerent eos, & sanarent omnem morbum, & omnem languorem. Hinc in nomine Iesu, & per fidem in nomen ipsius sanantur morbi, Act. 3. verf. 6. & 16. & cap. 4. verf. 10. & 9. v. 34. & Spiritus impuri eiiciuntur, Act. 16. v. 18. Ex quibus omnibus admiadmirandis operibus liquidò constat, Christum potentia diuina, ac infinita virtute illa omnia præstitisse, ac proinde verum & æternum Deum esse. Deus det Aduersariis nostris spiritum sanctum suum, cuius luce illustrentur & illuminentur mentes ipsorum, vt in operibus illis admirandis Christi æternam potentiam & sapientiam videant, & in verbo veritatem agnoscant, & amplectantur.
units.tr: Moreover, he did not only himself, by his own power and virtue, which he had in himself, perform such astonishing miracles; he also granted to others, namely his disciples, the power and faculty of working such miracles in his name and by his virtue: Matt. 10:1, "Then, calling his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity." Hence diseases are healed in the name of Jesus and through faith in his name (Acts 3:6, 16; Acts 4:10; Acts 9:34), and unclean spirits are cast out (Acts 16:18). From all these admirable works it is clearly established that Christ accomplished all these things by divine power and infinite virtue, and therefore that he is the true and eternal God. May God give our opponents his Holy Spirit, by whose light their minds may be enlightened and illumined, so that in those admirable works they may see the eternal power and wisdom of Christ, and may recognise and embrace the truth in the Word.

units.la: Argumentum alterum de Dominio, ac potestate Christi.
units.tr: The second argument, concerning the dominion and power of Christ.

units.la: Antequam verò hoc argumentum à nobis proponatur, monendus mihi est Oftorrodius, duplicem esse dominatum ac potestatem Christi. Vnum essentialem, æternum, tribus personis diuinis communem, & essentiæ diuinæ proprium, quo Christus secundùm diuinam naturam cum Patre & Spiritu sancto regnat in omnibus, & potestatem habet super omnia ab æterno in æternum. Alterum verò dispensatione voluntaria assumptum, & per gratiam vnionis communicatum, adeóque temporarium, & personæ singularem, quo ille in vnitate personæ, & operationum, regnat in omnibus, & potestatem habet super omnia in Ecclesia, cuius principium & finis in tempore, cum principio & consummatione Ecclesiæ est coniunctum. Atque de priore, non posteriore nobis hic est sermo. Vnde tale exurgit Argumentum:
units.tr: Before we put forward this argument, Ostorrodius must be reminded by me that the dominion and power of Christ is twofold. The first is essential, eternal, common to the three divine persons, and proper to the divine essence. By it Christ, according to the divine nature, reigns over all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and has power over all things from eternity to eternity. The second is taken up by voluntary dispensation and communicated through the grace of union, and so is temporary and proper to the person. By it he reigns over all things in the Church, in the unity of his person and operations, and has power over all things there; its beginning and end in time are joined with the beginning and consummation of the Church. It is of the former, not the latter, that we speak here. Hence the following argument arises:

units.la: Qui supremum & absolutum habet ius in res omnino omnes, adeoque absolutam & legitimam potestatem, & autoritatem, de rebus omnibus, vtpote suis, ex mero voluntatis arbitrio disponendi, ita vt sit supremus rerum omnium Dominus, & prorsus ille etiam est verus & æternus ille Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whoever has the supreme and absolute right over absolutely all things, and therefore absolute and lawful power and authority over all things, to dispose of them as his own by the mere decision of his will, so that he is the supreme Lord of all things, is also altogether the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Christus supremum & absolutum habet ius in res omnino omnes, adeoque absolutam & legitimam potestatem, & autoritatem de rebus omnibus, vtpote suis ex mero voluntatis arbitrio disponendi, ita vt sit supremus rerum omnium Dominus, & prorsus.
units.tr: But Christ has the supreme and absolute right over absolutely all things, and therefore absolute and lawful power and authority over all things, to dispose of them as his own by the mere decision of his will, so that he is the supreme Lord of all things, and altogether.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus & æternus ille Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Maioris propositionis veritatem ostendit Scriptura, Actor. 17. verf. 24. Deus qui fecit mundum, & omnia, quæ in eo sunt, quum sit cœli ac terræ Dominus in manufactis templis non habitat. 1. Timoth. 6. 15. Quem temporibus suis ostendet ille beatus & solus Princeps, Rex Re-
units.tr: The truth of the major premise is shown by Scripture. Acts 17. v. 24: "God, who made the world and all things that are in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands." 1 Tim. 6. v. 15: "Which he will show in his own times, the blessed and only Potentate, King of kings, and

units.la: L gum, & Dominus Dominorum. Vide etiam Pfal.24.v.1.& 50.v.10.11. 12. 1.Chron.29.verf.11.2. Matth.11.v.25. Iud.v. 4. Iob.9.v.12.14.33. Ef.45.v.9.& passim alibi.
units.tr: Lord of lords." See also Ps. 24. v. 1; Ps. 50. v. 10, 11, 12; 1 Chron. 29. v. 11; Matt. 11. v. 25; Jude v. 4; Job 9. v. 12, 14, 33; Isa. 45. v. 9, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: Assumptionis autem veritatem hac ratione demonstramus.
units.tr: We demonstrate the truth of the minor premise by the following reasoning.

units.la: Qui cælum ac terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt creauit; ille etiam supremum & absolutum ius habet in res omnino omnes, adeoque absolutam & legitimam potestatem, & autoritatem de rebus omnibus vt pote suis, ex mero voluntatis arbitrio disponendi, ita vt sit supremus rerum omnium Dominus, & plane αὐτοκράτωρ.
units.tr: Whoever created heaven and earth and all things that are in them, that one also has the supreme and absolute right over absolutely all things, and therefore absolute and lawful power and authority over all things, to dispose of them as his own by the mere decision of his will, so that he is the supreme Lord of all things, and plainly autocrat [αὐτοκράτωρ].

units.la: Atqui Christus cælum ac terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt creauit, quemadmodum superiori capite demonstrauimus, & Apostolus illud disertis verbis testatur Hebr. capit.1. verf.10. Tu Domine in initio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cæli.
units.tr: But Christ created heaven and earth and all things that are in them, as we demonstrated in the previous chapter. The Apostle also testifies to this in plain words, Heb. chap. 1. v. 10: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands."

units.la: Ergo Christus supremum & absolutum ius habet in res omnino omnes, adeoque absolutam & legitimam potestatem de rebus omnibus, vt pote suis, ex mero voluntatis arbitrio, disponendi, ita vt sit supremus rerum omnium Dominus, & prorsus αὐτοκράτωρ.
units.tr: Therefore Christ has the supreme and absolute right over absolutely all things, and therefore absolute and lawful power and authority over all things, to dispose of them as his own by the mere decision of his will, so that he is the supreme Lord of all things, and plainly autocrat [αὐτοκράτωρ].

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo tertio hanc quæstionem proponit, An nimirum ex potentia & potestate Christi diuina aliqua in ipso natura euinci ac demonstrari possit: quam ipsam quæstionem αὐτοπραγματικῶς tractat, argumento negationis inde sumpto, quod videlicet omnis potentia atque potestas Christo, ab ipso Deo Patre, & quidem maxima ex parte, vt præmium obedientiæ, fit data, atque concessa.
units.tr: In chapter thirteen of his Institutions, Ostorrodius proposes this question: whether, namely, some divine nature in Christ can be proved and demonstrated from the divine power and authority of Christ. He treats this very question in a practical manner [αὐτοπραγματικῶς], using an argument from denial drawn from the fact that all power and authority is given and granted to Christ by God the Father himself, and indeed for the most part, as the reward of obedience.

units.la: Argumentum ipsius tale est:
units.tr: His argument runs as follows:

units.la: Qui omnem suam potentiam ac potestatem ab alio, & quidem maximam ex parte, vt præmium præstitæ a se obedientiæ accepit, ille nulla ratione potest esse idem ipse, cui nullam ob causam dari quicquam potest, nempe vnus Deus.
units.tr: Whoever has received all his power and authority from another, and indeed for the most part as the reward of obedience rendered by him, cannot in any way be that same one to whom nothing can be given for any reason, namely the one God.

units.la: Atqui Christus omnem suam potentiam ac potestatem ab alio, & quidem maximam partem, vt præmium præstitæ a se obedientiæ, accepit.
units.tr: But Christ has received all his power and authority from another, and indeed for the most part as the reward of obedience rendered by him.

units.la: Ergo Christus nulla ratione potest esse ille idem, cui nihil quicquam dari potest, nempe vnus ille Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ cannot in any way be that same one to whom nothing can be given, namely that one God.

units.la: Resp. Quia hoc argumentum generale est, verba autem illa de praemio, partem tantum respiciunt, ex qua de toto in vniuersum, nihil concludi potest, ideo illis hic omissis, & responsioni ad argumentum particulare reseruatis, ad argumentum respondemus per distinctionem. Christus enim suam potentiam & potestatem accepisse dicitur ab alio, id est, qui alius sit, aut ratione essentiae, habeatque essentiam a Christi essentia, siue specie, siue numero differentem: aut, qui eandem numero habeat essentiam, sed modum in ea subsistendi diuersum, & sit alia persona: aut qui ita sit alius vt & essentiam, siue specie, siue numero ab essentia Christi differentem, & alium subsistendi modum habeat, qua ratione humana aliqua persona a persona diuina differt, & differret persona Christi, si φιλὸς ἀνθρωπῷ esset, vt Aduersarii contendunt. Deus deinde dicitur vel ὁμοούσιος, & essentialiter de tota Trinitate, vel ὑποστατικῶς de persona Patris, Filii, ac Spiritus sancti. Hisce igitur (nihil dicam hoc loco de voluntaria Christi dispensatione, & liberrima οἰκονομία, cuius respectu multa de Christo praedicantur, quae tamen ipsius Deitati nihil derogare possunt) distinctionibus ad intelligentiam syllogismi necessariis, promissis, liquido constat consequentiam nullam in argumentatione esse. Si enim dicatur in hunc modum: Quicunque omnem suam potentiam & potestatem ab alio accipit, nempe Deo, id est, qui ita alius est a Filio, at non tantum modo subsistendi, sed etiam essentia, siue numero diuersa, siue specie disparata aut contraria differat, ille revera unus cum illo, qui nullas ob causas accipere quicquam a quoquam potest, Deus esse nequit, quacunque etiam ratione vocabulum Deus accipiatur. At hoc sensu minor erit salsissima, quippe in qua sit futura manifesta principii petitio. Haec enim est ipsa principalis controuersia: An nimirum Christus eandem cum Patre essentiam diuinam communem habeat, & proprietate personali, & incommunicabili ab eodem distinguatur? Huius negationem dum sibi concessam sumit Ostorrodius, maxima falsitate, & fraude ludit. Sin vero Deus intelligatur relate, vt vnus Deus ὑποστατικῶς significet vnum Deum Patrem, tum argumentum totum conceditur, nec sententiam nostram impugnat: certissimum n. est nec Filium, nec Spiritum S. neque vllum subiectum aliud, quodcunque illud sit, praeter primam sacrosanctae Trinitatis personam, vnum illum Deum Patre esse. Sin vero denique in hunc modum dicatur: Quicunque omnem suam potentiam accipit ab alio, id est, ab alia quidem persona, quae tamen eandem cum altero essentiam, non specie, sed numero habeat: ille non potest esse unus ille Deus, id est, communem habere essentiam Dei, cui nullam ob causam dari quicquam potest: tum assumptio quidem fuerit vera, at propositio cum conclusione, etiam in rebus physicis hisce, & naturalibus, nedum in divinis, & hyperphysicis, salsissima. Non ne enim homo homini tum essentiam, tum personae aequalitatem, tum etiam proprietates humanas cæteras communicare potest? Hoc igitur cur Deo Patri derogaremus? An vero Abel, qui & essentiam, & aequalitatem personae ac operationum ab Adamo sibi communicatam habuit, eandem essentiam non aeque habiturus, & in numerum hominum referendus fuisset, etiamsi Adamus a nullo principio superiori extitisset? Sed ignorat Oftorrodius genus istud principiorum, habere nempe aliquid a se ipso, vel ab alio, ad causam efficientem referendam esse, quae ipsum effectum nunquam ingrediatur, & circa quem etiam numero eundem varii causae efficientis modi occupari possint. Sublatis igitur omnibus ambiguitatum cespitibus, ad hunc deveniendum est cardinem: An Christus ideo non potuit esse verus ac aeternus Deus, id est, habere cum Patre communem essentiam divinam, cui nihil dari a quoquam possit, quia videlicet omnem suam potentiam & potestatem a Deo Patre suo acceperit? Nos negamus constantissime, affirmare autem videtur Oftorrodius, eo quod opposita sint inter se, Deum esse, id est, habere essentiam divinam, cui ob summam perfectionem, & simplicitatem nihil accedere, aut decedere possit, & tamen a Patre omnem potentiam & potestatem accepisse. Sed rem penitus intuenti nulla contrarietas apparebit, cum Filius Dei per generationem æternam, essentiam divinam, & cum illa potentiam & potestatem acceperit, unde utrumque de Christo verissime, & sine ulla contradictione praedicabitur, quod & Deus sit, cui nihil dari a quoquam aut ullam ob causam possit, & quod omnem suam potentiam ac potestatem a Patre acceperit: sed illud ratione essentiae, hoc respectu personae, quæ respectuum diversitas omnem contradictionem & contrarietatem tollit.
units.tr: Reply. Since this argument is general, while the words about the reward concern only a part, from which nothing can be concluded about the whole in general, we set those words aside here, reserving them for the response to the particular argument, and we answer the argument by distinction. Christ is said to have received his power and authority from another, that is, from one who is other either in respect of essence, having an essence different from Christ's essence, whether in species or in number; or who has the same essence in number but a different mode of subsisting in it, and is another person; or who is so other that he differs both in essence, whether in species or in number, from Christ's essence, and also has a different mode of subsisting. By this last reasoning some human person differs from a divine person, and the person of Christ would differ in this way if he were a friend of man [φιλὸς ἀνθρώπῳ], as our opponents contend. Next, God is said either homoousios [ὁμοούσιος], essentially, of the whole Trinity, or hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς], of the person of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. With these distinctions, which are necessary for understanding the syllogism (I will say nothing here about Christ's voluntary dispensation and most free economy [οἰκονομία], in respect of which many things are predicated of Christ which nonetheless detract nothing from his Deity), it is clearly established that there is no valid inference in the argument. For if it is put this way: "Whoever receives all his power and authority from another, namely from God, that is, from one who is other than the Son not only in mode of subsisting but also differs in essence, whether numerically diverse or specifically disparate or contrary, is in reality not one with him who for no cause can receive anything from anyone, and so cannot be God, in whatever sense the word God is taken." But in this sense the minor premise will be most false, since it would be a manifest petitio principii. For this is the very principal controversy: whether Christ has the same divine essence in common with the Father, and is distinguished from him by a personal and incommunicable property. While Ostorrodius takes the denial of this as conceded to him, he plays with the greatest falsehood and deceit. But if God is understood relatively, so that "one God" signifies hypostatically one God the Father, then the whole argument is conceded and does not attack our view. For it is most certain that neither the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor any other subject whatever, apart from the first person of the most holy Trinity, is that one God the Father. But if finally it is put in this form: "Whoever receives all his power from another," that is, from another person who nevertheless has the same essence, not in species but in number, "cannot be that one God," that is, have the common essence of God, to which nothing can be given for any cause: then the assumption indeed would be true, but the proposition with its conclusion would be most false, even in these physical and natural things, let alone in divine and hyperphysical ones. For can a man not communicate to another man his essence, equality of person, and his other human properties? Why then should we deny this to God the Father? Or would Abel, who received his essence, equality of person and of operations from Adam, not have the same essence equally, and should he not be reckoned in the number of men, even if Adam had not come from any higher principle? But Ostorrodius is ignorant of that kind of principle: that having something from oneself or from another must be referred to the efficient cause, which never enters into the effect itself, and about which various modes of efficient cause may be concerned, numerically the same. Therefore, with all the stumbling blocks of ambiguity removed, we must come to this pivotal question: whether Christ therefore could not be the true and eternal God, that is, have the divine essence in common with the Father, to which nothing can be given by anyone, because he received all his power and authority from God the Father. We constantly deny it. Ostorrodius, however, seems to affirm that these are opposed to one another: that he is God, that is, has the divine essence, to which nothing can be added or taken away because of its supreme perfection and simplicity, and yet has received all power and authority from the Father. But to one who looks at the matter thoroughly, no contrariety will appear. The Son of God, by eternal generation, received the divine essence and with it power and authority. Whence both things can be predicated of Christ most truly and without any contradiction: that he is God, to whom nothing can be given by anyone or for any cause, and that he has received all his power and authority from the Father. The former is said in respect of essence, the latter in respect of person, and this difference of respects removes all contradiction and contrariety.

units.la: Nihilominus tamen Oftorrodius, quasi propositio maior extra omnem controversiae & dubitationis aleam constituta esset, ad probationem assumptionis progreditur, cuius refutationem, licet destrudestructo fundamento, nempe propositione, non opus esset, ut quicquam de illa ageremus, perstringemus tamen, quò tum responsionis Sophisticae falsitas, tum doctrinae nostrae veritas eò magis elucescat.
units.tr: Nevertheless Ostorrodius, as if the major premise were placed beyond all chance of controversy or doubt, goes on to prove the minor. Its refutation would need no treatment from us, since the foundation, namely the major premise, has been destroyed. Still, we will touch on it, so that both the falsity of his sophistical reply and the truth of our doctrine may shine forth all the more clearly.

units.la: Ad concinnandam itaque assumptionis illius probationem, potentiam ac potestatem Christi pro ratione diuersi temporis dupliciter consIderat, ante resurrectionem Christi, & post resurrectionem eius, ac in coelum ascensum. Quod attinet ad potentiam Christi, quam exeruit ante resurrectionem suam, tale argumentum nostrorum Doctorum videtur proponere.
units.tr: To work out the proof of that minor premise, he considers the power and authority of Christ in two ways, according to the different times: before Christ's resurrection, and after his resurrection and ascension into heaven. As for the power Christ exercised before his resurrection, our teachers seem to put forward this argument.

units.la: Quicunque potentiam habet miracula patrandi, ille est verus ac aeternus Deus. Psal. 72. v. 18. Benedictus sit Iehouah Deus, Deus Israelis, qui facit mirabilia solus.
units.tr: Whoever has the power to work miracles is the true and eternal God. Psalm 72:18: Blessed be Jehovah God, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders.

units.la: Atqui Christus ante resurrectionem potentiam habuit miracula patrandi, quia non tantum aegrotis sanitatem restituit, & mortuos resuscitauit, verùm etiam mari ac ventis, imò & malis Spiritibus imperauit, qui omnes ipsi obedierunt.
units.tr: But Christ, before his resurrection, had the power to work miracles, because he not only restored health to the sick and raised the dead, but also commanded the sea and the winds, and even the evil spirits, and all of them obeyed him.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus ac aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum respondet Aduersarius negando consequentiam, ratione negationis ducta ab absurdo. Si enim, inquit, Christus ideo verus esset Deus, quia miracula patrauit, sequeretur etiam omnes, quotquot unquam miracula ediderunt, unum illum & aeternum Deum esse. Hoc autem, quia manifestè falsum sit, liquidò inde quoque constare, verba Psalmi à Trinitariis non rectè intelligi, quippe quorum sensus sit, non quòd nemo miracula edere possit, praeter unum illum ac verum Deum, sed quòd omnia vera miracula à solo Deo proficiscantur, & ille solus potentiam à se ipso habeat eiusmodi miracula patrandi. Ac proinde si quis ex miraculis Christi diuinam in Christo naturam probare vellet, eum demonstrare oportere, Christum à se ipso potentiam illa patrandi habuisse. Quòd autem nihil à se ipso fecerit, aut etiam facere potuerit, Christum ipsum de se verbis disertis testari, Ioh. 5. v. 19. & 30. Ac proinde Christum nulla miracula à se ipso, id est, propria virtute, sed Patrem illa omnia per ipsum patrasse, Act. 2. v. 22.
units.tr: The adversary replies to this argument by denying the consequence, and he uses a reduction to absurdity. For if, he says, Christ were therefore the true God because he worked miracles, it would follow that all who have ever worked miracles are that one and eternal God. Since this is manifestly false, it is plainly clear from this that the words of the Psalm are not rightly understood by the Trinitarians. Their sense, as they take it, is not that no one can work miracles except that one true God, but that all true miracles proceed from God alone, and that he alone has the power of working such miracles from himself. Accordingly, if anyone wished to prove the divine nature in Christ from Christ's miracles, he would have to show that Christ had the power of working them from himself. That Christ did nothing of himself, or could do nothing, Christ himself testifies about himself in plain words, John 5:19 and 30. And so Christ worked no miracles by himself, that is, by his own power, but the Father performed all of them through him, Acts 2:22.

units.la: Resp. Ἀλόγως & ἀμαθῶς omnia ab Aduersario tractantur: quum enim assumptionem syllogismi sui probandam sibi sumpserit, quid opus fuit aut argumenta nostra recensere, aut refutare? Videamus tamen qua fide ab ipso vtrumque praestetur. Argumentum nostrum quod attinet, certè vitiosè proponitur ab ipso, ipsius potissimo neruo omisso. Non enim simpliciter ab ipso facto, hoc est, patratione miraculorum, sed à virtute, ex qua illa proficiscebantur, & quam in ipso Christo residere, res ipsa loquitur, & ipsi Samosatenianæ sectæ principes fatentur, argumentamur, Christúmque ideo verum & æternum Deum esse affirmamus, non quia simpliciter miracula patrauerit, sed quia in illis faciendis ita propriam ipsius virtutem exeruit, vt aliis quoque, nempe Apostolis, dispensationem miraculorum sua autoritate commiserit, quemadmodum ab initio huius capitis demonstrabimus. Absurdum igitur illud quod affingit consequentiæ nostræ Qstorrodius, non argumento nostro, sed ignorantiæ ipsius est impingendum, qui contra iustæ comparationis leges, terminos impares, Christum nempe, & cæteros, qui vnquam miracula patrarunt, in affectione impari, nempe patratione miraculorum, imperitissimè coniungit. Tum demum enim ex nostro argumento sequeretur, omnes quotquot vnquam miracula (vera intelligo, nec de præstigiis Diaboli quicquam dico) ediderunt, vnum illum verum Deum esse, si videlicet demonstraretur, eadem non tantum, sed in ipsis remanente virtute, quemadmodum Christus fecit, miracula non solùm patrasse, sed propria autoritate aliis quoque miracula patrandi potestatem dedisse. At quàm falsum hoc sit, discatOstorrodius à suo præceptore Fausto Socino, qui in libello suo aduersus Francifcum Dauidis de inuocando Christo pagina 72. & 73. in hunc modum scribit: Apostolorum potestas in eo potissimum diuersa à Chr: si potestate fuit, quod ipse virtute Patris in se manente res fecit & facit, illi vero virtute quidem eadem, sed non in ipsis, verum in Christo residente faciebant, in cuius nomine operabantur. Et cùm hoc pluribus Scripturæ locis confirmasset, tandem concludens, Ex quibus, inquit, præter multa alia quæ adferri possent, apparet Christum potestatem in se ipso habuisse ea faciendi, quæ faciebat, quantumuis admiranda opera, atque vt id crederetur, voluisse. Et paulò post: Ex quibus manifestum fit, inquit, virtutem, quæ miracula ab Apostolis fiebant, in ipsis Apostolis non fuisse, sed in nomine & potestate Iesu Christi omnia facta esse. Vide etiam de hoc miraculorum à Christo & Apostolis patratorum discrimine ipsum Ostorrodium in Institutionibus capite decimo nono, pag.113. Hinc liquidò constat, nulla ratione illud absurdum ex nostro argumento educi aut confici posse: quod cùm ita sit, qua fronte audet Ostorrodius tam manifesto innixus elencho affirmare, Verba Psalmi à nobis, quos per inuidiam Trinitarios appellat, male intelligi, aut explicari? Nos enim quum vera miracula à solo Deo proficisci cum Dauide affirmamus, non simpliciter de ipso effecto, aut quauis efficiente causa, sed de ipsa virtute primaria loquimur, ex qua illa omnia, quacunque etiam interueniente causa instrumentali, aut administra, fluunt, eámque in solo Deo residere affirmamus. Quod verò Ostorrodius addit, Deum illam virtutem à se ipso habere, verum quidem est, & huc etiam respicit Dauid, sed Deus de essentia &, non autem Trinitarius de hac aut illa persona sacrosanctæ Trinitatis intelligitur, quo ipso veritas sententiæ nostræ minimè euertitur, vt in responsione nostra ad argumentum Aduersarii demonstrabimus, quod tale est:
units.tr: Reply. Everything the adversary handles is done irrationally and ignorantly [Ἀλόγως καὶ ἀμαθῶς]. Since he has taken upon himself the task of proving the minor premise of his own syllogism, what was the point of either reviewing our arguments or refuting them? Still, let us see with what good faith he does both. As for our argument, he certainly sets it out badly, having left out its chief strength. We do not argue merely from the deed itself, that is, from the working of miracles, but from the power from which they proceed, which resides in Christ himself, as the thing itself makes plain and as the leaders of the Samosatene sect themselves admit. We affirm that Christ is therefore the true and eternal God, not because he simply worked miracles, but because in working them he so exercised his own power that he also committed to others, namely the apostles, the dispensing of miracles by his own authority, as we shall show from the beginning of this chapter. So the absurdity that Ostorrodius attributes to our inference is to be charged not to our argument but to his own ignorance. Contrary to the laws of a fair comparison, he most unskilfully couples unequal terms: Christ and all the others who ever worked miracles, in an unequal affection, namely the working of miracles. Only then would it follow from our argument that all who have ever worked miracles (I mean true ones; I say nothing here about the tricks of the Devil) are that one true God, if it were shown that they not only performed the same works as Christ, but also, with the same power remaining in them, gave others the power to work miracles by their own authority. But how false this is, let Ostorrodius learn from his teacher Faustus Socinus, who in his little book against Francis David, On Invoking Christ, pages 72 and 73, writes in this way: The power of the apostles differed from that of Christ chiefly in this, that he by the power of the Father did and does things while remaining in himself, whereas they indeed worked by the same power, but not residing in themselves, rather residing in Christ, in whose name they worked. And when he had confirmed this by several passages of Scripture, concluding at last he says: From these, among many other things that could be cited, it appears that Christ had in himself the power to do the things he did, however admirable the works, and that he willed this to be believed. And a little later: From these it is manifest, he says, that the power by which miracles were done by the apostles was not in the apostles themselves, but that all things were done in the name and power of Jesus Christ. See also Ostorrodius himself on this distinction between the miracles worked by Christ and those worked by the apostles, in the Institutions, chapter nineteen, page 113. From this it is clearly established that by no reasoning can that absurdity be drawn or made out of our argument. Since this is so, with what face does Ostorrodius dare, leaning so plainly on this refutation, to assert that the words of the Psalm are badly understood or explained by us, whom out of spite he calls Trinitarians? For when we affirm with David that true miracles proceed from God alone, we are not speaking simply of the effect itself, or of any efficient cause whatever, but of the primary power itself, from which all those works flow, even when some intervening instrumental or subordinate cause is involved, and we affirm that this power resides in God alone. As for Ostorrodius adding that God has that power from himself, this is indeed true, and David also has this in view; but God is understood according to essence, and not as a Trinitarian, that is, of this or that person of the most holy Trinity. By this very fact the truth of our view is in no way overturned, as we shall demonstrate in our reply to the adversary's argument, which runs as follows:

units.la: Si ex operibus illis miraculosis diuina aliqua in Christo natura demonstrari posset, tum Christus à se ipso vim ac potentiam habuisset illa miracula patrandi.
units.tr: If some divine nature in Christ could be demonstrated from those miraculous works, then Christ would have had the power and might to work those miracles from himself.

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum, Iohan. cap.5. verf.19. Amen Amen dico vobis, non potest Filius à semetipso operari, nisi viderit Patrem operantem: quacunque autem ille facit, Filius pariter facit. &c verf.30. Non possum ego à me ipso facere quicquam. Actor. cap.2. verf.22. Viri Israelitæ, audite sermones istos, Iesum illum Nazarenum, virum à Deo approbatum, apud vos præstantibus factis, & miraculis & signis, quæ edidit per eum Deus, in medio vestri, sicut ipsi nostis.
units.tr: But the consequent is false: John 5:19, Verily, verily, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does. And verse 30: I can of myself do nothing. Acts 2:22: Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by mighty deeds, and wonders, and signs, which God did through him in the midst of you, as you yourselves know.

units.la: Ergo & antecedens falsum est.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Resp. Falsam esse consequentiam, & ne quidem in rebus hisce physicis & naturalibus veram.
