Tu enim Ostorrodi, homo es, nec opinor, inficiaberis, humanásque actiones exeris virtute humana, an verò ex illis ad humanam tuam essentiam, ac naturam, tanquam ex effecto proprio, ad causam propriam non licebit argumentari, eò quòd nec operandi vim & facultatem, nec eius principium, naturam nempe & essentiam humanam abs te ipso habeas, sed parentibus tuis illa omnia accepta referre teneariis? Nonne vides te, tibi, naturæ, & tuæ, & vniuersæ iniuriam facturum, si salsissimos illos tuos canones, tanquam infallibilia κριτήρια, & certissimam iudicandi normam obtrudere voluceris? Atque hanc propositionis falsitatem demonstrasse licet sufficeret, quia tamen illa chorda perpetuò oberrat Osiorrodius, assumptionem quoque vna cum dictis Scripturæ examinabimus. Christum igitur secundùm naturam diuinam consideramus vel οὐσίας, seu ratione essentiæ, & quatenus est Deus absolutè, eandem cum Patre ac Spiritu sancto essentiam habens, vel ὑποστατικῶς, quatenus secundùm relationem Filius est à Patre. Priori respectu si consideretur Christus, tum falsa est minor. Vt enim Christus ratione essentiæ est αὐτόθεος & ἀγέννητος, ita etiam proprietates essentiales, & virtutem operandi diuinam à nullo habet, quia ipsa essentia est primum principiū omni principio alio etiam generationis, processionis, & ordinis carens. Neque minor locis illis Scripturæ confirmatur, quæ de Christo non quatenus Deus absolutè, sed quatenus filius est, loquuntur, vt postea ostendemus.
units.tr: Reply. The consequence is false, and it is not even true in these physical and natural matters. For you, Ostorrodius, are a man, and I do not think you will deny that you exercise human actions by human power. Yet may one not argue from those actions to your human essence and nature, as from a proper effect to its proper cause, on the ground that you have neither the power and faculty of acting nor its principle, namely your nature and essence as a human, from yourself, but are bound to credit all of these to your parents? Do you not see that you would do wrong to yourself, to your nature, and to the whole world, if you were willing to force upon us those most salty canons of yours as infallible criteria [κριτήρια] and the most certain norm of judgment? Although it would be enough to have demonstrated the falsity of this proposition, since Ostorrodius keeps harping on that same string, we shall also examine the minor premise along with the passages of Scripture he cites. We consider Christ according to his divine nature either as to his substance, or essence [οὐσίας], that is, according to his essence, and insofar as he is God absolutely, having the same essence as the Father and the Holy Spirit; or hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς], insofar as the Son is from the Father according to relation. If Christ is considered in the former respect, then the minor is false. For just as Christ is by essence self-God [αὐτόθεος] and unbegotten [ἀγέννητος], so he also has his essential properties and divine power of working from no one, because the essence itself is the first principle, lacking any other principle of generation, procession, or order. Nor are those passages of Scripture that speak of Christ not as God absolutely, but as Son, of less weight in confirming this, as we shall show afterwards.

units.la: Sin verò posteriori respectu Christus consideretur, falsa est propositio maior. Non enim sequitur patrationem miraculorum diuinam in Christo naturam demonstrare non posse, quia videlicet Christus illam virtutem à se ipso non habuerit: quia principium illud singulare, quod est persona, quæ est à Patre, & agit à Patre, principium agendi & operationum omnium commune, quod est essentia diuina omni principio carens, minimè tollit. Locus ex Iohanne agit de Christo, quatenus persona est à Patre genita, & iensus est: Deus Pater, vt est à se, tanquam principium deitatis, & qui essentiam à nemine communicatam habet, ita etiam à se ipso operatur, & virtutem ac potentiam à se ipso operandi habet. Esse enim à se, & operari à se ipso, se inuicem consequuntur. Vt autem Filius non est à se ipso, hoc est, essentiam diuinam nō à se ipso habet, sed à Patre per generationem æternam, ita etiam non à semet ipso operatur, hoc est, non habet virtutem illam & potentiam à se, sed à Patre sibi communicatam. Hoc autem vt ipsam essentiam, quæ illius potentiæ est principium, non tollit, ita quoque diuinæ Christi naturæ nihil præiudicare potest, quia illam virtutem licet à Patre, in se ipso tamen manentem habet, sic vt per se etiam qua Filius, etsi non à se operetur, sed à Patre: quo ipso ab omnibus creaturis cuidentissimè distinguitur, quarum nulli virtus illa, vt per se agat, est communicata: Per ipsum enim, nempe Deum, vimus, monemur, & sumus. Act. 17. v. 28. Quod verò Act. 2. 22. Deus, nempe Pater, per Christum illa miracula fecisse dicitur, id eo sensu est intelligendum, quo etiam per ipsum mundum, & omnia condicondidisse dicitur, qua de re, quia capite octauo prolixè egimus, hic repetitione non est opus. Quantum verò ad illam potestatem (quam in hoc argumeto cum potentia Oftorrodius imperitè confundit) quæ Christi resurrectionem ex mortuis, & ascensionem in cœlos est consequuta, & in eo consistit, quod Christus omnem potestatem in cœlo, ac in terra, imo claues inferorum, & mortis habeat, Apocal. 1. v. 18. & sit omnium Dominus, sit moderator, atque administrator, de illa inquam potestate, responsio Aduersarii hoc syllogismo formari potest.
units.tr: But if Christ is considered in the latter respect, the major premise is false. For it does not follow that the divine nature cannot be demonstrated from the working of miracles in Christ, on the ground that Christ did not have that power from himself. For that singular principle, which is the person who is from the Father and acts from the Father, does not in the least remove the principle of acting and of all operations, which is the divine essence, lacking any principle. The passage from John speaks of Christ as far as he is the person begotten of the Father and sent. God the Father, as he is from himself, is the principle of the Godhead, and since he has the essence communicated by no one, so he also acts from himself and has the power and might of acting from himself. For to be from oneself and to act from oneself follow one another. But just as the Son is not from himself, that is, does not have the divine essence from himself but from the Father by eternal generation, so he also does not act from himself, that is, he does not have that power and might from himself but has it communicated to him by the Father. Yet just as this does not remove the essence itself, which is the principle of that power, so it can prejudice nothing of the divine nature of Christ, because although he has that power from the Father, he nonetheless has it remaining in himself, so that through himself, even as the Son, although he does not act from himself but from the Father, he is most clearly distinguished by this very fact from all creatures, to none of whom that power has been communicated so as to act through itself. For "in him, that is God, we live, move, and have our being" (Acts 17:28). As for Acts 2:22, where God, namely the Father, is said to have done those miracles through Christ, this is to be understood in the same sense in which he is said to have created the world and all things through him; on which matter, since we treated it at length in chapter eight, there is no need to repeat it here. As for that power (which Ostorrodius unskilfully confuses in this argument with power in general), which followed Christ's resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven, and consists in this, that Christ "has all power in heaven and on earth, indeed the keys of hell and of death" (Rev. 1:18), and is Lord of all, governor and administrator, I say, concerning that power, the Adversary's answer can be formed into this syllogism:

units.la: Si ex illa Christi potestate demonstrari posset, esse in Christo aliquam diuinam naturam, tum Christus illam potestatem à se ipso haberet.
units.tr: If it could be demonstrated from that power of Christ that some divine nature is in Christ, then Christ would have that power from himself.

units.la: Atqui hanc potestatem non habet à se ipso, sed eam vt præmium obedientiæ ad mortem vsque crucis præstitæ à Patre accepit, Phil 2. v. 6. Eph. 1. verf. 20. Hebr. 2. v. 9. Matth. 28. v. 18. Act. 2. v. 36. Rom. 14. v. 9.
units.tr: But he does not have this power from himself, but received it from the Father as the reward of obedience rendered even to the death of the cross (Phil. 2:6; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 2:9; Matt. 28:18; Acts 2:36; Rom. 14:9).

units.la: Ergo ex illa Christi potestate non potest demonstrari esse aliquam in ipso diuinam naturam.
units.tr: Therefore from that power of Christ it cannot be demonstrated that some divine nature is in him.

units.la: Resp. Potestatem Christi, vt & dominatum eius, duplicem esse: vnum essentialem, æternum, & tribus personis diuinis commune: alterum verò temporarium, & dispensatiuum, cuius administrationem ex libera voluntate, & œconomia suscepit. Connexum autem falsum est, si de priore dominatu agat, quam falsitatem supra in priore connexo demonstrauimus. Sin de posteriore intelligatur, nititur falsa hypothesi, quia noftrũ demonstrationis argumentum à priore, non à posteriore dominio & potestate sumimus. Assumptio similiter, si de priore agat, falsa est, nec citatis locis probatur, quia in illis de alio dominio agitur. Sin verò de posteriore intelligatur, vt certè intelligitur, tum nihil facit contra nos, nec locis illis Scripturæ confirmatur, quæ omnia agunt, non de illa potestate, ac dominio, quod Christo est essentiale, adeóque cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto commune, sed de singulari illo, quod Mediator noster, ac <bl>διανομή</bl> dispensatione gratiæ recepit ad salutem sui corporis, nempe Ecclesiæ. Vt autem munus Christi mediatorium, deitati Christi nihil præiudicat, ita etiam hoc dispensatiuum dominium, alterum illud & essentiale minime tollit: vnde necesse non est, vt ad illa loca Scripturæ quidquam respondeamus. Manet igitur Christo Mediatori nostro sua miraculorum gloria, virtus, atque potestas, suum dominium, ius, atque autoritas, cuius luci ac splendori Ostorrodius cum Sociniana turba, frustra tenebras offundere conatur suis sophismatum & blasphemiarum praestigiis.
units.tr: I reply: the power of Christ, as also his dominion, is twofold: one essential and eternal, common to the three divine persons; the other temporary and dispensatory, whose administration he undertook from free will and by the economy. The connection is false if it speaks of the former dominion, a falsity which we demonstrated above in the earlier connection. If it is understood of the latter, it rests on a false hypothesis, because our argument of demonstration is taken from the former dominion and power, not from the latter. Likewise the assumption, if it speaks of the former, is false, nor is it proved by the passages cited, because in those passages another dominion is spoken of. But if it is understood of the latter, as indeed it is understood, then it does nothing against us, nor is it confirmed by those passages of Scripture, which all speak not of that power and dominion which is essential to Christ and therefore common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but of that singular power which our Mediator and the dispensation (οἰκονομία) of grace received for the salvation of his body, namely the Church. But just as the mediatorial office of Christ prejudices nothing of the Godhead of Christ, so also this dispensatory dominion in no way removes that other, essential one; hence there is no need for us to answer anything to those passages of Scripture. Therefore to Christ our Mediator remains his glory, power and might in miracles, his dominion, right and authority, to whose light and splendour Ostorrodius, with the Socinian crowd, vainly tries to cast shadows by the juggling tricks of his sophisms and blasphemies.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: In quo argumentum tertium ab operibus Dei proponitur, ac defenditur.
units.tr: In which the third argument, from the works of God, is put forward and defended.

units.la: RESTAT vt tertium genus operationum diuinarum, saluationis nempe, persequamur. Hic igitur quaeritur: An ex eo quod Christus in Scripturis est Saluator, ac Seruator noster dicitur, diuina aliqua in ipso natura demonstrari possit? Nos affirmamus; Ostorrodius autem Institutionum suarum capite duodecimo negat. Affirmationis nostrae duo argumenta in medium proferemus.
units.tr: It remains to pursue the third kind of divine operation, namely that of salvation. Here the question is: Can something divine in Christ's nature be demonstrated from the fact that Christ is called our Saviour and Preserver in the Scriptures? We affirm it; Ostorrodius, however, denies it in chapter twelve of his Institutions. We shall set out two arguments for our affirmation.

units.la: Primum igitur nostrum argumentum tale est.
units.tr: Our first argument is this.

units.la: Quicunque est Saluator noster, atque Seruator, ille etiam est verus ac aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whoever is our Saviour and Preserver is also the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Christus est Saluator noster, atque Seruator.
units.tr: But Christ is our Saviour and Preserver.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus & aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Maiorem propositionem nostri demonstrant, tum aliis argumentis, quibus euincitur Seruatorem mundi ac Saluatorem esse omnipotentem, omniscium, aeternum, & omnium rerum, caeli, terraeque, & omnium quae in eis sunt, supremum gubernatorem ac dominum, quae ipsius Dei essentialia sunt attributa: tum etiam illo Dei apud Esai. cap. 43. 11. testimonio Deus iustos saluans & seruans non est praeter me. Assumptionis veritas demonstratur testimonio tum Christi, qui Ioh. 10. verf. 28. inquit, Ego vitam aeternam do eis, nec peribunt in aeternum, nec rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea. Tum Patri. Act. 4. verf. 12. Nec est in alio quoquam salus, nec enim aliud nomen est sub caelo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oportet nos salvos fieri. teat nos seruari. Vnde necessario concluditur, aut Christum esse verum & æternum Deum Israelis, aut certè duos esse Saluatores, ac Seruatores, quod est absurdum atque blasphemum.
units.tr: Our side demonstrates the major premise both by other arguments, which prove that the Saviour and Preserver of the world is almighty, all-knowing, eternal, and the supreme governor and lord of all things in heaven and earth and all that is in them, which are the essential attributes of God himself; and also by that testimony of God in Isaiah 43:11, I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour. The truth of the minor premise is shown by the testimony of Christ, who says in John 10:28, I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. It is also shown by the testimony of the Father, in Acts 4:12, Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. From this it follows necessarily that either Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel, or else there are two Saviours and Preservers, which is absurd and blasphemous.

units.la: Ad argumentum ipsum non respondet Aduersarius, sed statim ad locum Esaiæ transuolat, quasi illo nobis erepto, totum nostrum argumentum corrueret. Dicit igitur primò, Christum eo tempore, quo Deus per Prophetam hæc verba enuntiauit, nondum extitisse, ac proinde Deum vnum illum saluatorem bene dici potuisse.
units.tr: The Adversary does not answer the argument itself, but at once flies to the passage from Isaiah, as if once that were wrested from us, our whole argument would collapse. He first says that Christ had not yet existed at the time when God spoke these words through the Prophet, and therefore it could rightly be said that God alone is the one Saviour.

units.la: Resp. Falsam esse hanc Ostorrodii exceptionem, & Christum verum illum & æternum Deum Israelis iam ab æterno extitisse, supra capite octauo, vbi eum huius vniuersi mundi conditorem esse, prolixè demonstrauimus, & capite sequente amplius confirmaturi sumus. Secundò ait, Verba illa, Præter me, non ita intelligenda esse, quasi nullus alius præter vnum Deum Seruator esset, sed quod omnis vera salus, per quemcunque illa etiam in nos deriuetur, à solo Deo proficiscatur, nec seruare quisquam possit, nisi is per quem Deus salutem præstet, quia in sacris literis quibusdam aliis illud nomen SERVATOR tribuatur, dicanturque de illis, quod Deus illos in Seruatores populo suo excitauerit ac dederit, vtex Iud.3. v.9. & locis aliis liquet. Quod si obiiciatur illos de quibus in prædictis locis agitur, non æternos Seruatores, quemadmodum Christus est, sed tantum temporarios esse, ac proinde magnum inter illos, & Christum discrimen sit statuendum, respondere se illam exceptionem ad rem nihil facere, quum apud Esaiam, non de æterna, sed de temporaria salute, vel saltem de vtraque in genere agatur: quamuis, si antecedentia, & consequentia Dei verba diligenter perpendantur, facile videre sit, illum locum de temporaria salute intelligendum esse.
units.tr: Reply. This objection of Ostorrodius is false: Christ, the true and eternal God of Israel, has existed from eternity. We have demonstrated this at length above, in chapter eight, where we showed that he is the Creator of this whole world, and we shall confirm it further in the following chapter. Secondly, he says that those words, "beside me," are not to be understood as if no other Saviour existed besides the one God, but that all true salvation, through whomever it is then conveyed to us, comes from God alone, and no one can save unless it is through him by whom God grants salvation; because in the sacred books the name SAVIOUR is given to certain others too, and they are said to have been raised up and given by God as Saviours to his people, as is clear from Judges 3:9 and other places. But if it is objected that those of whom these passages speak were not eternal Saviours, as Christ is, but only temporary, and that therefore a great difference must be drawn between them and Christ, he replies that this exception has nothing to do with the matter, since in Isaiah the subject is not eternal but temporal salvation, or at least salvation in general; although, if God's preceding and following words are weighed carefully, it is easy to see that the passage must be understood of temporal salvation.

units.la: Resp. Indubitata manet illa propositio nostra, primum & æternum salutis siue temporariæ, siue æternæ autorem esse vnum illum & æternū Deum Israelis, cuius veritatem agnoscit, etiā ipse Ostorrodius, nec inficias ibit vllus, qui vnum solum verum & æternum Deum nobiscum agnoscet & confitebitur, sic vt certissima illa argumenta, quibus hoc euidentissimè demonstrari poterit, recensere non sit necessarium. Atque Christum vtriusque salutis autorem esse primū ac æternum hinc liquet, tum quia ipse in initio terram fundauerit, & opera manuum ipsius sunt cœli, Hebr.1.v.10. Idem autem est mundi huius seruator, & gubernator æternus, qui eius extitit creator, tum etiam, quia ille nobis dat vitam æter-nam, & liberat nos à morte æterna. Ioh.1. verf.28. quam vitam, licet à Patre acceptam, in fe ipso tamen habet, Ioh.5. verf.26. Nec est in alio quoquam salus, aut aliud nomen sub cælo, quod datum fit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Vnde necessario sequitur Christum verum, vnum, & æternum illum Deum Israelis esse. Tertio ait, Libenter fe concedere, vt verba illa Dei apud Esaiam de salute æterna intelligantur, quum manifestum fit Christum Dei filium, non extra Deum Patrem suum saluatorem nostrum esse: & ipsemet omnem suam doctrinam, omniaque opera Deo Patri suo ascribat. Et quid multis nobis opus est? inquit, nonne fatis expresse Deum ipsum in Mediatorem excitaffe, misse, & erexisse dicitur? Act.13. v.23. & 5.31. Ef.19. verf.20. 1.Ioh.4. v.14. Ex eo igitur quod Christus Dei filius saluator noster dicitur, non id quod Aduersarii volunt, sed fi bene perpendatur, qua ratione Christus mediator noster dicatur, contrarium potius sequitur, siquidem vnus ille Deus hoc à fe ipso habet, nec vlla ratione de ipso prædicari potest, quod ille ad officium illud excitatus, missus, & euectus fit, quemadmodum de Christo dicitur. Atque sic quasi re bene & præclare gesta, cuiufta ac confessa iactabundus clamat Oftorrodius, manifestum hinc fieri, quàm frequenter aduersarii proprio ipsorum gladio percutiantur & iugulentur. Nos argumentum Oftorrodii ad formam reducemus, vt liquido constare possit, vtra pars falsitatis illo convincatur.
units.tr: Reply. Our proposition stands undoubted: that the first and eternal author of salvation, whether temporal or eternal, is that one eternal God of Israel. Ostorrodius himself acknowledges its truth, and no one who acknowledges and confesses with us the one true and eternal God will deny it, so that there is no need to recount the most certain arguments by which this could be most clearly demonstrated. That Christ is the first and eternal author of both kinds of salvation is clear from this: he founded the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of his hands (Hebrews 1:10); and he who is the eternal Preserver and Governor of this world is the same who was its Creator. It is also clear because he gives us eternal life and delivers us from eternal death (John 1:28, as printed), a life which, though received from the Father, he nevertheless has in himself (John 5:26). Neither is there salvation in any other, nor any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. From this it necessarily follows that Christ is the true, one, and eternal God of Israel. Thirdly, the Adversary says that he willingly concedes that God's words in Isaiah may be understood of eternal salvation, since it is manifest that Christ, the Son of God, is our Saviour not apart from God his Father, and that he himself ascribes all his teaching and all his works to his Father God. And why do we need many words? he says. Is it not sufficiently plain that God himself is said to have raised up, sent, and set forth the Mediator? (Acts 13:23; 5:31; Ephesians 1:20; 1 John 4:14). Therefore, from the fact that Christ the Son of God is called our Saviour, if it is weighed carefully, it follows, not what our opponents want, but rather the contrary, by the same reasoning by which Christ is called our Mediator; for that one God has this from himself, and in no way can it be said of him that he was raised up, sent, and brought forward to that office, as is said of Christ. And so, as if a matter had been well and splendidly accomplished and confessed by all, Ostorrodius boasts loudly: it is thereby made manifest how often our opponents are struck down and slain with their own sword. We shall reduce Ostorrodius's argument to form, so that it may be clear which side is convicted of falsehood by it.

units.la: Illud igitur tale est.
units.tr: The argument, then, runs as follows.

units.la: Qui est verus vnus ille, & æternus Deus, ille non potest ab alio in Saluatorem excitari, mitti, ac euehi.
units.tr: He who is the true, single and eternal God cannot be raised up, sent and exalted by another as Saviour.

units.la: Atqui Christus à Deo in Saluatorem excitatus, missus, atque euectus est: Act.13. verf.23. & 5. verf.31. Ef.19. verf.20.1. Iohan.4. verf.14.
units.tr: But Christ has been raised up, sent and exalted by God as Saviour: Act. 13. vers. 23. and 5. vers. 31. Ef. 19. vers. 20. 1. Iohan. 4. vers. 14.

units.la: Ergo Christus non est vnus ille æternus, ac verus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not that single, eternal and true God.

units.la: Resp. Crambem multoties coctam reponit Oftorrodius, qui perpetua ambiguitate & contrariorum elencho ludit. Deus enim essentialiter & οὐσιωδῶς si intelligatur, certissimum est à nemine illam æternam essentiam in Saluatorem mitti, & excitari posse, quia illa primum est Ens, quod principium & ordinis & generationis excludit. At vero si perfonaliter, de persona filii nomen Deus prædicetur, negamus Deum filium nulla ratione à Deo Patre in Saluatorem excitari ac mitti potuisse. Deus igitur absolutè sic consideratus, & quà Deus simpliciter à nemine mitti potuit: at mitti potuit, & missus est filius fecundùm beneplacitum gratiæ gloriosæ ipsius, & dispensationem illam misericordiæ, qua Deus homo factus est, & manifestatus in carne propter nos homines voluntariè & propter salutem nostram. Maior itaque propositio de Deo loquitur absolutè: Minor verò de fecunda persona diuina, & quidem fecundùm œconomiam voluntariam consideratam: unde omnis oppofitio tollitur, & quatuor termini in Aduersarii argumento deprehenduntur. Idem enim ipse, qui diuina virtute constituit, eligit, exaltat, atque mittit vt æternus Deus, diuino consilio, ac dispensatione voluntaria, constitutus est, electus, missus, atque exaltatus, nimirum vt Mediator, & homo factus in tempore ad consummationem optatissimæ salutis nostræ. Atque fecundùm hanc œconomiam ac voluntariam dispensationem Christus in citatis locis à Deo Patre missus & excitatus dicitur. Ab œconomia autem illa gratiosa, ad conditionem naturæ, non dari consequentiam, nec ea quæ de Christo ratione officii Mediatoris dicuntur, & diuinæ illius, ac liberrimæ dispensationis, qua inter Deum & homines, medio veluti loco constituitur, diuinę ipsius naturæ quicquam derogare posse iam supra demonstrauimus. Ex quibus omnibus patet, Christum æternum Deum & saluatorem dici ratione essentiæ & decreti de saluandis electis: electum verò, ac missum à Patre, ratione personæ, secundum liberam illam œconomiam consideratæ, & respectu executionis: quæ respectuum diuersitas & contrarietatem tollit, & clypeum porrigit, quo plumbea illa tela Ofiorrodii retundantur, simúlque vana iactatione sibi Aduersarium gratulari ostendit.
units.tr: Reply. Ostorrodius serves up a cabbage that has been cooked many times over, and he plays with constant ambiguity and with the refutation of opposites. For if God is taken essentially and οὐσιωδῶς [essentially], it is most certain that no one can send or raise up that eternal essence as Saviour, since it is the first Being, which excludes any beginning of order or generation. But if God is taken personally, and the name God is predicated of the person of the Son, we deny that the Son, as God, could in no way have been raised up and sent as Saviour by God the Father. So God, considered absolutely and as God simply, could be sent by no one; yet the Son could be sent, and was sent, according to the good pleasure of his glorious grace and that dispensation of mercy by which God was made man and was manifested in the flesh for us men, willingly and for our salvation. The major premise, then, speaks of God absolutely; the minor speaks of the second divine person, and indeed of him as considered in the voluntary economy. Thus every opposition is removed, and the four terms that are found in our opponent's argument are shown up. For the same one who, by divine power, establishes, chooses, exalts and sends himself as the eternal God, was, by divine counsel and voluntary dispensation, appointed, chosen, sent and exalted, namely as Mediator, and made man in time for the accomplishment of our most desired salvation. It is according to this economy and voluntary dispensation that Christ is said in the cited places to have been sent and raised up by God the Father. But we have already shown above that no conclusion can be drawn from that gracious economy to the condition of nature, nor can what is said of Christ in respect of his office as Mediator, and of that divine and most free dispensation by which he is set, as it were, in the middle between God and men, take anything away from the divine nature itself. From all these things it is clear that Christ is called eternal God and Saviour in respect of his essence and of the decree concerning the saving of the elect, but is chosen and sent by the Father in respect of his person, considered according to that free economy, and in respect of its execution. This diversity of respects removes the contradiction, and holds up a shield by which the leaden darts of Ostorrodius are turned aside, while at the same time it shows that the opponent rejoices in his empty boasting.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum secundum tale est.
units.tr: Our argument, in its second form, is as follows.

units.la: Qui propria autoritate ac potestate hominibus peccata remittit, ac remittere potest, ille est verus & æternus ille Deus Israelis.
units.tr: He who by his own authority and power forgives sins to men, and is able to forgive them, is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Christus non tantùm vt minister, sed [propria autoritate peccata remittit, ac remittere potest. Ergo Christus est verus ille & æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: But Christ forgives sins, and is able to forgive them, by his own authority, not only as a minister but as [God]. Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Maior propositio inde demonstratur, quia videlicet solus Deus is est, in quem peccatur, Psal. 51. v. 6. Tibi, tibi (o Deus) soli peccavi, & malum in oculis tuis feceram: ac proinde solus vt summus Iudex peccata remittendi potestatem habet: Esai. 43. verf. 12. Ego, ego sum, qui deleo praevaricationes tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordor. Marc. 2. 7. Quis potest peccata remittere, nisi solus Deus? Christus autem sibi non ministerium remissionis peccatorum, sed potestatem, & authoritatem competere, non modo distertis verbis asseruit, sed etiam miraculo evidentissimè comprobavit, Matth. 9. 6. Vnde manifestissimè liquet, Christum verum ac æternum illum Deum Israelis esse. Quia autem ad hoc posterius argumentum nihil respondet Ostorrodius, ideo ad sequentia progredimur.
units.tr: The major premise is proved as follows: it is God alone against whom sin is committed, Ps. 51. v. 6. Against thee, thee only (O God), have I sinned, and done evil in thy sight; and therefore only he, as supreme Judge, has the power of forgiving sins. Is. 43. vers. 12. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I do not remember your sins. Mark 2. 7. Who can forgive sins but God alone? But Christ asserted that the power and authority to forgive sins belong to himself, not merely a ministry of forgiveness; he did not only say so in plain words but also proved it most clearly by a miracle, Matt. 9. 6. Hence it is most clearly evident that Christ is that true and eternal God of Israel. Since Ostorrodius makes no reply at all to this second argument, we proceed to what follows.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: In quo argumentum quartum pro æterna Filii Deitate proponitur ac defenditur.
units.tr: In which the fourth argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is put forward and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum quartum pro aeternitate Iesu Christi æterna Deitate, sumitur à proprietate Dei essentiali, nempe æternitate, quæ in Scripturis Christo tribuitur: vnde in hunc modum argumentamur.
units.tr: Our fourth argument for the eternal Deity of Jesus Christ is drawn from an essential property of God, namely eternity, which is ascribed to Christ in the Scriptures. We argue in this way.

units.la: Qui est æternus, ac proinde expers temporis, principii atque finis, omnique tempore antiquior, omni fine posterior, & absolutè citra successionem totus simul, ille est verus ac æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whatever is eternal, and so is free of time, beginning and end, is older than all time, later than every end, and altogether simultaneous, without succession, is the one true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Christus est æternus, omnique principio temporis caret.
units.tr: But Christ is eternal and has no beginning in time.

units.la: Ergo Christus est vnus ille, ac verus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is that one true God of Israel.

units.la: Maior propositio est extra controuersiam. Minorem autem hac ratione demonstramus.
units.tr: The major premise is beyond dispute. We demonstrate the minor as follows.

units.la: Quicunque extitit ante creationem mundi, & eius iacta fundamenta, ille est æternus.
units.tr: Whatever existed before the creation of the world and the laying of its foundations is eternal.

units.la: Atqui Christus extitit ante creationem mundi, & eius iacta fundamenta damnarunt. damenta.
units.tr: But Christ existed before the creation of the world and the laying of its foundations.

units.la: Ergo Christus est aeternus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is eternal.

units.la: Maioris veritas inde confirmatur, quia esse ab aeterno, & esse ante iacta mundi fundamenta in Scripturis sacris sunt ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄρχεσθαι. Sic Eph.1. v.4. Elegit nos Deus in Christo ante quam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, id est, ab aeterno. nota enim sunt Deo ab auo omnia opera sua. Act.15. 18. Et Petrus dicit Christum praeordinatum ante iacta mundi fundamenta, quod iterum de aeternitate est intelligendum. Prou.8.22. & 23. Dominus possedit me, inquit Sapientia, in initio viarum suarum, antequam quicquam faceret. i. ante omne tempus ab aeterno ordinata sum, ante principium, ante primordia terrae. Extitisse autem Christum ante creationem mundi, & iacta eius fundamenta, ex sequentibus demonstratur. Primò, quia Ioh. 1. v.1. ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ dicitur, id est, ante tempus, locum, creationem, & res creatas omnes subsistebat. Qui enim iam in principio erat, eum ante principium fuisse necesse est. Quod autem Aduersarii illud principium non ad principium eorum omnium, quae principium habent in tempore, adeoque primum ipsius temporis terminum, momentum seu punctum, quo coeperunt esse tempus, locus, creatio, & res creatae tempore & loco: sed de initio praedicationis Euangelii restringendum, ac referendum censent, insulsum est, illamque interpretationem ac determinationem, nec subiecto, nec praedicato, nec adiunctis eorum conuenire, tam euidenter est à nobis demonstratum, ut hic diutius illis immorari non sit necesse. Secundò, quia v.3. omnia per hunc sermonem facta esse dicuntur, omniaque per ipsum condita, quae in caelo sunt, & quae in terra. Col.1.16. Et ipse creator caeli terraeque esse perhibetur, Hebr.1. 10. Qui autem δημιουργὸς est, & rerum omnium opifex, atque creator, eum ante res omnes creatas, adeoque ab aeterno extitisse, qua fronte inficiari audet Osiorrodius? Tertiò, quia se gloriam apud Patrem habuisse, antequam hic mundus existeret, ipse profitetur, Ioh. 17. v.5. Vnde quoque ipsum ab aeterno extitisse necessario sequitur: siquidem abest tertii adiecti, ut loquuntur, adest secundi adiecti necessaria ac perpetua datur consequentia. Deinde ad eandem aeternitatem demonstrandam, nonnulli ex nostris, etiam illum locum Ioh.8. v.58. ubi Christus, priusquam Abraham fieret, se fuisse affirmat, adducunt.
units.tr: The truth of the major premise is confirmed by the fact that to be from eternity and to exist before the foundations of the world were laid are, in the sacred Scriptures, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄρχεσθαι [from the beginning]. So Eph. 1:4: "God chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid," that is, from eternity. For "all his works are known to God from of old," Acts 15:18. And Peter says that Christ was "foreordained before the foundation of the world," which again must be understood of eternity. Prov. 8:22-23: "The Lord possessed me," says Wisdom, "in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything," that is, "I was ordained from eternity, before all time, before the beginning, before the first things of the earth." That Christ existed before the creation of the world and the laying of its foundations is shown from what follows. First, because John 1:1 says that ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ [he was in the beginning], that is, before time, place, creation and all created things he subsisted. For he who already was in the beginning must have been before the beginning. As for our opponents' claim that this "beginning" is not the beginning of all things that have a beginning in time, and so not the first limit of time itself, the moment or point at which time, place, creation and created things began to be, but must be restricted and referred to the start of the preaching of the Gospel, that is foolish; and that this interpretation and restriction fits neither the subject, nor the predicate, nor their adjuncts, we have demonstrated so plainly that there is no need to dwell on them longer here. Second, because at v. 3 "all things are said to have been made through this Word, and all things that are in heaven and on earth were created through him" (Col. 1:16), and he is said to be the Creator of heaven and earth (Heb. 1:10). Whoever is δημιουργός [maker] and the workman and creator of all things must have existed before all created things, and so from eternity; with what brazenness does Ostorrodius dare to deny this? Third, because he himself professes that he "had glory with the Father before this world existed" (John 17:5). From this it also necessarily follows that he existed from eternity: for where the third adjunct, as they say, is absent, the second adjunct is present, and a necessary and perpetual consequence is given. Moreover, to demonstrate the same eternity, some of our people also cite that passage John 8:58, where Christ affirms that he was "before Abraham was."

units.la: Osiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite octauo, hanc quaestionem proponit, An nimirum Christus ab æterno extiterit? quod negat: quia, inquit, illo concesso, necessario inde concluderetur ipsius diuina natura, adeoque ipsum æternum illum Deum esse. Argumentum autem negationis hoc adfert, quia nullus Scripturæ locus adduci posset, in quo Christus, aut Dei Filius ab æterno extitisse distertis verbis scribatur. Hoc vt demonstret, adducit locum illum Iohan. 8. verf. 58. vbi Christus antequam Abraham fieret extitisse dicitur, & cui loco plurimum à Trinitariis ait tribui, ad æternitatem Christi demonstrandam. Eodem autem in loco, nihil de æternitate agi, sed tantum affirmari Christum ante Abrahamum fuisse, ac proinde, locum illum nihil ad propositum facere. Vnde in hunc modum concludit, Si hic locus illam æternitatem demonstrare non potest, quid igitur de cæteris sentiendum?
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter eight of his Institutions, poses this question: "Did Christ, then, exist from eternity?" and denies it, "because," he says, "if this were granted, it would necessarily follow that his divine nature, and so that he is that eternal God, is concluded." His argument for the denial is this: "because no passage of Scripture could be cited in which it is written in plain words that Christ, or the Son of God, existed from eternity." To prove this, he adduces that passage John 8:58, "where Christ is said to have existed before Abraham was," and which, he says, is very much attributed by the Trinitarians to demonstrate the eternity of Christ. In that same place, however, nothing is said about eternity, but only that Christ was before Abraham; therefore that passage does nothing for the point at issue. From this he concludes in this way: "If this passage cannot demonstrate that eternity, what then should be thought of the others?"

units.la: Resp. Tria hîc ab Aduersario proponuntur, quæ nobis ordine sunt excutienda, argumentum negationis, exemplum, & quam nectit inde consequentia.
units.tr: Answer. Three things are put forward here by our opponent, which we must examine in order: the argument from negation, the example, and the consequence he draws from them.

units.la: Argumentum negationis tale est.
units.tr: The argument from negation is as follows.

units.la: Si nullus Scripturæ locus adduci potest in quo Christus ab æterno extitisse scribatur, tum etiam falsum est, Christum æternum esse.
units.tr: If no passage of Scripture can be cited in which it is written that Christ existed from eternity, then it is also false that Christ is eternal.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp. Negatur consequentia: Quamuis enim non iisdem quasi syllabis dicatur Christus ab æterno extitisse, dicitur tamen pluribus planè æquipollentibus: quemadmodum supra luculenter à nobis est ostensum. Nonne enim Deus ante omnia secula, ante omne tempus, ante creationem, & omnes res creatas fideles in Christo ad vitam æternam, ac salutem elegit? Hoc ipsum tamen cum his iisdem verbis in sacris literis nusquam scriptum repe-riatur, tum ideo minus verum fuerit? Falsitatem igitur suę consequentiæ agnoscat Aduersarius, quæ tum demum vera censenda esset, si id quod nos affirmamus nec iisdem verbis, nec phrasibus æquipollentibus, neque etiam necessaria consequentia in Scripturis haberetur, quod falsum esse ex antecedentibus liquet.
units.tr: Answer. The consequence is denied. For although it is not said in the same syllables that Christ existed from eternity, it is said in several entirely equivalent expressions, as we have shown clearly above. For does not Scripture say that God chose the faithful in Christ before all ages, before all time, before the creation and all created things, for eternal life and salvation? Yet if this same thing is nowhere written in Holy Scripture in these same words, is it therefore less true? Let our opponent, then, acknowledge the falsity of his consequence, which would be true only if what we affirm were found in the Scriptures neither in the same words, nor in equivalent phrases, nor by necessary consequence; and that this is false is clear from what has gone before.

units.la: Locum vero illum Ioh. 8. verf. 58. quod attinet, in quo Christus argumento à natura sua <bl>ἐσφαντωμένη</bl> desumpto Iudæorum ineptiam refellit, qui de persona Christi tanquam homine solo iudicabant: cabant: fateor equidem de æternitate verbis expressis nihil ibi contineri, aut si quis etiam cum contumaciori rem habeat, ex ipso textu eam demonstrari forte non posse. Sed quid tum inde? cùm propterea statim ipsa doctrina euertitur de æterna Filii deitate, quæ ex aliis etiam scripturæ testimoniis hauritur? An verò interpretatio loci tantùm alicuius singularis? Si illud affirmauerit Ostorrodius ineptus fuerit, & plane insulsus ac opus habuerit helleboro: si posterius, nihil veritati nostræ doctrinæ eo ipso præiudicabitur.
units.tr: As for that passage John 8:58, in which Christ, by an argument drawn from his own nature (ἐσφαντωμένη [ensnaring/captious]), refutes the folly of the Jews, who judged the person of Christ as a mere man: I grant indeed that nothing about eternity is contained there in express words, or that if someone dealt with a more obstinate person, it perhaps cannot be demonstrated from the text itself. But what follows from that? Since the doctrine of the eternal deity of the Son, which is drawn also from other testimonies of Scripture, is not thereby immediately overturned. Or is the interpretation of one single passage all there is? If Ostorrodius should assert the former, he would be foolish and plainly silly, and in need of hellebore; if the latter, nothing is thereby prejudiced against the truth of our doctrine.

units.la: Verùm (vt de tertio quoque agamus) maior adhuc est imperitia, quod Aduersarius ex vno illo particulari scripturæ testimonio, de cæteris in vniuersum omnibus concludiit, quasi verò illo concesso, quod locus ille de æternitate nihil agat, nec cæteros, qui allegari possunt, aut solent, eandem docere, sequeretur, quasi verò vnus scripturæ locus, alterius, in quo rex diuersa agitur, lex existere posset. Et quamuis æternitas ipsius Filii, ad quam tamen in sua responsione Christus haud dubiè respicit, si cum occæcatis, & præfractis illis ingeniis sit agendum, ex illo loco fortasse demonstrari nequeat, ille tamen vel solus Samosatenianorum thesin, qua affirmant, Christum tum demum exis"tere cœpisse, cùm ex Maria virgine nasceretur, adeoque in ipsius persona, nullam nisi humanam naturam agnoscunt, fortissimè euertit. Si enim Christus iam ante Abrahamum fuit, certè ipsum antequam ex Maria nasceretur extitisse, adeóque duas in ipso naturas esse necesse est. Prius affirmat ipse Christus, posterius igitur agnoscat Aduersarius, nisi sibi negati potius quàm ipsi Christo affirmanti, fidem haberi impiè postulauerit.
units.tr: But (to speak of the third point as well) it is even greater ignorance that the opponent concludes from that one particular testimony of Scripture about all the others in general, as if, granting that this passage says nothing about eternity, it would follow that the other passages which can be or usually are cited do not teach the same; as if one passage of Scripture could exist as the law of another, which deals with a different matter. And although the eternity of the Son itself, to which Christ undoubtedly refers in his reply, perhaps cannot be demonstrated from that passage if one must deal with those blinded and obstinate minds, yet that passage alone most strongly overturns the thesis of the Samosatenes, by which they affirm that "Christ began to exist only when he was born of the Virgin Mary, and so they acknowledge in his person no nature but the human." For if Christ was already before Abraham, certainly he existed before he was born of Mary, and so there must be two natures in him. Christ himself affirms the former; let our opponent therefore acknowledge the latter, unless he impiously demands that credence be given to the one who denies rather than to Christ himself who affirms.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum nostrum respondet Ostorrodius, ne illud quidem, quod nempe Christus ante natiuitatem ex virgine Maria extitérit, demonstrari posse, quia male verba illa Christi ex Graeco textu à Luthero Germanicè sint reddita, quasi ita haberent, Amen amen dico vobis, priusquam Abraham fieret, ego sum. Graecum enim textum ita habere, ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι, ἐγὼ εἰμί, quem ita oportet interpretari: Amen amen dico vobis, priusquam Abraham fiat ego sum: id est, Amen amen dico vobis, priusquam Abraham fiat, scilicet Pater multarum gentium (hæc enim vera est nominis Abrahami notatio & interpretatio, testante Scriptura Gen.17.v.5.) hoc est, antequam regnum cœlorum ad gentes, qui iam per fidem Abrahami filij sunt facti, transferatur, ego sum, nempe lux mundi, id est, Messias, quem se esse veris antecedentibus profitebatur, nempe 12.24.28.
units.tr: Ostorrodius replies to this argument of ours: "Not even that, namely that Christ existed before his birth from the Virgin Mary, can be demonstrated, because those words of Christ have been badly rendered into German by Luther from the Greek text, as if they read: 'Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am.' For the Greek text reads thus: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι, ἐγὼ εἰμί, which must be interpreted thus: 'Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham comes to be, I am': that is, 'Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham comes to be, namely the Father of many nations (for this is the true notation and interpretation of the name Abraham, as Scripture attests, Gen. 17:5), that is, before the kingdom of heaven is transferred to the nations, who through the faith of Abraham have already become his sons, I am,' namely the light of the world, that is, the Messiah, whom he professed himself to be from the preceding true statements," namely 12, 24, 28.

units.la: N
units.tr: N

units.la: Resp. Si verba ipsa per se, & ipsorum constructio consideretur, certissimum est illa utramque interpretationem admittere, nempe quod & sit Christus ante natum Abrahamum, & quod sit antequam fiat Abrahamus, & aoristum illum secundum cum Aduerbio πρὶν construction um, modo tempus praeteritum, modo futurum significare, ex locis similibus scripturae, & usu phrasews illius πρὶν γενέσθαι, aliorumque similium apud authores Graecos est manifestum. Sic enim Iohan.14.verf.29 Καὶ νῦν εἴρηκα ὑμῖν πρὶν γενέσθαι, ἵνα ὅταν γένηται, πιστεύσητε, id est, Et nunc dixi vobis priusquam fiat, vt cum factum fuerit, credatis: quod idem hisce verbis enuntiatur, Iohan.13.v.19. λέγω ὑμῖν πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι, &c. Quemadmodum etiam Eustathius illius aduerbii πρὶν significationem explicat, vt in eius παρεκβολὰς in Iliad. Homeri libro primo pagina quadragesima secunda videre est. Sic apud Homerum Odyss. ε πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι, antequam patria terra adueniat: & Odyss. ο πρὶν εἰς οἶκον ἐλθεῖν, priusquam domum veniam. Herodian. lib.3. πρὶν διαβῆναι γενέσθαι τὸ παραχθεῖν, priusquam diuulgetur facinus. Et paulo post: πρὶν ἐκπυσεῖσθαι τῷ δήμῳ γενέσθαι, priusquam populo innotescat. In quibus locis ille aoristus tempus futurum denotat, sed & praeteritum tempus per illum significari sequentia ostendunt exempla. Plato in Ep. τὴν δὲ πασῶν πρὶν ἀποθανεῖν παρεκκλησθῆναι ἀπὸ τῆς ἐργὴν γενέσθαι, quodvis supplicium perpeti maluit potius, quam vt scelerum ipsorum socius fieret. Thucydides, πρὶν ἐπυνθάνεσθαι γενέσθαι, priusquam auditus fuisset. Similem constructionem vide Matt.capite primo, verf.18: πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτοὺς, εὑρέθη ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, id est, priusquam ipsi conuenissent, inuenta est vterum ferre ex Spiritu sancto. Actor.7. verf. 2. πρὶν ἢ κατοικῆσαι αὐτὸν ἐν Χαρράν, id est, priusquam habitaret in Charrhan. 2.Macchab.13. verf.13. πρὶν εἰσβαλεῖν τοῦ βασιλέως τὸ στράτευμα εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν, καὶ γενέσθαι τῆς πόλεως ἐκρατεῖν, id est, priusquam exercitus Regis Iudaeam inuaderet, & vrbe potiretur: & alibi tum apud septuaginta interpretes, tum apud alios Graecos Oratores, & Poetas passim. Quum igitur manifestum sit, verba illa Christi vtroque modo explicari posse, verborum autem Christi sensum non esse varium, multiplicem, aut ambiguum, sed vnum atque simplicem: ideo quis verborum illorum Christi verus ac genuinus sit sensus, ex scopo dicentis, antecedentibus & consequentibus, nobis erit iudicandum. Quamuis igitur Christus in antecedentibus contra Iudaeos veritatem sui in uneris afferens se verum illum, ac Patribus promissum Messiam esse, lucem ac saluatorem mundi testatus sit. Haec tamen verba non ad ipsum officium, sed dignitatem personę tuendam referen- da esse, inepta illa, & inscita Iudæorum ab instituto sermone digressio, & blasphemia, quam digrediendo in veritatem naturæ divinę in Christo, euomuerunt, & quorum impiam asseverationem Christum refellere oportuit, luculenter euincit. Postquam enim ille de aduentu suo in carnem ad munus Mediationis peragedum dixisset Iudæis, Abraham Pater vester gestiuit, vt videret diem hunc meum, & vidit, atque gauisus est. Iudæi à verbis Christi, & sensu ipsorum digredientes regesserunt Christo hoc argumentum. Qui nondum annos natus est quinquaginta, eum Abrahamum vidisse est impossibile. Atqui tu nondum annos natus es quinquaginta. Ergo impossibile est te vidisse Abrahamum. Et quoniam illi de Christo iudicarunt, tanquam homine solum, respondet Christus, se non esse ψιλὸν ἀνθρωπον, sed humana conditione superiorem agnoscendum, & licet persona ipsius, qua homo, nondum sit quinquagenaria, personam tamen æternam esse, quæ iam substiterit ante Abrahami tempora: & quo personæ immutabilem veritatem secundum esse ipsius amplius confirmaret, non dicit, ego fui, aut eram, sed diuino modo loquitur, πρὸ ἀμνπιλόλον demonstrante, Antequam Abraham fieret, vel esset, ego sum. Hac Iudæorum impudenti impietate sic profligata per Christi responsionem, eo insaniæ ac furoris ipsi eruperunt, vt lapides humo sustulerint in eum coniecturi. Ex quibus omnibus etiam liquido constat illa Christi verba optimè à Luthero reddita esse.
units.tr: Answer. If the words themselves are considered by themselves, and their construction, it is quite certain that they admit both interpretations: that he is Christ before Abraham was born, and that he is before Abraham comes to be. The aorist, joined with the adverb πρίν in this second construction, sometimes signifies past time and sometimes future, as is clear from similar places of Scripture and from the usage of the phrase πρὶν γενέσθαι and similar phrases among Greek authors. Thus in John 14:29: "And now I have told you before it comes to pass, so that when it comes to pass you may believe" [Καὶ νῦν εἴρηκα ὑμῖν πρὶν γενέσθαι, ἵνα ὅταν γένηται, πιστεύσητε]. The same thing is said in these words in John 13:19: "I tell you before it comes to pass" [λέγω ὑμῖν πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι]. Eustathius also explains the meaning of the adverb πρίν, as can be seen in his commentary on the first book of Homer's Iliad, page forty-two. So in Homer, Odyssey ε: "before the patrimonial land is reached" [πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι]; and Odyssey ο: "before I come home" [πρὶν εἰς οἶκον ἐλθεῖν]. Herodian, book 3: "before the deed is divulged" [πρὶν διαβῆναι γενέσθαι τὸ παραχθεῖν]. And a little later: "before it is made known to the people" [πρὶν ἐκπυσεῖσθαι τῷ δήμῳ γενέσθαι]. In these places the aorist denotes future time, but the following examples show that past time is also signified by it. Plato, in the Epistles, says he preferred to suffer any punishment rather than become a partner in their crimes. Thucydides: "before it was heard of" [πρὶν ἐπυνθάνεσθαι γενέσθαι]. A similar construction is found in Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit" [πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτοὺς, εὑρέθη ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου]. Acts 7:2: "before he lived in Charran" [πρὶν ἢ κατοικῆσαι αὐτὸν ἐν Χαρράν]. 2 Maccabees 13:13: "before the king's army invaded Judaea and got control of the city" [πρὶν εἰσβαλεῖν τοῦ βασιλέως τὸ στράτευμα εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν, καὶ γενέσθαι τῆς πόλεως ἐκρατεῖν]; and elsewhere, both in the Septuagint and in other Greek orators and poets everywhere. Since, therefore, it is clear that those words of Christ can be explained in either way, and the sense of Christ's words is not varied, manifold or ambiguous, but one and simple, we must judge which is the true and genuine sense of those words from the purpose of the speaker and from what precedes and follows. Although Christ, in the preceding words, asserting against the Jews the truth of his own witness, declared that he is the true Messiah promised to the Fathers, the light and saviour of the world, nevertheless the foolish and unlearned digression of the Jews from the subject of discourse, and the blasphemy which they vomited forth in that digression against the true divine nature of Christ, and whose impious assertion Christ had to refute, clearly shows that these words are not to be referred to his office but to the defence of his dignity as a person. For after he had told the Jews of his coming in the flesh to perform the office of mediator, "Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad," the Jews, departing from Christ's words and their sense, threw back this argument at him: "He who is not yet fifty years old cannot have seen Abraham. But you are not yet fifty years old. Therefore it is impossible that you have seen Abraham." And since they judged of Christ as of a mere man, Christ answers that he is not a mere man (ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον), but must be acknowledged as superior to the human condition. Although his person as man is not yet fifty years old, the person is eternal and had already subsisted before the time of Abraham. To confirm more firmly the unchangeable truth of his person according to his being, he does not say "I was" or "I used to be," but speaks in a divine manner, showing it by saying: "Before Abraham was, or existed, I am." With this impudent impiety of the Jews routed by Christ's answer, they then burst out into such madness and fury that they picked up stones from the ground to throw at him. From all these things it also clearly appears that those words of Christ were very well rendered by Luther.

units.la: Atque hinc etiam corruit, quod subiicit Oftorrodius, parum, nempe, quod ad hanc disputationem attinet, referre sive admittatur, illE quem adseri verborum Christi sensus, sive minus, quia sufficiat quod illa verba aliter ex Græco textu verti possint, quam vero à Trinitariis sunt reddita, ac proinde manifestum sit, ex illis ne quidem illud quod Christus ante Mariam virginem extiterit, ne dñ quod ab æterno fuerit, demonstrari posse. Attamen si quis de genuina huius loci interpretatione plura desideret, eum ex aliis Samosatenianorum scriptis, præsertim vero ex disputatione sua aduersus Georgiu Tradelium Syndicu Augustanu, vbi de hoc ipso prolixè disputat petenda esse: quia, vt iā suprà monuimus, vera ac solida interpretatio, & genuinus scripturæ sensus non ex verborum tantum cortice, sed maximè rerum ipsarum, quæ tractatur medulla, ac natura, antecedentium item & consequentium circumstantiis, ac scopo ipso dicentium, ex aliis denique scripturæ testimoniis hauritur neque sequitur,si verba huius aut illius cōtextus sint ambigua,nullum tamē certū sensum in quo fit acquiescēdum aliunde depromi posse. Farraginem autem omniū scriptorū quib- Sociniana illa turba suos errores tueri conatur, hactenus neq; videre, neque consequi datū est,in futilissima vero illa aduersus præstantissimum virum D.Georgium Tradelium disputatione, nihil quod ad hunc præsentem locum attinet continetur,quod non abunde à nobis fit refutatum,& quicunque sine præiudicio librum illum legerit, plus audaciæ, impudentiæ, & procacitatis,quàm solidæ eruditionis,pietatis & candoris Christiani in illo deprehēdet.
units.tr: Hence also falls what Ostorodius adds: that it matters little, as far as this dispute is concerned, whether one admits the sense of Christ's words or not, since it is enough that those words can be translated from the Greek text differently from how they have been rendered by the Trinitarians; and therefore it is clear that from them one cannot even demonstrate that Christ existed before the virgin Mary, let alone that he existed from eternity. Yet if anyone desires more on the genuine interpretation of this passage, he should seek it from other writings of the Samosatenians, especially from his disputation against Georg Tradelius, syndic of Augsburg, where he discusses this very point at length. For, as we have already noted above, the true and solid interpretation and the genuine sense of Scripture are drawn not merely from the bark of the words but chiefly from the marrow and nature of the things treated, from the circumstances of what precedes and follows, from the very purpose of the speakers, and finally from other testimonies of Scripture. Nor does it follow that if the words of this or that context are ambiguous, no certain sense in which one may rest can be drawn from elsewhere. The farrago of all the writings by which that Socinian crowd tries to defend its errors we have so far neither been able nor had the opportunity to see or follow. But in that most futile disputation against the most excellent man, Georg Tradelius, there is nothing relevant to this present passage that has not been abundantly refuted by us. And whoever reads that book without prejudice will find in it more audacity, impudence and insolence than solid learning, piety and Christian candour.

units.la: Et hæc de illis Christi verbis. Sed pergit Aduersarius,& dicit,se cateris Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ ad Christi æternam existentiam demonstrandam adducuntur, silentio prætheritis, in gratiam veritatis studiosi,breuiter,attamen euidenter demonstraturum esse quod Christus ab æterno non extiterit. Argumentum autem ipsius,si ad formam redigatur,tale erit.
units.tr: And so much for those words of Christ. But the adversary goes on and says that, passing over in silence the other testimonies of Scripture that are adduced to demonstrate Christ's eternal existence, he will, for the sake of those who study the truth, briefly but clearly demonstrate that Christ did not exist from eternity. If his argument is reduced to form, it will be this:

units.la: Quicunque vere concipitur & generatur, illius persona ipsa concipitur ac generatur,sic vt ille tum demum persona esse incipiat, quæ priusquam conciperetur ac gigneretur,non fuit. Hoc enim ipsum est concipi atque nasci.
units.tr: Whoever is truly conceived and begotten, his very person is conceived and begotten, so that he only then begins to be a person who, before he was conceived and begotten, was not. For this is precisely what it is to be conceived and to be born.

units.la: Atqui Christus vere,non autem typice in utero virginis Mariæ conceptus,atque ab ipsa genitus est,testante Scriptura sacra.
units.tr: But Christ was truly, and not merely typically, conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary and born of her, as holy Scripture testifies.

units.la: Ergo Christus seu Filius Dei,secundum personam ipsam conceptus atque genitus est,sic vt tu demū persona esse inceperit,nec extiterit priusquam in Maria conciperetur,ac ab eadē gigneretur,aut certè contra veritatem duo Filij Dei erunt statuendi.
units.tr: Therefore Christ, or the Son of God, was conceived and begotten according to his very person, so that he only then began to be a person and did not exist before he was conceived in Mary and begotten by her; or else, contrary to the truth, two Sons of God must be posited.

units.la: Hoc argumentum affirmat Oftorrodius, tam firmum atque euidens esse,vt certò sciat,illud à Trinitariis nunquam solidè refutatum iri, modò constanter in illius veritatis professione perseuerare velint, quòd filius Dei verè in vtero virginis sit conceptus, & ab ea genitus.
units.tr: Ostorodius affirms that this argument is so firm and evident that he is certain it will never be solidly refuted by the Trinitarians, provided only that they steadfastly persevere in professing this truth: that the Son of God was truly conceived in the womb of the virgin and born of her.

units.la: Resp. His omnibus,quæ de conceptionis & generationis initio, progressu, & complemento, item de termino duplicis generationis,nempe & naturæ,à Philosophis & scholasticis vere traduntur, omissis,ad argumentum breuiter & perspicuè respondebimus, erroris causam primo omnium moftraturi. Veritatem naturæ diuinæ,& eiusdem attributum essentiale,nempe æternitatem,imperitè negat, atque impugnat Oftorrodius, sumpta ratione vel à natura humanæ. humana, vel initio personae Θεάνθρωπου in forma Dei, & forma serui certo tempore simul subsistere incipientis. Quia enim natura diuina & humana ratione totius personae inter se non pugnant, sed consentiunt, ideo etiam neutra naturarum recte negatur sumpto ab altera natura aut tota persona argumento. Quicunque igitur vere concipitur & generatur, illius persona ipsa concipitur, nec esse incipit, priusquam concipiatur & gignatur, videlicet in illa generatione, quae efficiente, materia, atque terminatione naturalis est, hoc est, quando per generationem non tantum suppositum naturā ipsam accipit, sed ipsa etiā natura suppositō naturali vi principii naturalis terminatur naturaliter, adeoq; & natura & suppositum producitur à concipiente & gignente. In generatione vero singulari & supernaturali, quae & principium efficientis causae, & terminū naturae, nempe suppositum habet supernaturale, quod vi conceptionis & generationis nec producitur, nec suum esse accipit, qualis est generatio & conceptio filii Dei in vtero virginis Mariae, locum habere non potest. Christus enim seu filius Dei conceptus quidem est in vtero virginis Mariae, & ex ea genitus nec incepit existere, priusquam ex illa gigneretur, nempe tota persona Θεὸς ἀνθρώπος in forma Dei, & serui simul subsistens, quia tota persona est genita, sed tamen, quia nec totum personae, quod ad vtramque naturam, ac propriā humanae vero per gratiam vnionis communicatum, vi illius conceptionis aut generationis fuit productum: inde minime sequitur Christum, seu filium Dei, ne quidem secundum naturam diuinā ab æterno, aut ante natiuitatem ex Maria virgine extitisse. Personae n. diuinae, quae natura humana ἀνυπόστατος, ac propria personalitate destitutam, in ipso virginis vtero ex gratia in personae suae vnitatem asciuit & coniunxit, æternitati illa vnio & coiunctio ex gratia, & in tempore facta, nihil praeiudicare potest. Vnde & ignoratione elenchi fallit Aduersarius, & à distributo ad non distributum, seu à parte ad totum, si in hoc mysterio ita loqui liceat imperitè concludit. Inde tamen non sequitur aut Mariam non genuisse totum Christum, & personam eius: aut non genuisse verum ac perfectum hominem: aut denique duos Filios Dei statuendos esse. Non primum: quia enim illa vnio naturae humanae cum persona τοῦ λόγου facta fit in ipso Mariae virginis vtero, animáque & corpus Christi in ipso λόγῳ creata fuerint, & sic ipsa natura humana Christi in se ἀνυπόστατος, à diuina autem in vnitatem personae assumpta, & facta ἐνυπόστατος, ne ad momentum quidem extra λόγῳ subsisterent: hinc recte Maria virgo tota persona genuis-se, & ipsa Θεοτόκος à S. Patrib. dicitur. Non secundum: licet n. illud suppo-situm quo terminata est humana Christi natura, vi conceptionis produ-ctum non fuerit, nec à principio naturali profectum, vtpote di-uinum & aeternum, non humanum & temporale, inde tamen nō se-quitur Mariam virginem hominem perfectum non genuisse: quia suppositum ipsum non est ex causis intrinsecis naturae conceptae ac genitae, sed extra eas, nec de genere materiae aut formae, adeoque nec pars, sed terminus naturae, quemadmodum ipsum punctum nec pars, nec causa est, sed terminus & πέρας (vt vocat Euclides) li-neae, quae interdum absque puncto actu existit, ideo à qualitate huius suppositi, tanquam termini ad qualitatem, aut imperfectionem naturae humanae, quam determinat suppositum illud diuinū, nulla datur consequentia. Nec recte in suo genere vnquam defe-se aliquid dicitur, quod ipsi à superiore principio dignius ac praestantius naturali suppeditatur, & communicatur. Non denique tertium, quia diuersae rationes filiationis diuersos Christos aut Filios Dei nō constituunt. Filii enim titulus, quia nomen est concretum, proprie non essentiae ac naturae ratione, quatenus videlicet illa à suppposito distinguitur, sed ratione suppositi Christo tribuitur: quia vero Filii Dei hypostasis seu suppositum est numero, vnū, nempe diuinum, ideo etiam vnus tantum Christus & Filius Dei dicitur. Et quia illa hypostasis duabus diuersis competit naturis, diuinae videlicet naturae per generationem aeternam, primo ac per se, & ab aeterno: humanae vero naturae, nec primo, nec per genera-tionem, nec per se, aut ratione principii naturalis, sed per gratiam vnionis, qua ipsa assumpta est in vnitatem personae & hypostasis diuinae in tempore, ideo diuersę filiationis diuersę rationes emer-gunt, Christūsque secundum naturam diuinam FiliusDei dicitur, natura primo ac per se, & genitus ab aeterno: secundum naturā ve-rò humanam, ex gratia vnionis hypostaticae, & filius factus in tem-pore. Vt autē duae illae in Christo naturae, & diuersae illae filiationis rationes, non conficiunt duo suppositā, ita quoque nec duos filios aut Christos inferunt: quia nomina concreta non nisi multiplica-tis suppositis ipsis multiplicantur, quod ipsum tantus doctor ac disputator, qui vniuersam Christi Ecclesiam in arenam ac certa-men prouocare, & vt verius dicam turbare non erubescit, ignora-re non deberet.
units.tr: Answer. Setting aside everything that the philosophers and schoolmen rightly say about the beginning, progress and completion of conception and generation, and likewise about the term of the twofold generation, namely of nature and of person, we will answer the argument briefly and clearly, first showing the source of the error. Ostorodius rashly denies and attacks the truth of the divine nature and its essential attribute, eternity, by taking his argument either from the human nature or from the beginning of the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος] person, who begins to subsist at a certain time together in the form of God and the form of a servant. For since the divine and human natures do not clash but agree within the whole person, neither nature is rightly denied on the basis of an argument taken from the other nature or from the whole person. Whoever is truly conceived and generated, that person himself is conceived, and he does not begin to exist before he is conceived and begotten. This holds in that generation which is natural in its efficient cause, matter and termination, that is, when through generation the supposit does not merely receive the nature, but the nature itself is naturally terminated in a natural supposit by the power of a natural principle; thus both nature and supposit are produced by the one who conceives and begets. But in a singular and supernatural generation, which has a supernatural principle of efficient cause and a supernatural supposit as the term of the nature, a supposit which by the power of conception and generation is neither produced nor receives its being, such as the generation and conception of the Son of God in the womb of the Virgin Mary, this rule cannot apply. For Christ, or the Son of God, was indeed conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary and begotten of her, and he did not begin to exist before he was begotten of her; namely the whole person, God-man [Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος], subsisting together in the form of God and of a servant, because the whole person is begotten. Yet because neither the whole person, as regards both natures, nor what was communicated to the human nature through the grace of union, was produced by the power of that conception or generation, it by no means follows that Christ, or the Son of God, did not exist even according to the divine nature from eternity, or before his nativity from the Virgin Mary. For the human nature, which in itself was without subsistence [ἀνυπόστατος] and destitute of its own personality, was taken by the divine Person, from grace, into the unity of his person in the very womb of the Virgin, and was joined to him; that union and conjunction, made from grace and in time, can prejudice nothing concerning eternity. Hence the Adversary also errs through ignorance of the elenchus, and concludes rashly, if it is permissible to speak thus in this mystery, from what is distributed to what is not distributed, or from part to whole. Yet it does not follow from this that Mary did not bear the whole Christ and his person, or did not bear a true and perfect man, or that two Sons of God must be posited. Not the first: for since that union of the human nature with the person of the Word [τοῦ λόγου] took place in the very womb of the Virgin Mary, and the soul and body of Christ were created in the Word itself, so that the human nature of Christ, in itself without subsistence [ἀνυπόστατος] but taken up into the unity of the divine person and made subsisting in him [ἐνυπόστατος], did not subsist even for a moment outside the Word; hence the Virgin Mary rightly bore the whole person, and she is called God-bearer [Θεοτόκος] by the holy Fathers. Not the second: for although that supposit by which the human nature of Christ is terminated was not produced by the power of conception, nor proceeded from a natural principle, being divine and eternal and not human and temporal, it does not follow from this that the Virgin Mary did not bear a perfect man. The supposit itself is not one of the intrinsic causes of the nature conceived and begotten, but lies outside them, and belongs neither to the kind of matter nor of form; it is therefore not a part but the term of the nature, just as a point is not a part or cause of a line but its term and end [πέρας] (as Euclid calls it), a line which at times exists in act without a point. Therefore no consequence follows from the quality of this supposit, as the term relates to the quality or imperfection of the human nature, which that divine supposit determines. Nor is it rightly said that anything is lacking in its own kind, when something more worthy and excellent is supplied and communicated to it from a higher, natural principle. Finally, not the third: for diverse grounds of sonship do not constitute diverse Christs or diverse Sons of God. The title "Son" is a concrete name, and it is attributed to Christ not properly on the ground of essence and nature, insofar as these are distinguished from the supposit, but on the ground of the supposit. And since the hypostasis or supposit of the Son of God is one in number, namely the divine one, therefore Christ is called only one Christ and one Son of God. And since that hypostasis belongs to two diverse natures, to the divine nature by eternal generation, first and through itself, and from eternity, but to the human nature neither first, nor through generation, nor through itself, nor by reason of a natural principle, but through the grace of the hypostatic union, by which it was taken into the unity of the divine person and hypostasis in time, therefore diverse grounds of diverse sonship arise: Christ is called Son of God according to the divine nature, by nature first and through itself, and begotten from eternity; but according to the human nature, from the grace of the hypostatic union, and made a son in time. Just as those two natures in Christ, and those diverse grounds of sonship, do not make two supposits, so neither do they introduce two Sons or two Christs; for concrete names are multiplied only when the supposits themselves are multiplied. This a teacher and disputant of such stature, who does not blush to challenge the whole Church of Christ into the arena and contest, or, to speak more truly, to disturb it, ought not to be ignorant of.

units.la: Atque supAtque hic est nodus ille Gordius, quem ne Alexander quidem Trinitarius expedire potest, ut misello suo populo Ostorrodius iactabundus audet persuadere. Illum an soluerimus, doctus & æquus iudicet lector. Manet itaque inconcussa thesis nostra, Filium nempe Dei Dominum Iesum Christum ab æterno, ante omne principium creationis, ante omne tempus, locum, & res creatas omnes, extitisse: cuius veritatem Sociniana turba allatrabit quidem, sed labefactabit aut euertet nunquam. Nunc ad alia progrediendum.
units.tr: And here is that Gordian knot which not even Alexander the Trinitarian could untie, though boastful Ostorodius dares to persuade his poor little people that it can be. Let the learned and fair reader judge whether we have loosed it. Our thesis therefore remains unshaken: that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, existed from eternity, before every beginning of creation, before all time and place, and before all created things. The Socinian rabble will indeed bark at this truth, but they will never weaken or overthrow it. Now let us proceed to other matters.

units.la: CAPVT XIV. In quo argumentum quintum pro æterna Filii Deitate proponitur ac defenditur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. In which the fifth argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is put forward and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum quintum, quo æterna ac diuina Christi natura demonstratur, inde desumitur, quòd Christus in sacris literis cum eiusmodi circumstantiis Deus appellatur, quæ nulli creaturæ tribui aut cōpetere possunt: Vnde sic concludimus,
units.tr: Our fifth argument, by which the eternal and divine nature of Christ is demonstrated, is drawn from this: that in the sacred writings Christ is called God in such circumstances as cannot be attributed or belong to any creature. Hence we conclude thus:

units.la: Qui in sacris Scripturis non attributiue tantum, sed etiam subiectiue Deus appellatur, sic vt nomen illud DEVS, non tantum prædicati, sed etiam subiecti locum obtineat, ille est verus atque æternus Deus.
units.tr: Whoever in the holy Scriptures is called God not only attributively but also subjectively, so that the name GOD holds the place not only of predicate but also of subject, is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui Christus in sacris Literis non attributiue tantum, sed etiam subiectiue Deus appellatur, hoc est, nomen DEVS ita de Christo enuntiatur, vt non tantum prædicati, sed etiam subiecti locum occupet.
units.tr: But Christ in the holy Scriptures is called God not only attributively but also subjectively; that is, the name GOD is so predicated of Christ that it occupies the place not only of predicate but also of subject.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus atque æternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Maioris veritas inde liquet, quòd nullus scripturæ locus extat, in quo nomen Deus de vlla creatura enunciatur, vt locum subiecti in enunciatione obtineat. Christū autem quod in assumptione affirmamus hoc nomine peculiari ratione indigitari, ex scriptura sacra cuidentissimè liquet. Vocatur enim primò Deus non tantum attributiuè, vt Iohan. 1. v. 1. Erat sermo ille Deus. Iohan. 20. v. 28. Respondit Thomas, & dixit ei, Dominus meus, & Deus meus. Rom. 9. v. 5. Christus qui est Deus supra omnes laudandus in secula. 1.Ioh.5. ver.20. Scimus Filium Dei venisse, & dedisse nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus illum, qui verax est, & sumus in vera ce illo, in Filio eius Iesu Christo: hic est verus Deus, & vita aeterna. Iud. ver.5. Impij, qui Dei nostri gratiam transferunt ad lasciuiam, & solum illum verum Deum, ac Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum negant. Verùm etiam subiectiuè: vt, Tit.2. v.31. Expectates beatam illam spem, & illustrem illum aduentum gloriae magni illius Dei, ac Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi. 1.Timot.3.v.16. Deus conspicuus est factus in carne. Hebr.1.ver.9. O Deus, vnxit te Deus tuus oleo laetitiae vltra consortes tuos. Quae omnia veritatem in Christo naturae diuinae firmissimè demonstrant. Deinde non simpliciter Deus, sed Deus magnus appellatur, quod epitheton soli vero ac aeterno Israelis Deo competere euidenter liquet, ex ipsa nominis ratione qua Dauid passim in Psal. reddit, ab operib. & miraculis stupendis, quae à nulla creatura, sed à solo Deo patrari possunt, desumptâ. Ps.77.v.14. O Deus, in sanctitate via tua est, quis fortis, magnus, & Deus? & 15. Tu o fortis mirificè ostendisti in populis robur tuum. & deinceps ad finem vsq; Psalmi. & 86.v.8.9.10. Non est par tibi inter vilos Deos, ô Domine, neque sunt paria operibus tuis opera: omnes gentes, quas affictis venientes incurruant se coram te Domine, & honorè habent nomini tuo: quia magnus es, atque mirificus, tu Deus, solus es, & 96.v.3.4.5. Narrate in gentib. honorem eius, in omnib. populis mirabilia eius opera, Magnum Iehouam, & laudatum valdè, reuerendum esse supra omnes Deos: nam omnes dii populorum sunt idola, Iehoua verò caelos fecit. Ex quib. liquidò cōstat, Christū nō tantū ratione dignitatis & officii Deum à Patre factū, sed ratione essentię verū atq; æternū Deum, & Iehouā Israelis esse. Tertiò, hisce æquipollent illa quod appellatur Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium, Apoc.17.14. & 19.16. Item Dominus, & rex gloriae. 1.Cor.2.8. quae nomina veritatē doctrinae nostrae fortiter euincunt, si cum veteris Testamenti scripturis conferantur, vbi eadem vero illi Iehouae, & Deo Israelis tanquam propria tribuuntur. Vide Psal.95.3. & 24.8.10. Quibus adde Act.7.2. 1.Tim.6.15. & alia. Ex quibus omnibus liquidò constat, Christum non tantùm ratione dignitatis ac officii Deum esse factum, sed ratione essentiae ac naturae verum atque aeternum Iehouam Israelis.
units.tr: The truth of the major premise is clear from the fact that there is no passage of Scripture in which the name God is said of any creature so as to hold the place of subject in the statement. That Christ, whom we affirm in the minor premise to be designated by this name in a peculiar way, is most clearly shown from holy Scripture.
