For he is called God first not merely attributively: John 1:1, "That Word was God"; John 20:28, "Thomas answered and said to him, My Lord and my God"; Rom. 9:5, "Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever"; 1 John 5:20, "We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life"; Jude v. 4, "Ungodly men who turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and deny the only true God and our Lord Jesus Christ." But also subjectively: Titus 2:13, "Looking for that blessed hope and glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ"; 1 Tim. 3:16, "God was manifested in the flesh"; Heb. 1:9, "O God, thy God has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows." All of these most firmly demonstrate the truth of the divine nature in Christ. Next, he is called not simply God but great God, an epithet which clearly belongs only to the true and eternal God of Israel, from the very reason of the name, which David everywhere in the Psalms draws from works and stupendous miracles that can be performed by no creature but only by God. Ps. 77:14, "O God, thy way is in holiness; who is so great a God as our God?"; v. 15, "Thou, O Strong One, hast wonderfully shown thy strength among the peoples," and so on to the end of the Psalm; Ps. 86:8-10, "There is none like thee among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like thy works. All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord, and shall glorify thy name; for thou art great and doest wonders; thou art God alone"; Ps. 96:3-5, "Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples. Great is Jehovah and greatly to be praised, to be feared above all gods; for all the gods of the peoples are idols, but Jehovah made the heavens." From which it is plainly established that Christ is God, and Jehovah of Israel, not only by reason of dignity and office, having been made God by the Father, but by reason of essence, the true and eternal God. Thirdly, equivalent to these are the names King of kings, and Lord of lords, Rev. 17:14 and 19:16; likewise Lord and King of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8. These names strongly prove the truth of our doctrine if they are compared with the Scriptures of the Old Testament, where the same are attributed as proper to that very Jehovah and God of Israel. See Ps. 95:3 and 24:8, 10. To these add Acts 7:2, 1 Tim. 6:15, and others. From all of which it is plainly established that Christ has become God not only by dignity and office, but is by essence and nature the true and eternal Jehovah of Israel.

units.la: Oftorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo hanc quaestionem proponit: An nimirum ex eo, quod Christus Deus sit, diuina eiusdem natura demonstrari possit? Nos affirmamus, & veritatem asserassertionis nostræ ex Scripturis luculenter demonstrauimus. Ille negat, & quia hanc quæstionem tractat αὐτοκατακρίτως, primò omnium argumentum nostrum proponit, cuius forma talis esse potest.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in the tenth chapter of his Institutes, poses this question: Whether, indeed, from the fact that Christ is God, his divine nature can be demonstrated? We affirm it, and have clearly demonstrated from the Scriptures the truth of our assertion. He denies it, and since he treats this question in a self-condemning manner [αὐτοκατακρίτως], he first of all puts forward our argument, whose form may be as follows:

units.la: Quicunque in Scripturis sacris Deus appellatur, ille diuinam habet naturam: aut certè non verus: sed falsus, & nomine tenus Deus fuerit, quod de Christo dici minimè potest.
units.tr: Whoever is called God in the sacred Scriptures has the divine nature; or else he is not truly God, but false, and is God only in name; which cannot be said of Christ.

units.la: Atqui Christus in Scripturis sacris Deus appellatur:
units.tr: But Christ is called God in the sacred Scriptures:

units.la: Ergo Christus diuinam naturam habet.
units.tr: Therefore Christ has the divine nature.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum respondet, Christum in sacris literis non ideo Deum appellari (quamuis ad hoc ipsum, nempe assumptionem nostram, demonstrandum multa loca allegentur, quæ non de Filio, sed de Patre sint intelligenda, quemadmodum ex Scriptis ipsorum nempe Socinianorum, sit manifestum) quasi ille Deus altissimus esset, sed quia à Deo diuinam potestatem ac gloriam acceperit, quandoquidem Deus, testante Apostolo, nomen illi dedit, quod est supra omne nomen, vt in illo nomine Iesu flectatur omne genu, Phil. 2. v. 9. Propter illud itaque nomen, id est, propter potentiam illam, imperium, potestatem, atque gloriam, quæ omnia plané sunt diuina, ipsum Deum esse, & appellari, ac proinde falsum esse, Christum propterea quod Dei nomine indigitatur, diuinam naturam habere, hoc est, Deum altissimum esse, quemadmodum Aduersarii interpretantur. Hæc responsio sic formari potest, quo vis argumenti eò magis elucescat.
units.tr: To this argument he replies that Christ is not called God in the sacred writings on that account (although many passages are cited to prove this very assumption, namely ours, which are to be understood not of the Son but of the Father, as is clear from their own writings, namely those of the Socinians) as though he were the most high God, but because he has received divine power and glory from God, since God, as the Apostle testifies, gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, Phil. 2:9. Therefore, because of that name, that is, because of that power, dominion, authority and glory, which are all plainly divine, he himself is called God and is God; and consequently it is false that Christ, because he is designated by the name of God, has the divine nature, that is, is the most high God, as our opponents interpret. This response can be formulated thus, so that the force of the argument may shine forth all the more.

units.la: Si Christus in Scripturis sacris Deus appellatur tantùm propterea, quod Deus illi nomen dedit, in quo omne genu est flectendum, tum sequitur falsum esse Christum ideo Deum vocari, quia diuinam naturam habeat, & sit Deus altissimus.
units.tr: If Christ is called God in the sacred Scriptures only because God gave him the name in which every knee must bow, then it follows that it is false that Christ is called God because he has the divine nature and is the most high God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Resp. I. argumentum nostrum mala fide ab Aduersario proponi, non enim ideo affirmamus, Christum diuinam naturam habere, atque Deum altissimum esse, quia quouis modo & nudè Deus in Scripturis dicatur, sed quia nomen illud Christo cum eiusmodi circunstantiis tribuitur, quas in nullam creaturam, sed in solum, verum illum, ac vnum Deum competere, apud omnes sanæ mentis iudices est extra controuersiam, qua de re supra in assumptionis nostræ demonstratione egimus. II. Nostros ad confirmandam illam enunciationem, quod Christus in Scripturis Deus appelletur, multa Scripturæ testimonia adducere, quæ non de Filio,
units.tr: Reply. First, our argument is put forward by the adversary in bad faith. For we do not affirm that Christ has the divine nature and is the most high God because God is named in the Scriptures in any way whatever, bare, but because that name is given to Christ in such circumstances as, beyond dispute among all sound-minded judges, belong to no creature but to the one true and only God; a matter we discussed above in the demonstration of our assumption. Second, to confirm the statement that Christ is called God in the Scriptures, our side adduce many testimonies of Scripture which are not to be understood of the Son but truly of God the Father; he ought not to have affirmed this so rashly,

units.la: O verùm de Deo Patre sint intelligenda, non tam temerè affirmare, aut eiusdem scriptæ antistitum testimonio fulcire, sed re ipsa coprobare debuisset, cum nullo iure, vt veritatis hostibus sine ratione aliquid affirmantibus, vel iuratis etiam, fidem vt habeamus, possimus adigi. III. Negamus, id, quod in assumptione affirmatur, ideo videlicet Christum in sacris literis Deum appellari, quia Deus Pater nome supra omne nomen, i. potestatem, gloriam, ac potentiam diuinam in ipsum contulerit: nec quicquam ab Aduersario adsertur, quo illa sententia stabiliatur, aut confirmetur: quamuis ad tantum errorem stabiliendum, quid quæso in medium adduci possit? Non enim ideo Christum nomine illo diuino indigitari, quod Pater ipsi in tempore, propter obedientiam præstitam, nomen supra omne aliud nomen, hoc est, gloriam, ac potestatem contulerit diuinam, sed quod ipse Christus, verus ille Iehouah, gloriam essentialem iam ante iacta mundi fundamenta apud Patrem habuerit, quod verò ille ab æterno à Patre genitus, & naturæ huius & gratiæ, seu creationis, & regenerationis, ac restaurationis autor fuerit, Patríque coæternus, & coæqualis existat, ex antecedentibus capitibus liquet: Atque hæc etiam causa est, quod nomen hoc ipsum Χριστός Christo cum eiusmodi circumstantiis tribuatur, quæ nulli creaturæ competere possunt, vt à natura diuina Christi ad hoc diuinum nomen, & vicissim ab hoc ad illam, necessaria detur consequentia.
units.tr: nor to have buttressed it with the testimony of the leaders of his own sect, but to have proved it in fact, since by no right can we be bound to give credence to the enemies of truth, who assert something without reason, even when they swear to it. Third, we deny that what is asserted in the minor premise holds, namely that Christ is called God in the sacred writings for this reason: that God the Father conferred on him the name above every name, that is, power, glory and divine might. Nor is anything brought forward by our opponent by which that opinion is established or confirmed; though, to establish so great an error, what, pray, could be brought forward? For Christ is designated by that divine name not because the Father conferred on him in time, on account of obedience rendered, the name above every other name, that is, glory and divine power, but because Christ himself, the true Jehovah, had essential glory with the Father already before the foundations of the world were laid; and that he, begotten by the Father from eternity, was the author of this nature and of grace, that is, of creation, regeneration and restoration, and is co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, is clear from the preceding chapters. And this too is the reason why this very name Christ [Χριστός] is attributed to Christ in such circumstances as cannot belong to any creature, so that from the divine nature of Christ to this divine name, and conversely from this name to that nature, a necessary consequence is given.

units.la: Hanc autem responsionem suam, dicit Ostorrodius duabus potissimum obiectionibus impugnari. I. Si Christus prædicta ratione Deus esset, sequeretur illum esse Deum factum, quod ex Scripturis sacris, vt pote quæ nunquam doceat, Christum à Patre Deum factum esse, demonstrari non potest. II. Si Christus non haberet diuinam naturam, hoc est, vnus ille Deus esset, duo Dii contra Scripturam, quæ vnum tantum Deum esse disertè, & sapissimè affirmat, statuentur.
units.tr: Ostorrodius says that this answer of his is attacked chiefly by two objections. I. If Christ were God in the aforesaid sense, it would follow that he was made God, which cannot be shown from the sacred Scriptures, since they never teach that Christ was made God by the Father. II. If Christ did not have the divine nature, that is, if he were that one God, then two Gods would be set up, contrary to Scripture, which states plainly and very often that there is only one God.

units.la: Ad primam obiectionem respondet, licet iisdem verbis ac syllabis in Scripturis non legatur, quod Deus Pater Christum Deum constitue-rit, inde tamen minime sequi, ipsum propterea à Deo constitutum ac factum Deum non esse. Primò, Si enim hoc ideo verum esset, quia totidem literis ac syllabis in sacris Scripturis non legi-tur, tum neque Aduersarij sua dogmata de Trinitate personarum de duabus in Christo naturis, & alia demonstrare possent. Vnde satis manifestum fit illos suis obiectionibus non veritatem sed victoriam, quaerere. Secundò, quia res ipsa per se clara est, quòd Deus ipsum Iudicem, Dominum, ac Regem constituerit, ipsique omnem potestatem, non tantùm in terra, sed etiam in cœlo, ac proinde diuinam dederit, in hunc finem, vt omnis lingua ipsum Dominum suum agnoscat, & confiteatur, omnéque genu non hominum tantùm, sed etiam Angelorum, tam malorum, quam bonorum, in nomine illius, flectatur, cùmque sicut Patrem honorent. Quem honorem diuinum esse, nemo inficias ire potest. Ex quibus omnibus sequi existimat, Deum Patrem ipsum Christum etiam Deum constituisse. Tertiò, quia etiam alij Dij veri, Psal. 82. vers. 6. facti sunt Dij, qui tamen facti esse nusquam legantur.
units.tr: To the first objection he replies: although it is not read in Scripture in the very same words and syllables that God the Father constituted Christ God, it does not follow from this that he was therefore not constituted and made God by God. First, if this were true because it is not read in Scripture in exactly the same letters and syllables, then neither could our opponents prove their doctrines of the Trinity of persons, of the two natures in Christ, and other things. Hence it is quite plain that in their objections they seek not the truth but victory. Second, because the matter is clear in itself, that God constituted him Judge, Lord and King, and gave him all power, not only on earth but also in heaven, and therefore divine power, to this end: that every tongue should acknowledge and confess him as its Lord, and that every knee, not only of men but also of angels, both evil and good, should bow in his name, and that they should honour him as they honour the Father. No one can deny that this honour is divine. From all these things he thinks it follows that God the Father constituted Christ also God. Third, because other true gods too, Psalm 82:6, were made gods, yet nowhere is it read that they were made.

units.la: Resp. Quum in hisce exceptionibus palmarium penè argumentum contineatur, quo Sociniani venerandam Christi Saluatoris nostri diuinitatem impugnare solent, ideò tres illas responsiones ordine disponemus, quò commodius ad singulas responderi possit, & simul vtra pars litigantium in veritatis aut inanis victoriæ studium incumbat, magis elucescat.
units.tr: Reply. Since almost the chief argument by which the Socinians usually attack the venerable divinity of our Saviour Christ is contained in these objections, we will therefore arrange those three answers in order, so that a reply can be made to each more conveniently, and at the same time it may become clearer which side of the disputants is intent on the pursuit of truth and which on empty victory.

units.la: Argumentum igitur primum tale est.
units.tr: The first argument, then, is this.

units.la: Si Christus ideò non esset Deus factus & constitutus, quia videlicet hoc ipsum sacra Scriptura totidem verbis ac syllabis non docet: tum etiam Aduersarij nullum argumentum ex Scriptura Sacra habebunt quò dogmata sua de Trinitate, déque duabus in Christo naturis, & alia demonstrare possent: quia videlicet illi ipsi fatentur res quidem ipsas in Scripturis contineri, licet verba & modus docendi, quibus res illas proponunt, & ab hæreticorum fraudibus distinguunt, totidem syllabis ibidem non legantur:
units.tr: If Christ were not made and constituted God for the reason that sacred Scripture does not teach this very thing in the same words and syllables, then our opponents too will have no argument from Holy Scripture by which they could prove their doctrines of the Trinity and of the two natures in Christ, and other things; for they themselves admit that the things indeed are contained in Scripture, although the words and manner of teaching, by which they set those things forth and distinguish them from the frauds of heretics, are not read in the same syllables there:

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum, vel saltem ab Aduersarijs non concedi-tur: Ergo etiam antecedens falsum est.
units.tr: But the consequent is false, or at least is not conceded by our opponents: therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Resp. I. nostram obiectionem mala fide ab Aduersario proponi, ac proinde argumento suo falsam hypothesin substerni. Non enim ideò tantum negamus & abominamur thesin illam Socinianam, qua illi Christum propter datum ipsi nomen supra omne nomen, hoc est, potestatem, gloriam, ac potentiam diuinam Deum factum esse à Patre affirmant, contra veritatem ac pietatem omnem, quia videlicet illa totidem verbis ac syllabis in Scripturis sacris non legitur, quasi interea res ipsas illis contineri taciti confiteremur, aut concederemus, sed ideo quia res ipsa quæ ab Aduersariis defenditur, cum veritate diuina, Scripturæ sacræ libris comprehensa pugnat manifestissimè, ac proinde etiam voces ac verba thefeos illius non sono tantum, sed etiam sensu toto, à verbis Scripturæ discrepant ac dissentiunt, sic vt neque res, neque verba in sacris literis comprehendantur. Pugnat, inquam, assertio illa cum veritate diuina, quia illa Christum in tempore à Deo Patre Deum factum esse affirmat: hæc vero eundem ab æterno apud Patrem gloria conspicuum fuisse, vniuersum hunc mundum condidisse, ipsique Patri æqualem esse testatur. At vero dicat mihi quasi Oftorrodius, qua ratione (vt ex multis vnum vrgeam) Deus in tempore factus, creatura ᾿Αλοΐς, & finita, in quam nihil quod per se & absolute infinitum est, cadere potest, Deo æterno creatori immenso, infinito, omnes alios qui verè sunt Dii constituenti, & potestate ac autoritate instruenti, par & æqualis esse queat? Atque hæc est falsa illa hypothesis cui superstruit argumentum etiam falsum, siue fundamentum eius, siue materiam respicias. II. Hinc igitur totus syllogismus corruit, cuius complexio à quæstionis scopo longissime aberret: nō enim quæritur, An ideo tàtum Christus nō sit Deus factus à Patre, quia hoc ipsum totidem verbis ac syllabis in Scripturis sacris non legitur, quod illa dianoia concluditur? Sed an Christus sit Deus factus à Patre, cùm tamen hoc ipsum in sacris literis sive verba, sive res verbis comprehensas respicias, nusquam doceatur? qui est sensus obiectionis, & argumenti illius, quo Doctores Ecclesiarum nostrarum, Photiniam illam thesin impugnant, cum quo etiam illa conclusio Aduersarii minimè pugnat, ac proinde aerem, non verò nostram doctrinam pungit. Vnde si ad modum primum syllogismi connexi hunc ipsum reduxeris, assumptio falsa fuerit. III. Ex iis quæ dicta sunt etiam liquet, connexum ipsum manifesto comparatorum elencho laborare, cùm verba dogmatis illius Christiani de Trinitate personarum diuinarum, sono tantum, nō sensu, à verbis Scripturæ, quæ rem ipsam euidenter docet, differat, à cuius Scripturæ veritate thesis Sociniana, & verbis & re ipsa maximè discrepat. IV. Quia & assumptio falsa est, duas enim in Christo naturas, hoc est, Christum, non hominem tàtum, sed etiam verum Deum esse, ScriScriptura sacra toties disertis verbis inculcat, quoties eum veri hominis, veríque Dei nomine indigitat, qua de re in antecedentibus iam egimus. Ex hisce autem omnibus Christianus & æquus Lector iudicet, Samosatenianíne an vero nos victoriam magis, quàm veritatem quæramus, quáve conscientia & æquitate illam calumniam Ostorrodius nobis impingat.
units.tr: Reply. I. That our objection is put forward by the opponent in bad faith, and that his argument therefore rests on a false hypothesis. For we do not deny and abominate that Socinian thesis, by which they affirm that Christ was made God by the Father on account of the name given him above every name, that is, power, glory and divine might, contrary to truth and all piety, merely because it is not read in the sacred Scriptures in the very same words and syllables, as if we tacitly confessed or conceded that the things themselves are contained in them. Rather we do so because the thing defended by our adversaries fights most clearly with the divine truth comprehended in the books of Holy Scripture, and therefore the very voices and words of that thesis differ and disagree from the words of Scripture not only in sound but in their whole sense, so that neither the matter nor the words are contained in the sacred letters. That assertion, I say, fights with divine truth, because it affirms that Christ was made God by God the Father in time, whereas Scripture testifies that he was from eternity conspicuous in glory with the Father, created this whole universe, and is equal to the Father himself. But let Ostorrodius, as it were, tell me by what reasoning (to press just one of many) God made in time, a creature, finite and created, into whom nothing that is in itself and absolutely infinite can fall, could be equal and like to the eternal Creator, immense and infinite, who constitutes all other beings that truly are gods and furnishes them with power and authority? And this is that false hypothesis on which he builds a false argument too, whether you look at its foundation or its matter. II. Hence the whole syllogism collapses, and its structure wanders very far from the scope of the question. For the question is not: Whether Christ is not made God by the Father only because this very thing is not read in the sacred Scriptures in the same words and syllables, which is the conclusion of that reasoning? But whether Christ was made God by the Father, although, whether you look to the words or to the matter comprehended in the words, this is nowhere taught in the sacred letters? This is the sense of the objection and of the argument by which the teachers of our Churches attack that Photinian thesis; with it that conclusion of the adversary does not agree at all, and so it strikes the air rather than our doctrine. Hence, if you reduce this to the first mood of the connected syllogism, the assumption will be false. III. From what has been said it is also clear that the connection itself labours under a manifest comparison of the elenchus, since the words of that Christian doctrine of the Trinity of the divine persons differ from the words of Scripture, which clearly teaches the thing itself, in sound only and not in sense; and the Socinian thesis differs most from the truth of that Scripture both in words and in fact. IV. Because the assumption is also false: for Holy Scripture repeats in plain words that there are two natures in Christ, that is, that Christ is not only man but also true God, as often as it names him by the name of true man and true God, a matter we have already treated in the preceding sections. From all these things let the Christian and fair reader judge whether it is Samosatenian or we who seek victory more than truth, and with what conscience and fairness Ostorrodius fastens that calumny upon us.

units.la: Argumentum secundum tale est.
units.tr: The second argument is as follows.

units.la: Si Deus Christum Iudicem, Regem, ac Dominum constituit, omnémq; potestatem non tantùm in terra, sed etiam in cælo, ac proinde divinam ipsi tr didit, ac donauit, eo fine, ut omnis lingua eum Dominum suum agnoscat, omnéque genu non hominum tantum, sed etiam Angelorum, tam malorum, quàm bonorum, in nomine ipsius, flectatur, eúmque sicut Patrem omnes honorent: sequitur etiam hoc ipsi datum ac donatum esse, quod sit & vocetur Deus, & per consequens, Deum Patrem ipsum Deum fecisse & constituisse.
units.tr: If God has appointed Christ as Judge, King and Lord, and has given and granted him all power not only on earth but also in heaven, and therefore divine power, so that every tongue should acknowledge him as its Lord, and every knee should bow in his name, not only of men but also of angels, both evil and good, and all should honour him as they honour the Father: it follows that it has also been given and granted to him that he is and is called God, and consequently that God the Father has made and appointed him God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum, Ioh. 5. verf. 22. Act. 10. verf. 42. & 17. verf. 3. Act. 2. verf. 36. Matth. 28. verf. 18. Phil. 2. verf. 9. Iohan. 5. verf. 23.
units.tr: But the first is true: John 5:22. Acts 10:42 and 17:3. Acts 2:36. Matt. 28:18. Phil. 2:9. John 5:23.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore so is the second.

units.la: Rationem consequentiæ hanc subiungit, Quia, videlicet maius sit Deum esse, quàm Dominum, sicut etiam ipsa deitas sine dominio consistere non potest.
units.tr: He adds this reason for the inference: because being God is greater than being Lord, just as Deity itself cannot exist without dominion.

units.la: Syllogismus talis erit.
units.tr: The syllogism will be as follows.

units.la: Si maius, seu plus est esse Deum, quàm esse Dominum, nec Deitas sine dominio quicquam est, aut subsistere potest, tum si Deus Christum Iudicem ac Dominum constituit, sequitur eundem etiam Christum à Deo Patre Deum factum esse.
units.tr: If being God is greater, or more, than being Lord, and Deity is nothing, or cannot subsist, without dominion, then, if God has appointed Christ Judge and Lord, it follows that the same Christ has also been made God by God the Father.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore so is the second.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam propter homonymiam regni, ac dominii Christi, quod duplex est, essentiale vnum, & commune Patri, Filio, ac Spiritui sancto: mediatorium, & personale alterum, ex dispensatione voluntatis à Christo acceptum, quod proprium est personæ Christi. Si de priore loquatur Ostorrodius, tum connexum verum, & assumptio falsa fuerit, nec locis illis citatis demonstrari potest, quia illa nō de supremo illo, vni- uersali, indepēdēte, ac Deo naturali, & essentiali dominio, sed de personali οἰκονομικῷ, mediatorio, & acquisito, ac supremo illi subor- dinato, loquuntur, quod Deus Christo donauit, ἡ σκηνή, vt loquitur Apostolus Phil. 2. 9. Et Christus ex dispensatione volunta- ria suscepit, idem Patri traditurus, cùm prius æquè, ac gloriam suam, vt pote sibi essentiale, iam ab æterno habuerit. Si verò de posteriore sit sermo, assumptionem quidem veram ac connexum falsum esse dicimus. Ex eo enim quod Christus sit factus Dominus, non sequitur propterea factum esse Deum, quia hæc sunt maximè dissimilia: Nam Deus est natura, Dominus voluntate & instituto, si nempe ad personale hoc & dispesatiuum Dominium respexeris: Deus est absolutè, Dominus relatè, & respectu nostri: Deus est essentialiter, Dominus accidentariè: Deus est formaliter secundum naturam diuinam suam, Dominus secundum vtraque in vnitate personæ ἀνθρώπου: quæ omnia inter se conturbat Ostorrodius imperitissimè. A ratione enim totius personæ Christi ἀνθρώπου, ad naturam ipsius alteram: aut ex opere voluntariæ dispensationis, atque consilii, ad opus, conditionem, & ius naturale, non datur consequentia. Sed videamus ipsam rationem, quæ connexum illud fulcitur ab Ostorrodio. Maius quid, seu plus est, inquit, esse Deum, quàm Dominum: sicuti etiam ipsa Deitas sine dominio nihil quicquam esse, nec subsistere potest. Duo verò quum sint hic interrogata, illa seorsim explicabimus, antequam ad illum prossyllogismum respondeamus. Prius igitur quod attinet, An, videlicet maius quid & excellentius sit esse Deum, quàm esse Dominum, suspicor in verbis Ostorrodii per typographicum errorem omissam esse particulam negatiuam non, sic vt sententia Aduersarii hæc sit, quum non sit excellentius quid esse Deum, quàm esse Dominum, sequitur si Christus à Deo Patre factus, & constitutus sit Dominus, eundem etiam Christum à Deo Patre factum esse Deum. Po- sterius autem, quod nempe Deitas absque dominio nihil plane sit, neque consistere possit, est ambiguum, propter duplex dominium di-ib uinum, essentiale nimirum ac summum: & œconomicum, il-li sique subordinatum. De illo verum fuerit, quod affirmatur quia est attributum essentiale Dei, quod negari nisi Deo negato non potest. De isto falsum, quia à mera ac libera voluntate Deo Dei pendet, quæ efficere potuisset, vt tale dominium nunquam extitisset, sine naturæ diuinæ præiudicio vllo. Quod si igitur, vt ad prossyllogismum respondeamus, nullus sit error typographicus, certissimum est connexum esse salsissimum cùm à minore ad maius, in hoc argumentationis genere, nulla datur consequentia, nec qui efficit id quod minus est, adeóque facilius, statim etiam effecisse dicetur id quod maius est, ac proinde difficilius, præsertim in rebus illis, quæ non sunt eiusdem generis. Si verò error typographicus sit commissus, tum distinguendum est dominium Dei essentiale, primum, summum, ac inde pendens, ab illo quod est œconomicum, & priori illi subordinatum: Si de priori & essentiali dominio verba Aduersarii intelligantur, verissima erit minor, sed consequentia falsa, quia Syllogismus principalis de posteriore dominio loquitur, vt paulò ante ostendimus. Sin verò de posteriore, & œconomico dominio verba illa accipiantur, propositio vera, assumptio autem falsa fuerit, quia Deus est solus herus, solus princeps, Rex regum, & Dominus dominantium, Matth. 11. vers. 25. Act. 17. vers. 20. 1. Tim. 6. vers. 15. propter cuius naturæ præcellentiam, & necessariam aliarum rerum ab illa dependentiam, nullum est bonum vel ius in creaturis, quod non sit illius dominio essentiali & æterno subiectum. At verò hoc alterum dominium non est naturale, sed œconomicum, nec fluit simpliciter ex ipsa naturali Dei excellentia supra res omnino omnes, sed ex libera eiusdem voluntate, neque est summum illud, primum, & αὐτοῦ, sed proximum, & subordinatum: nec denique æternum, sed vt laborando, patiendo, moriendo, ac præmium redemptionis pro nobis persoluendo à Christo reuera est comparatum: ita quoque tandem quantum ad exercitium siue actum processorium, vt loquuntur, aliqua saltem ex parte ab eodem depo-netur, 1. Cor. 15. vers. 24. 28. Ex quibus omnibus assumptionis falsitas satis elucescit, & sic totum corruit argumentum.
units.tr: Reply. The inference is false, on account of the ambiguity of the kingdom and dominion of Christ, which is twofold: one is essential and common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; the other is mediatorial and personal, received by Christ from the dispensation of the will, and proper to the person of Christ. If Ostorrodius is speaking of the former, then the connection may be true but the assumption false, and it cannot be shown from the passages cited, because those passages do not speak of that supreme, universal, independent and natural and essential dominion of God, but of the personal, economic [οἰκονομικῷ], mediatorial and acquired dominion, subordinate to that supreme one, which God gave to Christ, and which the Apostle speaks of in Phil. 2:9 [ὑπερύψωσεν]. Christ took this up by a voluntary dispensation, though he was to hand it over to the Father again; for before, he had equally, as something essential to himself, both his glory and this dominion from eternity. But if the discussion is about the latter, we say that the assumption is indeed true and the connection false. For from the fact that Christ has been made Lord it does not follow that he has therefore been made God, since these things are most dissimilar. For God is so by nature, while Lord is so by will and appointment, if indeed you look to this personal and dispensatory dominion. God is absolutely, Lord relatively and with respect to us; God is essentially, Lord accidentally; God is formally according to his divine nature, Lord according to both natures in the unity of the person of the man [ἀνθρώπου]. Ostorrodius most ignorantly confuses all these things. From the reasoning of the whole person of Christ as man, to his other nature, or from the work of voluntary dispensation and counsel, to the work, the condition and the natural right, no inference follows. But let us look at the reasoning itself, which Ostorrodius uses to support that connection. Being God, he says, is something greater, or more, than being Lord: just as Deity itself cannot be or subsist as anything without dominion. Since two things are asked here, we shall explain them separately before we answer that prosyllogism. First, then, as to whether being God is something greater and more excellent than being Lord, I suspect that through a typographical error the negative particle non has been omitted from the words of Ostorrodius, so that the opponent's position is this: since being God is not something more excellent than being Lord, it follows that if Christ has been made and appointed Lord by God the Father, the same Christ has also been made God by God the Father. As to the second point, namely that Deity without dominion is nothing at all and cannot subsist, it is ambiguous, on account of the twofold divine dominion: the essential and supreme, and the economic, subordinate to it. Of the former it is true, as it is affirmed, because it is an essential attribute of God, which cannot be denied unless God is denied. Of the latter it is false, because it depends on the mere and free will of God, which could have brought it about that such a dominion had never existed, without any prejudice to the divine nature. If, then, in order to answer the prosyllogism, there is no typographical error, it is quite certain that the connection is most false, since in this kind of argument no inference is given from the lesser to the greater, nor is it said that he who has brought about what is less, and therefore easier, has at once also brought about what is greater, and therefore more difficult, especially in matters which are not of the same kind. But if a typographical error has been committed, then a distinction must be drawn between the essential, primary and supreme dominion of God, which depends on that, and the economic dominion, which is subordinate to the former. If the words of the opponent are understood of the first and essential dominion, the minor premise is most true, but the inference is false, because the principal syllogism speaks of the latter dominion, as we showed a little above. But if those words are taken of the latter, economic dominion, the proposition is true but the assumption false, because God alone is master, alone prince, King of kings and Lord of lords, Matt. 11:25; Acts 17:20; 1 Tim. 6:15. On account of the pre-eminence of that nature and the necessary dependence of other things upon it, there is no good or right in creatures which is not subject to that essential and eternal dominion of his. But this other dominion is not natural but economic, and it does not flow simply from the natural excellence of God above all things, but from his free will, and it is not that highest, first and self-existent [αὐτοῦ] dominion, but a proximate and subordinate one; nor is it finally eternal, but was truly obtained by Christ through labouring, suffering, dying, and paying the price of redemption for us; and so, at last, as regards its exercise or the so-called processory act, it will be laid down by him in some part at least, 1 Cor. 15:24, 28. From all these things the falsity of the assumption is clear enough, and so the whole argument collapses.

units.la: Argumentum tertium tale est.
units.tr: The third argument is as follows.

units.la: Si alii etiam qui veri sunt dii, factisunt dii, nec tamen esse factidy vsquam legantur, tum sequitur falsum esse, quod Christus ideò non sit Deus factus, quia hoc ipsum totidem verbis ac syllabis in Scripturis sacris non legitur. Atqui sunt alii etiam veri Dii, Psal.8. verf.6. qui sunt Dÿ facti, nec tamen Dii facti esse vsquam leguntur:
units.tr: If other beings also, who are true gods, have been made gods, and yet nowhere are they read to have been made gods, then it follows that it is false that Christ is not made God because this very thing is not read in holy Scripture in so many words and syllables. But there are other true gods, Ps. 8. v. 6, who have been made gods, and yet nowhere are they read to have been made gods.

units.la: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, etc.

units.la: Resp. Οὐκ ἐστι θεὸς ἀλλ' ἢ εἷς, vt loquuntur, nec ad praesentem quæstionē quicquam facit syllogismus. Non enim ideò tantùm affirmamus Christum non esse Deum factum, quia hoc ipsum totidem verbis ac syllabis in sacris Literis non docetur: sed quia res ipsa, quibuscunque etiam verborum tegatur phaleris, cum veritate diuina, in Scripturis sacris comprehensa, pugnat è diametro: vt in responsione ad argumentum primum ostendimus. Ab hac quæstione, ceu scopo præfixo, cum aberret argumentum Aduersarii non obiectionem nostram, sed aerem impetit syllogismus ille. De veritate autem vtriusque propositionis videbimus in refutatione obiectionis nostræ secundæ, ad quam pergo.
units.tr: Reply: There is no God but one [Οὐκ ἐστι θεὸς ἀλλ' ἢ εἷς], as they say, and this syllogism has nothing to do with the present question. For we do not assert that Christ is not made God merely because this very thing is not taught in so many words and syllables in the sacred Scriptures. We assert it because the thing itself, whatever verbal trappings may cover it, is in direct contradiction with divine truth comprehended in the holy Scriptures, as we showed in our reply to the first argument. Since the adversary's argument strays from this question, which is set as its target, that syllogism does not strike our objection but beats the air. The truth of both propositions we will consider in the refutation of our second objection, to which I now proceed.

units.la: Ad secundam obiectionem nostram respondet Oftorrodius, negando assumptionem, quandoquidem, cùm Scriptura affirmat, vnum tantùm esse Deum, hoc ipsum non ita intelligendum sit, quasi simpliciter vnus tantum Deus esset: sed quòd vnus tantùm sit Dominus rerum omnium, & moderator, qui nullum alium se superiorem, & per omnia sibi æqualem habeat, vnde etiam expresse Deus Deorum nominetur. Deut.10. verf.17. quod fieri non potuisset, nisi res ita se haberet. Atque hanc explicationem dicit ab Apostolo Paulo disertis verbis confirmari, qui 1.Cor.8. verf.4. Etiamsi, inquit, sint, qui dicantur Dii, in cœlo & in terra (sicut sunt Dii multi, & Domini multi) nobis tamen vnus Deus est Pater ille à quo omnia. Vnde concludit, vnum tantùm esse Deum, quatenus ab illo omnia, nec absurdum esse, si quis etiam alium à quo non sint omnia, nempe Christum Deum suum agnoscat & colat, modò ipsum non vnum illum Deum esse existimet, quemadmodum etiam in eo nihil est absurdi, quod Apostolus eodem in loco dicit, Christianos vnum tantum Dominum habere, licet multi alii sint Domini, qui interdum etiam Christianorum sint Domini, vt alibi ab Apostolo nominantur. Argumentum si ad formam redigatur, tale est.
units.tr: To our second objection Ostorodius replies by denying the minor premise: since, when Scripture affirms that there is only one God, this must not be understood as though there were simply only one God, but that there is only one Lord and ruler of all things, who has no other superior to himself and equal to himself in all respects, whence he is also expressly named God of gods. Deut. 10. v. 17. This could not have happened unless things were so. And he says that this explanation is confirmed in plain words by the Apostle Paul, who says at 1 Cor. 8. v. 4: Even if there are those who are called gods, in heaven and on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father from whom are all things. Hence he concludes that there is only one God, insofar as all things are from him; nor is it absurd, if someone acknowledges and worships another, from whom not all things are, namely Christ, as his God, provided he does not think that Christ is that one God. In the same way there is nothing absurd in what the Apostle says in the same place, that Christians have only one Lord, although there are many other lords, who sometimes are even lords of Christians, as the Apostle names them elsewhere. If the argument is reduced to form, it is as follows.

units.la: Si, quum Scriptura sacra dicit, vnum tantum esse Deum, illud ita intelligendum est, non quasi vnus tantum Deus esset, nec præter eum vlli alii, sed quod vnus tantum sit rerum omnium Dominus, & supremus gubernator, tum sequitur non esse absurdum, si quis etiam alium, nempe Christum Deum suum agnoscat, modò
units.tr: If, when holy Scripture says that there is only one God, this is to be understood not as though there were only one God, and no other besides him, but that there is only one Lord of all things and supreme governor, then it follows that it is not absurd if someone acknowledges another also, namely Christ, as his God, provided

units.la: Notes in the right margin are largely illegible and are not transcribed. modò ipsum non vnum illum Deum esse existimet.
units.tr: Notes in the right margin are largely illegible and are not transcribed. provided he does not think that Christ is that one God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum,
units.tr: But the former is true,

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the latter too.

units.la: Minor habet ἀφον, ἡ Ξεοῦς illam ita probat, quòd sacra Scriptura sibi ipsi esset contradictura, si, cum illa vnum tantùm Deum verum affirmat, hoc ita intelligeretur, quasi simpliciter vnus tantùm verus Deus esset, quoniam in ea de multis diis legitur, qui tamen falsi dii non sint. Istam autem probat illis Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ Deuter.10. v.17. & 1.Cor.8.v.4. leguntur.
units.tr: He proves the minor premise in this way: that holy Scripture would contradict itself if, when it affirms that there is only one true God, this were understood as though there were simply only one true God, since in it we read of many gods, who are nonetheless not false gods. He proves this from those testimonies of Scripture which are read at Deut. 10. v. 17 and 1 Cor. 8. v. 4.

units.la: Resp. Meram esse λογμαχίαν, quia hæc omnia ad præsentem quæstionem plane nihil faciunt. Dum enim nos sententiam Aduersariorum impugnamus, nō simpliciter ab ipso nomine Dei, quod de subiectis modò vere, modò falsò, modò vniuocè, modò æquiuocè prædicatur, argumentum nostrum desumimus, sicuti falsò ab Ostorrodio proponitur. Sed quum sacra Scriptura modo peculiari, & eiusmodi cum circumstantiis, Christum Dei nomine indigitet, aliáque tum opera, tum epitheta de ipso passim enuntiet, quæ in ψλὸν ἀνθρωπον cadere non possunt: sed Christi diuinam naturam euidenter demonstrant, verissimè inde concludimus, ab Aduersariis, Christum, vnum illum & æternum cum Deo Patre Deum esse, negantibus, duos, non sibi inuicem subordinatos, sed æquales Deos, contra Scripturam sacram, vnum tantùm verum Deum agnoscentem, introduci, præsertim cùm Christus in sacris literis Deo Patri æqualis esse perhibeatur, ipsiq; supremum rerum omnium Dominium, iure tum creationis, tum prouidentiæ, & conseruationis, ac gubernationis, asseratur, de quibus omnibus iam in antecedentibus prolixè actum est. Eat igitur Ostorrodius, & voci altissimi se solum Iehouam, Deum ac Dominum, nec alium præter se esse affirmanti, obstrepat, nec absurdum fore, si quis præter illum Iehouam etiam alium colat, Deumque suum agnoscat, ampliùs ogganniat. Nec appendix illa, quam consequentiæ assuit, Aduersarium ab impietate illa liberat: quum enim hæc ipsa ἀρχὴν illud ψεῦδος sit, contrà quod cum Aduersariis contendimus, ideo illam hypothesin sui argumenti, quam statuit Ostorrodius, manifestè principium petit, ac idem contingit illi, quod iis, qui vtroque genu in luto defixi hærent, & quo magis alterum extrahere nituntur, eo altius alterum defigunt. Adde quod locus ille ex 1.Cor.8.v.4. de iis dominis ac diis agit, qui ex sola hominum opinione dii ac domini sunt, & nuncupatione sola per impiam abusionem, & diaboli nequitiam ipsis attributa, dii ac domini cefentur, vt ex scopo Apostoli,& membrorum oppofitione liquidò constat. De elencho comparatorum,quem Aduersarius in ipso argumento committit, dum videlicet ita contra Scripturæ veritatem ratiocinatur, ac fi Christi & cæterorum omnium, qui dii efle dicuntur, ratio conditióque æqualis effet, hic non differam,cùm ostendisse sufficiat,eum non argumentum nostrum,sed proprium commentum atque delirium impugnare.
units.tr: Reply: This is a mere war of words [λογομαχίαν], because all these points have nothing at all to do with the present question. For when we attack the opinion of our adversaries, we do not draw our argument simply from the name of God, which is predicated of subjects sometimes truly, sometimes falsely, sometimes univocally, sometimes equivocally, as Ostorodius wrongly proposes. But since holy Scripture designates Christ by the name of God in a peculiar manner, and with such circumstances, and everywhere ascribes to him both works and epithets which cannot apply to a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον], but clearly demonstrate Christ's divine nature, we rightly conclude against our adversaries, who deny that Christ is that one and eternal God with God the Father, and who introduce two gods, not subordinate to one another but equal, contrary to holy Scripture, which acknowledges only one true God. This is especially so since Christ is said in the sacred writings to be equal to God the Father, and supreme dominion over all things is ascribed to him by right of creation, providence, preservation and government, all of which have already been treated at length in the preceding sections. Let Ostorodius therefore go on and clamour against the voice of the Most High declaring that he alone is Jehovah, God and Lord, and that there is none other besides him; let him bawl further that it would not be absurd if someone worshipped, besides that Jehovah, another also, and acknowledged him as his God. Nor does that appendix which he has attached to the conclusion free the adversary from that impiety. For since this very principle [ἀρχὴν] is that very falsehood [ψεῦδος] against which we contend with our adversaries, Ostorodius's hypothesis for his argument, which he sets up, plainly begs the question. The same happens to him as to those who stick in the mud with both knees, and the more they strive to pull one out, the deeper they sink the other. Add that the passage from 1 Cor. 8. v. 4 deals with those lords and gods who are gods and lords only by the opinion of men, and who are called gods and lords only by name, through impious abuse and the malice of the devil, as is clear from the Apostle's purpose and the contrast of the members. I will not here discuss the comparison of the adversary's own making, which he commits within the argument itself, namely that he reasons against the truth of Scripture as though the case of Christ and of all the others who are said to be gods were the same and equal. It is enough to have shown that he is attacking not our argument but his own invention and delirium.

units.la: Hac autem ipsa occasione,nempe citati illius loci ex 1. Cor. 8. verf.4. obiter,ait,animaduertendum esse,quòd non Christus, sed solus Pater ibi Deus esse dicatur.
units.tr: On this very occasion, namely the cited passage from 1 Cor. 8. v. 4, he remarks in passing: it should be noted that it is not Christ but only the Father who is said to be God there.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si 1.Cor.8. v. 4.non Christus,sed solus Deus Pater vnus ille, & verus Deus appellatur,tum etiam solus Deus Pater vnus ille verus Deus est,non autem Christus.
units.tr: If, first, Christ is not called God, but only that one Father is called the one and true God, then it follows that only that one Father is the one true God, and not Christ.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est:dicit enim Apostolus: Etiamsi sint, qui dicantur dii in cælis & in terra, nobis tamen vnus Deus est Pater ille,a quo omnia.
units.tr: But the first premise is true, for the Apostle says: Even if there are those who are called gods in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God, that Father from whom all things come.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second premise is true as well.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam vnà cum assumptione esse falsam: Illam, quia cùm Deus verus opponitur fictis numinibus,falsis diis,ac idolis,tum oratio superlatiua, aut exclusiua,de vna persona vsurpata, non excludit alias diuinitatis personas, sed creaturas & fictitia numina, quibus Deus verus siue in vna, siue in pluribus personis opponitur. Vera igitur esset maior, si Deus Pater non tantùm distinguete,sed etiam oppositè,& disparatè ad filium, Deus appellaretur,quod est falsum.Hanc,quia nô solus Pater,sed etiam filius vnus ille Deus ac Dominus dicitur, cùm non tantùm Pater, sed etiam filius, iis, qui sola hominum opinione, & diaboli fraudibus, Dii ac Domini censentur, opponitur.Et quemadmodum, cùm Christus appellatur vnus Dominus,Pater non excluditur:sed vnum commune dominium Patris ac filii intelligitur: sic è diuerso, quum vnus Deus appellatur Pater, non excluditur filius,sed vna communis essentia diuina intelligenda est, vt rei ipsius veritas euincit.
units.tr: Reply. The consequence, together with the assumption, is false. As for the consequence, because when the true God is set against feigned deities, false gods, and idols, a superlative or exclusive expression applied to one person does not exclude the other persons of the Godhead. It excludes creatures and fictitious deities, to which the true God is opposed, whether in one person or in several. The major premise would therefore be true only if God the Father, distinguished from the Son and set over against him in an opposing and disparate way, were called God, which is false. As for the assumption, because the Son is called the one God and Lord, not only the Father. He is set against those who are counted as gods and lords by human opinion alone and by the deceptions of the devil. Just as, when Christ is called the one Lord, the Father is not excluded but a common dominion of Father and Son is understood, so conversely, when the Father is called the one God, the Son is not excluded. Rather, one common divine essence is to be understood, as the truth of the matter itself makes plain.

units.la: Hunc autem errorem(nempe consequentiæ,obiectionis secundæ)indeb...
units.tr: Ostorrodius says that this error (namely of the consequence, the second objection) arises from this source,

units.la: [Marginal notes in the right margin are too faint and cut off to be read.] dæ)inde proficisci ait Oflorrodius,quod hactenus arbitrati sint vt nos, nomen illud Deus, vnico illi vero Deo tanquam proprium in Scripturis tribui,quod tamen falsum esse ex iis,quæ hactenus dicta sunt,appareat. Quanquam verum sit, quod nomen illud, licet revera sit nomen appel-latiuum, vni tamen Deo simpliciter, & absolutè per modum loquendi, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocetur, id est, per excellentiam, non secus ac si proprium eius nomen esset,passim tribuatur.
units.tr: ...arises from this source, Ostorrodius says, because hitherto they have thought, as we do, that the name God is ascribed in the Scriptures to that one true God as his own proper name; yet this is shown to be false from what has been said so far. Although it is true that this name, though in reality it is an appellative, is nevertheless ascribed everywhere to the one God simply and absolutely, by a mode of speaking called kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], that is, by pre-eminence, just as if it were his proper name.

units.la: Resp.Quo æquitatis titulo tu,Oflorrodi,argumentum nostrum erroris insimules,ex iis,quæ hactenus ab vtraque parte dicta sunt, Christianus Lector iudicet. Rem ipsam quantum concernit (ad singulas enim tuas cauillationes,& fallacias,atque principii petitiones,ex quibus totus pene Institutionum tuarum liber est consutus, respondere nimis foret prolixû) esto quod nomen Deus nô sit proprium seu characteristicum & indiuiduale,sed appellatiuum & connotans,vt loquuntur scholastici,nihilominus tamen verissimè impugnatur & expugnatur sententia Samosateniana,hoc argumento nostro,quod videl-quia Christus in scripturis sacris Deus appellatur cum eiusmodi circumstantiis, quæ neque in Angelos, neque in Magistratibus,nec vllam creaturam aliam, quocunq; etiâ iure, Dei nomine, indigitetur, cadere possint, necessariò sequatur, aut Christum vnum illum æternum Deum Israelis esse,aut certè duos Deos, contra veritatem scripturæ, esse introducendos,nec vlla ratione exceptione illa infringitur,quòd nomen Deus nô proprium sit,seu characteristicum,sed appellatiuum. Quum enim per nomina appellatiua,si proprie de subiectis enuncientur,licet directè aliquid illis spectetur,subiecta tamen ipsa,per propriam & necessariam consequentiam intelligantur,ipsáque substantia non solùm nomine proprio & characteristico , sed etiam appellatiuo & connotante significetur : Christo autem nomen illud Deus proprie in scripturis sacris tribuatur , necessariò inde sequitur, eodem ipso nomine, Christi naturam diuinam, non autem potestatem tantùm, gloriam ac potentiam , ex gratia ipsi à Patre concessam significari : ac proinde cum ille naturam & essentiam diuinam habeat , necessariò alterutrum ex consequentibus supradictis inde concludi. Assumptionis autem nostræ vtriusque veritas, ex cuius demonstratione etiam consequentiæ nostræ necessitas magis elucescet, inde patet, tum quod Christus non tantùm attributiue,sed etiam subiectiuè Deus,& quidè magnus,item ἀγαθὸς & benedictus in secula, articuloque praefixo, & aliis cum circumstantiis appellatur, vt ab initio huius capitis demonstrauimus, & cum quibus nomen illud nec Angelis, nec Magistratibus in Scripturis tribuitur. Et quoniam Angeli, ac Magistratus, non nisi per communicationem gratiae, applicationem, & similitudinem, quia videlicet ad regendum hunc mundum sint Ministri Dei, dominio ac potestate ipsis à Deo ex gratia concessa, dii dicuntur, ideo illis etiam impropriè & metaphoricè hoc nomen tribuitur: Ac proinde, si proprie loqui velimus, falsa est illa assueratio Ostorrodii, videlicet non esse absurdum si plures dominos ac deos praeter vnum illum, rerum omnium supremum Dominum agnoscamus.
units.tr: Reply. By what title of fairness you, Ostorrodius, accuse our argument of error, let the Christian reader judge from what has so far been said on both sides. As to the matter itself: to answer each of your quibbles and fallacies, and your petitions of the principle, from which almost the whole of your Institutes is stitched together, would be too lengthy. Granted that the name God is not proper or characteristic and individual, but appellative and connotative, as the scholastics say, the Samosatenian opinion is nonetheless most truly refuted and overthrown by this argument of ours: namely, that since Christ is called God in the holy Scriptures with such circumstances as cannot apply to angels, to magistrates, or to any other creature, by whatever right it may be designated by the name of God, it necessarily follows either that Christ is that one eternal God of Israel, or else that two Gods must be introduced, contrary to the truth of Scripture. Nor is this argument overturned in any way by the exception that the name God is not proper or characteristic but appellative. For when appellative names are predicated properly of subjects, then although something is directly referred to them, the subjects themselves are nonetheless understood by a proper and necessary consequence, and the substance itself is signified not only by a proper and characteristic name but also by an appellative and connotative one. Since the name God is properly attributed to Christ in the holy Scriptures, it necessarily follows from the same name that the divine nature of Christ is signified, and not merely a power, glory and might granted to him by the Father out of grace. Consequently, since he has the divine nature and essence, one of the consequents mentioned above must necessarily be concluded from this. The truth of both parts of our assumption, from whose demonstration the necessity of our consequence becomes clearer still, is evident as follows: Christ is called not only attributively but also subjectively God, and indeed great, likewise good [ἀγαθὸς] and blessed for ever, with the article prefixed and with other circumstances, as we showed at the beginning of this chapter; and this name is not given in Scripture to angels or magistrates with such circumstances. And since angels and magistrates are called gods only through the communication of grace, by application and by likeness, because they are ministers of God for governing this world, with dominion and power granted to them by God out of grace, this name is therefore given to them improperly and metaphorically. Accordingly, if we wish to speak properly, that assertion of Ostorrodius is false, namely that it is not absurd if we acknowledge several lords and gods besides that one supreme Lord of all things.

units.la: Atque ex his etiam liquet, falsum esse id quod subiungit Aduersarius, nempe nomen DEVS, vni illi vero & aeterno Deo per excellentiam, non secus ac si proprium eius nomen esset, passim in Scripturis tribui, quia ratio est rerum congenerum & homogenearum & de quibus nomen idem, & res nomine significata, praedicatur proprie, licet alicui ex illis excellentius res ipsa, ac proinde etiam nomen competat: quas res Aristoteles, lib. 2. de ortu & interitu, homonymas appellat: qualis homonymia inter substantiam & cetera praedicamenta, si ad ens conferantur, obseruetur, quod de illa primo & per se, de cæteris vero secundum quid praedicatur. Deus autem & res creatae cum non sint entia homogenea, sed toto genere differant, modus ille loquendi, si analogus fit iudicandum, excludetur. Deinde vt Deus simpliciter, & absolute propter naturalem suam excellentiam rerum omnium est dominus, & potestatem, ac auctoritatem in res vniuersas habet, creaturae autem, puta Angeli, aut Magistratus, quicquid iuris, potestatis, vel auctoritatis vspiam habent, à Deo per communicationem gratiae acceperunt: ita quoque Dei nomen illi vniuocè ac proprie, his vero æquiuocè, & improprie tribuitur, quia à subiecto suo de quo vniuocè praedicatur, per abusionem quandam ad subiectum, toto genere differens, æquiuocè transfertur. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, nihil ad impugnandam veritatem doctrinae ipsius, & argumenti nostri, praeter inania sophismata, & commenta ab Ostorrodio adferri, falsóque concludi, tum ex solutione obiectionum nostrarum ab ipso allata liquidò constare, quòd Filius Dei in Scripturis sacris non ideo DEVS appelletur, quasi ille ipse Deus altissimus esset, sed propter maiestatem, & gloriam. gloriam ac potestatem diuinam,quam Pater in ipsum contulerit : tum etiam manifestum fieri, quod ex eo minime sequatur, Christum ideò diuinam habere naturam, quod nomen Dei in sacris literis ipsi tri-buatur.
units.tr: And from these points it is also clear that what the opponent adds is false, namely that the name GOD, to that one true and eternal God, by excellence, is attributed everywhere in Scripture just as if it were his proper name. For the reason is that things of one kind and homogeneous, of which the same name is predicated and the thing signified by the name, are predicated properly, even if the thing itself, and therefore also the name, belongs more excellently to one of them. Aristotle, in book 2 of On Generation and Corruption, calls these things homonyms. A homonymy of this kind is observed between substance and the other categories when they are compared with being, since it is predicated of substance first and per se, but of the others only in a certain respect. But God and created things are not homogeneous beings; they differ in their whole kind, so that mode of speaking, if it is to be judged analogical, is excluded. Further, since God simply and absolutely, by his natural excellence, is Lord of all things and has power and authority over all things, while creatures, such as angels or magistrates, have whatever right, power or authority they possess anywhere from God through the communication of grace, so the name of God is likewise attributed to God univocally and properly, but to them equivocally and improperly, because it is transferred equivocally, by a certain misuse, from its subject, of which it is predicated univocally, to a subject differing in its whole kind. From all of these points it appears that nothing is brought forward to overthrow the truth of our doctrine and of our argument except empty sophisms and inventions from Ostorrodius, and that he falsely concludes, both that it is clear from the solution of our objections which he himself has given that the Son of God is not called God in the Scriptures because he himself is the most high God, but on account of the majesty and glory glory and divine power which the Father has conferred upon him; and that it is also manifest that it does not follow from this that Christ has the divine nature because the name of God is attributed to him in the sacred letters.

units.la: Hac prima quæstione sic pertractata, aliam adhuc eodem capi-te decimo proponit,eámque duplicem: Primò videlicet, An Chri-stus in Scriptura sacra Iehouah appelletur? Secundò, An si nomine illo indigitetur,diuina ipsius natura inde demonstrari possit? Nos vtrum-que affirmamus. Ostorrodius vtrumque negat. Et priorem quæ-stionem, quantum concernit, certissimum est toties Christum in Veteri Testamento Iehouam appellari, quoties in Nouo Testa-mento à Christo ipso, & Apostolis ea de ipso exponuntur, quæ de solo vero Iehouah, & Deo Israelis enunciantur, qua de re in capite octauo prolixè egimus. Præter illa autem euidentissima Scripturæ testimonia, etiam hæc sequentia tum Christiano le-ctori,tum Aduersario consideranda proponimus: Iud.13.16.&22.23.Gen.32.v.29.30. Ierem.23.v.6. & 33.v.16. ex quibus, vt & aliis liquidò constat,illum de quo agitur,non Angelum creatum,sed Christum fuisse, in quo plena deitas resideret.
units.tr: Having treated this first question in this way, he proposes another in the same tenth chapter, and that a twofold one. First, namely, Is Christ called Jehovah in holy Scripture? Second, If he is designated by that name, can his divine nature be demonstrated from it? We affirm both. Ostorrodius denies both. As far as the first question is concerned, it is most certain that Christ is called Jehovah in the Old Testament as often as those things are said about him in the New Testament by Christ himself and by the Apostles which are said of the true Jehovah alone and of the God of Israel; we dealt with this at length in the eighth chapter. Besides those most evident testimonies of Scripture, we propose the following passages for consideration both by the Christian reader and by the opponent: Judg. 13.16. & 22.23. Gen. 32.29.30. Jer. 23.6. & 33.16. From these and others it is plainly established that the one of whom we speak was not a created angel but Christ, in whom the full deity dwells.

units.la: Contra verò affirmat Ostorrodius,Christum nullo in loco Scriptu-ra expressè Iehouam appellari. Hoc vt demonstret dicit locum il-lum Ierem. 23. v. 6. & cap. 33. v. 16. repetitum non de Christo,sed de Iuda, & Israele, vel de Iuda, & Hierosolymis intelligendum esse, sicuti vnusquisque qui locum illum diligentius inspexerit, facilè intel-liget.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, on the contrary, maintains that Christ is nowhere in Scripture expressly called Iehouah. To prove this, he says that the passage in Jeremiah 23:6 and chapter 33:16, which is repeated there, is not to be understood of Christ but of Judah and Israel, or of Judah and Jerusalem, as anyone who examines that passage more carefully will easily understand.

units.la: Resp. Imò verò locum illum de Christo intelligendum esse,vis verborum, & eorundem constructio, vt & res ipsa euidenter e-uincunt.Sed quid tum,si vnus ille locus Veteris Testamenti,non de Christo, sed de Iuda,de Israele & Hierosolymis est intelligen-dus? num inde sequetur nullum aliud extare Testimonium in locis aliis, quo Christum nomine Iehouah indigitari demonstre-tur? At cõficienda tibi hæc est cõsequentia omniũ absurdissima, si veritatem doctrina nostræ infringere velis isto argumēto tuo.
units.tr: I answer: on the contrary, that passage must be understood of Christ, as both the force of the words and their construction, and the matter itself, clearly prove. But suppose that this one passage of the Old Testament must not be understood of Christ but of Judah, Israel and Jerusalem. Would it follow that no other testimony exists in other places by which Christ is shown to be designated by the name Iehouah? Yet if you wish to overturn the truth of our doctrine by this argument of yours, you must draw the most absurd of all conclusions.

units.la: Quæstionem verò secundam,quod attinet,constanter affirma-mus, Christi æternam deitatem inde euidenter demonstrari,non quidem ex eo quod Christus simpliciter in Scripturis sacris Ie-houah dicitur, sed quod hoc nomen ipsi cum eiusmodi circum-stantiis tribuitur, quæ in nullam creaturã, sed solùm creatorem;
units.tr: As for the second question, we firmly affirm that Christ's eternal deity is clearly demonstrated from this, not indeed because Christ is simply called Iehouah in the sacred Scriptures, but because this name is given to him with such circumstances as belong to no creature, but only to the Creator;

units.la: vnum illum æternum ac verum Deum competunt. Huius autem rei, propter ea quæ capite octauo adduximus luculentissimum, Iudæis omnibus, & Socinianis, ac quotquot lucidissimæ veritati tenebras offundunt, suis stropharum & sophismatum præstigiis, extat testimonium Hebr.1. verf.10. vbi cœli terræque creatio, & Matth.9.v.4. vbi potestas remittendi peccata, Christo tribuitur, quæ tamen Iehouah creator, Sanctus, & Rex Israelis, Ef.43.v.15. 16.25. & alibi paflim sibi soli tanquam propria vendicat, & quæ nulli creaturæ competere possunt. Ex quibus manifestum, ex eo ipso nomine Iehouah, Christi æternam ac diuinam naturam luculenter demonstrari posse.
units.tr: circumstances which belong to that one eternal and true God alone. Of this, the most luminous proof, on the basis of what we have adduced in chapter 8, is available to all Jews and Socinians, and to all who cast darkness over the most lucid truth with the magic tricks of their twists and sophisms: Hebrews 1:10, where the creation of heaven and earth, and Matthew 9:4, where the power of forgiving sins, are attributed to Christ; yet Iehouah, creator, Holy One and King of Israel (Isaiah 43:15, 16, 25), and elsewhere throughout, claims these for himself alone as his own, and they cannot belong to any creature. From this it is evident that from the very name Iehouah the eternal and divine nature of Christ can be shown clearly.

units.la: Hanc vero ipsam quæstionem ἀνταρτικῶς tractat Qstorrodius, & suæ negationis hanc adfert rationem, quòd videlicet etiam Angelis creatis nomen illud Iehouah tribuatur, quos tamen vnum illum Deum non esse confiat, ac proinde multò magis ipsum Christum, qui ipsorum Angelorum princeps est ac Dominus, eo nomine, licet non sit vnus ille, & æternus Deus, appellari posse.
units.tr: Ostorrodius treats this very question by way of counter-argument [ἀνταρτικῶς], and he offers this reason for his denial: namely, that the name Iehouah is also given to created angels, who are certainly not that one God; and therefore, much more, Christ himself, who is the prince and Lord of these angels, can be called by that name, even though he is not that one and eternal God.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si etiam Angeli creati nomine Iehouah appellantur, nec tamen vnus ille & æternus Deus sunt, tum multò magis ipse Christus, qui princeps est ac Dominus omnium Angelorum, Iehouah appellari potest, licet non sit vnus ille & æternus Deus.
units.tr: If angels, though created, are also called by the name Iehouah, and yet they are not that one and eternal God, then much more can Christ himself, who is the prince and Lord of all the angels, be called Iehouah, even though he is not that one and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum, vt liquet ex eo, quod is, qui ex rubo loquutus est cum Mose Exod.3. aliquoties Iehouah appellatur, cum tamen non ipse Iehouah, sed Angelus Iehouæ fuerit, vt ex v.2 cap. eiusdem, & Act.7. v.30. liquet:
units.tr: But the antecedent is true, as is clear from the fact that he who spoke out of the bush with Moses (Exodus 3) is called Iehouah several times, although he was not Iehouah himself but the Angel of Iehouah, as is clear from verse 2 of the same chapter and from Acts 7:30.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the consequent is true as well.

units.la: Resp. I. Connexum esse falsum, quia manifesto comparatorum elencho laborat, & hypothesi falsa. Elenchus comparatorum est, quia à minori ad maius hoc loco nulla datur consequentia. Cùm enim vnum de duobus prædicatur, aut cùm quæritur, an aliquid de duobus enuntiari possit, tum si prædicetur de eo cui illud inesse, magis est verisimile, non illico prædicabitur de eo, cui idem competere, minus est verisimile. At vero Angelos nomine Iehouah appellari, & tamen non esse Deum æternum, vel infanti videbitur verisimilius, quàm si Christum tot nominibus excellentiorem Angelis, vtpote illorum principem, ac Dominum. minum, Iehouæ nomine indigitari, & tamen non esse Deum æternum dixeris. Et quia alia est ratio Christi, qui omnes res creatas sua excellentia & præstantia superat infinitè, alia Angelorum, qui Christo ipsorum Domino, principi & creatori sunt subiecti, ideò si quid de his prædicatur, quod perfectionem aliquam denotat simpliciter, multò magis id de Christo enuntiari posse optimè concluseris: non autem perfectionem vllam ipsi derogabis, eò quod illa in Angelos non cadat. Contra autem infallibilem illam consequentiam confeceris, quod etiamsi Christus ideò Deus æternus esse dicatur, quia nomen Iehouah de illo prædicatur, non tamen sequatur Angelos quoque vnum illum & æternum Deum esse, quia videlicet eodem titulo nominis Iehouah insigniantur, idque propter excellentiam illam qua Christus exuperat rerum creatarum naturam vniuersam. Hypothesis deinde falsa est, quia non simpliciter à nomine Iehouah argumentamur, sed quia Christo cum eiusmodi circunstantiis illud nomen tribuitur, quæ nonnisi vni illi & æterno Deo conuenire possunt, vti paulo ante ostendimus. II. Tantum abesse vt assumptio illis Scripturæ locis quæ adducuntur confirmetur, vt etiam contrarium, nempe Angelum illum non esse Spiritum creatum, sed ipsum Iehouam, æternúmque ac verum Deum, euidentissimè inde demonstretur. Nulla enim creatura, nullúsque spiritus creatus est Deus Abraham, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi, qui populum eduxit ex Aegypto, quod est apud omnes Atheismi non reos extra controuersiam. Atqui Angelus ille de quo ibi agitur est Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacobi, qui populum Israeliticum duxit ex Aegypto: vide Exod. 3. v. 6. 7. 8. 15. 16. 17. Act. 7. v. 30. Ergo Angelus ille non est spiritus creatus, sed ipse Iehouah, verúsque & æternus Deus. Atque hac ipsa ratione Ostorrodio iugulum proprio gladio præscinditur. Et sic manet inuictum argumentum nostrum, vere videlicet Christum, æternum illum & vnum Iehouam à nobis credi, atque adorari, quia passim in scripturis sacris Dei & Iehouæ nomine indigitetur.
units.tr: I answer, first: the connection is false, because it suffers from a manifestly faulty comparison and from a false hypothesis. It is a faulty comparison, because here there is no valid inference from the lesser to the greater. For when one of two things is predicated, or when it is asked whether something can be said of two things, then if it is predicated of the one to whom it belongs, it is more probable; it does not follow at once that it will be predicated of the one to whom the same thing belongs, which is less probable. Yet that angels are called by the name Iehouah and yet are not the eternal God would seem more probable even to an infant than if you were to say that Christ, who is by so many names more excellent than the angels, being their prince and Lord, is designated by the name Iehouah, and yet is not the eternal God. And since the nature of Christ, who infinitely surpasses all created things in his excellence and pre-eminence, is one thing, and the nature of the angels, who are subject to Christ their Lord, prince and creator, is another; therefore if something is predicated of these that simply denotes some perfection, you may rightly conclude that it can be said of Christ much more. Nor will you detract from him any perfection on the ground that it does not apply to the angels. On the other hand, you have drawn that infallible consequence the other way: that even if Christ is called the eternal God because the name Iehouah is predicated of him, it does not follow that the angels are also the one and eternal God, simply because they are marked with the same title of the name Iehouah, and this on account of that excellence by which Christ surpasses the whole nature of created things. Moreover, the hypothesis is false, because we do not argue from the name Iehouah simply, but because that name is given to Christ with such circumstances as can belong only to that one and eternal God, as we showed a little earlier. (2) So far is the assumption from being confirmed by the passages of Scripture that are adduced, that the contrary, namely that this angel is not a created spirit but Iehouah himself, the eternal and true God, is most clearly demonstrated from them. For no creature, no created spirit, is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, who led the people out of Egypt; this is beyond dispute among all who are not guilty of atheism. But that angel of whom the passage speaks is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, who led the Israelite people out of Egypt: see Exodus 3:6, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17; Acts 7:30. Therefore that angel is not a created spirit, but Iehouah himself, the true and eternal God. And by this very reasoning the throat of Ostorrodius is cut with his own sword. And so our argument stands unconquered: that we believe and worship Christ as that eternal and one Iehouah, indeed as truly God, because he is designated throughout the sacred Scriptures by the names of God and Iehouah.

units.la: CAPVT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: In quo argumentum sextum pro æterna Filii Deitate, proponitur, atque defenditur.
units.tr: In which the sixth argument for the eternal deity of the Son is set out and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum sextum, quo æternam Filii & Domini nostri Iesu Christi deitatem demonstramus, inde desumitur, quòd ipsi in sacris literis invocatio tribuitur, quam unus ille & æternus Deus sibi propriam vendicat.
units.tr: Our sixth argument, by which we demonstrate the eternal deity of the Son and our Lord Jesus Christ, is drawn from the fact that the Scriptures attribute to him invocation, which the one and eternal God claims as his own.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Qui religioso cultu, & vera cum fiducia animi, non tantùm iure invocari potest, sed etiam ex iussu & mandato Dei à nobis invocari debet: ille est unus ille, verus, atque æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whoever can rightly be invoked with religious worship and a true trust of the mind, and indeed ought to be invoked by us by the command and mandate of God, is that one, true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Filius Dei, dominus noster Iesus Christus, non tantùm iure potest, sed etiam ex iussu, & mandato Dei, debet à nobis religioso cultu, & vera cum fiducia animi, invocari.
units.tr: But the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, can not only rightly be invoked by us with religious worship and a true trust of the mind, but ought also to be invoked by the command and mandate of God.

units.la: Ergo Christus est unus ille verus, atque æternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is that one true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Propositionem utramque duplici ratione probabimus. Primò videlicet ipsa Aduersariorum confessione: deinde Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis. Ex eo autem, si demonstretur Christum, non tantùm iure posse, sed etiam debere à nobis invocari, necessario sequi, Christum verum atque æternum Deum esse, ipse Faustus Socinus, Samosatenianæ turbæ princeps & Antesignanus confitetur, in Epistola ad Ministros Transsyluaniæ, præfixa libro suo, de invocando Christo, aduersus Francisцum Dauidis, verba hæc sunt: Verùm ubi in responsione scriptum esse resciuerunt, nullum extare in sacris literis præceptum de Christo invocando, id est, de precibus nostris nominatim ad ipsum Christum dirigendis, & propterea invocandi verbo in hunc sensum accepto, posse nos quidem iure Christum invocare: non tamen id facere teneri, non pauci ex ipsis (nempe fratribus eius Polonis) id quod etiam Transsyluanis fratribus ab initio euenerat, non mediocriter sunt offensi. Et quamuis sapius illis, & voce & scripto ostendeostenderim, nihil esse cur hic offendi quisquam debeat,imò hanc esse so-lam rationem, & iis,qui Christo inuocationem non concedunt, & iis,qui ex Christi inuocatione, eum vnum illum Israelis Deum esse colligunt, os obstruendi:tamen vt ipsi, &c. Sed & assumptionis veritas Aduersa-riorum confessione, euidenter confirmatur. Sic enim Georgius Blandrata in Epistola ad Socinum, quæ prædicto libello, pagina decima septima continetur, inter cætera scribit: Nec dubito quin Aduersarij triumphum sint reportaturi, si inuocandi Christi non aliqua probabitur necessitas, quam ego certò probare multis argumentis, & fi-dei analogia contendam. Ex perpetuo videlicet sacerdotio, ex fide, ex accepta potestate, donisque absque mensura, ex Dei Patris gloria, ex consolatione nostra,ab exemplis Apostolorum,ab ipsa adoratione,quæ necessario inuocationem requirit. Et paulò post: Probetur igitur,membra Christi suum caput & ducem, regémque suo ordine inuocare debere, nisi Deo & Christo iniuriam facere velint, & summam sibi ipsis iniuriā inferre. Faustus Socinus eiusdem libri pag. 4. Quod ad rem ipsam,ait, ipso nomine secluso, pertinet, dico satis apparere inuocatum fuisse Christum,& inuocatione,quæ cultum & fiduciam,qua aliquid petitur,complectatur, ei in Scriptura S.fuisse tributam, ex eo quod Paulus in initio omnium suarum Epistolarum non à Deo Patre nostro tantum, sed à Domino quoque Iesu Christo,gratiam, pacem, & alicubi misericordiam iis, ad quos scribit: precatur, & easdem Epistolas plerumque ita concludit, Gratia Domini,&c. 1.Thess.3.11, 2.Cor.12.8.9. Et pag.30.postquam demonstrasset ex scripturis,Christum dum hic mortalis ageret,sa-tis frequenter inuocatum fuisse, addit: In his enim omnibus locis ab eo vera cordis fiducia, & in multis cultu quoque exteriore adhibito, ea petita sunt, quæ à solo Deo alioqui peti possunt, nec tamen eorum quis-quam,qui id fecerunt,eo nomine à Christo reprehensus est. Imò præterquā quod omnibus quæ petierunt gratificatus est, aliqui etiam ex ipsis vehe-menter ob id ipsum sunt commendati. Quum autē ipsi Socino ex mul-tis scripturæ locis Christum cum fiducia animi & religioso cultu inuocatum esse demonstranti,Francifcus Dauidis,exemplum qui-dem,& mandatum nullum proferri, regereret, respondit pag.27. Quanquam exempla sanctorum hominum, inquiens, dum Spiritu Dei aguntur,nisi expressum Dei verbum repugnet,nobis pro regula actionum nostrarum esse & possunt & debent. Ex quibus omnibus luculenter apparet, ipsos etiam Aducrsarios, vtriusque propositionis nostræ veritatem agnoscere, ac proinde eos doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum, non tam veritatis indagandæ, defendendæ, ac illustrandæ, quàm oppugnandæ diuinæ Christi naturæ, & victoriæ obtinendæ studio, suis sophismatum telis impetere.
