Verùm utraque propositionem etiā ipsa Scriptura confirmat, & maiorem quidem, dum inuocatione illā, quæ ex fide, & vera animi fiducia pēdet, diuinæ maiestati, si quidquā aliud propriā assignat, vt Ioel. 2.32. Quicunque inuocauerit nomen Iehoua saluus erit. Ps.50.15. Inuoca me in die tribulationis tuæ, eruā te, & tu glorificabis me. Prou. 18.10. Turris fortis nomen Iehoua, ad ipsam confugiet iustus, & seruabitur. Deut.6.13. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli seruies. Adoratum autem Christum, nec posse tantùm iure, sed debere etiam à nobis inuocari, ex iussu & mandato Dei, exempla testantur, Mat.8.2.5.25.& 9.27.& 14.130. & 15.22.& 17.15. Marc.5.22. & 10.47. Luc.17.5. Ioh.4.47. Et ipsi tanquā Domino nostro seruire nos teneri, liquet ex Col.3.24. Rom. 14.11. Ephes.6.5.6. Ex quibus omnibus necessariò, Christum vnum illum, & verum Iehouam esse, sequitur. Quod autem Socinus dicit, posse nos quidem Christum inuocare, sed tamen illud facere non teneri, præterquam quod toties damnatam infert ἀλλότριον, etiam ab ipsismet Samosatenianis, & scripturæ sacræ autoritate, satis sperspicuè refellitur.
units.tr: We will prove both premises in two ways. First, by the very confession of our opponents; then by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. That, if it is shown that Christ can rightly be invoked by us, and ought to be invoked, it necessarily follows that Christ is the true and eternal God, Faustus Socinus himself, the prince and standard-bearer of the Samosatene crowd, confesses in his Epistle to the Ministers of Transylvania, prefixed to his book on the invocation of Christ, against Francis David. His words are these: But when they learned that it is written in the reply that there is no precept in the Holy Scriptures about invoking Christ, that is, about directing our prayers by name to Christ himself, and that therefore, with "invoke" taken in this sense, we may indeed rightly invoke Christ, but are not bound to do so, not a few of them (namely his Polish brethren), as had happened from the beginning also to the Transylvanian brethren, were not a little offended. And although I have often shown them, both by voice and by writing, that there is no reason why anyone should be offended here, but rather that this is the only way both to stop the mouths of those who deny invocation to Christ and of those who conclude from the invocation of Christ that he is that one God of Israel; nevertheless, so that they themselves, etc. But the truth of the assumption is also clearly confirmed by the confession of our opponents. For Giorgio Blandrata, in his Epistle to Socinus, which is contained in the aforesaid booklet on page seventeen, writes among other things: Nor do I doubt that the opponents will carry off the triumph, if no necessity of invoking Christ is proved, which I will certainly prove by many arguments and by the analogy of faith. Namely, from his perpetual priesthood, from faith, from the power he has received, from the gifts without measure, from the glory of God the Father, from our consolation, from the examples of the Apostles, and from adoration itself, which necessarily requires invocation. And a little later: Let it therefore be proved that the members of Christ ought to invoke their head, leader and king in their proper order, unless they wish to do injury to God and Christ and inflict the greatest injury on themselves. Faustus Socinus, in the same book, page 4: As far as the matter itself is concerned, he says, leaving the name aside, I say it is sufficiently clear that Christ was invoked, and that invocation, which embraces worship and that trust by which something is asked, was attributed to him in Holy Scripture, from the fact that Paul, at the beginning of all his Epistles, prays for grace and peace for those to whom he writes, not only from God our Father but also from the Lord Jesus Christ, and somewhere also mercy, and usually concludes the same Epistles thus: The grace of the Lord, etc. (1 Thess. 3:11; 2 Cor. 12:8, 9.) And on page 30, after he had shown from the Scriptures that Christ, while he lived as a mortal, was invoked quite frequently, he adds: For in all these places, with true trust of heart, and in many with outward worship also, those things were asked which otherwise can be asked only of God; yet none of those who did so was rebuked by Christ for that reason. Indeed, besides granting all that they asked, he also commended some of them highly for this very thing. When, however, Francis David, in reply to Socinus himself, who was showing from many passages of Scripture that Christ was invoked with trust of mind and religious worship, objected that no example and no command was brought forward, Socinus answered on page 27: Although the examples of holy men, inquiring while they are moved by the Spirit of God, can and ought to be for us a rule of our actions, unless an express word of God stands against them. From all these things it clearly appears that our opponents themselves recognise the truth of both of our premises, and that therefore they attack the doctrine of our Churches not with the aim of seeking out, defending and illuminating the truth, but with the aim of assailing the divine nature of Christ and winning the victory, using the weapons of their sophisms. But Scripture itself also confirms both premises, and the major indeed, since it assigns to the divine majesty, if it assigns anything to it as its own, that invocation which depends on faith and a true trust of the mind; as in Joel 2:32: Whoever shall invoke the name of Jehovah shall be saved. Ps. 50:15: Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. Prov. 18:10: The name of Jehovah is a strong tower; the righteous runs to it and is kept safe. Deut. 6:13: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone. That Christ has been worshipped, and that he ought to be invoked by us, not only rightly but also by the command and mandate of God, is attested by examples: Matt. 8:2, 5, 25; 9:27; 14:30; 15:22; 17:15; Mark 5:22; 10:47; Luke 17:5; John 4:47. And that we are bound to serve him as our Lord is clear from Col. 3:24; Rom. 14:11; Eph. 6:5, 6. From all these things it necessarily follows that Christ is that one and true Jehovah. But what Socinus says, that we may indeed invoke Christ but are not bound to do so, besides introducing the alien [ἀλλότριον] doctrine so often condemned, is sufficiently clearly refuted even by the authority of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum cap.14. hanc proponit quæstionem, An videlicet ex honore illo diuino, qui Christo competit, diuinam ipsius naturam demonstrari possit? Hāc quæstionem ille tractat ἀποδεικτικῶς, & primò omnium argumentum nostrū ex inuocatione, quæ Christo cōpetit, diuina, desumptū, hac forma proponit. Deus est solus adorandus. Christus est adorandus. Ergo Christus est verus ille Deus.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in chapter 14 of his Institutions, raises this question: whether the divine nature of Christ can be demonstrated from that divine honour which belongs to him? He treats this question demonstratively [ἀποδεικτικῶς], and first of all sets out our argument from the divine invocation that belongs to Christ, in this form: God alone is to be worshipped. Christ is to be worshipped. Therefore Christ is the true God.

units.la: Primò itaque respondet, quamuis nullibi scriptum sit disertis verbis, quòd solus Deus sit adorandus, tamen se id concedere, perinde ac si scriptum esset, nempe in illis verbis Deu. 6. v.13. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ipsi soli seruies, quemadmodum à Christo citantur, Matt. 4.10. quo in loco expressè mandatum est, non quidem quòd Deus solus sit adorandus, sed quòd ipsi soli sit seruiendum. Ac proinde respondere se, Christum tunc cùm illud mandatum sanciretur, nondum extitisse, ac proinde Deum tum temporis solum adorandum fuisse.
units.tr: He first replies that although it is nowhere written in express words that God alone is to be worshipped, yet he concedes this as if it were written, namely in those words of Deut. 6:13, You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone, as they are cited by Christ in Matt. 4:10, where it is expressly commanded not that God alone is to be worshipped, but that he alone is to be served. And accordingly he replies that Christ had not yet existed when that command was given, and therefore at that time God alone was to be worshipped.

units.la: Resp. At verò nolumus in tam graui causa abste, Ostorrodi, iboriof precariò quicquam obtinere, tu rigidè persequitor ius tuum, nosón veri-ιτὰ. veritatis causam aduersus tuas impressiones strenuè tuebimur. Affirmas igitur nullibi extare , quòd Deus solus sit adorandus. Vbi primò omnium ambiguitate ludis manifesta : scis enim aliam esse adorationem religiosam , quæ prima Decalogi tabula præcipitur, & θρησκεία dicitur , ciuilem ac politicā aliam,ac proinde ipsam adorationem inuocatione latius patere,& hanc sub illa tanquam speciem sub genere comprehendi. De adorationis cultu igitur si loquaris in genere, vt ille non soli Deo, sed Angelis etiā & hominibus competit, ita nusquam legitur scriptum, quòd Deus solus sit adorandus.At verò si adoratione intelligas religiosam,quæ filialē seruitutem comitem habet,falsitatem assertionis tuæ euincit, vel vnicus ille locus Deut. 4.13.qui à Christo Matth. 4.10.citatur.Aut enim ibi Deus significare vult,se solum adorandum esse,& præter eum, nullum alium , aut simpliciter vult sibi cultum adorationis tribui debere. Atqui non posterius,idque duplici de causa:Primò, quia Deum religioso cultu honorandum esse, extra controuersiā erat,sed quærebatur,num eiusdem cultus alios quoque socios habere posset.Secundò : Qui populum Israeliticum ex Aegypto eduxit,ille etiam est adorandus : Atqui solus Deus populum eduxit ex Acgypto:Ergo solus etiam Deus ibi adorari iubetur. Sequitur ergo prius , nempe Deū in illo loco iubere,vt ille solus adoretur. Deinde cui seruiendū est, ille etiā solus est religioso cultu afficiēdus,quia religiosè aliquem colere,nihil aliud est, quàm voluntati ipsius,pio animi affectu obediendo inseruire. Atqui soli Deo seruiedum esse,Christus citato loco expressè docet. Ergo solus etiam Deus religioso cultu honorandus. Non igitur ex Aduersarii gratuita concessione,sed rei ipsius veritate obtinemus, nempe solum Deum inuocandum esse,cætera loca à nobis adducta piis aliorum meditationibus relinquentes. Insuper quicunque à nobis inuocatur ,illum etiam omniscium,& omni loco præsentem esse oportet,cū necesse sit ipsum omnia omniū hominū corda scrutari: siue omnia nostra dicta,facta, & cogitata distinctè, & singulatim omni loco & tempore perspicere,quippe absque qua speciali & distincta rerum omnium cognitione, nullus nos inuocantes exaudire posset: Atqui nemini præterquàm vni illi vero & æterno Deo Israelis omniscientia & omnipræsentia tribuitur, aut etiam tribui potest.
units.tr: Reply: But in so weighty a cause we do not want you, Ostorodius, to gain anything by mere petition; you rigorously pursue your right, and we will vigorously defend the cause of truth against your assertions. You affirm, therefore, that it is nowhere found that God alone is to be worshipped. Here, first of all, you play with an obvious ambiguity. For you know that there is one religious worship [θρησκεία], which is commanded in the first table of the Decalogue, and another civil and political worship, and so worship in general extends more widely than invocation, which is comprehended under it as a species under a genus. If, then, you speak of worship in the general sense, in which it belongs not only to God but also to angels and men, then indeed nowhere is it read that God alone is to be worshipped. But if you understand by worship that religious worship which has filial service as its companion, the falsity of your assertion is proved by that single passage, Deut. 4:13 (or 6:13), which Christ cites in Matt. 4:10. For either God there means that he alone is to be worshipped, and that no other besides him is, or he simply means that worship of adoration ought to be paid to himself. But not the latter, and for two reasons. First, because it was beyond controversy that God is to be honoured with religious worship; the question was whether he could have other partners in that same worship. Second: He who brought the people of Israel out of Egypt is also to be worshipped. But God alone brought the people out of Egypt. Therefore God alone is commanded to be worshipped there. It follows, then, that the former holds, namely that God in that place commands that he alone be worshipped. Next, whoever is to be served, he alone is also to be honoured with religious worship, since to worship someone religiously is nothing other than to serve his will with a devout disposition of mind. But Christ, in the passage cited, expressly teaches that God alone is to be served. Therefore God alone is also to be honoured with religious worship. Therefore we obtain, not from the gratuitous concession of our opponent but from the truth of the matter itself, that God alone is to be invoked, leaving the other passages we have adduced to the pious meditations of others. Moreover, whoever is invoked by us must also be omniscient and present in every place, since he must necessarily search the hearts of all men, and clearly perceive all our words, deeds and thoughts, each one, in every place and time; for without such a special and distinct knowledge of all things, no one could hear those who invoke him. But omniscience and omnipresence are attributed, or can be attributed, to no one except that one true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Reg.8. verf.39.Tu solus nosti corda hominum : Ierem.17.v.9. Ego Dominus scrutans corda & renes. Psalm.139.v.6.7.8.9. Quò ibo à Spiritu tuo, &c.Ergo etiam nemo præter vnum illum & æternum Deum Israelis religiose est inuocandus. Tanto itaque Socinus æquior est Oftorrodio,quanto magis ingenuè nemini nisi vniDeo inuocationis cultum deberi,agnoscit,dum profitetur, necessario consequuturum,quod Christus verus sit Deus, si ipsum inuocari debere,concedatur.Secundo,quod verò Oftorrodius dicit, Christum tum temporis,quum illud mandatum à Deo sanciretur,nondum extitisse, eo tam manifestè principium , de quo disceptatur, petit vt prolixiore refutatione minim e indigeat. Quid?quod ne in Christum quidē cadit inuocationis religiosæ honos,si ratione efsetiæ fit cùm essentialia illa Dei attributa,quæ ad inuocationem requiruntur,in nullam creaturam transfundi possint.
units.tr: 1 Reg. 8. vers. 39. Thou alone knowest the hearts of the children of men. Jer. 17. vers. 9. I the Lord search the heart and try the reins. Ps. 139. vers. 6, 7, 8, 9. Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? etc. Therefore no one apart from that one eternal God of Israel is to be invoked with religious worship. Socinus is thus fairer than Ostorodius, in that he frankly acknowledges that the worship of invocation is owed to no one but the one God. He professes that it would necessarily follow that Christ is the true God, if it were granted that he ought to be invoked. Secondly, as for Ostorodius's claim that Christ did not yet exist at the time when God enacted that command, this assumes the very point in dispute so plainly that it needs no lengthy refutation. Moreover, the honour of religious invocation does not even fall upon Christ, if, by reason of essence, those essential attributes of God that invocation requires cannot be transferred to any creature.

units.la: Secundo,respondet Aduersarius,mandatum illud Dei per diuinum honorem qui Christo tribuitur non infringi, quoniam, qui honorat Filium etiam Patrem honorat,id est Deum ipsum,vt liquet ex verbis illis Christi, Pater neminem iudicat, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio,vt omnes honorent Filium,quemadmodum Patrem honorant:qui non honorat Filium,neque Patrem honorat qui misit eum,Ioh. 5.v. 22. & 23. Quia verò nemo nostrûm est,qui neget id quod citatis Scripturæ locis affirmatur, nec illud cum iusto Dei mandato pugnat,quod Christus inuocandus esse affirmatur, sed quod Aduersarii Christo religiosum inuocationis cultum vendicant,quem tamen vnû illum,ac verum Deum Israelis esse negant,ideo subiungit Oftorrodius,Primò,non propterea tamen inquiens Deum ab illo honorari, qui Christum honorat, quasi Christus Deus ipse esset(vt excipere quis posset)sed ideo quia omnis honos,qui Christo exhibetur ad gloriam Dei spectat, vt testatur Apostolus Phil. 2 verf. 11.ac proinde diuinus ille honor, non in Christo, sed in Deo Patre ipsius tanquam vltimo scopo requiescat.Secundo, inquit, ex illa exceptione sequuturum Filium Dei ipsum Patrem esse, quoniam in loco illo quem citauimus, non Dei, sed Patris tantum nomen expresse legitur.
units.tr: Secondly, my opponent replies that God's command is not violated by the divine honour that is given to Christ, since "he who honours the Son also honours the Father," that is, God himself, as is clear from those words of Christ: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father; he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him" (John 5. vers. 22, 23). But since none of us denies what is affirmed by the scriptural passages cited, and since that does not conflict with God's just command that Christ is to be invoked, the problem lies rather in the fact that our opponents ascribe to Christ the religious worship of invocation, while they deny that he is that one true God of Israel. Therefore Ostorodius adds: First, he says, "not for this reason is God honoured by the one who honours Christ, as if Christ were God himself" (which someone might object), "but because all honour paid to Christ looks to the glory of God, as the Apostle testifies" (Phil. 2. vers. 11), "and so that divine honour rests not in Christ but in God the Father as its ultimate goal. Secondly," he says, "from that exception it would follow that the Son of God is the Father himself, since in the passage we cited, only the name of the Father, and not of God, is expressly read."

units.la: Resp. Ad primum : quum dominium & seruitus,id est, cultus atque honor,perpetuam relationem,& affectionem erga se inuicē habeant,Malach.1.v.6.ideo qua ratione Christus est Dominus, atq; Rex noster, eadem etiam ratione ipsi cultus & honor à nobis debetur. Atqui Christus duplici ratione Dominus noster est, & dominium in nos possidet ,primò videlicet iure naturæ & creationis:deinde iure gratiæ & redemptionis. Illud dominium est æternum,essentiale : hoc temporarium, acquisitum & œconomicum, vt iam sæpius demonstrauimus. Ergo etiam duplici iure, honor,cultus,& reuerentia, ipsi à nobis debetur, tum vt creatori, tum vt redemptori nostro. Vt autem priori ratione Dominus est ratione essentiæ suę,quatenus est ens primum,supremum,& à nullo alio principio pendens,priore vero ratione Dominus est ex voluntaria dispensatione à Deo Patre constitutus,electus, atque missus : ita etiam honor , qui ipsi tanquam supremo rerum omnium Domino & creatori tribuitur,in ipso tanquā vltimo fine requiescit:qui vero ipsi tribuitur vt Χριστῷ, & in regni huius œconomici administratione , quasi vicarium Patris agenti, is non in ipsum solum , sed in eum etiam qui misit ipsum , & cui tandem regnum illud est traditurus , redundat. Elenchum igitur oppositionis admittit Aduersarius , dum illas duas honoris causas ita inter se opponit, quasi vna posita, altera euerteretur. Vt enim œconomica illa dispensatio,naturam diuinam Christi nō euertit,ita etiam honor ille & cultus , qui Christo propter regiam mediatorii officii maiestatem debetur, illum,qui ipsi iure naturæ competit,minimè tollit. De priori cultu atque honore agitur in illo loco Iohannis, vnde etiam vera & æterna Christi deitas,necessaria consequentia illius honoris causa esse affirmatur. Primò,quia quo honore afficimus Deum Patrem,eodem quoque afficiendus est Filius:seu,Qua cultus ratione profequimurPatrem,eadem etiam colere debemus ipsum filium. Atqui Patrem colimus, & honoramus,vt æternum ac verum Deum Israelis,creatorem & conseruatorem nostrum,& supremum rerum omnium Dominum.Ergo etiam Filium,Domi-num nostrum Iesum Christū colere & honorare debemus , vt æternum ac verum Deum Israelis,creatorem, & conseruatorē nostrū, ac supremum rerum omnium Dominum. Harum.n.conditionum, quamcunque exceperis , nunquam Filium & Patrem æquali honore affeceris. Secundò,quia quicunq; ideo honoratur & colitur,vt honor tamē & cultus per ipsum ad superiorem aliquem tēdat, ille etiam non æquali cultu atque honore cum illo est afficiendus. Atqui Christus æquali honore cum Patre est afficiēdus.Ergo non ideo tātum honoratur & colitur, vt honor & cultus per ipsum ad superiorem,nempe Patrem, tendat:quod statuunt Samosateniani. Nemo itaque honorare dicitur à Christo Filium, qui non etiam honorat Patrem,non ea ob causam,quam affingit Aduersarius, sed quia sicut Pater non est sine filio, & qui negat filium, etiam Patrem negat, 1. Ioh. 2. v. 22. ita qui Filium non veneratur, nec Patrem venerari poterit. De posteriore cultu & honore agit Paulus ad Phil. 2. v. 11. ut omnes loci illius circunstantiæ apertissimè euincunt.
units.tr: Reply. To the first point: since lordship and servitude, that is, worship and honour, bear a perpetual relation and affection towards each other (Mal. 1. vers. 6), therefore, for the same reason that Christ is our Lord and King, the same worship and honour are owed to him by us. But Christ is our Lord in a twofold way, and he holds lordship over us: first, by the right of nature and creation; then by the right of grace and redemption. That lordship is eternal and essential; this one is temporary, acquired and economic, as we have often demonstrated already. Therefore honour, worship and reverence are owed to him by us under a twofold right, both as to our creator and as to our redeemer. Just as he is Lord by the former reason, by virtue of his essence, insofar as he is the first and supreme being, depending on no other principle, so by the latter reason he is Lord by the voluntary dispensation of God the Father, who appointed, chose and sent him. So too the honour that is paid to him as supreme Lord and creator of all things rests in him as its ultimate end; but the honour paid to him as Christ [Χριστῷ], and in the administration of this economic kingdom, as acting in the place of the Father, does not terminate in him alone, but also redounds to him who sent him, and to whom at last that kingdom will be handed over. Therefore my opponent admits the fallacy of opposition, since he sets these two grounds of honour against each other as if, once one were posited, the other would be overthrown. For just as that economic arrangement does not overthrow the divine nature of Christ, so that honour and worship which is due to Christ on account of the royal majesty of his mediatorial office does not in the least remove that which belongs to him by the right of nature. The former worship and honour is what is meant in that passage of John, from which the true and eternal deity of Christ is also affirmed as a necessary consequence of that honour. First, because the honour with which we honour God the Father must be given equally to the Son; or, in the manner in which we pay worship to the Father, we must in the same way worship the Son. But we worship and honour the Father as the eternal and true God of Israel, our creator and preserver, and the supreme Lord of all things. Therefore we must also worship and honour the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, as the eternal and true God of Israel, our creator and preserver, and the supreme Lord of all things. For whatever condition you may except, you will never have honoured the Son and the Father with equal honour. Secondly, because whoever is honoured and worshipped in such a way that the honour and worship paid through him tends towards some superior being, that one is not to be given equal worship and honour with that superior. But Christ must be given equal honour with the Father. Therefore he is not honoured and worshipped merely so that honour and worship pass through him to a superior, namely the Father, as the Samosatenians maintain. Thus no one is said by Christ to honour the Son who does not also honour the Father, not for the reason the opponent invents, but because, just as the Father is not without the Son, and whoever denies the Son also denies the Father (1 John 2. vers. 22), so whoever does not venerate the Son cannot venerate the Father either. Paul treats of the latter worship and honour in Phil. 2. vers. 11, as all the circumstances of that passage most clearly prove.

units.la: Ad secundum resp. negando consequentiam, qua vix ineptior alia dari potest. Honor enim & cultus, qui Deo Patri, Filio, ac Spiritui sancto debetur, fundamentum, & causam non habet in persona diuina, aut modo subsistendi, vnicuique trium illarum personarum, sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, peculiari, sed in essentia, vnde si nec Patrem honorare dicatur is qui Filium non honorat, non sequitur Christum esse Deum Patrem ipsum, sed eundem cum ipso habere essentiâ, ac proinde vnum, & æternum cum ipso esse Deũ: quia honor ille nec Patri nec Filio competit quà Pater & qua Filius, simpliciter, & quatenus secundum illam rationem internam à se inuicē distinguuntur, sed in vnitate essentiæ, & quà Pater Deus est, Filius Deus est, & Spiritus sanctus Deus est. Quum n. duæ personæ considerantur, & coparantur in affectione aliqua, quæ idiomatica, aut characteristica non est, & quæ vni ex illis comparatis personis æque ac alteri inesse dicitur, tũ sequitur quidẽ prædicatum illud, quod ex illa affectione exurgit de vtraq; prædicari æqualiter, non autẽ nomen personæ comparatæ vnius de persona alterius enuntiari: Vt, si dicam Paulum æqualem cũ Petro docendi autoritatem habere, non sequitur inde Petrum esse Paulum, aut Paulum esse Petrum, sed Paulo æquè ac ipsi Petro nomen, dignitatem & autoritatem Apostoli conuenire. Ratio consequentiæ huius est, quod docendi illa potestas, illis non tribuitur quà Paulus ille est, & alter Petrus, sed quà sunt Apostoli. Sed absurdissimas hasce ineptias Ostorrodii quid moror, quibus si defitueretur, non haberet quicquam quo veritatem doctrinæ nostræ orthodoxæ impugnaret?
units.tr: To the second point I reply by denying the inference, than which a more absurd one could hardly be given. For the honour and worship that is owed to God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit does not have its ground and cause in the divine person, or mode of subsisting, which is peculiar to each of the three persons of the most holy Trinity, but in the essence. Hence, even if it is not said that he who does not honour the Son honours the Father, it does not follow that Christ is the Father himself, but that he has the same essence as the Father and therefore is one and eternal with him, one God. For that honour belongs neither to the Father as Father nor to the Son as Son, simply, or insofar as they are distinguished from each other by that internal reason; but it belongs to the unity of essence: insofar as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. For when two persons are considered and compared in respect of some affection which is not idiomatic or characteristic, and which is said to belong equally to one of the compared persons as to the other, then indeed the predicate that arises from that affection is predicated equally of both; but the name of one compared person is not stated of the person of the other. For example, if I say that Paul has equal authority of teaching with Peter, it does not follow that Peter is Paul, or Paul is Peter, but that the name, dignity and authority of apostle belong to Paul just as much as to Peter himself. The reason for this inference is that that power of teaching is given to them not insofar as this is Paul and that is Peter, but insofar as they are apostles. But why should I dwell on these utterly absurd fallacies of Ostorodius? Without them, would he have anything left with which to assail the truth of our orthodox doctrine?

units.la: Tertiò, quasi iam nobis prostratis, signa nostra sub aduersò Marte iacerent, triumphat Ostorrodius, qunm addit, mirandum esse, quod nos ex diuino Christi honore, deitatem ipsius demonstrare conemur, cum tamen contrarium inde euidentius concludi possit, quoniam videlicet Scriptura sacra testatur quod Deus ipsi Christo honorem illum communicauerit. Vnde tale nobis opponit Argumentum:
units.tr: Thirdly, as though we were already prostrate and our standards lay beaten by the adverse god of war, Ostorodius exults when he adds that it is remarkable that we try to demonstrate Christ's deity from the divine honour given to him, when the contrary could more evidently be concluded from it, namely that holy Scripture testifies that God himself communicated that honour to Christ. Hence he puts to us the following argument:

units.la: Nullus, quem propter eam honorare tenemur, quod Deus ipsi omne iudicium, & nomen supra omne nomen dederit, est vnus ille & verus Deus. Atqui Christus propter hanc ipsam causam diuino honore afficitur. Ergo Christus non est vnus ille & verus Deus.
units.tr: No one whom we are bound to honour for this reason alone, that God has given him all judgement and the name above every name, is that one and true God. But Christ is honoured with divine honour for this very cause. Therefore Christ is not that one and true God.

units.la: Maiorem propositionem, inquit, per se manifestam esse, quoniam vnum illum Deum non propterea honore & cultu afficimus, quod ipsi iudicium, & nomen supra omne nomen a quoquam sit concessum, sed hanc ob causam, quia videlicet omne iudicium, dominium, imperium, & potestatem in omnia, a se ipso habeat.
units.tr: The major premise, he says, is self-evident, since we do not honour and worship that one God for the reason that judgement and a name above every name have been granted to him by anyone, but for this reason, namely that he has all judgement, dominion, rule and power over all things from himself.

units.la: Minorem autem ait, omissis aliis innumeris locis, ex duobus sequentibus potissimum demonstrari, Ioh. 5. v. 22. 23. Pater (inquit Christus) neminem iudicat, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio, vt omnes honorent Filium, prout honorant Patrem, Phil. 2. v. 11. Deus ipsum exaltauit (inquit Paulus) ac dedit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, vt in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur. Vnde manifestum fieri, inquit, se ex honore illo diuino, contra confitetam naturam Christi, quam tamen alij ex eodem illo honore demonstrare conentur, optime argumentatum esse.
units.tr: As for the minor premise, he says, setting aside countless other passages, it is chiefly proved from the following two: John 5:22-23, "The Father (says Christ) judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son, that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father"; Phil. 2:11, "God has exalted him (says Paul) and given him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." From this, he says, it is plain that he has argued very well from that divine honour against the confessed nature of Christ, which others nevertheless try to prove from that same honour.

units.la: Resp. Negamus consequentiam, manifesto oppositorum elecho laborantem, qui vt magis elucescat, sic habeat Oflorrodius. Nullus, quem hanc solam ob causam honorare tenemur, quòd Deus ipsi omne iudicium dederit, esse vnum illum ac verum Deum, agnoscimus & confitemur: sed nos ob hac solam causam teneri Christum diuino honore afficere, constantissime negamus. Vt n. regnum ac dominium Christi duplex esse supra aliquoties demonstrauimus, essentiale ac æternum vnum, mediatorium & œconomicum alterum, diuinum vtrumque: ita etiam duas ob causas Christum diuino honore afficiendum esse sequitur, tum videl. propter naturæ diuinæ suæ maiestatem & excellentiam supra res omnino omnes: tum etiam quia iudex ac Dominus super omnia est a Deo Patre constitutus. Vt autem hæc regni ac dominii œconomici administratio naturam ipsam diuinam non tollit, ita quoque honor ille quem Christo ideo exhibere tenemur, quod Deus ipsum iudicem constituerit, honori illi diuino, qui ipsi ex naturali debetur iure, minimè præiudicat, vt iam ipsam propositionē merito falsam pronuntiemus. At vero vnus ille Deus, non eam ob causam a nobis colitur aut honoratur, quod ipsi iudicium omne, & nomen supra omne nomen a quoquam sit concessum. Verum quidem est nos vnum illum Deum, nomine videl. Dei ὡς σωδζ sumpto, non propterea colere aut honorare, sed quid hoc deitati Christi præiudicare potest? què nos vt creatorè nostrum, vt Deum absolute, in vnitate essentiæ diuinæ, & naturali gloria, aut maiestate contemplantes,non propter dominium illud,quod laborando, certando, patiendo, & moriendo sibi acquisiuit, sed propter gloriam illam, quam apud Patrem habuit, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi,propter supremam, & plane αὐτοῦσύσιον potestatem & autoritatem: denique propter summum & absolutum illud ius & dominium,quod in res omnino omnes habet,pia mente ac religiose colimus & veneramur. At quoniam ille salua æterna deitate sua,etiam œconomicum illud,& mediatorium regnum voluntaria dispensatione suscepit,cum etiā propterea religioso honore afficiendum credimus, quod ille mediator, & σταυρωθὲντος sanguine suo,& redemptione peracta, dominium in nos, & iudicium, omnémque potestatem in cœlo & in terra à Patre obtinuerit. Vt autem hoc dominium acquisitum,quod est personę ἀνθρώπου,cum altero illo & essentiali dominio, quod est naturæ diuinæ Christi,nō pugnat:ita etiam cultus hic, alteri illi minimè repugnat, aut quicquam ei præiudicare potest: quum naturam diuinam malè negari, rationibus desumptis ab iis, quæ de Christo ratione officii mediatorii prædicantur,iam aliquoties ostenderimus.
units.tr: Reply. We deny the inference, which labours under a manifest fallacy of opposites. To make this clearer, Ostorodius should put it thus: "No one whom we are bound to honour for this reason alone, that God has given him all judgement, is that one and true God." We acknowledge and confess this. But that we are bound to give Christ divine honour for this reason alone we most firmly deny. For just as we have shown several times above that the kingdom and dominion of Christ is twofold, one essential and eternal, the other mediatorial and economical, both divine, so it follows that Christ is to be honoured with divine honour for two reasons: first, namely, on account of the majesty and excellence of his divine nature above all things whatsoever; and second, because he has been appointed by God the Father as judge and Lord over all things. Now, just as this administration of the economical kingdom and dominion does not take away the divine nature itself, so also that honour which we are bound to render to Christ because God has appointed him judge does in no way prejudice that divine honour which is due to him by natural right. Thus we rightly pronounce the proposition itself false. But indeed that one God is not worshipped or honoured by us for the reason that all judgement and a name above every name have been granted to him by anyone. It is true that we do not honour or worship that one God, taking the name God in the absolute sense [ὡς], for this reason; but how can this prejudice the deity of Christ? For we, contemplating him as our Creator, as God absolutely, in the unity of the divine essence and in natural glory and majesty, worship and reverence him with a pious and devout mind, not because of that dominion which he acquired for himself by labouring, contending, suffering and dying, but because of that glory which he had with the Father before the foundations of the world were laid, because of his supreme and altogether self-existent [αὐτοούσιον] power and authority, and finally because of that highest and absolute right and dominion which he holds over all things whatsoever. But since he, without losing his eternal deity, also undertook by voluntary dispensation that economical and mediatorial kingdom, we believe that he is to be honoured with religious worship also for this reason: that as mediator, and by his crucified [σταυρωθέντος] blood and the completed redemption, he obtained from the Father dominion over us, judgement, and all power in heaven and on earth. Now, just as this acquired dominion, which belongs to the person of the man [ἀνθρώπου], does not conflict with that other, essential dominion which belongs to the divine nature of Christ, so also this worship does not conflict with that other, nor can it prejudice it in any way; since we have already several times shown that the divine nature is wrongly denied by arguments drawn from what is said of Christ in respect of his mediatorial office.

units.la: Tertiò denique per prolepsin refutans obiectionem quandam, Si quis vero,inquit hic exciperet, dicens sententiam nostram de diuino Christi honore,nempe quòd Deus eum ipsi dederit, pugnare cum eo quod Deus ipse dixit Esa. 42. vers. 8. Honorem meum alteri non dabo: respondemus primò,sententiam nostram cum illis verbis minimè pugnare,sed Aduersarios Scripturas ipsas inter se committere, locúmque vnum ex Prophetis multis perspicuis,& clarissimis Christi & Apostolorum verbis opponere,quo ipso nihil aliud quæritur, quàm vt per eiusmodi oppositiones, ea quæ clara per se lucent,per ea, quæ obscura sunt, Nouum Testamentum per Vetus, multa denique loca per vnicum aliquem explicentur. Secundò, Hanc eandem sententiam ipsorum, inquit,cum verbis Prophetæ Esaiæ minimè pugnare, siquidem Deus gloriam suam se alius non daturum affirmans,nomine aliorum, neque Christum, neque suorum quenquam complectatur, secus ipsum sibimet contradicturum esse, quum apud eundem Prophetam cap. 46. ver. vlt. Dabo in Sion salutem, & Israeli gloriam meam, sicuti verba ipsa in contextu Hebraico legun-tur.Insuper etiam contra verba sua fecisset,quoties fidelibus, & in Chri-stum credentibus, se illos gloriæ suæ participes reddituros esse promisit. Rom.5,v.2. 1.Thessal.2.v.12. 1.Pet.5.v.10.Apocal.3.v.21. & 21.v.11.11.v.12. Vnde sequitur, Deum per nomen illud aliis, eos tantùm intelle-{ xisse,qui ab ipso sunt alieni,vt sunt idola,& imagines,vnde etiam statim subiecit,nec laudem meam sculptilibus. Tertiò ait,Verba illa, non dare,in sacris literis interdum idem significare,ac non permittere, quemadmodum videre sit in Psal. 16. v. 10. non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, id est,vt Lutherus locum illum transtulit,nō permittes,vt sanctus tuus corrumpatur. Ac proinde etiam ita intelligi posse verba illa Dei, nempe quòd ille non sit permissurus, vt homines,propria autoritate gloriam ipsius aliis,nempe idolis ascribant: non vero,ita,quasi nec ipse,nempe Deus,pro libera voluntatis arbitrio,eandem aliis communicare posset. Quartò,satis liquere ait,sensum verborum illorumDei genuinum hunc esse,quod videlicet nolit gloriam suam ad alios transferri,nempe vt per alienationem ipse illa spolietur: quod ipsum honorem Christi non attingat, quum ille, testante Scriptura sacra, à Deo ipso ei sit concessus, nec Deus propterea sua gloria priuetur, sed potius maximo honori ipsi cedat,sicut supra ex verbis Christi & Apostoli sit demonstratum.
units.tr: Thirdly, finally, refuting by anticipation an objection, "But if anyone," he says, "should here object," saying "that our opinion about the divine honour of Christ, namely that God has given it to him, conflicts with what God himself said, Isa. 42:8, 'My honour I will not give to another'": we reply first, that our opinion does not conflict with those words at all, but that our adversaries set Scripture against itself, and oppose to the clear and most evident words of Christ and the Apostles one passage from the Prophets; by which very act nothing else is sought than that, through such oppositions, things which shine clearly by themselves should be explained by those which are obscure, the New Testament by the Old, and in short many passages by a single one. Second, that this same opinion of theirs, he says, does not conflict with the words of the Prophet Isaiah at all; for since God, affirming that he will not give his glory to another, does not include Christ or any of his people under the name of "others", otherwise he would contradict himself, since in the same Prophet, Isa. 46, last verse, "I will give salvation in Zion, and my glory to Israel," as the words themselves are read in the Hebrew context. Moreover, he would also have acted against his own words whenever he promised to make the faithful and those who believe in Christ partakers of his glory: Rom. 5:2; 1 Thess. 2:12; 1 Pet. 5:10; Rev. 3:21; 21:11; 21:12. Hence it follows that by the name "others" God meant only those who are alien to him, such as idols and images; hence also he immediately added, "nor my praise to graven things." Third, he says that the words "I will not give", in the sacred letters, sometimes signify the same as "I will not permit", as can be seen in Ps. 16:10, "You will not give your holy one to see corruption"; that is, as Luther translated that passage, "You will not permit your holy one to be corrupted." And therefore those words of God can also be understood in this way, namely that he will not permit men to ascribe his glory on their own authority to others, that is, to idols; but not in such a way as if God himself, by the free choice of his will, could not impart the same to others. Fourth, he says it is sufficiently plain that the genuine sense of those words of God is this: that he is unwilling for his glory to be transferred to others, namely so that by alienating it he himself would be deprived of it; this does not touch the honour of Christ, since he, as Holy Scripture testifies, has been granted it by God himself, and God is therefore not deprived of his glory, but rather it redounds to his greatest honour, just as has been demonstrated above from the words of Christ and of the Apostle.

units.la: Resp. Quos quaso recessus, & quas latebras non quærit Ostorrodius,vt splēdorem veritatis cœlestis effugiat? Quas etiam strophas, & quos dolos non censuit,vt misero suo popello,orthodoxam nostram doctrinam suspectam reddat? Qua enim mente, & quo fine,hunc vnicum locum Esaiæ,cæteris omissis omnibus, in examen producit,quasi aut illo solo niteretur doctrina nostra,fidésque Christiana suffulciretur, aut ex vno illo de cæteris omnibus, & argumentis, & Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ ad veritatem confirmandam à nobis adducuntur,esset iudicandum? aut deniq; cùm locus aliquis,& quidem è multis vnus aliter atque aliter explicari potest,statim doctrina ipsa euerteretur,& non tantùm loci alicuius singularis interpretatio? Sed premamus aliquandiu vestigia Aduersarii in tortuosis illis varię interpretationis anfractibus oberrantis. Qui igitur,ex nostrę Ecclesiæ doctoribus, locū illum Esaiæ ad inuocationis & religiosi cultus gloriam soli Deo asserendam adducunt, illi nomine aliū,quicquid ita à Deo alienum est,vt ad essentiam eius non pertineat: & nomine g'oriæ honorem inuocationis, & religiosi cultus,intelligunt, qui ipsi soli, tum ob naturæ ipsius supra res alias omnes excellentiam,tum ob veritatem, & constantiam in omnibus promissis,debetur, complectuntur: Atque hinc necessaria consequentia inferunt, aut Christum inuocari non oportere: aut cum certè eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ diuinæ participem esse. Quum autem prius ipsi Christo, tum sacrarum literarum autoritate, tum ipsa Aduersariorum confessione tribuatur, posterius, quod nempe eiusdē cum Deo Patre essentiæ diuinæ sit particeps, verissime concludunt, & sine Scripturæ sacræ, & Testameti vtriusque locos sibi inuicē opponendi malitia, aut studio nullo, quā impietate nimis temere & malitiosè nobis Ostorrodius impingit. Sed videamus etiam exceptiones ipsius. Ad primā itaque respondeo per iustissimā inficiatione: dū enim dogmata, & capita Christianæ fidei, Veteris etiam Testamenti autoritate fulcimus & confirmamus, nō scripturas scripturis opponimus, vt inuidiosè calūniatur Ostorrodius: sed scripturas ex scripturis explicamus & illustramus, Christi & Apostolorum exemplum sequuti, qui doctrinę Euangelicæ, & Noui Testamenti, ab ipsis promulgatæ, capita, Veteris Testamenti & Prophetarum testimoniis tam frequenter confirmarunt, vt ex illis allegationibus cum notis & characteribus libri ἀπόκρυφοι & canonici ab illis qui apocryphi dicuntur, discernantur, & ex canone expugātur pænè omnes, quotquot ad cōfirmādā veritatē doctrinæ Euāgelicæ, à Christo, aut Apostolis citati nūquā fuerunt. Cūm aūt Ostorrodius Vet. Testam. autoritatē, ad stabiliēdā fidei doctrinā adhiberi vetat, quo alio nomine, quàm quod Anabaptistarū furoré imitatus, illud plane repudiet, sese suspectū reddit? Ad secundum. Locus Ef. 46 v. vlt. nō probat, Deū illius gloriæ, de qua c. 42. agit, quenquam participem fecisse, quia Deus per metonymiam effecti gloriam suam in Sion positurus dicitur. Quum ille ad illustrandam gloriam suam, iustitiæ, veritatis, & constantiæ in promissione salutis Israelitis facta, se Hierosolymam seruaturum, & populum suum ab interitu vindicaturum, inque libertatem asserturum esse, pollicetur. Loca ex Nouo Testamento allegata, non loquuntur de illa gloria, quo vnius ac æterni Dei propria & essentialis est, sed de gloria electis, ac fidelibus ex gratia in Christo communicata, quæ primæ illius δόξης, & effectus est, & per quā nihil aliud, quàm vocatio efficax, iustificatio, sanctificatio, futura electorum felicitas, & gloriosa illa in vitam æternam transportatio intelligitur: ac proinde ad rem præsentem nihil faciunt. Hunc genuinum esse locorum illorum sensum, manifestè liquet ex 2. Pet. 1. v. 4. vbi naturæ diuinæ participes futuri esse dicimur naturæ diuinæ vocabulo significante primò, non substantiam diuinam, sed qualitates, æternam nempe veritatem, iustitiam, sapientiam, pacem, voluptate, ac vitam perpetuam, & quicquid nobis potest boni communicari, vt apparet ex antithesi qua mundi corruptionem illi naturę diuinę participationi opponit: Deinde non qualitates Deo essentiales ac proprias, sed insignem Dei effectum, & electorum cum Deo similitudinem, vt Apostolus Paulus diserte explicat 1.Cor. 15.v.49.dicens, quemadmodum gestauimus imaginem terreni, nempe Adami, dum corruptioni & mortalitati, ab ipso in nos deriuatę, obnoxii fuimus, in hac vita, ita etiā gestabimus imaginē cœlestis, cum videlicet inchoata illa in nobis imaginis diuinæ restauratio, & reparatio perficietur, vnde & similes Deo futuri dicimur 1.Ioh.3. v.2. Quemadmodū enim in hac vita per dona gratię Dei in Christo Iesu, dum renati, ac iustificati imaginem Patris nostri, iustè viuendo, exprimimus: ita in futuro seculo per dona glorię, vbi immortales glorificati, acverè felices fuerimus: diuinę naturę imaginē, & similitudinē referemus. Gloriamur igitur sub spe gloriæ Dei, i.de spe gloriosa, vita nēpe æterna, quam à Deo expectamus, quia certi sumus quod Deus nos glorificabit, & quod Christus trásformabit corpus nostrū humile, vt cōforme fiat corpori suo glorioso. Phil.3.v.21.Quū verò in Apocalypsi sessuri dicimur cum Christo in throno ipsius, nihil aliud intelligitur, quàm quod regni cœlestis cōfortes futuri simus, quod promittitur fidelibus. Matth.19.ver.28. quod nihil aliud est, quàm quod Apostolus dicit, quū apparuerit Christus vita vestra, tū & vos cū ipso apparebitis in gloria. Col.3.v.4. Vnde vanā esse illā Oftorrodii exceptionē, luculenter demōstratur. Ad tertia: Incerta illa cōiectura est, nō solida loci illius interpretatio: nec si illud non dare interdū idē significat, quod nō permittere, sequitur illico in loco isto Esaiæ verba illa Lo-Etten, eandē significationē habere. Antecedēs ex Ps.16. v.10. nō probatur: interpretatio enim illa Lutheri propria est, nec à natiua significatione verba illa Lo-Etten, ad aliā trāfertur quū verbū Ghathan etiā propria significatione permittere, aut exponere significet. Consequēs etiamsi concedatur, tamen illa interpretatio & expositio illius loci, sola opinione, eáque falsa nititur. Quum enim gloria Dei proprie accipitur, & essentialem proprietatem eius denotat, tam est impossibile Deum illam pro libertate arbitrii vlli creaturæ cōmunicare, quàm vllam creaturā Deo inuito eandem eripere posse, quia etiam Deus seipsum negare non potest. 2. Tim. 2. verf 13. Ad quartam: Duplex ibi est error: primo, falsa illa hypothesis, nempe Christum non esse vnum cum Patre Deum, eiusdémque essentiæ, & gloriæ cum eodem participem, quo ipso principium manifestè petitur. Secundò, homonymia est in vocabulo illo honoris, qui in loco illo Esaiæ decuius disceptatur sensu, sumitur pro honore, qui Deo competit, qua Deus est: in responsione vero Aduersarii pro eo qui Christo vt Σωτὴρ ὡς ἀνθρώπῳ & mediatori, propter regnum illud œconomicum, & dispensatiuum tribuitur. Vnde falsa interpretatio, quæ illis scopis dissolutis nititur.
units.tr: Reply. What hiding-places and what lurking-holes does Ostorrodius not seek, so that he may escape the brightness of the heavenly truth? What twists and tricks has he not devised, so that he may make our orthodox doctrine suspect to his wretched little flock? For with what purpose, and to what end, does he bring forward this one passage of Isaiah for examination, all the others being set aside, as though our doctrine rested on that alone, or the Christian faith were propped up by it alone, or as though everything else, all the arguments and testimonies of Scripture which we adduce to confirm the truth, were to be judged by that one passage? Or indeed, as though, because some passage, and one of many at that, can be explained in different ways, the doctrine itself were overturned at once, and not merely the interpretation of one particular passage? But let us for a little while follow the adversary's footsteps as he wanders through the winding turns of his varied interpretation. Those of our Church's teachers who bring that passage of Isaiah forward to assert the glory of invocation and of religious worship for God alone understand by the word other whatever is so foreign to God that it does not belong to his essence; and by the word glory they understand the honour of invocation and of religious worship, which is due to him alone, both because of the excellence of his nature above all other things and because of his truth and constancy in all his promises. From this they draw the necessary conclusion either that Christ ought not to be invoked, or that he is certainly a partaker of the same divine essence as the Father. Now since the former is ascribed to Christ himself, both by the authority of the sacred letters and by the very confession of our adversaries, the latter, namely that he is a partaker of the same divine essence as God the Father, is what they rightly conclude. And so, without any malice or deliberate purpose of setting the passages of Scripture and of both Testaments against one another, it is Ostorrodius who with too much rashness and malice hurls this impiety at us. But let us also see his objections. To the first, then, I answer with a most just denial: for when we support and confirm the points and heads of the Christian faith by the authority of the Old Testament too, we are not setting Scripture against Scripture, as Ostorrodius spitefully slanders; rather we are explaining and illustrating Scripture by Scripture, following the example of Christ and the Apostles, who confirmed the heads of the Evangelical doctrine and of the New Testament, which they themselves published, so often by the testimonies of the Old Testament and the Prophets, that by those citations, marked with the notes and characters of the books [apokryphoi] and canonical, the books called apocryphal by those men are distinguished, and almost all those books which were never cited by Christ or the Apostles to confirm the truth of the Evangelical doctrine are struck from the canon. But since Ostorrodius forbids the authority of the Old Testament to be used to establish the doctrine of the faith, under what other name, than that he is plainly imitating the fury of the Anabaptists and rejecting it outright, does he render himself suspect? To the second. The passage of Isaiah 46, last verse, does not prove that God has made anyone a partaker of that glory which he discusses in chapter 42, because God is said, by metonymy, to be going to place his glory in Zion. For he promises, to illustrate his glory of justice, truth and constancy in the promise of salvation made to the Israelites, that he will preserve Jerusalem and will vindicate his people from destruction and assert their liberty. The passages from the New Testament that are cited do not speak of that glory which is proper and essential to the one and eternal God, but of the glory communicated by grace in Christ to the elect and faithful, which is the first [doxa] and effect of that glory, and by which nothing else is understood than effectual calling, justification, sanctification, the future happiness of the elect, and that glorious translation into eternal life; and therefore they have nothing to do with the matter at hand. That this is the genuine sense of those passages is plainly clear from 2 Peter 1:4, where we are said to be going to be partakers of the divine nature, the word divine nature signifying first not the divine substance but qualities: namely eternal truth, justice, wisdom, peace, joy and everlasting life, and whatever good can be communicated to us, as appears from the antithesis by which he opposes to this partaking in the divine nature the corruption of the world. Then, it is not qualities essential and proper to God, but the remarkable effect of God and the likeness of the elect to God, as the Apostle Paul expressly explains in 1 Corinthians 15:49, saying just as we have borne the image of the earthly, namely Adam, while in this life we were subject to the corruption and mortality derived into us from him, so also we shall bear the image of the heavenly, namely when that restoration and reparation of the divine image, begun in us, is brought to completion; whence we are also said to be going to be like God, 1 John 3:2. For just as in this life, by the gifts of God's grace in Christ Jesus, when we have been born again and justified, we express the image of our Father by living righteously, so in the future age, by the gifts of glory, when we have been glorified as immortals and truly blessed, we shall reflect the image and likeness of the divine nature. We glory therefore in hope of the glory of God, that is, in the glorious hope, namely eternal life, which we expect from God, because we are certain that God will glorify us and that Christ will transform our humble body to be conformed to his glorious body, Philippians 3:21. But when in the Apocalypse we are said to be going to sit with Christ on his throne, nothing else is understood than that we shall be sharers in the heavenly kingdom, which is promised to the faithful, Matthew 19:28; which is nothing other than what the Apostle says: when Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory, Colossians 3:4. Whence that objection of Ostorrodius is clearly shown to be empty. To the third: that is an uncertain conjecture, not a solid interpretation of that passage; nor does it follow, if not to give sometimes means the same as not to permit, that the words [Lo-Etten] in that passage of Isaiah immediately have the same meaning. The antecedent is not proved from Psalm 16:10: for that interpretation is Luther's own, and the words [Lo-Etten] are not transferred from their native meaning to another, since the verb [Ghathan] too, in its proper meaning, signifies to permit or to expose. Even if the consequent be granted, that interpretation and exposition of the passage rests only on opinion, and a false opinion at that. For when the glory of God is taken properly, and denotes his essential property, it is as impossible for God to communicate it to any creature at the creature's free will, as it is for any creature to be able to snatch it from him against his will, because God too cannot deny himself, 2 Timothy 2:13. To the fourth: there is a twofold error there. First, the false hypothesis, namely that Christ is not one God with the Father, and a partaker of the same essence and glory with him; by which very thing a principle is plainly begged. Secondly, there is an equivocation in the word honour, which in the sense of the passage of Isaiah under discussion is taken for the honour that belongs to God as God; but in the adversary's reply it is taken for that which is ascribed to Christ as [Soter hos anthropo], as Saviour as man and as Mediator, on account of that economic and dispensatory kingdom. Hence the false interpretation, which rests on these loosened aims.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: In quo argumentum septimum pro æterna Filii Deitate proponitur ac defenditur.
units.tr: In which the seventh argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is set forth and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM septimum, quo demonstramus Christum verum & æternum Deum esse, eiusdémque essentiæ cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto participem desumitur, tum ex illis Scripturæ locis quæ Christum ita vnum cum Deo Patre esse affirmant, vt necessariò inde concludatur illa non tantùm de voluntatis consensu, sed de vnitate essentiæ, & omnipotentiæ intelligenda esse, Ioh.10.v.28.29.30. Ego vitam æternam do eis, & non peribunt in æternum, nec rapiet eas quisquam à manu mea. Pater meus qui eas dedit mihi, maior omnibus est, neque potest eas quisquam rapere è manu Patris mei. Ego & Pater vnum sumus. Ioh.15.v.11. Pater sancte, serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint vnum prout & nos. Et v.21. Vt omnes vnum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, vt & ipsi in nobis sint. Et v.22. Et ego gloriam quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis, vt sint vnum sicut & nos vnum sumus: tum ex illis, quæ illā ἀπαράλλακτος & communionem personarum docent, vt Ioh.14.v.10. Pater qui in me manet, ipse facit opera, & v.11. credite mihi me in Patre, & Patrem in me esse. Vnde ita argumentamur.
units.tr: The seventh argument, by which we show that Christ is the true and eternal God and shares the same essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is drawn both from those passages of Scripture which affirm that Christ is so one with God the Father that it must necessarily be understood that these statements refer not merely to agreement of will but to unity of essence and omnipotence: John 10:28-30: I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand. My Father who gave them to me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one. John 17:11: Holy Father, keep them through your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are. And v.21: That they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us. And v.22: And the glory which you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one, just as we are one. And also from those passages which teach the indistinguishable likeness [ἀπαράλλακτος] and communion of the persons, as John 14:10: The Father who abides in me, he does the works, and v.11: believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me. From these we argue thus.

units.la: Qui cum Deo Patre vnum est, non tantùm vnitate concordiæ, & voluntatis consensu, sed etiam vnitate naturæ, & essentiæ, ille est verus verus atque aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whoever is one with God the Father not only by unity of concord and agreement of will, but also by unity of nature and essence, is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Christus vnum est cum Deo Patre , non tantùm vnitate concordia,& voluntatis consensu,sed etiam vnitate natura,& essentia.
units.tr: But Christ is one with God the Father not only by unity of concord and agreement of will, but also by unity of nature and essence.

units.la: Ergo Christus est verus,atque aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Maior propositio est extra controuersiam: Assumptionem ita demonstramus.
units.tr: The major premise is beyond dispute. We demonstrate the minor premise as follows.

units.la: Quicunque ita vnum est cum Deo Patre, vt sit eiusdem cum ipso potentia,ille cum Deo Patre vnum est,non tantùm vnitate concordia, & voluntatis consensu ,sed etiam vnitate essentia, at natura:
units.tr: Whoever is so one with God the Father that he has the same power as him is one with God the Father not only by unity of concord and agreement of will, but also by unity of essence and nature.

units.la: Atqui Christus ita vnum est cum Deo Patre, vt sit eiusdem cum ipso omnipotentia.
units.tr: But Christ is so one with God the Father that he has the same omnipotence as him.

units.la: Ergo Christus cum Deo Patre vnum est,non tantùm vnitate concordia & voluntatis consensu , sed etiam vnitate essentia, ac natura.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is one with God the Father not only by unity of concord and agreement of will, but also by unity of essence and nature.

units.la: Maioris propositionis veritas inde liquet, quod ipsę proprietates Dei essentiales nihil aliud sint, quàm ipsa Dei essentia , à qua non nisi ratione conceptus nostri distinguuntur. Assumptio autem ex scopo Christi,& argumentorum serie,quibus certitudinem & securitatem fidei,suis electis,confirmat,euidenter demonstratur. Neminem enim posse oues Christi ex manibus eius eripere , hoc argumento demonstrat. Si oues meas nemo poterit eripere ex manu Patris mei,tum etiam nemo ex manu mea illas eripiet. Atqui nemo poterit oues meas ex manu Patris mei eripere, quia videlicet ille maior est omnibus. Ergo etiam nemo poterit illas eripere ex manu mea. Connexum syllogismi hoc probat argumento : Si Pater oues meas mihi dedit, & ego & Pater vnum sumus, tum si nemo poterit illas eripere ex manu Patris mei , nec ex mea illas eripere poterit. Atqui prius est verum. Ergo & posterius. Hoc autem argumento connexum illud demonstrari non potest , nec quicquam ex illo concluditur nisi illud vnum sumus,non tantum voluntatis consensum , sed etiam vnam esse virtutem , manum, atque omnipotentiam Patris & Filii significet, vt quiuis pia mentis indagine illa perpen dens facilè animaduertit. Ex quibus omnibus necessariò sequitur , Christum eiusdem esse cum Deo Patre essentiæ ac naturæ, & proinde verum illum , & æternum Israelis Deum.
units.tr: The truth of the major premise is clear, because the essential properties of God are nothing other than the very essence of God, from which they are distinguished only by our manner of conceiving them. The minor premise is plainly shown from the purpose of Christ and the sequence of the arguments by which he confirms the certainty and security of faith in his elect. For by this argument he proves that no one can snatch Christ's sheep out of his hands: If no one will be able to snatch my sheep out of my Father's hand, then neither will anyone snatch them out of my hand. But no one will be able to snatch my sheep out of my Father's hand, because he is greater than all. Therefore neither will anyone snatch them out of my hand. He proves the connection of this syllogism by the following argument: If the Father has given me the sheep, and I and the Father are one, then if no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand, neither can anyone snatch them out of mine. But the first is true. Therefore the second is too. Yet this connection cannot be demonstrated by such an argument, nor can anything be concluded from it, unless we are one signifies not merely agreement of will but also that the Father and the Son have one power, one hand and one omnipotence, as anyone who weighs these words with a pious mind readily perceives. From all these things it necessarily follows that Christ is of the same essence and nature as God the Father, and therefore the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum cap 9.hanc quæstione͂ pro- ponit, An ex vnitate Patris ac Filÿ,ficta illa(vt non sine blasphemia appellat)natura diuina Christi demonstrari possit,quod ille negat,atque ad priora illa loca Scripturæ, quæ Christum vnum esse cum Deo Patre affirmat,respondet primò,Verum quidem esse,quod Christus cum Deo Patre vnum sit,sed non vnus.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in chapter 9 of his Institutes, raises this question: Can the divine nature of Christ, that fictitious nature (as he calls it, not without blasphemy), be demonstrated from the unity of Father and Son? He denies that it can. To the earlier passages of Scripture which affirm that Christ is one with God the Father, he responds first: It is true that Christ is one with God the Father, but not one.

units.la: Resp.Aduersarium manifesta æquiuocatione ludere. Quum enim affirmatur, vel negatur, quod Christus vnus sit cum Deo Patre,tum nomen Dei vel ϑεωδὸς, vel ὑπόστατικὸς intelligitur, & sensus est,vel Christum eandem cum Patre ὑπόστασιν habere,& vnam cum ipso eandémque personam esse : aut Christum eandem cum Patre essentiam habere, acproinde vnum & æternum cum illo Deum esse. Si posteriori modo verba intelligantur,Christus non est vnus cum Deo Patre,sed vnum,quod vocabulum essentiam denotat in hac enunciatione:sin priore, Christus cum Deo Patre & vnus est, & vnum : vt sic pro diuerso illo sensu Christum esse vnum cum Deo Patre affirmetur,& negetur sine contradictione vlla. Quum igitur ad vnitatem essentiæ demonstrandam non sit necessarium vt Christus vnus cum Deo Patre esse dicatur, quam quæso consequentiam inde conficiet Ostorrodius, quod non vnus, sed vnum cum Patre esse perhibetur?Nullam,nisi futilem,pro suo more.
units.tr: Reply: The opponent is playing with an obvious equivocation. When it is affirmed or denied that Christ is one with God the Father, the name God is taken either in the sense of the divine being [θεότης] or of the hypostasis [ὑπόστασις]. The sense is either that Christ has the same hypostasis as the Father and is one and the same person with him, or that Christ has the same essence as the Father and so is one and the same eternal God with him. If the words are understood in the latter way, Christ is not one with God the Father but one thing (unum), a word which in this statement denotes essence. But if they are understood in the former way, Christ is both one with God the Father and one, so that, in these different senses, it is affirmed and denied without any contradiction that Christ is one with God the Father. Since to demonstrate unity of essence it is not necessary that Christ be called one with God the Father, what consequence, I ask, will Ostorodius draw from the fact that he is said to be not one but one thing with the Father? None, except a futile one, as is his custom.

units.la: Secundò,respondet, etiamsi scriptum esset, quod Christus vnus sit cum Patre, tamen inde non sequi, quòd vnius sit essentiæ, quoniam Apostolus etiam de Christianis affirmauit Galat. 5.vers.28.quod illi vnus sint in Christo Iesu, quod de alia, quàm de essentia vnitate sit intelligendum,ac proinde multò minùs ex eo colligi posse, quòd Deus Pater, & Christus non quidem vnus,sed vnum esse dicantur.
units.tr: Secondly, he responds: Even if it were written that Christ is one with the Father, it would not follow from this that he is of one essence, since the Apostle also affirmed of Christians (Galat. 5.vers.28) that they are one in Christ Jesus; this must be understood of a unity other than unity of essence, and therefore it can much less be gathered from this that God the Father and Christ are said to be not indeed "one" but "one thing."

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Si ex loco Apostoli demonstrari non potuit,quòd Christiani vnum sint ratione essentiæ, de quibus tamen affirmatur, quòd sint vnus in Christo, tum multo minus vnitas essentiæ Patris ac Filÿ ex eo demonstrari potest, quod tantum vnum,non autem vnus esse dicantur.
units.tr: If it could not be shown from the apostle's passage that Christians are one in respect of essence, although it is affirmed of them that they are one in Christ, then much less can the unity of essence of the Father and the Son be shown from this, that they are said to be only "unum" and not "unus".

units.la: At qui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Respondeo, primò, falsam esse consequentiam, quæ manifesto comparatorum elencho laborat. I. quia existimat Ostorrodius maiorem fore argumenti efficaciam, si Deus Pater & Christus, non vnum tantum,sed etiam vnu dicerentur,quod est falsum. De quibus enim Apostolus affirmat.quòd sint vnus in Christo, de iis dicit Christus,quod in se ipso & Patre vnum sint, Iohan.17. verf. 11.& 21. Ergo idem vtriusque vocabuli sensus,momentum, atque pondus, & fallax ab vno ad alterum, tanquam à maiori ad minus consequentia. II. quia non sola ac nuda vocabuli illius significatione nititur argumentum nostrum, quod falsò praesupponit Adversarius,sed scopo,serie,& analogia argumentorum Christi,quibus ille salutis certitudinem ouibus suis promittit, & ex quibus necessario illa vnitas,non tantum concordiae & consensus, sed omnipotentiae & essentiae demonstratur,vt ab initio huius capitis demonstrauimus,quibus accedit ipsa tum Christi luculeta verborum illorum,Ego & pater vnum sumus, explicatio & interpretatio, tum ipsorum Iudeorum confirmatio. Quum enim Iudei lapides humo sustulissent, in Christum conieciuri, eo quod se vnum cum patre professus esset, respondet Christus, Si illos dixit deos ad quos sermo Dei factus est,& non potest solui Scriptura,me quem Pater sanctificauit, & misit in mundum,vos dicitis blasphemare,quia dixi,Filius Dei sum. Christus igitur filium Dei esse,& esse vnum cum Deo patre,vnum idemque esse testatur. Filius autem Dei est,quia ab aeterno genitus a Patre,ac Deus ipse est, vt Iudaei ipsi Christi verba interpretantur Ioh. 10. vv. 33. dicentes,Ob bonum opus te non lapidamus,sed ob blasphemiam, id quia tu homo cum sis,facis te ipsum Deum. III. quum vnù idem- que de diuersis enunciatur subiectis,tum pro subiectorum diuersitate,de diuerso vocabuli sensu est iudicandum. Diuersa autem sunt subiecta illa,de quibus vnitas illa praedicatur. Apostolus enim ad Gal.3.v.28.de spirituali illa cum Christo fidelium coniunctione & vnitate loquitur,quae nullo personarum respectu,omnes quotquot induuerunt in Christum, sine discrimine generis,dignitatis, aut sexus, per fidem,vinculo nempe Spiritus sancti, ita vniuntur cum Christo, vt cum ipso vnus velut Christus constituantur, eius nomen ac personam coram Deo gerentes, eáque causa vt Christus in ipsi eis accepti, quum omnium eius sint participes. At Christus Iohan. capite vigesimo, verf.28. 29,30. non de hac coniunctione spirituali, quae fidelium cum Christo est propria, sed de manu & omnipotentia Dei loquitur,cuius respectu se vnû cum Deo patre profitetur. Aliter ergo hic,& aliter ibi vnitatis illud vocabulum esse interpretandum, argumentorum quæ ibi tractantur diuer sitas,euidenter demonstrat. Sed hæreat ille Aduersarius in externo verborum cortice. Deinde fallum est non posse etiam ex illo Apostoli loco demonstrari Christianos essentia unum esse. Quod enim fideles unum sunt inter se,hoc inde habent, quod prius unū sunt cum Christo, eúmque per baptismum induerunt. Vnum autem cum Christo fiunt per fidem, & Christum per baptismum induunt tantummodo illi, qui ratione humanæ essentiæ,& inter se,& cum Christo unum sunt. Hebr.2.vers.14. Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps est factus eorundem. Vnum igitur sunt etiam ratione essentiæ, licet non numero,sed specie.
units.tr: I answer, first, that the inference is false, and it plainly suffers from a faulty comparison. (1) Ostorrodius supposes that the argument would have more force if the Father and Christ were called not only unum but also unus, which is false. Of those whom the apostle says are one in Christ, Christ says that they are one in himself and the Father (John 17:11 and 21). So the meaning, weight and force of the two words are the same, and the inference from one to the other is fallacious, as if from the greater to the less. (2) Our argument does not rest on the bare meaning of the word, as the opponent wrongly presupposes, but on the scope, sequence and analogy of Christ's arguments, by which he promises his sheep the certainty of salvation, and from which that unity is necessarily shown, not only of concord and agreement but of omnipotence and essence, as we demonstrated at the beginning of this chapter. To this is added the explanation and interpretation of Christ's own clear words, I and the Father are one, and the confirmation given by the Jews themselves. For when the Jews had picked up stones to throw at Christ, because he had professed that he was one with the Father, Christ replies: If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of me, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God? Christ therefore testifies that he is the Son of God, and that he is one with God the Father, one and the same. He is the Son of God because he was begotten from the Father from eternity, and he is God himself, as the Jews themselves interpret Christ's words in John 10:33, saying: We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God. (3) When one and the same thing is said of different subjects, its sense must be judged by the difference of the subjects. The subjects of which this unity is affirmed are different. For the apostle in Galatians 3:28 speaks of that spiritual conjunction and unity of believers with Christ, by which, with no regard to persons, all who have put on Christ, without distinction of race, rank or sex, are united with Christ through faith, by the bond of the Holy Spirit, so that they are constituted with him as one, as it were Christ, bearing his name and person before God, and for that reason are accepted in him as Christ, since they share in all that is his. But Christ in John 20:28, 29 and 30 does not speak of this spiritual conjunction, which is proper to believers with Christ, but of the hand and omnipotence of God, in respect of which he professes that he is one with God the Father. The difference of the arguments treated in each place therefore clearly shows that the word "unity" must be interpreted in one way there and in another here. But let the opponent cling to the outer husk of the words. Further, it is false that it cannot be shown from that passage of the apostle that Christians are one in essence. For that believers are one among themselves they have from this, that they are first one with Christ and have put him on through baptism. Now only those who are one with Christ and with one another in respect of human essence become one with Christ through faith and put on Christ through baptism. Hebrews 2:14: Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise was made partaker of the same. Therefore they are also one in respect of essence, though not in number but in kind.

units.la: Tertiò, quærit Oftorrodius, An non omnes fideles non tantum inter se,sed etiam cum Deo & Filio ipsius unum sint. Ioh.17.v.21. Vnde tamen nemo concludere posset,quod unitate essentiæ sint unum.
units.tr: Thirdly, Ostorrodius asks: Can it not be said that all believers are one not only among themselves but also with God and his Son? John 17:21. Yet from this no one could conclude that they are one in unity of essence.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si omnes fideles non tantum inter se,verum etiam cum Christo unum sunt, nec tamen ulla essentiæ unitas inde sequitur, tum ex eo etiam quod Christus cum Deo Patre unum esse dicitur, falsò colligitur,quod unus sit cum ipso unitate essentiæ.
units.tr: If all believers are one not only among themselves but also with Christ, and yet no unity of essence follows from this, then it is falsely inferred from the fact that Christ is said to be one with God the Father that he is one with him in unity of essence.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum:
units.tr: But the first is true:

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. I. Aduersarium mala fide interpretari argumentum nostrum,quod non tantum nudis illis Christi verbis nititur,quibus se unum cum Deo Patre profitetur, sed affectione ad illud connexum quod Christus verbis illis vult demonstrare,de qua in explicatione nostri argumenti egimus. Si igitur sensus conclusionis in responsione Oftorrodiana sit, quod ex nudo illo prædicato quo Christus unus cum Deo Patre esse dicitur, illa unitas essentiæ demonstrari nequeat,totum Syllogismum consedimus abfq; argumenti nostri præiudicio vllo, quod hac ratione ab Aduersario nec impugnatur, nec euertitur. II. Consequentiam esse falsam,quæ tū demum vera esset, si fideles eadem ratione qua Christus unum cum Deo Patre esse dicerentur,quod est falsum. Non enim vult Christus simplicirer, vt Apostoli sint unum,sicut Pater & filius,sed vt illam vnitatem naturæ & essentiæ, vnitate charitatis & concordiæ Christianæ imitentur, cum non de æqualitate, sed deb bat sed de similitudine ibi loquatur. III. Assumptionem quoque falsam esse, iam paulo ante ostendimus. Nihil ergo praeter aniles, & futiles argutias, ad argumentum nostrum labefactandum, Ostorrodius hactenus attulit.
units.tr: Reply. (1) The opponent interprets our argument in bad faith. It rests not only on Christ's bare words by which he professes that he is one with God the Father, but on the force connected with them, which Christ wants to demonstrate by those words; we treated this in the explanation of our argument. So if the sense of the conclusion in Ostorrodius' reply is that from the bare predicate by which Christ is said to be one with God the Father that unity of essence cannot be demonstrated, we have overturned the whole syllogism without any prejudice to our argument, which by this line of reasoning is neither attacked nor overturned by the opponent. (2) The inference is false; it would be true only if believers were said to be one with God the Father in the same way as Christ, which is false. For Christ does not mean simply that the apostles should be one as the Father and the Son are, but that they should imitate that unity of nature and essence by the unity of Christian love and concord, since there he speaks not of equality but of likeness. (3) The assumption is also false, as we have already shown a little earlier. Ostorrodius has therefore so far brought forward nothing but childish and trifling quibbles to weaken our argument.

units.la: Ad posteriora vero Scripturae loca respondet Ostorrodius: Primo, si inde concluderetur unitas essentiae inter Patrem, & filium, tum etiam sequi personam Patris essentialiter esse in persona Filii, & personam Filii in persona Patris. Hoc autem cum fit impossibile, nec ab ipsis Adversariis concedatur, quoniam personas Trinitatis nulla ratione inter se permixtas, aut confusas, sed distinctas esse affirmant, sed, ad vitandam praesertim Deorum pluralitatem, immeationem quandam, & unius personae in alteram, quasi in circulum influentiam mutuam confinxerunt, quam illi Graece περιχώρησιν, Latine vero circumincessionem appellarunt, manifeste inde sequitur verborum Christi alium esse sensum, quam ab illis statuitur.
units.tr: As to the later passages of Scripture, Ostorrodius replies: First, if it were concluded from them that there is unity of essence between the Father and the Son, then it would also follow that the person of the Father is essentially in the person of the Son, and the person of the Son in the person of the Father.
