But since this is impossible, and is not conceded even by our opponents, who affirm that the persons of the Trinity are in no way mixed or confused with one another but distinct, yet, chiefly to avoid a plurality of gods, have devised a certain interpenetration, a mutual influence of one person into another, as if in a circle, which they called in Greek perichōrēsis and in Latin circumincession, it is clearly evident from this that the sense of Christ's words is other than they take it to be.

units.la: Resp. Περιχώρησιν illam, seu ἐμπεριχώρησιν ἀδιαίρετον, id est arctissimam illam unionem personarum, quapropter unam & eandem numero essentiam, quam totam singulae personae possident, singulae personae in singulis esse, adeoque singulae in singulis manere, possidere, & glorificare singulas dicuntur, nō cōfinxerunt nostri, ut cavillatur Ostorrodius: sed contra Tritheitas aliosque veritatis hostes sancte tradiderunt. Quum enim una numero sit essentia, personae vero, seu hypostases tres incommunicabili proprietate inter se distinctae, περιχώρησις illa per se consequitur. Unde negat ipse Ostorrodius a nobis doceri, quod tamen multis in locis Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctores perspicue docuerunt, unam nempe personam revera in alia esse, eamque totam semper, & insepara-biliter permeet, & circumplectatur. Falsa igitur cum sit assumptio, conclusio per se ruit.
units.tr: Reply. Our writers did not invent that perichōrēsis [περιχώρησις], or indivisible emperichōrēsis [ἐμπεριχώρησιν ἀδιαίρετον], that is, that most intimate union of the persons, on account of which the one and the same essence in number, which each person possesses wholly, is said to be in each person, so that each person is in each, and so each dwells in, possesses and glorifies each. They handed it down faithfully, as a safeguard against the Tritheists and other enemies of the truth, not as Ostorrodius slanders. For since the essence is one in number, while the persons, or hypostases, are three, distinguished among themselves by an incommunicable property, that perichōrēsis follows of itself. Hence Ostorrodius denies that we teach what our teachers have nevertheless clearly taught in many places in our churches: that one person is truly in another, and always wholly and inseparably penetrates and embraces it. The assumption is therefore false, and the conclusion falls by itself.

units.la: Secundo, respondet Ostorrodius, Verborum illorum Christi, quibus affirmat, quod ipse in Patre sit, & Pater in ipso, sensum esse hunc, quod ille cum Patre sit, & Pater cum illo, quoniam particulae illius in multae sint significationes, & inter cetera etiam idem valeat quod cum, ut pluribus exemplis demonstrari posset. Particula autem in hoc loco ut placuisse Christo, ut summum illum voluntatis consensum, inter ipsum & Patrem ostenderet. II. Quia etiam legatur de veris Christi discipulis, quod illi sint in Christo, & Christus in ipsis, quoniam ipse Christus Ioh. 19. v. 20. dicat, In illo die vos cognoscetis me esse in Patre meo, & vos in me,& me in vobis. Quemadmodum igitur ille nihil aliud significare velit Christus, quam si diceret, nos arctissi me coiungemur, vosque meus populus, & mea membra eritis, ego autem caput & Dominus vester, curam vestri habiturus, nunquam vos deseram: ita quoque Deum in Christo, & Christum in Deo fuisse, quoniam Christus Dei erat 1.Cor. 3.v.23. Deum autem Christi Deum, ac caput, Eph.1.v.17. 1.Cor.11.v.3. ac pro inde ipsum nunquam dereliquerit, sed semper cum ipso fuerit, & opera a Christo edita, per ipsum Christum patrauerit. Tertio, aliquoties in Scriptura affirmari, quod vere fideles Christi, in Deo, & Deus in ipsis maneat.
units.tr: Secondly, Ostorrodius replies: The sense of those words of Christ, by which he affirms that he is in the Father and the Father in him, is this: that he is with the Father and the Father with him, since that particle has many meanings, and among others also the same as "with", as could be shown by many examples. The particle "in" in this place, however, shows that it pleased Christ to show the highest consent of will between himself and the Father. (2) Because it is also said of Christ's true disciples that they are in Christ and Christ in them, since Christ himself says, John 14:20, In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. Just as Christ wants to mean nothing other by this than if he had said: we shall be most closely joined, and you will be my people and my members, while I shall be your head and Lord, will take care of you, and will never forsake you; so also God was in Christ and Christ in God, since Christ was God's (1 Cor. 3:23), and God was the God and head of Christ (Eph. 1:17; 1 Cor. 11:3), and so he never left him, but was always with him, and accomplished through Christ the works done by Christ. (3) Thirdly, it is affirmed several times in Scripture that true believers in Christ remain in God, and God in them.

units.la: Resp. Falsam esse illam Oftorrodii interpretationem, ex collatione illius dicti Christi, cum interrogatione Philippi, luculenter apparet. Quomodo enim quaeso satisfaceret Christus Philippo petenti, ut offenderet sibi Patrem, si respondisset, Pater mecum est, & Deus meus est, qui me nunquam dereliquit, & opera quae ego facio per me edit? Non igitur genuina haec verborum Christi explicatio est, sed violenta detorsio, & audax depravatio. Ad primam probationem, respondeo, nullam esse consequentiam hanc, particula in aliquando idem significat, quod cum: ergo etiam hic idem denotat: quamuis ne antecedens quidem ab ipso probetur. Ad secundam quod attinet, negamus unam & eandem esse rationem fidelium cum Christo, quae sit Christi cum Deo: unde similitudinem inter duas illasunionis species, perperam ad aequalitate earum de pertrahit Oftorrodius. Filius enim natura est in Patre, & Pater in ipso, in nobis vero participatione, gratia, & communione Spiritus. 1.Ioh.4.v.13. Ex hoc cognoscimus quod in eo manemus, & ipse in nobis, quoniam de Spiritu suo dedit nobis. Aequalitatem illam testimonia ex Apostolo allegata non probant, quia in illis agitur de Christo, non quatenus Deus est absolute, sed quatenus secundum dispensationem voluntariam consideratur, nosq; sibi adiungit ad consummationem salutis nostrae. Secundum hanc igitur oeconomiam, Christus dicitur esse Dei Patris, deinde etiam secundum naturam assumptam, sicut totius naturae humanae conditio Deo est subiecta. Tertio, secundum corpus Ecclesiae, quae sibi tanquam capiti adunauit, suo sanguine redemptam. Hanc genuinam esse locorum illorum Pauli interpretationem, ex instituto ibi sermone euidenter liquet. Ab oeconomia autem illa voluntaria dispensatione, ad naturam Christi diuinam, de quae hioid hic agimus, nullam dari consequentiam saepius iam ostendimus. Ad tertiam respondemus, idem quod ad secundam, nempe à conditione hominum etiam fidelium, ad conditionem, & vnitatem diuinam, nullam confici consequentiam iustam, vt iam ostendimus. Manet igitur indissolubilis illa essentiae vnitas Patris atque filii, ad cuius vinculum soluendum aut secandum, frustra sophismatum suorum cultellum acuit Ostorrodius.
units.tr: Reply. That Ostorrodius's interpretation is false clearly appears from comparing that saying of Christ with Philip's question. For how, I ask, would Christ have satisfied Philip, who asked that he show us the Father, if he had answered: The Father is with me, and he is my God, who never forsook me, and the works that I do, he does through me? This, therefore, is not the genuine explanation of Christ's words, but a violent twisting and a bold distortion of them. As to the first proof, I answer that this inference is not valid, since the particle "in" sometimes means the same as "with": therefore it means the same here too, although not even the antecedent is proved by him. As to the second, we deny that the fellowship of believers with Christ is one and the same kind as the fellowship of Christ with God; hence Ostorrodius wrongly draws a likeness between the two kinds of union into an equality of them. For the Son is by nature in the Father, and the Father in him; but in us it is by participation, grace, and the communion of the Spirit (1 John 4:13): By this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. The testimonies cited from the Apostle do not prove that equality, because in those passages the subject is Christ not as he is God absolutely, but as he is considered in his voluntary dispensation, and as he joins us to himself for the completion of our salvation. According to this economy, therefore, Christ is said to be of God the Father, and then also according to the assumed nature, just as the condition of the whole human nature is subject to God. Third, according to the body of the Church, which he has joined to himself as its head, redeemed by his blood. That this is the genuine interpretation of those passages of Paul is plain enough from the purpose of the discourse there. But from that voluntary economy to the divine nature of Christ, which is what we are discussing here, no consequence follows, as we have often already shown. As to the third, we answer the same as to the second: namely, that from the condition of men, even believers, no just consequence can be drawn to the divine condition and unity, as we have already shown. That indissoluble unity of essence of the Father and the Son therefore remains; to loosen or cut its bond, Ostorrodius sharpens the little knife of his sophisms in vain.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: In quo argumentum octauum pro aeterna Filii Deitate proponitur, atque defenditur.
units.tr: In which the eighth argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is set forth and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum octauum, quo demonstramus Christum Iesum, verum illum vnum & aeternum cum Patre Deum Israelis esse, non autem φλὸν tantum ἀἰδιατον, inde desumitur, quod etiam in Christum credere, hoc est, certam & indubitatam fiduciam collocare debemus, vt postea ostendemus.
units.tr: ARGUMENT Our eighth argument, by which we demonstrate that Christ Jesus is the true and one eternal God of Israel together with the Father, and not merely a bare eternal [ψιλὸν ἀΐδιον], is drawn from this: that we must also believe in Christ, that is, place a certain and undoubted trust in him, as we will show afterwards.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum tale est.
units.tr: Our argument runs as follows.

units.la: In quem tenemur credere, & omnem cordis fiduciam collocare, ille est verus & aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: He in whom we are bound to believe, and in whom we must place all the trust of our heart, is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui in Christum tenemur credere, & omne cordis fiducia collocare. Ergo Christus est verus & aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: But we are bound to believe in Christ, and to place all the trust of our heart in him. Therefore Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Maior propositio inde demonstratur: 1. ex Eph. 4. v. 5. 6. Vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus, & Pater omnium, qui est super omnia, & per omnia, & in omnibus vobis. Vbi Paulus haec tria sic connectit, vt ab vno ad alterum ratiocinetur, vt quia vna est fides, ex eo vnum esse Deum demonstret: quia vnus est baptismus, inde quoque vnam esse fidem ostendat. Vnde conficitur, quod si varia sint fidei genera, plures etiam esse Deos oporteat, quod est impium. Varia autem fidei genera constituentur, si in aliu aliquem, quam in vnum Deum credere teneamur. 2. Qui solus iustificat impium, in eum etiam solum est credendum: Atqui Deus solus iustificat impium, Ro. 4. v. 5. & 8. v. 33. Es. 43. v. 25. Ergo in solum Deum est credendum. 3. Qui solus est καρδιογνώστης, & Dominus conscientiæ nostræ, sic vt eam obligare possit ad fidem & obedien-tiam ex fide,in illum etiam solù est credendū. Atqui solus Deus est κα̱ςιπωόμ̱ς 1. Reg.8. vers. 39. Dominus & Iudex conscientiæ,qui solus eam potest obligare ad fidem & obedientiam ex fide: Ergo in solū Deū est credendum. 4. Cuius verbū solum est obiectum fidei, in eum solum etiam est credendum. Atqui solum Dei verbum est obiectum fidei,quia fides est ex auditu, auditus autē per verbum Dei. Rom.10 v.17.Ergo etiam in solum Deum omnis fiducia cordis est collocanda.5. Qui solus potest foedus nobiscum pagere de rebus spiritualib. immortalitate,vita æterna,& cæteris donis,eadémq; nobis præstare,in eū etiā solum est credendū:quia hæc fides est conditio illa, sub qua ille in fœdere nobis vitā æter-nam promittit,& ad quam in eodem nos obligamur.Atqui solus Deus is est,Gen 8.Ier.31.v. 32. Deut.5. v.2.Ergo,&c.6. Qui solus est inuocandus,& cui soli est seruiendum religioso cultu , in illum etiam solum est credendum. Atqui solus Deus Israelis est inuocandus,& eí soli religioso cultu est seruiendum. Matth.4.v.10. Ergo, &c. 7.Quia solus Deus succurrit nobis in afflictionibus,& ab ipso solo est salus expectanda Ps.62.v.26.& Psal.37.v.4.5.6 39. 40.Ergo in illo solo fiducia est collocanda.8. Quia vere fideles,& sancti fiduciam suam in solo Deo posuerunt,vt Dauid Ps.13.v.6. & 15.v.2.57.v.2.9. Quia maledictus vir ille qui fiduciam habet in homine, & statuit carnem brachium suum. Ier.17. v.5. Alia infinita argu-menta omittimus, quibus veritas huius propositionis contra Samosatenianos demonstrari potest.
units.tr: The major premise is proved in the following ways. (1) From Eph. 4:5–6: One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all. Here Paul connects these three things so that he reasons from one to the next: since there is one faith, he shows that there is one God; since there is one baptism, he shows that there is also one faith. From this it follows that if there were different kinds of faith, there would also have to be several gods, which is impious. Different kinds of faith would arise if we were bound to believe in some other being than the one God. (2) He who alone justifies the ungodly is the only one in whom we are to believe. But God alone justifies the ungodly: Rom. 4:5; 8:33; Isa. 43:25. Therefore we are to believe in God alone. (3) He who alone is the searcher of hearts and the Lord of our conscience, so that he can bind it to faith and to obedience from faith, is the only one in whom we are to believe. But God alone is the one who searches the heart, the Lord and Judge of conscience, who alone can bind it to faith and to obedience from faith: 1 Kings 8:39. Therefore we are to believe in God alone. (4) He whose word alone is the object of faith is the only one in whom we are also to believe. But the word of God alone is the object of faith, since faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God: Rom. 10:17. Therefore all the trust of the heart is also to be placed in God alone. (5) He who alone can make a covenant with us concerning spiritual things, immortality, eternal life and the other gifts, and can grant them to us, is the only one in whom we are also to believe, because this faith is the condition under which he promises us eternal life in the covenant, and to which we are bound in the same covenant. But God alone is such a one: Gen. 8; Jer. 31:32; Deut. 5:2. Therefore, etc. (6) He who alone is to be invoked, and to whom alone religious worship is to be rendered, is the only one in whom we are also to believe. But the God of Israel alone is to be invoked, and to him alone religious worship is to be rendered: Matt. 4:10. Therefore, etc. (7) Because God alone helps us in afflictions, and salvation is to be expected from him alone: Ps. 62:26; Ps. 37:4–6, 39, 40. Therefore trust is to be placed in him alone. (8) Because true believers and saints have placed their trust in God alone, as David did: Ps. 13:6; 15:2; 57:2, 9. Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm: Jer. 17:5. We omit the countless other arguments by which the truth of this proposition can be demonstrated against the Samosatenians.

units.la: Assumptionem demonstrant plurima Scripturæ testimonia, Ioh. 3.ver.16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum,vt Filium suum vnigenitum dederit,vt quisquis credit in eum,non pereat, sed habeat vitā æternā, v.18. Qui credit in eum,non condemnatur, qui vero non credit, iam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen vnigeniti Filii Dei, vers.36. Qui credit in Filium habet vitam æternam: qui vero non credit Filio, non videbit vitam. Iohan. c.6.vers.29.Hoc illud est opus Dei, vt credatis in eum, quem misit ille. vers.40. Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me,vt omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æter-nam 1. Iohan. c.5.vers.10.Qui credit in Filium Dei , habet testimo-nium in se ipso : qui non credit Deo , mendacem eum facit. & vers. 13: Hæc scripsi vobis qui creditis in nomen Filii Dei,vt sciatis vos vi-tam æternam habere, & vt credatis in nomen Filii Dei. Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius apparet, Christum Saluatorem nostrum, non ψλοῦ tantum αὐθρώπου, sed æternum ac verum Deum esse.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved by very many testimonies of Scripture. John 3:16: God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. v. 18: He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. v. 36: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe the Son shall not see life. John 6:29: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. v. 40: This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. 1 John 5:10: He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; he who does not believe God makes him a liar. And v. 13: I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God. From all these passages it appears more clearly than the noonday light that Christ our Saviour is not merely a [ψιλὸς] man, but the eternal and true God.

units.la: Osiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo quinto, hanc quæstionem non sine audaci temeritate proponit, An nimirum ex fide in Christo fiͤta illa, in ipso diuina natura, demonstrari possit. Hanc autem quæstionem negat, & cum negationis rationem adferre possit nullam, ad vnicum ex pluribus argumentis nostris eludendum se confert pro more & ingenio suo. Inquit igitur, Sic argumentantur Aduersarij, Maledictus vir ille, qui siduciam habet in homine, sicut scriptum est, Ierem. cap. 17. vers. 5. Quum igitur manifestum sit, quod nos in Christum tencamur credere, sequitur ipsum non humana tantùm, sed etiam diuina natura constare, propter quem in ipsum credere possimus. Atque ad hoc argumentum respondet, Primò, nos denuo Scripturam Scripturæ opponere, atque veritatem ipsam, quantum in nobis est, opprimere, quamuis ex ignorantia hoc à nobis fieri existimet.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in the fifteenth chapter of his Institutions, puts this question, not without bold rashness: whether, namely, the divine nature in him can be demonstrated from that faith in Christ. He denies this question, and since he can offer no reason for the denial, he betakes himself, as is his habit and disposition, to evading one of our many arguments. He says therefore: Thus our opponents argue: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man," as it is written (Jer. 17:5). Since it is clear, then, that we are bound to believe in Christ, it follows that he consists not only of a human nature but also of a divine nature, on account of which we can believe in him. And to this argument he replies: First, that we again oppose Scripture to Scripture, and suppress the truth itself as far as we can, although he thinks this is done by us out of ignorance.

units.la: Resp. Hic denuo malitiosè & fraudulenter agit Aduersarius, & quo magis inuisam atq; contemptam reddat apud populū suum, doctrinam Ecclesiæ nostræ, vnicum illum Scripturæ locum sic in aciem producit, quasi vel illo solo & vnico niteretur veritas sententiæ nostræ, vel statim ipsa doctrina, quam tamen ex pluribus aliis hauriri, initio huius capitis ostendimus, euerteretur, si locus illæ Ieremiæ aliter atque aliter explicari possit. Rem ipsam quod attinet, non soluit argumentum nostrum, sed conuitiatur Ostorrodius, dum scripturam scripturæ à nobis opponi audacter nimis affirmat, qua de re in capite antecedente egimus. Egregius verò ille iudex ignorantiæ nostræ est, qui bonarum disciplinarum imperitus librum ex meris fallaciis confutum, & vel sexcentis elenchis scatentem, in apricum protrudere non erubescit. Secundò, dicit, Si hoc argumentum ipsorum sit firmum, tum non tantùm sequetur id quod illi concludunt, verum etiam omnes illos qui vnquam in hominem crediderunt, maledictos esse, imò etiam Deus ipse maledictionis huius autor constituetur, quippe qui Israelitis præceperit, vt perpetuò in Mosem crederent, vt ex veritate textus Hebraici videre est, Exod. 19. vers. 9. & 19.31. Insuper etiam regem Josaphatum, adhortatum esse populum Israeliticum, vt in Deum, & Prophetas eius crederet, 2.Par. 20. vers. 20. Cauendum autem, ait, ab illis versionibus, quæ in citatis locis habent, Mosi, & Prophetis, non autem in Mosem & Prophetas, quemadmodum textus Hebraicus habet, qui plane eodem modo de Mose, ac Prophetis, quo de ipso Deo loquitur.
units.tr: Answer. Here again the adversary acts maliciously and deceitfully. In order to make our church's doctrine more hated and despised among his own people, he brings forward that single passage of Scripture as if the truth of our view rested on it alone, or as if the doctrine itself would be overthrown if that passage of Jeremiah could be explained in one way or another, although, as we showed at the beginning of this chapter, the doctrine is drawn from many other passages. As for the matter itself, Ostorrodius does not solve our argument, but reviles; when he boldly asserts that we oppose Scripture to Scripture, we dealt with that charge in the preceding chapter. Truly, he is a remarkable judge of our ignorance, who, unskilled in the good disciplines, is not ashamed to bring forward a book refuted by mere fallacies and teeming with countless refutations. Second, he says: "If this argument of theirs were sound, then not only would what they conclude follow, but also all those who have ever believed in a man would be cursed; indeed God himself would be made the author of this curse, since he commanded the Israelites to believe in Moses forever, as is seen from the truth of the Hebrew text" (Exod. 19:9, 19; 31). Moreover, he also says that King Jehoshaphat exhorted the people of Israel to believe in God and in his prophets (2 Chron. 20:20). We must beware, he says, of those versions which in the cited passages have "to Moses and the prophets," and not "in Moses and the prophets," as the Hebrew text has, which speaks of Moses and the prophets in exactly the same way as of God himself.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs thus.

units.la: Si maledictus est, quicunque credit in hominem, sequitur maledictos esse, qui unquam in hominem crediderunt.
units.tr: If whoever believes in a man is cursed, it follows that all who have ever believed in a man are cursed.

units.la: Atqui consequens est absurdum, ut liquet tum ex locis citatis, tum ex eo, quod Deus hac ratione maledictionis illius statueretur autor.
units.tr: But the consequence is absurd, as is clear both from the passages cited and from the fact that God would thereby be made the author of that curse.

units.la: Ergo & prius.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Resp. Primo, In quem credimus, in eum fiduciam animi nostri collocamus, quod nobis non tantum de rebus corporalibus prospecturus, sed etiam vitae ac salutis aeternae participes sit redditurus: quod quia Scriptura soli Deo tribuit, inde infallibiliter concluditur, non nisi in unum verum Deum credendum esse. Quū itaque Ostorrodius populū Hæraliticū à promissione rerum spiritualiū, ac vitæ æternæ excludat, sed carnalem opulentiam, ac felicitatē temporalem ipsis metā præfigat, ut liquet ex Institutionū ipsius c.15. pag. 149. Neque etiam fidem Israelitis tribuere potest iustificantem, quæ maximè vitæ æternæ lætitiā in Christo, & per Christū cōsequēdā respicit, & quam nos in argumento nostro credendi verbo cōplectimur. Atque hoc licet ad nugas eius refellendas sufficeret abundè, loca tamen Scripturæ quæ ab ipso citantur, etiam examinabimus. Secundo itaque negamus assumptionem, quæ illis Scripturæ locis minimè probatur. Falsum enim est, credere in aliquem, vel in aliquid apud Hebræos semper idem significare, quod fiduciam in aliquid, vel in aliquem collocare, ut multis Scripturæ testimoniis illud demonstrari potest, ex quibus nos pauca quædam colligemus. Iob.24. v.22. inquit Iob, Detraxit fortes in fortitudine sua, & cum steterit, non credet vitæ suæ, ולא־יאמין בחיים Velo Iaamin bachaiin, id est, metuet vitæ suæ. Deut.28. v.66. Et erit vita tua tibi suspensa e regione, ac pauebis nocte, & die, neque credes vitæ tuæ, ולא תאמין בחייך Velo taamin bechaiacha, id est, exclusus à Dei tutela, & ad quasli-bet noxas te expositum videns, perpetuo metu ac pauore corripieris. 1.Sam. 27.12. Et credidit Achis Dauidi, dicens abominando abominatus est populum suum Israelem. ויאמן אכיש בדוד Vaiamen Achisch be Dauid, i.fidem habuit Dauidi narranti stragem à se factā. Vide etiam Prou.26. v.25. Ierem.12. v.6. Mich.7. v.5. Sic Dauid Psal.119. v.66. Bonitatem sensus, & scientiam tuam doce me, quia præceptis tui credidi. credidi. כי במצותיך האמנתי Ci bemitsvotačha haamanti. At Dauid fidu-ciam suam non in lege,ac mandatis Dei,quasi perfecta obedien-tia,operum integritate,vitæque puritate,iudicio Dei,respondere posset,sed in misericordia & benignitate diuina,collocauit.Pf.25. Delicta iuuentutis mea,& ignorantiæ ne memineris,secundum miseri-cordiam tuam memento mei tu: & v.11. Propter nomen tuum,Iehouah,condonabis iniquitatem meam,nam magna est. Vide Pf.32.v.5.& 33.v.5.& 43.2.& 130.3. Unde etiam beatitudinem hominis, non in obedientiam legalem,sed imputationem iustitiæ, h.e. gratuitam peccatorum remissionem transcribit,Pfal.32.v.1. Rom.4.7. Qui igitur Hebraeæ linguæ cognitione vel leuiter tinctus est, is nouit credere in aliquem, vel in aliquid apud Hebraeos interdum nihil aliud significare,quàm credere alicui, vt miranda sit,non tantùm stupida insciitia Ostorrodii,sed etiam audax temeritas,& procacitas, qua audet falsas appellare versiones illas, in quibus Phrasis illa יאמינו ביהוה וברשה Iaamin ba Iehouah uBemosčhah, Crediderunt Deo & Mosi, reddunturt. Fraudis enim & falsitatis ab ipso accusatur ipse Apostolus Paulus, qui illud Gen.15.v.6: Credidit Abraham Deo,& imputatum est ei ad iustitiam. והאמין בה'. Vehaamin balehouah, hoc modo est interpretatus: ἐπίστευσεν Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. Credidit Abraham Deo,& imputatum est ei pro iustitia: Rom.4.v.3: 17.Gal.3.6.Iac.2.23. & Christus ipse, Iudæos non in Mosem, sed Mosi credidisse affirmat Ioh.5.v.46. Sic in Nouo Testamento phrases illæ, credere in Deum, credere Deo, credere in Christum, credere Christo, credere in nomen Christi, credere nomini Christi & credere quod Iesus sit Christus, ac Filius Dei, eodem sensu vsurpatur, Ioh.1.2:50. & 2.v.10.23.& 3.v.15.16.18.36.& 4.v.15.& 5.v.24. 46.& 5.69.& 8.v.45. 46.& 10.v.38 & 11 v.27. & 12.v.44. & 14.11 Act.8.v.37. Ro.4.v.3. Gal.3.v. 6.Iac.2.v.23.1.Ioh.3.v.23.1.Ioh.5: v.1.5.10.13.& alibi passim.
units.tr: Answer. First, we place the trust of our mind in the one in whom we believe, since we expect him to care not only for bodily needs but also to make us sharers in life and eternal salvation. Because Scripture ascribes this to God alone, it infallibly follows that one must believe only in the one true God. Since, therefore, Ostorrodius excludes the Hebrew people from the promise of spiritual things and eternal life, and sets before them only carnal wealth and temporal prosperity, as is clear from his Institutes, ch. 15, p. 149, he cannot attribute to the Israelites a justifying faith, which looks above all to the joy of eternal life in Christ and through Christ, and which we embrace in our argument on believing in the Word. Although this alone would be quite enough to refute his trifles, we shall nevertheless examine the passages of Scripture he cites. Secondly, then, we deny the assumption, which is not at all proved by those passages. For it is false that to believe in someone, or in something, always means among the Hebrews the same as placing one's trust in something or someone. This can be shown by many testimonies of Scripture, from which we shall gather a few. Job 24:22: Job says, He drags off the strong by his strength, and when he has risen he will not believe in his life, [ולא־יאמין בחיים], that is, he will fear for his life. Deut. 28:66: And your life shall hang in doubt before you, and you shall dread night and day, and you will not believe your life, [ולא תאמין בחייך], that is, cut off from God's protection and seeing yourself exposed to every harm, you will be seized with constant fear and terror. 1 Sam. 27:12: And Achish believed David, saying, He has made himself utterly abhorred by his people Israel, [ויאמן אכיש בדוד], that is, he gave credence to David's account of the slaughter he had made. See also Prov. 26:25, Jer. 12:6, Mic. 7:5. So David, Ps. 119:66: Teach me goodness of judgment and knowledge, for I have believed in your commandments, [כי במצותיך האמנתי]. But David placed his trust not in the law and commandments of God, as though by perfect obedience, integrity of works and purity of life he could answer the judgment of God, but in the divine mercy and kindness. Ps. 25:7: Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance; according to your mercy remember me, you; and v. 11: For your name's sake, O Jehovah, pardon my iniquity, for it is great. See Ps. 32:5, 33:5, 43:2, 130:3. Whence David also pronounces blessed the man not for legal obedience but for the imputation of righteousness, that is, the free forgiveness of sins: Ps. 32:1; Rom. 4:7. Therefore whoever has even slightly tasted the knowledge of the Hebrew language knows that to believe in someone, or in something, among the Hebrews sometimes signifies nothing other than to believe someone. So one must marvel not only at Ostorrodius's stupid ignorance but also at his bold rashness and insolence, in that he dares to call false those versions in which the phrase [ויאמינו ביהוה ובמשה] is rendered they believed in the LORD and in Moses. For the Apostle Paul himself is accused by him of fraud and falsehood, since he rendered Gen. 15:6, Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness [והאמין בה׳], in this way: [ἐπίστευσεν Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην], Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness: Rom. 4:3; Gal. 3:6; Jas 2:23. Christ himself affirms that the Jews believed not in Moses but Moses: John 5:46. So in the New Testament the phrases to believe in God, to believe God, to believe in Christ, to believe Christ, to believe in the name of Christ, to believe the name of Christ, and to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God are used in the same sense: John 1:12; 2:50 (?); 2:10, 23; 3:15, 16, 18, 36; 4:15; 5:24, 46; 5:69; 8:45, 46; 10:38; 11:27; 12:44; 14:11; Acts 8:37; Rom. 4:3; Gal. 3:6; Jas 2:23; 1 John 3:23; 1 John 5:1, 5, 10, 13, and elsewhere throughout.

units.la: Ergo,Credere in Deum,& Credere Deo:Credere in Christum,& credere Christo,recipsa vnum sunt,licet phrasis posterior sit generalior,& sæpe etiā fidem tātūm historicam denotet, nō autem πιστεύειν illam iustificantis fidei,quam phrasis prior exprimit, quæ proinde frequentius in Nouo Testamento habetur,licet illa apud nullum autorem classicum tam Græcum, quàm Latinum,reperiatur,sed Christo, Apostolis, & Theologis Christianis sit peculiaris. Ergo non ex vi phraseos Hebraicæ, sed ex diuersitate obiectorum in quæ fides tendit,de ipsa fide est iudicandū. Quātū igitur ad locū primū ab Ostorrodio citatum attinet, qui ita habetur Exod.14. ver.31. Vidit Israel manum magnam, quam fecit Iehouah in Aegyptios, timuitque populus Iehouam, crediderunt autem Iehouæ, & Mosi seruo eius. ויאמינו ביהוה ובנשה עבדו Vaiaamin⁎ baiehouah ⁎ʾemoscħaħ għaßlo: Respondeo non collocasse eos vllam in Mose fiduciam, sed credidisse verbo & promissionibus Dei, cuius verbi ipse Moses erat preco & administer. Testatur hoc ipse Dauid Psal 106 v.12. vbi eandem historiam recenset, inquiens, Tum crediderunt verbis eius, cantauerunt laudes eius: ויאמינו כדכרו Vaiamin⁎ bidßirav. Per fidem autem illam, timorem ac reuerentiam significari in scripturis, est notissimum, sic vt verba illa, Crediderunt Deo & Mosi, nihil aliud quàm priorum sint exegesis. Ad locum secundum qui habetur Exod.19.v.9. in hunc modum, Dixit Iehouah ad Mosem, Ecce ego venio ad te, in densitate nubis, vt audiat populus tuus, dum loquar tecum, & etiam tibi credant in perpetuum ּ וגם־בך יאמינו לעור Vegham becha iaamin⁎ le-gholam. respondeo, Deum, qui antea loquutus erat cum Mose, remoto populo, iam illustri gloriæ suæ symbolo, palam se facturum promittere, quod Moses à Deo missus sit, quódque lex non à Mose prodierit, sed quod fideliter ille tradat per manus id quod à Deo acceperit, ac proinde effecturum, vt populus Israeliticus ipsi, tanquam legato suo fidem habeat, & debitam obedientiam ac reuerentiam præstet, Iohan. 9. vers.29. Nos scimus, quod Mosi loquutus est Deus: id est, certissimè nouimus ipsum à Deo missum esse, variis & multiplicibus signis id approbantibus. Atque hic idem sensus est loci tertii, qui 2. Paral.20. vers.20. extat: Dixit Iehosaphat, audite me, Iehuda, & habitatores Ierusalem, credite Iehouæ Deo vestro: האמינו ביהוה haaminu baiehouah, Credite Prophetis eius, האמינו בנביאיו haaminu binßiav. Fidem enim haberi vult Prophetis, tanquam legatis Dei, & non ex se, sed Dei ipsius ore loquentibus, sicuti ad discipulos inquit Christus Luc.10. vers.16. non autem fiduciam vllam in ipsos collocari. Quicquid enim autoritatis ac dignitatis Spiritus Dei imi scriptura, siue Sacerdotibus, siue Prophetis, siue Apostolis aut eorum successoribus defert, id totum proprie, non hominibus ipsis, sed verbo Dei datur, cuius ministerium illis est concessum. Secus credat Ostorrodius in homines, nos in te solo, Domine Deus spem & fiduciam nostram collocamus, neque confundemur in sæternum.
units.tr: Therefore, to believe in God and to believe God, to believe in Christ and to believe Christ, are in fact one and the same, although the latter phrase is more general and often denotes merely historical faith; it does not, however, denote that πιστεύειν of justifying faith which the former phrase expresses, and which is therefore more frequently found in the New Testament, though it is not found in any classical author, Greek or Latin, but is peculiar to Christ, the Apostles and the Christian theologians. Therefore the nature of the faith is to be judged not from the force of the Hebrew phrase but from the diversity of the objects toward which faith is directed. As regards the first passage cited by Ostorrodius, which is found at Exod. 14:31: Israel saw the great hand which Jehovah wrought against the Egyptians, and the people feared Jehovah, and they believed Jehovah and his servant Moses [ויאמינו ביהוה ובמשה עבדו], I answer that they placed no trust in Moses, but believed the word and promises of God, of which word Moses himself was the herald and minister. David himself bears witness to this, Ps. 106:12, where he recounts the same history, saying: Then they believed his words, they sang his praises [ויאמינו לדבריו]. That this faith signifies fear and reverence in the Scriptures is most well known, so that those words, they believed God and Moses, are nothing other than an explanation of the former. As for the second passage, which is found at Exod. 19:9, in this manner: Jehovah said to Moses, Behold, I come to you in the thickness of a cloud, that your people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever [וגם בך יאמינו לעולם], I answer that God, who had previously spoken with Moses apart from the people, now promises, with the illustrious symbol of his glory, to make it plain that Moses had been sent by God, and that the law did not come from Moses but that he faithfully passed on through his hands what he had received from God; and therefore that he would bring it about that the Israelite people would have faith in him as God's ambassador, and would render him due obedience and reverence: John 9:29, We know that God spoke to Moses; that is, we know most certainly that he was sent by God, as this was approved by various and manifold signs. And this same sense is the meaning of the third passage, which occurs at 2 Chron. 20:20: Jehoshaphat said, Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, believe Jehovah your God [האמינו ביהוה], believe his prophets [האמינו בנביאיו]. For he wants faith to be placed in the prophets as God's ambassadors, who speak not from themselves but from the very mouth of God, just as Christ says to his disciples, Luke 10:16; but he does not want any trust to be placed in them. For whatever authority and dignity the Spirit of God in Scripture confers on priests, prophets, apostles or their successors, all of it is properly given not to the men themselves but to the Word of God, whose ministry has been committed to them. Let Ostorrodius believe in men otherwise; we place our hope and trust in you alone, O Lord God, and we shall not be confounded forever.

units.la: Tertiò, respondet Ostorrodius, Deum apud Ieremiam non simpliciter, sed tantum plicitèr cum pronunciare maledictum, qui in hominem credit, sed cum tantùm, qui humanis vel propriis viribus ita fidit, vt per illam fiduciam animum suum à Deo auertat, quemadmodum ipsa verba hoc manifestè indicat. Atque hanc restrictione, qua euerti existimat probatione maioris propositionis nostræ, accómodat ad fidem in Christum, & dicit, tatum abesse ab illis, quod humanis Christi viribus cófundant, vel per fidem in Christum hominem animi ipsorum à Deo recedant, vt multò magis per illam fidem ad Deum conuertantur, cuius potentia, quæ in Christo est, illi confidant, siquidem fides in Christum nihil aliud aliquid sit, quàm ipsa fides in Deum, Iohan. 12. vers. 44. non quidem propterea, quod Christus sit ipse Deus, sed quia, per Christum, in ipsum Deum creditur, 1. Pet. 1. vers. 21.
units.tr: Thirdly, Ostorrodius replies, God does not pronounce a curse simply on the one who believes in man, as he does in Jeremiah, but only on the one who trusts in human or his own strength in such a way that by that trust he turns his mind away from God, as the words themselves plainly indicate. He applies this restriction, by which he thinks our proof of the major premise is overturned, to faith in Christ, and says that it is far from the case that they trust in Christ's human powers or that by faith in Christ as a man their minds turn away from God. Rather, by that faith they are turned more and more towards God, since they trust in the power that is in Christ, for faith in Christ is nothing other than faith in God itself (John 12:44), not because Christ is God himself, but because through Christ we believe in God himself (1 Pet. 1:21).

units.la: Resp. Verba illa in quibus refugium quærit Aduersarius, non limitationem antecedentium, sed & manifestam continent, causámque cur maledictus sit ille, qui fiduciam habet in homine, & carnem statuit brachium suum, hanc reddunt, quia videlicet animus noster per eiusmodi fiduciam à Deo, in quem solum, vt pote creatorem, patrem, & conseruatorem vnicum recumbere ipsum oportebat, necessariò auertatur, Deúsque honore & gloria sua spolietur, cum in alio quàm in ipso solo salus quærítur, vt passim apud Prophetas est videre. Sed quid tum? si maximè illud maledictionis fulmen Aduersarios non feriret, & ille ipse genuinus verborum illorum esset sensus, qui ab Aduersario adfertur: minimè tamen inde sequeretur, illos saluo Dei honore, in quàm alium qui non sit verus & æternus Deus, credere, & fiduciam animi collocare posse, cuius rei veritatem argumentis pluribus in propositionis nostræ demonstratione ostendimus. Ita aduersus nos disputat Ostorrodius, quasi locus ille vnicus fundamentum esset doctrinæ nostræ, quæ, illo destructo, necessariò corrueret, vt iam suprà monuimus. In ipsa verò applicatione duplicem errorem committit Ostorrodius, petitionem nempe principii manifestam, & oppositorum elenchum ipsi veritate ipsa longè familiariorem. Principiũ petit, dum πρϏτερον illud φυσεως, nempe Christum natura φιλον esse ανθρώπον, & per Christum, etiamsi ratione sententiæ suæ nudus esset homo, in Deum ipsum credi, fidémque nostram deduci quod demonstrandum ipsi erat, priusquam illud suę interpretationis statueret fundamentum. Elēchum oppositorum committit, dum videlicet ista duo, quod Christus ipse Deus sit, & quod per Christum in Deum ipsum credamus, ita inter se opponit, quasi hoc posito, illud necessario evertertur, cùm tamen ab iis, quæ de Christo ratione voluntariæ dispensationis & liberrimę illius œconomiæ dicuntur, ad negandam diuinam eiusdem naturam, nulla detur consequentia, vt iam sæpius demonstrauimus, & in sequente responsione amplius ostendemus.
units.tr: Reply. Those words, in which the adversary seeks a refuge, do not merely limit what precedes; they plainly contain both the curse and the reason why he is cursed who puts his trust in man and makes flesh his arm. That reason is that our mind, through such trust, must necessarily be turned away from God, on whom alone it ought to rest as creator, father and sole preserver, and God is robbed of his honour and glory when salvation is sought in anyone other than himself, as is seen everywhere among the Prophets. But what follows? Even if that thunderbolt of a curse did not strike our opponents, and even if the meaning given by the adversary were the genuine sense of those words, it would by no means follow that they could, without loss of God's honour, believe in and place the trust of their mind in another who is not the true and eternal God. We have shown the truth of this by many arguments in our demonstration of the proposition. Thus Ostorrodius argues against us as if that one passage were the foundation of our doctrine, which, once it was destroyed, would necessarily collapse, as we have already observed. In the application itself, Ostorrodius commits two errors: a manifest begging of the question, and a fallacy of opposites, which is much more familiar to him than to the truth itself. He begs the question when he assumes the πρότερον φύσεως [prior by nature], namely that Christ is by nature a man, and that through Christ, even if by the reasoning of his own view Christ were a mere man, we believe in God himself and our faith is led to him. This was what he had to demonstrate, before setting up that foundation for his interpretation. He commits the fallacy of opposites when he sets these two propositions against each other, namely that Christ himself is God and that through Christ we believe in God himself, as if, once the one is posited, the other is necessarily overturned. Yet no consequence follows from what is said of Christ in respect of his voluntary dispensation and most free economy towards the denial of his divine nature, as we have often demonstrated already and will show more fully in the following reply.

units.la: Quarto, & vltimò, inquit, ex ipsa fide in Christum, si illa bene intelligatur, firmissimum ipsis suppeditari argumentum, quo contrarium sententia nostra, quod nempe Christus non sit vnus ille Deus, demonstrari possit.
units.tr: Fourthly and lastly, he says, from faith itself in Christ, if it is rightly understood, there is supplied to them a most firm argument by which the contrary of our view, namely that Christ is not that one God, can be demonstrated.

units.la: Argumentum autem tale est.
units.tr: But the argument is as follows.

units.la: Qui verus ac æternus Deus est, per eum non creditur in alium aliquē, sed fides in ipsum, tanquam vltimum finem ac scopum recumbit, nec vlterius tendit, cùm ille sit altissimus.
units.tr: He who is the true and eternal God is not believed in as some other being through him; rather, faith rests on him as on the ultimate end and goal, and does not go further, since he is the highest.

units.la: Atqui per Christum creditur in alium, nempe Deum, sic vt fides non in ipsum Christum, tanquam vltimum finem ac scopum recumbat, quippe qui non est altissimus, sed vlterius tendit, nempe in ipsum Deum, sic vt merito dicere possis, eum, qui credit in Christum, non in ipsum Christum, sed in Deum credere, vt Christus disertis verbis testatur Ioh.12. v. 44. Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui misit me. Hoc autem ipsum de Deo vero dici non potest, quod nempe is, qui in ipsum credit, non in ipsum, sed in alium quempiam credat.
units.tr: But through Christ we believe in another, namely God, so that faith does not rest on Christ himself as the ultimate end and goal, since he is not the highest, but goes further, namely to God himself. So you may rightly say that the one who believes in Christ believes not in Christ himself but in God, as Christ testifies in plain words (John 12:44): He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me. But this very thing cannot be said of the true God, that is, that the one who believes in him does not believe in him but in some other.

units.la: Ergo Christus non est vnus ille verus atque æternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not that one true and eternal God.

units.la: Resp. Deus cùm consideratur absolutè in se, ac natura sua, verissimè statuitur vltimus finis atque scopus in quem omnis nostra fiducia, & προφιλα recumbit, quo sensu propositio illa maior est verissima. At quia in assumptione, varia permiscentur interrogata, & quædam sunt æquiuoca, quædam autem falsa, ordine ad singula respondebimus. Christus igitur, vt de subiecto agamus ante omnia, consideratur à nobis dupliciter, vel secundùm naturam diuinam absolutè, vel quatenus secundùm liberam dispensationem & voluntatem factus est homo, adeóque est συνεργός & mediator inter Deum, & Ecclesiam eius, cuius ille est constitutus caput atque Dominus. Quia igitur Deus absolutè vnum cum Deo Patre essentia, συστάσει, & omnipotentia, vt capite decimo sexto demonstrauimus, ea tenus per ipsum in nullum alium superiorem creditur, sed in ipso veluti vltimo termino suo fiducia nostra omnis requiescit. quiescit. Est enim ille Deus, ille benedictus in secula Iehoua, ac Deus Israelis, creator coelorum, terrae formator, ac opifex, vt nos capite decimo, ac decimoquinto demonstrauimus, & quem proinde Ostorrodius non sine blasphemia Altissimum illum esse negat. Sin vero secundum liberrimam illam oeconomiam & voluntariam dispensationem consideretur, per ipsum quidem in Deum credimus, inter cuius gloriae & maiestatis magnitudinem, & nostri ingenii tenuitatem ille semedium statuit: non tamen credimus in alium, qui videlicet ratione naturae ac essentiae alius sit a Christo, non autem oeconomiae illius, ac voluntariae dispensationis, & officii mediatorii, solo respectu. Hinc est, quod duo illa, nempe credere per Christum in Deum, & quod Christus ipse Deus sit, male inter se opponantur, vel saltem a se inuicem separentur, cum tamen prius illud ab hoc posteriore, tanquam causa necessario dependeat. Ideo enim per Christum in Deum credimus, quia Christus ipse est imago Dei inconspicui, Col. 1. verf. 15. in quo Deus nobis incomprehensibilis, & lucem habitans inaccessam se hominibus manifestat, & quasi in speculo aliquo contemplandum exhibet, quem Christus tanquam perfectissima imago repraesentare minime posset, nisi eiusdem cum ipso essentiae, maiestatis, & gloriae vnus verus & aeternus Deus esset. Secundum hanc eandem oeconomiam, non consideratur simpliciter vt altissimus, quia cum esset in forma Dei, & aequalis Deo, ipse exinaniuit se, ac Patre minorem constituit, propter salutem nostram, sed absque naturae diuinae omni praeiudicio. Atque secundum hanc ipsam voluntariam dispensationem (secundum quam ille locus 1. Pet. 1. v.21. etiam est intelligendus) Christus dixit eum qui credit in se, non in se, sed in eum, qui miserit ipsum, credere. Disertè enim ibi tanquam mediator, de se, & sua dispensatione protestari voluit, non agere se propriam causam, nec venisse proprio arbitratu, sed missum esse a Patre, nec loquutum esse a se ipso, adeoque non in se, sed in Patrem credere eos, qui in se credunt. A voluntaria autem illa dispensatione, ad ipsius diuinae naturae conditionem non dari consequentiam, iam multoties inculcauimus. Atque sic in fumum abit euanida illa Ostorrodii gloriatio, qua se doctrinam nostram argumento ab ipsa fide sumpto solide confutasse, & in cineres ac fauillas quasi redegisse, plebeculae suae persuadere conatur.
units.tr: Reply. When God is considered absolutely, in himself and in his own nature, he is most truly set up as the ultimate end and goal on whom all our trust and refuge rests, and in that sense the major premise is most true. But because the assumption mixes together various matters asked about, some of them ambiguous and some false, we will answer each point in order. First, to deal with the subject before all else: Christ is considered by us in two ways, either absolutely according to his divine nature, or in so far as, by his free dispensation and will, he has become man, and so is the συνεργός [fellow-worker] and mediator between God and his Church, of which he has been appointed head and Lord. Therefore, since God is absolutely one with God the Father in essence, συστάσει [substance], and omnipotence, as we demonstrated in chapter sixteen, to that extent he is not believed in through himself as some superior other; rather, all our trust rests in him as in its final term. For he is that God, that blessed one, Jehovah for ever, and the God of Israel, creator of the heavens and maker and framer of the earth, as we demonstrated in chapters ten and fifteen. Ostorrodius, not without blasphemy, denies that he is that Most High. But if he is considered according to that most free economy and voluntary dispensation, then indeed through him we believe in God, and he stands as mediator between the greatness of God's glory and majesty and the weakness of our understanding. Yet we do not believe in another who is, by reason of nature and essence, other than Christ; the difference lies in respect of his economy, voluntary dispensation and mediatorial office alone. Hence it is that those two things, namely to believe through Christ in God, and that Christ himself is God, are wrongly set against each other, or at least separated from each other, although the former necessarily depends on the latter as on its cause. We believe in God through Christ because Christ himself is the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15), in whom God, who is incomprehensible to us and dwells in unapproachable light, makes himself known to men and presents himself to be contemplated as in a mirror. Christ could not represent him as the most perfect image unless he were the one true and eternal God, one with him in essence, majesty and glory. According to this same economy, Christ is not considered simply as the Most High, for although he was in the form of God and equal to God, he emptied himself and made himself less than the Father for our salvation; yet this is without any prejudice to the divine nature. And according to this same voluntary dispensation (according to which that passage in 1 Pet. 1:21 also must be understood), Christ said: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me. For there, speaking clearly as mediator, he wished to testify about himself and his dispensation: that he was not pleading his own cause, nor had he come of his own accord, but had been sent by the Father, nor had he spoken from himself; and so those who believe in him believe not in him but in the Father. We have often insisted already that no consequence follows from that voluntary dispensation to the condition of the divine nature itself. And so that boast of Ostorrodius, by which he tries to persuade his common people that he has solidly refuted our doctrine by an argument taken from faith itself, and has reduced it, as it were, to ashes and dust, vanishes into smoke.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: In quo argumentum nonum,& vltimum, pro æterna Filii Deitate, proponitur, ac defenditur.
units.tr: In which the ninth and last argument for the eternal Deity of the Son is set forth and defended.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM nostrum nonum & vltimum, quod demonstramus contra Arianos, Samosatenianos,& Ebionitas, Christum non esse ψιλὸν tantùm ἄνθρωπον, sed verum atque æternum Deum, ex illis scripturæ locis desumitur, quæ affirmant, Christum ex supernis oriundum,è Patre exiuisse, & in mundum ita venijsse, vt tamen in cælo & in terra simul existat, Ioh.16.ver.28. Exiui à Patre,& veni in mundum,iterum relinquo mundum,& vado ad Patrem. & 17.vers.8. Et ipsi vere norunt me à te exiuisse, & crediderunt me à te missum esse. Exiuit inquam Christus à Patre primò per generationem æternam. Mich.5.ver.2. exire enim ab aliquo sæpe significat generari ab aliquo, vel originè ducere. Heb.7.v.5. A fratribus suis,licet egressis (ἐξηλυθότας) ex lumbis Abrahæ. Deinde in tempore per incarnationem, exinaniens se, forma serui accepta,& personam, seu officium mediatorium suscipiens. Item Iohan.8.vers.23. Vos ex inferis estis,ego ex supernis sum. Iohan.3.v.13. Nullus enim ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit è cœlo, Filius hominis,qui est in cœlo: & 6.v.38.50.51.58. è cœlo descendisse dicitur, v.62. inquit Christus. Si igitur conspiceretis Filium hominis ascendentem eò ,vbi erat prius? Ex quibus omnibus necessariò sequitur, Christum non humana duntaxat natura constare, sed immensum ac infinitum,ac proinde verum & æternum Deum esse.
units.tr: Our ninth and last argument, by which we show against the Arians, the Samosatenes and the Ebionites that Christ is not a mere ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον [mere man], but the true and eternal God, is drawn from those passages of Scripture which affirm that Christ came forth from on high, went out from the Father, and came into the world in such a way that he nonetheless exists in heaven and on earth at the same time: John 16:28, I came forth from the Father and have come into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father; and 17:8, And they have truly known that I came out from you, and they have believed that you sent me. Christ went out from the Father, I say, first by eternal generation (Micah 5:2; for to go out from someone often means to be begotten of someone, or to derive one's origin from him). Heb. 7:5, from their brothers, though they had come out (ἐξηλυθότας) from the loins of Abraham. Then in time, by the incarnation, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, and assuming the person, or mediatorial office. Likewise John 8:23, You are from below, I am from above. John 3:13, For no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven; and in 6:38, 50, 51, 58 he is said to have descended from heaven; in v. 62 Christ says, If then you were to see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? From all these things it necessarily follows that Christ does not consist of human nature alone, but is immense and infinite, and therefore is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo sexto hanc quæstionem proponit, An nimirum ex eo,quòd Scriptura dicit Christum in mundum venijsse, &c. diuina in ipso natura demonstrari possit? quod ille negat,neque nos simpliciter affirmamus. Non enim inde argumentamur, quòd Christus simpliciter in mundum venisse,aut missus esse dicitur, quod ipsum etiam Apostolis in sacris literis tribui iam ante Ostorrodium docuerunt nos præceptores nostri,sed quod exiuisse ipsum à Patre, & in mundum esse missum Scriptura. ptura affirmat. Statum igitur controuersiæ cum perperam propo- nat Aduersarius, aerem petunt quotquot adfert argumenta: quod ipsum licet ad euertendum hoc caput ipsius decimum sextum a- bunde sufficeret, lubet tamen ipsius refponfiones examinare.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter sixteen of his Institutions, proposes this question: whether, from the fact that Scripture says Christ came into the world, etc., the divine nature in him can be demonstrated. He denies this, and we do not simply affirm it. For we do not argue from the fact that Christ is simply said to have come into the world or to have been sent, which our teachers taught even before Ostorrodius was ever heard of is also attributed to the apostles in the sacred writings; rather we argue from the fact that Scripture affirms that he went out from the Father and was sent into the world. Since the adversary has wrongly stated the point at issue, all his arguments beat the air, which would be quite enough to overturn this sixteenth chapter of his; nevertheless it pleases us to examine his replies.

units.la: Primo igitur dicit, hoc nobis in more positum esse, vt ex peculiaribus modis loquendi noua dogmata, & nouas doctrinas cudamus.
units.tr: First, then, he says that it is our habit to coin new dogmas and new doctrines from peculiar modes of speaking.

units.la: Resp. At vero hoc meræ & putidæ est calumniæ nota, quam tu Ecclesiis nostris contra omnem Christianam æquitatem inuris. Eo fundamento nititur doctrina nostra, quòd hactenus conuellere tota illa Samosatenianorum turba, suis insultibus & impressionibus temerario quidem, sed tamen infelici ausu est conata. Et tu ipse Oftorrodi dum calamū aduersum nos stringis, nihil nisi crassam ignorantiam & insecitiam tuam prodis, nobisque loco Christianarum in Religione orthodoxa institutionum, nihil nisi farraginem quādam ex Elenchis, fallaciis ac sophismatibus meris consutam obtrudis, in qua etiam legenda, nedum refutanda, pudet fere bonas horas collocare.
units.tr: Reply. This is the mark of a pure and foul calumny, which you heap upon our churches against all Christian fairness. Our doctrine rests on this foundation: the whole Samosatene rabble has so far tried to overturn it with its attacks and assaults, rash indeed, but unhappy in their daring. And you yourself, Ostorrodius, while you draw your pen against us, reveal nothing but your crass ignorance and stupidity; and instead of Christian institutions in the orthodox religion, you thrust upon us nothing but a hodgepodge stitched together from fallacies, sophisms and mere quibbles, in which it is almost a shame to waste good hours even by reading, let alone by refuting.

units.la: Secundo, respondet, falsos quoque Prophetas in mundum exiuisse dici, 1. Iohan. 4. v. 1. & Christum ipsum dixisse, se misisse Apostolos in mundum, quemadmodum ipse à Patre sit missus, Iohan. 17. v. 18. qui tamen nō fuerint extra mundum, priusquam in illum exiuerint, vel missi fuerint. Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: Second, he replies that false prophets too are said to have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1), and that Christ himself said he had sent the apostles into the world, just as he himself was sent by the Father (John 17:18); yet these men were not outside the world before they went out into it or were sent. His argument is this:

units.la: Si etiam falsi Prophetæ in mundum exiuisse, & ipsi Apostoli à Christo in mundum missi dicuntur, quemadmodum Pater ipsum Christum misit, qui tamen extra mundum non fuerunt, cum in eum exirent, aut mitterentur: tum etiam ce eo, quod Christus in hunc mundum missus esse dicitur, non sequitur ipsum extra mundum iam extitisse, priusquam in eum mitteretur.
units.tr: If false prophets are also said to have gone out into the world, and the apostles themselves are said to have been sent into the world by Christ, just as the Father sent Christ himself, who nevertheless were not outside the world when they went out into it or were sent; then also, from the fact that Christ is said to have been sent into this world, it does not follow that he had already existed outside the world before he was sent into it.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Quia Aduersarius statum controuersiæ perperam propo- suit, ideò hoc argumentum nihil contra nos concludit, sed à scopo aberrat. Non enim ideò dicimus Christum verum & æternum Deum esse, vel iam extra mūdum extitisse, priusquam in eum mitteretur, quia videlicet in mundum à Patre missus dicitur. Quum etiam Iohannes à Deo missum esse Scriptura testetur, sed quia se exiuisse prius à Patre, & postmodum in mundum veniisse affirmat, Iohan. 16. v. 28. Atque hæc consequentia, non prior illa Aduersarii erat infringenda.
units.tr: Reply. Because the adversary has wrongly stated the point at issue, this argument proves nothing against us, but goes wide of the mark. For we do not say that Christ is the true and eternal God, or that he already existed outside the world before he was sent into it, because he is said to have been sent into the world by the Father, since John too is testified in Scripture to have been sent by God; rather we say it because he affirms that he went out from the Father first and afterwards came into the world (John 16:28). And this inference, not the adversary's earlier one, was the one that needed to be attacked.

units.la: Tertiò, respondet per concessionem, etiāsi videlicet hoc largiatur nobis quòd Christus extra mundum fuerit, ex eo tamen, quòd Christus à Patre egressus, & in hunc mundum ab eodem missus esse dicitur, minimè sequi, quòd Christus aliam etiam naturam praeter humanam habuerit, priusquam ex Maria Virgine nasceretur, nedum quod unus ille ac aeternus Deus fuerit. Atque hanc suam consequentiam stabilire conatur sequentibus rationibus. Primò, quia demonstrari non possit, quòd Christus ante natiuitatem ex Maria virgine à Patre extiterit, & in hunc mundum missus fuerit. Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: Third, he replies by conceding, namely that, even if we grant that Christ was outside the world, it nevertheless does not follow from the fact that Christ is said to have gone out from the Father and to have been sent into this world by him that Christ had another nature besides the human before he was born of the Virgin Mary, much less that he was that one and eternal God. And he tries to establish this inference by the following reasons. First, because it cannot be demonstrated that Christ came forth from the Father and was sent into this world before his birth of the Virgin Mary. His argument is this:

units.la: Si non potest demonstrari quòd Christus ante natiuitatem ex Maria virgine à Patre egressus, & in hunc mundu missus sit, tu ex eo quod à Patre egressus, & ab eo in hunc mundu missus dicitur, non sequitur quod ante natiuitatem illam ex virgine, aliā naturam praeter humanam habuerit, nedum quod unus ille, & aeternus Deus fuerit, etiamsi concedatur, quod ex tra hunc mundum fuerit.
units.tr: If it cannot be demonstrated that Christ, before his birth of the Virgin Mary, went out from the Father and was sent into this world, then from the fact that he is said to have gone out from the Father and to have been sent by him into this world, it does not follow that before that birth of the Virgin he had a nature other than the human, much less that he was that one and eternal God, even if it be conceded that he was outside this world.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. At vero non sponte & ex liberalitate aliqua hoc nobis concedis, sed inuitus, & veritatis vi coüictus, fateri cogeris, quod Christus extra mūdū fuerit, quia scriptura hoc tā euidēter & manifestè docet, vt nulla fróte negare istud audeas, vtrūq; nouo figmēto & nescio quo sōniātis cerebri delirio, simplicissimā scripturę veritatē adulterare & corrūpere adnitaris, qua de re postmodū videbimus, nūc ratiūculas tuas, quibus falsā illā tuā consequētiam stratuminare conaris, examinaturi. Et quantum ad primā attinet, negamus assumptionē illius. Si enim Christus non tantum priusquam ex Maria virgine, sed ab omni æternitate, ante omnes res creatas, & ante omnem locū exti tit, sequi tur ipsū secundùm voluntariam suam dispensationē à Patre egresū, & in mundū hunc ab eodē missum esse, antequā ex Maria virgine nasceretur. Atqui prius affirmat Apostolus, Phil. 2. v. 6. Quū in forma Dei esset (ὁ ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ τῷ Θεῷ) forma serui assumpsit: vnde liquet, Christum, antequam humanam naturam in vnitatem suæ personæ assumeret, verum fuisse ὑ φύσει μένον. Formam enim Dei, & hominis, veram & perfectā essentiam veri Dei, & veri hominis significare, capite 20. demonstrabimus. 1. Tim. 3. verf. 16. Deus conspicuus est factus in carne, iustificatus est in spiritu. Eandem etiam assumptionem nostram demonstrauimus omnibus illis argumentis, quibus Christum verum, & æternum Deum Israelis esse, euincimus. Ergo posterius quoque concedatur nobis, necesse est.
units.tr: Reply. Indeed you do not concede this to us freely or out of any generosity, but unwillingly, and compelled by the force of the truth you are forced to admit that Christ was outside the world, because Scripture teaches this so plainly and manifestly that you dare not deny it in any way. Hence you try to corrupt and adulterate the simplest truth of Scripture with a new fiction and some delirium of a dreaming brain, which we will see later; for now let us examine the little arguments with which you try to shore up your false inference. And as far as the first goes, we deny its assumption. For if Christ existed not only before he was born of the Virgin Mary, but from all eternity, before all created things and before all place, it follows that, according to his voluntary dispensation, he went out from the Father and was sent by him into this world before he was born of the Virgin Mary. But the first is affirmed by the Apostle, Phil. 2:6, Who, being in the form of God (ὁ ὑπάρχων ἐν μορφῇ τῷ Θεῷ), took the form of a servant. Whence it is clear that Christ, before he assumed human nature into the unity of his person, was truly existing by nature [ὑπάρχον φύσει]. For we will demonstrate in chapter 20 that the form of God and of man signifies the true and perfect essence of true God and true man. 1 Tim. 3:16, God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit. We have also demonstrated this same assumption by all those arguments by which we prove that Christ is the true and eternal God of Israel. Therefore it is necessary that the second also be granted to us.

units.la: Secundò, ad probandam suam consequentiam dicit contrarium ex Scripturis demonstrari posse, quòd nempe Christus tum demum egressus sit è Patre, & ab eo in mundum missus, postquam ex Maria virgine natus esset: quoniam Dominus ipse dixerit, Filium hominis descendisse è cœlo, & in cœlo fuisse, Ioh.3.v.13.& 6.v.62. quod fieri non potuerit, antequam nasceretur, nisi quis cum Mennonitis, id est, Anabaptistarum quadam secta, contra omnem veritatem afferere velit, Christum qua homo in utero virginis Maria cœlitus descendisse.
units.tr: Second, to prove his inference he says that the contrary can be demonstrated from the Scriptures, namely that Christ went out from the Father and was sent by him into the world only after he had been born of the Virgin Mary, since the Lord himself said that the Son of Man came down from heaven and was in heaven (John 3:13; 6:62); which could not have happened before he was born, unless someone, with the Mennonites, that is, a certain sect of Anabaptists, were willing to assert against all truth that Christ as man had come down from heaven into the womb of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si Christus tum demum egressus est à Patre, & ab eo in mundum missus, postquam ex Maria virgine nasceretur, tum ex eo quod à Patre egressus, & in hunc mundum missus esse dicitur, non sequitur, quod ante natiuitatem ex Maria virgine, aliam naturam præter humanam habuerit, nedum quod unus ille & æternus Deus fuerit:
units.tr: If Christ went out from the Father and was sent into the world only after he was born of the virgin Mary, then from the fact that he is said to have gone out from the Father and been sent into this world, it does not follow that before his birth from the virgin he had any nature other than the human, much less that he was that one and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ioh.3.v.13.& 6.v.62. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true: John 3:13 and 6:62. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Quæcunque in scripturis sacris de Christo dicuntur, & prædicantur de ipso, vel quatenus Deus est, & dicuntur de ipso, secundum divinā eius naturam, vel quatenus est Mediator inter Deum & homines: ac dicitur de tota persona secundum naturam vtramque ipsius. Quæ cùm ita sint, vel puero apparet, consequentiam esse falsam, quippe cuius antecedens de humana Christi natura, consequens verò de diuina loquatur. Falsò autem negari naturam vnam, sumpto, ex naturæ alterius ratione, argumento, iam supra cap.7. prolixè demonstrauimus. Quamuis igitur Christus secundum humanam ipsius naturā, post natiuitatem ex Maria Virgine, à Patre egressus sit, & ab eo in hunc mundum missus: hoc tamen nihil impedit, quo minus ex eo ipso, quod exiuisse à Patre, & in hūc mūdū missus esse dicitur (quod ipsū secundum diuinā eius naturā intelligendū esse, peculiaris illa phrasis, quæ de nullo alio quàm de Christo legitur, cū illis, quę initio huius cap. adiecimus, manifestè euincit) demonstrari possit, ipsū antequā ex Maria virgine nasceretur, extitisse, verūmq; & æternum Deum esse, vt quiuis facilè animaducertit. Assumptionem syllogismi, quantū cōcernit, & in ea pluribus confirmanda, frustrà desudat Osiorrodius, cùm non in ipsa, sed in consequentia error delitescat. Non enim quaeritur inter nos & Aduersarios, An Christus homo, id est secundum humanam naturam ipsius, post natiuitatem demum ex virgine Maria in mundum hunc sit missus, quod cum sit extra controuersiae aleam, frustra ab Aduersario confirmatur. Sed an vllum inde argumentum contra diuinam Christi naturam desumi possit? Vel, an inde sequatur, naturam diuinam Christi inde demonstrari non posse, quod Christus ante natiuitatem ex Maria virgine extiterit, adeo- que verus & aeternus sit Deus Israelis, qua de re altum est apud Oftorrodium silentium? Quamuis illam propositionem, in se alioquin vera, duo illa testimonia minime confirment, quippe quae per Synecdochen, qua & pars pro toto ponitur, in subiecto, & in attributo toti personae tribuitur in concreto, quod alterius naturae proprium est, toti Christo, ab altera natura, nempe humana denominato tribuunt, quod diuinae ipsius naturae est proprium, quam Synecdochen, Ecclesiastici scriptores, κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων & ἀντιδόσεως appellant. Secundum illam enim solam in caelo & in terra simul est, humana ipsius natura vtpote finita, certi loci cancellis, ac limitibus perpetuo circumscripta.
units.tr: Answer. Whatever is said or predicated of Christ in the sacred Scriptures is said either in respect of his being God, and is said of him according to his divine nature, or in respect of his being the Mediator between God and men, and is said of the whole person according to either of his natures. Since this is so, even a child can see that the inference is false, because its antecedent speaks of Christ's human nature and its consequent of his divine nature. Moreover, we have already shown at length, above in chapter 7, that to deny one nature on the ground of the other, by an argument of this kind, is false. So although Christ, according to his human nature, went out from the Father and was sent into this world only after his birth from the virgin Mary, this does not prevent it from being shown, from the very fact that he is said to have gone out from the Father and been sent into this world (which must be understood of his divine nature, as that peculiar phrase, read of no one but Christ, clearly proves together with the passages we cited at the beginning of this chapter), that he existed before he was born of the virgin Mary, and is true and eternal God, as anyone can easily perceive. As for the assumption of the syllogism, insofar as it concerns us, Osiander labours in vain to confirm it at length, since the error lies not in the assumption but in the inference. For the question between us and our opponents is not whether Christ, that is, according to his human nature, was sent into this world only after his birth from the virgin Mary. That is beyond dispute, so our opponent's confirming it is pointless. The question is whether any argument against Christ's divine nature can be drawn from it. Or whether it follows that Christ's divine nature cannot be demonstrated from the fact that he existed before his birth from the virgin, and so is the true and eternal God of Israel; on this point Osiander is conspicuously silent. Although the proposition, true in itself, is in no way confirmed by those two testimonies, they are assigned by synecdoche (in which a part is put for the whole) to the whole person, both as subject and as predicate, in the concrete. They attribute to the whole Christ, and name him from the other nature, namely the human, what belongs to his divine nature. Church writers call this synecdoche the communication of properties [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων] and the exchange [ἀντιδόσεως]. For by this alone is his human nature, being finite and always bounded by the limits of a particular place, in heaven and on earth at the same time.

units.la: Tertio, Oftorrodius, quasi re bene praeclareque gesta, euicta atque demonstrata, mirandum esse, inquit, nos Christo illud ipsum affirmanti fidem non adhibere. An vero Deo quicquam est impossibile? Et num ab expresso Dei verbo ad fictam illam communicationem idiomatum, & vnionem personalem recedemus? Absit. Atque eandem illam assumptionem confirmare conatur, duobus adhuc scripturae locis. Ioh. 18. v. 37. Ad hoc natus sum, & ad hoc veni in mundum, vt testimonium dem veritati. Vnde concludit, cum priore loco natiuitatis, posteriore vero aduentus in mundum, mentio fiat, natiuitatem ex virgine missionem in mundum praecessisse. Gal. 4. v. 4. Deus misit Filium suum factum ex muliere. Vnde in hunc modum ratiocinatur: Si Deus misit Filium suum, postquam ex Maria virgine natus esset, vt Apostoli verba testantur, sequitur hoc factum esse, postquam iam homo esset, adeoque non ante, sed post natiuitatem.
units.tr: Third, Osiander, as if the matter were well and splendidly done, proved and demonstrated, says that it is strange that we do not give credence to Christ when he affirms this very thing. Is anything impossible for God? And will we depart from the express word of God to that fictitious communication of properties and personal union? Far from it. He also tries to confirm the same assumption with two more passages of Scripture. John 18:37: For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. From this he concludes that, since the first passage mentions birth and the second the coming into the world, the birth from the virgin preceded the sending into the world. Gal. 4:4: God sent his Son, made of a woman. From this he reasons thus: If God sent his Son after he had been born of the virgin Mary, as the words of the Apostle testify, it follows that this happened after he was already a man, and so not before but after his birth.

units.la: Resp. Imo maximopere mirandum est Socinianos tantae lucis veritatis, suis sophismatum & anilium subtilitatum praestigiis tenebras tam pertinaciter offundere, nec tot argumentis, tot stupendis miraculis, tantisque operibus, quibus Christus suam diuinitatem asseruit, fidem adhibere velle. Ipsa vero Dei omnipotentia ad quam confugis, Oftorrodi, quid hac in parte tibi patrocinari potest? Nihil esse apud Deum impossibile, nouimus, & sanctè credimus, sed anne propterea sequitur Christum qua homo, ante solennem illum & visibilem in cœlum ascensum in ipsis cœlis fuisse? Minimè vero: Etiam te non minus ac Paulum, aut Eliam, in cœlos euehere potuisset Deus, & potest etiamnum, an ergo sequitur inde, te cœlestem illam Regiam vnquam ingressum esse? non sane: eam enim ibi diuinam Christi gloriam coram conspexisses, quam nunc tam studiose impugnas, ex ignorantiane an malitia, tu videris. Ab omnipotentia autem ad ipsum factum, nisi accedat voluntas Dei, non dari consequentiam, tantus Doctor, qui vniuersam Christi Ecclesiam ad certamen prouocare audet, ignorare non deberet. Quod vero Oftorrodius illam communicationem idiomatum, quæ ex vnione personali fluit, quoue nomine Patres Orthodoxi illam synecdochen, quam paulo ante explicauimus, appellarunt, à nobis fictam dicit, nósque à veritate diuina ad figmentum illud delabi affirmat, facit ille quidem pro consueta temeritate sua, vt conuitiis lacessat, quod argumentis refutare non potest. Si illa Synecdoche, vel ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία, confi-cta est, dicat mihi quæso Oftorrodius, quomodo Scriptura affirmet Deum Ecclesiam suo sanguine redemisse, & Dominum gloriæ crucifixum esse? Si vero existimet illam tropologicam verborum à natiua significatione in aliam mutationem, cum simplici Scripturæ veritate consistere non posse, ineptior est, quàm vt refutatione dignus censeatur. Scripturæ vero illa testimonia nihil concludunt, nisi Christum secundùm humanam naturam ipsius, post natiuitatem, ex Maria Virgine, in hunc mundum missum esse, quod ipsum credimus, & lubens confitemur, absque doctrinæ nostræ omni præiudicio, vt iam sæpius ostendimus.
units.tr: Answer. Indeed it is most remarkable that the Socinians should, with the tricks of their sophisms and their old-wives' subtleties, so stubbornly cast darkness over so great a light of truth, and be unwilling to give credence to so many arguments, so many astonishing miracles and such great works by which Christ asserted his divinity. But what, Osiander, can the very omnipotence of God, to which you flee, do to help you in this matter? We know and piously believe that nothing is impossible with God. But does it follow from this that Christ, as a man, was in the heavens themselves before his solemn and visible ascension into heaven? By no means. God could have carried you up into heaven no less than Paul or Elijah, and still can; does it therefore follow that you ever entered that heavenly kingdom? Certainly not. For you would have seen there that divine glory of Christ which you now so zealously assail, whether from ignorance or malice, let you judge. But a teacher as great as you, who dares to challenge the whole Church of Christ, ought not to be ignorant that from omnipotence to the actual deed there is no valid inference unless the will of God be added. As for Osiander calling that communication of properties, which flows from the personal union, and which the Orthodox Fathers named by the synecdoche I explained a little while ago, a fiction of ours, and asserting that we have fallen from divine truth into that fabrication: he does this, in keeping with his usual rashness, so that he may assail with insults what he cannot refute with arguments. If that synecdoche, or communication of properties [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία], is a fabrication, let Osiander tell me, I pray, how Scripture affirms that God redeemed the Church with his blood, and that the Lord of glory was crucified? But if he thinks that this tropological change of words from their native meaning cannot agree with the plain truth of Scripture, he is too foolish to be thought worthy of refutation.
