Those testimonies of Scripture conclude nothing except that Christ, according to his human nature, was sent into this world after his birth from the Virgin Mary. This we believe and gladly confess, without any prejudice to our doctrine, as we have already shown many times.

units.la: Quarto, respondet ad illum locum Ioh. 3. v. 13. in quo affirmatur, quod Christus simul in cœlo & in terra extiterit, ac dicit, Verba Christi aliter reddi posse, nempe hoc modo, Filius hominis, qui in cœlo erat, quemadmodum in hunc locum Beza & Erasmus annotauerint: ac proinde libenter se fateri, Christum Filium Dei in cœlis fuisse, & inde venisse, sed non ante, verum post natiuitatem ex Maria virgine.
units.tr: Fourth, he answers the passage John 3:13, in which it is affirmed that Christ was at the same time in heaven and on earth, and says: The words of Christ can be rendered otherwise, namely in this way: the Son of man, who was in heaven, as Beza and Erasmus have noted on this passage. And so I gladly confess that Christ the Son of God was in heaven and came thence, but not before, only after his birth from the virgin Mary.

units.la: Resp. Vtrouis modo participium illud ὤν reddatur, siue est, siue erat, sensus tamen idem est, Christum nempe secundùm naturam
units.tr: Answer. Whichever way the participle ὤν is rendered, whether is or was, the sense is nonetheless the same: that Christ, namely according to his

units.la: V
units.tr: V

units.la: diuinam è cœlo descendisse, vbi iam prius fuerit, nempe in principio apud Deum, vt Ioh.1.v.1.dicitur, id est, ante iacta mundi fundamenta, & ab æterno, vt capite decimo tertio demõstrauimus, quod ipsum humanæ ipsius naturæ cõpetere nullo modo potest. Quod verò Ostorrodius addit libenter se fateri Christum hominem, id est, secundum humanam naturam, in cœlis fuisse, & iam tum venisse inde, cùm verba illa enuntiaret, facile crediderim, cùm nullæ aliæ latebræ ad effugiendam veritatis lucem, nisi in eiusmodi figmētis, & deliriis ostendantur, quorum ille quæuis amplesceretur potius, quàm vt tributa gloria Deo, errorẽ suum agnosceret. Quũ enim lubricę illæ anguillæ videret, se alia ratione euadere nõ posse, quin in veritatis vinculis constringantur, audaciter affirmat Christum qua homo ante mortem & passionem in cœlos ascendisse, indeque à Patre de voluntate ipsius edoctum, iterum descedisse, ac proinde illo descensu, & ascensu, quæ illi nepe confinxerunt, verba illa Christi Ioh.3.13.&6.v.62. intelligeda esse. Sed videamus quibus rationibus illẽ noua illa Samosatenianā doctrinā stabilire conetur.
units.tr: divine nature, came down from heaven, where he had already been before, namely in the beginning with God, as is said in John 1:1, that is, before the foundations of the world were laid, and from eternity, as we demonstrated in chapter 13. This cannot in any way belong to his human nature. As for Osiander's addition that he gladly confesses that Christ as man, that is, according to his human nature, was in heaven and had already come thence when he uttered those words, I can readily believe it, since no other hiding places for escaping the light of truth are to be found except in such fictions and delusions. He would embrace any of these rather than give glory to God by acknowledging his error. Seeing that those slippery eels could not otherwise escape without being bound in the chains of truth, he boldly asserts that Christ as man ascended into heaven before his death and passion, and was taught by the Father about his will there, and descended again; and therefore that John 3:13 and 6:62 must be understood by that descent and ascent, which he has invented for them. But let us see by what arguments he tries to establish this new Samosatene doctrine.

units.la: Quinto itaque Christũ quà homo in cœlis fuisse, &inde descēdis- se probaturus, hanc obiectionem sibi proponit refutandam: nēpe, Si Christus homo, id est secundum humanam naturam ipsius, in cœlis fuit, postquam ex Maria virgine nasceretur, & inde etiam descēdit, se-quitur, ipsum etiam prius descēdisse. Atqui hoc ipsum cum in sacris literis scriptum non reperiatur, nec prius verum esse videtur. Ad hanc obiectionem respondet Ostorrodius, primò, negando ex eo, quod de ascensu Christi in cœlos, priusquam inde veniret, nihil in Scripturis sacris legatur, sequi, eum propterea in eos nec ascendisse, nec assumptum fuisse, & dicit sufficere, quod illud per consequentiam ab ipsis demonstretur. Si enim in cœlo fuerit, postquam homo natus esset, necessariò inde sequi ipsum etiam in cœlos ascendisse, ac eò assumptum esse.
units.tr: Fifthly, then, wishing to prove that Christ as man was in heaven and descended from there, he sets before himself this objection to refute: namely, If Christ as man, that is according to his human nature, was in heaven after he was born of the virgin Mary, and also descended from there, it follows that he also descended before. But this itself, since it is not written in the sacred letters, does not seem true either. To this objection Ostorrodius replies, first, by denying that from the fact that nothing is read in the holy Scriptures about Christ's ascent into heaven before he came from there, it follows that he therefore did not ascend thither or was not taken up; and he says it is enough that this is demonstrated from them by consequence. For if he was in heaven after he was born a man, it necessarily follows that he also ascended into heaven and was thus taken up.

units.la: Resp. Fortiter sanè iugulat se ipsum Ostorrodius verissima obiectione illa. Christum enim secundùm humanam ipsius naturam ante mortem ac passionem in cœlum ascendisse, inde descendisse, falsum est, nec ex Scripturis sacris demonstrari potest. Consequẽ- tiam verò Aduersarii qua figmentũ illud stabilire conatur, quantum attinet, eius nos assumptionem negamus, eámq. ex Scripturis nobis ostēdi postulamus, quũ ex iis quæ de Christo à natura humana denominato prædicantur, minimè sequatur eadem ipsi secundum humanam naturam separatim competere.
units.tr: Reply. Ostorrodius certainly cuts his own throat boldly with that most true objection. For that Christ, according to his human nature, ascended into heaven before his death and passion and descended from there, is false, and cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures. As for the adversary's consequence, by which he tries to establish that fiction, so far as it concerns us we deny his assumption and ask that it be shown to us from the Scriptures, since from what is predicated of Christ as denominated from his human nature it by no means follows that the same things belong to him separately according to his human nature.

units.la: Secundo,negat ille assumptionem obiectionis ab ipso propositæ, & affirmant legi in Scripturis,quodChristus quà homo in cœlum ascenderit,nempe, Ioh. 3. v. 13. Nemo ascendit in cœlum,nisi qui descendit è cœlo,Filius hominis,qui erat in cœlo. Quum autem Christus hoc de se affirmauerit,priusquam visibiliter in cœlum eueƈtus fuit, inde sequi affirmat Christum hominem, id est, secundùm humanam ipsius naturam,ante visibilem illam in cœlum ascensionem, illuc ascendisse, & inde descendisse.
units.tr: Secondly, he denies the assumption of the objection he himself proposed, and affirms that it is read in the Scriptures that Christ as man ascended into heaven, namely John 3:13: No one ascends into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who was in heaven. Since Christ affirmed this of himself before he was visibly taken up into heaven, he argues that it follows that Christ as man, that is according to his human nature, ascended thither and descended from there before that visible ascension into heaven.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is of this kind.

units.la: Si Christus ante visibilem suam in cœlum ascensione affirmauit,quod secùdum humanam naturam suam in cœlum ascenderit, tum etiam verum est illum ascendisse,ac proinde falsum est,quod illud in Scripturis non legatur.
units.tr: If Christ, before his visible ascension into heaven, affirmed that according to his human nature he had ascended into heaven, then it is also true that he ascended; and therefore it is false that this is not read in the Scriptures.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter too.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem esse falsam,quę illis Christi verbis minimè possit demonstrari,cum ex eo,quod Christus homo dicatur in cœlum ascendisse,aut descendisse,ibique fuisse, minimè sequatur secundum humanam naturam ipsius illud factum esse,nec quæ de Christo ab altera natura in cōcreto denominato prædicantur,statim quo que de eadē illa natura à qua denominatur,in abstracto enuntiari possint. Vt enim ex eo,quod Deus suo sanguine Ecclesiam redemisse,& Dominus gloriæ crucifixus esse dicitur,impium esset concludere,ipsâ deitatem Christi mortuam,passam,atque crucifixam esse:ita ex eo quodChristus à natura humana denominatus in concreto dicitur in cœlum ascendisse,inde descendisse, ibidem fuisse,absurdum esset affirmare, humanam Christi naturam in cœlum ascendisse,inde descendisse,& ibidem fuisse,nisi quis priorem etiam consequentiam, contra omnem pietatem,atque veritatem concedere velit.
units.tr: Reply. The assumption is false, which cannot be demonstrated from those words of Christ, since from the fact that Christ as man is said to have ascended into heaven, or descended, or to have been there, it by no means follows that this happened according to his human nature; nor can what is predicated of Christ concretely, from another nature by which he is denominated, be at once stated in the abstract of that very nature from which he is denominated. For just as, from the fact that God is said to have redeemed the Church with his own blood, and the Lord of glory to have been crucified, it would be impious to conclude that the deity of Christ died, suffered and was crucified; so from the fact that Christ, denominated concretely from his human nature, is said to have ascended into heaven, to have descended thence, and to have been there, it would be absurd to affirm that the human nature of Christ ascended into heaven, descended thence and was there, unless someone wishes to grant the former consequence too, contrary to all piety and truth.

units.la: Tertiò,inquit etiam expediuisse,rationémque postulasse,vt Christus secundùm humanam naturam ante visibilem illum in cœlum ascensum illuc eueheretur. Si enim Moses Christi typus montem sanƈtum conscenderit,ibidemque cum Deo,vel Angelo eius,aliquandiu conuersatus, & colloquutus fuerit,prius quà Deus per ipsum populo suo tabulas lapideas & ea quæ ad religiosum Dei cultum,qui externis,& corporalib.in rebus totus consistebat,speƈtabant,ipsi præscriberet, multo magis Christus per quem Deus mysterium Euangelij mūdo reuelare, & cultū sui plane spiritualem præscribere voluit,in cœlos ascendere, aliquandiu ibi cum Deo conuersari,& de volūtate ipsius edoceri debuit,quod nempe loqui, quidve facere deberet, quemadmodum Christus ipse testatur, quod ex se ipso nihil fecerit, aut loquutus sit, sed quemadmodum Pater ipsum docuerit, & ipsi in mandatis dederit, Iohan. 8. versu 28. 29. & 12. versu 49.
units.tr: Thirdly, he says it was also expedient, and reason demanded, that Christ according to his human nature should be carried up there before that visible ascent into heaven. For if Moses, a type of Christ, ascended the holy mountain, and there conversed and talked for some time with God or his Angel, before God through him prescribed to his people the tablets of stone and those things which pertained to the religious worship of God, which consisted wholly in external and bodily things, much more Christ, through whom God wished to reveal the mystery of the Gospel to the world and prescribe a wholly spiritual worship of himself, ought to ascend into heaven, to converse there for a while with God, and be taught about his will; namely, what he ought to say or do, just as Christ himself testifies that he did nothing or spoke nothing of himself, but as the Father taught him and gave him commands, John 8:28-29 and 12:49.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is of this kind.

units.la: Si Moses typus Christi montem sanctum conscendit, ibique apud Deum, vel Angelum eius aliquandiu conversatus est, priusquam Deus ipsi praescriberet ea, quae ad religiosum cultum spectarunt: multo magis ipse Christus in coelos ascendere, & ibi a Patre de voluntate ipsius edoceri debuit, quia cultus per Mosem praescriptus, tantum externus fuit, & in rebus corporalibus consistebat: Cultus autem per Christum praescriptus, mere est spiritualis.
units.tr: If Moses, a type of Christ, ascended the holy mountain and there conversed for some time with God or his Angel, before God prescribed to him those things which pertained to the religious worship: much more ought Christ himself to ascend into heaven and there be taught about his will by the Father, because the worship prescribed through Moses was only external, and consisted in bodily things. But the worship prescribed through Christ is purely spiritual.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the former is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the latter too.

units.la: Resp. Primo, negando consequentiam, quae nititur falsa hypothesi, & manifesta principii petitione, qua semper praesupponitur illud Χριστὸς Christum nempe ratione naturae, & essentiae suae, non verum & aeternum Deum, sed ϕῶς esse ἀνθρωπον: quod cum falsum sit, nemo non manifestum illum in argumento Ostorrodiano comparatorum elenchum deprehendit, & summam dissimilitudinem inter personas illas comparatas animadvertit. Christus enim aeterni Patris aeternus filius, in principio apud Deum fuit, & in sinu eius extitit ab aeterno, Iohan. 1. versu 1. & 18. Moses non item, unde ab uno ad alterum non perpetuo datur consequentia.
units.tr: Reply. First, by denying the consequence, which rests on a false hypothesis and a manifest begging of the question, in which it is always presupposed that Christ, by reason of his nature and essence, is not the true and eternal God but a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον]; which, since it is false, everyone sees at once is the manifest refutation of the comparisons made in Ostorrodius's argument, and notices the great dissimilarity between the persons compared. For Christ, the eternal Son of the eternal Father, was in the beginning with God, and has existed in his bosom from eternity, John 1:1 and 18. Moses is not so; hence there is no constant consequence from the one to the other.

units.la: Nec Aduersarium iuuat, quod Moses Christi typus fuit, quia ille non quoad personam & naturam, sed in quibusdam, quae spectabant officium atque munus mediatorium, Christum repraesentauit. Deinde falsum est quod affirmat in consequentiae probatione, nempe cultum per Mosem praescriptum tantum externum, & in rebus duntaxat corporalibus situm fuisse. Si enim Moses nihil aliud officii habuit quam ut populum Israeliticum ad Deum externis ritibus ac ceremoniis colendum induceret, quae causa est cur Deus in lege Israelitis lata, ut ipsum diligerent ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & ex omnibus viribus suis, postulauit? cur ex fide iustificatus dicitur Abraham, si ad obedientiam Deo praestandam externus cultus sufficiebat? Falsitatem illius dogmatis Samosateniani euertunt exempla omnium quotquot fidei nomine,& e recenio in Veteri Testamento celebrantur, vt prolixiore refutatione minime indigeat.
units.tr: Nor does it help the adversary that Moses was a type of Christ, since he represented Christ not in respect of person and nature, but in certain things which concerned the mediatorial office and function. Next, what he affirms in proving the consequence is false, namely that the worship prescribed through Moses was merely external and lay only in bodily things. For if Moses had no other office than to induce the people of Israel to worship God with external rites and ceremonies, what is the reason that God in the law given to the Israelites demanded that they love him with the whole heart, the whole soul and all their strength? Why is Abraham said to be justified by faith, if external worship was enough for rendering obedience to God? The examples of all who are celebrated in the Old Testament in the name of faith overthrow the falsehood of that Samosatenian dogma, so that it needs no lengthy refutation.

units.la: Quarto & vltimo inquit Aduersarius, ne quis hoc inusitatum & impossibile esse arbitretur,hominem videlicet priusquam moriatur, in cœlum ascendere,& iterum inde venire,considerandum esse exemplum Pauli,qui de se ipso testatus sit,quod in tertium vsque cœlum,& in paradisum raptus fuerit, 2. Cor.12.v.2. 4. Arbitrari autem Deum descendisse de cœlo,aut illuc ascendisse,omni rationi repugnare, quoniam cœlum thronus,& terra scabellum pedum ipsius est,Actor.7.ver.49. Ef.66.versu 1.
units.tr: Fourthly and lastly, says the adversary, lest anyone think this unusual and impossible, namely that a man should ascend into heaven before he dies and come down again from there, let the example of Paul be considered, who testified of himself that he was caught up into the third heaven and into paradise, 2 Cor. 12:2. 4. But to think that God descended from heaven, or ascended thither, is repugnant to all reason, since heaven is his throne and the earth the footstool of his feet, Acts 7:49; Isa. 66:1.

units.la: Resp.Exemplum Pauli non iuuat Aduersarium,non enim quæritur, an possibile sit, vel vsitatum, hominem aliquem à Deo in cœlum euehi, & rursus inde descendere, sed an Christus ante mortem & passionem suam, secundùm humanam ipsius naturam,in cœlum ascenderit,& inde rursus descenderit?quod ipsum ex Scripturis nunquam poterunt probare, nisi ex vno Pauli exemplo propositionem vniuersalem conficere velint, contra disciplinam Logicam.Quod verò ait rationi repugnare, si quis arbitretur, Deum descendere de cælo, aut in cœlum ascendere, eo ipso verbum Dei mentis humanæ excæcatæ deliriis subiicit, nec sententiam nostram, sed ipsam scripturam sacram impugnat, quæ Deum de cœlis descendisse palàm affirmat Gen.11.v.6.7.Exod.3.v.8.& 9. v.18.20. Num.11.v.17.25.& 12.v.5 Mich.1.v.3. De verborum sensu vt agamus,non postulat vlla necessitas,cùm sufficiat,ad refutandum Aduersarium, illud in scripturis de ipso Deo dici, quamuis de locali descensu illa intelligere vetet Dei simplicitas, ac immensitas,& apud Ioh.3.v.13. per ascensionem in cœlum, nihil aliud, quàm penetrationem ad inaccessam diuinitatis lucem,& cœlestium diuinæ voluntatis arcanorum cognitionem: per descensum autem ipsam incarnationem intelligendam esse, loci illius circunstantiç satis euidenter euincant.Atque sic hactenus vtramque nostram thesin de duabus in persona Christi naturis, eiusdémque æterna Deitate, à sophismatibus & blasphemiis Aduersarii vindicauimus: ille idem Dominus noster Iesus Christus largiatur nobis spiritum suum sanctum, spiritum illum veritatis, qui nos deducat in omnem veritatem, mentem & intelleεtum nostrum luce illius illuminet,vt cracula ipsius purè,& sanctè intelligamus: sapientiam concedat nobis, ut veritatem agnitam adversus mendaciorum praestigias, constanter, & sincerè tueamur, ad nominis sui gloriam, Ecclesiæ aedificationem, & animarum nostrarum æternam salutem: Amen.
units.tr: Reply. The example of Paul does not help the adversary. For the question is not whether it is possible, or customary, for some man to be carried up by God into heaven and come down again from there; but whether Christ, before his death and passion, ascended into heaven according to his human nature and descended again from there. This they will never be able to prove from the Scriptures, unless they wish to construct a universal proposition from the single example of Paul, contrary to the rules of logic. As for his saying that it is repugnant to reason if anyone thinks that God descends from heaven or ascends into heaven, by that very statement he subjects the word of God to the delusions of a blinded human mind, and he attacks not our opinion but the holy Scripture itself, which openly affirms that God descended from heaven, Gen. 11:6-7; Exod. 3:8-9; 18:20; Num. 11:17, 25; 12:5; Mic. 1:3. There is no need to inquire into the sense of the words, since it is enough, to refute the adversary, that it is said in the Scriptures of God himself, although God's simplicity and immensity forbid understanding that as a local descent; and that in John 3:13 the ascent into heaven means nothing other than penetration into the inaccessible light of the divinity and knowledge of the heavenly secrets of the divine will, while the descent is to be understood as the incarnation itself, the circumstances of that place make sufficiently clear. And so far we have vindicated both of our theses, concerning the two natures in the person of Christ and his eternal deity, from the sophisms and blasphemies of the adversary. May that same Lord Jesus Christ grant us his Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, who leads us into all truth, and illuminate our mind and understanding with the light of that Spirit, so that we may understand his oracles purely and holily; may he grant us wisdom, that we may steadfastly and sincerely defend the truth once recognised against the deceptions of lies, to the glory of his name, the building up of the Church, and the eternal salvation of our souls: Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: De Spiritu Sancto, tertia Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis persona.
units.tr: Of the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Most Holy Trinity.

units.la: QVIA in antecedentibus capitibus, de æterna Iesu Christi deitate, adversus Ostorrodium disputavimus, doctrinæ ipsius ratio postulat, ut de Spiritus sancti æterna deitate, αὐζήτως subiiciamus. Hic ergo quaeritur inter nos & Ostorrodium, cæterósque Samosatenianos, Vtrum Spiritus sanctus sit verum ὑφισάμεν, verâque persona, personali proprietate à Patre ac Filio distincta, & simul verus, ac æternus Deus, eiusdem cum Patre & Filio essentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis particeps? An verò tantum modo per modum qualitatis in Deo existat? Nos prius affirmamus, posterius negamus. Vt autem assertio nostra melius intelligatur, omnis vocabulorum πολυσημία & æquivocatio tollenda est. Nomen igitur Spiritus Sancti in Scripturis, & apud scriptores Ecclesiasticos, dupliciter accipitur, vel de substantia increata, vel de accidente aliquo ex gratia Electis à Deo concesso. De substantia increata enuntiatur, aut absolutè, & communiter, seu ὀνωδῶς de Patre, filio, ac Spiritu sancto, respectu videlicet proprietatum essentiæ, quæ tribus illis personis est communis, Ioh. 4. verf. 24. aut relatiuè, & singulariter, seu ὑφισατικῶς de tertia persona Trinitatis, quæ ὑπὸ ὑπάρξεως, & proprietate personali, à Patre ac filio distinguitur. De accidente autem in hominibus, & effecto tertiæ personæ in sacrosancta Trinitate cùm enuntiatur, tum motum, donum, aut virtutem aliquam Spiritus sancti significat, Iohan. 7. versu 38. 39. Qui credit in me, sicut dixit Scriptura, flumina aquæ vivæ ex ventre ipsius fluent. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu illo, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum, nondum enim erat Spiritus Spiritus Sanctus, quia Iesus nondum erat glorificatus. Vbi Spiritus proprie ὑπόστασιν Spiritus sancti significas pro χαρίσματα, id est, gratuitis, quorū Spiritus sanctus autor est, beneficiis, & salutaribus effectis, accipitur, unde Spiritus gratia Zachar. 12. v. 9. & Hebr. 10. v. 29. vocatur. Nos in praesente disputatione, nomē Spiritus S. in secunda significatione accipimus, ac dicimus, Spiritum sanctum esse personam in sacrosancta & individua Trinitate subsistentem, ordine tertiam, & secundum hypostasin a Patre, & Filio distinctam, & ab utroque σωαΐδιως emanantem, sive procedentem, aeternum, immensum, & infinitum, verúmque, ac unum illum Deum Israelis, eiusdem cum Patre ac Filio essentiae, maiestatis & gloriae participem. Atque hic quidem duo illa definitionis membra adversus Osiorrodium nobis sunt demonstranda: 1. quod Spiritus sanctus sit verum ὑφίσταμενον, verāque persona, à Patre ac Filio secundum hypostasin distincta. 2. quod sit verus ac aeternus Israelis Deus.
units.tr: Since in the preceding chapters we have disputed against Ostorodius concerning the eternal deity of Jesus Christ, the order of his teaching requires that we now treat, in the same way, the eternal deity of the Holy Spirit. The question between us and Ostorodius and the other Samosatenians is therefore this: Whether the Holy Spirit is a true subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] and a true person, distinguished from the Father and the Son by a personal property, and at the same time a true and eternal God, sharing the same essence, glory and majesty with the Father and the Son; or whether he exists in God only by way of a quality? We affirm the former and deny the latter. So that our assertion may be better understood, every ambiguity and equivocation of terms must be removed. The name Spirit of God in the Scriptures and among the ecclesiastical writers is taken in two ways: either of an uncreated substance, or of some accident bestowed by God on the elect as grace. Said of the uncreated substance, it is used either absolutely and in common, that is, essentially [οὐσιωδῶς], of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit with respect to the properties of the essence, which are common to those three persons (John 4:24); or relatively and singularly, that is, hypostatically [ὑφιστατικῶς], of the third person of the Trinity, who is distinguished from the Father and the Son by his hypostasis and personal property. When it is said of an accident in human beings, and of an effect of the third person in the Holy Trinity, it signifies a motion, a gift, or some power of the Holy Spirit (John 7:38, 39): He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this he spoke of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. Here "Spirit" does not properly signify the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, but is taken for the gifts [χαρίσματα], that is, the benefits and saving effects of which the Holy Spirit is the author; hence he is called the Spirit of grace (Zech. 12:9; Heb. 10:29). In the present disputation we take the name Holy Spirit in the second sense, and we say: The Holy Spirit is a person subsisting in the holy and undivided Trinity, third in order and distinct in hypostasis from the Father and the Son, proceeding eternally from both, eternal, immense and infinite, a true and one God of Israel, a partaker of the same essence, majesty and glory with the Father and the Son. Here the two parts of this definition must be demonstrated against Ostorodius: (1) that the Holy Spirit is a true subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] and a true person, distinct in hypostasis from the Father and the Son; (2) that he is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: 1. Primum membrum evidentissimè demonstratur ex illis attributis, quae omnium verè Philosophorum, & gentium non mo-nstrosarum consensu, solis rebus subsistentibus quae sub ratione personae concipiuntur, tribui solent. Cùm enim essentia, seu existentia, vita, intelligentia, voluntas, & potentia conuenit, id merito personae nomine indigitatur, verúmque est ὑφισάμενον, non vero aliquid secundum modum qualitatis, aut proprietatis in Deo existens: quę propositio tam certa est ac vera, vt nihil personae nomine appellari possit, si illa negetur, quia haec omnia soli rei subsistenti, ac personae, & quidem actu primo conueniunt, ac tribui possunt. Atqui Spiritui sancto conuenit 1. essentia, seu existetia, quia est in Deo, & à Deo emanat, ac à filio mittitur, 1. Cor. 2. versu 11. Iohan. 1 5. versu 26. 2. vita, quia incubat aquis, vt gallina pullis, Genes. 1. versu 2. Estque autor vitae animalis, & spiritualis viuentibus, Iohan. 33. versu 4. Spiritus Dei fecit me, & spiraculum omnipotentis viuificauit me. Iohannes 3. versu 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum Dei. Roman 8. versu 2. Lex Spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu liberauit me à lege peccati, & mortis: & versu 11. Sed si Spiritus eius, qui excitauit Iesum à mortuis, habitat in vobis, is, qui excitauit Christum ex mortuis, viuificabit etiam mortalia vestra corpora, per inhabitantem eius Spiritum in vobis. 3. intelligentia, quia scrutatur profunditates Dei, 1. Corinth. 12. versu 11. Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. 4. voluntas, quia distribuit sua dona prout vult, 1.Cor.12.v. 11. Sed omnia haec efficit unus ille & idem Spiritus dividens privatim singulis sicut vult. 5.potentia, qua Prophetæ, aliíque sancti, & ipse adeò Messias instruitur, & corroboratur. Mich 3. vers 8. Verumtamen ego repletus sum fortitudine Spiritus Domini, iudicio & virtute, ut annuntiem Iacob sceleus suum, & Israel peccatum suum. Eph.3 v.16. Ut det vobis pro divitiis suæ gloriæ, ut fortiter corroboremini per Spiritum suum in interiore homine. Ef.11. versu 2. Super quo quiescet Spiritus Iehovah, Spiritus sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, Spiritus consilii, & potentiæ, Spiritus scientiæ, & reverentiæ Iehovæ. Ex quibus omnibus necessario sequitur, Spiritum sanctum esse verum ὑφιστάμενον veramque personam, non autem aliquid secundum modum qualitatis, aut proprietatis in Deo existens.
units.tr: 1. The first part is most evidently demonstrated from those attributes which, by the agreement of all true philosophers and of the non-monstrous nations, are customarily ascribed only to subsisting things conceived under the notion of a person. For when essence or existence, life, understanding, will and power belong to something, it is rightly designated by the name of person; and it is a subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον], not something existing in God merely in the manner of a quality or property. This proposition is so certain and true that nothing can be called a person if this is denied, since all these things belong to and can be ascribed to a subsisting thing and a person, and to it chiefly and in the first act. But the following belong to the Holy Spirit: (1) essence or existence, since he is in God and proceeds from God, and is sent by the Son (1 Cor. 2:11; John 15:26). (2) Life, since he broods over the waters as a hen over her chicks (Gen. 1:2), and is the author of animal and spiritual life to the living (John 3:4 [sic]): The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life. (John 3:5): Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. (Rom. 8:2): The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death. (Rom. 8:11): But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. (3) Understanding, since he searches the depths of God (1 Cor. 2:10, 11): The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. (4) Will, since he distributes his gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11): But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who divides to each one individually as he wills. (5) Power, by which the prophets and other saints, and the Messiah himself, are equipped and strengthened (Mic. 3:8): But truly I am filled with the power of the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin. (Eph. 3:16): That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might through his Spirit in the inner man. (Isa. 11:2): The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord. From all these it necessarily follows that the Holy Spirit is a true subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] and a true person, and not something existing in God merely as a quality or property.

units.la: Deinde,id ipsum etiam probatur ex iis attributis, quæ nulli rei quàm subsistenti, ac personæ, actu secundo convenire possunt. Quicunque enim creat, conservat, vivifi cat, scientia, fide, charitate, spe, timore Domini, fortitudine, patientia, aliisque virtutibus instruit, docet, ducit in omnem veritatem, est paracletus, distribuit dona, irruit in Samsonem, recedit à Saule, mittit Prophetas, vocat & constituit Apostolos, descendit corporea specie tanquam columba super Christum, loquitur in Apostolis, annuntiat futura, tentatur ab Anania & Sapphira, testatur in cœlo cum Patre & filio, irascitur, blasphemia & contumelia afficitur: is inquâ cui ista omnia tribuuntur, verum est ὑφιστάμενον veráque persona, non autem qualitas tantum, ac proprietas divina. Atqui spiritui sancto illa omnia tribuuntur, Iob 33. v. 4. Iud.14. verf.6. 1.Sam.16. versu 14. Ef. 1.v.2. Luc.12.v.12. Ioh.16.v.13. Luc.1.v.33. Ef.61.v.1. Act.20.28. Act.13.v.2. & 16.v.7. & 20. versu 22. Matth.10. versu 20. Ioh.16. versu 13. Luc.3.22. 1.Cor.12. versu 11. Act.5. versu 9. 1.Ioh.5. versu 7. Ef.63. versu 10. Matth.12. versu 31 32. Hebr.10. versu 29.
units.tr: Next, the same is also proved from those attributes which can belong to nothing but a subsisting thing and person in the second act. For whoever creates, preserves and quickens; who instructs and teaches in knowledge, faith, love, hope, the fear of the Lord, fortitude and patience, and other virtues; who leads into all truth; who is the Paraclete; who distributes gifts; who rushes upon Samson; who departs from Saul; who sends prophets; who calls and appoints apostles; who descends in bodily form like a dove upon Christ; who speaks in the apostles; who foretells the future; who is tempted by Ananias and Sapphira; who bears witness in heaven with the Father and the Son; who is angered, and is blasphemed and insulted: he, I say, to whom all these things are ascribed, is a true subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] and a true person, and not merely a divine quality or property. But all these things are ascribed to the Holy Spirit: Job 33:4; Judg. 14:6; 1 Sam. 16:14; Isa. 1:2; Luke 12:12; John 16:13; Luke 1:33; Isa. 61:1; Acts 20:28; Acts 13:2; Acts 16:7; Acts 20:22; Matt. 10:20; John 16:13; Luke 3:22; 1 Cor. 12:11; Acts 5:9; 1 John 5:7; Isa. 63:10; Matt. 12:31, 32; Heb. 10:29.

units.la: Ergo Spiritus sanctus est verum ὑφιστάμενον, & vera persona, non autem aliquid tantum per modum qualitatis & proprietatis inni Deo existens.
units.tr: Therefore the Holy Spirit is a true subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] and a true person, and not merely something existing in God by way of a quality and property.

units.la: Tertiò, Si Spiritus sanctus est qualitas in Deo existens, tum est vel propria, vel essentialis, adeóque infinita, æterna, & immensa: aut est accidens tantum. Atqui non est Accidens, sic enim Deus compositus esset ex substantia, & sequeretur Deum non esse Deum, quod vel cogitare horrendum esset. Neque etiam est qualitas, seu proprietas Dei essentialis, quia Spiritus Dei accidens est in Christo secundùm Aduersariorum doctrinam, qui Christum ratione naturæ & essentiæ, ϑλὸν ἀξίωτον esse affirmant. quicquid autem est accidens in vno subiecto, id est impossibile, vt sit qualitas seu proprietas essentialis in alio subiecto. Impossibile enim est, vt persona creata finitáque, qualis ex ipsorum hypothesi est persona Christi, capax sit qualitatis seu proprietatis increatæ, infinitæ, & æternæ. Vnde sequitur Spiritum sanctum non esse meram qualitatem in Deo existentem.
units.tr: Thirdly, if the Holy Spirit is a quality existing in God, then it is either a proper or essential quality, and so infinite, eternal and immense, or it is merely an accident. But he is not an accident, for then God would be composed of substance, and it would follow that God is not God, which is horrible even to think. Nor is he an essential quality or property of God, because according to the doctrine of our opponents, who affirm that Christ, by reason of his nature and essence, is a mere man, the Spirit of God is an accident in Christ. And whatever is an accident in one subject cannot be an essential quality or property in another subject. For it is impossible that a created and finite person, such as the person of Christ is on their hypothesis, should be capable of an uncreated, infinite and eternal quality or property. Hence it follows that the Holy Spirit is not a mere quality existing in God.

units.la: Alterum vero membrum, quod videlicet Spiritus Sanctus sit verus & æternus Deus Israelis, solidè demonstrari potest, argumentis sequentibus. Primò, quia distertis verbis Deus Israelis appellatur 2. Sam. 23. v. 1. Hæc sunt verba nouissima, quæ dixit Dauid, Spiritus Domini loquutus est per me, & sermo eius per linguam meam, dixit Deus Israel, mihi loquutus est fortis Israelis, Dominator hominum. Vnde ita argumentamur.
units.tr: The second point, that the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God of Israel, can be firmly demonstrated by the following arguments. First, because he is named expressly the God of Israel in 2 Sam. 23. v. 1: These are the last words of David: The Spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue. The God of Israel said, the strong one of Israel spoke to me, the ruler of men. From this we argue as follows.

units.la: Qui dicitur à Dauide Deus Israel, fortis Israel, Dominator hominum, ille etiam est verus & æternus Deus Israel.
units.tr: He who is called by David the God of Israel, the strong one of Israel, the ruler of men, is also the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: Atqui Spiritus sanctus à Dauide dicitur Deus, & fortis Israel, Dominator hominum.
units.tr: But the Holy Spirit is called God by David, and the strong one of Israel, the ruler of men.

units.la: Ergo Spiritus sanctus est verus & æternus Deus Israel.
units.tr: Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: II. Ex Nouo Testamento, Matth. 28. v. 19. Baptizate in nomine Patris, Filij, ac Spiritus sancti. In cuius autem nomen baptizamur, is non nisi verus & æternus Deus est. Atqui baptizamur in nomen spiritus sancti. Ergo spiritus sanctus verus & æternus Deus est.
units.tr: II. From the New Testament, Matt. 28. v. 19: Baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But he into whose name we are baptized is none other than the true and eternal God. But we are baptized into the name of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Quod ad maioris confirmationem, & declarationem cõsequutionis attinet, Apostolus Paulus hæc tria, Deũ, fidem, baptisma, Eph. 4. ver. 5. 6. ita coniungit (sicut iam supra explicuimus) vt quia vna est fides, ex eo vnum esse Deum demonstret, & quia vnus est baptismus, inde quoque vnam esse fidem ostendat. Fides enim in vnum Deum spectare & conferri debet, ac in eo hærere: vnde conficitur, quod si varia sint fidei genera, plures etiam esse deos oporteat. Quia verò sacramentum fidei est baptismus, ipsius vnitatem nobis confirmat ex eo quod vnus est. Hinc etiam conficitur, vt nõ nisi in vnum Deum baptizari liceat, quia eius amplectimur fidem, in cuius nomen baptizamur. Ex quibus manifestè liquet, Christũ, quum in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti baptizari précépit, nihil aliud voluisse, quàm in Deum Patrem, Filium,ac Sp. S. credendum esse, quod ipsum nihil aliud est, quàm aperte testari, Patrem, Filium,ac Sp. S. vnum Deum esse. Deinde cui metitus est Ananias,ille est verus Deus,Act. 5. v. 4. Atqui Ananias mentitus est Spiritui sancto, Act. 5. v.3. Ergo Spiritus sanctus est verus Deus.
units.tr: As for the confirmation and clarification of this inference, the Apostle Paul joins these three things, God, faith, and baptism, in Eph. 4. v. 5, 6 (as we have already explained above), so that, because there is one faith, he shows from this that there is one God, and because there is one baptism, he likewise shows from this that there is one faith. For faith ought to look to and be directed toward one God, and cling to him; hence it follows that if there were different kinds of faith, there would also have to be several gods. Since baptism is the sacrament of faith, it confirms to us its unity from the fact that it is one. From this too it follows that we may be baptized only into one God, because we embrace the faith of him into whose name we are baptized. From these things it is plainly clear that Christ, when he commanded baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, wanted nothing other than that we believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and this is nothing other than to testify openly that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. Further, he whom Ananias lied to is the true God, Acts 5. v. 4. But Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Acts 5. v. 3. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true God.

units.la: III. Ex collatione Veteris,ac Noui Testamenti. De quo in Nouo Testamento à Christo & Apostolis ea exponuntur, quæ in Veteri Testamento, de vero & æterno Deo Israelis,dicta sunt,ille est verus & æternus Deus Israelis. Atqui de Spiritu sancto in Nouo Testamento ea exponuntur, quæ in Veteri Testamento de vero, & æterno Deo Israelis dicta sunt. Ergo Spiritus sanctus est verus, & æternus Deus Israelis. Minor demonstratur Esa. 6. versu 7 8.9. 10. Et audiui vocem Domini dicentis, quem mittam, & quis ibit nobis? Cui dixi, en ego, mitte me: Et dixit, Vade, vt dicas populo isti, audite indesinenter, at ne intelligatis, & videte indesinenter, neque cognoscatis. Act. vlt. versu 25. 26. Quum autem inter se disscordes essent, discesserunt, quum Paulus hoc verbum dixisset, Rectè sane Spiritus sanctus locutus est per Esaiam Prophetam Patribus nostris, dicens, Vade ad populum istam, & dic, Auditu audietis, & non intelligetis, & videntes videbitis, & non cernetis. Deinde omnes Prophetæ, cùm sermones ad populum facerent, plerúmque ita aspicabantur. Hæc dicit Dominus: Act.2. Pet 1. v.25. Acti à Spiritu sancto, loquuti esse dicuntur olim sancti Dei homines. Exod. 4. versu 11. 12. Tum dixit Iehoua illi, quis statuit os homini, aut quis statuere potest mutum aut surdum, aut sensibus valentem, aut cæcum? nónne ego Iehouah? Nunc itaque ito, & ego adero ori tuo, & docebo te, quæ loquuturus es. Matth.10. v. 20. Non vos estis qui loquimini, sed Spiritus Patris vestri is est, qui loquitur in vobis.
units.tr: III. From a comparison of the Old and New Testaments. Whatever things in the New Testament are said by Christ and the Apostles of which the things said in the Old Testament about the true and eternal God of Israel are asserted, that one is the true and eternal God of Israel. But things are asserted in the New Testament about the Holy Spirit which are said in the Old Testament about the true and eternal God of Israel. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God of Israel. The minor premise is demonstrated from Isa. 6. verses 7, 8, 9, 10: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? To whom I said, Here am I, send me. And he said, Go, and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; see indeed, but do not perceive. Acts last chapter, verses 25, 26: When they disagreed among themselves, they departed, after Paul had spoken this word: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers, saying, Go to this people and say, By hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. Then all the prophets, when they addressed the people, were usually regarded in this way: Thus says the Lord. 2 Pet. 1. v. 25: Moved by the Holy Spirit, the holy men of God are said to have spoken of old. Exod. 4. verses 11, 12: Then the LORD said to him, Who made man's mouth? Or who makes the mute or deaf, the seeing or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall say. Matt. 10. v. 20: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

units.la: IV. Ab operibus diuinis. Qui est creator cœli, terræ atq; hominum, & iustificat nos ac saluat, ille est verus, & æternus Deus Israelis Ier.10.v.11. Ef.44.v.10. Pf.96.v.5. Pfal.51.v.6. Ef.43.v.12. quiq; reddit nos diuinæ naturæ participes, in eo naturam diuinam, eúmque Deum esse necesse est. Atqui Spiritus sanctus est creator cœli & terræ, Pfal 33.v.6. Verbo Iehoua cœli facti sunt, & spiritu oris eius totus exercitus eorum. Et 104.v. 30. Te emittente Spiritum tuum recreantur, denique renouas faciem terræ, Iob. 26. v.13. Spiritu suo cœlos ornauit, Et hominis, Iob.33.v.9. Spiritus Dei fecit me, & spiraculum omnipotentis vivificauit me. Deinde iustificat nos ac saluat, 1. Cor. 6. 10. verf. 11. v.11.Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis in nomine Domini, & per spiritum Dei nostri. Denique reddit nos naturae diuinae participes, 2.Petr.1.versu 9.Ergo Spiritus sanctus, est verus & aeternus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: IV. From the divine works. He who is the creator of heaven, earth, and men, and who justifies and saves us, is the true and eternal God of Israel: Jer. 10. v. 11; Isa. 44. v. 10; Ps. 96. v. 5; Ps. 51. v. 6; Isa. 43. v. 12. And he who makes us partakers of the divine nature must have the divine nature and be God. But the Holy Spirit is the creator of heaven and earth, Ps. 33. v. 6: By the word of the LORD were the heavens made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth. And Ps. 104. v. 30: When you send forth your Spirit, they are created; and you renew the face of the earth. Job 26. v. 13: By his Spirit he adorned the heavens. And of man, Job 33. v. 9: The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life. Further, he justifies and saves us, 1 Cor. 6. v. 11: But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord and by the Spirit of our God. Finally, he makes us partakers of the divine nature, 2 Pet. 1. v. 4. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God of Israel.

units.la: V.Ab attributis Dei essentialibus.Cui tribuuntur in Scripturis sacris essentialia Dei attributa, & proprietates diuinae, ille est verus & aeternus Deus:Atqui Spiritui sancto,tribuuntur, in scriptura sacra, essentiales Dei proprietates, & attributa diuina, vt infinitas,omniscientia,omnipotentia,aeternitas,atque immensitas. Infinitatem enim Spiritus sancti probat eius,tum omniscientia, qua etiam profunditates Dei scrutari dicitur,omniaque nosse, quae in Deo sunt, 1.Cor.2.v.10.11. tum eius omnipotentia, qua cuncta creauit, & conseruat,vt paulo ante demonstrauimus. Aeternitatem illius solide euincit,tum rerum omnium creatio. Quicquid enim ante omnia, quae facta sunt, extitit:id aeternum est,tum tituli quibus insignitur:virtus enim altissimi,& Digitus Dei nuncupatur, Luc.1. v.35. & 11.v. 20. qui tituli rei principium temporis habenti,conuenire nequeunt. Immensitatis denique luculentissimum testimonium est, quod nemo a Spiritu Dei fugere possit: & Spiritus Domini in sanctis omnibus, tanquam in templo, habitare dicitur, Psal.139.v.7. 1.Cor.6.19. Ex quibus omnibus liquido iam constat, Spiritum sanctum non esse qualitatem aliquam,aut proprietatem diuinam,sed verum ὑφισάμενον, verumque, aeternum, & unum esse cum Patre,& filio Deum adorandum,& religiose colendum.
units.tr: V. From the essential attributes of God. He to whom the essential attributes and divine properties of God are ascribed in the holy Scriptures is the true and eternal God. But the Holy Spirit is ascribed in Holy Scripture the essential properties of God and divine attributes, such as infinity, omniscience, omnipotence, eternity, and immensity. For the infinity of the Holy Spirit is proved both by his omniscience, by which he is said to search the depths of God and to know all things that are in God (1 Cor. 2. v. 10, 11), and by his omnipotence, by which he created and preserves all things, as we demonstrated a little earlier. His eternity is firmly established both by the creation of all things and by the titles by which he is marked: for he is called the power of the Most High and the finger of God (Luke 1. v. 35; 11. v. 20), which titles cannot belong to a being that has a beginning in time. Finally, the most striking testimony to his immensity is that no one can flee from the Spirit of God, and that the Spirit of the Lord is said to dwell in all the saints as in a temple (Ps. 139. v. 7; 1 Cor. 6. v. 19). From all these things it now clearly stands that the Holy Spirit is not some quality or divine property, but a true subsisting being [ὑφιστάμενον], and a true and eternal God, one with the Father and the Son, to be worshipped and devoutly honoured.

units.la: Osiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite quarto,pagina trigesima secunda,sectione quarta,inquit Sp. S. non esse personam ab vno illo vero Deo,nempe Patre,distinctam,sed tantum potentiam ipsius,non quidem quamlibet, sed eam tantum per quam Deus aliqua ratione sanctificat. Atque ad hoc ipsum demonstrandum,non multis Scripturae testimoniis opus esse,sed verba Christi,quibus Luc.24. versf.49. inquit, Vos manete in urbe Hierusalem vsquequo induamini virtute ex alto, euidenter illud demonstrare,quum virtus ex alto nihil aliud sit, quam virtus, seu potentia altissimi,adeoque veri,& unius Dei.
units.tr: Osiander, in the fourth chapter of his Institutes, page thirty-two, section four, says: The Holy Spirit is not a person distinct from that one true God, namely the Father, but only his power, not any power whatever, but only that by which God sanctifies in some way. And to demonstrate this very point, he says, many testimonies of Scripture are not needed, but the words of Christ, in which (Luke 24, verse 49) he says, "You remain in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high," clearly demonstrate it, since power from on high is nothing other than the power or might of the Most High, and so of the true and one God.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si spiritus sanctus in scripturis sacris dicitur virtus altissimi, seu virtus ex alto, tum sequitur,cum non esse personam a Patre distinctam,sed tantum potentiam Dei,non quidem quamlibet,sed eam tantum per quam Deus aliquo modo sanctificat: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If the Holy Spirit is called in the sacred Scriptures the power of the Most High, or the power from on high, then it follows that he is not a person distinct from the Father, but only the power of God, not any power whatever, but only that power by which God sanctifies in some way. But the first is true. Therefore the second is also.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse salsissimam, ac duplici elencho oppositorum nempe, & notationis, laborare. Esse enim virtutem Dei, & esse personam minime inter se opponuntur, sic ut posito eo, quod Spiritus sanctus sit virtus altissimi, inde sequatur Spiritum sanctum non esse personam divinam, verumque ὑφεστῶν. Huius ratio haec est, quod Spiritus sanctus non eam ob causam Virtus Dei ex alto dicitur, quod sit qualitas aliqua in Deo, sed ab effecto, quia videl. per eum δύναμις, hoc est, virtutes miraculosae edūtur, & quia illae virtutum & miraculorum istorum efficax est causa per quam Deus agit. Quod vero annectit Oftorrodius, Spiritum sanctum esse eam tantum potentiam Dei, quae aliqua ratione sanctificat, aeque falsum est, ut ex iis, quae in argumento nostro membri primi, & tertio membri secundi, de Spiritu sancto, demonstravimus, manifeste liquet. Quibus & hoc accedit, quod idem Spiritus sanctus digitus Dei nuncupatur, Luc. 11. ver. 20. At digitus Dei non in omnibus actionibus suis sanctificat, ut liquet ex Exod. 8. verf. 16 & 17. & 19. ubi digitus Dei puluerem terrae in pediculos per totam Aegyptiorum terram conuertisse dicitur, quod non sanctificare, sed maledicere & punire est.
units.tr: Reply. The inference is most absurd, and it suffers from a double fallacy of opposites, namely of the notation. For being the power of God and being a person are in no way opposed to each other, so that, granting that the Holy Spirit is the power of the Most High, it would follow that the Holy Spirit is not a divine person but a real subsistence [ὑφεστῶν]. The reason for this is that the Holy Spirit is called the power of God from on high not because he is some quality in God, but from his effect: namely, because through him powers [δύναμις], that is, miraculous works, are brought forth, and because he is the efficient cause of those powers and miracles through which God acts. As for what Ostorrodius adds, that the Holy Spirit is only that power of God which sanctifies in some way, it is as false as is clearly shown by what we demonstrated in our argument concerning the first member and the third member of the second, about the Holy Spirit. To these is added the fact that the same Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, Luke 11:20. But the finger of God does not sanctify in all its actions, as is clear from Exodus 8:16, 17 and 19, where the finger of God is said to have turned the dust of the earth into lice throughout the whole land of the Egyptians, which is not to sanctify but to curse and punish.

units.la: Secundo, dicit Oftorrodius, quicquid ex sacris literis ad demonstrandam Spiritus sanctitatem adduci possit, illud hac ratione contineri, quod videlicet in scriptura sacra Spiritui sancto ea tribuantur, quae proprie personis tantum conueniunt. Ad hanc autem rationem respondet negando consequentiam, & negationis suae hanc rationem adfert, quia videlicet de multis rebus, in Scripturis, ea quae personarum sunt propria, enuntiantur, quae tamen perse non sint. Quum itaque Spiritus sanctus virtus sit ac potentia Dei, mirandum non esse, inquit, quod ipsi multa, quae Dei propria sunt, tribuantur. Atque hinc etiam esse, quod per nomen Spiritus sancti ipsum Deum sapius intelligere oporteat.
units.tr: Secondly, Ostorrodius says, whatever can be brought from the sacred writings to demonstrate the holiness of the Spirit is contained in this, namely that in Scripture those things are attributed to the Holy Spirit which properly belong only to persons. To this argument he replies by denying the inference, and he gives this reason for his denial: because in the Scriptures many things are said of things which are not persons in themselves, yet which are proper to persons. Since therefore the Holy Spirit is the virtue and power of God, it is not to be wondered at, he says, that many things which are proper to God are attributed to him. And hence too it is that by the name of the Holy Spirit one must often understand God himself.

units.la: Argumentum Oftorrodij tale est.
units.tr: The argument of Ostorrodius is this.

units.la: Si in scripturis sacris multa rebus, quae tamen personae non sunt, ea tribuuntur, quae personis sunt propria, tum etiam ex eo, quod attribuat personarum, & rerum subsistentium propria, de Spiritu sancto praedicantur, minime sequitur, Spiritum sanctum personam divinam esse.
units.tr: If in the sacred Scriptures many things which are not persons are given those things which are proper to persons, then also from the fact that the attributes proper to persons and to subsisting things are predicated of the Holy Spirit, it by no means follows that the Holy Spirit is a divine person.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp.Si qualitatibus nonnullis in Scripturis sacris, vel actiones, vel nomina substantiarum & personarum propria,proprie, & iisdem de causis tribuuntur,quibus attributa illa, quæ rerum subsistentium sunt propria, de Spiritu sancto enunciantur, tū consequetia vera fuerit,sed minor falsa. Primo, quia nomina substantiarum & subiectorum in Scripturis sacris sæpe adiunctis, hoc est, qualitatibus in subiectis inhærentibus, & qualitatū actionibus, tribuuntur per αὐξωσιν &emphaticam metonymiam:quia videlicet non tantum ipsæ substantiæ, per eiusmodi qualitates, veluti per instrumenta,sunt efficaces,sed etiam,& quidem maximè,quia qualitates illæ formis ipsis substantiarum dant,ut sic agant,quod exemplo carnis & spiritus,quatenus illa natiuam corruptionem , hic vero inchoatam regenerationem , denotat : veteris item & noui hominis, fit manifestum. At vero hoc de Deo Patre & Spiritu sancto dici minime potest. Secundo , quum in Scripturis sacris iis rebus quæ ὑποστάσεις non sunt,ea tribuuntur,quę proprie personarum,tum improprias prædicationes illas esse demonstrari poterit. Spiritui sancto autem in scripturis sacris proprie tribui ea , quæ non nisi rerum subsistentium hypostasibus seu personis conueniunt , ex tribus illis quæ nos adduximus argumentis,euidentissimè liquet. Tertio, quia ipsum spiritum sanctum,non tantum personam , sed etiam verum & æternum Deum esse demonstrauimus.Ex quibus omnibus liquidò constat consequentiam Aduersarii manifestò compa-ratorum laborare elencho , ac proinde vanam esse atque futilem.
units.tr: Reply. If, in the sacred Scriptures, actions or names proper to substances and persons are attributed properly, and for the same reasons, to certain qualities, as those attributes which are proper to subsisting things are said of the Holy Spirit, then the inference would be valid, but the minor premise would be false. First, because the names of substances and subjects in the sacred Scriptures are often joined with their adjuncts, that is, with the qualities inhering in subjects and with the actions of the qualities, and are attributed by way of amplification and emphatic metonymy: namely because not only the substances themselves are effective through such qualities, as through instruments, but also, and indeed chiefly, because those qualities give to the forms of the substances themselves that they act in such a way. This becomes clear from the example of flesh and spirit, insofar as the former denotes native corruption, the latter the inchoate regeneration; likewise of the old and new man. But this can by no means be said of God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Secondly, since in the sacred Scriptures those things which are not hypostases are given what is properly of persons, it will be possible to show that those predications are improper. But that in the sacred Scriptures the Holy Spirit is properly given those things which belong only to the hypostases or persons of subsisting things, is most clearly evident from the three arguments which we have adduced. Thirdly, because we have demonstrated that the Holy Spirit himself is not only a person but also the true and eternal God. From all these things it is plainly established that the inference of our opponent manifestly suffers from a fallacy of comparison, and therefore is empty and futile.

units.la: Hactenus itaque demonstrauimus veritatem doctrinæ, nostræ, de vera & æterna Filii ac spiritus sancti Deitate, ad quam obscuran-dam , & nobis eripiendam,nihil hactenus ab Osiorrodio nisi phaleratas nugas vanissimorum sophismatum & anilium fallaciarum allatum esse,liquidò constat. Dominus noster Iesus Christus veritatem suam à mendacio hominum vindicet, & seductas à veritatis tramite animas à tyrannide satanæ,tenebrarúmque potestate,ad se reuocet , lucémque suam admirabilem ipsi cum Patre,ac spiritu sancto sit laus,& honor in secula.
units.tr: Thus far we have demonstrated the truth of our doctrine concerning the true and eternal Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit; and it is plainly established that, in order to obscure this and snatch it from us, Ostorrodius has so far brought nothing but the gaudy trifles of most vain sophisms and old-wives' fallacies. May our Lord Jesus Christ vindicate his truth from the lies of men, and recall to himself souls seduced from the path of truth, away from the tyranny of Satan and the power of darkness; and to him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise and honour, and his wonderful light, for ever.

units.la: CAPVT XX. De Incarnatione Filij Dei.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. On the Incarnation of the Son of God.

units.la: NOS Christum Θεάνθρωπον dicimus esse personam, in qua duae naturae divina & humana hypostaticè, sed ἀτρέπτως, ἀσυγχύτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, & ἀχωρίστως unitae, unum singulare προσωπον Iesum Christum constituunt, ad ea omnia peragenda, quibus perfectè salus nostra obtineatur. Rom.1.v.3.4. De Filio suo facto ex semine Dauid, secundum carnem: declarato filio Dei potenter secundum spiritum sanctificationis, per resurrectionem a mortuis, nempe Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Et cap.9.v.5. Quorum sunt Patres, & ex quibus est Christus, quod ad carnem attinet, qui est supra omnes Deos laudandus in saecula. 1. Tim.3.v.16. Et sine controuersia magnum est pietatis mysterium, Deus conspicuus factus est in carne, iustificatus est in spiritu, conspectus est ab Angelis, praedicatus est Gentibus, fides illi habita est in mundo, susum receptus est in gloriam. Hebr.2.v.17. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, ut misericors esset, & fidelis Pontifex in iis, quae apud Deum (agenda sunt) ad expiandum peccata populi. Hebr.5.verf.1. Nam omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumitur, & pro hominibus constituitur in iis, quae apud Deum (agenda sunt) ut offerat donaria, & victimas pro peccatis.
units.tr: We say that Christ is the God-man [Theanthropon], a single person in whom the two natures, divine and human, are united hypostatically, yet without change [atreptōs], without confusion [asynchytōs], without division [adiairetōs], and without separation [achōristōs]. They constitute one singular person [prosōpon], Jesus Christ, to carry out all those things by which our salvation is fully obtained. Rom. 1:3-4: "Concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, namely Jesus Christ our Lord." And Rom. 9:5: "Of whom are the fathers, and of whom Christ came according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever." 1 Tim. 3:16: "And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory." Heb. 2:17: "Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people." Heb. 5:1: "For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins."

units.la: Ad huius autem Redemptoris nostri pleniorem cognitionem consequendam, in persona ipsius suppositum, in suppposito naturas, in naturis unionem, in unione officium, & denique in officio statum rite dignoscere nos oportet. De veritate tum suppositi, quod est secunda sacrosanctae Trinitatis persona ab aeterno subsistens: tum etiam naturae eius diuinae, iam in antecedentib.contra Aduersarium disputauimus: de officio autem infra suo loco acturi. Et quum in eo consentiamus, quod in Christo sit vera humana natura, hoc est, plena, integra, & perfecta essentia veri animi, ac veri corporis, cum omnibus utriusque proprietatibus: in hoc autem discrepemus, quod illi negato & suppositio diuino, & natura diuina, naturam humanam Christi in se constituant: nos vero ἀνυπόστατον, id est, propria, humana, & creata personapersonalitate destitutam, in λόγῳ perpetuam subsistentiam habere, affir-mamus, restat ut duarum illarum naturarum, diuinę nempe & humanæ vnionem contra Aduersarios, demonstremus. Verbum itaque, id est, secundam personam sacrosanctæ Trinitatis naturam humanam, ex substantia Mariæ virginis assumptam, & ἀνυπόστατον, ac propria personalitate destitutam, in personæ suæ vnitatem, sibi coniunxisse credimus, & sequentibus rationibus, ac scripturæ testimoniis, demonstramus.
units.tr: To attain a fuller knowledge of this our Redeemer, we ought rightly to distinguish in his person the suppositum, in the suppositum the natures, in the natures the union, in the union the office, and finally in the office the state. We have already disputed against our opponent in the preceding chapters about the truth of the suppositum, which is the second person of the most holy Trinity, subsisting from eternity, and also about his divine nature; we shall treat of his office in its proper place below. And since we agree that in Christ there is a true human nature, that is, a full, entire and perfect essence of a true soul and a true body, with all the properties of each; but we differ in this, that they, denying both a divine suppositum and a divine nature, hold that the human nature of Christ constitutes itself as a person; whereas we affirm that it is anhypostatic, that is, lacking its own proper, human and created person, lacking personality, in the Word having perpetual subsistence. It remains for us to demonstrate against our opponents the union of those two natures, the divine and the human. Therefore we believe that the Word, that is, the second person of the most holy Trinity, has joined to itself in the unity of his person the human nature, taken from the substance of the Virgin Mary, which is anhypostatic and destitute of its own personality; and we demonstrate this by the following arguments and testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM I. Si Christus est persona æterna, & æternus Deus, eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ, potentiæ, maiestatis, & gloriæ particeps, omnisque mutationis expers, & in tempore homo factus, & ex Maria virgine natus, & vnus tantum est Christus, vnica etiam persona & hypostasis Christi, tum sequitur, Verbum, id est, secundam personam sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, humanam naturam ἀνυπόστατον, & propria personalitate destitutam, in personæ suæ vnitatem assumpsisse. Secus enim humana natura, aut extra λόγον vagaretur omni personalitate destituta, quod est absurdum, aut propriam humanam, & creatam haberet hypostasin, & sic duo Christi, & duo filij Dei constituerentur, quod est impium. Atqui antecedens totum est verum. Veram enim & æternam Dei-tatem Filij, capitibus antecedentibus euidenter asseruimus. Natum vero esse Christum in tempore ex Maria virgine, & vnum tantum esse Christum, vnicamque personam & hypostasin Christi, apud vtramque est extra controuersiam: sic vt illa argumenta, & scripturæ testimonia, quibus veritas integra & perfecta naturæ humanæ Christi, aduersus Marcionitas, Manichæos, Arianos, Anabaptistas, & similis farinæ homines, in medium adferre, ad discutiendam illam, de qua disceptatur, quaestionem, non sit necessarium. Atque ad hanc primam rationem referenda sunt omnia argumenta, quibus Christum, non tantum verum hominem, sed etiam verum ac æternum Deum esse, demonstratur, de quibus in antecedentibus egimus. Ergo & consequens est verum. ARGVMENTVM II. desumitur ex Iohan. I. v. 14. Vbi Sermo caro factus esse dicitur. Per Sermonem autem intelligi verum & æternum Deum, id est, secundam personam sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, Filium nempe Dei, cœli ac terræ, cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto, creatorem, supra capite decimotertio demonstrauimus. Carnis vero nomine, quum de homine enuntiatur, primò, & per se ipsam substantiam, & naturam humanam, deinde vero fragilitatem, & mortalitatem, caeterasque proprietates accidentales, quae statum & conditionem hominis sequuntur, significari, ex scripturis sacris est manifestum. Vt Gen. 6. v. 12. Aspiciens Deus terram, & ecce corrupta erat, quia corruperat omnis caro viam suam, super terram, id est, omnis homo: Ioel. 2. v. 18. Eritque postea, vt effundam Spiritum meum super omnem carnem, id est, omnem hominem, vt verba sequentia manifestè docet. Sic Psal. 16. v. 10. & Act. 2. v. 31. Et quoties Christus carnem pro mundi vita dare dicitur, caro humanam Christi naturam significat. Vnde etiam Rom. 1. v. 3. Filius Dei factus ex semine Dauidis appellatur secundùm carnem, id est, secundùm humanam naturam. Ex quibus, vt & aliis pluribus Scripturae locis euidenter apparet, vocem carnis interdum, & quidem frequenter totum hominem, totásque Christi humanam naturā denotare. Es autem 40. v. 6. & Psal. 78. v. 39. idem nomen carnis ipsam fragilitatē, & imbecillitatem hominis, id est, hominē fragilem, imbecillem, & mortale significat, vt locorum circunstantię euidenter euincunt, sic vt Ioh. 1. v. 14. per carnis vocem, ipsa humana natura, cum defectibus, & infirmitatibus, statum, & conditionem hominis, sequentibus, & quas Christus Mediator, sine peccato assumere potuit, significet. Liquet hoc euidenter, ex Act. 2. v. 31. vbi caro Christi corruptionem non sensisse dicitur. At vero caro Christi, humanam eius naturam significat, secundùm quam Christus mortuus est reuera, & quidem morti obnoxiā, quia hoc dicitur de carne Christi, quae apud inferos, id est, in sepulchro vinculis mortis constringebatur, tantisper donec ex mortuis excitaretur. Sic 1. Pet. 4. v. 1. Christus carne pro nobis passus est dicitur, quod necessariò de humana eius natura passioni mortis obnoxia, est intelligendum. Denique factus est ὁ λόγος ille caro, vel per inhabitationem in carne, assistentiam, affectum, dignitatem & gratiam, aut per conuersionem, & commixtionem, vel sermonis in carnem, & cum carne, vel carnis cum sermone, & in sermonem: aut denique per vnionem personalem, qua videlicet λόγος naturam humanam in se ὑπόστασιν, & propria personalitate destitutam, in personae suae vnitatem sibi coniunxit. Non prius, sic enim contra scripturam & pietatē omnem, duo Christi, duóque Filii Dei cum Nestorio constituerentur. Non secundùm, quia plané est impossibile. Ergo
units.tr: ARGUMENT I. If Christ is an eternal person and eternal God, partaker of the same essence, power, majesty and glory with the Father, free from all change; and he was made man in time, and born of the Virgin Mary; and there is only one Christ, and the one person and hypostasis of Christ is also one; then it follows that the Word, that is, the second person of the most holy Trinity, has assumed the human nature, which is anhypostatic and destitute of its own personality, into the unity of his person. Otherwise the human nature would either wander outside the Word, destitute of all personality, which is absurd, or it would have its own human and created hypostasis, and thus two Christs and two sons of God would be constituted, which is impious. But the antecedent is wholly true. For we have clearly asserted in the preceding chapters the true and eternal divinity of the Son. That Christ was born in time of the Virgin Mary, and that there is only one Christ, one person and hypostasis of Christ, is beyond controversy between us both; so that there is no need to bring forward, against the Marcionites, Manichaeans, Arians, Anabaptists and men of that stripe, those arguments and testimonies of Scripture by which the full and perfect truth of the human nature of Christ is proved, in order to discuss the question under dispute. And to this first argument must be referred all the arguments by which it is shown that Christ is not only true man but also true and eternal God, which we have treated in the preceding chapters. Therefore the consequent is also true. ARGUMENT II. is taken from John 1:14, where it is said that the Word was made flesh. That by the Word is meant the true and eternal God, that is, the second person of the most holy Trinity, the Son of God, creator of heaven and earth with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we demonstrated above in the thirteenth chapter. But that the name flesh, when said of man, signifies first the very substance and nature of man, and then his frailty and mortality and the other accidental properties that follow the state and condition of man, is clear from the sacred Scriptures. As in Gen. 6:12: And God looked upon the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, that is, every man; Joel 2:28: And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, that is, upon every man, as the following words clearly show. So also Ps. 16:10 and Acts 2:31. And as often as Christ is said to give his flesh for the life of the world, flesh signifies the human nature of Christ. Hence also Rom. 1:3, the Son of God made of the seed of David, is called according to the flesh, that is, according to the human nature. From these, and from many other passages of Scripture, it is evident that the word flesh sometimes, and indeed frequently, denotes the whole man and the whole human nature of Christ. But in Isa. 40:6 and Ps. 78:39 the same word flesh signifies the very frailty and weakness of man, that is, a man who is frail, weak and mortal, as the circumstances of those passages clearly prove; so that in John 1:14, by the word flesh, the human nature itself, with its defects and infirmities, and the state and condition of man that follow it, which Christ the Mediator could assume without sin, is signified. This is clear from Acts 2:31, where it is said that the flesh of Christ did not see corruption. But the flesh of Christ signifies his human nature, according to which Christ truly died, and indeed was subject to death, because this is said of the flesh of Christ which lay in hell, that is, in the sepulchre, bound with the bonds of death, until he should be raised from the dead. Thus 1 Pet. 4:1 says that Christ suffered in the flesh for us, which must necessarily be understood of his human nature, subject to the passion of death. Finally, that ho logos [the Word] became flesh either by indwelling in the flesh, by assistance, affection, dignity and grace; or by conversion and mixing, either of the Word into the flesh and with the flesh, or of the flesh into the Word; or finally by personal union, by which the Word joined to himself the human nature, which lacks a hypostasis of its own and its own personality, into the unity of his own person. Not the first, for thus two Christs and two Sons of God would be constituted with Nestorius, contrary to Scripture and all piety. Not the second, because it is plainly impossible. Therefore

units.la: Ergo ... (marginal notes at right edge are cut off and largely illegible) Ergo verum est postremum & tertium.
units.tr: Therefore the last and third view is true.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM III.desumitur ex illis Scripturæ locis, in quibus Christus semè Abrahæ assûpsisse, carnis & sanguinis particeps factus, in carnem venisse, & corpus ipsi adaptatum esse dicitur, Hebr. 2. v. 14. Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, ut per mortem aboleret eum qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, Diabolum: & v. 16. 17. Non enim videlicet Angelos assumpsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumpsit. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, ut misericors esset, & fidelis pontifex in iis, quæ apud Deum (agenda forent) ad expiandum peccata populi. Et cap. 10. v. 5. Quapropter ingrediens in mundum, dicit, Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus adaptasti mihi. 1. Ioh. 4. v. 3. At quicunque Spiritus non confitetur Christum in carnem venisse, ex Deo non est. Ex quibus omnibus, unio illa hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo solide demonstratur, nisi quis impios Nestorii vel Eutychetis errores amplecti malit.
units.tr: ARGUMENT III. is taken from those passages of Scripture in which Christ is said to have taken hold of the seed of Abraham, to have become a partaker of flesh and blood, to have come in the flesh, and a body to have been prepared for him. Heb. 2:14: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil. And vv. 16-17: For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. And Heb. 10:5: Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me. 1 John 4:3: And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God. From all these, that hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ is solidly demonstrated, unless someone prefers to embrace the impious errors of Nestorius or Eutyches.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM IV.& cuidentissimum suppeditat nobis Apostolus Paulus Phil. 2. v. 5. 6. 7. inquiens, Christus, cum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam duxisse parem esse cum Deo, sed se ipsum exinaniuisse, forma servi accepta, similem hominibus factum. Ubi vocabulum μορφὴ non figuram tantum, & speciem Deitatis, vel statum quendam tertium, quem Samosatenianī dignitatis statum appellant, sed ipsam ὑπόστασιν & essentiam divinam, & in antithesi non submissionem tantum & humiliationem seu conditionem servilem & κένωσιν, sed ipsam naturam humanam, veramque essentiam veri ac perfecti hominis omnibus proprietatibus essentialibus vestitam, significare, sequentibus argumentis solide euincitur. Primo, Si Paulus Apostolus verbis illis suis, qui cum esset in forma Dei, &c. quid fuerit Dominus noster Iesus Christus, ante τὸν ἀνθρώπων, seu incarnationem ostendit, tum euidenter manifestum fit formam Dei non esse intelligendam, de humanæ naturæ specie gloriosa, & divina. Atqui verum est antecedens: nam Apostolus diserte dicit, Christum, cum in forma Dei esset. (Fuit autem in ea æterno, cum Patri Filius sit ὡμοούσιος, ut superioribus capitibus ostendimus,) sese exinaniuisse, & formam servi, id est, humanam naturam assumpsisse. Ergo verum etiam est consequens. Secundo, Si forma Dei idem est hoc loco, quod essentia Dei, tum satis manifeste apparet, non esse accipiendam de accidentali humanæ naturæ in Christo forma. Atqui prius est verum. Si enim aliud esse forma Dei, & aliud essentia Dei, tum Deus esset αὐτόθεος, quod est ἀδιάκτος, & ἄπειρος. Et vnumquod que per suam formam, in natura generis, vel speciei, esse dicitur. Ergo & posterius verum est. Tertio, Inter modos dicendi per se, tertius est earum propositionum, in quibus ipsum subsistere ὑφιστάμενον dicitur de singulari ὑφεστημένῳ: Sed Paulus dicit Christum Iesum etiam ante incarnationem fuisse in forma Dei: dicit enim ὃς ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων: Sequitur igitur Christum ὑποστασιν seu personam fuisse ante incarnationem, & μορφῆς δούλου appellatione, essentiam diuinam designari. Quarto, Quod est par Deo est etiam ἴσον, ratione essentiae: Atqui nemo potest dici par Deo respectu accidentalis formae: Certissimum igitur est μορφὴ θεοῦ non esse accidentalem formam, sed ipsam Dei essentiam. Quinto, De nulla creatura, etiam rationali, multo minus de forma accidentali, dici potest, parem eam esse cum Deo. Quis enim est par Iehouæ Deo nostro, qui altissime habitat? Psal. 113. v. 5. Et quis est Deus fortis par tibi? Mich. 7. v. 18. Atqui de Christo dicitur, quod par sit Deo ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ, Philip. 2. versu 6. Sexto & vltimo: Accidentalis forma humanae in Christo naturae, nec est ὑφιστάμενον, nec sola agit, quia actiones, sunt τὰ ὑφιστάμενα, & accidentia sine fulcris substantiarum non sunt, ne dum aliquid agunt. Atqui Christus in forma Dei primo est persona: deinde idem se exinaniuit, unde sequitur formam Dei in Christo accidentariam formam non esse. Minor probatur, quia de persona Filii dicitur: Ipse se, de actione autem eiusdem dicitur, exinaniuit, nempe quod ad vsum, non autem quod ad hypostasin & naturam ipsam diuinam. Atque haec de forma Dei: sequuntur argumenta de forma serui. Primo, Si forma Dei in Christo non est accidentalis forma, sed ipsa Deitas, tum in eodem forma serui est eius humanitas personali ter illa vnita, non autem accidentalis forma. Atqui prius iam est demonstratum. Ergo & posterius verum est: alioquin sequeretur Deitati accessisse formam accidentalem, quod est absurdum.
