Et sicut se habet is qui est in forma Dei ad τὸ θεῖον, ita is qui in forma serui est se habet ad τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. Atqui Deus verus is est, qui in forma Dei est: Ergo & verus homo est, qui in forma serui est. Unde liquet formam Dei de Deitate, formam autem serui de humana natura intelligi debere. Secundo, Nemo nisi substantialis formae formæ ratione,dici potest en ὁμοίωμα ἀνθρώπων ςῶμα. Significat enim similitudo naturæ humanæ εἰκὼν ἡ εἰκόνα ἐπωνύμιον, conformationem,& veritatem ipsam, vt in illo dicto Mosis: Vixerat autem Adam centum triginta annos cum gigneret (Filium) in imagine sua, secundum similitudinem suam: & vocaret nomen eius Sethum, Genef. 5. versu 3. Christus autem similis hominibus factus est, quam assumptionem ipsemet Paulus exposuit, Rom.8. versu 3. Hebr.2. versu 11.14.16.17. Sequitur igitur μορφὴ θεοῦ hoc loco substantialem hominis formam significare. Tertiò, Cuicunque tribuuntur propria & conditiones soli humanæ naturæ propriæ, eidem & naturæ veritas tribuitur. Atqui formæ serui,in Christo , illæ conditiones tribuuntur. Habitu enim compertus est vt homo, de quo verè dicitur ἐν ἀνθρώπου σχήματι ... ac nota est illa vox Pauli consolationis plenissima: Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum in omnibus similiter, absque peccato, Hebr. 4.v.15. Formæ itaque serui appellatione,naturam humanam Christi designari,certum est,qui totius vitæ,mortisque suæ schemate tanquam αὐτὸς τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως testatum fecit, se verum esse & nobis ὁμοούσιον hominem. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissimè colligitur,æterni Patris æternum Filium,naturam humanā ἀνυπόστατον, ac propria personalitate destitutam, in personæ suæ vnitatem,sibi vnione hypostatica,coniunxisse.
units.tr: ARGUMENT IV. The Apostle Paul gives us a most plain proof in Philippians 2:5–7, saying: Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men. That the word μορφή here means not merely a figure and appearance of Deity, or some third state, which the Samosatenians call a state of dignity, but the very substance [ὑπόστασις] and divine essence, and that in contrast it signifies not merely submission, humiliation, a servile condition and kenosis [κένωσις], but the human nature itself, and the true essence of a real and perfect man clothed with all his essential properties, is proved by the following arguments. First, if the Apostle, in the words who, being in the form of God, etc., shows what our Lord Jesus Christ was before he became man, that is, before the incarnation, then it is clearly evident that the form of God is not to be understood of the glorious and divine form of human nature. But the antecedent is true, for the Apostle plainly says that Christ, when he was in the form of God, (and he was in it from eternity, since the Son is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father, as we have shown in the earlier chapters), emptied himself and took the form of a servant, that is, assumed human nature. Therefore the consequent is also true. Second, if the form of God in this place is the same as the essence of God, then it appears quite plainly that it is not to be taken of the accidental form of human nature in Christ. But the first is true. For if the form of God were one thing and the essence of God another, then God would be autotheos [αὐτόθεος], which is without beginning [ἀδιάκτος] and infinite [ἄπειρος]. And each thing is said to exist through its form, in the nature of its genus or species. Therefore the latter is also true. Third, among the modes of predication per se, the third is that of propositions in which the subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] is said of the individual subsisting thing [ὑφεστημένον]. But Paul says that Christ Jesus was in the form of God even before the incarnation, for he says who, being in the form of God [ὃς ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων]. It follows, then, that Christ was a substance [ὑπόστασις], or person, before the incarnation, and that by the expression form of a servant the divine essence is not designated. Fourth, what is equal to God is also equal [ἴσον] in respect of essence. But no one can be called equal to God with respect to an accidental form. It is therefore most certain that form of God [μορφὴ θεοῦ] is not an accidental form but the very essence of God. Fifth, of no creature, even a rational one, and much less of an accidental form, can it be said that it is equal to God. For who is like Jehovah our God, who dwells on high? Psalm 113:5. And who is a God strong like you? Micah 7:18. But of Christ it is said that he is equal to God in the form of God [ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ], Philippians 2:6. Sixth and last: an accidental form of human nature in Christ is neither a subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον] nor does it act alone, since actions belong to subsisting things, and accidents do not exist without the supports of substances, much less act. But Christ is first a person in the form of God, and then the same person emptied himself; hence it follows that the form of God in Christ is not an accidental form. The minor is proved, because the person of the Son is spoken of as himself, but his action is spoken of as emptied, namely with respect to use, and not with respect to the hypostasis and the divine nature itself. So much for the form of God. The arguments about the form of the servant follow. First, if the form of God in Christ is not an accidental form but Deity itself, then in the same way the form of the servant is his humanity personally united to that Deity, and not an accidental form. But the first has already been demonstrated. Therefore the latter is also true; otherwise it would follow that an accidental form had been added to the Deity, which is absurd. And as he who is in the form of God stands toward the divine [τὸ θεῖον], so he who is in the form of a servant stands toward the human [τὸ ἀνθρώπινον]. But he who is in the form of God is true God. Therefore he who is in the form of a servant is also a true man. Hence it is clear that the form of God must be understood of the Deity, and the form of a servant of human nature. Second, no one can be called a likeness of men [ὁμοίωμα ἀνθρώπων] except by reason of a substantial form. For likeness [ὁμοίωσις] of human nature signifies image [εἰκών] or the image-name [εἰκόνα ἐπωνύμιον], conformation, and the very truth, as in that saying of Moses: And Adam had lived one hundred and thirty years, when he begat (a son) in his own image, after his likeness, and called his name Seth, Genesis 5:3. But Christ was made in the likeness of men, which assumption Paul himself explains, Romans 8:3, Hebrews 2:11, 14, 16, 17. It follows, therefore, that form of God [μορφὴ θεοῦ] in this place signifies the substantial form of man. Third, to whomever the properties and conditions belonging only to human nature are attributed, to him the truth of that nature is also attributed. But to the form of the servant in Christ those conditions are attributed. For he was found in habit as a man, of whom it is truly said in the appearance of a man [ἐν ἀνθρώπου σχήματι] ... and that most full word of Paul of consolation is well known: For we have not a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who was tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15. It is certain, therefore, that by the expression form of a servant the human nature of Christ is designated, he who through the whole pattern of his life and death, as the very author [αὐτὸς] of the incarnation, showed that he is a true man and consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with us. From all these things it is most clearly gathered that the eternal Son of the eternal Father joined to himself, by hypostatic union, into the unity of his own person, a human nature which was anhypostatic [ἀνυπόστατον] and destitute of its own personality.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM V. desumitur ex Col. 2.v.9. vbi in Christo omnis plenitudo diuinitatis habitare dicitur corporaliter. Vnde ita argumentamur: In quocunque homine inhabitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter,ille non tantum est verus homo, sed etiam verus & æternus Deus, operationesque diuinas per se facit: Ad omnem enim plenitudinem Dei, pertinet etiam ipsum esse Dei & operationes diuinas facere,ipsámque plenitudinem operationum diuinarum habere,per se,non communicatione gratiæ. Atqui in Christo,quem verũ hominẽ esse,extra controuersiã est, inhabitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter. Ergo Christus non tantũ est verus homo, sed etiã verus & æternus Deus,operationesq;diuinas facit,& plenitudinem operationum diuinarum habet. Quum autem Christus sit verus & æternus Deus,ac verus perfectusq; homo, & vnus tantũ sit Christus,ac vnica hypostasis Christi,sequitur æternum Dei Filiũ, naturam humanam in se ἀνυπόστατον, & propria personalitate destitutam,in personę suę vnitatẽ assumpsisse.Ex quibus omnibus facile apparet cuiuis candido & pio lectori, & qui animi oculis pertinacis præiudicii glaucoma non obducit, nostram de Incarnatione filii Dei, & duarum in ipso naturarum hypostatica vnione, veram, orthodoxam, & ex ipsis scripturarum fontibus haustam esse, quicquid Aduersarii oggánniant.
units.tr: ARGUMENT V. is drawn from Colossians 2:9, where it is said that in Christ all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Hence we argue thus: In whatever man all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, that man is not only a true man but also a true and eternal God, and performs divine works by himself: for the whole fullness of God includes also the very being of God, and performing divine works, and having the fullness of divine works in itself, by itself, not by communication of grace. But in Christ, whom it is beyond controversy to be a true man, all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Therefore Christ is not only a true man but also a true and eternal God, and performs divine works and has the fullness of divine works. Since, however, Christ is a true and eternal God and a true and perfect man, and there is only one Christ and one hypostasis of Christ, it follows that the eternal Son of God assumed into the unity of his own person a human nature which in itself was anhypostatic and destitute of its own personality. From all these things it readily appears to every sincere and pious reader, and to anyone whom the cataract of stubborn prejudice does not cloud over in the eyes of the mind, that our doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God, and of the hypostatic union of the two natures in him, is true, orthodox, and drawn from the very fountains of Scripture, whatever our adversaries may bluster.

units.la: Oftorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo septimo, hanc quæstionem proponit, An videlicet Christus filius Dei humanam naturam assumpserit. Quod confidenter negat, & primo omnium tantam blasphemiam ex malè sani pectoris gurgustio exhalat, vt palam profiteri audeat, nos videlicet doctrinam illam de Incarnatione filij Dei, quam nempe traditur, secundam personam sanctæ Trinitatis humanam naturam assumpsisse, tanquam tremendum aliquod mysterium suscipere & agnoscere, quod verum est: ab ipsis autem (nempe Samosatenianis) purum & putum hominum superstitiosorum figmentum iudicari. Resp. Vanum certè hoc, audaxque & intolerandæ impietatis de re tanta iudicium: sed quid mirum, stultitiam, figmentum, & delirium illud videri Oftorrodio, cæterisque qui ex Socini, & infelicis impurique illius Pauli Samosateni officina prodierunt discipulis, cùm animalem hominem nec capacem esse rerum spiritualium, nec percipere posse veritatis illius lucem, quæ à solo spiritu suum habent ortum, diuus Paulus disertis verbis affirmauerit? Verum & ipsum fundamentum, quo innixus Oftorrodius, de toto mysterio, tam impiam euomere audet blasphemiam, examinemus. Si enim, inquit, verum esset illud, nempe quod Ecclesiastica Christiana de ipsa Incarnatione docent, sequeretur in Christo non humanam tantùm, sed etiam diuinam naturam esse. Resp. Falsa principii petitio, qua in assumptione supponitur ipsa principalis rei controuersæ quæstio, tanquam concessa & euicta. Egregia verò, docta, & Samosateniano ingenio digna argumentandi ratio illa qua sacrosanctæ & individuæ Trinitatis veritatem impugnare pertinaciter sit positum, fine iudicio, sinèque discrimine reiiciuntur & negantur omnia, quæcunque cum illa doctrina cōsentire videtur, quod prium est illis, qui διδάσκοντες ... Secundò, inquit Oftorr. Si vera esset illa de Incarnatione doctrina, inde sequeretur (vt alia plurima argumenta, quibus falsitas commenti illius demonstratur, silentio prætereantur) Euangelistam, in primis autem Matthæum & Lucam, qui studiosè nobis historiam natiuitatis Christi descripserint, inuidia, vel insignis negligentia accusandos esse, eo quod de de re tanti momenti, & ad salutem necessaria scitu (ut docent Aduersarij) vel nihil, vel pauca, eáque obscuris admodum verbis tradiderint, quod tamen falsum sit, cum sanctos illos Dei viros non fortuito, & casu, ac temere, sed ex instinctu Spiritus sancti, historiam Euangelicam conscripsisse constet. Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter seventeen of his Institutes, puts forward this question: whether, namely, Christ the Son of God assumed human nature. This he denies with confidence, and first of all breathes out from the cesspit of an ill-sound heart so great a blasphemy that he dares openly to profess that we, namely, receive and acknowledge that doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God, which is taught, that the second person of the holy Trinity assumed human nature, as some dreadful mystery, which is true, but that it is judged by them (namely the Samosatenians) to be the pure and simple fiction of superstitious men. Answer: this judgment about so great a matter is certainly empty, bold, and of intolerable impiety. But what wonder that Ostorrodius, and the others who have come out of the workshop of Socinus and of that unhappy and impure Paul of Samosata, his disciples, should regard that doctrine as foolishness, fiction, and delirium, since the divine Paul has stated in plain words that the natural man is neither capable of spiritual things nor able to perceive the light of that truth, which has its origin from the Spirit alone? But let us also examine the very foundation on which Ostorrodius leans, when he dares to pour out so impious a blasphemy concerning the whole mystery. For if, he says, that were true, namely what the Christian Church teaches about the incarnation itself, it would follow that in Christ there is not only a human but also a divine nature. Answer: this is a false begging of the question, in which the very principal matter in dispute is assumed as granted and proved. And that reasoning, learned and worthy of the Samosatenian genius, by which the truth of the most holy and undivided Trinity is stubbornly attacked, rejects and denies without judgment and without distinction everything which seems to agree with that doctrine, which is characteristic of those who teach ... Second, says Ostorrodius, if that doctrine of the incarnation were true, it would follow (to pass over in silence many other arguments by which the falsity of that invention is shown) that the evangelists, and chiefly Matthew and Luke, who have diligently described to us the history of the birth of Christ, must be accused of envy or of remarkable negligence, because they have handed down concerning a matter of such importance, and necessary to know for salvation (as our adversaries teach) either nothing or little, and that in very obscure words, which is nevertheless false, since it is established that those holy men of God wrote the evangelical history not by chance, accident, or rashly, but under the impulse of the Holy Spirit. The argument is of this kind.

units.la: Si vera est, & ad salutem scitu necessaria illa de Incarnatione Christi doctrina, tum inuidiæ, vel saltem insignis negligentiæ accusandi essent Euangelistæ, in primis autem Matthæus & Lucas, qui historiam nativitatis Christi studiose conscribentes, de re tamen tam mirabili, & ad salutem scitu necessaria, nihil, vel pauca, eadémque obscuris admodum verbis, tradiderunt.
units.tr: If the doctrine of the Incarnation of Christ is true and necessary to know for salvation, then the Evangelists would have to be accused of envy, or at least of striking negligence, and above all Matthew and Luke, who, while diligently writing the history of Christ's birth, have related on so marvellous a matter, necessary to know for salvation, either nothing or little, and that in very obscure words.

units.la: At qui posterius falsum est, cum certum sit sanctos illos Dei viros non fortuito, casu, aut temere, sed ex instinctu Spiritus sancti historiam Euangelicam conscripsisse.
units.tr: But the latter is false, since it is certain that those holy men of God wrote the Gospel history not by chance, accident or rashly, but under the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ergo etiam prius est falsum.
units.tr: Therefore the former is also false.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam cum Marco, Matthæo, & Lucæ propositum fuerit humanitatis Christi historiam præcipuè pertexere, & genealogiam ipsius, & conceptionem, statum Saluatoris, ac vitam in his terris actam describere, quod præstiterunt vtique diligentissimè ac fidelissimè. Ostorrodius autem à testimonio negatiuo eóque particulari falsam necit consequentiam, & suo more scopas obtrudit dissolutas. An quaeso aut sermones illi de regeneratione cum Nicodemo, de aqua viva cum Samaritanis, de pane vitæ cum turba, de bono pastore, & bonis ouibus, de resurrectione cum Martha, de Spiritu sancto paracleto, cum discipulis peracta vltima coena, de fide cum Thoma, & aliis rebus grauissimis falsitatis sunt arguendi, propterea quod nec in Matthæi, nec Marci, nec Lucæ, sed Iohannis tantummodo historia recensean-tur? aut Matthæus, Marcus, & Lucas inuidiæ, aut negligentiæ insimulandi, eo quod sermonum illorum mentionem nullam fecerint? Vtrumque horum consequentium cum sit impium, & falsum, quid de consequentia Ostorrodii plane simili statuendum sit, quiuis facile animaduertit.
units.tr: Answer: The inference is false. Since Mark, Matthew and Luke intended chiefly to set out the history of Christ's humanity, and to describe his genealogy, his conception, the state of the Saviour and the life he led on this earth, which they certainly carried out most diligently and faithfully. But Ostorodius, from a negative testimony, and a particular one at that, draws a false inference, and in his usual manner foists on us loose brooms. Pray tell, are those discourses about regeneration with Nicodemus, about the living water with the Samaritans, about the bread of life with the crowd, about the good shepherd and the good sheep, about the resurrection with Martha, about the Holy Spirit the Paraclete with the disciples at the last supper, about faith with Thomas, and other most weighty matters, to be charged with falsehood because they are recounted not in Matthew, nor Mark, nor Luke, but in John alone? Or are Matthew, Mark and Luke to be accused of envy or negligence because they made no mention of those discourses? Since both of these inferences are impious and false, anyone can readily see what must be concluded about Ostorodius's inference, which is plainly similar.

units.la: CAPUT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: In quo tria illa testimonia ex Ioh.1.versu 14.1. Ioh.4. versu 3. Hebr.2. v.16. quæ ad demonstrandam Incarnationis, veritatem à nobis citantur, contra exceptiones Ostorrodij, defenduntur.
units.tr: In which those three testimonies, John 1:14, 1 John 4:3 and Hebrews 2:16, which we cite to prove the truth of the Incarnation, are defended against the objections of Ostorodius.

units.la: OSTORRODIVS in Socinianæ religionis Institutionibus suis, quatuor potissimum illa testimonia Scripturæ, quæ ad demonstrandam veritatem vnionis hypostaticæ, duarum naturarum in Christo, ex Ioh 1.versu 14. 1.Iohan.4. versu 3. Hebr.2.versu 16. Philip.2.verf.5.6.7. à nostræ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus citantur, eludere conatur,& tria quidem priora capite decimo octauo, postremum verò capite decimo nono aggreditur, consuetis sophismatum telis instructus. Nos χ̄ν πόδας vestigia illius prememus.
units.tr: In his Institutes of the Socinian Religion, Ostorodius sets out to undermine the four principal passages of Scripture that our Church's teachers cite to prove the truth of the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ: John 1:14, 1 John 4:3, Hebrews 2:16 and Philippians 2:5–7. He tackles the first three in chapter eighteen and the last in chapter nineteen, armed with his usual weapons of sophistry. We follow closely in his footsteps.

units.la: Quantum ad primum testimonium attinet,quod Ioh.1.v.14.hỉce verbis legitur ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, id est, Et sermo caro factus est,duo conatur demonstrare Aducrsarius. Primum aliter verba illa Euangelista,ex Græco textu,verti posse: Deinde si maximè ita vertenda sint, aliter tamen,quam Aduersarii ea interpretentur, exponi illa posse. Et lectionem quidem quantum concernit, primò affirmat,nullam necessitatem vrgere,vt verba illa Euangelistæ ita reddantur,Et verbum caro factum est, quandoquidem verbum illud Græcum ἐγένετο non tantùm factum est,sed etiam erat,vel fuit significet, quo sensu vsurpatum reperiatur in Scripturis,Iohan.1.versu 6.Marc.1.v.4.Luc.1.verf.5.& 24.versu 19.Rom.11.v.34.Sic vt verba illa Ioh.ita legi possint,& verbum caro erat. Atque hinc manifestum esse, inquit,locum illum nostro proposito minimè inseruire,nisi demonstretur ipsum omnino eo modo,quo vulgò consueuit,reddenda esse.
units.tr: As for the first testimony, John 1:14, which reads in Greek ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο [ho logos sarx egeneto], that is, "And the Word was made flesh," the adversary tries to show two things. First, that the Evangelist's words can be translated from the Greek text in another way. Second, that even if they must be translated in this way, they can still be explained differently from how our opponents explain them. As for the reading, he first asserts that there is no necessity to render the words of the Evangelist as "And the Word was made flesh," since the Greek verb ἐγένετο means not only "was made" but also "was" or "existed." It is used in that sense in Scripture at John 1:6, Mark 1:4, Luke 1:5, Luke 24:19 and Romans 11:34. So John's words could be read as "and the Word was flesh." From this, he says, it is clear that the passage does not serve our purpose, unless it is first shown that it must be rendered in the usual way.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is as follows.

units.la: Si verba illa Euangelistæ aliter ex Græco textu verti possunt & verbum verbum illud Grœcum, non tantum factum est, sed etiam erat vel fuit significat, tum locus ille Iohannis, demonstranda Incarnationi inseruire non potest, aut rationes afferenda sunt, quibus ostendatur, illam ipsam genuinam verborum esse transfigurationem.
units.tr: If those words of the Evangelist can be translated otherwise from the Greek text, and if that Greek verb means not only "was made" but also "was" or "existed," then that passage of John cannot serve to prove the Incarnation, unless reasons are given to show that this rendering is the genuine translation of the words.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first part is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Quum autem hactenus rationes multæ versionis illius allatæ sint, sequitur, locum illum ad demonstrandam Incarnationem nihil facere.
units.tr: Now, since many reasons for that translation have been offered so far, it follows that the passage does nothing to prove the Incarnation.

units.la: Resp. Negatur consequentia, tum quia per se falsa est, tum quia nititur falsa illa sub sumptione, qua affirmat Ostorrodius temere, nullis evidentibus rationib. hactenus à Theologis nostris, istâ loci versione stabilitam esse. Hæc falsitas quo magis deregatur, & significatio genuina verbi ὁ λόγος, & rationes quib. versionē illam, quam temere eludit Ostorrodius, stabiliant, sunt perpendendæ. Verbum itaque σὰρξ ἐγένετο, aut significat esse factum, & σαρξ factus, expressámque ortus notationem habet, quæ est significatio propria: aut metaleptice significat, esse, quia res in natura sunt, ex quo sibi factæ sunt, & tamen vi naturali vocis manet eadem ortus principii, quæ notatio, sive connotatio. Sic quando dicitur ἐγένετο fuit homo, notatur fuisse hominem, sed connotatur factum fuisse hominem, quia nullus homo non factus, ortum & principium habens alium.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is denied, both because it is false in itself and because it rests on the false minor premise, by which Ostorodius rashly claims that our theologians have so far established this rendering of the passage without any clear reasons. To expose this falsehood more fully, we must weigh the genuine meaning of the word ὁ λόγος and the reasons by which that rendering, which Ostorodius rashly evades, is supported. The verb σὰρξ ἐγένετο either means "was made," and so "made flesh," with the express notion of origin, which is its proper meaning; or it means by metalepsis "was," because things exist in nature since they have come into being, while by the natural force of the word the notion of origin and beginning remains, as a connotation. Thus when one says ἐγένετο fuit homo [egeneto fuit homo], the sense is "was a man," but the connotation is "had been made a man," because no man exists who was not made, having an origin and beginning from another.

units.la: Restat igitur ut loquutio hæc aut proprie exponatur, Verbum caro factum est, vel metaleptice, Verbum caro erat, aut fuit, quam ipsam interpretationem in sequentibus conatur Ostorrodius retinere. Nostri autem alteram defendunt, & sequentes afferunt rationes. Primò, quia propria est. Secundò, quia etiamsi daretur figurata interpretatio, tamen id ipsum quod Samosatenses fugiunt, connotatione complectitur. Tertiò, quia sic Iohannes ipse distinguit in hac narratione tota ab imperfecto ἦν, quod est secundi adiecti, seu esse subiecti notatur, sine ratione ulla principii vel ortus illius. Nam de simplici esse dicit Iohannes, In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum: In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum: Erat lux illa vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum: In mundo erat. Hæc omnia verbo ὧν exprimuntur. Sed de eo quod factum est, aut quod ex ante facto est, altero verbo semper vtitur, nempe γίνεσθαι. Omnia inquit per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est, & mundus per ipsum factus est: qui autem receperunt ipsum, dedit eis potestatem vt Filij Dei fierent.
units.tr: It remains, then, that this expression must be explained either properly, as The Word was made flesh, or metaleptically, as The Word was flesh, or was, which is the interpretation Ostorrodius tries to keep in what follows. Our people, however, defend the other and offer the following reasons. First, because it is the proper meaning. Second, because even if a figurative interpretation were allowed, it would still include, by connotation, the very thing the Samosatenes try to escape. Third, because John himself, throughout this whole narrative, distinguishes the imperfect ἦν [ēn], which marks the predicate or simple being of a subject with no reference to any beginning or coming into being. For John speaks of simple being: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. That was the true light, which lighteneth every man coming into this world. He was in the world. All of these are expressed by the verb ὢν [ōn]. But about what was made, or came from something previously made, he always uses the other verb, namely γίνεσθαι [ginesthai]. All things, he says, were made by him, and without him was not any thing made that was made, and the world was made by him; but as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God.

units.la: Quarto, & vltimo, quia etiamsi hoc isto verbo γίνεσθαι significare-tur, tamen si pone sequitur nomen substantiuum, fieri significat, ac non esse simpliciter & necessario, vt quum aqua facta vinum dicitur Ioh.2.ver.8. quum quæsit Apostolus, Ergo quod bonum est mihi factum est mors, Rom.7.v.13. & quum dicit, Christus factus est nobis Deo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, & redemtio, 1.Cor.1.v.30. Christus pro nobis factus est execratio, Gal.3.v.13. & similia multa. Ex quibus omnibus tum interpretationis nostræ veritas, tum Aduersarii tergiversatio meritas, ac vanitas meridiana luce clarius elucescit.
units.tr: Fourth and last, because even if this verb γίνεσθαι signified the sense claimed for it, yet when a substantive noun follows it means to become, not simply and necessarily to be. So it is when water is said to be made wine (John 2:8); when the Apostle asks, Was then that which is good made death unto me? (Rom. 7:13); when he says, Christ is made unto us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30); Christ was made a curse for us (Gal. 3:13); and many similar passages. From all of these, both the truth of our interpretation and the evasion of our opponent, and the emptiness of it, shine out more clearly than the noonday light.

units.la: Deinde vero suam versionem verbi γίνεσθαι confirmare nituntur Ostorrodius, hoc argumento, quod videlicet illa cum antecedentibus & consequentibus verbis magis consentiat, quod probare conantur hac ratione.
units.tr: Next, Ostorrodius and his people try to confirm their rendering of γίνεσθαι by this argument, namely that it agrees better with the words both before and after, which they try to prove as follows.

units.la: Si iam in antecedentibus Euangelista verbis affirmatum fuit Christum esse hominem, tum verba illa, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, si ita vertantur, & Verbum caro factum est, cum antecedentibus minime cohærere poterunt, sed turbato ordine iusto peruertuntur, cum quibus tamen si ita reddantur, & verbum caro erat, optime consentiunt, nectuntur, ac proinde prior versio reijcienda est, posterior autem retinenda.
units.tr: If it has already been affirmed in the Evangelist's preceding words that Christ is man, then the words ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο [ho logos sarx egeneto], if rendered thus, The Word was made flesh, can by no means cohere with what goes before, but the proper order is disturbed and overturned. Yet if they are rendered thus, the Word was flesh, they agree very well and are linked on to what precedes. Therefore the former rendering is to be rejected and the latter retained.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first premise is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Assumptionis καταμαρτυρία talis est.
units.tr: The confirmation of the minor premise runs as follows.

units.la: Si omnia illa, quæ Euangelista in antecedentibus, præsertim autem à vers.6. vsque ad hæc verba, de quibus disceptatur, dixit, ad illud tempus sunt referenda, quo Christus iam natus, ac præ inde homo fuit, imo quo iam Euangelium prædicauerat, à quibusdam receptum, ab aliis autem reiectum: tum sequitur iam in antecedentibus verbis affirmatum esse, quod Christus verus homo.
units.tr: If all the things which the Evangelist said in the preceding verses, especially from verse 6 down to these words under dispute, are to be referred to the time when Christ was already born and so already man, indeed when the Gospel had already been preached, received by some and rejected by others, then it follows that it was already affirmed in the preceding words that Christ is true man.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum:
units.tr: But the first premise is true:

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Quò veritas, falsitásque argumenti Ostorrodiani eò evidentius elucescat, de scopo ipso Apostoli, & tractationis ipsius, verborúmque ordine, iusta analysi altius paulo est inquirendum. Consilium igitur Diui Iohannis in conscribenda hac historia Euangelica, hoc fuisse, ut ea quae ab aliis Euangelistis de Christo Seruatore nostro non fuerant diserte exposita, in primis autem veritatem personae illius aduersus falsas illas haereses, quas Satan, ad labefactandam doctrinam Euangelii, excitauerat, quamplurimas, afferat, Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctores ex antiquissimis doctoribus, in primis autem Irenęo, Polycarpi, qui ipsius Iohānis auditor fuit, discipulo luculenter demonstrant. Unde statim ab initio capitis primi, veritatem tum personae Θεάνθρωπου, tum officii et muneris mediatorii, & redemptionis per ipsum factae, asserit, argumentis, & testimoniis evidentissimis, ac luculentissimis, integris primis triginta quatuor versibus, quam ipsam assertionem deinceps sequentibus capitibus fusius persequitur. Quae ad personam ipsam spectant, de qua etiam praesens institutur controversia, & ita tractat, ut primo res illas diuinas recenseat, quae ad personam Christi in se pertinent: deinde ad manifestationem triplicem illius Λόγου aeterni descendat, quarum prima facta est per opera, quorum alia in creandis rebus, alia in sustentandis, & regendis per vitam & lucem illius, licet repudiatam, tum à mundo communiter, tum à Iudaeorum gente seruiliter, & turpissimè, secunda per Verbum, tertia denique per carnis, seu humanae naturae assumptionem. Atque ita diuinitatem τοῦ Λόγου seu filii Dei, tum ab essentialibus proprietatibus diuinis, per adiunctam nempe aeternitatem, relatum Patrem coaeternum, appellationem, & nomen Dei proprium, & naturalem ipsius, propriámque lucem ac vitam viuificantem, tum effectis, creatione videlicet, sustentatione, & gubernatione, illustratione denique tum communi secundùm naturam, tum singulari secundùm iustificationis gratiam, quibus ipsis priora manifestationis genera, per quae Λόγος ille mundo est manifestatus, comprehenduntur. Hisce verò omnibus versu decimo quarto, ordine pulcherrimo & naturae conueniente subiicitur tertium manifestationis factae in carne assumpta personali, in temporum demum plenitudine, postquam operibus, & verbis diutissime omnes sollicitauissent. Atque hunc pulcherrimum sanctissimae narrationis illius ordinem frustrà turbare.
units.tr: Answer. So that the truth or falsity of the Ostorrodian argument may appear more clearly, we must inquire a little more deeply, by a sound analysis, into the Apostle's purpose, the treatment of the subject itself, and the order of the words. The design of divine John in writing this evangelical history was, therefore, to set forth those things about our Saviour Christ which the other Evangelists had not expressly stated, and above all to set forth, against the many false heresies which Satan had stirred up to undermine the doctrine of the Gospel, the truth of that Person. Our church teachers demonstrate this clearly from the most ancient teachers, especially Irenaeus, the disciple of Polycarp, who was himself a hearer of John. Hence, right at the beginning of the first chapter, throughout the first thirty-four verses, he asserts the truth both of the person, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπου], and of the office, mediatorial function, and redemption accomplished through him, with the most evident and luminous arguments and testimonies; and in the following chapters he pursues this assertion more fully. These things concern the person himself, who is also the subject of the present controversy, and he treats them so that first he recounts the divine things which belong to the person of Christ in himself. Then he comes down to the threefold manifestation of the eternal Word [Λόγου]. The first was made by works, some in creating things, others in sustaining and governing them through his life and light, which, though rejected both by the world in general and by the Jewish nation in a servile and most shameful way, was still a manifestation. The second was made through the Word, and the third through the assumption of flesh, that is, of human nature. And so he shows the divinity of the Word, or Son of God, both from the essential divine properties, namely the eternity attached to him, the coeternal Father related to him, his title and proper name of God, and his natural and own light and life that quickens, and from his effects, namely creation, sustaining, governing, and finally illumination, both common according to nature and singular according to the grace of justification. These earlier kinds of manifestation, by which that Word was made known to the world, are all included in these. To all of them, in verse 14, in the most beautiful order and fitting to nature, is added the third manifestation, made in the assumed flesh in a personal union, at last in the fullness of time, after they had for a very long time troubled everyone with works and words. It is in vain that these innovators try to disturb this most beautiful order of that most holy narrative

units.la: conantur nouatores illi, cum institutum consilium ipsorum, eo ipso penitus euertatur. Atque hinc iam facilis est ad argumentum responsio, cum falsitas assumptionis utriusque, & connexi, in syllogismo principali, manifeste detegatur. Falsum est connexum, quia etiam posito antecedente, nulla tamen ordinis verborum perturbatio inde sequeretur, quum Hebraeorum more in Scripturis enuntientur multa commodissime, & sine confusione ne vlla. Exemplum huius rei perspicuum habemus hoc ipso in carpite, versu decimo, vbi Christus primo in mundo fuisse, & deinde mundum creasse dicitur, cum tamen mundus ab ipso conditus sit in principio, ante res creatas omnes, ante omne tempus, & priusquam in mundo essentia, praesentia, regente & sustinente omnia potenterque verbo suo esse posset. Qui igitur verba illa antecedentia In sua venit, de Christo secundum humanam ipsius naturam intelligenda esse existimant ii haec ipsa, de quibus disputatur optime interpretantur, quod illis modus exprimetur, quo videlicet Christus ad sua venerit, idque ordine satis commodo. Sed talia sunt arma Aduersariorum, qui pro mendacio certantes, veritatem diuinam ipsam oppugnant. Verum assumptio quoque utriusque syllogismi falsa est, quum tertium illud genus manifestationis, quae facta est per carnis seu humanae naturae, in vnitatem personae ἀπὸ λόγου assumptionem, hoc ipso demum versu explicatur antecedentibus omnibus ad diuinitatem Christi, cuius lux, & splendor, licet totum mundum, & maxime, tum ante, tum post lapsum, & maxime Israelem etiam annuntiatione gratiae illuminauerit, tamen a toto mundo communiter, & maxima parte Israelitici populi reiectus est, solis credentibus iisque paucis, cum ampliectentibus, ac proinde ὁμοούσιος iure donatis, demonstrandam pertinentibus, ex breuissima & verissima analysi a nobis monstrata, liquet.
units.tr: Those innovators attempt this, though by the very same act their own chosen plan is utterly overturned. And so the answer to the argument is now easy, since the falsity of both the assumption and the connection in the principal syllogism is plainly exposed. The connection is false, because even if the antecedent is granted, no disturbance of the order of words would follow from it, since in the Scriptures, after the manner of the Hebrews, many things are stated most conveniently and without any confusion at all. We have a clear example of this in this very chapter, verse 10, where Christ is said first to have been in the world and then to have made the world, when in fact the world was made by him in the beginning, before all created things and before all time, and before he could be in the world, present, governing and sustaining all things and powerful by his word. Those who think that the preceding words, "He came to his own," are to be understood of Christ according to his human nature, interpret these very things under dispute very well, because they state the manner in which Christ came to his own, and do so in a fairly suitable order. But such are the weapons of our adversaries, who, fighting for a lie, assail the divine truth itself. Moreover the assumption of both syllogisms is false too, since that third kind of manifestation, which was made through the flesh or human nature, in the assumption of the Word [ἀπὸ λόγου] into the unity of the person, is explained in this very verse, after all the preceding manifestations of the divinity of Christ. His light and splendour, though it illumined the whole world, and especially Israel, both before and after the fall, by the announcement of grace, nevertheless was rejected in general by the whole world and by the greater part of the Israelite people, and was embraced only by believers, and those few. And this is clear from the very brief and most true analysis we have shown, which is pertinent to proving that they were of one substance [ὁμοούσιος] and were given the right accordingly.

units.la: Vt autem Oftorrodius suam versionem amplius stabiliat, dicit, Euangelista nomine carnis, non simpliciter hominem, sed hominem vilem, abiectum, infirmum, ac proinde perfequutionibus, miseriis, & ipsi morti ignominiosa obnoxium, denotare voluisse. Carnis enim vocabulum infirmitates humanas significari, ex quibusdam Scripturae testimoniis ostendit, ad quam tamen significationem confirmandam lol cus ille Hebraeor. 2. versu 14. perperam ab Oftorrodio explicatum, qua de re nobis paulo post erit agendum. Atque hanc ipsam causam sam fuisse dicit, ob quam a proprio populo receptum non fuerit, licet lul vitaque. vitaque hominum exiterit, videlicet caro, id est, vilis abiectúsque homo fuerit.
units.tr: But in order to strengthen his version further, Ostorodius says: "The Evangelist, by the name of flesh, meant to denote not simply a man, but a base, abject, weak man, and therefore one liable to persecutions, miseries and even to a shameful death." He shows from certain testimonies of Scripture that the word flesh signifies human infirmities; but to confirm this meaning Ostorodius wrongly explains that passage of Hebrews 2:14, a matter about which we shall have to speak a little later. And he says that this very cause was the reason why he was not received by his own people, although he was the light and life of men, namely, that he was flesh, that is, a base and abject man.

units.la: Resp. Quantum ad vocabulum carnis, & eius significationem concernit, de illo capite antecedente argumento nostro secundo egimus, ac ostendimus, omnino carnis nomine intelligendam quidem esse naturam, & essentiam hominis, verum non nudam, & nudè consideratam, sed qualitatibus illis vestitam, quas nos infirmitatis proprietates, easque temporarias, & accidentales, nec ex ipsis naturæ principiis fluentes, sed statum & conditionem hominis consequentes, appellamus. Quum igitur τὸν λόγον, factum esse carnem cum Evangelista docemus, assumpsisse eum, in unitatem hypostaseos suæ, unione personali, humanam naturam dicimus, sed non nudam, verùm omnibus proprietatibus non essentialibus tantùm, sed etiam accidentariis, vestitam, factúmque hominem affirmamus, sed infirmum, sed abiectum, sed morti ipsi obnoxium, sicuti ad sananda corporis animique nostri vulnera, necessarium erat. Hoc sensu, & hac significatione, nomen carnis, si accipiat Aduersarius, sic ut illo vocabulo & substantiam ipsam, & accidentia complectatur, certamen inter nos de hoc nomine nullum erit, sed stat immota sententia nostra, cum verbum σὰρξ non erat, sed factum est, vertendum esse, iam demonstrauimus, quâ ipsa significatione, hæc sententia cum antecedentibus optimè cohæret, hoc videlicet modo, ut sensus sit, λόγον illum, postquam operibus variis, & verbo, mundum in primis autem Iudæos sollicitauerit, tandem in plenitudine temporum, humanam naturam, cum adiacentibus illis infirmitatibus, assumpsisse, & per eam in mundo comparuisse homine per omnia excepto peccato fratribus similem, & sic salutis nostræ causa, ex summa cœlestis gloriæ celsitudine, ad tam vilem & abiectam conditionem descendisse. Sin verò Aduersarius ex eo, quod nomine carnis etiam adiunctæ infirmitatum qualitates intelligendæ sunt, ipsam essentiam humanam remouendam existimet, tum se crassissimum oppositorum elenchum committere, & positis accidentibus ad tollendam substantiam, vitiosissimè argumetari, meminerit. Atque hæc ipsa humiliatio, & exinanitio filii Dei, causa quidem fuit, (ut de appendice Oftorrodianæ explicationis, obiter aliquid monea-mus) cur à Iudæis Saluator reiectus fuerit, sed non vera, nō sola, nec per se, sed per accidēs tantùm illi cōtēptū gignens 1. Cor. 1. 23. & 24.
units.tr: Reply. As far as the word "flesh" and its meaning are concerned, we dealt with that in the chapter preceding our second argument, and we showed that by the name "flesh" must indeed be understood the nature and essence of man, yet not bare, nor considered as bare, but clothed with those qualities which we call the properties of weakness, and these temporary and accidental, not flowing from the very principles of nature, but following upon the state and condition of man. Therefore, when with the Evangelist we teach that "the Word became flesh," we say that he assumed human nature into the unity of his own hypostasis by a personal union, yet not bare, but clothed not only with its essential properties but also with its accidental ones; and we affirm that he became man, but weak, abject and liable to death itself, as was necessary for healing the wounds of our body and soul. In this sense and meaning, if the adversary takes the name "flesh" so that by that word it embraces both the substance itself and its accidents, there will be no dispute between us over this name; our view stands unshaken, since we have already shown that the word σάρξ must be rendered not "was" but "became" [ἐγένετο], and in that very meaning this sentence fits well with what precedes, namely in this way: that the Word, after he had stirred up the world, and above all the Jews, by various works and by his word, at last in the fullness of time assumed human nature with those attendant infirmities, and through it appeared in the world, like his brethren in all things except sin, and so for the sake of our salvation descended from the height of heavenly glory to so base and abject a condition. But if the adversary thinks that, because the name "flesh" is to be understood with the attached qualities of infirmity, the human essence itself must be removed, then let him remember that he commits a most gross refutation of opposites, and reasons most faultily by positing the accidents in order to abolish the substance. Moreover this very humbling and emptying of the Son of God was indeed the cause (let us note in passing something about the appendix to Ostorodius's explanation) why the Saviour was rejected by the Jews, but not the true cause, nor the sole one, nor in itself, but only accidentally producing contempt for him: 1 Cor. 1:23 and 24.

units.la: Veram enim huius reiectionis causam si inuestigare voluerit Ostorrodius, Iudaeorum superbam malitiam, & natiuas mentis humanae, quae, post lapsum, non est capax eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nec ea percipere potest, tenebras contempletur. Sed haec de uersione, uerborumque significatione dicta sufficiant, nunc ad concessionem eius progrediendum, qua dicit, Etiam si communis illa, & vulgata versio, qua verba illa, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο reddantur, Et sermo caro factus est, concedatur, minime tamen inde sequi, ea sic explicanda esse, quemadmodum a Trinitariis exponuntur, quoniam etiam aliter exponi possint, nempe quod non simpliciter homo sit factus, sed quod is qui potens erat operibus & sermonibus, Luc. 24. verf. 19. & propter summam potentiam miracula patrandi Deo par, ac in forma Dei erat, Phil. 2 v. 6. aliis hominibus, imo etiam peccatoribus similis sit factus, eo quod se omnis generis miseriis, calamitatibus, & morti ignominiosae subiecerit, quemadmodum etiam Apostolus in re pene eadem, similibus verbis, de ipso loquens, usus sit, nempe quod factus sit maledictio, Galat. 3. 13. quódve Deus ipsum miserit, in similitudine carnis, peccato obnoxium, Rom. 3. versu 3. & peccatum fecerit, 2. Cor. 5. versu 21.
units.tr: For if Ostorodius wished to investigate the true cause of this rejection, let him look at the proud malice of the Jews, and the natural darkness of the human mind, which after the fall is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God, nor can it perceive them. But let what has been said about the version and the meaning of the words suffice; now we must proceed to his concession, by which he says: "Even if that common and popular version, by which the words ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο [ho logos sarx egeneto] are rendered 'And the Word was made flesh,' be granted, it does not follow at all that they must be explained as the Trinitarians expound them, since they can also be explained otherwise, namely that he who was mighty in works and words (Luke 24:19), and because of his supreme power able to work miracles, equal to God and in the form of God (Phil. 2:6), was made like other men, indeed even like sinners, because he subjected himself to every kind of misery, calamity and shameful death, just as the Apostle too, speaking of him in almost the same matter and with similar words, used the expression that he was made a curse (Gal. 3:13), and that God sent him in the likeness of flesh subject to sin (Rom. 3:3), and that he made him sin (2 Cor. 5:21)."

units.la: Resp. Ex dictis apparet Ostorrodium vocabulum carnis ad accidentia, seu qualitates accidentarias, non vero ad substantiam, restringere: quod si vere & recte ab ipso fiat, tum sequetur vel per subiectum ipsum, de quo accidentia illa praedicantur, nempe λόγον, intelligendam esse substantiam essentiam nempe, ac naturam humanam, de qua sola qualitates illae enuntiari possunt, vel per vocabulum illud carnis accidentarias illas qualitates ita significari, ut tamen ipsa substantia tanquam subiectum proprium, essentia nempe humana, cui soli inesse, & de qua sola praedicari possunt, necessario connotetur, cum impossibile sit, infirmitates illas accidentarias, de natura vel persona divina, extra duarum naturarum personalem unionem enuntiari posse. Atqui prius omnino falsum, & per λόγον, intelligendam esse secundam personam sacrosanctae Trinitatis, filium nempe coaeternum Patris aeterni, verumque cum Patre, ac Spiritu sancto, coeli terraeque conditorem, supra capite decimo, & decimotertio, luculenter demonstrauimus. Ergo verum est posterius, videlicet nomine carnis ita notari qualitates accidentarias, ut tamen ipsum subiectum, substantia nempe, seu essentia humana necessario connotetur, quo ipso veritas in-
units.tr: Reply. From what has been said it appears that Ostorodius restricts the word "flesh" to the accidents, or accidental qualities, and not to the substance. If he does this truly and rightly, then it follows either that through the subject itself, of which those accidents are predicated, namely the Word, the substance, that is, the essence and nature of man, must be understood, since only of the human nature can those qualities be said; or else that by the word "flesh" those accidental qualities are so signified that the substance itself, as their proper subject, namely the human essence, in which alone they inhere and of which alone they can be predicated, is necessarily connoted, since it is impossible for those accidental infirmities to be predicated of the divine nature or person outside the personal union of the two natures. But the first is altogether false, since by the Word must be understood the second person of the most holy Trinity, the Son coeternal with the eternal Father, and true God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the creator of heaven and earth; this we have clearly demonstrated above in chapters 10 and 13. Therefore the second is true, namely that by the name "flesh" the accidental qualities are so noted that the subject itself, the substance, that is the human essence, is necessarily connoted; by this very fact the truth of our interpretation is not overturned but established.

units.la: tas inras interpretationis noftrę non euertitur,sed stabilitur.Sed falsam esse hanc vocabuli illius explicationem,& nomine carnis non tantum infirmitatem,& fragilitatem accidentariam, sed ipsam essentiam & naturam humanam, vna cum illis accidentibus,intelligēdam esse, ex capite vigesimo,& iis,quæ paulo ante docuimus,manifeste liquet. Loca Scripturæ,quæ ab Aduersario citantur,explicatione ipsius plane nihil patrocinantur:duo enim priora, nec de carne, nec de iis quæ carnis vocabulo significantur, quicquam agunt,licet illa recte ex Phil.2. v.6. adducta, falsa interpretatione corrumpantur.Quod autem Christus maledictio,& peccatum factus, ac in similitudine carnis peccato obnoxia missus esse dicitur, ad passionem, non ad qualitates accidentarias carnis referendum esse,vel cæcus animaduertit, unde ea quæ ad prædicamentum qualitatis pertinent,vitiosissimè,ex iis, quæ ad categoriam passionis sunt ferenda, probare conatur Qstorrodius, miserrimus ille Logicus.
units.tr: ...of our interpretation is not overturned but confirmed. That this explanation of the word is false, and that by "flesh" we must understand not merely accidental weakness and frailty but the human essence and nature itself, together with those accidents, is clear from chapter 20 and from what we taught a little earlier. The passages of Scripture that the opponent cites do not support his explanation at all. The first two have nothing to do with the flesh, nor with what is signified by the word "flesh," although the passage quoted from Philippians 2:6 is corrupted by a false interpretation. That Christ is said to have been made a curse and sin, and sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, refers to his suffering and not to the accidental qualities of the flesh; even a blind man can see this. Hence Ostorrodius, that most wretched logician, tries very faultily to prove what belongs to the category of quality from what must be referred to the category of suffering.

units.la: Atque ex hisce omnibus etiam euanescit conclusio Aduersarii, qua videlicet reiectam ac refutatam,falsámque interpretationem nostram pronuntiat. Et hæc de primo testimonio, quantum attinet ad sequendum quod 1. Iohan. 4.uersu 3. Hisce verbis legitur, hoc est, Et omnis Spiritus, qui negat Christum in carnem venisse, ex Deo non est, primo quibus potest argumentis,confutat sententiam,& explicationē nostram: deinde proponit & confirmat suam. Iohannes, inquit, scribit in sua Epistola eodem modo: Omnis Spiritus qui confitetur Iesum Christum, qui in carne venit, ex Deo est. Sic enim verba illa in Graeco textu leguntur,quae cum in translationibus quibusdam ita sint corrupta, ut non tantum venisse, pro qui venit, sed etiam in carnem pro in carne legatur, ideo fraus una ex altera fraude nata est, ut existimatum fuerit, Filium Dei aliquando sine carne, id est sine humana natura extitisse, aliquo modo autem in carnem venisse, vel humanam naturam assumpsisse. Detecta igitur fraude,simul liquet alterum illum dolum, hoc est commentum, seu figmentum illud Incarnationis Christi, ex verbis illis Iohannis, probari non posse. Atque versionem illam suam confirmare nititur testimonio cuiusdam Lutherani,nomine Thomae Naogeorgi, qui verba illa Graeca eodem modo quo Aduersarius transluisse dicitur.
units.tr: And from all this the opponent's conclusion also vanishes, the conclusion by which he declares our interpretation rejected and refuted and false. So much for the first testimony, as far as it concerns the next passage, 1 John 4:3. The words are read thus: "and every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh is not of God." He first attacks our teaching and explanation with every argument he can muster, and then he sets out and confirms his own. "John," he says, "writes in his epistle in the same way: 'every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ who came in the flesh is of God.'" For these are the words as they are read in the Greek text, and in some translations they have been so corrupted that the reading is not only "came" for "who came," but "into the flesh" for "in the flesh." Thus one deceit has been born from another, so that it has been thought that the Son of God at one time existed without flesh, that is, without human nature, and that in some way he came into the flesh or assumed human nature. Once this deceit is exposed, it is also clear that the other trick, that is, the invention or fiction of the incarnation of Christ, cannot be proved from those words of John. He seeks to support his version by the testimony of a certain Lutheran named Thomas Naogeorgus, who is said to have translated the Greek words in the same way as the opponent.

units.la: Resp. Primo falsum est in Graeco textu haberi, Et omnis Spiritus qui cõfitetur &c.ex Deo est.Legitur enim, ὁ πᾶν πνεῦμα, ὁ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ &c. οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστι. id est, Et quicunque spiritus non confitetur Iesum Christum,&c. ex Deo non est. Deinde merum est conuitium, quod dicit, textum originalem à nobis corruptum,& fraudem aliquam vsurpatam esse cum illud Ἰησοῦν reddamus venisse, & non qui venit, perinde enim est, quantum ad nostram controuersiam concernit, vtrouis modo verba illa vertantur, cũm argumento nostro nihil inde derogetur,semperque maneat illud,quod Apostolus affirmat,nempe Christum,seu Filium Dei,in carnem venisse quod ad stabilien-dam doctrinæ nostræ veritatem abundè sufficit. Nostros denique verba illa ἐν σαρκὶ non in carnem,sed in carne vertere oportuisse, non simpliciter affirmare,sed argumentis &rationibus solidis demonstrare Ostorrodius debuisset, vnde perse corruit conclusio illius, quam tàm præclaro superstruit fundamento. Et Iohannem certè veritatem humanæ naturæ,in persona Christi Ἰησοῦ, verbis illis Ἰησοῦ ἐν σαρκί, significare voluisse, ex scopo ipsius facilè est videre, qui fuit, confutare illos, qui Filium Dei non veram humanam naturam,sed tantùm phantasma aliquod assumpsisse, falsò docuerunt. Testimonium Thomæ Naogeorgi,viri alioquin doctissimi, nec Aduersariorum sententiam confirmat, nec nostram euerrit, cùm tantùm ipsi in controuersis dogmatibus, aut Scripturarum explicatione tribui debeat, quantum salua sacrarum literarum autoritate, priuato alicui & docto interpreti tribui potest, & ἀδ ἀδ quo in huius aut illius loci particularis explicatione,proChristia-na nostra libertate,salua amicitia, & sine omni præiudicio,dissen-tire possumus.
units.tr: Reply. First, it is false that the Greek text has "And every spirit that confesses, etc., is of God." For it reads: "πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ..., οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστι," that is, "and every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ, etc., is not of God." Next, it is mere abuse when he says that we have corrupted the original text and practised some fraud in rendering "Ἰησοῦν" as "came" and not "who came." For so far as our controversy is concerned, it makes no difference in which way those words are translated; nothing is taken away from our argument, and what the Apostle affirms always remains: that Christ, that is, the Son of God, came in the flesh, which is quite enough to establish the truth of our doctrine. Finally, that our people ought to have translated "ἐν σαρκί" as "in the flesh" and not "into the flesh," Ostorrodius should have not simply asserted but demonstrated by solid arguments and reasons; and thus his conclusion, which he builds on so splendid a foundation, collapses of itself. That John certainly meant to signify the reality of human nature in the person of Christ, "Jesus," by the words "Jesus in the flesh," is easy to see from the purpose of the passage, which was to refute those who falsely taught that the Son of God assumed not a true human nature but only some phantasm. The testimony of Thomas Naogeorgus, a man otherwise most learned, neither confirms the opponents' view nor overturns ours; for it ought to be given to him only in controverted doctrines or in the interpretation of Scripture as much as, with the authority of Holy Writ intact, may be given to any private and learned interpreter; and in the explanation of this or that particular passage we may, in Christian freedom, with friendship preserved and without any prejudice, disagree with him.

units.la: Tertium
units.tr: The third

units.la: Tertium testimonium habetur Hebræor.2. vers.16, hisce verbis ἐπιλαμβάνεται, ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται, id est, Non enim videlicet Angelos assumpsit,sed semen Abrahæ assumpsit. Hic itaque Ostorrodius reprehendit tum versionem Germanicam Lutheri, tum consequentiam nostram, quam ex hoc loco deducimus. Versionem reprehendit, eò quòd Lutherus verba illa reddiderit,ad se assumpsit,cum tamen verbum illud Græcum ἐπιλαμβάνεται nihil aliud quam simpliciter assumit, aut recipit,significet, assumi autem vel recipi aliquid possit ab aliquo, etiamsi ad se, vel in se illud nolens suscipiat assumat. Atque hinc fictam illam incarnationem Christi, nulla ratione ex hoc loco, probari posse, inquit, cùm hic tantùm de simplici assumptione, aut receptione fidelium in cœlos, agatur, & quidem ea potissimum quamquam quam Christus perfecit, postquam in cœlos receptus, & Sacerdos factus esset, quæ vt tempus illius sit a incarnationis nihil attingat, sed ad hac præsentia secula sit referenda, & vsque ad reditum, vel educationem Christi duret. Hanc igitur ipsam assumptionem nihil significare dicit, quàm curam illam salutis fidelium, & auxilium quid ipsis ferat, tenentibus verbis sequentibus, quia non Angeli, sed semen Abrahæ, id est, illi qui per Christum in Deum credunt, quippe verum semen Abrahæ, indigeant, vt videre sit, Roman. 9. verf. 16. Galat. 3. verf. 29. Hunc autem loci illius sensum, & hanc significationem genuinam esse illius seminis Abrahæ inde demonstrari inquit, quia vocabulum semen hoc loco sit nomen collectiuum, & multitudinem denotet, vt ex eo appareat, quod illud Angelis opponatur. Quum itaque Christus non omnes fideles, aut multos homines, sed vnam tantum essentiam humanam assumpsisse statuatur, ex hoc vel solo falsitatem commenti illius de Incarnatione demonstrari.
units.tr: The third testimony is Hebrews 2:16, in these words: "ἐπιλαμβάνεται, ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται" [ἐπιλαμβάνεται, ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται], that is, "For he certainly did not take hold of the angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham." Here Ostorrodius finds fault both with Luther's German version and with the inference we draw from this passage. He finds fault with the version because Luther rendered those words as "took to himself" [ad se assumpsit], whereas the Greek word "ἐπιλαμβάνεται" [ἐπιλαμβάνεται] signifies nothing more than simply "takes" or "receives," and something may be taken or received by someone even if he does not wish to take it to himself or into himself. And from this, he says, the fictitious incarnation of Christ cannot be proved in any way from this passage, since here there is spoken only of the simple assumption or reception of the faithful into heaven, and indeed especially of that assumption which Christ accomplished after he was received into heaven and made priest; this does not touch the time of his incarnation but must be referred to the present age and lasts until the return or the bringing up of Christ. He therefore says that this very assumption signifies nothing but that care for the salvation of the faithful and the help it brings them, as the following words show: "not the angels but the seed of Abraham," that is, those who believe in God through Christ, who are the true seed of Abraham, as may be seen in Romans 9:16 and Galatians 3:29. He says that this sense of the passage and this genuine meaning of "seed of Abraham" are shown by the fact that the word "seed" here is a collective noun and denotes a multitude, as appears from its being set over against the angels. Since, then, it is maintained that Christ assumed not all the faithful or many men but a single human essence, the falsity of that fiction about the incarnation is demonstrated from this point alone.

units.la: Resp. Quantum ad versionem Lutheri, & significationem ipsam verbi ἀπολαμβάνειν attinet, si rei significatæ veritatem, ac totius enunciationis sensum spectes, optimè à Luthero verbum illud redditum esse. Quum enim ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι in genere quamlibet assumptionem per se denotet, & hoc loco de ipso λόγῳ, seu æterno filio Dei, enuntietur, quod nempe semen Abrahæ, id est, humanam naturam assumpserit, ideo habita ratione partium materialium, huius enuntiati, antecedentis nempe & consequentis, seu subiecti & prædicati, verbum illud λαμβάνειν optimè assumpsit ad se, nempe in vnitate personæ suæ, Germanicè redditur, & significatio generalis, speciali subiecto verissimè accomodatur, cùm illâ ipsam vnionem, seu assumptionem in persona τοῦ λόγου factam esse, multis solidissimis argumentis, nostri demonstrauerint, & nos quoque cap. 20. ostenderimus. Significationem autem illam, quam ex suo cerebro huic verbo affingit Oftorrodius, nempe quod curam aliquam, aut solicitudinem significet, si ex probato aliquo autore nobis confirmauerit, lubens ex hoc testimonio doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum de Incarnatione filii Dei probari non posse confitebor. Quod verò alteram partem responsionis concernit, qua plane euerti existimat argumentum nostrum Aduersarius, hac forma disponi illa potest.
units.tr: Reply. As far as Luther's version and the very meaning of the word "ἀπολαμβάνειν" [ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι] are concerned, if you look to the truth of the thing signified and to the sense of the whole statement, Luther has rendered that word very well. For since "ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι" [ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι] in general denotes any assumption whatever, and here it is said of the Word itself, that is, of the eternal Son of God, that he took hold of the seed of Abraham, that is, assumed human nature, therefore, having regard to the material parts of this statement, its antecedent and consequent, or subject and predicate, the word "λαμβάνειν" [λαμβάνειν] has been very well taken to himself, that is, in the unity of his person, in German, and the general signification is most truly adapted to the particular subject, since our own writers have demonstrated by many very solid arguments that this very union, or assumption, was made in the person of the Word [τοῦ λόγου], and we too have shown it in chapter 20. But if the opponent should confirm for us from some approved author that signification which Ostorrodius fashions for this word out of his own brain, namely that it signifies "some care" or "solicitude," then I will gladly confess that the doctrine of our Churches concerning the incarnation of the Son of God cannot be proved from this testimony. As for the other part of his reply, by which the opponent thinks our argument is completely overturned, it may be arranged in this form:

units.la: Semen Abrahæ hic significat multos homines, id est, omnes fideles, qui per Christum in Deum credunt, Rom. 4. v. 16. Gal. 3. v. 29.
units.tr: "The seed of Abraham here signifies many men, that is, all the faithful who believe in God through Christ" (Rom. 4:16; Gal. 3:29).

units.la: Atqui Christus (secundum doctrinam Aduersariorum non multos homines, aut omnes fideles qui per Christum in Deum credunt, sed vnam naturam, seu indiuiduam essentiam humanam in personæ suæ vnitatem assumpsit:
units.tr: "But Christ (according to the doctrine of the opponents) assumed not many men, or all the faithful who believe in God through Christ, but one nature, or one individual human essence, into the unity of his person":

units.la: Ergo Christus in personæ suæ vnitatem femen Abrahæ non assumpsit, nec femen Abrahæ ipsam naturam humanam aut vnum numero essentiam significat.
units.tr: Therefore Christ did not take the seed of Abraham into the unity of his person, and the seed of Abraham does not signify human nature itself, or one essence numerically one.

units.la: Maioris hanc probationem adfert.
units.tr: He offers proof of the major premise.

units.la: Quia videlicet femen hoc loco fit nomen collectiuum, & multitudinem aliquam denotet, quod ex eo appareat, quia nempe Angelis opponatur.
units.tr: For clearly the word "seed" here becomes a collective noun and denotes some multitude, as appears from the fact that it is set over against the angels.

units.la: Resp. Propositionem maiorem esse falsam, vnà cum probatione, quæ manifesto paralogismo, ex puris particularibus constante, laborat. Non enim sequitur, si nomen feminis Rom. 4. v. 16. Galat. 3. versu 29. aut aliis etiam in locis est collectivum, ac multitudinem, hoc est, omnes fideles in Deum per Christum credentes, significat. Ergo etiam in hoc præsente loco eandem significationem obtinet, cùm vnum idémque vocabulum in Scripturis sacris, pro varietate subiectorum, de quibus enuntiatur, varias significationes obtinere, ipsis etiam pueris notum sit, à quarum vna ad alteram, nulla datur consequentia, & ipsimet Aduersarii vocabulo mundus, in vno eodémque versu decimo Euangelii Iohannis, triplicem significationem affingant, nec ab vna ad alteram consequentiam concedere velint. Et ipsum semen, vtrumque interdum fit nomen collectivum, & sumatur pro tota posteritate alicuius fine fidei respectu, aut conditione vlla, vt Genef. 12. versu 7. Semini tuo dabo terram hanc. Sic Genef. 15. versu 5. & 26. versu 3. & aliis lo-cis plurimis: tamen non semper collectiuè, sed interdum etiam pro vnico indiuiduo vsurpatur. Genef. 3. v. 15. Semen mulieris (id est Christus) conteret caput serpentis. Et 4. versu 25. Cognouit adhuc Adam vxorem suam, quæ peperit Filium, vocauitque nomen eius Seth, dicens, posuit mihi semen aliud Deus pro Abel, quem occidit Cain. Sic etiam semen Abrahæ non semper collectiuè pro tota posteritate Abrahami, vt Roman. 9. versu 7. Neque quia sunt semen Abrahæ, ideò omnes sunt filii, nec etiam pro credentibus omnibus, sed interdum etiam pro vnico Abrahæ filio, nempe Christo sumitur, vt: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes Gentes terræ, Gen. 22. v. 18. & 26. verf. 4.
units.tr: Reply: The major premise is false, and so is its proof, which suffers from an obvious paralogism, resting on purely particular premises. For it does not follow that because the word "seed" in Rom. 4:16 and Gal. 3:29, or in other places too, is collective and signifies a multitude, that is, all the faithful who believe in God through Christ, it therefore has the same meaning in this present passage. Even children know that one and the same word in holy Scripture takes different meanings according to the variety of the subjects of which it is predicated, and that no inference can be drawn from one of these meanings to another. Your own people, in the one verse tenth of John's Gospel, attach a threefold meaning to the word "world" and will not concede an inference from one meaning to another. The word seed itself is sometimes a collective noun, and is taken for the whole posterity of someone with respect to faith or some condition, as in Gen. 12:7, "To your seed I will give this land." So too in Gen. 15:5, 26:3 and very many other places. Yet it is not always collective; sometimes it is used even of a single individual. Gen. 3:15, "The seed of the woman" (that is, Christ) "shall crush the head of the serpent." And Gen. 4:25, "Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying, God has appointed me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." So also "seed of Abraham" is not always collective, for the whole posterity of Abraham, as in Rom. 9:7, "Nor because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children," nor for all believers. Sometimes it is taken for the one son of Abraham, namely Christ, as in "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," Gen. 22:18 and 26:4.

units.la: A ct.3.versu 25.vbi per femen Abrahæ nemo alius quàm solus Christus intelligitur, quemadmodum Apostolus Paulus disertè illud explicat, inquiens, Abrahæ dictæ sunt promissiones, & femini eius: Non dicit,Et feminibus,vt de multis,sed vt de vno: Et semini tuo,qui est Christus. Gal.3. versu 16. Atque hoc ipso in loco, nempe Heb. 2. versu 16.semen Abrahæ,non collectiue,&pro multitudine aliqua, sed pro vnico indiuiduo,natura nempe,& essentia humana,ex antecedentibus,si illa iusta analysi expendatur accuratius,firmissimè confirmatur. Posteaquàm enim Apostolus versu nono huius capitis, doctrinā ipsam, de Incarnatione, & humanæ naturæ assumptione, (cuius veritas inde demonstratur, quod Christus paulò minor Angelis factus esse dicitur,quibus homo quatenus homo, id est, humanæ naturæ respectu, paulò est inferior : & quia inter Angelicam,& humanam naturam descendendo,quemadmodum inter Deum, & Angelum ascendendo nulla natura est intermedia) & causam tum ipsius incarnationis, quæ est, vt mortem peroqui petisset, tum mortis ipsius, nempe decretum diuinum, quo Christus electis in Sacerdotem ordinatus est, vt sacrificio mortis expiaret omnium illorum peccata, quæ ipse, vt sponsor in se receperat,proposuisset,versibus autem sequetibus, quatuor nempe 10.11.12. & 13. ad obiectiones quasdam,per prolepsin, instituto Apostolico accommodatissimam, diluendas, responsionémque suam ad illas tum ratione à pari desumpta, tum testimoniis Christi, & Scripturarum confirmandam digrederetur: tandem versu 14. & 15. ad eandem illam doctrinam de Incarnationis ac mortis Filii Dei causa redit, eámque rursus salutem Electorum statuit sidonobis impetratam, tum per abolitionem, & abrogationem Satanicæ tyrannidis, & diabolici imperii,quod in nos exercebatur,& diiberationem Electorum ab eadem illa potestate, qui propter conscientiam peccatorum suorum perpetuo metu mortis trepidabant,quo ipso beneficium liberationis illius amplificatur. Quæ antecedentibus de Incarnatione Filii Dei dixerat, ea ipsa versu 16. Scripturæ testimonio confirmat, quæ videlicet passim estatur Christum,naturam humanam,seu carnem, & sanguinem posteris Abrahæ, non autem Angelicam naturam assumptuum esse, quia videlicet hominis causa in hoc redemptionis negotio agebatur, non Angelorum, quorum ii qui à Deo defecerunt promissionem salutis nullam habentes, nec in gloriam adducendi, nec Deo Patri reconciliandi per Christum erant: ii vero qui in integritate perseuerarunt, sacrificio illo Christi non indigebant, vbi denuo beneficium illud Christi erga electos, egregia disparatorum antithesi amplificatur: subiunctis deinde ac repetitis in reliquis duobus versibus ipsius incarnationis causis tum subordinatis, tum etiam superioribus, quibus illa doctrina concluditur. Quod vero in eodem illo loco nomen feminis Angelis opponitur, ex eo non sequitur, collectiue illud ibidem vsurpari, neque vlla ratione consequentia illa stabiliri potest, praesertim cum non vna essentia multis subsistentibus Angelis, sed vna natura, seu essentia humana vni naturae Angelicae opponatur, quam ipsam naturam humanam Apostolus nomine feminis Abrahami exprimere voluit, tum vt maiorem fidem suae doctrinae, testimonio Scripturae ipsius, in qua praecipuae promissiones ipsi Abrahamo factae esse leguntur, adducto, conciliare etiam vt Christum vere hominem, natum ex homine, Abrahami nempe posteritate, secundum veritatem promissionum, doceret. Ex quibus omnibus meridiana luce clarius elucescit, interpretationem Oftorrodianam falsam atque confictam esse. Quę vero idem Aduersarius suae interpretationi, de Christo, inspergit, falsa, portentosa, & nuper ex male sopito cerebro Socioniano prognata, quasi ille tum demum Sacerdos constitutus esset, postquam in coelos euectus fuisset, de iis in sequentibus, in loco de officio Christi, vbi de eiusdem Sacerdotio ex professo agendum erit, volente & auxiliante Domino, dispiciemus, nunc ad testimonium quartum ab Aduersario imposituris, ac deliciis vindicandum, perrecturi.
units.tr: Acts 3:25, where by "seed of Abraham" no one is understood but Christ alone, as the Apostle Paul explains it plainly, saying, "The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed." He does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one: "and to your seed, which is Christ," Gal. 3:16. And in this very place, namely Heb. 2:16, the seed of Abraham is firmly confirmed to mean not collectively, nor for some multitude, but a single individual, namely human nature and essence, if the preceding context is weighed more carefully by a proper analysis. For after the Apostle, in verse nine of this chapter, has set out the doctrine itself concerning the Incarnation and the assumption of human nature (whose truth is shown by the fact that Christ is said to have been made a little lower than the angels, to whom man as man, that is with respect to human nature, is a little inferior, and because between angelic and human nature, as between God and angel in ascent, there is no intermediate nature), and the cause both of the incarnation itself, namely that he might undergo death, and of death itself, namely the divine decree by which Christ was ordained High Priest for the elect, so that by the sacrifice of death he might expiate the sins of all those whom, as surety, he had taken upon himself and undertaken to bring forward; then in the following verses, 10, 11, 12 and 13, he goes on, by a prolepsis most suited to the Apostolic method, to dissolve certain objections, and to confirm his answer to them both by an argument from the like and by the testimonies of Christ and of the Scriptures. Finally, in verses 14 and 15, he returns to the same doctrine of the cause of the incarnation and death of the Son of God, and again sets forth the salvation of the elect as obtained for us, both by the abolition and abrogation of Satanic tyranny and the devilish dominion exercised over us, and by the deliverance of the elect from that same power, who for the sake of the awareness of their sins were trembling in perpetual fear of death. By this the benefit of that deliverance is magnified. What he had said above about the Incarnation of the Son of God, he confirms in verse 16 by the testimony of Scripture: that Christ assumed, as is everywhere stated, not the angelic nature, but the human nature, or flesh and blood, of the posterity of Abraham. For the work of redemption was carried on for the sake of man, not of angels, of whom those who fell away from God had no promise of salvation, neither to be brought into glory nor to be reconciled to God the Father through Christ; while those who persevered in integrity had no need of that sacrifice of Christ. Here again the benefit of Christ toward the elect is magnified by a striking antithesis of the dissimilar. Then, in the remaining two verses, he adds and repeats the causes of the incarnation, both subordinate and superior, by which that doctrine is concluded. But that in the same passage the name "seed" is set over against "angels" does not show that it is used collectively there, and no reasoning can establish that inference, especially since it is not one essence subsisting in many angels that is opposed to one angelic nature, but one nature or essence, human, that is opposed to the one angelic nature. The Apostle wished to express this human nature by the name "seed of Abraham," both to make his doctrine more credible by adducing the testimony of Scripture itself, in which the chief promises are read as made to Abraham, and to teach that Christ was truly man, born of a man, of the posterity of Abraham, according to the truth of the promises. From all these things it shines out more clearly than the noonday light that the Ostorodian interpretation is false and invented.
