As for what the same opponent adds to his interpretation about Christ, false, monstrous, and recently born from a badly lulled Socinian brain, as if he had been constituted Priest only after he was carried up into heaven, we will examine it, the Lord willing and helping, in the following pages, in the place on the office of Christ where the Priesthood of the same is to be treated professedly. Now we proceed to the fourth testimony that the opponent has to impose and to defend with his delights.

units.la: CAPVT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: In quo testimonium quartum, quod ad demonstrandam Incarnationis veritatem ex Philip. 2. versu 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. citatur ab exceptionibus Aduersarii, vindicatur.
units.tr: In which the fourth testimony, cited to prove the truth of the Incarnation from Philippians 2:5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11, is defended against the objections of the Adversary.

units.la: QVARTVM VTR...
units.tr: THE FOURTH TESTIMONY (running head garbled in the scan)

units.la: VARTVM testimonium nostrum,quod impugnat Ostorrodius,Phil.2.v.5.6.7.his verbis legitur, Itaque is sit affectus in vobis,qui fuit & in Christo Iesu,qui cùm esset in forma Dei , non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo,sed ipse exinaniuit se,forma serui accepta,similis hominibus factus,& habitu compertus vt homo, ipse se submisit factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Quapropter etiam Deus ipsum extulit in summam sublimitatem , ac donauit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen ,vt ad nomen Iesu omne genu se fleflat cœlestium ac terrestrium , & subterraneorum , omnisque lingua confitea-tur,Dominum esse Iesum Christum, ad gloriam Dei Patris. Ostorto-dius Institutionum suarum capite decimo nono promittit,se pro-baturum esse,ex his ipsis Apostoli verbis ,non tantùm doctrinam illam, de Incarnatione demonstrari non posse,sed etiam contrariam, nempe Socinianam, explicari & confitmari, vnde etiam singula verba ordine explanare,id est, obtorto collo ad falsitatem dogmatis sui palliandam , detorquere conatur. Vt igitur ad hoc ipsum fundamentum veritatis conuellendum commodam sternat viam,primo omnium inquit,Apostolum verbis illis, Is sit affectus in vobis ,qui fuit & in Christo Iesu,nos hortari,vt Christum in re illa , quam postea explicat,imitemur,atque sequamur,vnde manifestum sit, ipsum de re aliqua nota loqui voluisse, cum alioquin ipsam vt exemplum introducere non potuisset.Ex quo pluribus verbis concludit,de Incarnatione eo in loco nihil tractari:nos reiectis verborum integumentis , argumentum ad formam syllogisticam reuocabimus , quo& illius falsitas,& responsionis nostræ veritas, eo magis elucelcant : Tale igitur est.
units.tr: Our testimony that Ostorodius attacks, Philippians 2:5–7, reads in these words: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." Ostorodius, in chapter nineteen of his Institutes, promises that he will prove from these very words of the Apostle not only that the doctrine of the Incarnation cannot be demonstrated, but also that the contrary doctrine, namely the Socinian, is explained and confirmed. Hence he also tries to expound each word in order, that is, to twist them by main force so as to cover the falsity of his dogma. So, to clear a convenient path for overturning this very foundation of the truth, he says, first of all, that the Apostle, by the words "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus," exhorts us to imitate and follow Christ in that matter which he afterwards explains, whence it is plain that he meant to speak of some known matter, since otherwise he could not have introduced it as an example. From this he concludes at greater length that nothing is treated there concerning the Incarnation. We, setting aside the wrappings of words, will reduce the argument to syllogistic form, so that both its falsity and the truth of our answer may stand out more clearly. It goes like this:

units.la: Si Paulus,in loco illo citato , loquitur de re aliqua cognita & familiari,tum nihil ibi agit de Incarnatione:
units.tr: If Paul, in the passage cited, speaks of some known and familiar matter, then he deals there with nothing about the Incarnation.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum.
units.tr: But the first is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is too.

units.la: Connexi hanc affert probationem.
units.tr: He adds a proof of the connection.

units.la: Si doctrina de Incarnatione ita est obscura , vt etiam ipsi doctissimi Trinitarij fateantur se modum illius explicare non posse , tum certè , Si Paulus citato loco de re aliqua cognita & familiari loquitur,nihil ibi de Incarnatione agit. Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If the doctrine of the Incarnation is so obscure that even the most learned Trinitarians admit they cannot explain its manner, then certainly, if Paul in the cited passage speaks of some known and familiar matter, he deals there with nothing about the Incarnation. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Assumptionis καταδυνη talis est.
units.tr: The assumption (minor premise) is as follows.

units.la: Si Paulus illis verbis nos hortatur, ut Christum in ea re, quam in sequentibus explicat, imitari ac sequi debeamus, tum omnino sequitur, ipsum ibidem de re aliqua nota, & familiari, loqui: secus enim illam, ut exemplum, introducere minime potuisset.
units.tr: If Paul, by those words, exhorts us to imitate and follow Christ in that matter which he explains in what follows, then it certainly follows that he is speaking there of some known and familiar matter, for otherwise he could not have introduced it as an example.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Conclusionem vero ipsam principalem, nempe Paulum in loco citato nihil de incarnatione Christi agere, amplius probare conatur, testimonio Iohannis Caluini, qui in explicatione verborum illorum Apostoli, inter caetera, in hunc modum scripserit: Paulus hic non docet, quid fuerit Christus, sed qualiter se gesserit.
units.tr: He tries further to prove the principal conclusion itself, namely that Paul in the passage cited does not deal with the Incarnation of Christ at all, by the testimony of John Calvin, who, in explaining those words of the Apostle, among other things wrote in this way: "Paul here does not teach what Christ was, but how he conducted himself."

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam, una cum καταδυνη eiusdem, quae ab ignoratione modi, quem Scriptura ipsa Ecclesiam nunquam & nusquam docuit, ad negationem ipsius rei, vitiosissime concludit, ut supra capite septimo multis exemplis ex ipsa scriptura petitis, luculenter ostendimus. Mysterii illius, quo aeterni Patris, aeternus filius, per hypostaticam unionem naturae humanae factus homo dicitur, tantam altitudinem esse profitentur omnes sanio-res, ac modestiores Theologi, ut ad eius θεότη, & exactissimam, caus-aeque ipsius formalis plenam cognitionem, nulla humani ingenii acies, in hac quidem mortali vita, in qua natiuae caecitatis tenebris adhuc circumfusi, ex parte tantum cognoscimus, pertingere pos-fit: at vero qui inde ad negationem ipsius rei argumentari voluerit, nonnisi summam inscitiam, aut peruersi ingenii maliriam prodiderit. Si enim rerum physicarum quas haec natura suo ambitu, & peripheria complectitur, & quas videre, tangere, & sensibus percipere licet, formas & difficillimas, & raras inuentu, cognitúque perspicacissimi quique iudicarunt, quas tamen negare hominis esset insani, qua fronte quaeso Oftorrodius veritatem Incarnationis rei omnem humanae mentis captum superantis, totiúsque naturae cancellos, & limites transcendentis, impugnare audet, sumpta videlicet inde ratione, quod etiam doctissimi Theologi nostri, se modum formamque eius explicare non posse, profitean-tur? Sed quia de his capite septimo sufficienter actum est, ad probationem batione̅m assumptionis progredior, cuius quidem antecedens ambiguum est admodum, atque absurdum. Quum enim in assumptione affirmat, Paulum illis verbis nos hortari, vt Christum in re illa, quæ in sequentibus explicatur, imitemur, atque sequamur rem aut similem, aut plane eandem nobis imitandam proponi intelligit Ostorrodius, comparationem aliquam similium ab Apostolo institui existimat, quorum vtrumque est falsum. Non enim similium comparatio, sed à maiori ad minus, ibi instituitur: & sensus est, Cùm tantus misericordiæ affectus in Christo fuerit, qui tamen verus & æternus Deus est, vt nostræ salutis causâ, eousque se demiserit, vt ex summo maiestatis, ac gloriæ diuinæ fastigio, ad ignominiam se deiecerit, & humanam naturam assumpserit, atque homo factus, omnis generis miserias, mortemque ipsam ignominiosâ subierit, quàtò minus igitur nos, qui nihil sumus, superbire, & arrogantia, ac φιλαυτίᾳ efferri debeamus? Si enim ea, quâ Aduersarius statuit, & comparatio ab Apostolo proponeretur, & imitatio Christi à nobis postularetur, necessariò inde sequeretur, omnes Christianos omnes in forma Dei subsistere, pares Deo esse, ac formam serui assumere, & ea præstare, quæ à Christo ibi facta leguntur, quia imitari Christum secundùm doctrinam ipsorum, nihil aliud est, quàm præcipuas qualitates in eare, de qua agitur, ita exprimere, vt similitudo inter vtrumque appareat, & vterque eiusdem generis qualitates habere dicatur, licèt imitandum perfectiores eas habeat, sicuti his ipsis verbis Samosatenianorum Antesignanus ille Faustus Socinus, in libro de Iesu Christo Seruatore, capite quarto, id definit. Testimonium Caluini, quod sententiæ suæ patrocinari existimat Ostorrodius, in explicatione verborum illorum, de quibus iam agitur, nusquam legitur. Imo verò tantum abest, vt Valentinus Smalcius neget, ibi doceri, quid Christus fuerit, vt etiam in explicatione versu 6. in hunc modum scripserit. Porrò in his verbis asseri æternam eius (Christi) diuinitatem, qui non videt, prorsus cæcus. Et paulò post. Sicut ergo à suis virtutibus cognoscitur Deus, opera eius testimonia sunt æternæ eius diuinitatis, Rom. 1. vers. 20. Sarite diuina Christi essentia, probatur, ex Christi maiestate, quam ante omnia sempiternam cum Patre habebat, antequam se ipsum humiliaret. Mihi certissimum est argumentum, à gloria ad essentiam: quæ duo inseparabilia sunt. Postea verò in explicatione versu 7. cum videret Marcionitas... tas verbis illis, In similitudine hominum constitutus, ad probandum multa suum phantasma abuti, inquit, sed nullo negotio refelli possunt: quia hic Paulus (nempe his verbis) nihil aliud disputat, nisi qualiter se gesserit Christus, aut qua conditione versatus sit in mundo. Qui veneritin homo, tamen aliis dissimilis censebitur, si ita se gerat, quasi exemptus esset ab aliorum nlege. Hoc in Christo fuisse Paulus negat, sed ita vixisse, ut quivis ex hominum numero appareret: & tamen longe aliud erat quam homo. Et paulo post, Sicut prius asseruit, reipsa fuisse Deum, Patri aequalem: ita hic commemorat tanquam abiectum, & communis fortis habitum fuisse. Ex quibus omnibus apparet manifestissime, quàm falsis rationibus sententia Aduersariorum nitatur. Nos ad sequentia pergemus.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is false, and together with its minor premise it draws the most faulty conclusion from ignorance of the manner, which Scripture itself never and nowhere taught the Church, to the denial of the thing itself. As we have clearly shown in chapter seven with many examples taken from Scripture itself, all the more sober and modest theologians profess that the mystery by which the eternal Son of the eternal Father is said to have become man through the hypostatic union with human nature is so high that no keenness of human intellect, in this mortal life in which we are still surrounded by the shadows of natural blindness, can reach its divinity and its most exact formal cause; we know only in part. But whoever argues from this to a denial of the thing itself shows nothing but utter ignorance or a perverse wickedness of mind. For if the most acute men have judged the forms of physical things, which this nature embraces within its compass and periphery, and which may be seen, touched and perceived by the senses, to be both most difficult and rarely discovered, yet to deny them would be the act of a madman, then with what face, I ask, does Ostorodius dare to attack the truth of the Incarnation, a matter surpassing all the grasp of the human mind and transcending the bounds and limits of all nature, taking as his reason that even our most learned theologians profess that they cannot explain its manner and form? But since this has been dealt with sufficiently in chapter seven, I proceed to the proof of the assumption, whose antecedent is very ambiguous and absurd. For when he asserts in the assumption that Paul, by those words, exhorts us to imitate and follow Christ in that matter which is explained in what follows, Ostorodius understands that a matter either similar or altogether the same is set before us for imitation, and he thinks that the Apostle draws some comparison of similar things; both of these are false. For the comparison is not one of like things but an argument from the greater to the less. The sense is this: since in Christ there was such a feeling of mercy that he, though he is true and eternal God, so lowered himself for our salvation that from the highest summit of divine majesty and glory he cast himself down into dishonour, took upon himself human nature, and, made man, underwent every kind of misery and death itself, even the shameful death, how much less ought we, who are nothing, to be proud and to be puffed up with arrogance and [φιλαυτία] self-love? For if the comparison, as the Adversary lays it down, were what the Apostle proposed, and imitation of Christ were demanded of us, it would necessarily follow that all Christians subsist in the form of God, are equal to God, take the form of a servant, and perform those things which Christ is there read to have done. For, according to their doctrine, to imitate Christ is nothing other than to express the principal qualities in the matter under discussion in such a way that a likeness between the two appears, and both are said to have qualities of the same kind, even though the imitated one has them in a more perfect degree, as the chief of the Samosatenians, Faustus Socinus, defines it in these very words in his book on Jesus Christ the Saviour, chapter four. The testimony of Calvin, which Ostorodius thinks supports his opinion, in the explanation of those words under discussion, is nowhere to be found. Indeed, Valentinus Smalcius is so far from denying that what Christ was is taught there that in explaining verse 6 he wrote in this way: "Moreover, that his eternal divinity is asserted in these words, whoever does not see this is utterly blind." And a little later: "As God is known from his powers, and his works are testimonies of his eternal divinity (Romans 1:20), so the divine essence of Christ is proved from the majesty of Christ, which he had, eternal with the Father, before he humbled himself." For me the argument from glory to essence is most certain, since these two are inseparable. Afterwards, in explaining verse 7, when he saw that the Marcionites abused the words "being made in the likeness of men" to prove their fancy in many ways, he says: "but they can be refuted without any trouble, because here Paul (namely in these words) discusses nothing other than how Christ conducted himself, or in what condition he lived in the world. One who has come as a man will nevertheless be counted dissimilar to others if he so conducts himself as though he were exempt from the law of others. Paul denies that this was in Christ, but that he so lived as to appear one of the number of men; and yet he was far other than a man." And a little after: "As he earlier asserted that he was in truth God, equal to the Father, so here he recalls that he took on a lowly and common condition of life, as one despised." From all these things it appears most plainly with how false arguments the opinion of the Adversaries rests. We shall proceed to what follows.

units.la: Secundo, progreditur ad verba illa, quibus Apostolus dicit, Christum in forma Dei fuisse, per quam ipsammet essentiam Dei intelligendam esse, capite vigesimo luculenter & solide demonstrauimus: primo quidem, inquit, nos ad illam explicationem stabilien-dam, & confirmandam rationibus vti, non ex Scriptura, sed Philosophia & ratione communi desumptis.
units.tr: Secondly, he goes on to those words in which the Apostle says that Christ was in the form of God. We have clearly and solidly shown in the twentieth chapter that this refers to the very essence of God. First, he says, we rely on reasons drawn not from Scripture but from philosophy and common reason to establish and confirm that explanation.

units.la: Resp. Si maximè rationibus Philosophicis stabiliatur interpretatio nostra, an propterea falsa censenda fuerit? Principia, ad quae utrique parti in controuersiis fit recurrendum, si tanquam lex, regula, atque norma, debeant esse communia, qua fronte rationem ex Philosophia, & rationis humanae lumine petitas, respuent audebunt illi, qui ad illud ipsum tribunal in omnibus fere controuersiis prouocare, & ex legibus eiusdem, & modo illius de rebus superiorum sententiarum perpetuò iudicare, contra rationem, & ipsum naturae ordinem, solent? Verum an explicatio nostra, solius Philosophiae, & rationis, an vero etiam Scripturarum sacrarum, nitatur fundamento, tum ex Theologorum nostrorum scriptis, & capite vigesimo refutationis nostrae, syncerum iudicium. Deinde, inquit, rationes ipsas interpretationis nostrae consistere non posse, quia Apostolus vocabulum formae haud dubie non Philosophicè, sed vsu vulgari vsurpauerit, ac proinde non ipsam essentiam, sed tantum figuram illo significari. Primo quia etiam Lactantius ipse illud ita reddiderit, & Caluinus expresse scripserit, quod nihil aliud significet, dum forma, inquit, significat figuram vel apparentiam, vt vulgò loquuntur. Secundo quia etiam in sequentibus eadem vocabulum formae, loco figurae vsurpetur, vbi tamen non ipsam naturam, sed turam taram, seu essentiam, verum externam tantum speciem denotet. Tertio quia etiam Marcus 16. v. 12. nomen formae eodem sensu vsurpetur qui ipse locus ex Graeco textu sic reddi debeat: postea autem cum duo ex illis ambularet, manifestauit se illis alia forma. Unde manifeste demonstrari inquit nomen formae in Scripturis, pro externa specie, & figura vsurpari.
units.tr: Reply. Suppose our interpretation were supported chiefly by philosophical arguments. Would it therefore be judged false? If the principles to which both sides must appeal in controversies ought to be common, as a law, rule and standard, with what face will those men refuse reasons taken from philosophy and the light of human reason? They are the same men who, in almost every controversy, call upon that very tribunal and constantly judge the statements of the older writers about divine things by its laws and its methods, against reason and the very order of nature. But whether our explanation rests on the foundation of philosophy and reason alone, or also on the Holy Scriptures, may be judged fairly from the writings of our theologians and from the twentieth chapter of our refutation. Next, he says, the arguments for our interpretation cannot stand, because the Apostle undoubtedly used the word "form" not in a philosophical sense but in common usage, and so it signifies not the essence itself but only an outward figure. First, because Lactantius himself so rendered it, and Calvin expressly wrote that it signifies nothing else, since "form", he says, signifies figure or appearance, as people commonly speak. Second, because in the following verses the same word "form" is used in place of "figure", where it denotes not the nature itself, but an outward appearance only, not the essence. Third, because also in Mark 16:12 the name "form" is used in the same sense, and that passage ought to be rendered from the Greek text thus: "afterwards, as two of them walked, he showed himself to them in another form." From this he says it is plainly shown that in Scripture the name "form" is used for an outward appearance and figure.

units.la: Resp. Si maxime Apostolus, nomen formae, pro externa specie & figura sumpsit, an propterea no etiam philosophica significatione vocem illam vsurpauit? Plato certe, Aristoteles, & Theophrastus, aliique Philosophi, nomine μορφῆς aliquoties τὸ εἶδος seu externam figuram & speciem denotare voluerunt, unde etiam illa diuisio formae in externam & internam, seu accidentalem & essentialem, apud nonnullos obtinuit, quibus haec proprie, altera vero improprie, formae nomine indigitari consueuit. Sed videamus quantae sint rationes illae, quibus probare conatur Apostolum nomen forma, non philosophice, id est, proprie, sed vulgari significatione, improprie vsurpasse. Ad primam itaque dico, quamuis nos Lutheri versione nec stare, nec cadere velimus, tamen, quia nome illud Germanicum, quo Lutherus vocabulum forma reddidit, tam internam & essentialem, quam externam & accidentalem denotat, versio illa Samosateno minime patrocinatur. Caluinum quod attinet, dicit ille quidem, formam significare figuram seu apparitiam: quia simul statuit, & extra Deum talem formam, non fallacem, neque commentitam non reperiri, & formam illam ipsam maiestatem, & gloriam diuinam significare, necessario etiam per illam Dei formam proprietatem essentialem intelligit: secus enim frustra Diuinam Christi naturam inde demonstrare conaretur, qua de re sententiae ex Commentariis illius, a nobis paulo ante citatae, legantur. Ad secundam, respondeo falsum esse, quod ab illo affirmatur, nempe in sequentibus nomen formae, ipsam figuram & speciem tantum significari, qua de re iam capite vigesimo egimus, & paulo post agendum erit amplius. Ad tertiam quod attinet, fatemur nomen forma interdum in Scripturis, vt & in loco, quem citauit. Aduersarius, figuram & speciem externam significare: sed negamus, eam ob causam, etiam hoc loco, de quo agimus, idem vocabulo illo denotari. Quum enim nomen μορφωσις, deriuatum a nomine μορφὴ ipsam formae impositionem, & apud Hesychium ac Suidam idem quod μορφή significet, & tamen interdum non veram imaginem ac figuram, sed fictam aliquam laruam, & fallacem ꝑ ementitámque speciem denotet,vt Rom.2.v.20.& 2. Tim.3. v.5. ideò ab vno loco ad alterum non datur consequentia.Quia, cùm vnum idémque nomen in Scripturis sacris varias habet significationes,tum non sequitur, si in hoc significatu vsurpetur hoc aut illo loco, ideo etiam eodem vsurpari in alio. Secus enim Marcion aliquis,aut Manichęus, formam illam & figuram, qua Christus duobus discipulis compa-ruit, Marc.16. versu 12. inanem tantùm speciem,& phantasma,ex duobus illis locis Roman.nempe 2.versu 20.vbi μορφωσις externam veritatis speciem significat, & 2. Timoth.3 .versu 5 vbi idem nomen fictam pietatis levanem denotat, significare tam probabiliter concluserit,quam Oftorrodius formam Dei Phil.2. versi.6. figuram tantum Deitatis denotare ex Mar.16. v.12. verè probauerit.
units.tr: Reply. Suppose the Apostle took the word "form" for an outward appearance and figure. Does it follow that he did not also use that word in its philosophical sense? Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus and other philosophers certainly meant by morphē [μορφῆς] sometimes the eidos [τὸ εἶδος], that is, the outward figure and kind. Hence the division of form into external and internal, or accidental and essential, has prevailed among some writers, with the first properly called "form" and the second improperly. But let us see how strong those arguments are by which he tries to prove that the Apostle used the word "form" not philosophically, that is, properly, but in a common sense, improperly. First, then, I say that although we do not wish to stand or fall with Luther's translation, yet, because the German word by which Luther rendered "form" denotes both the internal and essential and the external and accidental, that translation does not in the least favour Samosatenus. As for Calvin, he indeed says that form signifies figure or appearance. But at the same time he holds that outside God no such form exists that is not deceptive or feigned, and that this form signifies the very majesty and glory of God. So he necessarily understands by that form of God an essential property. Otherwise he would labour in vain to prove from it the divine nature of Christ. On this matter, let the passages from his Commentaries which we cited a little earlier be read. Second, I answer that it is false, as he affirms, that in the following verses the word "form" signifies only the figure and appearance. We have already dealt with this in the twentieth chapter, and it must be treated more fully a little later. As for the third, we grant that the word "form" sometimes in Scripture signifies figure and outward appearance, even in the passage the Opponent cited. But we deny that for this reason it has the same meaning in the passage we are discussing. For since the noun morphōsis [μορφωσις], derived from morphē [μορφὴ], denotes the giving of form itself, and in Hesychius and Suidas means the same as morphē, yet sometimes it denotes not a true image and figure but some feigned mask and a false and pretended appearance, as in Romans 2:20 and 2 Timothy 3:5, there is no valid inference from one passage to another. For since one and the same word in the holy Scriptures has various meanings, it does not follow that because it is used in one sense in this or that passage, it is therefore used in the same sense in another. Otherwise some Marcion or Manichaeus might conclude, with as much probability, that the form and figure in which Christ appeared to the two disciples in Mark 16:12 was merely an empty appearance and phantasm, on the ground of those two passages in Romans 2:20, where morphōsis [μορφωσις] signifies the outward appearance of truth, and 2 Timothy 3:5, where the same word denotes a feigned semblance of godliness. Ostorodius has proved this about the "form of God" in Philippians 2:6, that it denotes only a figure of deity from Mark 16:12, no more truly than they would.

units.la: Tertiò, argumentum nostrum, quod ex illis Pauli verbis dedu-cimus, quibus Christus Deo æqualis esse dicitur, hac forma proponit.
units.tr: Third, our argument, which we draw from those words of Paul by which Christ is said to be equal to God, we set out in this form.

units.la: Nulla creatura Deo est æqualis.
units.tr: No creature is equal to God.

units.la: Christus Deo est æqualis:
units.tr: Christ is equal to God.

units.la: Ergo Christus non est creatura: & consequenter,cùm quicquid est,aut creator sit,aut creatura,idem etiam est ipse creator,diuinámque habet naturam.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not a creature. And consequently, since whatever exists is either creator or creature, he is himself the creator and has the divine nature.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum respondet Oftorrodius primò, sequi ex illo Christum non esse hominem,cùm negét ipsum esse creaturam.
units.tr: To this argument Ostorodius replies, first, that it follows from it that Christ is not a man, since he denies that he is a creature.

units.la: Ratiocinatio talis est.
units.tr: The reasoning goes like this.

units.la: Quod argumentum affirmat Christum non esse creaturam, id etiam affirmat Christum non esse verum hominem.
units.tr: Whatever argument affirms that Christ is not a creature also affirms that Christ is not a true man.

units.la: Atqui argumentum prædictum affirmat prius:
units.tr: But the aforementioned argument affirms the former.

units.la: Ergo etiam affirmat posterius: & per consequens est fictum.
units.tr: Therefore it also affirms the latter, and consequently it is false.

units.la: Resp. nofler ex malitia,an ex crassa aliqua ignorantia merito quis dubitauerit. Quid enim aut malitiosius est,aut magis imperitum,quàm quę de subiecto secundum quid & certo respectu,dicuntur vere,atque pie,ea de toto subiecto & simpliciter interpretari? Christum ex numero creatarum rerum exim-mus cum scriptura,quę ipsi rerum omnium creationem adscribit, secundùm naturam eius diuinam, & nihilominus creaturam affirmaaffirmamus, verúmque hominem, sed secundùm naturam eius alteram, nempe humanam. An ignorat Oftorrodius contraria de eodem subiecto enuntiari posse, modò illud non fiat secundùm idem, & ad idem, & eodem tempore ? Sed ita lubet ipsi naturam Christi impugnare, & σοφιστὴν sumptis armis, & rationibus ab alterius naturæ videlicet humanæ conditione, quem eram iam in antecedentibus satis luculenter perstrinximus, & confutavimus.
units.tr: Reply: we may well ask whether this comes from malice or from some gross ignorance. For what is more malicious, or more unskilled, than to take what is said truly and piously of a subject in a certain respect and in a certain sense, and to interpret it of the whole subject without qualification? We exempt Christ from the number of created things with Scripture, which ascribes the creation of all things to him, according to his divine nature; and yet we affirm that he is a creature and a true man, according to his other nature, namely the human. Does Ostorodius not know that contraries can be predicated of the same subject, provided this is not done in the same respect, towards the same thing, and at the same time? But he wishes thus to attack the nature of Christ, and, taking up arms as a sophist [σοφιστὴν], argues from the condition of the other, the human, nature, which we have already sufficiently and clearly touched upon and refuted in what precedes.

units.la: Secundò, respondet ad propositionem maiorem, per distinctionem, eámque duplicem, & dicit intelligendam esse æqualitatem, aut naturalem, aut quæ ex libera Dei voluntate fit communicata, & eam verum vel absolutam esse, & perfectam, vel non absolutam, ac imperfectam: propositionem itaque maiorem, si loquatur de naturali, & perfecta absolutáque æqualitate, veram, sed minorem, nisi fallaciam æquivocationis committat, falsam esse. Si autem intelligatur æqualitas imperfecta, & ex libera voluntate à Deo concessa, tum minorem propositionem esse veram, maiorem verò falsam : Primò, quia Deus possit aliquam creaturam sibi facere æqualem, licet non absolutè & in omnibus. Secundo, quia ipsi etiam Aduersarii (nempe nos) statuant Christum, quà creatura est, per unionem personalem naturæ divinæ, & humanæ, ita glorificatum esse, ut de ipso omnes proprietates divinæ naturæ prædicari possint, ipsáque divina potentia præditus divino cultu & honore affici debeat.
units.tr: Second, he replies to the major premise by a distinction, and a twofold one. He says that equality must be understood either as natural, or as communicated by the free will of God; and that the first is true or absolute and perfect, while the second is not absolute but imperfect. Accordingly, if the major premise speaks of a natural, perfect and absolute equality, it is true; but the minor premise, unless he commits the fallacy of equivocation, is false. If, however, equality is understood as imperfect and granted by God's free will, then the minor premise is true and the major false. First, because God could make some creature equal to himself, though not absolutely and in all things. Second, because our opponents themselves (that is, we) hold that Christ, as a creature, has been so glorified through the personal union of the divine and human natures that all the properties of the divine nature can be predicated of him, and that he, endowed with divine power, ought to receive divine worship and honour.

units.la: Resp. Quum omnis æqualitas sit relatio, & huius quidem, de qua inter nos & Aduersarium disceptatur, subiectum ac terminus, Deus & Christus, tanquam relatum & correlatum statuatur, idcò, tum argumenti nostri momentum, pondus, atque inuicta veritas, tū responsionis Oftorrodianæ anilis subtilitas, & manifesta falsitas eò magis elucescat, fundamentum relationis illius inda gandum, ac vera æqualitatis istius causa nobis inquirenda est, & ostendendum quidnam sit illud in quo, & propter quod Christus æqualis esse dicatur. Fundamentum autem huius æqualitatis non posse, quàm ipsas proprietates essentiales Dei, ex eo subiiliud esse non posse, quàm ipsas proprietates essentiales Dei, ex eo colligitur, quod omnes cæteræ cōparationes, quæ in actionibus & effectis fundantur, in illas ipsas proprietates veluti omnium actionum principia resoluatur, quod vsque adeò verum est, vt inter duarum causarum, puta Dei & Christi actiones, nisi ex illo principio, virtute nempe divina, proficiscatur, nulla vnquam æqualitas statui possit,cum vnius essentiæ proprias actiones, nemo nisi quiuis eiusdem est essentiæ,æqualiter præstare queat, semperque attendum illud Prophetæ, Et quis est par Iehouæ Deo nostro, qui alibi habitat? Ps. 113. v. 5. Cùm igitur Christus Deo Patri æqualis dicitur, necessario hoc fit respectu rei alicuius, quæ Deo tanquam proprietas aliqua essentialis competit, cùm accidens nullum in ipsum cadat. Hæc autem ipsa in Christo, secundùm doctrinam Adversariorum, qui ipsum φιλον tantùm ἀνθρωπον esse statuunt, non essentialis, seu essentialis, sed συμβεβηκòς, & accidentalis, quia ipsius essentiæ, & naturæ humanæ, illámque comitantium infirmitatum respectu, nobis per omnia excepto peccato, est similis, teste Apostolo Heb. 2. vers. 17. & 4. vers. 15. Rursum vel omnes proprietates diuinæ intelliguntur, vel vna aut altera tantùm, eæque vel ipsæ, vel earundem communicata aliqua ὑπόστασις. Atqui Christus ratione communicatæ illius ὑποστάσεως, Deo Patri æqualis dici non potest, tum quia illa creata, & finita est, vtpote creaturæ finitæ compe- tens: tum quia tantum differt ab ipsa Dei essentiali proprietate quantum radius à Sole, vmbra ab ipso corpore, & imago aliquâ adumbrata ab ipso prototypo. Neque etiam vnius aut alterius proprietatis respectu æqualis Deo dicitur, primò, quicquid est accidens in vno subiecto, id non potest esse proprietas essentialis in alio subiecto, & vice versa, secus manifestâ implicaretur contradictio: Atqui omnes proprietates Dei sunt essentiales Deo: Ergo non possunt esse accidentia in Christo, & per confequês, si ille φιλος fit ἀνθρωπος illarum respectu Deo æqualis dici non potest. Secundò, quia vna proprietas essentialis diuinæ naturæ sine cæteris omnibus communicari non potest. Si enim in ente creato omnes proprietates essentiales sunt ὁμόγονοι, ὁμοούσιοι & ὁμοφυεῖς, hoc est, simul oriuntur, existunt, & corrumpuntur: quantò minus ipsæ proprietates diuinæ, quæ propter absolutam Dei simplicitatem, neque inter sese, neque ab ipsa diuina natura, realiter differunt, sed secundùm nostrum duntaxat concipiendi modum, à se se inuicem separari possunt. Deinde cui vna proprietas essentialis naturæ diuinæ communicatur, ei etiam ipsam essentiâ diuinâ communicari necesse est: cui autê essentia diuina communicatur, ei necesse est omnes etiam illius essentiales proprietates communicari, cũ hæc sint inuicem sint ἀχώριστα, imo nihil aliud sint, quàm ipsa simplicissima essentia Dei. Sequitur ergo Christum non vnius tantùm, aut alterius terius sed omnium proprietatum essentialium Dei, respectu, Deo Patri æqualem dici, ac proinde naturæ & essentiæ suæ ratione, non nudū tātum esse hominē, sed verum, atque æternum Deum, secus enim nec proprietates illæ Christo competerent, vt iam demonstrauimus, nec inter ipsum & Deum, illarum respectu vlla æqualitas statui posset. Cui euidentissimæ rationi, etiam hoc accepti dit, quod haud dubie, omnium piorum iudicio, nudam creaturam cum Deo creatore æquare velle, ratione, aut respectu vllo, nihil aliud est, quàm summa cū impietate, Deū ex sohii & maiestatis suæ celsitudine, in creaturarum numerum deturbare, diuinitatem ipsi inuito, temerario, & nefario primorum nostrorum parentum auferre, & creaturam, creatori sociam adiungere. Ex hisce vero omnibus tria illa necessario consequuntur, primo falsam, & ex celebri Socipiano confictam esse distinctionem illā æqualitatis cū Deo Patre in naturalem, seu absolutam, & perfectam, & in nō absolutā ac imperfectam, & ex libera voluntate à Deo communicatam. Secundò falsò negari ab Aduersario assumptionem nostram, qua Christum Deo Patri absoluta, perfecta, & naturali æqualitate, æqualem esse affirmamus. Cum enim illam æqualitatem inde exurgere ostenderimus, quod omnes proprietates essentiales Dei, de Christo prædicentur, necessario inde sequitur eandem perfectam, absolutam, & Christo naturalem esse, à Patre non ex libera voluntate, sed natura secundum actionem voluntatis communicatam, quamuis proprie loquendo non ipsa æqualitas, sed res aliqua, vnde æqualitas, aut inæqualitas exurgit, communicari dicatur. Tertiò falsam esse ratiōnem Aduersarii primam, qua videlicet affirmat, posse Deum aliquam creaturam sibi æqualem facere, licet non absolutè, & in omnibus. Quia enim omnis æqualitas cum Deo in perfecta omnium proprietatum diuinarum communicatione consistit, harum autem nullius creatura vlla capax esse possit, etiam falsum ac plane impossibile est, Deum vllam creaturam ratione vlla sibi æqualem facere posse.
units.tr: Reply: since all equality is a relation, and since in this relation, about which we dispute with our opponent, the subject and the term, God and Christ, are set forth as relatum and correlate, therefore, so that both the weight and the invincible truth of our argument, and the senile subtlety and manifest falsity of Ostorodius' reply may stand out all the more clearly, we must investigate the ground of that relation and the true cause of this equality, and show what it is in which, and on account of which, Christ is said to be equal. Now the ground of this equality cannot be anything other than the essential properties of God themselves. This follows from the fact that all other comparisons, which are founded on actions and effects, are resolved into those very properties as the principles of all actions. This is so true that, between the actions of two causes, namely God and Christ, no equality can ever be established unless it proceeds from that principle, namely divine power; for no one, except one who is of the same essence, can equally perform the proper actions of one essence. And we must always keep in mind that word of the prophet: "Who is like Jehovah our God, who dwells on high?" (Ps. 113. v. 5). Since therefore Christ is said to be equal to God the Father, this necessarily happens with respect to some thing which belongs to God as an essential property, since no accident falls upon him. Now this very thing in Christ, according to the teaching of our opponents, who hold that he is merely a man [φιλον ἀνθρωπον], is not essential but accidental (συμβεβηκòς), since with respect to the essence and human nature, and the infirmities that accompany it, he is like us in all things except sin, as the Apostle witnesses (Heb. 2. vers. 17 and 4. vers. 15). Again, either all the divine properties are meant, or only one or another of them, and these either themselves or some hypostasis communicated of them. But Christ, by reason of that communicated hypostasis, cannot be said to be equal to God the Father: first, because it is created and finite, as belonging to a finite creature; second, because it differs from the essential property of God itself only as a ray differs from the sun, a shadow from the body, or a shadowy image from its archetype. Nor is he said to be equal to God with respect to one or another property. First, whatever is an accident in one subject cannot be an essential property in another subject, and vice versa; otherwise a manifest contradiction would follow. But all the properties of God are essential to God. Therefore they cannot be accidents in Christ, and consequently, if he is merely a man, he cannot be said to be equal to God with respect to them. Second, because one essential property of the divine nature cannot be communicated without all the others. For if in a created being all essential properties are co-originate, co-essential and co-natural [ὁμόγονοι, ὁμοούσιοι, ὁμοφυεῖς], that is, they arise, exist and perish together, how much less so are the divine properties, which, on account of the absolute simplicity of God, do not really differ from one another or from the divine nature itself, but can be separated from each other only in our manner of conceiving them. Further, to whomever one essential property of the divine nature is communicated, the divine essence itself must also be communicated to him; and to whomever the divine essence is communicated, all its essential properties must necessarily be communicated as well, since these are inseparable [ἀχώριστα] from one another, and indeed are nothing other than the most simple essence of God itself. It follows, therefore, that Christ is said to be equal to God the Father not with respect to only one or another property, but with respect to all the essential properties of God; and consequently, by reason of his nature and essence, he is not merely a man but a true and eternal God. Otherwise those properties would not belong to Christ, as we have already shown, nor could any equality between him and God with respect to them be established. To this most evident reasoning must be added this too: that to wish to make a bare creature equal to God the Creator, in any reason or respect, is, beyond doubt by the judgement of all the godly, nothing other than, with the greatest impiety, to cast God down from the height of his sovereignty and majesty into the number of creatures, to take away from him, against his will, by a rash and wicked act like that of our first parents, his divinity, and to join a creature as companion to the Creator. From all these things, however, three conclusions necessarily follow. First, that the distinction of equality with God the Father into natural or absolute and perfect, and into non-absolute and imperfect communicated by free will, is false and invented by the famous Socinus. Second, that our assumption, by which we affirm that Christ is equal to God the Father with an absolute, perfect and natural equality, is falsely denied by the opponent. For since we have shown that this equality arises from the fact that all the essential properties of God are predicated of Christ, it necessarily follows that the same equality is perfect, absolute and natural to Christ, and is communicated not by the free will of the Father but by nature, according to the action of the will; although, properly speaking, it is not equality itself but some thing from which equality or inequality arises that is said to be communicated. Third, that the opponent's first reason, namely that God could make some creature equal to himself, though not absolutely and in all things, is false. For since all equality with God consists in the perfect communication of all the divine properties, and since no creature is capable of any of these, it is also false and plainly impossible that God could make any creature equal to himself in any respect.

units.la: Rationem alteram, qua Ostorrodius negationem assumptionis nostrae per fictam illā distinctionem stabilire conatur, quātum cernit, qui duarum naturarum in Christo, diuinæ nempe & humanæ, eiusmodi vnionem hypostaticam confingunt, qua essentiales Dei proprietates realiter, seu reipsa, humanæ naturæ
units.tr: The second argument, by which Ostorrodius tries to establish the denial of our assumption through that invented distinction, is, as far as I can see, one that those who fashion a hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ, the divine and the human, must also make. By this union the essential properties of God are communicated really, or in fact, to the human nature considered in itself and in the abstract,

units.la: in sese,ac abstracto consideratæ,sint communicatæ,adeóque verè ac proprie de Christo qua homo,i. humanitate ipsius,prædicetur, illi quidem viderint quomodo se tum ex Eutychetis, tum etiam vestris laqueis expediant. Ostorrodius sub illo figmento tutus delitescere nequit. Nos enim vt ex rei veritate docemus, duas illas naturas in Christo diuinam & humanam personaliter vnitas esse, salutis vtriusque proprietatibus [Greek], [Greek]: ita etiam cum Scriptura sacra tradimus, & confitemur, totiius personæ Christi ab humana natura, vocabulo concreto [Greek] denominatæ, quæcunque sunt Dei propria tribui, sed Christo ab humanitate voce concreta denominato, & [Greek] non [Greek], secundùm humanitatem in abstracto, considerato: quod loquendi genus à veteribus [Greek], à recentioribus communicatio idiomatum appellatum, sententiæ Aduersarii nullatenus patrocinatur. Quod verò eundem Christum hominem religioso cultu veneramur, adorandum & inuocandum censemus, hoc est, adorationem & inuocationem nostram ad ipsam quoque carnem, id est, humanam Christi naturam dirigimus, ex eo non sequitur id quod vult Aduersarius, nempe posse Deum aliquam creaturam sibi, licèt non absolutè, & in omnibus, æqualem reddere, cùm honorem illum humanæ Christi naturæ tribuamus, non simpliciter, sed [Greek], id est, non quatenus est simpliciter, & in sese creatura, sed respectiuè, quatenus est Filii Dei caro, in qua sicuti se mundo exhibere voluit, & implere [Greek], nostræ salutì comparandæ necessaria, sic nunc quoque vult vt Seruator, Rex, & Gubernator noster agnosci, coli, & inuocari, eiusque nobis per fidem spiritua-liter apprehensæ interuentu nos quotidie ex fide in fidem, ac tandem ad beatam illam immortalitatem perducere. Atque hinc etiam euanescit id quod Aduersarius initio sectionis quartæ subiungit, nempe Trinitarios demonstrare non posse, quod Christus Deo per omnia sit æqualis. Cuicunque enim omnes proprietates Dei essentiales tribuuntur, ille etiam Deo Patri per omnia est æqualis: Atqui Christo omnes proprietates Dei essentiales tribuuntur, quia illarum respectu Deo Patri æqualis dicitur, vt paulò ante demonstrauimus: Ergo Christus Deo Patri per omnia est æqualis, æqualitate absoluta, & perfecta.
units.tr: so that they are truly and properly predicated of Christ as man, that is, of his humanity. Let them see how they extricate themselves from this snare, both the snare of Eutyches and your own. Ostorrodius cannot hide safely behind that fiction. We teach, as the truth of the matter requires, that the two natures in Christ, the divine and the human, are united in one person, each retaining the properties of its own nature. We also teach and confess, in accordance with holy Scripture, that all the proper attributes of God are ascribed to the whole person of Christ, named from his human nature by a concrete term. But they are ascribed to Christ named from his humanity by a concrete term, and not to the humanity considered in the abstract, according to his human nature. Scripture speaks in this way, and the ancients called it the communication of properties (communicatio idiomatum). This manner of speaking gives no support at all to the opinion of our opponent. As for our worshipping this same Christ as man with religious reverence, and holding that he is to be adored and invoked, that is, that we direct our adoration and invocation to his very flesh, that is, to the human nature of Christ, it does not follow from this what our opponent wants, namely that God can make some creature equal to himself, although not absolutely and in all respects. For we give that honour to the human nature of Christ not simply, but in a relative sense; that is, not insofar as it is a creature simply and in itself, but relatively, insofar as it is the flesh of the Son of God. In that flesh he willed to show himself to the world and to fulfil what was necessary for the acquiring of our salvation. In the same way he now also wills to be acknowledged, worshipped and invoked as our Saviour, King and Governor. Through his intercession, apprehended spiritually by us through faith, he daily leads us from faith to faith, and at last to that blessed immortality. Hence also vanishes what our opponent adds at the beginning of the fourth section, namely that Trinitarians cannot show that Christ is equal to God in all things. For whoever has all the essential properties of God ascribed to him is also equal to God the Father in all things. But all the essential properties of God are ascribed to Christ, since he is said to be equal to God the Father with respect to those properties, as we showed a little above. Therefore Christ is equal to God the Father in all things, with an absolute and perfect equality.

units.la: Quarto dicit Aduersarius, formam illam Dei, nihil aliud esse quàm figuram, speciémque & apparentiam, sicut, cùm Christus dicitur ... turn in forma Dei fuisse, nihil aliud sit intelligere, quàm quod fuerit similis Deo, seu Deo similis: quum autem ipsa æqualitas illa cum Deo, de qua loquitur Apostolus, nihil aliud sit, quàm ipsa forma Dei, idcirco necessario sequi, quod illa æqualitate nihil aliud significetur, nisi quod Christus Deo similis fuerit, non quidem similitudine perfecta, & ex qua ipsum etiam Deum esse consequatur.
units.tr: Fourthly, our opponent says that the form of God is nothing other than a figure, an appearance and a semblance, so that when Christ is said ... to have been in the form of God, this means nothing more than that he was like God, or similar to God. But since that very equality with God, of which the Apostle speaks, is nothing other than the form of God itself, it necessarily follows, so he says, that by this equality nothing more is signified than that Christ was like God, not indeed with a perfect likeness from which it would follow that he is God himself.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: Argumentum tale est.

units.la: Si æqualitas illa cum Deo, de qua loquitur Apostolus, nihil aliud significat, quam figuram externam, apparentiam & similitudinem aliquam cum Deo, tum sequitur non significare naturam ac essentiam divinam, & per consequens divinam Christi naturā ex illa æqualitate demonstrari non posse.
units.tr: If that equality with God of which the Apostle speaks signifies nothing other than an external figure, appearance and some likeness with God, then it follows that it does not signify the nature and essence of God, and consequently the divine nature of Christ cannot be demonstrated from that equality.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Rationem consequentiæ hanc adfert:
units.tr: He brings forward the reason for the consequence as follows:

units.la: Si ille, qui est sicut Deus, vel Deo similis, non potest esse ipse Deus, nec divinam naturam habere, tum si æqualitas illa nihil aliud significat, quam figuram externam, apparentiam & similitudinem cum Deo, tum sequitur illam non significare ipsam naturam, ac essentiam divinam.
units.tr: If one who is as God, or like God, cannot himself be God nor have the divine nature, then if that equality signifies nothing other than an external figure, appearance and likeness with God, it follows that it does not signify the nature and essence of God itself.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Assumptionem syllogismi principalis hac ratione pobare conatur.
units.tr: He tries to prove the assumption of the principal syllogism by this argument:

units.la: Si ipsa forma Dei nihil aliud significat quàm figuram externam, apparentiam & similitudinem aliquam cum Deo, non verò ipsam essentiam, seu naturam divinam: & ipsa æqualitas illa cum Deo, nihil aliud est quam ipsa forma Dei: tum sequitur ipsam quoque æqualitatem nihil aliud significare, quàm eandem figuram externam, apparentiam, & similitudinem aliquam cum Deo, non verò ipsam essentiam ac naturam divinam.
units.tr: If the form of God itself signifies nothing other than an external figure, appearance and some likeness with God, and not the essence or divine nature itself; and that equality with God is nothing other than the form of God itself; then it follows that equality too signifies nothing other than the same external figure, appearance and some likeness with God, and not the essence and divine nature itself.

units.la: Atqui prius utrumque verum est. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But both the first points are true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Resp. Primò, falsam esse consequentiam prosyllogismi, quo connexum syllogismi principalis probare conatur Aduersarius: quæ falsitas, ut eo manifestius appareat, duplex attendenda est distinctio: prima quòd nomen Deus modò οὐσιῶς seu essentialiter, modò ὑποστατικῶς seu personaliter, pro hac nempe aut illa sacrosanctæ Trinitatis persona vsurpatur, & Christo quidem oppositum ipsum Patrem denotat: altera quod similia sunt diuersi generis, neque ad vnum eundemque locum dialecticum referuntur. Sunt enim vel τὰ ὁμοίως ἐχόντα, vel τὰ ὁμοίως ὑπάρχοντα, id est, vel similiter se habet, vel similiter insunt. In illis spectatur ipsa tantum ἀξίωσις, habitudo, & non proportio: in his vero nulla proportio, sed ipsa ἐν τῷ ὑπάρξει, & quasi inexistentia: unde illa ad locum similium, haec ad locum pariter referuntur. Iam vero si Christus est similis Deo, id est, essentiae diuinae, nomine videlicet Dei ὁμοούσιος sumpto, tum certum est non habere ipsum eandem numero essentiam Dei: sed hoc sensu instituta similitudo falsa est, & Arriana. Si autem Christus similis dicatur Deo Patri, genere similium posteriori, tum omnino falsa est consequentia. Demonstratur haec distinctio ex Iohannis capite 5. versu 19. Quaecunque Pater facit, haec etiam Filius ὁμοίως, id est, pariter facit. Hoc autem si secundum naturam similium esset intelligendum, tum mundo illi, quem Pater creauit, alium similem à Filio conditum esse, sequeretur. Secundo, falsum esse eiusdem syllogismi principalis assumptionem, quae altero prosyllogismo minime confirmari potest, quia propositionis minoris, in illo pars valde manifesta falsitate laborat. Nam ὡς φῶς τοῦ ἥλιος non specie tantum, figuram, umbratilem aliquam apparentiam & similitudinem, sed ipsam essentiam diuinam cum omnibus proprietatibus suis significare, supra capite vigesimo multis argumentis demonstrauimus, quorum robur sophisticis Aduersarii exceptionibus labefactari non potest, ex iis, quae initio huius capitis diximus, satis super que liquet, itaque Aduersarius principium illud frustra petat. Aequalitatem vero illam non esse idem quod forma Dei (quae efficitur altera assumptionis in prosyllogismo pars) ex eo solide euincitur, quod aequalitas est relatio, forma autem Dei, relationis illius fundamentum, & aequalitatis causa, propter quam videlicet Christus Deo Patri aequalis est, & dicitur. Atque haec sunt illa terribilia argumenta, quibus ex hoc ipso loco, sententiam nostram confirmatam esse Oftorrodius pollicetur, quae quàm sint vana aut futilia, ex iis quae dicta sunt, liquido constat.
units.tr: Answer. First, the consequence of the prosyllogism, by which the Adversary tries to prove the connection of the principal syllogism, is false. To make this falsity plainer, a twofold distinction must be noted. The first is that the name God is used sometimes essentially [οὐσιωδῶς] and sometimes personally [ὑποστατικῶς], that is, for this or that person of the most holy Trinity; and as opposed to Christ it denotes the Father himself. The second is that things which are alike belong to different kinds, and are not referred to one and the same dialectical place. For some things are "those that are similarly disposed" [τὰ ὁμοίως ἐχόντα], and others are "those that similarly belong" [τὰ ὁμοίως ὑπάρχοντα], that is, they either stand in a similar relation or similarly inhere. In the former case only the relation itself is considered, a habitude and not a proportion; but in the latter there is no proportion, but the very being-in [ἐν τῷ ὑπάρξει] and, as it were, inexistence; whence the former are referred to the place of likes and the latter to the place of things equally shared. Now if Christ is like God, that is, like the divine essence, the name God being taken as consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος], then it is certain that he does not have the same numerical essence as God; but in this sense the comparison drawn is false and Arian. If, however, Christ is said to be like God the Father, belonging to the latter kind of likes, then the consequence is altogether false. This distinction is shown from John chapter 5, verse 19: "Whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in like manner [ὁμοίως], that is, equally." But if this were to be understood according to the nature of things that are alike, it would follow that another world like that which the Father created had been made by the Son. Second, the assumption of the same principal syllogism is false, and it cannot be confirmed by the other prosyllogism, because the part of the minor premise in it suffers from a very manifest falsity. For that Christ is "the brightness of the glory" [ὡς φῶς τοῦ ἥλιος] signifies not merely a shape, a shadowy appearance and likeness in appearance, but the divine essence itself with all its properties, we have demonstrated by many arguments above in chapter twenty, whose force cannot be weakened by the sophistical objections of the Adversary; and from what we said at the beginning of this chapter it is sufficiently and abundantly clear. So the Adversary seeks that principle in vain. That equality is not the same as the form of God (which is the second part of the assumption in the prosyllogism) is solidly proved from the fact that equality is a relation, while the form of God is the foundation of that relation and the cause of equality, on account of which Christ is equal to God the Father and is said to be so. And these are those "terrible" arguments by which Ostorrodius promises that our view is confirmed from this very passage; how empty or trifling they are is clear from what has been said.

units.la: Quinto, Sententia nostra sic quibus potuit rationibus refutata, explicat, quanam in re forma illa Dei & aequalitas, id est (ut illi fingit) figura diuinitatis, & similitudo cum Deo sita fit, quam illi in duobus illis capitibus ponit. Primò, quod Christus virtutem & potentiam in se habuerit, opera illa faciendi, quae nemo à se, nisi solus Deus, efficere potest, ut quod tam absens, quam praesens, omnibus creatura turbat. turis super terram, imo etiam Diabolis, & denique rebus inanimatis, vt mari, ventis, morbis, & ipsi morti imperauerit quicquid volucrit, quae etiam omnia ipsi obediuerint. Secundò, quod propter diuinam illam potentiam, vbique aliquos habuerit, qui ad ipsum, sicuti ad Deum ipsum, confugerint, auxilium eius implorauerint, vt ex parte diuina reuerentia ipsum prosequuti fuerint, adorauerint, & coram ipso prociderint.
units.tr: Fifthly, our opinion, having been refuted by the arguments we could bring, explains in what matter that form of God and equality, that is (as he imagines) the figure of divinity and likeness to God, consists; which he sets out in two heads. First, that Christ had in himself the power and might to perform those works of doing which no one can do of himself except God alone, so that, being as absent as present, he disturbed all creatures on the earth, indeed even the devils, and finally inanimate things, such as the sea, winds, diseases, and death itself, commanding whatever he wished, and all of these obeyed him. Second, that on account of that divine power he had some everywhere who fled to him as to God himself, sought his help, and, out of divine reverence, followed him, worshipped him, and fell down before him.

units.la: Resp. Vt de eo nihil dicam, quod Osiorrhodius ad hanc suam interpretationem stabiliendam, ne quidem adfert, sed cerebri Sociniani figmenta illa nobis tanquam oracula obtrudit, quantum ad primum caput attinet, ipse Osiorrhodius proprio gladio miserè iugulatur. Quod enim confitetur Christum virtutem ac potentiam miracula patrandi in se ipso habuisse, ex eo Christum verum ac aeternum Deum esse, ipsámque essentiam, ac naturam diuinam habere, solidè euincitur, idque hoc modo:
units.tr: Reply. I will say nothing here about the proofs Ostorrodius offers to establish his interpretation; he brings forward the figments of the Socinian brain as if they were oracles. As far as the first point goes, Ostorrodius is cut down by his own sword. For his admission that Christ had in himself the power and might to work miracles, once granted, firmly proves that Christ is the true and eternal God and has the essence and divine nature. It is proved in this way:

units.la: Qui praestat illa miracula, quae solus Deus à se ipso efficere potest, & in se habet virtutem ac potentiam miracula illa patrandi, ille etiam habet ipsam essentiam, ac naturam diuinam, & per consequens est verus atque aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Whoever performs those miracles which only God can effect by himself, and has in himself the power and might to work those miracles, also has the very essence and divine nature, and consequently is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui Christus praestat illa miracula, quae solus Deus à se ipso efficere potest, & virtutem ac potentiam miracula illa patrandi, in se ipso habet.
units.tr: But Christ performs those miracles which only God can effect by himself, and has in himself the power and might to work those miracles.

units.la: Ergo Christus ipsam etiam essentiam ac naturam diuinam habet, & per consequens est verus atque aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ also has the very essence and divine nature, and consequently is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Propositio minor inter nos & Aduersarios extra controuersiam est, maiorem sic probo:
units.tr: The minor premise is beyond dispute between us and our opponents. I prove the major as follows.

units.la: Si diuina miraculorum patratio est opus Dei ad extra, quod à sola essentia Dei proficiscitur, tum sequitur, quicunque praestat illa miracula, quae solus Deus à se ipso efficere potest, & virtutem miracula illa patrandi in se ipso habet, eum etiam ipsam essentiam, ac naturam habere, & per consequens verum atque aeternum Deum esse.
units.tr: If the divine working of miracles is an external work of God, which proceeds from the essence of God alone, then it follows that whoever performs those miracles which only God can effect by himself, and has in himself the power of working those miracles, also has the essence and nature itself, and consequently is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Assumptionis necessaria veritas inde liquet, quod operationum diuinarum ad extra, vt loquuntur, aliud principium praeter essentiam diuinam monstrari non potest, cui etiam tanquam causae propriae, omnia miracula vera sunt ascribenda: vnde necessario sequitur, cùm Christo illæ ipsæ operationes tribuantur, necessario eidem causam ipsam,nempe essentiam diuinā tribuen- dam esse,quum operationes essentiæ diuinæ proprias,nemo,nisi e- iusdē essentiæ particeps præstare possit. Hisce addo & illud,quod cùm ipsa potentia Dei,qua miracula patrantur, & quæ in Christo est,sit essentialis proprietas Dei,quæ à cæteris proprietatibus omnibus sit αὐτοῦ, necessario sequi Christo omnes proprietates diuinas competere,ac proinde,non vnius potentiæ ac virtutis illius miracula patrandi tantùm,sed omnium attributorum diuinorum respeƈtu, Deo Patri æqualem esse,atque dici. Cætera, quæ ad hoc argumentum pertinent,aut contra nos ab Aduersario excipi pos- sent,capite vndecimo prolixè pertraƈtauimus. Quantum verò attinet ad caput alterum, in quo Ostorrodius æqualitatem illam si- tam esse dicit,nempe cultum, & inuocationem, honorémque di- uinum,qui Christo non ex parte tantùm competit,ex ipso æterna Christi deitas,natura,ac essentia diuina solidè euincitur, quemad- modum capite decimo quinto prolixè demonstrauimus. Denique tota illa Aduersarii interpretatio falsa hypothesi,&manifesta prin- cipii petitione nititur,dum videlicet illam æqualitatem nihil nisi formam externam &speciem,seu aliquam similitudinem denota- re,falsò præsupponit, qua de re paulo ante egimus: vt iam frustra sibi contra illam suam interpretationem obiectionem confingat, & in ea refutanda desudet,quæ omnia, quia destructo fundamen- to,per se corruunt,examinare non est opus.
units.tr: The truth of the assumption is clear from the fact that no principle of divine external operations, as they are called, can be shown other than the divine essence, to which all true miracles are to be ascribed as their proper cause. Hence it necessarily follows that, since these same operations are attributed to Christ, the cause itself, namely the divine essence, must necessarily be attributed to him as well, since no one except a participant in that same essence can perform operations proper to the divine essence. To these things I add this: since the power of God by which miracles are wrought, which is in Christ, is an essential property of God, and is his own [αὐτοῦ] in distinction from all the other properties, it necessarily follows that all divine properties belong to Christ, and therefore that he is said to be equal to God the Father not only in respect of that power and virtue of working miracles, but in respect of all the divine attributes. The other matters pertaining to this argument, or which our opponent could raise against us, we have treated at length in the eleventh chapter. As for the second point, in which Ostorrodius says that this equality consists in worship, invocation and divine honour, which belong to Christ not merely in part, the eternal deity, nature and divine essence of Christ is firmly proved from it, as we demonstrated at length in the fifteenth chapter. Finally, that whole interpretation of our opponent rests on a false hypothesis and a manifest begging of the question, in that it falsely presupposes that this equality signifies nothing but an external form and appearance, or some likeness, as we treated shortly before. So he vainly contrives for himself an objection against that interpretation of his own, and labours to refute it; but since the foundation is destroyed, all these things fall of their own accord, and there is no need to examine them.

units.la: Sexto pergit Aduersarius,& conatur explicare,quo sensu Chri- stus æqualitatem illam, non rapinam arbitratus sit, & simul pro- bare conatur inde amplius,æqualitatē illam non nisi similitudine aliquam cum Deo,ex gratia Christo communicatam denotare. Et primò quidem sententiam orthodoxam refutat:deinde paraphra- sin & interpretationem Samosatenianam, quibus potest rationi- bus,confirmat. Sententiam nostram de illa æqualitate quantum concernit,inquit Aduersarius, Si illa vera fit,cum Apostolum nihil ad rem,seu scopum præsentem loquutum esse, quia de Deo nulla ratione dici possit,quod suam diuinitatem non pro rapina habuerit.
units.tr: Sixthly, the opponent goes on and tries to explain in what sense Christ thought that equality was not robbery, and at the same time tries to prove further that that equality denotes nothing but some likeness to God, granted to Christ by grace. And first indeed he refutes the orthodox view, then he confirms his own paraphrase and the Samosatenian interpretation by whatever arguments he can. As far as concerns our view of that equality, says the opponent, if it were true, then the Apostle would have spoken nothing to the point or to the present purpose, since it could not be said of God that he did not regard his divinity as robbery.

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Si per illam æqualitatem intelligatur ipsa essentia, vel natura Dei, tum sequitur Apostolum nihil ad rem & scopum præsentem loquu- tum esse, cùm diceret, Christum illam æqualitatem non rapinam arbitratus. arbitratum esse.
units.tr: If by that equality is understood the very essence or nature of God, then it follows that the Apostle spoke nothing to the point and to the present purpose when he said that Christ did not regard that equality as robbery.

units.la: Atqui consequens est absurdum: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is absurd. Therefore the antecedent is too.

units.la: Rationem consequentiae hanc reddit.
units.tr: He gives this reason for the consequence.

units.la: Si de Deo nulla ratione dici potest, quod diuinam suam naturam, & essentiam non sit rapinam arbitratus: tum si per illam aequalitatem intelligatur ipsa essentia, vel natura Dei, sequitur Apostolum nihil ad rem aut scopum praesentem loquutum esse, quum diceret, Christum aequalitatem non rapinam arbitratum esse.
units.tr: If it cannot be said of God that he did not regard his divine nature and essence as robbery, then if by that equality is understood the very essence or nature of God, it follows that the Apostle spoke nothing to the point or to the present purpose when he said that Christ did not regard equality as robbery.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Resp. Consequetiam esse falsam, vnà cum prosyllogismi assum-ptione: quum enim per rapinam Deum esse idem sit, quod falsa & ambitiosa vsurpatione Deum esse venditare, hoc autem de Deo vel cogitare impium esset, omnino inde sequitur, secundùm pietatem Christianam optimè dici, Deum verum non per rapinam, falsò & ambitiosè nomen & potestatem Dei vsurpare, quod ipsum argumento & scopo Apostoli maximum pondus atque momentum addit. Quum enim negat in eo, quod Christus Deo Patri aequalis sit, vllum fuisse ἁρπαγμόν, aut Christum ambitione aliqua monomè illud Dei vsurpasse, tatae obiectioni & blasphemiae commodissimè ansam omnem praescindit, dum ostendit Christum, non aliqua superbiâ humiliatum fuisse à Patre, & praecipitatum in erram, quod sua conditione non contentus, aequalitatem cum Deo per rapinam occupare voluerit, sed quamuis verus Deus, & omnia Patri aequalis esset: nihilominus tamè sponte salutis no-strae causa seipsum exinaniuisse. Atque hic est verus & genuinus eorum illorum sensus, scopo Apostolii accommodatissimus, veritati Oflorrodius frustra tenebras offundere conatur.
units.tr: Reply. The consequence is false, together with the assumption of the prosyllogism. For since to be God by robbery is the same as to boast of being God by a false and ambitious usurpation, and to think this of God would be impious, it wholly follows that, according to Christian piety, it is rightly said that the true God did not usurp the name and power of God falsely and ambitiously by robbery [ἁρπαγμόν]; and this gives the greatest weight and importance to the argument and purpose of the Apostle. For when he denies that in that which Christ is equal to God the Father there was any robbery [ἁρπαγμόν], or that Christ in any ambition usurped that which belongs to God, he most conveniently cuts off every occasion of that objection and blasphemy, while he shows that Christ was not humbled by the Father through any pride, nor cast down into the depths because, not content with his condition, he wished to seize equality with God by robbery; rather, although he was true God and equal to the Father in all things, nevertheless he willingly emptied himself for the cause of our salvation. And this is the true and genuine sense of those words, most suited to the purpose of the Apostle; Ostorrodius labours in vain to cast shadows over it.

units.la: Deinde verò suam paraphrasin, & interpretationē subiungit, inuiens: Sin verò nostra admittatur interpretatio, tum admodum eleganter loquutus est (Apostolus) quasi diceret, Christum dignitatem illam quae fuerit sicut Deus, non pro rapina habuisse, id est, non mordicus retinuisse more illorum, qui aliquid per rapinam, aut vim occupant, sed donum illam exist imasse, ac proinde eandem cum Deo sic placeret, se-fuisse, illaque se euacuasse. Idcirco & vos Christum hac in parte imitari debetis, & multis illis Dei donis spiritualibus, quae possidetis, non ad superbiam & arrogantiam abuti, nec eos, qui illis destituuntur propter contemnere, sed per ea aliis inseruire, & cum fraterna charitas id exigit, ita nos gerere, quasi illa non haberemus. Quoniam illa non a vobis ipsis habetis, sed Deus illa vobis donauit.
units.tr: Then he adds his own paraphrase and interpretation, saying: But if our interpretation is admitted, then the Apostle spoke most elegantly, as if he were saying that Christ did not regard that dignity which he had, being as God, as robbery; that is, he did not cling to it tightly, like those who seize or grab something by robbery or force, but counted it a gift, and therefore was pleased to be thus equal with God, yet emptied himself. So you too ought to imitate Christ in this respect, and not abuse the many spiritual gifts of God which you possess for pride and arrogance, nor despise those who lack them, but serve others by them, and, as brotherly love demands, conduct yourselves as if you did not have them. For you do not have them from yourselves, but God has given them to you.

units.la: Resp. Nos vero iam in antecedentibus demonstrauimus, per illam ἰσότητα non dignitatem aliquam, aut similitudinem accidentariam, sed aequalitatem in ipsis proprietatibus essentialibus diuinis fundatam, esse intelligendam, unde perpetua principii petitione ludit Aduersarius, dum illam aequalitatem interpretatur, aequalitatem & similitudinem non essentialem, sed accidentariam, & Christo ex gratia a Deo communicatam, candemque interpretationem suae paraphrasi tanquam fundamentum substernit. Deinde, falsum est, quod dicit Aduersarius, nempe illam explicationem suam scopo Apostoli magis quam nostram conuenire. Quum enim Paulo propositum fuerit, nos ad veram ταπεινοφροσύνην horta-ri, & stimulari, exemplo sese humiliantis Christi, ideo tanto maius pondus & momentum habet in se argumentum hortationis illud, quanto in maiori celsitudinis & dignitatis gradu Christus constitutus fuisse, vere dicitur. Quia vero extra controuersiam est, maiorem esse splendorem maiestatis, & gloriae diuinae essentialis, quam dignitatis alicuius, & similitudinis cum Deo accidentariae, ac proinde etiam longe excellentius humiliationis exemplum nobis in Christo proponi, si non tantum in diuinitatis aliqua figura externa, & vmbratili similitudine ille constitutus, nostrae salutis causa, sese humiliauerit, ideo luce meridiana clarius euadit ibi nostram, non autem Aduersarii interpretationem veram atque genuinam esse. Sed expendamus rationes illas, quibus suam explicationem Aduersarius fulcire conatur.
units.tr: Reply. We have already shown in what precedes that by that equality [ἰσότητα] is to be understood not some dignity or accidental likeness, but equality founded in the essential divine properties themselves. Hence the opponent plays with a perpetual begging of the question, since he interprets that equality as an equality and likeness not essential but accidental, communicated to Christ by God out of grace, and he lays this same interpretation beneath his paraphrase as its foundation. Next, it is false, as the opponent says, that his explanation agrees with the purpose of the Apostle better than ours. For since it was Paul's purpose to exhort and stir us to true humility [ταπεινοφροσύνην] by the example of Christ humbling himself, the argument of this exhortation has so much the greater weight and importance, the higher the rank of majesty and dignity in which Christ is placed. And since it is beyond dispute that the splendour of the majesty and glory which is essentially divine is greater than any dignity and accidental likeness to God, and therefore a far more excellent example of humiliation is set before us in Christ, if he, for the sake of our salvation, humbled himself not merely while placed in some external figure of divinity and shadowy likeness, then it becomes clearer than noonday light that our interpretation, not the opponent's, is true and genuine. But let us weigh those reasons by which the opponent tries to support his explanation.

units.la: Hanc igitur suam explicationem probare & stabilire conatur verbis sequentibus, quibus Christus se ipsum exinaniuisse, formam serui assumpta, perhibetur, ac dicit, illud ipsum χένωμα nempe, quo Christus similitudinem suam cum Deo (accidentariam autem falso intelligit) non rapinam duxit, cum permouisse, ut formam, seu figuram serui aut mancipii alicuius assumpserit, & hac ratione semetipsum exinanierit. Si autem Christus diuinam suam formam, pro diuina natura habuerit, id est, se ipsum verum Deum esse nouerit, tum hoc ipsum nec permouere, nec tale nefectum in ipso gignere potuisset, ut se ipsum exinaniret.
units.tr: Hence he tries to prove and establish this explanation of his by the following words, in which Christ is said to have emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He says that this very κένωμα, namely that Christ did not count his equality with God (which he falsely takes to be accidental) a thing to be grasped, induced him to assume the form or figure of a servant or slave of some kind, and in this way to empty himself. But if Christ had regarded his divine form as his divine nature, that is, had known himself to be true God, then this very knowledge could neither have moved him nor produced in him such a disposition that he would empty himself.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is of this kind.

units.la: Affectus ille in Christo, quo cum Deo Patre non duxit rapinam, permouit ipsum, ut formam serui aut mancipii alicuius assumpserit. sumpserit, & hac ratione se ipsum exinaniverit.
units.tr: That disposition in Christ, by which he did not count it robbery to be equal with God the Father, moved him to assume the form of a servant or slave of some kind, and in this way to empty himself.

units.la: Atqui, quod Christus formam illam divinam, essentiam ac naturam divinam, id est, semetipsum Deum esse, existimaverit, ipsum permovere non potuit, ut assumendo formam servi vel mancipii alicuius seipsum exinaniret.
units.tr: But that Christ thought himself to be that divine form, the divine essence and nature, that is, to be God himself, could not have moved him, by assuming the form of a servant or slave of some kind, to empty himself.

units.la: Ergo illud ipsum non est illud, de quo loquitur Apostolus, nec per ipsa natura & essentia Dei est intelligenda.
units.tr: Therefore that very thing is not what the Apostle speaks of, nor is it to be understood of the very nature and essence of God.

units.la: Assumptionem stabilire conatur duabus rationibus: I. quia aberrarent illa verba a scopo Apostoli: quae enim esset illa ratiocinatio, inquit, quoniam Christus suam aequalitatem cum Deo non pro rapina, sed natura sua reputavit, ideo se ipsum exinanire voluit? II. quia potius contrarium inde sequeretur, nempe Christum seipsum noluisse exinanire, quoniam non tantum non docuerit ipsum illud facere, sed etiam nulla ratione fieri potuerit, siquidem nulla iusta causa reddi posset, ob quam Deus rerum omnium Dominus, seipsum exinaniret, & manifestum sit, quod Deus se ipsum nec humiliare, nec ulla ratione exinanire queat.
