Et sic sententia sua nostrae assumptioni opposita (nempe quod affectus ille, quem ipsi Christo tribuunt, id ipsum in illo efficere potuerit, quod & docuerit ipsum, & commode fieri potuerit, ut quoniam similitudine sua non pro rapina, sed Dei dono reputaverit, cum Deo placeret, tanquam mancipii aliquod fieret, & sic seipsum exinaniret) & ratione secunda repetita concludit, hoc in loco nec de Incarnatione Christi, nec de duabus in ipso naturis, quicquam agi.
units.tr: He tries to establish the assumption by two reasons: (1) because those words would stray from the Apostle's purpose; for what kind of inference, he says, would it be: since Christ did not count his equality with God a robbery but his own nature, therefore he willed to empty himself? (2) because the opposite would rather follow from it, namely that Christ did not will to empty himself, since not only did the text not teach him to do that, but it could not be done in any way, since no just cause could be given why God, the Lord of all things, should empty himself, and it is plain that God can neither humble himself nor empty himself in any way. And so he sets his own opinion against our assumption (namely that the disposition which they attribute to Christ himself could have produced in him that which both taught him and could fittingly be done, so that, since he did not regard his equality with God as a robbery but as a gift of God, he should, in pleasing God, become as it were a slave, and so empty himself), and with the second reason repeated he concludes that nothing is treated in this place either of the Incarnation of Christ or of the two natures in him.

units.la: Resp. Propositionem maiorem esse falsam, quia ubi verba illa Apostoli non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo, nec ipse etiam affectus ille qui in Christo fuisse dicitur causam impellente humiliationis Christi continent, sed pertinent ad desumptionem ipsius subiecti, nempe Christi, in quo affectus ille fuisse dicitur, explicantque summa illa dignitatis, excellentiae, & maiestatis celsitudine, ex qua Christus Mediator noster, nostrae salutis causa se demisit. Non enim quod Christus cogitaverit, aut noverit se divinam illam naturam, & maiestatis gloriaeque cum Deo Patre aequalitatem, non per rapinam, aut aliquam iniuriam occupasse, sed ipsa φιλανθρωπία & studio voluntati Patris satisfaciendi, ipsum ad illam humiliationem permoverunt: ut quiuis qui verborum seriem atque constructionem paulo altius perpendit, facile animadvertit. Hinc igitur corruit ipsa assumptio, & eius ratio prima: ad secundam rationem respondeo,
units.tr: Reply. The major premise is false, because where those words of the Apostle, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, do not contain the disposition that is said to have been in Christ as the impelling cause of Christ's humiliation, but refer to the description of the subject itself, namely Christ, in whom that disposition is said to have been, and they set out that supreme height of dignity, excellence and majesty from which Christ our Mediator lowered himself for the sake of our salvation. For it was not because Christ thought, or knew, that his divine nature and equality of majesty and glory with God the Father had not been seized by robbery or some wrong, but it was his love of mankind and his zeal to satisfy the Father's will that moved him to that humiliation, as anyone will readily see who weighs the sequence and construction of the words a little more deeply. Hence the assumption itself falls, and its first reason. To the second reason I reply that

units.la: ignorationis elenchi paralogismo illam laborare: ὁ γὰρ φύσεως, ... ὁ δὲ οἰκονομίας λόγος, vt rectè inquit Nazianzenus oratione 1. de λόγω. Si igitur spectes τοῦ λόγου naturam, & quidem absolutè, ἡ ἀσώματος ... non potest de eo dici, quod fe summiserit, aut quod exaltatus fit, vel quod aliquid in tempore acceperit quia naturæ Dei, quæ summè perfecta, & beata ἀπαθὴς & ἀδιάφθορος, ac immutabilis est, nec ei accedere quicquam, nec etiam decedere potest. At fi illa consideretur relatiuè, respectu officii Mediatoris τῆς οἰκονομίας, ea videlicet ratione, qua à Patre datus & missus dicitur, verissimè, & ἀπόστολος, & υἱὸς ipsi tribuitur. At verò hæc eadem Christo posteriori, non priori respectu dicuntur, vnde elenchus manifestè patet.
units.tr: it labours under the paralogism of ignoring the point at issue (elenchus): as Nazianzen rightly says in his first oration on the Word, the account of nature [ὁ γὰρ φύσεως ...] is one thing, the account of the economy [ὁ δὲ οἰκονομίας λόγος] another. So if you look at the nature of the Word absolutely, [ἡ ἀσώματος ...] it cannot be said of him that he humbled himself, or that he was exalted, or that he received anything in time, because he is the nature of God, which is most perfect and blessed, [ἀπαθὴς καὶ ἀδιάφθορος], and immutable, and nothing can be added to it or taken away from it. But if he is considered relatively, with respect to the office of Mediator [τῆς οἰκονομίας], namely in the way in which he is said to have been given and sent by the Father, then he is most truly called both apostle and Son. But these same things are said of Christ with respect to a later, not an earlier, state, and so the fallacy is manifest.

units.la: Septimò, interpretatur nobis Oftorrodius, quid significetur verbis illis quibus Christus tum formam serui assumfisse, tum in similitudine hominum factus, & habitu compertus vt homo perhibetur. Eoq; primum quod attinet, primo dicit formam serui non ipsam humanam naturam significare, sed instar serui alicuius esse, & serui nomine non fa- mulu simpliciter, sed mancipiu aliquod denotari, qua ipsa significatione nomen δούλου fere semper in scripturis vsurpetur. Et opponi ibi formam serui forma Dei, qua ipsa antithesi magna illa ac vera humilitas Christi declaratur, nempe quod ille, qui fuerit sicut altissimus (quid enim altius ipso Deo) factus sicut abiectissimus, cum mancipio nihil sit abiectius, quod omnibus iniurijs & iniquitatibus expositum, omnia ferre cogitur, nec fe vel vnico verbulo vlcisci potest, vel audet.
units.tr: Seventhly, Ostorodius explains to us what is meant by those words by which Christ is said both to have assumed the form of a servant and to have been made in the likeness of men and to have been found in fashion as a man. As to the first of these, he says first that the form of a servant does not signify the human nature itself, but is to be a servant of some kind, and by the name of servant is meant not a mere attendant but some slave, which meaning the word δοῦλος [δούλου] is almost always used for in the Scriptures. And that the form of a servant is set over against the form of God, by which antithesis that great and true humility of Christ is declared: namely that he who was made as the Most High (for what is higher than God himself?) was made as the lowest, since nothing is lower than a slave, who, exposed to every injury and wrong, is compelled to bear everything and cannot or dares not avenge himself by a single word.

units.la: Resp. Nos quidem antithesin illam agnoscimus, & profitemur Apostolum immensam illam gloriam & maiestatem Christi, imi qua Christus erat ante assumptam carnem, extremæ abiectionis & humiliationis quæ fuit nostri causa assumpta, iam certe opponere, vt hinc à quanta gloria, & ad quantam ignominiam se sponte demiserit Filius Dei, propter salutem nostram, eò clarius elucescat. Sed tamen negamus formam serui hic nudum accidens, & meram conditionem seruilem denotare, & asserimus per illam formam significari ipsam essentiam, ac naturam humanam, vna cum omnibus proprietatibus tum essentialibus & æternis, tum accidentariis & temporalibus: quare iam in antecedentibus prolixè egimus, ac veritatem solidissimis rationibus demonstrauimus, vt per se euanescat illa iactatio Aduersariorum, qua Scripturas longè clarius, facilius, atque solidius: se ac suis, quàm nobis explicari gloriatur.
units.tr: Reply. We indeed acknowledge that antithesis, and we affirm that the Apostle sets against that immense glory and majesty of Christ which he had before he took on flesh the extreme abasement and humiliation which he took on for our sake, so that it may shine out all the more clearly from how great a glory, and to how great a shame, the Son of God voluntarily lowered himself for our salvation. But still we deny that the form of a servant here denotes a bare accident and mere servile condition, and we assert that by that form is signified the very essence and nature of man, together with all its properties, both essential and eternal and accidental and temporal. Wherefore we have already dealt at length with this in the preceding sections, and demonstrated the truth by the most solid arguments, so that the boast of our opponents, by which they glory that the Scriptures are explained far more clearly, easily and soundly by themselves and their followers than by us, may vanish of its own accord.

units.la: Secundò, promittit se rationes & argumenta, quibus nos conabimur demonstrare, per formam serui humanam naturam denotari, licet vnicum tantùm in medium producat, nempe illud quod exsequentibus verbis desumitur, quibus Christus in similitudine hominum factus, & habitu repertus vt homo, dicitur, & Paulus ipse, quidnam per formam serui intelligat, seipsum explicare, à nobis perhibetur. Ad hoc autem argumentum respondet primò nos sum-mere pro concesso, id quod tamen nobis demonstrandum incumbit, nempe Apostolum Paulum his verbis, quid per formam serui intellexerit, explicare. Quamuis enim certum sit Apostolum verba illa in eum finem subiunxisse, vt antecedentia eò facilius intelligerentur, nō tamē inde sequi, illa antecedentium explicationem esse, quoniā manifestum sit, nō semper, imò rarissimè, sequentia verba antecedentium explicatione cōtinere, quā-uis eò referantur, vt illa, nempe antecedentia explicare debeant.
units.tr: Secondly, he promises reasons and arguments by which we shall try to demonstrate that the form of a servant denotes human nature, yet he brings forward only one, namely that which is drawn from the following words, in which Christ is said to have been made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man, and it is claimed by us that Paul himself explains what he means by the form of a servant. To this argument he replies, first, that we take for granted what nevertheless lies on us to prove, namely that the Apostle Paul, by these words, explains what he understood by the form of a servant. For although it is certain that the Apostle added those words for the purpose of making what went before easier to understand, it does not follow from this that they are an explanation of what went before, since it is manifest that following words do not always, indeed very rarely, contain an explanation of the preceding words, even though they are related to them so that they ought to explain them.

units.la: Resp. Illam Aduersarii responsionem falsam esse, atque absurdam. Falsam, quia nostri per formam serui, & similitudinem hominum, vnum idemque, nempe naturam, & essentiam humanam significari, solida ratione euincunt, atque demonstrant. Si enim μορφὴ significat ἰδέαν εἰκόνα ὁμοίωσιν, conformationem, & veritatem humanæ naturæ, tum certè idem significatur per verba antecedentia, & formam serui, & idem per illa significari his ipsis verbis antecedentium in se complectentibus, demonstratur. Atqui veritas antecedentis liquet ex Genes. 5. versu 3. Vixerat autem Adam centum triginta annos, cum gigneret (Filium) in imagine sua secundùm similitudinem suam, & vocaret nomen eius Sethum, vbi imago, & similitudo non accidentaria, sed essentialis intelligitur. Vnde etiam liquet verum esse ipsum consequens. Absurdam dico responsionem illam, quia ex puris constat particularibus, non enim sequitur, si in quibusdam Scripturæ locis, sequentia verba antecedentium ἐξήγησιν non complectantur, etiam hoc in loco verba illa formam serui assumpsit, per similitudinem hominum non declarari. Sed insuper aut manifestè sibi contradicit Ostorrodius in responsione illa, aut magna cum blasphemia grauissimi erroris crimen impingit sanctissimis illis Dei Viris, qui tanquam notarii Dei polici, Verbum Dei nobis obsignarunt, obsignatumque Ecclesiæ radiderunt. Si enim in hoc aut illo verborum contextu, sequentia verba eò referantur & spectent, vt priora & antecedentia per illa explicentur, tum aut reuera eadem priorum verborum continent ἐχφράσιν & explicationem, aut certè à dictantis fine aberra-runt illi, qui verba illa tanquam Dei Amanuenses Ecclesiæ tradi-derunt: Atqui hoc posterius falsum est & impium. Illi enim fan-cti Dei viri à Spiritu sancto acti, ac proinde extra omnem erroris aleam constituti fuerunt. Ergo verum est alterum, & sic necessariò infi-Aduersarius sibi contradicit. Sed illas ineptias vel puer aliquis ani-maduertat.
units.tr: Reply. That answer of our opponent is false and absurd. False, because our side proves and demonstrates by solid reasoning that by the form of a servant and the likeness of men one and the same thing is meant, namely the nature and essence of man. For if μορφή [μορφὴ] signifies idea, image, likeness, the conformation and truth of human nature, then certainly the same is signified by the preceding words, and the same is shown by those very words, which comprehend within themselves the preceding words. And the truth of the antecedent is clear from Genesis 5:3: Now Adam had lived one hundred and thirty years, and begot (a son) in his own image, after his likeness, and called his name Seth, where image and likeness are understood not accidentally but essentially. Whence it is also clear that the consequent is true. I call that answer absurd, because it rests on mere particulars: it does not follow that, if in some passages of Scripture following words do not contain an explanation [ἐξήγησιν] of the preceding ones, then in this place too the words he took the form of a servant are not explained by the likeness of men. But moreover, either Ostorodius plainly contradicts himself in that reply, or with great blasphemy he charges the most sacred men of God, who, as faithful notaries of God, sealed the Word of God for us and handed it over, sealed, to the Church, with the crime of a most serious error. For if in this or that context of words the following words are so related and pointed to that the earlier and preceding ones are explained through them, then either they really contain the same statement and explanation of the earlier words, or certainly those men who handed these words down to the Church as God's amanuenses have strayed from the purpose of the one who dictated them. But the latter is false and impious. For those holy men of God were moved by the Holy Spirit, and therefore were placed beyond every chance of error. Therefore the former is true, and so of necessity our opponent contradicts himself. But even some boy could notice these silly claims.

units.la: Deinde respondet, si maximè concederetur, verba illa Pauli antece-dentium esse explicationem, nihilominus tamen non demonstrari id, quod in quæstione est positum, nempe Christum humanam naturam assumpsisse, id est, cùm Deus esset, hominem factum esse, quia Apostolus non dicat, factus est homo, sed, factus est sicut homo. Hoc autem nihil aliud esse, quàm quod Christus factus sit, sicut quiuis alius homo: quem admodum etiam Lutherus verba illa reddiderit. Quidquid autem hoc ipso significetur, promittit se paulò post expositurum esse.
units.tr: Next he replies that even if it were granted that those words of Paul are an explanation of what precedes, it still would not be shown what is at issue in the question, namely that Christ assumed human nature, that is, that being God he was made man. For the Apostle does not say "he was made man" but "he was made in the likeness of man." This, he says, means nothing more than that Christ was made just like any other man, as Luther also rendered those words. Whatever is signified by this phrase itself, he promises to explain shortly afterwards.

units.la: Resp. At nos vtrumque iam in antecedentibus demonstrauimus, nempe, verba hæc Apostoli & manifestè declarare quid per formam serui fit intelligendum, & simul veritatem doctrinæ nostræ de Incarnatione Filii Dei confirmare. Quum enim per similitudinem illam intelligere oporteat ἰδίαν ἢ εἰκόνα non accidentariam, sed essentialem, ac proinde ipsam naturam & essentiam humanam quam Filius Dei ἐν μορφῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων assumpsit, vt multis rationibus iam euicimus, necessariò per formam Dei, ipsam naturam & essentiam Dei significari, & sic filium Dei æternum, naturam humanam in se ἀνυπόστατον, in personæ suæ vnitatem assumpsisse sequitur. Sed quod paulo ante nobis falsò impingere conatus est Osiandrius, id iam verissimè in ipsum retorquere licebit, fumere videbitur pro concesso id, quod certis rationibus demonstrandum fuerat, nempe verbis illis, quibus Christus in similitudine hominum factus esse dicitur, nihil aliud significari, quàm quod factus sit sicut quiuis alius homo, cuius interpretationis falsitatem iamdiu multoties refutauimus.
units.tr: Reply. But we have already shown in what precedes both things: that these words of the Apostle clearly declare what is to be understood by the form of a servant, and at the same time confirm the truth of our teaching about the incarnation of the Son of God. For since that likeness must be understood as an image or form [ἰδίαν ἢ εἰκόνα] that is not accidental but essential, and therefore the very nature and essence of man which the Son of God assumed while he was "in the form of God" [ἐν μορφῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων], as we have already proved by many arguments, it necessarily follows that by "the form of God" the very nature and essence of God is meant, and so that the eternal Son of God assumed into the unity of his person a human nature which in itself was non-subsistent [ἀνυπόστατον]. But what Osiandrius tried to fasten on us a little earlier, that can now most truly be turned back upon him. He will seem to take for granted what ought to have been demonstrated by sound arguments, namely that by those words, in which Christ is said to have been made "in the likeness of men," nothing else is signified than that he was made just like any other man. We have refuted the falsity of this interpretation many times already.

units.la: Tertio dicit, per verba illa, quibus Christus habitu compertus dicitur vt homo non posse denotari naturam humanam: quoniam hominis natura sit interior hominis forma, habitus autem exterior figura, non quidem corporis, sed vitæ & actionum. Vnde concludit, nos demonstrare non posse, quod forma serui ipsam naturam humanam significet.
units.tr: Thirdly, he says that by those words, by which Christ is said to have been found in human fashion as a man, it cannot be denoted that human nature is meant; since the nature of man is the inner form of man, whereas fashion is an outer figure, not of the body but of life and actions. From this he concludes that we cannot demonstrate that the form of a servant signifies human nature itself.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs thus.

units.la: Si habitus ille humanus non significat ipsam naturâ humanam, tum sequitur demonstrari non posse, quod forma serui naturam & essentiam humanam significet.
units.tr: If that human fashion does not signify human nature itself, then it follows that it cannot be demonstrated that the form of a servant signifies the nature and essence of man.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Assumptionis hanc rationem adfert.
units.tr: He offers this reasoning for the minor premise.

units.la: Natura humana est interior hominis forma.
units.tr: Human nature is the inner form of man.

units.la: Atqui habitus non est interior illa hominis forma, sed figura aeterna, non quidem corporis ipsius, verum ipsius vitæ schema.
units.tr: But fashion is not that inner form of man, but an outward figure, not indeed of the body itself, but the mode of his life.

units.la: Ergo habitus ille humanus non significat ipsam essentiam & naturam humanam.
units.tr: Therefore that human fashion does not signify the very essence and nature of man.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam duplici de causa, primò, quia explicatio eius ex aliis etiam argumentis, quàm iis, quæ [illegible, ~12 letters], per æquipollentes phrases significatam denotant, hauriri potest. Quamuis igitur habitus ille humanus, quo Christus vt homo compertus esse dicitur, primò atque per se non ipsam naturam & essentiam, cuius perfectio in forma interiori consistit, sed vitæ perpessionum atque mortis Christi schema significet; quia tamē de illo prædicatur qui formam serui assumpsit, & proprietates conditionesque soli humanæ naturæ proprias significat, inde per formam serui tanquam proprium subiectum ipsam naturam & essentiam humanam denotari, verissimè concluditur. Cuicunque enim tribuuntur propria & conditiones soli humanæ naturæ propriæ, eidem & naturæ humanæ veritas tribuitur. Atqui forma serui in Christo illæ conditiones tribuuntur, nempe quòd habitu compertus fit vt homo. Ergo forma serui appellatione, naturam humanam Christi designari certum est, & sic habitus ille humanus non quidem primò ac per se, sed tamen secundario & consequenter humanam naturam designat.
units.tr: Reply. The inference is false, for two reasons. First, because its explanation can be drawn from other arguments than those which [illegible] denote by equivalent phrases. Although, therefore, that human fashion by which Christ is said to have been found as a man signifies first and in itself not the nature and essence (whose perfection consists in the inner form) but the outward appearance of the sufferings and death of Christ, nevertheless, because it is predicated of him who assumed the form of a servant, and signifies properties and conditions proper to human nature alone, it is most truly concluded from this that through the form of a servant, as its proper subject, the nature and essence of man is denoted. For to whomever the properties and conditions proper to human nature alone are attributed, to that same subject the reality of human nature is also attributed. But to the form of a servant in Christ these conditions are attributed, namely that he was found in fashion as a man. Therefore it is certain that by the term "form of a servant" the human nature of Christ is designated, and thus that human fashion designates human nature not indeed primarily and in itself, but nevertheless secondarily and by consequence.

units.la: Secundò, Si maximè verum esset totum antecedens, & habitus ille humanus nulla ratione naturam humanam denotaret, non tamen sequeretur simpliciter, nos demonstrare non posse per formam serui ipsam essentiam hominis significari, sed hoc tantum concluderetur, nempe hoc argumento, quod ex illis verbis deprompitur, illud non probari. Hac autem consequentiæ falsitate demonstrata, non opus est, vt ad assumptionem & probationem eius quicquam respondeamus, aut etiam sequelam illam examinemus, quibus sect. 10. tum probare conatur, habitum illum humanum non naturâ humanâ Christi, sed fortem & conditionem communem, qua
units.tr: Second, even if it were most true that the whole antecedent holds, and that human fashion in no way denoted human nature, it would still not simply follow that we cannot demonstrate by the form of a servant that the essence of man is signified; but only this would be concluded, namely that the argument drawn from those words is not proved. Once the falsity of this inference has been demonstrated, there is no need for us to answer the assumption and its proof, or even to examine the sequel by which he tries, in section 10, to prove that this human fashion signifies not the human nature of Christ but a common lot and condition,

units.la: tanquam alius quiuis abiectus homo, æstimatus fuit, significare tum eadem verba prolixa paraphrasi exponi, quam tamen falsam esse, & falso principio niti, ex antecedentibus euidenter liquet.
units.tr: by which he was esteemed like any other abject man; and that the same words are explained by a lengthy paraphrase. That this is false, and rests on a false principle, is plain enough from what has gone before.

units.la: Atque sic hactenus primam partem verborum Apostoli, abdas Aduersarii corruptelis & sophismatis vindicauimus, & ostedimus nihil ab Ostorrodio adferri, quo argumentum nostrum, ex hoc loco desumptum, pro immota Incarnationis veritate, labefactari ulla ratione possit: restat igitur vt nos ad alteram partem illorum verborum progrediamur, qua exaltatio Christi Mediatoris, ac Redemptoris nostri explicatur, & qua doctrinam nostram de Incarnatione Filii Dei, penitus euerti, atque solide refutari Ostorrodius nimis temere & audacter profitetur.
units.tr: And so far we have vindicated the first part of the Apostle's words from the corruptions and sophisms of the Adversary, and have shown that Ostorrodius brings forward nothing by which our argument, drawn from this passage, for the unshaken truth of the incarnation could in any way be weakened. It remains, therefore, that we proceed to the second part of those words, in which the exaltation of Christ our Mediator and Redeemer is explained, and by which Ostorrodius rashly and boldly professes that our doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God is utterly overturned and solidly refuted.

units.la: In huius autem rei explicatione tria omnino tractantur ab Aduersario: primò enim certa argumenta, ex illa Christi exaltatione, nectit, quibus nostram illam de Incarnatione Filii Dei, conuelli atque refutari existimat. Secundo explicat, quanam in re exaltationem illam Christi considerent ipsi Samosateniani doceant: Tertio, grauissimam illam blasphemiam à doctrina ipsorum amoliri conatur, qua videlicet Christus ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος[?], & nudus merúsque homo constituitur. Quantum ad primum membrum attinet, quatuor argumentis sententiam nostram impugnat, ad quæ sigillatim respondebimus.
units.tr: In the explanation of this matter the Adversary treats three things altogether. First, he links certain arguments drawn from that exaltation of Christ, by which he thinks our doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God can be torn down and refuted. Second, he explains in what respect the Samosatenes themselves teach that this exaltation of Christ is to be considered. Third, he tries to remove from their doctrine that most grievous blasphemy by which Christ is made a mere [ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος] and bare man. As far as the first part is concerned, he attacks our view with four arguments, to which we shall reply one by one.

units.la: Argumentum primum tale est.
units.tr: The first argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si Christus homo (nempe quà homo) is est, quem Deus propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, in summam exaltauit sublimitatem, tum sequitur antecedentia omnia, quæ Apostolus de Christo homine (id est humana ipsius natura) intelligenda esse.
units.tr: If Christ as man (namely, as man) is he whom God, because of the obedience he rendered even unto the death of the cross, has exalted to the highest sublimity, then all the things the Apostle says must be understood of Christ as man, that is, of his human nature, follow.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Assumptionem in hunc modum probat;
units.tr: He proves the assumption in this way:

units.la: Is, qui propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, in summam euectus est sublimitatem, aut est Deus ipse, aut Christus homo (aut denique perfectam illam idiomatum communicationem (licet enim [illegible, ~6 letters] illum [illegible, ~5 letters] appellat) diuinæ naturæ Christi tribuit, bui intelligitur, quod proprie ipsius naturæ humanæ competit.
units.tr: He who, because of the obedience rendered even unto the death of the cross, has been raised to the highest sublimity, is either God himself, or Christ as man, or (finally) the perfect communication of idioms, which attributes to the divine nature of Christ what properly belongs to his human nature.

units.la: Atqui non primum: quoniam enim Deus est ipse altissimus, ideo exaltari nulla ratione potest: nec secundum: primò quia [illegible, ~8 letters] Christi Christus verus Deus est, tum ne quidem humana ipsius natura propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam quicquam dari potuit, quia etiam secundum humanam naturam ab ipso statim conceptionis momento totius maiestatis diuinæ per vnionem hypostaticam particeps fuit, ipsis Aduersariis sic docentibus: Secundò, Si Deus (id est Christus secundum naturam diuinam suam) se humiliasset, naturam videlicet humanam assumendo, humanitas autem exaltata fuisset, tum alius sic demissset, ac humiliasset: alius autem humiliationis præmium adeptus esset, quod inquam & absurdum est.
units.tr: But not the first: for since God is the Most High, he cannot in any way be exalted. Nor the second: first, because if Christ is true God, then not even his human nature could have received anything on account of the obedience rendered, since, according to his human nature too, he partook of all divine majesty from the very moment of conception through the hypostatic union, as the Adversaries themselves teach. Secondly, if God (that is, Christ according to his divine nature) had humbled himself by assuming human nature, and the human nature had then been exalted, then one would have humbled and abased himself, and another would have obtained the reward of the humiliation; which, I say, is also absurd.

units.la: Ergo verum est secundum, nempe per eum, qui propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, in summam euectus est sublimitatem, Christum hominem intelligendum esse.
units.tr: Therefore the second is true: namely, that by him who, because of the obedience rendered even unto the death of the cross, has been raised to the highest sublimity, Christ as man is to be understood.

units.la: Resp. Primò, connexum causæ elencho laborare, quo præsuppositur falsa illa hypothesis, quasi videlicet Christus propter solam illam obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, exaltationis illud præmium obtinuisset. Non enim eò solum, quod secundum humanam naturam se ipse summiserat legi, & iustitiæ Dei actus erat obediens vsque ad mortem crucis: sed tum propter inanitionem deitatis, qua videlicet se per dispensationem voluntariam, forma serui accepta inaniuerat: tum propter acerbissimas perpessiones humanitatis eius, totámque obedientiam totius perpessionis (quæ omnia Ostorrodius ad stabiliendum suum dogma austutissimè dirimit) Deus ipsum in tantam extulit sublimitatem, nempe diuinitatem ab illa sui inanitione potentissimè vindicans, qua se ipse inaniuerat dispensatione voluntaria ertóque consilio nobis salutari: & humanitatem ab infirmitate perpessionibus illius euehendo adeò magnificè, vt præter illam gratiam, quam in diuinitate Christi personaliter obtinet humanitas supra res creatas omnes, etiam in se omnem plenitudinem gratiæ, veritatis & gloriæ possideat, quantam natura creata potest percipere, & quantam nulla alia præter hanc perpipit. Secundò, quum Christus homo is dicitur esse, quem Deus propter obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis præstitam, in summam extulit sublimitatem, intelligitur aut sola humana natura Christi, diuinitate illius exclusa, aut tota persona mediatoris nostri, secundum humanam naturam, ab altera tamen, nempe humana denominata. Si posteriori sensu intelligeretur connexum,
units.tr: Reply. First, the argument is weak in its connection, since it presupposes the false hypothesis that Christ obtained that reward of exaltation solely because of the obedience he rendered even unto the death of the cross. For it was not only that, according to his human nature, he subjected himself to the law and was obedient to the justice of God unto the death of the cross; but God also raised him to such sublimity because of the emptying of his deity, by which he emptied himself through a voluntary dispensation, taking the form of a servant, and because of the most bitter sufferings of his humanity and the whole obedience of the whole suffering (all of which Ostorrodius cunningly sets aside to establish his dogma). God powerfully vindicated his deity from that self-emptying, by which he emptied himself through a voluntary dispensation and a plan salutary for us; and he raised his humanity from the weakness of its sufferings so magnificently that, beyond that grace which the humanity personally possesses in the divinity of Christ, it possesses in itself, above all created things, every fullness of grace, truth and glory which created nature can receive, and which no other nature except this one can receive. Secondly, when Christ is called the man whom God has raised to the highest sublimity because of the obedience rendered even unto the death of the cross, the connection is understood either of the human nature of Christ alone, with his deity excluded, or of the whole person of our Mediator according to his human nature, though named from the other, namely from the human nature. If the connection were understood in the latter sense,

units.la: omnino falsum esset: cum diuina Christi natura non ideo exclu-datur quod toti personæ ab humanitate in concreto denomina-tæ, ea tribuantur,quæ sunt naturæ vtriusque in personæ vnitate. Sin vero priori modo intelligatur illud, quo etiam ab Aduersa-riis id intelligi certum est, tum negamus assumptionem, cuius proinde probatio nobis est examinanda. Diffunctum igitur pro-syllogismi negamus: nec enim Deus solus, nec homo solus, sed Deus-homo, & tertium namque lemma, quod vitiosissi-ma distributione annectitur, per medium abnegationis, vt vocant Logici, ex illa diffunctione resecamus, ille est, qui propter admi-randam illam κένωσιν, & exinanitionem secundum vtramque na-turam factam, in illam gloriæ celsitudinem & maiestatem est eue-ctus à Deo Patre, quemadmodum in antecedentibus euidentissi-ma apodixi ostendimus. Ad probationem primi lemmatis quod attinet, iam aliquoties illa superioribus capitibus à nobis est refu-tata, vbi ostendimus ab iis, quæ Christo ratione deitatis suæ absolute, simpliciter, in se, & ἀσυγχύτως consideratæ, verissimè prædicantur, ad negationem eorum, quæ de ipso ratione officii, & secundum voluntariam dispensationem, & œconomiam enunciantur, nullam dari consequentiam. Quicunque igitur est altissimus, illeelli non potest exaltari, videlicet in quantum vt altissimus considera-tur. Christus autem secundum diuinam naturam suam est altissi-mus, sed respectu diuinitatis suæ simpliciter & absolutè confide-ratæ, non autem ratione officii, & dispensationis, ac voluntariæ œconomiæ, secundum quam de ipso eodem Dei Filio & ὑπὸ, & ὑπόστασις prædicatur, sine contradictione vlla. Tertium lemma distinctionis, quamuis duobus prioribus assumptis, atque con-iunctis per se remouentur, rationibus tamen duabus ab Aduer-sario allatis minimè conuellitur. Negatur enim consequentia illa, si Christus sit verus Deus, tum humana ipsius natura, propter obe-dientiam præstitam, nihil dari potuisse, eo quod illa vnionis hypostati-cæ beneficio statim ab ipso conceptionis momento, totius maiestatis diuinæ particeps fuerit. Nam licet diuina persona humanæ naturæ fit vnita hypostaticè, nihil tamen quod diuinum est, & naturæ di-uinæ proprium, per illam vnionem in naturam humanam est translatum, quia vnio illa vt saluis, & distinctis, ac inconfusis ipsis naturis, ita etiam proprietatibus diuinis est facta cum propria extra subiectum suum proprium non communicetur, sine subiecti ipsius commu-nicatione. nication. Sic anima intelligēs suas proprietates ingressa in corpus non amittit eas, sed ita in se seruat, vt per vnionem animæ cū corpore communes quidem sint corporis, sed tamen in subiecto suo permanentes, nulla ratione extra illud transfusæ. Cùm enim ex corpore & anima persona vna constituta sit, suæ proprietates corpori, suæ item animo vel menti permanent propriæ, sed in vnione tamen sunt communes, quamuis integris in vtroque proprietatibus. Vt autem anima corpori est adiuncta per vnionem naturale: ita natura diuina Christi est humanæ adunata per vnionem gratiæ. Communicantur ergo in persona, quæ in natura vtraque propria permanent: sed communicantur, non transportatione, aut transfusione, non effusione, aut confusione, quia propria esse desinerent, verùm vnione personali integris in vnitate personæ remanentibus cuiusque naturæ proprietatibus. Atque hæc est vera communicationis ratio: si alii à veritate illa discedentes, communicationem eiusmodi statuunt, quæ fiat effusione, aut diffusione, illorum error doctrinæ nostræ, nullo æquitatis titulo, potest esse præiudicio. Verùm alterius quoque rationis, qua tertium illud disiunctionis lemma tollitur, consequentia nulla est: non enim sequitur: Si Christus secundum naturam diuinam, seu qua Deus, sese humiliauit, secundum humanam autem naturam exaltatus est, sic vt humiliatio de Christo secundum naturam diuinam proprie, exaltatio autem per communicationem idiomatum (quæ tamen responsio, quicunque etiam illius autor extiterit, aut per illam obiectionem infirmam refutare conetur, neque cum veritate ipsius rei, neque cum mente, & genuino verborum Apostoli sensu, ratione vlla consentit) prædicetur, quippe quæ proprie humanitati ipsius competat, tum alium se humiliasse, alium autem humiliationis præmium obtinuisse & reportasse. Sic enim sequeretur in Christo esse alium, & alium, duæque distinctæ personæ Christi, & duo filii Dei cum Nestorio introducerentur: cùm tamen propter duas naturas vnitas, sit quidem in Christo aliud & aliud, sed propter vnitatem hypostaseos diuinæ (humana enim natura in se est ἀνυπόστατος) non alius & alius, sed vna eademque persona Mediatoris ac redemptoris nostri. Quem consequentiæ errorem crassissimum vel indicasse tantum sufficit.
units.tr: it would be altogether false, since the divine nature of Christ is not excluded merely because those things which belong to the nature of each are attributed to the whole person, named concretely from the humanity, in the unity of the person. But if it is understood in the former way, which is certainly how the Adversaries understand it, then we deny the assumption, whose proof must therefore be examined. So we deny the disjunctive premise of the syllogism: for it is neither God alone nor man alone, but God-man. And we cut out of that disjunction the third proposition, which is joined by a most faulty distribution, through what the logicians call the mediation of negation: that is, he who, because of that wondrous kenosis and emptying made in both natures, has been raised by God the Father to that height and majesty of glory, as we have shown by the most evident demonstration in the preceding chapters. As for the proof of the first proposition, we have already refuted it several times in the earlier chapters, where we showed that from those things which are rightly and absolutely predicated of Christ in respect of his deity, considered simply, in himself, and without confusion, no consequence follows to the denial of those things which are stated of him in respect of his office, and according to his voluntary dispensation and economy. Therefore, whoever is the Most High cannot be exalted, namely insofar as he is considered as the Most High. But Christ according to his divine nature is the Most High, yet with respect to his deity considered simply and absolutely, not with respect to his office, dispensation and voluntary economy, according to which the same Son of God is predicated, without any contradiction, both as subordinate and as hypostasis. The third proposition of the disjunction, though it is removed by the two preceding premises taken together, is not in the least overturned by the two reasons brought by the Adversary. For that consequence is denied: that if Christ is true God, then his human nature could not have received anything on account of the obedience rendered, because from the very moment of conception it partook of all divine majesty through the benefit of the hypostatic union. For although the divine person is united hypostatically to the human nature, nothing that is divine and proper to the divine nature has been transferred into the human nature through that union, because that union was made in such a way that the natures remain whole, distinct and unconfused, and likewise their divine properties, which are not communicated outside their proper subject without communication of the subject itself. Thus the understanding soul, entering the body, does not lose its properties, but keeps them in itself, so that through the union of soul with body they are indeed common to the body, yet remain in their own subject and are in no way poured out beyond it. For since the person is constituted one from body and soul, its properties remain proper to the body, and likewise to the soul or mind, yet in the union they are common, though each keeps its properties whole. And just as the soul is joined to the body by a natural union, so the divine nature of Christ is joined to the human nature by a union of grace. Therefore the properties are communicated in the person, while they remain proper to each nature; but they are communicated not by transportation or transfusion, not by effusion or confusion (for then they would cease to be proper), but by personal union, the properties of each nature remaining whole in the unity of the person. This is the true manner of communication. If others, departing from that truth, establish a communication that takes place by effusion or diffusion, their error cannot be any prejudice to our doctrine, by any title of fairness. But the consequence drawn from the other reason, by which the third proposition of the disjunction is removed, is also invalid. For it does not follow that: if Christ according to his divine nature, or as God, humbled himself, and according to his human nature was exalted, in such a way that the humiliation is properly predicated of Christ according to the divine nature, but the exaltation by communication of idioms (which answer, whoever its author may be, and whatever weak objection he may try to refute it with, agrees neither with the truth of the matter, nor with the mind and genuine sense of the Apostle's words, in any way), and is properly predicated because it belongs properly to his humanity, then one person humbled himself and another obtained and carried away the reward of the humiliation. For thus it would follow that in Christ there is one and another, and two distinct persons of Christ, and two sons of God would be introduced with Nestorius; whereas, since he is one because of the two natures, there is indeed in Christ "the one" and "the other," but by the unity of the divine hypostasis (for the human nature in itself is anhypostatic) it is not "one and another," but one and the same person of our Mediator and Redeemer. It is enough merely to point out this most gross error of consequence.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM II. depromit Ostorrodius ex illis Apostoli verbis, quibus Christus à Deo Patre in illam sublimitatem gloriæ
units.tr: ARGUMENT II. Ostorrodius draws it from those words of the Apostle by which Christ is said to have been raised by God the Father to that height of glory

units.la: ac potentia diuina, nonnisi certam ob causam, obedientiam videlicet ad mortem vsque crucis praestitam, eusebius esse dicitur. Vnde quum non a se ipso, sed a Deo Patre Dominus factus sit, sequi existimat ipsum verum & aeternum Deum non esse.
units.tr: and divine power, only for a certain reason, namely the obedience rendered even to the death of the cross, is said to have been bestowed. Hence, since the Lord was made not of himself but by God the Father, he thinks it follows that he is not the true and eternal God.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Verus atque aeternus Deus, est a se ipso rerum omnium Dominus, nec ab vllo alio dominium suum obtinuit.
units.tr: The true and eternal God is the Lord of all things from himself, and has obtained his dominion from no other.

units.la: Atqui Christus non est a se ipso rerum omnium Dominus, sed a Deo Patre, & quidem nonnisi certam ob causam, nempe obedientiam ad mortem vsque crucis praestitam, dominio illo in res omnes est donatus:
units.tr: But Christ is not the Lord of all things from himself, but from God the Father, and indeed only for a certain reason, namely the obedience rendered even to the death of the cross, he has been granted dominion over all things.

units.la: Ergo Christus non est verus atque aeternus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is not the true and eternal God.

units.la: Resp. Hoc ipsum argumentum iam supra capite septimo, in responsione ad exceptionem quartam, & capite vndecimo, in responsione ad argumentum Aduersarii, prolixè est refutatum. Summa haec est. Christus consideratur duobus modis, respectu vi-delicet personae, aut officii mediatorii, & oeconomiae, seu dispensationis voluntariae. Personae autem, secundum naturam diuinam, aut humanam, aut vtramque simul. Si ad naturam diuinam respexeris, ea aut secundum se contemplanda est, aut secundum originem principiumque ipsius. Deinde dominium in res omnes est duplex, vnum essentiale, absolutum, summum, & αὐτοδέσποτον, alterum vero acquisitum, & priori subordinatum. Ad hanc igitur normam Aduersarii argumentationem examinemus. Verus & aeternus Deus, est a se ipso rerum omnium Dominus, nec ab vllo alio dominium suum obtinuit, verum est enuntiatum, sed nomine Dei essentialiter sumpto, at intellecto personaliter & ὑποστατικῶς, vera est propositio, sed tantum de Deo Patre, non autem de Deo Filio, aut Deo Spiritu sancto. Vt enim Pater solus est a se ipso, nec principium, fontem, aut originem ab vllo alio habet, ita etiam supremum illud, absolutum, & perfectum dominium (illud enim imi mins propositione intelligitur) a se ipso, siue absolute, & ratione essentiae, siue relate, & ως πρὸς τι consideretur, possidet, nec ab vllo alio superiori accepit. Vt autem Filius, qua filius, non est a se ipso, sed a Patre, tanquam origine, fonte, ac principio suo: & Spiritus sanctus, qua persona recipiens, videlicet ad personam Patris, ac filii a Patre.
units.tr: Reply. This very argument was already refuted at length above, in chapter seven, in the answer to the fourth exception, and in chapter eleven, in the answer to the adversary's argument. The gist is this. Christ is considered in two ways: with respect to his person, that is, his mediatorial office, and the economy or voluntary dispensation. The person, moreover, is considered according to the divine nature, or the human, or both together. If you look at the divine nature, it is to be contemplated either in itself or according to its origin and principle. Next, dominion over all things is twofold: one essential, absolute, supreme and self-ruling [αὐτοδέσποτον], the other acquired and subordinate to the first. Let us therefore test the adversary's argument by this rule. The proposition "The true and eternal God is the Lord of all things from himself, and has obtained his dominion from no other" is true when the name God is taken essentially, but understood personally and hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς]; the proposition is true, but only of God the Father, not of God the Son or God the Holy Spirit. For just as the Father alone is from himself, and has no source, fount or origin from any other, so too that supreme, absolute and perfect dominion (for it is understood in the proposition of the "most high") he possesses from himself, whether it is considered absolutely and in terms of essence, or relatively and as related to something [ὡς πρὸς τι], and he has received it from no superior. But the Son, as Son, is not from himself but from the Father, as from his origin, fount and principle; and the Holy Spirit, as a receiving person, namely in relation to the person of the Father and the Son, is from the Father.

units.la: Vt enim Pater solus est a se ipso. à Patre ac filio emanauit: ita quoque filius dominium idem iustè & perfectè possidet, sed acceptum ab alio, id est, alia persona (amplius quam dicimus Patrem, Deo tamen uno & eodem essentia cum filio. Spiritus Sanctus quoque idem possidet iustè, & perfectè, sed acceptum à Patre & filio. Hæc autem possidendi ratio, nec diuinitati Christi, nec Spiritus sancti, nec absolutæ perfectioni dominatus supremi & essentialis quicquam derogare potest, vt iam supra capite undecimo demonstrauimus, sed tantùm ordinem personarum dominantium ostendit. Assumptio deinde loquitur de dominio diuino posteriori (secus enim salsissima esset) quod ipsum Christo tribuitur non secundùm naturam diuinam simpliciter, & absolutè, sed secundùm naturam utramque ratione videlicet officii mediatorii, & liberrimæ œconomiomiæ, aut voluntariæ dispensationis. Unde tot serè termini, in argumentatione Ostorrodiana, quot verba numerantur.
units.tr: For just as the Father alone is from himself, the Son and the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father; so too the Son possesses the same dominion justly and perfectly, but received from another, that is, from another person (the Father, yet one God and of the same essence as the Son). The Holy Spirit likewise possesses it justly and perfectly, but received from the Father and the Son. Now this manner of possessing dominion detracts nothing from the divinity of Christ, or of the Holy Spirit, nor from the absolute perfection of supreme and essential lordship, as we have already shown above in chapter eleven; it shows only the order of the ruling persons. The assumption then speaks of the later divine dominion (otherwise it would be utterly insipid), which is attributed to Christ not simply and absolutely according to the divine nature, but according to both natures, namely by reason of the mediatorial office and the most free economy, or voluntary dispensation. Hence in Ostorrodius' argument there are almost as many terms as there are words.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM III.
units.tr: ARGUMENT III.

units.la: desumit Aduersarius ex illis Apostoli verbis, quibus Christus ab ipso Deo exaltatus esse dicitur, unde concludit Christum ab uno illo Deo, qui ipsum exaltauit, manifestè distinguí, ac proinde unum illum Deum esse non posse.
units.tr: The adversary takes it from those words of the Apostle by which Christ is said to have been exalted by God himself, whence he concludes that Christ is clearly distinguished from that one God who exalted him, and therefore that he cannot be that one God.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Qui distinguitur ab uno illo Deo, ille non est ipse unus iste Deus: At qui Christus manifestè distinguitur ab uno illo Deo: Ergo Christus non est unus ille Deus.
units.tr: He who is distinguished from that one God is not himself that one God. But Christ is clearly distinguished from that one God. Therefore Christ is not that one God.

units.la: Minor sic probatur.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved thus.

units.la: Qui ab uno illo Deo exaltatus esse dicitur, ille ab uno illo Deo distinguitur: secus enim ille qui exaltatur, & ille qui exaltat, unus idémque essent: At qui Christus ab uno illo Deo exaltatus esse dicitur: Ergo Christus ab uno illo Deo distinguitur.
units.tr: He who is said to have been exalted by that one God is distinguished from that one God; otherwise he who is exalted and he who exalts would be one and the same. But Christ is said to have been exalted by that one God. Therefore Christ is distinguished from that one God.

units.la: Resp. Deus dicitur dupliciter ἐπωδῶς, & ὑπερσατικῶς, essentialiter personaliter: Si essentialiter sumatur nomen Deus, tum distinguenda est propositio: Qui enim distinguitur à Deo, videlicet ratione essentiæ, & realiter, ille certè non est unus ille ac verus Deus: sed hoc sensu assumptio est falsa, nec illo prosyllogismo demonstratur, quia nomen Deus ibi ὑπερσατικῶς, de persona videlicet Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis prima, nempe Patre prædicatur. Qui vero distinguitur ab vno illo Deo non re, sed ratione tantum i.relatione, modo bom subsistendi, & proprietate personali, denique certi officii respectu, quę nullum discrimen essentiale inferunt, ille nihilominus est vnus ille & verus Deus. Sic in rebus physicis, ipsa nempe hominis animæ mine, quæ in vnoquoqne homine tantum vna est numero, tres facultates ac definitione diuersa differentes, ratione quidem ab ipsa anima distinguuntur, & tamen re ipsa nihil aliud sunt quam ipsa anima intelligens, sentiens ac videns, animaq; vt totum essentiale de singulis facultatibus prædicatur. Atque hoc sensu vera est assumptio, sed propter falsitatem propositionis, conclusio euanescit. Sin vero nomen Deus sumatur personaliter, quemadmodum reuera sumitur ab Apostolo, tum qui distinguitur ab vno illo Deo, nempe Patre, qui est vnus ille Deus, ille non est vnus illi Deus, nempe Pater, quod ipsum de Christo credimus & affirmamus, quod proprietate idiomatica seu personali à Patre distinguatur. ac proinde non vna eademque numero sit persona Patris ac filii, licet Filius cum Patre ac Spiritu sancto propter vnitatem essentiæ, sit vnus idemque verus Deus. Atque ob æquiuocationem illas varias totum destruitur argumentum, cui tamen velut solido fundamento Aduersarius innititur.
units.tr: Reply. God is spoken of in two ways, essentially [οὐσιωδῶς] and personally [ὑποστατικῶς]. If the name God is taken essentially, then the proposition must be distinguished: "He who is distinguished from God", namely by reason of essence and really, "is certainly not that one and true God." But in this sense the assumption is false, and it is not demonstrated by that prosyllogism, because the name God there is used personally [ὑποστατικῶς], that is, predicated of the first person of the most holy Trinity, namely the Father. "He who is distinguished from that one God", however, is distinguished not in reality but only in reason, that is, by relation, by the mode of subsisting, by personal property, and finally by respect to a certain office, which bring no essential difference; "he nevertheless is that one and true God." So in natural things, the very soul of man, which in each man is only one in number, has three faculties differing in definition and in kind: they are distinguished from the soul itself in reason, and yet in reality they are nothing other than the soul itself understanding, feeling and seeing, and the soul is predicated as a whole essence of each faculty. In this sense the assumption is true, but because the proposition is false, the conclusion vanishes. But if the name God is taken personally, as it is indeed taken by the Apostle, then he who is distinguished from that one God, namely the Father, who is that one God, is not that one God, namely the Father. This we believe and affirm of Christ, that he is distinguished from the Father by idiomatic or personal property, and so the person of the Father and the Son is not one and the same in number, although the Son, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, by unity of essence, is one and the same true God. And because of these various equivocations the whole argument is destroyed, though the adversary leans on it as on a solid foundation.

units.la: Hanc autem responsionem nostram, qua videlicet dicimus nomen Deus non essentialiter, sed ὑποστατικῶς pro prima sacrosanctæ Trinitatis persona, sumedum esse, excipit Aduersarius petitione principii laborare, cum afferamus plures vna persona diuinas esse, quod tamen nondum sit concessum, neque hactenus a nobis demonstratum.
units.tr: The adversary objects to this reply of ours, by which we say that the name God is to be taken not essentially but hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς] for the first person of the most holy Trinity, that we are guilty of begging the question, since we assert that there are several divine persons in one person, which has not yet been granted, nor hitherto demonstrated by us.

units.la: Resp. Hanc exceptionem esse falsam. Quum enim Aduersarius doctrinam orthodoxam de sacrosanctæ Trinitatis mysterio sibi reuideri fuisse fingendam sumpserit, vnicam tantum personam diuinam esse, ipsi de monstrandum erat. Sed quid quæso ad destruendam illam veritatem præter meras & futilissimas nugas ab ipso est allatum, quas etiam ipsi pueri facile refutarent? Pollicitus est Faustus Socinus in suo peculiari libro solidis argumentis & rationibus, quod vnica tantum sit persona diuina, demonstraturum esse, sed hactenus nihil praeter inanes verborum & promissionum ampullas præstitit. Veritatem deinde doctrinæ nostræ, Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctores tam luculenter & solide demonstrarunt, vt Ariana & Socinia progenies, allatrare illam, euertere autem & labefactare numquam possint. quam possint. Quum igitur illa ipsa veritas aduersus omnes im- munis oportunos quantumuis hostium impetus incorcusla & victrix sem- per emerserit, & instar florentis alicuius palmulæ, nulli inimico- rum oneri succubuerit, qua fronte petitionis principii nos insimu- lare potest Ostorrodius quod suas sophismatum & cavillationum nebulas, illius luce & splendore dispellamus? Sed Lector candidus & Christianus iudex esto.
units.tr: Reply. This objection is false. For since the adversary has taken it upon himself to pretend that the orthodox doctrine of the mystery of the most holy Trinity must be revised, it was for him to show that there is only one divine person. But what, I ask, has he brought forward to destroy that truth, apart from mere and most trifling nonsense, which even boys could easily refute? Faustus Socinus promised in his special book to demonstrate with solid arguments and reasons that there is only one divine person, but hitherto he has produced nothing but empty words and bombastic promises. Moreover, the teachers of our Churches have demonstrated the truth of our doctrine so clearly and solidly that the Arian and Socinian brood may bark at it, but can never overturn or weaken it. Since that very truth has always emerged unshaken and victorious against all the assaults of enemies, however many and however timely, and like some flourishing little palm has never yielded to the burden of any foe, with what face can Ostorrodius accuse us of begging the question because we disperse his clouds of sophisms and cavils by its light and splendour? But let the reader be candid and the judge a Christian.

units.la: Quartum argumentum desumit ex verbo ἐχρίσατο, quod hoc lo- co donum gratuitum significat, quod videlicet Deus in Christum pro- pter obedientiam præstitam ex gratia contulerit. Unde concludit exal- tationem Christi non tantum gloriæ ac maiestatis diuinæ declarationem & manifestationem, sed veram eleuationem ad summum imperium, ma- iestatem, ac gloriam diuinam, significare, quod sectione decima ter- tia aliquot rationibus demonstrare conatur.
units.tr: The fourth argument is drawn from the word ἐχρίσατο [echrisato], which here signifies a free gift, namely that God bestowed it on Christ out of grace on account of the obedience rendered. From this he concludes that the exaltation of Christ signifies not merely a declaration and manifestation of divine glory and majesty, but a true elevation to supreme dominion, majesty and divine glory; this he attempts to demonstrate by several arguments in the thirteenth section.

units.la: Resp. Duplici vitio hoc argumentum quartum laborare. Pri- mo, quia non concluditur id quod intendit Aduersarius, nempe hoc ipso loco doctrinam de Incarnatione filii Dei plane de- clarari. Secundo, quia nos ipsi fatemur, exaltationem Christi non tan- tum maiestatis & gloriæ diuinæ declaratione ac manifestatione, sed insuper etiam potente ex mortuis resurrectione, gloriosa in cœlum ascensione, sessione denique regia ad dextram Patris cœ- lestis, per quam plenitudine gloriæ, potestatis, imperiique in cœlo et in terra super omnia & in omnia creata significatur, definien- dam esse. Unde etiam probationes ipsius in medium producere non est necessarium.
units.tr: Reply: This fourth argument labours under a double fault. First, because it does not conclude what the adversary intends, namely that the doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God is plainly declared in this very passage. Second, because we ourselves confess that the exaltation of Christ is to be defined not merely as a declaration and manifestation of divine majesty and glory, but moreover as the mighty resurrection from the dead, the glorious ascension into heaven, and finally the royal session at the right hand of the heavenly Father, by which is signified the fullness of glory, power and dominion in heaven and on earth over all things and in all created things. Hence it is also not necessary to bring forward his proofs of this.

units.la: Hactenus etiam primum membrum disputationis Ostorrodia- nus, quam ex posteriore verborum Pauli parte extruere conatur, à Vdcobis est examinatum: sequitur iam secundum, in quo explicat Aduersarius, quidnam sit illa exaltatio Christi, qua ita à Deo eue- ctus fuerit, & quam Apostolus proponit, quum inquit, Donauit i- lli nomen, quod est supra omne nomen. Et primo dicit, verbis illis si- gnificari, Deum (quemadmodum idem testatur Apostolus Ephes. i.) ad dextram suam collocatum supra omnes principatus, potestates, dominia, potentiam, & omnia, quæ nominari possunt, non tantum in hoc, sed etiam in futuro sæculo, omnibusque eius pedi- bus subiectis, caput Ecclesiæ ipsum in omnibus constituisse: sic vt nulla sublimis Christi potestas monstrari possit, quæ ipsi non sit data, vt ipsi homini Christo tribui nequeat, & per consequens propter diuinam illam poteftatemac gloriam, diuina in Christo effentia acna-tura nullo modo astrui possit.
units.tr: So far the Vdcobis has examined the first part of the disputation which Ostorrodius attempts to build from the latter part of Paul's words. Now follows the second part, in which the adversary explains what that exaltation of Christ is, by which he was so lifted up by God, and which the Apostle sets forth when he says: "He gave him a name which is above every name." And first he says that by those words is signified that God (as the same Apostle testifies, Ephesians 1) placed him at his right hand above all principalities, powers, dominions, might, and everything that can be named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, and, with all things put under his feet, appointed him head of the Church over all things. Thus no lofty power of Christ can be shown which has not been given to him, which cannot be ascribed to the man Christ himself, and consequently, on account of that divine power and glory, the divine essence and nature in Christ cannot in any way be established.

units.la: Resp.Ipsum antecedens,Christum videlicet per illam exaltatio-nem, ad tantam dignitatis, gloriæ & maiestatis diuinæ celsitudi-nem & sublimitatem à Deo Patre eue&tum esse, vt non solum caput Ecclesiæ,sed etiam Rex, & Gubernator cœli ac terræ, om-niúmque rerum creatarum constitutus,cum ipso,subiectis illi re-bus omnibus,omnia tam in cœlo,quàm in terra regat, atque gu-bernet,agnoscimus,credimus,atque confitemur,sed negamus cō-sequentiam,quia infertur,primò,illa omnia de Christo homine, ibi est,qua homo,seu humanitate ipsius prædicari: Secundò, ex diuinæ Christi potestate, ac gloria, diuinam ipsius naturam & essentiam demonstrari nullo modo posse, quorum neutrum ex illo antece-dente,legitima consequentia deducitur: quæ enim quæso est illa consequentia:Deus Christum in summam gloriæ,potestatis,ac imperij plenitudinem extulit: Ergo & summi illa potestas de Christo, quâ homo, id est,humanitate ipsius prædicatur, & ex diuina potentia Christi diuina ipsius natura & essentia demonstrari nullo modo potest? nullaillan sane, cùm nullo vero medio consequentia illa falsa conficiatur.
units.tr: Reply: We acknowledge, believe and confess the antecedent itself, namely that Christ, through that exaltation, was raised by God the Father to such a height of dignity, glory and divine majesty that he was constituted not only head of the Church but also King and Governor of heaven and earth and of all created things, ruling and governing all things both in heaven and on earth with all those things made subject to him. But we deny the consequence, because it is inferred, first, that all those things are predicated of Christ as man, that is, in respect of his humanity; second, that from the divine power and glory of Christ his divine nature and essence cannot in any way be demonstrated. Neither of these follows by legitimate consequence from that antecedent. For what, I ask, is that consequence: "God raised Christ to the highest fullness of glory, power and dominion; therefore those supreme things are predicated of Christ as man, that is, of his humanity, and from the divine power of Christ his divine nature and essence cannot in any way be demonstrated"? Surely there is no such consequence, since that false conclusion is drawn by no true middle term.

units.la: Quantum enim ad primum attinet, quum illa omnia de Christo mediatore respectu officii ipsius prædicentur,cuius partes ille non tantum secundum humanam,sed etiam secundum diuinam suam naturam præstitit(vtraque enim,diuina nempe& humana natura personam Christi constare,iam supra demonstrauimus)necessariò etiam sequitur,gloriam illam,potestatem, ac maiestatem de ipso non tantum secundum humanam,sed etiam diuinam naturam eo nuntiari.Quantum verò ad alterum consequens attinet,caueri oportet æquiuocationem manifestam,dominatum enim diuinum ac potestatem quæ Christo tribuitur, duplicem esse ostendimus, essentialem,summum, & plane independentem, qui ex naturali Dei supra res omnino omnes excellentia, originem & quasi fundamentum habet,alterum verò accidentarium,& priori subordinatum,Christóque vt mediatori competentem: illum Pater ipsi communicauit per generationem ab æterno: hunc ipsi tanqu am vicario ex gratia largitus est in tempore: prior potestas est propria essentialis diuina,Patri,Filio,ac Spiritui sancto in vnitate essentiæ communis est,hæc verò donum est gratuitum, soli filio ratione officii, & voluntariæ dispensationis,& œconomiæ,à Patris,& Spiritus sancti persona distincto, competens. Et quamuis nec haec quidem in creaturam nudam cadere possit, tamen non ex hac sola, sed maxime ex priore illa, quae essentialis, ac æterna Dei proprietas est, diuinam Christi naturam luculenter demonstramus qua de re iam in antecedentibus egimus.
units.tr: For as far as the first point goes, since all those things are predicated of Christ the Mediator with respect to his office, whose parts he performed not only according to his human but also according to his divine nature (for we have already demonstrated above that both natures, divine and human, constitute the person of Christ), it necessarily follows that that glory, power and majesty are declared of him not only according to his human but also according to his divine nature. As for the other consequence, care must be taken against a manifest equivocation, for we have shown that the divine dominion and power which is given to Christ is twofold: one essential, supreme and wholly independent, which has its origin and, as it were, foundation in the natural excellence of God above all things whatsoever; the other accidental and subordinate to the former, and competent to Christ as Mediator. The Father communicated the former to him by eternal generation; the latter he bestowed upon him in time, as upon his vicar, out of grace. The former power is the proper essential divine attribute, common to the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the unity of essence; the latter is a free gift, competent to the Son alone by reason of office and voluntary dispensation and economy, distinct from the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit. And although not even this latter can fall upon a mere creature, yet we demonstrate the divine nature of Christ clearly not from this alone, but chiefly from that former power, which is the essential and eternal property of God; concerning which matter we have already treated in the preceding sections.

units.la: Deinde refutat Ostorrodius superstitiosum illum cultum, quo videlicet audito nomine Iesu caput aperiendum, aut genua flectenda esse, multi arbitrantur, &, per Apostoli verba, metaphoricam genuflexionem, interiorem nempe cultum, & reuerentiam animi intelligendam esse, verissime docet, quae proinde illis medita relinquimus, qui nescio quam religiosam pietatem & sanctitatem per externos illos ritus affectant.
units.tr: Next Ostorrodius refutes that superstitious worship by which many think that at the hearing of the name Jesus the head must be uncovered or the knees bent, and he most truly teaches that, through the words of the Apostle, a metaphorical genuflexion is to be understood, namely inward worship and reverence of mind. Let those who affect I know not what religious piety and holiness through those outward rites keep these things to themselves.

units.la: Tertio finem illius exaltationis, quam ad gloriam Patris factam esse docet Apostolus, explicat, & dicit, finem Deo Patri, in exaltando Christo hunc propositum fuisse, ut non tantum summa eius potentia, & diuitiarum excellentia, verum etiam infinita eius bonitas, gratia, & misericordia erga genus humanum innotesceret: Deum vero illum finem assequutum non esse, si Christo nihil revera dederit, sed ille omnia iam antea habuerit.
units.tr: Third, he explains the purpose of that exaltation which the Apostle teaches was done for the glory of the Father, and says that the purpose of God the Father in exalting Christ was that not only his supreme power and the excellence of his riches, but also his infinite goodness, grace and mercy towards the human race, might become known; and that God did not in fact attain that purpose if he had given Christ nothing in reality, but Christ had already possessed all things beforehand.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument runs as follows.

units.la: Exaltationis illius, qua Christus à Deo Patre in summam gloriam, maiestatis, ac potentia diuina sublimitatem euectus fuit, finis est gloria Dei, misericordia ipsius, diuitiarum, potentia, & bonitatis, gratiaque erga genus humanum manifestatio & declaratio.
units.tr: The exaltation by which Christ was raised by God the Father to the highest glory and to the sublimity of divine majesty and power has as its end the glory of God, his mercy, riches, power and goodness, and the manifestation and declaration of his grace towards the human race.

units.la: Atqui ex illa exaltatione, qua Christo nihil datum esse dicitur, quod antea non habuerit, talis manifestatio & declaratio non oritur.
units.tr: But from that exaltation, in which Christ is said to have received nothing he did not already have before, no such manifestation and declaration arises.

units.la: Ergo hæc non est vera illa exaltatio, de qua Apostolus loco hoc præsente loquitur.
units.tr: Therefore this is not that true exaltation of which the Apostle speaks in the passage before us.

units.la: Resp. Totum argumentum à nobis concedi, sed nihil illud concludere, cum nos potentiæ ac maiestatis diuinæ in Christo declaratione sola, exaltationem Christi minimè definiamus, sed illam vnicam tantùm gradum eius constituamus, & veram illam gloriæ, potentiæ, imperii, ac potestatis plenitudinem, tota persona capitis, & Mediatoris nostri, exaltatione illa collatam,
units.tr: Reply. We grant the whole argument, but it proves nothing, since we do not define Christ's exaltation solely by the declaration of divine power and majesty in Christ. We regard that declaration as only one degree of it, and we hold that the true fullness of glory, power, dominion and authority is conferred by that exaltation upon the whole person of our Head and Mediator,

units.la: Ec ad salutem nobis,qui natura filii irae atque mortis fumus,necessa- riam agnoscamus.Sed tueantur fe illi,qui contra Scripturae veri- tatem augustissimum illud exaltationis , tam angustis cancellis circumscribunt,illos nominare debuisset Aduersarius, ne simpli- cioribus falsitatis illud crimen integris Ecclesiis impingendi oc- cafio & ansa praebeatur.
units.tr: and we acknowledge it as necessary for our salvation, we who by nature are children of wrath and of death. But let those defend themselves who, contrary to the truth of Scripture, confine that most august exaltation within such narrow limits. The Adversary ought to have named them, so that the simpler sort are not given an occasion or pretext for laying that charge against the Churches as a whole.

units.la: Deinde ex iisdem illis verbis,quibus gloria illa Dei,exaltationis illius finis esse perhibetur ab Apostolo , inquit, citra contradictio- nem,& plane ἀλλοτριότητος[?] sequi,Christum non esse vnum illum & aeter- num Deum, quoniam videlicet Deus Christum non simpliciter exalta- uerit ideo,vt illo honore afficeretur,sed vt omnis ille honor, qui Christo propter exaltationis dignitatem exhibetur , ad gloriam ipsius Dei tan- quam autore illius honoris deriuetur,& sic ille honor non in ipso Christo, sed in Deo Patre terminetur, & per Christum Deum ipse honore- tur. Ad hoc ipsum autem argumentum iam capite decimoquin- to,& decimofeptimo sufficienter respondimus,vt hic nulla repe- titione fit opus.
units.tr: Next, from those same words by which the Apostle says that the glory of God is the end of that exaltation, he says that it follows, without contradiction and plainly, from estrangement [ἀλλοτριότητος] that Christ is not that one and eternal God. For God, he says, did not exalt Christ simply in order that Christ might be honoured by it; rather, all the honour that is paid to Christ on account of the dignity of his exaltation is derived back to the glory of God himself as the author of that honour. Thus that honour terminates not in Christ himself but in God the Father, and God is honoured through Christ. We have already answered this very argument sufficiently in the fifteenth and seventeenth chapters, so there is no need to repeat it here.

units.la: Atque hactenus de genuina loci illius Apostoli interpretatione actum est , nunc vltimo loco blasphemiam illam & impietatem palliare conatur Aduersarius, cuius euidenter conuincuntur eo ipso , quod Christum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον & hominem solum esse , ex doctrina ipsorum necessario consequatur,& dicit , cùm quis purus & solum homo esse perhibeatur ,duobus modis illud intelligi posse , & ratione essentiae, & ratione qualitatum. Si ratione essentiae illud intelligatur , tum fatemur , inquit, essentiam Christi, vtpote veri hominis, non aliam nisi humanam esse. Sin vero ratione qualitatum , & qualis ille homo fit , consideretur , dicimus Christum non nudum,purum,& solum hominem esse,sed aliquid amplius,quam caeteri homines,praesertim ab eo tempore,quo Deus Pater ipsum propter obedientiam praestitam exaltauit , ita vt iam reliquis hominibus opponi possit,non secus ac si illes homo amplius non effet.
units.tr: So much for the genuine interpretation of that passage of the Apostle. Now, in the last place, the Adversary tries to disguise that blasphemy and impiety, which are plainly refuted by the very fact that, on their doctrine, it necessarily follows that Christ is a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον] and only a man. He says: "When someone is said to be pure and only a man, this can be understood in two ways, either in respect of essence or in respect of qualities. If it is understood in respect of essence, then we grant that the essence of Christ, as of a true man, is no other than human. But if it is considered in respect of qualities, and of what sort of man he is, we say that Christ is not a bare, pure and only man, but something more than other men, especially from the time when God the Father exalted him because of the obedience he rendered. So that he can now be set over against the rest of mankind, as if he were no longer a man."

units.la: Resp. Vt de ipso disiunctionis vitio,quo laborat ipsa distinctio, nihil agam , dico primo , illam ipsam distinctionem nihil ad remmm facere,nec palliandae, aut excusandae impietati doctrinae Samofatenianae quicquam momenti adferre. Quamuis enim Christus propter excellentiam ipsi per exaltationis gratiam collatorum donorum , puta sapientię, potentiae,fulgoris,gloriae,maiestatis,alio- rumque , & plurium, quàm vlli vel Angeli,vel homines acceperint, longè supra communem humanæ naturæ fortem & condi- tionē cōstitutus & euectus esse verissimè ab illis agnoscatur:sem- per tamen grauissimū illud impietatiscrimē ipsis intēratur æquis- simè, docere videlicet illos,Christum ratione essentiæ ac naturæ suæ φλο᾽ ἀνθρωπον, & hominem solùm esse,cùm non ad naturam & essentiam Christi, sed eiusdem accidentia,gratiam videlicet Dei, qui in tantam gloriæ celsitudinem euectus est,dona,& qualitates illæ accidentariæ sint referendæ. Nam quum & hæ ipsç creatæ sint, ac finitę, humanam Christi naturam minimè destruentes, i- deò etiam Christum à ceteris hominibus distinguunt quidem, sed ex catalogo hominum minimè expungunt aut eximunt. Se- cundò,falsum esse consequens illud,quod ex distinctione illa in- fert Aduersarius,Christum videlicet(intelligē qua homo est,vel se- cundùm essentiam & naturam humanam ipsius : secus enim ad quęstionem præsentem nihil illa faciunt) ceteris hominibus ita op- poni posse, quasi ille homo esse desisset, neque argumentis vllis,aut Scripturę testimoniis probari posse.
units.tr: Reply. Leaving aside the faulty disjunction on which this distinction itself rests, I say first that this distinction has nothing to do with the matter and adds no weight to excusing or palliating the impiety of the Samosatene doctrine. For although it is truly acknowledged by them that Christ, because of the excellence of the gifts conferred upon him through the grace of exaltation (wisdom, power, splendour, glory, majesty, and many more than any angel or man has received), has been raised far above the common lot and condition of human nature, nevertheless that most grave crime of impiety remains fully attached to them, namely that they teach that Christ, in respect of his essence and nature, is a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον] and only a man, whereas those gifts and accidental qualities are to be referred not to the nature and essence of Christ but to its accidents, namely the grace of God who raised him to such height of glory. For since these are created and finite, they do not destroy the human nature of Christ. They therefore indeed distinguish Christ from other men, but they by no means strike him off or exclude him from the roll of mankind. Second, the consequence which the Adversary draws from that distinction is false, namely that Christ (understood as man, that is, in respect of his human essence and nature, for otherwise these distinctions do nothing to the present question) can be set over against other men as if he had ceased to be a man, and this cannot be proved by any arguments or testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: Hoc ipsum tamen consequens duobus exemplis ex Scriptura petitis demonstrare conatur. Primum habetur in illis Apostoli verbis Gal.1.v.1. Paulus Apostolus non ab hominibus, neque per homi- nem,sed per Iesum Christum ac Deum Patrem. Alterum Marc.16.v 7. Abite,dicite discipulis eius,& Petro:Et Act.5.v.29. Respondês Petrus, & Apostoli dixerunt, Vbi propter eminentiam & prærogatiuam, qua Petrus alios Apostolos superauerit, ita ipsum distinctè nominari dicit, quasi inter Apostolos ipse non esset recensendus,cùm tamen ipse quoque Apostolus fuerit.Vnde infert multò magis ipsum Christum,qui non mo- do omnes homines, sed omnes etiam cœlestes principatus, ac potestates, potentia,& dignitate, quàm longissimè superet, ex numero hominum eximendum esse,& illis opponendum.
