units.tr: Yet the Adversary tries to prove this very consequence from two examples taken from Scripture. The first is in the Apostle's words in Gal. 1:1: Paul an apostle, not of men, nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father. The second is Mark 16:7: Go, tell his disciples and Peter; and Acts 5:29: But Peter and the apostles answered. From these, he says, it is clear that Peter is named separately, as if he were not to be counted among the apostles, on account of the eminence and prerogative by which he surpassed the other apostles, although he was himself an apostle too. From this he infers that Christ much more, who surpasses not only all men but also all heavenly principalities and powers in power and dignity by the widest margin, must be removed from the number of men and set over against them.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum:Christum in illo Pauli loco non qua homo est, aut secundùm humanam naturam ipsius, nec etiam respectu do- morum humanę ipsius naturę collatorum,sed Σωτήρων,& quà etiam verus Deus est, hominibus opponi.Quid ? ex eo ipso loco diuina Christi natura solidè euincitur.Si enim Paulus nō ab hominibus, neque per hominem , sed per Iesum Christum,qui verus Rex , & Caput est Ecclesię , constitutus est Apostolus, necessariò inde se- quitur Iesum Christum φλο᾽ ἀνθρωπον & hominem solùm non esse, sed verum insuper, æternúmque Deum. Atqui prius affirmat Apostolus: Ergo consequens etiam concedat Samosatenus, aut litem ipsi Apostolo intentet, necesse est. Ad alterum: falsum esse, Petrum gradu vel auctoritate cæteros Apostolos superasse: iure quidem ætatis, & temporis quo vocatus est ad ministerium, primus erat: sed ratione vocationis, & auctoritatis Apostoli æquales fuere omnes. Qui plura hac de re desiderat, videat doctissimas animaduersiones Francisci Junii, Guilielmi Vitakeri, Sibrandi Lubberti, Matthæi Sutliui in libros Bellarmini de Pontifice Romano, in quibus fabulosum illud commentum ita refellitur, ut qui doctissimis illis meditationibus aliquid adiicere vellet, nonnullas Athenas (quod dicitur) deferre videretur. Quod igitur Petrus Apostolus in duobus illis citatis locis distincte nominatur, eo ipso nec vocationis, nec gradus, nec auctoritatis in munere Apostolico prærogatiua, sed vel singularis aliquis eius feruor, vel ætatis ordo, & temporis, quo ante reliquos ad munus Apostolicum vocatus fuit, ratio, vel etiam aliæ circumstantiæ innuuntur, ut manifesto caus elencho interpretatio Aduersarii laborare deprehendatur. Hoc vero destructo antecedente, ipsum consequens, quod illo fundamento nititur, per se & sponte corruit.
units.tr: Reply. As to the first: in that passage of Paul, Christ is set over against men not as man, nor in respect of his human nature, nor even in respect of the gifts conferred on his human nature, but as Saviour [Σωτήρ], and as he is also true God. Indeed, from that very passage the divine nature of Christ is soundly established. For if Paul was made an apostle not by men, nor by man, but by Jesus Christ, who is the true King and Head of the Church, it necessarily follows that Jesus Christ is not a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον] and only a man, but also true and eternal God. The Apostle affirms the first; therefore the Samosatene must either grant the consequence or bring a lawsuit against the Apostle himself. As to the second: it is false that Peter surpassed the other apostles in rank or authority. By right of age and of the time at which he was called to the ministry he was indeed first, but in respect of the calling and authority of an apostle all were equal. Anyone who wants more on this matter should consult the most learned observations of Franciscus Junius, Guilielmus Vitakerus, Sibrandus Lubbertus and Matthaeus Sutlivius on the books of Bellarmine concerning the Roman Pontiff. In those works that fabulous invention is so thoroughly refuted that anyone who wished to add anything to those learned reflections would seem to be carrying owls to Athens, as the saying goes. Therefore, that Peter the apostle is named separately in those two passages cited does not point to any prerogative in calling, rank or authority in the apostolic office. It points rather to some singular fervour of his, or to the order of his age and the time at which he was called to the apostolic office before the others, or to other circumstances. So the Adversary's interpretation is shown to labour under a manifest fallacy. And once this premise is destroyed, the conclusion that rests upon it falls of its own accord.

units.la: Quæ Aduersarius eiusdem capitis sectione decimaseptima, ad eandem impietatem sententiæ suæ tegendam adfert, partim ab initio huius capitis sunt refutata, partim vero ad examen capitis quadragesimi primi, vbi reliqua ex professo tractantur ab Aduersario, differemus, disputationi de persona Iesu Christi Σαυθρώπε hic, finem imponentes.
units.tr: The further arguments which the Adversary brings, in the seventeenth section of this same chapter, to cover up the same impiety of his opinion, have partly been refuted at the beginning of this chapter, and partly we will defer to the examination of the forty-first chapter, where the Adversary deals with the rest in set form. Here we bring to an end the disputation about the person of Jesus Christ.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: DE OFFICIO IESV CHISTI Mediatoris: et primum De Prophetico.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF JESUS CHRIST THE MEDIATOR: and first, concerning the Prophetic office.

units.la: HACTENVS veritatem diuinæ naturæ in persona Christi inuictam, aduersus vanissimas illas Paulinistarum strophas, ex verbo Dei defendimus: sequitur nunc, vt de amplissimo & excellentissimo eiusdem Saluatoris ac Mediatoris nostri officio, breuiter contra Aduersarium nostrum agamus. Vt autem hæc nostra assertio ita sit dilucidior & illustrior, non tantum ipsos Aduersarii errores confutabimus, sed etiam quid de illo salutifero munere credendum sit, & tradendum in Ecclesiis, ex ipsis Scripturarum sacrarum fontibus, breuiter ostendemus, vt simul, hoc iacto veritatis fundamento, doctrinæ Samosatenianæ falsitas tum clarius, tum etiam facilius corruat. Officium igitur Christi munus Mediatoris ipsi à Patre iniunctum, & voluntarie à Filio susceptum, vt præstaret illa omnia, quibus Deus Pater electis suis reconciliaretur, ipsique pro peccatis nostris satisfieret, ita merito suo salutem ac vitam æternam nobis acquireret & communicaret, unde etiam Saluator, Redemptor, & Seruator noster, Iesus item & Christus dicitur. A Patre hoc munus ipsi iniunctum esse dicimus: Neque enim quisquam sibi sumit hunc honorem, sed qui vocatur à Deo sicut & Aaron: ita & Christus non sibi hunc honorem tribuit, vt fieret Pontifex, sed is, qui dixerat ei, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, Hebr.5. v.4. & 5. Unde etiam non tantum Spiritu sancto, & quidem præ omnibus consortibus ipsius unctus, hoc est, Sanctus sanctorum factus, & non modo aliquibus Spiritus sancti donis, sed ipso toto Spiritu citra mensuram donatus est; Ioh.3. v.34. Eorum etiam missio illius triplici peculiari signo à Deo comprobata fuit cœli videlicet apertione, Spiritus sancti in specie corporea, super ipsum demissione, & voce ipsa Patris ad illum delata, qua extra omnium, qui vnquam ad munus aliquod à Deo sunt electi. uocati,ordinem,singulari priuilegio est eucétus. Hoc idem deinde munus,quod ita proprium est ipsius, vt neque ex integro neque ex parte aliqua sua,ad vllum alium transferri potest, Christus secundum vtramque naturam diuinā & humanam exequitur, distinctionis quidem,hoc est,agente vnaquaque natura id quod suum est,& sequatur, vt naturarum,sic etiam actionum discrimine, attamen non separatim,ac diuise, sed vtriusque actionibus, ad vnum idemque perficiendum concurrentibus. Huius insuper officii partes duas constituimus, primam videlicet,Iustitiae salutis, et vitae aeternae per expiationem peccatorum, perfectissimo satisfactione & redemptionis persoluto λυτρῳ factam,meritum,impetrationem & acquisitionem:alterā verò salutis,& iustitiae merito obedientiae & satisfactione pro peccatis acquisitae,communicationē,& distributionem,quibus duob.actibus,tanquam partibus essentialibus integra officii illius vis perfectè comprehenditur. Hinc per se & necessario sequitur munus Christi triplex agnoscendum & asserendum esse,Propheticum nempe,Sacerdotale,& Regium,quemadmodum etiam ei in Scripturis eadem tria illa officia distinctè & diserte tribuuntur. Et Christum quidem Saluatorem nostrum Prophetam esse, inde demonstratur, quod Messiam Prophetam futurum, per tribus in Veteri Testamento prædixit Moses, Deuter. 18. versu 11 Prophetam e medio tui, & fratribus tuis, sicut ego sum,suscitabit tibi Iehouah Deus,ei audscultate.& versu 18. Prophetam suscitabo eis, e medio fratrum ipsorum,sicut tu es,&indam verba mea ori eius,vt eloquatur eis,quicquid præcepero ipsi. Et Esaias cap. 42. 6.& 7. Ego Iehouah vocaui te iuste,vt confirmem manum tuam, & custodiens te, tradam in fœdus populi,in lucem gentium: Ad aperiendum oculos cæcos,ad educendum claustro vinctum,è carcere sedentes in tenebris: Et cap. 6.v. 1. Spiritus Domini Iehouae super me,eo quod vnxit Iehouah me ad Euangelizandum mansuetis misit me,ad sanandum contritos animo, ad proclamandum captiuis libertatem,& vinctis aperturam ergastuli. Christum autem has prædictiones de se intelligendas, & se Prophetam ii mundū misso esse ipse testatur Luc.1 v.21.Hodie impleta est Scriptura in auditibus vobis:Ioh.18.v.37.Ego ad hoc natus sum,& ad hoc veni in mundu,vt dem testimonium veritati. Hanc autem Prophetiam Christi definimus, quod sit officium eius, quo ille arcanum Dei consilium & veritatem,de redemptione generis humani,& reconciliatione cum Deo,aliáq; omnia ad salutem obtinendam scitu necessaria,hoc ipsum minib.patefecit,tum prædicatione veritatis & Euangelii externa,quæ scripturis Veteris Testamenti, & omnis generis signis, quibus [?] octrinæ alicuius diuina veritas demonstrari potest, per scientiam [?] videlicet Dei solius propriæ, qualis est cordium inspectio, arcanorumque aliorum revelatio, & futurorum prædictio, declaratione [?] per potentiam soli Deo competentem insignis, prodigiis ac virtutibus monstratam, per summam denique tolerantiam, qua ad [?] signandam veritatem Euangelii, & promissionum Patribus factarum, atrocissimam & ignominiosissimam mortem crucis volens [?] sponte subierit, confirmauit, tum etiam illuminatione interna [?] per Spiritum sanctum, qua mentes electorum ita illustrauit, ut veritatem in verbo, & potentiam in operibus viderent, agnoscerent, [?] ad salutem ipsorum amplecterentur: quod idem munus nunc in [?] coelis ad dextram Dei Patris sedens, per externum ministerium, & Spiritus sancti virtutem fide lissimè exequitur.
units.tr: So far we have defended from the Word of God the truth of the divine nature in the person of Christ, which is unconquered, against those most empty Paulinist fabrications. It now follows that we deal briefly with our Adversary concerning the most ample and excellent office of the same Saviour and Mediator of ours. So that this our assertion may be clearer and more illustrious, we will not only refute the Adversary's own errors, but also briefly show, from the very fountains of the holy Scriptures, what must be believed about that saving office and taught in the Churches. Thus, with this foundation of truth laid, the falsity of the Samosatenian doctrine may fall both more clearly and more easily. The office of Christ, then, is the function of Mediator enjoined on him by the Father and voluntarily undertaken by the Son, to perform all those things by which God the Father might be reconciled to his elect and satisfaction made to him for our sins, and so by his merit acquire and communicate salvation and eternal life to us. Hence also our Saviour, Redeemer and Preserver is called Jesus and Christ. We say that this office was enjoined on him by the Father: No one takes this honour upon himself, but he is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself by becoming high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you, Heb. 5 vv. 4 and 5. Hence also he was anointed not only with the Holy Spirit, and that above all his fellows, that is, made the Holy of holies, and endowed not merely with some gifts of the Holy Spirit but with the whole Spirit without measure; John 3 v. 34. His mission was also confirmed by God with a threefold special sign: namely, the opening of the heavens, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him in bodily form, and the voice of the Father itself addressed to him, by which he was distinguished with a singular privilege beyond the order of all who have ever been chosen, called or appointed by God to any office. This same office, which is so proper to him that it cannot be transferred to any other, either wholly or in any part of it, Christ carries out according to both natures, divine and human. The distinction of natures remains, that is, each nature acts in what is its own and is not confused, and so the actions are distinct as the natures are; yet they are not separate or divided, but the actions of both concur to accomplish one and the same thing. Moreover, we set up two parts of this office: the first, namely the merit, impetration and acquisition of righteousness, salvation and eternal life through the expiation of sins, brought about by a most perfect satisfaction and by the payment of redemption, the ransom [λύτρῳ]; and the second, the communication and distribution of the righteousness and salvation acquired by the merit of obedience and by satisfaction for sins. By these two acts, as essential parts, the whole force of that office is perfectly comprehended. Hence it follows of itself and necessarily that the threefold office of Christ must be acknowledged and asserted: the Prophetic, the Priestly, and the Kingly, just as in the Scriptures these same three offices are distinctly and expressly attributed to him. That Christ our Saviour is a Prophet is shown first by the fact that Moses foretold through three that the Messiah would be a Prophet in the Old Testament, Deut. 18 v. 11: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet from among you, from your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen; and v. 18: I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, that he may speak to them whatever I command him. Also Isaiah ch. 42 vv. 6 and 7: I, the LORD, have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and keep you, and give you as a covenant to the people, as a light to the nations, to open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners from the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness from the prison; and ch. 61 v. 1: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the meek; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. That Christ himself understood these predictions as concerning himself, and that he was sent into the world as a Prophet, he testifies, Luke 1 v. 21: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing; and John 18 v. 37: For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. We define this prophetic office of Christ as that office by which he made known to men himself, that secret counsel and truth of God concerning the redemption of the human race and its reconciliation with God, and all other things necessary to be known for obtaining salvation. He did this both by the external preaching of the truth and of the Gospel, which he confirmed by the Scriptures of the Old Testament and by every kind of sign by which the divine truth of any teaching can be demonstrated, namely by the knowledge that belongs to God alone, such as the inspection of hearts and the revelation of other hidden things and the prediction of future events, by a notable display of power that belongs to God alone, shown by miracles and powers, and finally by the greatest patience, by which, to seal the truth of the Gospel and of the promises made to the Fathers, he willingly underwent the most atrocious and most ignominious death of the cross. He also did it by the internal illumination of the Holy Spirit, by which he so enlightened the minds of the elect that they saw and recognised the truth in the word and the power in the works, and embraced them for their salvation. This same office he now carries out most faithfully, sitting in heaven at the right hand of God the Father, through the external ministry and the power of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sed Christum non tantùm Prophetam, & Prophetarum omnium principem, verùm etiam summum Sacerdotem esse, Scriptura ipsa [?] manifestè docet. Messiam enim olim Patribus promissum, fore Sacerdotem Veteris Testamenti scripturæ euidenter demonstrant, [?] Sacerdotis nomen, tum etiam rem nomine illo significatam, [?] sertè ipsi tribuentes. Psalm. 110. vers. 4. Iurauit Ichouah, & non pœnitebit, tu es Sacerdos in seculum, secundùm ordinem Melchisedek. Ef. 53. vers. 4. & 5. Veruntamen morbos nostros ipse pertulit, & dolores ipsos nostros baiulauit, quamuis non æstimemus plagam affectum, percussum à Deo & afflictum. Nā ipse dolore afficitur à defectionibus nostris, atteritur ab iniquitatib. nostris, castigatio pacis nostræ impositur ei, & tumice ut sit curatio nobis: & v.6. Iehouah coïecit in ipsum iniquitates omnium nostrum: & v.7. Exigitur (pœna) & ipse affligitur, neque aperit os suum, parua pecus ad mactationem ducitur, & velut ouis coram tonsoribus obmutescēs, neq; aperit os suum. & v.10.11.12. At Iehouah delectatus est conterere ipsum morbo affecit, quàdoquidē exponebat se ipse sacrificium pro peccato, videbit semē, prolongabit dies, & delectatio Iehoua per eū prosperabitur. Exceptū modestis seipsu vides satiabitur, cognitione sui iustificabit seruus meus iustus multos, quoniam iniquitates ipse baiulauit. Idcirco partem dabo ei pro multis, vt cū robustis partiatur prædā, pro eo quod prō- [?] tradidit in mortem se ipsum, & cum defectoribus annumeratus est: nā ipse peccatum multorum perferēs pro defectoribus intercessit. Iesum autem [?] Christum verum esse Sacerdotem, scriptura Noui Testamēti aperti-ssimè testatur, dum ipsi & nomen sacerdotis, & omnia ad munus sacerdotale pertinentia, disertis verbis tribuit. Hebr. 5. vers. 5. & 6. Christus non sibi hunc honorem tribuit, ut fieret Pontifex, sed is qui dixerat ei, Filius meus es tu, ego genui te. Sicut & alibi dicit, Tu es Sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedec. Et cap.2. verf.17. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, ut misericors esset, & fidelis Pontifex in iis quae apud Deum (agenda forent) ad expiandum peccata populi. Et cap.8. ver.3. Omnis Pontifex ad offerenda dona & victimas constituitur, unde necesse fuit, hunc quoque habere quod offerret. Et cap.10. verf.11.12. Omnis Sacerdos quotidie adstat operans, & eandem saepius offerens hostias, quae nunquam possunt auferre peccata. Hic vero una pro peccatis oblata victima in perpetuum sedet ad dextram Dei. Matth.10.28. Item Marc.10.45. Filius hominis non venit ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ministraret, daretque animam suam in redemptionis pretium pro multis. Act.20.28. Deus (id est, filius Dei Christus) Ecclesiam acquisivit proprio sanguine. Rom.3. verf.24.25. Iustificantur gratis, per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Et cap.5. verf.10. Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii eius, nempe mortem illam cruentam in cruce. Galat.3. verf.13 Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio, nempe in cruce. Ephes.1.v.7. In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum, ex divitiis ipsius gratia. Et 5.verf.2. Christus tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo in odorem bonae fragrantiae. 1.Timoth.2.verf.6. Qui dedit semetipsum redemptionis pretium (ἀντίλυτρον) pro quibusvis. 1.Petr.1.verf.18.19. Redempti estis non caducis rebus, argento, vel auro, sed pretioso sanguine tanquam agni immaculati & inculpati, nempe Christi. Sed omnia illa locca, & scripturae testimonia in quibus Christo & titulus Sacerdotis, & res nomine significata tribuitur, recensere nimis prolixum foret. Hoc autem sacerdotium Christi definimus, quod sit Officium Christi, quo ille personae ac vitae sanctitate perfectissimus, seipsum hominem inculpatum, per Spiritum aeternum, in sacrificium verum ac propriè propitiatorium & divinitus absolutum, in cruce Deo obtulit, extinctóque peccato & morte, & deleto chirographo, in sanctuarium caelestc, cuius ille minister est, ingressus, sedauit iram Dei, gratiam & reconciliationem peperit, & una pro peccatis oblata sui victima remissionem peccatorum, aeternam redemptionem & spiritum gratiae impetrauit, maledictionem abstulit, iustitiam seculorum, & vitam aeternam, quin & Ecclesiam, cui ista bona omnia communicantur, summámque super omnia in coelo & in terris.
units.tr: But Scripture itself plainly teaches that Christ is not only the Prophet and the chief of all the prophets, but also the high priest. The Scriptures of the Old Testament clearly demonstrate that the Messiah promised to the Fathers would be a priest, attributing to him both the name of priest and the reality signified by that name. Psalm 110. v. 4: The LORD has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. Isaiah 53. vv. 4 and 5: Surely he has borne our sicknesses and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. v. 6: The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. v. 7: He was oppressed and he was afflicted, yet he did not open his mouth; he is led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearers is dumb, so he does not open his mouth. vv. 10–12: Yet it pleased the LORD to crush him and to make him sick; when he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. He shall see the travail of his soul and be satisfied; by his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will give him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; for he bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors. That Jesus Christ is the true priest, the Scripture of the New Testament most openly testifies, since it attributes to him, in express words, both the name of priest and all things pertaining to the priestly office. Heb. 5. vv. 5 and 6: Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you. As he says elsewhere: You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek. And ch. 2. v. 17: Therefore he had to be made like his brethren in all things, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the things pertaining to God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. And ch. 8. v. 3: Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it was necessary that this one also should have something to offer. And ch. 10. vv. 11 and 12: Every priest stands daily ministering and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this one, having offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down at the right hand of God. Matt. 20. 28; likewise Mark 10. 45: The Son of man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many. Acts 20. 28: God (that is, the Son of God, Christ) purchased the Church with his own blood. Rom. 3. vv. 24 and 25: They are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. And ch. 5. v. 10: We were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, namely that bloody death on the cross. Gal. 3. v. 13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, namely on the cross. Eph. 1. v. 7: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace. And ch. 5. v. 2: Christ gave himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God as a fragrant aroma. 1 Tim. 2. v. 6: Who gave himself a ransom price [ἀντίλυτρον] for all. 1 Pet. 1. vv. 18 and 19: You were redeemed not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, namely Christ. But to recount all those passages and testimonies of Scripture in which the title of priest and the reality signified by it are attributed to Christ would be too lengthy. We define this priesthood of Christ as that office by which he, most perfect in the holiness of his person and life, offered himself, a man without fault, through the eternal Spirit, on the cross to God as a true sacrifice, properly propitiatory and divinely accepted. Having abolished sin and death and blotted out the handwriting, he entered into the heavenly sanctuary, of which he is the minister. There he appeased the wrath of God, obtained grace and reconciliation, and by one sacrifice of himself offered for sins he obtained the remission of sins, eternal redemption and the Spirit of grace. He took away the curse, and obtained the righteousness of the ages, eternal life, and the Church, to which all these good things are communicated; and the highest power over all things in heaven and in earth, and the whole right to eternal life, together with all things necessary both for giving and for receiving it. Having obtained these for us, he intercedes unceasingly before...

units.la: [Marginal notes are cut off or show-through and are not reliably legible; not transcribed.] in terra potestatem, acquisiuit, & totum ius in vitam æternam, & quæcunque ad illam tum dandam, tum accipiendam sunt necessaria, adeptus pro nobis indesinenter intercedit apud Patrem, & simul nos aduersus accusationes, quas nobis, & conscientiæ nostræ intentat Aduersarius defendit.
units.tr: ...on earth, acquired power, and the whole right to eternal life, and everything necessary both for giving and for receiving it. Having obtained these, he unceasingly intercedes for us with the Father, and at the same time defends us against the accusations which the Adversary brings against us and against our conscience.

units.la: Restat munus Christi regium: In quo considerandum est, Messiam non Prophetam tantum, & Sacerdotem, sed insuper etiam Regem, & quidem inter Reges eximium, imo Regum omnium Dominum Patribus promissum esse, Ierem. 23. versu 5. Ecce dies venturi sunt, dictum Iehouæ, quibus excitabo Dauidi germen iustum, qui regnabit Rex, secundabitur que, ac exercebit ius & iustitiam in terra: Ezech. 37. versu 24. Et seruus meus Dauid Rex erit super iustos, ac pastor unicus erit omnibus ipsis, Psalm. 45. versu 7. & 8. Solium tuum ò Deus in seculum, & sempiternum, sceptrum rectum, sceptrum regni tui. Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti improbitatem, propterea unxit te, ò Deus, Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis: & 89. versu 28. Primogenitum constituam eum, excelsum supra Reges terræ. Et Psal. 2. v. 12 Et nunc Reges, & Iudices terræ, osculemini Filium. & 72. v. 9. 10. 1 Dominabitur à mari uno ad alterum, & à flumine quaque fines terræ, coram eo honorem exhibentes incurvabunt se barbari, & inimici eius pulverem lingent. Reges Oceani, & insulani munus reddent, Reges Schebæ, & Sebæ donarium offerent. Denique incurvabunt se ei omnes Reges, omnes Gentes seruient ei. Iesum Christum vero Regem regum esse, & Dominum dominantium: testatur scriptura tum diuersis verbis titulum illum ipsi tribuens, Apocal. 17. versu 14. Hi cum agno pugnabunt, & Agnus vincet eos, quoniam Dominus dominorum est, & Rex regum. Et 19. versu 13. & 16. Vocetur nomen eius Sermo Dei: Habebatque in vestimento, & in femore suo nomen scriptum, Rex regum, & Dominus dominantium, tum etiam affirmans, Dominium ac potestatem in cœlo, & in terra, auctoritatemque in omnem carnem, ut omne genus se coram eo flectat, ipsi traditam esse, & ipsos Angelos ministros ei datos ad exequendum mandata ipsius. Matth. 28. versu 18. Act. 2. versu 36. Hebræorum 1. versu 6. & 14. Psalm. 110. versu 1.
units.tr: There remains Christ's kingly office. In regard to it we must consider that the Messiah was promised to the Fathers not only as Prophet and Priest but also as King, and indeed as an outstanding king, even the Lord of all kings. Jer. 23. verse 5: Behold, the days are coming, says the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous branch, who shall reign as king, prosper, and execute judgment and righteousness in the land. Ezek. 37. verse 24: My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd. Psalm 45. verses 7 and 8: Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. You love righteousness and hate wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. And Psalm 89. verse 28: I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. And Psalm 2. verse 12: Now therefore, O kings, be wise; kiss the Son. And Psalm 72. verses 9 and 10: He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth. Those who dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring tribute; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. All kings shall bow down before him; all nations shall serve him. That Jesus Christ is the King of kings and the Lord of lords, Scripture testifies, ascribing that title to him in various words. Rev. 17. verse 14: These will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings. And Rev. 19. verses 13 and 16: His name is called The Word of God; and on his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords. Scripture also affirms that dominion and power in heaven and on earth, and authority over all flesh, so that every kind bows before him, have been given to him, and the angels themselves have been given to him as ministers to carry out his commands. Matt. 28. verse 18; Acts 2. verse 36; Heb. 1. verses 6 and 14; Psalm 110. verse 1.

units.la: Porro regnum hoc Christi, quod plane spirituale est, definimus, quod sit officium Christi, quo ipse salutis, iustitiæ, ac vitæ æternæ, prophetia sua demonstrat, & sacerdotio partæ, electos reddit participes, ex statu nempe peccati, & miseriæ, ad gratiosi fœderis sanguine suo confirmati,participationem, verbo, & spiritu illos vocando:Deinde ctiam omnia bona,tùm ad hanc animalem,tùm ad spiritualem vitam necessaria,fidelibus communicat,Ecclesiam suam potenter tuetur,atque conferuat,& hostes eius reprimit,atque coercet : denique tanquam Iudex vniuersorum à Deo constitutus, sententiam iustificationis Electis suis pronunciaturus, eósque vita æterna donaturus est, aducrfus reprobos verò sententia condemnationis prolata, eos æternis pœnis afficiet.
units.tr: Moreover, we define this kingdom of Christ, which is wholly spiritual, as the office of Christ by which he, through his prophetic work, makes known salvation, righteousness and eternal life, and, through the priesthood he has obtained, makes the elect partakers of them. That is, he calls them by word and Spirit from the state of sin and misery into participation in the covenant of grace confirmed by his blood. Then he also gives to the faithful all the goods needful both for this animal life and for spiritual life, powerfully defends and preserves his Church, and restrains and checks its enemies. Finally, appointed by God as Judge of all, he will pronounce the sentence of justification upon his elect and grant them eternal life, but against the reprobate he will pronounce the sentence of condemnation and subject them to eternal punishments.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius euadit, Meffiam, id est,Iesum Christum,Dominum ac Saluatorem nostrum, promissum illum Patribus,Prophetam, Sacerdotem, ac Regem esse, & ad salutem nobis ærernam impetrandam, & communicandam,illas muneris Prophetici,Sacerdotalis,ac Regii, functiones, quas recensuimus,necessario requirit: sic vt, qui Iesum Christum, vel Prophetam,vel Sacerdotem,vel Regem esse, negare non erubescit,eundem quoque cum impiis Iudæis, promissum Patribus, & nobis præstitum Meffiam, Dominumque nostrum esse,necessario inficias ire teneatur, & qui munerum illorum Christi, actionem, & functionem illam expungit, eundem Saluatorem,ac Redemptorem,imo Iesum, & Christum, minimè agnoscat. Hanc officiorum Christi descriptionem fufius perfequutus sum, quàm instituti nostri ratio, quæ potissimum est, ferre videatur: sed quia doctrina Samofatenianorum summæ impietatis hinc solidissimè conuincitur, ideo operam illam non inutiliter me collocaffe confido.
units.tr: From all these things it becomes clearer than noonday light that the Messiah promised to the Fathers, that is, Jesus Christ our Lord and Saviour, is Prophet, Priest and King, and that to obtain and communicate eternal salvation to us he necessarily requires those functions of the prophetic, priestly and kingly office which we have reviewed. Hence whoever is not ashamed to deny that Jesus Christ is Prophet, or Priest, or King, is necessarily bound also to deny, with the impious Jews, that he is the Messiah promised to the Fathers and given to us, and our Lord. And whoever strikes out the action and function of those offices of Christ certainly does not acknowledge him as Saviour and Redeemer, indeed not even as Jesus and Christ. I have pursued this description of Christ's offices more fully than the plan of my work, which is chiefly concerned with other matters, seems to allow; but since the teaching of the Samosatenes is most solidly refuted by it, I trust that I have not spent this effort in vain.

units.la: Quia enim Scriptura sacra disertis verbis testatur,promissum Meffiam vere,ac proprie Prophetam,Sacerdotem,& Regem futurum esse: ideo quicunque Iesum Christum vel Prophetam,vel Sacerdotem,vel etiam Regem vere ac proprie esse negat, ille eundem cum impiis Iudæis, promissum istum Meffiam esse inficiatur, & qui ex officio ipsius expungit functiones, & actiones illas, quas nos ad generis humani redemptionem necessarias esse demonstrauimus,& Christo Mediatori in Scripturis tribui ostendimus, ille eundem nec Saluatorem, nec Redemptorem, imo nec Iesum nec Christum esse agnoscit.
units.tr: For since holy Scripture testifies in plain words that the promised Messiah will truly and properly be Prophet, Priest and King, whoever denies that Jesus Christ is truly and properly Prophet, or Priest, or even King, denies with the impious Jews that he is that promised Messiah. And whoever, from his office, strikes out those functions and actions which we have shown to be necessary for the redemption of mankind, and which we have shown are ascribed to Christ the Mediator in the Scriptures, does not acknowledge him to be Saviour or Redeemer, indeed not even Jesus or Christ.

units.la: Atqui Ofiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite quadragesimo,sectione octaua, & sequentibus, Christum vere & proprie Sacerdotem esse negat, & Sacerdotium Christi nihil aliud, quàm Regni ipsius spiritualis administrationem esse docet, & capite vicesimo, & sequentibus multas actiones, & functiones ex officio Christi expungit, quae & Christo Mediatori in Scripturis tribuuntur, & ad Redemptionem generis humani sunt necessariae:
units.tr: But Ostorrodius, in chapter forty of his Institutes, section eight and those following, denies that Christ is truly and properly a Priest, and teaches that the priesthood of Christ is nothing other than the administration of his spiritual kingdom; and in chapter twenty and those following he strikes out of Christ's office many actions and functions which are ascribed to Christ the Mediator in the Scriptures and are necessary for the redemption of mankind.

units.la: Ergo Ostorrodius Iesum Christum, promissum illum Messiam esse, cum impiis Iudaeis negat, & eundem nec Salvatorem, nec Redemptorem, imò nec Iesum, nec Christum esse agnoscit.
units.tr: Therefore Ostorrodius, with the impious Jews, denies that Jesus Christ is that promised Messiah, and does not acknowledge him to be Saviour or Redeemer, indeed not even Jesus or Christ.

units.la: Atque sic hactenus, quid de officio Christi Mediatoris sentiamus, & doceamus, ex ipsa Scriptura sacra, breviter ostendimus: sequitur igitur ut errores Aduersarii recensseamus. Ostorrodius itaque Institutionum suarum capite vicesimo officium Christi ita definit, quod ille nobis voluntatem Dei, de aeterna salute nobis danda, patefecerit, eamque ad finem & exitum suum perducat. Et huius officii Christi duas esse dicit partes, manifestationem videlicet voluntatis diuinae, propter quam Propheta appelletur, & administrationem, seu exequutionem voluntatis diuinae, propter quam functionem Rex nominetur: atque hisce duobus actibus seu partibus totam officii Christi vim contineri existimat.
units.tr: And so far we have briefly shown, from holy Scripture itself, what we think and teach concerning the office of Christ the Mediator. It follows, then, that we should review the errors of the Adversary. Accordingly, in chapter twenty of his Institutes Ostorrodius defines the office of Christ thus: that he has revealed to us the will of God concerning the eternal salvation to be given us, and brings it to its end and outcome. And he says that there are two parts of this office of Christ, namely the manifestation of the divine will, on account of which he is called Prophet, and the administration or execution of the divine will, on account of which function he is named King; and he thinks that the whole force of Christ's office is contained in these two acts or parts.

units.la: Resp. Definitionem ac distributionem officii Christi falsam & imperfectam esse. Falsa est, quia nititur falsa illa hypothesi, Deum nimirum absque vllo intercedente merito, & satisfactione Christi nobis peccata remittere, ac vitam aeternam daturum esse, cuius rei falsitatem iam ante in descriptione muneris Christi sacerdotalis ostendimus, & infra suo loco amplius demonstrabimus. Imperfecta igitur etiam est, quia omittuntur actus praecipui, ad munus illud, & salutis nostrae apotelesma perficiendum, necessario requisiti. Si enim illa vel definitio, vel distributio sufficiens esset, tum & Sacerdotium Christi expungendum, & Christus ipse efficacia tantum, non autem efficacia & merito, id est reconciliatione nostri cum Deo, satisfactione pro peccatis nostris, redemptione à peccato, & morte aeterna, iustitiaeque ac vitae aeternae acquisitione, ac imprecatione, & acquisitae salutis communicatione, siue distributione simul Saluator; Mediator denique tantùm Dei apud homines, non verò hominum etiam apud Deum agnoscendus esset, quod tamen falsum, & erroneum esse ipsa Scriptura luculenter docet, cuius nos non omnia huc pertinentia,sed pauca duntaxat testimonia annotabimus: Rom.3. v.24.& 25.Iustificantur autem gratis,eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu:quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius,ad declarandam iustitiam suam, per remissionem peccatorum praecedentium.2. Cor.5.verf.19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi,non imputando ipsis peccata ipsorum.Matth. 10. ver.28. Filius hominis non venit ut ministraretur sibi, sed ut ministraret, daréque animam suam in redemptionis pretium pro multis. Hebr.5. v.1. Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumitur, & pro hominibus constituitur in iis, quae apud Deum (agenda sunt) ut offerat dona, ria,& victimas pro peccatis.& v. 9.10. Et consecratus, factus est autor salutis aeternae,omnibus qui ipsi auscultant. Cognominatus à Deo Pontifex secundum ordinem Melchisedeck. Hebr. 7. versu 24. 25. Ipse propterea quod in aeternum manet,perpetuum habet sacerdotium. Unde & seruare prorsus potest eos,qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, semper viuens,ut interpellet pro eis,& 9.v.12. Neque per sanguinem hircorum, & vitulorum,sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium,aeternam redemptionem nactus.Ex quibus omnibus, vt & aliis infinitis Scripturae locis, euidenter apparet, Christum non tantùm patefactione voluntatis diuinae, & salutis aeternae communicatione, & distributione, sed etiam eiusdem acquisitione,& impetratione,Mediatorem, ac Saluatorem nostrum extitisse.
units.tr: Reply. The definition and division of Christ's office is false and imperfect. It is false, because it rests on the false hypothesis that God forgives us our sins and will give us eternal life without any intervening merit and satisfaction of Christ. The falsity of this we have already shown in the description of Christ's priestly office, and we will demonstrate it more fully in its proper place below. It is therefore also imperfect, because it omits the principal acts which are necessarily required to complete that office and the accomplishment [ἀπότελεσμα] of our salvation. For if that definition or division were sufficient, then the priesthood of Christ would have to be struck out, and Christ himself would have to be acknowledged as Saviour only by efficacy, not by merit and efficacy, that is, by reconciling us to God, by satisfaction for our sins, by redemption from sin and eternal death, by acquiring righteousness and eternal life, and by intercession, and by communicating or distributing the salvation thus acquired; and he would have to be acknowledged only as Mediator of God before men, and not also of men before God. That this is false and erroneous Scripture itself teaches plainly. We will note not all the passages that bear on this, but only a few testimonies: Rom. 3. verses 24 and 25: They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, because in his forbearance he had passed over former sins. 2 Cor. 5. verse 19: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. Matt. 10. verse 28: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Heb. 5. verse 1: Every high priest is taken from among men and is appointed on behalf of men in the things pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. And verses 9 and 10: And having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek. Heb. 7. verses 24 and 25: But he, because he continues forever, has a permanent priesthood. Therefore he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. And Heb. 9. verse 12: He entered once for all into the holy place, not by means of the blood of goats and calves, but by means of his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. From all these passages, and from countless other places of Scripture, it is clearly evident that Christ is our Mediator and Saviour not only by the manifestation of the divine will and by the communication and distribution of eternal salvation, but also by its acquisition and obtaining.

units.la: Deinde tria illa capita ordine tractat Aduersarius, & primò ostendit Christum propter illam voluntatis diuinae patefactionem, Prophetae nomine in Scripturis sacris indigitari: Secundò demonstrare conatur Christum propter officium illud Propheticum, Filium Dei, & Deum nominari potuisse, & nominatum quoque esse:tertiò explicat, quibusnam in rebus officium illud Christi consistat, & quare Deus nobis talem Prophetam dederit & excitauerit. Et quoniam de primo capite nulla est inter nos & Aduersarium controuersia,modò voluntatem illam Dei,cuius interpres Christus Propheta fuit,dextrè explicer,ideò illo omisso ad examen quaestionis secundae progredimur. Illa igitur quantum concernit,Christum propter officium ipsum Propheticum primò Filium Dei appellari potuisse,& appellatum quoque esse. esse, ex illis Christi verbis Ioh. 10. ver. 34.35. & 36. Nonne scriptum est in lege vestra, Ego dixi Dii estis? Si illos dixit Deos ad quos sermo Dei factus est, & non potest solvi Scriptura: Quem Pater sanctificavit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis, Tu blasphemas, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum? de- nique monstrare conatur in hunc modum:
units.tr: Next the adversary takes those three heads in order. First he shows that Christ, on account of that revelation of the divine will, is designated by the name of Prophet in the holy Scriptures. Secondly he tries to demonstrate that Christ, on account of that prophetic office, could be called, and was called, the Son of God and God. Thirdly he explains in what things that office of Christ consists, and why God has given and raised up such a Prophet for us. Since there is no controversy between us and the adversary about the first head, provided I explain properly that will of God of which Christ the Prophet was the interpreter, I pass over it and proceed to examine the second question. As far as it concerns Christ himself on account of the prophetic office, the adversary says that he could be called, and was called, the Son of God, and this from the words of Christ in John 10:34-36. "Is it not written in your law, I said, You are gods? If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, You blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?" Finally he tries to show it in this way:

units.la: Si Christus propter sanctificationem fuit, & missionem in hunc mundum seipsum Filium Dei appellavit: tum sequitur ipsum etiam propter officium Propheticum, seipsum nomine Filii Dei indigitasse.
units.tr: If Christ, on account of his sanctification and his mission into this world, called himself the Son of God, then it follows that he also, on account of the prophetic office, designated himself by the name of Son of God.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Ratio consequentiae haec est.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is this.

units.la: Si ipsa missio Christi nihil aliud est, quam officium ipsius Propheticum, seu munus annuntiandi Euangelium, & sanctificatio Christi, nihil aliud, quam copia vel plenitudo Spiritus sancti, a quo unctus est, in hunc finem, ut Euangelizaret, tum vera est prior illa consequentia.
units.tr: If the very mission of Christ is nothing other than his prophetic office, or the function of proclaiming the gospel, and the sanctification of Christ is nothing other than the abundance or fullness of the Holy Spirit, by whom he was anointed to this end, that he might preach the gospel, then that former consequence is valid.

units.la: At qui missionem Christi nihil aliud esse, quam munus ipsius Propheticum, dicit ex illis Scripturae locis, nempe Deut. 18. v. 18. Act. 2. v. 22. & 7. v. 37. Iohan. 7. v. 16. & 8. v. 18. & 12. v. 48.49. in quibus Christus a Patre in Prophetam missus esse dicitur, demonstrat. Christum autem in hunc finem a Spiritu sancto unctum esse, ut euangelizaret, ex Luc. 4. v. 18. ostendit.
units.tr: But that the mission of Christ is nothing other than his prophetic function he demonstrates from those passages of Scripture in which Christ is said to have been sent by the Father as Prophet: Deut. 18. v. 18.; Acts 2. v. 22.; 7. v. 37.; John 7. v. 16.; 8. v. 18.; 12. v. 48.49. And he shows from Luke 4. v. 18. that Christ was anointed by the Holy Spirit to this end, that he should preach the gospel.

units.la: Ergo vera est prior illa consequentia.
units.tr: Therefore that former consequence is valid.

units.la: Resp. Rem ipsam quantum concernit, dubium no est, quin Christus tribus illis argumentis, sanctificatione nimirum, id est, unctione Spiritus sancti, & donorum omnium collatione, quibus ille in sculpto aliquo sigillo a Patre signatus, & a reliquis omnibus segregatus fuit, missione deinde in hunc mundum, & ad munus mediatorium ordinatione: denique operibus divinis (quae Oros Florrodius in hac argumentatione omittit callide) Iudaeorum calumniam solide refutaverit, & simul etiam se verum aeternumque Deum esse, euidenter demonstraverit, non tamen sequitur illam vel sanctificationem, vel missionem, vel denique opera & miracula illa ab ipso patrata, causam esse, quare filius Dei exstiterit & appelletur, sive naturam eius divinam sive humanam respicias, quia ipsius nominis impositi veritas, non ex solis causis, sed etiam aliis argumentis arguitur & demonstratur, quemadmodum ex illa ipsa Christi cum Iudaeis disputatione cuidenter apparet. Non enim ex sola sanctificatione & missione, sed etiam, & quidem potissimum,
units.tr: Reply. As to the matter itself, there is no doubt that Christ, by those three arguments, namely sanctification (that is, the anointing of the Holy Spirit and the bestowal of all gifts, by which he was sealed by the Father as with a carved seal and set apart from all others), then his mission into this world and his appointment to the mediatorial office, and finally by the divine works (which Ostorrodius craftily omits in this argument), solidly refuted the calumny of the Jews, and at the same time clearly demonstrated that he is the true and eternal God. Yet it does not follow that that sanctification, or that mission, or finally those works and miracles performed by him, is the cause why he existed and is called the Son of God, whether you look at his divine or his human nature. For the truth of the name imposed is proved and demonstrated not from causes alone but also from other arguments, as is clear from that very disputation of Christ with the Jews. For he demonstrates that he is the true Son of God and the true and eternal God not from sanctification and mission alone, but also, and indeed chiefly,

units.la: ex operibus diuinis tanquam certissimis deitatis argumentis,ab effectu proprio desumptis se verum Dei filium, & verum æternúmque Deum esse demonstrat, vt ex versu trigesimo septimo, & trigesimo octauo eiusdem capitis liquidò constat, quæ tamen operum diuinorum patratio,nec filiationis, (vt ita loquar) nec ipsius deitatis Christi causa,sed vtriusque effectus, index, & certissimum est τεκμήριον. Ad argumentum autem ipsum quantum concernit,vtraque assumptio est falsa. Non enim propter illam sanctificationem aut missionem sibi ipsi Filii Dei nomen imponit, sed illis argumentis se verum Dei filium esse demonstrat, sic vt si maximè inde quoque nominis illius rationem desumi concedatur, illa tamen nec prima fit, nec sola, nec etiam præcipua. Non enim quæ sui rei ipsius veritatem demonstrant aut declarant, nominis propter ea impositi causa existunt. Christus enim etiam per resurrectionem ex mortuis filius Dei declaratus esse dicitur Roman. capite primo, versu quarto: cùm tamen iam ante mortem,filius Dei re & nomine, non autem propter resurrectionem illo nomine indigitatus fuerit. Et Christum naturæ diuinæ respectu filium Dei esse propterea, quòd ab æterno genitus fit à Patre, iam supra capite 9. demonstrauimus: naturæ verò humanæ respectu, filiationis causam esse primam ac propriam, præter vnionis gratiam, sanctificationem, non quidem illam, qua à Spiritu sancto in Prophetam, Sacerdotem, & Regem vnctus est, sed eam qua peculiari ac singulari ratione & modo in vtero Virginis conceptus, & ex ea genitus, ac proinde purissimus, nullaque peccati originalis impuritate, labe & contagione infectus fuit, ipse Angelus Domini disertis verbis testatur, Luc.cap.1.versu 35. Spiritus sanctus(inquiens) super veniet in te,&virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi,quapropter & quod nascetur in te sanctum,vocabitur Filius Dei. Deinde falsum est quod in sua assumptione profyllogismi affirmatur, nempe missionem Christi nihil aliud esse,quàm munus ipsius Propheticum,vel officium annuntiādi Euangelii,quia missio à Patre profecta,nihil aliud quàm ordinatio,vocatio, & electio Christi fuit, ad munus mediatorium exequendum,ordinationem autem,vocationem,& electionem aliquod munus,ab ipso munere quàm maximè differre, ipsi etiam pueri norunt. Et locis citatis nihil aliud demonstrari potest, quàm Christum à Deo Patre in Prophetam electum ac missum, & à spiritu sancto in Prophetam,Regem,& Sacerdotem vnctum esse,vnum de aliis ab de argumentatio tota cuanefcit.
units.tr: from the divine works, as most certain marks of deity, drawn from their proper effect, as is plain from verses 37 and 38 of the same chapter. Yet the performance of those divine works is the cause neither of his sonship (if I may so speak) nor of his deity, but is an index and most certain token (τεκμήριον) of each. As far as the argument itself is concerned, both assumptions are false. For it is not on account of that sanctification or mission that he gives himself the name of Son of God; by those arguments he demonstrates that he is the true Son of God. So even if it were granted that the reason for the name is also drawn from these, yet this is neither the first, nor the only, nor even the principal reason. For those things which demonstrate or declare the truth of a thing are not the causes of the name imposed on account of them. Christ is said to be declared Son of God through the resurrection from the dead, Romans 1:4, yet even before his death he was Son of God in reality and by name, and was designated by that name not on account of the resurrection. And that Christ is the Son of God with respect to his divine nature, because he was begotten from eternity by the Father, we have already demonstrated above in chapter 9. With respect to his human nature, the first and proper cause of his sonship is, besides the grace of union, sanctification. This is not the anointing by which he was consecrated by the Holy Spirit as Prophet, Priest and King, but that by which, in a peculiar and singular manner and mode, he was conceived in the womb of the Virgin and born of her, and therefore was most pure, infected by no stain, blemish or contagion of original sin. The Angel of the Lord himself testifies this in plain words, Luke 1:35: "The Holy Spirit," he says, "will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also that which is born holy in you will be called the Son of God." Next, what is asserted in his assumption of the prosyllogism is false, namely that the mission of Christ is nothing other than his prophetic function or the office of proclaiming the gospel. For the mission proceeding from the Father was nothing other than the ordination, calling and election of Christ to execute the mediatorial office, and that ordination, calling and election is some function quite different from the prophetic function itself, as even boys know. From the cited passages nothing can be demonstrated except that Christ was chosen and sent by God the Father as Prophet, and anointed by the Holy Spirit as Prophet, King and Priest; with that one of the other points, the whole argument vanishes.

units.la: Secundò,inquit Oftorrodius, ex iisdem Christi verbis demonstrari, ipsum Christum propter officium Propheticum, Deum etiam non inari posse, & hoc probare conatur duabus rationibus. Primò, quia Christus citauerit illa verba ex Psal. 82. v. 6. vbi Deus dixit, Ego dixi Dij estis, & filii excelsi omnes, & tale extruit argumentum:
units.tr: Secondly, says Ostorrodius, it can be shown from the same words of Christ that Christ himself, on account of the prophetic office, can also be called God; and he tries to prove this by two arguments. First, because Christ quoted those words from Psalm 82:6, where God said "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High," and he constructs such an argument:

units.la: Si illi Dij nominari potuerunt, ad quos tantum factum est Dei sermo, quanto magis igitur ille, Christus, Deus appellari potuit, per quem Deus ipse nobis est loquutus, & què, ad confirmandum ipsius munus, tanta & plane diuina potentia conuestiuit, ut (quemadmodum supra demonstratum est) in forma Dei, & Deo similis fuerit?
units.tr: If those could be called gods to whom only the word of God came, how much more then could that Christ be called God, through whom God himself spoke to us, and whom, to confirm his office, he clothed with so great and plainly divine power that (as has been shown above) he was in the form of God and like God?

units.la: Atqui prius verum est, & liquet ex textu. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true, and is clear from the text. Therefore also the latter.

units.la: Resp. Christum verum Deum esse, & vere etiam Deum appellari non tantum posse sed etiam debere, religiosè & sancte credimus, confitemur, sed negamus, hoc nomen ipsi propter officium vel Propheticum, vel Sacerdotale, vel Regium impositum esse, vel etiam imponi potuisse. Ad argumetum respondemus consequentia esse falsam, primò, quia nititur falsa hypothesi illa (de forma Dei & potentia Christi diuina in antecedentib. prolixè actû est) Iesum Christum videlicet non esse verum illum & æternum Israelis Deum, quę hypothesis cum sit falsa, liquidò constat, à scopo verborum Christi longissimè aberrare Aduersarii argumentatione, quippe qua longè aliud cōcludatur, quàm quod Christus disputatione illa demonstrare instituerat. Christus enim, cōtra Iudæos, æternam suam deitatem argumentis euidentissimis astruere voluit, Ostorrodius vero inde cōcludit, Christum propter officium Propheticum, Deum appellari posse, sed Deum in tempore factum, propter datum nempe ipsi nomen supra omne nomen, hoc est, potestatem, gloriam, atque potentiam diuinam ipsi concessam, vt ipse Aduersarius mentem suam Institutionum capite decimo prolixius explicauit. Non igitur tantum ipsius sanctificationis, secundùm magis & minus, sed etiam naturæ ipsius, personarum, comparatio à Christo instituitur. Deinde falsa est eadem illa consequentia, quia Ostorrodius diuidit membra connunctissima argumentationis Christi, & subdolè omittit argumentum præcipuum, quod Christus ad afferendam deitatem suam aduersus Iudæorum calumnias, vsurpauit & adduxit, operationes nempe diuinas, ipsam naturam diuinam Christi manifestissimè testificantes. Cætera quæ ad labefactandum & diluendum hoc idem argumentum facere possent, breuitatis causa omitto.
units.tr: Reply. We religiously and devoutly believe and confess that Christ is true God, and that he can and indeed ought to be truly called God; but we deny that this name was imposed on him, or could have been imposed, on account of the prophetic, priestly or royal office. We reply to the argument that the consequence is false. First, because it rests on that false hypothesis (discussed at length above, about the form of God and the divine power of Christ), namely that Jesus Christ is not the true and eternal God of Israel. Since this hypothesis is false, it is clear that the adversary's argument wanders far from the aim of Christ's words, since it concludes something quite different from what Christ had set out to demonstrate in that disputation. For Christ, against the Jews, wanted to establish his eternal deity by most evident arguments, whereas Ostorrodius concludes from this that Christ, on account of the prophetic office, can be called God, but a God made in time, namely on account of the name given to him above every name, that is, the power, glory and divine might granted to him, as the adversary himself explains his mind more fully in chapter 10 of his Institutes. Therefore the comparison is instituted by Christ not only of his sanctification according to more and less, but also of his nature and persons. Next, the same consequence is false, because Ostorrodius divides the most closely connected members of Christ's argument, and craftily omits the principal argument which Christ used and adduced to assert his deity against the calumnies of the Jews, namely the divine works, which most manifestly testify to the divine nature of Christ. The other things that could serve to weaken and dissolve this same argument I omit for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Deinde inquit, Iohannem Euangelistam, sine omni dubio, Christum nullam aliam ob causam, quam propter officium ipsius Propheticum, tale nimirum, quale ipsi impositum erat, id est, miranda potentia coeflitum, Dei nomine appellasse, cum inquit Ioh. 1. v. 2. Sermo erat Deus: sic enim verba illa ex textu Graeco vertenda esse, quoniam nomen Deus ibi non subiecti, sed praedicati locum occupet, hoc est, Iohannes non quid Deus, sed quid Verbum fuerit explicare voluerit. Et addit, certum esse, quod Christus Dei filius vel nullam aliam ob causam, vel certe potissimum propter officium ipsius Propheticum, a Iohanne Sermo nominatus fuerit, nempe quia & Deus per ipsum loquutus sit nobis, & quemadmodum per sermonem hominis ipsius voluntas significatur, ita etiam nos homines per Christum voluntatem Dei perceperimus. Eam vero quam Trinitarij de causis illis, ob quas Iohannes Christum Sermonem appellauerit, affirment, nihil nisi meras coniecturas, eaque Philosophicas magis quam Theologicas, ac proinde merito profabulis habendas esse. Denique concludens inquit, Cum igitur propterea quod Propheta fuerit, a Iohanne Sermo appellatus sit, facile inde colligi, ipsum Iohannem propter qualitates muneris Prophetici, Christum nomine illo indigitasse, nempe vt hac ratione excellentiam muneris illius commendaret, & ob oculos omnium poneret.
units.tr: Next he says: John the Evangelist, without any doubt, called Christ God for no other reason than his prophetic office, which was of such a kind as had been laid upon him, that is, on account of the wonderful power of heavenly things, when he says in John 1:2, "The Word was God." For the words must be rendered this way from the Greek text, since the word God there occupies the place of the predicate, not the subject; that is, John meant to explain not what God was but what the Word was. He adds that it is certain that Christ, the Son of God, was named the Word by John for no other reason, or at least chiefly, on account of his prophetic office, namely because God spoke to us through him, and just as a man's will is made known through his speech, so we men perceive the will of God through Christ. But the reasons which the Trinitarians give for John calling Christ the Word are nothing but mere conjectures, and philosophical ones rather than theological, and therefore rightly to be counted as fables. Finally, concluding, he says: Since, then, it is easy to infer from the fact that he was a prophet that John called him the Word, it follows that John, on account of the qualities of the prophetic office, designated Christ by that name, namely so as to commend the excellence of that office and set it before the eyes of all.

units.la: Resp. Duo hic vel imperite, vel ad nectendos captionum laqueos callide confundit Oftorrodius, nempe Christum propter officium Propheticum a Iohanne Dei nomine appellatum esse, & Iohannem cap. 1. verf 2. eundem Christum propter officium Propheticum Sermonem nominasse, quum tamen prius tantum ipsi demonstrandum incumberet, sed quum nulla ratione se enuntiatum illud fulcire posse animaduerteret, illo relicto, ad alterum astute transiliit. Rem ipsam quod attinet, agnoscimus apud Iohannem nomen λόγος subiecti, nomen vero Θεός praedicati locum obtinere: hanc enim constructionem, & seriem orationis, & articulus, denique ipse scopus Euangelistae, veraм & genuinam esse demonstrant: sed negamus Christum a Iohanne propter officium Propheticum, quibuscunque etiam qualitatibus illud coueftitum esse intelligatur, Deum appellatum esse, nec quicquam in medium adferre poterit Aduersarius, quoniam vanam illam interpretationem suam stabiliat. Describit enim ibidi non officium, sed ipsam personam πρὸς τὸν θεόν, & descriptionis argumentationem. menta, non ab ipsius officii mediatorii epithetis, sed ipsius personæ diuinæ proprietatibus, & operationibus desumit. Qui enim in principio erat, id est, ante iacta fundamenta mundi, & ab æterno, ante omne tempus, ante creationem, & res creatas omnes, & erat apud Deum, & Deus erat, denique per quem cælum, terra, & omnia quæ in eis sunt, creata sunt, ille certe non propter officium aliquod certo ac definito tempore ipsi impositum, Deus à Iohanne nominari potuit. Atqui sermo ille, de quo agit Ioannes Euangelista, In principio erat, id est, ante iacta mundi fundamenta, & ab æterno ante omne tempus, ante creationem, & res creatas omnes, quemadmodum nos capite decimotertio demonstrauimus: Et erat apud Deum, & erat Deus, vt ipse Ioannes testatur, Ergo Sermo ille non propter officium Propheticum, à Iohanne Deus est appellatus. Alterum nominationem nimirum quantum concernit, & rationem quare videlicet Filius Dei, id est, Verbi, vel Sermonis nomine à Iohanne fit indigitatus, agnoscimus quidè eum etiam ab effectu illo, quod videlicet ipsam voluntatè Dei nobis reuelaueritac patefecerit, ac proinde etiā ab ipso munere Prophetico desumi: Hæc. n. ratio vera est, & ex ipsis Scripturis sacris hausta: sed negamus eā vel solā esse, vel sufficientem ad tanti mysterii explicationē. Sic enim Filius Dei accidentarius tantùm, non autem essentialis, & absolutus Patris sermo constitueretur, quod est falsum. Quòd verò Oftorrodius illa omnia, quæ à doctissimis & antiquissimis Patribus, & aliis exquisitissimæ eruditionis, & doctrina admirabili clarissimis viris de causis & ratione nominis illius in medium sunt prolata, non tantùm falsitatis accusare, sed etiam in fabularum inanium numerum referre non erubescit, eo ipso certè summam, & petulantem, impotentis & ægrotātis animi immodestiam prodit, præsertim cùm boni & sancti illi viri, illas explicationes, non vt olim Sybillæ folia, obtrudere conati sint, sed tanquam meditationes, & explicationes priuatas Ecclesiæ iudicio candidè, & modestè subiecerint: eandem igitur modestiam in Aduersario desidero, temerariam illam audaciam abominor: & sic ipsa quoque conclusio evanescit.
units.tr: Reply. Here Ostorrodius confuses two things, either unskilfully or cleverly, to set snares of deception: namely, that Christ was called God by John because of his prophetic office, and that John, in chapter 1 verse 2, called the same Christ the Word because of his prophetic office. Yet he had only to demonstrate the first, and when he saw that he could not support his assertion by any argument, he left that aside and cleverly leapt to the other. As to the matter itself, we acknowledge that in John the word Logos [λόγος] is the subject and the word Theos [Θεός] holds the place of the predicate; for this construction, the sequence of the sentence, the article, and finally the very purpose of the Evangelist show that this is the true and genuine reading. But we deny that Christ was called God by John because of his prophetic office, whatever qualities that office may be understood to have had, and the Adversary can bring forward nothing to support that empty interpretation of his. For in the same place John does not take the description from the epithets of the mediatorial office, but from the properties and operations of the divine person himself. For he who was in the beginning, that is, before the foundations of the world were laid, and from eternity, before all time, before creation and all created things, and was with God [πρὸς τὸν θεόν], and was God, and through whom heaven, earth and all that is in them were created, certainly could not be called God by John on account of some office laid upon him at a certain and defined time. But that Word of whom the Evangelist John speaks was in the beginning, that is, before the foundations of the world were laid, and from eternity before all time, before creation and all created things, as we demonstrated in chapter thirteen; and was with God, and was God, as John himself testifies. Therefore that Word was not called God by John because of the prophetic office. As far as the naming is concerned, and the reason why he is designated by John as the Son of God, that is, the Word or Speech, we grant that he was so named also from that effect, namely that he revealed and made known to us the will of God, and therefore also from the prophetic office itself. For this reason is true and drawn from the holy Scriptures themselves; but we deny that it is the only reason, or a sufficient one, for the explanation of so great a mystery. For in that case the Son of God would be constituted as only an accidental, and not an essential and absolute, Word of the Father, which is false. But that Ostorrodius is not ashamed not only to accuse of falsehood all those things which the most learned and most ancient Fathers, and other men of most exquisite learning and admirable doctrine, have brought forward concerning the causes and reason of that name, but even to count them among empty fables, this surely reveals a supreme and wanton immodesty of an impotent and sick mind, especially since those good and holy men did not try to force those explanations upon us like the leaves of the Sibyl, but submitted them frankly and modestly to the judgment of the Church as private meditations and explanations. I therefore desire the same modesty in the Adversary, and abhor that rash audacity; and thus his conclusion too vanishes.

units.la: Tertiò explicat Oftorrodius, quanam in re officium illud Christi Propheticum consistat, & quare Deus eiusmodi Prophetam nobis dederit, atque excitauerit, cuius rei hanc adfert rationem, quod nempe Deus, cùm absque reuelatione diuina, decretum, & voluntas Dei, de omnibus illis, qui vere, & ex animo resipiscunt, ex mortuis refuscitan- dis atque saluandis, scitu tamen necessaria, nobis innotescere non po- tuerit, Filium suum Iesum Christum, in hunc mundum miserit, vt nobis decretum illud, & voluntatem Dei Patris, reuelaret, vt ex Ioh. 1. vers. 18. liquido constat. Quibus verbis Ostorrodius verum quidem finem vnctionis, & vocationis Christi, ad munus Propheticum indicat, sic tamen, vt sub flexiloquis verborum ambagibus, maximi illius erroris, quo meritum mortis Christi impugnatur, venenum clam semper inspergat, de quo in sequentibus nobis erit agendum.
units.tr: Thirdly, Ostorrodius explains in what the prophetic office of Christ consists, and why God has given and raised up such a Prophet to us, and of this he gives this reason: namely that God, since, without divine revelation, the decree and will of God concerning all those who truly and from the heart repent, concerning their raising from the dead and their salvation, which is nevertheless necessary to know, could not become known to us, sent his Son Jesus Christ into this world, so that he might reveal to us that decree and the will of God the Father, as is clear from John 1:18. In these words Ostorrodius indicates the true purpose of Christ's anointing and calling to the prophetic office; yet in such a way that, under the winding circumlocutions of his words, he always secretly sprinkles the poison of that greatest error, by which the merit of Christ's death is assailed, which we shall have to treat in what follows.

units.la: Atque hanc ipsam causam esse dicit, quare videlicet Filius Dei in Scripturis imago Dei inconspicui 2. Cor. ver. 4. Col. 5. ver. 15. Splendor gloriæ, & Character personæ ipsius Heb. 1. vers. 3. dicatur, nempe, quia ille Deum inuisibilem, hoc est, voluntatem, & potentiam (nam essentiam diuinam hominibus ostendere, vt impossibile, ita etiam consiliy diuini respectu, plane inutile foret) quantum videlicet cognitio eius ad salutem scitu necessaria est, visibiliter monstrauerit. Hinc etiam esse addit, quod Christus dixit, Qui conspicit me, conspicit eum, qui misit me, id est Deum, Ioh. 12. v. 45. Hoc enim, nempe conspicere Deum de intuitu voluntatis diuinæ, non autem essentiæ Dei, quam nullus hominum videre potest 1. Tim. 6. v. 16. ex sequentibus manifestum esse ait, præsertim vero ex v. 45. 49. Hinc denique progreditur ad refutationem sententiæ illorum, qui ex illis Scripturæ dictis, in quibus, qui Christum viderunt, etiam Patrem vidisse dicuntur, eundem Christum Dei Filium, eiusdem cum Deo Patre essentiæ, esse, demonstrare conantur, quam sententiam multis absurdis grauare studet.
units.tr: And he says that this very cause is why the Son of God is called in the Scriptures the image of the invisible God (2 Cor. 4; Col. 1:15), the brightness of glory, and the express image of his person (Heb. 1:3); namely, because he made visible the invisible God, that is, his will and power (for to show men the divine essence would, as it is impossible, so also with respect to the divine counsel be altogether useless), as far as the knowledge of him is necessary to salvation. From this, he adds, comes also what Christ said: He who sees me sees him who sent me, that is God (John 12:45). For this, namely to see God, concerns the regard of the divine will and not the essence of God, which no man can see (1 Tim. 6:16); this is clear from what follows, especially from verses 45 and 49, he says. Finally, he proceeds from this to refute the opinion of those who try to demonstrate, from those sayings of Scripture in which those who saw Christ are also said to have seen the Father, that this same Christ, the Son of God, is of the same essence as God the Father; an opinion which he labours to burden with many absurdities.

units.la: Resp. Quum vox imaginis Dei, etiam cum de Christo prædicatur, sit πολύσημος & æquiuoca, ideo homonymiam illam prius tollii oportet, priusquam explicare possimus commodè, quare videlicet, & quo sensu, Christus ab Apostolo, nomine illo indigitetur. Vt enim Christi considerandi triplex est ratio, vel secundum naturam diuinam, & qua Deus est, vel secundum naturam humanam, & qua homo est, vel denique secundum œconomiam ac dispesationem voluntariam, & qua Θεάνθρωπος, ac Mediator est: ita quoque imago Dei, in sacris literis, triplici respectu, de illo prædicatur, vt Deo videlicet, & secundum naturam diuinam ipsius: deinde vt homini, & secundum naturam humanam ipsius: denique vt Θεανθρώπῳ aos Mediatore, & secundum voluntariam illam œconomiam, ac dispensationem. Diuinæ naturæ respectu, character, & imago Dei, Patris essentialis, perfecta, coæterna, & consubstantialis, quia cum Patre eiusdem essentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis, à Patre per generationem æternam sibi communicatæ est particeps. Hæc imago simpliciter de ipsa essentia, seu diuina natura Filii Dei prædicatur, & relationem non ad nos, sed ad Deum Patrem habet, unde essentialis imago à Theologis nuncupatur. Quanquam accuratè loquendo Christo diuinæ naturæ respectu, imaginis appellatio, non abssq; κατ' ἐχνῶσιν aliqua tribuatur. Cum illa proprie sùpta, distinguatur à re, cuius est imago, tum fundamenti, tum extremorum respectu: Christus autem à Patre hypostasi quidem differat, in essentia verò siue fundamento summa sit vnitas, atque adeò τωύτης. Humanæ naturæ respectu, Christus imago Dei dicitur, non quidem essentialis, seu propter essentiæ similitudinem, & æqualitatem, sed per gratiam conceptionis è Spiritu Sancto, & vnionis cum λόγω, quæ creata quidem est, sed gradibus, & numero, donorum sapientia, iustitia, potentia, & gloria omnibus Angelis, & hominibus in immensum antecellens. Atque hæc imago, quia cum ipsa natura humana Christi originem suam habuit, imago Dei naturalis dici potest. Respectu muneris Mediatorii, & qua προφήτης, ac Mediator, id est, Propheta, Sacerdos, ac Rex noster est, imago Dei dicitur per gloriam virtutis (vt loquitur Irenæus) quam Diuus Paulus Hebr. 1. v. 3. ἀπαύγασμα καὶ χαρακτὴρ videlicet Dei Patris appellat, quia videlicet in Christo Mediatore ac διαδρώτης operum diuinorum virtus, splendor, & excellentia ita refulget, vt in ipso, ceu lucidissimo speculo, Patris cœlestis potentia gloriosa, voluntas paterna, misericordia, & φιλανθρωπία, erga genus humanum summa, & πολυτρόπως illa σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ contemplanda nobis proponitur. Quum igitur Christus imago Dei inconspicui dicitur, non imaginem essentialem, seu, quæ de ipsa essentia directè prædicatur, sed eam, quæ per gloriam virtutis conspicitur, intelligendam esse, iudicant doctissimi quidam Interpretes, quorum sententiæ hac in re libentissimè subscribo, quoniam illa cum ipso epistolæ illius scopo verissimè conuenit. Hinc tamen æterna Christi Deitas nihilominus euidentissimè demonstratur, quia virtutis similitudo (vt inquit Hilarius) non potest esse dissimilis ipsi naturæ, & perfecta Dei sapientia, bonitate, iustitia, misericordia, & potentia representandis, nulla creatura sufficeret. Quantum autem ad verba Christi, quæ habentur, Ioh. 12. verf. 45. attinet, verissimum est, non de Physico aliquo aspectu corporis,& intuitu, sed de iustitiæ, misericordiæ, potentiæ,ac gloriæ diuinæ in Christo crucifixo, & ad dexteram gloriæ diuinæ euecto,nobis exhibitę,cognitione spirituali,& contemplatione,quę per fidem est,illa intelligeda esse, Deum enim nemo vidit vnquam,sed Filius vnigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris,enarrauit nobis,nempe consilium & voluntatem ipsius Ioh.1. ver.18.qui habitat lucem inaccessam, quam nullus hominum vidit,nec videre potest. 1 Tim.6 verf.16.quod ipsum de essentia diuina,& omnibus eius attributis est intelligendum. Atque vt opera creationis, quæ omnia,& singula,etiam minutissima diuinitatis euidentissima vestigia in se complectuntur,non ipsam diuinitatem, potentiam neque Dei,bonitatem , ac sapientiam in se oculis corporis nostri concipiendam præbent,sed animos nostros sursum ad ipsum autorem extollunt, nobisque occasionem, & amplissimam materiam præbent,altiori mentis indagine,illam bonitatem, ac potentiam considerandi , ita etiam per opera redemptionis à Christo facta infinita Dei misericordia,bonitas,ac φιλανθρωπία, in Christo videlicet crucifixo,& glorificato,oculis animi,per fidem cōtemplanda, & conspicienda, proponitur , Commendat enim suam erga nos charitatem Deus,quod,cum adhuc essemus peccatores,Christus pro nobis mortuus sit. Rom.5.ver.8. &,Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum daret,Ioh.3 ver.16.De cognitione ergo, & visione, quæ per fidem est, Christus loquitur, quibus tamen verbis, euidentissimum nobis suppeditatur argumentum , ad diuinam Christi naturam astruendam, cum perfecta Dei sapientia, misericordia, & bonitate repræsentandis nulla creatura (vt iam diximus ) sufficere posset. Atque hæc ipsa mens est Theologorum nostrorum,qui ex illo dicto,Christum eiusdem cum Deo Patre essentiæ esse , demonstrare conati sunt, vt acrem verberent illa absurdorum tela , quæ in nos iaculatur Ostorrodius. Qui aliter sentiunt,& docent, Deúmque in ipso corpore Christi, vere & physicè conspici posse, existimant, illi viderint, quomodo se ex Anthropomorphitarum crassissimo errore,& ab Aduersario obiectorum absurdorū tricis expediant.
units.tr: Reply. Since the word "image of God," even when it is predicated of Christ, is polysemous and equivocal [πολύσημος], we must first remove this ambiguity before we can conveniently explain why and in what sense the Apostle designates Christ by that name. For just as Christ may be considered in three ways, either according to his divine nature, by which he is God, or according to his human nature, by which he is man, or finally according to the voluntary economy and dispensation, by which he is the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος] and Mediator, so too the image of God is predicated of him in the Scriptures in three respects: first in relation to God, and according to his divine nature; then in relation to man, and according to his human nature; and finally in relation to the God-man, that is, the Mediator, and according to that voluntary economy and dispensation.
