In respect of the divine nature, Christ is the essential, perfect, coeternal and consubstantial character and image of the Father, because, being of the same essence, glory and majesty as the Father, he is a partaker of what has been communicated to him by the Father through eternal generation. This image is predicated simply of the essence itself, or the divine nature of the Son of God, and it has a relation not to us but to God the Father; for this reason theologians call it the essential image. Yet, speaking strictly, the title of image is given to Christ in respect of the divine nature not without some catachresis [κατ' ἐχνῶσιν]. For the image, taken properly, is distinguished from the thing of which it is the image, both with respect to its ground and with respect to its extremes; but Christ differs from the Father indeed in hypostasis, yet in essence, or ground, there is the highest unity, and therefore identity [τωύτης]. In respect of the human nature, Christ is called the image of God, not indeed essentially, that is, on account of likeness and equality of essence, but by the grace of his conception from the Holy Spirit and his union with the Word [λόγω]. This human nature is indeed created, but it surpasses all angels and men immeasurably in degrees and number of gifts: wisdom, righteousness, power and glory. And since this image had its origin together with the human nature of Christ itself, it may be called the natural image of God. In respect of the office of Mediator, and as he is Prophet [προφήτης] and Mediator, that is, our Prophet, Priest and King, he is called the image of God through the glory of virtue (as Irenaeus says), which the divine Paul calls the brightness and express image [ἀπαύγασμα καὶ χαρακτὴρ] of God the Father (Heb. 1:3). This is because in Christ the Mediator and executor [διαδρώτης] of the divine works, the virtue, splendour and excellence of God shine forth in such a way that in him, as in a most bright mirror, the glorious power of the heavenly Father, the paternal will, mercy, and the highest love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία] toward the human race, and that wisdom of God which is manifold in its ways [πολυτρόπως σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ], are set before us to be contemplated. Therefore, when Christ is said to be the image of the invisible God, certain most learned interpreters judge that we must understand not the essential image, that is, what is predicated directly of the essence itself, but the image which is seen through the glory of virtue. I most gladly subscribe to their opinion in this matter, since it agrees most truly with the very purpose of that epistle. Yet from this the eternal Deity of Christ is nonetheless most evidently demonstrated; for, as Hilary says, the likeness of virtue cannot be unlike the nature itself, and no creature would be sufficient to represent the perfect wisdom, goodness, righteousness, mercy and power of God. As for the words of Christ in John 12:45, it is most true that they must be understood not of some physical aspect or sight of the body, but of a spiritual knowledge and contemplation, which is through faith, of the righteousness, mercy, power and divine glory exhibited to us in Christ crucified and exalted to the right hand of divine glory. For no one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him to us, namely his counsel and will (John 1:18); who dwells in light unapproachable, which no man has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6:16), which itself must be understood of the divine essence and all its attributes. And just as the works of creation, which all and each, even the smallest, contain within themselves the most evident traces of divinity, do not present to the eyes of our body the Deity itself, the power of God or the goodness and wisdom of God, but raise our minds upward to the author himself, and give us the occasion and very ample matter for considering that goodness and power by a deeper inquiry of the mind; so also through the works of redemption accomplished by Christ, the infinite mercy, goodness and love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία] of God is set forth in Christ crucified and glorified, to be contemplated and beheld by the eyes of the mind through faith. For God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8); and God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son (John 3:16). Christ therefore speaks of knowledge and sight which is through faith; and yet in these words there is supplied to us a most evident argument for establishing the divine nature of Christ, since no creature (as we have already said) could suffice to represent the perfect wisdom, mercy and goodness of God. This is indeed the very mind of our theologians, who have tried to demonstrate from that saying that Christ is of the same essence as God the Father, so that they might hurl back those absurd darts which Ostorodius casts at us. As for those who think otherwise and teach otherwise, and who suppose that God can be seen truly and physically in the very body of Christ, let them see for themselves how they may extricate themselves from the most gross error of the Anthropomorphites and from the tangles of absurdities objected by our opponent.

units.la: Quoniam vero Aduersarius ab initio capitis vigesimi,functionem muneris Prophetici, reuelatione diuinæ voluntatis definiuit (quæ tamen definitio,aut imperfecta est, nisi videlicet etiam illa reuelatio intelligatur , quæ fit per illuminationem Spiritus sancti internam : aut ambiguitate ludit) ideo sectione quinta pergit, & voluntatis diuinae cognitionem in duobus illis capitibus posi-tam esse docet, nempe primo quidnam Deus nobis per Christum promiserit, secundo quidnam per eundem nobis mandauerit, quae sigillatim capitibus sequentibus persequitur. Quae vero sub finem subiunguntur falsa enthymemata, & in loco de Libero Arbitrio examinabuntur.
units.tr: But since our opponent, at the beginning of the twentieth chapter, defined the function of the prophetic office as the revelation of the divine will (a definition which is either imperfect, unless it is understood to include also that revelation which takes place through the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, or else it plays on an ambiguity), therefore in the fifth section he goes on and teaches that the knowledge of the divine will is contained in those two chapters, namely: first, what God has promised us through Christ; second, what he has commanded us through the same. These he pursues point by point in the following chapters. As for the false enthymemes which are added toward the end, they will be examined in the place about free will.

units.la: CAPVT XXIV. De promissionibus diuinis, & vita aeterna: vbi simul explicatur quaestio illa controuersa, An videlicet promissiones Dei, in Veteri Testamento, tantum temporales, an vero etiam Spirituales, fuerint.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. On the divine promises and eternal life, where at the same time the controverted question is explained: whether the promises of God in the Old Testament were merely temporal or were also spiritual.

units.la: STORRODIVS itaque primam cognitionis illius partem, quae est de promissionibus diuinis explicaturus, capite vigesimo primo, quatuor illas theses proponit: primo, Deum nobis per Christum vitam aeternam promisisse: secundo, vitam aeternam, & remissionem peccatorum, vnum ac idem, non autem res diuersas esse: tertio praedicationem Euangelii solam, posse hominem absque interna Spiritus Sancti illuminatione, & operatione, a peccatis converti, sic vt homo etiam proprij arbitrij viribus aliquid boni praestare queat: quarto promissiones Veteris Testamenti tantum corporales fuisse, spiritualibus in Nouo demum Testamento promulgatis: quas ille ordine explicat, & demonstrare conatur.
units.tr: Storrodius, then, intending to explain the first part of that knowledge, which concerns the divine promises, sets out in his twenty-first chapter four theses: first, that God has promised eternal life to us through Christ; second, that eternal life and the remission of sins are one and the same, and not different things; third, that the preaching of the Gospel alone, without the inward illumination and operation of the Holy Spirit, can convert a man from sins, so that a man may by the powers of his own free will accomplish something good; fourth, that the promises of the Old Testament were merely bodily, spiritual promises being published only in the New Testament. He explains these in order and tries to demonstrate them.

units.la: Quaestio prima extra controuersiae aleam est constituta, secundam quod attinet, vt ad illam solide responderi possit, ante omnia, quid vitae aeternae nomine significetur, nobis est explicandum. Vita igitur aeterna duobus modis dicitur, vna absoluta, in se & essentialis, quae est creaturae viuentis secundum essentiam in se: altera quae consideratur secundum affectionem, creaturæ viuentis ad principium æternum vitæ, Deum, qui propterea etiam μετωνυμικῶς in Scripturis vita æterna appellatur. Secundum vitam illam essentialem, qua creaturæ viuunt in sese, omnes tam mali quam boni, æternum victuri sunt, quia vitam illam æternam, omnes ab uno principio habent, prout inde à creatione mundi, imaginem illius impressam habuerunt: at de hac non instituitur præsens disputatio. Secundum alterum vero modum, quem in habitu, & affectione esse indicauimus, siue relatione ad Deum, qui, vt anima corporis vita, ita animæ ipsius anima est, ac vita, adeoque principium æternum æternæ vitæ, pii tantummodo victuri sunt in Christo Iesu, quæ proinde de piis prædicata, κατ' ἐξοχὴν vita æterna dicitur, quia tum vitam illam essentialem in sese habent, tum vitam illam in Christo, communicatione gratiæ. Hæc autem vita æterna quemadmodum non uno momento, sed per certos gradus, atque progressus in nobis perficitur: ita etiam modo initium illius futuræ, hoc est, sensum illum fauoris Dei, significat, ex remissione peccatorum, & sanctificationis dono perceptum, sed languidum adhuc, & qui denum in altera vita plene vigebit, & perficietur, interdum vero denotat statum hominum electorum beatissimum, in altero seculo, & plenum fauoris diuini sensum, cum excellentia glorię cœlestis coniunctum. Prioris significationis exempla sunt hæc, Ioh. 5. v. 25. Veniet tempus, & nunc est, quum mortui audient vocem Filii Dei, & qui audierint viuent: Ioh. 6. v. 47. Amen Amen dico vobis, qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam: & v. 52. 54. Nisi comederitis carnem Filii hominis, & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Qui edit carnem meam, & bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam æternam. Posterioris significationis exempla sunt ista Matth. 25. v. vlt. Et abibunt isti in supplicium æternum, iusti vero in vitam æternam. Rom. 2. v. 6. 7. Deus reddet vnicuique secundum opera ipsius: iis quidem, qui per tolerantiam operis boni, gloriam & honorem, & immortalitatem quærunt, vitam æternam: & alibi passim. Prior significatio vera quidè est, sed impropria, ac tropica, quia initium tantum, & primum quasi gradum declarat vitæ illius futuræ, & æternæ felicitatis, qua non nisi glorificatis corporibus nostris, & abstersis omnibus lachrymis ab oculis nostris, & restaurata in nobis perfecte imagine Dei, perfruemur. Posterior & vera, & propria est, qua significatione vitam æternam intelle-ctam, sic describere possumus, quod sit status hominum electorum beatifbeatissimus, in altero seculo, in æternum, duraturus, per quem illi in cœlum recepti, & apud Christū, sanctosque Angelos degentes, ab omnibus miseriis liberi, fruetur perfecto gaudio, & pleno sensu fauoris illius, itemq. perfecta gloria, tum ex sanctitate animarum, tum ex claritate corporū, & perfecta imaginis Dei restauratione. Huius definitionis singulæ partes ex ipsa Scriptura sacra demonstrantur, vide Ioh. 17. verf. 24. & 24. verf. 2. 3. 1. Thess. 4. verf. 17. Phil. 3. verf. 23. Heb. 10. verf. 19. Luc. 23. verf. 43. Luc. 16. verf. 22. Apoc. 21. verf. 4. 1. Cor. 13. verf. 9. 10. 12. 1. Ioh. 3. verf. 2. Apoc. 22. verf. 4. Psal. 17. verf. vlt. & 16. verf. 11. Matth. 8. ver. 11. Apocal. 21. verf. 3. & 19. ver. 9. 1. Cor. 15. ver. 42. Phil. 3. verf. vlt. Dan. 12. verf. 3. Matth. 13. ver. 43.
units.tr: The first question is beyond dispute. As for the second, so that a solid answer can be given to it, we must first explain what is meant by the name eternal life. Eternal life is spoken of in two ways. One is absolute, in itself and essential, which belongs to a living creature according to its essence in itself. The other is considered according to the disposition of the living creature toward the eternal principle of life, God, who is therefore also called eternal life in the Scriptures by metonymy [μετωνυμικῶς]. All men, both evil and good, are destined to live forever according to that essential life by which creatures live in themselves, since all have that eternal life from one principle, having borne its image impressed upon them from the creation of the world. But the present disputation is not concerned with this. According to the other meaning, which we have shown to lie in the habit and disposition, or relation to God, who is to the soul what the soul is to the body, and is the soul and life of the soul itself, and so the eternal principle of eternal life, only the godly will live in Christ Jesus. This is therefore predicated of the godly and is called eternal life pre-eminently [κατ' ἐξοχήν], because they have both that essential life in themselves and that life in Christ through the communication of grace. Now this eternal life is brought to completion in us not in a single moment but by certain degrees and progressions. Thus it signifies at first the beginning of that future life, that is, the sense of God's favour, received from the remission of sins and the gift of sanctification, but as yet feeble, and which will at last flourish and be perfected fully in the other life. Sometimes, however, it denotes the most blessed state of the elect men in the next age, and a full sense of the divine favour joined with the excellence of heavenly glory. Examples of the former meaning are these: John 5:25, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and they that hear shall live; John 6:47, Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life; and vv. 52, 54, Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood hath eternal life. Examples of the latter meaning are Matthew 25:46, And these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal; and Romans 2:6-7, God will render to every man according to his deeds: to them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life; and elsewhere throughout. The former meaning is indeed true, but improper and tropical, since it declares only the beginning, as it were the first step, of that future life and eternal happiness, which we shall enjoy only when our bodies are glorified, all tears are wiped from our eyes, and the image of God is perfectly restored in us. The latter meaning is both true and proper, and in this sense we can describe eternal life as the state of the most blessed elect in the other age, lasting forever, by which they, received into heaven and dwelling with Christ and the holy angels, free from all miseries, enjoy perfect joy and a full sense of that favour, and likewise perfect glory, both from the holiness of their souls and from the brightness of their bodies and the perfect restoration of the image of God. Each part of this definition is demonstrated from Holy Scripture itself: see John 17:24; 1 John 3:2 (cf. John 17:2-3); 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 10:19; Luke 23:43; Luke 16:22; Revelation 21:4; 1 Corinthians 13:9-10, 12; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4; Psalm 17:15; Psalm 16:11; Matthew 8:11; Revelation 21:3 and 19:9; 1 Corinthians 15:42; Philippians 3:21; Daniel 12:3; Matthew 13:43.

units.la: Ex hisce omnibus manifeste iam liquet, remissionem peccatorum, non esse unum ac idem quod vita externa, siue priore, siue posteriore significatione hæc intelligatur. Si enim posteriori significatu, vitæ æternæ vocabulum accipiatur, pro sensu videlicet fauoris Dei, tum remissio peccatorum, ab illa tanquam causa abeffectu differt, quum non sit ipsemet sensus, sed eius causa efficiens, ac procreans. Si vero posteriore sensu accipiatur, tum tanto magis differt remissio peccatorum à vita æterna, quanto plures causæ ad huius perfectionem, & complementum, quàm initium eius requiruntur, quas nos in definitione recensuimus. Quamuis igitur per remissionem peccatorum ipsa mors æterna auferatur, & cohibeatur à fidelibus, quod ipsum vrget Aduersarius, minimè tamen inde sequitur, remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam plane vnum ac idem esse, cum illi huius definitio ex Scripturis sacris collecta, nullatenus competere possit, licet hæc illam, necessario quidem, sed tamen non immediatè, verum aliarum etiam causarum, vt sanctificationis, resurrectionis, & glorificationis interuentu, consequatur. Quos enim Deus prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit, quos vero vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit, quos autem iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit, Rom. 8. verf. 30. Et quemadmodum reatus, qui opponitur remissioni peccatorum, non ipsa damnatio æterna est, sed damnationis causa, nisi gratia Dei conferatur, ita quoque, remisssio peccatorum, non ipsa vita æterna est, sed medium, & causa cum aliis eandem efficiens.
units.tr: From all these things it is now plainly clear that the remission of sins is not one and the same as eternal life, whichever meaning of the latter is understood. If the word eternal life is taken in the latter sense, namely for the sense of God's favour, then the remission of sins differs from it as cause from effect, since it is not the sense itself but its efficient and producing cause. If it is taken in the latter sense, then the remission of sins differs from eternal life all the more, in that more causes are required for its perfection and completion than for its beginning, and we have listed these in the definition. Although, then, through the remission of sins eternal death itself is taken away and restrained from believers, which is the very point the Adversary presses, it does not at all follow that the remission of sins and eternal life are altogether one and the same. The definition of eternal life, gathered from the Holy Scriptures, cannot apply to the remission of sins in any way, even though the remission necessarily results in eternal life, but not immediately; it results through the intervention of other causes as well, such as sanctification, resurrection and glorification. For whom he did predestinate, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified (Romans 8:30). And just as guilt, which is opposed to the remission of sins, is not eternal damnation itself but the cause of damnation, unless the grace of God is granted, so also the remission of sins is not eternal life itself but a means and a cause which, together with the others, produces the same.

units.la: Quæstionem, seu thesin tertiam infrà in loco de Libero Arbitrio examinabimus: quartam, & vltimam, promissiones videlicet Veteris Testamenti temporales tantummodo fuisse, spirituales vero in nouo demum testamento, & quidem per Christum, ex Virgine Maria natum, primo omnium promulgatas esse, repudiamus, & ex ipsa Scriptura sacra Populum Israeliticum sub Veteri Testamento, eiusdem nobiscum foederis socium, eorundemque bonorum, & promissionum spiritualium consortem fuisse, non quidem omnibus, quae ex illa adduci possent, sed paucis tantum, argumentis, demonstrabimus.
units.tr: We will examine the third question or thesis below, in the place on free will. The fourth and last, namely that the promises of the Old Testament were merely temporal and bodily, while spiritual promises were first published in the New Testament, and indeed through Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, we reject. And we will demonstrate from Holy Scripture itself that the Israelite people under the Old Testament were partners in the same covenant with us and sharers in the same good things and spiritual promises. We will do this not with all the arguments that could be drawn from it, but with a few only.

units.la: Argumentum primum: desumitur ab ipsius foederis forma, seu lege, & utraque eius parte, tam Dei, quàm hominum respectu. Sic enim semper cum Patribus in Veteri Testamento pepigit Dominus, Ero vobis in Deum, & vos mihi eritis in populum, Leu. 26. v.12. quae ipsa formula ad promissiones Noui Testamenti à Paulo accomodatur, 2. Cor. 6. v.16. 17.18. quae consensio Templo Dei cum simulacris? nam vos templum estis Dei viuentis sicut dixit Deus. Habitabo in eis & inambulabo, & ero illorum Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Quapropter exite è medio illorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus, & impurum ne attingite, hinc ego excipiam vos: & ero vobis pro patre, & vos eritis mihi pro filiis, ac filiabus dicit Dominus omnipotens. Deum autem habere propitium totius felicitatis caput est, unde etiam Dauid beatum pronunciat populum, cuius Dominus est Deus, Psalm. 144. v.15. & beatam gentem, quam in hereditatem sibi elegit. Psal. 33. v.12. Veram autem beatitudinem idem Propheta Dauid, non in terrena aliqua felicitate, sed remissione peccatorum, & gratuita iustitiae imputatione, quae donum Dei est, non corporale, sed spirituale, collocat, Psal. 32. v.12 Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtectae sunt peccata, Beatus vir cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. Quum igitur populo Israelitico, certissimas, de remissione peccatorum, promissiones factas esse constet, & Aduersarius ipse, remissionem peccatorum, & vitam aeternam, vnum, ac idem non autem res diuersas, esse, doceat, ideo non tantum ex sacris literis, sed ipsa etiam Aduersarii hypothesi, promissiones in Veteri Testamento, non temporales tantum, & corporales, sed etiam spirituales, ac aeternas, & Iudaeis non carnalem opulentiam, ac felicitatem, metam propositam, fuisse, ad quam aspirarent, sed eosdem per diuinas vitae aeternae promissiones, in spem immortalitatis fuisse cooptatos, manifeste sequitur.
units.tr: First argument: it is drawn from the very form of the covenant, or its law, and from both parts of it, with respect to both God and men. For the Lord always made his covenant in this way with the fathers in the Old Testament: I will be your God, and you shall be my people (Leviticus 26:12). This very formula is applied by Paul to the promises of the New Testament, 2 Corinthians 6:16-18: And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? For ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, and will be a father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty. Now to have God propitious is the head of all happiness; hence David also pronounces blessed the people whose God is the Lord (Psalm 144:15), and the nation that he chose for his inheritance (Psalm 33:12). But the same prophet David places true blessedness not in any earthly happiness but in the remission of sins and the free imputation of righteousness, which is a gift of God, not bodily but spiritual: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin (Psalm 32:1-2). Since it is therefore certain that the most assured promises of the remission of sins were made to the Israelite people, and since the Adversary himself teaches that the remission of sins and eternal life are one and the same and not different things, it clearly follows, not only from the sacred letters but also from the Adversary's own hypothesis, that the promises in the Old Testament were not merely temporal and bodily but also spiritual and eternal; and that the goal set before the Jews was not carnal wealth and prosperity to aspire to, but that they were enlisted through the divine promises of eternal life into the hope of immortality.

units.la: Argumentum secundum, desumitur à testimoniis Christi, & Apostolorum, Ioh. 5. v. 46. Si crederetis Mosi, crederetis mihi: de me enim ille ille scripsit. Act.10.v. 43. Huic testimonium dant omnes Prophetæ, re-missionem peccatorum accepturum, per nomen eius, quicumque credide-rit in eum. Rom. 10. ver.16. Sed non omnes auscultarunt Euangelio: Esaias enim dicit, Domine quis credidit sermoni nostro? aut igitur per sermonem illum, quem Esaias prædicauit, intelligitur Euange-lium, aut male locus ille ab Apostolo allegatur, quod est absurdū. 1.Pet. 1. ver.10. De qua salute inquisierunt, & scrutati sunt Prophetæ Rom.1. ver.2. Quod (Euangelium) ante promiserat per Prophetas, in Scripturis sanctis. Et cap.3. versi. 21.22. Nunc vero absque lege, iustitia Dei patefaćta est, comprobata testimonio Legis, ac Prophetarum, iustitia inquam Dei, per fidē Iesu Christi, in omnes & super omnes qui credunt. Quicquid insuper Paulus (& per consequens cæteri quoq; Apostoli) dixit & prædicauit, illud Prophetæ & Moses prædixerunt, Act.26.v.22. Sed auxilium à Deo natus, perstitit in hunc usque diem, testificans tum paruis, tum magnis, nec quicquam dicens extra ea, quæ Prophetæ, ac Moses, futura prædixerunt. Paulum autem, non de rebus corporalibus, sed de vita æterna & Christo crucifixo & gratia Dei nobis per illum oblata concionatum esse, certius est, quam vt probatione vlla indigeat: Galat. 4. versu 1. Quandin hæres infans est, nihil differt à seruo, quamuis sit Dominus omnium. Cùm enim certissimum sit, Ecclesiam Israeliticam, quæ sub Veteri Testamento fuit, ibi cum Ecclesia Christiana conferri, necessariò inde sequitur, Patres sub Veteri Testamento, eiusdem hæreditatis spe, suffultos, & eiusdem adoptionis nobiscum participes fuisse, alioquin illa comparatio, & similitudo Pauli, ad rem planè nihil faceret. Quum igitur ex illis omnibus euidenter ac solidè demonstretur, Patres in Veteri Testamento, doćtrina & promissionibus Euangelicis minimè caruisse, inde certissimum est, promissiones illas in Veteri Testamento, non tantùm temporales fuisse, cùm doćtrina Euangelii spiritualis sit, & hominum corda non in præsentis vitæ lætitia detineat, sed ad spem vitæ æternæ euehat, vt testatur Apostolus, Ephef.cap.1. ver.13. Posteaquam Euangelio credidistis, obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ, in redemptionem acquisitæ possessionis. Huc etiam refer promissiones de semine mulieris caput serpentis contrituro, primis Parentibus factas & posteris sæpissimè confirmatas.
units.tr: Second argument, drawn from the testimonies of Christ and the Apostles. John 5:46: If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote of me. Acts 10:43: To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name. Rom. 10:16: But not all obeyed the gospel, for Isaiah says, Lord, who has believed our message? Either the message that Isaiah preached means the gospel, or the Apostle quotes that passage wrongly, which is absurd. 1 Pet. 1:10: Concerning this salvation the prophets made inquiry and searched. Rom. 1:2: (The gospel), which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. And chap. 3:21-22: But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been revealed, attested by the Law and the Prophets: the righteousness, I say, of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all and upon all who believe. Whatever Paul (and consequently the other Apostles also) said and preached, the Prophets and Moses had foretold. Acts 26:22: But having obtained help from God, I have stood to this day, testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the Prophets and Moses foretold would come to pass. That Paul preached not of bodily things but of eternal life, of Christ crucified, and of the grace of God offered to us through him, is more certain than that it needs any proof. Gal. 4:1: As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant, though he is lord of all. Since it is quite certain that the Israelite Church, which existed under the Old Testament, is there compared with the Christian Church, it necessarily follows that the Fathers under the Old Testament, sustained by the hope of the same inheritance, were partakers with us in the same adoption; otherwise that comparison and likeness of Paul would have nothing to do with the matter. Since, therefore, from all these things it is clearly and solidly demonstrated that the Fathers in the Old Testament lacked neither the doctrine nor the promises of the Gospel, it is most certain that those promises in the Old Testament were not merely temporal, since the doctrine of the Gospel is spiritual and does not hold men's hearts in the joys of the present life but lifts them up to the hope of eternal life, as the Apostle testifies, Eph. 1:13: After you believed the gospel, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the possession that has been acquired. To this also refer the promises made to our first parents of the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, and very often confirmed to their posterity.

units.la: Hh
units.tr: Hh

units.la: Argumentum tertium desumitur ab effectu Euangelii & promissionum spiritualium proprio. Si enim Patres in Veteri Testamento habuerunt promissiones tantum temporales, non autem Euangelicas ac spirituales, vtique nec gratia Christi seruati sunt, quia salus non est, nisi per gratiam Christi: gratia Christi vero, non nisi per Euangelium. Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Iohann.14. ver.6. Atqui Patres seruati sunt gratia Christi, sicut & nos, Act.15. ver.10.11. Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum, impositο iugo seruici Discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus? Imo per gratiam Iesu Christi credimus nos seruari, sicut & illi: Vnde sequitur non tantum promissionibus temporalibus affixos illos fuisse, sed ipsis per promissiones Euangelicas aditum ad vitæ æternæ possessionem patefactum esse.
units.tr: Third argument, drawn from the effect proper to the Gospel and to spiritual promises. For if the Fathers under the Old Testament had only temporal promises and not evangelical and spiritual ones, then surely they were not saved by the grace of Christ either, since there is no salvation except through the grace of Christ, and the grace of Christ comes only through the Gospel. No one comes to the Father except through me, John 14:6. But the Fathers were saved by the grace of Christ, just as we are, Acts 15:10-11: Now therefore why do you put God to the test by laying on the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are. Hence it follows that they were not only bound to temporal promises, but that through the evangelical promises access to the possession of eternal life was opened to them.

units.la: Argumentum quartum. Si Patres in Veteri Testamento, tantum temporales, non autem Euangelicas & spirituales promissiones habuerunt, tum vtique etiam fide caruerunt: quomodo enim inuocabunt cum, in quem non crediderunt: quomodo autem credent quod non audierint? Fides est ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum (id est Euangelium) Dei. Rom.10. ver.14.17. Atqui fidem Patres habuerunt, tum, quia fides illorum prolixè celebratur. Hebr.11. tum etiam quia Abraham, qui signum accepit circumcisionis signaculum (σφραγίδα) iustitiæ fidei, Rom.4. ver.11. per fidem iustificatus,& pater omnium credentium esse dicitur, Rom.4.v.9. & sequentibus.
units.tr: Fourth argument. If the Fathers under the Old Testament had only temporal promises and not evangelical and spiritual ones, then surely they also lacked faith: for how will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe what they have not heard? Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word (that is, the Gospel) of God. Rom. 10:14, 17. But the Fathers did have faith, both because their faith is celebrated at length in Heb. 11, and also because Abraham, who received the sign of circumcision, a seal [σφραγίδα] of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11), is said to have been justified through faith and to be the father of all who believe (Rom. 4:9ff.).

units.la: Argumentum quintum & vltimum, desumitur à Sacramentorum in Veteri Testamento significatione.
units.tr: Fifth and last argument, drawn from the meaning of the sacraments in the Old Testament.

units.la: Si enim Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti, eiusdem gratiæ,ac fauoris diuini, cuius Sacramenta Noui Testamenti, symbola, sigilla ac σφραγίδες sunt,tum sequitur etiam promissiones in Veteri Testamento, non temporales tantum, sed etiam spirituales & Euangelicas fuisse, quia Sacramenta nihil aliud,quam quod verbo promittitur, obsignare & confirmare possunt: & Sacramenta Noui Testamenti promissionum spiritualium de remissione peccatorum, sanctificatione, & vita aterna signa sunt & sigilla, Rom.6. ver.3.4. An ignoratis nos, quotquot baptizati sumus, in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius esse baptizatos? Sepulti igitur sumus vnà cum eo per baptismum in mortem: vt sicut excitatus est Christus ex mortuis in gloriam Patris, ita & ita & nos noua vita ambulemus. Tit.3.verf. 5. Non ex operibus iustis, quæ fecerimus nos, sed ex sua misericordia seruauit nos per lauacrum regenerationis, & renouationem Spiritus sancti. 1.Corinth.10.ver.16. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis,quem frangimus,nonne communio corporis Christi est? 1. Corinth.12. verf.13. Per vnum Spiritum nos omnes in vnum corpus baptizati sumus, & omnes vna potione potati sumus in vnum Spiritum.
units.tr: For if the sacraments of the Old Testament were symbols and seals, and the pledges, as it were, of the same grace and divine favour of which the sacraments of the New Testament are symbols and seals (and seals [σφραγίδες]), then it follows that the promises in the Old Testament were not only temporal but also spiritual and evangelical. For sacraments can do nothing other than seal and confirm what is promised in the word; and the sacraments of the New Testament are signs and seals of the spiritual promises concerning the remission of sins, sanctification, and eternal life. Rom. 6:3-4: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. Titus 3:5: Not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit. 1 Cor. 10:16: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? 1 Cor. 12:13: For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, and all were given one drink in one Spirit.

units.la: Atqui Sacramenta veteris Testamenti, eiusdem gratiæ, ac fauoris diuini, cuius sacramenta Noui Testamenti symbola & sigilla extitisse, affirmat non obscure Paulus, quum Patres per legitimum sacramentorum vsum eiusdem rei significatæ, cuius & nos participes factos esse, diuersis verbis testatur,1.Corinth.cap.10. verf. primo,secundo, tertio & quarto:Nolui vos ignorare,fratres,inquiens, quod Patres nostri omnes sub nube fuerunt, & omnes per mare transierunt, & omnes in Moysen baptizati sunt nube, & mari, & omnes eandem esscam spiritualem ederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Biberunt enim ex sequente spirituali petra: Petra verò erat Christus. Et quamuis cibus ac potus ille subsidium fuerit vitæ corporalis, quo Dominus præsenti corporis necessitati succurrebat, tamen quum iisdem certissimis signis testari voluerit, se illis tanquam populo peculiari & electo Deum adesse, dubium nullum est, quin vltra terrenam vtilitatem, habuerint etiam in illis spiritualis vitæ euidentissimum argumentum.
units.tr: But that the sacraments of the Old Testament were symbols and seals of the same grace and divine favour of which the sacraments of the New Testament are symbols and seals, Paul clearly affirms, when he testifies in various words, in 1 Cor. 10:1-4, that the Fathers, through the lawful use of the sacraments, became partakers of the same thing signified, of which we too are partakers. I would not have you ignorant, brothers, he says, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. And although that food and drink were a support of bodily life, by which the Lord met the present needs of the body, yet since he wished to attest by these very certain signs that he was present with them as with his peculiar and chosen people, there is no doubt that beyond earthly usefulness they also had in them the most evident proof of spiritual life.

units.la: Quanquam verò doceamus, & affirmemus easdem Veteris ac Noui Testamenti promissiones extitisse, & populum Israeliticum eiusdem fœderis, eorundémque bonorum spiritualium nobiscum fuisse consortem, atque per fidem in Messiam venturum in eandem cœlestem hæreditatem collimasse, minimè tamen diffitemur, easdem promissiones spirituales, seculari vel temporali modo circumuestitas, & sub beneficiis terrenis ceu speculo contemplandas, ac quodammodo degustandas exhibitas fuisse: sic vt illud substantiâ vnum ac idem fœdus, diuersis modis propositum & administratum fuerit,quas differentias accidentales in administrandi ratione,& circumstantiis positas ipsi vnitati substantiali nihil derogare Theologi nostri passim & luculenter docuerunt.
units.tr: Although we teach and affirm that the same promises existed in the Old and New Testaments, and that the Israelite people were partakers of the same covenant and of the same spiritual goods with us, and aimed through faith in the coming Messiah at the same heavenly inheritance, yet we by no means deny that those same spiritual promises were presented clothed in a worldly or temporal form, and set forth to be contemplated under earthly benefits as in a mirror, and in some measure to be tasted beforehand. Thus the one covenant, substantially one and the same, was proposed and administered in diverse ways; and our theologians have taught often and clearly that these accidental differences, lying in the manner of administering and in circumstances, take nothing away from the substantial unity itself.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capite quinto,& vigesimo primo,contrariam sententiam tuetur,ac docet,Christum post suum demum in carnem & in mundum hunc aduentum,promissiones Euangelicas, ante natiuitatem ipsius ex Maria Virgine omnibus ignotas, reuelasse,ac proinde promissiones illas in Veteri Testamento, temporales tantum, non autem spirituales ac aeternas fuisse, & consequenter, non accidentale tantum,sed substantiale discrimen, inter Vetus & Nouum Testamentum, si res promissas spectes, statuendum esse: quam erroneam sententiam suam, aliquot argumentis, tum ex sacris literis, tum à testimonio & autoritate humana desumptis, demonstrare conatur:nos singula examinabimus.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in chapters five and twenty-one of his Institutes, defends the contrary opinion and teaches that Christ, only after his coming in the flesh and into this world, revealed the evangelical promises, which were previously unknown to all before his birth from the Virgin Mary; and therefore that those promises in the Old Testament were only temporal and not spiritual and eternal, and consequently that, if one looks at the things promised, a substantial and not merely accidental difference must be posited between the Old and New Testaments. He tries to demonstrate this erroneous opinion of his by several arguments, drawn partly from the Holy Scriptures and partly from human testimony and authority. We will examine each of them.

units.la: Argumentum primum desumit ex 2.Tim.1. verf.10. Patefacta nunc est (gratia) per illustrem illum aduentum Saluatoris nostri Iesu Christi, qui mortem quidem aboleuit,vitam autem in lucem produxit, ac immortalitatem,per Euangelium. Et Ioh.1.v.18. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, Filius vnigenitus,qui est in sinu Patris,ipse enarrauit. Ex quibus verbis sequi existimat Aduersarius,Christum hominem primum fuisse,qui & quidem in Nouo demum Testamento,vitam aeternam reuelauerit per praedicationem Euangelij:& proinde cum illo omnes,qui ante natum ex Virgine Maria Christum extitierunt, latuerit, ideo promissiones Veteris Testamenti temporales tantum fuisse.
units.tr: The first argument is drawn from 2 Tim. 1:10: But is now made manifest (grace) by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. And from John 1:18: No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him. From these words the adversary concludes that Christ, as a man, was the first to reveal eternal life, and that only in the New Testament, through the preaching of the gospel; and therefore, since all who existed before Christ was born of the Virgin Mary remained in the dark, the promises of the Old Testament were merely temporal.

units.la: Resp.Consequentiam esse falsam,quia Christus per illustrē suum in carnem aduetum, vitam æternam ac immortalitatem in lucem produxisse dicitur non quod Patres in veteri Testamento, omnibus promissionibus,de vita æterna cōsequenda,caruerint,sed quia in ipsius demum persona extitit solida promissionum veritas, quæ in veteri Testamento,non nisi sub variis rituum ac ceremoniarum typis ac figuris obscurè adumbrata fuit : deinde quia gratiæ illius splendor, per eundem Christi illustrem aduentum , etiam Gentibus illuxit , diruta videlicet maceria illa, quæ tam diu misericordiam Dei, intra Israeliticæ Reipublicæ fines conclusam tenuerat, & annuntiata per ipsum pax est etiam iis qui procul erant, non secus atque iis qui propè coniunc̄ti,vt simul in vnum populum coalescerent. Quia itaque Christus palam aduentu suo exhibuit, quæ Prophetæ olim obscurè prædixerant,omnesque salutis nostræ numeri in carne ipsius impleti sunt, ipsis etiam Gentibus in societatem fœderis ascitis : ideo hæc viua rerum exhibitio, iure merito- que noui quasi & singularis præconii nomen obtinuit & hoc sensu nunc per Christum manifestatum dicitur à Paulo id, quod prius ex parte tantùm ostensum fuerat.Ex quibus omnibus simul sequi-tur, Paulum ibi loqui de Euangelio non late, sed stricte accepto, quatenus videlicet omnium promissionum complementum, ad-eoque plenam rei exhibitionem significat, in quam etiam Patrum fides olim respiciebat. Locum alterum ex Iohanne citatum, quan-tum attinet, etiamsi verba illa non tantùm de externo corporei oculi aspectu, sed de cognitione & notitia Dei, sint intelligenda, ta-men illorum sensus alius esse nõ potest, quàm neminem vnquam ante Christi aduentum claram illam apertámque notitiam Dei in Christo habuisse. Viderunt quidem homines, & cognouerunt Deum aliquo modo per naturę lucem: viderunt quoque eum fui, hoc est, Iudæi per lucem Verbi, legis nimirum, & promissionum Euangelicarum quæ fuerunt de Christo venturo: viderunt Iudæi adumbratum figuris, & sacrificiis variis, sed clare & perspicuè ante Christum manifestatum in carne non viderunt, sed Filius vnige-nitus nobis plenam illam cognitionem reuelauit, consilium videlicet, & voluntatem Patris, de salute nostra, clarissimè nobis ex-ponendo. Ex his autem sequitur quidem nostram conditionem Patrum in Veteri Testamento, potiorem esse, sed illos omni vi-tæ æternæ consequendæ spe destitutos fuisse, minimè colligitur.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is false. Christ is said to have brought eternal life and immortality to light by his illustrious coming in the flesh, not because the Fathers in the Old Testament lacked all promises of eternal life to be obtained, but because the solid truth of the promises came into existence in his own person, whereas in the Old Testament it was only obscurely shadowed under the various types and figures of rites and ceremonies. Further, because the splendour of that grace, through the same illustrious coming of Christ, also shone upon the Gentiles, the wall of partition having been broken down, which had so long kept God's mercy shut up within the borders of the Israelite commonwealth; and peace was preached to those who were far off no less than to those who were near, so that they might grow together into one people. Therefore, since Christ by his coming openly displayed what the prophets had long foretold obscurely, and all the parts of our salvation were fulfilled in his flesh, the Gentiles themselves being admitted into the fellowship of the covenant, this living exhibition of things rightly obtained the name of a new and unique proclamation; and in this sense Paul says that what had been shown only in part before is now made manifest through Christ. From all this it follows together that Paul is speaking of the gospel not in the broad sense but in the strict sense, namely as signifying the fulfilment of all the promises, and so the full exhibition of the thing, toward which the faith of the Fathers also looked in former times. As for the second passage cited from John, even if those words are to be understood not only of the outward sight of the bodily eye but of the knowledge and acquaintance of God, their sense cannot be other than this: that no one before Christ's coming had that clear and plain knowledge of God in Christ. Men indeed saw and knew God in some measure by the light of nature; they also saw the Son, that is, the Jews, by the light of the Word, namely the law and the evangelical promises concerning the Christ who was to come; the Jews saw him shadowed in figures and various sacrifices; but they did not see him clearly and plainly manifested in the flesh before Christ. The only begotten Son has revealed to us that full knowledge, namely the counsel and will of the Father concerning our salvation, setting it out most clearly for us. From this, however, it follows that our condition is indeed better than that of the Fathers under the Old Testament, but it is by no means inferred that they were deprived of every hope of obtaining eternal life.

units.la: Argumentum fecundum desumit ex Hebr. 7. ver. 19. Nihil ad perse-ctionem conduxit Lex, verum introductio ad spem meliorem, per quam appropinquamus Deo. Quod autem per illam αντιχριστου melioris spei, Euangelium, seu Nouum fœdus significetur, inde colligi posse, inquit Ad-uerfarius, quòd per Euangelium spes melior fit introducta, illa, quæ sub Lege erat: & inde sequi affirmat, illi qui sub Lege su VeteriTeftamen-to fuerunt, nullam vitæ æternæ consequendæ spem factam esse, quum a-lioquin per fœdus nouum alia melior introduci non potuisset. Atque hanc ipsam spem ait, esse Spiritum & potentiam illam Dei, quæ Legi, & literæ in Scripturis sacris opponitur. 2. Corinth. 3. verf. 6. Qui fecit vt i-donei effemus Ministri Noui Testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus: nam litera occidit, sed Spiritus viuificat. Cætera, quæ huius loci explicationi ab Aduersariis subiunguntur, ac imminent, ad examen quæstionis tertiæ, in loco, de Libero Arbitrio, excutiendæ, reii-cimus.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from Heb. 7:19: For the law made nothing perfect, but the bringing in of a better hope [κρείττονος ἐλπίδος] did; by which we draw nigh unto God. The adversary says that that this better hope signifies the gospel, or the New Covenant, can be gathered from this, that through the gospel a better hope was introduced than that which was under the Law; and from this he affirms that those who lived under the Law in the Old Testament had no hope of obtaining eternal life, since otherwise another, better hope could not have been introduced through the New Covenant. And he says that this very hope is the Spirit and that power of God which is set against the Law and the letter of the sacred Scriptures. 2 Cor. 3:6: Who also hath made us able ministers of the New Testament; not of the letter, but of the Spirit: for the letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life. The rest, which the adversaries add to the explanation of this passage and which bear on it, we set aside for the examination of the third question, to be discussed in the place on Free Will.

units.la: Refp. Consequentiam esse fallam, quia Apostolus in loco citato, per Legem, nec promissiones Patribus factas, nec ipsam fœde-tis substantiam, sed eius accidentia, accessiones, & annexa, seu, vt loquuntur vulgò, accessoria, ceremonias nempe Sacerdotii Leuitici, intelligit, sicuti ex antecedentibus versibus, & ipso Apostoli scopo, liquidò constat. Versu enim duodecimo eiusdem capitis affirmat Apostolus, propter mutatum Sacerdotium Leviticum, etiam Legem mutatam esse, quam eandem Legem versu vndecimo, ordinem appellat. Et Apostolus demonstrans hoc ipso capite, Christum Pontificem Pontifici Leuitico, itemque sacerdotium Christi sacerdotio Leuitico longè præstare, argumentum inter cætera desumit ab vtilitate & effectu, quod videlicet Sacerdotio Christi populus sanctificatus sit, vti confirmatur ab ipso Paulo capite nono, Sacerdotio autem Leuitico nihil sanctificatum, tum quia carnale sit, id est, in cæremoniis positum, ac proinde constans ex mandato dissolubili, tum etiam, quia Lex (nempe cæremonialis) vmbram solummodo obtinens eorum bonorum, quæ futura erant, non ipsam imaginem rerum, iidem hostiis anniuersariis, quas offerunt, nunquam in perpetuum potest accedentes sanctificare: sed repetita tantum fit quot annis mentio peccatorum: nec potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata: Hebræorum capite decimo, versu primo, tertio & quarto. Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius apparet, per Legem illam, non ipsum fœdus Testamenti Veteris, sed tantùm œconomiæ Veteris circunstantias, ritus ac cæremonias tum ipsis Sacerdotibus, tum etiam populo obseruandas, & quæcunque cum sacerdotio Leuitico implicita erant, intelligenda esse. Hinc autem ex ipsa comparatorum natura, & iustę oppositionis legibus, euidenter demonstratur, per introductionem illam spei meliorIs, non ipsum Euangelium, vt falsò contendit Aduersarius, sed Sacerdotium Christi Melchisedecianum, intelligendum esse, quod sanctificatione nos perfecerit, cùm ipsi Sacerdotio Aaronico & Leuitico, non Euangelium, sed Christi Sacerdotium Melchisedecianum opponatur, & cum illo conferatur. Hoc sacerdotium Christi vocat Apostolus Spem meliorem, obiectiue, vt mihi quidem videtur, quia idem sacerdotium Christi iam olim bonum speratum fuit, longè præstantius quàm sacerdotium illud Aaronicum & Leuiticum, quemadmodum eadem metonymia felicitas secundùm promissionem sperata, capite 6.18. spes promissa appellatur, & fides, pro rebus creditis dicitur, Galat.cap.3. versu 23. Quamuis & illorum sententia non temerè fit reiicienda, qui statuunt SacerSacerdotium Christi, effeciuè spem melioremab Apostolo appellari, quòd videlicet populum Dei in spem meliorem, de Dei erga nos gratia, & fauore, quam vetus illud Leuiticum. & Aaronicum erexerit. Hanc spem meliorem superin troductam esse dicit Apostolus, id est, abolito cum sua Lege Sacerdotio Aaronico & Leuitico, nouum hoc, & prastantius Christi Sacerdotium substitutum, quod deinceps solum in Ecclesia vigere debeat, ne amplius per cæremonias legales Deus colatur. Deinde verò rationem euidentem ab effectu desumptam reddit Apostolus, quare Sacerdotium Christi spem meliorem appellauerit, quia videlicet per Sacerdotium Christi appropinquamus Deo: Christus enim merito, & intercessione sacrificii sui aditum nobis ad Deum parauit, imo ipse ceu manu in Dei conspectum nos adducit, sistens nos Deo Patri in filios: Heb.2.v.13. Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedisti mihi: Rom.5.v.2. Per Christum fidem habemus ..., id est accessionem, vel adductionem ad Deum. 1.Pet.3.18. Passus est pro peccatis nostris, iustus pro iniustis, vt nos ad Deum adduceret. Olim verò tam Sacerdotes, quàm populus procul arcebantur à sanctuario, quasi à Dei conspectu, cùm ingrediente Pontifice solo in Sanctuarium Sacerdotes à longe in atrio suo, populus longius in atrio extremo stare coacti fuerint, quia nondum patefacta fuerat via ad sacrarium, priore tabernaculo adhuc consistente. Hac igitur falsa destructa hypothesi, quod nempe per spem illam meliorem, Euangelium sit intelligendum, corruit per se conclusio illa, quod videlicet Patribus in veteri Testamento, nulla vita æterna spes affulserit: Sed quia idem argumento eodem Aduersarii, effici videtur, etiamsi in locum Euangelii Sacerdotium Christi substituatur, ideò argumentum illud, assumpto vtroque termino, dilucidè formabimus, & plenius ad illud respondebimus.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is false, because in the passage cited the Apostle understands by the Law neither the promises made to the Fathers nor the substance of the covenant itself, but its accidents, additions and appendages, or, as people commonly say, its accessories, namely the ceremonies of the Levitical priesthood, as is clear from the preceding verses and from the Apostle's own purpose. For in the twelfth verse of the same chapter the Apostle affirms that because the priesthood was changed, the law was changed also; and in the eleventh verse he calls this same law an order. Moreover, in demonstrating in this very chapter that Christ as priest far surpasses the Levitical priest, and the priesthood of Christ the Levitical priesthood, the Apostle draws his argument, among other things, from the usefulness and effect, namely that the people were sanctified by the priesthood of Christ. This is confirmed by Paul himself in chapter nine: but the Levitical priesthood sanctified nothing, both because it was carnal, that is, consisted in ceremonies, and therefore rested on a dissoluble commandment, and also because the Law (namely the ceremonial law), having only the shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offer year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect; for it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins (Heb. 10:1, 3, 4). From all these things it appears more clearly than the noonday light that by that Law is to be understood not the covenant of the Old Testament itself, but only the circumstances of the economy of the Old Testament, the rites and ceremonies to be observed both by the priests themselves and by the people, and whatever was bound up with the Levitical priesthood. Hence, moreover, from the very nature of the things compared and the laws of proper opposition, it is evidently demonstrated that by that introduction of a better hope is to be understood not the gospel itself, as the adversary falsely contends, but the Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ, which has made us perfect by sanctification, since the Aaronic and Levitical priesthood is opposed not by the gospel but by the Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ, and is compared with it. The Apostle calls this priesthood of Christ a better hope objectively, as it seems to me, because this same priesthood of Christ was already long ago hoped for as a good far more excellent than that Aaronic and Levitical priesthood; just as by the same metonymy the happiness hoped for according to the promise is called the promised hope in chapter 6:18, and faith is used for the things believed (Gal. 3:23). Yet the view of those is not rashly to be rejected who hold that the priesthood of Christ is called by the Apostle a better hope effectively, namely because it has raised the people of God to a better hope of God's grace and favour than that old Levitical and Aaronic priesthood did. The Apostle says that this better hope has been introduced, that is, when the Aaronic and Levitical priesthood with its law was abolished, this new and more excellent priesthood of Christ was put in its place, which alone ought henceforth to flourish in the Church, so that God should no longer be worshipped through legal ceremonies. Then the Apostle gives an evident reason drawn from the effect why he called the priesthood of Christ a better hope, namely because through the priesthood of Christ we draw near to God: for Christ, by the merit and intercession of his sacrifice, has prepared access for us to God; indeed he himself, as it were by the hand, leads us into the sight of God, presenting us to God the Father as sons: Heb. 2:13, Behold I and the children whom God hath given me; Rom. 5:2, By whom we have access by faith, that is, approach or introduction to God; 1 Pet. 3:18, Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God. But in former times both priests and people were kept far away from the sanctuary, as if from the sight of God: while only the high priest entered into the sanctuary, the priests were compelled to stand afar off in their own court, and the people further off in the outer court, because the way to the holy place had not yet been opened while the former tabernacle still stood. Therefore, with this false hypothesis destroyed, namely that by that better hope the gospel is to be understood, that conclusion falls of itself, namely that no hope of eternal life shone upon the Fathers in the Old Testament. But since by the same argument the adversary's conclusion seems to follow even if the priesthood of Christ is substituted in place of the gospel, we will therefore set out that argument clearly with both terms assumed, and answer it more fully.

units.la: Argumentum igitur tale est.
units.tr: So the argument runs as follows.

units.la: Si per Euangelium, vel Sacerdotium Christi, in Nouo Testamento, spes melior vitæ æternæ consequendæ, hominibus est facta, & introducta: tum sequitur Patribus, in Veteri Testamento, nullam spem vitæ æternæ consequendæ factam esse. Si enim etiam tum illam spē habuissent, tum per Euangelium, aut Sacerdotium Christi nulla melior introduci potuisset:
units.tr: If, through the Gospel or the Priesthood of Christ in the New Testament, a better hope of obtaining eternal life has been made and introduced for men, then it follows that no hope of obtaining eternal life was given to the Fathers in the Old Testament. For if they had already had that hope, then no better hope could have been introduced through the Gospel or the Priesthood of Christ.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Vtrumque conexum, tum syllogismi principalis, tum prosyllogismi esse falsum, vt vel puer aliquis agnoscit. Ex eo enim, quod sub Nouo Testamento, spes est melior, amplior & illustrior, quàm sub Veteri Testamento, minimè sequitur, sub hoc, nullam plane spem populo Dei affulsisse: quia fides, spes, & charitas, quatenus de hoc, aut illo subiecto praedicantur, ex eo rerum sunt genere, quae maius, minúsque recipiunt: & spes illa melior, seu melioris spei causa dicitur Sacerdotium Christi, non ratione Noui, aut diuersi obiecti, sed ratione claritatis, quia populus in Veteri Testamento, futura bona non nisi in vmbris, & figuris conspexit, quae nos hodie in ipsa imagine contemplamur. Quum denique demonstrauimus, per spem illam meliorem intelligendum esse Sacerdotium Christi Melchisedecianum, sequitur salsissimum esse id quod affirmat Aduersarius, nempe, spem iltam esse potentiam, & Spiritum illum Dei, qui in Scripturis sacris, Legi, & Litera opponitur, quam euidentem, & absurdam falsitatem, prolixius refutare, non est huius loci, atque instituti nostri.
units.tr: Reply. Both connections, that of the main syllogism and that of the prosyllogism, are false, as even a child can see. For from the fact that under the New Testament the hope is better, fuller and clearer than under the Old, it does not at all follow that no hope whatever shone upon the people of God under the Old. Faith, hope and love, as they are predicated of this or that subject, belong to the kind of things that admit of more and less. And that better hope, or the cause of the better hope, is said to be the Priesthood of Christ, not by reason of a new or different object, but by reason of clarity: the people under the Old Testament saw the future goods only in shadows and figures, which we today contemplate in the very image. Finally, since we have shown that by the better hope the Melchizedekian Priesthood of Christ is to be understood, it follows that what the Adversary affirms is most false, namely, that this hope is the power and Spirit of God, which in the holy Scriptures is opposed to the Law and to the letter. To refute at length this evident and absurd falsehood is not the place or the purpose of our work.

units.la: Argumentum tertium desumit ex Hebr. 8. ver. 6. At nunc (eo) excellentius sortitus est ministerium, quo praestantioris foederis est Mediator, quod praestantioribus promissis sanctum est. Ex quibus verbis apparere, inquit Aduersarius, Deum promissiones spirituales de vita aeterna, Nouo Testamento referuasse.
units.tr: The third argument he takes from Hebrews 8:6. But now he has obtained a ministry so much more excellent, by as much as he is the Mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. From these words, says the Adversary, it appears that God has reserved spiritual promises of eternal life for the New Testament.

units.la: Resp. Consequenter esse falsum: nouum enim foedus, seu Testamentum: quod foedus, & Testamentum vetus substantia alioquin vnum immutabile, & perpetuum, claritate cognitionis, ac illuminationis spiritualis, quantitate donorum Spiritus sancti, & amplitudine, superat, propterea quae praestantius appellatur, promissis praestantioribus sanctum esse dicitur, non quod Patribus, qui sub Lege, & caeremoniarum illo onere, tanquam sub tutela, ac paedagogia vixerunt, non eadem vitae aeternae spes affulserit, sed quia, etiamsi Deus illis eandem salutem, ac vitam aeternam promiserit, non tamen eadem, nec aequalis reuelationis spiritualis fuerit mensura, vel species: vnde haec ab Apostolo instituta coparatio, ad formam, hoc est, administrationis diuinae diuersitatem potius, quàm ad ipsam materiam est referenda.
units.tr: Reply. The consequence is false. For the New Testament, or covenant, surpasses the Old covenant and testament, which is otherwise one and unchangeable and perpetual, in the clarity of knowledge and spiritual illumination, in the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and in its scope; and for this reason it is called the better, and is said to be established upon better promises. This does not mean that the Fathers, who lived under the Law and under the burden of ceremonies, as under guardianship and a schoolmaster, did not have the same hope of eternal life. Rather, even if God promised them the same salvation and eternal life, the measure and kind of spiritual revelation were not the same or equal. Hence this comparison made by the Apostle is to be referred to the form, that is, to the diversity of the divine administration, rather than to the matter itself.

units.la: Argumentum quartum & vltimum per prolepsin & praeoccupationem tionem quandam, qua nouitatis crimen, & suspicionem à sua doctrina amoliri conatur, proponit, Vltimò etiam hoc sciendum esse inquiens, ipsos (uempe Samosatenianos) non primos extitisse : qui statuunt in Nouo tantum Testamento demum promissiones illas de vita aeterna, non autem in veteri quoque Testamento, quippe quod temporalia tantum promissa habuerit, falsas esse.
units.tr: The fourth and last argument, by way of prolepsis and anticipation, in which he tries to ward off from his doctrine the charge and suspicion of novelty, he sets forth thus: Finally this too must be known, he says, that they (namely the Samosatenians) were not the first to hold that those promises of eternal life are true only in the New Testament, and not also in the Old, since the Old had only temporal promises.

units.la: Resp. Quid tum Oflorrodiânum ergo tua conditio tolerabilior, aut crimen leuius esse putas tuum, quod falsam doctrinam tu ipse quidem non confinxeris, sed ab aliis traditam studiosè amplexus fueris atque propagaueris: Minimè vero: nec enim antiquitas, nec errantium multitudo, vt nosti, iustum parit errori patrocinium, neque hoc te excusare potest, quod alii tecum, vel ante te in eodem falsitatis luto hęserint. Quid post veritatem in mundo antiquius mendacio? Diabolus enim à principio in veritate non stetit, sed mendax est, & mendacii pater. Qui tamen partum hunc diabolicum edit, nempe mendacium, vetusta mendacii origine, ab illo crimine neutiquam liberatur. Errorem vestrum de Persona Christi, iam ante annos mille, & centenos aliquot, Paulus Samosatenus, Episcopus Antiochenę Ecclesiæ, in gratiam Zenobiæ, potetissimæ illius Arabiæ, Syriæ, & Phoeniciæ, Reginę, cui placere, & cuius aulæ seruire voluit, homo ambitione, & fastu turgidus, stabiliuit: an propterea vos, qui ex officina illius prodiistis, eiusdem blasphemiæ sectatores, sub Autoris, & Antesignani illius vestri præsidio, aduersus veritatis diuinæ, & eius propugnatorum, impetum ac tela, tuti latere potestis? Quærcum aliam abs te excuti, & alium refugii portum, quæri oportet.
units.tr: Reply. What then? Do you think, Ostorodius, that your position is more tolerable, or your crime lighter, because you did not yourself devise the false doctrine but eagerly embraced and spread what others had handed down? By no means. For neither antiquity nor the multitude of those who err, as you know, lends just protection to error, nor can it excuse you that others have stuck with you, or before you, in the same mire of falsehood. What is older in the world than a lie after the truth? For the devil did not stand in the truth from the beginning, but is a liar and the father of lies. Yet whoever brings forth this diabolical offspring, namely a lie, is by no means freed from that guilt by the ancient origin of the lie. Your error concerning the Person of Christ, more than eleven hundred years ago, was established by Paul of Samosata, Bishop of the Church of Antioch, to please Zenobia, the most powerful queen of Arabia, Syria and Phoenicia, whose court he wished to serve, a man swollen with ambition and pride. Can you then, who have come forth from his workshop and are followers of the same blasphemy, lie safe under the protection of that author and standard-bearer of yours, against the assault and weapons of divine truth and of its champions? You must seek some other excuse and some other refuge.

units.la: Sed audiamus, quæso, quosnam ille sententię iflius patronos ac socios nobis recenseat. Nam Robertus Bellarminus, inquit, præcipuus Iesuita, qui postea etiam Cardinalis factus est, lib. 2. de Pontifice Romano cap. 29. expresse affirmat, Patres (vt vocant) in eadem sententia fuisse, atque vt hoc demonstret, aliquot loca ex iis annotauit: & quoniam ipse eiusdem est sententiæ, eo ipso satis indicat Romanam Ecclesiam, candem quoque comprobare, vel saltem non improbare, acreycere.
units.tr: But let us hear, I beg you, whom he names to us as the patrons and allies of that opinion. For Robert Bellarmine, he says, the chief Jesuit, who was afterwards made a Cardinal, expressly affirms in book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 29, that the Fathers (as they are called) were of the same opinion; and to demonstrate this he noted several passages from them. And since he himself holds the same opinion, he thereby sufficiently indicates that the Roman Church also approves it, or at least does not disapprove of it and tolerates it.

units.la: Resp Εὕρη ἡ λοιπὸς τὸ πῶμα: dignum patella operculum, dignus Samosateniano cliente patronus Loiolota Bellarminus, qui, quanto præstantior est Iesuita, & ad amplioris dignitatis fastigium, à suo capite Pontifice nempe Romano, adultero & destructore isto Ecclesiæ,malo,& peruerso seruo,euectus,tanto certior,& immanior Dei,Christi,& Ecclesiæ hostis est: qua igitur fronte Aduersarius nobis pestilentissimam,& impurissimam Loiolitarum colluuiem omni pietati,paci,& tranquillitati inimicam,omnium vero turbarum,& seditionum tubam,& perpetuum quoddā incentiuum opponere audet? Nec Bellarmini igitur,nec Ecclesiæ illius Apostaticę Romanę consensum,vel moror,vel Aduersario inuideo:quę enim non pudet ipsi Deo creatori,& Christo Mediatori ac Saluatori nostro honorem & cultum debitum nefario ausu suffurari, & miseris creaturis,imo idolis ascribere,idolatria,tam nefanda & horrenda,qua nulli vel Gentiles, vel Iudæi modernam Ecclesiam Romanam superarunt,qui ille bonis illis & sanctis Patribus, qui sub Veteri Testamento vixerunt, promissionum spiritualium pabulum præscindere, & omnem illorum felicitatem terrenorum bonorum cācellis circumscribere,vereretur?Sed nisi Aduersarius perniciosissimis illis purpuratæ meretricis Babylonicæ procis, & adulatoribus,Loiolitis videlicet,& ipsi Ecclesiæ Romanę palliatę assentationis popysmata obtrudere potius,quàm illius autoritati, aut iudicio,reuera aliquid tribuere voluerit, quid causæ est, cur in articulo de Sacrosancta Trinitate, & æterna Christi, Spiritúsq; sancti deitate, in agnitionem & professionem veritatis, Ecclesiarum omnium Euangelicarum, & Pontificiarum autoritate non permoueatur? Hæc de dignitate, & fide citatorum testium, de rei ipsius veritate in antecedentibus egimus,sed quoniam lubuit Aduersario, tam honorificum in hac causa testem allegare, idem respondeo ipsi,quod à doctissimis Theologis nostris,qui libros illos Bellarmini,& crassissimos errores de filio illo perditionis, Pontifice nempe Romano,tam solidè & erudite refutarunt, vt in cineres & fauillas,eos redegisse videantur,scite admodum obiecerunt,nescire nempe ipsum,quid Vetus,& quid Nouum Testamentum sit, in magno errore,& in maximis tenebris illum versari, atque adeo ad ipsum Catechismum,quem ignorare videatur, relegandum esse.Sed pergimus cum Aduersario ad sequentia.
units.tr: Reply. [Εὗρε ὁ λοιπὸς τὸ πῶμα] A lid fit for the dish! Bellarmine the Loyolite is a fit patron for a client of Samosata. The more distinguished he is as a Jesuit, and the higher he has been raised to the summit of dignity by his head, the Roman Pontiff, that adulterer and destroyer of the Church, a bad and perverse servant, so much the more certain and savage an enemy of God, of Christ and of the Church is he. With what face, then, does the Adversary dare to set before us the most pestilential and foul sewer of the Loyolites, hostile to all piety, peace and tranquillity, and the trumpet of all disturbances and seditions, and a perpetual incitement? I therefore neither delay over Bellarmine's opinion nor over the consensus of that apostate Roman Church, nor do I grudge them to the Adversary. For are they not ashamed to steal, with a wicked daring, the honour and worship due to God the Creator and to Christ our Mediator and Saviour, and to ascribe it to wretched creatures, indeed to idols, with an idolatry so impious and horrible that neither Gentiles nor Jews have surpassed the modern Roman Church in it? Would such people hesitate to cut off the food of spiritual promises from those good and holy Fathers who lived under the Old Testament, and to hem in all their happiness within the bounds of earthly goods? But unless the Adversary wished to thrust upon us the flatteries of those most pernicious suitors and flatterers of the purple harlot of Babylon, namely the Loyolites and the Roman Church herself dressed in a cloak, rather than to attribute anything real to her authority or judgment, what reason is there why he is not moved by the authority of all the Evangelical and Pontifical Churches in acknowledging and confessing the truth on the article of the Most Holy Trinity and the eternal deity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit? We have already dealt, in the preceding sections, with the dignity and faith of the witnesses cited and with the truth of the matter itself. But since it pleased the Adversary to cite so honourable a witness in this cause, I give him the same answer that our most learned theologians gave, who refuted those books of Bellarmine and his gross errors about that son of perdition, the Roman Pontiff, so solidly and learnedly that they seem to have reduced them to ash and cinders. They pointedly observed that he does not know what the Old and the New Testament are, that he is in great error and in the greatest darkness, and that he should therefore be sent back to the Catechism, which he seems not to know. But we proceed with the Adversary to what follows.

units.la: CAPVT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: De Mandatis Christi.
units.tr: On the Commandments of Christ.

units.la: Vbi quæstio illa controuersa, An videlicet Christus legem Mosis moralem, à falsis interpretationibus & additamentis liberauerit,ac purgauerit:an verò nouis mandatis & additionibus interpolauerit, & auxerit;explicatur, veritas defenditur, & falsitas cum suis argumentis refellitur.
units.tr: Here the disputed question is examined and the truth defended: whether Christ cleansed and purified the moral law of Moses from false interpretations and additions, or whether he instead interpolated and enlarged it with new commandments and additions. The position is explained, the truth defended, and the falsehood refuted with its arguments.

units.la: VEMADMODVM autem Ostorrodius capite antecedente, Patres in Veteri Testamento promissiones tantum temporales,non autem spirituales & æternas habuisse, gratiámque & salutem æternam post Christi demum in carnem aduentum annuntiatam fuisse,affirmat : ita in sequentibus docet,per Christum in Nouo Testamento non tantum cæremonias, & politiam Mosis abrogatas, sed ipsam etiam legem moralem auctam & completam esse , sicut verbis illis Christi Matth.5. ver.17. Ne existimate,dicentes,me venisse, ut dissoluam legem,aut Prophetas, non veni ut dissoluam ,sed ut impleam: Præcepta moralia non tantum à variis & falsis Iudæorum ac Pharisæorum traditionibus, & commentis, quibus illa corruperant,vindicata à Christo,& repurgata, sed aliquot nouis mandatis aucta & completa esse perhibeantur. Quum autem hanc sententiam, & doctrinam suam Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capitibus decem, ita prolixè persequatur, & tot Pelagianorum,atq; Anabaptistarum commenta inferciat, vel centies à nostris refutata,vt omnia & singula, quæ decem illis capitibus adferuntur, excutere , nimis prolixum, & longum ac pene inutile foret: idcò operæpretium facturus esse mihi visus sum, fi'digitum, quod aiunt ad fontem intenderem, & quæ prolixis dicenda essent, ad generalia capita ita reuocarem, atque contrahe- rem, vt tamen illorum beneficio, singula facile refutari queant, Doctrinam videlicet nostram orthodoxam argumentis aliquot confirmando: errores autem Aduersarii breuiter iudicando, & vbi ille impegerit commonstrando.
units.tr: Just as Ostorodius asserts in the preceding chapter that the Fathers under the Old Testament had only temporal promises, not spiritual and eternal ones, and that grace and eternal salvation were first announced after Christ came in the flesh, so in what follows he teaches that through Christ in the New Testament not only the ceremonies and polity of Moses were abrogated, but the moral law itself was enlarged and completed, as in Christ's words at Matthew 5:17, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy but to fulfil." He claims that the moral precepts were not only vindicated and purged by Christ from the various false traditions and inventions of the Jews and Pharisees, by which they had corrupted them, but were also increased and completed by several new commandments. Since Ostorodius pursues this opinion and doctrine at such length over ten chapters of his Institutions, and stuffs in so many inventions of the Pelagians and Anabaptists, already refuted a hundred times by our people, a full examination of every single point in those ten chapters would be too long, and well-nigh useless. I have therefore thought it worth while, as they say, to point my finger at the source, and to reduce and condense what would need to be said at length into general heads, so that by their help each point can easily be refuted. That means confirming our orthodox doctrine by several arguments, briefly judging the adversary's errors, and showing where he has gone wrong.

units.la: Sententiam igitur nostram, qua docemus, & asserimus, Christum in Nouo Testamento, legem moralem per Mosen traditam, à fermento traditionum, & falsarum interpretationum quidem repurgasse, nullis autem nouis mandatis, aut additionibus auxisse, interpolasse, aut compleuisse, sequentibus argumentis, & rationibus demonstramus.
units.tr: Therefore we demonstrate our view, which teaches and asserts that Christ in the New Testament cleansed the moral law delivered through Moses from the leaven of traditions and false interpretations, but did not enlarge, interpolate or complete it with any new commandments or additions, by the following arguments and reasons.

units.la: Argumentum primum: Quod omnibus numeris, partibus atque gradibus absolutum, & perfectum est, illud etiam nulla ratione augeri, perfici, aut compleri vllis additamentis potest.
units.tr: The first argument: What is perfect in all its respects, parts and degrees cannot be increased, perfected or completed by any additions whatever.

units.la: Atqui lex moralis à Deo per Mosen tradita omnibus numeris, partibus, atque gradibus absoluta, & perfecta est: adhoc nempe, vt canon, regula, ac norma sit bonorum operum faciendorum, & perfectissima obedientia Deo ab homine præstanda, via denique iustitiæ & vitæ æternæ per illam, & quidem ex merito, & debito consequenda.
units.tr: But the moral law delivered by God through Moses is perfect in all its respects, parts and degrees: it is intended to be the rule, standard and norm of good works to be done and of the most perfect obedience to be rendered to God by man, and finally the way of righteousness and eternal life, to be attained through it by merit and as a due reward.

units.la: Ergo lex moralis nulla ratione augeri, perfici, aut compleri vllis additamentis potest.
units.tr: Therefore the moral law cannot be increased, perfected or completed by any additions whatever.

units.la: Propositio maior omnium eruditorum consensu certissima est. Assumptio verò ab ipsa perfectionis natura, ac definitione demonstratur.
units.tr: The major premise is most certain by the agreement of all learned men. The minor premise is proved from the very nature and definition of perfection.

units.la: Cuicunque enim in suo genere nihil addi potest, nec quicquam adimi, illud in suo genere omnibus numeris, partibus, atque gradibus, absolutum & perfectum est.
units.tr: For whatever in its own kind nothing can be added to, nor anything taken away from, is perfect in its own kind in all respects, parts and degrees.

units.la: Atqui doctrinæ legis moralis quicquam addi, aut ab illa detrahi etiam grauissimè prohibet Deus, Deut. 4. v. 1. 2. Nunc ergo Israel attende, ad statuta iudiciaque illa, quæ ego doceo vos facere, vt viuatis, & ingrediâ hereditario iure possideatis terram istam, quam Iehoua Deus maiorum vestrorum dat vobis.
