Ne addite ad verbum illud quod ego præcipio vobis, neque detrahite de eo, vt seruetis præcepta Iehoua Dei vestri, quæ ego præcipio vobis. Et cap. 12. vers. vltim. Quicquid ego vobis præcipio, id obseruabitis, vt faciatis, ad hoc nihil addes, ab eo nihil detrahes. Ergo lex moralis omnibus numeris, partibus, atque gradibus perfecta est.
units.tr: But God strictly forbids anything to be added to the doctrine of the moral law, or taken away from it, Deut. 4:1-2: "Now therefore, Israel, hearken unto the statutes and unto the judgements, which I teach you, for to do them, that ye may live, and go in and possess the land which the LORD God of your fathers giveth you. Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you." And Deut. 12:32, the last verse: "Whatsoever I command you, that shall ye observe to do: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it." Therefore the moral law is perfect in all its respects, parts and degrees.

units.la: Argumentum secundum. Quod perfectam salutis consequendae viam monstrat, & eam praescribit iustitiam, qua quis citra transgressionem functus, coram tribunali seuerae iustitiae Dei constitutus, iustus a Deo, & vitae aeternae praemio dignus in se, ex debito, secundum legem & citra gratiam, censetur & pronunciatur, ad ipsius salutem, & iustitiae, tum divinae, tum humanae gloriam, illud certe perfectissimum est, nec ulla ratione, aut ullis additamentis augeri, complerive potest:
units.tr: The second argument. What shows a perfect way of obtaining salvation, and prescribes that righteousness by which a man, without transgression, and standing before the tribunal of God's strict justice, is counted and pronounced righteous before God and worthy of the reward of eternal life, by debt, according to the law and apart from grace, for the glory of his salvation and of both divine and human justice, is certainly most perfect, and cannot be increased or completed by any means or any additions.

units.la: Atqui lex moralis a Deo per Mosen tradita, perfectam salutis consequendae viam monstrat, & eam praescribit iustitiam, qua quis citra transgressionem functus, &c.
units.tr: But the moral law delivered by God through Moses shows a perfect way of obtaining salvation, and prescribes that righteousness by which a man, without transgression, etc.

units.la: Ergo lex moralis perfectissima est, nec ulla ratione, aut ullis additamentis augeri, complerive potest.
units.tr: Therefore the moral law is most perfect, and cannot be increased or completed by any means or any additions.

units.la: Assumptionem quod attinet, & quidem legem moralem, perfectam salutis, & eiusmodi iustitiae, qualem descripsimus, consequendae, viam monstrare, inde liquet, tum quod ex eiusdem sententia, omnibus nobis in hoc elaborandum & incumbendum est, ut salute ac vita aeterna potiamur, & tamen nihil faciendum, quod non fit lege Dei praescriptum, ut ex Mose paulo ante demonstravimus. Hinc gratissima illa Mosis contestatio: Caelum & terram testor, quod tibi ostenderim hodie viam vitae & mortis, Deut. 30. ver. 19. Item, Et nunc Israel quid abs te postulat Deus tuus, nisi ut sibi penitus adhaereas, Deut. 10. ver. 12. quae plane inanis esset si lex moralis aliquo defectu, a Christo corrigendo, laboraret, nec perfectae iustitiae integerrimam regulam praescripsisset. Inanis etiam ista esset, & frustratoria promissio, Qui fecerit haec, vivet in ipsis, Levit. 18. ver. 5. Unde certe necessario sequitur, lege Dei tradi, quicquid ad salutem est necessarium, tum quod ipsa Scriptura diversis verbis idem affirmat, Rom. 4. v. 2. Nam si Abraham ex operibus iustificatus fuit, habet quod glorietur: & v. 4. Atqui ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. & cap. 2. ver. 13. Non enim qui audiunt legem, iusti sunt apud Deum, sed qui legem praestant iustificabuntur: & cap. 10. ver. 5. Moses enim describit iustitiam ex lege, quod qui praestiterit illa, vivet per illa: Et Christum legem illam moralem nullis nouis mandatis locupletare, nec quicquam in illa corrigere. voluisse, ex eo liquet euidentissimè, quod ille volentem ad vitam ingredi per bona opera, nihil aliud quàm legis mandata seruare iu-bet. Matth.19.v.17. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata: & Luc.10. v.28. Hæc fac, & viues. Quod verò ipso actu per legem nemo iustifi-catur, hoc non fit vitio aut natura ipsius legis moralis, quasi opera in illa præscripta Deo per se & in se grata non sint, nec ipsa strictè & rigidè sumpta iustitia, adeo vt qui ea fecerit, quæ lege illa præ-scribuntur,eo ipso citra absolutionem, aut gratuitam imputatio-nem iustus sit: sed per accidens, quia videlicet propter impoten-tiam & imbecillitatem carnis à nobis præstita non fuerit. Quem-admodum contrà legi cæremoniali iustificatio in scripturis adi-mitur,non quia præstita non est,sed simpliciter propter ipsius,non carnis peccatricis impotentiam, & quia neque opera ipsius, Deo per se grata sunt, vt ipsi iustitiæ nomine venire possint, neque il-lum respectum habent, vt absolutio à peccatis contra legem mo-ralem patratis,per illa obtineatur,vel ipsa gratiosè in iustitiam im-putentur.
units.tr: As for the minor premise, that the moral law shows the perfect way of obtaining salvation and such righteousness as we have described, this is clear, first, because by its own account we must all labour and strive to lay hold of salvation and eternal life, and yet nothing must be done that is not prescribed by the law of God, as we have shown from Moses just above. Hence Moses's most welcome solemn appeal: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death," Deut. 30:19. Likewise: "And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul," Deut. 10:12. These words would plainly be empty if the moral law laboured under some defect that Christ must correct, and if it had not prescribed the most entire rule of perfect righteousness. That promise would also be empty and fruitless: "Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgements: which if a man do, he shall live in them," Lev. 18:5. From this it certainly follows necessarily that whatever is necessary to salvation is delivered in the law of God. Scripture itself affirms the same thing in different words: Rom. 4:2, "For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory"; and 4:4, "Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt"; and Rom. 2:13, "For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified"; and Rom. 10:5, "For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them." And that Christ did not wish to enrich that moral law with any new commandments, nor to correct anything in it, is most evident from the fact that, when someone wishes to enter into life by good works, he bids him keep nothing but the commandments of the law: Matt. 19:17, "If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments"; and Luke 10:28, "This do, and thou shalt live." That no one is in fact justified by the law is not due to any fault or nature of the moral law itself, as though the works prescribed in it were not in themselves and by themselves pleasing to God, nor as though righteousness, strictly and rigidly taken, were not what it demands, so that whoever does what that law prescribes would thereby be righteous without absolution or gracious imputation. Rather it is accidental, because in us it is not performed on account of the impotence and weakness of the flesh. In contrast, justification is denied to the ceremonial law in the Scriptures, not because it is not performed, but simply because of the impotence not of the sinful flesh but of the ceremonial law itself; and because its works are not in themselves pleasing to God so that they could count as righteousness, nor do they have such regard that absolution from sins committed against the moral law could be obtained through them, or that they could themselves be graciously imputed as righteousness.

units.la: Argumentum tertium: Quod & in se perfectissima & integerrima omnis obedientiæ, iustitiæ, & sanctimoniæ regula ac norma est,& à nobis summam obedientiæ, & integritatis internæ & externæ perfectionem exigit ac requirit, adeo vt nihil virtutis aut operis boni à nobis præstari possit, ad quod non simus ex sententia illius obstricti & obligati; illud certè nullis additamentis perfici aut lo-cupletari potest:
units.tr: The third argument: What in itself is the most perfect and entire rule and norm of all obedience, righteousness and holiness, and demands from us the highest perfection of obedience and of inner and outer integrity, so that no virtue or good work can be performed by us to which we are not, by its judgement, bound and obliged; that certainly cannot be perfected or enriched by any additions.

units.la: Atqui legem Dei moralem perfectissimam & integerrimam debitæ à nobis Deo obedientiæ normam ac regulam esse, Dauid Ps. 119.passim testatur:eandem verò non tantùm in se perfectam esse, sed etiam à nobis summam obedientiæ & integritatis internæ & externæ perfectionem exigere ac requirere,ex eo liquet,quòd Chri-stus cœlestem perfectionem à nobis postulat Matth.5.v.48. Estote vos perfecti,vt Pater vester,qui est in cœlis,perfectus est. Et nos in ora-tione Dominica,Angelicam perfectionem petere iubemur,Matt. 6.v.10. Fiat voluntas tua sicut in cœlo, ita etiam in terra. Ita vt nihil virtutis aut boni operis à nobis præstari queat,ad quod non simus à sententia legis obligati,Luc.17.vers.10. Vos quum feceritis omnia, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite, serui inutiles sumus: nam quod debui-mus facere fecimus.
units.tr: Moreover, that the moral law of God is the most perfect and most complete rule and standard of the obedience owed by us to God, David testifies throughout Psalm 119. That the same law is not only perfect in itself but also requires and demands from us the highest perfection of obedience and of internal and external integrity is clear from the fact that Christ demands heavenly perfection from us, Matt. 5:48: Be ye therefore perfect, as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. In the Lord's Prayer we are also commanded to ask for angelic perfection, Matt. 6:10: Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth. Thus nothing of virtue or good work can be performed by us to which we are not bound by the sentence of the law, Luke 17:10: So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.

units.la: Ergo lex Dei moralis perfectissima est,& nulla ratione nullísq; addiadditamentis augeri, compleri, aut locupletari potest.
units.tr: Therefore the moral law of God is most perfect, and by no means can it be increased, completed, or enriched by any additions.

units.la: Argumentum quartum : Si Christus in Nouo Testamento perse- ctionem cœlestem à nobis postulauit, & Angelicam obedientiam ac conformitatem cum lege Dei petere iussit, & tamen omnium præceptorum compendium, totiusque iustitiæ speculū proponēs, eandem legis moralis summam, ad quam Moses in Veteri Testa- mento omnia Dei mandata aut præcepta reuocauit, & quidem iis- dem verbis repetiit & inculcauit, tum certissimum est, Christum in Nouo Testamento ad legem moralem nihil addidisse, neque vllis nouis mandatis illam adauxisse aut locupletasse.
units.tr: Fourth argument: If Christ in the New Testament demanded heavenly perfection from us, and commanded us to seek angelic obedience and conformity with the law of God, and yet, setting forth the summary of all precepts and the mirror of all righteousness, he repeated and impressed upon us, in the very same words, that same sum of the moral law to which Moses in the Old Testament referred all the commandments and precepts of God, then it is most certain that Christ in the New Testament added nothing to the moral law, and did not increase or enrich it by any new commandments.

units.la: Atqui Christus, in Nouo Testamento, perfectionem cœlestem à nobis postulauit, & Angelicam obedientiam & conformitate cum lege Dei petere iussit, vt in Argumento tertio demonstrauimus, & tamen omnium præceptorum compendium proponens, eandem legis moralis summam, ad quam Moses in Veteri Testamento, omnia Dei mādata ac præcepta reuocauit, & quidem iisdem verbis repetiit & inculcauit. Confer illud Matth. 22. v. 37. 38. 39. Marc. 12. v. 30. 31. Luc. 10. v. 27. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, ex tota anima tua, & ex omnibus viribus tuis, & proximum tuum sicut te ipsum. cum Deut. 6. v. 5. Leu. 19. v. 18.
units.tr: But Christ in the New Testament demanded heavenly perfection from us, and commanded us to seek angelic obedience and conformity with the law of God, as we have shown in the third argument; and yet, setting forth the summary of all precepts, he repeated and impressed upon us, in the very same words, that same sum of the moral law to which Moses in the Old Testament referred all the commands and precepts of God. Compare Matt. 22:37–39, Mark 12:30–31, Luke 10:27: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and thy neighbour as thyself, with Deut. 6:5 and Lev. 19:18.

units.la: Ergo Christus in Nouo Testamento ad legem Moralem nihil addidit, nec vllis nouis consiliis, argumentis, aut additamentis il- lam perfecit & locupletauit.
units.tr: Therefore Christ in the New Testament added nothing to the moral law, nor did he perfect or enrich it by any new counsels, arguments, or additions.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius elucescit, Christum nullam legis moralis ἐντολῆς aut correctionem instituisse, nec ad æternam Patris sui iustitiam quicquam addidisse, adeóque quum impleuisse legem dicitur, ipsum ab additionibus ac commentis Pha- risæorum, qui tortuosè illam depravabant, eam repurgatam, pristi- næ puritati restitu̇isse significari, vt hallucinentur vehementissime, quotquot arbitrantur, iustitiæ tantum initium ac tyrocinium tra- ditum olim fuisse in Lege, perfectionem vero in Euangelio doce- ri, Christūmque suos discipulos in altiorem perfectionis gradum extollere, quàm potuerit Moses crassum carnalémque populum, qui vix discendis elementis fuerit idoneus, qua opinione falsa, et- iam ex Veteribus quosdam deceptos fuisse, conslat. Præter so- lidissimas enim illas rationes, quibus paulò ante absolutissi- mam legis perfectionem demonstrauimus, sententiæ eidem no- stræ disputationis Christi tum occasio, tum series, cuidenter suffragatur. Quum enim Scribæ & Pharisæi legem à Christo per Euangelii prædicationem violari & euerti passim vociferarentur, Christus id ipsum quod sibi ab Aduersariis iniquè obiiciebatur, valide in ipsos retorquet, & illorum tum fucosam iustitiæ ostentationem, tum peruersam doctrinam, & falsam legis interpretationem perstringit: illà enim Deo secure illudebant, dum legis doctrina ad politicum ordinem translata, se laruata ac fictitia iustitia apud homines venditabant: hac verò discipulos suos quasi simias ad hypocrisin formabant, dum legem Dei ad externa tantum officia restringebant, quasi illis defungi sufficeret, & se ab homicidio iuste absolueret quisquis hominem manu non occideret: se purum & casti merito putaret coram Deo, quisquis rapto concubitu, aut clandestino adulterio corpus non pollueret. In ipsa deinde disputationis serie præcepta ista Legis non ita adducit Christus, ut in lege, si sensum spectes, habentur, sed ut erant à Scribis ac Pharisæis deprauata, & populo rudi inculcata perperam, ut Pharisaicam illam doctrinam in lucem educeret, & vitandam moneret, propterea non dicit in lege scriptum, sed dictum veteribus, non per Mosen, ut falsò affirmat Oltorrodius, sed à Scribis & Pharisæis, ac si diceret, Non est obscurum quod Scribæ & Pharisæi de præceptis contra homicidium, adulterium, & reliqua scelera latè sint commenti. Hactenus literalis sensus, & expositio inter vos per Scribas vulgata est, satis esse si quis tantum oculos, manus & pedes componat, ad fucosam bonorum operum speciem, manus ab homicidio ac vi abstineat, & alienum thorum illicito concubitu non contaminet, ut ut in turbidos affectus, iram, odium, invidiam, libidinem & concupiscentiam exardescat. Ego verò moneo vos legem non tantum in politico modo vitæ magistram esse, ad formandos mores externos, sed Spiritum, fidem, charitatem, & ipsissimum charitatis affectum exigi, ac proinde proximum violati non vi & manibus tantum, sed ipsis quoque animi insidiis, & adulterium committere non illos tantum qui uxores alienas corrumpunt, sed eos etiam, qui interni concupiscentiæ vštionibus inflammantur: quod ipsum de reliquis etiam præceptis est sentiendum, uti Christus per species fusius exponit. Neque illius interpretationis Pharisaicæ exemplum habes Ioh. 8. ver. 31. Nobis non licet, inquiunt hypocritæ sceleratissimi, interficere quenquam, cùm tamen ira, odio, & invidia perciti Christum tradiderint Pilato trucidandum & crucifigendum. Verba antecedentia idem euincūt, quod nos, aduersus Samosatenianos, affirmamus: posteaposteaquam enim Christus, se non ad destruendam, sed implendam legem venisse, affirmasset, subiicit verf. 18. Amen quippe dico vobis, donec praeterceat caelum & terra, iota unum, aut apex unus non praeterierit ex lege, donec omnia facta fuerint. Ex quibus verbis duo illa consequuntur euidenter, primo, Christum, quum in antecedentibus proximè verbis, se ad legem implendam venisse testatur, minimè significare voluisse, se legem per Mosen latam, illa ratione, aut illis novis praeceptis auxisse & locupletasse, alioquin haec aitiologiae loco subiecta asseueratio, praemissa verba, nullatenus comprobaret, quū fictae illius innouationis, & augmenti nulla ibi mentio fiat. Secundo, Christum ibidem non de exacta vitę humanę cum lege conformitate, sed solida doctrinę certitudine, & perpetua legis stabilitate, loqui, & docere, nihil videlicet in tota hac mundi machina, tam firmum esse ac stabile, quàm constans sit & immota legis veritas quæ veracissima certitudo de lege minimè enuntiari posset, nisi æterna illa & immutabilis piè sanctèque viuendi regula esset. Sic ex verf.19. vbi inquit Christus, Quisquis soluerit unum ex mandatis hisce minimis, & sic docuerit homines, minimus vocabitur in regno cœlorum: quisquis autem fecerit & docuerit, hic magnus vocabitur in regno cœlorum, manifestissimè liquet, Christum illo loco, non tam de obedientia legi praestanda, & vitę actionibus ad eius obsequium formandis, quàm de autoritate inuiolabili, & doctrinę ac interpretationis integritate & constantia, aduersus Scribas & Pharisæos disceptare. Vt iam constare posset Ostorrodio, quod quærit capite vigesimo tertio, quibusnam videlicet rationibus & argumentis suffulti, Christum illa capitis quinti parte, peruersam & falsam Pharisaeorum interpretationem, qua legis eneruabant autoritatem, perstringere, affirmemus? Vnde non est necesse, vt ad caput vigesimum secundum, & vigesimum tertium quicquam à me addatur amplius: attamen vt rei ipsius & doctrinæ nostræ veritas eò magis elucesceat, animaduersiones breues in duo sequentia capita, quibus praeceptum Decalogi septimum, & tertium, non tantùm vindicatum ab adulterina Pharisaeorum explicatione, sed auctum & locupletatum esse à Christo, contendit Aduersarius, subiiciemus.
units.tr: From all these things it shines out more clearly than the noonday sun that Christ did not institute any correction of the moral law's commandment [ἐντολῆς], nor did he add anything to the eternal righteousness of his Father. Therefore, when he is said to have fulfilled the law, this signifies that he cleansed it of the additions and fictions of the Pharisees, who had twisted it and corrupted it, and restored it to its original purity. Those are most greatly deceived who think that only the beginning and apprenticeship of righteousness was handed down of old in the Law, while perfection is taught in the Gospel, and that Christ raised his disciples to a higher degree of perfection than Moses could have raised a gross and carnal people, who were scarcely fit to learn the rudiments. It is established that some of the ancients too were deceived by this false opinion. For besides those most solid reasons by which we demonstrated just above the most complete perfection of the law, the occasion and the course of Christ's disputation clearly support our same view. For when the scribes and Pharisees everywhere cried out that the law was being violated and overthrown by the preaching of the Gospel, Christ turns back on them, with force, that very charge which was unjustly thrown at him by his adversaries, and lays bare both their showy display of righteousness and their perverse doctrine and false interpretation of the law. For by the one they mocked God with impunity, while they transferred the teaching of the law to the civil order and peddled among men a masked and feigned righteousness; by the other they formed their disciples like apes into hypocrisy, restricting God's law to external duties, as if it were enough to discharge these, and as if whoever did not kill a man with his hand were rightly acquitted of murder, and whoever did not defile a body by rape or secret adultery thought himself pure and chaste before God. Further, in the course of the disputation itself, Christ does not cite these precepts of the Law as they stand in the law, if you look at the sense, but as they had been corrupted by the scribes and Pharisees and wrongly impressed upon the untutored people. He did this in order to bring that Pharisaic doctrine into the light and to warn that it must be avoided. For this reason he does not say written in the law, but said to the ancients, not through Moses, as Ostorodius falsely asserts, but by the scribes and Pharisees, as if he were saying: It is not obscure that the scribes and Pharisees have widely invented teachings about the precepts against murder, adultery, and the other crimes. Up to this point, you have had the literal sense and exposition spread among you by the scribes: that it is enough if a man merely restrains his eyes, hands, and feet, so as to abstain from murder and violence with his hands, and not to defile another's bed by unlawful intercourse, provided that he is inflamed with turbulent passions such as anger, hatred, envy, lust and covetousness. But I warn you that the law is not only the teacher of outward morals in the civil conduct of life, but that it demands the Spirit, faith, love, and the very affection of love itself; and therefore that one does violence to his neighbour not only with force and hands, but also by the snares of the mind, and that not only those who corrupt other men's wives commit adultery, but also those who are inflamed by the internal stirrings of lust. The same must be felt about the other precepts as well, as Christ explains more fully through the particular cases. Nor do you have an example of that Pharisaic interpretation in John 8:31: We may not put any man to death, say these most wicked hypocrites, although, stirred by anger, hatred and envy, they handed Christ over to Pilate to be slain and crucified. The preceding words prove the same thing that we assert against the Samosatenians. For after Christ had affirmed that he came not to destroy but to fulfil the law, he adds in verse 18: For verily I say unto you, till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled. From these words two things clearly follow. First, when Christ in the immediately preceding words testifies that he came to fulfil the law, he by no means meant to say that he had increased and enriched the law given through Moses in that way, or by those new precepts; otherwise this assertion, subjoined as a reason for the words before it, would not prove them at all, since there is no mention there of any such fictitious renewal or increase. Second, Christ there is not speaking of an exact conformity of human life with the law, but of the firm certainty of doctrine and the perpetual stability of the law. Nothing in this whole machine of the world is so firm and stable as the constant and unmoved truth of the law; and that most true certainty could not be stated about the law unless it were an eternal and unchangeable rule of living piously and holily. So, from verse 19, where Christ says: Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven; but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven, it is most plainly clear that Christ in that passage was disputing, against the scribes and Pharisees, not so much about the obedience to be rendered to the law and the shaping of the actions of life to its observance, as about its inviolable authority and the integrity and constancy of its doctrine and interpretation. So Ostorodius may now understand what he asks in chapter twenty-three: By what reasons and arguments, namely, do we maintain that Christ, in that part of chapter five, condemns the perverse and false interpretation of the Pharisees by which they weakened the authority of the law? Hence there is no need for me to add anything further on chapters twenty-two and twenty-three. Nevertheless, so that the truth of the matter itself and of our doctrine may shine forth all the more, we will append brief observations on the two following chapters, in which the adversary contends that the seventh and third precepts of the Decalogue were not only vindicated from the adulterous explanation of the Pharisees, but were also increased and enriched by Christ.

units.la: Christum igitur praeceptum septimum, Non committes adulterium, seu Non moechaberis, correxisse, & perfectiorem iustitiam requisiuisse, Aduersarius Institutionum suarum cap. 24. argumentis quatuor astruere conatur.
units.tr: Therefore the Adversary, in chapter 24 of his Institutes, tries to show by four arguments that Christ corrected the seventh precept, Thou shalt not commit adultery, or Thou shalt not commit adultery, and required a more perfect righteousness.

units.la: Primum est, quia Christus Matth.5.vers.27.28.inquit, Audiuistis, quod di&um fuerit antiquis, Non committes adulterium: At ego dico vobis,quod quicunque aspexerit mulierem ad concupiscendum eam,iam adulterium commisit cum ea,in corde suo. Quum autem in lege Mosis nusquam scriptum extet, intuitum vxoris alienæ adulterium esse, necessario inde sequi existimat, Christum illis verbis legem illam Mosis correxisse, & perfectiorem iustitiam requisiuisse.
units.tr: First, because Christ says in Matthew 5:27-28: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, Thou shalt not commit adultery. But I say to you, that whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Since it is nowhere written in the law of Moses that looking at another man's wife is adultery, he thinks it must necessarily follow that by those words Christ corrected that law of Moses and required a more perfect righteousness.

units.la: Secundum est, quia Christus versu trigesimo primo & trigesimo secundo, dicit, Di&um est, quicunque repudiauerit vxorem suam, det illi libellum diuortii: At ego dico vobis,quod quisquis repudiauerit vxorem suam, nisi causa scortationis, facit eam mœchari, & quicunque repudiatam duxerit,mœchatur. Quum igitur lex simpliciter & absolute permiserit, vt vxor, quæ in oculis mariti gratiam non inueniret,id est,ipsi nō placeret, ab ipso dimitteretur, Christus autem nō nisi ob solam scortationem permittere illud voluerit: ideo manifestè hinc liquere, inquit, quod Christus legem illam veterè correxe-rit, imò penitus abrogauerit, non quidem quatenus aliquid mădauerit, sed quatenus aliquid permiserit, sic vt ne minima quidem sit suspicio, Christum genuinum legis sensum à peruersis Pharisæorum expositionibus vindicare,illis verbis,voluisse.
units.tr: Second, because Christ, in verses 31 and 32, says: It was said, whoever puts away his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you, that whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries her when she has been put away commits adultery. Since the law simply and absolutely allowed that a wife who did not find favour in her husband's eyes, that is, did not please him, should be dismissed by him, while Christ wished to permit this only on account of fornication, it is therefore plain from this, he says, that Christ corrected that old law, indeed utterly abrogated it, not indeed insofar as he commanded something, but insofar as he permitted something, so that there is not even the slightest suspicion that by those words he wished to vindicate the genuine sense of the law from the perverse expositions of the Pharisees.

units.la: Tertium est, quia homini Christiano non fit licitum,præter coniugem legitimo matrimonio iunctam, alias habere concubinas: (quod ex 1.Corinthior.capite septimo, versu quarto demonstrat) quum autem hoc nusquam in lege prohibitum fuisse legatur,imò quidam, qui tamen Deo placuerunt, nec ab eo puniti propterea fuerunt, præter vxores, alias concubinas habuisse, perhibeantur: idcirco,ait,inde sequi, Christum legem illam septimam perfectiorem red-didisse,& locupletasse.
units.tr: Third, because it is not lawful for a Christian man to keep concubines besides his wife joined to him in lawful marriage (which he proves from 1 Corinthians 7:4). But since it is read nowhere in the law that this was forbidden, and indeed some who nevertheless pleased God, and for that reason were not punished by him, are said to have had other concubines besides their wives, therefore, he says, it follows that Christ made that seventh law more perfect and enriched it.

units.la: Quartum & vltimum est, quòd hominem Christianum non deceat plures vna vxores simul habere(quamuis hoc ipsum in Nouo Testamento non fit prohibitum, sed ex multis colligatur circumstantiis, sub Euangelio hoc minime decere) quod tamen in ipsa lege nusquam vetitum fuerit.
units.tr: Fourth and last, that it does not befit a Christian man to have several wives at the same time (although this is not itself forbidden in the New Testament, but is gathered from many circumstances, that under the Gospel it is by no means fitting), which however was nowhere forbidden in the law itself.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum: Intuitum impudicum adulterium esse, quidem in lege Mosis scriptum non est, quia synecdochica est illa, quam Christus vsurpat, loquutio. Quamuis enim homines (vt optimè annotat doctissimus interpres) adulterii reos faciunt nō modo oculi, sed etiā cæcæ cordis vistiones: quia tamē vt plurimū oculi animos omi-nantur. animos suis lenociniis solicitant, & libido quasi per istas fores penetrat,ideo hac loquendi forma vsus est Christus, quum vellet concupiscentiam adulterii damnare. Attamen nihilominus res ipsa,quamChriftus fynecdochica sua loquutione designare voluit, disertis verbis in lege prohibetur, cuius praeceptum decimum expresse vetat, Ne quis vxorem proximi fui concupiscat.Somniaffe mihi videtur Oftorrodius, illa contra veritatem tam apertam scribens. Iudaei,prout fucosa Iustitiae larua mirifice sibi applaudiebantur,& in reputandis animae,& naturę nostrae corruptae infirmitatibus segnes,& socordes admodum erant,puros fe,& castos putabant,modo impuro concubitu corpus non polluerent, vt vt interea prauis desideriis, & lasciuientium cupiditatum affectibus, ipse animus eftuaret: Christus vero contra ex Decalogi praecepto decimo ostendit,adulteros esse coram Deo,non tantum qui alienas vxores corruperint,sed qui oculos polluerint impudico aspectu, at punctiones,ac titillationes admittendo fcortationem in animis conceperint. Et certe impudicus ille aspectus, quo quis in vxoris alienę amorem illicitum, ac desiderium inflammatur, & exardescit, motus est, aut bonus aut malus, aut indifferens.Atqui bonus non est,alioquin nec lege morali,nec à Christo prohiberetur,nec etiã indifferens dici potest,quoniam lex diuina nullam animi partem, nec vllas inclinationes, motus, aut operationes morales nobis relinquit liberas aut indifferentes, cùm nos iubet Dominum Deum diligere,ex toto corde,ex tota anima,& ex omnibus viribus nostris: Ergo necessario inde sequitur, illum malum ac prauum esse, & per consequens lege Dei prohibitum,alioquin ipsa lex diuina,perfecta iustitiae,integritatis,& sanctimoniae regula non effet,quod est contra veritatem, quā paulò ante euidentius, & luculentis argumentis,demonstrauimus. Hinc liquet vanitas argumenti primi quo Aduersarius veritatem impugnat: aut enim praeceptum decimum ex decalogo expungat oportet, & cum hypocritis illis Pharifeis, externam illam & simulatam obedientiam, ac fictitiam iustitiam stabiliat, aut Christum concedat genuinum legis sensum, à peruersis Iudaeorum explicationibus vindicaffe, & repurgaffe.
units.tr: Reply to the first: It is true that a lustful look is not written as adultery in the law of Moses, because the expression Christ uses is synecdochic. For although (as the most learned interpreter rightly notes) men make themselves guilty of adultery not only by the eyes but also by the visions of the blind heart, yet because the eyes mostly rule the minds and solicit them with their enticements, and lust penetrates as if through those doors, Christ used this form of speech when he wished to condemn the desire for adultery. Nevertheless the very thing which Christ wished to designate by his synecdochic speech is expressly forbidden in the law, whose tenth precept plainly says: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife. Ostorrodius seems to me to be dreaming when he writes things so contrary to such plain truth. The Jews, applauding themselves wonderfully in the disguise of a false righteousness, and being quite slack and careless in weighing the weaknesses of the soul and of our corrupt nature, thought themselves pure and chaste, provided they did not defile the body with impure intercourse, though meanwhile the soul itself boiled with wicked desires and the passions of wanton lusts. Christ, on the contrary, from the tenth precept of the Decalogue, shows that they are adulterers before God: not only those who have corrupted other men's wives, but those who have polluted their eyes with an immodest look and, by admitting pricks and tickles, have conceived fornication in their minds. And certainly that immodest look by which someone is inflamed and kindled with illicit love and desire for another's wife is either good, or bad, or indifferent. But it is not good, otherwise it would not be forbidden by the moral law or by Christ; nor can it be called indifferent, since the divine law leaves us no part of the mind, no inclinations, motions or moral operations free or indifferent, when it bids us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength. Therefore it necessarily follows that it is evil and depraved, and consequently forbidden by the law of God; otherwise the divine law would not be the perfect rule of righteousness, integrity and holiness, which is contrary to the truth that we demonstrated a little earlier more clearly and with luminous arguments. Hence the emptiness of the first argument by which the Adversary attacks the truth is plain: for he must either strike the tenth precept out of the Decalogue and, with those hypocritical Pharisees, establish that external and feigned obedience and fictitious righteousness, or he must concede that Christ vindicated and purged the genuine sense of the law from the perverse explanations of the Jews.

units.la: Ad fecundum: Lex Testamenti Veteris triplex fuit, moralis, ceremonialis,(de qua,vt pote abrogata nulla est controuersia)& iudicialis, seu politica. Si legem moralem dicat Aduersarius absolute, & simpliciter permisse, vt vxor quę marito
units.tr: To the second: The law of the Old Testament was threefold: moral, ceremonial (about which, as it has been abrogated, there is no controversy), and judicial or political. If the Adversary says that the moral law absolutely and simply permitted that a wife who to her husband

units.la: non placet,dimittatur,falsum affirmat,quia ad rei illius confirma-tionem,ex toto decalogo ne ne quidem afferri potest. Sin vero de lege politica hoc accipiatur, tum argumentum totum est ἀσεβὲς, quia praesentem quaestionem,quae est, An Christus in Novo Testamento legem Moralem per Mosen latam locupletauerit, correxerit, auxerit, & perfectiorem reddiderit; an vero genuina interpretatione, a peruersis Pharisaeorum expositionibus vindicauerit? & in qua non de politica lege,sed de morali est controuersia, nihil attingit, nec sententiam nostram impugnat. Et quamuis lege politica simpliciter & absolute permissum fuisset vxorem dimittere: haec tamen αὐτοχώρητος legi morali non posset esse praeiudicio. Quia non illa huius, sed haec illius regula ac norma esse debuit: & leges ciuiles, quoniam interdum ad hominum mores flectuntur, multa non bona saepe permittunt, propter subditorum malitiam, ne videlicet status Reipublicae perturbetur, sicuti nec omnia quae bona sunt ac Deo placent, iidem praecipiuntur. Hinc fit vt per leges ciuiles & politicas multa agere liceat absque reatu ciuili, quae tamen non absque culpa morali fiunt. At quanto salsius iudicabimus Aduersarii argumentum, cum ne politica quidem lex hoc simpliciter & absolute permittat, sed καθ' ὑπόθεσιν & αὐτοχώρητον, propter σκληροκαρδίαν videlicet, & duriticm cordis ipsorum, quam Moses ipse Israeli non semel exprobrauit. Liquet hoc quod affirmamus, ex ipsius Christi verbis Matth. cap. 19. verf. 8 inquientis, Moses ob duritiem cordis vestri permisit vobis dimittere vxores vestras: caeterum ab initio non fuit sic: quasi diceret: Non hoc vobis permisit, quasi rectum esset natura, sed sciens cordis vestri duritiem, leuius malum indulsit, ne grauius a vobis committeretur. Neque enim is probat diuortium, qui hoc maluit admitti, quam homicidium. Errorem igitur τῆς ἐπεξηγήσεως committit in hoc argumento Aduersarius, & in hac ipsa manifestam accidentis fallaciam. Quod denique Christus in eadem sua responsione contra illam petulantem coniugii violationem, & inueteratam diuortiorum licentiam, ad primam & puram Dei institutionem, tanquam ad fundamentum & legem prouocat, ex eo ipso solide demonstratur, Christum non nouam legem tulisse, sed turpem abusum sustulisse, ac proinde non vt nouum legislatorem, sed vt fidelem legis interpretem, & genuini sensus vindicem, consideranduu nobis esse.
units.tr: does not please should be dismissed, he asserts what is false, because not even one passage from the whole Decalogue can be cited to confirm that point. But if this is taken of the political law, then the whole argument is impious [ἀσεβὲς], because it touches nothing of the present question, which is: Did Christ in the New Testament enrich, correct, increase and make more perfect the moral law given through Moses, or did he vindicate it by genuine interpretation from the perverse expositions of the Pharisees? In that question the controversy concerns the moral, not the political, law, and the argument does not impugn our opinion. And although it had been permitted simply and absolutely by political law to dismiss a wife, that self-refuting [αὐτοχώρητος] permission could not be prejudicial to the moral law. For it was not the moral law that ought to be the rule of this, but the reverse; and civil laws, since they sometimes bend to men's morals, often permit many things that are not good, on account of the wickedness of subjects, namely so that the state of the commonwealth may not be disturbed, just as they do not command everything that is good and pleasing to God. Hence it comes that by civil and political laws many things may be done without civil guilt, which nevertheless are not done without moral fault. But how much more absurdly shall we judge the Adversary's argument, since not even the political law permits this simply and absolutely, but by way of supposition [καθ' ὑπόθεσιν] and conditionally [αὐτοχώρητον], on account of hardness of heart [σκληροκαρδίαν], namely the hardness of their heart, which Moses himself rebuked Israel for more than once. What we affirm is plain from the words of Christ himself in Matthew 19:8, saying: Moses, because of the hardness of your heart, permitted you to put away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. It is as if he said: He did not permit you this as though it were right by nature, but knowing the hardness of your heart, he indulged a lesser evil, so that a greater might not be committed by you. For he does not approve divorce who preferred that it be admitted rather than homicide. Therefore the Adversary commits an error of explanation [τῆς ἐπεξηγήσεως] in this argument, and in it a manifest fallacy of accident. Finally, that Christ, in the same reply, against that wanton violation of marriage and the inveterate licence of divorce, appeals to God's first and pure institution as to foundation and law, is solidly demonstrated by this very fact: Christ did not bring in a new law but removed a shameful abuse, and so we must regard him not as a new lawgiver but as a faithful interpreter of the law and a vindicator of its genuine sense.

units.la: Ad tertium & quartum: Vtriusque consequentia est falsa, quamuis enim Patres ob polygamiam, vel propterea quod concubinas habuerint, rint, reprehensos aut punitos fuisse à Deo nusquam legamus, illos tamen recte fecisse, aut lege morali illa concessa & permissa, non autem prohibita fuisse minime inde sequitur. Nam ne Iacobi quidem incestum, ut qui duas sorores simul duxerat reprehensum fuisse legimus, neque filiarum Lothi cum Patre concubitum, neque iniquissimum illud Davidis contra Mephibosceth indicium, & alia multa, quæ tamen peccata grauia contra legem Dei patrata fuisse constat. Atque hunc manifestum consequentiæ errorem notare sufficit, ut de polygamia Patrum pluribus differere minime sit necesse.
units.tr: To the third and fourth: Both consequences are false. For although we never read that the Fathers were rebuked or punished by God for polygamy or for keeping concubines, it by no means follows from this that they did right, or that the moral law conceded and permitted such things and did not forbid them. For we read that not even the incest of Jacob was rebuked, who had married two sisters at once, nor the intercourse of Lot's daughters with their father, nor that most unjust judgment of David against Mephibosheth, nor many other things, which nevertheless are known to have been grave sins committed against the law of God. It is enough to note this manifest error of consequence, so that there is no need to say more at length about the polygamy of the Fathers.

units.la: Et hæc de præcepto septimo aduersus adulterium lato: restat, ut de præcepto tertio quoque breuiter agamus.
units.tr: These things concern the seventh commandment, against adultery. It remains that we also briefly treat the third commandment.

units.la: Ostorrodius itaque Institutionum suarum capite 25. affirmat, Christum tertium decalogi præceptum de iuramento, non tantum a peruersa Pharisæorum interpretatione vindicasse & repurgasse, sed correxisse, locupletasse, & noui aliquid ad illud addidisse, quam suam sententiam probare conatur ex illis Christi verbis, Matth. 5. v. 33. 34. quibus inquit, Rursum audistis dictum: fuisse antiquis, non peierabis, sed reddes Domino, quæ tu iuraueris: Ego vero dico vobis: ne iuretis omnino: Ex quibus Christi verbis liquere ait Aduersarius, Christum aliquid ad legem illam per Mosem latam addidisse, quia Christus verba sua, verbis Mosis manifeste opposuerit, neque Moses vsquam dixerit, Non iurabis.
units.tr: Ostorodius, therefore, in chapter 25 of his Institutes, affirms that Christ did not merely vindicate and purge the third commandment of the decalogue from the perverse interpretation of the Pharisees, but corrected it, enriched it, and added something new to it. He tries to prove this opinion from those words of Christ in Matthew 5:33-34, in which, he says, You have heard that it was said to the ancients: you shall not swear falsely, but shall render to the Lord what you have sworn. But I say to you: do not swear at all. From these words of Christ, the Adversary says, it is clear that Christ added something to the law given through Moses, because he set his own words in plain opposition to the words of Moses, and Moses nowhere said, You shall not swear.

units.la: Resp. Primo falsum esse antecedens: nam Christum illa sua verba non ipsius Mosis verbis, sed peruersis, impiis, & falsis Pharisæorum expositionibus, quibus genuinum legis sensum adulterabant, & corrumpebant, in tota illa aduersus hypocritas & Sophistas illos disputatione, opposuisse, ex illis argumentis, quibus nos absolutam & summam legis moralis perfectionem demonstrauimus, liquide constat. Quum enim Deus præcepto illo tertio, non modo periuria damnasset, sed etiam iurandi leuitatem, ac temeritatem qua in rebus friuolis, & communi sermone, temere & conceptim nomen Dei arripitur, & reuerentiæ nominis diuini derogatur: Iudei autem in solis periuriis culpam transgressionis esse finxissent, sibi fas esse arbitrati, Dei nomine impune abuti, modo iurando neminem fallerent, ideo Christus fidus ille Scripturarum interpres, hunc crassum errorem, & impium abusum corrigit, ac reprehendit. Secundò, quoniam igitur particula illa omnino in verbis Christi non ad substantiam, sed ad formam iuramenti est referenda, & Christus (vt ipse Aduersarius fatetur, & aliquot argumetis probat) non quoduis, sed voluntarium, spontaneum ac temerarium, & quod sine iusta causa præstatur, Iuramentum prohibuit, Moses vero etiam vetuit, ne nomen Domini in vanum vsurpetur, hoc est, ne quis nomine Domini, sine causa, & temerè quisquam abutatur: ideò manifestum est Christum ad præceptum Mosis nihil addidisse, sed vnum idémque cum illo docuisse.
units.tr: Reply: First, the antecedent is false. It is clear from those arguments by which we demonstrated the absolute and supreme perfection of the moral law that Christ, in that whole disputation against those hypocrites and sophists, set his words not against the words of Moses himself, but against the perverse, impious and false expositions of the Pharisees, by which they adulterated and corrupted the genuine sense of the law. For in that third precept God condemned not only perjury but also the levity and rashness of swearing, by which the name of God is seized thoughtlessly and hastily in trivial matters and in everyday speech, and reverence for the divine name is diminished. The Jews, however, had pretended that the guilt of transgression lay only in perjury, and they judged it lawful to abuse the name of God with impunity, provided they deceived no one by swearing. Christ, therefore, that faithful interpreter of the Scriptures, corrects and rebukes this gross error and impious abuse. Secondly, since the particle omnino in the words of Christ must be referred not to the substance but to the form of the oath, and since Christ (as the Adversary himself admits and proves by several arguments) forbade not any oath whatever, but the voluntary, spontaneous and rash oath which is made without just cause, while Moses also forbade that the name of the Lord be taken in vain, that is, that anyone abuse the name of the Lord without cause and rashly, it is manifest that Christ added nothing to the precept of Moses, but taught the same thing as he did.

units.la: Ad hanc secundam responsionem excipit Aduersarius, & dicit, probari non posse, Mosen, idem illud, quod Christus Dominus prohibuerit, vetuisse, quia Moses vsus sit vocabulo Hebraico, quod falsò, mendaciter, non autem frustra, vel sine causa significet, vt manifestum sit ex aliis Scripturæ testimonijs, vt Exo.23. v.1. Non assumes rumorem falsum mendacij: & Deut.5.v 20. Non dices in proximum tuum testimonium falsum: quibus in locis nomen Hebraicum שוא falsum, vel mendacium significare, ac proinde liquere hinc ait, Christum mandatum illud Mosis, de iuramento, perfectius reddidisse, & libertatem illam sine causa, & sponte iurandi, quam Moses concesserat, modò falsò nemo iuraret, abrogasse.
units.tr: To this second reply the Adversary objects, and says that it cannot be proved that Moses forbade the same thing that Christ the Lord forbade, because Moses used a Hebrew word which signifies falsely or lyingly, not in vain or without cause, as is clear from other testimonies of Scripture, such as Exodus 23:1, You shall not raise a false report; and Deuteronomy 5:20, You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. In which passages the Hebrew word [שוא] means falsehood or lying, and hence, he says, it is clear that Christ made the commandment of Moses about swearing more perfect, and abrogated that freedom of swearing without cause and spontaneously which Moses had granted, provided that no one swore falsely.

units.la: Resp. Vanam reuera esse illam Aduersarii exceptionem, quæ enim est illa consequentia, nomen שוא quibusdam in locis significat falsum, & mendacium, ergò in præceptorum diuinorum catalogo idem nomen mendacium tantùm significat? At aliæ quoque sunt nominis illius significationes: ex puris igitur particularibus constat Aduersarii argumentum. Atque vt de rei veritate constet planius, tenendum est nomen שוא fœmininum genere, varias habere significationes. Interdum enim significat falsitatem, falsum mendacium, vt in duobus illis ab Aduersario citatis locis, & Psalm. 12.ver.2. Mendacium (שוא) loquitur quisque cum proximo suo Iob.31. v.5. Si ambulaui cum mendacio (שוא־עם) & festinauit ad dolū pes meus, i.Si non syncerè versatus sum, cum hominibus transigens, sed fucatè, aliud videlicet in ore, aliud in pectore clausum gerens. Ezec. 13.v.6. Viderunt vanum (שוא) id est Prophetiam vanam & falsam: vide etiam ver.7.& 8.& cap.12. v.24.& 21.v.29. Thr.2.v.14. & alibi. Interdum verò significationes habet alias, vt Ef.5.ver.48. Væ ijs qui attrahunt iniquitatem funibus vanitatis (שוא) & veluti funibus plaustri plaustri peccatum, id est, qui rationibus illicitis, aut vanis prætexti-tus, & illecebris peccata peccatis cumulant, & in illis se obstinant. Sic Iob.7. ver.3. Sic iure hereditario tradidi sum mihi mensibus va-nis (ירחי שוא) & noctes laboriosas patuerunt mihi, id est, hæreditate ac-cepi, veluti iure hæreditario obtinui mentes vanitatis, id est anxie-tatis, & molestiæ, seu menses molestos & cœlitus mihi constitutę, seu impositæ sunt noctes ærumnosæ. Iob.15.ver.31. Non credet qui vanitate (שוא) errat, quod vanitas (שוא) futura sit permutatio eius, id est, non credet per vanitatem, hoc est, rebus vanis, in quibus spem & fiduciam collocarat, deceptus, quod vanitas futura sit commuta-tio eius, id est, quod in vanitatem & nihilum sit redigendus totus ille prosper status, in quo erat. Quo in loco idem nomen diuer-sam significationem obtinet, priore siquidem loco res vanas signi-ficat, in quibus fiduciam collocabat, opes nempe gloriam & huius-modi mundana ac fluxa: posteriore vero vanitatem, in quam hæc omnia redigenda sunt, dum ex his decidens plane miser fiet, & calamitosus. Ef.1. versu 13. Ne addatis offerre sacrificium mendax (שקר) id est, vanum, irritumque, quo non delector, sed quod floccifacio. Et cap.30.versu 28. Spiritus eius torrens inundans, usque ad collum diuidit, ad ventilandum gentes in ventilabro vanitatis, id est ventilabro inutili, confracto, & futili, quod non paleam tantum, sed & bona, si qua semina insunt, excutit, quasi dicat, Deus omnes Israelis hostes perdet, & nihil relinquet. Hoc ipsum vero nomen שוא coniunctum cum verbo, aduerbialiter sumptum, vnanimi Hebræorum doctissimorum consensu idem significat, quod temere, vel frustrà, nulloque utili fine, vel sine causa: Psalm. 89.vers.48. Memento ego quid sim, quod tempus, propter quid frustra (שוא) creaueris omnes filios hominum. id est vt quid humani generis sobolem creasti? frustrane, nec vllo alio fine, quàm vt breuis exigat æui — Tempora perpetuo curarum exercita fluctu?
units.tr: Reply: The Adversary's objection is indeed empty. What is the inference? The word [שוא] signifies falsehood and lying in some places; therefore in the catalogue of divine precepts the same word signifies only lying? But that word has other meanings as well, so the Adversary's argument rests only on particular passages. To make the truth clearer, it must be remembered that the word [שוא] is feminine in gender and has various meanings. Sometimes it means falsity, a falsehood, a lie, as in the two passages the Adversary cites, and in Psalm 12:2, "Everyone speaks lying [שוא] with his neighbour"; Job 31:5, "If I have walked with falsehood [שוא־עם] and my foot has hastened to deceit", that is, if I have not dealt sincerely with men but deceitfully, having one thing in my mouth and another hidden in my breast; Ezekiel 13:6, "They have seen vanity" [שוא], that is, a vain and false prophecy; see also verses 7 and 8, chapter 12:24 and 21:29, Lamentations 2:14, and elsewhere. Sometimes, however, it has other meanings, as in Isaiah 5:18, "Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity" [שוא], "and sin as with cart-ropes", that is, those who by illicit reasons, pretexts and enticements heap sin upon sin and persist in them. So Job 7:3, "So I have been made to possess months of vanity [ירחי שוא], and laborious nights have been appointed for me", that is, I have received, as by hereditary right, months of vanity, that is, of anxiety and trouble, or troubled months appointed to me from heaven, or wearisome nights have been imposed on me. Job 15:31, "Let him not believe who errs through vanity [שוא] that vanity will be his recompense", that is, let him not trust, deceived by vain things, the things in which he placed his hope and trust, namely that his whole prosperous state, in which he was, will be turned into vanity and nothing. In this passage the same word has a different meaning in each place: in the first it signifies empty things in which he placed his trust, namely riches, glory and such worldly and fleeting things; in the second, vanity, into which all these are to be reduced, when he falls from them and becomes utterly wretched and miserable. Isaiah 1:13, "Do not add to bring a lying [שקר] offering", that is, a vain and void offering, in which I take no delight but which I hold cheap. And chapter 30:28, "His breath, like an overflowing torrent, reaches up to the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity" [שוא], that is, with a useless, broken and worthless sieve, which shakes out not only the chaff but also any good seed, as if to say that God will destroy all Israel's enemies and leave nothing. Moreover, this very word [שוא] joined with a verb and taken adverbially signifies, by the unanimous agreement of the most learned Hebrews, the same as rashly or in vain, to no useful end, or without cause. Psalm 89:48, "Remember what I am, why you have created all the sons of men in vain" [שוא], that is, why did you create the offspring of mankind? Is it in vain, with no other end than that it should spend its brief age, "times harassed by a perpetual flood of cares"?

units.la: Et Psal.127.v.1.2. Si Iehouah non ædificet domum, frustra (שוא) laborant ædificantes: Si Iehouah non custodiat ciuitatem frustra (שוא) vigilat custos: Frustra vobis est maturantibus surgere, tardantibus sedere, edentibus panem dolorum: sic dabit dilecto suo son ninn, id est, omnia sunt in manu Dei sita, frustrà, in cassum, & vana est omnis humana diligentia, industria, anxietas, & solicitudo, nisi diuina adsit, & faueat prouidentia, vanus est labor ædificantium, incassum excubat muris vigil custodia, nisi Dominus ipse vrbem ædificet & custodiat: frustra mane surgendo solem anteuertis, & vespere sero domum reuerteris, victum etiam quantumuis anxio labore vix parabis, & acquires: nisi Dominus benignam manum admouerit, qui in prouidentia ipsius acquiescentibus, iucundam ac tranquillam quietem largitur [Ier. 2. ver. 30. Frustra (Hebrew) percussi filios vestros, disciplinam non receperunt: i. frustra & verbis, & ferulis, ac castigationibus conatus sum illos in viam reducere, quia labor vterque vanus fuit & inutilis. & 4. ver. 30. Tu autem vastata quid facies? quod induis te coccino, quod ornas te ornamento aureo, quod pingis stibio oculos tuos: frustra (Hebrew) ornas te, contempserunt te amatores, animam tuam quærent, id est, hæc omnia nihil tibi proderunt. Et 6. ver. 29. Combustum sufflatorium, ab igne consumptum est plumbum frustra (Hebrew) conflauit conflator, & mali non sunt auulsi, i. vt conflator operam perdit aliquando dum studet, vt cōflando repurget argentum: sic Deus quum voluit repurgare scoriam Iuda, operam & oleum perdidit. Et 8. ver. 15. Quod oblitus est mei populus meus, frustra (Hebrew) adolent, & impingere eos faciunt, i. frustra & incassum obtendunt suas cæremonias, quod valde sacrificiis intenti sint, & peragant ea, quæ ad externum mei cultum pertinent. Et 46. v. 11. Ascende in Galaad, & tolle Balsamum, virgo filia Misraim, frustra (Hebrew) multiplicabis medicamina, sanitas non erit tibi: i. frustra ibis in Galaad pro comparanda resina, siue Balsamo: tanta enim erit strages in toto exercitu, vt nulla medicina iuuare possit, frustra igitur & in cassum multis medicaminibus vteris. Vnus ille locus est, in quo aduerbium illud Hebraicum, mendaciter & falso reddi potest: nempe Hof. cap. 10. ver. 4. Loquuntur verba execrando falso, pangendo fœdus: id est, omnes periuri, ac fœdifragi sunt, ac nouæ conspirationes quotidie inter ipsos pullulant. Ex hisce igitur omnibus iam liquido constat nomen illud (Hebrew) aduerbialiter sumptum, fere nunquam mendaciter, sed semper pene frustra, & nulla iusta de causa, ac in cassum, significare ita vt illa Mosis prohibitio non minus longe lateque se extendat, ac diffundat, quàm ipsius Christi mandatum, ideóque falsum esse quod affirmat Ostorrodius, nempe, aduerbium illud Hebraicum, in tertio decalogi præcepto, mendaciter, & falso, non autem temerè, frustra, & in vanum significare, ac proinde etiam futilem esse cõclufionem illam, quam ex falso illo exsculpit antecedente, Christum mandatum illud de iuramento, correxisse, & auxisse, libertatem videlicet illam sine causa & frustra ac sponte iurandi, quam Moses concessisse, salsissime affirmat, abrogando.
units.tr: Likewise Psalm 127:1-2, "If the LORD does not build the house, those who build it labour in vain" [שוא]; "If the LORD does not keep the city, the watchman stays awake in vain" [שוא]; "It is in vain for you to rise early and sit late, eating the bread of toil; so he gives to his beloved sleep" [שנה]. That is, all things lie in the hand of God; all human diligence, industry, anxiety and care is in vain and to no purpose unless divine providence is present and favours it. The labour of the builders is empty, the watch of the guard keeps vigil in vain, unless the Lord himself builds the city and keeps it. In vain you rise early and get up before the sun, and come home late in the evening; you will scarcely provide and acquire your food even with anxious toil, unless the Lord extends a kind hand, who gives a pleasant and tranquil rest to those who rest in his providence. Jeremiah 2:30, "In vain I have struck your sons; they have not received correction": that is, in vain I have tried by words, by rods and by chastisements to lead them back to the way, because both labours were empty and useless. And 4:30, "And you, when you are laid waste, what will you do? Though you clothe yourself in scarlet, though you adorn yourself with gold ornaments, though you paint your eyes with antimony, in vain you adorn yourself; your lovers despise you, they seek your life": that is, all these things will profit you nothing. And 6:29, "The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the smelter smelts, and the wicked are not removed": that is, as the smelter sometimes loses his labour while he strives to purify silver by smelting, so God, when he wished to purify the dross of Judah, lost his labour and oil. And 8:15, "Because my people has forgotten me, they offer sacrifices in vain and make them stumble", that is, they vainly and to no purpose put forward their ceremonies, because they are busy with sacrifices and perform those things which pertain to my external worship. And 46:11, "Go up to Gilead and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt; in vain you multiply remedies, there is no healing for you": that is, you will go to Gilead in vain to procure resin or balm, for the slaughter in the whole army will be so great that no medicine can help; so you use many remedies in vain and to no purpose. There is one passage in which that Hebrew adverb can be rendered lyingly or falsely, namely Hosea 10:4, "They speak words, swearing falsely, making a covenant": that is, all are perjured and covenant-breakers, and new conspiracies spring up among them daily. From all these things it is now clear that that word, taken adverbially, almost never means lyingly but nearly always in vain, without any just cause, to no purpose; so that Moses' prohibition extends as widely and broadly as the command of Christ himself. Therefore what Ostorodius affirms is false, namely that the adverb in the third commandment means lyingly and falsely, and not rashly, in vain and to no purpose; and it follows that his conclusion, which he most falsely draws from that false antecedent, is also futile: that Christ corrected and enlarged the commandment about swearing, abrogating, namely, that freedom of swearing without cause, in vain and spontaneously, which Moses had granted.

units.la: Atque haec lubuit ad illam quaestionem controversam, An videlicet Christus Matth.5. legem Moysis moralem a perversis Pharisaorum expositionibus repurgaverit, & genuino sensui restituerit, an vero novis praeceptis auxerit, correxerit, & locupletaverit? annotare. Eorum enim, quae in sequentibus capitibus septem tractantur, quaedam eiusdem sunt farinae cum antecedentibus iam refutatis, ac proinde iisdem responsionibus nostris diluuntur. Quaedam vero plane sunt ἀπροσδιόνυσα, & ad legem Moysis ἀδιάφορα penitus non pertinent: quaedam denique immiscentur vera & utilia, ex quibus tamen contra doctrinae nostrae veritatem nihil concludi potest.
units.tr: I have thought it worth noting these points on the controverted question, namely whether Christ, in Matthew 5, purged the moral law of Moses of the perverse expositions of the Pharisees and restored it to its genuine sense, or whether he added to it new precepts, corrected it, and enriched it. Of the matters treated in the seven following chapters, some are of the same kind as the points already refuted and so are answered by the same replies of ours. Some are plainly irrelevant [ἀπροσδιόνυσα] and have nothing to do with the law of Moses, being indifferent [ἀδιάφορα]. Some, finally, are mixed in with true and useful material, from which nothing can nevertheless be concluded against the truth of our doctrine.

units.la: Quae enim capite vigesimosexto de vindicta, disputat, ex illis Christi verbis Matt.5. ver.38.39. Audistis dictum fuisse, Oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente: Ego vero dico vobis, ne resistatis malo, sed quisquis te cadet in dextram tuam maxillam, obuerte ei alteram, videlicet praesentem controversiam nihil attingunt, quia in citato illo loco comparatio non cum lege morali, sed cum iudiciali, de qua nihil inter nos, & Aduersarium hac praesente disputatione disceptatur, est instituta. Deinde falsum quoque est antecedens illud Aduersarii, Moses, videlicet, privatam tantum vindictam prohibuisse, Christum vero & Paulum, etiam illa, quae per Magistratum fit, una cum litibus saecularibus coram tribunali politico, Christianis interdixisse. Paulus enim Christianis interdicit litibus, verum non omnino, sed primo, coram infideli Magistratu, quibus Euangelio dedecus infertur, & quasi impiorum sannis, exponitur Christi nomen. Liquet hoc quod dicimus ex 1.Cor.6. ver. ubi inquit Paulus, Sustinet aliquis vestrum negotium habens cum altero, iudicari sub iniustis, & non magis sub sanctis? Et ver.5. Ad erubescentiam vestram dico, adeo non est inter vos sapiens, ne vnus quidem qui possit diiudicare inter fratrem suum (& fratrem?) Unde manifestum est licere ad tribunal confessus Christiani, & hominum fidelium & sanctorum, contra fratrem prouocare, modo illud absque odio, & prauo in proximum affectu fiat, aut demonstrandum est Aduersario, Magistratum Christianum iustum, sanctum & fidelem non esse. Secundo, de causis quibusvis leuioribus, quod arguebat Corinthiorum φιλονεικίαν, turbidos animi affectus, impatientiam, & vindictę cupiditatem. Tertio, idque cum fratribus, & domesticis fidei, quibus oportebat ignoscere. Summa, litigandi libidinem reprehendit, & contendendi ardorem, ac iniurias leviores vult fratribus ignosci, paci Ecclesiae condonari, & mansuetudine tolerari, aut componi. Eadem etiam est Christi sententia, in loco citato, prohibentis vltionem priuatam, & ne quauis iniuria irritemur, & excandescamus in vindictæ cupiditatem. Alioquin si stricte ad literam malo non est resistendum, vtique (quod dictu blasphemum esset) Christus ipse in legem a se latam peccauit, qui percussus in maxillam vnam, non præbuit alteram, sed malo restitit, innocentiam suam tuendo, & iniustitiam redarguendo, Ioh.18. verf.23. Si male loquutus sum, ostende: sin autem bene, quid me percutis? Peccauit & Paulus, qui percussus in iudicio Pontifici iniusto vindictam a Deo minatur, Act. 23. v.3. Percutiet te Deus paries dealbate: Sequeretur etiam ingens, & misera ἀδελφία. Si enim malo simpliciter resistendum non esset, omniaque nostra prędæ, & direptioni relinquenda, omnis disciplina, non modo ciuilis, sed & œconomica, Ecclesiastica, & scholastica tolleretur, & horribilis licentia, ac impunitas scelerum inueheretur.
units.tr: As for what he argues in chapter 26 about vengeance, from Christ's words in Matthew 5:38–39, "You have heard that it was said, An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; but I say to you, do not resist evil, but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also," these have no bearing on the present controversy, because in that passage the comparison is made not with the moral law but with the judicial law, which is not in dispute between us and the Adversary in this discussion. Next, the Adversary's premise is also false, namely that Moses forbade only private vengeance, while Christ and Paul forbade Christians even those measures taken through the magistrate, together with secular lawsuits before the civil tribunal. Paul forbids Christians lawsuits, but not altogether; he forbids them, first, before an unbelieving magistrate, by which the gospel is disgraced and the name of Christ is exposed to the mockery of the impious. What we say is clear from 1 Corinthians 6, where Paul says: "Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints?" And in verse 5: "I say this to your shame: is there not among you a wise man who could decide between his brothers?" Hence it is plain that it is lawful to bring a complaint against a brother before the tribunal of a Christian and of faithful and holy men, provided it is done without hatred and an evil disposition toward the neighbour; or else the Adversary must show that a Christian magistrate is not just, holy and faithful. Second, Paul rebukes the Corinthians' contentiousness [φιλονεικία] over any trivial causes, their turbulent emotions, impatience and desire for revenge. Third, he does so with brothers and members of the household of faith, whom they ought rather to forgive. In sum, he reproves the lust for litigation and the ardour for contending, and wishes lighter injuries among brothers to be pardoned, condoned for the peace of the Church, and borne with gentleness or settled. Christ's judgment in the passage cited is the same: he forbids private vengeance, and that we be provoked by every injury and flare up in a desire for revenge. Otherwise, if we must not resist evil in the strict letter, then surely (a thing blasphemous to say) Christ himself sinned against the law he had given, since when struck on one cheek he did not offer the other, but resisted the evil, defending his innocence and rebuking the injustice: "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?" (John 18:23). Paul too would have sinned, who, struck in an unjust judgment by the high priest, threatens him with vengeance from God: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall" (Acts 23:3). There would also follow a huge and wretched confusion. For if evil were not to be resisted at all, and all our goods left to plunder and robbery, all discipline would be abolished, not only civil but domestic, ecclesiastical and scholastic, and a dreadful licence and impunity for crimes would be introduced.

units.la: Ea vero, quæ capite vigesimo septimo, de charitate, ex illis Christi verbis, Matth. 5. ver. 43. 44. Audistis dictum fuisse, Diliges proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Ego vero dico vobis, diligite inimicos vestros, benedicite ijs qui detestantur vos, benefacite ijs qui oderunt vos, & precamini pro ijs qui vos infestant, & persequuntur vos, conatur concludere Aduersarius falsa hypothesi & manifesta principii petitione, nituntur, quasi videlicet Christus nouum aliquod præceptum, verbis & mandato Mosis opponeret: Christum enim non inter suam & legis Mosaicæ doctrinam, sed inter legem prout falsis, & adulterinis Pharisæorum expositionibus depravata fuit, & genuinam suam interpretationem, illam comparationem instituere, hoc est, præcepta legis, non ita, vt in lege, si sensum spectes, habentur, sed vt erant a Scribis & Pharisæis depravata, & populo rudi perperam inculcata, adducere, ex eo liquet manifestissime, quod verba illa, odio habebis inimicum tuum, in Veteri Testamento, non tantum non extant vsquam, verum etiam illis plane contraria præcipiuntur, vt Leuit. 19. versu 18. Ne vlciscitor, neque iram asseruato in populares tuos, sed diliges proximum tuum, sicuti
units.tr: As for what he tries to conclude in chapter 27 about charity, from Christ's words in Matthew 5:43–44, "You have heard that it was said, You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy; but I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you," the Adversary relies on a false hypothesis and a plain begging of the question, as if Christ were setting some new precept against the words and command of Moses. For it is clear most manifestly from this that the comparison is not made between Christ's teaching and the Mosaic law, but between the law as it had been corrupted by the false and adulterated expositions of the Pharisees, and his own genuine interpretation; that is, he brings forward the precepts of the law not as they stand in the law when its sense is considered, but as they had been corrupted by the scribes and Pharisees and wrongly impressed on the uneducated people. This is most evident because the words "you shall hate your enemy" are nowhere to be found in the Old Testament; indeed, the very opposite is commanded there, as in Leviticus 19:18: "You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am Jehovah."

units.la: Non paginis indicatus, sed ab extremo margine saeculi suppressus. sicuti teipsum, Ego Iehouah, Exod. 23. ver. 4.5. Si offenderis bouem inimici tui, aut asinum eius errantem, omnino reducito eum ad illum : Si videris asinum oforis tui succumbentem oneri suo, dum abstines a deponendo (onere) illius, omnino deponito cum eo onus. Prouer. 25. ver. 21.22. Si esuriat ofor tuus, ciba eum pane, & si sitiat, da ei bibendum aquam, nam carbones ignis coacervabis super caput eius, & Iehouah rependet tibi. Ex quibus omnibus luculenter apparet, Christum illo in loco legem Moisis non correxisse, aut nouis praeceptis locupletasse, sed eius puritatem ab impuro Scribarum, Pharisaeorumque fermento vindicasse, genuinum videlicet eius sensum, tum a falsis interpretationibus, tum ab additamentis impiis Iudaeorum asserendo. Falsa interpretatio fuit, quod in his verbis, Diliges proximum tuum, appellatione proximi, aut amicum intelligebant, aut certe si qui amplius sapere videbantur, eum intelligebant, qui inimicus non esset. Additamentum fuit, quum dicerent contra autoritatem legis, habebis odio inimicum tuum. Utrumque evertit Christus commodissima interpretatione ὑπερ ... Nam primo affirmat illud aduersari Legi, quod dicitur, odio habebis inimicum tuum, quia tum iustitiae legis, & naturali iuri, Matth. 5. ver. 44. tum naturae, exemploque Dei ipsius aduersatur. verf. 45. Deinde vero aperte docet καθ' ἑλλήν, proximi appellatione omnes homines intelligendos, eosque non in se ipsis, sed in Deo considerandos esse, ac proinde omnes sine exceptione diligi oportere, quod exemplo suo, in omni tempore demonstrauit Deus, & Christus narratione euidentissima docuit. Luc. 10.
units.tr: Not indicated in the pages, but pushed down from the outer margin of the century. "As yourself. I am Jehovah." Exodus 23:4–5: "If you come upon the ox of your enemy, or his ass going astray, you shall certainly bring it back to him. If you see the ass of one who hates you lying under its burden, and you would refrain from unloading it, you shall certainly unload it with him." Proverbs 25:21–22: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink; for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Jehovah will reward you." From all these things it appears clearly that Christ in that place did not correct the law of Moses or enrich it with new precepts, but vindicated its purity from the impure leaven of the scribes and Pharisees, that is, asserting its genuine sense against both the false interpretations and the impious additions of the Jews. The false interpretation was this: by the word "neighbour" [proximus] in "you shall love your neighbour" they understood either a friend, or else, if some seemed to be wiser, one who was not an enemy. The addition was when, against the authority of the law, they said, "you shall hate your enemy." Christ overturned both by a most apt interpretation [ὑπερ ...]. For first he affirms that the saying "you shall hate your enemy" is contrary to the Law, because it opposes both the justice of the law and natural right (Matthew 5:44), and also the nature and example of God himself (verse 45). Then he plainly teaches that by the word "neighbour" all men are to be understood [καθ' ἑλλήν, proximi], and that they are to be considered not in themselves but in God, and therefore that all without exception are to be loved; this God has demonstrated by his example at all times, and Christ taught by a most evident narrative (Luke 10).

units.la: Aduersus responsionem nostram, & loca ex Veteri Testamento citata, duo excipit Aduersarius, primo inquit, Etiamsi verba illa, odio habebis inimicum tuum, in lege non reperiantur hodie : tamen potuisse fieri, ut aliquando in illa scripta fuerint : quemadmodum etiam illud de Christo, Et Nazaraeus vocabitur, nusquam apud Prophetas extet, etiamsi Matthaeus cap. 2. ver. 25. testetur, a Prophetis illud dictum fuisse. Secundo, etiamsi Salomon idem illud quod Paulus Rom. 12. ver. 20. de cibando inimico, etiam eo tempore, quo lex adhuc durauit, dixerit, tamen non praecepti aut mandati, quemadmodum apud Paulum, sed tantum exhortationis loco verba illa Salomonis habenda esse.
units.tr: Against our reply and the passages from the Old Testament cited, the Adversary raises two objections. First, he says: "Even if the words 'you shall hate your enemy' are not found in the law today, yet it may have happened that at some time they were written in it, just as also that about Christ, 'He shall be called a Nazarene,' appears nowhere among the Prophets, although Matthew (2:23) bears witness that this was spoken by the Prophets. Second, even if Solomon said the same thing that Paul says in Romans 12:20 about feeding an enemy, even at the time when the law still endured, nevertheless those words of Solomon are to be taken not as a precept or command, as in Paul, but only as an exhortation."

units.la: Respon. Ad primum, Exemplum esse dissimile, quia verba illa odio habebis inimicum tuum, nec proprie, nec figurate dicta in lege reperiuntur,imo pręcepta contraria ex Veteri Testamento à nobis sunt adducta : illa verò de Christo , Et Nazaræus vocabitur, etiamsi proprie & clarè, apud Prophetas non legantur dicta: tamen reperiuntur dicta obscurè & improprie,qua de re vide libri primi parallelum octauum Francisci Iunii.
units.tr: Answer. To the first: the example is not similar, because the words "you shall hate your enemy" are found in the law neither properly nor figuratively, but on the contrary we have adduced from the Old Testament precepts opposed to them. As for those words about Christ, "He shall be called a Nazarene," although they are not read as spoken by the Prophets properly and clearly, nevertheless they are found spoken obscurely and improperly; on this matter see the eighth parallel of the first book of Francis Junius.

units.la: Ad secundum: dicimus exceptionem secundam per primam evi-denter euerti:nam verba illa, Odio habebis inimicum tuum, affirma-re oportet scripta esse in lege,aut non scripta esse: Si dicat Aduer-sarius,aliquando in lege scriptum id fuisse,tum impium, & nefan-dum facinus imputat ipsi Salomoni, & Spiritui Sancto per ipsum loquenti,quasi ille,eo ipso tempore quo leges Mosaicæ, tanquam rescripta & mandata ipsius Dei, durare debuerunt,aliquid contra autoritatem diuinam vel legibus Dei plane contrarium præcipe-re,aut suadere voluerit. Quod cum absurdum sit & impium, ne-cesse est,vt fateatur verba illa in lege Mosis nunquam scripta suis-se. Quod si verum est,vt certissime est, manifestè apparet veritas sententiæ nostræ,qua affirmamus,verba illa, odio habebis inimicum tuum, non vt præceptum aliquod legale , sed vt impurum Iudæo-rum additamentum à Christo adduci, à quo vt & à falsa ipsius le-gis interpretatione, Christus genuinum sensum mandatorum di-uinorum vindicauerit. Quæ verò Oftorrodius in hoc & sequen-te vigesimo octauo capite de quatuor illis quæstionibus nullo ni-xus fundamento disserit : An videlicet liceat latronem occidere, si vita tutandæ non sit alia ratio? An Christianis liceat bellum gerere? An homini Christiano liceat Magistratus munere fungi? An Magi-stratui liceat gladio in maleficos animaduertere? Quarum tertiam ille concedit, modò ne sanguis vllus humanus, vlla de causa fun-datur, reliquas verò simpliciter negat, ea non est operæprecium hic operosè refellere,cùm eadem illa Anabaptistarum dogmata à nostris Theologis passim refutata legantur. Vide igitur Caluinum, Martyrem,Musculum & Aretium in locis Communibus,& com-mentaria nostrorum in libros Samuelis & Regum, item in Gene-sin, & caput decimum tertium Epistolæ ad Romanos , in primis verò Petrum Martyrem in caput secundum secundi libri Samue-lis. Denique scripta nostrorum aduersus Anabaptistas, in quibus de rebus illis prolixè disputarunt.
units.tr: On the second point: we say the second exception is plainly overturned by the first. For one must affirm either that the words You shall hate your enemy were written in the law, or that they were not. If the opponent says that they were written in the law at some time, then he imputes an impious and abominable crime to Solomon himself, and to the Holy Spirit speaking through him.
