He would have us believe that Solomon, at the very time when the Mosaic laws were meant to endure as the rescripts and commands of God himself, wished to prescribe or recommend something plainly contrary to divine authority and to the laws of God. Since this is absurd and impious, he must confess that those words were never written in the law of Moses. If that is true, as it most certainly is, the truth of our position is clearly evident. We affirm that the words you shall hate your enemy are not a legal precept but an impure addition of the Jews, which Christ rejected, and by which, as well as by their false interpretation of the law, Christ vindicated the genuine sense of the divine commands. As for what Ostorrodius argues in this chapter and the following twenty-eighth chapter about four questions, resting on no foundation at all, namely: Is it lawful to kill a robber if there is no other way of protecting life? Is it lawful for Christians to wage war? Can a Christian man hold the office of magistrate? Can the magistrate punish evildoers with the sword? Of these he concedes the third, provided no human blood is shed for any cause whatever, but he simply denies the rest. It is not worth the effort to refute these at length here, since those same dogmas of the Anabaptists are found refuted everywhere by our theologians. See therefore Calvin, Martyr, Musculus and Aretius in their Common Places, and our men's commentaries on the books of Samuel and Kings, likewise on Genesis and on chapter thirteen of the Epistle to the Romans; and above all Peter Martyr on the second chapter of the second book of Samuel. Finally, see the writings of our men against the Anabaptists, in which they have discussed those matters at length.

units.la: Locus de excommunicatione, & disciplina Ecclesiastica quem capite
units.tr: Locus de excommunicatione, & disciplina Ecclesiastica quem capite

units.la: capite vigesimo nono prolixè tractat Aduersarius, ad præsentem quæstionem & controuersiam non pertinet, sed planè alienus est, quia aliud est de lege morali, quæ singulis hominibus præstanda incumbit, omnésque & singulos obligat, aliud verò de totius Ecclesiæ regimine agere. Vtinâ verò hoc ab omnibus Ecclesiis, Principibus, ac Magistratibus Christianis impetrari posset, vt disciplinâ Ecclesiasticam, secundùm mandatum & canones Christi, atque Apostolorum instaurarent, instaurat àmque constanter & prudenter exercerent! Quod vt profligatissimis hisce temporibus tandem fiat, omnibus fidelibus Dei seruis, & Ecclesiarum Pastoribus, summis & ardentissimis precibus à Deo est contendendum.
units.tr: In chapter twenty-nine my opponent treats at length matters that do not bear on the present question and controversy at all, because it is one thing to deal with the moral law, which every person is bound to keep and which obliges each and all, and quite another to deal with the government of the whole Church. Would that all Churches, Christian princes and magistrates could be brought to restore church discipline steadily and wisely, and to exercise it, according to the commandment and canons of Christ and the Apostles! So that this may at last happen in these most corrupt times, all faithful servants of God and ministers of the Churches must press it on God with the most earnest and fervent prayers.

units.la: Quæ idem Aduersarius capite trigesimo & trigesimo primo de temperantia in victu, & modestia in amictu, de frugalitate item, & σωφροσύνη contra luxum, fastúmque insolentem, φιλαρχίαν deinde, & insatiabilem opum cumulandarum cupidinem ac intemperiem, procacitatem denique, & linguæ intemperantiam, disputat, si superstitione careant, minimè improbamus, & optamus illa vitia ab hominibus Christianis, & in Rempublicam Israeliticam ascitis, aliena, virtutes autem contrarias in iisdem maximè conspicuas esse.
units.tr: What the same opponent argues in chapters thirty and thirty-one, on temperance in food and modesty in dress, on frugality too, and sobriety [σωφροσύνη] against luxury and proud insolence, then on love of rule [φιλαρχία], on the insatiable desire to heap up wealth and intemperance, and finally on shamelessness and intemperance of the tongue, we do not in the least condemn, provided they are free of superstition. We wish that these vices were far from Christians and from the commonwealth of Israel, and we observe that the contrary virtues shine most clearly in those same men.

units.la: Sed interim petitionis principii ipsum arguo, quia falsò affirmat, Deum in veteri Testamento, vanos sermones, scurriles facetias, mendacia denique ipsa, & calumnias, ac maledicta, nusquam prohibuisse expresse. Contrarium enim ostendimus in antecedentibus, vbi legem Dei perfectam iustitiæ diuinæ normam esse demonstrauimus. Et lex illa, quæ præcipit, vt Deum diligamus ex toto corde nostro, ex tota anima nostra, & ex omnibus viribus nostris, proximum autem sicut nosmetipsos, num quæso profanandi nominis diuini licentiam, & conuitiis, contumeliísque in proximi famam & existimationem debacchandi petulantiam indulgeret? Dormitauit hîc Ostorrodius.
units.tr: But meanwhile I charge him with begging the question, because he falsely asserts that God in the Old Testament never expressly forbade empty words, buffoonish jests, nor indeed lies themselves, slanders and abuse. For we have shown the contrary in what precedes, where we demonstrated that the law of God is the perfect rule of divine righteousness. And does that law, which commands us to love God with all our heart, all our soul and all our strength, and our neighbour as ourselves, grant licence to profane the divine name, or indulgence to the insolence of raging with insults and abuse against a neighbour's good name and reputation? Ostorrodius has nodded off here.

units.la: Capite denique trigesimo secundo, vbi denuò de charitate agit, tria tractat Aduersarius. Primò probare conatur, longè perfectiorem charitatem erga proximum in Euangelio, quàm à lege requiri: quod vt ostendat, duplex discrimen inter charitatem Euangelicam (duplicem enim ille charitatem confingit) & charitatem legalem statuit, primum ratione obiecti circa quod charitas versari & occupari debeat, id est, respectu eorum qui à nobis sunt diligèdi, & dicit se difcrimen illud iam in antecedentibus demonstrasse, quia probauerit, sub Euangelio, quemuis hominem, cuiuscunque ordinis, conditionis, & religionis illesit, tam inimicum, qui male de te sit meritus, quam amicum, & qui bene tibi fecerit, proximi nomine intelligendum, diligendum, & omnibus amoris & charitatis Christianæ officijs prosequendum esse, quod ipsum, cum in lege nusquam præcipiatur, sed proximi nomine ille tantũ qui eiusdem cultus, religionis, ac fœderis cum Deo, socius fuit, intelligatur, ideo euidens in eo discrimen legis & Euangelij inde apparere concludit. Secundum ratione modi, quũ proximus à nobis diligi debeat, cuiusmodi respectu maximum inter charitatem legalem, & Euangelicam discrimen esse, duabus rationibus probare conatur. Prima est: Quamuis ipsum Euangelium nihil maius aut perfectius præcipere videatur illis, quæ à lege nobis iniunguntur, siquidem lex disertis verbis dicat, Diliges proximũ tuũ sicut temet ipsum: tamé verba illa legis, non secundum literalem sensum, sed restrictiuè intelligi oportere: quum autem verba illa in Euangelio, Diliges proximum tuum sicut temetipsum, non restrictiuè, sed vniuersaliter, & secundum literam sint accipienda, ideo sequi ait, ingens discrimen inter charitatem legalem, & Euangelicam statuendum esse. Sed attendatur quæso ratio, qua antecedens, verba videlicet illa in lege de proximo diligendo non vniuersaliter, sed restrictiuè sumenda esse probat. In Lege scriptum est, inquit, Oculum pro oculo. Si itaque præceptum illud, Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum, non restrictiuè, sed secundum literam, & vniuersaliter accipiendum esset, tum nullus oculum proximi pro suo postulare posset, quoniam quicunque alteri oculum excusserit, tamen cuperet suum propterea non eruì, sed delictum sibi condonari. Secunda est, quia Christus velit vt proximum nostrum magis quàm nosmet ipsos diligamus, ita vt pro ipso etiam mortem ipsam libenter subeamus, Iohan.15. verf.13. 1.Iohan.3. verf.16. de quo ipso nullum in tota lege præceptum extet, vnde etiam Christus illud suum, & nouum mandatum appellauerit.
units.tr: Finally, in chapter thirty-two, where he again treats of love, my opponent deals with three points. First he tries to prove that the love required toward neighbours in the Gospel is far more perfect than what the law requires. To show this he sets up a twofold distinction between Gospel love (for he invents a twofold love) and legal love. The first is by reason of the object on which love ought to be directed and exercised, that is, with respect to those whom we must love; and he says that he had already shown this distinction in the foregoing, since he proved that under the Gospel every man, of whatever rank, condition or religion, whether an enemy who has done you wrong or a friend who has done you good, is to be understood and loved under the name of neighbour and to be served with all the offices of Christian love. Since this is nowhere commanded in the law, but under the name of neighbour is understood only the one who shared the same worship, religion and covenant with God, he therefore concludes that a clear distinction between law and Gospel appears from this. The second distinction is by reason of the manner in which the neighbour ought to be loved; with respect to this he tries to prove that the difference between legal and Evangelical love is greatest, by two arguments. The first is this: Although the Gospel itself seems to command nothing greater or more perfect than what is enjoined on us by the law, since the law says in plain words, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, yet those words of the law must be understood restrictively, not according to the literal sense; but since those words in the Gospel, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, are to be taken not restrictively but universally and according to the letter, therefore he concludes that a huge distinction must be posited between legal and Evangelical love. But let us ask to see the reasoning by which he proves that the antecedent, namely that those words about loving the neighbour in the law are to be taken not universally but restrictively. It is written in the law, he says, An eye for an eye. If, therefore, that precept, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, were to be taken not restrictively but according to the letter and universally, then no one could demand an eye of his neighbour for his own, since whoever has knocked out another's eye would still wish that his own eye not be plucked out in return, but that his offence be forgiven him. The second is this: because Christ wills that we love our neighbour more than ourselves, so that we willingly undergo death itself for him, John 15:13; 1 John 3:16, a precept which is nowhere in the whole law, whence Christ also called it his own and new commandment.

units.la: Resp. Quia vnus est Dominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma omnium filiorum Dei, Veteris & Noui Testamenti: ideo charitatis virtus vtrobique vna specie est in omnibus, non multiplex, licet numero & gradu sit diuersa, prout vnicuique mensuram fidei, quę charitatis radix atque mater est, admetitur Dominus. Non igitur charitas alia Euangelica, alia legalis confingenda, quemadmodũ nec fides ipsa alia legalis, alia Euangelica recte dicitur, quam ἐκστιμῶν propterea appellat Apostolus, 1.Pet.1.v.1. Hinc duplex illud charitatis Euangelicæ & legalis discrimen, duplex otiosi & delirantis ingenii figmentum esse perspicitur. Nam primum quod attinet, à diuerso obiecto sumptum, negamus Aduersarium cap.27. demonstrasse, vllum, quod ad charitatis officium, legis & Euangelii discrimen, quasi videlicet nomen proximi, in Nouo Testamento, latius quàm in Veteri sumendū esset, & ibi quemuis hominem, hīc verò Israelitam tātum significaret. Illam enim significationis diuersitatem, inane & impium Pharisæorum sanctā Domini legē, salsissimis suis expositionibus petulanter depravantium, figmentū esse, animaduersiones nostræ, in caput 27. luculenter, opinor, demonstrant. Discrimen secundum, quod in charitatis & dilectionis modo ponit Aduersarius, quantum concernit, falsum est, verba illa diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum, in lege restrictiue, in Euangelio autem vniuersaliter, & secundum literam interpretanda esse. Quem enim sensum illorum verborum nobis daturus esset Aduersarius? cur in medium non protulit interpretationem, si non ipsummet eius puduit? Ratio subiuncta à talionis lege desumpta, præceptum charitatis nō restringit, quia poenam illā Deus permisit Iudicibus, non priuatis hominibus, cui Magistratus politici potestati, diuinitus concessæ, priuati hominis Christiani officium non potest esse præiudicio. Præceptum Christi de vita pro salute proximi impendenda, non additamentum aut nouum mandatum in se, sed veram legis ἐντολῆς complectitur, qua ostendit Dominus, quodnam sit verum & infallibile charitatis sincerae indicium & τυμῶν, nempe si quis pro fratre & proximo suo animam ponat. Quod verò Christus præceptum illud de mutua charitate inter Christianos, nouum & nouum appellat, sicut & Paulus legem Christi illud vocat Galat. capite sexto, versu secundo; id non propterea fit, quod ante Christum mandatum illud mutuæ dilectionis non extiterit, sed quia illud depravatis hominum moribus antiquatum, ipse nouus Magister renouauit, ac studiosissimè inculcauit, deinde à falsis Iudæorum additamentis, & tortuosis corruptelis depravatum, eius sensum pristinæ puritati restituit, ipso insuper opere & proprio exemplo perfectissimè impleuit, dum videlicet adhuc inimici essemus, pro nobis moriēdo, denique fidelibus per communicationem Spiritus S. hoc largitur, ut & ipsi illud præstare valeant. Aliud itaque est,ac nouum illud Christi mandatum charitatis in proponendi modo, non ipsa substantia, aut eius parte vlla. Vnde vetus doctrina dicitur à Ioh.1 Epist.2.v.8.nempe quoad substantiam ipsam,noua autem ibidem,quoad formam &modum tractandi,quia tenebrae præterceunt, ac lux vera iam lucet, illuminans nimirum corda, ac remouens animum ad hoc vt charitatis doctrina sit efficax.
units.tr: Answer. Because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism of all the sons of God, of the Old and New Testaments, therefore the virtue of love is one and the same in kind in both, not manifold, although it differs in number and degree, according as the Lord apportions to each the measure of faith, which is the root and mother of love. Hence love is not to be invented as one Evangelical and another legal, just as faith itself is not rightly called one legal and another Evangelical; the Apostle calls it elect [ἐκλεκτῶν] on that account, 1 Pet. 1. Thus that twofold distinction between Evangelical and legal love is plainly a twofold fiction of an idle and raving mind. For as to the first, taken from a different object, we deny that my opponent in chapter 27 showed any distinction between law and Gospel in the duties of love, as though the name of neighbour were to be taken more widely in the New Testament than in the Old, so that there it would mean any man whatever, but here only an Israelite. Our observations on chapter 27, I think, clearly demonstrate that this difference in meaning is an empty and impious invention of the Pharisees, who with their saltiest expositions wantonly corrupted the holy law of the Lord. The second distinction, which he places in the manner of love, is, so far as it concerns us, false: that the words You shall love your neighbour as yourself are to be interpreted restrictively in the law and universally and according to the letter in the Gospel. For what sense of those words would my opponent give us? Why did he not bring forward an interpretation, unless he himself was ashamed of it? The argument taken from the law of retaliation does not restrict the command of love, because God permitted that punishment to judges, not to private persons; the duty of a private Christian cannot prejudice the power of the civil magistrate, which was granted by God. Christ's precept about laying down one's life for the salvation of a neighbour is not an addition or a new commandment in itself, but embraces the true commandment [ἐντολῆς] of the law, in which the Lord shows what is the true and infallible sign [τεκμήριον] and proof of sincere love, namely if anyone lays down his soul for his brother and neighbour. As for Christ calling that precept of mutual love among Christians new, just as Paul calls it the law of Christ in Galatians 6:2, this is not because the commandment of mutual love did not exist before Christ, but because, though it had been made obsolete by corrupt human morals, the new Master himself renewed it and most diligently impressed it on us; then, after it had been depraved by the false additions and crooked corruptions of the Jews, he restored its sense to its original purity; moreover, by his own work and perfect example he fulfilled it, while we were still enemies, by dying for us; and finally he grants to believers, through the communication of the Holy Spirit, that they too may be able to perform it. Thus the new commandment of Christ differs from the old in the manner of proposing love, not in its substance or any part of it. Hence the old doctrine is called in 1 John 2:8 old as to its substance itself, but new there as to its form and manner of teaching, because the darkness is passing away and the true light already shines, illuminating hearts and moving the mind so that the doctrine of love may be effective.

units.la: Secundò occasione ex discrimine primo charitatis sub Lege, & Euangelio, hoc est,ex definitione proximi desumpta,disputat,quenam sit vera in Christum fides, ac quisnam proinde verus in Christo frater sit agnoscendus, sed quia illa omnia in capite quarto à nobis sunt examinata,supervacaneum esset,quicquam ad illa,hoc loco,addere.
units.tr: Secondly, on the occasion of the first difference between love under the Law and under the Gospel, that is, from the definition of "neighbour" he has taken up, he argues what the true faith in Christ is, and who therefore is to be acknowledged as a true brother in Christ. But since we examined all those matters in the fourth chapter, it would be superfluous to add anything to them here.

units.la: Tertiò & vltimò,illam tractationem de munere Christi Propheticò,eiusdémque promissionibus & mandatis concludit : sed quia ex salutis & iustificationis nostræ materia, meritum & satisfactionem Christi penitus excludit,eámque in solam obedientiam,quam secundùm normam præceptorum Christi præstare tenemur, pro impietate Sociniana transcribit, falsámque illam sententiam, in sequentibus demonstrare conatur:ideo promittit,se antequam vlterius progrediatur,capita quædam explicaturum & declaraturum esse, sine quorum vera notitia & intelligentia facile quis in perniciosam illam opinionem prolabatur,vt existimet,se nihilominus æternæ salutis participem fieri posse,etiamsi mandata Christi non seruet. Atque eiusmodi capita tria esse dicit: Primum est, An penes liberum hominis arbitrium sit necne,mandata Dei,quæ per Christum sanciuit,seruare?id est, An homo liberi arbitrij sui viribus, Dei mandata per Christum lata seruare possit,necne? Secundum est, An Deus ab æterno de vnoquoque hominum particulariter apud se decreuit, quinam saluari aut damnari debeant? Tertium est, An Deus nos,etiamsi Christi mandata non seruemus, modò in Christum credamus(loqui autem se ait de fide in Christum cum vulgo, quasi illa aliud & diuersum quid esset, quàm mandatorum Christi obseruatio) iustificare,hoc est,peccata remittere nobis velit necne? Quæ tria capita Aduersarius aliquot sequentibus capitibus prolixè tractat,nos contextum disputationis prosequemur, & omnia quæ ab ipso in medium adferuntur,ordine ac diligenter, gratia & auxilio Spiritus sancti freti,examinabimus.
units.tr: Thirdly and lastly, he concludes that treatment of Christ's prophetic office and of his promises and commands. But since he excludes entirely from the matter of our salvation and justification the merit and satisfaction of Christ, and transfers it solely to the obedience which we are bound to render according to the rule of Christ's precepts, in the manner of the Socinian impiety, and sets out to demonstrate that false opinion in what follows, he therefore promises that, before he proceeds further, he will explain and clarify certain heads, without a true knowledge and understanding of which anyone may easily slip into that pernicious opinion, namely that he can nevertheless become a partaker of eternal salvation even if he does not keep the commands of Christ. And he says there are three such heads: The first is, Whether it lies within man's free will or not to keep the commands of God which he has ratified through Christ? that is, Whether man, by the powers of his free will, is able to keep the commands of God given through Christ or not? The second is, Whether God from eternity decreed with himself, concerning each man individually, who ought to be saved or damned? The third is, Whether God, even if we do not keep the commands of Christ, provided only that we believe in Christ (he says he speaks of faith in Christ in the common manner, as though it were something other and different from the observance of Christ's commands), wishes to justify us, that is, to remit our sins, or not? The adversary treats these three heads at length in several following chapters; we shall follow the course of the disputation, and, relying on the grace and help of the Holy Spirit, we shall examine in order and carefully everything that he brings forward.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: In quo tum status controuersiæ de Libero hominis arbitrio proponitur, & explicatur, tum sententia orthodoxa de illo ex Scripturis demonstratur.
units.tr: In which the state of the controversy concerning free choice is set out and explained, and the orthodox view of it is demonstrated from the Scriptures.

units.la: OTA Aduersarÿ disputatio duabus partibus absoluitur, quarum prima de Libero hominis Arbitrio, & hac occasione de primi hominis tam ante, quàm post lapsum statu & conditione, déque imagine Dei in homine, denique de peccato originali: altera verò de liberi arbitrii viribus agit: illa capite trigesimo tertio, hæc verò capite trigesimo quarto continetur.
units.tr: The Adversary's disputation is completed in two parts. The first concerns Free Choice itself and, on this occasion, the state and condition of the first man both before and after the fall, the image of God in man, and finally original sin. The second deals with the powers of free choice. The first is contained in chapter thirty-three, the second in chapter thirty-four.

units.la: Partem huius disputationis primam, quæ est de ipso Libero hominis Arbitrio, quantum concernit, quæstionem controuersam in hunc modum proponit Aduersarius: An homo habeat liberum Arbitrium, nécne ? Sic enim verba illa Germanica, An homo habeat liberam voluntatem nécne?reddenda Latinè existimo, quum illam facultatē animæ, quæ à Latinis Liberum Arbitrium nominari consueuit, Germani liberam voluntatem appellare soleant. Sed parum interest, vtro modo verba illa interpretemur, rem ipsam & quæstionem controuersam quantum attinet, tot ambiguitatum & æquiuocationum integumentis inuoluta proponitur illa ab Aduersario, vt iis non sublatis, tota disputatio nostra vaga, incerta, ac plané ridicula futura esset. Quum enim ipsa tum Arbitrÿ, tum adiunċti eius, nempe Libertatis vox fit πολυσημος & ipsum de quo quæritur, Liberi Arbitrii subiectum, nempe Homo, non sit vnum quid & simplex, atque iisdem qualitatibus vestitum, sed eiusmodi circunstantiis diuersum, quibus præsupponuntur causæ tales, quæ status hominis tam diuersos efficiunt, vt ipsa quoque Arbitrii libertas, secundùm diuersitatem illorum necessariò variet, ipsum denique Liberi Arbitrii obiectum, seu materia circa quam, specie sit varia & multiplex, neque horum quicquam abAduersario in quæritur ... stione proposita definitum sit ac determinatum: ideo satis apparet ad illam absolutè & simpliciter responderi non posse: verùm ante omnia tum ipsius liberi Arbitrii definitionem, & boni obiecti distinctionem præmittendam, tum statuum hominis diuersitatem considerandam esse, quæ tria capita, quoad fieri poterit, breuiter & succinctè expediemus.
units.tr: As far as the first part concerns free choice itself, the Adversary puts the controverted question in this way: Does man have free choice or not? I think the German words, "Whether man has free will or not," are best rendered in Latin in this form, since Germans usually call that faculty of the soul which Latins are accustomed to call liberum arbitrium "free will." But it matters little which way we translate those words. The question itself, as far as the controversy goes, is put forward by the Adversary wrapped in so many ambiguities and equivocations that, if they were not removed, our whole disputation would be vague, uncertain and plainly ridiculous. For the word arbitrium and its attribute, the word libertas, are many-sensed [πολυσημος], and the very thing under inquiry, the subject of free choice, namely man, is not one simple thing clothed with the same qualities. He differs according to circumstances which presuppose such causes as make the states of man so different that the freedom of choice itself necessarily varies with them. Lastly, the object of free choice, that is the matter about which it is exercised, is manifold and various in kind, and none of these things has been defined or determined in the question as the Adversary proposes it. So it is clear enough that it cannot be answered absolutely and simply. Rather, before all else, we must first set out the definition of free choice itself and the distinction of the good object, and then consider the diversity of man's states. These three heads we shall dispatch as briefly and succinctly as we can.

units.la: Arbitrij itaque nomen, proprie sententiam Iudicis, quam in dirimenda controuersia inter partes litigantes pronuntiat, significans, ad res omnes, quæ tum in deliberationem, tum vel maximè in electionem cadunt, accommodari cœpit. Et illarum quidem rerum respectu, quæ in deliberationem cadunt, ad intellectum refertur, & nihil aliud est, quàm metis, siue intellectus, tum facultas, qua mens de aliqua re sibi proposita, id est, obiecto intelligibili, iudicare ac discernere potest: tum etiam ipsum iudicium, secundùm illam facultatem peractum, quo rem aliquam veram vel falsam, bonam vel malam esse iudicat. Illarum verò rerum consideratione, quæ in electionem ex deliberatione ortam cadere possunt, ad voluntatem refertur, & est voluntatis tum facultas, qua res ab intellectu sibi monstratas, aut eligere, appetere, ac desiderare potest ratione boni, aut repudiare, odisse & abominari, ratione mali: tum electionem ipsam, qua voluntas rem ab intellectu monstratam vel desiderat & prosequitur ratione boni, vel odit ac fugit ratione mali: quod voluntatis arbitrium, desiderium ac placitum, alias αὐτοκρατορία appellatur.
units.tr: The name arbitrium properly means the judgment of a judge, which he pronounces in settling a dispute between litigating parties, and it has come to be applied to all things that fall under deliberation or, above all, under choice. With regard to those things that fall under deliberation, it is referred to the intellect, and it is nothing other than the faculty of the mind by which it can judge and discern about some matter set before it, that is an intelligible object; and also the judgment itself, carried out by that faculty, by which it judges some thing to be true or false, good or bad. With regard to those things that can fall under choice, which arises from deliberation, it is referred to the will, and it is both the faculty of the will by which it can choose, desire or wish for things presented by the intellect under the aspect of good, or reject, hate and abominate them under the aspect of evil; and the choice itself, by which the will either desires and pursues the thing shown by the intellect under the aspect of good, or hates and flees it under the aspect of evil. This decision, desire and pleasure of the will is otherwise called self-determination [αὐτοκρατορία].

units.la: Libertas, quæ proprium Arbitrii adiunctum est, pro ratione duplicis operationis seu actus liberi arbitrii, primi nempe & secundi, in genere duplex est. Respectu actus primi varia est: primo, libertas a coactione seu vi, qua violetus principii externi impulsus & aduersantia voluntati impedimenta remouentur. Secundo, libertas ab omnimoda necessitate, qua voluntas non necessariò determinatur ad vnum obiectum actu immutabili. Tertiò, à iure ac imperio præcipientis, & obligatione præstandæ obedientiæ, qua quis legibus solutus, nullius superioris inspectionis curæ & gubernationi subiectus, sed plane è αὐτεξούσιον est. Quarto, libertas à peccato, & dominio illius, qua quis vel potest non peccare si velit, potest non peccare si velit, autem peccare si velit, vel non potest peccare, ac ne velle quidem. Quinto, libertas à miseria, qua quis propter miseriam & immunitatem ab omni malo culpæ, omnis quoque mali poenæ expers est. Sed de hoc vltimo, & tribus primis libertatis modis, nulla hic est quæstio, verùm dispiciendum est, de illa libertate, quæ est à peccato, & dominio illius, de qua inter nos & Aduersarium potissima est controuersia, vt postea apparebit. Respectu verò actus secundi, seu operationis liberi Arbitrii, quæ est electio, libertas rursus distinguitur in libertatem contrarietatis, seu specificationis: & libertatem contradictionis, siue exercitii: illa seligitur vnum ex duobus vel pluribus, ista vno proposito, illud acceptatur aut reiicitur: seu illa est libertas simpliciter aliquid volendi, vel non volendi: hæc autem sic vel aliter volendi.
units.tr: Libertas, which is the proper attribute of free choice, is in general twofold according to the twofold operation or act of free choice, namely the first and the second. With respect to the first act it is various: (1) freedom from coercion or force, by which the violence of an external impulse and the obstacles opposed to the will are removed; (2) freedom from all necessity, by which the will is not necessarily determined to one object by an unchangeable act; (3) freedom from the right and command of one who gives orders, and from the obligation to render obedience, by which a person is released from laws, subject to the care and government of no superior, and is wholly self-governing [αὐτεξούσιον]; (4) freedom from sin and its dominion, by which a person is able not to sin if he wills, is able to sin if he wills, or is not able to sin, nor even to will it; (5) freedom from misery, by which a person, on account of his freedom from misery and from every evil of guilt, is also free from every punishment of evil. But concerning this last, and the first three modes of liberty, there is no question here. We must examine rather that freedom which is from sin and its dominion, which is the chief point of controversy between us and the Adversary, as will appear later. With respect to the second act, the operation of free choice which is choice, liberty is again distinguished into freedom of contrariety or specification, and freedom of contradiction or exercise. By the former one chooses one of two or more things; by the latter, with one proposal, one accepts or rejects it. Or the former is the liberty simply to will or not to will something, while the latter is to will it in this way or that.

units.la: Bonum obiectu, seu materia circa quâ versatur liberū Arbitrium, duorum est generum. Primi generis sunt actiones illæ humiliores, quæ sensibus & rationi humanæ subiacent, nec captum nostrum naturalem superant. Eaeque rursum duplices: aut merę naturales cuiusmodi sunt actiones cum brutis nobis communes, vt comedere, bibere, dormire, & similes aliæ: aut insuper proæreticæ, quæ & morales siue ciuiles dicuntur, & quæ omnibus hominibus communes sunt, cuiusmodi sunt loqui, ratiocinari, exercere artes tam liberales, quàm mechanicas, quæque ad externam seu politicâ honestatem & sanctimoniâ pertinent. Secundi generis sunt actiones sublimiores, quæ salutares seu spirituales dicuntur: hæ sunt actiones supernaturales, vtpote nonnisi à principio supernaturali proficiscentes, & supernaturalem hominis finem, puta syncerum & spiritualem Dei cultum, & æternâ animarum nostrarum salutem concernentes, cuiusmodi sunt conuersio ad Deum, fides in Christum, vera sanctitas, & similia. Atque ad hæc obiecta, secundùm illas differentias distincta, non eodem modo se habere liberum hominis Arbitrium, vel pueris ipsis est notum.
units.tr: The object, or the matter about which free choice is concerned, is of two kinds. Of the first kind are those lower actions which lie within the reach of the senses and human reason and do not exceed our natural capacity. These again are of two sorts: either purely natural actions, such as we share with the brutes, like eating, drinking, sleeping and others of this kind; or, in addition, actions that are called moral or civil, which belong to all men, such as speaking, reasoning, practising the arts both liberal and mechanical, and those that pertain to external or civil honesty and decency. Of the second kind are the higher actions, which are called saving or spiritual. These are supernatural actions, since they proceed only from a supernatural principle, and they concern the supernatural end of man, namely the pure and spiritual worship of God and the eternal salvation of our souls. Such are conversion to God, faith in Christ, true holiness, and similar things. That free choice of man does not stand in the same relation to these objects, distinguished according to these differences, even children know.

units.la: Status hominis quadruplex est, status nempe primæ vitæ integritatis, in quo à Deo per creationem est constitutus: status insequutæ corruptionis, in quam per peccatum præcipitatus, à priore deturbatus fuit: status renouationis, & restauratæ iustitiæ, in quem per gratiam à Christo est restitutus: Status denique glorificationis, in quem ex misericordia suo tempore transportabitur.
units.tr: The state of man is fourfold: the state of the first integrity of life, in which he was established by God in creation; the state of the corruption that followed, into which he was cast down by sin and thrown out of the former state; the state of renewal and restored righteousness, into which he is restored by grace through Christ; and finally the state of glorification, into which he will be transferred in due time by mercy.

units.la: Ex hac libertatis, & ipsius tum obiecti, tum subiecti, tam varia ac necessaria distinctione, euidenter apparet, quàm varie ad quæstionem propositam ab Aduersario, responderi possit, & quam vagus totius disputationis cursus futurus esset, nisi certis suis terminis ac limitibus circumscriberetur : ac proinde statum controversiae aliter formandum esse. Atque vt in hac controversia non cuiusuis libertatis, sed eius tantum quae est à peccato & dominio illius, nobis hic est consideratio : ita quoque ad idem propositum nostrum magni momenti non est, dispicere, quaenam vires sint liberi Arbitrii, ad bona naturalia, animalia, & ciuilia intelligendum, volendum, ac faciendum, vnde illis omissis, de bono spirituali, quod veram religionem & cultum Dei, vitamque hominis spiritualem, quam secundum Deum viuere tenetur, concernit, agemus. Et quia de homine quatenus consideratur in statu illo post lapsum, quem nos corruptionis & peccati dominatis appellamus, prima (quamuis nec subiectum distinxerit) ab Aduersario instituitur controversia: ideo inquiremus cum ipso, ex Scripturis sacris, quas vires homo nondum renatus habeat, ad bona spiritualia, quae sola vere bona sunt, & Deo placentia, primo intelligendum, & volendum: deinde (quae est disputationis nostrae pars altera) faciendum, atque praestandum.
units.tr: From this so varied and necessary distinction of liberty, and of both its object and its subject, it is evident how variously the question proposed by the Adversary could be answered, and how vague the whole course of the disputation would be unless it were bounded by its own fixed terms and limits. Accordingly the state of the controversy must be formed differently. Just as in this controversy our concern is not with every kind of liberty but only with that which is from sin and its dominion, so also it is of no great importance to our present purpose to inquire what powers free choice has for understanding, willing and doing natural, animal and civil goods. Setting those aside, we shall deal with spiritual good, which concerns true religion and the worship of God, and the spiritual life of man, which he is bound to live according to God. And since the Adversary begins the first controversy concerning man as he is considered in that state after the fall, which we call the state of corruption and dominion of sin (though he does not distinguish the subject), we shall inquire with him, from the holy Scriptures, what powers man not yet reborn has, first to understand and will the spiritual goods, which alone are truly good and pleasing to God, and then (which is the second part of our disputation) to do and perform them.

units.la: Quantum igitur primam disputationis partem concernit, status controversiae inter nos & Socinianos hic erit: An homo non regenitus habeat liberum Arbitrium, ad bona spiritualia, quae veram religionem, pietatem, & verum Dei cultum concernunt, intelligendum, ac volendum? id est, An homo animalis, & nondum renatus, dum in via est animalis huius vitae, propriis naturae suae viribus, sine gratia Spiritus S. illuminantis intellectum, & renouantis cor, ac voluntatem ipsius, bonum spirituale, & veritatem caelestem intelligere, velle ac desiderare, & appetere possit? An vero liberum Arbitrium habeat tantum ad malum, sic vt bonum caeleste & supernaturale, resque spirituales suis viribus, nec percipere, nec velle aut appetere possit, sed auersetur illud, malum autem tantum appetat, atque velit? Vel, si forte Aduersarius liberi Arbitrii subiectum solam voluntatem esse statuat; An homo nondum renatus, bonum spirituale, vel ipsius rationis ductu intellectu, vel lumine supernaturali gratiae perceptu, propriis voluntatis suae viribus, eligere, velle, appetere ac desiderare possit? Et quia Aduersarius miserae collapsaeque naturae nostrae, & liberi (o vtinam!) Arbitrii nostri patrocinium, aduersus Christi gratiam, suscipit, alterutrius καταφαση tueri ipsum necesse est: Nos vtramque negamus, & negationem nostram euidentib. argumentis & rationibus, volete Domino, demonstrabimus, primo omniū singulatim, tū mētē,tū volūtatē & affectus hominis nondum renati:deinde vero vitā eius ex S.Scripturis describpturi.
units.tr: So, as far as the first part of the dispute is concerned, the state of the controversy between us and the Socinians will be this: Does a man not yet regenerate have free choice to understand and to will the spiritual goods that concern true religion, piety and the true worship of God? That is, can a natural man, not yet reborn, while he is still on the way of this natural life, by the powers of his own nature and without the Spirit of God illuminating his understanding and renewing his heart and will, understand, will, desire and seek spiritual good and heavenly truth? Or rather, does he have free choice only towards evil, so that he can neither perceive nor will nor seek heavenly and supernatural good and spiritual things by his own powers, but shuns them and seeks and wills only evil? Or, if the Adversary perhaps holds that the will alone is the subject of free choice: can a man not yet reborn, by the powers of his own will, choose, will, seek and desire spiritual good, which is perceived either by the understanding under the guidance of reason alone, or by the supernatural light of grace? And since the Adversary takes up the defence of our wretched and fallen nature, and of our free choice (O that he would not!) against the grace of Christ, he must maintain one of the two affirmations [κατάφασις]. We deny both, and, the Lord willing, we will demonstrate our denial with plain arguments and reasons: first, taking separately the mind, the will and the affections of the man not yet reborn, and then, afterwards, describing his life from the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Argumentum 1. quo demonstramus, hominem animalem, & nondum renatum, Spiritúque Christi destitutum, res spirituales absque illuminatione supernaturali,& solius naturę viribus, aut rationis communi lumine, intelligere ac percipere non posse,desumitur ex 1.Cor. 2. verf.14. Animalis homo non est capax eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia siquidem illi sunt, nec potest ea cognoscere, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Adesdum Christophore Ostorrodi, & quibus coloribus, primariam naturæ nostræ, cuius tu patrocinium tàm temerè suscipis.partem,diuus Paulus depingat, cōtemplator,& illius loci tū subiectum, tum attributum,& attributi,seu praedicati illius grauissimam rationem, & causam altius nobiscum & accuratius perpendito. Subiectum illius enuntiationis est Homo non quiuis, si statuum eius consideres diuersitatem, sed Homo animalis,& ψυχικὸς, conueniens videlicet epitheto tali,quo qualitas cuius,seu status,& conditio significatur ,per quem hominem ψυχικὸν nihil aliud intelligit,quàm hominem nondum regenitum,nec Spiritu sanctificationis donatum, quales sumus à natura omnes,quicunque naturali & carnali propagatione,ab Adamo descendimus, caro videlicet,filii irae,solius Adami terrestris imaginem gerentes, & in peccatis mortui. Hanc subiecti descriptionem veram ac genuinam esse , liquet tùm ex antithesi , qua versu sequenti homini ψυχικῷ,id est carnali, πνευματικὸν, seu spiritualem opponit : tum ex subiecti αἰτιολογίᾳ,qua rationem & causam,quare videlicet homo carnalis non potuit percipere illa quae sunt Spiritus Dei,hanc subiicit:quia spiritualiter diiudicentur: unde necessariò sequitur hominem ψυχικὸν, Spiritu Christi destitutum, ac proinde extra Christum, peccati & Satanae laqueis captiuum,& constrictum teneri. Qui enim Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est eius: Rom.8.ver.9. sed secundum carnem est,& quae carnis sunt sapit, verf.5. Attributum vero,seu praedicatum, quod de homine non renato enuntiat Paulus,idem ipsum est,quod nos in thesi ipsi tribuimus,& consistit in duobus, primò in ἀλογίᾳ, propter quam non est capax illorū,quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest illa intelligere, quae ἀλογίαι, i. ignorantiā rerum caelestium, & ad salutem scitu factuq; necessariarum praesupponit. Secūdo in ματαιότητι τῆς νοὸς,καὶ τῆς διανοίας i. vanitate illa mentis, & iudicii, qua verum esse falsum,contráq; iudicat, & ipsam Dei sapientiam excellentissimam, pro stultitia ducit, sicuti alibi etiam Paulus dicit, se prædicare Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis vero stultitiam. 1.Corin.1.v.2. Causam denique & rationem illius enuntiati, quod videlicet homo animalis non possit percipere, nec intelligere illa, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, reddit Apostolus, ab illius sapientiæ cælestis & cognitionis rerum spiritualium, causa efficiente propria, à qua illa ortum suum ducit, nempe Spiritu Dei, quo animalis homo est destitutus, quum inquit, Spiritualiter dijudicantur. Quibus verbis indicat Apostolus, illarum rerum spiritualium cognitionem, à solo spiritu Christi ortum habere, & eundem Spiritum Dei, à quo Euangelii doctrina profecta est, solum eiusdem esse interpretem, qui eam nobis patefaciat, ac proinde in ea iudicanda hominem necessario exercere, donec Spiritu Dei fit illuminatus. Quis enim hominum novit illa quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus, qui est in homine? ita etiam ea, quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei, 1.Cor.2.v.11.
units.tr: Argument 1. By which we demonstrate that the natural man, not yet reborn and destitute of the Spirit of Christ, cannot understand or perceive spiritual things without supernatural illumination, by the powers of nature alone or by the common light of reason. It is drawn from 1 Cor. 2:14: The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. Come now, Christoph Ostorodt, and consider with what colours the divine Paul paints the principal part of our nature, the part whose defence you so rashly take up; and weigh with me more deeply and carefully both the subject of that passage, and its predicate, and the very grave reason and cause of the predicate. The subject of that statement is not any man, if you consider the diversity of his states, but the natural man [ψυχικός], clearly suited to the epithet by which the quality, or state and condition, is signified. By the natural man [ψυχικός] he means nothing other than the man not yet regenerate and not given the Spirit of sanctification, such as we all are by nature, all who descend from Adam by natural and carnal propagation: flesh, namely, children of wrath, bearing only the image of the earthly Adam, and dead in sins. That this description of the subject is true and genuine is clear both from the antithesis, by which in the following verse he opposes to the natural man [ψυχικός], that is the carnal man, the spiritual man [πνευματικός]; and from the reason given for the subject, by which he states the ground and cause why the carnal man could not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: because they are spiritually discerned. Hence it necessarily follows that the natural man, destitute of the Spirit of Christ, and therefore outside Christ, is held captive and bound in the snares of sin and Satan. For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his (Rom. 8:9), but is according to the flesh, and minds the things of the flesh (v. 5). The predicate, however, which Paul states of the man not reborn, is the very thing we attribute to him in thesis, and it consists of two parts. First, in ignorance [ἀλογία], on account of which he is not capable of those things which are of the Spirit of God, nor can he understand them, which ignorance [ἀλογία], that is, ignorance of heavenly things, he presupposes as necessary to be known and done for salvation. Second, in the vanity of mind and understanding [ματαιότης τῆς νοὸς καὶ τῆς διανοίας], that is, that vanity of mind and judgement by which he judges truth to be falsehood and the reverse, and counts the most excellent wisdom of God as foolishness, as Paul also says elsewhere, that he preaches Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness (1 Cor. 1:23). Finally, the Apostle gives the cause and reason of that statement, namely that the natural man cannot perceive or understand those things which are of the Spirit of God, from the proper efficient cause of that heavenly wisdom and of the knowledge of spiritual things, from which it takes its origin, namely the Spirit of God, of whom the natural man is destitute, when he says: they are spiritually discerned. By these words the Apostle indicates that the knowledge of those spiritual things has its origin in the Spirit of Christ alone, and that the same Spirit of God, from whom the doctrine of the Gospel has come forth, is alone its interpreter, the one who lays it open to us; and that therefore the man who has not yet been illuminated by the Spirit of God must necessarily fail in judging it. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:11).

units.la: Hinc tale argumentum contra Aduersarium extruo.
units.tr: From this I construct the following argument against our opponent.

units.la: Nullus homo ψυχικὸς, seu animalis, & non renatus capax est eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest res spirituales intelligere, sed pro stultitia illas ducit, quia videlicet à solo Dei Spiritu diiudicantur, quo illi sunt destituti, 1.Corinth. 2.verf. 11.14.
units.tr: No natural man (ψυχικὸς [animal]), that is, one who is not reborn, is capable of the things of the Spirit of God. He cannot understand spiritual matters, but counts them foolishness, because they are judged only by the Spirit of God, which such a man lacks (1 Cor. 2:11, 14).

units.la: Atqui omnes quotquot naturali & carnali propagatione, ab Adamo descendunt, sunt homines ψυχικοί, id est, animales & carnales, antequam videlicet Spiritu Dei renouentur & regenerentur: nisi fortassis, quod absurdum ex huius assumptionis negatione necessario sequeretur, Aduersarius, cælestè illud παλιγγενεσίας, & renascentiæ beneficium, nobis ἀνώθεν, & ipsum Spiritum Dei, non ab ipsa regeneratione supernaturali, sed à propagatione carnali esse, contra veritatem Scripturæ affirmare velit.
units.tr: But all who descend from Adam by natural and carnal propagation are natural and carnal men (ψυχικοί, that is, animal and carnal), until they are renewed and regenerated by the Spirit of God. Unless perhaps our opponent wishes to maintain, against the truth of Scripture, that the heavenly benefit of rebirth (παλιγγενεσία) and the Spirit of God, which come to us from above (ἄνωθεν), come not from supernatural regeneration itself but from carnal propagation. The denial of this assumption would necessarily lead to that absurdity.

units.la: Ergo nullus homo, quicunque naturali & carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendit, antequam per Spiritum Sanctum renouetur ac regeneretur, capax est eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest res spirituales, & quæ salutis nostræ, ac redemptionis demptionis mysterium concernunt intelligere, sed pro ftul-titia illas ducit.
units.tr: Therefore no man who descends from Adam by natural and carnal propagation is capable of the things of the Spirit of God until he is renewed and regenerated by the Holy Spirit. He cannot understand spiritual matters, or the mystery of our salvation and redemption, but counts them foolishness.

units.la: Argumentum 11. desumitur ex 2. Cor.3.ver.5.Non quod idonei fi-mus ex nobis ipsis,ad cogitandum quicquam tanquam ex nobis ipsis.sed quod idonei fumus,id ex Deo est.Et Rom. 8.verf.7.Intelligentia carnis inimicitia est aduersus Deum: Nam legi Dei non subiicitur, siquidem ne potest quidé. Vbi Paulus rursum humano intelleEtui omne lumen intelligentiæ, in rebus spiritualibus adimit, & docet non habere hominem animalem, priusquam Spiritus diuini luce illustretur,tantùm in fe luminis,vt naturali rationis& intelleEtus fuę duEtu, vel cogitare tantummodò aliquid boni possit, sicuti alibi Deus ipse testatur. Omne figmentum cogitationum hominis (scilicet nondum renati,ad malum tantùm esse,ídque omni tempore, Gen.6.v. 5. Hisce Scripturæ testimoniis suffragantur etiam illa, in quibus nobilissima hominis pars, nempe anima, insipientiæ & vanitatis titulis insignitur, & homines ipsi obtenebrati mente, amentes & stulti,quin & tenebræ appellantur, Rom.1. verf.21.22. Propterea quod cùm Deum cognouerint, Deum tamen non glorificauerunt, neque gratias ei egerunt, sed vanifacti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est desipiens cor illorum, quum fe profiterentur esse sapientes,stulti facti sunt,Eph.4. v.17.18. Ne amplius versemini,sicut reliquæ Gentes versantur in vanitate mentis suæ, cogitationem habentes obscuratam,& abalienatam à vita Dei,propter ignorantiam quæ est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis ipsorum. Et 5. ver.8.Eratis olim tenebræ,nunc autem lux in Domino. Tit.3.verf.3. Eramus quondam & nos amentes,rebelles, errantes, seruientes cupiditatibus, ac voluptatibus variis in malitia & inuidia degentes,alij alios odio prosequentes. Iohann. 1. verf.5.Lux in tenebris lucet, sed tenebræ non comprehenderunt ipsam. Quibus adde & illa testimonia, in quibus ipsa etiam mente renouari homo dicitur, & Dei, rerúmque diuinarum cognitio, & notitia humani intelleEtus viribus adimitur, & foli reuelationi, atque illuminationi spirituali,adscribitur: Rom.12. ver.2. Ne confi-gurcmini seculo isti, sed transformemini per renouationem mentis ve-ftræ. Ephef.1.ver.17.18.Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi Pater ille gloriæ, det vobis Spiritum sapientiæ,&reuelationis per agnitionem ipsius illuminatis oculis metis vestræ, vt sciatis quæ fit spes illa vocationis ipsius, Matt.11.ver.27.Nemo nouit Filium nisi Pater,neque Patrem quisquam nouit nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius reuelari. & 16. ver.17. Beatus es Simon Bar-Iona, quia caro, & sanguis hoc non retexit tibi, sed Pater meus, qui est in cœlis. Act. 16. ver. 14. Dominus aduaperuit cor Lydiæ, vt attenderet ea, quæ dicebantur à Paulo. Rom. 8. ver. 56. Nam qui secundum carnem sunt, quæ carnis sunt sapiunt, qui vero secundum Spiritum, quæ sunt Spiritus: nam intelligentia carnis mors est, intelligentia vero Spiritus, vita & pax. Plura hac ipsa de re vide caput primum huius defensionis nostræ.
units.tr: The fifth argument is drawn from 2 Cor. 3:5: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God." And from Rom. 8:7: "The carnal mind is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be." Here Paul again takes away from the human understanding all light of insight in spiritual matters, and teaches that the natural man does not have such light before he is illumined by the light of the divine Spirit. Of himself he has only so much light that, by the guidance of his natural reason and understanding, he can think of some good, as God himself testifies elsewhere: "Every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart is only evil continually" (Gen. 6:5), that is, of the man not yet reborn. Other testimonies of Scripture agree with these, in which the noblest part of man, namely the soul, is marked with the titles of folly and vanity, and men themselves are said to be darkened in mind, senseless and foolish, and even called darkness. Rom. 1:21-22: "Because when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful, but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened; professing themselves to be wise, they became fools." Eph. 4:17-18: "This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart." And Eph. 5:8: "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord." Titus 3:3: "For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another." John 1:5: "The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not." To these add those passages in which man is said to be renewed even in his mind, and the knowledge of God and of divine things is taken away from the powers of the human understanding and ascribed solely to revelation and spiritual illumination: Rom. 12:2: "Be not conformed to this world, but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Eph. 1:17-18: "That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him; the eyes of your understanding being enlightened, that ye may know what is the hope of his calling." Matt. 11:27: "No man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him." And Matt. 16:17: "Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed this unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven." Acts 16:14: "Whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken by Paul." Rom. 8:5-6: "For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit. For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." More on this very matter may be seen in the first chapter of this our defence.

units.la: HANC vero mentis cæcitatem, vertiginem atque suffusionem sequi grauissimorum affectuum syndromen, & tantam voluntatis ac cordis peruersitatem, vt id quod vere bonum est, odio prosequatur, malum vero tantum appetat, atque velit, liquet primo ex iis Scripturæ testimoniis, in quibus cor ipsum hominis fraudulentum, peruersum, incircumcisum, durum & lapideum dicitur frequentissime, Ierem. 4. ver. 4. Circumcidite vos Iehouæ, & amouete præputia animi vestri, viri Iehudæ, & habitatores Ierusalaimorum: & 9. ver. 26. Omnes ista gentes præputiatæ sunt, etiam tota domus Israelis præputiati sunt corde: & 17. ver. 9. Fraudulentum cor ipsum supra omnia & mortiferum est, quis cognoscat ipsum? Ezech. 36. ver. 26. Et dabo vobis cor nouum, & Spiritum nouum ponam in medio vestri, & amouens cor lapideum è carne vestra, indam vobis cor carneum. Act. 7. ver. 51. Duri ceruice, & incircumcisi corde & auribus, vos semper Spiritui Sancto obnitimini. Ex corde hominis egrediuntur cogitationes malæ, cædes, adulteria, fornicationes, furta, falsa testimonia, obtrectationes. Matth. 15. ver. 19. Secundo, ex iis Scripturæ testimoniis, quibus homo in hoc statu existens, dicitur sub potestate peccati & Satanæ, variarumque voluptatum, & cupiditatum in seruitutem redactus & captiuatus esse, Rom. 6. ver. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. An nescitis, quod cui sistitis vos ipsos seruos ad obediendum, eius serui estis cui obeditis, vel peccati ad mortem, vel obedientiæ ad iustitiam? Gratia autem sit Deo, quod fuistis serui peccati, sed ex corde obediistis in formam doctrinæ, cui estis traditi, & liberati à peccato mancipati estis iustitiæ: itaque sicut sistitis membra vestra serua impuritati, & iniquitati, ad iniquitatem, ita nunc sistite membra vestra serua iustitiæ ad sanctimoniam. Quum enim serui esse-tis peccati, liberi eratis iustitiæ. 2 Tim. 2. verf. 25. 26. Cum lenitate erudientem eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti, & quando det eis Deus, vt respipiscentes, agnoscant veritatem, & elapsi ex Diaboli laqueis, à quo captiui tenentur, &c. 2. Pet. 2. verf. 19. Libertatem eis pollicendo, quum ipsi serui sint corruptionis: siquidem à quo quis superatus est, huic etiam etiam in seruitutem est addictus. Atqui omnes homines non renati, superantur à peccato & Sathana: Ergo omnes homines non renati peccato & Sathanæ in seruitutem sunt addicti. Iohan. 8. ver. 34. Quisquis committit peccatum, seruus est peccati. Tit. 3. ver. 3. Eramus quondam & nos amentes, rebelles, errantes, seruientes cupiditatibus ac voluptatibus variis, in malitia & invidia degentes. Hisce iunguntur & illa Scripturæ loca, in quibus sola Dei misericordia, & Christi gratia ab illa seruitute liberari, & in veram libertatem vindicari, dicimur, Iohann. 8. ver. 36. Si vos Filius in libertatem vindicauit, verè liberi eritis: 2. Corinth. 3. ver. 17. Dominus Spiritus ille est: vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, ibi libertas: Tit. 2. ver. 14. Qui dedit semet ipsum pro nobis, vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum: Et 3. versu 4. 5. Sed postquam bonitas, & erga homines amor apparuit Seruatoris nostri Dei, non ex operibus iustis quæ fecerimus nos, sed ex sua misericordia seruauit nos, per lauacrum regenerationis ac renouationis Spiritus sancti. Quum igitur ibi demum vera sit libertas, vbi Spiritus Dei est, & illi soli verè liberi sint, quos Filius Dei in libertatem vindicauerit: sequitur arbitrium nostrum in statu corruptionis, ad bonum, liberum non esse, nósque omnes priusquam Spiritu libertatis à Domino nostro Iesu Christo donemur, seruituti Sathanæ & peccati mancipatos esse, quandoquidem certissimum est, omne id naturæ nostræ deesse, quod Spiritus Sancti beneficio nobis præstitum & communicatum esse, Scriptura testatur. Quum deinde totus homo, antequam gratiæ Christi per fidem particeps reddatur, peccati imperio & Sathanæ dominio subiacere, diuinis testimoniis perhibeatur, ipsam certè voluntatem quæ præcipua eius sedes est, eiusdem seruitutis vinculis constringi necesse est. Tertiò, ex iis Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ describunt nobis beneficia Christi per Spiritum Sanctum voluntati collata, & remedia gratiæ, quibus cordis vitiositas corrigitur & sanatur. Quum enim nos omnibus illis beneficiis nudos & vacuos esse intelligatur, quæ nobis ex gratia & misericordia sua largitur Dominus, ideo ex ingenti illo bonorum cumulo, quæ Spiritus Sancti beneficio credentibus obtingunt, qualis & quanta sit penuria nostra, euidenter elucescet. Quum igitur Apostolus Eph. 2. ver. 10. dicit: Nam ipsius opus sumus, conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quæ præparauit Deus, vt in ijs versaremur, dubium non est, quin solum Deum spiritualis nostrae vitae autorem faciat,quod ipsum paulo ante disertis verbis docuit, quum v. 4.5.6. inquit, Sed Deus,qui dines est misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam, qua dilexit nos, etiam quum per offensas mortui effemus,vna viuificauit nos per Christum, cuius gratia estis seruati,vnáque excitauit,vnáque collocauit in cælis in Christo Iesu. Sic Phil.1.ver.6. Persuasum habens hoc ipsum fore, vt qui cœpit in vobis bonum opus, perficiat vsque ad diem Iesu Christi. Quo in loco Apostolus per boni operis principium conuersionis nostrae, quae in voluntate est,originem : per complementum vero,perfeucrantiae donum designat, vtrumque vero beneficium gratiae diuinae in solidum adscribit. Sic Ezech.capite trigesimosexto, versu vigesimosexto,& vigesimoseptimo. Dabo vobis, inquit Dominus: cor nouum, Spiritum nouum, ponam in medio vestri, & auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, & dabo vobis cor carneum: & Spiritum meum ponam in medio vestri, & faciam vt in præceptis meis ambuletis. Alia infinita omitto,quum vero excitatis testimoniis appareat, Dominum nos in peccatis & offensis nostris mortuos,viuificare bonum in cordibus nostris non tantum inchoare & perficere,sed etiam operari in nobis velle,id est, bonam voluntatem, creare etiam cor nouum, auferre lapideum, dare carneum, sequitur voluntatem hominis penitus corruptam esse,totámque transformari ac renouari oportere, vt ad boni electionem aspirare possit.
units.tr: That this blindness, dizziness and clouding of the mind is accompanied by a grievous disorder of the affections, and by such a perversity of will and heart that a man hates what is truly good and desires and chooses only evil, is plain first from those passages of Scripture in which the heart of man itself is very often called deceitful, perverse, uncircumcised, hard and stony. Jer. 4:4: "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem." Jer. 9:26: "All these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart." Jer. 17:9: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" Ezek. 36:26: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." Acts 7:51: "Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost." Matt. 15:19: "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies." Second, it is plain from those passages of Scripture which say that man, in this state, is brought into bondage and captivity under the power of sin and Satan, and under the various lusts and desires. Rom. 6:16-20: "Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey, whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you. Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness. As ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness. For when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness." 2 Tim. 2:25-26: "In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; and that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will." 2 Pet. 2:19: "While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption; for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage." Therefore all men who are not reborn are overcome by sin and Satan; therefore all men who are not reborn are delivered over to bondage under sin and Satan. John 8:34: "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." Titus 3:3: "For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy." To these are joined those passages of Scripture in which we are said to be delivered from that bondage, and set free into true liberty, by the mercy of God and the grace of Christ alone. John 8:36: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." 2 Cor. 3:17: "Now the Lord is that Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Titus 2:14: "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works." And Titus 3:4-5: "But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost." Since, therefore, true liberty is found only where the Spirit of God is, and only those are truly free whom the Son of God has set free, it follows that our will in the state of corruption is not free towards the good, and that all of us, before we are given the Spirit of liberty by our Lord Jesus Christ, are delivered over to the bondage of Satan and sin. For it is most certain that everything which Scripture says was bestowed on us and communicated to us by the benefit of the Holy Spirit is lacking in our nature. Since, further, the whole man, before he is made partaker of the grace of Christ through faith, is by divine testimony said to be subject to the rule of sin and the dominion of Satan, the will, which is his chief seat, must certainly be bound with the chains of this same bondage. Third, it is plain from those passages of Scripture which describe for us the benefits of Christ, bestowed on the will through the Holy Spirit, and the remedies of grace by which the wickedness of the heart is corrected and healed. For since we are understood to be naked and empty of all those benefits which the Lord bestows on us from his grace and mercy, therefore from that vast heap of good things which come to believers by the benefit of the Holy Spirit, it will be clearly evident what and how great our poverty is. Since, then, the Apostle says (Eph. 2:10): "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them," there is no doubt that he makes God alone the author of our spiritual life. He had taught this in plain words a little earlier, when he says (vv. 4-6): "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, by whose grace ye are saved; and hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus." So too Phil. 1:6: "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." In this place the Apostle ascribes the origin of our conversion, which lies in the will, to the beginning of the good work, and the gift of perseverance to its completion, and he attributes both benefits wholly to divine grace. So too Ezek. 36:26-27: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes." I omit countless other testimonies. But since the passages cited make it clear that the Lord, who quickens us when we are dead in sins and offences, not only begins and completes the good in our hearts but also wills to work in us, that is, to create a good will, to give a new heart, to take away the stony and give the fleshly, it follows that the will of man is wholly corrupt, and must be wholly transformed and renewed, if it is to be able to aspire to the choice of good.

units.la: Atque hæc de intellectus humani vertigine ac cæcitate: & voluntatis, cordisque peruersitate ac rebellione, ex Scripturis sacris desibasse sufficiat: restat vt totius vitae hominis,in peccato constituti,faciem contemplemur, quam nobis Scriptura sacra multis in locis luculentissimè describit,vt Rom.3.versu 9.& sequent. Ante criminati sumus Iudaeos & Graecos omnes esse sub peccato,sicut scriptum est,Non est iustus,ne vnus quidem, non est qui intelligat, non est qui exquirat Deum, omnes deflexerunt, simul inutiles facti sunt, non est qui faciat quod bonum est, non est vsque ad vnum: sepulchrum apertum guttur eorum,linguis suis ad dolum vsi sunt,venenum aspidum, sub labijs eorum, quorum os diris & amarulentia plenum est, veloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem, contritio & calamitas in vijs eorum,& viam pacis non cognouerunt, non est timor Dei coram oculis eorum. Et Ephef.2.versu 1.2.3. Et vos quum essetis mortui in offensis & peccatis,in quibus olim versati estis,vt est vita mundi huius, secundùm principem, principem, cui potestas est aëris, & Spiritus nunc agentis in hominibus contumacibus, inter quos & nos omnes conuersati sumus olim in cupiditatibus carnis nostræ, facientes quæ carni & cogitationibus libebant, eramúsque natura filii iræ, vt etiam reliqui. Porrò manifesta sunt opera carnis, quæ sunt adulterium, scortatio, impuritas, proteruia, idololatria, veneficium, inimicitiæ, lis, æmulationes, iræ, contentiones, dissidia, hæreses, inuidiæ, cædes, ebrietates, commessationes, & his similia. Galat. capite quinto, versu decimonono, vigesimo & vigesimo primo. Et Ephef. capite quarto, versu 17. 18. 19. Ne amplius versemini, sicut reliquæ Gentes versantur in vanitate mentis suæ, cogitationem habentes obscuratam, & abalienatam à vita Dei, propter ignorantiamque est in ipsis, ex obduratione cordis eorum: qui postquam dedoluerunt, semetipsos dediderunt proteruiæ, ad certatim patrandam impuritatem omnem. Iohann. capite quinto, versu vigesimoquinto. Amen, Amen dico vobis, venit tempus, & nunc est, quum mortui audient vocem Filii Dei, & qui audient, viuent. Hisce adde illa scripturæ loca, in quibus homines nondum renati, tanquam malæ arbores, non nisi malos fructus proferre, iuxta carnem incedere, & propterea Deo non posse placere, dicuntur: Matth. 7. versu 18. Non potest arbor bona malos fructus ferre, neque arbor putris fructus bonos ferre: & 12. versu 35. Bonus homo e bono thesauro cordis profert bona, & malus homo ex malo thesauro profert mala. Rom. 8. versu 5. Nam qui ex carne sunt, quæ carnis sunt sapiunt, qui verò secundum Spiritum, quæ sunt Spiritus. Et ver. 8. Ergo qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Item, in quibus opera illorum, vtpote extra fidem & Christi gratiam, facta, licet alioqui sæpè speciosa tanquam immunda & inutilia traduntur: Vt Es. 64. ver 10. Sumus, vt immundus omnes nos, & sicut panniculus omnes iustitiæ nostræ, diffluimúsque velut folium omnes nos, & iniquitates nostræ velut ventus auferunt nos. Rom. 14. ver. 23. Quicquid non est ex fide, id peccatum est. Heb. 11. ver. 6. Atqui fieri non potest, vt sine fide quisquam Deo placeat: Ioh. 15. v. 4. 5. Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructu à semetipso, nisi maserit in vite, ita nec vos nisi in me maseritis. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites, is, qui manet in me, & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructu multum: nam absque me nihil potestis facere. Ex quib. omnib. luculenter apparet, homine animale, priusquam Sp. S. gratia imbuatur, peccati iugo, ac seruitute Satanæ totû opprimi: imo in peccatis & iniquitate penitus mortuũ esse, nec aliud quicquã nisi peccare posse, sic vt tota ipsius vita nihil aliud, nisi perpetuum quoddam sit peccatorum curriculum, antequam Deus ipsi gratia sua illuxerit. Quemadmodum enim, qui mortuus est morte corporali, nullo munere hominis viui potest fungi, neq; sensum, vitam, vigorem, aut vires vllas hominis viuentis in se habet: ita quoque homo, qui mortuus est spiritualiter in peccatis, nullas actiones hominis virtute & beneficio Spiritus Sancti viuentis efficere valet, neque etiam vires vllas in se ad malum fugiendum & bonum præstandum habet. Concludimus igitur cum Scriptura sacra, hominis non regeniti mentem & intellectum tantis ignorantiæ & cæcitatis tenebris obrutum esse, vt res spirituales, quæ videlicet veram pietatem, purúmque Dei cultum concernunt, priusquam luce supernaturalis gratiæ cœlitus illuminetur, etiam cum docentur, percipere non possit, voluntatem vero eiusdem à bono tam auersam & tanta nequitia imbutam esse, vt nisi à Spiritu Sancto flectatur, bonum spirituale ac Deo placens, nec velle aut eligere queat, malum autem tantùm appetat, atque velit, sic vt in ipsius voluntate, nec semen vllum virtutis, nec vlla ad virtutem inclinatio post vniuersalem illam humani generis apostasiam remanserit.
units.tr: And let it suffice to have drawn these points from the holy Scriptures about the dizziness and blindness of the human intellect, and about the perversity and rebellion of the will and heart. It remains that we consider the whole face of human life, while a man is held under sin, which Holy Scripture describes most vividly to us in many places, as in Rom. 3, verse 9 and following: "We have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, as it is written: There is none righteous, no, not one; there is none who understands, there is none who seeks after God. They have all turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, no, not one. Their throat is an open grave; they have used their tongues to deceive; the venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes." Also Eph. 2, verses 1, 2, 3: "And you, when you were dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked, according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we also all once lived in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest." Gal. 5, verses 19, 20, 21: "Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalries, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these." Eph. 4, verses 17, 18, 19: "No longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles walk, in the futility of their minds, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, due to the hardening of their hearts; who, having become callous, have given themselves over to sensuality, to work every kind of impurity greedily." John 5, verse 25: "Truly, truly, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live." To these add those passages of Scripture in which men not yet reborn are said, like bad trees, to bring forth only bad fruit, to walk according to the flesh, and therefore not to be able to please God: Matt. 7, verse 18: "A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit." And Matt. 12, verse 35: "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and an evil man out of his evil treasure brings forth evil things." Rom. 8, verse 5: "For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit." And verse 8: "So those who are in the flesh cannot please God." Likewise, passages in which their works, done outside faith and the grace of Christ, are called unclean and useless, though otherwise often splendid: as Isa. 64, verse 6: "We are all become like one unclean, and all our righteousnesses are like a filthy rag; we all wither like a leaf, and our iniquities carry us away like the wind." Rom. 14, verse 23: "Whatever is not of faith is sin." Heb. 11, verse 6: "But without faith it is impossible to please God." John 15, verses 4, 5: "As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing." From all these things it appears plainly that the natural man, before he is imbued with the grace of the Holy Spirit, is wholly oppressed by the yoke of sin and the bondage of Satan; indeed, he is utterly dead in sins and iniquity, and can do nothing but sin, so that his whole life is nothing but a continual course of sins, until God shines upon him with his grace. For just as one who is dead in bodily death cannot perform any function of a living man, and has in himself no sense, life, vigour, or any powers of a living man, so too a man who is spiritually dead in sins is not able to perform any actions of a man living by the power and benefit of the Holy Spirit, nor does he have in himself any powers to flee evil and perform good. We conclude therefore with Holy Scripture that the mind and understanding of the unregenerate man is so overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance and blindness that he cannot perceive spiritual things, which concern true piety and pure worship of God, even when they are taught, until he is illuminated from heaven by the light of supernatural grace; and that his will is so turned away from good and so steeped in such wickedness that, unless it is bent by the Holy Spirit, it cannot will or choose the spiritual good that pleases God, but desires and wills only evil; so that in his will there remains no seed of virtue, and no inclination to virtue, after that universal apostasy of the human race.

units.la: CAPVT XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: In quo Aduersarij argumenta refutantur, & simul de primi hominis statu, & conditione tam ante, quàm post lapsum; de imagine item Dei in homine; denique de peccato originali, agitur.
units.tr: In which the adversary's arguments are refuted, and at the same time the state and condition of the first man, both before and after the fall, is discussed; likewise the image of God in man; and finally original sin is treated.

units.la: STORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite trigesimo tertio, contrariam sententiam tuetur ac docet, Hominem etiam post lapsum, & nondum regenitum, ab ipsa natura, & creationis beneficio, liberum arbitrium, seu liberam voluntatem habere, secundum quam quam (vt capite trigesimoquarto seipsum explicat) cupere, ac vel-le possit, debi am praeceptis Dei obedientiam praestare, licet illud solius naturae viribus & sine gratia, efficere re ipsa non queat.
