Et hanc suam sententiam hoc argumento demonstrare conatur, quod videlicet primus homo, ex quo nos omnes propagati ac derivati sumus, ac proinde naturae ipsius participes, a natura & ipsius creationis beneficio, liberum arbitrium, seu liberam voluntatem habuerit, sicut omnes Theologi confiteantur, & res ipsa evidenter evincat.
units.tr: Storrodius, in chapter thirty-three of his Institutes, defends and teaches the contrary opinion: that man, even after the fall and not yet regenerate, has free choice or free will from nature itself and the benefit of creation, by which he can desire and will (as he explains himself in chapter thirty-four) to render obedience to God's precepts, although he cannot actually accomplish this by the powers of nature alone and without grace. He tries to prove this opinion by the following argument: that the first man, from whom we all have been propagated and derived, and so are partakers of his nature, had free choice or free will from nature and the benefit of creation, as all theologians confess and the matter itself clearly proves.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism is as follows.

units.la: Si primus homo a natura, & ipsius creationis beneficio, liberum arbitrium, seu liberam voluntatem (id est, desiderium, & inclinationem ad servandum praecepta Dei) habuit, tum sequitur, nos omnes quoque liberum arbitrium, seu liberam voluntatem, ab ipsa natura habere:
units.tr: If the first man had free choice or free will (that is, desire and inclination to keep God's precepts) from nature and the benefit of creation, then it follows that we all also have free choice or free will from nature itself:

units.la: Atqui primus homo ab ipsa natura, & creationis beneficio, liberum arbitrium & liberam voluntatem habuit, ut probatur tum consensu omnium Theologorum, tum rei ipsius evidentia, & manifesta veritate: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: But the first man had free choice and free will from nature and the benefit of creation, as is proved both by the consensus of all theologians and by the evidence of the thing itself and its manifest truth. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Connexi probatio haec est.
units.tr: The proof of the connection is this.

units.la: Si nos omnes ab Adamo propagati, & ex illo derivati, ac proinde naturae ipsius participes sumus, tum, si Adamus a natura & ipsius creationis beneficio, liberum arbitrium & liberam voluntatem habuit, ad bonum eligendum: sequitur etiam nos idem liberum arbitrium, eandemque voluntatis libertatem habere:
units.tr: If we all have been propagated from Adam and derived from him, and so are partakers of his nature, then, if Adam had free choice and freedom of will to choose the good from nature and the benefit of creation, it follows that we also have the same free choice and the same freedom of will:

units.la: Atqui prius est verum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter also.

units.la: Resp. Connexum esse falsum, neque subiuncto prosyllogismo demonstrari, propter eiusdem consequentiae falsitatem. Quamvis enim libenter fateamur, & ex Scriptura ipsa constet, Adamum liberrimo arbitrio ad bonum & ad malum ante lapsum praeditum, imo summis institiae & sanctimoniae, omniumque virtutum ornamentis ac dotibus ipsius creationis beneficio instructum fuisse, nosque omnes ab ipso tanquam stirpe ac radice, licet propagemur, minime tamen inde sequitur, eundem virtutum cumulum, candemque arbitrii libertatem, per generationem naturalem, ab ipso in posteros deriuari. Quum enim ille, priusquam posterorum suorum vllum genuisset, tunesto suo lapsu, omne virtutum, quibus eluxit, iustitiaeque & sanctimoniae decus, seque ipsum & liberum suum arbitrium perdiderit, & sic vniuersam naturam horribili vitiositate corruperit, imaginem Dei, ad quam conditus fuit, misere deformauerit, denique peccandi necessitatem sibi & posteris suis contraxerit; ideo non illa primaeua arbitrii libertas, nec virtutum, iustitiaeque & sanctimoniae originalis splendida possessio, sed tristis peccati seruitus, vitiorumque omnium turma & luxurians illa concupiscentiae indomitae hydra, cum peccandi necessitate in posteros dimanauerunt, sic vt naturae quidem ipsius Adami (non enim naturam ipsam, sed naturae sanitatem & integritatem peccando amisit) per generationem participes reddamur, sed corruptae, vitiatae & sanctitate originali spoliatae, miserrimisque languoribus & morbis, & omnigenarum miseriarum fluctibus penitus oppressae. Dum ergo Ostorrodius conditionem hominis, in peccati squaloribus & corruptionis statu constituti, ab ipsius creationis splendore & primaeuae integritatis felicitate, praepostere aesti mandam ducit, ingentem suam insciitiam & imperitiam prodit.
units.tr: Answer: the connection is false, and it cannot be demonstrated by the added prosyllogism, because the consequence itself is false. For although we gladly admit, and it is clear from Scripture itself, that Adam before the fall was endowed with the most free choice toward good and evil, and indeed had been furnished by the benefit of creation with the highest justice and holiness and the adornments and gifts of all virtues, and although we are all propagated from him as from stock and root, it by no means follows that the same store of virtues and the same freedom of choice flowed down to his posterity through natural generation. For since he, before he had begotten any of his posterity, by his wretched fall lost all the virtue in which he shone, and the glory of justice and holiness, and himself and his free choice, and so corrupted all nature with horrible vitiosity, miserably deformed the image of God in which he had been made, and finally contracted for himself and his posterity the necessity of sinning; therefore it was not that original freedom of choice, nor the splendid possession of original virtue, justice and holiness, that flowed down to his posterity, but the sad servitude of sin, the whole brood of vices, and that luxuriant hydra of unbridled concupiscence, together with the necessity of sinning. So we are indeed made partakers of Adam's nature by generation (for he lost not nature itself but the soundness and integrity of nature by sinning), but we are corrupted, vitiated and stripped of original holiness, and utterly overwhelmed by the most wretched sicknesses and diseases and the waves of every kind of misery. Therefore, while Ostorrodius judges the condition of man, placed in the filth of sin and the state of corruption, by the splendour of his creation and the happiness of his original integrity, putting the cart before the horse, he betrays his own great ignorance and inexperience.

units.la: Ad hanc responsionem nostram qua dicimus, hominem primum quidem libertate arbitrii donatum & immortalem, iustumque ac sanctum a Deo conditum fuisse, sed peccando libertatem illam & rectitudinem, cum immortalitate perdidisse, ac proinde per generationem, dotes illas in posteros propagare non potuisse, excipit Aduersarius, ac dicit, duo in illa fumi pro concessi, quae ex sacris Scripturis demonstrari non possint, primo videlicet, hominem primum immortalem, sanctum & iustum a Deo creatum fuisse: deinde vero, hanc primam ipsius naturam, per peccatum corruptam ac depravatam esse, quia vero illa duo capita, ex Scripturis sacris demonstrari non possint, ideo totam, inquit, ratiocinationem illi super struam, falsam, argumentum vero pro arbitrij libertate allatum, validum ac firmum esse.
units.tr: To this answer of ours, in which we say that man was indeed created by God endowed with freedom of choice, immortal, just and holy, but by sinning lost that freedom and uprightness together with immortality, and so could not transmit those gifts to posterity by generation, the adversary objects, saying that "there are two things taken for granted in it which cannot be demonstrated from holy Scripture: first, that the first man was created by God immortal, holy and just; and second, that this first nature of his was corrupted and depraved by sin. Since those two points cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures, the whole reasoning built upon them is false, but the argument brought for freedom of choice is valid and firm."

units.la: Resp. Falsam esse illam Aduersarii exceptionem: atque vt tum datae responsionis nostrae solida veritas, tum vero exceptionis Ostorrodianae falsitas eo magis appareat, duae illae quaestiones discutiendae, & cum Aduersario diligentius sunt considerandae: primo, An primus homo immortalis, sanctus & iustus a Deo conditus fuerit?
units.tr: Answer: the adversary's objection is false. And so that the solid truth of our answer, and the falsity of Ostorrodius's objection, may appear all the more clearly, those two questions must be discussed and carefully considered with the adversary. The first is: Was the first man created by God immortal, holy and just?

units.la: Secundo,
units.tr: Secondly,

units.la: Secundò, An idem primus homo, naturam generis humani peccando corruperit, ac vitiauerit? Seu, quod idem est, An humana natura per peccatum Adami sit corrupta ac depravata? Nos de utraque tum sententiam nostram explicaturi & confirmaturi, tum ad contradicentis Aduersarii exceptiones responsuri, non quidem ipsius naturæ & doctrinæ, sed contextus, quem refutamus ordinem sequuturi sumus.
units.tr: Secondly: Did the same first man corrupt and vitiate the nature of the human race by sinning? Or, which is the same thing: Is human nature corrupted and depraved through the sin of Adam? In explaining and confirming our opinion on both points, and in answering the adversary's objections, we will follow not the order of his nature and doctrine but the order of the text that we are refuting.

units.la: Quæstionem vero primam quantum concernit, quum illa de diuersis & quidem eiusmodi attributis instituatur, quę non sunt eiusdem generis, sed illorum primum, nempe immortalitas, ad statum hominis externum, reliquæ vero duę, nempe iustitia & sanctimonia, ad naturam ipsius referantur, ac proinde non iisdem tantum, sed diuersis etiam argumentis de subiecto demonstrentur: ideo illam in duas partes distinguemus, quarum prima de immortalitate primi hominis, altera vero de iustitia & sanctimonia originali eiusdem tractabimus.
units.tr: As far as the first question is concerned, since it is raised about different attributes, and of such a kind that they are not of the same genus, but the first of them, namely immortality, refers to man's external state, while the other two, namely justice and holiness, refer to his nature itself, and so are proved about the subject not only by the same arguments but also by different ones: therefore we will divide it into two parts, of which the first will treat of the immortality of the first man, and the second of his original justice and holiness.

units.la: Partem primam quod attinet, videlicet, An Adamus immortalis a Deo conditus fuerit? quum ipsius attributi nomen, nempe immortalitas, sit æquiuocum, & variis modis dicatur, propter subiectorum quibus tribuitur diuersitatem, & eiusdem causas varias ac diuersas, ideo priusquam argumenta illa, quibus respondeo nostra stabilitur, proferantur. primò omnium vocis ipsius πολυσημία tollenda: deinde quid tum nos, tum Aduersarii hac de re sentiant, paucis exponendum est.
units.tr: As for the first part, namely, Was Adam created immortal by God? Since the name of the attribute itself, immortality, is equivocal and is used in various ways, on account of the diversity of the subjects to which it is attributed and its various and different causes, therefore, before the arguments by which our answer is established are put forward, the polysemy [πολυσημία] of the word must first be removed. Then what both we and the adversaries think on this matter must be set out briefly.

units.la: Quicquid itaque immortale dicitur, id vel ἁπλῶς, & simpliciter, vel κατά τι, & secundum quid, seu, ut Thomas Aquinas loquitur, ex parte causæ efficientis tale dicitur. Quod ἁπλῶς & simpliciter immortale dicitur, id nunquam moritur, unde immortalitas ipsi verissime tribuitur, licet diuersimodè, videlicet, vel πρῶτος, primò, per se, in se, ex se, & ἀνεπιδεκτος, quo modo solus Deus immortalis dicitur (quia nec moritur unquam, neque etiam ratione: aut respectu vi-lo, vtpote vitam in seipso æternam ab æterno, habens in æternum: mori potest, unde etiam ἀθάνατος & ἀδιαφθορος in sacris literis appellatur, qui mori, ac corrumpi non possit, quíque solus habet immortalitatem videlicet perfectam, & à se ipso, vt videre est 1. Tim. 1. v. 17. & 6. v. 16. Item Rom. 1. v. 23. tum quia prorsus est ἀφθαρτος: tũ quia omnis passionis expers est, nõ modo quia propter infinitatẽ essẽtiæ, nihil quod est extra ipsum, in illum agere potest: sed etiam, quia propter simplicitatem suam vllius causæ externæ actionem recipere nequit.) Vel ἐπομένως, & per communicationem, ac quasi ὑπὸ-ρολὼ vitæ illius quomodo immortalia dicuntur, quæ in fe & potentia sua, propter essentiæ mutabilitatem (nam simplex & omnimoda immortalitas solius Dei propria est) mutabilia, mortalia, ac corruptibilia sunt, etsi absolutam Dei potentiam spectes, in nihilum redigi possunt, quippe ex nihilo creata, actu tamen eo modo nunquam mutantur, aut moriuntur, propterea quòd Deus vult substantiam illorum perpetuò in suo esse, vt loquuntur, conferuare. Quæ hoc modo immortalia sunt, talia sunt, vel beneficio & consilio creationis, vt Angeli & animæ rationales: vel iustitia Dei remunerante, eáque vel benignitate illius, & per μετάδοσιν, seu glorificationem, vt Spiritus Beatorum, fiue Angelorum, fiue hominum, ipsique etiam homines, ad sempiternam gloriam translati: vel seueritate & ira puniente, vt reprobi ac damnati ad mortem æternam, qui licet à vita Dei gratiosa in sempiternum exclusi, vitam tamen essentialem æternum, sed abominandum in modum, sunt vicuri. Quod vero κατὰ τι, & fecundum quid, seu ex parte causæ efficientis immortale dicitur, illud est, quod in fe quidem φύσει est, atque ex contrariis ac inter fe pugnantibus qualitatibus conflatum, & neque simpliciter nequit mori, neque etiam certo ac absoluto Dei decreto, sed ex singulari pacto ac fœdere, certáque sub conditione non moritur. Atque hunc vltimum immortalitatis modum Adamo in statu innocentiæ constituto tribuimus, videlicet non impotentiam moriendi, sed potetiam nō moriendi, imò vitam perpetuam, fi debitam obedientiam præstitisset. Fuit igitur Adamus quidem corruptibilis, ac mortalis, primò fecundum id, quod est ex contrariis, & inter fe pugnantibus elementis conflatum: deinde fecundum solutionem vnionis hypostaticę, qua anima & corpus adunata inter fe constituunt vnum ὑφιστάμενον: tertiò, in fe, & potentia sua: sed fuit etiã immortalis, & ἀθάνατος, potentia gratiæ Dei in Christo, fecundum veritatem promissionis diuinæ, fi ille debitam obedientiam præstitisset, & ἀναμάρτητος in illa gratia Dei substitisset, nec ab ea difceffiffet, in qua subsistebat conditionaliter. Et hunc immortalitatis modum intelligimus, cùm Adamum immortalem creatum fuisse dicimus, non autem quamlibet & omnimodam immortalitatem ei tribuimus. Hanc sententiæ nostræ veritatem euidentibus,ac solidis argumentis demonstrabi- mus , cum prius quid Aduersarii hac de re sentiant, breuiter ex- posuerimus.
units.tr: Whatever is called immortal is so either absolutely and simply [ἁπλῶς], or in a certain respect [κατά τι], or, as Thomas Aquinas puts it, on the side of the efficient cause. That which is called immortal absolutely and simply never dies, and so immortality is most truly attributed to it, though in different ways. Either it is so first, primarily, through itself, in itself, from itself, and incapable of receiving [ἀνεπίδεκτος] any change, in which way God alone is called immortal, because he neither ever dies nor can die in any way or with respect to anything, having eternal life in himself from eternity to eternity. Hence he is also called in the sacred letters immortal [ἀθάνατος] and incorruptible [ἀδιάφθορος], one who cannot die or be corrupted, and who alone has immortality, namely perfect and from himself, as may be seen in 1 Tim. 1. v. 17 and 6. v. 16; likewise Rom. 1. v. 23. He is both altogether incorruptible [ἄφθαρτος], and free from all passion, not only because, on account of the infinity of his essence, nothing outside himself can act upon him, but also because, on account of his simplicity, he cannot receive the action of any external cause. Or, by consequence [ἐπομένως] and by communication, and as it were by a kind of hypo-rrhoe [ὑπορροή] of that life; in this way those things are said to be immortal which are in themselves and by their own power, on account of the mutability of their essence (for absolute and all-embracing immortality belongs to God alone), mutable, mortal and corruptible. Yet if you regard God's absolute power, they can be reduced to nothing, since they were created out of nothing; nevertheless in act they never change or die in this way, because God wills to preserve their substance perpetually in its being, as they say. Those things which are immortal in this way are so either by the benefit and design of creation, like angels and rational souls; or by the rewarding justice of God, and that either by his goodness, through impartation [μετάδοσιν], or glorification, like the Spirits of the Blessed, whether of angels or of men, and men themselves translated to eternal glory; or by punishing severity and wrath, like the reprobate and the damned, who, although excluded forever from the gracious life of God, will nevertheless live an essential eternal life, but in an abominable manner. But that which is called immortal in a certain respect [κατὰ τι], or according to what, that is, on the side of the efficient cause, is that which is indeed immortal by nature [φύσει] in itself, but compounded of contrary and mutually conflicting qualities. It neither can absolutely not die, nor does it fail to die by a certain and absolute decree of God, but by a singular pact and covenant, and under a certain condition it does not die. And we attribute this last mode of immortality to Adam as constituted in the state of innocence: not an inability to die, but a power not to die, and indeed perpetual life, if he had rendered due obedience. Adam was therefore indeed corruptible and mortal: first, according to that which is compounded of contrary and mutually conflicting elements; second, according to the dissolution of the hypostatic union, by which soul and body joined together constitute one subsistence [ὑφιστάμενον]; third, in himself and by his own power. But he was also immortal and deathless [ἀθάνατος], by the power of God's grace in Christ, according to the truth of the divine promise, if he had rendered due obedience and had persisted sinless [ἀναμάρτητος] in that grace of God, not departing from that in which he subsisted conditionally. It is this mode of immortality that we understand when we say that Adam was created immortal; we do not attribute to him any and every kind of immortality. We shall demonstrate the truth of this opinion of ours by evident and solid arguments, once we have briefly set out what the adversary thinks on this matter.

units.la: Ostorrodius hoc ipso capite trigesimo tertio, negat immortali- tatem. Adamo,etiam in statu innocentiæ constituto, vlla ratione natu- ralem fuisse,sed creatum fuisse ipsum à Deo natura mortalem, sicut et- iam in statu gratiæ constitutus,non tantum in se & potentia sua corru- ptibilis fuerit,sed etiam re & actu ipso moriturus fuisset,quamuis Deus ipsum à morte conseruare, vel etiam mortuum resuscitare iterum po- tuisset. Ac proinde ipsum peccando non mortalitatem, vt pote natura- lem ipsi, sed mortem ipsam, ac moriendi necessitatem contraxisse,sic vt ipsi Christiani ac sideles qui moriuntur, nō moriantur propter peccatum, sed ideo,quia mortalitas ipsi Adamo & omnibus qui naturæ ipsius par- ticipes sunt factì,naturalis fuerit,& sit etiamnum.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in this same thirty-third chapter, denies that Adam, even in the state of innocence, was immortal by any natural right. He was created by God mortal by nature, just as a man in the state of grace is not only corruptible in himself and by his own power, but would also actually die, although God could have kept him from death or raised him again once dead. Therefore by sinning Adam did not contract mortality, as something natural to him, but death itself and the necessity of dying. So Christians and believers who die do not die because of sin, but because mortality was natural to Adam and to all who have become sharers in his nature, and it remains so still.

units.la: Sed quænam Samosatenianorum de immortalitate Adami sit sententia, clarius longè exponit Faustus Socinus libro tertio, de Iesu Christo seruatore, capite octauo, vbi inter cætera in hunc modum scribit : Mors naturalis, quatenus naturalis est, & omnibus communis, non est stipendium peccati, sed naturæ nostræ, quam ipsemet Adamus in ipsa creatione accepit, propria sequela. Peccati autem sti- pendium, est moriendi necessitas & mors æterna. Id vel ex eo patet, quod Christus nos,qui illi fidem habemus,ab omni prorsus peccato, id est, peccati pœna,& reatu liberauit,& tamen naturalem mortem non ade- mit,sed æternam duntaxat,& moriendi necessitatem. De æterna morte non est qui ambigat : de moriendi autem necessitate, admonere nos pos- sunt ÿ, ex nobis, quos viuos offendet postremus Christi aduentus, qui mortem non gustabunt. Idem enim iudicium faciendum est de omnibus, quod de paucis illis. Nam si moriendi necessitatem Christus non sustulif- set, ne illi quidem pauci mortem effugere possent. Moriuntur igitur cateri fideles:non quia propter peccatum eos mori necesse sit,cum peccati reatus penitus sublatus fuerit,sed propter mortalitatē,quæ etiam ante peccatum & sine peccato homini,vtpote corpus animale habenti, & ex terra,ab ipso initio formato, naturalis erat, vt recte inprimis animad- uertit,& latè exposuit Augustinus de Genesi ad literam libri 6.cap.19. vsque ad postremum caput 29:Beneficio igitur Christi à moriendi neces- sitate liberati sunt,qui ipsi confidunt,alioqui mortem necessario subitu- ri. Hinc manauit illa in Epist. ad Hebr. sententia,capite nono ad finem. Statutum est hominibus semel mori. Ibi enim hominis ex decreto diui-no, conditio, quam ab Adamo traximus, citra Christi beneficium confide-ratur. Quanquam verbum ἀπόκειται, quod vetus interpres conuertit, sta-tutum est, euentum, & rei naturam potius quàm diuinum decretum declarat. Quod autem mors naturalis, quatenus naturalis est, pœna pec-cati non sit, latissimè à nobis alio loco disputatum est: nempe in libello de mortalitate primi hominis aduersus Puccium. Quem librum hactenus nec videre, nec consequi potui.
units.tr: But the view of the Samosatenians on Adam's immortality is set out much more clearly by Faustus Socinus in the third book, On Jesus Christ the Saviour, chapter eight, where among other things he writes as follows: Natural death, insofar as it is natural and common to all, is not the wages of sin, but a consequence proper to our nature, which Adam himself received in his very creation. The wages of sin, however, are the necessity of dying and eternal death. This is clear from the fact that Christ freed us, who have faith in him, from every sin, that is, from the penalty and guilt of sin, and yet he did not take away natural death, only eternal death and the necessity of dying. No one doubts about eternal death. As for the necessity of dying, those of us whom the last coming of Christ finds alive, who will not taste death, can teach us. The same judgment must be made about all as about those few. For if Christ had not removed the necessity of dying, not even those few could escape death. Therefore the other believers die, not because it is necessary for them to die on account of sin, since the guilt of sin has been wholly taken away, but on account of mortality, which was natural to man even before sin and without sin, since he has an animal body and was formed from the earth at the beginning. This was rightly noticed first, and fully explained, by Augustine in his Literal Commentary on Genesis, book 6, chapter 19, to the last chapter, 29. Therefore those who trust in Christ are freed from the necessity of dying by his benefit; otherwise they would necessarily have to undergo death. From this came that saying in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter nine, near the end: It is appointed for men once to die. For there the condition of man, which we drew from Adam, is considered by divine decree apart from the benefit of Christ. Yet the word ἀπόκειται, which the old translator rendered "it is appointed," declares an outcome and the nature of the thing rather than a divine decree. That natural death, insofar as it is natural, is not a penalty of sin, has been discussed by us at much greater length elsewhere: namely in the little book on the mortality of the first man, against Puccius. I have not yet been able to see or obtain this book.

units.la: Quæ itaque vtriusque partis hac de re sit sententia, per breues antitheses declarabimus.
units.tr: Let us, then, state the view of each side on this matter in brief antitheses.

units.la: Sententia orthodoxa. Sententia Socinianorum.
units.tr: The orthodox opinion. The Socinian opinion.

units.la: 1. Adamus, in statu innocentiæ, mortalis fuit & immortalis: mortalis potentia, & in se, ac natură sua, immortalis vero gratia conditoris & beneficio pacti, seu fœderis, nec moritu-rus fuisset, si in gratia perstitis-set, & Deo adhæsisset ἀναμάρτητος.
units.tr: 1. Adam, in the state of innocence, was both mortal and immortal: mortal in his power and in himself and by his nature, but immortal by the grace of the Creator and by the benefit of the covenant, or pact, and he would not have died if he had persevered in grace and had clung to God, [ἀναμάρτητος] sinless.

units.la: 2. Deus non potuisset tantùm, sed etiã voluisset, ipsum à mor-te conseruare, si non peccasset, nec refuscitatione à mortuis o-pus fuisset.
units.tr: 2. God not only could have, but would have, kept him from death if he had not sinned, and there would have been no need of raising him from the dead.

units.la: 3. Non tantùm mors æterna, & moriendi necessitas, sed etiam mors corporalis, & quicquid mortis nomine in sacris literis appellatur, peccati pœna ac sti-pendium, ac proinde mors cor-poralis, non ipsius naturę, quam
units.tr: 3. Not only eternal death and the necessity of dying, but also bodily death, and whatever is called death by the name in the sacred writings, is the penalty and wages of sin; and therefore bodily death is not a consequence of his nature, which

units.la: 1. Adamus etiam in statu innocen-tia constitutus, nec in se, aut à na-tura, nec beneficio gratiæ, aut pa-cti, seu fœderis, cum ipso initi, im-mortalis fuit, sed moriturus fuisset, etiamsi non peccasset.
units.tr: 1. Adam, even when placed in the state of innocence, was not immortal, either in himself or by nature, or by the benefit of grace, or by the pact or covenant made with him; he would have died even if he had not sinned.

units.la: 2. Deus potuisset quidem, si voluis-set ipsum à morte conseruare, vel etiam mortuum iterum refusci-tare.
units.tr: 2. God could indeed have kept him from death, if he had willed, or even raised him again once dead.

units.la: 3. Mors corporalis non peccati pœ-na vel stipendium, sed homini na-turali & ipsius natura, quam A-damus in ipsa creatione accepit, propria sequela est. Ipsa autem mors æterna, cum moriendi neces-sitate (Ostorrodius addit mortem Adamus in ipsa creatione accepit, sed contra naturam & peccati ipsius, sequela est.
units.tr: 3. Bodily death is not a penalty or wages of sin, but a consequence proper to natural man and to his nature, which Adam received in his very creation. Eternal death itself, however, together with the necessity of dying (Ostorrodius adds death which Adam received in his very creation, but is a consequence contrary to nature and to that of sin itself).

units.la: Christus non moriendi necessitatem, sed damnationem aeternam, à fidelibus sustulit, qui proinde moriuntur, non propter aliquam mortalitatem, quæ Adamo etiam ante peccatum naturalis fuisse confingitur, sed quia statutum est omnes homines propter peccatum mori, verum beneficio & efficacia passionis Christi, mortis naturalis vis & efficacia, in sanctis, fracto aculeo immutatur.
units.tr: Christ removed from believers not the necessity of dying but eternal damnation. Therefore believers die, not on account of some mortality which is pretended to have been natural to Adam even before sin, but because it has been decreed that all men die on account of sin; yet, by the benefit and efficacy of Christ's passion, the power and efficacy of natural death is changed in the saints, its sting having been broken.

units.la: ipsam) peccati poena, ac stipendium est.
units.tr: itself) is the penalty and wages of sin.

units.la: Fideles moriuntur, non quia propter peccatum eos mori necesse sit, cum moriendi necessitas sublata sit per Christum: sed propter mortalitatem, quæ etiam ante peccatum, & sine peccato homini, utpote corpus animale habenti, & ex terra, ab initio formato naturalis erat.
units.tr: Believers die, not because it is necessary for them to die on account of sin, since the necessity of dying has been removed through Christ; but on account of mortality, which was natural to man even before sin and without sin, since he has an animal body and was formed from the earth at the beginning.

units.la: Nos veritatem sententiæ, ac thesium nostrarum, ita demonstrabimus, ut simul falsitas doctrinæ Socinianæ, manifeste omnibus appareat.
units.tr: We will demonstrate the truth of our view and our theses in such a way that the falsehood of the Socinian doctrine will at the same time be plain to everyone.

units.la: Argumentum I. desumitur à natura imaginis divinæ. Imago enim (prout nos imaginis nomen hic sumimus, nempe pro eo quod ad exemplar, & ἀρχέτυπον alterius efformatur) est quod aliquid repræsentat, hoc est, vel à prototypo est expressum, vel ad ipsius typum efformatum, id est, vel eandem participat speciem, quomodo filius est imago patris, vel saltem eam adumbrat, ac demonstrat sicut statua Cæsaris imago illius vocatur. Imago autem Dei in homine per creationem quum effulserit, sic ut maiestatem divinam, perfectionemque adumbraverit, seu repræsentaverit, & quidem simillime, (quia imago erat iuxta similitudinem, id est, Deum quàm proximè referens) proprietates nempe illas, quæ communicabiles dicuntur, Deus autem sit immortalis, iustus, sanctus, & verax: ideo sine dubio etiam ipse Adamus, ad imaginem Dei conditus, beneficio ipsius conditoris, non tantum iustus, sanctus & verax conditus fuit, sed etiam immortalis futurus fuisset, si non peccasset.
units.tr: Argument I. is drawn from the nature of the divine image. For an image (as we take the word "image" here, namely for that which is formed after a model and an archetype [ἀρχέτυπον] of another) is something that represents something, that is, either is expressed from its prototype or is formed after its likeness: either it shares the same species, as the Son is the image of the Father, or at least it shadows forth and displays it, as Caesar's statue is called his image. Now since the image of God in man shone forth at creation, so as to shadow forth or represent the divine majesty and perfection, and indeed most closely (because it was an image according to likeness, that is, referring to God as nearly as possible), namely those properties which are called communicable, and since God is immortal, just, holy, and true, therefore without doubt Adam himself, created in the image of God, was made by the benefit of his Creator not only just, holy, and true, but would also have been immortal, if he had not sinned.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum respondet Aduersarius, ac dicit, Primò, Si homo primum immortalitate, & iustitia Deo similis fuisset conditus, tum ipsum nulla ratione mori, aut peccare potuisse, quoniam Deus ita immortalis ac iustus est, ut nulla ratione mori, aut peccare possit. Quod autem homo ea ratione immortalis, aut iustus conditus non fuerit, ex eo manifestum esse ait, quod & peccauerit, & mortuus sit. Vnde concludit, similitudinem illam & imaginem Dei, non immortalitatem, aut iustitiam, sed aliud aliquid fuisse, quod etiamnum in homine conspiciatur & reperiatur. Atque huic argumento tantum tribuit Aduersarius, ut nulla sententiae suae ἀνταπόδοσις opus esse, exi stimet.
units.tr: The Adversary responds to this argument, and says: First, if man had been created like God in immortality and righteousness, then he could in no way have died or sinned, since God is so immortal and just that he can in no way die or sin. That man was not created immortal or just in this way is clear, he says, from the fact that he both sinned and died. From this he concludes that that likeness and image of God was not immortality or righteousness, but something else, which is still seen and found in man. And the Adversary attributes so much to this argument that he thinks no rejoinder [ἀνταπόδοσις] to his own view is needed.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si imago illa Dei & similitudo, ad quam homo fuit conditus, significaret iustitiam, & immortalitatem, sic ut homo, immortali, ate & iustitia Deo similis creatus fuisse dicatur, tum neque morit neque peccare potuisset.
units.tr: If that image of God and likeness, to which man was created, signified righteousness and immortality, so that man could be said to have been created like God in immortality and righteousness, then he could neither have died nor been able to sin.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum esse, patet ex euentu: Ergo & antecedens: & consequenter illa imago Dei, ac similitudo, aliud quid fuit, quod etiamnum in homine reperitur.
units.tr: But the consequent is plainly false, as the outcome shows. Therefore the antecedent is false too, and so that image of God and likeness was something else, which is still found in man.

units.la: Connexi hanc probationem subiicit.
units.tr: He adds a proof of the connection.

units.la: Si Deus nulla ratione peccare, aut mori potest, tum si homo iustitia & immortalitate ipsi similis creatus fuit, & imago ac similitudo illa Dei, ad quam conditus Adamus fuit, immortalitatem & iustitiam significat, sequitur ipsum nec mori, nec peccare potuisse.
units.tr: If God can in no way sin or die, then, if man was created like him in righteousness and immortality, and that image and likeness of God to which Adam was created signifies immortality and righteousness, it follows that he could neither die nor sin.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Resp. Connexum vtrumque falsum esse: Sequeretur enim ex antecedente, hominem primum, beneficio imaginis diuinae, nec mori, neque peccare potuisse, si videlicet illa imago Dei ad quam conditus fuit, non tantum similitudinem aliquam, & analogiam immortalitatis, iustitiae & sanctimoniae diuinae, ac communicatam quandam συμπάθειαν, sed etiam aequalitatem, eorundem attributorum in se complecteretur. Sed quia hominem Dei imaginem, in primaeuae integritatis statu fuisse dicimus, non propter essentiae diuinae, quae immutabilis est, similitudinem, sed propter quarundam proprietatum non aequalitatem, sed conuenientiam & analogiam, ac proinde conditionem Adami etiam in ipso naturæ & creationis primordio, sentimus longissimè abfuisse à conditione Dei, & adumbrare solùm, ac quasi lineamentis quibusdam repræsentare imaginem Dei potuisse, ideò vehementer fallit Oflorrodius, dum inter πὸ ὁμοίως ἐχονϚ & τὸ ὁμοίως ἐπίχονϚ, discrimen nullum facit.
units.tr: Reply: both the connections are false. It would follow from the antecedent that man, by the benefit of the divine image, could neither die nor sin, if indeed that image of God to which he was created comprised not merely some likeness and analogy of immortality, righteousness and divine holiness, and a certain shared sympathy [συμπάθεια], but also equality in those same attributes. But since we say that man was the image of God in the state of original integrity, not because of any likeness to the divine essence, which is unchangeable, but because of certain properties which were not equal to God's but agreed with them and were analogous to them; and since we hold that Adam's condition, even at the very beginning of his nature and creation, was far removed from the condition of God, and could only adumbrate the image of God, or represent it as in certain outlines; therefore Ostorodius is greatly mistaken in making no distinction between being alike in state [τὸ ὁμοίως ἔχον] and being alike in relation [τὸ ὁμοίως ἐπίχον].

units.la: Secundo imaginem & similitudinem illam Dei, non immortalitatem, iustitiam, & sanctimoniam significare, ex eo etiam manifestum esse dicit, quod homo etiam postquam iam peccavit, ad similitudinem & imaginem Dei conditus esse dicitur: In quibus locis illa imago Dei, nulla ratione de immortalitate & iustitia intelligi potest, utpote quas dotes, ipsis etiam Aduersarijs confitentibus, homo statim, atque peccavit, perdidit.
units.tr: Second, he says it is also clear from this that that image and likeness of God does not signify immortality, righteousness and holiness: man is said to have been created in the likeness and image of God even after he had already sinned. In these passages that image of God cannot in any way be understood as immortality and righteousness, since, as even our opponents concede, man lost these gifts as soon as he sinned.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si homo, etiam postquam peccavit, ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei creatus, vel factus esse dicitur, tum illa imago & similitudo Dei, immortalitatem & iustitiam, nulla ratione significare potest: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If man, even after he sinned, is said to have been created or made in the image and likeness of God, then that image and likeness of God can in no way signify immortality and righteousness. But the former is true; therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Connexi hanc probationem subiungit.
units.tr: He adds a proof of the connection.

units.la: Si homo, statim atque peccavit immortalitatis, & iustitiæ dotes penitus amisit, tum, si etiam postquam peccavit, nihilominus ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei creatus esse dicitur, sequitur certè imaginem & similitudinem illam Dei, nulla ratione immortalitatem & iustitiam significare posse. Atqui prius verum est, ipsis Aduersarijs confitentibus: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If man, as soon as he sinned, wholly lost the gifts of immortality and righteousness, then, if nevertheless he is said to have been created in the image and likeness of God even after he sinned, it certainly follows that that image and likeness of God can in no way signify immortality and righteousness. But the former is true, as our opponents concede; therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam utramque esse falsam, atque ut illa falsitas eò magis & euidentius appareat, notandum est, ut imago Dei tres quasi partes in se complectitur, substantiam videlicet incorpoream, & immortalem cum suis facultatibus intelligendi, atque volendi: deinde perfectissimas ac præstantissimas illas animæ rationalis dotes ac qualitates, iustitiam puta, & sanctimoniam, cum summa illa felicitate & beatitudine in qua constituerat ipsum Dominus: deniq; ius & dominium in creaturas reliquas, quo ille maiestate diuinâ repræsentabat, & quodâmodo repræsetat, & adûbrat etiânû, ita quoque hominem nomine imaginis diuinæ indigitari posse, ratione nominis vel ab omnibus illis tribus partibus simul atque coniunctim, vel ab vna, aut altera tantùm ex illis desumpta. Et quia nec ipsam Dei imaginem, primorum parentum lapsu penitus deletam, sed miserè corruptam ac deformatam esse dicimus, nec integram animæ substantiam, aut rationem omnem, iudicium atque intelligentiam, sed animæ sanitatem, præstantissimas videlicet illas qualitates ac dotes ipsius, quibus ipsam Deus in creatione ornauerat, sublatas & extinctas esse docemus: ideò nihil impedit, quominus etiam post peccatum, homo propter illas imaginis diuinæ reliquias, ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei factus esse dicatur, salua doctrina nostra.
units.tr: Reply: both consequences are false. So that this falsity may appear all the more clearly and evidently, it should be noted that the image of God embraces, as it were, three parts. The first is an incorporeal and immortal substance with its faculties of understanding and willing. The second is those most perfect and excellent gifts and qualities of the rational soul, namely righteousness and holiness, together with that supreme happiness and blessedness in which the Lord had established him. The third is the right and dominion over the other creatures, by which he represented, and in a way still represents and adumbrates, the divine majesty. Thus man can also be designated by the name of the image of God, whether the name is taken from all three parts together and jointly, or from only one or another of them. And since we say that the image of God itself was not wholly blotted out by the fall of our first parents, but was wretchedly corrupted and deformed; and since we teach that it was not the whole substance of the soul, nor all reason, judgement and understanding, that was lost, but the soundness of the soul, namely those most excellent qualities and gifts with which God had adorned it at creation, which were removed and extinguished; therefore nothing prevents, while our doctrine stands, that even after the fall man should be said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, on account of those remnants of the divine image.

units.la: Quamuis igitur homo etiam post peccatum & immortalitatis, iustitiæque originalis dotes peccato perditas, ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei factus esse dicitur, minimè tamen inde sequitur imaginem & similitudinem Dei, iustitiam, sanctimoniam, & immortalitatem hominis in primæua integritate constituti, significare non posse. Vt enim homo ante lapsum ad imaginem Dei conditus esse dicebatur, non tamen propter ipsam animæ substantiam, & splendidam in res creatas cæteras autoritatem & dominii potestionem, sed maximè propter virtutum omnium, quibus conspicuus erat chorum & cumulum: ita post lapsum, peccato videlicet virtutibus omnibus profligatis, ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei factus esse perhibetur, argumento non ab illo nobilissimæ & bonis omnibus ac virtutibus exaggeratæ imaginis diuinæ splendore, sed ab eiusdem, vt & dominii, & supra creaturas cæteras dignitatis ac excellentiæ reliquiis desumpto. Sic Gen. 9. ver. 6. Qui effundit, inquit Iehouah, sanguinem hominis, per hominem sanguis illius effunditur, quoniam ad imaginem suam hominem fecit Deus. Vbi Deus reliquias illius imaginis diuinæ, quam effinxerat principiò in nobis, & indignissimè deformatam à nobis, misericorditer se conseruaturus significat, & destruere prohibet. Sic 1. Corint. 11. ver. 7. Vir quidem non debet velare caput suum, quum sit imago, & gloria Dei, & mulier gloria viri est. Quo in loco vir, ob imperium ac dominium, quod in res omnes, atque etiam in mulieres obtinet, imago Dei appellatur, quum alias ipsam etiam mulierem ad imaginem Dei conditam esse, constat. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissimè liquet, connexum vtrumque Aduersarii falsum esse. Tum demum ex eo, quod homo etiam post peccatum, catum, & perditam immortalitatem,ac iustitiam originalem, ad imaginem,& similitudinem Dei factus esse dicitur, sequeretur il-lam imaginem Dei ac similitudinem, immortalitatem, & iusti-tiam significare non posse, si videlicet solam immortalitatem, & iustitiam illa imagine significari doceremus,quod cum falsum sit, ideò totum argumentum euanescit.
units.tr: Although, therefore, man even after sin is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, though the gifts of immortality and original righteousness were lost through sin, it by no means follows that the image and likeness of God cannot signify the righteousness, holiness and immortality of man as constituted in original integrity. For just as before the fall man was said to be created in the image of God, not, however, on account of the substance of the soul itself, nor his splendid authority and dominion over the other created things, but chiefly on account of all the virtues in which he was conspicuous as a whole and in their fullness; so after the fall, with sin having overthrown all the virtues, he is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, the argument being drawn not from the splendour of that most noble image of God, enriched with all good things and virtues, but from the remnants of that same image, such as its dominion and its dignity and excellence above the other creatures. Thus Gen. 9. ver. 6: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image," says Jehovah. There God signifies that he will mercifully preserve the remnants of that divine image which he had at first formed in us and which we have most unworthily deformed, and he forbids them to be destroyed. Thus 1 Cor. 11. ver. 7: "A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man." In this passage the man is called the image of God because of the authority and dominion which he holds over all things and even over women, although it is clear that the woman too was created in the image of God. From all of these it is most manifestly plain that both connections of our opponent are false. Then, from the fact that man, even after sin, with immortality and original righteousness lost, is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, it would follow that that image and likeness of God cannot signify immortality and righteousness, if indeed we taught that only immortality and righteousness were signified by that image. Since this is false, the whole argument vanishes.

units.la: Tertiò suam sententiam, quànam in re statuenda sit imago illa,exponens, dicit illam sitam esse primo,ac præcipuè in dominio, ac imperio illo,quod Deus homini in res creatas alias contulit,vt videre sit ex Gen. 1.vers.26. Posteà dixit Deus faciamus hominem ad imagi-nem nostram, secundùm similitudinem nostram, qui dominetur piscibus maris, & in volucres cœli, & in pecudes, & in vniuersam terram, atque in omnia reptilia reptantia super terram: Deinde in ratione, sine cuius vsu nemo rebus creatis dominari possit.
units.tr: Third, in setting out his own view of where that image is to be located, he says that it lies first and chiefly in that dominion and rule which God gave man over the other created things, as may be seen from Gen. 1. ver. 26: "Afterwards God said, Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, who shall rule over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over the cattle, and over the whole earth, and over all the creeping things that creep upon the earth." Then he locates it in reason, without the use of which no one could rule over created things.

units.la: Resp. Imaginem, ac similitudinem Dei,ad quam homo conditus fuit,etiam in dominio illo,ac imperio quod accepit à Deo in creaturas cæteras, atque in rationis lumine rectè constitui, minimè negamus, nec locus ex Mose citatus aliud probat, sed illam non in solo dominio, aut ratione, sed insuper, & quidem præcipuè in iustitia,& sanctimonia originali, quærendam esse ex illis argumentis,quibus hominem à Deo iustum, & sanctum creatum esse paulò post demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Reply: we by no means deny that the image and likeness of God, to which man was created, is rightly placed in that dominion and rule which he received from God over the other creatures, and in the light of reason; nor does the passage cited from Moses prove anything else. But we seek it not in dominion or reason alone, but further, and indeed chiefly, in original righteousness and holiness, as we shall demonstrate shortly from those arguments by which man is shown to have been created by God righteous and holy.

units.la: Argumentum I I. desumitur à reparatione per Christum facta: Quod n. in Christo recuperamus, id in Adamo habuimus, & amisimus: Atqui in Christo recuperamus corpora immortalia,ac spiritualia 1 Cor.15.42. Seminatur corpus corruptioni obnoxium, excitatur incorruptum: & 53.54. Oportet hoc corruptioni obnoxium, induere incorruptam naturam, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem: quum autem hoc corruptioni obnoxium indueret incorruptam naturam, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tum fiet illud, quod scriptum est, Absorpta est mors ad victoriam. Ergo talia corpora habuimus in Adamo, ac proinde ipsum quoque tale, nempè spirituale, & immortale,habuisse,necesse est.
units.tr: Argument II is drawn from the restoration effected through Christ. What we recover in Christ, we had in Adam and lost. But in Christ we recover immortal and spiritual bodies: 1 Cor. 15. ver. 42: "It is sown a body subject to corruption; it is raised incorruptible." And vers. 53, 54: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality; and when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory." Therefore we had such bodies in Adam, and so he too must necessarily have had such a body, namely a spiritual and immortal one.

units.la: Argumentum I I I. desumitur à mortis ipsius natura, & effectu: Quod enim est contra naturam hominis, & illam plane destruit, id non est homini naturale. Quicquid enim proprie homini naturale est,id vel essentiam hominis constituit, vel perficit,& ex principiis, & causis essentialibus oritur: Atqui mors corporalis, est contra naturam hominis, & illam destruit: Ergo mors corporalis homini non est naturalis.
units.tr: Argument III. is drawn from the nature and effect of death itself. What is contrary to the nature of man and plainly destroys it cannot be natural to man. Whatever is properly natural to man either constitutes or perfects the essence of man and arises from its essential principles and causes. But bodily death is contrary to the nature of man and destroys it. Therefore bodily death is not natural to man.

units.la: Argumentum III. desumitur à proprio peccati effectu: Si enim mors non animæ tantùm & æterna, sed etiam corporalis, cum omnibus suis adiunctis, tum consequentibus, vt vanitate, & omnis generis ærumnis, tum signis innumeris mortem istam antecedentibus, & quicquid mortis nomine, in Scripturis, appellatur, ex Dei voluntate, & iustitia, peccati effectus, stipendium, atque pœna est: tum necessario sequitur, Adamum, si in primæua integritate, & innocentia perstitisset, ex eadem Dei voluntate, & iustitia, quantumuis in se mortalem, nùquam tamen moriturum fuisse: Atqui mortem non animæ tantùm, & æternam, sed etiam corporalē, cū omnib. coniunctis antecedentibus, & cõsequentibus, & quicquid mortis nomine in Scripturis sacris appellatur, ex Dei volūtate & iustitia, peccati effectum, stipendium, atqș pœnam esse demonstratur: primò: Ex Rom. 5. v. 12. 13. 14. Sicut per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors peruasit, in quo omnes peccauerunt: nam vsque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo, peccatum vero esse non putatur, non existente lege: regnauit autem mors ab Adam vsque ad Mosen, in eos etiam qui non peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam. Quibus verbis ostendens Apostolus, quare propter Adamum omnes moriantur, seu quare mors per delictū n Adami inuecta in mundum, in omnes homines ineuitabili vi peruaserit, non illam recenset causam quam Sociniani confingunt, quod videlicet mors corporalis homini naturalis & ipsius naturæ quam Adamus in creatione acceperat, sequela sit, sed veram mortis originem patefacit, nempe peccatum, cùm omnes peccasse affirmat. Sicuti etiam alibi mortem stipendium peccati esse docet. Rom. 6. ver. 23. Quod si igitur solum peccatum mortis causa meritoria est, & ipsi aditum in mundum patefecit, necessario sequitur Adamum, nisi peccasset, nunquam moriturum fuisse. Illud enim, cuius sola & vnica causa est peccatum, esse non potest, nisi peccatum fit, vel fuerit, cùm à remotione causæ efficientis propriæ ac solitariæ, omnium gentium non barbarum consensu necessaria detur consequentia: Sed mors est illud, cuius sola & vnica cáusa est peccatum. Ergo mors Adamum inuadere non potuisset, nisi ille prius peccasset. Secundò, ab ipsius pacti, seu fœderis diuini cum Adamo initi, & comminationis, si debitam obedientiam non praestaret, natura,ac veritate: Gen.2.v. 17.Ex arbore scientia boni & mali non comedes : nam quacunque die comederis ex illa,moriendo morieris. Hac enim comminatione diuina non tantum mortem aeternam,aut moriendi necessitatē,sed quicquid mortis nomine,in sacris Scripturis,appellatur,intelligendum esse,ex eo liquet manifestissimè, quòd mortis nomine hic significatur,quicquid vitæ,& summæ illi felicitati, qua Adamus in statu innocentiæ constitutus perfruebatur, si peccaret,aduersaturū erat: quum certissimum sit, Deum ipsi priuationem praesentis status, & bonorum,quæ possidebat,& illis contrariorum malorum miseriam, minari, illorúmque omnium comminatione à peccato, & inobedientia deterrere ipsum voluisse. Quia vero vitæ , & felicitati Adami aduersabatur, non modò aeterna mors, aut moriendi necessitas, sed ipsa etiam mors corporalis,cum omnibus suis antecedentibus, consequentibus, atque effectis, quippe quæ omnia & singula, naturam ipsius euersura, & destructura erant, si peccaret: ideò euidenter hinc apparet, non tantum æternam mortem, aut moriendi necessitatem,sed quicquid mortis nomine in Scripturis appellatur, illa comminatione diuina contineri. Hisce adde & illud, quod phrasis ista,moriendo morieris, in Scriptura, communiter, de quauis morte vsurpatur. De corporali, Gen.26. verf.11.Qui te-tigerit hominem ipsum,aut uxorem eius,moriendo morietur. Exod. 21.v. 16.Qui maledixerit patri suo, aut matri suae, moriendo morietur: & sic in reliquis sanctionibus poenarum ciuilium, 2.Sam.1.verf.12.Filius qui natus est tibi, morte moriatur. De spirituali verò,& corporali simul:Ezech.3.verf.18. Cum dixero impio, Moriendo morieris,&c. Cùm itaque illa comminatio non specialis sit, sed indefinita, & aequipollens vniuersali, de quauis morte, ideò sequitur omnes mortis miserias,phrasi illa intelligendas esse. Ex hisce igitur omnibus necessariò sequitur,Adamum,quantumuis in se mortalem, ac φθαρτὸν, nunquam tamen moriturum fuisse, si in primæua integritate & innocentia perstitisset ἀθάνατον.
units.tr: Argument III. is drawn from the proper effect of sin. If death is not only the death of the soul and eternal death, but also bodily death with all its attendant and consequent evils, such as vanity and every kind of distress, and the countless signs that precede that death, and whatever is called death in Scripture, is the effect, wages and punishment of sin, by the will and justice of God, then it follows necessarily that Adam, had he persevered in his original integrity and innocence, would never have died, even though he was mortal in himself, by the same will and justice of God. But that death is not only of the soul and eternal, but also bodily, together with all its attendant and consequent evils, and whatever is called death in the holy Scriptures, is the effect, wages and punishment of sin, by the will and justice of God, is shown as follows. First, from Rom. 5. vv. 12–14: As through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned. For until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no law. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam. In these words the Apostle shows why all die because of Adam, or why death, brought into the world through the sin of Adam, spread to all men with unavoidable force. He does not give the cause that the Socinians invent, namely that bodily death is natural to man and a consequence of the nature which Adam received at creation. Instead he discloses the true origin of death, namely sin, when he affirms that all have sinned. Likewise he teaches elsewhere that death is the wages of sin, Rom. 6. v. 23. If, then, sin alone is the meritorious cause of death, and has opened the way for it into the world, it follows necessarily that Adam, had he not sinned, would never have died. For that whose sole and only cause is sin cannot exist unless sin has happened or will happen, since by the removal of its proper and only efficient cause the consequence is necessary, as all civilized peoples agree. But death is that whose sole and only cause is sin. Therefore death could not have seized Adam unless he had first sinned. Secondly, from the nature and truth of the covenant or divine agreement made with Adam, and of the threat, should he not render the due obedience: Gen. 2. v. 17: Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for in the day that you eat of it, dying you shall die. That this divine threat means not only eternal death or the necessity of dying, but whatever is called death in the holy Scriptures, is made very clear by the fact that the word death here signifies whatever would be opposed to life and to that supreme happiness which Adam enjoyed in the state of innocence, if he sinned. For it is most certain that God threatened him with the loss of his present state and of the goods he possessed, and with the misery of the evils contrary to them, and wished to deter him from sin and disobedience by threatening all of these. And since bodily death, with all its antecedents, consequents and effects, opposed the life and happiness of Adam, not only eternal death or the necessity of dying, but bodily death itself would have overturned and destroyed his nature, had he sinned. Therefore it is evident that not only eternal death or the necessity of dying, but whatever is called death in the Scriptures, is contained in that divine threat. Add to this that the phrase dying you shall die is commonly used in Scripture of any kind of death. Of bodily death, Gen. 26. v. 11: He who touches this man or his wife shall surely die. Exod. 21. v. 16: He who curses his father or his mother shall surely die; and so in the other sanctions of civil penalties; 2 Sam. 1. v. 12: The son who is born to you shall surely die. Of both spiritual and bodily death together, Ezek. 3. v. 18: When I say to the wicked, You shall surely die, etc. Since, then, that threat is not specific but indefinite, and equivalent to a universal one, concerning any kind of death, it follows that all the miseries of death are to be understood under that phrase. From all these things it follows necessarily that Adam, though mortal and corruptible in himself, would never have died had he persevered in his primal integrity and innocence, being immortal.

units.la: Hinc etiam corruit hypothesis, ac fundamentum illius confictæ distinctionis,qua post peccati mortísque in mundum introitum inter mortalitatem, & moriendi necessitatem discrimen faciunt Samosateniani, illámque naturæ ipsius, hanc verò peccati sequelam esse affirmant : quia mortalitas in statu corrupto, nihil aliud est quàm moriendi necessitas. Vt enim homo ante lapsum erat mortalis in se, & natura sua, ac poterat mori etiam ipso actu, quia peccare poterat, & sic gratia Dei qua à morte conseruabatur, excidere, sed tamen moriturus nûquam fuisset, nisi peccando gratia Dei indignum se fecisset: ita homo post lapsum, ita est mortalis, vt necessariò moriatur & non posset non mori. Quum igitur ex argumetis allatis constet, Adamum si non peccasset, nunquam moriturum fuisse, & peccati poenam esse, quicquid mortis nomine in Scripturis sacris appellatur: ideò manifestè liquet, in corruptionis hoc, & peccati dominantis statu, inter mortalitatem & moriendi necessitatem discrimen nullum esse.
units.tr: Hence also collapses the hypothesis and foundation of that invented distinction by which the Samosatenians, after the entry of sin and death into the world, make a difference between mortality and the necessity of dying, and affirm that the former belongs to the nature of man, and the latter is a consequence of sin. For mortality in a corrupt state is nothing other than the necessity of dying. Just as man before the fall was mortal in himself and by his nature, and could even actually die, since he could sin and so fall from the grace of God by which he was preserved from death, yet he would never have died unless by sinning he had made himself unworthy of the grace of God; so man after the fall is so mortal that he necessarily dies and cannot but die. Since, then, it is established by the arguments adduced that Adam, had he not sinned, would never have died, and that whatever is called death in the holy Scriptures is the punishment of sin, it is clearly manifest that in this state of corruption and dominant sin there is no difference between mortality and the necessity of dying.

units.la: Deinde, si moriendi necessitas peccati poena est, mors autem corporalis Adamo etiam ante peccatum, & sine peccato naturalis fuit, ideò quia corpus animale habuit, tum sequitur moriendi necessitatem, ipsi etiam ante peccatum & sine peccato naturalem, ac proinde inter Adamū in statu integritatis ac innocentiæ, & in statu peccati constitutum, cæterósque peccatores omnes, quoad poenam corporalem & moriendi necessitatē discrimē nullum fuisse, & sic peccati poenā ipsi innocēti, & iustissimo inflictam esse, quum mortalitas ex animalitate nihil aliud sit, quam moriendi necessitas, quia necessitas materiæ corruptibilis, facit necessariam corruptionem, & mortem, vnde etiam Philosophi materiam ὕλην ap-pellarunt. Atqui consequens cum sit falsum, impium, & iustitiæ diuinæ plane contrarium: Ergo & antecedens falsum est censendum. At Deus potuisset quidem, si voluisset, inquit Ostorrodius, Adamum à morte immunem conseruare.
units.tr: Further, if the necessity of dying is the punishment of sin, but bodily death was natural to Adam even before sin and without sin, because he had an animal body, then the necessity of dying was also natural to him before sin and without sin. Consequently there was no difference, as regards bodily punishment and the necessity of dying, between Adam constituted in the state of integrity and innocence and all other sinners in the state of sin. Thus the punishment of sin would have been inflicted on him, though innocent and most just, since mortality arising from animality is nothing other than the necessity of dying, because the necessity of corruptible matter produces necessary corruption and death; hence the philosophers also called matter [ὕλη]. But since the consequent is false, impious, and plainly contrary to the justice of God, the antecedent must also be judged false. But God could indeed, says Ostorrodius, have preserved Adam free from death, if he had willed.

units.la: Resp. Quid tum? Hoc causam Socinianam non iuuat, nec abfur-ditatē sententiæ illius tegit, cùm à posse, ad esse, vt loquuntur, nomen detur consequentia. Aut enim voluit Deus Adamum in se, & natura sua mortalem, sua omnipotetia à morte conseruare, quandiu in sua integritate & innocentia perseueraffet, aut non voluit. Sic voluit, qua fronte affirmare audent Socistiani, Adamum etiam, non peccasset, moriturum tamen fuisse, mortemque corporalem non peccati, sed naturæ ipsius, quam Adamus in creatione accepit, sequelam esse? Nonne quæcunque Deus vult facit in cœlo, & in terra, & in omnibus abyssis, Psal. 135. 6. Si verò Deus noluit id beneficii in Adamum conferre, sola potentia diuina sine voluntate Dei coniuncta, neque ipsum à mortis sæuitia & iniuria actu ipso liberasset, nec discrimen inter Adamum in statu integritatis, & in statu peccati constitutum. cæterósque peccatores omnes vllum fecisset, nisi forte exístimet Aduersarius peccato Adami, illam Dei potétiam diminutam, aut Deum illa spoliatum esse, quum ipse etiamnum, si absolutam eius omnipotétiam spectes,omnes quantumuis impios, si vellet à morte saluos & immunes conseruare,imò res ipsa(si verû sit quod Socinus affirmat)conseruet quotquot Christi aduentus,in vltima iudicii die,superstites deprehédet, inter quos multos etiá impios, vt paulò post demonstrabimus,futuri sunt,inter quos proinde, & Adamum in statu innocentiæ omnium virtutum ornamentis instructum,quò ad pœnam corporalem, secundùm Aducrsariorum doctrinam, discrimé nullum erit,quum satis ex iis quæ dicta sunt, appareat solam Dei potentiam sine voluntate, statuum & conditionum hominis discrimen nullum consistere. Quod verò Oftorrodius addit & dicit,verba illa comminationis, Gen.2. v.17.& illa Apostoli Rom.5. v.12. quibus mors per peccatum in mundum intrasse dicit, non de mortalitate naturali,sed de morte ipsa, & moriendi necessitate intelligenda esse,nodum non soluit,sed cogringit. Si enim mors ipsa corporalis pœna peccati est, seu, si hæc pœna peccati est, quod mors ipso actu in mundum intrauerit,& Adamus moriturus fuisset, etiamsi non peccasset, sequitur Deum Adamo innocenti pœnam peccati inflicturum, & ipsum iniuste puniturum fuisse, quod cum blasphemum sit & impium, ideo doctrina Aduersariorum de mortalitate primi hominis,falsitatis & erroris grauissimi luculeter & solide conuincitur.
units.tr: Reply. And what of that? This does not help the Socinian cause, nor does it cover the absurdity of their opinion, since the inference is called, as they say, from can to is. For either God willed to preserve Adam, who was mortal in himself and by his nature, from death by his omnipotence, as long as he persevered in his integrity and innocence, or he did not will it. If he willed it, how do the Socinians dare to affirm that Adam, even had he not sinned, would still have died, and that bodily death is the consequence not of sin but of the nature which Adam received at creation? Does not Psalm 135. 6 say that whatever God wills he does, in heaven and in earth and in all the depths? But if God did not will to confer that benefit on Adam, then the divine power alone, without the will of God joined to it, would neither have actually freed him from the violence and injury of death, nor would it have made any difference between Adam constituted in the state of integrity and all other sinners in the state of sin, unless perhaps the Adversary thinks that God's power was diminished by Adam's sin, or that God was deprived of it. For even now, if you consider his absolute omnipotence, he could preserve from death all the wicked, if he willed to save and free them; indeed the very fact (if what Socinus affirms is true) will preserve all those who are found alive at the coming of Christ on the last day of judgment, among whom, as we will show shortly, there will be many wicked people. Among these, then, Adam, instructed in the ornaments of all virtues in the state of innocence, will make no difference as regards bodily punishment according to the doctrine of the Adversaries, since it appears sufficiently from what has been said that the power of God alone, without his will, establishes no difference between the states and conditions of man. As for what Ostorrodius adds and says, that those words of the threat, Gen. 2. v. 17, and that saying of the Apostle, Rom. 5. v. 12, by which he says death entered the world through sin, are to be understood not of natural mortality but of death itself and the necessity of dying, this does not untie the knot but tightens it. For if bodily death itself is the punishment of sin, or if this is the punishment of sin, that death entered the world in fact, and Adam would have died even had he not sinned, it follows that God would have inflicted the punishment of sin on the innocent Adam and would have punished him unjustly. Since this is blasphemous and impious, the doctrine of the Adversaries concerning the mortality of the first man is clearly and solidly refuted as a most grievous falsehood and error.

units.la: Quod deinde thesi quarta affirmat Socinus, nimirum Fideles non mori propterea,quod propter peccatum eos mori necesse sit,quum Christus illam necessitatem moriendi sustulerit,falsum est: Quum enim & necessitas moriendi,& mors ipsa, ac quicquid mortis titulo in sacris literis indigitatur,peccati pœna & stipendium sit,ac proinde nemo moriatur nisi ob causam mortis, nempe peccatum, vt aliquot argumentis ac rationibus à nobis est demonstratum:ideo necessariò hinc sequitur fideles,non propter aliquam mortalitatem,quam Samosateniani etiam ante peccatum,& sine peccato Adamo naturalem fuisse confingunt, sed quia propter peccatum illos mori necesse sit,quemadmodum etiam Apostolus affirmat Heb.9. verf.27. Statutum est,inquiés,hominibus,vt semel moriantur, id est,ab ipso Deo statutum est propter peccatum, vt omnes lex illa & coditio mortis maneat,vnde etiam omnib. moriendi necessitas incubit. Ratio autè quam subiungit,ab illorum exemplo & conditione desumptam, quos postremus Christi aduentus, viuos offendet ( nam de argumento altero, An videlicet fideles, per Christum à moriendi necessitate liberati sint, vt & de duab.illis rationibus,quib. in thefin quartam inspersis,obiter demonstrare conatur, mortalitatem hominis, etiam ante peccatum & sine peccato naturalem fuisse, paulò post in responsione ad argumeta Ostorrodii dispiciemus) fideles à moriendi necessitate non vindicat, quia duplici inde consequente absurdo, falsitatis manifestæ conuincitur. Si enim moriendi necessitas poena peccati est, à qua per solum Christum liberamur, ideò si illi, quos superstites offendet Christi aduentus, liberati sunt per Christū à mortis necessitate, sequitur inde primò, illos solos per Christum à poena peccati liberatos esse, quum cæteros omnes, qui ante diem iudicii è viuis excedunt, necessitas moriendi manęat, vt in antecedentibus solidè est demonstratum. Secundò, non solos fideles, sed multos etiam impios ac reprobos, per Christum, à poena peccati liberatos esse, quia inter illos quos Christus in vltima iudicii die viuos inueniet, multi erunt impii ac reprobi: Mat.24.v.40.41. Tum duo erùt in agro, vnus accipietur & alter relinquetur: duæ molentes in pistrino, vna accipietur & altera relinquetur, Luc.17.v.34. Duo erunt in vno lecto, vnus accipietur & alter relinquetur: & 18.ver. 8 Veruntamen Filius hominis, quum venerit, num reperturus est fidem in terra? Vnde etiam apparet, ex paucis illis, quibus viuis supremus ille dies superueniet, de ordinaria & communi hominum conditione iudicium faciendum non esse, quandoquidem omnibus ante Christi aduentum morientibus, moriendi necessitas incumbit, teste Apostolo Heb.9.ver. 27. Statutum est hominibus, vt semel moriantur, postea iudicium. Ex quibus liquet, paucos illos non ideò mortem non gustaturos esse, quòd Christus illos potius quàm alios, à moriendi necessitate liberauerit, sed quia dies supremus illis superueniet. Mutabuntur tamen in oculi nictu, quæ mutatio, quum fieri nequeat, quin aboleatur prior natura, merito mortis species cēsetur, licet in morte ordinaria reputari non possit, quum non sit animæ à corpore solutio.
units.tr: As for Socinus's fourth thesis, namely that the faithful do not die because it is necessary for them to die on account of sin, since Christ has removed that necessity of dying, it is false. Since both the necessity of dying and death itself, and whatever is designated by the name of death in the sacred writings, are the punishment and wages of sin, and therefore no one dies except for the cause of death, which is sin, as we have demonstrated by several arguments and reasons, it necessarily follows that the faithful die not because of some mortality which the Samosatenians imagine was natural to Adam even before and without sin, but because it is necessary for them to die on account of sin. The Apostle also affirms this: Heb. 9. v. 27. "It is appointed, he says, for men to die once", that is, it was appointed by God himself on account of sin, so that this law and condition of death remains, whence the necessity of dying also presses on all men. The reason he adds, taken from the example and condition of those whom the last coming of Christ will find alive, does not free the faithful from the necessity of dying, and it is refuted by two manifestly false consequences. (As for the second question, whether the faithful have been freed from the necessity of dying through Christ, and the two reasons, which he inserts into the fourth thesis, by which he briefly tries to show that man's mortality was natural even before sin and without sin, we shall examine shortly in the reply to Ostorodius's arguments.) For if the necessity of dying is the punishment of sin, from which we are freed through Christ alone, then, if those whom the coming of Christ finds alive have been freed by Christ from the necessity of death, it follows, first, that only they have been freed by Christ from the punishment of sin, while the necessity of dying remains for all the others who depart from the living before the day of judgment, as has been solidly demonstrated above. Second, it follows that not only the faithful but many also of the ungodly and reprobate have been freed from the punishment of sin through Christ, since among those whom Christ finds alive on the last day of judgment there will be many ungodly and reprobate: Matt. 24. v. 40-41. "Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left; two women grinding at the mill; one will be taken and the other left"; Luke 17. v. 34. "Two will be in one bed; one will be taken and the other left"; and 18. v. 8: "Nevertheless, when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" From this it also appears that no judgment about the ordinary and common condition of men should be made from those few to whom that last day will come while they are alive, since the necessity of dying presses on all who die before the coming of Christ, as the Apostle testifies, Heb. 9. v. 27. "It is appointed for men to die once, and after that the judgment." From these things it is clear that those few will not fail to taste death because Christ freed them from the necessity of dying rather than others, but because the last day will overtake them. Yet they will be changed in the twinkling of an eye, and since that change cannot happen without the former nature being abolished, it is rightly regarded as a kind of death, although it cannot be counted as ordinary death, since it is not a separation of the soul from the body.

units.la: Ex hisce verò omnibus euidenter tum doctrinæ, ac thesium nostrarum veritas, tum sententiæ Socinianæ falsitas, apparet, vnde etiam hæc de quæstionis primæ parte prima, nimirum, An Adamus à Deo immortalis conditus fuerit? dicta sufficiant: Nunc ad partem alteram progredior. Quæstionis itaque primæ partem alteram, An videlicet Deus homInem iustum & sanctum creauerit? quantum concernit, quum illius termini nulla ambiguitate laborët, nec explicatione vlla indigeat, ideò missis ambagibus omnibus, recta, ad tententiæ nostræ qua affirmamus, Deum hominem primum, iustum, & sanctum, creasse, illámque iustitiam originalem, non tantum possibilitatem quandam Dei mandata obseruandi, aut propensionem solummodo ad virtutes fuisse, sedipsam virtutem omnium, quæcunque in Decalogo præcipiuntur, aut requiruntur, possessionem, & cumulum, in se continuisse, confirmationem: progrediemur, quam sequentibus argumentis adstruimus.
units.tr: From all these things it is evidently clear both the truth of our theses and the falsity of the Socinian opinion, and so what has been said about the first part of the first question, namely whether Adam was created immortal by God, is enough. Now I proceed to the second part. As far as concerns the second part of the first question, whether God created man just and holy, since its terms are free of any ambiguity and need no explanation, I therefore set aside all circumlocutions and go straight to the confirmation of our opinion, by which we affirm that God created the first man just and holy, and that this original righteousness was not merely some possibility of keeping God's commandments, nor only a propensity toward the virtues, but itself contained within it the possession and fullness of all the virtues which are commanded or required in the Decalogue. We shall proceed to establish this by the following arguments.

units.la: Argumentum I. desumitur ab ipsa imagine diuina, & eius per Christum reparatione: Quod enim Christi gratia, in nobis reparatur, ac restauratur, id fuit illa imago Dei, ad quam Deus hominem primitus creauerat: quia amissa, ac deleta per peccatum, imagine Dei, opus erat instauratione, ac reparatione, per ipsum Christum: Atqui reparatur, & restauratur in nobis Christi gratia, vera Dei agnitio, iustitia, sanctimonia, & gloria, Ephes. 4. uerf. 24. Induere nouum illum hominem, qui secundum Deum conditus est ad iustitiam, & sanctimoniam veram, Col. 3. uerf. 10. Et induueritis nouum illum hominem, qui renouatur in agnitionem congruentem imagini eius, qui ipsum condidit. 1. Cor. 1. ver. 30. Factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. 2. Cor. 3. v. 18. Nos omnes, retecta facie, gloriam Domini, vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur, ex gloria in gloriam, tanquam à spiritu Domini: Ergo vera illa Dei agnitio, iustitia, sanctimonia, & gloria, est illa Dei imago, ad quam homo primitus fuit conditus. Quum autem imago illa homini naturalis fuerit, necessario inde sequitur, Deum hominem iustum, ac sanctum condidisse.
units.tr: Argument I. It is drawn from the divine image itself and its restoration through Christ. For what is restored and renewed in us by the grace of Christ was that image of God in which God first created man, since, when the image of God was lost and destroyed through sin, there was need of its renewal and restoration through Christ himself. But the grace of Christ, the true knowledge of God, righteousness, holiness and glory are restored and renewed in us: Eph. 4. v. 24: "to put on the new man, who after God has been created in righteousness and true holiness"; Col. 3. v. 10: "and have put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him"; 1 Cor. 1. v. 30: "God has made him to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption"; 2 Cor. 3. v. 18: "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." Therefore that true knowledge of God, righteousness, holiness and glory is that image of God in which man was first created. Since that image was natural to man, it necessarily follows that God created man just and holy.

units.la: Argumentum II. desumitur ab ipsius creationis perfectione, & legis diuinæ rigore: Ecclesiastes enim cap. 7. v. 30. Hominem rectum à Deo conditum fuisse testatur: vnde necessario sequitur, Adamum nulla virtute, in qua illa rectitudo consistat, caruisse, & à lege Decalogi, quæ recti est regula, nulla in re aberrasse. Quum verò omnium illarum virtutum, quæ à lege exiguntur, chorum, iustitiæ, & sanctimoniæ nomine appellare, soleat Apostolus, lex etiam ipsa iustos, & sanctos nullos pronunciet, nisi qui omnib. illis virtutibus, quæ in illa præcipiuntur, polleat: necessario sequitur Adamum iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ originalis dotibus perfectissimis, ipsius creationis beneficio, excelluisse.
