Hisce addc argumentum quartum, ab ipsa Dei legislatoris iustitiam desumptum: nisi enim Deus hominem tam iustum, sanctum ac perfectum condidisset, quàm lex, quæ summam, & absolutissimam iustitiam, ac sanctimoniam exigit, requirit, sequeretur Deum ipsi legem præscripsisse, natura ipsius perfectiorem, & ita summam iniquitatem, & iniustitiam, in ipsum exercuisse, quod cum salsissimum sit, & impium, sequitur verissimam esse sententiam nostram, qua docemus, Adamum, creationis beneficio, iustitiæ, & sanctimoniæ, omniumque virtutum ornamentis instructum, id est, iustum, & sanctum à Deo creatum fuisse.
units.tr: Argument II. It is drawn from the perfection of creation itself and the strictness of the divine law. For Ecclesiastes 7. v. 30 testifies that man was created by God upright. Whence it necessarily follows that Adam lacked no virtue in which that uprightness consists, and did not go astray in any matter from the Decalogue, which is the rule of what is right. Since the Apostle is accustomed to call the whole company of virtues required by the law by the names of righteousness and holiness, and the law itself pronounces none to be just and holy except one who excels in all those virtues which it prescribes, it necessarily follows that Adam excelled, by the benefit of his creation, in the most perfect endowments of original righteousness and holiness. To these add a fourth argument, drawn from the righteousness of God himself as lawgiver: for unless God had created man as just, holy and perfect as the law, which demands and requires the highest and most absolute righteousness and holiness, it would follow that God had prescribed to him a law more perfect than his own nature, and so had exercised the greatest iniquity and injustice against him. Since this is most false and impious, it follows that our opinion is most true, by which we teach that Adam, by the benefit of creation, was furnished with the adornments of righteousness, holiness and all the virtues, that is, that he was created by God just and holy.

units.la: Argumentum III. Desumitur à fine primi hominis. Si enim Adamus conditus erat, vt Deum agnoscere & colere, sequitur ipsum virtutibus naturalibus, id est, iustitia & sanctimonia originali, quarum beneficio id præstaret, & sine quibus nullus verus Dei cultus esse potest, à Deo instructum fuisse, nisi dicamus Deum, quod singulis rebus creatis per naturam contulit, nempe vt viribus idoneis ad operationes suas edendas polleant, cum homini, id est, operi præstantissimo, denegasse, quod est absurdum. Atqui de fine illo hominis, nemo sanctus est qui dubitet: Ergo etiam alterum necessariò sequitur.
units.tr: Argument III. It is drawn from the end of the first man. For if Adam was created so that he might know and worship God, it follows that he was furnished by God with natural powers, that is, with original righteousness and holiness, by whose benefit he could accomplish this, and without which there can be no true worship of God; unless we say that God denied to man, who is the most excellent of his works, what he has given by nature to each created thing, namely that they should be strong with suitable powers for carrying out their operations; and that is absurd. But no one who is sound would doubt that end of man. Therefore the other also necessarily follows.

units.la: Atq; sic hactenus veritatem doctrinæ nostræ, tū de immortalitate, tum de iustitia & sanctimonia originali primi hominis, certis atque evidentibus argumentis demonstrauimus, argumentáque nostra, ab exceptionibus Aduersarii vindicauimus: Restat nunc, vt argumenta & rationes eiusdem, quibus mortalitatem primi hominis (nam de iustitia & sanctimonia originali <bl>καταβολῆς</bl> nihil tractat) astruere conatur, examinemus.
units.tr: And so far we have demonstrated the truth of our doctrine, both concerning the immortality and concerning the original righteousness and holiness of the first man, by certain and evident arguments, and we have defended our arguments against the objections of the adversary. It remains now that we examine the arguments and reasons by which he tries to establish the mortality of the first man (for he says nothing about the original [καταβολῆς] righteousness and holiness).

units.la: Hominem primum itaque, etiam ante peccatum mortalem fuisse, sequentibus argumentis & rationibus demonstrare conatur Oftorrodius.
units.tr: Ostorodius tries to prove by the following arguments and reasons that the first man was mortal even before sin.

units.la: Argumentum I. ex fine creationis, Ad quem Deus hominem ordinauit, desumitur, qui fuit vt liberos gigneret, Gen.1.ver.28. Et benedixit eis Deus, & dixit eis Deus, fructificate, & multiplicamini, & replete terram, & subiicite eam vobis, &c. Illi autem, qui immortales sunt, nullos liberos gignunt: quod manifestum esse dicit, tum ex rationis lumine, tum disertis Christi verbis, Luc.20. verf.35.36. Qui vero digni habiti fuerint, qui æuum illud consequantur, & resurrectionem nem ex mortuis, neque ducunt vxores, neque nuptum dantur, neque enim mori possunt amplius: pares enim Angelis sunt, & filii sunt Dei, quum sint filii resurrectionis.
units.tr: Argument I. It is drawn from the end for which God created man, to whom God ordained him, which was that he should beget children (Gen. 1:28): "And God blessed them, and God said to them, Be fruitful and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it, etc." But those who are immortal beget no children, as is plain both from the light of reason and from the clear words of Christ (Luke 20:35-36): "But they who are counted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage; neither can they die any more, for they are equal to the angels, and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection."

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Qui immortales sunt, nullos liberos gignunt: Atqui homo primus liberos genituru* fuisset, etiam si non peccasset, utpote ad hoc, nempe ut gigneret, defnatu: Ergo primus homo etiam sine peccato, non immortalis, sed mortalis fuit.
units.tr: Those who are immortal beget no children. But the first man would have begotten children even if he had not sinned, since he was destined for this very purpose, namely to beget. Therefore the first man, even without sin, was not immortal but mortal.

units.la: Argumentum II. Desumitur ex causis conseruantibus, nempe cibis, quibus hominem statim ab initio vsum fuisse constat, ex Gen. i. v. 29. Dixit denique Deus, Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam producentem semen, quae est in superficie omnis terrae, & omnem arborem, in qua est fructus arboris producentis semen, vobis erit in escam. Ipse cibus autem nihil cum immortalitate commune habeat: 1. Cor. 6. v. 13. 14. vbi Paulus affirmat, Deum & ventrem, & escam aboliturum, nos vero potentia sua suscitaturum esse:
units.tr: Argument II. It is drawn from the means of preservation, namely food, which it is established that man used from the very beginning (Gen. 1:29): "Then God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat." But food has nothing in common with immortality (1 Cor. 6:13-14), where Paul affirms that God will destroy both the belly and meats, but will raise us up by his power.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Quicunque esca, & cibis vtuntur, illi natura sunt mortales: Atqui primus homo etiam ante peccatum, & sine peccato cibo vsus fuit: Ergo homo primus etiam ante peccatum & sine peccato, natura mortalis fuit.
units.tr: Whoever uses food and nourishment is by nature mortal. But the first man used food even before sin and without sin. Therefore the first man, even before sin and without sin, was by nature mortal.

units.la: Argumentum III. Desumit a natura corporis humani, quod est animale, id est, tale corpus homo primus habuit, cuius vita erat ipsa anima: 1. Cor. 15. v. 45. Factus est prior homo Adam in animam viuentem: tale autem corpus mortale esse testatur Apostolus, 1. Cor. 15. v. 42. 43. 44. Seminatur corpus corruptioni obnoxium, excitatur incorruptum: seminatur ignominiosum, excitatur gloriosum, seminatur infirmum, excitatur potens, seminatur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale, est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale.
units.tr: Argument III. It is drawn from the nature of the human body, which is animal, that is, the first man had such a body that its life was the soul itself (1 Cor. 15:45): "The first man Adam was made a living soul." But the Apostle testifies that such a body is mortal (1 Cor. 15:42-44): The body is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Qui habet corpus animale, seu tale, cuius vita est ipsa anima, ille natura est mortalis :
units.tr: He who has an animal body, that is, such a body whose life is the soul itself, is by nature mortal.

units.la: Atqui Adamus etiam integer,& fine peccato, habuit corpus animale, seu cuius vita ipsa anima fuit :
units.tr: But Adam, even in his integrity and without sin, had an animal body, that is, one whose life was the soul itself.

units.la: Ergo Adamus etiam integer,& fine peccato,fuit mortalis.
units.tr: Therefore Adam, even in his integrity and without sin, was mortal.

units.la: Argumentum IV. Desumit à materia hominis, ex qua homo creatus fuit,quia videlicet natura terrenus, id est, ex terra factus erat : terrenum autem,& mortalem esse, Apostolo Paulo unum ac idem est,ut euidenter liquet ex 1.Cor.15. ver.47.48.49.50. Primus homo è terra terrenus:fecundus homo ipse Dominus è cœlo. Qualis terrenus ille, tales & qui terreni sunt, & qualis ille cœlestis, tales & qui cœlestes sunt: Et sicut gestauimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus etiam imaginem cœlestis.Hoc autem dico,fratres, carnem & sanguinem non posse regni Dei hereditatem consequi,neque corruptionem consequi incorruptæ naturæ hæreditatem.
units.tr: Argument IV. It is drawn from the matter from which man was created, namely because he was by nature earthly, that is, made from earth. But for the Apostle Paul, earthly and mortal are one and the same, as is clear from 1 Cor. 15:47-50: "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption."

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Qui natura sua terrenus, id est, ex terra factus est, ille etiam natura sua est mortalis.
units.tr: Whoever is earthly by his nature, that is, made from earth, is also mortal by his nature.

units.la: Atqui Adamus, etiam ante peccatum, & fine peccato, natura terrenus,id est,ex terra factus erat:
units.tr: But Adam, even before sin and without sin, was earthly by nature, that is, made from earth.

units.la: Ergo Adamus, etiam ante peccatum & fine peccato, naturâ mortalis fuit.
units.tr: Therefore Adam, even before sin and without sin, was mortal by nature.

units.la: Argumentum V. Desumit ab exemplo Christianorum, qui & ipsi sunt mortales, quod fieri non posse, inquit, fi mortalitas non naturalis, sed pœna peccati effet : & ita Diabolus, vtpote autor peccati, causa, & autor ipsius mortalitatis haberi posset, cum tamen Christus fidelium peccata sustulerit,& ad hoc venerit,ut opera Diaboli dissolueret, 1.Iohan. 3.verf.8.
units.tr: Argument V. It is drawn from the example of Christians, who are themselves mortal. This, he says, could not happen if mortality were not natural but the punishment of sin; and so the Devil, as the author of sin, could be regarded as the cause and author of mortality itself. Yet Christ has taken away the sins of believers and came for this purpose, that he might destroy the works of the Devil (1 John 3:8).

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Si ipsi Christiani, & fideles, quorum peccata Christus sustulit, mortales tamen sunt,tum sequitur mortalitatem non peccati pœnam, sed homini naturalem esse.
units.tr: If Christians and believers themselves, whose sins Christ has taken away, are nevertheless mortal, then it follows that mortality is natural to man and not the punishment of sin.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also true.

units.la: Argumentum VI. & vltimum: Desumitur ex eo,quod inter cateras arbores, quas Deus, ut homo illis vescaretur, in horto Hedenis plantauerat, tauerat, etiam arbor vita, vna fuerit: Si autem primus homo natura, inquit Oftorrodius, immortalis fuisset, tum Deus ipsi frustra arborem vitae in escam & cibum dedisset, quod nulla ratione affirmari potest, quoniam Deus solus sapiens est, ac proinde nihil vnquam fine causa facit.
units.tr: Argument VI, and the last: It is drawn from the fact that among the other trees which God had planted in the garden of Eden, so that man might eat of them, there was also one tree of life. "But if the first man," says Ostorodius, "had been immortal by nature, then God would have given him the tree of life for food and nourishment in vain; and this cannot be affirmed for any reason, since God alone is wise and therefore never does anything without cause."

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus:

units.la: Si primus homo natura sua immortalis fuisset, tum Deus frustra inter cateras arbores horti, etiam arborem vitae, in cibum, & escam, ipsi dedisset:
units.tr: If the first man had been immortal by his nature, then God would have given him, in vain, the tree of life among the other trees of the garden for food and nourishment.

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is false. Therefore so is the antecedent.

units.la: Resp. Tollenda ante omnia æquiuoca ipsius prædicati, de quo disceptatur significatio. Quemadmodum enim immortalitas, vel actum tantum, vel potentiam & actum moriendi simul excludit: sic etiam mortalitas, vel potentiam tantum moriendi, vel potentiam & actum cum moriendi necessitate, eáque vel ex ipsius naturæ conditione, vel superioris iudicis sententia ac decreto orta, coniunctum significat. Hoc est, Vt immortale aliquid dicitur, vel quod non moritur, potest tamen certo aliquo respectu mori: vel quod nec actualiter morte vnquam corripitur, nec etiā mori vnquam potest: ita quoque mortale aliquid dicitur, vel quod non tantum potest mori, sed etiam actu, & quidem necessario moritur, nec potest non mori, vel quod in fe, & potetia sua potest quidem mori, ex certa tamen hypothesi, & potentiæ contrariæ, causæque alicuius impedientis, ne naturalis illa potentia in actum deducatur, interuentu, non moritur. Atque ex hac verissima distinctione euidenter liquet, cuius & quanti ponderis ac momenti sint illa, quæ ab Aduersario doctrinæ nostræ opponuntur, argumēta. Nam fi illis eam impugnet primi hominis immortalitatem, qua ex creationis ipsius beneficio, à mortis spiculis tutus fuisse existimetur, vt quandiu in statu integritatis constans perstitisset, non tantum non moriturus fuisset, sed nec in fe, ac potentia sua mori potuisset, sed omnimodam moriendi impotentiam habuisset, omnia, quotquot adferuntur argumenta, sunt ἀπεσφάλμενα. Quia omnes vnanimi consensu credimus, atque docemus, immortalitatem Adamo, necquidem ipsius creationis beneficio, ἁπλῶς & simpliciter, ac πρώτως, primò, per fe, ac in fe, & ἐπιφανῶς à Deo collatam esse vnquā, sed illum simul corruptibilem ac incorruptibilem, mortalem & immortalem fuisse, attamen diuerso respectu docemus. Corruptibilem videlicet ac mortalem, primò fecundum id quod est ex cōtrariis , ac inter se pugnantibus elementis conflatum : deinde se-cundùm solutionem vnionis hypostaticæ,qua anima & corpus v-nita inter se vnum constituunt ὑφιστάμενον : denique in se & poten-tia sua, incorruptibilem verò ac immortalem potentia gratiæ Dei, secundùm veritatem promissionis diuinæ, si debitam Deo creatori obedientiam præstitisset, & ἀναμάρτητος in illa gratia subsi-stisset.Sin verò etiam alterum immortalitatis modum , qui in po-tentia ad vtrumque actum, moriendi videlicet, & non moriendi, sed certis conditionibus per Dei gratiam ac omnipotentiam , aut iustitiam,iudiciúmque iustum,ad hunc autem illum euentum determinata ponitur,suis rationibus conuellat, & afferat ac concludat,hominem primum,si eius natura potentiáque naturalis respiciatur, non tantùm mori potuisse, sed etiam, licet non peccasset, moriturum tamen fuisse, tum falsa est omnium & singulorum argumentorum consequentia. Nihil enim aliud quàm potentiam naturalem moriendi, quam & nos Adamo vnanimi consensu tribuimus,euincunt,hoc est,demonstrat, hominem primum in se & potentia sua naturali consideratum mori potuisse, sed beneficio illo gratiæ diuinæ , quæ ipsum aduersus mortis imperium , quan-diu in integritate perfisteret ἀθανασία, præmunitum fuisse, ac proinde mortalem & immortalem, sed mortalem imbecillitate naturæ , immortalem verò beneficio gratiæ diuinæ extitisse , paulo ante ostendimus,minimè euertit. Hoc vt appareat manifestius,ad singula Aduersarii argumenta , sigillatim & ordine , sed breuiter tamen respondebimus.
units.tr: Reply. First, the ambiguity of the predicate under dispute must be removed. For just as immortality excludes either the act alone or both the power and the act of dying, so mortality signifies either only the power of dying, or the power and the act together with the necessity of dying, and that necessity arising either from the condition of the nature itself or from the sentence and decree of a higher judge. That is to say: something is called immortal either because it does not die, yet can die in some respect, or because it is never actually seized by death, nor can it ever die at all. Likewise something is called mortal either because it not only can die but actually and necessarily dies, and cannot not die, or because in itself and by its own power it can indeed die, but under a certain hypothesis, and through the intervention of a contrary power and some hindering cause preventing that natural power from being brought into act, it does not die. From this most true distinction it is plainly evident how great and of what weight are the arguments which the Adversary opposes to our doctrine. For if by these arguments he would overthrow the immortality of the first man, by which, through the benefit of his creation, he is thought to have been safe from the darts of death, so that as long as he remained in the state of integrity he would not only not have died but would have been unable to die in himself and by his own power, but would have had a complete inability to die, then all the arguments that are brought forward are wrong [ἀπεσφάλμενα]. For we all believe with one accord, and teach, that immortality was never bestowed on Adam by God simply and absolutely [ἁπλῶς], and primarily [πρώτως], first, through himself and in himself, and manifestly [ἐπιφανῶς], by the benefit of creation itself; but we teach that he was at once corruptible and incorruptible, mortal and immortal, yet in different respects. He was corruptible and mortal, first according to what he was composed of, elements that are contrary and mutually opposed; then according to the dissolution of the hypostatic union, by which soul and body, united, constitute one subsisting thing [ὑφιστάμενον]; and finally in himself and by his own power. He was incorruptible and immortal by the power of God's grace, according to the truth of the divine promise, if he had rendered due obedience to God his creator and had persisted without sin [ἀναμάρτητος] in that grace. But if he should refute, with his own arguments, and should assert and conclude, that the first man, if his nature and natural power are considered, could not only die but would also have died even had he not sinned, which is the other mode of immortality, that which is placed in a power toward both acts, namely dying and not dying, but determined to this or that outcome by certain conditions, through God's grace and omnipotence, or his justice and just judgment, then the consequence of all and each of the arguments is false. For they prove nothing beyond the natural power of dying, which we too ascribe to Adam with one accord; that is, they demonstrate that the first man, considered in himself and in his natural power, could die. But that he was fortified by that benefit of divine grace against the dominion of death, so that as long as he persisted in integrity he was immortal [ἀθανασία], and that he was therefore mortal and immortal, mortal by the weakness of his nature but immortal by the benefit of divine grace, as we have shown a little earlier, is in no way overturned. To make this clearer, we will reply to each of the Adversary's arguments, one by one and in order, but briefly.

units.la: Ad primum igitur,secundum,tertium & quartum,quæ eiusdem planè sunt generis,farinæ,atque valoris,quantum concernit,respon-deo,propositiones illas maiores omnes esse falsas:nihil enim aliud ex mediis illis quatuor concludi potest , quàm Adamum potentia,& in se ac natura sua mortalem fuisse : inde tamen non sequitur,eundem,etiamsi non peccasset, moriturum tamen fuisse, quia nos illam immortalitatem , quam contra Samosatenianos asseri-mus, non à conditione aut viribus hominis , sed potentia Dei, & statu gratiæ ac fœderis , hoc est , veritate promissionis diuinæ , si homo debitam obedientiam præstitisset, suspendimus. Hanc igi-tur suis argumentis conuellat oportet Aduersarius , si doctrinam nostram euertere velit.
units.tr: As for the first, second, third and fourth arguments, which are entirely of the same kind, stuff and worth, I answer that all their major premises are false. These four premises can conclude only that Adam was mortal by his power and by his own nature. It does not follow from this that he would have died even if he had not sinned. We do not make his immortality, which we assert against the Samosatenians, depend on the condition or powers of man, but on the power of God, on the state of grace and covenant, that is, on the truth of God's promise, which we hold to be suspended on man rendering the obedience he owed. The Adversary must therefore overthrow this doctrine with his arguments if he wishes to overturn our teaching.

units.la: Ad quintum, dico consequentiam esse falsam : ad probationem vero, ὅτι vero,qua Christus fideles à peccatis ipsorum liberasse, & illa sustulisse dicitur,respondeo primo Christum duplici modo nos in hac vita à peccato liberare, primò redimedo nos ab eius reatu,remissionem videlicet peccatorum, per sanguinem suum impetrando: deinde mortificando illud ipsum in nobis,& nos ab ipsa peccati seruitute redimendo. Illo beneficio peccati reatū tollit, ne illud imputetur nobis:hoc verò vim eius enervat,& radicem amputat, ne amplius dominetur nobis, Rom.8.1. Nulla est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu:& 6.14. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur. Tit. 2.14. Christus dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. At quia mortificatio illa & regeneratio in hac vita nec momentanea est, hoc est, non uno momento perficitur, sed per quotidiana incrementa,in dies prouehitur ac promouetur: nec perfecta ob concupiscentiæ originalis labem,perpetuò in hac vita nobis inhærētem, ideo peccatorum illæ reliquiæ in sanctis remanentes, poenarum quoque reliquias, inter quas etiam est ipsa mors corporalis, secum trahunt. Secundò, mortem ipsam corporalē duplici modo esse considerandam, primò per se,qualis natura sua est: secundò quatenus est per Christū immutata. Per se considerata mors, verè est stipendium peccati,Christi, omniumque membrorum ipsius hostis, & maledictio legis,imò porta,suburbanum, ac vestibulum inferni, & cruciatuum æternorum initium. Altero verò respectu nequaquam talis est, quia vi mortis Christi, desiit esse maledictio, plaga atque poena,quippe quæ nobis facta est quies à peccato,via & transitus ad vitam æternam, ac portulæ instar, per quam, ex hoc ergastulo & lachrymarum valle,ingredimur in cœlestem Regiam:hinc est quod Salomon dicit Eccles.7.v.1. Melior esse homini, nempe electo ac fideli, diem quo moritur,quàm quo nascitur. Die enim ortus nascuntur ac producuntur homines in huius vitę miseriā:post vbi per morte,morte Christi penitus immutatā, hinc demigrat,tū verò introeunt in æternā illā & gloriosam felicitatem,omnibus Dei sanctis æternum associādi. Atqui hoc de impiorū morte dici non potest,quibus nec nasci, nec mori bonum est. Quàm falsa itaque sit illa consequentia, vel ex illis iam dictis liquet, vt non sit necesse,de autore mortis multum contendere. Mortis autor est certo respectu Diabolus,quia peccati quę mortis causa meritoria,autor ac suasor est,non verò mortalitatis ipsius:hoc est,autor extitit actus,& necessitatis non potentiæ moriendi,quæ duo iniquè confundit Aduersarius. Hæc enim de conditione naturæ est, altera peccati stipendium atque pœna est, quam summus & iustus iudex peccatoribus infligit. Atque hæc opera Filius Dei in nobis destruit, hic gratiosa inchoatione, in altera verò vita gloriosa consummatione ac perfectione.
units.tr: As for the fifth argument, I say that the inference is false. As for the proof, the claim [ὅτι] that Christ is said to have freed the faithful from their sins and taken them away, I answer, first, that Christ frees us from sin in this life in two ways. First, he redeems us from its guilt, that is, he obtains for us the forgiveness of sins through his blood. Second, he mortifies sin itself in us and redeems us from the very slavery of sin. By the former benefit he takes away the guilt of sin, so that it is not imputed to us. By the latter he weakens its power and cuts off its root, so that it no longer rules over us: Rom. 8.1, There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus; and 6.14, Sin shall not have dominion over you. Titus 2.14, Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. But because this mortification and regeneration in this life is not instantaneous, that is, it is not completed in a single moment, but advances and grows day by day, and is not perfect because of the stain of original concupiscence, which clings to us perpetually in this life, therefore the remnants of sin that remain in the saints also drag along with them remnants of punishments, among which is bodily death itself. Secondly, bodily death must be considered in two ways: first in itself, as it is by its own nature, and second, as it has been changed by Christ. Considered in itself, death truly is the wages of sin, the enemy of Christ and of all his members, the curse of the law; indeed it is the gate, the suburb and the vestibule of hell, and the beginning of eternal torments. In the other respect it is by no means such, because by the power of Christ's death it has ceased to be a curse, a blow and a punishment. Rather, it has become for us a rest from sin, a way and passage to eternal life, and, like a little gate, the means by which we pass out of this prison and valley of tears into the heavenly kingdom. Hence Solomon says, Eccles. 7.1, Better is the day of death than the day of birth for man, namely for the elect and faithful. For on the day of birth men are born and brought forth into the misery of this life; but when they die, through the death of Christ, which has been wholly changed, they depart from here, and then they enter into that eternal and glorious happiness, to be joined forever with all God's saints. But this cannot be said of the death of the wicked, for whom it is good neither to be born nor to die. How false that inference is can be seen from what has already been said, so that there is no need to dispute at length about the author of death. In a certain respect the devil is the author of death, because he is the author and instigator of sin, which is the meritorious cause of death, but he is not the author of mortality itself. That is, he was the author of the act and of the necessity of dying, not of the power to die, and the Adversary wrongly confuses these two. For the latter belongs to the condition of nature, while the former is the wage and punishment of sin, which the supreme and just judge inflicts on sinners. The Son of God destroys these in us: the former by a gracious beginning here, and the latter by a glorious completion and perfection in the other life.

units.la: Ad sextum & vltimum, Resp. Totum argumentum,prout ab Aduersario proponitur,concedi potest, quia est ἀπροσδιόνυσον, nec quicquam aduersus doctrinæ nostræ veritatem concludit. Non enim natura aut potentia sua,sed gratia Dei, & certa sub conditione,hominem primum immortalem fuisse docemus. Vnde igitur arbor vitæ sic dicta fuerit ab effectúne,an verò significationis causa? superfluum esset hoc loco disputare. Quæ verò Aduersarius sub finem sectionis quintæ, eiusdem capitis trigesimi tertii, de sensu illorum duorum locorum Gen.2.vers.17.& Rom.3.ver.12.annectit, de iis nos in sententiæ nostræ demonstratione tam prolixè egimus, vt nulla hic repetitione sit opus.
units.tr: As for the sixth and last argument, I answer: the whole argument, as the Adversary puts it forward, may be granted, since it is irrelevant [ἀπροσδιόνυσον] and concludes nothing against the truth of our doctrine. For we teach that the first man was immortal not by his own nature or power, but by the grace of God and under a certain condition. Whether the tree of life was so called from its effect or rather for the sake of its signification is superfluous to dispute here. As for what the Adversary adds at the end of the fifth section of the same thirty-third chapter, about the meaning of those two passages, Gen. 2.17 and Rom. 3.12, we have treated these matters at such length in demonstrating our position that there is no need to repeat them here.

units.la: Hactenus igitur primam quæstionem controuersam, An videlicet Deus hominem primum immortalem, iustum, & sanctum creauerit absoluimus. Sequitur nunc,vt quæstionem alteram, An nimirum primus homo naturam totius generis humani peccando corruperit, ac vitiauerit: scu,quod idem est, An natura humana per peccatum Adami sit corrupta ac vitiata? breuiter persequamur.Et quia Aduersariis negantibus, nos affirmamus, peccato primorum parentum, omnibus iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ originalis virtutibus expulsis atque profligatis,ita corruptam ac vitiatam esse totam naturam humanam,vt omnes, quotquot carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendunt,nascantur filii iræ,iniusti,atque ad Deum agnoscendum ac amandum , & ad ea quæ Deo placent faciendum ineptissimi ac impotentissimi,ad omne autem malum natura sua propensissimi, ac nisi per Christum liberentur, in æternas tandem pœnas detrudendi : neque etiam in ipsis quæstionis propositæ terminis, quicquam latet ambiguitatis: ideo missis omnibus ambagibus,nos statim ad ipsam doctrinæ nostræ κατασκευὴν conferemus.
units.tr: So far, then, we have settled the first controverted question, namely, whether God created the first man immortal, just and holy. We now go on briefly to pursue the second question, namely, whether the first man by sinning corrupted and vitiated the nature of the whole human race; or, which is the same thing, whether human nature has been corrupted and vitiated through the sin of Adam. Since the Adversaries deny and we affirm that, by the sin of our first parents, all the virtues of original righteousness and holiness were driven out and destroyed, and the whole human nature was so corrupted and vitiated that all who descend from Adam by carnal propagation are born children of wrath, unjust, utterly unfit and powerless to acknowledge and love God and to do what pleases him, and by nature most prone to every evil, and, unless they are freed through Christ, are at last thrust down into eternal punishments; and since there is nothing ambiguous even in the very terms of the question proposed, we will set aside all circumlocutions and at once turn to the proof of our own doctrine.

units.la: Argumentum 1. desumitur ex illis Scripturæ testimoniis,quę naturæ nostræ corruptæ fructus atque effectus proprios nobis describūt Gal.5.v.19.20.21. Manifesta sunt opera carnis,quæ sunt adulterium,fornicatio,impuritas, proteruia, idololatria, veneficium, inimicitia, tia, lis, æmulationes, ira, contentiones, dissidia, hæreses, invidia, cædes, ebrietates, comessationes, & his similia, Matth. 15. vers. 19. Exinde egrediuntur cogitationes malæ, cædes, adulteria, fornicationes, furta, falsa testimonia, obtrectationes. Atque horum vitiorum non unum aut alterum, sed omnes in universum homines reos peragendos esse, sequentia euincunt testimonia. Psalm. 14. ver. 2. 3. Iehouah prospexit e cœlis supra filios, ut videat, an sit intellegens, quærens Deum: omnes declinauerunt, pariter fœtuerunt, non bonum faciens, ne vnus quidem. Tit. 3. 3. vers 3. Eramus quondam & nos amentes, rebelles, errantes, seruientes cupiditatibus & voluptatibus variis, alij alios odio prosequentes. Ephes. 2. vers. 1. 2. 3. Et vos quum essetis mortui in offensis & peccatis, in quibus olim versati estis, vt est vita mundi huius, secundum principem, cui potestas est aëris, & Spiritus nunc agentis in hominibus contumacibus, inter quos & nos conuersati sumus, olim in cupiditatibus carnis nostræ, facientes quæ carnis & cogitationibus libebant. Hæc vero omnia ex natura ipsa emanasse, non consuetudine aut imitatione acquisita esse, ex eo manifeste demonstratur, quod Paulus subiicit, Eramúsque natura filij iræ, sicut & reliqui. Vnde liquido constat, ipsam naturam peccati, & concupiscentiæ veneno totam infectam, & miserè corruptam ac depravatam esse, creationis alioquin origine & beneficio rectam, præstantissimisque iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ originalis donis abundè instructam, vt in antecedentibus à nobis est demonstratum. Huius vero vniuersalis corruptionis, aliud si potest Aduersarius principium & causam, præter communem illam totius generis humani in & cum Adamo apostasiam, & sequutum inde iustum Dei iudicium, ex Scripturis sacris, nobis ostendat. Quod vero dicunt Aduersarii, nos ideo natura filios iræ dici, quia Adamus posteros suos genuerit, cum iam filius iræ ob peccatum esset, illud, si dextre interpreteris, verum est, sed falsum quod addunt, nempe, non tamen ideo sequi, naturam ipsam vitiatam ac corruptam, aut nos naturâ ipsa peccatores esse. Nunquam enim Deus iniquitatem primorum parentum in tota natura vlcisceretur, nisi tota natura per illum vitiata & peccato infecta esset, neque nos originis ac naturæ ipsius vitio, Dei iræ, culpæ vindici, obnoxii essemus, nisi hoc peccati & corruptionis stigma atque cauterium ipsi naturæ Adamus principium eius impressisset.
units.tr: Argument 1. is drawn from those testimonies of Scripture which describe for us the fruits and proper effects of our corrupted nature. Gal. 5.19–21: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, strife, contempt, quarrels, emulations, wrath, contentions, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and the like. Matt. 15.19: Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders. And that not one or two of these vices, but all men in general are guilty of them, is shown by the following testimonies. Ps. 14.2–3: The LORD looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see if there were any that understood, that sought God. They are all gone aside, they are together become filthy; there is none that does good, no, not one. Titus 3.3: For we ourselves also were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another. Eph. 2.1–3: And you, when you were dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked, according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we also all once lived in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind. Now that all these things flowed from nature itself, and were not acquired by custom or imitation, is clearly shown by what Paul adds: And we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. Hence it is plain that nature itself is wholly infected with the poison of sin and miserably corrupted and depraved, although by its origin in creation it was otherwise upright and richly endowed with the most excellent gifts of original righteousness and holiness, as we have demonstrated above. Moreover, if the Adversary can, let him show us from the holy Scriptures some other principle and cause of this universal corruption, apart from the common apostasy of the whole human race in and with Adam, and the just judgment of God that followed from it. As for what the Adversaries say, that we are therefore called children of wrath by nature, because Adam begat his posterity when he was already a child of wrath on account of sin, this is true if you interpret it rightly, but what they add is false, namely, that it does not follow from this that nature itself is vitiated and corrupted, or that we are sinners by nature itself. For God would never have avenged the iniquity of our first parents upon the whole of nature, unless the whole of nature had been vitiated and infected with sin through him; nor would we be liable, through the fault of origin and of nature itself, to the wrath of God, the avenger of guilt, unless Adam, the beginning of that nature, had stamped this brand and cautery of sin upon nature itself.

units.la: Argumentum II. desumitur ex eo, quòd, ante regenerationis gratiam, omnes, quotquot carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendimus, peccati mancipia, & serui diaboli sumus, Rom. 6. v. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. An nescitis, quod cui vos sistitis seruos ad obediendum, eius serui estis, cui obeditis, vel peccati ad mortem, vel obedientiae ad iustitiam? Gratia autem sit Deo, quod fuistis serui peccati, sed ex corde obedistis eiformae doctrinae, cui estis traditi, & liberati à peccato, mancipati estis iustitiae: itaque sicut exhibuistis membra vestra seruire impuritati, & iniquitati ad iniquitatem: ita nunc sistite membra vestra seruire iustitiae, ad sanctimoniam. Quum enim serui essetis peccati, liberi eratis iustitiae. Ioh. 8. v. 34. Quisquis committit peccatum, seruus est peccati. 2. Tim. 2. v. 25. 26. Cum resipiscentes agnoscant veritatem, & elapsi ex Diaboli laqueis, à quo captiui tenentur & Tit. 3. v. 3. Eramus quondam & nos amentes, rebelles, errantes, seruientes cupiditatibus, & voluptatibus variis. 2. Pet. 2. v. 19. Libertatem eis pollicendo, quàm ipsi serui sint corruptionis, siquidem à quo quis superatus est, huic etiam in seruitutem est addictus. Ex quibus liquet manifestissime, naturam hominis depravatam, miserum diaboli mancipium esse. Quum autem ipse Satanas, nec iuris, aut potestatis quicquam habere possit in quenquam, nisi peccatorum vinculis undique implicatum: ideo euidenter hinc apparet, naturam ipsam peccati contagione infectam, & culpę grauissimę compedibus constrictam esse. Neque est quod obiiciat quispiam, non naturę corruptę vitio, sed arbitrii libertate, & pec andi consuetudine hanc contractam esse seruitutem. Quicquid n. omnibus & singulis hominib., in statu corruptionis, & dominantis peccati, commune est, id non consuetudine, aut imitatione acquisitum esse, sed ex naturę corruptę lacunis emanasse, vel stupidissimus quisquam fatebitur: Atqui omnes, & singulos homines, priusquam Sp. Christi, in vera libertate vindicetur, peccati mancipia & seruos esse, tum ex communi vitę humanę descriptione, quà paulo ante ex Scrip. collecta tradidimus, tum ex testimoniis à nobis iam citatis liquet euidentissime: primo quod ex Apostolo Rom. 6. v. 16. cōstat hominē vnūquēq; vel peccati ad mortē, vel obedietię ad iustitiā seruū esse. Homine vero vilum, priusquam à Spiritu S. renouetur, ac regeneretur, & ipsius Christi morte, ab illa peccati seruitute liberetur, obedientiae ad iustitiam seruire, non opinor, quenquam ex Aduersariis tam impudentem esse, qui affirmare audeat: seruitutem igitur illam ex ipsius naturę corruptę origine nobis incumbere, fateatur necesse est. Secundo, quicunque committit peccatum, id est, carnis desideriis mancipatus est, ille servus est peccati, & a quo quis superatus est, huic in servitutem addictus est: Atqui nos omnes, antequam per lavacrum regenerationis ac renovationis Spiritus sancti emundemur, committimus peccatum, id est, carnis desideriis addicti sumus, & cupiditatum impetu superamur, ut ex Ephes. 2. v. 3. Tit. 3. v. 3. liquet, quippe carnales & venundati sub peccato, Rom. 7. v. 14. quod testimonium ex Aduersariorum hypothesi addo: sequitur igitur omnes & singulos ante regenerationis gratiam, sub tyrannide & dominio Satanae, captivos detineri. Hinc adde, quòd ibi demum vera est libertas, ubi spiritus Christi est, & illi soli vere liberi sunt, quos Filius Dei in libertate vindicaverit, quo spiritu Dei natura destituti sumus: unde necessario sequitur, nos omnes, priusquam spiritu libertatis à Domino nostro Iesu Christo donemur, servituti Satanae & peccati totos mancipatos esse.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the fact that, before the grace of regeneration, all of us who descend from Adam by natural propagation are slaves of sin and servants of the devil, Rom. 6:16-20: Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness? But thanks be to God that you who were slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness. Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness, leading to further lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. John 8:34: Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. 2 Tim. 2:25-26: If perhaps God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive. Titus 3:3: For we too were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, slaves to various passions and pleasures. 2 Pet. 2:19: They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for whoever is overcome by someone, to that one he is also enslaved. From these passages it is perfectly clear that the depraved nature of man is a wretched slave of the devil. Since Satan himself can have no right or power over anyone except one entangled on every side in the bonds of sins, it is evident from this that nature itself, infected by the contagion of sin and bound in the fetters of the gravest guilt, is so enslaved. Nor can anyone object that this slavery was contracted not through the vice of a corrupted nature but through the freedom of the will and the habit of sinning. For even the most stupid person will admit that whatever is common to all and each of men in a state of corruption and dominant sin is not acquired through custom or imitation but has flowed from the corrupt source of nature. Yet that all and each man, before being set free by the Spirit of Christ into true liberty, are slaves and servants of sin is made most evident both from the common description of human life that we gave a little earlier, drawn from Scripture, and from the testimonies we have already cited: first, because from the Apostle, Rom. 6:16, it is established that every man is a slave either of sin unto death or of obedience unto righteousness. But that a man, before he is renewed and regenerated by the Holy Spirit and set free from that slavery of sin by the death of Christ himself, should serve obedience unto righteousness, I do not think any of our opponents is so shameless as to dare to assert. It must therefore be admitted that that slavery lies upon us from the origin of our corrupt nature itself. Second, whoever commits sin, that is, is given over to the desires of the flesh, is a slave of sin, and whoever is overcome by someone is enslaved to that one. But all of us, before we are cleansed by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, commit sin, that is, we are given over to the desires of the flesh and are overcome by the onslaught of our lusts, as is clear from Eph. 2:3 and Titus 3:3, namely that we are fleshly and sold under sin, Rom. 7:14; I add this testimony on the hypothesis of our opponents. It follows, then, that all and each man, before the grace of regeneration, are held captive under the tyranny and dominion of Satan. Add to this that true liberty exists only where the Spirit of Christ is, and that only those are truly free whom the Son of God has set free; we are destitute of the Spirit of God by nature. From this it necessarily follows that all of us, before we are given the Spirit of liberty by our Lord Jesus Christ, are wholly enslaved to the servitude of Satan and of sin.

units.la: Argumentum I I I. desumitur ex Psal. 51. v. 7. ubi Dauid ingenuè confitetur, se in iniquitatibus genitum, & in peccato conceptum esse à matre. Nec certè arguit ibi matris aut patris peccata, sed quò Dei erga se benignitatem magis commendet, propriae peruersitatis confessionem à prima natiuitate repetit. Quum autem hoc Dauidi peculiare non fuerit, sequitur, communem generis humani sortem sub eius exemplo notari, omnésque qui ab impuro eius semine descendunt, peccati contagione infectos nasci. Quis enim daret mundum de immundo? Iob. 14. v. 5.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from Ps. 51:7, where David frankly confesses that he was born in iniquities and conceived in sin by his mother. Certainly he is not there accusing his mother's or his father's sins; rather, in order to commend more strongly God's kindness toward him, he traces back to his first birth the confession of his own perversity. Since this was not peculiar to David, it follows that under his example the common lot of the human race is noted, and that all who descend from his impure seed are born infected with the contagion of sin. For who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Job 14:5.

units.la: Ad hunc locum ex Psalmo citatum excipit Aduersarius, ac dicit, hoc testimonium Dauidis esse impertinens, nec quicquam ad rem facere, primò, quia sit figurata & hyperbolica loquutio, quod duabus rationibus probare conatur. Prima est, quia Dauid ibi non unius peccati, sed multorum, & quidè eiusmodi mentionem faciat, quae sint transgressiones, id est, peccata actualia, in quibus nemo concipi potest. Secundus est, quia modus iste loquendi, in Scripturis sacris non sit inusitatus, aut nouus, ut Psal. 58. versu 4. Abalienant se improbi inde à vulua, aberrant inde ab vtero loquentes mendacium: & 48. vers. 8. Noui te omnino acturum esse perfidè, ac defectorem ex utero vocari te. Iohan. 9. vers. 34. Tu in peccatis natus es totus, & tu doces nos. Atque hyperbolica hac loquendi forma peccata actualia, inquit, amplificari & exaggerari solere. Secundò, quia Dauid illo in loco, non de aliis hominibus, sed tantum de semetipso loquatur, & quam uis in omnib us hominibus, nullo excepto, sit peccandi potentia, inquit, qua omnes peccare possunt (Deus enim omnibus liberum arbitrium tam ad bonum, quam ad malum, indidit) dici tamen non potest, propterea omnibus & singulis ineffabiles cupiditates & inclinationes ad peccandum, quia videlicet in multis hæ reperiuntur.
units.tr: To this passage from the Psalm our opponent objects, and says that this testimony of David is irrelevant and has nothing to do with the matter; first, because the expression is figurative and hyperbolical, which he tries to prove on two grounds. The first is because David there is speaking not of one sin but of many, and makes mention of such things as are transgressions, that is, actual sins, in which no one can be conceived. The second is because this manner of speaking is not unusual or new in the holy Scriptures, as in Ps. 58:3: The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from the belly, speaking lies; and Ps. 48:8 (LXX): I knew that you would surely act faithlessly, and that you would be called a deserter from the womb. John 9:34: You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us? And, he says, by this hyperbolical form of speech actual sins are wont to be magnified and exaggerated. Second, because David in that place speaks not of other men but only of himself; and although in all men, none excepted, there is a power of sinning by which all can sin (for God gave all a free will toward good as well as toward evil), it cannot therefore be said that unspeakable desires and inclinations to sin are present in all and each, merely because they are found in many.

units.la: Resp. Ineptam esse illam Aduersarii exceptionem: sed causas ipsas examinabimus, propter quas locum ex Psalmo allegatum, ἀντιθέτως esse affirmat. Prima est, quia figurata & hyperbolica sit illa loquutio. Atqui hoc falsum est, & falsum esse, ex ipsius Aduersarii verbis euidenter demonstratur. Hyperbolica illa loquendi forma, inquit, peccata actualia amplificari & exaggerari solent. Paulo post vero, hanc ipsam responsionem quasi corrigens, addit, quamuis credibile est, Danidem, non ut exaggeraret, sed ut excusaret peccata sua, ita loquutum, id est, in describenda infirmitate humana (obserua quaeso Lector ineptam & dormitantis animi exegesin) ἀσφαλῶς, id est, illa locuendi formula vsum esse, quae res vel maiores, vel minores quam sunt, reddunt: quasi peccatum ipsi homini agnatum esset, non autem, quod reuera ita sit. Hinc ita concludo, primo, ex verbis Aduersarii: Hyperbolica loquendi formula peccata actualia exaggerari & amplificari solent: Atqui Dauid loco citato peccata sua non amplificare aut exaggerare, sed excusare voluit. Ergo illa loquendi forma, qua quis in peccato conceptus, aut ab utero ipso malus esse dicitur, non est, saltem illo in loco, hyperbolica. En tibi Aduersarium contradictionis manifestæ vinculis intricatum.
units.tr: Reply. That exception of the opponent is absurd. But let us examine the very reasons for which he asserts that the passage cited from the Psalm is ἀντιθέτως [by contrary sense]. The first is because that expression is figurative and hyperbolical. But this is false, and its falsity is clearly shown from the opponent's own words. That hyperbolical form of speech, he says, is wont to magnify and exaggerate actual sins. A little later, however, as if correcting this very answer, he adds: although it is credible that David spoke thus not to exaggerate but to excuse his sins, that is, in describing human weakness (please observe, reader, the absurd interpretation of a drowsy mind), ἀσφαλῶς [safely/surely], that is, he used that form of speech which makes things either greater or smaller than they are, as if sin were innate in man himself and not, as is really the case. Hence I conclude thus: first, from the opponent's own words: the hyperbolical form of speech is wont to exaggerate and magnify actual sins; but David in the passage cited wished not to magnify or exaggerate his sins, but to excuse them. Therefore that form of speech by which someone is said to have been conceived in sin, or to be evil from the very womb, is not hyperbolical, at least in that place. See, the opponent is entangled in the bonds of a manifest contradiction.

units.la: Deinde vero ex ipsius hyperboles genuino fine atque vsu, qui duplex tantum est, vt etiam Aduersarius agnoscit, vel μείωσις nimirum, vel ἐπίτασις, id est, vel amplificatio vel extenuatio. Atqui neuter vsus scopo Dauidis conuenit: non primus, quia culpam, fatente Aduersario, non exaggerare, sed deprecari voluit: non secundus, quia ille ingenuæ confessioni, & resipiscentiæ veritati ac synceritati plane repugnat: unde liquet, verba illa Dauidis, non hyperbolica, sed vera ac propria esse, & Aduersarium Rhetoricam vel male didicisse, vel saltem infeliciter nobis profiteri. Rationem vero primam quantum concernit: falsum est, Dauidem in loco citato non vnius peccati, sed multorum, & quidem eiusmodi, mentionem facere, quæ sint peccata actualia: vtrumque enim nomen Hebraicum, non pluralis, sed singularis est numeri, quod discere debuisset Aduersarius, priusquam hoc tam audacter affirmaret. Beghauon enim & Bechete nomina mina sunt singularis numeri, quorum illud nempe ghavon, iniquitatem, seu peruersitatem: hoc vero nempe chete peccatum significat: illud in plurali, cum plures iniquitates designat ghavonim, vel ghavonoth: hoc vero chataim, vel chatoth, & chataoth, habet. Vnius itaque peccati mentionem facit Dauid, nempe originalis, sed quod omnium peccatorum actualium fons, origo, & mater est, atque omnia peccata actualia δυνάμει in se, tanquam in radice, complectitur. Quod vero idem ratione secunda dicit, illam loquendi formulam in sacra Scriptura nec inusitatam, nec nouam esse, id veritatem doctrinæ nostræ magis confirmat, licet peccata actualia interdum illa exaggerarentur. Non enim omnis amplificatio statim hyperbolica est, cuius argumenta etiam, vt plurima Scripturæ sacræ exempla id luculenter docent, à veríssimis rei circumstantiis, causis, & effectis desumuntur. Sic Ef. 48. v. 8 defectorem ex vtero, Iehovah domum Israelis appellat: quasi diceret: Noui ingenium vestrum & quod prauaricantes prauaricaremini, peccata peccatis accumulates, si quid ab vtero, ipsisque ab incunabulis, prauaricator, nominisque mei contemptores, filius iratus natus, & in peccati labe conceptus. Sic Dauid Pf. 58. v. 4. aulicorum Saulis improbitatem, & nequitiam grauiter, sed tamen verissimè amplificat, à naturali & ipsis ingenita, corruptione, quæ in alienatione, & aberratione à Deo est posita. Quod vero Iudæi Ioh. 9. v. 34. ad illum, qui à natiuitate cæcus erat, dixerunt, ipsum peccatorem natum esse totum, ad peccatorum actualium, ipsius amplificationem referri non potest. Quum enim illi natiuę istius cæcitatis causam in peccato, non vero in gloriæ, & potentiæ diuinæ illustrandæ fine, quærendam esse opinarentur, ideo ipsum etiam à natiuitate peccatorem esse, feroci contemptu, & odio, proclamauerunt, vel ipsum nondum natum, illam cæcitatem promeruisse, vel propter parentum peccata illam inflictam sustinere, arbitrati. Et notum est illud μετεμψύχωσις delirium, quo multi ex Scribis imbuti fuerant, animas vna vita defunctas, in noua migrare corpora, atque illic priorum scelerum pœnas pendere, existimantibus: vnde etiam illum cæcitate afflictum, ab vtero matris cum scelerum suorum nota prodiisse, calumniabantur. Alteram vero causam, propter quam locum ex Psalmo citatum, ἀσεβαδιάνυτον esse cauillatur Aduersarius, quantum concernit, illa tota est inepta. Quamuis enim ibi non de omnibus hominibus in genere, sit sermo, nihil tamen impedit, quò minus communis hominum conditio sub eius exemplo notetur, nisi reliquorum originem ipsius Dauidis puriorem & sanctiorem esse, Aduersarius demonstrauerit. Omnes vero & singulos homines prauis cupiditatibus & desideriis flagrare, & ad peccandum indefinetèr solicitari, nec ex potentia peccandi, quam etiam Adamus ante lapsum, quippe libero ad vtrumque obiectû, bonum & malum, arbitrio præditus, habuit, sed inobedientia sua in peccandi necessitatè cóuertit, nec ex paucorû quorundā exèplo, qui prauas cōcupiscētiæ vstiones in corde sentiūt, sed ex cōmuni omniū seruili cōditione, qua ab origine iub peccati dominantis iugo, & Sathanę imperio, captiui detinētur, & peccādi necessitate, demōstramus, vt ex toto hoc cap. cōstat. Alio itaq; ariete opˢest Aduersario, si testimoniū illud expugnare velit.
units.tr: Next, from the genuine purpose and use of hyperbole itself, which is twofold only, as the Opponent also acknowledges: either diminution [μείωσις] or intensification [ἐπίτασις], that is, either amplification or extenuation. Now neither use fits David's purpose. Not the first, because, as the Opponent admits, he wished not to magnify his sin but to plead against it. Not the second, because that plainly clashes with a frank confession and with the truth and sincerity of repentance. Hence it is clear that David's words are not hyperbolical but true and literal, and that the Opponent has either learned rhetoric badly or at least professes it to us unhappily. As for the first reason, it is false that David in the passage cited mentions many sins, and such as are actual sins. Both Hebrew nouns are singular, not plural, which the Opponent ought to have learned before affirming so boldly. Beghauon and Bechete are nouns of the singular number. The former, namely ghavon, means iniquity or perversity; the latter, namely chete, means sin. When several iniquities are meant, the former becomes ghavonim or ghavonoth, and the latter takes the forms chataim, chatoth and chataoth. David therefore mentions one sin only, namely original sin. Yet this is the fount, origin and mother of all actual sins, and it embraces all actual sins potentially [δυνάμει] within itself, as in a root. As for his second reason, that this manner of speaking is neither unusual nor new in Holy Scripture, this confirms our doctrine all the more, even if actual sins were sometimes so exaggerated. For not every amplification is at once hyperbolical. Its grounds, as very many examples in Holy Scripture plainly show, are drawn from the most true circumstances, causes and effects of the matter. Thus Isaiah 48:8 calls the house of Jehovah's people a rebel from the womb, as if to say: I know your disposition, that you have been rebels, transgressing again and again, that from the womb, indeed from the cradle, you were a transgressor and a despiser of my name, a son born in wrath and conceived in the stain of sin. So David, Psalm 58:4, forcefully but most truly amplifies the wickedness and malice of Saul's courtiers, drawing it from their natural corruption, which is innate in them and consists in estrangement and aberration from God. As for the Jews' words in John 9:34, said to the man who had been blind from birth, that he was altogether born in sin, these cannot be referred to an amplification of actual sins. The Jews supposed that the cause of that congenital blindness was to be sought in sin, not in the purpose of displaying God's glory and power. Therefore, with fierce contempt and hatred, they declared that he was a sinner from birth, or else thought that he had merited that blindness before he was born, or that he was bearing it as a punishment inflicted for his parents' sins. It is well known that the delirium of metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις] had infected many of the scribes, who held that souls which had departed in one life passed into new bodies and there paid the penalties of their earlier crimes. Hence they also slandered him, saying that he had come forth from his mother's womb already marked with the stain of his own sins. As for the other reason why Aduersarius carps that the passage cited from the Psalm is impious [ἀσεβαδιάνυτον], it is entirely pointless as far as it concerns the matter. For although the Psalm does not speak of all men in general, nothing prevents the common condition of man from being noted under David's example, unless the Opponent shows that the origin of others is purer and holier than David's. We show, moreover, that all and each of men burn with depraved lusts and desires and are endlessly stirred to sin. This is not due to the power of sinning, which Adam too had before the fall, being endowed with a free will toward both good and evil, but which by his disobedience he turned into the necessity of sinning. Nor is it shown from the example of a few who feel depraved stirrings of concupiscence in the heart, but from the common servile condition of all, by which from their origin they are held captive under the yoke of the reigning sin and under the dominion of Satan, and by the necessity of sinning, as this whole chapter makes clear. So the Opponent must use another ram if he wishes to batter down that testimony.

units.la: Argumentum IV. desumitur ab exemplo infantum.
units.tr: Argument IV is drawn from the example of infants.

units.la: Quum enim mortem quamuis, peccati pœnam ac stipendium esse, ex Scripturis S. iam supra demonstrauerimus, ipsorū autem quamplurimi, antequā vllo rationis vsu polleant, moriantur: idcirco necesse est illos vel actuali, vel natiuæ ac hæreditariæ corruptionis iniquitate obstringi. Nisi.n. & ipsi peccassent, & tamen morerentur, tum reuera filius etiā innocēs portaret iniquitatem patris, neque illa tantùm anima quæ peccauit, moreretur: quod falsum & absurdum esse, non solùm Dei ipsius demonstratur testimonio, sed etiā Aduersariorum confessione probatur. Quū verò plurimi infantes moriantur, priusquā ob defectum rationis peccatum aliquod actuale perpetrare queant, necessariò sequitur, illos originalis peccati contagione infectos, ac proinde naturā hominis ipsam, peccato vitiatā atque corruptā esse. Et certè in ipsis infantibus natiuum esse malarum cupiditatū fontem, eo ipso illi ostendunt, quod, quàm primùm per ætatē licuerit, magno impetu in vitia feruntur. Quin & oppositā priuātia, idem, quod nos affirmamus, euincunt. Quicunque enim renascuntur, & à peccatis abluuntur, illos peccato ante contaminatos fuisse, necesse est, priuatione habitum semper præsupponēte. Atqui multi infantes renascūtur, & à peccatis abluuntur, multos siquidem ex illis saluari, & in regnū cælorum ingredi, dubium non est: regnum autem Dei nemo nisi renatus videre potest, Ioh. 3. v. 3. 5. Vnde necessariò sequitur infantes, vtpote qui actuali culpa non sunt obstricti, originali peccato obnoxios esse.
units.tr: For although we have already shown above from the Holy Scriptures that death is the punishment and wages of sin, very many infants die before they have any use of reason. Therefore they must be bound by guilt, either actual or by natural and hereditary corruption. For if they had not sinned and yet died, then indeed the innocent son would bear the iniquity of the father, and it would not be only the soul that sinned that died. That this is false and absurd is shown not only by the testimony of God himself but is also proved by the confession of the Opponents. Since very many infants die before they can commit any actual sin through lack of reason, it necessarily follows that they are infected with the contagion of original sin, and therefore that human nature itself is vitiated and corrupted by sin. Indeed, that in infants themselves there is a native source of evil desires they show by this very fact, that as soon as their age allows, they are carried with great force into vices. Moreover, the opposite privation proves the same thing that we affirm. For all who are born again and washed from sins must have been previously contaminated by sin, since privation always presupposes a habit. But many infants are born again and washed from sins; for that many of them are saved and enter the kingdom of heaven is beyond doubt; and no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again (John 3:3, 5). Hence it necessarily follows that infants, who are not bound by actual guilt, are liable to original sin.

units.la: Argumentum V. desumitur ab vsu & necessitate παλιγγενεσίας, seu regenerationis ac renouationis Spiritus S. Nisi.n. natura nostra, & omnes
units.tr: Argument V is drawn from the use and necessity of palingenesia [παλιγγενεσία], that is, the regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. For if our nature and all

units.la: omnes eius facultates, non modò omnibus gratiæ ornamētis spoliatę, verùm etiā habituali nequitia imbutę essent, tum ad salutem ac vitam æternam consequendam, sola iustificatione &remissione peccatorum, non autem renouatione ac regeneratione, h.e. mortificatione carnis, ac veteris hominis, & viuificatione {spiritus}, ac noui hominis indigeremus, id est, vt præstemus, & velimus id quod bonum est, ac Deo placet, non opus esset veterem cordis duritiem remoueri & nouam quandam mollitiem informari, bonam voluntatem, & cor nouū, sublato illo, quod nobis à natura inest, lapideo, in nobis à Deo per Spir. S. creari, veterem nostrum hominem cum Christo crucifigi, eundem cum suis factis exui, carnem vnà cum affectibus & concupiscentiis suis crucifigi, cordis nostri præputiū circumcidi, nos à peccato, ne amplius in nobis regnet ac dominetur, & lege peccati ac mortis liberari, membra nostra terrestria mortificari, vetus fermentum in nobis expurgari, nos denique per baptismum, cum Christo in mortem sepeliri. Atqui ad salutem ac vitam æternam consequendam, & vt præstemus atque velimus, id quod bonum est ac Deo placet, non sola iustificatione & remissione peccatorum, sed etiam renouatione ac regeneratione, hoc est, mortificatione carnis & viuificatione spiritus opus esse, adeòque nos omnibus illis, quas recensuimus, Spiritus sancti actionibus & beneficiis indigere, sequentia scripturæ sacræ testimonia euidenter demonstrant, Ezech. 36. verf. 26, 27. Dabo vobis cor nouum & spiritum nouum ponam in medio vestri, & amouens cor lapideum, è carne vestra, indam vobis cor carneum, & spiritum meum ponâ in medio vestri, quo faciam, vt in statutis meis ambuletis, & iura mea obseruetis, facientes ea. Deut. 10. v. 16. Circumcidatis præputium cordis vestri, & ceruicè vestram ne obduretis amplius. & 3. v. 6. Circūcidet Iehouah Deus tuus animum tuum: & animum feminis tui, ad diligendum Iehouā Deū tuum, ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, vt viuas, Ier. 4. v. 4. Circūcidite vos Iehouæ, & amouete præputia animi vestri, viri Iehudæ, & habitatores Ierusalaimorum. Col. 2. 11. In quo etiam circumcisi estis, circumcisione quæ fit sine manibus, dū corpus carnis peccato obnoxiæ, exuistis, per circumcisionem Christi. Rom. 6. 4. Sepulti igitur sumus vnà cum illo per baptismū in mortē: vt quemadmodum excitatus est Christus, ex mortuis, per gloriā Patris, ita & nos in nouitate vitæ ambulemus, v. 6. Illud scientes, quod ille vetus noster homo cum illo crucifixus est, vt eneruetur corpus peccati, ne posthac seruiamus peccato, versu 11. & 12. Ita etiam vos colligite,vos ipsos tum mortuos esse peccato,tum vero viuere Deo,per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum : Ne regnet igitur peccatum in mortali corpore vestro, vt obediatis peccato in cupiditatibus corporis, verf.14. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur, non enim estis sub lege,sed sub gratia, verf.18. Liberati à peccato,mancipati estis iustitiae. Rom.8 verf.2. Nam lex spiritus vitae, qui est in Christo Iesu,liberauit me à lege peccati & mortis. Col.3. verf.5. Mortificate membra vestra terrestria,fornicationem,impuritatem,mollitiem,cupiditatem malam,& auaritiam,quae est idololatria, verf.9.10. Ne mentimini alius alium,quum exueritis veterem illum hominem cum factis ipsius, & induerit nouum illum, qui renouatur in agnitionem congruentem imagini illius,qui ipsum condidit. 1.Cor.5. verf.7. Expurgate vetus fermentum, vt sitis noua massa,sicut estis fermenti expertes. Galat.5.verf.29. Qui enim sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum affectibus & concupiscentiis. Ex quibus omnibus necessario sequitur, naturam humanam non modo omnibus gratiae diuinae ornamentis, ob peccatum spoliatam, sed nequitia etiam habituali imbutam, ac vitiatam esse, ac proinde nos non tantum actuali, sed etiam habituali iniquitate obstringi.
units.tr: all its faculties were not only stripped of every ornament of grace but also steeped in habitual wickedness, then we would need only justification and the forgiveness of sins to attain salvation and eternal life, and not renewal and regeneration, that is, the mortification of the flesh and of the old man and the quickening of the new man. That is, we would not need that, in order to do and will what is good and pleasing to God, the old hardness of heart should be removed and a new softness formed in us; that a good will and a new heart should be created in us by God through the Holy Spirit, with the stony heart taken away which is naturally in us; that our old man should be crucified with Christ, and stripped off along with his deeds; that the flesh should be crucified together with its affections and lusts; that the foreskin of our heart should be circumcised; that we should be freed from sin, so that it no longer reigns and rules in us, and from the law of sin and death; that our earthly members should be mortified; that the old leaven should be purged out of us; and, finally, that through baptism we should be buried with Christ into death. But that to attain salvation and eternal life, and to do and will what is good and pleasing to God, we need not only justification and forgiveness of sins but also renewal and regeneration, that is, the mortification of the flesh and the quickening of the Spirit, and that we therefore need all those works and benefits of the Holy Spirit which I have listed, is clearly shown by the following testimonies of Holy Scripture: Ezek. 36:26-27: I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh; and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my judgments and do them. Deut. 10:16: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked. And Deut. 30:6: The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. Jer. 4:4: Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Col. 2:11: In whom also you are circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ. Rom. 6:4: Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death, that as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6:6: Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that henceforth we should not serve sin. Rom. 6:11-12: So you also reckon yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Rom. 6:14: Sin shall not have dominion over you; for you are not under the law, but under grace. Rom. 6:18: Being freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness. Rom. 8:2: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death. Col. 3:5: Mortify therefore your earthly members: fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. Col. 3:9-10: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created him. 1 Cor. 5:7: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Gal. 5:24: And those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts. From all of which it necessarily follows that human nature was not only stripped of all the divine ornaments of grace on account of sin, but also steeped in habitual wickedness and corrupted, and therefore that we are bound not only by actual but also by habitual iniquity.

units.la: Argumentum VI. desumitur ab imaginis diuinae, hoc est, iustitiae & sanctimoniae originalis priuatione,& vitiositatis,inclinatio-nisque ad malum,ac praui habitus successione. Si n. ob & per peccatum, intellectus hominis spoliatus est eximia illa sapientia spirituali, & cognitione Dei,ac voluntatis eius,rerumque spiritualium,ad purum Dei cultum & vitam aeternam pertinentium,e contra autem tantis ignorantiae atque caecitatis tenebris obrutus,vt non tantum res spirituales etiam cum docentur, suis tamen viribus percipere non possit, sed verum insuper esse falsum, contraque imo ipsam excellentissimam Dei sapientiam,vanam & meram stultitiam esse iudicet:si deinde hanc mentis caecitatem ac vertiginem, sequitur cordis ac voluntatis prauitas & peruersitas, qua id quod vere bonum est,ac Deo placet,naturae suae viribus,non amplius potest appetere, malum autem tantum appetit, atque vult : si denique illi mentis caecitati, & cordis peruersitati, ex aequo respondet vitium omnium impotentia, ad id quod vere bonum est praestandum, & malum quo decet modo omittendum. Hoc est,si homo antequam per Spiritum sanctum renouetur ac regeneretur, nullas plane in se vires habet,ad id quod vere bonum est, intelligendum, volendum,ac ... dum, ac faciendum : tum vere sequitur naturam ipsam hominis per & ob peccatum miserè vitiatam & corruptam esse. Adamum enim per creationis beneficium tantis gratiæ ornamentis instru-ctum fuisse, ut perfectam Deo obedientiam, si voluisset, præstare potuisset, iam ante à nobis est demonstratum. Atqui intellectum hominis spoliatum esse eximia illa sapientia spirituali, & cognitione salutari Dei, & voluntatis ipsius rerumque spiritualium, tum ad purum Dei cultum, tum ad vitam æternam pertinentium, e contra autem, crassissimis ignorantiæ ac cæcitatis tenebris obrutum, liquet manifestissimè tum ex illis epithetis, quæ in scriptura sacra de ipsa mente & intellectu humano enuntiantur : quæ omnia ad tria illa capita revocari possunt, primò videlicet ad ἄγνοια, id est, ignorantiam, seu σκότος, & densas illas ignorantiæ nubes ac tenebras menti incumbentes, ipsámque adeo obtenebrantes, ut nihil loci relinquant vitæ Dei, quam Apostolus depingit, Ephes. 4. ver. 18. Cogitationem habentes obscuratam, & abalienatam à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam quæ est in ipsis, ex obduratione cordis illorum: unde etiam Gentes Deum ignorare dicuntur, 1. Thes. 4. verf. 5. Atque hinc est quod Iohannes dicit, Filium Dei venisse, & dedisse nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus illum qui verax est, 1. Iohan. 5. verf. 20. Et Paulus precatur Ephesiis à Deo πνευματικῶς ... illorum ut sciant quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, & quæ opes gloriæ hæreditatis ipsius in sanctis, Ephes. 1. verf. 18. Secundo ad illam ἀξιωμάτων, qua propter offusas ignorantiæ & cæcitatis tenebras, res spirituales, etiam cum docentur, sine Spiritus sancti interna illuminatione, homo percipere non potest, ut disertis verbis testatur Apostolus 1. Corinth. 2. v. 14. Animalis homo, inquiens, non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, neque potest illa percipere, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Tertio ad illam μωρίαν, id est, vanitatem illam mentis, cogitationum, & iudicii, qua homo verum esse falsum contráque iudicat, imò ipsam excellentissimam Dei sapientiam, in quam ipsi etiam Angeli cupiunt introspicere, 1. Petr. 1. verf. 12. meram & vanam stultitiam esse dicit, 1. Cor. 2. verf. 14. Animalis homo non est capax illorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia siquidem sunt illi, neque potest illa percipere, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur: & 1. Cor. 1. v. 23. Nos autem prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis verò stultitiam: tum vero ex propriis & proximis mentis nostræ & intellectus humani effectis, qui pessimi fructus putridam radicem,& foetidissimi riuuli im purum fontem arguunt. Quum enim Apostolus testatur, φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, id est, sapientiam carnis inimicitiam esse aduersus Deum, id quod in homine est sapientissimū è diametro,cum mete & voluntate Dei pugnare indicat. Sed illam vanitatē mentis nostrę clarissimè ab effectis describit ipse καρδιογνώστης, qui omne figmentum cogitationum cordis humani tantummodo malum esse omni tempore testatur, Gen.6.v.5.& 8.vers.21.quibus verbis non tantum potentia aliqua peccandi,aut pronitas ad malum,sed ipsa nequitia figmentorum cordis, hoc est,cogitationum,inclinationum,appetituum,& actionum omnium,ex cordis officina prodeuntium,denotatur. Quæna vero illa figmenta cordis sint,Christus ipse perspicuè docet,quum ex corde,inquit,egrediuntur cogitationes malæ,cædes,adulteria,scortationes,furta,falsa testimonia, obtrectationes.
units.tr: Argument VI. is drawn from the privation of the divine image, that is, of original righteousness and holiness, and from the vitiation, the inclination to evil, and the succession of a depraved habit. For if, through and because of sin, the intellect of man has been stripped of that eminent spiritual wisdom and knowledge of God, of his will, and of spiritual things pertaining to the pure worship of God and to eternal life; and, on the contrary, has been overwhelmed by such darkness of ignorance and blindness that it cannot, by its own powers, perceive spiritual things even when they are taught, but rather judges what is true to be false, and even the most excellent wisdom of God itself to be vain and sheer folly; and if this blindness and giddiness of mind is followed by perversity and corruption of heart and will, so that it can no longer desire by the powers of its nature what is truly good and pleasing to God, but desires and wills only evil; and if, finally, this blindness of mind and perversity of heart is matched by an impotence of all things, so that one cannot perform what is truly good and cannot omit evil as one ought; then it truly follows that the very nature of man has been wretchedly vitiated and corrupted through and because of sin. That Adam, through the gift of creation, was furnished with such ornaments of grace that, had he willed, he could have rendered perfect obedience to God, has already been demonstrated by us earlier. But that the intellect of man has been stripped of that eminent spiritual wisdom and of the saving knowledge of God, of his will and of spiritual things pertaining both to the pure worship of God and to eternal life, and, on the contrary, has been overwhelmed by the thickest darkness of ignorance and blindness, is clear most manifestly both from those epithets which Holy Scripture applies to the mind and understanding of man, all of which can be traced back to three heads. First, to agnoia [ἄγνοια], that is, ignorance, or skotos [σκότος], and those dense clouds and shadows of ignorance which lie upon the mind and so darken it that they leave no room for the life of God, which the Apostle depicts: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart (Eph. 4:18). Whence also the Gentiles are said not to know God (1 Thess. 4:5). And hence John says that the Son of God has come and has given us a mind, that we may know him who is true (1 John 5:20). And Paul prays to God for the Ephesians, spiritually [πνευματικῶς], that they may know what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints (Eph. 1:18). Second, to that ... [ἀξιωμάτων], by reason of which, with ignorance and blindness cast over them, a man cannot perceive spiritual things, even when they are taught, without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle clearly testifies: The natural man, he says, does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor. 2:14).
