Third, to that moria [μωρία], that is, the vanity of mind, of thought, and of judgment, by which a man judges what is true to be false and, on the contrary, judges even the most excellent wisdom of God, into which the angels themselves desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12), to be sheer and empty folly; so the Apostle says: The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him (1 Cor. 2:14); and: We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness (1 Cor. 1:23). Then, too, it appears from the proper and immediate effects of our mind and of the human understanding, which, like the worst fruits, show a rotten root and a most foul stream from an impure fountain. For when the Apostle testifies that the phronema tēs sarkos [φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς], that is, the wisdom of the flesh, is enmity against God (Rom. 8:7), he indicates that what is most wise in man is diametrically opposed to the mind and will of God. But the very searcher of hearts [καρδιογνώστης] describes that vanity of our mind most clearly from its effects, testifying that every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil at all times (Gen. 6:5; and 8:21). By these words is denoted not merely some power of sinning or a proneness to evil, but the very wickedness of the imaginations of the heart, that is, of all its thoughts, inclinations, appetites and actions, which proceed out of the workshop of the heart. What these imaginations of the heart are, Christ himself plainly teaches, when he says: Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders.

units.la: Osiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite trigesimo tertio, sectione quinta ,ad hoc testimonium ex Genesi citatum excipit, ac dicit,ibi non de originali,sed actuali peccato,nec de naturali,sed voluntaria agi cupiditate, & inclinatione ad peccandum. Atque hanc exceptionem ratione stabilire conatur:quia videlicet Deus Gen.8.v.21.nihil aliud significare voluerit,quâ malitiam hominis, propter quam tum hominem ipsum, tum totam terram perdiderat, in posterum ipsum non amplius permoturam esse,vt propter illam,terram, & quicquid viuit super ipsam,execrare & pessumdare velit. Peccatum autem actuale, non originale, illius malitia nomine designari, quia peccatum actuale, non vero originale, illius maledictionis & perditionis causa extiterit. Atque hanc ipsam malitiam nomine malorum figmentorum cordis indigitari in Scripturis sacris,vt Gen.6.ver.5.videre sit. Atque malitiam actualem,non originalem illius καταχυσμοῦ causam fuisse, exemplo Noachi demonstrare conatur. Statim, inquit,sequitur in eodem capite sexto, Noach autem inuenit gratiam in oculis Iehouah:quare? num propterea quòd ille solus inter cæteros homines peccato originali non fuerit infectus? Audi quid scriptura dicat,Noach vir iustus,inquit illa,integer fuit in generationibus suis, cum Deo ipso ambulauit. Atque hinc necessarió sequitur,inquit Gen.8.v.21.non de originali,sed actuali peccato tractari.
units.tr: Osiorrodius, in section five of chapter thirty-three of his Institutions, takes exception to this testimony cited from Genesis. He says that the passage is not about original sin but about actual sin, and is concerned not with natural but with voluntary desire and inclination to sin. He tries to establish this exception by reasoning that God, in Genesis 8:21, meant nothing else than the wickedness of man, on account of which he had destroyed both man himself and the whole earth, and that he would no longer be moved in future to curse and destroy the earth and everything that lives upon it because of it. He argues that this wickedness is to be understood as actual sin, not original sin, because it was actual sin and not original sin that caused that curse and destruction. That this same wickedness is indicated in Holy Scripture by the name of the evil figments of the heart, he says, may be seen in Genesis 6:5. He tries to show by the example of Noah that actual wickedness, not original, was the cause of that deluge [καταχυσμοῦ]. Immediately, he says, there follows in the same sixth chapter: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of Jehovah." Why? Was it because he alone among the other men had not been infected with original sin? Hear what Scripture says: "Noah was a just man," it says, "and perfect in his generations; with God himself he walked." And from this, he says, it necessarily follows that Genesis 8:21 deals not with original but with actual sin.

units.la: Argumentum,si Aduersarii mentem bene sim assequutus,tale erit:
units.tr: If I have grasped the opponent's meaning correctly, the argument will be this:

units.la: Si Gen.8.vers.21.non agitur de peccato originali,sed de actuali, tum locus locus ille est ἀπρεσοδιόντος, neque potest originale peccatum ex illo demonstrari:
units.tr: If Genesis 8:21 is not about original sin but about actual sin, then that place is ambiguous [ἀπροσδιόριστος], and original sin cannot be proved from it.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second is also.

units.la: Probatio assumptionis huius est:
units.tr: The proof of this assumption is as follows:

units.la: Si Deus Gen. 8. ver. 21. nihil aliud significare voluit, quàm malitiam hominis, propter quam tum hominem ipsum, tum totam terram diluvio perdiderat, ipsum in posterum nunquam permoturam esse amplius, ut propter illam, terram, & quicquid viuit super ipsam, execrare & pessumdare velit: tum sequitur in illo loco non de originali, sed de actuali peccato agi:
units.tr: If God in Genesis 8:21 meant nothing else than the wickedness of man, on account of which he had destroyed both man himself and the whole earth by the flood, that he would no longer ever be moved again to curse and destroy the earth and everything that lives upon it because of it, then it follows that that passage is not about original but about actual sin.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second is also.

units.la: Consequentiae probationem hanc adfert:
units.tr: He offers this proof of the consequence:

units.la: Si peccatum actuale, non vero originale, illius maledictionis & perditionis causa extitit: Deus autem Genes. 8. verf. 21. nihil aliud significare voluit, quàm malitiam hominis, ob quam tum hominem ipsum, tum totam terram diluvio perdiderat, ipsum in posterum nunquam permoturam esse amplius, ut propter illam, terram, & quicquid viuit super ipsam, execrare & pessumdare velit: tum sequitur illo in loco, malitia illius nomine, non originale, sed actuale peccatum designari, ac proinde non de originali, sed de actuali peccato ibidem agi.
units.tr: If actual sin, and not original sin, was the cause of that curse and destruction; and God in Genesis 8:21 meant nothing else than the wickedness of man, on account of which he had destroyed both man himself and the whole earth by the flood, that he would no longer ever be moved again to curse and destroy the earth and everything that lives upon it because of it; then it follows that in that place the wickedness is designated by that name, not original but actual sin, and therefore that there it is not original but actual sin that is treated.

units.la: Atqui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true. Therefore the second is also.

units.la: Hanc assumptionem ultimam demonstrare conatur exemplo Noachi, Gen. 6. v. 8. & 9. in hunc modum.
units.tr: He tries to prove this last assumption by the example of Noah, Genesis 6:8 and 9, in the following way.

units.la: Si non actualis, sed originalis malitia illius diluvij & exitij causa extitisset, tum sequeretur, Noachum ideo invenisse gratiam in oculis Iehouah, quia ille solus inter cateros homines, originali labe non fuerit infectus:
units.tr: If it was not actual but original wickedness that was the cause of that flood and destruction, then it would follow that Noah found grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he alone among other men had not been stained by original corruption.

units.la: Atqui non propter illam immunitatem à peccato originali, sed quia iustus & integer fuit, & cum Deo ipso ambulauit, gratiam invenit in oculis Iehouah:
units.tr: But he did not find grace in the eyes of Jehovah on account of that immunity from original sin, but because he was just and perfect and walked with God himself.

units.la: Ergo actualis, non vero originalis malitia, illius exitij & diluvij causa extitit.
units.tr: Therefore actual, and not original, wickedness was the cause of that destruction and flood.

units.la: Resp. Primò, Consequentiam syllogismi principalis esse falsam: quia rei veritas de qua disceptatur, non tantùm ex illis Scripturae sacrae testimoniis demonstratur, quae illam simpliciter esse, vel non esse affirmant, sed ex iis etiam, quae illius causas, effecta, subiecta, proprietates, & circunstantias alias describunt. Quum itaque Deus Gen.6. v. 5. & Gen.8. v. 21. malitiæ arguat, quicquid ex cordis non regeniti officina proficiscitur vnquam, omnésque inclinationes, cogitationes, appetitus, & actiones inde emanantes, nequitiæ accusat: Paulus vero 2.Corinth.3. verf.5. illam tantumque languorem nobis tribuat, vt non tantùm nihil boni cogitemus vnquam, sed ne cogitare quidem possimus, ideo necessariò sequitur ipsum cor hominis corruptum, depravatum, & nequitia ac malitia originali, tanquam lepra aliqua infectu esse. Quales enim sunt causæ propinquæ, particulares, & propriæ, tales etiam esse illarum effectus, & contrà, vel pueris notum est. Et quis crediderit purum ac limpidum esse fontem illum qui non nisi fœtidissimas & impuriffimas aquas perpetuò egerit, aut bonam esse arborem illam, quæ non nisi perniciosissimos & pestiferos fructus ædit? Sed videamus, quibus argumentis assumptionem stabiliat. Secundò itaque respondemus consequentiam profyllogismi esse falsam, neque subiuncto epilogismo stabiliri, quippe cuius assumptio manifesta falsitate laborat, & oppositionum elencho ludit. Nam nec sola actualis, neque sola originalis malitia separatim, sed vtraque illius interitus & exitii causa meritoria extitit. Si enim solum actuale peccatum, nō vero originale quoque illius interitus causa extitisset, sequeretur non solam animam quæ peccauit, mortuam, sed filios innocentes patrum iniquitatem tulisse, id est, propter parentum scelera, impietatem, & iniquitatem, diluuio deletos pœnas dedisse. Nam in illo diluuio plurimos etiā infantes, qui omnis rationis vsu caruerunt, ac proinde peccatum actuale committere non potuerūt, interiisse, dubium nullum est.
units.tr: Reply. First, I say that the consequence of the principal syllogism is false, because the truth under dispute is demonstrated not only from those testimonies of Holy Scripture which simply affirm that it is or is not, but also from those which describe its causes, effects, subjects, properties, and other circumstances. Since therefore God, in Genesis 6:5 and Genesis 8:21, charges with wickedness whatever ever proceeds from the workshop of the unregenerate heart, and accuses of wickedness all the inclinations, thoughts, desires, and actions that emanate from it; and since Paul, in 2 Corinthians 3:5, attributes to us such weakness that we not only never think anything good but are not even able to think, it necessarily follows that the heart of man itself is corrupted, depraved, and infected with original wickedness and malice, like some leprosy. For whatever the proximate, particular, and proper causes are, such also are their effects, and conversely; even boys know this. And who would believe that that fountain is pure and clear which never sends forth anything but the foulest and most filthy waters, or that that tree is good which bears nothing but the most pernicious and deadly fruit? But let us see with what arguments he supports the assumption. Secondly, then, we reply that the consequence of the prosyllogism is false, and that it is not established by the appended epilogism, since its assumption labours under manifest falsity and plays with the refutation of opposites. For neither actual wickedness alone nor original wickedness alone separately, but both together, were the meritorious cause of its ruin and destruction. For if actual sin alone, and not original sin also, had been the cause of its ruin, it would follow that not only the soul which sinned died, but that innocent children bore the iniquity of their fathers, that is, that on account of their parents' crimes, impiety, and iniquity they paid penalties by being destroyed by the flood. For there is no doubt that in that flood very many infants also perished, who had no use of reason and therefore could not commit actual sin.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum & absurdum esse, Aduersarius modò sibi constare velit, haud inuitus fatebitur: Ergo & antecedentis, id est, assumptionis illius falsitatem agnoscat. Solum verò actuale, non autem originale quoque peccatum, vnà cum multiuariæ nequitiæ ipsius fructibus, diluuii causam fuisse, vltimo qui adfertur profyllogismo non demonstratur, tum quia totus est ἀσεβής, & falsa nititur hypothesi. Nemo enim nostrum affirmat, solum originale peccatum, illius exitii ac diluuii causam meritoriam & ἀποκαρπτικὴν fuisse, neque peccatum originale in illo negotio, peccato actuali quisquam nostrum opponit, sed vtrumque impurum nempe fontem, cum scatetibus inde fœtidis aquis, & radicem putridam, tridam cum fructibus putridis omnes optimè coniungunt : tum etiam quia vtraque eius præmissa falsa est. Manifestæ enim falsitatis arguimus consequentiam : primò, quia crasso causæ laborat elencho. Ex eo enim quod peccati originalis effectus proprius, iusti videlicet diuini iudicii vltio ac vindicta in ipsum Noachum nō redundauit, minimè sequitur, hoc immunitati ipsius, à peccato originalis contagione, imputādum esse, aut Noachū hæreditaria illa labe infectum non fuisse. Remoto enim effectu proprio, ad remotionem causæ, per extrinsecus obiectum obstaculum impeditæ, hoc est, à negatione actus secundi, à causis externis cohibiti ad negationem actus primi, neque in Theologicis, neque in naturalibus rebus dari consequentiam, extra dubitationis aleā iampridem fuit constitutum. Ex eo enim quod magnes, quem in manibus teneo, allio inunctus, ferrum non attrahit, non sequitur magnetem vim attrahendi non habere, aut in manibus meis non esse, cùm saluo actu primo, actus secundus per causam extrinsecam fuerit cohibitus. Sic manibus alicui arctissimè conuinctis, suspenditur apprehensionis actus, sed inde tamen non sequitur, manus nullam vim & facultatem apprehendendi habere: & ex eo quod ardentissimus ille ignis in fornace Babylonica, tres illos Israelitas non adussit, & consumpsit, concludi nulla ratione potest, ignem illum vim adurendi non habuisse, aut verum ignem in illa fornace accensum nō fuisse. Sic ex eo quod maledictus est omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, & tamen nulla est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu : non sequitur fideles in se consideratos, nullius culpæ & peccati reatu teneri. Si enim dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, mendaces sumus, & veritas Dei non est in nobis, i. Iohan. 1. verf. 8. Ex eo itaque quod peccatum originale vnà cum actuali impietate illius exitii causa extitisse, & Noachus tamen cum reliqua hominum impiorum colluuie non interiisse dicitur, minimè sequitur, Noachum illa contagione originali polutum non fuisse. Quemadmodum enim ignis in fornace illa Babylonica verus & naturalis ignis fuit, licet flagrantissimus eius feruor diuina potentia ita repressus & extinctus fuerit, vt eodem tres illi Israelitæ non modò non conflagrarint, sed ne capillus quidem capitis ipsorum læsus aut adustus fuerit : ita quoque peccatum originale ipsum quoque Noachum infecerat ( quis enim daret mundum ex immundo?) etiamsi gratia Dei remittentis ipsi imputatum
units.tr: But the consequence is false and absurd; the opponent, if he wishes to remain consistent with himself, will admit this without reluctance. Therefore he must also acknowledge the falsity of the antecedent, that is, of that assumption. That actual sin alone, and not original sin also, together with the many fruits of its wickedness, was the cause of the flood, is not demonstrated by the last prosyllogism which is offered, both because it is wholly ungodly [ἀσεβής] and rests on a false hypothesis. For none of us affirms that original sin alone was the meritorious and destructive [ἀποκαρπτικὴν] cause of that destruction and flood, nor does any of us set original sin over against actual sin in that matter; rather, we all rightly join both together: the impure fountain, with its foul waters bubbling forth from it, and the putrid root, with its putrid fruits. And the consequence is also refuted because each of his premises is false. For we charge the consequence with manifest falsity: first, because it labours under a gross refutation of cause. For from the fact that the proper effect of original sin, namely the vengeance and punishment of the just divine judgement, did not fall upon Noah himself, it by no means follows that this must be ascribed to his immunity from the contagion of original sin, or that Noah was not infected with that hereditary stain. For that, with the proper effect removed, the cause is removed by an external obstacle that impedes it, that is, from the negation of the second act to the restraint of the first act by external causes, there is no valid consequence either in theological or in natural matters, has long since been established beyond the reach of doubt. For from the fact that a magnet, which I hold in my hands, does not attract iron when it has been smeared with garlic, it does not follow that the magnet has no power of attraction, or that it is not in my hands, since the second act has been restrained by an external cause while the first act remains intact. So, when a person's hands are tightly bound, the act of grasping is suspended; yet it does not follow from this that the hands have no power and faculty of grasping. And from the fact that that most fierce fire in the Babylonian furnace did not burn and consume those three Israelites, it can by no reasoning be concluded that that fire had no power to burn, or that the true fire had not been kindled in that furnace. So too, from the fact that everyone is cursed who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, and yet there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, it does not follow that believers, considered in themselves, are held under no guilt of fault and sin. For if we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth of God is not in us, 1 John 1:8. Therefore, from the fact that original sin, together with actual impiety, was the cause of that destruction, and yet Noah is said to have perished not with the rest of the impious mass of men, it by no means follows that Noah was not polluted by that original contagion. For just as the fire in that Babylonian furnace was a true and natural fire, although its most blazing heat was so restrained and quenched by divine power that those three Israelites were not only not set on fire but not even a hair of their heads was harmed or scorched, so also original sin had infected Noah himself (for who would make the clean out of the unclean?), even though it was imputed to him by the grace of God remitting it...

units.la: Sc
units.tr: Sc-

units.la: non fuerit, nec ipsi fraudi esse, aut cum reliqua impiorum caterua, in idem exitium rapere non potuerit. Secundo, quia si consequentia illa esset veritatis necessariæ, tum ex sententia Aduersarii sequeretur, Noachum plane ἀμαρτωλὸν fuisse, id est, omni peccato actuali caruisse: Si enim ex eo quod peccatum originale illius diluuii, & exitii causa θεοκαταρκτικὴ, & meritoria fuisse statuitur, sequitur Noachum ideo inuenisse gratiam in oculis Iehouah, quia videlicet vnus ex omnibus reliquis hominibus peccati originalis labe non fuerit infectus: tum si peccatum actuale, non vero originale, vt vult Aduersarius, illius diluuii causa fuit, necessario Noachus ideo inuenit gratiam in oculis Iehouah, quia videlicet solus ille, ab omni actualis peccati culpa immunis fuerit. Vtriusque enim consequentiæ eadem est necessitas & veritas, quia ex remotione causæ, ad remotionem effectus vtraque nititur. Atque consequens falsum esse, hoc est, ἀμαρτωλὸν ipsi Noacho attribui non posse, ipsa Scriptura sacra luculenter docet. Si enim iniquitatem obseruaueris Domine, inquit Psalmista, quis consistet? Psal.130.v.3. Ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo, quia non esset iustus coram te vllus viuens, Psal.143.v.2. & 1.Ioan.1 v.8. Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, mendaces sumus, & veritas Dei non est in nobis. Ergo & antecedens id est, consequentiam Aduersarii falsam esse, necesse est. Atque hæc de connexo. Assumptionem vero, quæ ex partibus constat discretis, quantum concernit, libenter fatemur Noachum non ideo inuenisse gratiam in oculis Iehouah, quia ille solus peccato originis non fuerit infectus, sed dicimus, eandem manifesto caussæ elencho laborare. Nō enim ideo gratiam in oculis Iehouah meruisse Noachus dicitur, quia iustus fuit, sed ideo iustus fuit, quia gratiam in oculis Iehouah inuenit, quod duabus solidissimis rationibus demonstratur. Prima est, quia ex testimoniis modo citatis apparet, Deum si cum Noacho intrare in iudicium voluisset, & iniquitates ipsius obseruasset, nō minus ipsum, quam reliquos homines diluuio perdere potuisse, vnde sequitur ipsum ex gratia, & misericordia Dei, non autem merito, aut iustitia operum seruatum fuisse. Secunda est, quia Noachus iustus ibi dicitur, iustitia non inhærente, & operum, seu legali, sed Euangelica, & quæ per fidem est, Hebr.11. v.7. Per fidem admonitus oraculo Noe, ea, quæ nondum videbantur, veritus, apparauit arcam, ad salutem domus suæ: per quam condemnauit mundum & eius, quæ secundum fidem est, iustitia, factus est est hæres. Quia vero iustitiæ Euangelicæ applicatio, i. iustificatio, gratiæ diuinæ, ac misericordiæ, non causa, sed effectus est, Rom.3. 24. Iustificantur autem gratis, eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu: ideo sequitur, Noachum non ideo inuenisse gratiam in oculis Iehouah, quia iustus fuerit, sed ideo iustum fuisse, quia gratiam in oculis Iehouah inuenerit. Apparet itaque nihil ab Aduersario allatum esse, quod nostrum argumentum labefactare possit. Sed pergamus in assumptionis nostræ demonstratione.
units.tr: was not, nor could he be dragged into the same destruction with the rest of the ungodly. Secondly, if that inference were of necessary truth, then on the opponent's view it would follow that Noah was plainly ἀμαρτωλός [sinless], that is, free from all actual sin. For if, because original sin is posited as the cause of that flood and of its destruction, both the divine judgment and the meritorious cause, it follows that Noah found grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he alone, among all other men, was not infected with the stain of original sin, then, if actual sin and not original sin was the cause of the flood, as the opponent wants, Noah must have found grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he alone was immune from the guilt of every actual sin. Both inferences have the same necessity and truth, since each rests on the removal of the cause leading to the removal of the effect. That the consequent is false, that is, that Noah cannot be called ἀμαρτωλός [sinful], is clearly taught by Holy Scripture itself. "If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities," says the Psalmist, "who shall stand?" Psalm 130:3. "Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified." Psalm 143:2; and 1 John 1:8: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Therefore the antecedent, that is, the opponent's inference, must be false. So much for the connection. As for the assumption, which consists of separate parts, we freely admit that Noah did not find grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he alone was not infected with original sin; but we say that the same assumption is refuted by a manifest proof of cause. For Noah is not said to have merited grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he was righteous; rather he was righteous because he found grace in the eyes of Jehovah. This is shown by two very solid reasons. The first is that, as appears from the testimonies just cited, if God had wished to enter into judgment with Noah and had marked his iniquities, he could have destroyed him no less than the rest of mankind in the flood. From this it follows that Noah was preserved by grace and the mercy of God, and not by merit or the righteousness of works. The second is that Noah is called righteous there by a righteousness not inherent, not of works or of the law, but evangelical, which is through faith (Heb. 11:7): "By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house, by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith." Because the application of evangelical righteousness, that is, justification, is an effect of divine grace and mercy and not its cause (Rom. 3:24: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus"), it follows that Noah did not find grace in the eyes of Jehovah because he was righteous, but was righteous because he found grace in the eyes of Jehovah. It is clear, then, that the opponent has brought forward nothing that can shake our argument. But let us go on to the demonstration of our assumption.

units.la: Mentis igitur cæcitatem, <bl>τυφλωσιν</bl>, & vanitatem, de qua hactenus egimus, sequi <bl>τ πνευματι τ καρδίας</bl>, i. cordis ac voluntatis obduratione, prauitatem ac peruersitatem, vt homo non regenitus, id quod vere bonum est, & Deo gratum, non amplius possit appetere, sed auersetur, malum autem tantum appetat atque velit: Mentis denique cæcitati, & cordis malitiæ ex æquo respondere viriũ omnium impotentiam & imbecillitatem, vt nisi vires nouæ per Spiritum S. in nobis gignatur, neque id quod vere bonum est, præstare, neque malum quo decet modo omittere ac vitare possimus, cap. 26. ex ipsis scripturæ sacræ fontibus demonstrauimus. Ex quibus necessario sequitur, naturam humanam per peccatum splendidis illis iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ originalis ornamentis spoliatam, ac proinde miserè fœdatam atque corruptam esse.
units.tr: Therefore the blindness of mind (τύφλωσιν) and the vanity of which we have so far spoken must be followed by the hardening of the heart and will (τῷ πνεύματι τῆς καρδίας), that is, by a depravity and perversity such that the unregenerate man can no longer desire what is truly good and pleasing to God, but shrinks from it, and desires and wills only evil. Moreover, the impotence and weakness of all men must correspond equally to the blindness of mind and the malice of heart, so that unless new powers are begotten in us through the Holy Spirit, we can neither do what is truly good nor avoid evil as we ought. We demonstrated this in chapter 26 from the very sources of Holy Scripture. From these points it necessarily follows that human nature, through sin, has been stripped of those splendid ornaments of original righteousness and holiness, and therefore has been miserably defiled and corrupted.

units.la: Huius autem vniuersalis & natiuæ corruptionis non posset reperiri exordium, nisi ad primum omnium parentem, tanquam ad fontem ascendamus, ex Adami & Christi comparatione planum facit Apost. Rom.5.12. Quemadmodum per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intrauit, ac per peccatum mors, & sic in omnes homines mors pertransiit, quia omnes peccauerunt: & v. 18.19. Sicut per vnam offensam reatus venit in omnes homines, ad condemnationem: ita per vnam iustificationem beneficium redundauit in omnes homines ad iustificationem vitæ. Sicut per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per vnius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi. Et 1. Cor. 15.21.22. Quia, n. per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio mortuorum: Sicut enim in Adamo omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes viuificabuntur. Quũ autem certissimum sit, exque scripturis sacris ipsis constet, iustitiam Christi non tantum vt exemplum nobis imitandam propositam, sed ipsa communicatione nostram esse, indeque vitæ æternæ nos participes reddi, Christíque vita & resurrectio nobis non tantum vt exemplum & similitudo, sed vt causa, pignus, & hypostasis vitæ æternæ ac resurrectionis nostræ proponatur: ideo necessariò sequitur ipsam Adami inobedientiam, & inde consequuntam corruptionem, non imitatione tantùm & exemplo, sed imputatione, & propagatione carnali, in posteros deriuatam esse.
units.tr: The beginning of this universal and innate corruption cannot be found unless we ascend to the first parent of all, as to a source. The comparison of Adam and Christ makes this plain in the Apostle (Rom. 5:12): "As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." And verses 18–19: "As by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation, so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." And 1 Cor. 15:21–22: "For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive." Since it is most certain, and it is established from Holy Scripture itself, that the righteousness of Christ is set before us not only as an example to be imitated, but is ours by communication itself, and that thereby we are made partakers of eternal life; and since Christ's life and resurrection are set before us not merely as an example and likeness, but as the cause, pledge and substance of our eternal life and resurrection, it necessarily follows that Adam's disobedience, and the corruption that followed from it, has been derived to his posterity not merely by imitation and example, but by imputation and carnal propagation.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capite trigesimo tertio, sectione quinta, ad testimonia Pauli ex Epistolæ ad Romanos capite quinto allegata duo excipit: & primò dicit, quosdam peccatum originale ex illis verbis probare conari, qua in vulgata versione leguntur, in quo omnes peccauerunt, perinde quasi Apostolus dixisset, in Adamo omnes peccasse: Sciendum verò esse, quod textus Græcus habeat ἐφ' ᾧ (quod vetus Interpres reddiderit in quo) quod nihil aliud significet, quàm quia, vel quoniam, sicuti Lutherus quoque locum illum transtulerit, vel quatenus. Sensum itaque genuinum verborum illorum Pauli hunc esse, omnes videlicet homines morti plane obnoxios esse, quoniam, vel quatenus omnes peccauerunt. Hoc autem non de peccato originali, sed de malis operibus, id est, peccatis actualibus, intelligi deberet, sicuti manifestum fit ex verbis sequentibus, quibus dicit Apostolus, peccatum vsque ad legem in mundo fuisse, peccatum verò vbi lex non est, non imputari.
units.tr: In section five of chapter thirty-three of his Institutes, Ostorodius takes exception to two points about the testimonies of Paul from Romans chapter five. First, he says that some try to prove original sin from those words which are read in the Vulgate version, "in whom all have sinned," as though the Apostle had said, "in Adam all have sinned." But it must be understood that the Greek text has ἐφ' ᾧ (which the old translator rendered "in whom"), which signifies nothing other than "because," or "since," as Luther also translated that passage, "or" "inasmuch as." So the true sense of those words of Paul is this: that all men are plainly liable to death, since, or inasmuch as, all have sinned. But this ought to be understood not of original sin but of evil works, that is, actual sins, as is manifest from the words that follow, in which the Apostle says that sin was in the world until the law, but that sin is not imputed where there is no law.

units.la: Resp. Eodem sensu recidit, siue illud ἐφ' ᾧ reddas pro ὅτι, eo quòd, quia, quandoquidem, vel quatenus, siue per elliptin idem pronomen, ad nomen antecedens, nempe Adamum referas. Certissimum enim est, & ex ipsa disputationis serie manifeste apparet, causam ibi & rationem, quare mors tanta cum potentia & violentia in omnes & singulos homines sæuiat, hanc reddi, quia videlicet omnes peccauerunt, nempe in vno illo homine Adamo, quippe in quo omnes mortui sunt, 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 22. Falsum enim est illo in loco non de peccato originali id est, peccato Adami, qui tanquam stirps, radix & principium totius generis humani, totum genus humanum repræsentabat, imputatione & propagatione in nos deriuato, sed de peccatis actualibus, quæ singulis hominibus propria sunt, agi. Nam ad ipsum primorum parentum delictum necessariò ascendendum, & tanquam ad originem ac principium penetrandum esse, ex eo liquet euidentissimè, quod non adulti tantum, sed etiam infantes, in quos tamen peccatum actuale non cadit, peccati eo ipso accusantur & conuincuntur, quod & illi peccati pœnæ & stipendio, nempe morti sunt obnoxii: infantes siquidem nõnisi in parentibus peccati & iniquitatis rei peragi possint, & singulí quoguli quoque parentes proximi, ia olim ab ipso conceptionis & nativitatis momento, peccatores & rei exiterint. Quomodo vero illa Aduersarii assumptio, qua affirmat versu illo duodecimo, non de originali, sed de actuali tantum peccato disputari, ex vers. 13. stabiliri queat, non video. Occurrit enim ibi Apostolus per prolepsin, illi obiectioni, cua doctrina illa de universali illo reatu, quo per Adami inobedientiam ἁμαρτία constitutum est Deo, totum genus humanum, impugnari poterat hoc modo, Vbi non est lex, ibi neque peccatum est: Aliqui ab Adamo usque ad Mosen non erat lex: Ergo neque peccatum: Et tum contraria conclusioni assertione, omnes videlicet peccasse, ne illis quidem qui ante legem Mosis fuerunt, exceptis, id quod prius dixerat, tuetur, tum ad propositionem respondet per negationem, & subiectam correctionem: Cum non est lex, inquiens, peccatum non ἐλλογεῖται: id est, cum non est lex, peccatum quidem non agnoscitur, non reputatur, non existimatur esse peccatum, etiamsi peccatum revera sit: quamvis igitur ante Mosen, non existimabatur esse peccatum, quia tunc nondum erat lex lata, tamen peccatum in mundo fuisse, vt vers. 14. probat ex effectu & poena, ac stipendio peccati, nempe morte. Per ἀμαρτίαν vero, quae vsque ad legem in mundo fuisse dicitur, non actuale tantum, sed originale quoque, id est, quod uis peccatum, inprimis vero reatum illum primi peccati intelligendum esse, ex verbis illis sequentibus liquido constat, quibus mors regnasse dicitur in eos quoque qui non peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam, hoc est, non solum in adultos, qui, vt Adam transgressus est legem illam singularem, de fructu certae arboris non edendo: sic ipsi transgressi sunt legem moralem, siue inscriptam cordibus, siue ore Dei pronunciatam, ac per Mosen latam, in sua quisque persona: sed etiam in infantes, quorum nullus in sua ipsius persona vllam legem transgredi potuit, quum nullus per infirmitatem aetatis, legem vllam intelligere, aut ratione inter rectum & prauum discernere atque diiudicare potuerit.
units.tr: Reply. It comes to the same sense whether you render that ἐφ' ᾧ as ὅτι, because, since, seeing that, or inasmuch as, or whether, by ellipsis, you refer the same pronoun to the preceding noun, namely Adam. For it is most certain, and clearly appears from the very sequence of the argument, that the cause and reason why death rages with such power and violence against all and each man is given here: namely, because all have sinned, that is, in that one man Adam, in whom all have died (1 Cor. 15:22). For it is false that in that passage the subject is not original sin, that is, the sin of Adam, who, as the stock, root and beginning of the whole human race, represented the whole human race, and whose sin is derived to us by imputation and propagation, but that it concerns actual sins which belong to each individual man. That we must necessarily ascend to the very offence of our first parents, and penetrate to it as to the origin and beginning, is most evident from the fact that not only adults but also infants, on whom actual sin does not fall, are for that very reason accused and convicted of sin: they too are liable to the punishment and wage of sin, namely death. For infants can only be conceived and born from parents who are guilty of sin and iniquity, and each of their immediate parents likewise was a sinner and guilty from the very moment of conception and birth. But how that assumption of the opponent, by which he affirms that in verse twelve the discussion is of actual sin only, and not of original sin, can be established from verse 13, I do not see. For the Apostle there meets, by prolepsis, an objection with which the doctrine of that universal guilt, by which sin is reckoned to the whole human race before God through Adam's disobedience, could be attacked in this way: "Where there is no law, there is no sin. But from Adam to Moses there was no law. Therefore there was no sin." And so, first he maintains the contrary of the conclusion, namely the assertion that all have sinned, not excepting even those who lived before the law of Moses, which is what he had said before; then he answers the premise by a negation and a corrective clause: "Where there is no law," he says, "sin is not reckoned" (οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται): that is, where there is no law, sin is indeed not acknowledged, not reckoned, not considered to be sin, even though it really is sin. So although before Moses sin was not thought to be sin, because the law had not yet been given, nevertheless sin was in the world, as verse 14 proves from its effect, punishment, and wage, namely death. By the sin which is said to have been in the world until the law, one must understand not only actual sin but original sin as well, that is, the guilt of that first sin above all. This is clear from the following words, in which death is said to have reigned even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression. That is, death reigned not only over adults, who, as Adam transgressed that single law concerning not eating the fruit of a certain tree, likewise transgressed the moral law, whether written in their hearts or pronounced by the mouth of God and given through Moses, each in his own person; but also over infants, none of whom could transgress any law in his own person, since no one, because of the weakness of his age, could understand any law or discern and judge between right and wrong by reason.

units.la: Secundo respondet ad verba illa vers. 19. quibus per inobedientiam vnius hominis multi peccatores constituti dicuntur, & inquit, peccatorem in sacris literis, ex vsu Hebraeae linguae, non semper verum peccatorem, sed eum quoque cum quo perinde agitur, ac si peccati vere reus esset, & aliquid mali perpetrasset, denotare, vt videre fit ex 1. Reg. 1. vers. 21. vbi Regina Bathsheba, metuens ne ipsa cum filio Salomone, post obitum Regis Dauidis ab Adonia occideretur, his verbis Regem compel-lasse legitur: Cum occubuerit Dominus meus Rex cum patribus suis, futurum est ut sim ego, & filius meus Salomo peccatores. Quibus Regina Bathsheba significare voluerit, post obitum Dauidis futurum esse, non quidem ut illa cum filio aliquid mali patrare teneretur, sed ut perinde tractaretur, ac si quid sceleris & flagitij commisisset. Nomine vero peccatorum in illo Apostoli loco, non veros peccatores, sed eos designari, qui in illo peccatorum habiti & tractati sunt, ex antithesi illa, quas per obedientiam unius multi dicuntur iusti constituendi esse liquere, quandoquidem illi nō quatenus bona praestiterint opera, sed quatenus vitam aeternam consequuntur, pro iustis habeantur, ita ut iustorum nomine illo in loco, nulli alij denotentur, quam qui sunt sicut iusti, nempe perfecti, quemadmodum Christus erat, quippe cum quibus Deus perinde atque cum Christo agit, quamvis tales revera non sint. Quia itaque posteri Adami non minus quam ipse Adam, morti sunt obnoxij, idque propter peccatum Adami, ideo Apostolum dixisse inquit, illos per inobedientiam Adami peccatores constitutos esse, nempe quia perinde ipsis cesserit, ac si ipsimet peccassent, quemadmodum Adamus peccavit. Denique obseruandum esse dicit similitudinem illam quae hac nre est inter Christum & Adamum, nempe quod sicut omnes, qui ex Adamo originem ducunt, eiusdem conditionis sunt cum ipso participes, cui ille cum posteros suos generare inciperet, fuit obnoxius, ita etiam omnes in Christum credentes, quatenus tales sunt, a Christo ipso proficiscuntur, ac proinde vitae aeternae participes redduntur. Argumentum ad formam redactum tale erit. Si Rom. 5. verf. 19. nomine peccatorum non intelliguntur veri peccatores, & qui culpae alicuius ac peccati reatu tenentur, sed tales cum quibus perinde agitur, ac si peccatores essent, & mali quid commisissent: tum ex illo loco peccatum originis demonstrari non potest: Atqui prius verum est. Ergo & posterius. Assumptionem probare conatur duabus rationibus, Prima est: Si nomen peccatorum ex usu Hebraeae linguae in sacris literis non semper flagitiosum aut sceleratum, sed interdum etiam illum significat, qui non secus tractatur, ac si scelus aliquod & flagitium commisisset, tum Roman. 5. verf. 19. nomine peccatorum, non veró peccatores, sed tales designantur cum quibus perinde agitur, quasi peccafi peccatum aliquod commissent.
units.tr: Second, he answers those words of verse 19, by which it is said that "through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners," and says that in the Holy Scriptures, according to the usage of the Hebrew language, the word "sinner" does not always mean a true sinner, but also one with whom people deal as though he were truly guilty of sin and had committed some wrong. He says this is seen in 1 Kings 1:21, where Queen Bathsheba, fearing that she and her son Solomon would be killed by Adonijah after the death of King David, is read to have addressed the king in these words: "When my lord the king shall sleep with his fathers, it will come about that I and my son Solomon will be sinners." By these words Queen Bathsheba meant that after David's death she and her son would be treated as though they had committed some crime or wickedness, not that they would be bound to do any wrong themselves. In that passage of the Apostle, the word "sinners" designates not true sinners but those who were regarded and treated as sinners, as is clear from the contrast that through the obedience of one many are to be made righteous. For they are counted righteous not because of the good works they have done but because they obtain eternal life. So in that place the word "righteous" designates no others than those who are "as righteous," namely perfect, just as Christ was, since God deals with them just as He deals with Christ, although they are not truly such. Therefore, since the posterity of Adam, no less than Adam himself, are subject to death, and this on account of Adam's sin, the Apostle, he says, said that they were made sinners through the disobedience of Adam, namely because it was reckoned to them just as if they themselves had sinned, as Adam sinned. Finally, he says that one must observe the similarity that exists between Christ and Adam here: just as all who trace their origin from Adam share the same condition to which he was subject when he began to beget his descendants, so too all who believe in Christ, insofar as they are such, proceed from Christ Himself, and therefore are made partakers of eternal life. The argument, reduced to form, will be this: If in Romans 5:19 the word "sinners" does not mean true sinners, who are held bound by the guilt and reatus of some fault, but those with whom people deal as though they were sinners and had done wrong, then the sin of origin cannot be demonstrated from that passage. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also true. He tries to prove the minor premise by two reasons. The first is this: If, according to the usage of the Hebrew language in the Holy Scriptures, the word "sinners" does not always mean the wicked or criminal, but sometimes also means those who are treated as though they had committed some crime and wickedness, then in Romans 5:19 the word "sinners" designates not true sinners but those with whom people deal as though they had committed some sin.

units.la: Atqui prius verum si‌sse liquet ex 1.Reg.3.v.21.
units.tr: But the former is clearly true, as is shown by 1 Kings 3:21.

units.la: Ergo & posterius verum est.
units.tr: Therefore the latter is also true.

units.la: Secunda est:
units.tr: The second is:

units.la: Si in antithesi nomine iustorum, non designantur illi, qui reuera sunt iusti, sed qui ideo iusti dicuntur, quia regnum cœlorum consequuntur, hoc est, qui perinde habentur, ac si vt Christus ipse, iusti ac perfecti essent, ac proinde vt Christus ipse à Deo Patre, tractantur: tum nomine peccatorum, non veri peccatores, sed illi designantur, cum quibus non secus agitur, ac si peccassent, hoc est, qui propter Adami peccatum, pœna peccati non minus ac ipse Adam, subiiciuntur.
units.tr: If in the contrast the word "righteous" designates not those who are truly righteous but those who are called righteous because they obtain the kingdom of heaven, that is, those who are regarded as though they were perfect and just, as Christ himself was, and therefore are treated by God the Father as Christ himself is treated, then the word "sinners" designates not true sinners but those with whom people deal as though they had sinned, that is, those who, on account of Adam's sin, are subjected to the punishment of sin no less than Adam himself.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse falsam, neque duabus rationibus allatis demonstrari posse. Ad primam enim respondeo primò, consequentiam esse falsam. Ex eo namque, quòd nomine peccatorum in scripturis sacris interdum non vere flagitiosi, sed illi denotantur, cum quibus perinde agitur, quasi sceleris aliquid ac flagitii commisissent, minimè sequitur, hoc quoque, de quo disceptatur, loco, non de veris peccatoribus, sed iis tantùm agi, qui instar peccatorum habentur, ac tractantur. Sunt puræ particulares, ex quibus nihil certi concluditur. Secundò, assumptionem quod attinet, distinguendum esse inter iudicium, ac tribunal diuinum, & inter iudicium ac tribunal humanum. Illud enim semper iustum ac verax est, & omnis iniquitatis expers. Nam iustus est Iehouah in omnibus viis suis, Psalm 145.vers.17. qui diligens iustitiam, odio prosequitur omnem iniquitatem, Psalm. 45.vers.8. qui improbat improbum, reddendo viam eius in caput eius, & iustificando iustum, reddendo ei secundùm iustitiam eius. 1.Reg.8.vers.32. Coram quo maledictus est, quicunque peruertit ius peregrini, pupilli, aut viduæ. Deuteron.cap.17.vers.19. Cui abominationi est, quicunque absoluit improbum, & condemnat iustum. Prou.17.ver.15. Cuius iudicium non ... aut ... sed ... est. Roman.cap.2.vers.2. Quanta verò iniquitas & iniustitia sæpenumero in tribunali hominum exerceatur, tum exemplis plurimorum, iudicium ex auarities, aut alio aliquo affectu prauo peruertentium, quæ historiæ sacræ recensent, tum quotidiana experientia comprobatur. Nomine itaque peccatorum interdum etiam illos indigitari, qui licet culpæ expertes, poenas tamen luunt, lubens concedo, sed illud in iudicio ac tribunali humano, eóque iniquo fieri affirmo, vt exemplum Bathsabæ ab Aduersario allegatum, de iniuriis abAdonia sibi imminentibus, apud Dauidem conquerentis, luculenter ostendit, in iudicio vero ac tribunali diuino, foli illi peccatores nominantur ac habentur, qui reuera culpæ alicuius reatu tenentur, neque contrarium vllius exempli inductione demonstrari potest. Quum itaque locus ille Roman 5. ver.19. de tribunali diuino, non humano agat ( vt enim per obedientiam Christi iustificamur, non coram humano, sed diuino tribunali: ita etiam per inobedientiam Adami non hominibus, sed Deo constituimur) ideo necessario sequitur, nomen peccatorum in loco allegato à nobis, vere ac proprie sumendum esse. Hisce adde, quod sententia Aduersarii Deum ipsum summæ iniustitiæ accusat. Si enim in iudicio ac tribunali diuino, propter Adami transgressionem posteri eius, qui tamen peccatores non sunt, nec mali quicquam commiserunt, nihilominus pro peccatoribus habentur, & morte puniuntur, tum filius portabit iniquitatem parentis, nec illa tantum anima, quæ peccauit, mortua est, & Deus iustum ac innocentem condemnare & multare dicetur. Atqui consequens falsum est & impium: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: I reply: the minor premise of the main syllogism is false, nor can it be demonstrated by the two reasons brought forward. To the first I reply, first, that the consequence is false. For from the fact that in the sacred Scriptures the word "sinners" sometimes designates not those who are truly wicked but those with whom people deal as though they had committed some crime and wickedness, it by no means follows that in the passage under dispute too, it is not about true sinners but only about those who are held and treated as sinners. These are pure particulars, from which nothing certain is concluded. Second, as regards the minor premise, a distinction must be made between the divine judgment and tribunal and the human judgment and tribunal. For the former is always just and true, and free of all iniquity. "For Jehovah is righteous in all his ways" (Psalm 145:17); "he who loves righteousness hates every iniquity" (Psalm 45:8); "he who condemns the wicked, bringing his way upon his head, and justifying the righteous, rewarding him according to his righteousness" (1 Kings 8:32). "Cursed before whom is anyone who perverts the judgment of the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow" (Deuteronomy 27:19, cap. 17 as printed). "He is an abomination to whom anyone who acquits the wicked and condemns the righteous" (Proverbs 17:15). "Whose judgment is not ... but ... is" (Romans 2:2, cap. 2). But how great iniquity and injustice is often practised in the tribunal of men, is proved both by the examples of very many people who have perverted judgment through avarice or some other wicked passion, which the histories of sacred Scripture recount, and by daily experience. So I gladly concede that by the word "sinners" sometimes those are also indicated who, though free of guilt, nonetheless suffer punishments; but I affirm that this happens in human judgment and tribunal, and an unjust one at that, as the example of Bathsheba cited by our opponent clearly shows, when she complained to David of the injuries about to be inflicted on her by Adonijah. In the divine judgment and tribunal, however, only those are named and regarded as "sinners" who are truly held bound by the guilt of some fault, and no instance can be adduced to demonstrate the contrary. Since therefore that passage, Romans 5:19, treats of the divine tribunal and not the human one (for just as we are justified through the obedience of Christ before the divine and not the human tribunal, so too through the disobedience of Adam we are "constituted" not before men but before God), it necessarily follows that the word "sinners" in the passage cited by us must be taken truly and properly. Add to this that the opponent's opinion accuses God Himself of the highest injustice. For if in the divine judgment and tribunal, on account of Adam's transgression, his posterity, who are not sinners and have committed no wrong, are nevertheless regarded as sinners and punished with death, then the son will bear the iniquity of the father, and not only the soul that sinned will be dead, and God will be said to condemn and punish the just and innocent. But the consequent is false and impious. Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Ad rationem secundam respondeo, vtramque eius propositionem esse falsam. Consequentiæ enim falsitas demonstratur ex verbis Apostoli Rom.5. verf.15. Non vt offensa, ita etiam est quod Deus gratificatur. Cuius discriminis causa est manifesta: Quia enim generare Adamus non poterat, quin vna cum reatu qualitatem vitiosam simul in posteros transfunderet; Christus vero non generatione aliqua naturali iustitiam suam nobis communicet, sed tum imputatione obedientiæ suæ, ab omni reatu & pœna nos liberet, tum paulatim tantum, & per quotidianos progressus, potentia sui Spiritus nos regeneret ac transformet: hinc est, quod iustitia & iniquitas, Rom.5.verf.19. opponuntur quidem tanquam duarum diuersarum causarum disceptantes effectus, sed quia iustitia de qua in illo capite agitur, non simpliciter ipsi corruptioni, sed tum actiuæ corruptionis Adami, tum consequutæ inde vitiositatis reatui opponitur: idcirco ex eo, quod nomine iustorum designantur, qui per imputatam, non vero subiectiue inhærentem iustitiam iusti sunt, minime sequitur, nomine peccatorum nos propterea tantum indiindigitari, quia Adami delictum nobis imputetur, non autem quia ipsa etiam corruptionis labes in nos transfundatur. Assum-ptio autem eiusdē prosyllogismi multis, iisque grauissimis erroribus scatet: Nam primo falsum est, per iustos ibi non vere iustos, sed eos tantum, qui iustorum instar, a Deo tractantur, intelligendos esse. Agitur enim de illis, quos Deus ex mera misericordia, & gratia, per remissionem peccatorum, seu iustitiam Christi imputatam iustificat: At quoscunque Deus iustificat, & quibuscunque peccata remittit, seu quorumcunque iniquitates teguntur, & quicunque per sanguinem Christi ab omnibus peccatis ipsorum mundantur, ii non titulo tenus aut κατ' ὄνομα, sed reipsa & κατ' ἀληθειαν iusti sunt. Non enim in imaginaria & inani fictione, aut δικαίως illa iustitiæ Christi imputatio consistit, sed in eadem prorsus veritate, qua impositio peccatorum nostrorum in Christum, qui nunquam propter illa factus fuisset κατάρα, seu execratio, nec eadem sustulisset, nisi re ipsa imputata illi fuissent, nemo siquidem execrabilis est Deo, nisi propter peccatum, id est, quatenus peccator vel est, vel censetur. Et quanquam illa iustitia, qua coram tribunali diuino iustificamur, subiectiuè sit in ipso Christo, non tamen plane est extra nos, quia Christus in nobis habitat, vt caput nostrum, per communicationem spiritus, in quo iustitia ipsius nostra fit, per fidem, quod autem fide habetur, id vere habetur, quia fides certis & infallibilibus verbi diuini promissionibus nititur. Secundo falsum etiam est, illos ideo iustos appellari, quia vitam æternam consequuntur: non enim vitæ æternæ adeptio, iustificationis, sed hæc illius causa efficiens est: ideo si-quidem regnum coelorum consequimur, quia Deus nos ex mera misericordia propter iustitiam Christi iustificat, & regni cœlestis hæreditate dignos iudicat, vt tota doctrina Euangelica luculenter docet. Tertio, falsum est, eos qui in illo loco iusti a Paulo nominantur, non secus ac ipsum Christum iustos & perfectos ceseri. Necessario enim sequeretur illos non minus quam ipsum Christum, esse redemptores ac saluatores mundi, quod falsum est & impium. Iusti itaque credentes illo in loco ideo dicuntur, quia singulis quidem iustitia Christi imputatur, ita ac si eam singuli pro se, non vero pro aliis præstitissent. Quarto falsum est, eosdem perinde haberi & tractari a Deo Patre, quemadmodum Christus ipse habetur atque tractatur. Deus enim nos natura filios iræ, in peccatis natos & conceptos, ac maledictioni æternæ obnoxios, ex mera misericordia propter sanguinem Chri-sti, peccata nostra expiantis, iustificat, sanctificat, re-generat,& glorificat : cum Christus natura & vita ἀϊδιότητα, ne-que sanctificationis,neque renouationis beneficio indigeat. De-inde Deus Christum propter obedientiam præstitam, in summam extu-lit sublimitatem, ac donauit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, vt ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat cœlestium, ac terrestrium, & sub-terraneorum : Philip.cap.2.vers.9.10. Dedit ipsi omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, Matth.cap.28.vers.18. Constituit ipsum caput corporis Ecclesiæ, principium, & primogenitum ex mortuis, vt in omnibus primas teneat:Coloss.capite primo,versu decimo octauo. Quæ omnia singulis electis & credentibus contingere, aduersus Scripturæ di-uinæ veritatem affirmādum,aut crassissimi erroris, & notoriæ sal-sitatis,assumptio illa accusanda, est. Comparationis illius, quam Paulus inter Christum & Adamum instituit,explanatio, quam ar-gumento suo attexuit Aduersarius, ex impuris Pelagianorum la-cunis hausta est, & falsam illam esse, ex responsione nostra, mani-feste apparet.
units.tr: I answer the second argument by saying that both of its premises are false. The falsity of the consequence is shown from the words of the Apostle in Rom. 5:15: But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. The reason for this difference is plain. Adam could not beget children without passing on a corrupt quality along with the guilt. Christ, however, does not communicate his righteousness to us by any natural generation. He frees us from all guilt and punishment by the imputation of his obedience, and he regenerates and transforms us only gradually, through daily progress, by the power of his Spirit. Hence righteousness and unrighteousness are set against each other in Rom. 5:19 as the effects of two different causes. But the righteousness spoken of in that chapter is opposed not simply to corruption itself, but both to the active corruption of Adam and to the guilt of the vice that follows from it. So it does not follow, from the fact that they are called righteous because they are reckoned righteous through an imputed righteousness, not one inherent in them, that we are designated sinners only because Adam's offence is imputed to us, and not also because the stain of corruption itself is passed on to us. The assumption of this prosyllogism, moreover, is full of many and very serious errors. First, it is false that by the righteous are meant there not those who are truly righteous, but only those who are treated by God as if they were righteous. The passage speaks of those whom God justifies out of pure mercy and grace, by the forgiveness of sins and the imputed righteousness of Christ. Yet whoever God justifies, whose sins he forgives, whose iniquities he covers, and who are cleansed from all their sins by the blood of Christ, these are righteous not merely in name or [κατ' ὄνομα], but in fact and [κατ' ἀλήθειαν], in truth. For the imputation of Christ's righteousness does not consist in an imaginary and empty fiction, or in mere appearance [δοκήσει], but in the very same truth by which our sins were laid upon Christ. He would never have been made a curse [κατάρα], or execration, for them, nor would he have taken them away, unless they had really been imputed to him. For no one is accursed by God except on account of sin, that is, insofar as he is, or is reckoned to be, a sinner. And although the righteousness by which we are justified before the tribunal of God is inherent in Christ himself as its subject, it is not wholly outside us, since Christ dwells in us as our head, through the communion of the Spirit, and his righteousness becomes ours through faith. What is held by faith is truly held, because faith rests on the certain and infallible promises of the divine Word. Second, it is also false that they are called righteous because they obtain eternal life. Attaining eternal life is not the cause of justification; rather, justification is its efficient cause. We obtain the kingdom of heaven because God, out of pure mercy, justifies us for the sake of Christ's righteousness and judges us worthy of the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, as the whole Gospel teaching clearly shows. Third, it is false that those whom Paul calls righteous in that place are reckoned to be perfect and righteous just as Christ himself is. For it would necessarily follow that they were no less redeemers and saviours of the world than Christ himself, which is false and impious. Believers are therefore called righteous in that place because the righteousness of Christ is imputed to each one, as if each had performed it for himself and not for others. Fourth, it is false that they are regarded and treated by God the Father in the same way that Christ himself is regarded and treated. For God, out of pure mercy, justifies, sanctifies, regenerates and glorifies us, who by nature are children of wrath, born and conceived in sins and liable to eternal damnation, on account of the blood of Christ, which expiates our sins. Christ, however, has eternity by nature and life [ἀϊδιότητα], and needs neither the benefit of sanctification nor that of renewal. Moreover, God, because of the obedience rendered by Christ, exalted him to the highest height and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth (Phil. 2:9-10). He has given him all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18). He has appointed him head of the body of the Church, the beginning, and the firstborn from the dead, so that he may have the first place in all things (Col. 1:18). To maintain that all these things happen to each of the elect and believers is contrary to the truth of divine Scripture, and that assumption must be condemned as a gross error and a notorious falsehood. The explanation of the comparison that Paul draws between Christ and Adam, which our opponent has added to his argument, is drawn from the impure cesspools of the Pelagians, and from our reply it is plainly evident that it is false.

units.la: Testimonia quæ Aduersarius, ex historia Iobi,ad probandam il-lam natiuæ corruptionis labem allegata,eiusdem capitis trigesimi tertii,sectione quinta refutat, suo valori & ponderi relinquo, ne-que sine discrimine quæuis axiomata, quæ ibi extant, aut cuius-uis ibi loquentis dicta, ad dogma aliquod stabiliendum, adduce-da esse iudico, cùm Deus ipse capite vltimo, versu septimo & o-ctauo inter ἀχρότατον Iobi, & reliquorum cum ipso disceptantium, discernat,& illum recte,hos vero non item,de se loquutos esse, pronun-tiet, atque alia per Dei gratiam, magno pondere & numero, αὐτῆς & ἀξιόπιστα nobis suppetant testimonia, quibus & huius de pec-cati originalis hæreditaria labe,& aliorum fidei nostræ capitum & articulorum veritatem solidè stabilire & asserere queamus, & ex ipsius quoque Iobi verbis,de naturæ nostræ corruptione haud ob-scurè constet.
units.tr: The testimonies that the opponent cites from the history of Job to prove that stain of original corruption, I leave to their own worth and weight. Their refutation is given in the fifth section of the thirty-third chapter. I judge that no axioms found there, nor the words of any speaker there, should be brought forward without discrimination to establish any doctrine, since God himself, in the last chapter, verses 7 and 8, distinguishes between Job and the others who disputed with him, and declares that the former spoke rightly about himself, but the latter did not. By God's grace we have other testimonies at hand, of great weight and number, and trustworthy, by which we can firmly establish and assert the truth of this doctrine of the hereditary stain of original sin and of the other articles and heads of our faith. From the very words of Job also, it is not obscurely established that our nature is corrupt.

units.la: Atque sic hactenus veritatem doctrinæ nostræ de miseranda il-la naturæ humanæ corruptione ac depravatione, ex Scripturis ip-sis demonstrauimus, & ab exceptionibus Aduersarii vindicaui-mus:restat igitur vt eiusdem quoque argumenta, quibus ille sen-tentiam suam,qua negat,naturam humanam per Adami delictum vi-tiatam atque depravatam esse,stabilire conatur,quanta sieri poterit breuitate,excutiamus.
units.tr: And so far we have demonstrated from the Scriptures themselves the truth of our doctrine of the wretched corruption and depravity of human nature, and have vindicated it against the opponent's objections. It remains, therefore, that we examine, as briefly as possible, the arguments by which he tries to establish his view, which denies that human nature was vitiated and depraved through Adam's offence.

units.la: Hanc itaque sententiam suam eodem capite trigesimo tertio, sectione quarta, tribus argumentis demonstrare nititur. Primum est, quia nulla causa adferri posset, quare humana natura per Adami transgressionem corrumpi ac vitiari debuerit.
units.tr: In the same thirty-third chapter, fourth section, he sets out to prove this view with three arguments. The first is this: because no cause could be given why human nature should have been corrupted and vitiated through Adam's transgression.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus:

units.la: Si nulla causa offendi potest, quare propter actiuam illam Adami transgressionem, tota natura humana corrumpi ac vitiari debuerit, tum sequitur illam propter Adami delictum minime corruptam ac vitiatam esse:
units.tr: If no cause can be offered why the whole of human nature ought to have been corrupted and vitiated because of that active transgression of Adam, then it follows that it was not corrupted and vitiated at all because of Adam's offence.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter also.

units.la: Resp. Vtramque propositionem esse falsam. Consequentia enim falsa est, quia non in diuinis tantum & hyperphysicis, verum etiam in physicis hisce & inferioribus rebus, de multarum rerum veritate, aliorum argumentorum & mediorum adminiculo, non autem per solas causas nobis constat, quarum tamen causas ignoramus, qua de re in antecedentibus primis capitibus egimus. Illum igitur malorum actualium omnium fontem, originalem nempe nequitiam, quae & foetidis suis fructibus nimium sese prodit, & in Scripturis ipsis tam graphice nobis depingitur, qua fronte negandam putat Aducrsarius, etiamsi causa eius ostendi non posset? Verum & assumptio falsa est: nam quare propter actiua illam primorum parentum transgressionem totum genus humanum primaeuae iustitiae ornamentis ac dotibus spoliatum, & virtutum illarum priuationem omnium vitiorum turma insequuta fit, causa assignari potest certissima, nempe iustissima Dei voluntas, & comminationis, qua lex illa sancita est, veritas. Hac enim lege & conditione Deus amplissimas illas iustitiae & sanctimoniae originalis dotes in Adamum contulit, vt eas sibi, suisque vniuersis aut perseuerando conseruaret, aut patrando peccatum perderet.
units.tr: Answer: Both premises are false. The consequence is false, because the truth of many things, not only in divine and supernatural matters but also in these physical and lower things, is known to us not solely through causes, whose causes we do not know, but with the help of other arguments and means. On this point we have spoken in the earlier chapters. Shall the opponent, then, deny with such a bold face the original wickedness, the source of all actual evils, which reveals itself all too clearly in its foul fruits and is so vividly depicted for us in the Scriptures themselves, even though its cause cannot be shown? Moreover, the assumption is also false. For the reason why, through that active transgression of our first parents, the whole human race was stripped of the ornaments and gifts of original righteousness, and the deprivation of those virtues was followed by a whole troop of vices, can be assigned with certainty: namely, the most just will of God and the truth of the threat by which that law was sanctioned. For by this law and condition God bestowed those most ample gifts of original righteousness and holiness upon Adam, so that he and all his descendants might keep them by persevering, or lose them by committing sin.

units.la: Argumentum Aduersarii secundum est, quia fieri non potuerit, vt per eandem illam primorum parentum actiuam transgressionem tota natura humana corrumperetur, cum vnus actus non faciat habitum.
units.tr: The Opponent's second argument is that it could not happen that the whole human nature was corrupted through that one active transgression of our first parents, since a single act does not produce a habit.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows:

units.la: Si fieri non potuit vt propter vnicam illam primorum parentum actiuam transgressionem, tota natura humana corrumperetur, sequitur illam etiam propterea corruptam non esse:
units.tr: If it was not possible that, because of that single active transgression of our first parents, the whole human nature was corrupted, it follows that it was not corrupted on that account.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Assumptionis probatio hæc est:
units.tr: The proof of the minor premise is this:

units.la: Si unus actus non facit habitum, tum fieri non potuit, ut propter unicam illam primorum parentum transgressionem actiuam tota natura humana corrumperetur.
units.tr: If a single act does not produce a habit, then it was not possible that, because of that single active transgression of our first parents, the whole human nature was corrupted.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem esse falsam, ad probationis connexum respondeo, consequentiam negando: Etiamsi enim unus actus per se, & immediate habitum gignere non possit, inferre tamen potest priuationem, quam postea habitus contrarius vel per se, vel extrinsecæ causæ interuentu insequitur. Quum itaque nos naturæ humanæ corruptionem, non solo vitiositatis, & ad malum inclinationis, habitu, sed antecedente iustitiæ & rectitudinis originalis priuatione, quæ actiuam transgressionem vt iusta tanti flagitii vindicta, iusto Dei iudicio sequuta est, definiamus, ideo consequens istud ex illo antecedente confici non potest. Deinde unus actus non facit habitum, videlicet effectu, aut productione, sed potest facere habitum merito, quemadmodum Adamus transgressione legis diuinæ, meruit donorum illorum, quibus enituit priuationem, quam habitus vitiosus postea sequutus est. Tertio antecedens verum est de actione quæ fit à causa secundum consuetum naturæ ordinem, non autem de iis, quæ peculiari iudicio diuino disponuntur, aut puniuntur.
units.tr: Answer: I hold the minor premise to be false, and I deny the consequence of the proof. For although a single act cannot of itself and immediately beget a habit, it can bring about a privation, which a contrary habit afterwards follows, either of itself or through the intervention of an external cause. Since we define the corruption of human nature not only as the habit of vice and the inclination to evil, but as the prior privation of original justice and righteousness, which followed the active transgression as the just punishment of so great a crime, by the just judgment of God, this consequence cannot be drawn from that antecedent. Further, a single act does not produce a habit by its effect or production, but it can produce a habit by merit, just as Adam, by transgressing the divine law, merited the privation of those gifts in which he had shone, a privation which the vicious habit afterwards followed. Third, the antecedent is true of an action which is performed by a cause according to the customary order of nature, but not of those things which are ordained or punished by a special judgment of God.

units.la: Tertium & vltimum Aduersarii argumentum est, quod inter cateras pœnas, quas Deus primis parentibus, propter peccatum & inobedientiam irrogare decreuerat, huius pœnæ plane nulla mentio fiat, vt quiuis locum illum Gen. 3. inspiciens facile animaduertere possit.
units.tr: The Opponent's third and last argument is that among the other punishments which God had decided to inflict on our first parents for their sin and disobedience, there is plainly no mention of this punishment, as anyone who looks carefully at that passage of Genesis 3 can easily notice.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows:

units.la: Si inter illas pœnas, quas Deus primis parentibus propter peccatum & inobedietiam ipsorum irrogare decreuerat, huius corruptionis plane nulla fit mentio, tum sequitur naturam humanam per & propter idem peccatum minime corruptam esse.
units.tr: If among those punishments which God had decided to inflict on our first parents for their sin and disobedience there is plainly no mention of this corruption, then it follows that human nature was not corrupted through and on account of the same sin.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true; therefore the latter also.

units.la: Resp. Antecedens esse falsum: In illa enim comminatione, per mortem intelligi, quicquid mortis nomine in Scripturis sacris appellatur, supra luculeter & solide à nobis est demonstratum. Quia vero non corporalis tantum, sed etiam spiritualis mors, hoc est, non modo discessus animæ à corpore, verum etiam totius hominis à gratiosa Dei, qui animæ nostræ vita, & cuius Spiritus animæ nostræ stræ anima est, vita & communione separatio, mortis nomine indi-gitatur: ideo necessario sequitur illam naturę humanę corruptio-nem, hoc est, priuationem imaginis diuinæ, & auersionem à Deo, cum reatu iræ & maledictionis diuinæ, sub illa mortis commina-tione comprehēdi, quippe quæ separationem illam, à vita & com-munione Dei gratiosa, & priuationem eius Spiritus sub se com-plectitur. Hinc enim est, quod omnes mortui in peccatis, & filij iræ nasci dicimur ab Apostolo Ephef.2.v.1.Et sic auersi à Deo mortui vocantur.Matth.8.v.22.Sine vt mortui sepeliant suos mortuos.1.Tim. 5.v.6.Vidua quæ in luxu viuit, viuens mortua est.Atque ex hisce omnibus (vt tandem redeat vnde digressa est, disputatio nostra) eui-denter apparet veritas solida tum responsionis nostrę ad illud Ad-uersarii argumentum, ab initio huius capitis propositum, quo ex primæua parentum primorum integritate, & creationis splendo-re, libertatem arbitrii humani etiam in statu dominantis peccati, contra scripturæ sacræ veritatem astruere voluit: tum etiam sen-tentiæ & complexionis illius, qua asserimus & concludimus, ho-minis non regeniti mentem & intellectum tantis ignorantiæ & cæcitatis tenebris obrutum esse, vt res spirituales, quę videlicet ve-ram pietatem, purúmque Dei cultum concernunt, priusquam lu-ce supernaturalis gratiæ cœlitus illuminetur, etiam cum docen-tur percipere non possit, voluntatem verò eiusdem à bono tam auersam, & tanta nequitia imbutam esse, vt nisi à spiritu sancto re-nouetur & flectatur, bonum spirituale, ac Deo placens, nec velle nec eligere queat, malum autem tantùm appetat atque velit, sic vt in ipsius voluntate, nec semen vllum virtutis, nec vlla ad virtu-tem inclinatio, post vniuersalem illam generis humani apostasiam, remanserit. Ad sequentia igitur progredior.
units.tr: Answer: The antecedent is false. For in that threat, that by death is meant whatever is called death in the holy Scriptures, has been clearly and solidly demonstrated by us above. And since death is named not only bodily death, that is, the departure of the soul from the body, but also spiritual death, that is, the separation of the whole man from the gracious God, who is the life of our soul and whose Spirit is the soul of our soul, from life and communion with him, it necessarily follows that the corruption of human nature, that is, the privation of the divine image and the aversion from God, together with the guilt of divine wrath and curse, is comprehended under that threat of death, since it embraces under itself that separation from the gracious life and communion of God and the deprivation of his Spirit. Hence it is that the Apostle says we are all dead in sins, and children of wrath by nature (Ephes. 2. v. 1), and so those turned away from God are called dead: Suffer the dead to bury their dead (Matth. 8. v. 22); She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives (1 Tim. 5. v. 6). And from all these things (so that our discussion may at last return to where it had digressed) there clearly appears the solid truth both of our answer to that argument of the Opponent, proposed at the beginning of this chapter, by which, from the original integrity of our first parents and the splendour of their creation, he wished to assert the freedom of the human will even in the state of dominant sin, against the truth of holy Scripture; and also of that statement and conclusion of ours, by which we assert and conclude that the mind and understanding of unregenerate man is so overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance and blindness that it cannot perceive spiritual things, which concern true piety and pure worship of God, even when they are taught, until it is illumined from heaven by the light of supernatural grace; and that his will is so averted from good and so steeped in such wickedness that, unless it is renewed and bent by the Holy Spirit, it can neither will nor choose spiritual good that pleases God, but desires and wills only evil, so that in his will there remains, after that universal apostasy of the human race, no seed of virtue and no inclination to virtue. I therefore proceed to what follows.

units.la: CAPVT XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: In quo de Liberi Arbitrii viribus agitur, & tum sententia orthodoxa explicatur ac demonstratur, tum falsa Aduersarij doctrina, & argumenta, quibus illam stabilire conantur,refutantur.
units.tr: In which the powers of free choice are discussed. The orthodox opinion is both explained and demonstrated, and the false doctrine of our opponent, together with the arguments by which he tries to establish it, is refuted.

units.la: HACTENVS primam partem huius disputationis, quæ fuit de ipso Libero hominis Arbitrio, absolui- mus: sequitur nunc pars altera, quæ est de liberi Arbitrii viribus. Vt vero hanc quoque eò dilucidius & breuius persequi possimus,primò omnium doctrinæ Oftorrodianæ de proposita hac materia, analysin præmittemus: deinde proposito controuersiæ statu, veritatem doctrinæ nostræ confirmabimus,& errores Aduersarii diluemus.
units.tr: Up to now we have finished the first part of this disputation, which concerned free choice itself. Now follows the second part, which concerns the powers of free choice. So that we may pursue this part too more clearly and briefly, we shall first set out an analysis of Ostorrodius' doctrine on the matter in hand. Then, having stated the point of the controversy, we shall confirm the truth of our doctrine and refute the errors of our opponent.

units.la: Oftorrodius itaque Institutionum suarum capite trigesimoquarto,quæstionem illam, quaenam sint liberi Arbitrij vires ? ita tractat vt primò suam ea de re sententiam exponat,certis positis hypothesibus,quarum vltimam duabus rationibus probare conatur, sectione prima: deinde quia homini ad hoc, vt debitam legi diuinæ præstare possit obedientiam, aliquod auxilium diuinum, necessarium esse agnoscit,quid & quotuplex illud auxilium diuinum fit, & in genere, quænam adminicula homini sint necessaria, quibus adiutus,legi diuinæ satisfacere possit,explicat sectione secunda & tertia. Denique subiecta complexione duplici,generali videlicet & speciali,totam disputationem concludit,sectione tertia.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in chapter thirty-four of his Institutes, treats the question "what are the powers of free choice?" as follows.
