First, he sets out his own opinion, with certain hypotheses laid down, the last of which he tries to prove by two arguments (section one). Then, since he acknowledges that man needs some divine aid in order to render the obedience owed to the divine law, he explains what this divine aid is, how many kinds there are, and in general what helps man requires in order to satisfy the divine law when aided by them (sections two and three). Finally, he concludes the whole disputation with a double summary, general and special (section three).

units.la: Primum,nempe sententiam Aduersarii quantum concernit,dicit ille primò, quamuis neget naturam humanam per primorum parentum peccatum corruptam esse, libenter se tamen concedere, propemodum in omnibus hominibus vehemens desiderium, & magnam inclinationem & propensionem ad peccandum inesse, non quidem propter illud peccatum,sed quia homines semetipsos, per propria peccata & malitiam corruperint & depravauerint, illámque malitiam vi feminis in posteros suos transfuderint. Secundò, Eam ob causam se sentire,omnes ferè homines mines, à natura exiguas vires habere, ad Dei præcepta seruandum, voluntatem autem illa seruādi, vnumquemque ex propria sua natura habere posse, imò si quis eam non habeat, hoc ex consuetudine peccandi profecti, quæ in homine efficiat, vt non tātum peccet, verùm etiam iniquitate delectetur, ac proinde nullo obedientiæ præceptis diuinis præstandæ studio aut desiderio ducatur. Vires autem hominis, quamuis ad seruandam Dei legem sint exiguæ & imbecilles, tamen non vsque adeò infirmas aut exiguas esse, quin homo diuino auxilio adiutus, veram obedientiam præceptis diuinis præstare possit. Tertiò, Deum nulli illorum, quibus legem suam præstandam innuxit, auxilium suum ad illam obedientiam præstandam necessarium denegare, quod duabus rationibus probare conatur, de quibus suo loco & ordine agemus.
units.tr: First, as far as concerns the opponent's view, he says: "Although he denies that human nature has been corrupted through the sin of our first parents, he is willing to grant that in almost all men there is a vehement desire, a great inclination and propensity to sin. This is not indeed on account of that sin, but because men have corrupted and depraved themselves through their own sins and malice, and have transmitted that malice to their posterity by way of seed." Secondly, "For that reason I perceive that almost all men have from nature only small powers for keeping God's precepts, but that each one can have the will to keep them from his own nature. Indeed, if anyone does not have this will, it arises from the habit of sinning, which makes a man not only sin but also take delight in iniquity, and so he is not driven by any zeal or desire to perform the divine commands. The powers of man, although small and feeble for keeping God's law, are nevertheless not so weak or small that a man, aided by divine help, cannot render true obedience to the divine precepts." Thirdly, that God denies to none of those to whom he has enjoined his law the aid necessary for rendering that obedience. He tries to prove this by two arguments, which we shall deal with in their own place and order.

units.la: Caput verò secundum quod attinet, nempe quænam adminicula homini sint necessaria, vt debitam legi diuinæ obedientiam præstare queat, ea tum ex parte Dei, tum ex parte nominis considerare videtur Aduersarius. Ex parte enim Dei auxiliū recenset duplex, vnum externum, alterum internum. Externum auxilium consistere dicit vel in adiunctis legi promissionibus boni alicuius, cuius adipiscendi desiderio & spe, homo ad omnem legis difficultatem superandā incitetur, & promoueatur: vel in comminationibus mali alicuius, cuius formidine à transgressione legis diuinæ deterreatur: facilius autem, seu vehementius hominem per promissiones, quàm comminationes ad aliquid præstandum impelli, ac proinde cum in Nouo Test. multò præstantiores extent promissiones, quàm in V. Testamento, idcoo obedientiam facilius præstari legi diuinæ sub Nouo, quàm sub Veteri Test. Internum verò auxilium duplex quoque esse affirmat, primū cùm Deus, id quod obedientiam ipsi præstantibus promisit, aliquatenus etiam cordibus illorum inscribit: secundū verò, cùm Deus mentem hominis illuminat, vt voluntatem eius rectè intelligat, quæ in externo verbo, propter varias causas, quæ in hominis vita incidunt, expressè comprehendi non possit. De hoc autē posteriori auxilio intelligēda esse illa loca, in quib. Dauid petit, vt Deus ipsum voluntatem suam doceat, vt Ps. 143. v. 8. 10. & Psal. 119. de priori autem intelligenda esse illa loca, in quibus mentio fit Spiritus S. quem Deus tanquam pignus aliquod, & arrhabonem futuri & alicuius magni boni nobis largitur, vt 2. Cor. 1. v. 22. & cap. 5. v. 5. Eph. 1. v. 13. 14. Atque ex hoc duplici auxilio interno, prius propriè ad Nouum, posterius verò ad Vetus Testamentum pertinere, quoniam sicut in Nouo Testam. vera bona promissa sint, ita etiā in Veteri, voluntas Dei, de bonis operib. non tam clarè vt in Nouo sit manifestata. Ex hisce vero omnibus manifestum esse, inquit, quod auxilium illud externum verum sit auxilium, quoniam interius nihil aliud sit, quàm μπμόσωσις, & obsignatio exterioris, praecipuè vero, quia interius illud nemini obtingat, (agit autem hic de vocatione Dei ordinaria, non extraordinaria) nisi qui exterioris tam participes factus fuerit. Neminem enim, in corde suo, de promissionibus illis, per Spiritum sanctum certiorem fieri, nisi audito externo Dei verbo, promissionibus divinis fidem habuerit, quandoquidem Spiritus sanctus credentibus & obedientibus detur, Act. 5.3.2. Eph. 1.13. Atque haec de auxilio divino. Adminiculum ex parte hominis quantum concernit, dicit Aduersarius, neminem Dei verbum, ac voluntatem perfectè intelligere posse, nisi totis viribus Dei voluntatem reuelatam facere adnitatur, quoniam, vt Salomon inquit, Timor Domini est initium sapientiae. Prou. 1.v.7.
units.tr: As to the second point, namely what helps are necessary for man to be able to render due obedience to the divine law, the opponent seems to consider these both on God's part and on man's part. On God's part he lists a twofold aid, one external and the other internal. He says the external aid consists either in the promises of some good attached to the law, by the desire and hope of obtaining which a man is roused and advanced to overcome every difficulty of the law, or in the threats of some evil, by the fear of which he is deterred from transgressing the divine law. But a man is more easily, or more vehemently, impelled to do something by promises than by threats. Therefore, since the promises of the New Testament are far more excellent than those of the Old, obedience to the divine law is more easily rendered under the New Testament than under the Old. The internal aid, he likewise affirms, is also twofold: first, when God also writes on the hearts of those who render him obedience, to some extent, what he has promised; second, when God illumines the mind of man so that he rightly understands his will, which cannot be expressly comprehended in the external word on account of various causes that arise in human life. Those passages in which David asks that God teach him his will, such as Ps. 143:8, 10 and Ps. 119, are to be understood of this latter aid. Those passages in which mention is made of the Holy Spirit, whom God bestows on us as a pledge and earnest of something future and great, such as 2 Cor. 1:22; 5:5; Eph. 1:13-14, are to be understood of the former. And of this twofold internal aid, the former pertains properly to the New Testament, the latter to the Old, since just as true good things were promised in the New Testament, so also in the Old, but the will of God concerning good works was not so clearly manifested as it is in the New. "From all these things," he says, "it is manifest that this external aid is a true aid, since the internal aid is nothing other than a reminder [ὑπόμνησις] and a confirmation of the external. Especially, it is manifest because that internal aid comes to no one (here he is speaking of God's ordinary calling, not his extraordinary one) unless he has been made a partaker of the external. For no one is assured in his heart of those promises through the Holy Spirit, unless, having heard the external word of God, he has believed the divine promises, since the Holy Spirit is given to those who believe and obey." Acts 5:32; Eph. 1:13. So much concerning divine aid. As far as the aid on man's part is concerned, the opponent says that no one can perfectly understand God's word and will unless he strives with all his powers to do the revealed will of God, since, as Solomon says, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Prov. 1:7.

units.la: Ex his omnibus liquet, statum controuersiæ (conclusionem enim suo reseruabimus loco) in tribus hisce quaestionibus positum esse, primò, An in homine, quandiu est in statu dominantis peccati, sint reliquae vllae vires (quanta enim sit non plurimorum tantum, sed omnium hominum, quotquot carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendunt, natiua prauitas, cupiditatum & desideriorum prauorum peruersitas, & vndenam illa corruptio ac depravatio suam ducat originem, capite antecedente prolixè à nobis est ostensum, & ea quę de Veteris ac Noui Testamenti discrimine ab Aduersario adferuntur, capite vigesimo quarto à nobis sunt refutata) aut vlla voluntatis inclinatio & desiderium, quoad opera pietatis, & debitam legi diuinae obedientiam praestandam, aspiret, aut aspirare possit, sic vt vires illae tantum excitandae sint & confirmandae, non autem restaurandae ac renouandae? An vero liberi Arbitrij vires in homine per peccatum ita sint extinctae, atque deletae, vt in ipso nec semen vllum virtutis, nec vlla in voluntate ad virtutem, aut operam pietatis inclinatio sit reliqua, ita vt non excitandae tantum & confirmandae sint vires, sed nouae δυνάμεις & potentia, quae debitam legi diuinae praestet obedientiam, creanda ac restauranda? Nos prius negamus, posterius affirmamus: Aduersarius contrà prius affirmat, posterius negat. Secundò, An homo in statu peccati dominantis constitutus, solo Dei auxilio externo in promissionibus & comminationibus sito opus habeat, vt debitam praeceptis diuinis obedientiam, & opera pietatis praestare queat? An vero praeter externam verbi diuini praedicationem, interna Dei gratia, hominem rerem renouans, ac regenerans, carnem mortificans, & Spiritum vivifi-cans, nouasque vires in nobis creans, sine qua externum illud auxi-lium efficax non sit ad salutem, requiratur? Nos prius negamus, poste-rius affirmamus: Aduersarius contra prius affirmat, posterius ne-gat. Tertiò: An Deus omnibus & singulis, quibus legem suam præstan-dam iniunxit, auxilium necessarium, ac sufficiens ad præcepta Dei ser-uandum, largiatur? Nos negamus, Aduersarius affirmat. Hasce tres quæstiones, quanta fieri poterit breuitate persequuturi, verita-tem sententiæ nostræ ex Scripturis sacris demonstrabimus, & sal-sitatem contrariam ex iisdem confutabimus. Quia verò duæ priores coincidunt, sic vt vna thesi demonstrata, vel refutata, al-tera quoque demonstretur, vel refutetur: ideò illas etiam co-niunctim tractabimus.
units.tr: From all this it is clear that the state of the controversy (for we shall reserve the conclusion for its proper place) rests on three questions. The first: whether in man, as long as he is in the state of dominant sin, any remaining powers exist. (How great the innate depravity is, not only of most men but of all men as many as descend from Adam by carnal propagation, and the perversity of depraved lusts and desires, and whence that corruption and depravity takes its origin, we have shown at length in the preceding chapter. And what the opponent brings forward about the difference between the Old and New Testaments we refuted in the twenty-fourth chapter.) Does any inclination and desire of the will, as regards works of piety and the rendering of due obedience to the divine law, aspire, or can it aspire, so that those powers need only be aroused and strengthened, not restored and renewed? Or rather, are the powers of free choice in man so extinguished and destroyed by sin that in him there remains neither any seed of virtue nor any inclination of the will to virtue or to works of piety, so that not only must the powers be aroused and strengthened, but new powers and capacities, which render due obedience to the divine law, must be created and restored? We deny the former and affirm the latter; the opponent, on the contrary, affirms the former and denies the latter. The second: whether man, placed in the state of dominant sin, needs only the external aid of God, consisting in promises and threats, in order to be able to render due obedience to the divine precepts and works of piety. Or rather, besides the external preaching of the divine word, is the internal grace of God required, renewing and regenerating man, mortifying the flesh, quickening the spirit, and creating new powers in us, without which that external aid is not effective for salvation? We deny the former and affirm the latter; the opponent, on the contrary, affirms the former and denies the latter. The third: whether God bestows on all and each of those to whom he has enjoined his law the aid necessary and sufficient for keeping God's precepts. We deny; the opponent affirms. Since we are going to pursue these three questions with as much brevity as possible, we shall demonstrate the truth of our view from the holy Scriptures, and refute the contrary falsehood from the same. But since the first two coincide, so that when one thesis is demonstrated or refuted the other is demonstrated or refuted too, we shall therefore treat them also together.

units.la: Argumentum primum,quo demonstramus, non exiguas tantùm, aut imbecilles, sed nullas plane in homine, post lapsum, ante regenerationis gratiam, vires esse reliquas, nec vllam inclinationem aut desiderium, cuius instinctu ad opera pietatis aspirare possit, ac proinde auxilium Dei, & gratiam regenerationis, non tantùm ex-terna verbi prædicatione, eiusque confirmatione, sed arcana etiam Spiritus Sancti virtute & efficacia definiendum esse, desumitur ex illis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis in quibus homo, priusquam per spiritum sanctum renouetur ac regeneretur, mortuus in peccatis, & alienatus à Deo, ac vita Dei gratiosa, & Republica Israelitica, hostis item, & inimicus Dei appellatur, Ephes. 2. versu 1. Et vos quum essetis mortui in offensis, & peccatis, & versu 3. inter quos & nos omnes conuersati sumus olim in cupiditatibus carnis nostræ, facien-tes quæ carni & cogitationibus libebant, eramusque natura filii ira, vt etiam reliqui: & versu quinto, etiam quum per offensas mortui esse-mus, vna viuificauit nos per Christum. Ioan. 5. vers. 25. Amen amen di-co vobis, veniet tempus, & nunc est, quum mortui audient vocem filii Dei, & qui audient viuent. Ephes. 4. vers. 17. 18. Ne amplius versemi-ni, sicut reliquæ Gentes versantur, in vanitate mentis vestræ, cogitatio-nem habentes obscuratam, & abalienatam à vita Dei, propter igno-rantiam, quæ est in ipsis, ex obduratione cordis ipsorum. & 2. vers. 12. Vos illo tempore fuisse absque Christo, alienos à Republica Israelitica, & extraneos à pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, & Dei expertes in mundo. Coloss. 1. vers. 21. Itaque vos quondam abalienatos, & hostes mente operibus malis intenta, nunc sane reconciliauit: & vers. 13. Vósque mortuos in peccatis & præputio carnis vestra,cum eo viuificauit condonatis vobis omnibus peccatis.
units.tr: The first argument, by which we show that after the Fall and before the grace of regeneration, man has not merely small or feeble powers but none at all, and no inclination or desire by whose impulse he could strive toward works of piety. From this it follows that God's help and the grace of regeneration must be defined as not only the external preaching of the Word and its confirmation, but also the hidden power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit. This is drawn from those testimonies of Holy Scripture in which man, before he is renewed and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, is called dead in sins, alienated from God and from the life of God's grace and from the commonwealth of Israel, and likewise an enemy and foe of God. Ephesians 2:1: And you, who were dead in trespasses and sins, and verse 3: Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others; and verse 5: even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ. John 5:25: Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. Ephesians 4:17, 18: That ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. and 2:12: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. Colossians 1:21: And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled; and verse 13: And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses.

units.la: Hinc ita argumentamur.
units.tr: From this we argue as follows.

units.la: Quicunque in peccatis plané sunt mortui,abalienati à Deo, & vita Dei,imò hostes,inimici, & expertes Dei, in illis penitus nullæ sunt vires ad opera pietatis præstanda, nulláque ad resipiscentiam aut obedientiam mandatis diuinis præstandam inclinatio aut propensio, ac proinde non externo tantùm auxilio, sed interna potissimum Spiritus sancti gratia & virtute ipsis opus est, ad hoc, vt debitam legi diuinæ obedientiam præstare queant:
units.tr: Whoever are wholly dead in sins, alienated from God and from the life of God, indeed enemies, foes and strangers to God, have absolutely no powers at all for performing works of piety, and no inclination or propensity to render repentance or obedience to the divine commands. Therefore they need not only external help but chiefly the inward grace and power of the Holy Spirit, so that they may render the obedience due to the divine law.

units.la: Atqui nos omnes, quotquot carnali propagatione ab Adamo descendimus,à natura tales esse,ex testimoniis allegatis constat:Ergo,&c.
units.tr: But all of us who descend from Adam by carnal propagation are by nature such, as is evident from the testimonies cited. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Consequentiæ necessaria veritas ex eo patet, quod sicut per mortem naturalem vita priuati, nulla ad sanitatem, vitámque recuperandam,aut actiones hominis viuentis edendas, inclinatione ducuntur:ita mortuus morte spirituali,& alienatus à vita Dei,ad Deũ amádum,& opera pietatis præstanda nulla ratione inclinare aut propendere & aspirare potest. Nam si aliquæ in homine quátumuis imbecilles &exiguæ vires reliquæ essēt,&in volutate vlla quantumuis languida & torpescens inclinatio,ad virtutem illum instigaret, tum quidem languidi, infirmi, & ægroti, non autem mortui in peccatis dici possemus. Cùm denique hostes & inimici Dei, & filii iræ simus natura, quomodo quæso vllo præceptorum eius seruandorũ,& obedientiæ ipsi præstandæ studio duceremur?
units.tr: The necessary truth of the consequence is plain from this: just as a person deprived of life by natural death is moved by no inclination to recover health and life or to perform the actions of a living man, so one who is dead in the spiritual death and alienated from the life of God can in no way incline, tend or aspire to love God and perform works of piety. For if any powers in man, however feeble and small, remained, and if any inclination in the will, however faint and sluggish, incited him to virtue, then we could indeed be called weak, infirm and sick, but not dead in sins. Finally, since by nature we are enemies and foes of God and children of wrath, by what means, I ask, would we be led to keep his precepts and to eagerness for rendering obedience to him?

units.la: Argumentum secundum desumitur ex illis Scripturæ testimoniis in quibus nos filii,& serui Diaboli,ac peccati, & ea tantùm quæ carnis sunt, sapere perhibemur,omnéque figmentum cogitationum nostrarum ad malum tantum esse dicitur, idque omni tempore, Rom. 6.16. An nescitis quod cui sistitis vos ipsos seruos ad obedidum,eius serui estis,cui obeditis,vel peccati ad mortè,vel obedientiæ ad vitam?& v.19.20. Sicut stitistis membra vestra serua in puritati & iniquitati, ad patrandum iniquitatè: ita nunc sistite membra vestra serua iustitiæ ad sanctimoniam:quũ enim serui essetis peccati, liberi eratis iustitiæ.1.Ioh.3.8. Qui committit peccatum,ex Diabolo est: & v.10. Per hoc manifesti sunt filij Dei, & filij Diaboli, quisquis non exercet iustitiam,non est ex Deo,&qui non diligit fratrem suum.2.Tim.2.26.vt refipifcentes agnoscant veritatem, & elapsi ex Diaboli laqueis, à quo captiui tenentur,mentis sanitatem recipiant. Rom.8.v.5.6.7. Qui secundum carnem sunt,quæ carnis sunt sapiunt:nam intelligetia carnis mors est,& inimicitia aduersus Deum: legi enim Dei non subiicitur, nam ne potest quidem. Gen.6.v.5. Omne figmetum cogitationum cordis humani tantummodo ad malū est,idque omni tepore. Hinc ita argumetamur:
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from those testimonies of Scripture in which we are said to be the sons and servants of the Devil and of sin, and to savour only the things of the flesh, and in which every figment of our thoughts is said to be only evil, and that at all times. Romans 6:16: Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? and verses 19, 20: As ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness, and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness. For when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness. 1 John 3:8: He that committeth sin is of the devil; and verse 10: In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother. 2 Timothy 2:26: that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will; and that they may come to repentance and acknowledge the truth, and that, escaping from the snares of the Devil by whom they are held captive, they may recover their soundness of mind. Romans 8:5–7: For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; for to be carnally minded is death, and the carnal mind is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. Genesis 6:5: Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. From this we argue thus:

units.la: Quicunque sunt serui peccati,& mancipia,ac filii Diaboli, & ea tantum, quæ carnis sunt sapiunt, & quorum omnis intelligentia inimicitia est aduersus Deum,omnéque figmentum cogitationum ad malum tantùm est, idque omni tempore,in illis nullæ sunt vires ad bona opera præstanda, nec vlla ad pietatem inclinatio,aut propensio, ac proinde non externo tantum Dei auxilio, sed interna,& arcana Spiritus sanẚti vi,& efficacia indigent,vt ad Deum conuersi debitam ipsi obedientiam præstent: Atqui tales à natura sumus omnes, vt ex testimoniis recitatis apparet:Ergo,&c.
units.tr: Whoever are servants of sin and slaves, and sons of the Devil, and savour only the things of the flesh, and whose whole understanding is enmity against God, and every figment of whose thoughts is only evil, and that at all times, have in them no powers for performing good works, nor any inclination or propensity toward piety. Therefore they need not only the external help of God but the inward and hidden power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, if they are to be turned to God and render him the obedience due. But all of us are such by nature, as appears from the testimonies recited. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Propositionis maioris veritas inde manifesta est, quod filii & serui Diaboli sunt,quos ille totos sibi vendicare potest, quibus peccatum dominatur,qui peccato addicti,& mãcipati sunt, ac toti sub potestate Satanæ constituti, ipsi toti militant, seruiunt,& tantummodo id,quod ipsi lubet,faciunt,quid autem ille vnquam nisi malum voluit?Quum denique illud ipsum, quod in homine non regenito est præstatissimum, nempe ipsum φρόνημα, inimicitia sit aduersus Deum, quæ reliqua esset in ipso inclinatio, aut propensio, cuius instinctu ad pietatem, & obedientiam incitaretur? Quod si denique vllæ in homine vires essent reliquæ, aut de operibus pietatis exercendis seria cogitatio mentem eius subiret vnquam, tum non posset omne figmentum cogitationum hominis, ad malum tantum esse, neque homo ipse ea tantum quæ carnis sunt sapere dici posset.
units.tr: The truth of the major premise is manifest from this: those who are sons and servants of the Devil are those whom he can claim wholly as his own, over whom sin rules, who are given over to sin and enslaved to it, and who, wholly under the power of Satan, fight wholly for him and serve him and do only what he pleases. But what has he ever wished except evil? Finally, since that very thing which is most excellent in the unregenerate man, namely the mind itself [φρόνημα], is enmity against God, what inclination or propensity would remain in him by whose impulse he might be stirred to piety and obedience? And if any powers remained in man, or if any serious thought about exercising works of piety ever entered his mind, then the whole figment of man's thoughts could not be only evil, nor could man be said to savour only the things of the flesh.

units.la: Argumentū III. desumitur ex illis scripturæ testimoniis, quæ natiuā mentis nostræ cæcitatē, h.e. ἀγνοίαν ἀδυναμίαν & ματαιότητα τῆς νοός, describunt:itè in quibus Deus per Spiritū S.mentē nobis illuminare dicitur,Eph.1.v.17.18. Deus Domini nostri I.Christi, Pater ille gloriæ,det vobis spiritum sapientiæ & reuelationis, per agnitionem ipsius, illuminatis oculis mentis vestræ, vt sciatis quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, & quæ opes gloriæ hæreditatis ipsius in sanctis, 1.Cor.2.vers.14. Animalis homo non est capax illorum,quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: sunt enim eistultitia,neque potest ea percipere,quia spiritualiter diiudicantur.2.Cor.3. v.5.non quod idonei simus ex nobis ipsis,ad cogitandum quicquam velut ex nobis ipsis,sed quod idonei sumus,id ex Deo est. Act.16.v.14. Quaedam autem mulier nomine Lydia,quae purpuram vendebat in vrbe Thyatirorum, Deum colens nos audiuit, cuius Dominus adaperuit cor, vt attenderet ea quae dicebantur à Paulo.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from those testimonies of Scripture which describe our natural blindness of mind, that is, ignorance [ἀγνοίαν], impotence [ἀδυναμίαν] and vanity [ματαιότητα] of the mind [τῆς νοός]; and in which God is said to enlighten our minds through the Holy Spirit. Ephesians 1:17, 18: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: the eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, 1 Corinthians 2:14: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 2 Corinthians 3:5: not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God. Acts 16:14: And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.

units.la: Hinc ita argumentamur.
units.tr: From this we argue as follows.

units.la: Qui ne quidem capax est eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei, neque potest res spirituales etiam cum docentur percipere,nec idoneus est ad cogitandum aliquid boni, nisi per Spiritum sanctum mens ipsius illuminetur, sed pro stultitia ipsam etiā excellentissimam Dei sapientiam ducit, ille multo minus vllis pollet viribus, quibus opera pietatis exercere queat, aut vllo pietatis & obedientiae desiderio ducitur,ac proinde non excitari tantùm, & confirmari vires in ipso oportet, sed nouam δωάμιν & potentiam ipsi conferri,vt resipiscat, & praeceptis diuinis obtemperet.
units.tr: Whoever is not even capable of the things of the Spirit of God, and cannot perceive spiritual things even when they are taught, and is not fit to think anything good unless his mind is enlightened by the Holy Spirit, but counts as foolishness even the most excellent wisdom of God, has far less strength by which he could perform works of piety, or by which he could be led by any desire for piety and obedience. Therefore in him not only must his powers be stirred up and strengthened, but a new power [δύναμιν] must be conferred on him, so that he may repent and obey the divine precepts.

units.la: Atqui nos omnes à natura tales esse,tum ex citatis testimoniis, tum ex capite primo huius defensionis nostrae, euidenter liquet:Ergo,&c.
units.tr: But that all of us are by nature such is clear, both from the testimonies cited and from the first chapter of this our defence. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Veritas consequentiae est manifesta:Quum enim non gratia regenerans, sed ipsa ratio per gratiam excitata, & confirmata istius ad pietatis opera inclinationis fundamentum ab illis naturae & liberi Arbitrii patronis statuatur, illa verò nisi radiis lucis coelestis, & spiritualis gratiae illustretur, in rebus spiritualibus, quae veram pietatem, purumque Dei cultum, & vitam aeternam concernunt, planè caecutiat, necessario omnis, quae illi superstruitur, & inniti confingitur ad pietatem inclinatio & propensio, corruit. Quum deinde Apostolus palam affirmet, non posse nos viribus nc ltris vel cogitare aliquid boni, vera autem Christi & rerum coelestium notitia nos imbuat, & ad veram obedientiam nos fleCtat sanCtus Dei spiritus, necessario inde sequitur, non excitari tantùm confirmarique torpescentes & languentes in nobis vires reliquas, sed nouam potentiam nouásque vires in nobis creari ac restaurari. Quum denique homo animalis nō sit capax illorum,quae sunt spiritus Dei,neque res spirituales etiam cum docentur(docentur autem additis promissionibus & comminationibus)percipere possit, manifestum est,homini, vt resipiscere & voluntati diuinae obedire possit, non tantùm externo illo, sed maximè interno Spiritus sancti auxilio opus esse. Et mirum est, Aducrsarium, internam illuminationem ad Vetus tantùm Testamentum ablegare, cùm tamen ex ipsius sententia, in illo tantùm terrenæ promissiones, ac intellectu faciles, in Nouo verò Testamento, res longè sublimiores tradatur. Sed eiusmodi contradictionum laqueis se inuoluant necesse est, quicunque in gratiam & φιλανθρωπίαν Dei ineffabilem naturæ studio & cæca admiratione ducti sunt iniuriosi.
units.tr: The truth of the consequence is evident. For since it is not regenerating grace but reason itself, roused and strengthened by grace, that these defenders of natural free will set up as the foundation of the inclination to works of piety, and since reason, unless it is illumined by the rays of heavenly light and spiritual grace, is plainly blind in spiritual matters, which concern true piety, pure worship of God and eternal life, it necessarily follows that the inclination and propensity to piety which is built upon reason and invented to rest on it collapses. Next, since the Apostle plainly affirms that we cannot of our own powers even think anything good, but that the true knowledge of Christ and of heavenly things imbues us, and the holy Spirit of God bends us to true obedience, it necessarily follows that the remaining powers in us, which are sluggish and languid, are not merely roused and strengthened, but that new power and new strength are created and restored in us. Finally, since the natural man is not capable of those things which are of the Spirit of God, and cannot perceive spiritual things even when they are taught (and they are taught with added promises and threats), it is clear that for man to repent and be able to obey the divine will he needs not only that external help but above all the internal help of the Holy Spirit. And it is remarkable that the Adversary sends the internal illumination away to the Old Testament only, since by his own view only earthly promises, easy to grasp, are handed down in that, while in the New Testament far more sublime things are delivered. But those who are led by a love of nature and a blind admiration into an unspeakable grace and philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] of God must necessarily entangle themselves in such snares of contradiction.

units.la: Argumentum quartum & vltimum desumitur ex iis Scripturæ testimoniis, in quibus Deus dicitur cor nostrum natura tardum, Luc. 24. verf. 25. vanum, Psal. 5. verf. 10. Ephes. 4. ver. 17. durum, Rom. 2. verf. 5. fraudulentum supra modum, Ierem. 17. v. 9. lapideum, Ezech. 36. ver. 26. emollire, aperire, conuertere, circumcidere, auferre, nos regenerare ac renouare, cor carneum dare, ad imaginem suâ creare, non perficere tantùm, sed etiam velle in nobis operari. 2. Paral. 34. v. 27. Quia mollitus est animus tuus, ita depressisti te à facie Dei, cùm audiuisses verba eius contra locum hunc, & contra habitatores eius, & deprimens te coram me, lacerasti vestimenta tua, & fleuisti coram me, ideo etiam ego exaudiui. Act. 27. v. 14. Deus adaperuit cor Lydiæ, vt attenderet ad ea, quæ dicebantur à Paulo. Luc. 1. v. 16. 17. Multos filiorum Israel conuertet ad Dominum Deum ipsorum: nam ipse præcedet in conspectu eius, cum Spiritu & virtute Eliæ, vt conuertat corda patrum in filios, & rebelles ad prudentiam iustorum, vt paret Domino populum instructum. Ierem. 31. verf. 18. Conuerte me, vt conuertar, quia tu es Iehoua Deus meus. Deuter. 30. verf. 6. Circumcidet Iehoua Deus tuus animum tuum, & animum feminis tui, ad diligendum Iehouam Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, vt viuas. Col. 2. verf. 11. In quo circumcisi estis, circumcisione quæ fit sine manibus. Ezec 36. v. 26. 27. Et dabo vobis cor nouum, & spiritum nouum ponam in medio vestri, & amouens cor lapideum è carne vestra indam vobis cor carneum, & spiritum meum ponam in medio vestri, quo faciam, vt in statutis meis ambuletis, & iura mea obseruetis facientes ea. Ioh. 3. verf. 5. Nisi quis regenitus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, non potest introire in Regnum Dei: & 6. verf. 44. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Tit. 3. verf. 5. Ex sua misericordia seruauit nos per lauacrum regenerationis, & renouationem Spiritus sancti. Phil. 2. verf. 13. Deus is est, qui efficit in vobis & vt velitis, & vt efficiatis, pro gratuita sua beneuolentia. Hinc ita argumentamur.
units.tr: The fourth and last argument is drawn from those testimonies of Scripture in which God is said to make our heart by nature slow, Luke 24. v. 25; vain, Ps. 5. v. 10; Eph. 4. v. 17; hard, Rom. 2. v. 5; deceitful beyond measure, Jer. 17. v. 9; stony, Ezek. 36. v. 26; and that he softens, opens, converts, circumcises, takes away, regenerates and renews us, gives a heart of flesh, creates us in his own image, and not only completes but also works in us the will itself. 2 Chron. 34. v. 27: Because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and against its inhabitants, and humbled yourself before me, and rent your garments and wept before me, therefore I also have heard you. Acts 16. v. 14: The Lord opened the heart of Lydia, so that she attended to the things that were said by Paul. Luke 1. v. 16, 17: He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God; for he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready a people prepared for the Lord. Jer. 31. v. 18: Turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are the LORD my God. Deut. 30. v. 6: The LORD your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. Col. 2. v. 11: In whom you were circumcised with a circumcision which is made without hands. Ezek. 36. v. 26, 27: And I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit in the midst of you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my spirit in the midst of you, so that you walk in my statutes and keep my judgments and do them. John 3. v. 5: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the Kingdom of God; and 6. v. 44: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. Titus 3. v. 5: According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Phil. 2. v. 13: It is God who works in you both to will and to do, for his good pleasure. From this we argue thus.

units.la: Si Deus cor nostrum natura tardum, vanum, durum, fraudu- lentum, & lapideum emollit, aperit, conuertit, circumcidit circumcisione,quæ fit sine manibus, aufert, & dat carneum, nos per Spiritum S.renouat ac regenerat,atque adChristum trahit, bonum denique in cordibus nostris non tantùm in- choat & perficit,sed etiam operatur ipsum velle, id est,bonâ voluntatem, tum certè sequitur in voluntate hominis, nul- lam esse propensionem aut inclinationem, qua ad repiscen- tiam aut virtutesChristianas aspiret,nec vires vllas reliquas, ad opera pietatis præstanda, ac ipsum proinde non externo tantùm auxilio & adiumento, sed potissimùm arcana Spiri- tus sanƈti vi & efficacia indigere.
units.tr: If God softens, opens, converts, circumcises (with a circumcision made without hands), takes away, and gives flesh instead of our heart, which by nature is slow, vain, hard, deceitful and stony, and renews and regenerates us through the Holy Spirit, and draws us to Christ, and finally not only begins and completes the good in our hearts but also works in us the very willing, that is, the good will, then it certainly follows that in the will of man there is no propensity or inclination by which it aspires to repentance or Christian virtues, and that no remaining powers are left for performing works of piety; and so man needs not only external help and assistance, but chiefly the hidden power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Atqui antecedentis veritas patet ex allegatis scripturæ testi- moniis:
units.tr: But the truth of the antecedent is plain from the testimonies of Scripture cited.

units.la: Ergo & consequens verum est.
units.tr: Therefore the consequent is also true.

units.la: Connexi veritas necessaria manifesta est ex eo, quòd scriptura sacra testatur cor nouum, hoc est, nouam quandam cordis natu- ram aut dispositionem nobis diuinitus dari, & cor nostrum natu- ra lapideum esse demonstrat, quod mutari oporteat, antequam ad recipiendam gratiam possit esse aptum. Quod autem dari nobis necesse est, id certè non habemus: cor nouum necesse est nobis da- ri, vt ambulemus in præceptis Dei: eam igitur aut vim aut volun- tatem à natura non habemus. Imò natura hęc omnis in contrariũ inclinat ac propendet, cum nullũ nobis nisi lapideum à natura cor insit. Quemadmodum enim in lapide nulla inclinatio est, qua molle- scat, sed noua lapidi natura opus est, si ex lapide carnem fieri velis: ita nos oportet, vt vocibus & legibus diuinis deleƈtemur, cœlesti gratia renouari, veterem cordis duritiem remoueri, nouam quan- dam mollitiem informari. Si deinde nolumus venire antequam nos Pater ad Filium trahere incipiat, quicquid est in nobis bonæ voluntatis, gratiæ tribuendum est. Quid enim opus esset aut no- uam voluntatem in nobis creari, si naturali instinƈtu, ad pietatis & sanƈtimoniæ studium propenderemus, aut nos à Patre ad Filium trahi, si naturali quadam inclinatione & sponte veniremus, nec a- liud nobis necessarium esset, nisi duntaxat vocari, aut admoneri, aut expergefieri? Verissimum enim est, quod dixit Augustinus có- tra duas Pelagii epistolas libr. 1. cap. 19. Non dixit, inquiens, nisi Pater duxerit eum,vt illic aliquo modo intelligamus praecedere voluntatem. Quis trahitur si iam volebat? & tamen nemo venit,nisi velit. Trahitur ergo miris modis,vt velit,ab illo,qui nouit intus in ipsis hominum cordibus operari,non vt homines, quod fieri non potest, nolentes credant, sed vt volentes ex nolentibus fiant. Ergo vis quædam arcana Spiritus adhibenda est, quæ nos volentes, ex inuitis & nolentibus faciat, quę nisi accesserit aliunde,nunquam ad Christum veniemus. Has autem actiones soli auxilio Dei externo minime competere posse, luce meridiana clarius elucescit. Si enim sola externa verbi praedicatione ad nos conuertendos Deus vteretur, quid (vt ex plurimis iam ante propositis argumentis vnum tantum repetam) opus erat, vt cor Lydiæ diuinitus aperiretur, quo attenderet ea quæ à Paulo dicebantur?
units.tr: The necessary truth of the connection is evident from this: Holy Scripture testifies that a new heart, that is, a certain new nature or disposition of the heart, is given to us by God, and it shows that our heart is by nature stony and must be changed before it can be apt to receive grace. That which must be given to us, we certainly do not have; a new heart must be given to us so that we may walk in the precepts of God. Therefore we do not have that power or that will by nature. Indeed, all of nature inclines and tends the opposite way, since by nature we have nothing in us but a stony heart. For just as in a stone there is no inclination by which it softens, but a new nature is needed if you wish to make flesh out of stone, so we must be delighted by the divine voices and laws, be renewed by heavenly grace, have the old hardness of heart removed, and have a certain new softness formed. Next, if we are unwilling to come until the Father begins to draw us to the Son, whatever good will is in us must be ascribed to grace. For why would there be any need for a new will to be created in us, if we inclined by natural instinct to the pursuit of piety and holiness, or if we were drawn by the Father to the Son, if we came by some natural inclination and spontaneously, and nothing else were necessary for us except to be called, or admonished, or awakened? For what Augustine said against the two letters of Pelagius, book 1, chapter 19, is most true: He did not say, he says, unless the Father has drawn him, so that we may understand in some way that the will goes before. Why is he drawn if he already wished? And yet no one comes unless he is willing. He is therefore drawn in wonderful ways, so that he may be willing, by him who knows how to work inwardly in the very hearts of men, not so that men who are unwilling may believe, which cannot happen, but so that those who are unwilling become willing. Therefore a certain hidden power of the Spirit must be applied, which makes us willing out of the unwilling and reluctant, and which unless it comes from elsewhere, we shall never come to Christ. That these actions cannot belong to the external help of God alone is clearer than the midday light. For if God used only the external preaching of the Word to convert us, why (to repeat just one of the many arguments already put forward) was it necessary for the heart of Lydia to be opened by God, so that she would attend to the things that were said by Paul?

units.la: Ex hisce vero omnibus euidenter apparet, verissimum esse id, quod nos contra Aduersarium affirmauimus, nempe in homine non regenito, quandiu versatur in statu animalis huius vitæ, & peccati dominantis, nec inclinationem, desiderium, aut propensionem, qua ad Christum, veramque respiscentiam, & vitæ sanctimoniam contendat & aspiret, nec vires vllas ad opera pietatis praestanda, reliquas esse: ac proinde verum, sufficiens & efficax Dei auxilium, quo ad Christum & veram respiscentiam conuertimur, non tantum in externa illa verbi praedicatione, verum etiam in interiori Spiritus Sancti virtute, vi, & efficacia, qua illuminatis oculis mentis nostræ, voluntati noua sanitas restituitur, nouæque vires in nobis gignuntur, consistere.
units.tr: From all of this it is clearly evident that what we affirmed against the Adversary is most true: in the unregenerate man, for as long as he remains in the state of this animal life and of dominant sin, there remains neither any inclination, desire or propensity by which he strives and aspires towards Christ and true repentance and holiness of life, nor any power at all for performing works of piety. It follows that the true, sufficient and efficacious help of God, by which we are turned to Christ and true repentance, consists not only in that external preaching of the Word but also in the inward power, force and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, by which, our eyes of mind being enlightened, a new health is restored to the will and new powers are begotten in us.

units.la: Distinguendum vero est inter regenerationis, & conuersionis primum initium, & eius progressum, atque incrementum secundum quod discrimen ipsi etiam gratiæ diuinæ effectus variant. Hinc enim est, quod arrhabo ille, & obsignatio Spiritus Sancti, de quo 2.Cor.1. verf.22. & c.3. verf.5.Ephes.1.v.13. agitur, ex causis salutis,& respiscentiâ operantibus minime quidè fit excludendus, inter auxilia tamen illa quibus respiscentia,& renouatio in nobis inchoatur, veráque & iustificans fides in nobis gignitur, recenseri minime potest, quia ille arrhabo Spiritus fidè in nobis non gignit, sed sequitur,confirmat & comitatur,vt tum ex Aduersarii confessione,tum ex locis scripturæ ab ipso citatis liquidò constat,& illorum vltimo, nempe Ephes.1. v.13. disertis verbis affirmatur. In quo enim,inquit Apostolus,postquam credidistis,obsignati estis Spiritu illo promissionis sanctò, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ. Quod Ostorrodius sectione tertia, de studio obedientiæ Deo præstandæ, quod ille adminiculum ex parte hominis statuere videtur, subiungit illis, si in se considerentur, libenter assentimur, neque illa veritatem doctrinæ nostræ impugnant. Agunt enim non de primo conuersionis initio, de quo hic quæritur, & quod nos diuinæ gratiæ in solidum adscribimus, sed de eius incremento & progressu, deque plena, solida, perfecta, & salutari Dei cognitione, quæ studium & affectum pié viuendi necessario includit, vt locus ab Aduersario ex Prou. 1. vers. 2. allegatus, docet, & Paulus testatur, qui omnes eos Deum ignorare affirmat, qui diuinæ voluntati, iam aliquatenus cognitæ non obtemperant. Tit. 3 vers. 16.
units.tr: We must distinguish between the first beginning of regeneration and conversion and its progress and increase, and the effects of divine grace also vary according to this difference. Hence that pledge and sealing of the Holy Spirit, of which 2 Cor. 1 verse 22 and chapter 3 verse 5, and Eph. 1 verse 13 speak, is by no means to be excluded from the causes working salvation and repentance. Yet it cannot be counted among those aids by which repentance and renewal are begun in us and true, justifying faith is begotten in us, because that pledge of the Spirit does not beget faith in us but follows, confirms and accompanies it. This is clear both from the Adversary's own confession and from the passages of Scripture he cites, and above all from the last of them, Eph. 1 verse 13, which affirms it in plain words: "In whom, says the Apostle, after you had believed, you were sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance." As for what Ostorrodius adds in his third section, on the zeal for obedience to be rendered to God, which he seems to set up as an aid on man's part, we readily assent to those things when they are considered in themselves, and they do not impugn the truth of our doctrine. For they do not treat of the first beginning of conversion, which is the question here, and which we ascribe wholly to divine grace, but of its increase and progress, and of the full, solid, perfect and saving knowledge of God, which necessarily includes zeal and affection for living piously, as the passage from Prov. 1 verse 2 cited by the Adversary shows, and as Paul bears witness, who declares that all those are ignorant of God who do not obey the divine will already known to them in some measure. Tit. 3 verse 16.

units.la: Atque hæc de duabus primis quæstionibus disseruisse sufficiat, ad tertiam & vltimam (nam Aduersarius ad defensionem sententiæ suæ nullum adfert argumentum) progrediendum nobis est, & dispiciendum, An Deus omnibus & singulis hominibus, quibus legem suam præstandam iniunxit, auxilium necessarium, ac sufficiens, ad seruandum præcepta ipsius, suppeditet, ac largiatur. Quæstio sublimis & ardua, multisque disputationum ventilationibus agitata, ac proinde accurata disquisitione dignissima: sed quia illa potius ad locum de prædestinatione, de qua capite sequente nobis agendum est, quàm ad hanc præsentem disputationem pertinet: ideò nos breuitati studentes, quid de hac re sentiendum sit, ex gratiæ sufficientis & necessariæ definitione, & vocationis euentu, iudicabimus. Auxilium itaque illud Dei, quod nihil aliud est, quàm vocatio diuina (loquor de illa qua ad Deum conuertimur) est actio Dei gratiosa, qua Deus ex mera sua misericordia & φιλανθρωπία electos ad vitam æternam, sed per peccatum à Deo & vita eius gratiosa alienatos, tempore à se constituto, ex statu miseriæ & peccati dominatis, ad benedictionum spiritualium communionem in Christo efficaciter euocat, hoc est, per externam verbi prædicationem, & internam Spiritus sancti operationem, illos in peccatis mortuos viuificat, mentem natiuæ cæcitatis tenebris obrutam luce spiritualis sapientiæ & cognitionis illuminat, cor lapideum aufert, carneum suppeditat, illósque viribus ad opera pietatis exercēda necessariis instructos, sibi consecrat in populum peculiarem studiosum bonorum operum, & sic regenerat in spem viuam per resurrectionem Iesu Christi ex mortuis, in hæreditatem, quæ nec perire potest, nec contaminari, nec marcescere, illis in cœlo seruatam. Hoc vero auxilium diuinum illa definitione ex scripturis ipsis κατ᾽ἀξίαν collecta descriptum, non omnibus illis obtingere, à quibus ille obedientiam, & vitæ innocentiam postulat, euidenter liquet ex euentu, & demonstrat hoc idem refractariorum, incredulorum; & in sua nequitia ac impietate pertinaciter pereuntium multitudo, quos æternum exitium nunquam maneret, si Deus illos gratiæ illius participes reddidisset, aut participes reddere voluisset, sic vt pluribus argumentis, quibus eadem veritas doctrinæ nostræ demonstrari posset, recensendis tutò supersedere queamus.
units.tr: So much for the first two questions. We must now proceed to the third and last (for the Adversary brings no argument at all in defence of his opinion), and examine: "Whether God supplies and bestows the necessary and sufficient help for keeping his precepts to all and each of the men to whom he has enjoined the keeping of his law." It is a lofty and difficult question, debated in many contests of disputation, and therefore most worthy of careful inquiry. But because it pertains rather to the place on predestination, which we must treat in the following chapter, than to this present disputation, we, aiming at brevity, will judge what is to be thought about this matter from the definition of sufficient and necessary grace and from the outcome of the calling. That help of God, then, which is nothing other than the divine calling (I speak of that by which we are turned to God), is a gracious action of God, by which God, out of his mere mercy and love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], effectually calls the elect, who through sin are alienated from God and from his gracious life, at a time he has appointed, out of the state of misery and dominant sin, into the fellowship of spiritual blessings in Christ. That is, by the external preaching of the Word and the internal working of the Holy Spirit, he makes alive those who are dead in sins, illuminates the mind, overwhelmed by the shadows of native blindness, with the light of spiritual wisdom and knowledge, takes away the stony heart and gives a fleshy one, and, having equipped them with the powers necessary for exercising works of piety, consecrates them to himself as a peculiar people zealous for good works, and so regenerates them unto a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, unto an inheritance which can neither perish, nor be defiled, nor fade away, reserved in heaven for them. Now that this divine help, described in that definition collected from the Scriptures themselves according to worth [κατ᾽ἀξίαν], does not fall to all those from whom he demands obedience and innocence of life, is plainly evident from experience, and it is demonstrated by the multitude of the refractory, the unbelieving, and those who, obstinate in their wickedness and impiety, perish, who would never face eternal destruction if God had made them partakers of that grace, or had been willing to make them partakers. So we may safely forbear to recount the many arguments by which the same truth of our doctrine could be demonstrated.

units.la: Ostorrodius sectione prima eiusdem capitis, duabus rationibus probare conatur, Deum nulli hominum, à quibus obedientiam præceptis suis præstandam postulat, auxilium suum denegare. Prima est, quia Deus alioquin illos, qui suis mandatis non obediunt, iuste punire, quemadmodum facere soleat, non posset.
units.tr: In the first section of the same chapter, Ostorrodius tries to prove by two reasons that God denies his help to no men from whom he demands obedience to his precepts. The first is that otherwise God could not justly punish those who do not obey his commands, as he is accustomed to do.

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument runs thus:

units.la: Si Deus non suppeditat omnibus illis, quibus obedientiam mandatis suis præstandam imperat, auxilium necessarium, quo adiuti, voluntati ipsius satisfacere possint, tum eos, qui præcepta ipsius non seruant, nullo iure punire potest: Atqui consequens falsum esse, ex eo liquet, quod ille tales punit: Ergo & antecedens falsum est.
units.tr: If God does not supply to all those whom he commands to render obedience to his commands the necessary help, by which, being aided, they may be able to satisfy his will, then he cannot justly punish those who do not keep his precepts. But the consequent is plainly false, as is clear from the fact that he does punish such people. Therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Connexi hæc probatio adfertur:
units.tr: The following proof is attached to this:

units.la: Si nemo iure vllo propterea multari potest, quod non præstiterit id, quod præstare non potuit, tum si Deus non suppeditat omnibus illis, quibus obedientiam mandatis suis præstandam imperat, auxilium necessarium, quo adiuti voluntati ipsius satisfacere possint, sequitur, ipsum, eos qui præcepta ipsius non seruant, nullo iure puniri posse: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If no one can justly be punished for failing to perform what he was not able to perform, then, if God does not supply to all those whom he commands to render obedience to his commands the necessary help, by which, being aided, they may be able to satisfy his will, it follows that he cannot justly punish those who do not keep his precepts. But the first is true. Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp. Connexum vtrumque esse falsum, & ne quidem in foro hominum politico semper valere regulam, neminem videlicet iuste propterea puniri posse, quod non præstiterit id, quod præstare tamen non possit. Si quis enim pecuniæ summam commodato ab aliquo accipiat, eámque aliquando insumat, & dilapidet cum omnibus quæ possedit bonis, nihilominus etiamsi soluendo non sit, iure meritóque ad solutionem debiti à creditore vrgetur, & à Magistratu furti reus peragitur, iusteque punitur. Si itaque Deus nunquam sufficientibus viribus, atque virtutibus, quæ ad perfectam legi diuinæ obedientiam præstandam requiruntur, hominem instruxisset, sic vt homo eam, quam Deus ab ipso requirit, obedientiam ne quidem in primæuæ integritatis statu, & creationis ipsius splendore constitutus, præstare potuisset, tum Deus illos, qui mandata ipsius transgrediuntur, nullo iure punire posset, quia tulisset homini legem naturæ ipsius perfectiorem, & ita summam iniustitiam in ipsum exercuisset. Sed quia homo omnibus illis virtutibus, & gratiæ adminiculis, quibus suffultus Deo perfectam obedientiā, si voluisset, præstare potuisset, à Deo ornatus fuit excellentissime, per impietatem petulanter semet ipsum spoliauit: ideò Deus, & iuste ipsum punire potest, quoties officium negligit, & iure optimo exactissimam obedientiam ab ipso postulat. Homo enim etiamsi peccando gratiæ illa ornamenta perdiderit, Deum tamen iure suo creationis, propter quod ipsi obedientia debetur à creatura, spoliare minimè potuit. Quod itaque Deus illa obedientiæ officia homini, omnibus licet viribus destituto imperat, hoc facit vt creator, quo iure propter peccatum hominis non excidit: quod vero ipsum ab officio recedentem punit, hoc facit vt iustus iudex, scelerúmque vindex: quod denique gratiæ suæ non omnibus & singulis denuò confert, hoc facit vt summus & liberrimus rerum omnium Dominus, qui nemini debitor est, Roman. cap. 9. versu decimoquinto, Miserebor cuius misertus fuero, & commiserabor, quem commiseratus fuero. Et cui liberum est gratiam dare quantam, & quibus velit. Matth. cap. vigesimo, ver. decimoquinto, An non licet mihi quod volo facere in meis? Ex præceptis itaque, & pœnis diuinis, non quod homo possit, sed quid debeat: item non vires, sed imbecillitatem hominis, Ostorrodius æstimare discat.
units.tr: Answer. Both the connection and the premises are false. The rule, that no one can justly be punished for failing to do what he could not do, does not always hold even in the civil courts of men. Suppose someone borrows a sum of money from another, spends it, and squanders it along with all his goods; even though he is not solvent, the creditor rightly and justly presses him for payment of the debt, and the magistrate prosecutes him as a thief and justly punishes him. So if God had never equipped man with sufficient strength and virtues, which are required for the perfect performance of obedience to the divine law, so that man, even in the state of his original integrity and in the splendour of his creation, could not have rendered the obedience God requires of him, then God could not justly punish those who transgress his commands, because he would have imposed on man a law more perfect than his nature, and so would have done the greatest injustice to him. But because man was supremely adorned by God with all those virtues and aids of grace, by which, supported, he could have rendered perfect obedience if he had willed, and wantonly stripped himself of them through impiety, therefore God can justly punish him whenever he neglects his duty, and with the best right he demands the most exact obedience from him. For even though man has lost those gifts of grace by sinning, he could by no means strip God of his right as creator, on account of which obedience is owed to him by the creature. Therefore, that God commands man, though deprived of all strength, to perform these duties of obedience, he does as creator, a right which man's sin has not forfeited; that he punishes man when he withdraws from duty, he does as a just judge and avenger of crimes; and that finally he does not bestow his grace again on all and each, he does as the supreme and most free Lord of all things, who owes nothing to anyone: Romans 9:15, "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show compassion on whom I will show compassion," and "to whom it is lawful to give grace, as much as, and to whom, he wills." Matthew 20:15, "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own?" From God's precepts and punishments, therefore, let Ostorrodius learn to judge not what man can do, but what he ought to do; likewise not man's strength, but his weakness.

units.la: Ratio Aduersarii secunda est: quod Deus non eiusmodi legem tulerit, quam nemo hominum præstare possit, quoniam lex, testante Paulo Roman. cap septimo, versu decimo, homini ad vitam est data, nemo autem, teste eodem Paulo Rom.10.5.per legem viuit, nisi qui praestiterit illam.
units.tr: The opponent's second argument is that God has not enacted such a law as no man can perform, since the law, as Paul bears witness in Romans 7:10, was given to man for life; "but no one," as the same Paul testifies, Romans 10:5, "lives by the law unless he has performed it."

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument runs thus:

units.la: Si lex homini data est ad vitam, id est, eo fine vt homo per eius praestationem vitam aeternam consequatur, tum sequitur Deum non eiusmodi legem tulisse, quam plane nullus hominum seruare possit.
units.tr: If the law was given to man for life, that is, to the end that man might obtain eternal life by performing it, then it follows that God has not enacted such a law as plainly no man could keep.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est, Rom.7. v.10.
units.tr: But the first is true, Romans 7:10.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Connexi probatio haec est:
units.tr: The proof of the connection is this:

units.la: Si nemo per legem viuit, nisi qui praestiterit illam, lex autem homini data est ad vitam, id est, eo fine, vt homo per eius praestationem, vitam aeternam consequatur, tum sequitur Deum non eiusmodi legem tulisse, quam plane nullus hominum seruare possit:
units.tr: If no one lives by the law unless he has performed it, but the law was given to man for life, that is, to the end that man, by performing it, might obtain eternal life, then it follows that God has not enacted such a law as plainly no man could keep.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est, Rom. 10. v.5.
units.tr: But the first is true, Romans 10:5.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp. Primo, totum argumentum esse ἀπογοδιόνιον: non enim quaeritur, An Deus eiusmodi legem tulerit, quae ab hominibus seruari possit? Sed, An Deus omnibus & singulis hominibus, quibus obedientiam legibus suis praestandam imperauit, sufficiens auxilium suppeditet, quibus adiuti illam praestare possint? cuius καταφασιν argumentum Adversarii non probat. Secundo, assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse falsam. Legem enim homini post lapsum non in eum finem datam esse, vt per eam iustitiam & vitam aeternam obtineret, inde liquet, quod hoc pacto Deus promissionem Euangelicam antè datam irritam fecisset. Roman. capite quarto, versu decimotertio & decimoquarto. Non enim per legem promissio cessit Abrahae, aut semini eius, vt haeres esset mundi, sed per iustitiam fidei: etenim qui ex lege, sunt haeredes, inanis facta est fides, & vana reddita est promissio. Roman. capite vndecimo, versu sexto, Quod si per gratiam, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia iam non est gratia: sin ex operibus, iam non est gratia, alioquin opus iam non est opus. Galat. cap. 3. versu 17. Hoc autem dico pactionem ante confirmatam à Deo respectu Christi, lex post annos quadringentos & triginta cepit, non facit irritam, vt aboleat promissionem, nempe aliam, & quidem contrariam salutis proponendo, & verè ex lege esset iustitia. Galat. 3. verf. 21.22. Num igitur lex addita est aduersus promissiones Dei ? Absit : nam si data fuisset lex, quæ posset viuificare, verè ex lege esset iustitia: sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus. Denique legis repetitę finis esset iustitia ad salutem operanti, non Christus ad iustitiam credenti, nisi per accidens. Roman. capite 10. versu 4. Nam finis legis est Christus ad iustitiam cuiuis credenti. Quin hoc ipsum Deus per modum promulgandi legem, non obscurè significatum voluisse videtur, quippe qui terribilis fuit, & formidabilis, ac percellédis abigendisque potius Israelitis, quàm alliciendis comparatus, adhibitis tonitru, fulgure, nube densa, sonitu tubæ vehementi valde cum trepidatione, & fumo totius montis, adeò vt non tantùm populus metu perculsus recesserit à monte, sed & ipse Moses exterritus fuerit, & tremebundus. Exod. 19. ver. 16. Fuit verò die illo tertio, quum cœpisset mane, vt essent soni, & fulgura, & nubes densa super illum montem, sonitúsque tuba vehemens valdè, adeò vt trepidaret totus ipse populus, qui erat in castris, & capite 20. versu 18. 19. Ipse autem populus totus percipiebat illos sonos, & fulgura, & sonum tubæ, montémque ipsum fumantem, percipiénsque populus commoti sunt loco, & steterunt procul: dixerunt itaque Mosi, loquere tu nobiscum, & audiemus, sed ne loquatur Deus nobiscum ne moriamur. Hebr. 12. v. 21. Et Moses (adeò terribile erat visum, quod apparebat) dixit, Expauefactus sum, ac tremebundus. Quæ omnia non possunt esse signum Dei placabilis, & promissionem vitæ æternæ promulgantis. Hisce adde, quod ipsa lex, quia quum ex fide non fit, impossibili ea conditione vrget nos, cuius præstandæ facultatem ipsa non suppeditat, ne quidem potest nos iustos sistere coram tribunali Dei, non sua, sed carnis nostræ vitiofitate impedita. Rom. 8. v. 3. Quum enim legis impotentia nihil posset in carne, Deus suoipsius Filio misso conformato carni peccato obnoxia, idque pro peccato condemnauit peccatum in carne. Quum eo vsque aduersetur Legi caro nostra, vt ei cũ vniuersa sua intelligentia nec velit, nec possit subiici, Rom 8. v. 7. Intelligentia carnis inimicitia est aduersus Deum. Legi enim Dei non subiicitur, nam nec potest quidem. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum est, non ideo datam esse Legem, vt nos iustificet, sed vt nos imbecillitatis nostræ conuictos ad fidem Christi dirigat, Gal. 3. v. 24. Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christum, vt ex fide iustificaremur. Quum verò Paulus Rom. 7. v. 10. Legem ad vitam esse dicit, non ipsum legislatoris, decalogum reperepetentis, finem,sed legis ipsius vim & naturam respicit, quæ vitam & iustitiam quidem in se complectitur, eiusque consequendæ viam ac rationem nobis monstrat, sed sub conditione homini post lapsum impossibili,quam passim vrget contra illos, qui ex operibus legis iustificari volentes,nec seipsos nouerunt,nec vim ac naturam legis perspectam habent.
units.tr: Answer. First, the whole argument is [ἀπογοδιόνιον], beside the point. For the question is not, "Did God enact a law that men could keep?" but, "Does God supply sufficient help to all and each of those to whom he has commanded obedience to his laws, by which, being aided, they may be able to render it?" The opponent's argument does not prove the affirmative of this question, [κατάφασιν]. Second, the minor premise of the main syllogism is false. That the law was not given to man after the fall for the purpose of obtaining righteousness and eternal life through it is clear from the fact that in this way God would have made void the gospel promise given before. Romans 4:13–14: "For the promise to Abraham or to his seed that he should be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is made of no effect." Romans 11:6: "And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if of works, then it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work." Galatians 3:17: "This I say: the covenant previously confirmed by God in respect of Christ, the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not make void so as to abolish the promise," namely another one, and one indeed contrary, proposing salvation; and righteousness would truly be by the law. Galatians 3:21–22: "Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid. For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be by the law. But the Scripture has concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe." Finally, the purpose of the law, when it is repeated, would be righteousness for salvation to the one who works, not Christ for righteousness to the one who believes, except incidentally. Romans 10:4: "For the end of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes." Indeed God seems to have intended this very thing, not obscurely indicated by the manner of promulgating the law: it was terrible and dreadful, and prepared rather to strike terror into and drive away the Israelites than to attract them, with thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a very loud blast of a trumpet, great trembling, and smoke from the whole mountain, so that not only did the people, struck with fear, withdraw from the mountain, but Moses himself was terrified and trembling. Exodus 19:16: "Now on the third day, when morning came, there were thunderings and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and a very loud blast of a trumpet, so that all the people who were in the camp trembled." And chapter 20, verses 18–19: "Now all the people perceived the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking; and when the people saw it, they were moved and stood afar off. And they said to Moses, 'You speak with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die.'" Hebrews 12:21: "And so terrible was the sight that Moses said, 'I am exceedingly afraid and trembling.'" None of these things can be a sign of a God who is placable and who proclaims the promise of eternal life. Add to these that the law itself, since it is not of faith, presses us with an impossible condition, the means of fulfilling which it does not supply, and so cannot even set us upright as righteous before the judgment seat of God, being hindered not by its own fault but by the vice of our flesh. Romans 8:3: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh." Since our flesh is so opposed to the law that with its whole mind it neither wills nor is able to be subject to it, Romans 8:7: "The mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be." From all these things it is evident that the law was not given to justify us, but to lead us, convicted of our weakness, to faith in Christ. Galatians 3:24: "The law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith." But when Paul says in Romans 7:10 that "the law is unto life," he does not look to the purpose of the lawgiver, who reiterated the decalogue, but to the force and nature of the law itself, which indeed embraces life and righteousness in itself, and shows us the way and method of attaining them; but under a condition impossible for man after the fall, which it presses everywhere against those who, wishing to be justified by the works of the law, neither know themselves nor have a clear view of the force and nature of the law.

units.la: Hisce vero omnibus Aduersarius sectione tertia duas conclusiones subiicit,vnam specialem,quam ex disputatione hac de Liberi Arbitrii viribus educit, & qua affirmat, in grauissimo errore versari omnes fere Euangelicos,in primis autem Caluinistæ ( hoc enim nomine inuidiose nos indigitat ) Schwenckfeldianos, Perfectistas, & magnam partem Anabaptistarum ( cum quibus nos iniquissime coniungit ) sentientes, hominem (videlicet animalem & nondum renatum ) ex auditu verbi Dei externo nihil proficere posse, nisi ipsum Spiritus Sanctus interna quadam vi erudiat, & fidem ac obedientiam in ipso operetur: alteram generalem, qua totam disputationem de Libero hominis Arbitrio concludens, ait : Certum igitur esse quod homo etiam post lapsum Adami, libero polleat arbitrio, quódue vires eius naturales, ab eo tempore, non sint attenuatæ, aut diminutæ, nisi quatenus homines frequenter peccando habitum & consuetudinem peccandi contraxerint, & sic seipsos corruperint, illámque corruptionem in posteros deriuauerint,& etiamnum deriuent.
units.tr: In the third section, the Adversary sets two conclusions before these points. One is a special conclusion, which he draws from this disputation about the powers of free will, and by which he affirms that almost all Evangelicals are in the gravest error, especially the Calvinists (for this is the name by which he invidiously points at us), together with the Schwenckfeldians, the Perfectists, and a great part of the Anabaptists (with whom he most unjustly joins us), who hold that man (namely the natural man, not yet reborn) can gain nothing from the external hearing of the Word of God unless the Holy Spirit himself instructs him by some inward power and works faith and obedience in him. The other is a general conclusion, with which he ends the whole disputation about man's free choice: "It is certain, therefore, that man, even after the fall of Adam, possesses free will, and that his natural powers from that time have not been weakened or diminished, except insofar as men, by sinning often, have contracted a habit and custom of sinning, and so have corrupted themselves, and have passed on that corruption to their posterity, and still pass it on."

units.la: Resp. Primam quod attinet, salsissimam esse illam,ex capite primo, & vigesimo sexto huius defensionis nostræ liquidò, & tam manifeste constat, vt illis hoc loco quicquam addere, superfluum foret. Altera vero, destructis à nobis, quibus nititur, præmissis, sponte quoque corruit. Concludimus igitur nos cum sacris literis, hominem animalem,& nondum renatum, extra gratiam salutarem in statu peccati dominantis, per & propter corruptionem originalem ab Adamo in omnes posteros deriuatam omni libertate Arbitrii ita spoliatum esse, vt,nisi Spiritus sancti gratia, & interna illuminatione, arcanáque vi & virtute illuminetur ac renouetur, neque res spirituales intelligere, neque id quod vere bonum est velle ac perficere possit. Deo omnipotenti, & clementissimo Patri,qui pro gratuita sua benevolentia,per lauacrum regenerationis, & renouationem Spiritus sancti in nobis efficit, & vt velimus,& vt efficiamus id quod bonum est, & ipsi placet, sit laus & gloria in secula.
units.tr: Reply. As for the first conclusion, it is quite plainly and so manifestly false, as is clear from the first and twenty-sixth chapters of this our defence, that it would be superfluous to add anything to them here. The second, however, falls of its own accord once the premises on which it rests, which we have overthrown, are destroyed. We therefore conclude, with the sacred writings, that natural man, not yet reborn, outside saving grace, in the state of dominant sin, through and because of the original corruption derived from Adam into all his posterity, is so stripped of all freedom of choice that, unless he is illuminated and renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, by inward illumination and by the hidden power and virtue of that Spirit, he can neither understand spiritual things nor will and perform what is truly good. To almighty God, and to the most merciful Father, who, by his free goodness, through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit within us, brings it about both that we will and that we do what is good and pleasing to him, be praise and glory for ever.

units.la: CAPUT XXIX. DE AETERNA DEI PRAEDESTINATIONE.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX. CONCERNING THE ETERNAL PREDESTINATION OF GOD.

units.la: VERITATEM doctrinæ nostræ, quæ est de Aeterna Dei prædestinatione, contra Aduersarium propugnaturus, primo omnium sententiæ orthodoxæ summam proponam, deinde Aduersarii errores referam ac perstringam. Nec tamen est, quod quis planam omnium eorum, quæ ad integram huius loci tractationem pertinent, explicationem à me expectet, cùm instituti ac propositi nostri ratio, quæ ἀπαντητικὴ potissimum est, hoc non ferat, & illa tractatum integrum ac prolixum requirant. Et quum penè de tota hac doctrina, vel saltem plerisque aut multis capitibus, quæ in hanc doctrinam incidunt, discrepantes inter se, & diuersæ admodum Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum sint sententiæ, animus non est patrocinium suscipere illorum, quæ priuatus vllus ea de re docuit aut scripsit, sed dispicere, vtrum illa absurda, quæ Aduersarius ex doctrina de Prædestinatione, in genere ac indefinitè sic nominata (nullam enim certam ea de re doctrinam recenseт) elicere ac educere conatur, sententiæ illi, quam Ecclesiæ nostræ reformatæ publicè profitentur, & quæ in Harmonia confessionum extat, iure meritóque impingi possint ac debeant, cuius summam breuiter proponemus.
units.tr: Intending to defend the truth of our doctrine of the eternal predestination of God against our opponent, I shall first set out the sum of the orthodox view and then report and expose the opponent's errors. No one should expect from me a plain explanation of everything that belongs to a full treatment of this topic, since the character of my undertaking and purpose, which is by way of reply [ἀπαντητικὴ] above all, does not allow it, and such matters require a full and lengthy treatment. Since nearly the whole of this doctrine, or at least most of the points that fall under it, are disputed, and the opinions of the ecclesiastical writers differ widely, my intention is not to take up the defence of whatever any private individual has taught or written on the subject. Rather, I shall examine whether those absurdities which the opponent tries to draw out of the doctrine of predestination, named thus in general and indefinitely (for he sets out no certain doctrine on the matter), can rightly and properly be charged against that view which our reformed Churches publicly profess and which stands in the Harmony of Confessions. I shall briefly set out its sum.

units.la: Prædestinatio igitur, iuxta sententiam confessionis Helueticæ, est, qua Deus ab æterno prædestinauit, vel elegit liberè, & mera sua gratia, nullo hominū respectu, sanctos, quos vult saluos facere in Christo, iuxta illud Apostoli Ephes. capite primo, versu quarto, Deus elegit nos in ipso, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi: & 2. Timoth. capite primo, versu nono & decimo: Qui saluos fecit nos, & vocauit vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, quæ data est quidem nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia, sed patefacta nunc est per illustrem illum aduentum Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Vel iuxta confessionem Gallicam: Prædestinatio est,qua Deus ex hac corruptione & damnatione vniuersali,in qua omnes homines natura sunt submersi, alios quidem eripere, quos videlicet æterno & immutabili suo consilio, sola sua bonitate & misericordia,nullóque operum ipsorum respectu,in Iesu Christo elegit: alios vero in ea corruptione ac damnatione relinquere, in quibus nimirum iustè suo tempore damnandis iustitiam suam demonstret, sicut in aliis diuitias misericordiæ suæ declarat.
