Vel denique iuxta confessionem Belgicam : Prædestinatio est, qua Deus (postquam tota Adami soboles sic in perditionem & exitium primi hominis culpa,præcipitata fuit ) se ipsum talem demonstrauit, ac præstitit,qualis est reuera,nimirum & misericordem,& iustum, misericordem quidem eos damnatione & interitu liberādo & seruando quos in æterno suo consilio pro gratuita sua bonitate ,per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum elegit absque vllo operum ipsorum respectu : Iustum verò,alios in illo suo lapsu & perditione relinquendo,in quem ipsi sese præcipites dederunt. Ab istis definitionibus nō discrepat illa qua definitur prædestinatio,quòd sit æternū,immutabile,ac liberū Dei decretū,quo ex libere voluntatis beneplacito alios ad æternā salutem,pro gratuita sua misericordia elegit :alios ad æterna damnatione,pro sua iustitia repudiauit. Vnde hanc prædestinationem duplicem esse dicimus, aliam ad vitam, aliam verò ad mortē,& illam electionem, hāc vero reprobationē appellamus. Electio est æternū Dei decretū , quo ex beneuolo voluntatis suæ affectu, quosdā homines ex humano genere corrupto, lapsóq;ad salutē & vitā æternā,omniáq; media quibus ad finē illū perduci,& sine quibus finē illū cōsequi nō possunt in Christo elegit,vt in eis summā suam misericordiam demonstret.Reprobatio verò est decretum iræ Dei, quo ex liberrimo voluntatis suæ beneplacito decreuit,quosdam in communi corruptione & miseria relinquere , eósque vt suo ipsorum facto & vitiōsitate mersos , in peccato & extra vnionem Christi positos, ad mortem æternam condemnare, ad iram ac iustitiam suam declarandum. Vtriusque verò decreti, tum electionis, tum reprobationis causam impulsi-uam in solum Dei miserendi vel non miserendi beneplacitum transcribimus,sic vt quemadmodum causam ꝏ qua Deus ad decretum illud faciendum compulsus est,nec fidem præuisam, nec præuisa bona opera,nec quicquam eorum,quæ ab homine sumi possent, sed solum & vnicum Dei beneplacitum esse, cum scriptura afferimus : ita ipsius reprobationis causam impellentem extra Dei voluntatem nusquam,ne quidem in ipso peccato quǫren-dam esse docemus. Vtrique denique decreto electionis & reprobationis suam subiungemus exequutionem,cuius actus eo ordine & modo peragi dicimus,quo in & a decreto sunt ordinati: quamuis inter decretum electionis & decretum reprobationis, & vtriusque exequutionem, quod ad effecta & fructus attinet, ingens discrimen esse,sanctè credamus ac doceamus, quum electio causa sit & eius quǫ expectatur in futura vita gloriæ (vt cum Thoma Aquinate loquar) & eius quæ percipitur in præsenti gratiæ: reprobatio autem non fit causa eius, quæ est in hac vita culpæ, sed eius quæ in futuro & iusto Dei iudicio redditur, poenæ. Hoc est: Electione detur electis vt & boni sint, & bonum assequantur: reprobatione vero reprobis non vt mali sint,sed vt malum assequantur, quod est bonum iustumque iudicium Dei. Atque hæc doctrinæ illius de prædestinatione, quam profitentur Ecclesiæ orthodoxæ, summa est: dispiciendum igitur nunc est,num illa absurda,quæ ab Aduersario recensentur,illi doctrinæ iustè necne impingi possint ac debeant?
units.tr: Predestination, then, according to the view of the Helvetic Confession, is that by which God from eternity predestined, or freely chose, by his mere grace and without regard to any human merit, the saints whom he wills to save in Christ, according to the Apostle's words in Ephesians chapter 1, verse 4: God chose us in him before the foundation of the world; and in 2 Timothy chapter 1, verses 9 and 10: Who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began, but has now been made manifest through the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Or, according to the Gallic Confession: predestination is that by which God, out of this general corruption and condemnation in which all men are sunk by nature, rescues some, namely those whom he chose in Jesus Christ by his eternal and unchangeable counsel, by his goodness and mercy alone, with no regard to their works; and leaves others in that corruption and condemnation, in whom he justly shows his justice in his time for their condemnation, just as in others he declares the riches of his mercy. Or finally, according to the Belgic Confession: predestination is that by which God (after the whole offspring of Adam had been thus plunged into perdition and ruin by the fault of the first man) showed and presented himself as he truly is, namely both merciful and just: merciful indeed in delivering and preserving from damnation and destruction those whom he chose in his eternal counsel by his free goodness through Jesus Christ our Lord, without any regard to their works; but just in leaving the others in that their fall and perdition into which they had cast themselves. Nor does that definition differ from these, which defines predestination as the eternal, unchangeable and free decree of God, by which, from the good pleasure of his free will, he chose some to eternal salvation out of his free mercy, and rejected others to eternal damnation for his justice. Hence we say that this predestination is twofold: one to life, the other to death; and we call the former election and the latter reprobation. Election is the eternal decree of God, by which, from the kindly affection of his will, he chose in Christ certain men out of the corrupt human race, fallen and lapsed, to salvation and eternal life, together with all the means by which they are brought to that end and without which they cannot attain it, so that he might display his supreme mercy in them. Reprobation, however, is the decree of God's wrath, by which, from the most free good pleasure of his will, he decided to leave certain men in the common corruption and misery, and to condemn them to eternal death, as sunk in sin and placed outside union with Christ by their own deed and wickedness, in order to declare his wrath and justice. Moreover, for the cause of each decree, both of election and of reprobation, we ascribe the impelling cause solely to the good pleasure of God in showing mercy or not showing mercy. Thus, as Scripture teaches us, the cause that moved God to make that decree was neither foreseen faith, nor foreseen good works, nor anything that could be taken from man, but only and alone God's good pleasure; and we teach that the impelling cause of reprobation is nowhere to be sought outside the will of God, not even in sin itself. Finally, we add to the decree of election and of reprobation their execution, whose acts we say are carried out in the order and manner in which they were ordained in and by the decree. Although we devoutly believe and teach that there is a great difference between the decree of election and the decree of reprobation, and between the execution of each, as regards effects and fruits, since election is the cause both of the glory hoped for in the future life (to speak with Thomas Aquinas) and of the grace received in the present, whereas reprobation is not the cause of the guilt that is in this life, but of the punishment that is rendered in the future and in God's just judgment. That is: by election it is given to the elect that they both be good and attain the good; by reprobation, however, it is not given to the reprobate that they be evil, but that they attain evil, which is the good and just judgment of God. This, then, is the sum of that doctrine of predestination which the orthodox Churches profess. We must now examine whether those absurdities which are recounted by the opponent can rightly and properly be charged against that doctrine.

units.la: Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum capite trigesimo quinto, disputationem suam de prædestinatione in duas partes distinguit, in quarum prima causas exponit, ob quas ille, sententiæ ac doctrinæ ipsi, qua statuitur æterno Dei decreto, de omnibus & singulis hominibus constitutum esse, quinam suo tempore ad salutem ac vitam æternam perduci, qui vero certò damnari debeant: in altera vero promittit, se ex infinitis scripturæ sacræ testimoniis vnicum allegaturum esse,quod sententiam illam falsitatis solidè conuincat.
units.tr: In chapter thirty-five of his Institutions, Ostorodius divides his disquisition on predestination into two parts. In the first he sets out the reasons for which he rejects and attacks that view and doctrine which holds that, by the eternal decree of God, it has been settled concerning all and each men who, in their time, are to be brought to salvation and eternal life, and who must certainly be condemned; in the second part, however, he promises that he will allege from the countless testimonies of Holy Scripture a single one which solidly refutes that view as false.

units.la: Partem primam quantum concernit,duas potissimum recenset causas, ob quas doctrinam illam de prædestinatione improbet ac impugnet. Prima est, quia posita & concessa illa sententia, necessariò omnis religio & cultus Dei euertatur: altera est, quia necessariò inde sequitur, Deo multa absurda & impia adscribenda & imputanda esse. Nos vtramque causam eo ordine, quo illæ ab Aduersario proponuntur, examinabimus, & vt eò diligentius appareat, quàm illæ nullius sint ponderis ac momenti, vtramque syllogisticè proponemus.
units.tr: As far as the first part is concerned, he lists chiefly two reasons for which he rejects and assails that doctrine of predestination. The first is that, once that view is posited and granted, all religion and worship of God is necessarily overthrown; the second is that it necessarily follows from it that many absurd and impious things must be ascribed and imputed to God. We shall examine each reason in the order in which the opponent proposes them, and, so that it may appear more clearly how utterly without weight or moment they are, we shall set out each in syllogistic form.

units.la: Argumentum igitur à causa prima desumptum,tale est:
units.tr: The argument drawn from the first cause, then, is as follows:

units.la: Quæ sententia ac doctrina vniuersam religionem Christianam, & totum Dei cultum euertit, illa falsa est, ac reiicienda.
units.tr: Whatever view and doctrine overthrows the whole Christian religion and the entire worship of God is false and must be rejected.

units.la: Atqui sententia ac doctrina illa de praedestinatione, qua docetur, aeterno Dei decreto de omnibus & singulis hominibus constitutum esse, quinam saluari, qui vero damnari debeant, vniuersam religionem,& totum Dei cultum euertit.
units.tr: But that view and doctrine of predestination, which teaches that by the eternal decree of God it has been settled concerning all and each men who are to be saved and who must be condemned, overthrows the whole religion and the entire worship of God.

units.la: Ergo sententia ac doctrina illa de praedestinatione falsa est, ac reiicienda.
units.tr: Therefore that view and doctrine of predestination is false and must be rejected.

units.la: Assumptionem hac ratione demonstrare conatur, quod ex sententia & doctrina illa de praedestinatione necessario sequatur, omnia, quaecunque ad pietatis officia spectant, non liberè, sed necessario fieri, quo posito, omnis conatus, omneque studium ac desiderium pietatis tollatur, quoniam in iis quae necessario fiunt, nec aliter se habere possunt, omnis opera, omnisque labor inutilis sit ac frustraneus: vbicunque autem omnis labor omneque studium pietatis cessat, ibi necessario omnis religio euertatur.
units.tr: He tries to demonstrate the minor premise in this way: that from that view and doctrine of predestination it necessarily follows that all things which pertain to the duties of piety are done not freely but necessarily; once this is posited, every effort, every zeal and every desire for piety is taken away, since in things which happen necessarily, and cannot be otherwise, all works and all labour are useless and vain; and wherever all labour and all zeal for piety cease, there the whole of religion is necessarily overthrown.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The prosyllogism is as follows.

units.la: Qua sententia omnem conatum omneque studium pietatis tollit, illa vniuersam religionem & totum Dei cultum euertit.
units.tr: Whatever opinion removes all effort and all zeal for piety overthrows the whole of religion and the entire worship of God.

units.la: Atqui praedicta illa sententia ac doctrina de praedestinatione, omnem conatum studiumque pietatis tollit.
units.tr: But that aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination removes all effort and zeal for piety.

units.la: Ergo praedicta illa sententia ac doctrina de praedestinatione, vniuersam religionem Christianam ac totum Dei cultum euertit.
units.tr: Therefore that aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination overthrows the whole Christian religion and the entire worship of God.

units.la: Assumptionis Epilogismus talis est:
units.tr: The epilogism of the assumption is as follows:

units.la: Ex qua sententia ac doctrina necessario sequitur, omnia illa, quae ad pietatis officia spectant, non liberè, sed necessario fieri, illa omnem conatum omneque pietatis studium tollit:
units.tr: From that opinion and doctrine there necessarily follows that all those things which pertain to the duties of piety happen not freely but by necessity; and this removes all effort and all zeal for piety.

units.la: Atqui ex praedicta illa sententia ac doctrina de praedestinatione necessario sequitur, omnia illa quae ad pietatis officium spectant, non liberè, sed necessario fieri:
units.tr: But from that aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination there necessarily follows that all those things which pertain to the duties of piety happen not freely but by necessity.

units.la: Ergo praedicta illa sententia ac doctrina de praedestinatione, omnem conatum, omneque studium pietatis tollit.
units.tr: Therefore that aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination removes all effort and all zeal for piety.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem in omnibus tribus syllogismis esse falsam. Haec enim doctrina de aeterna Dei praedestinatione, nec religionem cultumque Dei euertit, sed stabilit, nec conatum studiumque pietatis tollit, sed accendit, auget, & confirmat, nec libertatem creaturæ, necessitati euentibus decreto diuino impositæ opponit, sed subordinat commodissime: vnde libertas creaturæ in vltimo syllogismo necessitati, id est, infallibili certitudini, quam necessitatem consequentiæ appellant (eam enim necessitatem, quam coactionis vocant, excludimus ex hoc negotio) perperam opponitur, & doctrinæ illi falsò affingitur, quòd ex ea sequatur, omnia, quæ ad pietatis officia spectant, non liberè, sed absoluta necessitate fieri, cum tamen illis pietatis officiis & actionibus, & necessitatem, secundum quam necessariò, id est, infallibiliter euen-niunt, nec possunt non euenire, quæcumque Deus decreuit, & libertatem, secundum quam euenire vel non euenire possunt, sed diuerso respectu, illam videlicet necessitatem causæ primæ respectu, nempe Dei, qui non mutatur, hanc verò, videlicet libertatem respectu causæ secundæ, nempe creaturæ tribuit verissimè. Vt enim infallibilis prouidentiæ diuinæ certitudo, quæ Deum necessitatis, temeritatis, & omnis contingentiæ suspicione liberat, voluntatis humanæ in eligendo libertatem, & causarum secundarum naturam ac proprietatem non tollit, nec impedit, quò minùs actiones prouidentiæ diuinæ (quam hoc loco à prædestinatione distinguimus) moderamini subiectas & subordinatas contingenter & mutabiliter producant, unde etiam Dei autoris respectu necessitate immutabili existunt, causis secundis eosdem effectus pro naturæ suæ conditione vel liberè vel contingenter producentibus, à quibus etiam tanquam vel internis vel proximis nomen contingentiæ aut necessitatis obtinere solet: ita quoque licet decretum prædestinationis sit certum, firmum, ac penitus immutabile, sic vt omnia certo in tempore ita exequutioni mandentur, quemadmodum ab æterno à Deo sunt decreta, Deúsque tempore & modo apud se constituto omnia efficaciter operetur, quæcumque ad electorum salutem decreuit: illa tamen infallibilis euentuum certitudo & necessitas ab immutabili Dei prædestinantis veritate, sapientia, & omnipotentia dependens, studium ac desiderium pietatis non labefactat, sed gignit atque confirmat. Nam decretum illud prædestinationis vt vt immutabile & infallibile, tamen non simplex, nuda, aut simpliciter absolutum nobis occurrit, sed copulatum & comitatum potius, ac conuestitum causis secundis, omnibusque illis mediis, quibus electos suos ad vitam æternam perducere, Deus ante iacta mundi fundamenta constituit. Docet hoc euidenter illa Pauli exhortatio, secunda ad Timotheum, capite secundo, versu decimo nono: Stat quidem solidum Dei fundamentum, habens sigillum hoc, Nouit Dominus qui sint sui, sed discedat ab iniustitia, quisquis nomen Christi invocat. Et prima ad Thessalonicenses, capite quarto, versu septimo: Non vocauit nos Deus ad impuritatem, sed ad sanctificationem. Item ad Ephesios capite secundo, versu decimo: Ipsius opus sumus conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quae praeparauit Deus ut in iis versaremur. Et capite primo versu quarto: Elegit nos in ipso, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, ut simus sancti & inculpati coram eo per charitatem. Ex quibus omnibus, quam vanum ac futile sit Aduersarii argumentum, cuidenter apparet.
units.tr: Answer: The assumption is false in all three syllogisms. For this doctrine of the eternal predestination of God neither overthrows religion and the worship of God but establishes them, nor removes the effort and zeal for piety but kindles, increases and confirms them. Nor does it set the freedom of the creature over against the necessity that the divine decree imposes on events, but subordinates the one to the other most conveniently. Hence in the last syllogism the freedom of the creature is wrongly set against necessity, that is, infallible certainty, which they call the necessity of consequence (for we exclude from this business that necessity which they call of coercion). It is falsely attributed to that doctrine that from it there follows that all things pertaining to the duties of piety happen not freely but by absolute necessity. Yet God has most truly given to those duties and actions of piety both the necessity by which whatever God has decreed happens infallibly, and cannot fail to happen, and the freedom by which they can happen or not happen. These are given in different respects: that necessity with respect to the first cause, namely God, who does not change; and that freedom with respect to the second cause, namely the creature. For just as the infallible certainty of divine providence, which frees God from any suspicion of necessity, chance or all contingency, does not remove or hinder the freedom of the human will in choosing, nor the nature and property of secondary causes, so that they produce their actions, which are subject and subordinate to the direction of divine providence (which we here distinguish from predestination), contingently and changeably. Hence also with respect to God as author these actions exist with immutable necessity, while the secondary causes produce the same effects freely or contingently according to their nature, and from these, as internal or proximate causes, the names of contingency or necessity are usually obtained. So too, although the decree of predestination is certain, firm and wholly immutable, so that all things are carried out at the appointed time just as they were decreed by God from eternity, and God effectually works at the time and in the manner settled with himself everything he has decreed for the salvation of the elect, nevertheless that infallible certainty and necessity of events, depending on the immutable truth, wisdom and omnipotence of God who predestines, does not weaken the zeal and desire for piety but begets and confirms it. For that decree of predestination, however immutable and infallible, does not present itself to us as simple, bare or merely absolute, but rather as joined, accompanied and clothed with secondary causes and with all those means by which God, before the foundations of the world were laid, determined to bring his elect to eternal life. Paul's exhortation in his second letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse nineteen, clearly teaches this: Indeed the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity. And in his first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter four, verse seven: God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Likewise in Ephesians, chapter two, verse ten: We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. And in chapter one, verse four: He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. From all these things it clearly appears how vain and futile the adversary's argument is.

units.la: Venio nunc ad causae secundae, nempe grauissimarum illarum absurditatum quibus Deum ipsum a sententiae ac doctrinae illius asseclis, impie grauari affirmat Ostorrodius. Scelus certe grauissimum, quod illi doctrinae intentatur, quod cum ab illa amoliti fuerimus, maximae iniquitatis, & turpissimae iniuriae crimine Aduersarium constringemus. Quatuor autem absurditates sententiae illi impinguntur, nempe Iniquitas, seu Iniustitia: Hypocrisis, & fraus: Infscitia, seu Imprudentia: denique Malitia.
units.tr: I come now to the second point, namely the most grave absurdities with which Ostorodius impiously says God himself is burdened by the followers of this opinion and doctrine. Certainly it is the most serious charge that is brought against that doctrine; and once we have cleared it of this, we shall bind our opponent with the charge of the greatest iniquity and most shameful injustice. Four absurdities are imputed to that opinion: iniquity, or injustice; hypocrisy and deceit; ignorance, or imprudence; and finally, malice.

units.la: Argumentum generale inde desumptum tale erit.
units.tr: The general argument drawn from this will be as follows.

units.la: Quae sententia ac doctrina Deum ipsum iniquitatis seu iniustitiae, hypocrisis deinde, ac fraudis, infscitiae item ac imprudentiae, denique malitiae accusat, ea sine dubio impia est ac falsa:
units.tr: Whatever opinion and doctrine charges God himself with iniquity or injustice, then with hypocrisy and fraud, likewise with folly and imprudence, and finally with malice, is without doubt impious and false.

units.la: Atqui sententia ac doctrina illa de praedestinatione, qua docetur, aeterno Dei decreto constitutum esse de omnibus & singulis hominibus, quinam saluari, qui vero damnari debeant, Deum iniustitiae fraudisque, imprudentiae, hypocrisios, & malitiae accusat:
units.tr: But that doctrine of predestination, which teaches that by the eternal decree of God it has been settled who among all and each of mankind are to be saved and who ought to be damned, charges God with injustice, fraud, imprudence, hypocrisy and malice.

units.la: Ergo sententia ac doctrina illa de praedestinatione, impia est ac falsa.
units.tr: Therefore that doctrine of predestination is impious and false.

units.la: Assumptionis singula membra ordine probare conatur, & illam doctrinam quidem Deo iniquitatem & iniustitiam aspergere, inde probare vult, quia nihil iniquius excogitari possit, quam aliquem ideo puniri, quod non fecerit aut praestiterit id, quod tamen praestare ac facere rc minimè potuerit : Deum autem iuxta sententiam ac doctrinam illam eos punire,qui mali & immorigeri sint, in quorum tamen potestate minimè fuerit,ut illi Deo obedirent,siquidem immutabili Dei decreto constitutum sit, ne illi debita pietatis & obedientiæ officia præstarent, ac proinde Deum ideo punire homines,quod non faciant ac præstent id,quod tamen vt præstare non possent,Deus ipse decreuerit.
units.tr: He tries to prove the individual members of the minor premise in order. He wants to show from this that the doctrine casts iniquity and injustice upon God, because nothing more unjust can be imagined than for someone to be punished for not doing or providing what he was nevertheless quite unable to provide or do. But according to that doctrine God punishes those who are wicked and disobedient, although it was not in their power to obey God, since by God's unchangeable decree it has been determined that they should not perform the due duties of piety and obedience. So God punishes men for not doing what God himself has decreed they could not do.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The prosyllogism is as follows.

units.la: Ex qua sententia & doctrina sequitur, Deum homines ideo punire quod debita pietatis & obedientiæ officia non præstent, quod tamen vt præstare non possent, Deus æterno & immutabili decreto constituerit, illa Deum summa iniustitia & iniquitatis accusat:
units.tr: From that opinion and doctrine it follows that God punishes men for not performing the due duties of piety and obedience, which, though they could not perform them, God has settled by an eternal and unchangeable decree; that doctrine charges God with the highest injustice and iniquity.

units.la: Atqui ex prædicta sententia & doctrina de prædestinatione sequitur, Deum homines ideo punire, quod debita pietatis & obedientiæ officia non præstent, quæ tamen vt præstare non possent, Deus æterno & immutabili decreto constituerit.
units.tr: But from the aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination it follows that God punishes men for not performing the due duties of piety and obedience, which, though they could not perform them, God has settled by an eternal and unchangeable decree.

units.la: Ergo prædicta illa sententia, ac doctrina de prædestinatione Deum summa iniustitia, & iniquitatis accusat.
units.tr: Therefore that aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination charges God with the highest injustice and iniquity.

units.la: Consequentiæ hanc adfert rationem:
units.tr: He gives this reasoning for the consequence.

units.la: Si nihil iniquius est, nec etiam excogitari potest, quam aliquem ideo puniri, quod non præstiterit id, quod tamen nullo modo præstare potuit,tum ex qua sententia ac doctrina sequitur, Deum homines ideo punire, quod debita obedientiæ & pietatis officia non præstent,quæ tamen vt præstare non possent,Deus æterno & immutabili decreto constituerit, illa Deum summa iniustitia & iniquitatis accusat.
units.tr: If nothing is more unjust, nor can even be imagined, than for someone to be punished for not performing what he could in no way perform, then the doctrine from which it follows that God punishes men for not performing the due duties of obedience and piety, which, though they could not perform them, God has settled by an eternal and unchangeable decree, charges God with the highest injustice and iniquity.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est:
units.tr: But the former is true:

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore so is the latter.

units.la: Secundum assumptionis membrum, quod videlicet prædicta illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione, Deum hypocriseos ac fraudis accusat, ex eo probare conatur, quod Deus iuxta illam sententiam, etiamsi decreuerit, vt maxima pars eorum, quibus verbum Dei annunciatur, interiret, nihilominus tamen per Euangelij prædicationem, omnibus promiscuè salutem offerat, ac proinde aliud præseferat, quam vero in animo habeat, & apud se decreuerit, quod proprie nihil aliud sit. aliud sit quàm hypocrisis, & quidem eo intolerabilior, quod Deus eam in illis rebus exerceat, per quas homines decipiantur. Nam exempli gratia, inquit, Cùm quis audiens Deum per Euangelij prædicationem sibi sub conditione resipiscentia, remissionem peccatorum, ac vitam æternam promittere, omni conatu vitæ emendationi incumbit, in medio autem cursu corruit, quoniam videlicet Deo ita visum est, imò ne ulterius in illo cursu progrediatur, sed penitus concidat, & prosternatur, Deus ipsi gratiam subtrahat, atque ita causa existat, quod ulterius pergere nequeat.
units.tr: For the second member of the minor premise, that the aforesaid opinion and doctrine of predestination charges God with hypocrisy and fraud, he tries to prove from the fact that according to that opinion God, even though he has decreed that the greater part of those to whom the word of God is announced should perish, nevertheless offers salvation to all indiscriminately through the preaching of the gospel. So he displays one thing while holding in mind and having decided another, which is properly nothing other than hypocrisy, and all the more intolerable because God practises it in matters by which men are deceived. For example, he says: when someone, hearing that God promises him through the preaching of the gospel forgiveness of sins and eternal life on condition of repentance, applies himself with every effort to amendment of life, but in the middle of the course falls, because it has so seemed good to God, indeed so that he may not proceed further in that course but be utterly cast down and overthrown, God withdraws grace from him. Thus God becomes the cause that he cannot go on.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The prosyllogism is as follows.

units.la: Ex qua sententia ac doctrina sequitur, Deum etiamsi decreverit, ut maxima pars eorum, quibus verbum Dei annunciatur, pereat, nihilominus tamen omnibus non electis tantùm, verum etiam reprobis promiscuè, & communiter remissionem peccatorum, ac vitam æternâ sub conditione resipiscentia offerre, & ita homines decipere, dum videlicet reprobos vitam æternam sub resipiscentia conditione illis promittendo ad resipiscentiæ studium, & conatum excitet, in medio autem cursu gratiam illis subtrahendo prosternat: illa Deum hypocriseos, ac fraudis accusat.
units.tr: From that opinion and doctrine it follows that God, even though he has decreed that the greater part of those to whom the word of God is announced should perish, nevertheless offers to all indiscriminately, not only the elect but also the reprobate, forgiveness of sins and eternal life on condition of repentance, and so deceives men. For by promising eternal life to the reprobate on condition of repentance he stirs them up to zeal and effort for repentance, but in the middle of the course, by withdrawing grace from them, he casts them down. That doctrine charges God with hypocrisy and fraud.

units.la: Atqui ex sententia & doctrina illa de prædestinatione, sequitur prius:
units.tr: But from that opinion and doctrine of predestination the former follows.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore so does the latter.

units.la: Tertium assumptionis membrum, quod videlicet eadem illa sententia, ac doctrina de prædestinatione, Deo imprudentiam impingat, inde probare conatur, quod Deus (iuxta illam) per Euangelii prædicationem, omnes eos, qui illud audiunt, saltem in speciem, ad vitam aeternam perducere conatur, cum tamen inter illos multi sint, qui ex sententia ac vi infallibilis illius prædestinationis saluari minimè possint. Stultum verò esse, inquit, aliquid efficere conari, quod tamen, nullo modo fieri possit: & hanc imprudentiam tanto maiorem & crassiorem in Deo futuram esse, quod ille haud ignoret, hoc impossibile esse.
units.tr: The third member of the minor premise, that the same opinion and doctrine of predestination charges God with imprudence, he tries to prove from the fact that God (according to it), through the preaching of the gospel, endeavours to bring all who hear it, at least in appearance, to eternal life, although among them there are many who by the force of that infallible predestination cannot be saved at all. It is foolish, he says, to try to bring about what cannot in any way be done; and this imprudence will be all the greater and grosser in God, because he is not ignorant that this is impossible.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The first prosyllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Ex qua sententia, ac doctrina sequitur Deum conari aliquid efficere, quod tamen fieri minimè posset, illa Deum summa imprudentia ac inscitia accusat:
units.tr: From the view and doctrine just stated it follows that God, by such a doctrine, is charged with the greatest folly and ignorance, since he tries to bring about something that cannot in any way come to pass.

units.la: Atqui ex prædicta illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione prius sequitur: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the aforesaid view and doctrine of predestination comes first. Therefore so does the consequence.

units.la: Assumptionis epilogismus talis est:
units.tr: The epilogism of the assumption runs as follows:

units.la: Ex qua sententia ac doctrina sequitur, Deum per Euangelij prædicationem, omnes eos, qui illud audiunt, saltem in speciem, ad vitam æternam perducere conari, cum tamen inter illos multi sint, qui ex sententia ac vi infallibilis illius prædestinationis salvari minimè possint, ex illa etiam sequitur, Deum conari aliquid efficere, quod tamen nullo modo fieri possit.
units.tr: From this view and doctrine it follows that, through the preaching of the Gospel, God tries to bring all who hear it, at least in appearance, to eternal life, although among them there are many who cannot be saved by the terms and power of that infallible predestination. From this it also follows that God tries to bring about something that cannot in any way come to pass.

units.la: Atqui ex prædicta illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione sequitur prius: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But from the aforesaid view and doctrine of predestination the first follows. Therefore so does the second.

units.la: Quartum & vltimum assumptionis membrum, quod videlicet eadem illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione, Deum malitia accuset, inde probare conatur, quod ex illa necessariò sequatur, Deum peccati authorem esse, quum enim ille neminem nisi peccatorem, & ob peccatum condemnet, ideo ipsum non tantùm quinam condemnari, sed etiam quinam peccare debeant, decreuisse.
units.tr: The fourth and last member of the assumption, namely that this same view and doctrine of predestination accuses God of malice, he tries to prove as follows: from it there necessarily follows that God is the author of sin. For since he condemns no one except a sinner, and on account of sin, he has decreed not only who are to be condemned but also who must sin.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The prosyllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Ex qua sententia ac doctrina sequitur, Deum esse peccati autorem, illa Deum malitia accusat:
units.tr: From this view and doctrine it follows that God is the author of sin. By this, God is charged with malice.

units.la: Atqui ex prædicta illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione, sequitur, Deum esse peccati autorem:
units.tr: But from the aforesaid view and doctrine of predestination it follows that God is the author of sin.

units.la: Ergo eadem illa doctrina Deum malitia accusat.
units.tr: Therefore this same doctrine charges God with malice.

units.la: Assumptionis epilogismus talis est.
units.tr: The epilogism of the assumption runs as follows.

units.la: Ex qua sententia & doctrina sequitur, Deum non tantùm quinam condemnari, verùm etiam quinam peccare debeant, decreuisse, ex eadem sequitur, Deum esse peccati autorem.
units.tr: From this view and doctrine it follows that God has decreed not only who are to be condemned but also who must sin; from the same it follows that God is the author of sin.

units.la: Atqui ex prædicta illa sententia ac doctrina de prædestinatione, sequitur prius:
units.tr: But from the aforesaid view and doctrine of predestination the first follows:

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore so does the second.

units.la: Resp. Priusquam singulas illas probationes refutemus, quibus hæc doctrina vt plurimum iniquissimè grauari solet, duo nobis præpræmittenda videntur. Primò videlicet demonstrandum est, hanc ipsam doctrinam de æterna Dei prædestinatione, cuius summam & compendium initio huius capitis proposuimus, ex ipsis scripturæ sacræ fontibus haustam esse, ac proinde nullam illarum absurditatum iure illi impingi posse. Secundò ostendendum, Aduersarii totam disputationem falsa hypothesi niti, nec statum controversiæ bona fide ab ipso formari. Primum quod attinet, ipsam videlicet scripturam sacram euidenter docere, Deum quosdam homines ante iacta mundi fundamenta ad vitam æternam elegisse, reiectis cæteris, & damnationi æternæ destinatis, manifestè docet Paulus ad Ephesios capite primo, versu quarto & quinto: Elegit nos in ipso antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, vt simus sancti & inculpati coram eo per charitatem, qui prædestinauit nos, quos adoptaret in filios, per Iesum Christum in se, pro beneplacito affectu voluntatis suæ. At electio, vbi nulla est reiectio ac reprobatio, locum habere non potest. Sic eximium pro vtraque prædestinationis parte testimonium extat capite vigesimo quinto, versu vigesimo quarto, vbi regnum Dei ante iacta mundi fundamenta, benedictis Patris cœlestis paratum esse dicitur. & versu quadragesimo primo similiter ignis Diabolo & Angelis eius paratus esse perhibetur. Sic Actorum decimotertio, versu quadragesimo octauo, crediderunt dicuntur, quotquot ordinati sunt ad vitam æternam: ex quo loco cum non omnes crediderint, necessariò concluditur, non omnes ad vitam æternam electos esse. Et Christus ipse prædixit, totum genus humanum in vltimo iudicio in duas partes diuidendum esse, videlicet in ordinem benedictorum & saluandorum, & in ordinem maledictorum ac damnandorum, & illos quidem in regnum cœlorum ab æterno ipsis paratum, hos verò in ignem æternum, & Diabolo ac Angelis eius paratum, mittendos esse, Matth. 25. vers. 32. 33. 34. 41. quæ separatio ipsum æternum prædestinationis decretum necessariò præsupponit, quo Deus illis in tempore vitam æternam donare, hos verò perpetuo exitio deuuere apud se constituerit. Quæcumque enim Deus in tempore vult ac facit, ea etiam ab æterno voluit, & se facturum decreuit, quia nota sunt Deo ab æterno omnia opera sua, Act. 15. vers. 18. Quum denique Deus ab æterno decreuerit quibusdam ordinaria suppeditare media, quibus ex statu vitæ animalis, & dominantis peccati, ad vitæ æternæ hæreditatem emergere queant, alios verò in natiua corruptione, & inde iusto Dei iudicio confequuta maledictione relinquere, vnde gratia Dei per illustrem aduentum Iesu Christi fidelibus in Christo Iesu data esse dicitur ante tempora seculària, 2.Tim. 1.ver f.9.10. Sic mysteria regni coelestis à sapientibus abscondita, & infantibus detecta esse dicuntur, Matth. 11.verf.25. cuius discriminis causa in ἀδοξίαι Patris transcribitur verf.26& Christus ipse testatur Discipulis suis datum esse, quod nouerint mysteria regni coelorum, reliquis autem, id est,infidelibus datum non esse. Matt.13.verf.11.ideò liquidò,opinor, constat, illos ad vitam aeternam electos, hos verò damnationi aeternae addictos esse.
units.tr: Reply. Before we refute the individual proofs by which this doctrine is most unjustly burdened, two points seem to us to be set out in advance. The first is that this very doctrine of God's eternal predestination, whose substance and summary we proposed at the beginning of this chapter, has been drawn from the very sources of Holy Scripture, and therefore no such absurdity can rightly be charged against it. The second is that our opponent's whole disputation rests on a false hypothesis, and that he has not formed the state of the controversy in good faith. As to the first point, that Holy Scripture itself clearly teaches that God chose certain men to eternal life before the foundation of the world, the others being passed over and destined to eternal damnation, Paul plainly teaches in Ephesians chapter 1, verses 4 and 5: "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love, who predestined us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will." But election cannot take place where there is no rejection and reprobation. Likewise, there is an outstanding testimony for both parts of predestination in chapter 25, verse 34, where the kingdom of God is said to have been prepared from before the foundation of the world for the blessed of the heavenly Father, and in verse 41, where fire is likewise said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels. So in Acts 13, verse 48, it is said that as many as were ordained to eternal life believed; from this passage, since not all believed, it is necessarily concluded that not all are chosen to eternal life. And Christ himself foretold that at the last judgment the whole human race will be divided into two parts, namely the company of the blessed and the saved, and the company of the cursed and the damned, and that the former will be sent into the kingdom of heaven prepared for them from eternity, and the latter into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25, verses 32, 33, 34, 41). This separation necessarily presupposes the eternal decree of predestination, by which God determined to grant eternal life to those people in time, and to keep the others in perpetual ruin away from himself. For whatever God wills and does in time, he also willed from eternity and decreed to do, since all his works are known to God from eternity (Acts 15, verse 18). Finally, since God has decreed from eternity to supply some with ordinary means by which they may rise from the state of animal life and dominant sin to the inheritance of eternal life, while leaving others in their natural corruption and the curse that follows by the just judgment of God, hence the grace of God is said to have been given to the faithful in Christ Jesus before the ages, through the illustrious coming of Jesus Christ (2 Tim. 1, verses 9, 10). So the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom are said to have been hidden from the wise and revealed to infants (Matt. 11, verse 25), and the cause of this difference is ascribed to the Father's good pleasure [εὐδοκία] in verse 26. And Christ himself testifies that it has been given to his disciples to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but that to the rest, that is, to the unbelievers, it has not been given (Matt. 13, verse 11). Therefore, I think, it is plainly established that the former are chosen to eternal life and the latter are doomed to eternal damnation.

units.la: Alterum verò quod attinet, totam videlicet Aduersarii disputationem falsa hypothesi niti, statumque controuersiae subdolè, & inuidiosè ab ipso proponi, ex eo manifestè apparet,quod thesin illam, qua affirmatur, aeterno,& immutabili decreto, à Deo constitutum esse, de omnibus, quinam ex illis saluari, qui verò damnari, debeant, non directè impugnat sed πεῖσμα & consectarium illi assuit, nullis consequentiae iustae legibus, ex illa thesi deductum, quod videlicet Deus simul decreuerit, non tantum qui boni ac pietatis studiosi,sed etiam qui mali,& impii,existere deberent. Quum tamen illi ipsi, qui praescientiam lapsus, & reliquorum peccatorum, decreto illi de fine hominis vltimo, substernendam esse negant,maximam diuersitatem inter electionis,&reprobationis exequutionem, quod ad media vtriusque attinet statuendam, esse euidenter doceant,& Deum electionis quidem exequendae media, in destinatis ad vitam aeternam, velle,efficere,ac ἐνεργητικῶς operari, sic vt illa decretum electionis, tanquam effectus suam causam,sequantur,reprobationis verò exequendae media,nec velle,nec probare simpliciter, velle tamen illa iustis de causis non impedire, sed permittere, hoc est velle ista,non quoad approbationem,& effectionem à se, verum tantum quoad permissam quandam effectionem ab aliis, sic vt illa media non à voluntate Dei, & ipso decreto eiusdem, sed à voluntate, deficientis creaturae, pendeant; & decretum illud, non vt effectus suam causam, sed vt consequens suum antecedens sequantur,ostendant. Quae quum ambiguitate inuoluat Aduersarius,& confundat,euidenter apparet,statum controuersiae ab ipso peruerti, praesertim quum exquisitae συζητήσεως, & disquisitionis leges non permittant,vt consectaria, quae tanquam ἀτοπα, ac absurda, ex ipsa thesi controuersa eliciuntur, cum ipsa thesi, quae impugnatur ab aduersa parte confundantur, ne cum sententisententiam ac doctrinam Aduersarii refutare nequeat, ea illi affinGere videatur, quæ facile confodere & conuellere possit. Nos igitur consequentiam negamus, de qua in responsione ad profyllogismum vltimum pluribus agemus: nunc ad singula argumenta, quibus assumptionem suam stabilire conatur, ordine responsuri.
units.tr: As to the second point, that our opponent's whole disputation rests on a false hypothesis, and that the state of the controversy is set out by him in a deceitful and spiteful way, this is clear from the fact that he does not directly attack the thesis which affirms that God has determined by an eternal and unchangeable decree who among all men are to be saved and who are to be damned. Instead he attaches to it an appendage [πεῖσμα] and corollary, which by no lawful rule of consequence is drawn from that thesis: namely, that God has decreed at the same time that not only those who are zealous for goodness and piety, but also those who are evil and impious, should exist. Yet those very men who deny that foreknowledge of the fall and of other sins should be placed beneath the decree concerning man's final end, clearly teach that there is the greatest difference between the carrying out of election and of reprobation as far as their means are concerned. They teach that God, in carrying out election, wills, effects and works actively [ἐνεργητικῶς] the means in those destined for eternal life, so that the decree of election follows them as an effect follows its cause. But in carrying out reprobation, God neither wills nor simply approves the means, yet for just reasons he wills not to hinder them but to permit them. That is, he wills them not with respect to approval and effecting by himself, but only with respect to a certain permitted effecting by others; so that those means depend not on God's will and his decree, but on the will of the deficient creature. And they show that the decree follows not as an effect follows its cause, but as a consequence follows its antecedent. Since our opponent involves and confuses these points with ambiguity, it is plainly evident that he twists the state of the controversy, especially since the rules of exact argument and inquiry do not permit the corollaries which are drawn from the disputed thesis as absurd [ἄτοπα] and ridiculous to be confused with the thesis itself that is attacked by the other side. Otherwise he could not refute the opinion and doctrine of his opponent, and it would seem that he is ascribing to it things which he can easily overthrow and demolish. We therefore deny the consequence, which we shall discuss at more length in the reply to the last prosyllogism. Now we shall answer the individual arguments by which he tries to establish his assumption, in order.

units.la: Ad primum igitur respondeo, Assumptionem epilogismi simpliciter & vniuersaliter enuntiatam, esse falsam, vt capite antecedente à nobis est demonstratum, vbi ostendimus, Deum, quia homo omnibus illis virtutibus, & gratiæ diuinæ dotibus, quibus, ipsius creationis beneficio, tam excellenter instructus fuit, vt Deo perfectam obedientiam, si voluisset, præstare potuisset, per impietatem & inobedientiam, seipsum spoliauit, & iuste ipsum hominem punire posse, quoties debitæ obedientiæ officia non præstat, & iure optimo exactissimam obedientiam, etiamsi illam suo vitio suaque culpa præstare nequeat, ab ipso postulare: homo siquidem, licet peccando gratiæ collatæ ornamenta perdiderit, Deum tamen suo iure creationis, propter quod ipsi cultus & obedientia ab homine debetur, spoliare minime potuerit. Atque hoc ipsum, licet ad convellendum Aduersarii argumentum sufficiat, tamen profyllogismum ipsum quoque examinare lubet. Verùm quia connexi pars antecedens obscura laborat ambiguitate, ideo illam ante omnia tollemus. Non enim aliquid præstare posse, vt duobus modis dicitur, ita causæ eiusmodi præsupponuntur, pro quarum diuersitate, diuersum admodum de illa consequentia, vt & de assumptione, exstit iudicium. Nam quum homo debitæ obedientiæ, & pietatis officia, non posse præstare dicitur, duobus modis id intelligi potest, vel propter negationem potentiæ ac facultatis ad illa præstanda necessario requisitæ, vel propter negationem actus, qua videlicet potentia, facultas, & inclinatio per extrinsecum obstaculum impeditur, quo minus homo officium debitum actu ipso præstare possit. Si itaque Aduersarius per illam phrasin negationem actus intelligat, qua videlicet homo, qui alioquin inclinatione ac desiderio ad officium pietatis aspiret, & sufficientibus viribus ad illud præstandum sit instructus, sed vi illius decreti diuini, ac æternæ prædestinationis impediatur, quo minus actu & re ipsa munere suo fungi possit, tum consequentia vera est, sed assumptio falsa ac impia, quia Deus respipiscere, aut debitæ obedientiæ ac pietatis officia præstare volentem, minime impedit, sed iuuat, excitat, & confirmat, iuxta illud, Quisquis habet, ei dabitur, & reddetur abundantior: Matth. 13. verf. 12. & Phil. 1. verf. 6. Persuasum habens hoc ipsum, ut qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiat usque ad diem Iesu Christi: Et qui operatur velle Deus, idem etiam operatur perficere. Phil. 2. verf. 13. Et impium illud effatum, quod videlicet decretum praedestinationis, resipiscere volentibus, sit obstaculo, sententiae ac doctrinae Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quam ex ipsis Scripturae sacrae fontibus haustam esse demonstrauimus, falso impingitur. Sin vero Aduersarius per illam phrasin negationem facultatis, & virium, ad obedientiam Deo praestandam requisitarum, intelligat, tum huius quoque negationis causae, quae variae esse possunt, accurate sunt distinguendae. Decretum enim praedestinationis, quod iam ἀιτιαμίας illius causa statuetur, vel ut efficiens, vel ut deficiens illius impotentiae causa considerari potest, ac debet, hoc est, homo reprobus propter decretum praedestinationis, debita obedientiae officia praestare ideo non posse dicetur, vel quia Deus hominem nunquam sufficientibus viribus, ad debitam, quam exigit ab illo, obedientiam praestandam, instruxerit: vel quod eundem gratiae sufficientibus ornamentis ac dotib. ornauerit quidem, sed iisdem ipsum, ut praedestinationi exequedae viam sterneret, sine ante cedente peccati merito rursus spoliauerit: vel denique quod Deus hominem reprobum, qui seipsum imaginis diuinae, & iustitiae originalis gratia per inobedientiam priuauit, eadem non denuo exornare: sed in natiua miseria, & iniquitate derelinquere constituerit. Si priori modo decretum praedestinationis diuinae, illius ἀιτιαμίας causa statuatur, tu vera est consequentia, sed assumptio falsa. Hominem enim ante lapsum omnibus donis ac virtutibus, ad perfectam obedietiam diuinae voluntati praestandam, ipsius creationis beneficio, a Deo instructum fuisse, cap. 26. vigesimo septimo solide a nobis est demonstratum. Si secundo modo illius causae respectu decretum illud praedestinationis induatur, tum consequentia iterum vera, at assumptio falsa fuerit. Inobedientiam enim & impietatem hominis causam extitisse, quare illo iusto Dei iudicio dotib. illis imaginis diuinae, quibus excellucrat priuatus fuerit, in praedicto cap. ostendimus, & ex Scripturis ipsius qui cōstat illam humanae naturae corruptione, hominis peccatū, & inni obedientia infequuta esse. Si vero tertio modo & sensu phrasis intelligatur, tu assumptio quidem vera est, sed consequentia falsa, quia Deus liberrimus omniū Dominus, nemini gratiam restituere re tenetur, nec iniuriam nobis facturus fuisset, si totum genus humanum propter inobedientiam in aeternum exitium praecipitasset: &miseretur cuius vult misereri, Rom.9.verf.15. & ipsi liberum est gratiam dare quantam, &quibus vult: Matt.20. verf.15. An non licet mihi facere quod volo in meis? Ex quibus omnibus iam euidenter apparet, primam illam calumniam doctrinae nostrae, neutiquam impingi posse.
units.tr: To the first, then, I answer that the minor premise of the epilogism, stated simply and universally, is false. I demonstrated this in the preceding chapter, where we showed that God, having been stripped by man's impiety and disobedience of all those virtues and gifts of divine grace with which man was so excellently furnished by the benefit of creation that he could have rendered God perfect obedience had he wished, may justly punish man whenever he fails to perform the duties of due obedience, and may rightly demand the most exact obedience from him, even though man cannot render it through his own fault and guilt. For although by sinning man has lost the adornments of the grace bestowed on him, he could by no means deprive God of his right as Creator, by virtue of which worship and obedience are owed to God by man. This, though it is enough to overthrow the adversary's argument, we also wish to examine in the prosyllogism itself. But since the antecedent part of the connection suffers from an obscure ambiguity, we shall first remove it. For "to be able to do something" is used in two senses, and the grounds presupposed differ, and according to their difference the judgment on that consequence, and likewise on the minor premise, is quite different. For when it is said that man "cannot perform" the duties of due obedience and piety, this can be understood in two ways: either because of the lack of the power and capacity necessarily required for performing them, or because of the lack of the act, namely where the power, capacity and inclination are hindered by some external obstacle, so that man cannot actually perform the duty owed. If therefore the adversary understands by that phrase the lack of the act, namely where a man who otherwise aspires with inclination and desire to the duty of piety, and is furnished with sufficient strength to perform it, is nevertheless hindered by the force of a divine decree and eternal predestination from actually discharging his office in deed, then the consequence is true, but the minor premise is false and impious. For God does not hinder one who wishes to repent or to perform the duties of due obedience and piety, but helps, stirs up and strengthens him, according to that saying: "To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance" (Matt. 13:12); and Phil. 1:6: "being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will carry it on until the day of Jesus Christ"; and "for it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Phil. 2:13). And that impious assertion, that the decree of predestination is an obstacle to those willing to repent, is falsely hurled against the doctrine and teaching of our Churches, which we have shown to be drawn from the very fountains of holy Scripture. But if the adversary by that phrase understands the lack of power and of the strengths required for rendering obedience to God, then the causes of this lack, which may be various, must also be carefully distinguished. For the decree of predestination, which is set up as the cause of this inability, can be considered and ought to be considered either as the efficient or as the deficient cause of that inability. That is, a reprobate man will be said not to be able to perform the duties of due obedience because of the decree of predestination either because God never furnished him with sufficient strength to render the due obedience which he requires; or because God indeed adorned him with sufficient gifts of grace, but then stripped him of the same again, without any preceding merit of sin, in order to pave the way for carrying out predestination; or finally because God resolved not to adorn again with grace the reprobate man, who by disobedience had deprived himself of the grace of the divine image and original righteousness, but to leave him in his native misery and iniquity. If the decree of divine predestination is set up as the cause of this inability in the first way, then the consequence is true, but the minor premise is false. For we have solidly demonstrated in chapter 27 that man before the fall was furnished by God with all the gifts and virtues needed to render perfect obedience to the divine will, by the benefit of his creation. If the decree of predestination is considered in the second way with respect to that cause, then again the consequence is true, but the minor premise false. For we have shown in the aforesaid chapter that the disobedience and impiety of man was the cause why, by that just judgment of God, he was deprived of those gifts of the divine image by which he had excelled; and from Scripture itself it is clear that the corruption of human nature, the sin of man, and the disobedience that followed it, are the cause. But if the phrase is understood in the third way and sense, then the minor premise is indeed true, but the consequence false. For God, the most free Lord of all, is bound to restore grace to no one, nor would he have done us any injustice if he had cast the whole human race into eternal destruction because of disobedience: "he has mercy on whom he wills to have mercy" (Rom. 9:15), and it is lawful for him to give grace as much as and to whom he wills (Matt. 20:15): "Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is mine?" From all these things it now clearly appears that the first calumny against our doctrine cannot in any way be fixed upon it.

units.la: Ad 11.respondeo, Assumptionem esse salsissimam, & multiplici errore laborare. Nam primo falsum est, salutis gratia omnibus sine cuiusquam exceptione hominibus offerri. Quid enim statuendum esset de tot hominum myriadibus, prius ex hac vita excedentibus, quam de Christo minimum quicquam audiendo acceperint?quid de tot populis, ac gentibus, quos & ante aduentum Christi, Deus, vt loquitur Apostolus Act.14.verf.16. fuit in ipsorum viis (quae quia nihil nisi merae fuerunt tenebrae, non nisi ad exitium illos potuerunt ducere) per tot secula errare, & incedere, & iam pridem propter Euangelii contemptu deseruit, & adhuc hodie deserit? Quid denique de multis Indorum populis, qui pluribus post Christum natu sese culis, demum a Christianis indagati, ac reperti, de veritate, & luce Euangelii prius ne quidem nuntiu vllu acceperunt? Quod si Deo eandem voluntate ab initio mundi constitisse certum est, & ille omnibus nota esse voluit sua veritate, & salutis gratia, Cur igitur legem suam non etiam Getibus publicauit, sed inclusam in Iudeeq angustiis tenuit vitae lucem? Cur in praefatione legis tantum Israelitas, non vero omnes populos, aut populorum singulos copellauit? Quid sibi vult illud Mosis Gentis Israeliticae praerogatiuas recensentis Deut. 4. v.6. vbi inquit, Non esse Gentem, quae statuta & leges habeat, quibus regatur, quemadmodum populus ille? Cui & illud Dauidis encomiu respondet, Non ita fecit vlli populo, nec sua iudicia manifestauit illis Psal.14.v.20. Quin & Prophetas nec missos esse ad omnes gentes, neque omnib. Getibus scripsisse constat: & Paulus ipse non ignorauit, se prohibitum esse a Spiritu,ne in Asia verba de Christo faceret, & ne transiret in Bithyniam,quo pergebat,Act.16.v.6. Denique Christus ipse non omnes sed multos vocatos, & ex hisce paucos electos esse dicit, Matt,20.v.16. Et hoc speciale promittitur Ecclesiae donum,quod super ipsam orietur Dominus, & gloria eius illic conspicua erit, Esa.6.v.2. Quod si igitur nec tempore Mosis ac Prophetarum, nec tempore Christi, & Apostolorum omnibus & singulis, gratia illa & doctrina salutaris
units.tr: To the second, I answer that the minor premise is most false and labours under many errors. For, first, it is false that the grace of salvation is offered to all men without any exception. For what must be said of the countless multitudes of men who departed from this life before they had heard anything at all about Christ? What of so many peoples and nations, whom God, as the Apostle says, "allowed to walk in their own ways" (Acts 14:16)—which, since they were nothing but sheer darkness, could lead them only to destruction—for so many ages, and whom he long ago abandoned on account of contempt for the Gospel, and still abandons today? What finally of the many peoples of the Indies, who, discovered and found by Christians only many centuries after Christ, had never received any message at all of the truth and light of the Gospel? But if it is certain that God from the beginning of the world had the same will, and wished his truth and the grace of salvation to be known to all, why then did he not also publish his law to the Gentiles, but kept the light of life enclosed within the narrow bounds of the Jews? Why did he address in the preface of the law only the Israelites, and not all peoples or individual peoples? What does that saying of Moses mean, recounting the privileges of the Israelite nation (Deut. 4:6), where he says that there is no nation which has statutes and laws by which it is governed, like that people? To this the praise of David also corresponds: "He has not done so for any nation, nor made known his judgments to them" (Ps. 147:20). Indeed it is agreed that the prophets were not sent to all nations, nor wrote to all Gentiles; and Paul himself was not unaware that he was forbidden by the Spirit to speak the word about Christ in Asia, and not to go into Bithynia, where he was heading (Acts 16:6). Finally Christ himself says that not all but many are called, and of these few are chosen (Matt. 20:16). And this special gift is promised to the Church: "the Lord will arise upon her, and his glory will be seen there" (Isa. 60:2). If therefore neither in the time of Moses and the prophets, nor in the time of Christ and the Apostles, was that grace and saving doctrine offered to all and to each,

units.la: [marginal notes on the left edge are only partly legible and are not transcribed] oblata fuit,dicat & demõstret Oftorrodius,quomodo,& quo tempore illa vniuerfalitas coeperit ? Quo fine vero etiam in Ecclesia, gratia Dei per Euangelii prædicationem offeratur, qui tamen ad damnationem ƺternam sunt destinati,ex refponfione ad argumentum tertium patebit. Secundo præfupponitur hypothesis falsa, videlicet hominem reprobum , ac nondum regenitum proprio conatu vita emendationi incumbere posse. Homines enim ψχικὸι & extraChriftum constitutos,quales sunt reprobi omnes, nec intelligere, nec velle, nec perficere posse res bonas ac spirituales,quæ videlicet ad veram pietatem,verumque Dei cultum pertinent, capite vigefimo sexto & vigefimo septimo , prolixe & luculenter ex Scripturis ipsis est demonstratum : quem igitur conatum,aut quas vires, quodve desiderium ad percurrendum illud pietatis stadium Aduersarius illis tribuit?Vnde tertio falsum quoque est,Deum illos per gratiæ suæ subtractionẽ,ab illo conatu & studio auellere ac deiicere, quasi vero Deus iustissimus ille iudex,aut grauissimam illam pœnam,nempe gratiæ suæ priuationem, vlli infligat, nisi qui seipsum impietate & peccatis illa indignum reddiderit, & Deum prius deseruerit , aut resipiscere volentibus suo decreto obsistat. Semper enim verum est illud Christi,Quisquis habet,ei dabitur,& reddetur abundantior. Mat. 13. verf.12. Neque ideo tantum reprobi non credunt neque resipiscunt, quia Deus ipsis non omnia illa media suppeditare decreuit, quibus fides efficaciter in ipsis gignatur , verum maxime quia illi resipiscere nolunt,sed omnem Dei gratiam repudiant ac aspernantur. Vtrumque vide in sequentibus scripturæ dictis:Matth. capite 11.verf.25.26. Confiteor tibi Pater Domine cæli & terræ,quod abfcondeᵴ hæc à sapientibus & intelligentibus,& ea detexeris infantibus,etiam Pater,quia ita placuit tibi: & cap.13.verf.11. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni cœlorum, illis autem (nempe infidelibus & reprobis) non est datum. Rom.2.verf.4.5. An copiam benignitatis eius,& tolerantiæ, ac lenitatis contemnis , ignorans te benignitate Dei ad refipifcentiam deducit? Sed pro duritia & corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizas tibi ipfiiram,in diem iræ, & patefactionis iusti iudicij Dei. Iohan.12.verf. 37.38.39.40. Quum autem tot signa coram eis edidisset , non credebant in eum, vt sermo Efaiæ Prophetæ impleretur , quem dixit, Domine quis credit sermoni nostro,& brachium Domini cui reuelatum est? Propterea non poterant credere,quia iterum dixit Efaias , Excæcauit oculos eorum,& obduruauit corda eorum,ne videant oculis,& intelligant corde,& con- uerlam. uertantur, & sanem eos. Ex quibus omnibus iam iterum apparet, sententiam ac doctrinam nostram de praedestinatione, etiam a secundi criminis obiecti culpa immunem esse.
units.tr: offered, let Ostorodius say and demonstrate how and at what time that universality began. But for what purpose the grace of God is offered in the Church through the preaching of the Gospel even to those who have nonetheless been destined to eternal damnation, will become clear from the answer to the third argument. Second, a false hypothesis is presupposed, namely that a reprobate man, not yet regenerated, can by his own effort apply himself to the improvement of his life. For men who are natural (ψυχικοί) and placed outside Christ, such as all the reprobate are, can neither understand, nor will, nor accomplish good and spiritual things, which pertain to true piety and the true worship of God; this has been demonstrated at length and clearly from Scripture itself in chapters 26 and 27. What effort, then, or what powers, or what desire does the adversary attribute to them for running that course of piety? Hence, third, it is also false that God, by withdrawing his grace, tears them away and casts them down from that effort and zeal, as if that most just judge inflicted this most grievous punishment, namely the deprivation of his grace, on anyone except one who has made himself unworthy of it by impiety and sins, and has first forsaken God, or who opposes his decree to those willing to repent. For that saying of Christ is always true: "To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance" (Matt. 13:12). Nor do the reprobate therefore not believe and not repent merely because God has not decreed to supply them with all those means by which faith is effectively begotten in them; but chiefly because they are unwilling to repent, and reject and spurn all the grace of God. See both in the following sayings of Scripture: Matt. 11:25–26: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants; yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight"; and Matt. 13:11: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them (namely the unbelieving and reprobate) it has not been given." Rom. 2:4–5: "Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, forbearance and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But because of your hardness and your impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God." John 12:37–40: "Although he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he spoke: 'Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they should not see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.'" From all these things it again appears that our doctrine of predestination is free even from the guilt of the second charge brought against it.

units.la: Ad tertium respondeo, eius quoque assumptionem esse falsam: Deum enim conari illos, quos ad exitium, ac damnationem aeternam destinauit, ad resipiscentiam & salutem perducere, per Euangelii praedicationem, nullo modo ex praedicta sententia, ac doctrina de praedestinatione, sequitur, & per se quoque falsum est. Quoscunque enim Deus conatur, id est, vult in tempore, ad salutem ac vitam aeternam perducere, voluntate videlicet non signi tantum, sed etiam beneplaciti, ii quoque certo ad salutem perducuntur, quia quascunque vult Deus, ea facit in coelo, in terra, & omnibus abyssis, Psal. 135. verf. 6. & iis quoque omnia suppeditat media, & gratiae subsidia, quibus ad vitam aeternam perduci, & sine quibus salutem consequi non possunt: quum vero non tantum externam Euangelii praedicationem, sed maxime internam Spiritus sancti gratiam, illuminationem, virtutem & efficaciam homini necessariam esse, ad hoc, ut ad resipiscentiam permoveatur, & per veram fidem in Christum, remissionem peccatorum consequuntur ad vitam aeternam perducatur, ex iis, quae de liberi arbitrii viribus disseruimus, liquido constet, & Deus hominibus reprobis efficacem illam gratiam non largiatur: ideo euidenter apparet, ipsum licet etiam reprobis nonnullis gratiam & remissionem peccatorum, sub conditione fidei ac resipiscentiae, quam illi sua culpa nunquam praestare possunt, per externam Euangelii praedicationem offerat, minime hoc conari, ut reprobos ad resipiscentiam ac vitam aeternam perducat. Neque etiam hic finis Deo propositus esse confingendus est, quasi dum electos & reprobos communiter compellat voce Euangelii, eos quos iusto suo iudicio reprobauit, & ad damnationem aeternam destinauit, ex albo reproborum ac damnadorum, in album electorum ac saluandorum transferat, sed ut electi ministerio verbi ad destinatum finem, nempe vitam aeternam perducantur, reliquis vero omnis excusationis praetextus adimatur, quippe qui fateri cogantur se nec inuitos, nec coactos, sed spontanea voluntate gratiam oblatam repudiasse. Unde apparet Deum iustissimum iudicem no hypocritam, sed hypocritarum & hypocriseos vindicem ac vltorem esse. Et sic tertium quoque crimen, sententiae ac doctrinae nostrae de praedestinatione, ab Aduersario intentatum, ab illa amoliti fumus.
units.tr: To the third point I reply that its assumption is also false. It does not follow from the aforesaid teaching and doctrine of predestination that God endeavours, through the preaching of the Gospel, to bring to repentance and salvation those whom he has destined to destruction and eternal damnation. The claim is false in itself as well. For whomever God endeavours, that is, wills in time to bring to salvation and eternal life, by a will not only of sign but also of good pleasure, these are certainly brought to salvation, because "whatever the Lord pleases, he does in heaven, on earth, and in all the deeps" (Psal. 135. v. 6). To these he also supplies all the means and aids of grace, without which they cannot be brought to eternal life or attain salvation. Since it is clear from what we have argued about the powers of free will that man needs not only the external preaching of the Gospel but, above all, the inward grace, illumination, power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, so that he may be moved to repentance, obtain forgiveness of sins through true faith in Christ, and be brought to eternal life, and since God does not bestow that effective grace on reprobate men, it is plainly evident that God, although through the external preaching of the Gospel he offers even to some reprobate grace and forgiveness of sins on the condition of faith and repentance (which they can never render by their own fault), does not at all intend thereby to bring the reprobate to repentance and eternal life. Nor is this end to be imagined as proposed by God, as if, when he addresses the elect and the reprobate alike by the voice of the Gospel, he transfers those whom by his just judgment he has reprobated and destined to eternal damnation from the roll of the reprobate and the damned into the roll of the elect and the saved. Rather, the elect are brought by the ministry of the Word to the appointed end, namely eternal life, while every pretext of excuse is taken from the rest, who are forced to confess that they rejected the offered grace not unwillingly nor under compulsion, but by their own spontaneous will. Hence it is clear that God is the most just judge, not a hypocrite, but the avenger and punisher of hypocrites and hypocrisy. And so we have also removed from our doctrine and teaching of predestination the third charge brought against it by the Adversary.

units.la: Ad quartum, & vltimum: respondeo Assumptionem profyllogifmi esse falsam, epilogifmum vero fallaci ambiguitate laborare. Nam quum Deus decreuisse dicitur, quinam in tempore peccatores existere debeant, decretum vel de efficiendo, vel de permittendo peccato, & in exequutione ipsa, vel operatio Dei efficax, qua videlicet Deus peccatum approbet, efficiat, & ipsas causas fecundas, & creaturas peccantes ad malum perpetrandum inclinet, sic vt peccatum ipsum, decretum illud, & eius exequutionem, tanquam effectus suam causam sequatur, vel operans permissio, qua videlicet Deus peccatum, quod tamen vehementissime odit, improbat, atque punit, iustissimis de causis non vult impedire, sed permittit, denique creaturę peccantis in permissa miseria desertio, prsfupponitur. Si posteriori modo Deus decreuisse intelligatur, quinam peccatores existere debeant, cum peccatum permissioni diu nae vt causae imputari nequeat, consequentia falsa est, sed assumptio vera, fi priori modo intelligatur, tum consequentia quidem vera est, sed assumptio falsa, nec vel apparente tantum consequentia, ex prædicta Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententia de prædestinatione, impia illa, & plane blasphema thesis educi potest, quod videlicet Deus peccatum approbet, efficiat, ac ipsas causas fecundas ad peccandum inclinet, atque ita peccati autor, & causa existit. Causam enim tum lapsus primorum parentum, tum etiam reliquorum peccatorum omnium, veram proximam, ac propriam non in Dei decreto, sed libera hominis voluntate, quaeredam, & Adamu non vi aut instinctu alicuius decreti diuini, sed diaboli inftigatione, spontanea voluntate, liberrimóque arbitrio, & proprio cordis motu, impulsum, à Deo fe alienaffe, lapsúmque esse, Deũ item non tantũ iustissimis de causis, & fine omni culpa, lapsum illũ permiffiffe, verũ etiam quosdam in peccatis ac miseria derelinquere, nec illis media illa suppeditare, quibus ex illa emergant, sancte credimus, ac profitemur, nec tamē vllā culpam in Deum deriuari posse, tum ex Scriptura sacra, tũ confcietiæ humanæ testimonio, solide demonstramus: Illa enim docet Deum non tantum iustum esse in omnibus viis suis, Pfal. 145 v. 17. qui non velit iniquitatem, Pfal. 5. v. 5. qui diligens iustitiam, odio prosequatur iniquitatem, Pfalm. 45. v. 8. cum omnibus operantibus iniquitatem, Pfalm. 5. v. 5. & qui peccati autor nullo modo existat, Deu. 32. v. 4. Zichar. 8. v. 17. Iacob. 1. v. 13. 1, Ioh. 2. v. 16. verum etiam liberrimum, & nemini obligatum esse, sic vt peccatum permittere,& hominem peccatorem,in sua iniquitate, & miseria deserere possit,nec ipsum inde liberare teneatur, Rom. 9. v. 15. Miserebor cuius misertus fuero, & commiserabor, quem commiseratus fuero:& 11. v. 35. Quis prior dedit ei,vt retribuat ei? Matt. 20. v. 15. Anno licet mihi facere de meo,quod volo? Ipsa vero conscientia Deum omnis culpae expertè esse testatur, quia omnes sentimus, & fateri cogimur,nos nec coactos,nec inuitos, sed sponte cocupiscentiis carnis, & voluntati Satanae obsequi, studioque mali delectari, adeoque & concupiscere.& studiosè sectari,& cum delectatione perficere quod malum est : libera autem, & non coacta voluntas est in concupiscentia praecedente, in studio subsequente, & tandem in operis delectatione. Quum igitur docceamus Deum decreto providentiae,peccata permittere statuisse,& decreto praedestinationis ex illa corrupta generis humani massa quoidam ad vitam aeternam eligere, omniaque media ipsis suppeditare, quibus ad salutè perdu-cantur, alios vero in peccatis suis relinquere , & postmodum condemnare decreuisse, ac proinde praedestinatione electis dari vt boni sint,& bonum assequantur,reprobis vero non vt mali sint,sed vt malum assequantur : ideo euidenter apparet, illam blasphemiam, quod videlicet Deus peccati autor constituatur, doctrinae & sententiae Ecclesiarum nostrarum, non nisi per apertam & iniquissimam calumniam imputari posse. Et quia Aduersarius suum,quem refutamus,librum,illo titulo Institutiones Religionis Christianae, insigniuit, ideo hanc controuersiam, non tantum διαοκδ. sed etiam καθαοκδ. tractare debuisset, vt iustae νομικ. leges a docentibus exigunt.
units.tr: To the fourth and last point I reply that the assumption of the prosyllogism is false, and the epilogism labours under a fallacious ambiguity. For when it is said that God has decreed who in time ought to exist as sinners, the decree may be understood either concerning the bringing about or the permitting of sin. In the first case, the execution is God's efficacious operation, by which he approves sin, brings it about, and inclines the secondary causes and the sinning creatures themselves to perpetrate evil, so that sin itself, that decree and its execution follow as effects from their cause. In the second case, the execution is an operative permission, by which God, for most just reasons, does not wish to hinder sin, which nevertheless he most vehemently hates, disapproves and punishes, but permits. In this case the abandonment of the sinning creature to the misery permitted is presupposed. If God is understood to have decreed in the second way who ought to exist as sinners, the consequence is false, since sin cannot be imputed to God's permission as a cause, but the assumption is true. If it is understood in the first way, the consequence is indeed true but the assumption is false. Nor can that impious and plainly blasphemous thesis, namely that God approves and brings about sin, inclines the secondary causes themselves to sin, and so is the author and cause of sin, be drawn even in appearance from the aforesaid teaching of our Churches on predestination. For we piously believe and profess, and solidly demonstrate both from Holy Scripture and from the testimony of human conscience, that the true, proximate and proper cause of the fall of the first parents, and of all the other sins, lies not in God's decree but in the free will of man. Adam fell, turning away from God, not by the force or impulse of any divine decree, but by the instigation of the devil, by spontaneous will, by most free choice and by his own motion of heart. We also believe that God not only permitted that fall for most just reasons and without any fault, but also leaves some in sins and misery and does not supply them with the means by which they might rise out of it, and yet no blame can be derived to God. For Scripture teaches that God is not only just "in all his ways" (Psal. 145. v. 17), that he is one "who does not will iniquity" (Psal. 5. v. 5), "who, loving justice, pursues iniquity with hatred" (Psal. 45. v. 8), and "hates all who work iniquity" (Psal. 5. v. 5), and that he is in no way the author of sin (Deut. 32. v. 4; Zech. 8. v. 17; Jacob. 1. v. 13; 1 John 2. v. 16). It teaches too that he is most free and bound to no one, so that he can permit sin and leave the sinning man in his iniquity and misery, and is under no obligation to deliver him from it (Rom. 9. v. 15: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion on whom I have compassion"; Rom. 11. v. 35: "Who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him?"; Matt. 20. v. 15: "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own?").
