Conscience itself testifies that God is free of all fault, for we all feel, and are forced to confess, that we obey the lusts of the flesh and the will of Satan not unwillingly nor under compulsion, but spontaneously, and that we take delight in evil, desire it, eagerly pursue it, and carry it out with pleasure. The will is free and uncoerced in the preceding desire, in the subsequent zeal, and finally in the delight of the deed. Since therefore we teach that God by the decree of providence resolved to permit sins, and by the decree of predestination chose some out of that corrupt mass of mankind to eternal life, supplying them with all the means by which they are brought to salvation, but left others in their sins and afterwards resolved to condemn them, so that by predestination the elect are given to be good and to attain the good, while the reprobate are not given to be evil but to attain evil: it is therefore evident that the blasphemy, that God is made the author of sin, can be imputed to the doctrine and teaching of our Churches only through an open and most iniquitous calumny. And since the Adversary has adorned the book he refutes with the title Institutes of the Christian Religion, he ought to have treated this controversy not only in part but also as a whole, as the just laws of teachers require.

units.la: Atque haec de prima disputationis parte, progredien dum igitur nunc est ad secundam, in qua promittit Aduersarius se ex infinitis Scripturae sacrae testimoniis, unicum allegaturum esse, quod sententiam ac doctrinam illam de praedestinatione, falsitatis solide conuincat. Illud autem extare ait, 1. Iohan. capite 2. verf. 2. Et ipse (videlicet Christus) est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro (peccatis) totius mundi. Quibus verbis nihil aliud significari, inquit Aduersarius, quam Christum quantum in ipso est, paratum esse, non tantum ad illorum, qui iam in ipsum credunt, sed etiam ad reliquorum omnium miserandum, debitaque poenas peccatorum ipsorum ab illis remouendum:quod verum esse non possit, si praedestinationis decreto, multi à beneficij illius participatione sint exclusi.
units.tr: And this is enough on the first part of the disputation. We now proceed to the second, in which the Adversary promises that, from the infinite testimonies of Holy Scripture, he will cite one only, which solidly convicts that doctrine and teaching of predestination of falsity. He says that this is found in 1 John chapter 2 verse 2: "And he himself (namely Christ) is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the (sins of the) whole world." By these words, says the Adversary, nothing else is signified than that Christ, so far as it lies in him, is prepared not only to have mercy on those who already believe in him, but also to remove the punishment due for their sins from all the others. This cannot be true if, by the decree of predestination, many are excluded from participation in that benefit.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Si multi æterno Dei decreto & prædestinatione, à mortis Christi participatione sunt reiecti & exclusi, tum sequitur verum non esse, quod Christus paratus sit, non tantum ad illorum qui in ipsum credunt, sed etiam reliquorum omnium commiserandum, debitāsque peccatorum ipsorum pœnas, ab illis remouendum & tollendum.
units.tr: If, by the eternal decree and predestination of God, many are rejected and excluded from participation in the death of Christ, then it follows that it is not true that Christ is ready not only to take away from those who believe in him, but also from all the rest, the punishment due for their sins and to remove it from them.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum esse, ex citato Scriptura testimonio liquet: Ergo & antecedens falsum est.
units.tr: But that the consequent is false is clear from the cited testimony of Scripture. Therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Resp. Nos tum assumptionem ipsam examinabimus, tum genuinum postea citati ex Scriptura testimonii sensum exponemus. Assumptionem quod attinet, apparet hanc esse Aduersariorum sententiam: Christum videlicet ex æquo mortuum esse pro omnibus hominibus, nullo electorum & reproborum habito discrimine, ita ut omnes servari possent, si vellent, quod autem non omnes seruentur, causam esse, quod non omnes recipiant & amplectantur gratiam Christi, quod ut facerent, in ipsorum potestate erat. Liberum enim Arbitrium cum Pelagianis asserit, ut ex præcedente disputatione apparet. Nostrarum vero Ecclesiarum, & omnium orthodoxorum sententia est, Christum Dominum ac Seruatorem nostrum, perfectissimam quidem hostiam Deo Patri obtulisse, quae delendis omnium hominum peccatis sufficiens esset, nullo excepto, si & omnibus illa destinata esset, & omnibus esset datum ut Christum reciperent, & vera fide gratiam in eo datam amplecterentur. Iam vero ad solos electos pertinere Christi beneficium, quorum etiam fides propria sit ex Dei dono, ac peculiaris. Vt tota salus nostra gratuita Dei misericordia sit adscribenda. Illam vero Aduersarii sententiam refutant, & hanc orthodoxam demonstrant, nostri passim, euidentibus testimoniis, & grauissimis argumentis, ex scriptura ipsa desumptis, ex quibus nos aliquot tantum adducemus.
units.tr: Reply. We will examine both the assumption itself and then set out the genuine sense of the testimony cited from Scripture. As for the assumption, it appears that this is the opponents' view: that Christ died equally for all men, with no distinction made between elect and reprobate, so that all could be saved if they wished, and that the reason not all are saved is that not all receive and embrace the grace of Christ, which it was in their own power to do. For he maintains free will with the Pelagians, as is clear from the preceding disputation. But the view of our Churches and of all the orthodox is that Christ our Lord and Saviour offered to God the Father a most perfect sacrifice, which would have been sufficient to blot out the sins of all men without exception, if it had been intended for all and if it had been given to all that they should receive Christ and embrace with true faith the grace given in him. Now the benefit of Christ pertains to the elect alone, whose faith too is their own and peculiar, and is from the gift of God, so that our whole salvation is to be ascribed to the free mercy of God. Our writers everywhere refute the opponents' view and demonstrate this orthodox one, by clear testimonies and weighty arguments drawn from Scripture itself; of these we shall adduce only a few.

units.la: Axioma primum.
units.tr: First axiom.

units.la: Quos Deus per Christum seruare decreuit, iis etiam spem fecit eius rei per euidentes promissiones: Vnde beneficium mortis Christi ad eos solos spectat, ad quos etiam promissio eius pertinet. Sumus enim secundum promissionem hæredes, Gal. 3. vers. 29. Quod si vos estis Christi, nempe semen Abrahæ estis, & secundum promissionem hæredes.
units.tr: Those whom God has decided to save through Christ, to them he has also given hope of this by clear promises. Hence the benefit of Christ's death belongs only to those to whom his promise also belongs. For we are heirs according to the promise, Gal. 3. ver. 29. For if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.

units.la: Argumentum tale est.
units.tr: The argument is this.

units.la: Ad quos proprië pertinet promissio Redemptionis per mortem Christi factæ, pro iis etiam solis Christus mortuus est: Atqui ad solos electos promissio Redemptionis per mortem Christi factæ proprië pertinet. Ergo etiam pro solis electis Christus mortuus est.
units.tr: Christ died only for those to whom the promise of redemption made through the death of Christ properly belongs. But the promise of redemption made through the death of Christ properly belongs only to the elect. Therefore Christ died only for the elect.

units.la: Prosyllogismus Minoris.
units.tr: Prosyllogism of the minor.

units.la: Quicunque sunt filii Abrahæ, ad eos solos proprië pertinet promissio Redemptionis per mortem Christi factæ: Atqui soli electi sunt filii Abrahæ: Ergo etiam ad solos electos proprië pertinet promissio Redemptionis per mortem Christi factæ.
units.tr: Whoever are the sons of Abraham, to them alone properly belongs the promise of redemption made through the death of Christ. But only the elect are the sons of Abraham. Therefore the promise of redemption made through the death of Christ properly belongs only to the elect.

units.la: Maioris Epilogismus.
units.tr: Epilogism of the major.

units.la: Si soli Abrahamo, & semini eius, id est, Christo, & electis, qui in Christo sunt, promissio proprië est facta, tum quicunque sunt filii Abrahæ, ad eos solos proprië pertinet promissio Redemptionis per mortem Christi factæ: Atqui prius est verum, Gala.3. ver.16. Abrahæ dictæ sunt promissiones, & femini eius. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If the promise was made properly to Abraham and his seed, that is, to Christ and to the elect who are in Christ, then whoever are the sons of Abraham, to them alone properly belongs the promise of redemption made through the death of Christ. But the former is true, Gal. 3. ver. 16: The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Therefore the latter is also true.

units.la: Minoris Epilogismus.
units.tr: Epilogism of the minor.

units.la: Quicunque sunt ex fide, ii soli sunt filii Abrahæ, & soli benedicuntur cum fideli Abrahamo, Galat.3. verf.7. Noftis eos, qui ex fide sunt, esse filios Abrahæ. & verf.9. Itaque qui ex fide sunt benedicuntur cum fideli illo Abraham: Atqui soli electi sunt ex fide, Tit.1. verf.1. Paulus servus Dei, Apostolus autem Iesu Christi secundum fidem electorum Dei: Act. 13. v. 48. Crediderunt quot quot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Ergo soli electi sunt filii Abrahæ, & benedicentur in fideli illo Abraham.
units.tr: Whoever are of faith, they alone are the sons of Abraham and alone are blessed with faithful Abraham. Gal. 3. ver. 7: You know that those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham. And ver. 9: So those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham. But only the elect are of faith. Titus 1. ver. 1: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of the elect of God. Acts 13. ver. 48: As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Therefore only the elect are the sons of Abraham, and they will be blessed in faithful Abraham.

units.la: Axioma secundum.
units.tr: Second axiom.

units.la: Fidelium salus ab æterna Dei prædestinatione, gratuita ele[?] ætione dependet, eáque ceu basi & fundamento nititur, ob quam etiam causam certa est & immutabilis: Quos præsciuit, eosdem etiam prædestinauit, vt conformes fierent imagini Filij sui, vt sit primogenitus inter multos fratres: quos vero prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit: & quos vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit: quos autem iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit: & v. 38. 39. Mihi persuasum est, neque mortē, neque vitam, neque Angelos, neque Principatus, neque potestates, neque instantia, neque futura, neque sublimitate, neque profunditatem, neque vllam rem aliam creatam, posse nos separare à charitate Dei quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro: & 11. v. 29. Dona & vocatio Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα : 2 Tim. 1. v. 9. 10. Qui (Deus) seruauit nos, & vocauit vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, quæ data est nobis in Christo Iesu, ante tempora secularia, sed patefacta nunc est per illustrem illum aduentum Seruatoris nostri Iesu Christi, qui & mortem abolevit, & vitam in lucem produxit, ac immortalitatem per Euangelium: & 2. vers. 19. Solidum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, Nouit Dominus qui sint sui: Vide etiam Ioh. 6. v. 37. & 10. v. 26. 27. 28. 29. Eph. 1. v. 4. 5. 9. 11. & alibi.
units.tr: The salvation of believers depends on the eternal predestination of God, which is free election, and rests on it as its base and foundation; for this reason too it is certain and unchangeable. Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified. And ver. 38, 39: I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. And 11. ver. 29: The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα]. 2 Tim. 1. ver. 9, 10: (God) who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and the grace which was given us in Christ Jesus before the ages, but has now been made manifest through the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel. And 2. ver. 19: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. See also John 6. ver. 37, and 10. ver. 26, 27, 28, 29; Eph. 1. ver. 4, 5, 9, 11, and elsewhere.

units.la: Syllogismus primus.
units.tr: First syllogism.

units.la: Quos Deus non ad iram vt reprobos (Iud. v. 4 Subrepserunt quidam homines iam olim descripti, ad hanc damnationem impij, qui Dei nostri gratiam transferunt ad lasciuiam, & solum illum horum Deum, ac Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum negant, sed ad salutem per Christum obtinendam constituit, pro iis etiam solis Christus mortuus est, vt cum ipso viuant, docente id Apostolo, 1. Thess. 5. v. 9. 10. Non constituit nos ad iram, sed ad salutem obtinendam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui mortuus est pro nobis, vt siue vigilemus, siue dormiamus, simul cum eo viuamus:
units.tr: Those whom God has appointed not to wrath as reprobates (Jude 4: Certain men have crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ), but to obtain salvation through Christ, for them alone Christ also died, that they might live with him, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Thess. 5:9-10: God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, that whether we wake or sleep we should live together with him.

units.la: Atqui solos electos (nos inquit Apostolus) constituit Deus non ad iram, sed ad salutem obtinendam per Christum:
units.tr: But God appointed only the elect (we are speaking, says the Apostle) not to wrath but to obtain salvation through Christ.

units.la: Ergo pro solis electis mortuus est Christus, vt viuant cum ipso.
units.tr: Therefore Christ died for the elect alone, that they might live with him.

units.la: Syllogismus secundus.
units.tr: Second syllogism.

units.la: Pro quibus Christus se ipsum sanctificauit, id est, in Sacerdotem simul & victimam consecrauit, pro iis etiam mortuus est, se ipsum hostiam obtulit Deo.
units.tr: For those for whom Christ sanctified himself, that is, consecrated himself at once as priest and victim, for them also he died, offering himself as a sacrifice to God.

units.la: Atqui pro iis duntaxat se ipsum sanctifi cauit,id est,in Sacerdotem & hostiam consecrauit, quos ei Pater, vt suos redimendos ac seruados dedit, Ioh.17. v.16. Patefeci nomen tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi e mundo, tui erant, & eos mihi dedisti, & sermonem tuum seruarunt:& verf.19. Pro eis ego sanctifico me ipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem.
units.tr: But he sanctified himself, that is, consecrated himself as priest and sacrifice, only for those whom the Father gave him to be redeemed and saved as his own, John 17:6: I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world; they were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word; and verse 19: For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified through the truth.

units.la: Ergo Christus pro his etiā peculiariter est mortuus, & se ipsum in sacrificium obtulit.
units.tr: Therefore Christ also died in a peculiar way for these, and offered himself as a sacrifice.

units.la: Syllogismus tertius.
units.tr: Third syllogism.

units.la: Pro quibus Christus non orauit,pro iis multo minus mortuus est,quia hæ duæ partes sacerdotii Christi,& sacrificii eius nequaquam diuelli possunt:
units.tr: For those for whom Christ did not pray, for them much less did he die, because these two parts of Christ's priesthood and of his sacrifice can by no means be separated.

units.la: Atqui Christus pro reprobis non orauit, Iohan.17.verf.9. Ego pro eis rogo,non pro mundo rogo,sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt.
units.tr: But Christ did not pray for the reprobate: John 17:9: I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours.

units.la: Ergo multo minus pro iis mortuus est.
units.tr: Therefore much less did he die for them.

units.la: Syllogismus quartus.
units.tr: Fourth syllogism.

units.la: Pro quibus Christus est mortuus & resurrexit, ii reuera ἀνάστασιν sunt, & ἀκαταχρίτοι, Roman.cap.8.verf.33. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus (is est) qui mortuus est,qui etiam est dextram Dei, qui etiam postulat pro nobis: vnde apparet pro iis demum Christum esse mortuum, qui extra periculum condemnationis sunt:
units.tr: For those for whom Christ died and rose again, these are truly risen [ἀνάστασιν] and uncondemned [ἀκαταχρίτοι], Rom. 8:33: Who shall condemn? It is Christ who died, who is also at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. Whence it appears that Christ died only for those who are beyond the danger of condemnation.

units.la: Atqui nulli reprobi, sed soli electi sunt ἀνάστασιν,ἀκαταχρίτοι, & extra periculum condemnationis, vt Paulus diserte docet Roman.8.v.33. Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus (is est) qui iustificat.
units.tr: But none of the reprobate, only the elect, are risen [ἀνάστασιν], uncondemned [ἀκαταχρίτοι], and beyond the danger of condemnation, as Paul plainly teaches in Rom. 8:33: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies.

units.la: Ergo non pro reprobis,sed pro electis Christus est mortuus.
units.tr: Therefore Christ did not die for the reprobate, but for the elect.

units.la: Syllogismus quintus.
units.tr: Fifth syllogism.

units.la: Quos Deus sanguine Filii sui redemit, ex æterno suo consilio ac decreto, iis etiam suo tempore vocatis fidem dat, & resipiscentiam, vt ad Christum adducti, in eoque iustificati & sanctificati, seruentur. Roman.8.verf.30. Quos prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit: &quos vocauit,eos etiam iustificauit:quos autem iustificauit,eos etiam glorificauit. Et pro quibus Christus sese sanctificauit hostiam, ii etiam verè sanctificantur. Iohan.17. vers.19. Pro eis ego sanctifico me-ipsum,vt sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem. Efficacia enim mortis Christi, ab ipsa morte scparari nunquam potest, nec debet, quia Christus non frustra est mortuus: 2. Cor.5. vers.15. Qui hoc statu erimus,si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, nempe omnes fuisse mortuos, & (illum)pro omnibus mortuum esse,vt qui viuunt posthac,non sibi viuant, sed ei,qui pro ipsis mortuus est,& resurrexit.
units.tr: Those whom God redeemed by the blood of his Son, according to his eternal counsel and decree, to these also, when called in their time, he gives faith and repentance, so that, brought to Christ and in him justified and sanctified, they are preserved. Rom. 8:30: Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified. And for those for whom Christ sanctified himself as a victim, these are also truly sanctified. John 17:19: For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified through the truth. For the efficacy of Christ's death can never and must never be separated from the death itself, because Christ did not die in vain. 2 Cor. 5:15: Those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again, since one died for all, and therefore all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might not live for themselves.

units.la: Atqui ad Christum neque vocantur omnes homines, neque fide donantur,2. Thess.3. v.2. Fides non est omnium:& reprobi,qui nullam in Christo partem habent, non sanctificantur, sed moriuntur in peccatis suis: Iohan.8. v.21. Ego vado,& quaeretis me, & in peccatis vestris moriemini.
units.tr: But neither are all men called to Christ, nor are they granted faith: 2 Thess. 3:2: Not all have faith. And the reprobate, who have no part in Christ, are not sanctified but die in their sins: John 8:21: I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins.

units.la: Ergo Deus sanguine Filii sui non omnes,sed solos electos redemit,& Christus pro his solis sese sanctificauit, & mortuus est.
units.tr: Therefore God redeemed by the blood of his Son not all, but only the elect, and Christ sanctified himself and died for these alone.

units.la: Axioma tertium.
units.tr: Third axiom.

units.la: Nullum Dei consilium, aut decretum suo potest fine frustrari. Voluntati enim eius quis vtique resistat? Rom. 9. v.19. Neque enim sapientia est aut intelligentia, aut consilium aduersus Dominum, Prou.21. v.30. Neque poenitudine ducitur,aut vnquam mutatur: 1. Sam. 15. v. 29. Mal. 3. v. 6.
units.tr: No counsel or decree of God can be frustrated of its end. For who indeed resists his will? Rom. 9:19: For there is no wisdom or understanding or counsel against the Lord. Prov. 21:30: It is not swayed by repentance, nor is it ever changed. 1 Sam. 15:29; Mal. 3:6.

units.la: Hinc ita collige.
units.tr: From this, conclude thus.

units.la: Si Deus voluit omnium hominum,secundum singula indiuidua peccata semel purgari,morte Filii sui, & omnes seruari, nullo inter electos & reprobos habito discrimine: nihil obstare vnquam potuit, quo minus id etiam fieret, & ad destinatum atque optatum euentum deduceretur.
units.tr: If God willed that the sins of all men, each individual sin, be once purged by the death of his Son, and that all be saved, with no distinction made between elect and reprobate, then nothing could ever have prevented this from also being done and brought to the intended and desired outcome.

units.la: Atqui non fit hoc: Ergo etiam vt fieret,non ita simpliciter, & generaliter voluit:nempe vt maneat illud,quod per Prophetā dicitur · In monte Sion & Ierusalem erit euasio, sicut Dominus dixit,& in superstitibus (reliquiis) quos Iehouah vocat, Ioel.2. v.32.
units.tr: But this does not happen. Therefore, even in willing that it should happen, he did not will it simply and generally, namely so that there remains what is said through the prophet: On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the Lord has said, and among the survivors (the remnant) whom Jehovah calls. Joel 2:32.

units.la: Vnde consequitur(vt a refutatione assumptionis ad testimonii citati explicationem progrediamur) vniuersalem illam enuntiationem ac sententiam,quam Ostorrodius ex 1.Iohan.2.vers.2.allegat,& contra doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum de praedestinatione vrget,ad suam conditionem,nempe fidei restringendam,& cum indefinitè accipiendam, tum co modo explicandam esse, quo Spiritus suiti ritus ipse sanctus illius autor eam explicat, neque extra genuinum suum sensum esse detorquendam. Illic enim mundi vocabulum vni Genti Iudaeorum opponitur, ad quam Iohannem scribere, ex ipsa phrasi, & ex versu septimo eiusdem capitis intelligitur. Neque aliud vult Apostolus, quàm Christum non modò pro Iudaeorum, sed & pro omnium eorum, qui ex omnibus Gentibus per vniuersum mundum dispersis, seruandi sint, peccatis mortuum esse: vt si per mundum totum humanum genus indefinitè, deinde sub hoc ipso οιωεκδοχικῶς certam hominum speciem, nempe ipsos electos, ex toto mundo colligendos intelligas, nihil absurdi id sit futurum: quum de qualibet specie, ipsum totū genus prædicetur, & totum ipsum de præcipuis suis partibus. Sed hoc ita esse rectius ex ipsius Domini verbis intelligitur. Ioh. 13. v. 1. Ante festum autem Paschæ, sciens Iesus venijse horam ipsius, vt transiret ex hoc mundo ad Patrem, quum dilexisset suos, qui erant in mundo, vsque ad finem dilexit eos. Ioh. 17. v. 6. Patefeci nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi e mundo, tui erant, & mihi eos dedisti, & sermonem tuum seruarunt. & v. 9. Ego pro eis rogo, non pro mundo rogo, sed pro (iis) quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. v. 19. 20. Pro eis ego sanctifico me ipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem, non pro eis autem rogo tantum, sed & pro iis, qui per sermonem eorum creduturi sunt in me. Quo sensu igitur Deus mundum dilexisse dicitur, eodem etiam Christus Seruator noster propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi appellatur: Atqui Deus Ioh. 3. v. 16. ita mundum dilexisse dicitur, vt Filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, verùm eo sensu, vt amor ille Dei ad credentes in Christum restrin-gatur, vt ex citatis Scripturæ testimoniis apparet, ne putemus ad singula hominum indiuidua hoc referendum esse: Ergo etiā Chri-stus propitiatio pro eorū tantum peccatis est, quos Pater eis tanquam suos seruandos dedit, pro quibus ipse erat, & pro quibus ipse sanctificauit seipsum, id est, in sacrificium consecrauit, quique adeò per prædicationem Euangelii quouis tempore in ipsum sunt crediturí. Hisce omnibus adde, quòd, si Christus pro omnibus omnium hominum etiam reproborum & in sua incredulitate perseuerantium, peccatis factus est propitiatio, necessariò inde sequatur, ipsum etiam pro illorum incredulitate & contumacia satisfecisse, ac proinde neminem illorum vel in peccatis manere, vel propter illa damnari posse, quod manifeste falsum est. Oftorrodius tamen audaćter affirmat, mundi vocabulum nec solum Electorum cœtum significare, & hoc ipsum sine omni fundamento, & specie veritatis asseri inquit, neque uni Iudæorum Genti opponi, quum Apostolus non de Iudæis tantum qua Iudæis, sed in genere de omnibus iisdem quatur, qui iam in Christum credebant.
units.tr: Hence it follows (so that, after refuting the assumption, we may proceed to explain the cited testimony) that that universal statement and sentence which Ostorodius takes from 1 John 2:2, and urges against the doctrine of our Churches on predestination, must be restricted to its condition, namely faith, and taken indefinitely, and explained in the way that the Holy Spirit, the author of that passage, himself explains it, and must not be twisted beyond its genuine sense. For there the word world is opposed to the one nation of the Jews, to whom it is understood from the very phrasing, and from verse 7 of the same chapter, that John was writing. Nor does the Apostle mean anything other than that Christ died for the sins not only of the Jews but also of all those who are to be saved from all nations scattered through the whole world. So if you understand "the world" indefinitely as the whole human race, and then under this same word, synecdochically [συνεκδοχικῶς], a certain kind of men, namely the elect themselves to be gathered from the whole world, nothing absurd will follow, since the whole genus is predicated of each species, and the whole of its principal parts. But that this is so is more rightly understood from the Lord's own words. John 13:1: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end. John 17:6: I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world; they were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. And verse 9: I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. Verses 19-20: For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified through the truth; and I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. In the sense, therefore, in which God is said to have loved the world, in that same sense Christ our Saviour is called the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. Yet God is said in John 3:16 to have so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life; but in such a sense that this love of God is restricted to those who believe in Christ, as appears from the cited testimonies of Scripture, lest we think that it is to be referred to each individual man. Therefore Christ too is the propitiation only for the sins of those whom the Father gave him as his own to be saved, for whom he himself sanctified himself, that is, consecrated himself as a sacrifice, and who, through the preaching of the Gospel, will believe in him at any time. To all this add that if Christ became the propitiation for the sins of all men, including the reprobate who persevere in their unbelief, it would necessarily follow that he also satisfied for their unbelief and obstinacy, and so that none of them either remains in sins or can be condemned on account of them, which is manifestly false. Ostorodius, however, boldly affirms that the word world signifies not only the company of the elect, and that this is asserted without any foundation or appearance of truth, and that it is not opposed to the one nation of the Jews, since the Apostle is not speaking of the Jews only as Jews, but in general of all those who were already believing in Christ.

units.la: Resp. Mundi vocabulum in loco citato, indefinitè sumptum uni Iudæorum, sed fidelium Genti opponi, ad quam Ioannem præcipuè scribere, ex ipsa phrasi, & ex v.7. eiusdem capitis intelligitur, sub hoc ipso vero genere humano indefinitè per mundi vocabulū significato ipsos electos ex toto mundo colligendos intelligi debere, paulò ante luculenter à nobis est demonstratum. Et certe mundū non tantum totam istam machinam cœlo terràque constante, vt Ioh.1.v.9.10. neque tantum vniuersum genus humanum, vt Ioh.15.v.19. Elegi vos ex mundo, neque ipsam tantum impiorum & infidelium, reproborúmque turbam, ut Ioh.14.v.17. & 17.v.9. sed interdum etiam Electorum, ac fidelium cœtum, ex vniuerso mundo selectum significare tum ex collatione locorum Ioh.3. v.16.& Ioh.13.v.1 Ioh.17.v.6.9. paulò ante à nobis instituta, tum etiam ex aliis Scripturæ testimoniis euidenter apparet: vt Ioh.6.v.33. Panis ille Dei is est, qui de cœlo descendit, & dat vitam mundo. Hinc ita colligo. Quibus cœlestis ille panis vitæ dat vitam æternam, illi per Mundi vocabulum designantur: Atqui Christus cœlestis ille panis vitæ, solis fidelibus & electis suis quibus vitam æternam dat, Ioh.10.v.27.28. Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & ego eas agnosco, & sequuntur me. Et ego vitam æternam do eis, nec peribunt in æternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam è manu mea. Ergo per Mundi vocabulum illo in loco soli fideles & electi designantur. Denique fatetur hoc ipsum Samosatenianorum Antesignanus Georgius Eniedinus in Ioh.1. v.10. Mundus, inquiens, accipitur interdum pro hominibus Synecdochicè, & quidem nunc pro quibusdam, nunc pro piis, nunc etiam pro solis impiis. Unde apparet nihil absurdi, ex nostra loci illius, quem frustra adduxit Aduersarius, ad doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum conuellendam, expositione, consequi posse. Quæ insperg it disputationi suæ conuitia, nos prædestinarios, doctrinam verò illam de prædestinatione Calvinianam appellando, non moror, sed tacitus prætereo.
units.tr: Reply: The word "world" in the passage cited, taken indefinitely, is opposed not to the one nation of the Jews but to the nation of the faithful, to whom John writes especially; this is clear from the phrase itself and from verse 7 of the same chapter. Under this very human race, signified indefinitely by the word "world," the elect to be gathered from the whole world must be understood; this was clearly demonstrated by us a little earlier. And indeed "world" signifies not only that whole machine of heaven and earth (as in John 1:9-10), nor only the entire human race (as in John 15:19, "I have chosen you out of the world"), nor merely the crowd of the impious, unbelieving and reprobate (as in John 14:17 and 17:9), but sometimes also the assembly of the elect and faithful, selected from the whole world. This is evident from the comparison of passages in John 3:16, John 13:1 and John 17:6, 9, which we set out a little earlier, and also from other testimonies of Scripture, such as John 6:33: "The bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world." I argue thus: those to whom that heavenly bread of life gives eternal life are designated by the word "world." But Christ, that heavenly bread of life, gives eternal life only to his own elect and faithful, as in John 10:27-28: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Therefore in that passage the word "world" designates only the faithful and elect. Finally, Georgius Enyedinus, the forerunner of the Samosatenians, himself admits this very point on John 1:10: "The world," he says, "is sometimes taken synecdochically for men, and indeed now for some, now for the godly, now even for the impious alone." Hence it appears that nothing absurd can follow from our interpretation of that passage, which the Opponent has cited in vain in order to overthrow the doctrine of our Churches. As for the reproaches he has scattered through his disputation, calling us predestinarians and calling that doctrine of predestination Calvinistic, I do not dwell on them but pass them over in silence.

units.la: Tandem verò & coronidis loco, sectione quarta addit, & dicit, sententiam ac doctrinam Aduersariorum secum ipsa pugnare, quoniam illi illi in doctrina de prouidentia affirmént,omnia quaecunque fiunt, vel non fiunt, praesertim vero, quae salutem ac damnationem hominum concernunt, prius a Deo ita constituta ac ordinata esse, ac proinde necessario ita fieri, nec vlla ratione immutari posse: in doctrina vero de peccato primi hominis statuant, ipsum, vt pote libero Arbitrio praeditum, sponte, libere, ac petulanter peccasse. Quum autem ille libero Arbitrio praeditus fuerit, ac proinde peccatum cuitare potuerit, ideo ipsum minime necessario peccasse, cum libertas, ac necessitas peccandi sese mutuo tollant. Atque hoc omnibus falsis doctrinis contingere, inquit,vt quantumuis multis integumentis & inuolucris conuestiantur, atque ornentur, malum ipsarum fundamentum detegatur, & ipsarum Autores suis contradictionibus illas imprudenter euertant, & impugnent.
units.tr: At last, by way of a crown, in the fourth section he adds and says that the opinion and doctrine of the Opponents contradicts itself, because in the doctrine of providence they affirm that all things whatever that happen or do not happen, especially those that concern the salvation and damnation of men, have been first so constituted and ordained by God, and therefore necessarily come to pass thus and cannot be changed by any means; but in the doctrine of the sin of the first man they maintain that he, as endowed with free will, sinned willingly, freely and wantonly. Since, however, he was endowed with free will, and therefore could have avoided sin, he did not sin of necessity, since freedom and necessity of sinning mutually cancel each other. And this, he says, happens to all false doctrines: however many wrappings and covers they are dressed and adorned in, the bad foundation of them is laid bare, and their authors, through their own contradictions, carelessly overthrow and attack them.

units.la: Resp. Qua ratione necessitas, ac infallibilis certitudo euentuum rerum omnium, maximè verò earum, quae ad salutem ac damnationem hominum pertinent, libertatem causarum secundarum coniunctam ac subordinatam sibi habeat, neque harum naturam aut proprietatem tollat: quàm diuersae item tum prouidentiae, tum praedestinationis circa bonum & malum sint actiones, in responsionibus nostris ad argumenta Aduersarii, hoc ipso capite tam cuidenter & prolixe ostendimus, vt in putido illo cauillo operosius refutando, diutius immorari velle, penitus inutile & superfluum foret. Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius apparet, Aduersarium nullam iustam causam adferre potuisse, quare ab orthodoxa illa Ecclesiarum nostrarum de praedestinatione doctrina tantopere abhorreat, illámque tam hostili animo impugnet ac persequatur: sed ipsam contra omnes illius insultus inuictam, firmámque subsistere. Deus omnis boni autor, largiatur nobis gratiam, vt vocationem & electionem nostram, per exercitationem virtutum Christianarum firmam reddere studeamus, cuius nomen magnificum in secula sit benedictum.
units.tr: Reply: By what reasoning the necessity and infallible certainty of the outcome of all things, and especially of those that pertain to the salvation and damnation of men, has freedom of secondary causes joined and subordinated to it, and does not take away their nature or property, and how different the actions of providence and of predestination are with respect to good and evil, we have shown in this same chapter, in our replies to the arguments of the Opponent, so clearly and at such length that it would be wholly useless and superfluous to linger long in refuting that foul sophism at greater length. From all these things it appears more clearly than the noonday light that the Opponent could bring forward no just cause why he so greatly shrinks from that orthodox doctrine of predestination held by our Churches, and why he assails and persecutes it with such hostile spirit; rather, it stands unconquered and firm against all his assaults. May God, the author of every good, grant us grace so that, through the practice of Christian virtues, we may strive to make our calling and election sure, whose magnificent name be blessed for ever.

units.la: CAPVT XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: In quo doctrina orthodoxa de Fide iustificante explicatur, & ex Scripturis sacris demonstratur.
units.tr: In which the orthodox doctrine of justifying faith is explained and demonstrated from the holy Scriptures.

units.la: QVVM contraria iuxta se posita magis elucescât, ideo priusquam Aduersariorum, de Fide iustificante, errores recenseamus ac refutemus, primò omnium veritatem doctrinæ nostræ explicabimus, & ex scripturis ipsis demonstrabimus. Quia verò ipsum vocabulum fidei est πλεονασμον, variæque ac diuersæ admodum eius in S. Scripturis occurrunt significationes, idcirco ante omnia ex ambiguitatis illius involucris euoluendum & explicandum est subiectum ipsum, ut intelligatur quænam sit illa fides, de cuius natura inter nos disceptatur. Fides itaque dupliciter accipitur, improprie, vel proprie. Improprie tria significat. Primo, Articulos fidei, eósque vel omnes, id est, totam doctrinam Euangelii, vt 1. Timoth. 4. ver 1. Spiritus autem diserte dicit, fore, vt posterioribus temporibus defecsant quidam à fide, spiritibus deceptoribus attendentes, ac doctrinis dæmoniorum. Gal. 1. v. 23. Qui persequebatur nos aliquando, nunc annunciat fidem, quam olim vastabat. Vel quosdam tantum, & quasi præcipua Catecheseos Apostolicæ capita, vt Heb. 6. v. 1. 2. Quapropter omisso, qui in Christo rudes inchoat, sermone, non iacientes rursum fundamentum resipiscentia ab operibus mortuis, & fidei in Deum, Baptismatum doctrinæ, ac manuum impositionis, & resurrectionis mortuorum, & iudicij æterni. Secundo, Plenam eorum reuelationem, quæ olim sub inuolucris & obscuritate vmbrarum legis latebant: Galat. 3. v. 23. Antequam autem veniisset fides, sub legis præsidio tenebamur, conclusi in eam fidem, quæ erat reuelanda. Tertio, Manifestam & publicam de Christo declarationem omnibus factam: vt Act. 17. v. 31. Eo quod statuit diem, quo iustè iudicaturus est orbem terrarum, per eum virum, quem definiit, fide palam facta omnibus, illo à mortuis excitato. In significatione propria vocabulum fidei tam apud sacros, quàm profanos autores, interdum actiuè, interdum passiuè vsurpatur. Actiuè significat virtutem tutem vera dicendi, & promissa seruandi, seu dictorum, promissorumque veritatem & constantiam, tum Dei erga homines, Psal. 33. v. 4. Quia rectum est verbum Iehoua, & omne opus eius in fide, id est, veritate, & constantia. 2. Tim. 2. v. 13. Si infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, negare se ipsum no potest. 1. Ioh. 1. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est, & iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & purget nos ab omni iniquitate. Tum hominum erga sese. Prou. 14. v. 5. Testis optima fidei non mentitur, efflat autem mendacia testis falsus. Psal. 12. v. 2. Da salutem Iehouah: nam defuit beneficus, defecerunt fideles ex filiis hominum. Et haec nominis illius significatio nota est, & passim apud prophanos autores obuiam, vtinam apud Christianos esset in vsu. Passiue autem significat notitiam, ascensum, ac persuasionem animi, qua illa, quae ab aliis dicuntur aut nobis promittuntur credimus, quo sensu in negotio Iustificationis passim in sacris literis vsurpatur.
units.tr: Since opposites are shown up more clearly when set side by side, before we list and refute the errors of our opponents concerning justifying faith, we will first set out the truth of our doctrine in full and demonstrate it from the Scriptures themselves. Because the word faith itself is a pleonasm [πλεονασμός], and it occurs in the Holy Scriptures with many varied and quite different meanings, the subject itself must first be unfolded and explained from the wrappings of that ambiguity, so that it may be understood what that faith is whose nature is in dispute between us. Faith is therefore taken in two ways, improperly or properly. Improperly it has three meanings. First, it means the articles of faith, either all of them, that is, the whole doctrine of the Gospel, as in 1 Timothy 4:1: But the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will fall away from the faith, paying attention to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons. Or Galatians 1:23: He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith which he once tried to destroy. Or only some of them, and as it were the chief heads of the Apostolic catechesis, as in Hebrews 6:1-2: Therefore, leaving the initial word of Christ, let us go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, the teaching of baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. Second, it means the full revelation of those things which once lay hidden under veils and the obscurity of the shadows of the law: Galatians 3:23: But before faith came, we were kept under the guard of the law, shut up to that faith which was to be revealed. Third, it means the open and public declaration about Christ made to everyone, as in Acts 17:31: Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by the man whom he has appointed, having given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead. In its proper meaning the word faith is used, both by sacred and by profane authors, sometimes actively and sometimes passively. Actively it means the virtue of speaking truly and keeping promises, that is, the truth and constancy of words and promises, both of God toward men, Psalm 33:4: For the word of Jehovah is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness, that is, in truth and constancy; 2 Timothy 2:13: If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself; 1 John 1:9: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. And it means that of men toward one another, Proverbs 14:5: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. Psalm 12:2: Help, Jehovah, for the godly man ceases; the faithful have vanished from among the sons of men. This meaning of the name is well known and occurs everywhere in profane authors; would that it were in use among Christians. Passively, however, it means the knowledge, assent and persuasion of the mind by which we believe those things that are said by others or promised to us, and it is in this sense that the word is used throughout the Scriptures in the matter of justification.

units.la: Fides hac significatione intellecta, iterum duplex est, vel historiae vel promissionum. Fides historica est vniuersae veritatis tam legalis, quam Euangelicae mentis cognitio, seu fiduciae expers notitia, & quod ad veritatem attinet, mentis iudicium. Fides promissionum est vel miraculosa, vel temporaria, vel iustificans. Fides miraculorum est, de futuro aliquo euentu miraculoso per reuelationem, aut promissionem singularem Dei, certa persuasio, seu mentis cognitio, & voluntatis apprehensio. Fides temporaria est notitia, & assensus, qua fide illa praediti assentiuntur doctrinae Euangelii, eam profitentur, & cognitione eius delectantur, aliquam ve speciem bonorum operum edunt, & de ea propter certas ac temporarias causas gloriantur. Atque de hisce fidei speciebus non instituitur praefens controuersia. Fides iustificans est habitus infusus a Spiritu Sancto in animo hominis per internam illuminationem testificationemque, & verbi praedicationem externam, quo Christum Iesum Mediatorem Dei & hominum cum bonis, & donis ipsius omnibus, Spiritu & verbo oblatum, non tantum nouimus, sed & nobis singulariter praestitum, donatumque singulariter prehendimus, ac percipimus ad Dei gloriam, & animarum nostrarum salutem. Veritatem huius definitionis ex fidei causarum, effectorum, subiectorum, obiectorum, & adiunctorum analysi breuiter demonstrabimus.
units.tr: With this meaning of faith understood, it is again twofold, either of history or of promises. Historical faith is the knowledge of the whole truth, both of the law and of the Gospel, or a knowledge devoid of trust, and, so far as it concerns truth, a judgment of the mind. Faith of promises is either miraculous, or temporary, or justifying. Miraculous faith is a certain persuasion, or knowledge of the mind and apprehension of the will, concerning some future miraculous event, through a special revelation or promise of God. Temporary faith is the knowledge and assent by which those endowed with it assent to the doctrine of the Gospel, profess it, take delight in knowing it, do some sort of good works, and boast of it for certain temporary reasons. The present controversy does not concern these kinds of faith. Justifying faith is a habit infused by the Holy Spirit into the mind of man through inward illumination and testimony, and through the external preaching of the word, by which we not only know Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and men, offered together with all his benefits, in the Spirit and the word, but also lay hold of him and receive him, given to us individually and bestowed on us individually, to the glory of God and the salvation of our souls. We will briefly demonstrate the truth of this definition from an analysis of the causes, effects, subject, object and attributes of faith.

units.la: Causa efficiens fidei iustificantis principalis est Deus Pater in Filio, per Spiritum sanctum, qui donum hoc supernaturale nobis infundit intus nobis Christum offerendo,& mentem nostram lumine suo illustrando, animúmque testificatione sua obsignando, vt Christum oblatum videamus, & in illum vt Seruatorem nostrum certa fide credamus. Iohan. capite sexto, versu vigesimo nono:Hoc illud est opus Dei, vt credatis in eum, quem misit ille. Actorum decimosexto, versu decimoquarto:Dominus aperuit cor Lydiæ, vt attenderet ea, quæ dicebantur à Paulo. Roman. 12. ver. 3.Quemuis sapiat ad sobrietatem, prout cuique Deus partitus est mensuram fidei. Philip. 1. verf. 29.Quia vobis datum est in Christi negotio non solum in eum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi. Luc. capite vigesimo quarto, versu quadragesimo quinto:Tunc aperuit illorum mentem, vt intelligerent scripturas. Hebr. cap. 12. verf. 2. Intuentes in fidei ducem ac perfectorem Iesum. Ephef. capite 2. verf. 8.Gratia estis seruati per fidem, idque non ex vobis, Dei donum est. Instrumentalis est vel ordinaria, vel extraordinaria: Ordinaria est Verbum Dei secundum vtramque partem essentialem, id est tam Legem, quàm Euangelium, sed aliter secundum priorem, aliter secundum posteriorem. Nam Lex indirectè producit fidem, per vtriusque mali culpæ & poenæ agnitionem, quam directè præbet homini consternato, vt ipsum de propriis viribus desperantem ad Christum adducat. Galat. capite tertio, versu vigesimo quarto:Lex Paedagogus noster fuit in Christum, vt ex fide iustificaremur. Euangelium verò fidem gignit directè, ac proinde semen & potentia Dei vocatur, 1. Iohan. capite tertio, versu nono:Quisquis natus est ex Deo peccatum non committit, quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet. Roman. cap. 1. verf. 16.Euangelium potentia Dei est ad salutem cuiuis credenti: & capite decimo, versu octauo :Hoc est verbum illud fidei quod prædicamus: & versu decimoseptimo :Fides ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei: 1. Petr. capite primo, versu vigesimo tertio :Renati non ex semine mortali, sed ex immortali per sermonem Dei viui, & manentis in æternum. Huic verbo adduntur Sacramenta, quæ fidem genitam alunt, fouent & augent. Extraordinaria sunt miracula, siue opera Dei totius creatæ naturæ vires superantia, quibus tamen verbum Dei necesse est. Atque hæc instrumenta, quemadmodum non sunt contemnenda cum offeruntur, ita neque requirenda cùm auferuntur. Matth. 12. ver. 39.Natio mala & adulterina signum requirit, sed signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum illud Ionæ Prophetæ. Materia in qua, vel subiectum fidei iustificantis duplex est, commune, vel proprium. Subiectum commune est totus homo, animo & corpore constans, sed peccator, & peccata sua agnoscens. Neque fides enim, nec dona illa, quae fidem consequuntur, vlli nisi peccatori sunt necessaria, nec alii nisi peccatores in Christum credere iubentur, nec vllorum nisi peccatorum Christus est Mediator. Vide Matth.cap.1. verf.21.& cap.9.verf.12. Marc.cap.1.verf. 15.Matth.cap.11.verf.28. Iohan.cap.8.ver.24. Atque hinc est quod Iudei iustitiam ex lege quaerentes, in lapidem offendiculi impegisse dicuntur. Roman.cap.9.verf.31.32.Israelem vero, qui sectabatur legem iustitiae, ad legem iustitiae non pervenisse: quare? quia non ex fide, sed velut ex operibus legis: offenderunt enim ad lapidem offendiculi.
units.tr: The efficient cause of justifying faith is principally God the Father in the Son, through the Holy Spirit, who infuses this supernatural gift into us, offering Christ to us inwardly, illuminating our mind with his light and sealing our soul with his testimony, so that we see the offered Christ and believe in him with a sure faith as our Savior. John 6:29: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. Acts 16:14: The Lord opened the heart of Lydia, so that she attended to the things spoken by Paul. Romans 12:3: Let each think of himself with sober judgment, as God has assigned to each a measure of faith. Philippians 1:29: For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake. Luke 24:45: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. Hebrews 12:2: Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. Ephesians 2:8: For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God. The instrumental cause is either ordinary or extraordinary. The ordinary is the Word of God in both its essential parts, that is, both the Law and the Gospel, but in different ways according to each part. For the Law produces faith indirectly, through the recognition of the guilt and punishment of both evils, which it presents directly to the man who is dismayed, so that it may lead him to Christ, despairing of his own strength. Galatians 3:24: The law was our guardian until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith. The Gospel, however, begets faith directly, and therefore it is called the seed and power of God. 1 John 3:9: Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him. Romans 1:16: The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. And 10:8: This is the word of faith which we preach; and 10:17: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. 1 Peter 1:23: You have been born again not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God. To this word are added the sacraments, which nourish, cherish and increase the faith once begotten. The extraordinary instruments are miracles, or works of God that surpass the powers of all created nature, yet the word of God is necessarily joined with them. And these instruments, just as they are not to be despised when offered, so they are not to be sought when withdrawn. Matthew 12:39: An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. The matter in which, or the subject of justifying faith, is twofold, common or proper. The common subject is the whole man, consisting of soul and body, but a sinner, and acknowledging his sins. For neither faith nor those gifts which follow faith are necessary to anyone except a sinner, nor are any but sinners commanded to believe in Christ, nor is Christ the Mediator of any but sinners. See Matthew 1:21; Matthew 9:12; Mark 1:15; Matthew 11:28; John 8:24. Hence it is that the Jews, seeking righteousness by the law, are said to have stumbled at the stone of offense. Romans 9:31-32: Israel, who pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if by works of the law; for they stumbled at the stone of offense.

units.la: Subiectum proprium est tum mens, tum voluntas. Et mentem quidem fidei subiectum esse liquet ex iis appellationibus, quae fidei passim in Scripturis tribuitur, vt cum vocatur Scientia. Esai.capite quinquagesimo tertio, versu vndecimo, In scientia sui servus meus iustificabit multos: cognitio, Iohann.capite decimoseptimo, versu tertio: Haec est vita aeterna, vt te solum cognoscant verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Επίγνωσις, Coloss.cap.3.verf.9. Vt impleamini agnitione voluntatis eius, cum omni sapientia & intelligentia spirituali: & versu decimo, Omni opere bono fructum proferentes, & crescentes in agnitionem Dei. & capite tertio, versu decimo: Et induentis nouum illum hominem qui renouatur in agnitionem congruentem imagini eius, qui ipsum condidit: σωφία, seu intelligentia. Coloss. 2. verf. 2. vt consolationem accipiant ipsorum corda ipsis charitate compactis, & omni opulentia certo persuasae intelligentiae (τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως) ad cognitionem mysterii Dei, & Patris, & Christi. Nam σωφίαν hoc loco nec conscientiam, vt apud Herodianum libro quarto: nec iudicium illud mentis, id est, spiritualem illam ἀισθησιν, sed perspicaciam & prudentiam in rerum spiritualium diiudicatione, de qua agit Apostolus Philip.capite primo, versu secundo: & Coloss. capite primo, versu nono: & cui opponit 1. Corinth.cap.1. ver.19. τὴν σύνεσιν (videlicet ἀρχιλ) τῶν συνετῶν nempe ἀνθρώπων ψυχῶν: (quemadmodum Aristoteles naturalem illam animi facultatem definit Ethicor.libr.6.cap.10.quod σύνεσις fit ἕξις τοῦ καλῶς λογίζεσθαι, id est, quod σύνεσις fit habitus & facultas recte intelligendi, & iudicandi eas res, circa quas prudentia versatur, cui contraria est ἀσύνεσία, id est, stupiditas, & hebetudo ingenii) sed firmam ac solidam notitiam veritatis firmo sincero quae assensu, significare, ex omnibus loci illius circumstantiis euidenter apparet. Non solum intellectum theoreticum vero, seu practicam etiam, & effectiuum, id est, voluntatem fidei iustificantis subiectum ἐνεργητικὸν esse, apparet tum ex scripturae sacrae testimoniis, Roman. 10. veri. 9. Si credis in corde tuo, quod Deus eum excitauit ex mortuis, seruaberis: & 10. verf. 10. Corde creditur ad iustitiam, & ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. At cor Hebraica phrasi frequentissime facultatem animae volentem denotare, magis notum est, quam ut probatione vila indigeat: tum etiam, quia obiectum fidei non solum ut verum, sed etiam ut bonum nobis ac salutare agnoscere, appetere, & amplecti debemus. Neque euertit hanc doctrinam vulgatum illud axioma Philosophicum, Quod videlicet nullum accidens singulare possit esse in duobus subiectis, quia fidem non eodem modo natuimus in intellectu, quod est in voluntate: nam in isto fidem primo per se, ac proprie, in illa vero secundario, nempe ἐνεργητικῶς, quatenus eam mouet, & afficit, recidere dicamus. Quemadmodum enim scientia, qua bonum a malo internoscimus subiectiue inest menti, voluntati effectiue, cum elicit aut imperat actiones, quas ratio dictat: ita etiam fidei actus primus distinguendus est ab actu secundo: nam respectu essentiae est utique in intellectu tanquam in proprio subiecto: at respectu operationis, quae proprii locum in ea obtinet, nullamque prorsus mutationem ei adfert, etiam voluntati inest, nempe ut utramque renouet, ac bonorum suorum pro utriusque ratione & captu participem faciat.
units.tr: The proper subject is both the mind and the will. That faith has the mind as its subject is clear from the names that Scripture commonly gives to faith, such as knowledge. In Isaiah 53:11, By his knowledge my servant shall justify many. In John 17:3: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Coloss. 1:9 has knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις]: that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. At verse 10 he says: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God. At Coloss. 3:10: and have put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator. At Coloss. 2:2, wisdom or understanding [σωφία]: that their hearts may be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding [τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως], to the knowledge of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ. For here wisdom [σωφίαν] means neither conscience, as in Herodian book 4, nor that judgment of the mind, that is, the spiritual perception [ἀισθησιν]; it means keenness and prudence in judging spiritual things, the subject of the Apostle at Philippians 1:2 and Coloss. 1:9. It is opposed to 1 Cor. 1:19, the understanding [σύνεσιν] of the wise [τῶν συνετῶν], that is, of wise men. (Aristotle defines this natural faculty of the soul in Ethics book 6, ch. 10: understanding [σύνεσις] is a disposition for reasoning well, that is, a habit and faculty of rightly understanding and judging those things with which prudence is concerned, and its contrary is lack of understanding [ἀσύνεσία], that is, stupidity and dullness of wit.) Rather, it is a firm and solid knowledge of the truth, with a firm and sincere assent. This is evident from all the circumstances of that passage. That the will is also the subject of justifying faith, and is effective [ἐνεργητικὸν], not merely theoretical intellect but also practical intellect, is clear from the testimonies of Holy Scripture: Romans 10:9, If you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved; and Romans 10:10, With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. That "heart" in Hebrew idiom very often denotes the willing faculty of the soul is better known than to need any proof. Also, we ought to acknowledge, pursue and embrace the object of faith not only as true but also as good and salutary for us. Nor does the familiar philosophical axiom overturn this doctrine, that no single accident can be in two subjects. For faith is not inherent in the intellect and the will in the same way. We say that it falls first in the intellect, through itself and properly, but in the will secondarily, effectively [ἐνεργητικῶς], insofar as it moves and affects the will. Just as the knowledge by which we distinguish good from evil is inherent in the mind as its subject, but in the will as its effective cause, when it elicits or commands the actions that reason dictates, so also the first act of faith must be distinguished from the second act. For with respect to its essence it is indeed in the intellect as in its proper subject; but with respect to its operation, which holds its proper place in the will and brings no change to it at all, it is also in the will, namely so that it renews both and makes them partakers of its good things according to the capacity and grasp of each.

units.la: Obiectum etiam fidei iustificantis, seu materia circa quam haec fides versatur, generale aut speciale est totum Dei verbum nobis in Scripturis sacris patefactum, vltra quod fides iustificans non sapit. 1. Cor. 4. verf. 6. Haec autem, fratres, figura quadam transfuli ad me ipsum, & Apollo propter vos, ut in nobis discatis, supra id quod scriptum est, non supra sapere. Rom. 10. verf. 17. Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Verbi enim diuini veritas, fidei huius fundamentum ac fulcrum est, à quo si declinet, necessario corruit. Speciale obiectum est doctrina Euangelii, reconciliationem & sanctificationem per & propter Mediatorem Christum offerentis & conferentis. Quamuis igitur fidei iustificantis obiectum sit totius verbi diuini veritas, in promissionibus tamen Euangelicis solidam stabilitatem reperit.
units.tr: The object of justifying faith, or the matter with which this faith is concerned, is in general or in particular the whole Word of God revealed to us in the holy Scriptures, beyond which justifying faith does not go. 1 Cor. 4:6: But these things, brethren, I have figuratively transferred to myself and Apollos for your sake, that in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written. Romans 10:17: Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. For the truth of the divine word is the foundation and prop of this faith, and if faith departs from it, it necessarily falls. The specific object is the doctrine of the Gospel, which offers and confers reconciliation and sanctification through and for the sake of the Mediator, Christ. Although, then, the object of justifying faith is the truth of the whole divine Word, it finds its firm stability especially in the evangelical promises.

units.la: Forma fidei iustificantis est πίστις, seu certa persuasio, de veritate Euangelica, & salute per solum Christum obtinenda, firmúsquc assensus veritati illi adhibitus, ac proinde legitima ad obiectum suum proprium & adæquatum Christum videlicet ordinatio, secundum quam qui credit, illi arctissimè vnitur, adeò vt vnum cum Christo factus omnium illius bonorum communionem habeat, secundum demensum à Deo ordinatum. Atque hinc concludimus, charitatem, ac obedientiam, quam mandatis diuinis præstare tenemur, non magis esse formam fidei, quàm corpus animæ, per quod operatur, aut effectum causæ, nec fidem etiam, habitum spiritualem, ex fide, spe & charitate compositum, rectè appellari posse, qua de re in parte ἐνεργητικὴ pluribus nobis erit agendum.
units.tr: The form of justifying faith is faith [πίστις], that is, a certain persuasion about the evangelical truth and about salvation to be obtained through Christ alone, together with a firm assent given to that truth. Accordingly, it is a lawful ordering toward its own proper and adequate object, namely Christ, by which whoever believes is most closely united to him, so that, made one with Christ, he has communion in all his good things, according to the measure ordained by God. From this we conclude that love and the obedience which we are bound to render to the divine commands are no more the form of faith than the body is the soul, through which the soul acts, or than an effect is the cause. Nor can faith, as a spiritual habit composed of faith, hope and love, rightly be called faith either. We shall deal with this matter at more length in the part on the effective operations.

units.la: Effectus fidei iustificantis, quæ sunt ἐνέργειαι in ipso homine, varii recenseri possunt, nos paucorum enumeratione contenti erimus. Primum igitur ex fide nascitur filialis illa fiducia, quâ homo fidelis promissionem illam Dei, de reconciliatione, remissione peccatorum, ac vita æterna, per & propter Christum, impetranda, sibi per fidem specialem applicat, ac proinde tranquilla cum conscientia, & indubitata persuasione, de fauore, gratia, & amore Dei, accedit ad tribunal gratiæ, & remissionem peccatorum, vitámque æternam, à Deo, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, petit, Ephef.3.v.12. In quo habemus libertatem, & aditum cum fiducia, per fidem ipsius. Ex quibus verbis luculenter apparet, verum esse id quod præstantissimi Theologi, inprimis verò Caluinus, & Beza obseruarunt, nempe πεποίθησιν, id est fiduciam, à fide, tanquam effectum à causa, dissere, ac proinde à nonnullis perperam, pro fide, substitui ipsum fiduciæ nomen, quamuis illa duo, indissolubili nexu ac vinculo, quoties de fide iustificante agitur, cohæreant: Differunt enim πίστις & πεποίθησις, seu fides, ac fiducia, non tantùm vt causa & effectus, sicut ex citato testimonio liquet, & ex sequentibus amplius patefiet, verùm etiam, subiecto, actu, atque obiecto distinguuntur. Subiecto proprio: nam si essentiam, & actum primum ipsius fidei respicias, subiectum ipsius ἁγιωσύνης, & proprium est intellectus, nō quidem theoricus tantùm, sed etiam practicus: fiducia verò vtcunque radicem habeat in intellectu, sedem tamen proprie in corde figit, ibique aduersus omnes dubitationis ac desperationis insultus, castrametatur. Actu, quia fides ample[?]titur veritatem propositionis Euangelicæ indefinitè & singulariter quidem etiam, sed sub præscripta conditione, quo videlicet credit homo, Christum esse promissum illum salvatorem mundi, & suū quoque, si in ipsum credat: seu omnes credentes in Christum salvos esse: & se quoque, si in ipsum crediderit. Fiducia verò consequens propositionis, id est, promissum fidei præmium, nempe vitam æternam, sibi applicat absolutè ac speciali ter, propter certitudinem antecedentis, quia videlicet homo ille scit & sentit, se credere: ac proinde fides est assensus, seu certò persuasa intelligentia, & notitia de veritate sermonis Euangelici, propter infallibilem veritatem, & infinitam potentiam Dei: Fiducia verò est specialis applicatio, seu, de reconciliatione cum Deo, per mortem Christi facta, ac fidei præmio, vitæ videlicet æternæ, hæreditate consequenda, persuasio, propter fidem, tanquam necessarium antecedens, cui Deus salutem, & omnes benedictiones spirituales promisit ac destinauit, & sine qua, nec in filium adoptare, nec vitæ æternæ participem facere quenquam, decreuit. Et certè destinatum ac promissum ex Dei misericordia, & gratia, fidei præmium, ab ipsius fidei, velut requisitæ obedientiæ, obiecto, diligentes distinguendum esse, quis inficiabitur? Quum enim Deus ius ... remissionem peccatorum ac vitam æternam, cum omnibus benedictionibus spiritualibus, omnibus Ecclesiæ membris promiserit communiter, verùm non absolutè, sed sub conditione fidei quæ cum sit ... obiectum credendum necessariò præsupponit, inde manifestè liquet, specialem illam consequentis in propositione applicationem, atque absolutam de remissione peccatorum, ac vita æterna consequenda, certitudinem ac persuasionem fidei obiectum non esse, quia ordine naturæ, iustitiæ, decreti, ac fœderis diuini, obedientia fidei, ipsum obedientiæ, ac fidei præmium præcedit: secus enim prius crederemus & expectaremus promissum præmium, quàm officium cui illud promissum est præstaremus, quod est absurdum & contra fœderis diuini naturam, secundum quam bonum virtutis & iustitiæ, à creatura præstandum bonum conditionis & felicitatis à Deo promissæ, semper antecedit, & demonstratur veritas sententiæ nostræ, tum autoritate Iohannis capite primo Euang. versu duodecimo: Quotquot autem eum acceperunt, dedit eis dignitatem, ut filii Dei fierent, iis qui credunt in nomen eius, & cap. vigesimo, versu 31. Hæc scripta sunt ut credatis datis Iesum esse Christum, & vt credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Rom. 0. v. 9. Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Iesum, & credideris in ore tuo, quod Deus eum excitauit ex mortuis, saluus eris. Ioh. 6. v. 68.69. Respondit ei Simon Petrus, Domine ad quem ibimus? verba vitae aeternae habes, & nos credimus & cognouimus te esse Christum Filium illum Dei viuentis. En confessionem fidei Apostolicam.
units.tr: The effects of justifying faith, which are operations [ἐνέργειαι] in the man himself, can be listed in various ways. We shall be content with a short enumeration of a few. First, from faith is born that filial confidence by which the faithful man applies to himself, through a special faith, that promise of God concerning reconciliation, the forgiveness of sins, and eternal life, to be obtained through and for the sake of Christ. Consequently, with a tranquil conscience and an undoubting persuasion of God's favour, grace and love, he approaches the throne of grace and asks God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. Ephesians 3:12: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence through his faith. From these words it is clear, as the most eminent theologians, especially Calvin and Beza, have observed, that confidence [πεποίθησιν], that is, fiducia, differs from faith as an effect from its cause. Therefore some have wrongly substituted the name fiducia for faith, although the two cohere in an indissoluble bond whenever justifying faith is under discussion. For faith [πίστις] and confidence [πεποίθησις], or faith and fiducia, differ not only as cause and effect, as is clear from the cited testimony and will become clearer from what follows, but are also distinguished by their subject, act and object. By their proper subject: for if you consider the essence and first act of faith itself, its subject is the intellect, and its proper seat is not only the theoretical but also the practical intellect. Fiducia, however, though it has its root in the intellect, nevertheless properly fixes its seat in the heart, and there it encamps against all the assaults of doubt and despair. By their act: because faith embraces the truth of the evangelical proposition indefinitely and even singularly, but under the prescribed condition, namely that the man believes that Christ is that promised Saviour of the world, and his own Saviour too, if he believes in him; or that all who believe in Christ are saved, and that he too will be saved if he believes. But fiducia, which follows the proposition, that is, the reward of faith promised, namely eternal life, applies it to himself absolutely and specially, on account of the certainty of the antecedent, because that man knows and feels that he believes. Accordingly, faith is assent, or a certainly persuaded understanding and knowledge of the truth of the evangelical word, on account of the infallible truth and infinite power of God. Fiducia, however, is the special application, or the persuasion, of reconciliation with God made through the death of Christ, and of the reward of faith, namely eternal life to be obtained by inheritance, on account of faith as a necessary antecedent. God has promised and destined salvation and all spiritual blessings to faith, and he has decreed that without faith he will adopt no one as a son or make anyone a partaker of eternal life. And who will deny that the reward of faith, destined and promised by God's mercy and grace, must be distinguished from the object of faith as the required obedience? For since God has promised forgiveness of sins and eternal life, with all spiritual blessings, to all the members of the Church in common, but not absolutely; rather under the condition of faith, which of necessity presupposes the object to be believed, it is manifestly clear that this special application of the consequent in the proposition, and the absolute certainty and persuasion about the forgiveness of sins and eternal life to be obtained, is not the object of faith. For in the natural order, the order of justice, the order of God's decree and covenant, the obedience of faith precedes the reward of that obedience and of faith. Otherwise we would believe and expect the promised reward before performing the duty to which it was promised, which is absurd and contrary to the nature of the divine covenant, according to which the good of virtue and righteousness to be rendered by the creature always precedes the good of condition and happiness promised by God. The truth of our view is demonstrated both by the authority of John 1:12, But as many as received him, to them he gave the power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name, and of John 20:31, These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing you may have life through his name. Romans 10:9: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. John 6:68-69: Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Behold the apostolic confession of faith.

units.la: Sic Ioh. 4. v. 34. Ex urbe autem illa multi Samaritanorum crediderunt in eum. v. 42. Ipsi audiuimus & scimus hunc esse vere Seruatorem illum mundi Christum: & 11. v. 25.26.27. Dixit ei, nempe Martha, Ego sum resurrectio & vita, qui credit in me, etsi mortuus fuerit, viuet: Et quisquis viuit, & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum: credis hoc? Ait illi, etiam Domine, ego credo te esse Christum filium Dei, qui in mundum venturus erat. Nec alia fides in adultis baptizandis requiritur.
units.tr: So John 4:34. "Many of the Samaritans from that city believed in him." Verse 42: "We have heard for ourselves, and know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, Christ." And John 11:25–27: "Jesus said to her, Martha, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, shall live; and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this? She said to him, Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world." No other faith is required in adults who are to be baptized.

units.la: Act. 8. v. 36.37. Ait Eunuchus, En aquam, quid prohibet me baptizari? Dixit vero Philippus, Si credis ex toto corde, licet. Respondens ille, dixit, Credo Filium Dei esse Iesum Christum. In quibus locis, vt & alibi passim praemium fidei, ab ipsa fide, & eius obiecto, distertis verbis distinguit tum etiam exemplo Abrahae, qui tum demum postquam Dei verbo credidit, iustitiae laudem obtinuisse, non vero priusquam crederet iustificatus esse dicitur. Adde, quod obiectum fidei semper verum est, etiam antequam credamus. imo etiamsi illud nunquam nobis persuaderi pateremur, nihilominus tamen indubitatae ac infallibili veritati diuinae, nisi certitudinem, & ἀξιώσεως illius à fide adeóque nutu & arbitrio nostro, suspensam velimus, illa ἀπιστίᾳ nostra nihil derogaretur. Si enim nos infidi sumus, ille tamen fidus manet, negare seipsum non poterit. 2. Tim. capite secundo, versu decimo tertio.
units.tr: Acts 8:36–37: "The eunuch said, See, there is water; what prevents me from being baptized? Philip said, If you believe with your whole heart, you may. He answered, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." In these passages, as elsewhere throughout, Scripture explicitly distinguishes the reward of faith from faith itself and from its object. The example of Abraham does the same: he is said to have obtained the praise of righteousness only after he believed the word of God, and not to have been justified before he believed. Add that the object of faith is always true, even before we believe it. Indeed, even if we never allowed it to be persuaded to us, the divine truth, which is indubitable and infallible, would lose nothing, unless we made the certainty and worthiness [ἀξιώσεως] of that truth depend on faith, and so on our nod and judgement. Our unbelief [ἀπιστίᾳ] takes nothing from it: "If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself" (2 Tim. 2:13).

units.la: At vero priusquam in Iesum Christum credamus nec amici Dei nec filii ipsius, nec vitae aeternae haeredes sumus, vt pote filii irae, ac proinde maledictioni & damnationi aeternae obnoxii. Quandiu vero, imo per quot annos multorum aures externa Euangelii praedicatione verberantur, priusquam permoueri queant, vt fidem habeant ipsius veritati, & tamen credere interea semper iubentur? Ex quibus omnibus liquido, opinor, constat, obiectum fiduciae, & specialis illius applicationis, ab ipsius fidei, ac πληροφορίας obiecto, distinguendum, ac proinde ποιήσεως illam, seu fiduciam fidei iustificantis, nec formam, nec partem essentialem. sed effectum fructúmque esse. Hanc sententiam nostram confirmat vniuersa totius Euangelii veritas, quæ non nisi credentibus in Christum vitam ac salutem æternam promittit. Quemadmodum igitur Euangelium nobis promittit reconciliationem cum Deo Patre, remissionem peccatorum, ac vitam æternam: ita etiam de illis beneficiis consequendis & impetrādis certi esse possumus, quia omnis salutis nostræ certitudo verbo Dei & promissionibus ipsius nititur. Atqui Euangelium nec remissionem peccatorum, nec reconciliationem cum Deo Patre, nec vitam æternam promittit vllis, nisi sub conditione fidei, hoc est, nisi credat Christum esse promissum, ac præstitum illum Saluatorem mundi, & suum quoque, si hoc credat. Secundum sermonem Euangelicum enim verū est, Omnes in Christum credentes salvos futuros esse, sed non est verum de Petro & Paulo, nisi posita in illis conditione fidei, sub qua nobis vita æterna promittitur, hoc est, verum hoc est de illis non materialiter, sed formaliter consideratis, vt loquuntur Scholastici. Ergo nemo de salute certus esse potest, nisi stipulatam conditionem impleuerit, hoc est, crediderit Christum esse Saluatorem mundi, & suum quoque, si crediderit. Ex quibus omnibus necessario sequitur, fidem ac fiduciam, vitam æternam, velut obiectum, non eodem modo, considerare, quia illa, videlicet fides, coniungit consequens commune, nempe vitæ æternæ præmium, cum antecedente communi, nempe credentibus omnibus, generaliter (quia commune illud antecedens adiuncto conuestitum est ex libera Dei voluntate ac dispensatione requisito ad hoc, vt consequens seu prædicatum istud, de illo enuntiari possit) de suo subiecto vero, cui infusus est fidei habitus, specialiter, sed sub conditione, & non absolute: vtrumque vero propter naturam gratuiti fœderis, veritatem promissionis diuinæ, & omnipotentiam Dei: fiducia vero, commune illud consequens seu attributum de subiecto seu antecedente proprio enuntiat specialiter, simpliciter & absolute, propter certitudinem fidei, cuius conditione, subiectum conuestitum esse præsupponit. Ac proinde liquido etiam constat, credere in Christum, & credere me saluum futurum esse, non esse vnum & idem, quamuis hoc posterius, illud prius, necessario ac semper consequatur, quæ proinde indissolubili nexu copulo coniungóque, non vero separo aut seiungo, sed quia male confunduntur, distinguo.
