Or: justifying faith is a habit infused by the Holy Spirit into the human mind, by which we know, lay hold of and receive Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and men, with all his benefits, to the glory of God and the salvation of our souls. But good works are not a habit of this kind infused by the Holy Spirit; they are supernatural actions, which, the Holy Spirit working, proceed from the regenerate and justified out of true faith, and are done according to the law of God, to the glory of the divine name, the edification of our neighbour, and the confirmation of our faith and election. This definition cannot apply to justifying faith itself. Therefore justifying faith and good works are not one and the same. Or: things that differ in genus and form, or in specific difference, cannot be one and the same in reality and essence. Now justifying faith and good works differ in genus and form, or specific difference. In genus: because justifying faith, as a theological virtue, is an infused habit, whereas good works are not habits but actions. In form: because the form of justifying faith is full assurance [πληροφορία], or a certain persuasion concerning the truth of the Gospel message and of salvation to be obtained through Christ alone, and a firm assent given to that truth; and so it is a lawful orientation toward its own proper and adequate object, namely Christ. But the form of good works is good order [εὐνομία], that is, their agreement and conformity with the law of God, just as the form of sin and of an evil work is lawlessness [ἀνομία] and deviation from the law. Now, just as law and Gospel differ in form, so too the conditions of each covenant, the legal and the evangelical, differ in form; and therefore justifying faith is neither prescribed nor judged by the law, nor does it receive its form and specific difference from the law. For the law demands perfect righteousness and obedience, complete in every number and degree, and condemns even the least transgression to eternal curse; but faith begs for the pardon of sins and embraces it as promised through and for the sake of Christ. Hence it necessarily follows that justifying faith and good works cannot be one and the same in reality and essence. Secondly: if the effects that the holy Scriptures ascribe to justifying faith cannot in any way belong to good works or to charity, then it follows that justifying faith and good works, or charity, cannot be called one and the same in reality. Now the former is plainly true, as the holy Scriptures themselves clearly show. For it is through faith, not through good works or charity, that we obtain the right of the sons of God, that we are united with Christ and made partakers of all the benefits flowing from the power of his death, burial, resurrection and life. John 1:12: "As many as received him, to them he gave this dignity, that they should become the sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name." Romans 11:23: "And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, shall be grafted in." Romans 6:3, 4, 6, 8, 11: "Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have grown together with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly grow together also in the likeness of his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be made powerless, that we should no longer serve sin, etc. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him. So also you reckon yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God, through Christ Jesus our Lord." Galatians 2:20: "I am crucified with Christ. Yet I live, but not I; Christ lives in me; and the life that I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Ephesians 3:17: "May he grant you that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith." Colossians 2:10-13: "And you are complete in him, who is the head of all rule and authority; in whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, when you put off the body of the flesh subject to sin, through the circumcision of Christ; buried with him in baptism, in which also you were raised with him through the faith of God's effective working, who raised him from the dead, and when you were dead in sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, having forgiven you all your sins," etc. Colossians 3:1-3: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; mind the things above, not the things on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." And just as the bond of union with Christ, on the side of believers, is justifying faith itself, through which Christ dwells in our hearts, while on the side of Christ it is the Spirit of Christ himself, who flows from Christ our head into believers, and through whom the faithful are joined to Christ as members to the head; so the bond by which the faithful are joined to one another is charity itself, and mutual love and concord. Colossians 2:2: "That their hearts may be comforted, being knit together in love, and attain all the riches of full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery of God, both of the Father and of Christ." Then, "we live by faith, not by good works." Galatians 2:20: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me; and the life that I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." "Our hearts are purified by faith, not by good works." Acts 15:9: "He made no distinction between us and them, having purified their hearts by faith." Finally, we are justified through faith, not through good works. Romans 4:3-5: "What does the Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness. But to the one who works, the wage is not counted as grace but as debt; but to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness." And Romans 11:6: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work." Galatians 2:16: "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, but through faith in Jesus Christ, we also have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by the works of the Law, because by the works of the Law no flesh will be justified." He does not overturn this doctrine, that elsewhere we are also said to be justified by works and not by faith only, and Abraham is said to have been justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar. James 2:21, 24: Because the Apostle James attributes justification, salvation and eternal life to good works in such a way, and withholds them from faith alone, a metonymy of the effect must be recognised here in the word "works", so that the name of the effect is put for the cause, and works, the effects of faith, are put for faith, their efficient cause. The word "faith" is not taken properly, nor synonymously [σωσῳνύμως], but homonymously [ὁμωνύμως] and universally [καθολικῶς]; that is, James grants to his adversaries, against whom he disputes, that faith, though often vaunted in words, albeit falsely, may be called faith, but it is dead and ineffective for justifying. This clearly appears from the question and the thesis itself, which he sets out to prove: that faith without works is dead, useless, and altogether powerless to justify and save; a thesis which he states in verse 14 and afterwards demonstrates both by a comparison and by very weighty arguments. Thirdly, because justifying faith is opposed to doubt and unbelief, whereas good works are opposed not to doubt or unbelief but to impiety and evil deeds. Matthew 14:31: "Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him, and said to him, O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" Mark 9:24: "The father of the boy immediately cried out with tears, 'I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.'" Romans 2:6-8: "who will render to each according to his works: to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory, honour and immortality, that is, eternal life; but to those who are contentious, and do not obey the truth but obey unrighteousness, there will be indignation and wrath." Fourthly, things that differ in office and object cannot be one and the same in reality. Now justifying faith and charity differ in office and object, because justifying faith looks immediately to Christ in the Gospel, and without any help from other virtues assents to the truth of the Gospel message with a firmly persuaded understanding. John 6:68: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God." John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." 2 Thessalonians 2:11, 12: "God will send them a working of deception, so that they believe a lie, and so that all who did not believe the truth may be condemned." Titus 1:1: "Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness." Yet although faith also produces the constant fruits of good works, it does so mediately, and "working through charity"; hence it is also said to work through charity: Galatians 5:6. But charity itself is concerned and occupied with the good of the neighbour and with the virtues commanded by the precepts of the second table: Romans 13:8-10: "He who loves another has fulfilled the Law. For the commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet,' and whatever other commandment there is, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself.' Love does no wrong to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." From these things it necessarily follows that justifying faith and charity and good works are not one and the same in reality and essence. Fifthly, because one virtue cannot constitute the form and essence of another virtue. Now justifying faith and charity are introduced and commended throughout the holy Scriptures as different species of virtue: 1 Corinthians 13:13: "But now faith, hope and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity." Ephesians 6:23: "Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Colossians 1:3, 4: "We give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all the saints." 1 Thessalonians 1:3: "Constantly remembering before our God and Father your effective faith, your laborious charity, and your patient hope in our Lord Jesus." 1 Timothy 4:12: "Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity." And 6:11: "But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness." 2 Peter 1:5-7: "For this very reason, adding all diligence, supply in your faith virtue, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge temperance, and in temperance patience, and in patience godliness, and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love." 1 John 3:23: "This is his teaching: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as he commanded us," and elsewhere throughout. From all these passages it appears clearer than midday light that charity and good works cannot constitute the form of justifying faith. Sixthly and lastly: if faith and good works were to be made one and the same in reality and essence, then those two parts of theology, namely faith and the actions of faith, or wisdom and righteousness, and the true sense of God and his right worship, would be confused with one another; yet these two different parts are most plainly distinguished in the holy Scriptures. Acts 24:14-16: "I confess this to you, that according to the way which they call a sect, so I serve the God of my fathers, believing all things that are written in the Law and the Prophets, and having hope in God, which these men also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust. In this I also exercise myself to have a conscience without offence toward God and toward men." Mark 1:15: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near; repent and believe the Gospel." So Paul, Titus 3:8, commands that "those who have believed God should be careful to maintain good works"; that is, that they should direct all their cares and thoughts to the exercise of good works, by which their conduct, adorned and commended by its own distinctive graces, ought to be conspicuous, and they should excel in these, as befits those who wish to be seen to have believed God and kept themselves for him. And 1 John 3:23: "This is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son, and love one another, as he commanded." From these testimonies it clearly appears that our whole religion, and the sum of all Christian piety, rests on two heads: namely faith, which we exercise in the revealed Word of God in the holy Scriptures, and good works, or a good conscience before God; that is, obedience to what God demands of us in his Word, which we pursue with zeal, for the sake of the promised salvation, toward God. Now that faith, the actions of faith, that is, a right sense of God, should precede true worship of him in this order, is confirmed both by nature and by Scripture. For nature teaches that an act of the mind, such as the knowledge of God, is prior to an act of the will, such as the worship of God and the pursuit of piety and good works. Scripture plainly testifies that there can be no invocation of God without faith, and no faith without preaching. Romans 10:14: "How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?" And in Ephesians 4:18 the unbelieving Gentiles are said to be "alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them," as if this ignorance were not simple and harmless, but culpable and deliberate, joined with a wicked mind, and were the cause why those nations live impiously and do not duly worship God in hope of attaining eternal life. And Hebrews 11:6: "He who comes to God must hold firmly to these two things: that God exists, and that he rewards those who seek him." For clearly, one who does not know God's nature, works and will cannot worship him rightly and earnestly, since there is no desire for what is unknown. From all these things it most evidently appears that justifying faith must not indeed be separated from good works, as a cause from its effect and a tree from its fruits, but must be distinguished from them; and that the adversary has most imprudently confused the one with the other, against the very nature of faith and the authority of holy Scripture. Having thus set these things out, the arguments of the adversary himself, by which he tries to establish his absurd opinion, must now be examined by us in order.

units.la: Ad primum igitur respondeo, assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse falsam, neque subiuncto prosyllogismo demonstrari, quippe cuius connexum manifesta falsitate laboret. Quamuis enim Asaph Israelitici populi posteros,ad fidem verbi ac promissionum diuinarum veritati habendam, spemque ac fiduciam in solo Deo collocandam, hortatus fuerit, minimè tamen inde sequitur fidem, spem fiduciamque, & obedientiam, vnum ac idem esse: quemadmodum è contrà, ex eo quod incredulitati Israelitarum, sed metonymicè sumptæ, id est vniuersæ ipsorum impietati, virtutes illæ Christianæ, fides nimirum, & obedientia ex fide,ab Asapho opponuntur: sequi incredulitatem Israelitarum proprie,ac strictè sumptam,diffidentiæ,inobedientiæ,ingratitudinis,ac reliquorum scelerum nominibus definiendam esse, quis cum ratione dixerit? In Psalmo enim isto septuagesimo octauo, impia illa, & obstinata Israelitarum malitia ita ab Asapho describitur vt prima omnium scelerum causa, & origo, de potentia videlicet diuina, vaccillantis animi dubitatio, ex qua deindè diffidentia,-de gratia, & beneuolentiæ diuinæ erga illos affectu,cũ horrenda ingratitudine,impatientia frementis,ac in Deum impia cum audacia insurgentis animi,aliisque innumeris peccatis, emanauerunt, ab illo recenseatur, illius verò dubitationis fons, nempè summa cordis durities, & operum diuinorum impius contemptor,oscendatur, vnde factum fit, vt neque castigationibus vllis, nec stupendis illis à Deo patratis miraculis, nec denique ingentium quantumuis beneficiorum cumulis, ad fidem promissionibus diuinis habendam, & obedientiæ ac debitæ gratitudinis officia Deo pręstanda, flecti ac permoueri potuerint. Ac proinde non solam incredulitatem, sed incredulitatis etiam fœtidos fructus, prolixè enumerat Psaltes, quemadmodum etiam in sua admonitione fontem ipsum cum riuulis, nempe fidem cum pietatis & obedientiæ serio studio, ac impietatis odio, coniungit & iniungit,quæ omnia imperitè perturbantur & confunduntur ab Ostorrodio, cui proinde consequentia prosyllogismi probanda incumbit.
units.tr: To the first argument, then, I reply that the minor premise of the principal syllogism is false, and it cannot be proved by the attached prosyllogism, since its connection suffers from manifest falsity. For although Asaph exhorted the posterity of the Israelite people to hold to the faith of the word and the truth of the divine promises, and to place their hope and trust in God alone, it does not follow from this that faith, hope, trust and obedience are one and the same thing. Conversely, when Asaph sets against the unbelief of the Israelites (taken metonymically, that is, as their whole impiety) those Christian virtues, namely faith and obedience arising from faith, who could rightly say that the unbelief of the Israelites, taken properly and strictly, must be defined by the names of distrust, disobedience, ingratitude and the rest of their sins? In that seventy-eighth Psalm, Asaph describes the impious and obstinate wickedness of the Israelites as follows: the first cause and origin of all their sins is a wavering mind's doubt about the divine power, from which there then flowed distrust; doubt about God's grace and his goodwill towards them; a dreadful ingratitude; the impatience of a rebellious spirit; and an impious audacity rising up against God, along with countless other sins. The source of that doubt is shown to be the extreme hardness of heart and the impious contempt of God's works. Hence it came about that they could be moved and turned neither by any chastisements, nor by the astonishing miracles wrought by God, nor finally by heaps of however great benefits, to hold the divine promises as true and to render to God the duties of obedience and due gratitude. Therefore the Psalmist lists at length not only the unbelief but also the foul fruits of unbelief; and just as in his exhortation he joins and enjoins the very source together with its streams, namely faith together with earnest zeal for piety and obedience and hatred of impiety, all of which Ostorrodius confuses and mixes up through his lack of skill. He is therefore bound to prove the consequence of his prosyllogism.

units.la: Ad secundum respondeo, connexi consequentiam esse falsam, neque ratione annexa stabiliri & confirmari posse: nam de Daniele illa quidem testimonia perhibentur, quod & Deum studiosissimo cultu prosequutus sit,& fidem, spem, atque fiduciã in ipso solo collocauerit: sed tamen fidem Danielis nihil aliud fuisse quàm fiduciam in Deo collocatam, & obedientiam præceptis diuinis pręstitam,neque ex illo antecedēte sequitur, neque ex citato illo capite sexto, vllo modo demonstrari potest. Et mirum est,ex qua Logica Ostorrodius illam rationem nectendarum consequentiarum didicerit, vt cum duo vel plura diuersa prædicata de subiecto enunciantur,vel diuersa etiam officia alicui iniunguntur,illorum vnum alterius formam appellandum & constituendum esse? Argumenti tertij planè eadem est ratio. Niniuitæ enim & credidisse Deo,& vitam morésque serió emendasse leguntur,quis tamen iustis legibus inde concludet, fidem ac resipiscentiam re & essentia ipsa vnum ac idem esse? Resipiscentia igitur seria ac fide iustificante,bonorúmque operum studio peccatoribus ad consequendam remissionem peccatorum, vitámque æternam opus esse,Scriptura luculenter docet,& nos religiosè credimus, sed negamus ex illo Niniuitarum exemplo sequi,aut vllis aliis rationibus & argumentis fidem iustificantem,&bonorum operum studium ac resipiscentiam. tiam reipsa vnum ac idem esse, nec inter se tanquam causam & effectum distingui debere, demonstrari posse.
units.tr: To the second argument I reply that the consequence of the connection is false, and cannot be established or confirmed by an attached reason. For indeed the testimonies bear witness that Daniel worshipped God with the utmost devotion and placed his faith, hope and trust in him alone. But that Daniel's faith was nothing other than trust placed in God, and obedience rendered to the divine precepts, does not follow from that antecedent, nor can it be demonstrated in any way from the sixth chapter cited. And it is remarkable from what kind of logic Ostorrodius learned this rule for drawing consequences: that when two or more different predicates are stated of one subject, or different duties are laid upon someone, one of them must be called and treated as the form of the other. The third argument has exactly the same answer. For we read that the Ninevites both believed God and earnestly amended their life and morals; yet by what sound rules will anyone conclude from this that faith and repentance are one and the same thing in reality and in essence? Scripture teaches plainly, and we religiously believe, that serious repentance, justifying faith and zeal for good works are needed for sinners to obtain forgiveness of sins and eternal life. But we deny that it follows from the example of the Ninevites, or from any other reasons and arguments, that justifying faith, zeal for good works and repentance are in fact one and the same, or that they ought not to be distinguished from one another as cause and effect.

units.la: Ad quartum & vltimum respondeo: Falsum esse, quod in prima enuntiatione affirmatur, nempe fidem illam, ob quam hactenus sancti Dei homines Deo placuerint, talem fidem, proprie videlicet sic dictam, fuisse, qualem Aduersarius hactenus definiuit, cuius definitio proinde, non vt certa atque concessa ab illo praesupponenda, sed vt dubia, ac a nobis negata, demonstranda fuit. Quanquam enim sanctos illos Dei homines fiduciam ac spem suam in solo Deo collocasse, & cum vera fide seriam pietatis & obedientiae studium coniunxisse, libenter meritoque agnoscamus: tamen fidem ipsorum, qua coram Deo iustificati sunt, nihil aliud quam fiduciam, & hac nihil aliud quam obedientiam mandatis diuinis praestitam, fuisse, demonstrari minime potest: neque testimonium ex Heb. 11. verf. 6. sententiae illi patrocinatur: sensus enim est, Fieri non posse, vt recte seriòque Deum colat, qui illius naturam, voluntatem, & opera ignorat, quum ignoti nulla sit cupido: sicut e contrà fieri non potest, vt qui solidam habet Dei cognitionem, non etiam ad illum colendum, & vitam aeternam capessendam sese accingat. Ex quibus iam sententia ac doctrina Aduersarii euertitur, & fidem iustificantem, vero Dei cultu, & bonorum operum studio, ordine priorem esse, ac proinde vnum ac idem reipsa cum hoc esse non posse, tum ex hoc ipso citato loco, tum ex aliis etiam scripturae testimoniis luculenter demonstratur. Nam si quaerere Deum nihil aliud est quam ipsum timere & colere, debitamque obedientiam ipsi praestare, eos ipsos vero qui ad Deum accedunt, hoc est, vt volunt Aduersarii, Deo placent, seque ad Deum colendum, & debitam obedientiam ipsi praestandam accingunt, credere oportet Deum esse, & remunerari cultores suos: liquido constat fidem illam, studio obedientiae & cultus diuini ordine priorem esse. Deinde verum Dei cultum atque inuocationem absque fide praecedanea, neque hanc absque praedicatione esse posse, discerne docet Apostolus Rom. 10. v. 14. Quomodo inuocabunt eum in quem non crediderunt? quomodo autem credet de quo nec audierunt? quomodo autem audient absque praedicante? Ex quibus omnibus iam liquido constat, connexum principalis syllogismi esse falsum, neque subiuncto prosyllogismo demonstrari, quippe cuius connexum antiquitate, & latente sub hac, consequentiae falsitate, laborat. Nam Deo sine vero ipsius cultu & inuocatione placere nō posse,ambiguè dicitur:Vel enim intelligitur de causa sine qua non,vt loquuntur Logici,sic vt sen- sus sit,sidem illam quæ bonorum operum fructibus, atque orna- mentis destituta sit,nos nec iustificare,nec ad vitam æternam per- ducere posse:Vel intelligitur de iustificationis causa efficiente,eá- que vel meritoria, vel instrumentali. Si priori sensu accipiatur e- nuntiatum illud, tum consequentia falsa est & ridicula:non enim sequitur ex eo, quod fides nos non iustificat sine bonis operibus, id est,si bonis operibus careat,bona opera fidei ipsius essentiam atque formam constituere. Consequentiam enim hanc etiam rerum naturalium exempla falsitatis conuincunt: nam ex eo quod intel- lectus non intelligit sine voluntate, anima non ratiocinatur sine corpore,lux solis non sine calore ciusdem illuminat,& calor solis non sine luce illius calefacit, minimè sequitur, voluntatem intel- lectus humani,corpus animæ,& calorem lucis,lucem denique ca- loris naturam ac formā constituere.Sin vero posteriori sensu acci- piatur prædictum enuntiatū,falsa est assumptio,siue de meritoria, siue de iustrumentali causa intelligatur,quia iustificationis nostrę causam meritoriā ipsum sacrificium Christi,instrumentalem vero fidem esse,docet Apostolus, Rom.3.v.24.25.Iustificātur autem gra- tis,id est,eius gratia per redemptionem factam in IesuChristo,quem pro- posuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam, per remissionem præcedentium peccatorum. Ex quibus omnibus manifeste iam apparet,fidem iustificantem cum suis esse- ctis atque fructibus cōfundi ab Aduersario,nec quicquam ab ipso in medium prolatum esse,quo sententia ac doctrina ipsius stabili- ri possit. Quę autem de fine mortis Christi subiungit Aduersarius, de iis capitibus sequentibus disputatio instituetur.
units.tr: To the fourth and last argument I reply: what is affirmed in the first statement is false, namely that that faith, on account of which the holy men of God have hitherto pleased God, was faith properly so called, of the kind the Adversary has hitherto defined. His definition, therefore, was to be proved by us, since we deny it, and not presupposed by him as certain and granted. For although we gladly and rightly acknowledge that those holy men of God placed their trust and hope in God alone, and joined serious zeal for piety and obedience with true faith, yet it cannot at all be shown that their faith, by which they were justified before God, was nothing other than trust, and that trust nothing other than obedience rendered to the divine commands. Nor does the testimony of Heb. 11 verse 6 support that opinion. Its sense is this: it is impossible for one to worship God rightly and earnestly who is ignorant of his nature, will and works, since there is no desire for the unknown; just as conversely it is impossible for one who has solid knowledge of God not to gird himself also to worship him and to lay hold of eternal life. From these points the doctrine and teaching of the Adversary is overturned, and it is shown clearly, both from this very passage and from other testimonies of Scripture, that justifying faith is prior in order to true worship of God and to zeal for good works, and therefore that it cannot be one and the same in reality with them. For if to seek God is nothing other than to fear and worship him and render him due obedience, and those who approach God, that is, as the Adversaries wish, please God and prepare themselves to worship God and to render him due obedience, it must be believed that God exists and rewards those who worship him. It is plainly evident that that faith is prior in order to zeal for obedience and divine worship. Next, the Apostle in Rom. 10 verse 14 teaches us that true worship and invocation of God cannot exist without prior faith, and that faith cannot exist without preaching: How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? From all these points it is now clear that the connection of the principal syllogism is false, and cannot be demonstrated by the attached prosyllogism, since its connection suffers from the antiquity of the falsity hidden beneath this consequence. For the statement that God cannot be pleased without true worship and invocation of him is ambiguous. It is understood either of a cause without which not, as the logicians say, so that the sense is that faith which lacks the fruits and adornments of good works cannot justify us nor bring us to eternal life; or it is understood of the efficient cause of justification, whether meritorious or instrumental. If the statement is taken in the first sense, then the consequence is false and ridiculous. For it does not follow from the fact that faith does not justify us without good works, that is, if it lacks good works, that good works constitute the very essence and form of faith. Examples from natural things also refute this consequence: because the intellect does not understand without the will, the soul does not reason without the body, the light of the sun does not illuminate without its heat, and the heat of the sun does not warm without its light, it by no means follows that the will constitutes the nature and form of the human intellect, the body constitutes the nature of the soul, heat constitutes the nature of light, or light constitutes the nature of heat. But if the stated proposition is taken in the second sense, then the assumption is false, whether it is understood of the meritorious or of the instrumental cause. For the Apostle teaches in Rom. 3 verses 24 and 25 that the meritorious cause of our justification is the sacrifice of Christ itself, and the instrumental cause is faith: They are justified freely, that is, by his grace through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness through the remission of sins that are past. From all these points it now clearly appears that the Adversary confuses justifying faith with its effects and fruits, and that he has brought forward nothing by which his opinion and doctrine could be established. The discussion of what the Adversary adds about the purpose of Christ's death will be carried out in the following chapters.

units.la: Atque sic hactenus primam disputationis Ostorrodianæ par- tem, nempe <bl>καταδικαστικὴν</bl>, qua doctrinam suam de fide iustificante proposuit,& demonstrare conatus est,examinauimus: restat vt et- iam ipsam <bl>ἀνατρεπτικὴν</bl>, qua aliorum à sua discrepantem doctrinam ac sententiam conuellere ac refutare conatur, breuiter excutiamus.
units.tr: So far we have examined the first part of Ostorodius's disputation, the condemnatory [καταδικαστικήν] part, in which he set out his doctrine of justifying faith and tried to demonstrate it. It remains to examine briefly the second part as well, the refutative [ἀνατρεπτικήν] part, by which he tries to overturn and refute doctrines that differ from his own.

units.la: In hac autem <bl>ἀνατρεπτικὴ</bl> tum Pōtificiorum, tum nostram orthodo- xam de fide iustificante doctrinam impugnat.Et illam quidē nem- pe Pontificiorum, tum notitiam & cognitionem veritatis à fidei definitione excludentium, tum etiam filialem illam fiduciam, ab eadem separantium,sententiam,quātum concernit,cum illa multis iisque grauissimis erroribus scateat, ipsam suis autoribus & patronis defendendam ac propugnandam relinquo, nostrarum Ecclesiarum, ac orthodoxam, a telis, quibus illa impetit Oftorrodius, vindicaturus ac defensurus.
units.tr: In this refutative part he attacks both the doctrine of the Papists and our orthodox doctrine of justifying faith. As for the Papists' view, which excludes the knowledge and recognition of the truth from the definition of faith, and which also separates from faith that filial trust, I leave it to its own authors and patrons to defend and champion, since it teems with many very grave errors. I shall undertake to vindicate and defend our Churches' orthodox doctrine from the missiles with which Ostorodius assails it.

units.la: Hanc igitur quantum concernit, in maxima caecitate illos haerere inquit, qui etsi statuant fidem non per solum assensum, sed etiam fiduciam definiendam esse, tamen fiduciam illam ita interpretantur, quod videlicet per illam meritum & iustitiam Christi apprehendamus, id est, credamus Deum nobis peccata nostra remissurum esse, si firmiter statuamus, illa per mortem & passionem Christi deleta esse. Atque hanc fidei definitionem, seu formam potius, quatuor argumentis impugnat, quo ordine proponemus atque examinabimus.
units.tr: As far as this goes, he says that those are stuck in the greatest blindness who, although they hold that faith is to be defined not by assent alone but also by trust, nevertheless interpret that trust so that, namely, through it we lay hold of the merit and righteousness of Christ, that is, we believe that God will forgive us our sins if we firmly hold that they have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ. He attacks this definition of faith, or rather this formula, with four arguments, which we shall set out and examine in order.

units.la: Primum est: quia illa fidei definitio nulla ratione ex Scripturis sacris demonstrari possit.
units.tr: The first is: that this definition of faith cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures in any way. ## The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
Quae definitio fidei iustificantis ex Scripturis sacris demonstrari non potest, illa non est vera:
units.tr: A definition of justifying faith that cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures is not true:

units.la: Atqui haec fidei iustificantis definitio, quod videlicet per illam meritum ac iustitiam Christi apprehendamus, id est, credamus Deum nobis peccata nostra remissurum esse, si firmiter statuamus, ea per mortem ac passionem Christi deleta esse, ex Scripturis sacris demonstrari non potest:
units.tr: But this definition of justifying faith, namely that through it we lay hold of the merit and righteousness of Christ, that is, we believe that God will forgive us our sins if we firmly hold that they have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ, cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures:

units.la: Ergo illa fidei iustificantis definitio non est vera.
units.tr: Therefore that definition of justifying faith is not true.

units.la: Secundum est, quod in eadem illa fidei definitione pugnantia inter se affirmentur, nempe Deum peccata nostra nobis remissurum, eademque deleturum esse, si credamus illa per mortem & passionem Christi deleta esse: ex quo evidenter apparet, inquit, illam fidem non esse fidem illam, sine qua Deo nemo placere potest.
units.tr: The second is that in this same definition of faith contradictory things are affirmed, namely that God will forgive us our sins and also blot them out, if we believe they have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ; from which it clearly appears, he says, that this is not that faith without which no one can please God. ## The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
Quae definitio pugnantia inter se, & se invicem evertentia affirmat, illa non est vera:
units.tr: A definition that affirms things contradictory to one another, and mutually subversive, is not true:

units.la: Atqui illa fidei definitio, quod videlicet per illam meritum & iustitiam Christi apprehendamus, inter se pugnantia, & se invicem evertentia affirmat:
units.tr: But this definition of faith, namely that through it we lay hold of the merit and righteousness of Christ, affirms things contradictory to one another and mutually subversive:

units.la: Ergo illa fidei definitio non est vera.
units.tr: Therefore that definition of faith is not true.

units.la: Assumptionis hanc adfert probationem.
units.tr: The proof of the minor premise is given here.

units.la: Quae fidei iustificantis definitio affirmat, Deum peccata nostra nobis remissurum & deleturum esse, si videlicet credamus, illa per mortem & passionem Christi deleta esse, illa inter se pugnantia, ac se invicem euertentia affirmat:
units.tr: The definition of justifying faith affirms that God will forgive and blot out our sins if we believe that they have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ; it affirms things that are mutually contradictory and that overturn one another:

units.la: At qui illa fidei iustificantis definitio affirmat, Deum peccata nostra nobis remissurum ac deleturum esse, si videlicet credamus illa propter mortem ac passionem Christi deleta esse:
units.tr: But a definition of justifying faith which affirms that God will forgive us our sins and blot them out, if we believe they have been blotted out on account of the death and passion of Christ:

units.la: Ergo illa fidei iustificantis definitio pugnantia inter se, ac se invicem euertentia affirmat.
units.tr: Therefore that definition of justifying faith affirms things contradictory to one another and mutually subversive.

units.la: Tertium est: quod illa fides sic definita cum bonis operibus nihil commune habet, quae proinde definitione illa fidei non comprehenduntur, cum tamen fides illa in se complectatur.
units.tr: The third is that faith so defined has nothing in common with good works, and so is not comprehended by that definition of faith, although that faith nonetheless embraces them within itself. ## The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
Quae fides sua natura ac proprietate cum obedientia ac bonis operibus nihil commune habet, illa non est vera ac iustificans fides:
units.tr: Faith which by its nature and property has nothing in common with obedience and good works is not true and justifying faith:

units.la: At qui fides illa, qua meritum & iustitiam Christi amplectimur, id est, credimus Deum nobis peccata nostra remissurum, si firma persuasione statuamus, illa per mortem & passionem Christi deleta esse.
units.tr: But that faith by which we embrace the merit and righteousness of Christ, that is, we believe that God will forgive us our sins if we hold with firm persuasion that they have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ,

units.la: Ergo fides illa non est vera ac iustificans fides.
units.tr: Therefore that faith is not true and justifying faith.

units.la: Maioris probatio haec est.
units.tr: The proof of the major premise is this.

units.la: Si fides vera ac iustificans, ipsam obedientiam ac bona opera in se complectitur, tum quum fides sua natura ac proprietate cum obedientia ac bonis operibus nihil commune habet, illa non est vera ac iustificans fides:
units.tr: If true and justifying faith embraces within itself obedience and good works, then, since faith by its own nature and property has nothing in common with obedience and good works, that faith is not true and justifying faith:

units.la: At qui prius est verum: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true: therefore the consequent also.

units.la: Minoris probatio haec est.
units.tr: The proof of the minor premise is this.

units.la: In cuius fidei definitione nulla obedientia ac bonorum operum fit mentio, illa cum obedientia ac bonis operibus nihil commune habet: Atqui in definitione fidei illius, qua iustitiam ac meritum Christi apprehendimus, nulla fit mentio obedientiae ac bonorum operum: Ergo fides illa, cum obedientia ac bonis operibus, sua natura ac proprietate nihil commune habet.
units.tr: A definition of faith in which no mention is made of obedience and good works shows that faith has nothing in common with obedience and good works. But in the definition of that faith by which we apprehend the righteousness and merit of Christ, no mention is made of obedience and good works. Therefore that faith, by its nature and property, has nothing in common with obedience and good works.

units.la: Quartum est: quod si illa vera esset fides, necessario inde sequeretur, eos omnes qui ante Christi aduentum Deo placuerunt, eandem illam fidem habuisse. Hoc vero nullis Scripturæ testimoniis probari, sed contrarium inde demonstrari posse, quemadmodum vnicum illud caput vndecimum epistolæ ad Hebræos aperte testatur. Quamuis enim multorum ibi fiat mentio, qui in Deum crediderint, ac proinde ipsi placuerint, eorundemque fides ibi explicetur: tamen obedientia, iustitia ac meriti Christi, ne vnico quidem verbo mentionem ibi fieri. Atque vel vnicum exemplum Rahab, cuius fides, ob quam illa cum tota familia sua conseruata fuit, ibi recensetur, oculos hominibus aperire deberet, inquit, vt errorem suum agnoscerent. Quid enim illa, vtpote Ethnica, de obedientia & morte Christi scire potuit? Vnde sequitur, fidem ipsius hanc fuisse, non quod Christi iustitiam apprehenderit, sed quod fiduciam suam ac spem illam in Deo Israelis collocauerit, ipsum, si populo ipsius benefaceret, idremuneraturum esse, quemadmodum ex historia Iof. 6. & illis verbis Hebr. 11. verf. 31. Per fidem Rahab illa meretrix non periit, vna cum iis qui non obedierant, quum pacifice excepisset hospitio explorato-res, manifeste appareat.
units.tr: The fourth is: that if that were true faith, it would necessarily follow that all who pleased God before the coming of Christ had that same faith. But this cannot be proved by any testimony of Scripture; rather the contrary can be shown from it, as the single eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews plainly testifies. For although there is mention there of many who believed in God, and so pleased him, and their faith is explained there, yet not so much as a single word is said there about obedience, righteousness or the merit of Christ. Even the single example of Rahab, whose faith, on account of which she was preserved with her whole household, is listed there, ought to open men's eyes so that they recognise their error. For what could she, being a Gentile, know of the obedience and death of Christ? Whence it follows that her faith was not that she laid hold of the righteousness of Christ, but that she placed her trust and hope in the God of Israel, that he would reward her if she did good to his people, as is evident from the story in Iof. 6. and from those words of Heb. 11. vers. 31. "By faith the harlot Rahab did not perish with those who did not obey, when she had received the spies peaceably in her house." This is plainly evident.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Si illa fides, qua meritum & iustitiam Christi apprehendimus, vera & iustificans esset fides, tum inde sequeretur, omnes illos qui ante Christi aduentum Deo placuerunt, eadem illa fide praditos fuisse:
units.tr: If that faith by which we apprehend the merit and righteousness of Christ were a true and justifying faith, it would follow that all those who pleased God before the coming of Christ were endowed with that same faith.

units.la: Atqui consequens est falsum:
units.tr: But the consequent is false.

units.la: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is false too.

units.la: Assumptio sic probatur:
units.tr: The assumption is proved as follows.

units.la: Si omnes illos, qui ante Christi aduentum Deo placuerunt, eandem fidem habuisse, qua videlicet mortem, iustitiam ac meritum Christi apprehenderint, nullis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis probari, sed contrarium inde demonstrari potest: tum falsum est, illos fide illa praditos fuisse:
units.tr: If it could not be proved by any testimonies of holy Scripture that all those who pleased God before the coming of Christ had the same faith, namely that by which they apprehended the death, righteousness and merit of Christ, but the contrary could be demonstrated from it, then it is false that they were endowed with that faith.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est:
units.tr: But the former is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Huius assumptionis Ἐπιχείρημα duplex adfert: vna generalis, in hunc modum:
units.tr: The author offers a twofold argument [Ἐπιχείρημα] in support of this assumption. The first is general, in this form:

units.la: Si capite vndecimo epistola ad Hebraeos, multorum fit mentio, qui in Deum crediderunt, ac proinde ipsi placuerunt, & quorum fides ibi explicatur, & tamen obedientia, iustitia, ac meriti Christi, ne vnico quidem verbo fit mentio: tum omnes illos qui ante Christi aduentum Deo placuerunt, ea fide praditos fuisse, qua videlicet iustitiam & meritum Christi apprehenderint, non tantum nullis Scriptura sacra et testimonis probari, sed etiam contrarium inde demonstrari potest:
units.tr: If, in the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, there is mention of many who believed in God, and so pleased him, and their faith is set out there, and yet not so much as a single word is said about the obedience, righteousness and merit of Christ, then it is not only the case that it cannot be proved by any testimony of holy Scripture that all those who pleased God before the coming of Christ were endowed with that faith by which they apprehended the righteousness and merit of Christ, but the contrary can also be demonstrated from it.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the former is true. Therefore the latter is too.

units.la: Altera specialis in hunc modum:
units.tr: The second, special, argument runs thus:

units.la: Si Rahab meretrix, vtpote Ethnica, de morte & obedientia Christi nihil scire potuit, & fides ipsius haec fuit, non quod meritum & mortem Christi apprehenderit, sed quod fiduciam ac spem illam in Deo collocauerit, ipsum, si populo ipsius benefaceret, id remuneraturum esse: tum euidenter demonstratur, illos qui ante Christi aduentum Deo placuerunt, non fuisse ea fide praditos, qua videlicet iustitiam & meritum Christi apprehenderint:
units.tr: If Rahab the harlot, being a Gentile, could know nothing of the death and obedience of Christ, and her faith was not that she apprehended the merit and death of Christ, but that she placed her trust and hope in God, that he would reward her if she dealt kindly with his people, then it is plainly demonstrated that those who pleased God before the coming of Christ were not endowed with that faith by which they apprehended the righteousness and merit of Christ.

units.la: Atqui prius verum esse, ex historia Iosuae, cap. 6. & Hebr. 11. verf. 31. liquet: Ergo & posterius verum est.
units.tr: But the former is true, as is clear from the history of Joshua, chapter 6, and Hebrews 11:31. Therefore the latter is true too.

units.la: Resp. Quid de fidei iustificantis definitione sentiendum sit, quoue modo fiducia cum illa cohaereat, & hoc ipso, & antecedente capite, prolixe a nobis est explicatum. Qui vero fiduciam, id est, firmam illam persuasionem, qua quis remissionem peccatorum per mortem Christi partam, & redemptionem per illum factam, non minus ad se, quam ad caeteros electos pertinere statuit, atque ita promissiones Euangelicas sibi specialiter applicat, & applicando remissionis peccatorum, & omnium beneficiorum, morte Christi nobis partorum reipsa particeps redditur, fidei iustificantis formam constituunt, ac proinde illos qui certa cum fiducia ac firma persuasione credunt, Christi morte ac passione peccata ipsorum deleta esse, de Iictorum veniam ac remissionem peccatorum reipsa consequi statuunt: illi inter meritum & efficaciam mortis Christi, inter remissionis peccatorum aliorumque beneficiorum acquisitionem, & eorundem applicationem: denique inter decretum Dei, quo videlidelicet Deus ab æterno electos ac fideles non tantum ad vitam æternam, sed omnia etiam media quibus ad finem illum perducantur elegit, & decreti illius exequutionem, bonorumque ac beneficiorum omnium communicationem, accurate distinguunt, & ea quæ merito mortis Christi nobis acquisita, & æterna prædestinatione decreta sunt beneficia, ad fidei iustificantis obiectum, efficaciam vero, applicationemque eorundem, & decreti diuini exequutionem, quod ad remissionem peccatorum, & iustificationem attinet, ad fidei effectum atque consequens distincte referunt. Quæ distinctio iam amplam ad obiecta ab Aduersario argumenta respondendi materiam suppeditat.
units.tr: Reply. What ought to be thought of the definition of justifying faith, and how trust is joined to it, has been explained at length by us both in this chapter and in the one before. Those, however, who constitute the form of justifying faith as trust, that is, the firm persuasion by which someone holds that the forgiveness of sins obtained through the death of Christ, and the redemption made by him, pertain to himself no less than to the other elect, and so applies the evangelical promises specially to himself, and by applying them is in fact made a partaker of the forgiveness of sins and of all the benefits won for us by the death of Christ; and who therefore hold that those who believe with sure trust and firm persuasion that their sins have been blotted out by the death and passion of Christ do in fact obtain the pardon and remission of their sins: these writers carefully distinguish between the merit and the efficacy of the death of Christ, between the acquisition of the forgiveness of sins and of other benefits, and their application; and finally between the decree of God, by which God from eternity elected the faithful and the elect not only to eternal life but also to all the means by which they are brought to that end, and the execution of that decree and the communication of all good things and benefits. They refer what has been won for us by the merit of Christ's death, and what has been decreed as benefits by eternal predestination, to the object of justifying faith; but they refer the efficacy and application of these things, and the execution of the divine decree as far as forgiveness of sins and justification are concerned, to the effect and consequence of faith. This distinction now supplies ample material for answering the objections raised by our opponent.

units.la: Ad primum igitur respondetur, assumptionem esse falsam: quia credere in Christum, est credere Iesum Christum esse Seruatorem mundi, qui liberet populum suum à peccatis ipsius, Matth. 1. verf. 21. Vocabis nomen eius Iesum, ipse enim liberabit populum suum à peccatis ipsius. Iohan. cap. 4. verf. 39. 42. Ex urbe autem illa multi Samaritanorum crediderunt in eum: ipsi audiuimus, inquientes, & scimus hunc esse vere illum Seruatorem mundi, Christum. Actor. 8. verf. 36. 37. Ait Eunuchus, En aquam, quid prohibet me baptizari? Dixit vero Philippus, Si credis ex toto corde, licet. Respondens autem ille dixit, Credo Filium Dei esse Iesum Christum. Qua autem ratione Christus est ac dicitur Seruator noster, talem etiam nos ipsum per fidem amplectimur: Atqui Christus est ac dicitur Seruator noster, non tantum quatenus æternæ salutis viam ipse nobis annuntiauit, & voluntatem Patris, de nostri redemptione, plene nobis exposuit, eandemque exemplo vitæ, mortis & gloriosæ resurrectionis suæ, in sua ipsius persona nobis ostendit, multisque modis confirmauit, denique accepta à Patre plenissima potestate, in coelo ac terra, omnibus credentibus, in illo nouissimo die, daturus est vitam æternam, & abolita morte, omnibusque hostibus sibi subiectis, nos ab omni miseria liberatos, in societatem coelestis gloriæ adducturus: sed & quidem præcipuè, quatenus ipse vt sanctus Pontifex, & sancta victima, sua passione & morte, pro nostris peccatis, iusto Dei iudicio satisfecit, & poenas nobis ob peccata debitas, in se vt sponsorem nostrum deriuauit, denique amissam Dei gratiam, & vitæ æternæ præmium nobis est promeritus: vt capite vigesimo quarto demonstrabimus: Ergo Christum talem Seruatorem per fidem apprehendimus, atque amplectimur,credimusque per mortem,ac passionem ipsius peccata nostra expiata atque deleta esse, credendoque beneficiorum per mortem & sanguinem Christi nobis comparatorum reipsa participes reddimur. Quum deinde ipsimet Aduersarii, fiduciam seu confidentiam fidei iustificantis formam constituant,quæ πληροφορίαν ac persuasionem illam certam, qua'singuli credentes promissiones Euangelicas sibi particulariter applicant, & totum illum coelestium bonorum voluntate diuina fidelibus & electis decretum thesaurum ad se quoque pertinere statuunt, in se complectitur: ideo tum ex ipsa Scriptura sacra, tum Aduersariorum hypothesi, & sententia sequitur credere in Christum nihil aliud esse, quàm Deum nobis per fidem meritum & satisfactionem Christi apprehendentibus, peccata nostra remissurum vitæque æternæ hæredes effecturum esse.Ex quibus iam assumptionis falsitas cuidenter apparet.
units.tr: To the first, therefore, it is answered that the assumption is false, because to believe in Christ is to believe that Jesus Christ is the Saviour of the world, who will free his people from their sins, Matthew 1:21: You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins. John 4:39, 42: And many of the Samaritans of that city believed in him, saying, "We have heard him ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world, Christ." Acts 8:36, 37: The eunuch said, "See, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." Now, in the way in which Christ is and is called our Saviour, we too embrace him through faith. But Christ is and is called our Saviour not only in so far as he has declared to us the way of eternal salvation and fully expounded to us the will of the Father concerning our redemption, and has shown and confirmed this in many ways in his own person by the example of his life, death and glorious resurrection, and, having received from the Father the fullest power in heaven and on earth, will give eternal life to all believers on the last day, and, death being abolished and all enemies made subject to him, will lead us, freed from all misery, into the fellowship of heavenly glory; but also, and especially, in so far as he, as holy High Priest and holy victim, by his passion and death made satisfaction for our sins before the just judgment of God, and took upon himself, as our surety, the punishments owed to us for sin, and finally merited for us the restoration of God's favour and the reward of eternal life, as we shall show in chapter 24. Therefore we apprehend and embrace Christ through faith as such a Saviour, and we believe that our sins are atoned for and blotted out through his death and passion, and by believing we are made partakers in fact of the benefits obtained for us through the death and blood of Christ. Then, since our opponents themselves make trust, or confidence, the form of justifying faith, and include in it that full assurance [πληροφορίαν] and certain persuasion by which individual believers apply the evangelical promises to themselves particularly, and hold that the treasury of heavenly goods, decreed by the will of God for the faithful and the elect, pertains to them too: therefore it follows, both from Holy Scripture itself and from the hypothesis and opinion of our opponents, that to believe in Christ is nothing other than, through faith, laying hold of the merit and satisfaction of Christ, that God will forgive our sins and make us heirs of eternal life. From these points the falsity of the assumption now clearly appears.

units.la: Ad secundum respondetur,assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse falsam, neque subiuncto prosyllogismo demonstrari, quippe cuius connexum manifesta consequentiæ falsitate laboret, vt vel ex iis, quæ responsionibus hisce præmissa sunt manifeste apparet. Verba enim illa, nobis remissa ac deleta esse peccata nostra, item, nos iustificatos esse, & similia, quum vel respectu ipsius decreti diuini, vel exequutionis illius,quę fit per certa media,inter decretum diuinum,&exequutionem ipsius interuenientia,enuntientur,diuersum etiam sensum induunt,sic vt remissa nobis peccata esse dicantur, vel destinatione, & ordinatione Dei æterna,vel applicatione beneficii illius quæ fit per fidem in tempore, quod definiuit Dominus, sic vt electus aliquis, iustificatus, & non iustificatus dici queat,absque contradictione, sed illud respectu decreti diuini, hoc vero respectu exequutionis, & priusquam per fidem in Christum remissionem peccatorum reipsa consequatur. Huc pertinet illud Christi Ioh. 10. v.16. Alias oues habeo quæ non sunt ex hoc ouili, illas quoque oportet me adducere: nam vocem meam audient, fietque vnus grex, & vnus pastor. Vnde liquet, quum in fidei iustificantis definitione, fideles dicantur & credere per mortem, & passionem Christi deleta esse peccata ipsorum, & per fidem,remissionem peccatorum reipsa consequi, sed diuerso respectu, illud videlicet respectu decreti diuini, ac destinationis, hoc vero respectu exequutionis, & applicationis, quæ fit per fidem: ideo connexum profyllogismo. logismi, manifesto oppositorum elencho laborare.
units.tr: To the second it is answered that the assumption of the principal syllogism is false, and cannot be demonstrated by the appended prosyllogism, since its connection suffers from a manifest falsity of consequence, as is plain even from what has been set out in these replies. For the words "our sins have been forgiven and blotted out," likewise "we have been justified," and similar expressions, when they are spoken with respect either to the divine decree itself or to its execution, which takes place through certain means intervening between the divine decree and its execution, take on a different sense: so that sins are said to be forgiven us either by the eternal destination and ordination of God, or by the application of that benefit which is made through faith in time, as the Lord determined; so that someone may be called elect and justified, and also not justified, without contradiction, the former with respect to the divine decree, the latter with respect to its execution, and before he actually obtains the forgiveness of sins through faith in Christ. To this belongs that saying of Christ, John 10:16: I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also; and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd. Hence it is clear that, although in the definition of justifying faith the faithful are said both to believe that their sins have been blotted out through the death and passion of Christ, and through faith to obtain the forgiveness of sins in fact, these are said with different respects: the former with respect to the divine decree and destination, the latter with respect to the execution and application that is made through faith. Therefore the connection of the prosyllogism suffers from a manifest refutation of opposites.

units.la: Ad tertium, respondetur assumptionem esse falsam, vt manifeste liquet ex illa confessione Pauli, Act. 24. v. 14. 15. 16. Hoc tibi fateor, me secundum viam illam quam haeresin dicunt, ita seruire patrio Deo, vt qui credam omnia quae in lege, ac Prophetis scripta sunt, & spem habeam in Deo, fore, quam etiam ij ipsi expectant, resurrectionem mortuorum, tum iustorum, tum iniustorum. Interea vero ipse me exerceo ad conscientiam habendam sine offendiculo, apud Deum, & apud homines. Atqui vt praeceptum de fide in Christum, resipiscentiae, & bonorum operum praestandorum mandatum coniunctum habet. Mar. 1. v. 15. Expletum est tempus, & appropinquauit regnum coelorum, conuertimini, & credite Euangelio. Tit. 3. v. 8. Haec volo te asseuerare, vt bonis operibus operam dent, qui Deo crediderunt: 1. Ioh. 3. v. 23. Haec est, eius doctrina, vt credamus nomini Filii eius Iesu Christi, & diligamus alios, sicut mandauit nobis. & iustificatio cum sanctificatione beneficio perpetuo, ac indissolubili nexu, & vinculo copulatum est: Tit. 2. v. 14. Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, id est non tantum a reatu & poena, sed etiam imperio, ac dominio peccati, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. Mar. 1. 21. ipse seruabit populum suum a peccatis ipsius, nimirum tum remissionem peccatorum nobis impetrando, tum ipsa peccata in nobis abolendo, denique loco aeterni supplicii, vitam aeternam nobis conferendo. Ita quoque vera viua ac iustificans fides, veraque ac solida Dei notitia & cognitio nos semper ad verum Dei timorem, & cultum format ac instituit, & ad serium pietatis ac bonorum operum studium impellit, nec praestantissimis illis fructibus destitui potest. Matt. 7. v. 17. 18. Omnis arbor bona fert fructus bonos, putris autem arbor fert fructus malos: non potest arbor bona malos fructus facere, neque arbor putris fructus bonos ferre, Iac. 2. v. 17. 18. Fides, si opera non habeat, mortua est per se: quinimo dicet aliquis, Tu fidem habes, & ego opera habeo, ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi fidem meam ex operibus meis. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 3. 4. Per hoc scimus nos cum nosse, si mandata ipsius obseruamus, qui dicit, Noui eum, & mandata eius non seruat, mendax est, & in eo veritas non est. Ex quibus omnibus euidenter apparet inter fidem iustificantem, per quam salutem ac vitam aeternam in solo Christo quaerimus ac adipiscimur, & bona opera pietatisque studium, talem communionem, qualis est inter caulam, & effectum, inter frugiferam arborem, & suauissimos fructus, denique inter fontem,ac riuulos,statuendam & agnoscendam esse, ac proinde assumptionem syllogismi principalis merito falsitatis à nobis argui.Eius verò probationem quantum concernit,falsam esse propositionem illius maiorem, ex perfectæ definitionis legibus vel pueris constat. Si enim definitione colligenda sunt omnia, cum quibus ipsi definito aliqua communio intercedit, tum in definitionem causæ omnes tum internæ, tum externæ, effectus item omnes, subiecta, adiuncta, proprietates, & accidentia omnia, integrum, vt & membra, genus cum speciebus, coniugata & notatio congerenda erunt,quod est absurdissimum. In perfectissima hominis definitione,nullam facultatis ridendi,aut loquendi mętionem facimus : num igitur, homo nec loqui nec ridere propterea poterit?Ineptias igitur illas autori ipsarum relinquo.
units.tr: As to the third point, I reply that the minor premise is false, as is clear from Paul's own confession in Acts 24:14–16: I admit this to you, that according to the way which they call a sect, I so serve the God of my fathers, that I believe all things which are written in the law and the Prophets, and I have hope in God, which they themselves also look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust. And in this I myself also exercise myself to have a conscience without offence toward God and toward men. Yet the precept concerning faith in Christ is joined with the command of repentance and of doing good works. Mark 1:15: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of heaven is at hand; repent and believe the gospel. Titus 3:8: These things I want you to affirm constantly, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. 1 John 3:23: This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he commanded us. Justification is also joined with sanctification by a perpetual and indissoluble bond and tie. Titus 2:14: He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, that is, not only from guilt and punishment but also from the rule and dominion of sin, and purify for himself a special people, zealous for good works. Matthew 1:21: He will save his people from their sins, namely by obtaining for us the forgiveness of sins, by abolishing sins themselves in us, and finally by bestowing on us eternal life in place of eternal punishment. Likewise, true living and justifying faith, and true and solid knowledge and acquaintance with God, always shape and institute us to the true fear and worship of God, and drive us to a earnest zeal for piety and good works, nor can it be deprived of these most excellent fruits. Matthew 7:17–18: Every good tree bears good fruit, but a rotten tree bears evil fruit. A good tree cannot bear evil fruit, nor a rotten tree bear good fruit. James 2:17–18: Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself. Indeed someone will say, You have faith, and I have works; show me your faith from your works, and I will show you my faith from my works. 1 John 2:3–4: By this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says, I know him, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. From all of these things it is evident that between justifying faith, through which we seek and attain salvation and eternal life in Christ alone, and good works and the zeal for piety, there must be recognised and acknowledged such a communion as exists between cause and effect, between a fruitful tree and its sweetest fruits, and finally between a spring and its streams. Therefore the minor premise of the principal syllogism is rightly charged by us with falsehood. As for its proof, the major premise of that proof is false, which even boys know from the rules of a perfect definition. For if everything with which the defined thing has any communion were to be gathered into the definition, then all causes, both internal and external, all effects likewise, subjects, adjuncts, properties and all accidents, the whole, together with the parts, genus with species, cognates and etymology, would have to be collected together, which is most absurd. In the most perfect definition of man we make no mention of the faculty of laughing or of speaking: does man therefore not have the power to speak or to laugh? I therefore leave those absurdities to their author.

units.la: Ad quartum & vltimum respondetur, assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse falsam. Nam falsum esse id quod priore ipsius mebro dicitur nempè definitionem illam fidei iustificantis, quafidem, ac meritum & iustitiam Christi apprehendere dicimus, ex scripturis sacris demonstrari non posse, tum ex responsione nostra ad argumentum primum, tum verò ipsa Aduersariorum doctrina, qua illi fatentur, fidem omnium illorum: qui nunquam Deo placuerunt, & placere velint, specie vnam tantum esse,manifestè appareret. Si enim fides iustificans est,qua credimus in Iesum Christum, qui merito, & efficacia redemptor ac saluator noster est, vt infrà patebit, vna autem tantùm specie fides est in Veteri ac Nouo Testamento, quorum prius ante probauimus, posterius verò ipsimet Aduersarii confitentur, tum necessariò sequitur, omnes illos qui in veteri Testamento ante Christi in carnem adventum,Deo placuerunt,& iustificati sunt eadem illa fide seruato tamen vtriusque Testamenti discrimine, præditos fuisse. Ad posterius verò assumptionis membrum quod attinet, & iam illud falsitatis arguimus, nec subiunctis illis duabus rationibus probatur. Nam primum quantum concernit falsum illud est, tum quia ex testimonio particulari negatiuo, ad negationem rei alicuius, quæ ex aliunde petitis argumentis demonstrari potest, non datur consequentia, tum etiam, quod in hac controuersia maximè est animaduertendum, quia Apostolus Heb. 11. v. 1. definit fidem ὑπόστασιν ἐλπιζομένων, & ἔλεγχον οὐ βλεπομένων, quorum verborum sententia,quamuis nihil in se contineat à fidei iustificantis natura alienum, num,integram tamen ipsius definitionem non complectitur, vti exemplorum multorum quae subiiciuntur,inductione,& ad generalem illam definitionem accommodatione,liquidò constat.Eam enim solum fidei partem, ac proprietatem Apostolus persequitur, qua fides cum patientia coniungitur, eámque in se complectitur, quod tum verborum illorum, quibus praecedens caput clauditur, series & nexus, tum ea, quae subiunguntur exempla euidenter demonstrant, vnde iam connexum tantum esse apparet. Ad secundam vero rationem quantum attinet, quamuis libenter fateamur, Rahebam illam fide tam illustri, qualis est illa sub Euangelii luce, ac splendore & qua ipsammet personam Iesu Christi, ac functiones ipsius nouerit, praeditam non fuisse: quia tamen ipsi fides eaque vera, & viua tribuitur, quae sub vtroque Testamento Mediatore & Messia nititur, vt ex conuenientia vtriusque foederis apparet, sallsam dicimus esse minorem. Quomodo vero,& quibus mediis illa in cognitionem illam perducta fuerit, hoc docet ipse Dominus: Inuentus sum, inquiens, ab iis qui me non quaerebant, conspicuus factus sum iis, qui de me non interrogabant. Rom.10.v.20. Atque haec de fide iustificante dicta sint, Dominus Iesus illam nobis adaugeat.
units.tr: As to the fourth and last point, I reply that the minor premise of the principal syllogism is false. For what is said in its first member is false, namely that the definition of justifying faith, by which we say we grasp faith, merit and the righteousness of Christ, cannot be demonstrated from the holy Scriptures. This is clear both from our answer to the first argument and from the very doctrine of our adversaries, by which they confess that the faith of all those who never pleased God and do not wish to please him is one species only. For if justifying faith is that by which we believe in Jesus Christ, who is our redeemer and saviour by his merit and efficacy, as will be shown below, and there is only one species of faith in the Old and the New Testament (the former of which we proved before, and the latter the Adversaries themselves concede), then it necessarily follows that all those in the Old Testament who pleased God and were justified before the coming of Christ in the flesh were endowed with that same faith, the difference between the two Testaments being preserved. As for the second member of the minor premise, we also charge it with falsehood, and it is not proved by the two reasons subjoined. For first, as far as it concerns the falsehood of that member, it is false, both because no consequence follows from a particular negative testimony to the denial of something that can be demonstrated from arguments drawn from elsewhere, and also, which must be especially noted in this controversy, because the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen [ὑπόστασιν ἐλπιζομένων, ἔλεγχον οὐ βλεπομένων]. The sense of those words, although it contains nothing foreign to the nature of justifying faith, nevertheless does not embrace its whole definition, as is clearly evident from the induction of the many examples that follow and their application to that general definition. For the Apostle pursues only that part and property of faith by which faith is joined with patience, and includes that within itself, as the sequence and connection of the words with which the preceding chapter closes, and the examples that are subjoined, clearly demonstrate; hence it is plain that the connection is only partial. As for the second reason, although we gladly grant that Rahab did not have that illustrious faith, such as exists under the light and splendour of the gospel, and by which one knows the very person of Jesus Christ and his offices, nevertheless, since to her is attributed a true and living faith, which rests upon the Mediator and Messiah under both Testaments, as the agreement of the two covenants makes clear, we say that the minor is false. But how and by what means she was brought to that knowledge, the Lord himself teaches: I was found, he says, by those who did not seek me; I was made manifest to those who did not ask for me. Romans 10:20. And let these things be said concerning justifying faith; may the Lord Jesus increase it in us.

units.la: CAPVT XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: De Iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo: in quo sententia ac doctrina orthodoxa proponitur, & ex Scripturis sacris confirmatur.
units.tr: On the Justification of a Sinful Man before God: in which the orthodox doctrine is set out and confirmed from the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Eleberrimam illam, nobisque ad salutem ac vitam æternam consequendam plane necessariam, sed gravissimis, temporibus omnibus, controversiarum ac disputationum fluctibus & tempestatibus agitatam, De Iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo, doctrinam explicaturus, operæprecium facturus mihi videor, si primo omnium orthodoxam Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententiam, quanta fieri poterit breuitate & perspicuitate proponam, atque ex Scripturis sacris confirmem, deinde vero eandem ab erroribus & argumentis, quibus illam euertere & conuellere conatur Aduersarius, vindicem.
units.tr: Since I am about to explain the doctrine of the Justification of a sinful man before God, a most famous doctrine, absolutely necessary for us to attain salvation and eternal life, yet at all times tossed by the waves and storms of heavy controversies and disputes, I think I shall be doing useful work if, first of all, I set out the orthodox teaching of our Churches as briefly and clearly as possible and confirm it from the holy Scriptures. Then I shall defend that same teaching against the errors and arguments by which the Adversary tries to overturn and undermine it.

units.la: Verbo igitur iustificandi vt à definitione nominis, cuius explicatio rei ipsius tractationi multum lucis adfert, ducamus exordium, negamus significari talem motum ab iniustitia ad iustitiam, sicut quando in motibus physicis, vna qualitate expulsa, altera introducitur, quale vocis illius etymon confingunt ipsi Pōtificii, iustificationem idem quod per succedentem virtutis infusionem, peccati inhærentis expulsionem esse statuentes: neque talem compositionem, qualem putant iidem exigere rationem compositionis, vt in calefacere, viuificare, sanctificare, sic in iustificare pro iustum facere: sed, cùm ex communi phrasi & vsu linguæ tum Hebraicæ verbum צדק tum Græcæ, apud Paulum, ex cuius scriptis hæc iustificationis doctrina potissimū est desumpta verbum δικαιόω, quorum vtrumque iustificare significat, forense sit, & à tribunali politico ac ciuili, ad spirituale & diuinum translatum ac deductum, illud dicimus, in hac doctrina significare, in iudicio Dei, absoluere à peccatis, seu à reatu & pœna peccatorum, & iustum atque innocentem pronunciare. Hanc significationem demonstrat antiantithesis iustificationis & condemnationis sæpius repetita: Deut. 25. v.1. Si fuerit controuersia inter aliquos, ideoque accesserint ad iudicium, vt iudices sententiam de iis ferant: tum iustum pronunciaturi sunt eum qui iustus est, & condemnaturi eum qui iniustus est. 1. Reg. 8. v. 32. Tunc tu audito e cœlis, & conficiens iudicato seruos tuos, condemnando improbum, reddendo viam eius in caput eius, & iustificando iustum, reddendo ei secundum iustitiam eius. Roman. cap. 5. verf. 16. Iudicium quidem ex vno lapsu introiit ad condemnationem, donum autem ex multis lapsibus ad iustificationem. & v.18. Sicut per vnius lapsum iudicium introiit ad condemnationem: sic per vnius iustificationem donum iustitiæ in omnes homines introiit ad iustificationem vitæ: & cap. 8. v. 33. 34. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat, quis est qui condemnet? Quum vero in locis citatis condemnare non significet iniustum facere, vel iniustitiam infundere, sed iniustum ac reum pronuntiare: ideo ex contrariorum natura & ratione sequitur, iustificare aliquem non idem esse quod iustum facere, vel iustitiam infundere, sed à peccatis, seu reatu, & poenis peccatorum absoluere, iustumque ac innocentem pronuntiare. Sic Prou. 17. v. 15. Qui iustificat improbum, & qui condemnat iustum, abominationi Iehouæ sunt æque ambo. Atqui iudex iniquus minime abominationi Iehouæ futurus esset, si maxime iustificando impium qualitatem iustitiæ ipsi infunderet, seu iustum ipsum ex iniusto faceret.
units.tr: Let us therefore begin with the word to justify, taking our start from the definition of the term, whose explanation brings much light to the subject itself. We deny that it signifies such a movement from unrighteousness to righteousness as happens in physical motions, where one quality is expelled and another introduced. That is the etymology of the word which the Papists themselves invent, holding that justification is the expulsion of indwelling sin by the infusion of virtue which follows it. Nor does it mean a composition of the kind they think the rules of composition require, as in to warm, to quicken, to sanctify, so also to justify means to make just. Rather, both from the common phrase and usage of language, the Hebrew verb [צדק] and the Greek verb [δικαιόω], which Paul uses (and it is chiefly from his writings that this doctrine of justification is drawn), both of which mean to justify, have a forensic sense. They have been carried over and transferred from the civil and political tribunal to the spiritual and divine. We say that in this doctrine the word means to absolve from sins, that is, from the guilt and punishment of sins, in the judgement of God, and to pronounce a person just and innocent. This sense is shown by the antithesis of justification and condemnation, which is repeated often. Deut. 25. v. 1: If there is a dispute between some people, and they come to judgement, so that the judges may pass sentence on them, then they shall pronounce just the one who is just, and condemn the one who is unjust. 1 Kings 8. v. 32: Then hear from heaven, and act and judge your servants, condemning the wicked, bringing his way upon his own head, and justifying the just, rewarding him according to his righteousness. Rom. ch. 5, v. 16: The judgement came from one fall into condemnation, but the gift from many falls into justification. And v. 18: As through the fall of one the judgement came into condemnation, so through the justification of one the gift of righteousness came upon all men into justification of life. And ch. 8, vv. 33, 34: Who will accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? Since in the passages cited, to condemn does not mean to make unjust or to infuse unrighteousness, but to pronounce unjust and guilty, it follows from the nature and reason of opposites that to justify someone is not the same as to make him just or to infuse righteousness. It is to absolve from sins, that is, from the guilt and punishments of sins, and to pronounce him just and innocent. So Prov. 17. v. 15: He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, are both alike an abomination to Jehovah. Yet a corrupt judge would not be an abomination to Jehovah if, by justifying the wicked, he infused the quality of righteousness into him, or made the man himself righteous out of unrighteous.
