units.la: Vt autem duplex est promissio iustitiæ & salutis, vna in fœdere operum, qua agnoscimus Deum esse bonum, sed iis qui perfectam obedientiam lege requisitam præstant: altera in fœdere gratiæ, cuius conditio extra nos in solo Christo reperitur: seu, vt duplex est iustitia, (de iustitia vniuersali & quæ personæ est, loquor) legalis & operum vna, Euangelica & fidei altera: ita duplex quoque est iustitiæ applicatio, quæ iustificatio dicitur, vna legalis, quæ est acceptatio hominis illius, in cuius vita reperitur ea puritas & sanctitas, quæ testimonium iustitiæ, apud Dei seueri iudicis throni um meretur: seu qui operum suorum integritate rigido ac seuero Dei iudicio respondere potest. Quod quia impossibile, non quidem ex vitio legis, cuius promissiones nec incertæ sunt, nec fallaces, sed propter infirmitatem carnis, Roman. capite octauo, versu tertio, Quum legis impotentia nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio missio conformato carni peccato obnoxiæ, idque pro peccato, condemnauit peccatum in carne: ideo nulla etiam inde existere hominis coram Deo iustificatio potest. Altera vero Euangelica, qua iusti censentur, & a peccatis absoluuntur illi, qui operum iustitia exclusi Christum per fidem apprehendunt,cuius iustitia proinde tanquam veste induti, in Dei conspectu, non vt peccatores, sed tanquam iusti apparent. Atque de hac in praesentiarum agemus.
units.tr: Now there is a double promise of righteousness and salvation. One is in the covenant of works, by which we acknowledge that God is good, but promises it only to those who render the perfect obedience the law requires. The other is in the covenant of grace, whose condition is found outside us, in Christ alone. Likewise, there is a double righteousness (I am speaking of universal righteousness, which belongs to the person): one legal and of works, the other evangelical and of faith. So too there is a double application of righteousness, called justification: one legal, which is the acceptance of that man in whose life there is found that purity and holiness which deserves the testimony of righteousness before the throne of the stern judge of God, that is, of one who by the integrity of his works can answer the rigorous and severe judgement of God. Since this is impossible, not because of any fault in the law, whose promises are neither uncertain nor deceptive, but because of the weakness of the flesh (Rom. ch. 8, v. 3: Since the law was powerless in the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh), no justification of man before God can arise from this legal application. The other is evangelical, by which those are counted righteous and absolved from sins who, excluded from the righteousness of works, lay hold of Christ through faith. His righteousness, as if they were clothed in it, makes them appear before the sight of God not as sinners but as righteous. It is of this justification that we shall speak for the present.

units.la: Iustificatio igitur Euangelica est actio Dei gratiosa,indiuidua, & simul tota,qua ex mera sua gratia & misericordia, omnes,& solos electos,in se iniustos, ac propterea accusationi & maledictioni legis obnoxios , propter meritum Christi Euangelio oblatum , & fide apprehensum per remissionem peccatorum,& iustitiae Christi imputationem , iustos pronuntiat ac aestimat , ad misericordiae & gratiae suę gloriam,ac certam iustificati sanctificationem ac salute. Qua definitione iustificationis & causas omnes,tum internas,tum externas,& subiectum proprium complexi sumus.
units.tr: Evangelical justification, then, is a gracious act of God, individual and at the same time total. By his pure grace and mercy he pronounces and accounts just all and only the elect, who in themselves are unrighteous and therefore liable to the accusation and curse of the law. He does this on account of the merit of Christ, offered in the gospel and apprehended by faith, through the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, to the glory of his mercy and grace, and for the certain sanctification and salvation of the justified. In this definition of justification we have included all the causes, both internal and external, and its proper subject.

units.la: Causam efficientem iustificationis , eamque principalem designamus , cum iustificationem actionem Dei nuncupamus. Solus enim Deus est qui iustificat:Esa. 43. ver. 25. Ego ego sum qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me. Rom. 4. verf. 5. 6. Ei qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides sua pro iustitia. Sicut etiam Dauid pronuntiat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat iustitiam absque operibus: & verf. 8. Beatus vir, cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. Galat. 3. verf. 8. Prouidens autem Scriptura Deum ex fide iustificaturum Gentes, ante euangelizauit Abrahae, Benedicentur in te omnes gentes. Quamuis vero opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indiuisa, vt tota salutis series non minus vni personę quàm alteri in solidum referri debeat,ex ordine tamen causarum Patris gratia & misericordia impulsiua dicitur , tum ratione ordinationis Filii, vt esset victima & propitiatio,aliorúmque mediorum ad perfectionem gratiosi operis redemtionis: tum ratione applicationis beneficii nobis a Filio parti , idoneos nos reddens ad participationem sortis sanctorum. Actor. 15. ver. 11. Per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, credimus nos seruatum iri, quemadmodum & illos. Rom. 3. ver. 24. 25. Iustificantur gratis eius gratia, per redemptionem factam in Iesu Christo: quem proposuit Deus, vt esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam per remissionem praecedentium peccatorum. Rom. 4. ver. 16. Propterea ex fide est haereditas vt sit per fit per gratiam. Rom. 5. verf. 15. Si illius vnius lapsu multi mortui sunt, multò magis gratia Dei & donum per gratiam, quæ est vnius hominis Iesu Christi in multos redundauit: & v. 17. Qui redundantiam gratiæ, & doni iustitiæ accipiunt, in vita regnabunt per vnum Iesum Christum: & v. 21. Vt gratia regnaret per iustitiam in vitam æternam, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Roman. 11. v. 5. Ita igitur & hoc tempore referuatio secundum electionem gratiæ facta est. Gal. 2. v. 21. Non abrogo gratiam Dei, nam fi per legem est iustitia, ergo Christus frustrà mortuus est. Galat. 5. v. 4. Facti estis inanes Christi, quicunque per legem iustificamini à gratia excidistis. Ephef. 1. v. 5. 6. 7. Prædestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios, per Iesum Christum in sese, qua nos gratiosos effecit in illo dilecto in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius. & 2. v. 8. Gratia servati estis per fidem. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Qui seruauit nos, & vocauit vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris: sed ex suo proposito, & gratia, quæ data quidem est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. Tit. 3. v. 7. Vt iustificati ipsius gratia hæredes efficeremur secundum spem vitæ æternæ. Col. 1. v. 12. Gratias agentes Patri, qui idoneos nos fecit ad participandam sortem sanctorum in luce. Ex quibus testimoniis etiam liquet, per illam gratiam enim intelligendam esse gratiam infusam, seu qualitates nouas, ex illo diuite misericordiæ diuinæ fonte fluentes, sed gratuitum Dei beneplacitum, fauorem, ac dilectionem, qua Deus nos elegit, vocat, iustificat, & in filios adoptat, sic vt nec propter solam inhærentem nouitatem, nec partim misericordia, partim infusis donis, nos iustificari, luce meridiana clarius elucescat. Vnde iam doctrina illa Pontificiorum de præuisa fide, vel operibus, de viribus inhærentibus ex libero arbitrio, præparatione ac dispositione nostræ voluntatis, à malo ad bonum conuertente necessario corruit. Quamuis enim gratuitus ille Dei fauor, cum qualitatibus illis nouis, tanquam causa cum effectu sit coniunctus, ita vt diuelli non possint, cum omnis reconciliatus etiam renouetur, possunt tamen, ac debent in hoc negotio accuratissimè distingui, cum tanta sit oppositio gratiæ & operum non solum eorum, quæ naturali iudicio & liberi arbitrii conatu, extra Christi gratiam faciunt homines nondum regeniti, sed etiam eorum, quæ sunt fructus nouæ creaturæ, vt in vnum componi non possint, sed gratuita iustificatione stante, iustitia & meritum operum necessario euertatur. Non enim ex operibus iustis, quæ fecerimus nos, sed propter viscera misericordiæ suæ, seruauit nos Deus. Tit. 3. verf.
units.tr: We call God the efficient cause of justification, and the principal one, when we name justification the act of God. For God alone is the one who justifies. Isa. 43. v. 25: I, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake. Rom. 4. vv. 5, 6: To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. So also David pronounces blessed the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works. And v. 8: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Gal. 3. v. 8: The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: In you shall all the nations be blessed. Although the works of the Trinity ad extra are undivided, so that the whole series of salvation must be attributed no less to one person than to another, nevertheless, according to the order of causes, the grace and mercy of the Father is called the impelling cause. This is so both with respect to the appointment of the Son, that he should be the sacrifice and propitiation, and the other means to the completion of the gracious work of redemption, and with respect to the application to us of the benefit won by the Son, making us fit to share in the lot of the saints. Acts 15. v. 11: Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we shall be saved, just as they are. Rom. 3. vv. 24, 25: They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness by the remission of former sins. Rom. 4. v. 16: Therefore it is by faith, that it might be by grace, that the inheritance is given. Rom. 5. v. 15: If through the one man's fall many died, much more the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abounded to many. And v. 17: Those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. And v. 21: That grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Rom. 11. v. 5: So too at this present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. Gal. 2. v. 21: I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died in vain. Gal. 5. v. 4: You who are justified by the law have become estranged from Christ; you have fallen from grace. Eph. 1. vv. 5, 6, 7: He predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, in himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he has made us accepted in the Beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood. And ch. 2. v. 8: By grace you have been saved through faith. 2 Tim. 1. v. 9: Who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time. Titus 3. v. 7: That, being justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. Col. 1. v. 12: Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. From these testimonies it is also clear that by that grace we must understand not infused grace, that is, new qualities flowing from that rich fountain of divine mercy, but the free good pleasure, favour and love of God, by which God chose us, calls us, justifies us, and adopts us as sons. Thus it shines clearer than the midday sun that we are justified neither by the new quality inherent in us alone, nor partly by mercy and partly by infused gifts. From this it follows that the Papists' doctrine of foreseen faith or works, of inherent powers from free will, and of the preparation and disposition of our will, which turns itself from evil to good, necessarily collapses. For although that free favour of God is joined to those new qualities as cause is joined to effect, so that they cannot be separated (since every reconciled person is also renewed), they can and must nonetheless be most carefully distinguished in this matter. There is such an opposition between grace and works (not only those which unregenerate men perform outside the grace of Christ by natural judgement and the effort of free will, but also those which are the fruits of the new creature) that they cannot be combined into one. If justification is by free grace, the righteousness and merit of works is necessarily overthrown. Titus 3. v. 5: Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy God saved us.

units.la: 5. Luc. 1. verf. 78. Ephef. 1. verf. 5. Ei autem qui operatur mercedem Deus non imputat ex gratia & miseticordia, sed ex debito, Rom. 4. verf. 4. Nam si per gratiam, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia: aut si ex operibus, non ex gratia, alioquin opus non esset opus. Rom. capite vndecimo, versu sexto. Causa externe Deum mouens, siue ΑΦΟΡΙΣΤΙΚΗ noftrę iustificationis est IesusChriftus. Secunda ad Corinthios, capite quinto, versu decimo octauo & decimo nono: Hæc omnia sunt ex Deo, qui reconciliauit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, deditque ministerium reconciliationis: nempe quia Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum: & quidem tum meriti eius, tum efficaciæ & applicationis respectu, quare etiam à Scholasticis causa meritoria dicta est: de qua capite sequente nobis fusius erit agendum. Causa denique ΤΕΛΕΩΤΙΚΗ est ipse Spiritus sanctus, iustificationis illud beneficium interna testificatione sua nobis obsignans. Quem enim Deus in hac vita iustificat, eiusdem animo etiam per Spiritum sanctum mediante verbo gratiæ, testimonium reddit iustitiæ imputatæ, seu remissionis peccatorum, ac per consequens adoptionis, propter satisfactionem mediatoris. Roman. capite 8. versu decimo sexto, Ipse Spiritus testatur vnà cum spiritu nostro nos esse filios Dei. Ephes. capite primo, versu decimo tertio, In quo speraftis & vos, audito sermone veritatis, id est, Euangelio, in quo etiam posteaquam credidistis, obsignati estis Spiritu illo promissionis sancto, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ, dum in libertatem vindicemur ad laudem gloriæ ipsius.
units.tr: Luke 1:78. Ephesians 1:5. "To him who works, the reward is not reckoned as grace and mercy, but as debt," Romans 4:4. "For if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would not be grace. Or if it is by works, it is not by grace; otherwise work would not be work." Romans 11:6. The external cause moving God, or the determining cause [ΑΦΟΡΙΣΤΙΚΗ] of our justification, is Jesus Christ. 2 Corinthians 5:18-19: "All these things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their sins against them." This holds both with respect to his merit and with respect to the efficacy and application of it, which is why the Scholastics also called him the meritorious cause. We shall treat this more fully in the following chapter. Finally, the perfecting cause [ΤΕΛΕΩΤΙΚΗ] is the Holy Spirit himself, who seals this benefit of justification to us by his inward testimony. For to the one whom God justifies in this life, the Holy Spirit, through the word of grace, gives testimony to his mind that righteousness is imputed to him, that is, that his sins are forgiven, and consequently that he is adopted, on account of the mediator's satisfaction. Romans 8:16: "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." Ephesians 1:13: "In him you also, having heard the word of truth, that is the gospel, in whom also, after you believed, you were sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, until the redemption of those who are God's possession, to the praise of his glory."

units.la: Causæ iustificationis famulantes sunt tum offerens, nempe Euangelium (cuius sigilla sunt Sacramenta) quod annuntiando offert iustificationem, & potentia Dei est ad salutem cuiuis credenti, Roman. primo, versu decimosexto, tum apprehendens nempe fides, cuius ἐνέργεια duplex quum sit, vna, qua immediate sine aliarum virtutum adminiculo, in Euangelio Christum respicit: altera, qua mediatè per charitatem est efficax, nos remotis aliis virtutibus, non quidem à natura, sed ab actu fidei, iustificandi virtutem ac dignitatem priori ἀξία conferuandam & adscribendam esse censemus. Rom. capite quarto, versu vigesimo quarto & vigesimo quinto, Futurum est vt imputetur nobis scilicet fides ad iustitiam, qui credimus in eum, qui excitauit Iesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis, qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri. Galat. capite secundo, versu 20. Viuo per fidem filij Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit seipsum pro me.
units.tr: The causes of justification have their helpers: first the one who offers, namely the gospel (whose seals are the sacraments), which by proclaiming offers justification, and which "is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes," Romans 1:16; and then the one who apprehends, namely faith. Since its energy [ἐνέργεια] is twofold, one part looks immediately to Christ in the gospel, without the aid of other virtues; the other works mediately through love. We hold that, setting aside other virtues, the power and worth [ἀξία] of justifying must be ascribed and attributed to faith, not by its nature but by its act. Romans 4:24-25: "It shall be reckoned to us, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, faith for righteousness; who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification." Galatians 2:20: "I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

units.la: Materia iustificationis illius nostræ, est iustitia, satisfactio atque obedientia Christi, sic vt iustitia illa propter quam iustificamur, & peccatis nobis omnibus condonatis, hęredes vitæ æternæ censemur, subiectiuè sit in solo Christo, nostra autem per fidem fiat: Rom. 3. v. 24.25. Iustificantur gratis eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Iesu Christo, quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius. & 4. v.24. Futurum est vt imputetur nobis scilicet fides ad iustitiam, qui credimus in eum qui excitauit Iesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis: qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri: & 5. v. 9. Iustificati igitur eius sanguine seruabimur nunc multo magis per eum ab ira. & 10. Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filij eius. & 8. v. 3.4. Quod impossibile erat legi, quatenus infirmabatur per carnem, Deus fecit, Filio suo misso in similitudine carnis peccato obnoxia, idque pro peccato condemnauit peccatum in carne, vt illud iustis legis impleret in nobis. & 10. v. 6.7. Quæ ex fide est iustitia, ita dicit: Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Quis ascendet in cœlum? hoc est Christum ex alto deducere: aut quis descendet in abyssum? hoc est Christum ex mortuis reducere. prima ad Corinthios, capite primo, versu trigesimo: Christus factus est nobis à Deo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, & redemptio. secunda ad Corinthios, capite quinto, versu vltimo: Eum qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos fiamus iustitia Dei in ipso. Galat. 2. v. 20.21. Vitam quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem Filij Dei, qui dilexit me & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Non abrogo gratiam Dei. Nam si per legem est iustitia, igitur Christus frustra mortuus est. Et capite tertio, versu decimotertio & decimoquarto, Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio: Scriptum est enim, Execrabilis quisquis pendet in ligno, vt in gentibus benedictio Abrahæ extet in Christo Ie-su. vt promissum illum spiritum accipiamus per fidem. Ad Ephesios capite quinto, sexto, septimo: Prædestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios, per Iesum Christum in se secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suæ ad laudę gloriosæ suæ gratiæ, qua gratiosos nos effecit in illo dilecto, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum ex diuitę ipsius gratia. Rom. 4. versu 5. Ei qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad iustitiam. Ex quibus omnibus testimoniis luculenter apparet rem illam quę homini ad iustitiam imputatur per fidem, & quæ nos Deo gratos vitáque æterna dignos efficit, esse ipsam obedientiam & iustitiam Christi, quippe qua sola omnia electorum peccata sunt expiata, nobisque ad cælestem hæreditatem aditus patefactus. Et hac quidem sola fide, id est, propter sola n iustitiam & obedientiam Christi fide apprehensam, non autem partim fide, id est, propter imputatam satisfactionem Christi partim vero operibus, id est, propter iustitiam inhærentem, homine iustificari, ex sequentibus Scriptu-ræ testimoniis demonstratur: Roman 3. vers. 27. Vbi igitur gloriatio? Exclusa est. Per quam legem? Operum? Non. Imo per legem fidei: & v. 28. Concludimus igitur fide iustificari hominem absque operibus legis. Et 4. vers. 2. Si Abraham ex operibus iustificatus fuit, habet quod glorietur, at non apud Deum. Galat. 2. vers. 16. Scientes non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi: etiā nos in Iesum Christum credidimus, vt iustificaremur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Ephef. 2. vers. 8. 9. Gratia estis seruati per fidem, non ex operibus. Tit. 3. vers. 5. Non ex operibus iustis, quæ fecerimus nos, sed ex sua misericordia seruauit nos, &c. Phil. 3. ver. 9. Vt inueniar in eo non habens meam iustitiam, quæ est ex lege, sed eam quæ per fidem est Christi. Atque hinc est, quod Iudæis hac ruinæ causam extitisse tradit Apostolus, quod suam volentes iustitiam stabilire, iustitiæ Dei non fuerint subiecti. Ro-man. 10. vers. 3. Hic tamen obseruandum fidem nos iustificare, non quatenus consideretur absolutè vt qualitas, sed quatenus est relatum, respiciens & apprehendens suum correlatum, videlicet Christum cum iustitia ipsius, netonymia nimirum continentis pro re contenta, & adiuncti pro subiecto, vel potius instrumenti apprehensi vi, vt ita dicam, pro obiecto apprehenso: id est, nomine fidei intelligendam esse rem quempiam, quæ per fidem ad iustitiam homini imputatur. Nam proprie loquendo, id quod est in homine non dicitur ei imputari, sed id quod est extra hominem. Quum igitur fides sit qualitas in homine inhærens, iustitia vero, satisfactio & obedientia Christi quam fides apprehendit, extra hominem, inde fit vt illa homini imputetur per fidem, id est, accepta ei feratur, homoque eo loco habeatur, ac si ipsemet illam iustitiam ac obedientiam pro se præstitisset. Nec tamen hæc iustitia, licet subiecto & ortu extra nos sit in Christo, est imaginaria & inanis, quia actu & effectu nostra est imputatiue, & quidem dupliciter: primò communione videlicet illa, quam vinculo Spiritus habemus cum ipso qui est caput nostrum, & cuius membra sumus: secundò etiam applicatione, eáque duplici, Dei, & nostri: Dei, nobis imputando iustitiam Christi, vt paulò post ostendemus: nostri, eam apprehendendo & recipiendo fide: quarum illa licet non sit efficax absque hac, quia sunt simul tempore, hanc tamen ab illa, tanquā eius causa & fundamento dependere statuimus. Non enim vos me elegistis, inquit Christus, sed ego vos: Iohan. capite decimo quinto, versu decimosexto: Et nos diligimus eum, quia prior ipse dilexit nos. 1. Ioh. 4. v. 19. Vnde manifestissimè liquet, verissimum esse id quod asserimus, nempe iustificari nos iustitia non nostra: nam Iehoua est iustitia nostra: non infusa, quia facti sumus iustitia Dei in Christo: non inhærete, quia non debemus comperiri habentes iustitiam nostram: non informante, quia nullus viuens coram Deo iustificabitur: sed Christi, & quidem non exemplari eius, est enim factus nostra iustitia: non habituali, quia eius est originalis: minus essentiali, quia ἀκαταγνωστος, & incommunicabilis: sed actuali, quæ effectus est vtriusque, quam videlicet obedientia sua nobis peperit: Ierem. 33. v. 16. 2. Cor. 5. v. 21. Phil. 3. v. 9. Psal. 143. v. 2. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. Eph. 4. v. 8. Rom. 5. v. 19. Nec denique pugnat hæc doctrina, de merito, iustitia, & satisfactione Christi, cum iustificationis nostræ causa συνεργούμενη, mera videlicet Dei gratia, quia hoc modo iustificamur efficienter si nos respicias, quod nullum interueniat meritum nostrum: illo verò meritorie si Christum, cuius satisfactio & meritum nobis imputatur: vtroque autem modo, vt opera nostra excludantur. Ephes. 2. vers. 8. 9. Gratia estis servati per fidem, idque non ex vobis, donum Dei est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Sic Daniel non propter aliquam iustitiam propriam, sed propter Dominum & miserationes eius exaudiri cupit, Dan. 9. v. 17. 18. 19. Nunc audi, ausculta Deus noster orationi serui tui, & deprecationibus eius, & fac vt luceat faciès tua super sanctuarium tuum, quod desolatum est in Dominum, id est, Christum Mediatorem, quem Deus hæredem & Dominum omnium constituit: Inclina Deus mi aurem tuam, & audi, aperi oculos tuos, & vide desolationes nostras: non enim propter illam iustitiam nostram, nos procidentes deprecamur te, sed propter miserationes tuas amplissimas: Domine exaudi, Domine condona, Domine attende, & effice, ne tardato, propter te Deus mi, &c. Forma iustificationis nostræ in iustitiæ ac obedientiæ Christi applicatione, remissione videlicet peccatorum, & iustitiæ Christi imputatione consistit. Roman. 3. verf. 24.25. Iustificantur gratis,id est, eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu,quē proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam,per remissionem praecedentium peccatorum. Roman. 4. verf. 6.7.8. Dauid dicit, beatificationem esse hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam suam absque operibus,dicens:Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates,& quorum obtecta sunt peccata : Beatus vir cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. & verf. 5. Ei qui non operatur,sed credit in eum qui iustificat impium,imputatur fides sua ad iustitiam.& verf. 24.25. Futurum est ut imputetur nobis sc. fides ad iustitiam, qui credimus in eum qui excitauit Iesum Dominum nostrum a mortuis : qui traditus est propter lapsus nostros,& excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri. 1. Corint. 1. ver. 30. Christus factus est nobis a Deo sapientia,iustitia,sanctificatio,& redemptio. Eph. 1. v. 6.7. Deus per suam gratiam effecit nos gratiosos in illo dilecto, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Phil. 3. Vt inueniar in eo non habens iustitiam meam,quae est ex lege,sed eam quae per fidem est Christi. Ex quibus omnibus apparet formulam iustificationis nostrae causam in ablatione causae mortis secundae & ac imputatione eius, quod est principium vitae, consistere.
units.tr: The matter of that justification of ours is the righteousness, satisfaction and obedience of Christ. The righteousness on account of which we are justified, and with all our sins forgiven are reckoned heirs of eternal life, is subjectively in Christ alone, but is made ours through faith. Rom. 3. v. 24.25. They are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. And 4. v. 24. It shall be imputed to us (namely faith unto righteousness) who believe in him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification. And 5. v. 9. Being therefore justified by his blood, we shall be saved now much more through him from wrath. And 10. We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. And 8. v. 3.4. What was impossible for the law, insofar as it was weakened through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. And 10. v. 6.7. But the righteousness that is of faith speaks thus: Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down from above; or who will descend into the abyss? that is, to bring Christ back up from the dead. First Corinthians ch. 1, v. 30: Christ was made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Second Corinthians ch. 5, last verse: He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Galatians 2. v. 20.21. The life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died in vain. And in ch. 3, v. 13 and 14: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, since he became a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Ephesians ch. 5, 6, 7: He predestined us whom he would adopt as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he has made us graced in the beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace. Rom. 4. v. 5. To him who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed to righteousness. From all these testimonies it clearly appears that the thing which is imputed to man for righteousness through faith, and which makes us pleasing to God and worthy of eternal life, is the very obedience and righteousness of Christ, since by it alone all the sins of the elect are expiated and access to the heavenly inheritance is opened to us. And that a man is justified by faith alone, that is, on account of the righteousness and obedience of Christ apprehended by faith alone, and not partly by faith, that is, on account of the imputed satisfaction of Christ, and partly by works, that is, on account of inherent righteousness, is shown from the following testimonies of Scripture. Rom. 3. v. 27. Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No. But by the law of faith. And v. 28. We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. And 4. v. 2. If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of, but not before God. Gal. 2. v. 16. Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we also have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by the works of the law. Eph. 2. v. 8.9. By grace you are saved through faith, not of works. Titus 3. v. 5. Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, etc. Phil. 3. v. 9. That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ. And hence the Apostle tells us that the cause of ruin for the Jews was this: that, desiring to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God. Rom. 10. v. 3. Here, however, it must be observed that faith justifies us not insofar as it is considered absolutely as a quality, but insofar as it is a relation, looking to and laying hold of its correlate, namely Christ with his righteousness. This is metonymy, the container put for the contained and the adjunct for the subject, or rather (so to speak) the instrument for the object apprehended by its power. That is, by the name faith we are to understand some thing which is imputed to man for righteousness through faith. For properly speaking, what is in man is not said to be imputed to him, but what is outside man. Since therefore faith is a quality inhering in man, but the righteousness, satisfaction and obedience of Christ, which faith apprehends, is outside man, it follows that this is imputed to man through faith, that is, is carried to his account, and man is regarded in that position as if he himself had performed that righteousness and obedience. Nor is this righteousness, although in its subject and origin it is outside us in Christ, imaginary and empty, for in act and effect it is ours by imputation, and indeed in two ways. First, by that communion which we have with him who is our head and whose members we are, through the bond of the Spirit. Secondly, by application, and that twofold, of God and of ours: of God, by imputing to us the righteousness of Christ, as we will show a little later; of ours, by apprehending and receiving it by faith. Of these, although the former is not effective without the latter, since they are simultaneous in time, nevertheless we hold that the latter depends on the former as its cause and foundation. For you did not choose me, says Christ, but I chose you: John ch. 15, v. 16. And we love him, because he first loved us. 1 John 4. v. 19. Whence it is most clearly evident that what we assert is most true, namely that we are justified not by our own righteousness. For Jehovah is our righteousness: not infused, because we have been made the righteousness of God in Christ; not inherent, because we ought not to be found having our own righteousness; not informing, because no living man will be justified before God; but it is Christ's, and indeed not his example, for he has been made our righteousness; not habitual, because it is his original; not least essential, [ἀκαταγνωστος] and incommunicable; but actual, which is the effect of both, namely that which his obedience has won for us. Jer. 33. v. 16. 2 Cor. 5. v. 21. Phil. 3. v. 9. Ps. 143. v. 2. 1 Cor. 1. v. 30. Eph. 4. v. 8. Rom. 5. v. 19. Nor finally does this doctrine of the merit, righteousness and satisfaction of Christ conflict with the cooperating cause [συνεργούμενη] of our justification, namely the pure grace of God. For in this way we are justified efficiently if you look to us, since no merit of ours intervenes; but meritoriously if you look to Christ, whose satisfaction and merit is imputed to us; and in both ways our works are excluded. Eph. 2. v. 8.9. By grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast. Thus Daniel desires to be heard not on account of any righteousness of his own, but on account of the Lord and his mercies. Dan. 9. v. 17.18.19. Now hear, our God, the prayer of your servant and his supplications, and cause your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate, for the Lord's sake, that is, for Christ the Mediator, whom God has appointed heir and Lord of all. Incline your ear, my God, and hear; open your eyes and see our desolations: for not on account of that righteousness of ours do we fall down and pray to you, but on account of your very great mercies. Lord, hear; Lord, forgive; Lord, attend and act, and do not delay, for your own sake, my God, etc. The form of our justification consists in the application of Christ's righteousness and obedience, namely in the remission of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Rom. 3. v. 24.25. They are justified freely, that is, by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness through the remission of previous sins. Rom. 4. v. 6.7.8. David says that blessed is the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works, saying: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. And v. 5. To him who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed to righteousness. And v. 24.25. It shall be imputed to us (namely faith unto righteousness) who believe in him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences and raised for our justification. 1 Cor. 1. v. 30. Christ was made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Eph. 1. v. 6.7. God by his grace made us graced in the beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins. Phil. 3. That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ. From all these things it appears that the form of our justification consists in the removal of the cause of the second death and in the imputation of that which is the beginning of life.

units.la: Finis iustificationis nostrae duplex est, vnus summus ac remotus, qui est patefactio gloriae diuinae. Roman. 3. verf. 25. 26. Ad declarandam iustitiam suam praesenti tempore,vt sit ipse iustus,& iustificans eum qui est ex fide Iesu: quo gloria Dei in sapientissima illa iustitia, & misericordiae ac temperamento potissimum elucet: alter proximus,qui est non tantum pax conscientiae,quę hoc scuto ignita Sathanae tela extinguit,legisque execrationes retundit:1. Iohan. 5. verf. 5. Quis est qui vicit mundum,nisi qui credit Iesum esse filium Dei? Roman. 5. v. 1. Iustificati ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum,per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: verum etiam ipsa sanctificatio Spiritus,& denique vita aeterna. Eph. 1. verf. 4. Elegit nos in ipso antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, vt simus sancti & inculpati coram eo per charitatem. 2. Thess. 2. v. 13.14. Deus elegit vos ab initio ad salutem per sanctificationem Spiritus, & fidem habitam veritati, quo vocauit vos per Euangelium nostrum,ad obtinendam gloriam Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Tit. 3. v. 7. Vt iustificati ipsius gratia,haeredes efficeremur secundum spem vitae aeternae. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. Electi ex praenotione Dei Patris ad sanctificationem Spiritus,per obedientiam,& aspersionem sanguinis Iesu Christi. su Christi. Habac.2.v.4. Iustus ex fide viuet.
units.tr: The end of our justification is twofold. The first and highest end, which is more remote, is the manifestation of the glory of God (Rom. 3:25-26): To declare his righteousness at this present time, that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. In that most wise righteousness, and especially in the blending of mercy and justice, the glory of God shines forth. The second end is nearer: it is not only peace of conscience, which by this shield quenches the fiery darts of Satan and breaks the curses of the law (1 John 5:5): Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God? (Rom. 5:1): Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. It is also the sanctification of the Spirit, and finally eternal life (Eph. 1:4): He hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love. (2 Thess. 2:13-14): God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation, through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, whereunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. (Titus 3:7): That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. (1 Pet. 1:2): Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. (Hab. 2:4): The just shall live by his faith.

units.la: Subiectum denique iustificationis, sunt omnes & foli electi,sed peccatores,quia hi foli remissione peccatorum, & iustitiae Christi imputatione indigent,& peccata sua agnoscentes, detestantes, atque ad gratiam & misericordiam Dei per fidem in Christum Iesum Mediatorem ac Redemptorem nostrum confugientes: quia hi solum veniam peccatorum, gratiam, ac vitam aeternam per Christum cõsequuntur:denique cum Christo capite nostro per fidem uniti: quia hi tantùm communionem cum Christo habent, & vim mortis,sepulturae,vitae,ac resurrectionis ipsius participant, cum omnibus beneficiis, inter quae non vltimum locum obtinet gratuita iustificatio,inde in nos redundantibus. Roman.8.ver.30. Quos Deus praedestinauit,eos etiam vocauit:& quos vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit:quos autem iustificauit,eos etiam glorificauit.& verf.1.Nulla est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu:& ver.33.34. Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus is est qui iustificat : Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est, imò verò qui etiam excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam postulat pro nobis. Dominus Iesus, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius,remissionem peccatorum,& qui est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris,cum Deo Patre,& Spiritu sancto, laudetur in secula.
units.tr: The subject of justification, finally, is all and only the elect, but as sinners, because only these need the remission of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Acknowledging and detesting their sins, they flee to the grace and mercy of God through faith in Christ Jesus, our Mediator and Redeemer. Only these obtain forgiveness of sins, grace and eternal life through Christ. Finally, they are united by faith with Christ our head, and only they have communion with Christ and share in the power of his death, burial, life and resurrection, together with all the benefits which flow over to us from him, among which free justification holds no small place. (Rom. 8:30): Whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. And (Rom. 8:1): There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. And (Rom. 8:33-34): Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. May the Lord Jesus, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, and who is the propitiation for our sins, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praised for ever.

units.la: CAPVT XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: In quo sententia ac doctrina Aduersarij de Iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo, recensetur ac refutatur.
units.tr: In which the opponent's view and doctrine of the justification of a sinful man before God is set out and refuted.

units.la: STorrodius Institutionum suarum cap. 36. & 37. veritatem sententiae ac doctrinae orthodoxae, de Iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo impugnaturus, ac simul doctrinam Samosatenianorum (cuius summa haec est: Hominem videlicet à Deo iustificari, nihil aliud esse, quàm per gratuitam remissionem & condonationem, nullo Christi interueniente merito & satisfactione, deletis peccatis ipsius, iustum pronuntiari, & quasi iustum tractari: Seu: Hominem à Deo iustificari, quando Deus per gratuitam remissionem, nullo Christi merito aut satisfactione interueniente, peccatis ipsius deletis, iustum pronuntiat ipsum, & non secus ac si iustus in se esset, tractat, vitaeque aeternae praemio ornat. Ac proinde materiam iustificationis nostrae non esse iustitiam & satisfactionem Christi, sed fidem iustificantem, seu fiduciam, & confidentiam in Deum, per Christum, collocatam, id est, obedientiam praeceptis Christi praestitam, spe videlicet beatae immortalitatis consequendae, quae fides seu obedientia nobis à Deo pro iustitia imputetur. de qua postmodum agemus) explicaturus, ac propugnaturus, primò omnium causam exponit, cuius gratia de Libero hominis Arbitrio, de primi item hominis tam ante quàm post lapsum statu & conditione, denique de praedestinatione diuina, disputauerit ac disseruerit, eamque hanc esse dicit, vt manifestum fieret, nos debitam obedientiam auxiliante diuina gratia, quam Deus omnibus & singulis impertitur, praeceptis diuinis praestare posse. An vero Storrodius hunc finem & scopum suum assequutus sit, ex rationum & argumentorum vtrinque propositorum momentis inter se collatis, & iis quae capite 26. 27. 28. 29. de iisdem rebus tractauimus, fiat iudicium, in quibus capitibus enumeratas illas ab Aduersario quaestiones controuersas tam prolixè exposuimus,& veritatè tot ac tantis argumentis cõfir-mauimus,vt speremus, æquum Lectorem nihil amplius ea de re à nobis efflagitaturum esse:ad sequentia igitur progredior.
units.tr: Storrodius, in chapters 36 and 37 of his Institutions, sets out to attack the teaching of the orthodox view on the justification of a sinful man before God, and at the same time to explain and defend the doctrine of the Samosatenians (whose substance is this: that a man is justified by God in nothing other than being pronounced and treated as righteous through free remission and pardon, with no intervening merit or satisfaction of Christ, his sins being blotted out; or, in other words: that a man is justified by God when God, through free remission, with no intervening merit or satisfaction of Christ, blots out his sins, pronounces him righteous, treats him as if he were righteous in himself, and crowns him with the reward of eternal life. Accordingly, the matter of our justification is not the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ, but justifying faith, or trust and confidence in God through Christ, that is, obedience rendered to the precepts of Christ, in the hope of attaining blessed immortality; this faith or obedience is imputed to us by God as righteousness. We shall discuss this later). First of all, he sets out the reason for which he has argued and discoursed on the free will of man, on the state and condition of the first man both before and after the fall, and finally on divine predestination. He says that this was so that it might become clear that we are able, with the help of divine grace, which God imparts to all and each, to render due obedience to the divine precepts. Whether Storrodius has reached this aim and goal may be judged by weighing the force of the reasons and arguments put forward on both sides, and by the matters we treated about the same things in chapters 26, 27, 28 and 29, where we set out at such length the controverted questions listed by our opponent and confirmed the truth with so many and such great arguments that we hope a fair reader will demand nothing further from us on the subject. I therefore proceed to what follows.

units.la: Secundò transit ad ipsam doctrinam de Iustificatione, atque in tractatione illius ante omnia perstringit ac refutat sententiam ac doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quam passim à Theologis nostris in scriptis, cócionibus, ac disputationibus, & quoties sese occasio offert, stu-diosissimè inculcari dicit, eámque duabus illis thesibus comprehen-sam proponit: I. Deum nos non iustificare propter bona opera,sed propter meritū Filii ipsius Iesu Christi, i.propterea quòd Christus primò cùm nullus hominū legē perfectè seruare posset, Deo Patri pro nobis seu loco nostro obcdiuerit,atque ita legē pro nobis im-pleuerit:deinde Deo Patri pro omnibus peccatis nostris,tā futuris quā præteritis,morte ac passione sua plenissimè satisfecerit. II.Ac proinde Deũ,si vitā ac salutē æternam cõsequi velimus,nihil aliud à nobis postulare,nisi vt hoc firmiter credamus, illámq; obedien-tiam ac satisfactionem nobis applicemus. Atque hanc doctrinam, quam facile & iucundum ad vitam æternam consequendā compendium cõpleƈti cauillatur,falsa esse, hoc argumēto euincere conatur, quòd inde sequeretur,bona opera ad vitam æternam consequedam necessaria non esse,ac proinde omnes Prophetas, Apostolos,& Martyres,ac iustos Dei homines meritò stultitiæ damnandos,quòd in illo medio non acquiescen-tes, dies noctésque in hoc elaborauerint, vt seruarent præcepta Dei, ac eam ob causam etiam multas calamitates perpessi sint, imò multi cru-delissima & ignominiosissima supplicia subierint. Quum verò certissi-mum sit,illos omnes hac in re non errasse,ideò necessariò sequi, vel illam sententiam ac doctrinam Theologorum, de satisfactione Christi, falsam & erroneam esse: vel saltem ad vitam æternam consequendam, fidem illam, quæ meritum & satisfactionem illam Christi apprehendere dicimur,non sufficere ,sed insuper necessarium esse, vt præceptis diuinis obediamus.
units.tr: Secondly, he passes to the doctrine of justification itself, and in treating it he first of all attacks and refutes the teaching of our Churches, which he says is everywhere, in writings, sermons and disputations, and whenever the occasion arises, most diligently impressed by our theologians. He sets it out as comprised in two theses: (1) that God does not justify us on account of good works, but on account of the merit of his Son Jesus Christ, namely because Christ, since no man could keep the law perfectly, first rendered obedience to God the Father for us, or in our place, and so fulfilled the law on our behalf; then, by his death and passion, he fully satisfied God the Father for all our sins, both future and past. (2) Accordingly, God, if we wish to attain life and eternal salvation, asks nothing else of us than that we firmly believe this and apply to ourselves that obedience and satisfaction. This doctrine, which he sneeringly calls an easy and pleasant shortcut to attaining eternal life, he tries to prove false by this argument: that it would follow from it that good works are not necessary for attaining eternal life; and therefore all the Prophets, Apostles, and Martyrs, and the righteous men of God, would rightly be condemned as fools, because, not resting in that middle way, they laboured day and night to keep God's precepts, and for that reason suffered many calamities, and indeed many underwent the cruelest and most shameful punishments. Since it is most certain that they all erred in none of this, it necessarily follows that either that teaching of the theologians about the satisfaction of Christ is false and erroneous, or at least that the faith by which we are said to lay hold of that merit and satisfaction of Christ is not sufficient for attaining eternal life, but that it is also necessary that we obey the divine precepts.

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument runs as follows:

units.la: Ex qua sententia ac doctrina sequitur, bona opera ad vitam ac salutem æternam consequendam necessaria non esse, illa falsa est & erronea:
units.tr: From this teaching it follows that good works are not necessary for attaining eternal life and salvation; but that is false and erroneous.

units.la: Atqui ex illa sententia ac doctrina,qua docetur Deū iustificare nos non propter bona opera, sed propter obedientiam & satisfactionem Christi, Deū à nobis vitam ac salutem æternam cõsequi volētibus nihil aliud postulare, nisi in hoc firmiter credamus, illámque obedientiam & satisfactionem Christi nobis applicemus, sequitur, bona opera ad salutem ac vitam æternam consequendam necessaria non esse: Ergo sententia ac doctrina illa de iustificatione, falsa est ac erronea.
units.tr: But from that teaching, by which it is taught that God justifies us not on account of good works but on account of the obedience and satisfaction of Christ, and that God asks nothing else of those who wish to attain eternal life and salvation than that they firmly believe this and apply to themselves that obedience and satisfaction of Christ, it follows that good works are not necessary for attaining eternal life and salvation. Therefore that doctrine of justification is false and erroneous.

units.la: Connexi probatio hæc est:
units.tr: The proof of the connection is this:

units.la: Si bona opera ad salutem consequendam necessaria non essent, tum sequeretur omnes Prophetas, Apostolos, ac Martyres, & alios iustos ac sanctos Dei homines merito stultitiæ damnandos esse, quod illo facili medio, nempe fide, per quam obedientia & satisfactio Christi nobis applicatur, non contenti, in præstanda præceptis divinis obedientia, dies noctesque desudauerint, multas miserias & calamitates sustinuerint, denique crudelissima ac ignominiosissima supplicia subierint:
units.tr: If good works were not necessary for attaining salvation, it would follow that all the prophets, apostles, martyrs, and other righteous and holy people of God would rightly be condemned as fools, because they were not content with that easy means, namely faith, through which the obedience and satisfaction of Christ is applied to us, but instead toiled day and night to render obedience to the divine precepts, endured many miseries and calamities, and at last underwent the most cruel and shameful punishments.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum est: Ergo & antecedens, ac proinde sequitur, vel doctrinam ac sententiam illam de iustificatione quæ fieri dicitur per obedientiæ ac satisfactionis Christi imputationem, falsam esse, vel saltem præterfidem illam qua meritum Christi nobis applicatur, aliquid amplius ad salutem consequendam necessarium esse, nempe hoc ut præceptis divinis obediamus.
units.tr: But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent is too. It follows that either the doctrine and opinion of justification that is said to occur through the imputation of Christ's obedience and satisfaction is false, or at least that, besides that faith by which Christ's merit is applied to us, something more is necessary for attaining salvation, namely that we obey the divine precepts.

units.la: Resp. Quum doctrinam ac sententiam illam quam Aduersarius impugnat, partim nostram agnoscamus, partim vero ambiguitate laborare atque inuolui deprehendamus: ideo priusquam ad argumentum propositum respondeamus, exponendum est quidnam hac de re sentiant ac doceant Ecclesiæ nostræ. Et primam quidem thesin quantum concernit, cum illa duobus cōstet membris, quorum primo falsa iustificationis materia remouetur, posteriori vero, vera ac genuina causa, per quam iustificamur, asseritur, de singulis ordine ac sigillatim erit agendum. Membrum igitur primum quantum attinet, Deum videlicet nos non propter opera bona iustificare, non ex humano cerebro, sed verbi diuini fontibus hausta est doctrina illa, qua asseritur, ex operibus non iustificari coram Deo quenquam: vel sola fide, & non ex operibus Legis, hominem iustificari, vt ex sequentibus Scripturæ testimoniis liquidò constat. Rom. 3. ver. 27. 28. Vbi igitur gloriatio? Exclusa est. Per quam legem? Operum? Non. Imo per legem fidei. Concludimus igitur fide iustificari cari hominem absque operibus legis. Galat. 2. verf. 15. 16. Nos natura Iudaei, & non ex Gentibus peccatores, quum sciremus non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi: etiam nos in Christum Iesum credidimus, ut iustificaremur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Tit. cap. 3. verf. 5. Non ex operibus iustis, quae fecerimus nos, sed ex sua misericordia seruauit nos, &c. Phil 3. verf. 9. Ut inueniar in eo non habens iustitiam meam quae est ex lege, sed eam quae per fidem est Christi. Roman. 11. verf. 6. Nam si per gratiam, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia: aut si ex operibus, non ex gratia, alioquin opus non esset opus. Ex quibus, ut & aliis innumeris scripturae sacrae testimoniis euidenter apparet, primum doctrinae illius, quam Ecclesiae nostrae profitetur membrum, totidem verbis in sacris literis comprehendi. Suam igitur, quam Samoateniani inculcant ac tuentur, sententiam, nempe bonis operibus iustificari hominem, ex iisdem scripturis sacris demonstret, si posset, Osiorrodius. Scio testimonium Iacobi, qui Abrahamum ex operibus iustificatum esse, & hominem ex operibus, non vero ex fide tantum iustificari perhibet, a quibusdam ad stabiliendam operum iustitiam produci. Sed qui in illo enuntiato subiectum, id est, bonorum operum vocabulum proprie intelligendum esse censet, nec illo ipsam fidem bonorum operum feracem, & charitatis fructibus foecundam, vsitatissima in scripturis sacris effecti metonymia designari, ex ipsa quaestione quam ibi tractat Apostolus Iacobus, ac totius disputationis serie, non animaduertit, cum certe caecutire oportet ac necesse est. Neque discrimen illud inter opera legis, & opera fidei, item inter obedientiam legi praestandam, & eam quam praeceptis Christi praestare tenemur, quod vrgent Aduersarii, vel doctrinam nostram euertit, vel sententiam Aduersarii stabilit. Quum enim ipsi Aduersarii (quod in hac controuersia diligentissime est animaduertendum) doceant, ac mordicus tueantur, legem Mosis moralem, per Christum multis partibus correctam, auctam, interpolatam, ac nonnis praeceptis locupletatam esse, quis non videt exactiorem, perfectiorem, ac proinde etiam difficiliorem obedientiam a Christo, quam a Mose, praescriptam esse? Quum deinde Aduersarii profiteantur, hominem perfectam, & partibus, numeris ac gradibus omnibus absolutam obedientiam praeceptis Christi praestare posse, Paulus vero Rom. 8. ver. 3. palam affirmat, iustificationem ex operibus legis impossibilem esse, seu, neminem ex operibus legis iustisicari posse, non propter legis, sed carnis vitiositatem ac infirmitatem : i. quia praestita non fit, non vero quia iustitia quae in illa praescribitur, Deo grata non fit, quis non animadvertit, Ostorrodium ipsi Paulo directe contradicere, idque dupliciter? Primo videlicet, quia ex sententia Aduersarii necessario sequitur posse aliquem legis moralis iustitia circa transgressionem fungi, ac proinde coram tribunali seuerae iustitiae constitutum, iustum a Deo, ac vitae aeternae praemio dignum, in se, ex debito, & circa remissionis gratiam censeri ac pronuntiari. Quum enim doceat idem Aduersarius, praeceptis Christi praestantiorem ac perfectiorem iustitiam, quam in lege Mosis, praescribi, & hominem in hac vita ad summam iustitiae perfectionem, quam ille aequalitate cum iustitia Christi definit, pertingere posse, necessario inde sequitur, hominem in hac vita etiam illam obedientiam, quae in Lege Mosis praescribitur, perfecte & exacte praestare, ac proinde, modo praedicto, instificari posse. Qui n. effectu dare potest id, quod maius, ac difficilius est, ille etiam id quod minus ac facilius est, praestare posse, omnium non insanietium suffragiis censetur. Quu deinde homo per eiusmodi iustitiam, qua iustitiam in lege praescriptam perfectione superet, iustificari possit, iustificatio autem toti legi simul, & semel adimatur ab Apostolo: inde necessario sequitur, contra Apostolu, Legem iustificare non posse, non vitio ac infirmitate hominum in legem peccantium, sed Legis ipsius vitio, atque infirmitate. Quum vero utrumque consequens impium sit ac absurdum, inde quantopere Aduersarii a veritate aberret, fit manifestum. Sed progrediendum nobis est ad sequentia. Alterum igitur theseos nostrae membrum quod attinet, Deum videlicet nos propter meritum, obedientiam & satisfactionem, seu mortem & passionem Christi iustificare, solide ex Scripturis sacris demonstrauero, cum ex illis, per mortem Christi peccata nostra expiata, ac remissionem peccatorum nobis partam esse, probatum a me fuerit. Nam id quod expiata sunt peccata nostra, seu quo parta est nobis peccatorum remissio, est id ipsum, quod nobis ad iustitiam imputatur, seu propter quod iustitia nobis a Deo imputatur, seu denique propter quod iustificamur, id est, iusti a Deo habemur ac pronunciamur, quia remissio peccatorum & iustificatio reipsa unum ac idem sunt, ut ex verbis Pauli liquido colligat, Ro. 4. v. 6. 7. 8. vbi inquit, Dauid pronunciat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat iustitiam absque operibus, dicens: Beati quorum remissae remissa sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata: Beatus vir cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. Atqui mortem Christi esse id quo expiata sunt peccata nostra, & quo parta nobis est peccatorum remissio, sequentia scripturæ sacræ dicta diserte testatur: Mat. 20. v. 28. Filius hominis venit, vt daret animam suam in redemptionis pretium pro multis. Luc. 22. v. 20. & Matt. 26. v. 28. Hoc poculum est nouum illud Testamentum per meum sanguinem, qui pro vobis & pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Ioh. 1. v. 29. Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Rom. 3. 24. 25. Iustificatur autem gratis eius gratia per redemptionem factam in Iesu Christo, quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam per remissionem praecedentium peccatorum. Rom. 5. v. 9. 10. Iustificati igitur eius sanguine seruabimur nunc multo magis per eum ab ira. Nam si cum inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo, per mortem Filii eius &c. Galat. 3. v. 13. Christus redemit nos ab execratione legis, dum pro vobis factus est execratio. Scriptum est enim, Execrabilis omnis qui pendet in ligno. Tit. 2. v. 14. Qui tradidit semetipsum, vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate. Hebr. capite nono, versu vigesimosexto. Christus nunc semel in consummatione seculorum, ad abolendum peccatum per immolationem suiipsius, patefactus est. 1. Petr. 1. verf. 19. Redempti estis pretiosO sanguine, vtpote agni immaculati, & incontaminati: nempe Christi. & cap. 2. verf. 24. Christus peccata nostra pertulit in carne sua, super lignum. & cap. 3. verf. 18. Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, iustus pro iniustis, vt nos ad Deum adduceret. prima Iohannis, capite primo, versu septimo. Sanguis Iesu Christi filii eius purgat nos ab omni peccato. Ex quibus omnibus necessario sequitur, mortem & passionem Christi esse id ipsum, quod nobis ad iustitiam imputatur, seu, propter quod nobis iustitia imputatur, seu denique propter quod iustificamur, id est, iusti a Deo habemur, ac pronunciamur. Vnde iam apparet, ipsam thesin primam non a Theologis nostris confictam, sed ex ipsis Scripturis sacris haustam ac depromptam esse.
units.tr: Reply. Since we acknowledge that the doctrine and opinion which the Adversary attacks is partly ours, but find that it is also burdened with ambiguity and confusion, therefore, before we answer the argument proposed, we must set out what our Churches think and teach on this matter. As far as the first thesis is concerned, since it consists of two parts, of which the first removes the false matter of justification and the second asserts the true and genuine cause by which we are justified, each must be treated in order and separately. As far as the first part is concerned, namely that God does not justify us on account of good works, this doctrine, which asserts that no one is justified before God by works, but that a man is justified by faith alone and not by works of the law, is not drawn from human brains but from the fountains of the divine Word, as is clear from the following testimonies of Scripture. Rom. 3:27-28: Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No. But by the law of faith. We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Gal. 2:15-16: We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles, since we knew that a man is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. Titus 3:5: Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, etc. Phil. 3:9: That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ. Rom. 11:6: But if by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. And if of works, it is no longer of grace; otherwise work is no longer work. From these, as from countless other testimonies of holy Scripture, it is evident that the first part of the doctrine professed by our Church is contained in the Scriptures in just these words. Let Ostorrodius, then, if he can, demonstrate from the same holy Scriptures his own opinion, which the Socinians press and defend, namely that a man is justified by good works. I know the testimony of James, who says that Abraham was justified by works, and that a man is justified by works and not by faith only; some bring this forward to establish the righteousness of works. But whoever holds that in that statement the subject, that is the term "good works", must be understood properly, and does not notice that the faith itself, fruitful in good works and rich in the fruits of love, is designated by the very common metonymy found in the holy Scriptures, must certainly be blind, as is evident from the very question that the Apostle James treats there and from the whole sequence of the argument. Nor does that distinction, which the Adversaries press, between the works of the law and the works of faith, and likewise between the obedience owed to the law and that which we are bound to render to the precepts of Christ, either overthrow our doctrine or establish the opinion of the Adversary. For since the Adversaries themselves teach, and stubbornly defend (which in this controversy must be most carefully noted), that the moral law of Moses has been corrected in many parts, increased, interpolated, and enriched with some new precepts by Christ, who does not see that a more exact, more perfect, and therefore also more difficult obedience has been prescribed by Christ than by Moses? Since, moreover, the Adversaries profess that a man can render perfect obedience to the precepts of Christ, complete in all its parts, numbers, and degrees, while Paul plainly affirms at Rom. 8:3 that justification by works of the law is impossible, or that no one can be justified by works of the law, not because of the vice and weakness of the law but of the flesh, that is, because that obedience is not rendered, not because the righteousness prescribed in it is not pleasing to God, who does not see that Ostorrodius directly contradicts Paul himself, and in two ways? First, namely, because on the Adversary's view it necessarily follows that someone can fulfil the righteousness of the moral law with respect to transgression, and so, placed before the tribunal of strict justice, can be counted and pronounced righteous before God, and worthy of the reward of eternal life, in himself, by debt, and apart from the grace of forgiveness. For since the same Adversary teaches that a more excellent and more perfect righteousness than that in the law of Moses is prescribed by the precepts of Christ, and that in this life a man can attain to the highest perfection of righteousness, which he defines as equality with the righteousness of Christ, it necessarily follows that in this life a man can also render perfectly and exactly that obedience which is prescribed in the law of Moses, and therefore can be justified in the manner described above. For whoever can achieve what is greater and more difficult is judged, by the agreement of all sane people, able also to achieve what is less and easier. Second, since a man can be justified through that kind of righteousness, which surpasses in perfection the righteousness prescribed in the law, and since justification is taken away from the whole law at once and together by the Apostle, it necessarily follows, against the Apostle, that the law cannot justify, not through the vice and weakness of men who sin against the law, but through the vice and weakness of the law itself. But since both consequences are impious and absurd, it is made manifest how far the Adversaries wander from the truth. But we must proceed to what follows. As for the second part of our thesis, namely that God justifies us on account of the merit, obedience, and satisfaction, or the death and passion, of Christ, I will demonstrate this solidly from the holy Scriptures, since it has been proved by me from them that our sins have been expiated through the death of Christ and that the forgiveness of sins has been won for us. For that by which our sins are expiated, or by which the forgiveness of sins has been won for us, is the very thing which is imputed to us for righteousness, or on account of which righteousness is imputed to us by God, or finally on account of which we are justified, that is, we are held and pronounced righteous by God; because the forgiveness of sins and justification are in fact one and the same, as Paul clearly concludes from his words at Rom. 4:6-8, where he says: David pronounces blessed the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works, saying: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. But that the death of Christ is that by which our sins are expiated and by which the forgiveness of sins has been won for us is expressly attested by the following sayings of holy Scripture: Matt. 20:28: The Son of man came to give his life as a ransom for many. Luke 22:20 and Matt. 26:28: This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. John 1:29: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Rom. 3:24-25: They are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness by the forgiveness of previously committed sins. Rom. 5:9-10: Therefore, since we are now justified by his blood, we shall much more be saved through him from wrath. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, etc. Gal. 3:13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, when he became a curse for us. For it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Titus 2:14: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity. Heb. 9:26: Now once at the consummation of the ages he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. 1 Pet. 1:19: You were redeemed with precious blood, as of a lamb unblemished and undefiled, namely of Christ. And 2:24: Christ himself bore our sins in his body on the tree. And 3:18: Christ once suffered for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God. 1 John 1:7: The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. From all these it necessarily follows that the death and passion of Christ is the very thing that is imputed to us for righteousness, or on account of which righteousness is imputed to us, or finally on account of which we are justified, that is, held and pronounced righteous by God. Whence it now appears that the first thesis itself was not invented by our theologians but drawn and taken from the holy Scriptures themselves. As for the second thesis, which asserts that God demands and requires nothing else from us who desire to attain salvation and eternal life than that we apprehend and apply to ourselves through faith the merit, satisfaction, and righteousness of Christ, and therefore that good works are necessary for eternal life...

units.la: Thesin vero secundam quantum concernit, qua asseritur, Deum a nobis salutem ac vitam æternam consequi volentibus, nihil aliud postulare & exigere, nisi vt per fidem meritum, satisfactionem, & iustitiam Christi apprehendamus, nobisque applicemus, ac proinde bona opera ad vitam æternam consequendam necessaria non esse, non memini me illam apud Theologorum nostrorum vllum legisse, imo
units.tr: As for the second thesis, which asserts that God requires of those who wish to obtain salvation and eternal life nothing more than that they lay hold of the merit, satisfaction and righteousness of Christ by faith and apply them to themselves, and that therefore good works are not necessary for obtaining eternal life: I do not recall having read this in any of our theologians. Indeed, I dare to affirm with confidence that it is falsely attributed by Ostorodius to the teachers of our churches.

units.la: certò affirmare audeo, ipsam falsò Ecclesiarum nostrarum Do‑ctoribus ab Ostorrodio affingi. Distinguimus enim primò inter i‑psam iustificationem, ac vitam æternam, tanquam antecedens,& consequens,quia illa hanc ordine naturæ & tempore antecedit:vt patet tum ex dictis Pauli Rom. 8. v. 30. Quos iustificauit,eos etiam glorificauit.& 5. v. 18. ita per vnam iustificationem beneficium redun‑dauit in omnes homines ad iustificationem vitæ: tum ex eo, quod iu‑stificationis beneficium in huius vitæ spatia incidit,vt vel vnicum Abrahami exemplum demonstrat. Rei verò consequentis plures causas existere solere, quàm antecedentis,nemo ignorat. Deinde cum quid ad salutem consequendam necessarium dicitur, id vel vt causa vitæ æternæ meritoria, vel vt causa efficiens, & conditio, sine qua fieri non potest, vt quis salutem adipiscatur,necessarium esse intelligitur. Quantum igitur ad ipsam iustificationem attinet, exclusa omni operum iustitia, beneficium illud soli fidei, cum sa‑cra Scriptura in solidum adscribimus, causa & ratione duplici, tum quia non propter iustitiam inhærentem, ac bona opera, sed sola fide,id est, propter solam iustitiam ,& obedientiam Christi fi‑de apprehensam, quippe qua sola omnia electorum peccata sunt expiata,nobisque ad cœlestem hæreditatem aditus patefactus,ho‑minem coram Deo iustificari,id est,rem illam, quæ homini ad iu‑stitiam per fidem imputatur,& quæ nos Deo gratos,vitáque æter‑na dignos efficit, esse solam obedientiam & iustitiam Christi, ex Scriptura ipsa demonstrauimus : tum quia sola fides ex parte ho‑minis iustificandi est efficax illud organum & instrumentum, per quod videlicet illam iustitiam & obedientiam Christi apprehen‑dimus,nobisque applicamus. Illis enim tantum dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri, qui receperunt ipsum. Ioh.1. v.12. Vitam autem,ac salutem æternam, quantum attinet, bona opera ad illam conse‑quendam nobis omninò necessaria esse, palam profitemur vnani‑mi consensu omnes, non quidem vt causam meritoriam, sed vt causam efficientem, & conditionem, sine qua vitam ac salutem æternam adipisci minimè possumus. Matth. 5. v. 20. Nisi excellentior fuerit iustitia vestra, quàm Scribarum & Pharisæorum, nequaquam ingrediemini in regnum cœlorum. & capite septimo, versu vigesimo primo, Non omnis qui dicit mihi Domine,Domine,ingredietur in regnū cœlorum,sed qui facit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est, & capi‑te vigesimo quinto,versu trigesimo quarto, trigesimo quinto, trigesimo sexto, Venite benedicti Patris mei, hareditario iure possidete regnum paratum vobis inde a iactu mundi fundamentis: esuriui enim & dedistis mihi quo vescerer &c. Ro.8.13. Si secundum carne vixeritis, futurum est ut moriamini: si vero spiritu actiones corporis mortificetis, viuetis. & alibi passim. Hisce distinctionibus sic praemissis, vanitas argumenti, quo Aduersarius veritatem sententiae nostrae impugnat, manifeste apparet. Illam enim sententiam ac doctrinam, ex qua sequitur bonorum operum studium, & pietatis erga Deum, atque charitatis erga proximum officia, nulla ratione, nullóque modo ac respectu, ad salutem necessaria esse, quaeve ipsam fidem veris pietatis fructibus nudat, & cum bonorum operum contemptu coniuncta est, falsam atque erroneam esse credimus atque docemus, sed assumptionem syllogismi principalis negamus, neque Aduersarius illam probare unquam poterit. Illam vero sententiam atque doctrinā, quae principium, medium, atque finem iustificationis nostrae, in solam fidem transcribit, & bonorum operum, non quidem ut causae meritoriae, sed ut causae efficientis, & conditionis, sine qua nullus vitam ac salutem aeternam consequi potest, necessitatem agnoscit, verissimum esse, in antecedentibus a nobis est demonstratum. Atque haec ipsa doctrina ab Apostolis, ac Prophetis, quin & Christo ipso tradita & confirmata, (ut abunde ex Scripturis sacris probauimus,) & sanctissimorum Martyrum sanguine consignata est, ut ex historia eorundem liquido constat.
units.tr: We first distinguish between justification itself and eternal life, as antecedent and consequent, because justification precedes eternal life in the order of nature and in time. This is clear both from the words of Paul, Rom. 8. v. 30: Whom he justified, them he also glorified; and 5. v. 18: So by the one justification the benefit came upon all men unto justification of life; and from the fact that the benefit of justification falls within the span of this life, as even the single example of Abraham shows. Nobody is unaware that the consequent thing usually has more causes than the antecedent. Next, when something is said to be necessary for obtaining salvation, it is understood to be necessary either as the meritorious cause of eternal life, or as the efficient cause and the condition without which a person cannot attain salvation. So, as far as justification itself is concerned, we ascribe that benefit wholly to faith alone, excluding all righteousness of works, as Holy Scripture does, for two reasons. First, because a man is justified before God not on account of inherent righteousness or good works, but by faith alone, that is, on account of the righteousness and obedience of Christ alone, apprehended by faith; for by this alone all the sins of the elect are expiated and the way into the heavenly inheritance is opened to us. We have shown from Scripture itself that the thing which is imputed to a man for righteousness through faith, and which makes us acceptable to God and worthy of eternal life, is the obedience and righteousness of Christ alone. Second, because faith alone, on the part of the man being justified, is the effective organ and instrument by which we apprehend that righteousness and obedience of Christ and apply it to ourselves. For to them he gave power to become the sons of God, who received him (John 1. v. 12). As for eternal life and salvation, we all openly profess with one accord that good works are wholly necessary for attaining them, not indeed as the meritorious cause, but as the efficient cause and the condition without which we can by no means attain eternal life and salvation. Matt. 5. v. 20: Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall in no way enter the kingdom of heaven. And chapter 7, verse 21: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. And chapter 25, verses 34, 35, 36: Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat, etc. Rom. 8. v. 13: If you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live. And elsewhere throughout. With these distinctions laid down in advance, the emptiness of the argument by which the Opponent attacks the truth of our position clearly appears. We believe and teach that the opinion and doctrine from which it follows that the study of good works, the duties of piety toward God and of charity toward the neighbour, are in no way, in no manner or respect, necessary for salvation, or which strips faith of the true fruits of piety and is joined with contempt for good works, is false and erroneous. But we deny the assumption of the principal syllogism, and the Opponent will never be able to prove it. That opinion and doctrine, however, which transfers the beginning, middle and end of our justification to faith alone, and acknowledges the necessity of good works, not indeed as meritorious causes but as efficient causes and conditions without which no one can attain eternal life and salvation, has been shown by us in the preceding sections to be most true. And this very doctrine was handed down and confirmed by the Apostles and Prophets, and indeed by Christ himself (as we have sufficiently proved from holy Scripture), and has been sealed with the blood of the most holy martyrs, as is clear from their history.
