S. illuminatione, & renouatione, res spirituales, & quae tum verum Dei cultum, tum vitā, ac salutem aeternam concernunt intelligere: unde etiam causas fidei iustificantis, & resipiscentiae nostrae ac conuersionis, in solum vitae ac salutis aeternae natiuum desiderium, & eiusdem promissionem ac annuntiationem, atque veritatis annuntiatae confirmationem, transcribunt contra Scripturam sacram, quemadmodum ex iis,quæ supra de libero arbitrio,& eiusdem viribus,disseruimus, liquidò constat. Atque hinc est, quod Oslorrodius thesi septima spem vitæ æternæ consequendæ, dicit esse Spiritum illum, cuius virtute ac beneficio cupiditates,ac desideria carnis mortificemus, & ad vitæ integritatem ac sanctimoniam incitetur,vt hac ratione interna illa spiritus sancti renouatio,à causis refipiscentiam in nobis operantibus excludatur : cuiusrei confirmationem ac probationem ab Osiorrodio desidero. Tertiò, quia etiam sanctorum hominum exempla nobis imitanda,in Scripturis sanctis proponūtur: 1.Cor.11.v.1. Imitatores mei estote,sicut ego Christi. 1. Thess.1.v.6. Et vos imitatores nostri facti fuistis,& Domini,recepto sermone cum oppressione multa,cum gaudio Spiritus sancti,adeò vt fueritis exemplaria omnibus credentibus in Macedonia,& Achaia. Phil.3.v.17. Estote simul imitatores mei,Fratres,& eos considerate,qui ita incedunt, sicut habetis nos pro exemplari. Heb.13. Memores estote ducum vestrorum, qui locuti sunt vobis sermonem Dei,quorum imitamini fidem,considerantes, qui fuerit exitus conuersationis ipsorum. Quarto : Si Christus sic nobis vitæ suæ exemplo viam salutis ostendit, vt imitatione eius vitam nostram componentes ad salutem aspiremus,frustrà nobis illa salutis via est ostensa, cum nostra obedientia etiam quum ad summum, in hac vita, gradum peruenerit, longissimè à perfectione Christi absit: Phil. 3.v.12. Nedum vt iam metam apprehenderim, aut iam perfectus sim,sed persequor,experiens an quoque apprehendam, cuius rei causa etiam apprehensus sum à Christo Iesu. Sed hac de re capite sequente pluribus agendum erit. Quintò,quia multi quoque Martyres suo sanguine veritatem cælestem obsignando, Ecclesiæ salutem non parum promouerunt,unde etiam expressè pro Ecclesia , & salute , atque consolatione piorum premi,atque pati dicuntur:2.Cor.1.v.5.6. Sicut abundant perpessiones Christi in nobis: ita per Christum etiam abundat consolatio nostra: sive enim premimur, id fit pro vestra consolatione,ac salute,quæ efficitur in tolerantia earundem perpessionum,quibus & nos afficimur:sive consolationem accipimus, id fit pro vestra consolatione,ac salute : & spes nostra firma est de vobis, quod sciamus vos , sicut socii estis perpessionum , ita etiam i socios fore consolationis. Colos.cap.1. versu 24.Num gaudeo de iis,quæ patior pro vobis , & reliquias afflictionum Christi vicissim expleo in carne mea , pro corpore ipsius , id est , Ecclesia. 2. Timoth. 2. versu 10. Omnia hæc sustineo propter Electos,vt & ipsi salutem consequantur. quantur,quæ est in Christo Iesu cum gloria æterna.Sextò,quia ipsa formulæ ratio redemptionis nostræ in morte, & sanguine Christi, id est, expiatione peccatorum nostrorum per mortem & sanguinem Christi facta,cõsistit,vti paulò post demõstrabimus,ideo ipsa resurrectio Christi nõ ad ipsa redemptionis causam formalem,sed redemptionis & expiationis iam peractæ confirmationem est referenda. Roman. 4.versu 25.Christus traditus est propter lapsus nostros nimirum expiandos,& excitatus est propter iustificationem nostri,videlicet testificandam.1.Cor.15.versu 17.Si Christus non est excitatus,inanis est fides vestra : adhuc estis in peccatis vestris. Ex quibus omnibus denuò apparet hanc actionem , atque functionem , cum priori licet coniunctam, totius officii Christi naturam non complecti, multò minus verò ipsius redemptionis nostræ causam formalem constituere.
units.tr: Although this action of Christ is remarkable, and has very great importance for begetting and nurturing faith and hope in us, yet, even though it is joined with the former, it is solidly demonstrated by the following reasons and arguments that the whole nature and force of the mediatorial office, and the principal fruit of the death and passion of Christ the Saviour [σωτήρος], are not comprehended in it. First, namely, because other actions and functions besides these enumerated are also ascribed to Christ in Holy Scripture, and are assigned to him for carrying out the mediatorial office and for acquiring and communicating life and eternal salvation to us, as we shall show shortly. Second, because these two actions of Christ, namely the proclamation and confirmation of divine truth, are useless and ineffective for begetting faith and repentance in us, unless that inner teacher, the Spirit of Christ, comes, by whose illumination and renewal it finally comes about that we can discern with the eyes of our mind the truth in the doctrine of Christ and the divine power in his works and miracles. For natural man, being in the state of native blindness and under the dominion of sin, cannot perceive spiritual things, even when they are taught, without the spiritual light shining upon him; as we have shown at length in the first chapter, likewise in the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh. And in this very controversy one must carefully note that false hypothesis which our opponents presuppose in their disputations, namely that a man can understand spiritual things, and those that concern both the true worship of God and life and eternal salvation, even without the inner illumination and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Hence they also attribute the causes of justifying faith, of our repentance and conversion, solely to a natural desire for life and eternal salvation, and to its promise and proclamation, and to the confirmation of the truth proclaimed, contrary to Holy Scripture, as is clear from what we set out above concerning free will and its powers. And from this it is that Ostorodius, in his seventh thesis, says that the Spirit, by whose power and benefit we mortify the lusts and desires of the flesh and are stirred to integrity of life and holiness, is that which attains the hope of eternal life; so that by this reasoning the inner renewal of the Holy Spirit is excluded from the causes that work repentance in us. I require Ostorodius to confirm and prove this. Third, because the examples of holy men are also set before us for imitation in Holy Scripture: 1. Cor. 11. v. 1. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. 1. Thess. 1. v. 6. And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Phil. 3. v. 17. Brothers, join in imitating me, and consider those who walk so as you have us as a pattern. Heb. 13. Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you, and considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith. Fourth: If Christ so showed the way of salvation to us by the example of his life, that by imitating him we might shape our lives and aspire to salvation, then that way of salvation has been shown to us in vain, since our obedience, even when it has reached its highest degree in this life, is still very far from the perfection of Christ. Phil. 3. v. 12. Not that I have already obtained it, or am already perfect, but I press on, to see whether I may also lay hold of that for which I was laid hold of by Christ Jesus. But this matter will have to be treated at more length in the following chapter. Fifth, because many martyrs, by sealing heavenly truth with their blood, have greatly advanced the salvation of the Church; hence they are also said expressly to be afflicted and to suffer for the Church, and for the salvation and consolation of the godly: 2. Cor. 1. v. 5, 6. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. If we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effected in the endurance of the same sufferings that we also undergo; and if we receive consolation, it is for your consolation and salvation; and our hope for you is firm, knowing that as you are sharers in the sufferings, so you will also be sharers in the consolation. Col. 1. v. 24. Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for his body, that is, the Church. 2. Tim. 2. v. 10. I endure all things for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. Sixth, because the very manner of our redemption consists in the death and blood of Christ, that is, in the expiation of our sins made through the death and blood of Christ, as we shall show shortly; therefore the resurrection of Christ is to be referred not to the formal cause of redemption itself, but to the confirmation of the redemption and expiation already accomplished. Rom. 4. v. 25. Christ was delivered up for our trespasses, namely to be expiated, and was raised for our justification, namely to be attested. 1. Cor. 15. v. 17. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. From all these things it appears again that this action and function, although it is joined with the former, does not embrace the whole nature of Christ's office, much less does it constitute the formal cause of our redemption itself.

units.la: Tertia actio & functio,quæ Christo Mediatori in sacris scripturis tribuitur,pertinet ad officium ipsius Regium, quatenus videl. ipse accepta à Patre plenissima potestate in cœlo,& in terra,nobis credentibus in illo nouissimo die daturus est vitam æternam, & abolita morte omnibúsque hostibus sibi subiectis nos ab omni miseria liberatos in societatē cœlestis gloriæ adducturus est.Mat. 28. v.18.Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo,& in terra.Ephef.1. versu 20. 21.Efficacitatem roboris sui exeruit Deus in Christo, cum excitauit eum ex mortuis,& collocauit ad dextram suam in cœlis , longè supra omne imperium , ac potestatem , & potentiam, & dominium , & omne nomen , quod nominatur non solum in hoc seculo , verùm etiam in futuro: & omnia subiecit eius pedibus,eúmque constituit caput super omnia ipsi Ecclesiæ.quæ est corpus ipsius,& complementum eius , qui omnia implet in omnibus. Philip.2. versu 9.10. Quapropter etiam Deus ipsum in summam extulit sublimitatem , ac donauit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen , vt ad nomen Iesu omne genu se flectat , cœlestium, terrestrium , ac subterraneorum. Ioh.10.v.27.28.29.Oues mea vocem meam audiunt,& ego eas agnosco , & sequuntur me , & ego vitam æternam do eis,nec peribunt in æternum,neque rapiet eas quisquam è manu mea. Pater meus qui eas mihi dedit maior est omnibus , neque quisquam potest eas rapere è manu Patrũ mei. Iohan.17.versu 1.2.Pater venit hora illa,glorifica Filium tuum,vt & Filius tuus te glorificet , sicut dedisti ei autoritatem in omnem carnem , vt quotquot dedisti ei , det eis vitam æternam : 1. Corinth. 15. versu 25. 26. 27. Nam oportet eum regnare vsque quo omnes inimicos subiecerit pedibus eius, vltimus autem hostis aboletur mors, nam omnia subiecit sub pedes eius : quum autem dicit omnia esse subiecta, palam est hoc dici excepto eo qui subiecit ei omnia. Philipp.3.ver.21. E cælis Seruatorem expectamus Dominum Iesum Christum, qui transformabit corpus nostrum humile, vt conforme fiat corpori suo glorioso, pro efficacitate, qua potest etiam sibi subiicere omnia. Hebr.capite secundo,versu 8. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius : enimuero per hoc quod subiecit ei omnia, nihil omisit, quod non sit ei subiectum : at nunc nondum videmus ei subiecta esse omnia. Sed Iesum illum cernimus gloria & honore esse coronatum, qui paulisper fuit Angelis inferior factus propter mortis perpessionem, vt beneficio Dei mortem pro omnibus gustaret.
units.tr: The third action and function that the holy Scriptures ascribe to Christ the Mediator belongs to his kingly office, insofar as he, having received from the Father the fullest power in heaven and on earth, will give eternal life on the last day to us who believe in him, and, death having been abolished and all enemies made subject to him, will lead us, freed from every misery, into the fellowship of heavenly glory. Matt. 28.18: All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Eph. 1.20–21: God wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come; and hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all. Phil. 2.9–10: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth. John 10.27–29: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand. John 17.1–2: Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee: as thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him. 1 Cor. 15.25–27: For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death. For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he saith all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excepted, which did put all things under him. Phil. 3.21: We look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself. Heb. 2.8–9: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man.

units.la: Verùm ne hanc quoque actionem, cum prioribus duabus licet cõiunctam, integrum illud Christi Mediatoris nostri officium exprimere, ex eo liquet manifestissime, tum quia in Scripturis S. ipsi adhuc aliæ tribuuntur actiones & functiones ad exequendum munus illud mediatorium, & ad salutem ac vitam æternam nobis acquirendam & communicandā necessariæ, quemadmodum paulo post demonstrabimus : tum deinde, quia ad Mediatoris nostri officium pertinet, nō tantùm vitam ac salutem æternam nomine Patris nobis conferre atque largiri, verùm etiam eandem salutem nobis impetrare ac promereri: vt in sequentibus probabitur.
units.tr: But that this action too, although it is joined with the two previous ones, does not express the whole of that office of Christ our Mediator, is most clearly evident. First, because the holy Scriptures ascribe to him still other actions and functions, necessary for carrying out that mediatorial office and for acquiring and communicating salvation and eternal life to us, as we shall show a little later. Second, because it belongs to the office of our Mediator not only to confer and bestow eternal life and salvation on us in the name of the Father, but also to obtain and merit that same salvation for us, as will be proved in what follows.

units.la: Restant igitur duæ actiones atque functiones Sacerdotales aliæ, in quibus ipsa Sacerdotii Christi ratio proprie consistit, nimirum peccatorum nostrorum per satisfactionem expiatio, & pro nobis apud Deum intercessio : de quibus duabus actionibus iam sigillatim & ordine nobis erit agendum.
units.tr: There remain, therefore, two other priestly actions and functions, in which the very nature of Christ's priesthood properly consists: namely, the expiation of our sins through satisfaction, and intercession on our behalf before God. We must now treat of these two actions separately and in order.

units.la: Quantum igitur ad priorem actionem, nimirum expiationem peccatorum nostrorum concernit, quæ propriam atque principalem seruandi rationem in se complectitur, qua videlicet Iesus Christus vitam atque salutem æternam, nobis acquisiuit, & pepe-rit, illam dicimus esse Meritum, & satisfactionem Christi, qua videlicet ille vt sanctus Pontifex, & sancta victima per mortem ac passionem, pro peccatis nostris iusto Dei iudicio satisfecit & pœnas nobis ob peccata nostra debitas in se vt sponsorem nostrum deriuauit, & sic amissam Dei gratiam, & vitæ æternæ præmium nobis peperit, & promeritus est : Atque hanc ipsam sententiam, & doctrinâ nostrâ luculentis & grauibus rationibus argumentis, ex ipsa Scriptura desumptis, demonstrabimus.
units.tr: As for the former action, namely the expiation of our sins, which contains within itself the proper and principal manner of saving us, by which Jesus Christ obtained and procured for us life and eternal salvation, we call this the merit and satisfaction of Christ. By it he, as the holy High Priest and holy victim, through death and passion, made satisfaction for our sins by the just judgment of God, and in his capacity as our surety took upon himself the punishments due to us for our sins, and so won for us and merited the forfeited grace of God and the reward of eternal life. This very doctrine we shall demonstrate from Scripture itself, by clear and weighty arguments.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum primum desumitur ex illis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis, in quibus Christus in se iustus, & innocens. (1. Pet. 1. v. 19. redempti estis pretiosò sanguine agni immaculati & incontaminati Christi: & 2. v. 22. Qui peccatum non fecit, nec inuentus est dolus in ore eius) dicitur portasse iniquitates nostras, dolores nostros baiulasse, & propter illas vulneratus, afflictus, assus, execratio factus, denique mortuus esse: item in quibus castigatio pacis nostræ ipsi imposita, & iniquitates omnium nostrum in ipsum coniectæ, & similia perhibentur. Es. 53 v. 4.5.6.7. Verum tamen morbos nostros ipse pertulit, & dolores ipsos nostros baiulauit, quamuis non æstimemus plaga affectum eum, percussum à Deo & afflictum. Nam ipse dolore afficitur à defectionibus nostris, aduritur ab iniquitatibus nostris, castigatio pacis nostræ imponitur ei, & pumice eius fit curatio nobis. Iehouah coiecit in ipsum iniquitates omnium nostrum: Exigitur pœna, & ipse affligitur, neq; aperit os suum, vt parua pecus ad mactationem ducitur, & velut ouis coram tonsoribus suis obmutescens, neque aperit os suum: Et v. 10. 11. 12. At Iehouah delectatus conterere ipsum, morbo affecit quandoquidem seipsum exponebat sacrificium pro reatu, videbit semen, prolongabit dies, & delectatio Iehouæ per eum prosperabitur: Exemptum molestia seipsum videns satiabitur, cognitione sui iustificabit seruus meus iustus multos, quoniam iniquitates ipse baiulauerit. Idcirco partem dabo ei pro multis, vt cum robustis partiatur prædam, pro eo quod profundit in mortem seipsum, & cum defectoribus annumeratus est: nam ipse peccatum multorum perferens pro defectoribus intercessit. Sic 1. Pet. 2. v. 24. Qui peccata nostra ipsemet sustulit in corpore suo super lignum, vt peccatis mortui iustitiæ viueremus, cuius vibicibus sanati estis. Nam eratis velut oues errantes, sed conuersi nunc estis ad pastorem illum, & curatorem animarum vestrarum. Gal. 3. v. 13. Christus nos redemit ab execratione Legis dum pro nobis factus est execratio. Psal. 69. v. 5. reddidit quod non rapuit. Heb. 2. v. 9. Sed Iesum illum cernimus, gloria, & honore coronatum, qui paulo inferior erat Angelis factus, propter mortis perpessionem, vt beneficio Dei, pro omnibus mortem gustaret. Ioh. 10. versu 15. Ego animam meam pono pro ouibus. Et Iohan. 6. versu 51. Panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita. Rom. 4. versu 25. Christus traditus est propter lapsus nostros, & excitatus propter iustificationem nostri. 1. Corinth. 15. versu 3. tradidi vobis in primis quod & accepi, Christum vidclicet mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris secundum Scripturas.
units.tr: Our first argument is drawn from those testimonies of holy Scripture in which Christ, who was righteous and innocent in himself (1 Pet. 1.19: ye were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot; and 1 Pet. 2.22: who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth), is said to have borne our iniquities, carried our sorrows, and, wounded, afflicted, crushed, and made a curse on account of them, finally to have died; likewise those passages in which the chastisement of our peace was laid upon him, the iniquities of us all were laid upon him, and similar things are asserted. Isa. 53.4–7: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows; yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. Jehovah hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. Isa. 53.10–12: Yet it pleased Jehovah to bruise him; he hath put him to grief; when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Jehovah shall prosper in his hand. He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death, and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. So 1 Pet. 2.24: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls. Gal. 3.13: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. Ps. 69.4: I restored that which I took not away. Heb. 2.9: But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man. John 10.15: I lay down my life for the sheep. John 6.51: The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. Rom. 4.25: Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. 1 Cor. 15.3: For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures.

units.la: Argumentum tale est;
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Qui ipse innocens ac iustus per se morbos nostros ac dolores peccatorum nostrorum poenas pertulit,ac baiulauit,qui propter defectiones & iniquitates nostras à Deo plaga & dolore affectus,attritus,afflictus,& percussus est,in quem coniiciuntur iniquitates omnium nostrum , cui imponitur castigatio pacis nostrae,cuius tumice fit curatio nobis,qui peccata multorum pertulit , qui seipsum exposuit sacrificium pro reatu, qui pro nobis factus est execratio , & reddidit quod non rapuit,denique qui cum defectoribus annumeratus , pro nobis passus atque mortuus est : ille pro iis, id est, eorum loco,pro quibus illa omnia sustinuit , poenas subiit, & in se vt sponsorem ipsorum deriuauit : ac proinde ipsorū Seruator est,non tantum fidem , id est,resipiscentiam in illis operando,& vitā æternam ipsis communicando , sed etiam peecata ipsorum expiando,id est, pro illis satisfaciendo:
units.tr: He who was himself innocent and righteous bore our diseases and sorrows, and carried the punishments of our sins. He was struck, afflicted, bruised and smitten by God because of our transgressions and iniquities. The iniquities of us all were laid upon him, the chastisement of our peace was placed on him, and by his stripes we are healed. He bore the sins of many, and he offered himself as a sacrifice for guilt. He was made a curse for us, he restored what he had not taken, and finally he was numbered with the transgressors and suffered and died for us. He underwent punishment in place of those for whom he endured all these things, that is, in their stead, and he took them over into himself as their surety. Therefore he is their Saviour, not only by working repentance [resipiscentia] in them and by communicating eternal life to them, but also by expiating their sins, that is, by making satisfaction for them.

units.la: Atqui Iesus Christus morbos nostros , ac dolores , peccatorum nostrorum poenas pertulit, ac baiulauit : ille propter defectiones & iniquitates nostras à Deo plaga & dolore affectus,attritus,afflictus,& percussus est,in ipsum coniectæ sunt iniquitates omnium nostrum , ipsi imposita est , eius tumice fit curatio nobis, ille peccata nostra pertulit , & pro reatu illorum sacrificium se exposuit , ille pro nobis factus execratio reddidit quod non rapuit,denique pro nobis passus atque mortuus est.
units.tr: But Jesus Christ bore our diseases and sorrows, and carried the punishments of our sins. He was struck, afflicted, bruised and smitten by God because of our transgressions and iniquities. The iniquities of us all were laid upon him and placed on him, and by his stripes we are healed. He bore our sins and offered himself as a sacrifice for their guilt. He was made a curse for us, he restored what he had not taken, and finally he suffered and died for us.

units.la: Ergo Iesus Christus pro nobis & loco nostro poenas nobis ob peccata nostra debitas subiit , & in se,vt sponsorem nostrum deriuauit , ac proinde seruator noster est , non tantum quia resipiscentiam doctrina, innocentia vitæ,miraculis,passione, morte , & resurrectione , in nobis operatur, verùm etiam & quidē præcipuè,quia morte & passione sua peccata nostra expiauit,ac Deo pro illis satisfecit,& consequēter ideò potissimū etiam in hunc mundum venit,& à Deo patre missus est.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus Christ underwent, for us and in our place, the punishments due to us for our sins, and he took them over into himself as our surety. Therefore he is our Saviour, not merely because by his teaching, the innocence of his life, his miracles, his passion, death and resurrection he works repentance in us, but chiefly and above all because by his death and passion he expiated our sins and made satisfaction to God for them. Consequently, for this reason above all, he also came into this world and was sent by God the Father.

units.la: Assumptio habetur in citatis Scripturæ sacræ testimouiis : maioris verò propositionis veritas necessaria rationib. euidentissimis demondemonstratur. Quum enim portare iniquitates alicuius, nihil aliud sit, quàm poenas quæ peccato illius debebantur luere ac persoluere, quemadmodum ex illa contentione Israelitarum cum Deo, & Dei ipsius responso, manifestè liquet: Lam.5.v.7. Patres nostri peccarunt & non sunt, nos iniquitatem eorum portauimus, id est, propter peccata & flagitia ab ipsis patrata punimur. Ezech. 18.verf.20. Anima quæ peccauerit ipsa morietur: Filius non portabit iniquitatem Patris, neque Pater portabit iniquitatem filii: iustitia iusti super eum erit, & impietas impii super eum erit, td est, Filius non multabitur propter delicta Patris, neque pater propter peccata filii, sed anima, id est, homo ipse qui peccauit morietur: ideò necessario sequitur, eum qui peccata electorum ac fidelium tulit, in se, à Deo peccati vindice, coniecta, poenas ipsis ob peccata debitas persoluisse: & eum, qui peccata nostra sponte in se recepit, poenas nobis ob peccata debitas in se vt sponsore nostrum deriuasse. Quicunque deinde per se planè innocens, & iustus est, ita vt non tantum perfectissimam obedientiam lege requisitam citra omnem transgressionem, verùm etiam aliquid amplius quàm ipsa lex à nobis desideret & exigat, præstitit, ille non potest definito Dei consilio, & iusto eius iudicio, mortis præsertim tam crudelis ac ignominiosæ, qualem ipse Christus subiit, supplicio & maledictioni atque execrationi legis subiici, imò à Deo ipso conteri, affligi, & percuti, nisi aliena peccata, tanquam reus & sponsor expianda in se suscepepit: tum quia mors & quicquid mortis nomine in sacris Scripturis appellatur, solius peccati stipendium, & poena est, atque peccato, ex ordine iustitiæ, & veritate comminationis diuinæ debetur, quemadmodum capite vigesimo septimo fuse à nobis est demonstratum: tum etiam quia perfectissimæ obedientiæ, & operum iustitiæ, ex infallibili & constantissima veritate promissionis diuinæ, Fac hoc & vives. Luc.10.verf.28. Contrarium mortis, id est, vitæ ac felicitatis tā corporalis, quā spiritualis, præmiū est destinatū. Quæ promissio hactenus etiam in Angelis bonis & sanctis valuit, qui cū origine suâ seruates in veritate perstiterint, Deus nullū eorū hactenus morti vel destructioni mortis analogiā habeti, aut passioni alicui destructionē subiecit. Cū igitur agnus ille immaculatus, nēp e Christus qui peccatū nō fecit, & in cuius ore dolus inuentus nō est, & qui totā legē citra omnē transgressionem exactissimè præstitit, peccata tamē & delicta nostra baiulauerit, & propter illas à Deo plaga, & dolore affectus, attritus afflictus, & percussus, denique καταρὰ pro nobis factus, crudelissimæ & ignominiosissimæ mortis supplicium subiecit, quis non videt ipsum poenas peccatis nostris debitas persoluisse, ac in se vt vadem, & iponsorem nostrum derinasse, & illa omnia propter peccata nostra ipsi imputata, passum esse? Peccata enim nostra non nisi imputata ipsi tum execrationis quam sustinuit, tum mortis quam subiit, ei causa fuerunt, quemadmodum ipsum Adami delictum nonnisi per imputationem nostrum factum, nobis mortis, maledictionis & corruptionis natiua causa extitit. Neque hoc etiam insidit consequetiæ nostræ neruum, quod Matthæus cap. 8. v. 16 17. (Quum autem serum diei esset, obtulerunt ei demoniacos multos inquiens, & eiecit spiritus verbo, omnesque male affectos sanauit: vt impleretur quod dictum est per Esaiam Prophetam dicentem, ipse invaletudines nostras accepit & morbos portauit. ) illud vaticinium Esaiæ ad morborum corporalium sanationem citat & accommodat. Quum enim certissimum sit, Esaiam capite illo quinquagesimo tertio non de miraculis, sed morte Christi, nec de corporalibus beneficiis, sed de spirituali, & æterna gratia, per mortem Christi nobis parta differere, quemadmodum ex eo liquet manifestissime, quod ipse se pro peccatis sacrificium exposuisse, & in morte profudisse, atque cognitione sui multos iustificaturus esse dicitur, quorum iniquitatum in ipsum coniectarum etiam morbi illi corporis effectus, atque fructus extiterunt, & cuius spiritualis gratiæ ac sanationis animæ, symbolum fuit illa morborum curatio, inde manifeste apparet, Euangelistam ad effectum, eumque ex multis vnum, & ad symbolum transferre, quod causæ communis est, & rei ipsi, ac veritati conuenit. Nam id propter quod Christus plaga & dolore affectus, attritus & percussus, denique mortuus & καταρὰ factus est, illud ipsum est quod ille baiulauit, ac sustulit: Atque non corporales morbi, sed ipsa animarum nostrarum vulnera, id est, peccata fuerunt id, propter quod Christus plaga, & dolore affectus, attritus, percussus, denique mortuus, & καταρὰ factus est, ac poenas nobis debitas persoluit, & persoluendo à nobis sustulit: Ergo non corporales illi morbi, sed animarum nostrarum vulnera id ipsum sunt, quod Christus baiulauit ac sustulit.
units.tr: The minor premise is established by the testimonies of Holy Scripture cited above. The truth of the major premise is shown by the most evident reasons. For to bear another's iniquities is nothing other than to pay and discharge the penalties which were due to that person's sin, as is plain from that complaint of the Israelites against God and from God's own answer: Lam.5.v.7. "Our fathers sinned, and are not; we have borne their iniquities," that is, we are punished for the sins and crimes committed by them. Ezech. 18.verf.20. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him," that is, the son shall not be punished for the offences of the father, nor the father for the sins of the son, but the soul, that is, the man himself who sinned, shall die. It therefore necessarily follows that he who bore the sins of the elect and of believers, having had them laid upon him by God, the avenger of sin, paid to them the punishments due to them for their sins; and that he who of his own accord took our sins upon himself, as our surety, took over into himself the punishments due to us for our sins. Furthermore, whoever is plainly innocent and righteous in himself, so that he has rendered not only the most perfect obedience required by the law, without any transgression, but also something more than the law itself demands and exacts from us, cannot, by the fixed counsel of God and his just judgment, be subjected to the penalty, curse and execration of the law, least of all to a death so cruel and ignominious as that which Christ himself underwent, nor be bruised, afflicted and smitten by God himself, unless he took upon himself, as a guilty party and surety, the sins of others to be expiated. This is so, first, because death, and whatever is called death in the Holy Scriptures, is the wage and penalty of sin alone, and is owed to sin by the order of justice and by the truth of the divine threatening, as we demonstrated at length in chapter twenty-seven. Second, because for the most perfect obedience and the works of righteousness, by the infallible and unchanging truth of the divine promise, Fac hoc, and thou shalt live. Luke 10. v. 28. the opposite of death, that is, life and happiness both bodily and spiritual, is appointed as the reward. This promise has hitherto also held good for the good and holy angels, who, having persisted in the truth from their origin, God has hitherto never subjected to death, or to any analogue of death, or to any destruction through suffering. Since, therefore, that spotless Lamb, namely Christ, who did no sin, in whose mouth no guile was found, and who fulfilled the whole law most exactly without any transgression, nevertheless bore our sins and transgressions, and because of them was struck, afflicted, bruised and smitten by God, and finally was made a curse [κατάρα] for us and underwent the punishment of a most cruel and ignominious death, who does not see that he paid the penalties due to our sins, took them over into himself as our surety and bondsman, and suffered all these things, which were imputed to him on account of our sins? For our sins were the cause of his suffering the curse he endured and the death he underwent only by way of imputation, just as Adam's offence became the natural cause of death, curse and corruption for us only by the imputation of his act to us. Nor does the sinew of our argument fail in this, that Matthew, ch. 8, vv. 16–17 (When the even was come, they brought unto him many that were possessed with devils: and he cast out the spirits with his word, and healed all that were sick: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses) quotes and applies that prophecy of Isaiah to the healing of bodily diseases. For since it is quite certain that Isaiah in that fifty-third chapter treats not of miracles but of the death of Christ, and not of bodily benefits but of the spiritual and eternal grace obtained for us through Christ's death, as is very clearly evident from the fact that he is said to have offered himself as a sacrifice for sins, to have poured out his soul in death, and that by the knowledge of himself he would justify many, of whose iniquities laid upon him those bodily ills were also the effects and fruits; and since that healing of diseases was a sign [symbolum] of spiritual grace and of the healing of the soul, it plainly appears that the Evangelist transfers the prophecy from the effect, and one of many effects, to the sign, which is common to the cause and belongs to the thing itself and to the truth. For that on account of which Christ was struck, afflicted, bruised, and finally died and was made a curse, is precisely what he bore and took away. But it was not bodily diseases, but the very wounds of our souls, that is, our sins, on account of which Christ was struck, afflicted, bruised, and finally died and was made a curse, and paid the penalties due to us, and by paying them took them away from us. Therefore it is not those bodily diseases, but the wounds of our souls, which are the very thing that Christ bore and took away.

units.la: OSTORRODIVS instituionum suarum capite vigesimo septimo, sectione sexta, ad primi huius argumenti nostri partem exci-
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in the twenty-seventh chapter of his Institutes, section six, takes up the first part of this argument of ours, and says:

units.la: tem excipit, ac dicit : [Quum Scriptura sacra Christum pro nobis mortuum esse testatur, non significari, quasi Christus vice & loco nostro mortem obiisset: quandoquidem etiam cum pro peccatis nostris mortuus esse dicitur, non peccatorum nostrorum loco & vice mortuus esse intelligendus sit: imò nos ipsos, modò regni ipsius participes esse velimus, exemplo Christi, ad mortem paratos esse oporteat: sed quod ille causa nostri, horrendam atque crudelem illam mortem subierit, quemadmodum etiam cum pro peccatis nostris mortuus esse dicitur, nihil aliud significatur, quàm ipsum propter peccata nostra mortem oppetiisse. Hoc est Christum ideo pro nobis mortuum esse perhiberi, quia videlicet (vt Aduersarius sectione vt & thesi quinta eiusdem capitis explicat,) mors Christi nobis remissionem peccatorum, quam Deus nobis primò omnium per Christum, & quidem in æternum promisit, confirmauerit, (unde etiam sanguis Christi, noui & æterni fœderis sanguis appellatur: Matth.26.v.28.) & Christus nonnisi per illam ad resurrectionem, & illustrem ipsius potentiam, atque gloriam peruenire poterit, quandoquidem ipsum pati, & ita in gloriam introire oportuit, vt ipse testatur Luc.24.v.20.]
units.tr: "Although Holy Scripture testifies that Christ died for us, this does not mean that Christ died in our place and stead, since even when he is said to have died for our sins, he is not to be understood as having died in the place and stead of our sins. Rather, if we wish to be partakers of his kingdom, we ought to be ready for death after Christ's example. What it means is that he underwent that horrible and cruel death for our sake, just as when he is said to have died for our sins, nothing else is signified than that he met death because of our sins. That is, Christ is said to have died for us because, as the opponent explains in section five and thesis five of the same chapter, his death confirmed for us the forgiveness of sins, which God first of all promised us through Christ, and promised for ever (whence also the blood of Christ is called the blood of the new and eternal covenant: Matt. 26. v. 28.). Christ could attain to the resurrection and to the glorious display of his power and majesty only through that death, since it was necessary that he suffer and so enter into glory, as he himself testifies in Luke 24. v. 20."

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument is this:

units.la: Si Christus etiam pro peccatis nostris mortuus est, & tamen eo ipso non significatur, ipsum vice vel loco peccatorum nostrorum mortuum esse, & nos omnes exemplo Christi, ad mortem paratos esse oporteat: tum ex eo quod Christus pro nobis mortuus esse perhibetur, non sequitur ipsum vice & loco nostro mortuum esse.
units.tr: "If Christ also died for our sins, and yet by that very fact it is not signified that he died in the stead or place of our sins, and that all of us ought to be ready for death after Christ's example; then from the fact that Christ is said to have died for us, it does not follow that he died in our place and stead."

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: "But the first is true; therefore so is the second."

units.la: Resp. Christum etiam morte & passione sua promissiones per ipsum factas nobis obsignasse & confirmasse, lubeti animo fatemur: sed negamus hanc ipsam obsignationem & confirmationem præcipuam, aut solam causam mortis Christi, aut effectum, atque fructu præcipuum extitisse, quemadmodum nos tum ipso argumento nostro, tum confirmatione eius demonstrauimus, & à positione effecti vnius, ad remotionem fructuum, & effectorum aliorum, ex eadem causa existentium, nonnisi falsa nectitur consequentia. Ad argumentum Aduersarii vero quod attinet, dico connexum esse falsum. Quum enim duabus illis phrasibus pro aliquo mori & Mmm pro peccatis alicuius mori:diuersum quid significetur,atque diuersĕ indicentur causæ,quas confundit Ostorrodius,ideò à significatio-ne vnius ad significationem alterius,tanquam æquipollentem,nō datur consequentia. Vt enim peccatū ipsum nec moritur nec pœ-nas luit, sed causa impellens ac meritoria est ob quam peccator morte,aliisque pœnis plectitur: ita etiam qui moritur pro pecca-to alicuius,non moritur vice aut loco peccati. sed propter pecca-tum , vel à se, vel ab alio commissum , sibique tanquam sponsori imputatum. Quia vero peccatori ex ordine iustitiæ, & veritate comminationis diuinæ,mortis supplicium incumbit,ideò qui pro eiusmodi homine moritur, eius vice & loco moritur, pœnásque alteri debitas morte sua persoluit. Christus igitur cum mortuus dicitur pro peccatis nostris, causa impulsiua mortis, nempe pec-catorum nostrorum imputatio, sine qua peccata nostra ipsi mor-tis causa existere non potuerunt, denotatur & ille pro peccatis nostris non redimendis, sed expiandis, tollendis, atque delendis, vel propter peccata nostra quemadmodum alibi loquitur Apo-stolus, nempe Rom. 4.v.25.vbi Christum traditum in mortem pro-pter offensas nostras esse inquit , mortem oppetiisse, intelligitur. Quum vero Christus pro nobis mortuus esse perhibetur, intelli-gitur causa finalis, & in hac ipsa peccatorum expiatio, vel satis-factio,& sensus est,Christum pro nobis redimendis, id est, loco nostro mortuum esse, dum videlicet mortem pro nobis subiit, & ceu victima piacularis peccata nostra expiauit , sicuti pro nobis e-tiam factus peccatum dicitur. 2. Cor. 5.v.21. non poterat autem vi-ctima expiatoria esse , nisi & peccatum & pœnam eius in se reci-peret: vnde etiam ita pro omnibus mortuus esse perhibetur, vt nos videlicet propter mortem ipsius , quam loco nostro subiit, omnes mortui esse censeamur. 2.Cor.5. v.15. Quod vero Ostorro-dius dicit, Oportere etiam nos ad mortem exemplo Christi paratos esse, causam ipsius non iuuat, quum non ideò moriamur vt peccata nostra morte expiemus, sed vt per illam , virtute mortis Christi immutatam,veluti portam exuto hoc mortali, & tot infirmitati-bus obnoxio, corpore, in æternam animarum requiem ingredia-mur,qua de re iam capite vigesimo septimo aliquid egimus.
units.tr: Reply. We willingly admit that Christ, by his death and suffering, also sealed and confirmed the promises made through him. But we deny that this sealing and confirmation was either the chief or the only cause of Christ's death, or its chief effect and fruit, as we have shown both in our own argument and in its confirmation. From the positing of one effect, the inference to the exclusion of other fruits and effects arising from the same cause is only a false consequence. As for the opponent's argument, I say that its connection is false. For those two phrases, "to die for someone" and "to die for someone's sins", signify different things and indicate different causes, which Ostorrodius confuses. Therefore no inference can be drawn from the meaning of the one to the meaning of the other as if they were equivalent. Sin itself neither dies nor pays penalties; it is the impelling and meritorious cause on account of which the sinner is punished with death and other penalties. So too, one who dies for another's sin does not die in the place or stead of the sin, but because of a sin committed either by himself or by another and imputed to him as surety. Since, however, the penalty of death falls upon the sinner by the order of justice and the truth of the divine threat, whoever dies for such a man dies in his place and stead, and by his death pays the penalty owed to another. Therefore when Christ is said to have died for our sins, the impelling cause of his death is signified, namely the imputation of our sins, without which our sins could not have been the cause of death for him. It is understood that he died because of our sins, as the Apostle says elsewhere, Rom. 4. v. 25, where he says that Christ was delivered up to death because of our offences. But when Christ is said to have died for us, the final cause is understood, and in this the expiation or satisfaction of sins is involved. The sense is that Christ died for our redemption, that is, in our place, since he underwent death for us and, as a propitiatory victim, expiated our sins, just as he is said to have been made sin for us, 2 Cor. 5. v. 21. But he could not be an expiatory victim unless he took upon himself both our sin and its penalty. Hence he is also said to have died for all in such a way that, through his death, which he underwent in our place, we are reckoned to have all died: 2 Cor. 5. v. 15. As for what Ostorrodius says, that we too ought to be ready for death after Christ's example, this does not help his cause. We do not die in order to expiate our sins by our death, but so that through it, by the power of Christ's death, we may pass, as through a gate, out of this mortal body, which is subject to so many infirmities, into the eternal rest of our souls. We have already said something about this matter in the twenty-seventh chapter.

units.la: Argumentum secundum ad confirmandam veritatem sententiæ nostræ desumitur ex illis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis, quæ docent Christū esse summum nostrum sacerdotē, eundémque cum legali
units.tr: Second argument to confirm the truth of our position is drawn from those testimonies of Holy Scripture which teach that Christ is our supreme priest, and compare him with the legal high priest

units.la: Pontifice conferunt, & testantur morte ac sanguine ipsius, nostra peccata expiari, purgari, emundari, & ablui, ac proinde Christum tanquam victimam cum sacrificiis expiatoriis conferre solent, quemadmodum enim Pontifex legalis, populi sui peccata typicè expiabat,& pro ipso orabat,vt legimus Leu. capitib. 4.5.6.9.10.Sic Christus summus noster Sacerdos purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum facta intercedit pro nobis in coelo. Hebr.1.v. 3. Qui purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum facta sedit ad dextram maiestatis illius excelsissimæ : Rom.8.v.34. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est,qui mortuus est,imo vero qui etiã excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis, Heb.2.v.17. Vnde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri,vt misericors esset & fidelis Pontifex in iis quæ apud Deum agenda forent,ad expiandum peccata populi. Hebr.4.verf.14.15. Habentes igitur Pontificem magnum, qui penetrauit coelos Iesum Filium Dei teneamus hanc professionem. Non enim habemus Pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum in omnibus similiter absque peccato. & capite quinto,v.1. Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumitur, & pro hominibus constituitur in iis quæ apud Deum agenda sunt,vt offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis : & 7.v.24.25. At ille quod in æternum manet, perpetuum habet Sacerdotium, unde & seruare prorsus potest eos,qui per ipsum ad Deum accedunt.& v 27. Cui nō sit quotidie necesse,quèadmodum illis Pōtificib. prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi,id enim fecit semel,quū semetipsum obtulit,Eph.5.v.2.Versamini cū charitate,sicut & Christus dilexit nos & tradidit semetipsū pro nobis, oblatione ac victimã Deo in odore bonæ fragrātiæ:Et quèadmodū secūdū legē omnia sanguine vi ĉtimarū mūdabātur. Heb.9. v.22. etsi peccata nō reipsa isto sangui- ne expiarentur,Heb.10.v.4.Non enim potest sanguis taurorum & hircorū auferre peccata:ita Christi sanguis reuera expiat omniū credētiū peccata. 1.Io.1.v.7.Sāguis Iesu Christi Filÿ eius purgat nos ab omni peccato,& 2.vers.2.Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solùm ,sed etiam totius mundi : & 4.v.10. In hoc est charitas,non quod nos dilexerimus Deū,sed quod ipse dilexerit nos & miserit Filiū suum, vt esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Apocalyps.capite 1. versu 5.Iesus Christus est fidus ille testis, primogenitus ille ex mortuis,ac princeps regū terra,qui dilexit nos & lauit nos a peccatis nostris per sanguinem suum: quatenus videlicet ille ad remissionem peccatorum effusus est. Matth. 26. 28. Hoc est sanguis meus novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum: vel quatenus seipsum immaculatum obtulit Deo Patri. Hebr. 9. v. 14. Galat. 2. v. 20. Vivo autem non amplius ego, sed vivit in me Christus, & vitam, quam nunc vivo in carne, vivo per fidem Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. 1. Petr. 1. v. 19. Redempti estis pretioso sanguine, utpote agni immaculati & incontaminati, Christi. Atque ita est agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi, Ioh. 1. v. 29. Atque ita nos Deo reconciliavit, tollens id, quod Deum a nobis alienavit & separavit. Esa. 59. ver. 2. Iniquitates vestrae dividerunt inter vos, & Deum vestrum, & peccata vestra faciunt, ut occultet faciem a vobis, ne exaudiat. Rom. 5. v. 10. Nam si quum inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii eius, multo magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam illius. Unde etiam ἱλαστήριον sive ἱλασμὸς appellatur: Rom. 3. v. 25. Quem proposuit Deus placamentum (ἱλαστήριον) per fidem in sanguine ipsius. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 2. Ipse est propitiatio (ἱλασμὸς) pro peccatis nostris.
units.tr: They also testify that by his death and blood our sins are expiated, purged, cleansed and washed away. For this reason they usually compare Christ with the expiatory sacrifices. Just as the legal high priest typically expiated the sins of his people and prayed for them, as we read in Leviticus chapters 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10, so Christ our supreme Priest, by the purging of our sins accomplished through himself, intercedes for us in heaven. Heb. 1. v. 3. Who, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high. Rom. 8. v. 34. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Heb. 2. v. 17. Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. Heb. 4. v. 14, 15. Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. And in chapter 5, verse 1: Every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. And chapter 7, verses 24 and 25: But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him. And verse 27: Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself. Eph. 5. v. 2: Walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour. And just as according to the law all things were cleansed with the blood of victims (Heb. 9. v. 22), so, even if sins were not really expiated by this blood, for it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins (Heb. 10. v. 4), nevertheless the blood of Christ truly expiates the sins of all believers. 1 John 1. v. 7: The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. And chapter 2, verse 2: And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. And chapter 4, verse 10: Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Revelation chapter 1, verse 5: Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood. That is, insofar as he was poured out for the remission of sins. Matt. 26. 28: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Or insofar as he offered himself without blemish to God the Father. Heb. 9. v. 14. Gal. 2. v. 20: I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. 1 Pet. 1. v. 19: But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. And thus he is the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world (John 1. v. 29). And thus he reconciled us to God, taking away what had alienated and separated God from us. Isa. 59. v. 2: But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear. Rom. 5. v. 10: For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. Hence he is also called [hilastērion] or [hilasmos]: Rom. 3. v. 25: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation [hilastērion] through faith in his blood. 1 John 2. v. 2: He is the propitiation [hilasmos] for our sins.

units.la: Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: The argument runs thus:

units.la: Qui verus, summus, misericors, fidelis, magnus, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus, & sublimior caelis factus est Pontifex, sic ut non sit ipsi quotidie necesse, quemadmodum Pontificibus legalibus, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre: & tamen postquam ex hominibus assumptus, & pro hominibus constitutus est in iis, quae apud Deum agenda sunt, affectus etiam est sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, & tentatus in omnibus similiter absque peccato, & per Spiritum aeternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, oblationem & victimam in odorem bonae fragrantiae, ad expiandum apud Deum peccata populi, & agnus ille Dei est immaculatus & incontaminatus, qui sublatis peccatis nostris, quae Deu a nobis alienarunt, & benignam eius faciem auerterunt a nobis, pretioso suo sanguine in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum sic effuso, ut sit pro illis ἱλασμὸς, & propitiatio, qui nos purgat ac lavat ab omnibus peccatis nostris: atque ἱλαστήριον, seu propitiatorium illud est, in quo Deus tribunal suae gratiae erexit, & denique purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum ipsum facta sedet ad dextram maiestatis diuinæ excelsissimæ, vt interpellet pro nobis: ille peccata nostra in se vt victimam, & agnum piacularem deriuata, reuera expiauit, ac proinde seruator noster est, non tantum quia doctrina, innocentia vitæ, miraculis, & morte, ac passione sua nobis viam salutis annuntiauit, & annuntiatam confirmauit: verùm etiam, & quidem potissimum, quia peccata nostra reuera expiauit, & pro iis satisfecit.
units.tr: He who has become the true, supreme, merciful, faithful, great, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and higher than the heavens, a High Priest who has no need, as the legal high priests did, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins; and yet who, taken from among men and appointed for men in things pertaining to God, was touched with the feeling of our infirmities and was tempted in all points like as we are, without sin; and who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, an offering and a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savour, to make atonement before God for the sins of the people; and who is that Lamb of God, unblemished and undefiled, who, by taking away our sins, which had alienated God from us and turned his gracious face away from us, by pouring out his precious blood for the remission of our sins, has become for them [hilasmos] and propitiation, and who cleanses and washes us from all our sins; and who is that [hilastērion], or mercy seat, on which God erected the throne of his grace; and who, finally, by the purging of our sins accomplished through himself, sits at the right hand of the high Majesty of God, to intercede for us: this one, having taken our sins upon himself as a sin offering and a sacrificial lamb, truly expiated them; and therefore he is our Saviour, not only because he announced to us the way of salvation by his teaching, the innocence of his life, his miracles, and his death and passion, and confirmed what he announced, but also, and indeed chiefly, because he truly expiated our sins and made satisfaction for them.

units.la: Atqui Iesus Christus, est summus ille, misericors, fidelis, magnus, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & sublimior cœlis factus Pontifex, cui nõ fuit necesse, quemadmodum Pontifices legalibus, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre: & tamè postquâ ex hominib. assumptus fuit, & pro hominibus constitutus in iis, quæ apud Deum agenda sunt, affectus etiâ est sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, & tentatus in omnibus similiter absque peccato, & per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, oblationem, & victimam in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, ad expiandum apud Deum peccata populi: idem ipse est agnus Dei immaculatus, & incontaminatus, qui sublatis peccatis nostris, quæ Deum à nobis alienarunt, & benignam eius faciem à nobis auerterunt, pretioso suo sanguine in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum sic effuso, vt sit pro illis ἱλασμὸς, & propitiatio, nos purgat ab omni peccato: idem ipse ἱλαστήριον seu propitiatorium illud est, in quo Deus tribunal suæ gratiæ erexit, denique purgatione per seipsum facta, sedit ad dextram maiestatis diuinæ excelsissimæ, vt interpellet pro nobis:
units.tr: But Jesus Christ is that supreme, merciful, faithful, great, holy, innocent, undefiled High Priest, separated from sinners and made higher than the heavens, who had no need, as the legal high priests did, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins; and yet, taken from among men and appointed for men in things pertaining to God, he was touched with the feeling of our infirmities and was tempted in all points like as we are, without sin; and through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God, an offering and a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savour, to make atonement before God for the sins of the people. The same is the undefiled and undefiled Lamb of God, who, by taking away our sins, which had alienated God from us and turned his gracious face away from us, by pouring out his precious blood for the remission of our sins, has become for them [hilasmos] and propitiation, and cleanses us from all sin. The same is that [hilastērion], or mercy seat, on which God erected the throne of his grace; and finally, having accomplished purging through himself, he sits at the right hand of the high Majesty of God, to intercede for us.

units.la: Ergo Iesus Christus peccata nostra in se, vt victimam, & agnum piacularem deriuata, reuera expiauit, ac proinde Seruator noster est, non tantum quia viam salutis nobis annuntiauit, & doctrinam suam innocentia vitæ, miraculis, & morte, ac passione sua confirmauit, verùm etiam, & quidem potissimum, quia peccata nostra verè expiauit, & pro iis satisfecit.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus Christ, having taken our sins upon himself as a sin offering and a sacrificial lamb, truly expiated them; and therefore he is our Saviour, not only because he announced to us the way of salvation, and confirmed his teaching by the innocence of his life, his miracles, and his death and passion, but also, and indeed chiefly, because he truly expiated our sins and made satisfaction for them.

units.la: Antecedentis totius veritas ex eo demonstratur solidissimè, quod ipsis etiam Aduersariis non refragantibus, qui reuera, ac proprie Pontifex & Sacerdos est populi, sacerdotii Veteris Testamenti typo adumbratus, ille etiam peccata nostra coram Deo reuera expiauit,& cuius mors,ac sanguinis effusio,& victima Deo ad expiandum peccata populi oblata, sacrificiis expiatoriis, in Veteri Testamento adumbrata fuit, illa etiam reuera fuit sacrificium expiatorium,seu victima piacularis pro peccatis nostris,vti ex natura typi & antitypi, seu symboli ac figuræ, & rei significatæ certò constat:Atqui Christum reuera, & proprie Pontificem, ac Sacerdotem nostrum esse,ex eo demonstratur, tum quod Messiæ promisso in Veteri Testamento,& nomen Sacerdotis, & res nomine significata diuersis verbis tribuitur,quemadmodum cap.23.demonstrauimus:tu ex collatione dignitatis personæ,& sacerdotii. Est enim Messias Filius Dei primogenitus, & præcipua Sacerdotii dignitas, & præfectus domui Patris,Ps.2.v.7.Filius meus es tu,ego hodie genui te:& 89.v.28. Ego primogenitum constituam eum, excelsum supra Reges terra.Heb.3.v.5.6.Et Moses quidè fidelis fuit in tota domo ipsius vt famulus,ad testificanda,quæ post dicenda erant: At Christus vt Filius domui suæ præest:& 10.v.21. Habemus Sacerdotem magnum, præfectum domui Dei: & 9.v.24. Non enim in manufactum sacrarium ingressus est Christus, quod sit exemplar vero respondens, sed in ipsum cœlum,vt appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis:tum denique quia in Nouo Testamento,& titulus, & omnia ad munus Sacerdotale pertinentia ipsi tribuuntur, quemadmodum ex testimoniis paulò ante citatis euidenter apparet.Mortem verò Christi, & sanguinis ipsius effusionem, victimamque Deo ad expiandum peccata populi oblatam,sacrificiis expiatoriis in Veteri Testamento adumbratam fuisse,confirmat,primò Apostolus Hebr.8.v.4.5.Nam si esset in terra,inquit,ne Sacerdos quidem esset, manentibus illis Sacerdotibus qui secundum legem offerunt dona: vt qui exemplari, & umbræ deseruiunt rerum cœlestium,sicut diuinitus dictum est Mosi, quum esset absoluturus tabernaculum:Vide enim,inquit,vt facias omnia ad exemplar,quod ostensum est tibi in monte.Confirmat enim Apostolus hisce verbis argumentum illud,quo videl.Sacerdotii Christi supra Leuiticū Sacerdotiū eminentiā,& præstantiā demonstrauit,nempe quod Christus ingressus sit sanctuarium cœleste,& præstantius illo quod ingressus fuit Sacerdos Leuiticus,quippe quod terrenum, & manufactum fuerit: in hunc modum: Si Christus non esset in cœlis sed adhuc in terra, tum sequeretur eum ne Sacerdotem quidem esse:quia enim vmbræ rerum cœlestiū durant,donec res ipsæ exhibeatur:ritus autè illi Sacerdotii Leuitici vmbræ rerum cœlestium per Sacerdotium,id est,Sacrificium & intercessionem Christi exhibendarum,extiterunt,quamdiu Christus vixit in terra, tam diu etiam manere & vigere debuerunt sacerdotes Leuitici, quippe quorum sacerdotium demum per sacrificium seu mortem illius aboleri debuit, manentibus autem seu vigentibus sacerdotibus Leuiticis,sacerdotio Christi locus esse non potest, nimirum vt reipsa illo fungatur: Atqui consequens est absurdum. Ergo & antecedens.Secundò,Iohannes in Apocalypsi cap.13.uersu octauo. Vbi Christum propterea appellat agnum mactatum ab origine mundi,quia & Agnis, & aliis sacrificiis,quae ab initio mundi offerebantur,fuit denotatus & adumbratus.Tertiò,Res ipsa:Si enim sacrificia ista, typi Christi non fuissent, tum nulla ratione ipsis peccatorum expiatio, quae per mortem Christi demum reipsa praestita fuit,adscribi potuisset, quandoquidem testante Apostolo, Lex non potest accedentes sanctificare,alioquin desiissent offerri: nec potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Quum igitur effectus ille sacrificiis expiatoriis Veteris Testamenti tribuatur,vt ex Leuit.praesertim autem c.16.apparet,vbi cum de solenni illa expiatione,annuatim per duos hircos facienda,praecepit Deus, subiicit v.21.22.Nitens Aaron ambabus manibus suis super caput illius hirci,qui viuus erit,confitebitur super ipsum omnes iniquitates filiorum Israelis,& omnes defectiones eorum ex quibusq.peccatis eorū,&postquā imposuerit illa capiti istius hirci, emittet eum per hominē commodū in desertum:nam portabit hircus ille super se omnes iniquitates illorum in regionem inhabitabile:& v.30.Isto die expiationem faciet pro vobis,ad mundandū vos ab omnib.peccatis vestris,coram Iehoua mundabimini,necessario sequitur nisi ipsa scriptura secum differentiat, sacrificia illa vim,atq. virtute expiandi & purgandi peccata nostra nonisi symbolicè seu typicè & sacramentaliter habuisse, quatenus videl. umbrae, atq.symbola sanctae illius victimae corporis Christi extiterunt. Ex quibus omnibus luce meridiana clarius euadit, Christum vere, ac proprie sacerdotē noftrū,ac Pōtificē fuisse, & victimā ab ipso,Deo oblatā,victimā verā,eámq. piacularem, qua propitius nobis Deus fit redditus, extitisse. Hisce adde, quòd si Christus illa omnia quae ipsi in citatis Scripturae S. testimoniis tribuuntur praestando, tantummodò doctrinā suā confirmauit,& summū illū dignitatis,glorię &maiestatis gradū cōsequutus est,tū sequetur id,quod ipsi Adversarii alioquin fatētur,& auide amplectūtur,Christū videl.tātū Dei apud nos,non autem nostrum quoque apud Deum mediatorem esse,seu Christum non idcirco in hunc mūdum venisse, vt nostro nomine aliquid apud Deum perageret, quod est salsissimum, & ipsi Scripturæ sacræ plane contrarium. Qui enim Pontifex est ex hominibus assumptus, & pro hominibus constitutus in iis,quæ apud Deum videlicet agenda sunt, seipsum obtulit pro peccatis nostris victimam & oblationem Deo,in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, qui est propitiatio apud Deum pro peccatis nostris, qui sanguine suo deletis iniquitatibus nostris,quæ inter nos & Deum nostrum disterminarunt,&purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum facta,sedet ad dextram Dei, vt interpellet pro nobis, nihil ne ille pro nobis apud Deum præstare dicetur? Sed impium hoc quum sit,ideò salsissimam esse Aduersariorum doctrinam, vel infans iudicauerit.
units.tr: The truth of all that has been said is most solidly demonstrated by this, which even our opponents do not deny: he who is truly and properly the High Priest and Priest of the people, foreshadowed by the priesthood of the Old Testament, himself truly expiated our sins before God. And his death, the shedding of his blood, and the victim offered to God to expiate the sins of the people, which were foreshadowed in the Old Testament by the expiatory sacrifices, were also truly an expiatory sacrifice, or a sin-offering for our sins. This is certain from the nature of type and antitype, or of symbol and figure and the thing signified. But that Christ is truly and properly our Priest and High Priest is demonstrated in two ways. First, the promise of the Messiah in the Old Testament attributes to him both the name of Priest and the reality signified by that name, in various words, as we showed in chapter 23. Second, this follows from comparing the dignity of his person with the priesthood. For the Messiah is the firstborn Son of God and the chief dignity of the priesthood, and the ruler over the house of the Father. "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee" (Ps. 2:7), and "I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth" (Ps. 89:28). "And Moses was indeed faithful in all his house as a servant, to bear witness to those things which were to be spoken afterwards; but Christ as a Son over his own house" (Heb. 3:5-6). "We have a great High Priest, who is set over the house of God" (Heb. 10:21). "For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true, but into heaven itself, to appear now in the presence of God for us" (Heb. 9:24). Finally, this follows because in the New Testament both the title and all the functions belonging to the priestly office are ascribed to him, as is clear from the testimonies cited a little earlier. That the death of Christ, the shedding of his blood, and the victim offered to God to expiate the sins of the people were foreshadowed in the Old Testament by the expiatory sacrifices, is confirmed first by the Apostle in Heb. 8:4-5: "For if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law; they serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was divinely warned when he was about to complete the tabernacle: for, 'See,' he says, 'that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.'" The Apostle confirms with these words the argument by which he showed the superiority and excellence of Christ's priesthood over the Levitical priesthood, namely that Christ entered a heavenly sanctuary, which is more excellent than the one the Levitical priest entered, since that was earthly and made with hands. The argument runs like this: if Christ were not in heaven but still on earth, it would follow that he was not even a priest. For shadows of heavenly things last only until the things themselves are made present. The rites of the Levitical priesthood were shadows of heavenly things, to be made present through the priesthood, that is, the sacrifice and intercession, of Christ. So as long as Christ lived on earth, the Levitical priests had to remain and continue in office, since their priesthood was to be abolished only by his sacrifice or death. But while the Levitical priests remained or continued in office, there could be no place for Christ's priesthood to be actually exercised by him. This consequence is absurd; therefore the antecedent is also false. Second, John in the Apocalypse 13:8 calls Christ "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world," because he was denoted and foreshadowed both by lambs and by the other sacrifices which were offered from the beginning of the world. Third, the thing itself: if those sacrifices had not been types of Christ, then the expiation of sins, which was in fact accomplished by the death of Christ, could in no way be ascribed to them. For, as the Apostle testifies, "the law can never make the comers thereunto perfect," otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, and "it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" (Heb. 10:1, 4). Since that effect is ascribed to the expiatory sacrifices of the Old Testament, as appears especially from Lev. 16, where God, when he commanded the solemn expiation to be made each year by means of two goats, adds (vv. 21-22): "Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their transgressions in all their sins, and after he has put them upon the head of the goat, he shall send him away by the hand of a suitable man into the wilderness; for that goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities into a land not inhabited." And (v. 30): "On this day he shall make atonement for you, to cleanse you from all your sins; before the LORD you shall be clean." It follows necessarily, unless Scripture itself contradicts this, that those sacrifices had the power and virtue of expiating and cleansing our sins only symbolically, or typically and sacramentally, in so far as they were the shadows and symbols of that holy victim, the body of Christ. From all these things it becomes clearer than noon-day light that Christ was truly and properly our Priest and High Priest, and that he was the true victim offered to God by himself, the atoning sacrifice through which God is rendered propitious to us. Add to this that if Christ, by performing all those things which are ascribed to him in the cited testimonies of Holy Scripture, only confirmed his doctrine and attained to that highest degree of dignity, glory and majesty, then it would follow (which our opponents themselves otherwise admit and eagerly embrace) that Christ is only God's mediator with us, and not also our mediator with God; that is, that Christ did not come into this world to accomplish anything before God on our behalf. This is most false and plainly contrary to Holy Scripture itself. For if he who is taken from among men to be High Priest, and appointed for men in the things pertaining to God, offered himself as a victim and offering to God for our sins, a sweet-smelling savour, who is the propitiation before God for our sins, who by his blood has blotted out our iniquities which separated between us and our God, and who, having made purification of our sins by himself, sits at the right hand of God to make intercession for us, will it not be said that he did nothing for us before God? But since this is impious, even an infant could judge that the doctrine of our opponents is most false.

units.la: OSTORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite trigesimoseptimo ad hoc argumetum nostrum tria excipit. Primum est, sanguinem Christi ideo nos à peccatis nostris purgare dici, non quod in ipso sanguine Christi arcana quædam vis sit, ac virtus peccata nostra expurgandi: sed quia causa existat illius sine quo à peccatis nostris non lauamur,diuina videlicet potestatis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qua ille omnes eos, qui ipsi obediunt, à pœna ipsis ob peccata illorum debita liberare, id est, à morte æterna eripere, & beata immortalitate donare potest. Quandoquidem certum sit,Christum per sanguinis sui effusionem ad illam potestatem peruenisse.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in chapter 37 of his Institutes, raises three objections to this argument of ours. The first is this: the blood of Christ is said to cleanse us from our sins not because there is some secret power and virtue in the blood itself to purge our sins, but because it is the cause of that without which we are not washed from our sins, namely the divine power of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he is able to free from the punishment due to their sins all those who obey him, that is, to snatch them from eternal death and grant them blessed immortality. For it is certain that Christ attained that power through the shedding of his blood.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus:

units.la: Si Christus diuinam suam potestatem per sanguinis sui effusionem consequutus est,qua ille omnes eos,qui ipsi obediunt, à pœna,quam peccatis suis meruerunt,liberare, id est,à morte æterna eripere,& beata immortalitate donare potest:tum sanguis Christi ideo nos à peccatis purgare dicitur, non quod in ipso sanguine Christi arcana quædam vis ac virtus lateat,peccata nostra expurgandi,sed quia causa existit illius rei, sine qua non mundamur à peccatis nostris, nempe exaltationis Christi:
units.tr: If Christ, through the shedding of his blood, obtained that divine power by which he can free from the punishment that they have deserved by their sins all those who obey him, that is, snatch them from eternal death and grant them blessed immortality, then the blood of Christ is said to cleanse us from sins not because some hidden power or virtue lies in the blood of Christ itself for cleansing our sins, but because it is the cause of that thing without which we are not cleansed from our sins, namely the exaltation of Christ.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est:Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Christi sanguinem in se & natura sua cõsideratum, occultam quādam in se habere δύναμιν ac virtutem peccata nostra eluendi,& di,& nos ab illis purgandi,nec docet Scriptura,neque nos affirmamus,alioquin nec effusione illius,ad expianda peccata nostra,nec aspersione eiusdem,ad nos fanctificados opus fuisset: & liquet idè ipsum ex eo quod prædicatum in illa enuntiatione, Sanguis Iesu Christi purgat & lauat nos ab omni peccato,est metaphoricum, voce illa lauandi seu purgandi ab aquæ effectu, & lauacro quo sordes corporis eluuntur, ad sanguinem Christi, propter similitudinem effecti illius translata. Non igitur ipse sanguis Christi simpliciter, sed sanguis Dei,quo redempta Ecclesia dicitur, Act.20.v.18. & in remissionem peccatorum effusus, Matth.26.v.28. liberat nos à reatu & dominio peccati, quatenus videlicet est sanguis Agni illius Dei, in victimam expiatoriam, & odorem bonæ fragrantiæ Deo oblati. Hoc est,illa ipsa mors & effusio sanguinis Christi,seu obedientia & illa Christi, ad mortem vsque crucis & effusionem sanguinis Deo Patri præstita est, causa ob quam Deus credentes iustificat,& peccata ipsis remittit.Christum vero ad tantum maiestatis,gloriæ, & honoris gradum extulit. Vis enim illa nobis peccata remittendi, & nos per renouationem & regenerationem lauandi ac purgandi,ad causam iustificationis efficientè,nempe Deü referenda est,qui solus peccata remittit,& credentes per Spiritum sanctum renouatos ac regenitos sibi consecrat in populum peculiarem studiosum bonorum operum. Atque hinc manifestum est, consequentiam Aduersarii duplici vitio laborare: nam & falsa hypothesi nititur, dum videlicet affingit nobis sententiam, quæ nostra non est:& vnius caufę,cuius plures sunt effectus & fructus, effectum ac fructum vnum tollendo, sumpto ab effecti alterius veritate argumento & ratione, grauissimum oppositorum elenchum committit. Nam vterque effectus, nempe & remissio peccatorum, & exaltatio Christi, obedientiæ eiusdem, tanquam causæ efficienti in Scripturis sacris tribuitur. Et illa quidem, Rom.3. v.24.25. Iustificantur autem gratis eius gratia,per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu quem proposuit Deus placamétum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam per remissionem præcedentium peccatorum:& 5.v.9. Iustificati igitur eius sanguine, seruabimur nunc multo magis per eum ab ira. Hæc vero Philip. 2.ver.6.7.8.9. Qui cum esset in forma Dei non duxit rapinam partem esse cum Deo, sed ipse se exinaniuit forma serui accepta, similis hominibus factus, & habitu compertus ut homo,ipse se submisit, factus obediens vsque ad mor-
units.tr: Reply. The blood of Christ, considered in itself and in its own nature, does not have some hidden power [δύναμιν] and virtue for washing away our sins and cleansing us from them. Scripture does not teach this, nor do we affirm it. Otherwise, neither its shedding to make atonement for our sins nor its sprinkling to sanctify us would have been necessary. This is plain from the fact that the predicate in that statement, "The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses and washes us from every sin," is metaphorical. The word "washing" or "cleansing" is transferred to the blood of Christ from the effect of water and from the bath by which the dirt of the body is washed away, because of the likeness of the effect. So it is not the blood of Christ simply, but the blood of God, by which the Church was redeemed (Acts 20:28), and which was poured out for the forgiveness of sins (Matt. 26:28), that frees us from the guilt and dominion of sin, insofar as it is the blood of that Lamb of God, offered as an expiatory sacrifice and a sweet-smelling savour offered to God.
