Vnde necessario sequitur Christum per mortem & sanguinem suum non apud homines, sed apud Deum propitiationem, seu ἱλαστήριον & placamentum extitisse: & vice versa: Quem Christus, morte & passione sua propitium reddidit, apud eum etiam est propitiatio, & eius respectu propitiationis, ac reconciliationis in sacra Scriptura fit mentio: Atqui Christus non apud homines, sed apud Deum est propitiatio, quia non homini, sed Deo θυσίαν ἱλαστικήν, videlicet seipsum per spiritum aeternum inculpatum & incontaminatum obtulit: Ergo Christus morte & passione sua non hominem, sed Deum homini propitium reddidit. Tertio, à quo Christus propter iniquitates nostras, percussus, plaga affectus, afflictus, & attritus est, & cuius delectatio prosperatur, per mortem eius, cuius lacum vini furoris & irae ipse calcauit, atque cum cuius irae sensu nobis mortem obiit, eum certè nobis reconciliauit, & propitium reddidit: Atqui Christus à Deo propter iniquitates nostras ipsi imputatas, percussus, plaga affectus, afflictus & attritus est, ac prosperatur per mortem eius delectatio Iehouae, & calcauit lacum vini furoris & irae Dei, atque cum irae diuinę sensu mortem obiit, quemadmodum in antecedentibus demonstrauimus: Ergo Christus Deum nobis reconciliauit ac propitium reddidit. Quarto, cum Christus seipsum victimam & oblationem obtulit in odorem bonae fragrantiae, &cum animâ suam dedit λύτρον & in redemptionis pretium, eundem etiam reconciliauit. Atqui Christus non hominibus, sed Deo, seipsum oblationem & victimam obtulit in odorem bonae fragrantiae, & animam suam dedit in λύτρον ac redemptionis precium: Ergo Christus non homines Deo, sed Deum hominibus reconciliauit, id est, placatum & propitium reddidit. Ex quibus omnibus iam euidenter apparet, illum reconciliationis ac propitiationis modum & formam hominibus tribui & competere non posse, ac proinde in Scripturis sacris, reconciliationis & propitiationis, non hominum, sed Dei respectu, mentionem fieri. Neque euertit hac doctrinam, quod nos per Christum Deo reconciliati dicimur, seu, Deus nos sibi per Christum reconciliare legitur, quia reconciliari Deo nihil aliud est, quàm coram tribunali gratiae ipsius iustificari, & remissionem peccatorum consequi, vt patet tum ex Rom. 5. verf. 8. 9. 10. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quod cum adhuc essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus sit: iustificati igitur eius sanguine e seruabimur nunc multo magis per eum ab ira: Nam si cum inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii eius, multo magis reconciliati seruabimur per vitam ipsius. Reconciliati autem cum Deo, & iustificati coram ipso, vnum ac idem in illis verbis significare, ex disputationis Paulinae serie luculenter apparet: & 2. Corint. 5. verf. 18. 19. Hæc omnia sunt ex Deo, qui reconciliauit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, deditque ministerium reconciliationis: nempe quia Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum: quo in loco Apostolus reconciliationem illam, qua Deo reconciliamur remissione, seu non immi non imputatione peccatorum nostrorum, id est, iustificatione nostri coram Deo, disertis verbis definit: tum etiam quod nō tantùm pars offensa & irata, sed etiam pars offendens & lædens, qualis est, in illo quod inter Deum & nos extitit, dissidio, genus humanum parti offensæ reconciliari dicitur : vt Matth. 5. vers. 23. 24. Si munus tuum attuleris ad altare, & illic memineris fratrem tuum habere aliquid contra te, omitte illic munus tuum coram altare, & abi, primum reconciliator (Ϛλλάγης, quod explicandum restat) fratri tuo, & tum veniens offer munus tuum. Homo vero tum demum vero Dei amore accenditur, cum videlicet per illuminationem cœlestem natiuis mentis ipsius tenebris expulsis, intellectus vera Dei & benignitatis ipsius notitia tribuitur, & cor per internam Spiritus sanctì virtutem renouatur, & deleto illo, quo à natura flagramus, erga Deum, & omne id quod bonum est, odio, nouis viribus ad Deum amandum & colendum instruitur, qua de re in loco de Libero Arbitrio & eius viribus prolixè egimus. Atque hæc de ipsa thesi seu assumptione, quod argumentum ipsum, quo illa stabilitur ab Aduersario, concernit, quod videlicet Deus nobis non fuerit inimicus, sed nos dilexerit, si illud simpliciter & absolutè intelligatur, quasi videlicet Deus nos ita amore prosequutus sit, vt nulla ratione nobis fuerit offensus, quemadmodum sanctì illi Angeli, qui originem suam seruant ἀιαμεταπτωτ ab ipso diliguntur, tum assumptio prosyllogismi vltimi falsa est. Quamuis enim Deus nos tanquam creaturas suas dilexerit, & ante iacta mundi fundamenta nos ad vitam æternam elegerit, nihilominus tamen propter læsionem & offensionem maiestatis suæ, nobis vt peccatoribus, & morte ac damnatione æterna dignis, iustissimè offensus fuit, nec etiam nos nisi vt per Christum redimendos & reconciliandos, vnquam vel post lapsum, vel ante Christi mortem amauit. Hoc ipsum præclarè explicat Augustinus Tractatu 110. in Euangelium Iohannis: Habebat, inquiens, Deus erga nos charitatem, etiam cum inimicitias aduersum eum exercentes, operaremur iniquitatem, & tamen ei verissimè dictum est: Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Proinde miro & diuino modo, etiam quando nos oderat, diligebat. Oderat enim nos, quales ipse non fecerat: & quia iniquitas nostra opus ipsius non omni ex parte consumpserat, nouerat simul in vnoquoque nostrum, & odisse quod feceramus, & amare quod fecerat. Ex hac verò medii terminì limitatione & explicatione verissima apparet cōnexum prosyllogismi ultimi, falsum esse. Atque ex hac responsione simul apparet vanissimam ac salsissimam esse Oftorrodii exceptionem alteram, qua videlicet sectione nona capitis trigesimiseptimi affirmat, Christum Mediatorem Dei & hominum appellari, non quia Deum nobis reconciliauerit, sed quia voluntatem, ac decretum ipsius nobis annuntiauerit, vt noua illius refutatione non fit opus.
units.tr: Reply. The minor premise of the principal syllogism, which has two parts, is false. Its first part, which asserts that it is nowhere found in the sacred Scriptures that Christ reconciled God to us, is, if taken simply and absolutely, rightly denied by us as false. Although this very word, apollaxei [ἀπολλάξει], and the phrase chō tēn rhēsin [χ̄ τὴν ῥῆσιν] are nowhere read word for word in the sacred Scriptures, the thing itself is taught and impressed upon us in almost countless places of Holy Scripture by equivalent expressions. This is clear from the testimonies of Holy Scripture cited in our four preceding arguments, and it will become plainer still from what follows, and especially from those passages with which we shall go on to answer the two arguments of our opponent. As for the second part of the same minor premise, which says that for the attainment of salvation and eternal life it was not necessary that God be reconciled to us, since our opponents' position, stated and summed up as a disjunctive axiom, has only one part, namely the denial of our view, while the minor premise of the second principal syllogism embraces the thesis and opinion of our opponents, and both parts are confirmed by the same arguments, therefore, aiming at brevity, we shall join these two assumed statements, taking the whole thesis or proposition, and answer first the proposition and then the argument adduced to confirm it. The whole thesis or assumption, then, is this: Christ by his death and passion did not appease or make propitious God, as though God had been angry and hostile to us, but reconciled us, who had been enemies of God and had hated him, to God, and made us, as it were, friends. Or: For the attainment of salvation and eternal life, it was not necessary that God should be appeased and reconciled as if he had been angry and hostile to us, but that we, who had been enemies of God and had hated him, should be reconciled to him and become, as it were, friends. So that the manifest falsity of this thesis may be the more fully exposed, and the truth of our view and doctrine may shine more clearly, we must examine: which parties were at variance, and whether both of the parties at variance, or only one, and what offence and hostile feeling there was? Then: whether both, or only one, was reconciled, and therefore with respect to which party the reconciliation and propitiation are mentioned in Holy Scripture? Finally: whether the same mode of reconciliation belongs to and must be ascribed to both parties? The parties at variance, to be reconciled through Christ, are God and men. The prophet Isaiah testifies to this, saying: Your sins have separated between you and your God (Isa. 59:2). And Paul (1 Tim. 2:5): There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. And that man, before he is renewed and regenerated by the power of the Holy Spirit and brought to a true recognition of his native misery, is an enemy of God and pursues him with hostile mind, not so much as Creator but as the severe avenger of his laws: this, I believe, is settled beyond dispute between us and the Socinians. Moreover, we by no means deny that man, who must be brought from the state of his native corruption and dominant sin to the participation of grace and spiritual benefits, must be imbued with true and sincere love towards God; but how, by what method, and by whose power this comes about, we shall explain afterwards. But that not only man but also God was offended and angry with us, and must be reconciled to us through the death of Christ, appears from the following: first, because Isaiah, in the passage cited, says that the sins of men have separated them and their God, and caused him to hide his face from them, so that he does not hear. By these words the prophet teaches that our sins are like a wall interposed between God and us, that they deprive us of the grace of God and shut against us the door of his kindness, and therefore that God hates us with just hatred, unless perhaps our opponents think, against the infinite and most evident proofs, that God is not offended and angry with those from whom he turns away the face of his kindness and mercy, and to whose prayers he closes his ears. Likewise what David says: You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak lies; the man of blood and deceit the LORD abhors (Ps. 5:5–6). And (Ps. 11:5–6): The LORD tests the righteous, but the wicked and him who loves violence his soul hates; upon the wicked he will rain coals, fire and brimstone, and a burning wind shall be the portion of their cup. Prov. 11:20: Those of perverse heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those whose way is blameless are his delight. Prov. 17:15: He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD. Deut. 27:26: Cursed is he who does not abide by all the words of this law, to do them. Hence Paul calls all, as many as descend from Adam by natural and carnal propagation, children of wrath, that is, shut out from the grace and favour of God and liable to damnation (Eph. 2:3). Also from the terrible judgments of God, from the effects of God's wrath and the punishments of sins, and above all from the fact that God would have our sins expiated only through the most atrocious and ignominious punishment of Christ's death, joined with the most grievous sense of divine wrath. For if there was nothing more atrocious and grievous in that punishment and passion of Christ than death or common execution, let my opponents tell me why Christ shrank so from the cross, why, if you look at the kinds and bodily tortures, which were in particular more severe and cruel than those suffered by all the martyrs, he trembled with such dread, why blood dripped from his venerable face, and why at last on the cross he cried out that he was forsaken by God? We have the parties at variance regarding propitiation and reconciliation, and their mode and form. Now we must look and see whether God was appeased and reconciled to man, or man to God, through the death and cross of Christ. Since the mode and form of that reconciliation consists in satisfaction for our sins and in the sense of divine wrath, it becomes clearer than noonday light that whenever Holy Scripture makes mention of that reconciliation and propitiation, it signifies that God has been rendered propitious and appeased to us by the death of Christ. Moreover, Christ through death became hilasmos [ἱλασμὸς], that is, propitiation, and hilastērion [ἱλαστήριον], that is, the place of propitiation, before God, and so also reconciled him and made him propitious. And that it is not man who was made propitious to God, but God to man, through the death and blood of Christ, is most plainly shown by the fact that hilasetai [ἱλάσεται] and hileōs [ἵλεως], or hileōs eiē [ἵλεως εἴη], said of someone or of someone's sins, in Holy Scripture means to remit sins to someone, or no longer to remember someone's sins: Luke 18:13, O God, be merciful [ἱλάσθητί] to me, a sinner. That tax collector asked for and obtained forgiveness of sins, as appears from verse 14, where he is said to have gone down to his house justified. So Heb. 8:12: I will be merciful to their iniquities [ἵλεως ἔσομαι ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν] and I will remember their iniquities no more. Hence it necessarily follows that Christ by his death and blood became the propitiation, or hilastērion and place of appeasement, not before men but before God; and conversely, the one to whom Christ through his death and passion made propitious is also the one before whom there is propitiation, and it is with respect to him that propitiation and reconciliation are mentioned in Holy Scripture. But Christ is propitiation not before men but before God, because he offered himself, namely himself, to God and not to men, as a propitiatory sacrifice [θυσίαν ἱλαστικήν], through the eternal Spirit, unblemished and uncontaminated. Therefore Christ by his death and passion made God, not man, propitious to man. Third: Christ, smitten by God for our iniquities, struck, afflicted, humbled and crushed, and the pleasure of the LORD prospers in his hand, by whose death, the one whose wine-press of the wine of fury and wrath he himself trod, and with whose sense of wrath he died for us, certainly reconciled us to himself and made him propitious. But Christ was smitten by God for our iniquities imputed to him, struck, afflicted and crushed, and the pleasure of the LORD prospers through his death; and he trod the wine-press of the fury and wrath of God, and he died with the sense of divine wrath, as we have shown in what precedes. Therefore Christ reconciled God to us and made him propitious. Fourth: since Christ offered himself as victim and oblation for an odour of sweet fragrance, and gave his soul as lytron [λύτρον], a ransom and price of redemption, he also reconciled God. But Christ offered himself as oblation and victim for an odour of sweet fragrance, not to men but to God, and gave his soul as lytron [λύτρον], the ransom and price of redemption. Therefore Christ did not reconcile men to God, but God to men, that is, made him appeased and propitious. From all these things it is now clearly evident that this mode and form of reconciliation and propitiation cannot be ascribed or belong to men, and therefore that in Holy Scripture mention of reconciliation and propitiation is made with respect to God, not to men. Nor does what is read, that we are said to be reconciled to God through Christ, or God is read to reconcile us to himself through Christ, overturn this doctrine, because to be reconciled to God is nothing other than to be justified before the tribunal of his grace and to obtain remission of sins, as appears from Rom. 5:8–10: But God commends his love towards us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, being now justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. That to be reconciled with God and to be justified before him mean one and the same thing in those words is clear from the course of Paul's argument. And 2 Cor. 5:18–19: All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; namely, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them. In this passage the Apostle expressly defines that reconciliation by which we are reconciled to God as the forgiveness, or non-imputation, of our sins, that is, our justification before God. Also, it is not only the offended and angry party but also the offending and injuring party, which in the dispute between God and us is the human race, that is said to be reconciled to the offended party. So Matt. 5:23–24: If you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled [διαλλάγηθι, to be explained further] to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Man, however, is then truly kindled with the love of God when, through heavenly illumination, the native darkness of his mind has been driven out, the true knowledge of God and of his kindness is given to his understanding, and his heart is renewed by the inward power of the Holy Spirit, and that hatred towards God and all that is good, which by nature burns in him, is removed, and he is equipped with new strength to love and worship God. We have treated this matter at length in our place on free will and its powers. And so much for the thesis or assumption itself, insofar as it concerns the argument by which our opponent establishes it, namely that God was not hostile to us but loved us. If this is taken simply and absolutely, as though God loved us so that he was in no way offended by us, as those holy angels who keep their origin unchangeable are loved by him, then the minor premise of the last prosyllogism is false. For although God loved us as his creatures, and before the foundation of the world chose us to eternal life, nevertheless, on account of the injury and offence to his majesty, he was most justly offended with us as sinners, worthy of death and eternal damnation, nor did he ever love us, either after the fall or before Christ's death, except as those to be redeemed and reconciled through Christ. Augustine explains this admirably in Tractate 110 on the Gospel of John: God had love towards us even when we, practising enmity against him, did iniquity; and yet it was most truly said to him: You hate all who work iniquity. Therefore, in a wonderful and divine way, even when he hated us, he loved us. For he hated us as he had not made us; and because our iniquity had not wholly destroyed his work, he knew at once in each of us both to hate what we had done and to love what he had made. From this true limitation and explanation of the middle term it is clear that the connection of the last prosyllogism is false. And from this reply it is at the same time clear that the other exception of Ostorrodius is most empty and most foolish, namely that in the ninth section of chapter thirty-seven he affirms that Christ is called Mediator between God and men not because he reconciled God to us, but because he announced to us God's will and decree; there is no need for a new refutation of it.

units.la: Quintum & vltimum argumentum, quo veritas sententiae ac doctrinae nostrae confirmatur, desumitur ex illis Scripturae sacrae testimoniis, quae docent, Christum Seruatorem pretioso suo sanguine nos redemisse, & seipsum pretium redemptionis pro nobis dedisse. Matt. 20. v. 28. Mar. 10. v. 45. Filius hominis non venit vt sibi ministraretur, sed vt ministraret, daretque animam suam in redemptionis pretium (λύτρον) pro multis. 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Qui semetipsum dedit redemptionis pretium (ἀντίλυτρον) pro quibusuis. Coloss. capite primo, versu decimoquarto, In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, id est, remissionem peccatorum. 1. Cor cap. 6. versu decimonono & vigesimo. An ignoratis corpus vestrum esse templum Spiritus sancti, qui est, in vobis, quem habetis a Deo, neque esse vestri iuris? nam empti estis pretio: & 7. v. 23. Pretio empti estis, ne estote serui hominum. Act. 20. v. 28. Attendite vobis ipsos, & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus S. constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam proprio illo sanguine acquisiuit. Heb. 9. v. 12. Neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum, sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium, aeternam redemptionem nactus. 1. Petr. capite primo, versu decimooctauo & decimonono, Vt qui sciatis vos non caducis rebus argento vel auro fuisse redemptos, ex vana vestra conuersatione, ex Patrum traditionibus acceptα, sed pretioso sanguine, vt pote agni immaculati & incontaminati Christi, Tit. cap. 2. versu decimoquarto, Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. Apoc. 5. v. 9. Dignus es qui accipias librum & aperias eius sigilla, quoniam mactatus es & redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem tuum. Atque hinc est, quod per sanguinem Christi dicamur ab illa ventura ira liberati: Hebr. capite secundo, versu decimo quarto & decimo quinto. Quoniam pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis: ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, vt per mortem aboleret eum qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, Diabolum, & liberos redderet, quotquot metu mortis, per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti. prima IohanIohannis capite tertio, versu octauo. Ad hoc patefactus est Filius Dei, vt dissoluat opera Diaboli. Roman.capite 5. versu 9. Iustifica-ti eius sanguine seruabimur nunc multo magis per eum ab ira. Galat. capite tertio,versu 13. Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio. 1.Thessal.cap.1.versu 10. Vt expectaretis Filium eius e cælis, quem excitauit a mortuis, nempe Iesum,qui liberat nos ab ira illa ventura.
units.tr: The fifth and last argument, by which the truth of our doctrine and teaching is confirmed, is drawn from those testimonies of Holy Scripture which teach that Christ our Saviour redeemed us with his precious blood, and gave himself as the ransom price for us. Matt. 20. v. 28. Mark 10. v. 45. The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom [λύτρον] for many. 1 Tim. 2. v. 6. Who gave himself a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for all. Col. chapter 1, verse 14: In whom we have redemption through his blood, that is, the forgiveness of sins. 1 Cor. chapter 6, verses 19 and 20: Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price. And chapter 7, verse 23: Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men. Acts 20. v. 28: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. Heb. 9. v. 12: Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption. 1 Pet. chapter 1, verses 18 and 19: Knowing that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conduct received by tradition from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. Titus chapter 2, verse 14: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. Rev. 5. v. 9: Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood. And from this it is that we are said to be delivered by the blood of Christ from that coming wrath. Heb. chapter 2, verses 14 and 15: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. 1 John chapter 3, verse 8: For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Rom. chapter 5, verse 9: Being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. Gal. chapter 3, verse 13: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. 1 Thess. chapter 1, verse 10: To wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, namely Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

units.la: Argumentum tale est;
units.tr: The argument is as follows;

units.la: Qui morte & sanguine suo vere,ac proprie nos redemit à morte, damnatione, & maledictione æterna, & verum redemptionis pretium pro nobis persoluit, & sic à ventura ira nos liberauit, ille peccata nostra in se vt sponsorem nostrum deriuauit, ac proinde Seruator noster est, non tantum quia viam salutis nobis annunciauit, & doctrinam suam vitæ integritate, miraculis, morte, passione, & gloriosa resurrectione sua confirmauit: verum etiam, & quidem potissimum, quia peccata nostra expiauit, & pro iis satisfecit.
units.tr: Whoever truly and properly redeemed us from death, damnation and eternal curse by his death and blood, and paid the true price of redemption for us, and so delivered us from the coming wrath, has taken our sins upon himself as our surety; and therefore he is our Saviour, not only because he announced to us the way of salvation and confirmed his teaching by the integrity of his life, by miracles, by his death, passion and glorious resurrection; but also, and indeed chiefly, because he expiated our sins and made satisfaction for them.

units.la: Atqui Iesus Christus morte & sanguine suo vere ac proprie nos à morte, maledictione, & damnatione æterna redemit, & verum redemptionis pretium pro nobis persoluit, & ab ira ventura nos liberauit:
units.tr: But Jesus Christ truly and properly redeemed us from death, curse and eternal damnation by his death and blood, paid the true price of redemption for us, and delivered us from the coming wrath.

units.la: Ergo Iesus Christus peccata nostra in se vt sponsorem nostrum deriuauit, ac proinde Seruator noster est, non tantum quia viam salutis nobis annuntiauit, & doctrinam suam vitæ integritate, miraculis, morte, passione, & gloriosa resurrectione confirmauit: verum etiam, & quidem potissimum, quia peccata nostra expiauit, & pro iis Deo satisfecit.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus Christ took our sins upon himself as our surety, and therefore he is our Saviour, not only because he announced to us the way of salvation and confirmed his teaching by the integrity of his life, by miracles, by his death, passion and glorious resurrection; but also, and indeed chiefly, because he expiated our sins and made satisfaction to God for them.

units.la: Propositio maior extra controuersiæ & dubitationis aleam est posita, verum assumptionem negat Ostorrodius, & ad loca Scripturæ ad illam confirmandam allegata, Institutionum suarum capite trigesimoseptimo, sectione octaua, respondet, ac dicit, verbum illud Latinum redimere sæpissimè, præsertim in Scripturis sacris, nihil aliud significare quàm liberare, ac proinde Christum vel animam ipsius, redemptionis pretium appellari, non quod ille vera satisfactio, quæ instar debiti, alicui pro nobis fuerit persoluenda, exiterit, sed quia Christus seipsum, imò Deus ipse Christum morti tradidit, vt nos à peccatis, id est, pœna peccatorum liberaremur: Ioh.3.v.16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum nō pereat,sed habeat vitam æternam:Rom.5.v.8. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quod quum adhuc essemus peccatores,Christus pro nobis mortuus sit. Hoc autem nihil aliud esse, inquit,quàm quòd Christus ex mandato Dei seipsum seu animam,id est vitam suam impenderit ac dederit, vt hac ratione ipsemet ad beatam immortalitatem, & suam potestatem perueniret,per quam nos ad eandem immortalitatem perduceret.
units.tr: The major premise has been placed beyond the hazard of controversy and doubt, but Ostorrodius denies the minor premise, and in Institutes chapter 37, section 8, he replies to the passages of Scripture cited to confirm it, and says: the Latin word "redimere" very often, especially in the holy Scriptures, means nothing other than "to deliver"; and therefore Christ, or his soul, is called the price of redemption, not because he was a true satisfaction which had to be paid to someone in our place as a debt, but because Christ gave himself up, indeed God himself delivered Christ to death, so that we might be freed from sins, that is, from the punishment of sins: John 3. v. 16: So God loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Rom. 5. v. 8: But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. This, he says, is nothing other than that Christ, by the command of God, devoted and gave up himself, or his soul, that is his life, so that by this means he himself might attain to blessed immortality and his power, by which he might lead us to the same immortality.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism is this:

units.la: Si verbum illud latinum redimere,sæpissimè,præsertim in sacris Scripturis,nihil aliud significat,quàm liberare, tum Christus seu anima ipsius,redemptionis pretium appellatur, non quod ille vera sit satisfactio, quæ instar debiti, alicui fuerit persoluenda, sed quia Christus seipsum,imò Deus Christum morti tradidit,vt nos à peccatis,id est,pœna peccatorum liberaremur: seu, quia Christus ex mandato Dei, seipsum, seu animam, id est,vt suam impenderit ac dederit, vt ipsemet hac ratione ad beatam immortalitatem & summam potestatem peruenireт, per quam nos ad eandem immortalitatem perduceret:
units.tr: If the Latin verb redimere, very often, and especially in the sacred Scriptures, means nothing else than to liberate, then Christ, or his soul, is called the price of redemption, not because it is a true satisfaction, which would have to be paid to someone as a debt owed, but because Christ handed himself over, indeed God handed Christ over to death, so that we might be freed from sins, that is, from the punishment of sins; or, because Christ, by the command of God, devoted and gave himself, or his soul, that is, his life, so that by this means he himself might attain to blessed immortality and supreme power, through which he might lead us to that same immortality:

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergò & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true: therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam. Quamuis enim λύτρωσις seu redemptio interdum simplicem liberationem,quæ, fit nullo interueniente pretio,significet,indè tamē non sequitur, redimendi verbum,in iustificationis, & salutis nostræ negotio, eandem significationem obtinere, quum à specie ad speciem, & à particulari ad vniuersale nulla detur legitima consequentia. Deinde ἀντρωσιν,seu redemptionem illam hic non metaphoricè, aut metonymicè, sed proprie accipiendam esse,ex eo probatur,quia omnia verae ἀντρώσεως ac redemptionis requisita hic concurrunt, vt captiuum genus humanum,Christus redemptor, anima seu vita Christi, λύτρον, ac redemptionis pretium, denique is qui hoc redemptionis pretium accepit,nempe Deus, iudex ille, qui nos ex iusto iudicio, Diabolo tanquam carnifici,ac ministro suo tradidit. Tertiò,quia nullus nostrum dicit Christum seu animā Christi, esse ipsam satisfactionem, sed Christum σωτῆρα docemus esse satisfactorem, ac summum Sacerdotem & Pontificem, corpus ac vitam Christi victimam & redemptionis pretium, immolationem vero ac mortem ipsius satisfactionis formam, quæ distinguenda sunt, non confundenda. Quarto, quia satisfactio pro peccatis,& liberatio à peccatorũ poena,perperam inter se opponuntur, quandoquidem liberatio à peccatorum poena,satisfactionis illius finis atque effectus est,& Christus per sanguinem suum æternam redemptionem nactus esse dicitur. Quinto & vltimo,si mortis ac passionis Christi hic præcipuus fuisset finis, nimirum vt ille hac ratione, ad beatam immortalitatem,& summæ dignitatis ac potestatis fastigium eucheretur, tum Christus non tam pro nobis peccatoribus, quàm pro semetipso, mortuus esset, & seipsum victimam, ac ἀντίψυχον obtulisset, quod salsissimum esse, ex ipsa Scriptura sacra liquidò constat.
units.tr: Answer. The inference is false. For although λύτρωσις, or redemption, sometimes signifies simple liberation, which happens without any price intervening, it does not follow from this that the verb redimere, in the matter of our justification and salvation, has the same meaning; since no legitimate inference can be drawn from a species to a species, or from a particular to a universal. Next, that redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις] is not to be taken here metaphorically or metonymically, but properly, is proved from the fact that all the requisites of a true redemption and ransom come together here: the captive human race; Christ the Redeemer; the soul or life of Christ, the ransom [λύτρον] and price of redemption; and finally he who received this price of redemption, namely God, that judge who, by a just judgment, handed us over to the Devil as to an executioner and his minister. Thirdly, because none of us says that the soul of Christ is itself the satisfaction, but we teach that Christ the Saviour [σωτήρ] is the satisfier, and the supreme Priest and High Priest, that the body and life of Christ are the victim and price of redemption, and his immolation and death the form of the satisfaction; these things must be distinguished, not confounded. Fourthly, because satisfaction for sins and liberation from the punishment of sins are wrongly set against each other, since liberation from the punishment of sins is the end and effect of that satisfaction, and Christ is said to have obtained eternal redemption through his own blood. Fifthly and lastly, if the chief end of Christ's death and passion had been that he might by this means be raised to blessed immortality and to the summit of supreme dignity and power, then Christ would have died not so much for us sinners as for himself, and would have offered himself as victim and ἀντίψυχον, which is clearly most false, as is plain from Holy Scripture itself.

units.la: Atque sic hactenus veritatem sententiæ ac doctrinæ orthodoxæ de vera peccatorum nostrorum expiatione & pro illis satisfactione,per mortem & obedientiam Christi præstita, ex ipsis Scripturis sacris demonstrauimus, & contra Aduersarii cauillationes & sophismata defendimus: vnde iudicet Christianus & æquus lector, qua fronte,conscientia,ac pietate, Ostorrodius Institutionum suarum cap. trigesimo septimo, hanc doctrinam de merito & satisfactione Christi veteres & superstitiosas Pontificiorum fabulas redolere, affirmet. Restat autem vt functionem & actionem Sacerdotalem alteram, in qua etiam propriam Sacerdotii Christi rationem proprie consistere diximus,nimirum pro nobis apud Deum intercessionem exponamus: verum quia Aduersarius illius modum & rationem capite quadragesimo, in tractatu de regno Christi, exponit: ideo nos illius rei explicationem ad examen illius capitis reiiciemus, nunc argumenta illa quibus Aduersarius doctrinam orthodoxam labefactare & conuellere conatur, refutaturi.
units.tr: And thus far we have demonstrated from the holy Scriptures themselves the truth of the orthodox teaching concerning the true expiation of our sins and the satisfaction made for them through the death and obedience of Christ, and have defended it against the cavils and sophisms of our opponent. From this let the Christian and fair reader judge with what brazenness, conscience and piety Ostorodius, in chapter thirty-seven of his Institutions, affirms that this doctrine of the merit and satisfaction of Christ smells of the old and superstitious fables of the Papists. It remains, however, that we set forth the other priestly function and action, in which we have said the proper character of Christ's priesthood itself consists, namely intercession for us before God. But since our opponent expounds its manner and method in chapter forty, in the treatise on the kingdom of Christ, we shall therefore refer the explanation of that matter to the examination of that chapter, and now proceed to refute the arguments by which the opponent tries to shake and overthrow the orthodox doctrine.

units.la: CAPVT XXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXV.

units.la: In quo argumenta Aduersarij, quibus ille sententiam ac do-ctrinam orthodoxam,de vera peccatorum expiatione, & pro iis satisfactione, per mortem & sanguinem Christi fa-ćta,recensentur ac refutantur.
units.tr: In which the arguments of the Adversary are set out and refuted, by which he attacks the orthodox doctrine and opinion concerning the true expiation of sins, and the satisfaction made for them through the death and blood of Christ.

units.la: OSTORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite trigefimofexto, tria affert argumenta, quibus orthodoxam de satisfactione Christi doctrinam conuellere & astruere conatur,peccata nobis nulla interuenien-te satisfactione, ex mera liberalitate, misericordia, & gratia Dei remitti, quorum primum est,quod in sacris literis, illius satisfactionis, aut vllius rei ipsi æquipollentis, ne vnico quidem verbulo mentio fiat: imo necessarium sit, vt illius non aliquoties tantùm, sed frequentissimè in Scripturis S. mentio fiat : quandoquidem Aduersaræ illam in suis concionibus & scriptis, sine intermissione inculcent.
units.tr: Ostorrodius, in the thirty-sixth chapter of his Institutes, offers three arguments by which he tries to overturn the orthodox doctrine of Christ's satisfaction and to establish that sins are forgiven us, without any satisfaction intervening, from mere liberality, mercy and the grace of God. The first is this: in the holy writings there is not even the slightest mention, not so much as a single word, of that satisfaction or of anything equivalent to it. Indeed, it would be necessary that mention of it be made in the Holy Scriptures not just a few times but very frequently, since our opponents keep dinning it into their sermons and writings without pause.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows:

units.la: Cuius doctrinæ ac sententiæ in Scripturis sacris nulla plane fit mentio, illa falsa est & erronea:
units.tr: A doctrine or opinion of which there is absolutely no mention in the holy Scriptures is false and erroneous.

units.la: Atqui illius doctrinæ ac sententiæ, qua docetur Christum morte & passione sua, Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, sic vt peccata nostra per satisfactionem pro illis præstitam, à nobis auferantur, nulla plane in Scripturis S. fit mentio, sic vt neque satisfactio, nec quicquam quod satisfactioni æquipolleat, ibi doceatur:
units.tr: But the doctrine and opinion which teaches that Christ, by his death and passion, satisfied God for our sins, so that our sins are taken away from us through the satisfaction offered for them, has absolutely no mention in the holy Scriptures, so that neither satisfaction nor anything equivalent to it is taught there.

units.la: Ergo doctrina illa de satisfactione Christi, falsa est ac erronea.
units.tr: Therefore the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction is false and erroneous.

units.la: Resp. Quicquid neque quo ad verba & phrases, neque quo ad rem ac sententiam ipsam, quæ affirmatur aut negatur, in scripturis sacris, docetur, illud in religionis negotio minimè admittendum, sed tanquam falsum & erroneum repudiandum ac reiiciendum esse, religiosè credimus & affirmamus : sed hoc sensu intellectam assumptionem negamus. Quamuis enim hæ ipsæ phrases, quibus afferimus, Iesum Christum Deo pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, cisse , & peccata nostra in se vt vadem ac sponsorem nostrum deriuasse, in sacra Scriptura non extent,rem tamen ac sententiam, illis phra-sibus comprehensam ac significatam,necessaria consequutione ex Dei verbo deduci,ex apodixi nostra,quam capite antecedēte,ex sa-cris literis extruximus,manifestè apparet. Quod vero Aduersarius dicit, non satis fore , etiamsi aliquoties illius satisfactionis in Scripturis sacris, mentio sieret , sed necessarium esse , vt illa multoties & fre-quentissimè inculcaretur : eo ipso magnam & crassam suam imperi-tiam prodit ac palam facit,se naturam,maiestatem,autoritatem,& dignitatem Scripturæ sacræ plane ignorare. Quum enim ipsa veri-tas diuina, Scripturæ sacræ forma sit interior ac essentialis, totum subiectum & omnes,ac singulas eius partes informans,ac veluti a-nima , & vitalis spiritus viuificans,num ex rei,quæ ibi docetur,re-petitione crebriori , ipsi veritati quicquā accedere posse existima-bimus? Si verissimum, & extra omnem iustæ dubitationis aleam constitutum est, quicquid in Dei verbo continetur,nonne erroris aut mendacii Deum ipsum accusat,qui fidem rei ab ipso vel semel vel aliquoties affirmatæ,adhibere detrectet,etiamsi illius repetitio crebra non frequentetur? Atque hoc nimirum est Ecclesiis Christi, catechismos,& institutiones religionis Christianæ edere,in quibus omnis doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ fundamēta , nempe Scri-pturæ sacræ veritas,ac,αὐτοπιστία & ἀξιοπιστία,conuellantur.
units.tr: Answer. We religiously believe and affirm that whatever is not taught in the holy Scriptures, neither in words and phrases nor in the matter and substance itself that is affirmed or denied, is in no way to be admitted in matters of religion, but must be rejected and repudiated as false and erroneous. But we deny the minor premise in this sense. For although these very phrases, by which we assert that Jesus Christ satisfied God for our sins, and drew our sins upon himself as our surety and bondsman, do not occur in Sacred Scripture, the matter and substance comprehended and signified by those phrases is, by necessary consequence, deduced from the Word of God, as is clear from our proof, which in the preceding chapter we built from the sacred letters. As for what the Adversary says, that it would not be enough even if mention of that satisfaction were made in the holy Scriptures a number of times, but it would be necessary for it to be inculcated many times and very frequently, he thereby betrays and makes plain his great and gross ignorance, and shows that he entirely fails to understand the nature, majesty, authority and dignity of holy Scripture. For since divine truth itself is the inner and essential form of Holy Scripture, informing the whole subject and all its parts, and giving life to them as their soul and living spirit, will we think that any addition can be made to the truth itself by more frequent repetition of what is taught there? If it is most true and placed beyond all reasonable doubt that whatever is contained in the Word of God is true, does not he who refuses to accept as true a matter affirmed by God himself, once or several times, even if it is not often repeated, accuse God himself of error or lying? And this indeed is what it means to publish catechisms and summaries of the Christian religion for the Churches of Christ, in which the foundations of all Christian doctrine and religion, namely the truth of Holy Scripture and its autopistia [αὐτοπιστία] and axiopistia [ἀξιοπιστία], would be overthrown.

units.la: Argumentum Aduersarii secundum est,quod Scriptura sacra non tantum illius satisfactionis pro nostris peccatis præstita , mentio-nem nullam faciat , verum etiam doctrinam illam de satisfactio-ne , falsam esse demonstret , quandoquidem illa , peccata nobis ex mera gratia , & pro nihilo , scu non propterea quod aliquid pro il-lis solutum sit , remitti , ac condonari , passim doceat & affir-met.
units.tr: The Adversary's second argument is that Holy Scripture not only makes no mention of any satisfaction offered for our sins, but also shows and asserts that the doctrine of satisfaction is false, since it everywhere teaches and affirms that sins are forgiven and pardoned to us from mere grace, and for nothing, that is, not because anything has been paid for them.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism is this.

units.la: Si Scriptura sacra passim affirmat , ac docet , peccata nostra nobis ex mera gratia remitti , ac condonari , tum illa doctrina,qua affir-matur, remissionem peccatorum , ac vitam æternam nonnisi per satisfactionem Christi obtineri,falsa est ac erronea.
units.tr: If Holy Scripture everywhere affirms and teaches that our sins are forgiven and pardoned to us from mere grace, then the doctrine which affirms that the remission of sins and eternal life are obtained only through the satisfaction of Christ is false and erroneous.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est:
units.tr: But the first is true.

units.la: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp.Connexi consequentiam esse falsam,quippe quæ manifesto oppositorum elencho laboret. Vt enim gratia Dei, & meritum Christi minimè inter sese opponuntur, sed hoc vt causa salutis nostræ inferior, gratiæ diuinæ tanquam superiori subordinatur ac subalternatur: (nihil siquidem mereri potuit Christus, nisi ex mero Dei beneplacito, qui ab æterno constituit ipsum placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. 3. verf. 25. Et nos in illo ante iacta mundi fundamenta elegit. Ephes. 1. verf. 4.) sic etiam peccatorum nostrorum expiatio & satisfactio pro iis per mortem & sanguinem Christi præstita, gratuitam peccatorum remissionem minimè tollit, tum quia illa satisfactio non à nobis, sed à Christo Mediatore, vade, ac sponsore nostro exigitur: tum quia Deus illud, quo sibi satisfieri voluit, ac Filium Mediatorem, quif actus est victima & propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nobis gratis dedit, & peccato in carne ipsius condemnato, iniquitates nostras nobis non imputat, sed illas propter Christi gratis nobis remittit & condonat: tum denique quia hæc ipsa satisfactio, præstita quidem est à Christo iustitiæ diuinæ, sed non strictè, quæ secundum rigorem legis pœnâ debitam, ipsismet peccatoribus infligit: verum temperatæ, clementi misericordiæ & moderamine, atq; gratuita ordinatione iudicis cœlestis & clementissimi Dei ab æterno facta, atq; in Evangelio revelata, qua factum est, ut pœna peccatis nostris debita, non nobis ipsis irrogata, sed in Christum Mediatorem ac sponsorem nostrum deriuata fuerit. Atque hinc etiam euanescit, exceptionis illius, qua responsionem nostram, qua gratuitæ peccatorum remissioni, satisfactionem Christi propter respectuum diuersitatem, aduersari & opponi non posse dicimus, conuellere conatur Aduersarius, quam tamen exceptionem subiungere iubet.
units.tr: Answer. The connection of the consequence is false, since it plainly suffers from the fallacy of opposites. For the grace of God and the merit of Christ are by no means opposed to each other; rather, the latter, as the lesser cause of our salvation, is subordinated and made subject to divine grace as the higher cause. (For Christ could merit nothing except by the mere good pleasure of God, who from eternity set forth him as the propitiation through faith in his blood, Rom. 3. v. 25, and chose us in him before the foundation of the world, Eph. 1. v. 4.) So too the expiation of our sins, and the satisfaction for them made through the death and blood of Christ, does not abolish the free forgiveness of sins: first, because that satisfaction was not demanded of us but of Christ the Mediator, our surety and bondsman; second, because God himself gave us freely that by which he wished to be satisfied, namely his Son, the Mediator, who became the victim and propitiation for our sins, and, with sin condemned in his flesh, he does not impute our iniquities to us but freely forgives and pardons them for Christ's sake; and finally, because this satisfaction, though indeed offered by Christ to divine justice, was not offered in the strict sense, which according to the rigour of the law inflicts the penalty due on the sinners themselves, but in the tempered, merciful and gentle manner, and by the free arrangement of the heavenly Judge and most merciful God, made from eternity and revealed in the Gospel, by which it came about that the punishment due to our sins was not inflicted on ourselves but was transferred to Christ the Mediator and our surety. And from this too there vanishes the objection by which the Adversary tries to overturn our answer, in which we say that the satisfaction of Christ cannot be set against or opposed to the free remission of sins because of the difference of respects; yet he orders us to add this objection.

units.la: Ad hanc igitur responsionem nostram, qua dicimus, remissionē peccatorū respectu nostri gratuitam, morti vero ac passioni Christi, tanquam causæ meritoriæ tribuendam esse, excipit Osiorrodius, ac dicit: Hoc ipsum tamen confiteri non posse, quandoquidem id quod Christus præstitit, à nobis præstitum esse censeatur, cum Christus non pro se, sed pro nobis satisfecit, ac proinde dici non posse, quod Deus ex mera gratia & liberalitate nobis peccata nostra remiserit, accepta à Christo pro iis satisfactione. Et quoniam Deus id quod nos ipsi debebamus, accepe-rit, ideo nihil nobis ab ipso remissum esse: cum autem hoc falsum sit, ideo hanc doctrinam de satisfactione Christi directè cum sacris literis pugnare.
units.tr: To this answer of ours, in which we say that the remission of sins is free with respect to us, but is to be attributed to the death and passion of Christ as the meritorious cause, Ostorrodius objects and says: Nevertheless, this cannot be granted, since what Christ accomplished is deemed to have been accomplished by us, since Christ made satisfaction not for himself but for us; and therefore it cannot be said that God forgave us our sins out of mere grace and liberality, once satisfaction had been accepted from Christ for them. And since God is thought to have accepted from Christ what we ourselves owed, therefore nothing was remitted to us by him; but since this is false, this doctrine of Christ's satisfaction directly contradicts the sacred letters.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Siid quod Christus pro nobis praestitit, perinde habetur ac si nos ipsi id praestitissemus, ille autem Deo pro nostris peccatis satisfecit, & sic Deus, id quod nos ipsi debebamus accepit: tum sequitur Deum nobis peccata nostra ex mera gratia & liberalitate non remisisse, ac proinde illam respectuum diuersitatem, contrarietatem illam, quae est inter gratuitam peccatorum remissionem, & satisfactionem pro iis, non tollere:
units.tr: If what Christ has performed on our behalf is regarded just as if we had performed it ourselves, and he has satisfied God for our sins, so that God has received what we ourselves owed, then it follows that God has not forgiven our sins out of pure grace and generosity. Therefore that distinction of relations, that contrast which exists between the gratuitous forgiveness of sins and satisfaction made for them, is not removed.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp. Consequentiam esse falsam: sequeretur enim consequens ex illo antecedente, si Deus illam satisfactionem non a Mediatore, spōsore, ac vade nostro, sed a nobis ipsis exegisset, si illud ipsum λυτρον, quo Deus sibi satisfieri voluit, a nobis ipsis praestitum ac persolutum, non vero a Deo ex gratia & misericordia suppeditatum & subministratum esset: si denique Deus iure stricto nobiscum egisset, nec de illo quicquam remisisset, aut rigorem iustitiae suae ἐπιεικείας, & misericordiae moderamine non temperasset: quae omnia cum falsa sint, ut responsione antecedente demonstravimus, ideo falsitas consequentiae manifeste apparet.
units.tr: Reply. The inference is false. The consequent would follow from that antecedent only if God had demanded that satisfaction not from a Mediator, surety and guarantor, but from ourselves; if that very ransom [λύτρον], by which God willed to be satisfied, had been provided and paid by us ourselves, and not supplied and furnished by God out of grace and mercy; or if God had dealt with us by strict right and had remitted nothing of it, and had not tempered the rigour of his justice with forbearance [ἐπιεικείας] and the moderation of mercy. All these things are false, as we have shown in the reply to the antecedent. Therefore the falsity of the inference is plainly evident.

units.la: Argumentum Aduersarii tertium est, quod haec ipsa sententia ac doctrina de satisfactione, gloriam Dei supra modum minuat atque obscuret. Ex illa enim alterutrum horum absurdorum necessario sequitur, nempe Deum vel noluisse nobis, sine interueniente satisfactione, peccata nostra remittere, vel illud praestare non potuisse, quorum neutrum absque summa in Deum iniuria, dici possit. Si enim noluisset, tum necessario sequeretur, ipsum immisericordem esse, atque id ipsum non praestare, quod tamen nobis per Christum imperet ac praecipiat, nempe ut quisque nostrum fratri ex animo ignoscat. Si vero voluisset, & tamen non potuisset, tum sequi ipsum habere aliquem se superiorem, quod nihil aliud sit quam Deum omni sua potestate spoliare, & minorem libertatem ipsi quam homini alicui tribuere: quandoquidem liberum sit unicuique Domino, subditis ac seruis suis contra ipsum peccantibus debita illorum remittere possit, & hoc ipsi non vitio, sed laudi vertatur. Alias vero plurimas causas & rationes, quib. doctrina illa de satisfactione refutari possit, se intermittere dicit: eum vero qui plura desiderat, ad suam aduersus Georgium Tradelium disputationem & librum Fausti Socini de Iesu Christo Seruatore, remittit. Atque sic concludit, Peccata nostra non per satisfactionem, Sed gratuitam remissionem auferri atque deleri, ac proinde in negotio iustificationis nostri coram Deo, in illa satisfactione frustra fiducia collocari.
units.tr: The opponent's third argument is that this very doctrine of satisfaction greatly diminishes and obscures the glory of God. For from it one of two absurdities necessarily follows: either that God was unwilling to forgive us our sins without the intervening satisfaction, or that he could not grant it. Neither of these can be said without great injury to God. For if he was unwilling, then it necessarily follows that he is unmerciful and does not do what he nevertheless commands and enjoins upon us through Christ, namely that each of us should forgive his brother from the heart. But if he was willing and yet not able, then it follows that he has some superior over him, which is nothing other than stripping God of all his power and granting him less freedom than any man, since it is open to every lord to remit the debts owed to him by his subjects and servants who sin against him, and this is counted to him not as a fault but as a praise. As for the many other causes and reasons by which that doctrine of satisfaction could be refuted, he says he passes them over; but to one who desires more he refers him to his own disputation against George Tradelius and to the book of Faustus Socinus, On Jesus Christ the Saviour. And so he concludes: our sins are taken away and blotted out not by satisfaction but by gratuitous forgiveness, and therefore in the matter of our justification before God it is vain to place trust in that satisfaction.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Si peccata nostra nobis non remittuntur nisi interveniente satisfactione Christi, tum illud fit, quia Deus sine illius satisfactionis interventu peccata nobis remittere, vel noluit, vel non potuit.
units.tr: If our sins are not forgiven us except by the intervening satisfaction of Christ, then this comes about because God was either unwilling or unable to forgive us our sins without the intervention of that satisfaction.

units.la: Atqui utrumque consequens falsum est, & gloriam Dei minuit ac obscurat: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But each consequent is false and diminishes and obscures the glory of God. Therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Primi membri in assumptione probatio hæc est.
units.tr: The proof of the first member in the minor premise is this.

units.la: Si Deus noluit peccata nostra nobis remittere, nisi interveniente satisfactione Christi, tum sequitur ipsum immisericordem esse, & id ipsum non præstare, quod tamen nobis iniungit ac imperat, nempe ut quisque nostrum fratri delinquenti ex animo ignoscat.
units.tr: If God was unwilling to forgive us our sins unless by the intervening satisfaction of Christ, then it follows that he is unmerciful and does not do what he nevertheless enjoins and commands upon us, namely that each of us should forgive from the heart a brother who offends.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum est: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Membri secundi in assumptione Syllogismi principalis probatio hæc est.
units.tr: The proof of the second member in the minor premise of the principal syllogism is this.

units.la: Si Deus voluit, & tamen non potuit nobis peccata nostra remittere, nisi interveniente satisfactione, tum sequitur ipsum habere aliquem seipso superiorem, & minori potestate quàm hominem aliquem praeditum esse.
units.tr: If God was willing, and yet could not forgive us our sins unless by the intervening satisfaction, then it follows that he has someone superior to himself and is endowed with less power than some man.

units.la: Atqui consequens est absurdum: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is absurd; therefore the antecedent is also absurd.

units.la: Connexi Epilogismus hic est.
units.tr: The conclusion of the connected argument is this.

units.la: Si homo aut Dominus aliquis subditis ac servis suis contra ipsum delinquentibus, debitum remittere potest, & hoc ipsi non vitio, sed laudi vertitur, Deus autem voluit quidem, sed tamen non potuit nobis peccata nostra remittere, nisi ipsi satisfieret pro illis: tum sequitur, ipsum habere aliquem seipso superiorem & minori potestate, quàm hominem aliquem praeditum esse.
units.tr: If a man or some lord can remit the debt owed to him by subjects and servants who offend against him, and this is counted to him not as a fault but as a praise, but God was willing, yet could not, forgive us our sins unless satisfaction were made to him for them, then it follows that he has someone superior to himself and is endowed with less power than some man.

units.la: Atqui consequens falsum est: Ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent is also false.

units.la: Resp. Quum ipsa Scriptura sacra totum redemptionis mysterium, & vniuersam eius administrationem, ac salutis tum dispensationem, tum fundamentum, principium, medium, ac finem, in liberrimam Dei voluntatem, & ἀδιαὶ, tanquam primam ac supremam causam transcribat, ideo hic pedem sisto, & in hoc speculum fidei meae aspectum defigo, ne altius quàm fas est euol ado, in profundiorem, quàm meae & aliorum saluti conducat, labyrinthum se demergat: ac proinde quæstionem illam controuersam, An videlicet satisfactio pro peccatis nostris sit absolutè necessaria, & dependeat non tantum à necessitate, & infallibili certitudine decreti diuini, ac liberâ ordinationis, verum etiam à necessitate naturæ diuinæ, sicut Deus nullum peccatum condonare possit vlli, nisi plena satisfactione pro eo à Christo accepta? aliis, quibus vberior Spiritus sancti reuelatio contigit, tractandam & explicandam relinquo. Ego in libero illo decreto Dei, & gratuita exequutione ipsius, tantam φιλανθρωπίας opulentiam, tantumque misericordiæ & gratiæ diuinæ thesaurũ inuenio, vt habeat fides mea, quod contempletur, quod miretur, & in quo acquiescat, nec penetrare altius desideret, quod tamen absque præiudicio dictum, neque derogatum quicquam velim iis, quæ à præstantissimis atque clarissimis Viris hac de re scripta extant. Quanquam & hoc addam, neque absurdum illud, quasi videlicet superior aliquis Dominus, ac Legislator Deo præficiatur, ex doctrina & sententia illa, qua satisfactio pro peccatis nostris, à necessitate naturæ diuinæ suspenditur, 'iusta ac necessaria consequentia deduci, neque Aduersarios rationibus & argumentis illis, quibus nonnulli ex Ecclesiarum nostrarum Doctoribus illam sententiam de absoluta satisfactionis necessitate confirmarunt, satisfecisse. Nam illud, nimirum consequentiam illam quantum concernit, eam falsam ac minimè necessariam esse, ex veritissima tum libertatis, tum necessitatis distinctione, ac diuersarum vtriusque causarum consideratione, liquidò constat. Ex eo enim, quod Deus aliquid posse, vel non posse dicitur, nonnisi contra veritatem ac pietatem omnè colligitur, ipsum id posse, vel non posse, ex permissu, & interdicto superioris alicuius Domini, præsertim quum constet, Deum esse supremum rerum omnium Dominum, nemini obligatum, nulliúsque ductui obnoxium, & prorsus ἀντιθέτως. Non potest quidem Deus quædam facere, verum non propter extrinsecus impedimetum aliquod,sed quia illa cum perfectione, veritate, & excellentia naturæ diuinæ pugnant, & cum manifesta iniustitia, aut vitio naturali, aut quouis simili defectu coniuncta sunt, atque contradictionem vel in Deo, vel in rebus creatis inuoluunt. Causam igitur, cur Deus peccata impunita dimittere non possit,non in superius aliquod potestate diuina imperium ac magisterium, sed excellentiam ac perfectionem naturæ diuinæ,transcribunt Theologi nostri, qua fieri non possit,vt Deus iustitiam suam abneget vnquam,aut veritati renuntiet, mortis interminatione in homine peccatore non complendo.Posterius vero,nempe argumenta illa, quibus sententiam ac doctrinam suam confirmant illi,qui satisfactionem pro peccatis à necessitate naturæ diuinæ dependere statuunt, quantum concernit, certe quomodo Deus(vt ex rationibus illorum aliquot,vnicam tantum recenseam)id non puniat necessario, quod tamen naturali ac necessario odio prosequitur,ab Aduersariis nondum est ostensum: sed hæc aliis vberius explicanda relinquo. Ad primi vero membri in assumptione syllogismi principalis probatione respondeo, vtramque præmissam esse falsam, & consequentiam quidem, tum quia remissio peccatorum nostri respectu plane est gratuita, atque ex summa & ineffabili Dei misericordia profecta, qui satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris non à nobis,sed Christo Mediatore nostro exegit, eúmque nobis sponsorem ex gratia dedit, nobisque satisfactionem ipsius ad iustitiam imputat:tum etiam,quia inter illas ipsas iniquitates,quæ sunt in quauis transgressione & offensa proximi contra nos, distinguendum est, quarum vna contra Deum est, & mandata ipsius,ac peccatum proprie dicitur;contra hominem & bonum ac felicitatem ipsius altera,quæ iniuria ac noxa proprie appellatur:illa à solo Deo remittitur, hæc autem nos proximo condonare,& ex animo ignoscere iubemur, non quòd Deus impunitam ac inultam dimittere velit quamuis iniuriam, & nocendi libidinem ac petulantiam, qua in proximum sæuitur, sed quia vindicta & vltionem sibi reseruauit Dominus, nec peccata puniri vult, nisi ab iis,quos ille publica potestate &autoritate instruxit.Atque hæc consideranda fuissent Aduersario diligentius,priusquam illis rem tanti momenti superstrueret.Assumptio autem falsa est,quatenus videlicet absurdum esse affirmat, Deum id ipsum non præstare, quod nobis præstandum imperat atque iniungit: quasi vero Deus,qui summus est rerum omnium Dominus, ac supremum dominium obtinet in creaturas suas omnes, ad paria obedientiæ, & cultus officia hominib. obstringeretur, ad quæ ille homines iure tum creationis, tum redemptionis obligat? Hoc enim quæso quid aliud esset, quàm Deum ex supremi ac cœlestis imperii maiestate, & regia infra terrenæ ac humanæ potestatis dignitatem & autoritatem deturbare? Quæ omnia cum absurda sint, & impia, quàm vanum etiam, ac futile sit argumentum Aduersarii, euidenter apparet. Librum aduersus Georgium Tradelium, & alterum à Fausto Socino de Iesu Christo Seruatore, scriptum, quantum concernit, quum illa, quæ ibi continentur à Viris clarissimis & doctissimis Dn. Doctor. Dauide Pareo, Dn. Doct. Sibrando Lubberto, & Dn. Georgio Zarnouetio, refutata sint, ideo illa hic repetere velle, superuacaneum esset. Atque sic hactenus veritatem sententiæ orthodoxæ, de sacrificio, merito & satisfactione Christi, euidentissimis argumentis demonstrauimus, & ab exceptionibus Aduersarii, ac sophismatis vindicauimus. Deus omnis boni autor, largiatur nobis gratiam, vt autoritatem peccatorum nostrorum ex amplitudine, & dignitate pretii, quo redempti sumus, metientes, abnegata impietate, & mundanis cupiditatibus temperanter, & pie, & iuste, in hoc præsente seculo viuamus.
units.tr: Reply. Since Holy Scripture itself traces the whole mystery of redemption, its entire administration, and the dispensation of salvation, as well as its foundation, origin, means and end, to the most free will of God and his eternal [ἀΐδιον] counsel as the first and supreme cause, I here halt my step and fix the gaze of my faith on this mirror, so as not to fly higher than is right, nor plunge into a labyrinth deeper than is useful for my salvation and that of others. Accordingly I leave to others, to whom a fuller revelation of the Holy Spirit has been given, the controverted question to be treated and explained: whether satisfaction for our sins is absolutely necessary, and depends not only on the necessity and infallible certainty of the divine decree and free ordinance, but also on the necessity of the divine nature, so that God could pardon no sin to anyone unless full satisfaction for it had been received from Christ. For my part, in that free decree of God and in its gratuitous execution I find such abundance of love for mankind [φιλανθρωπίας], and so great a treasury of divine mercy and grace, that my faith has something to contemplate, to wonder at, and in which to rest, and does not desire to penetrate further. Yet I would say this without prejudice, and without wishing to detract anything from what the most excellent and distinguished men have written on this subject. Still I will add this: neither is the absurdity drawn by a just and necessary consequence from that doctrine and opinion, which makes satisfaction for our sins depend on the necessity of the divine nature, namely that some superior lord and lawgiver is set over God, nor have our opponents satisfied the arguments by which some of the teachers of our Churches have confirmed the opinion of the absolute necessity of satisfaction. For as far as that consequence is concerned, it is clearly established that it is false and by no means necessary, from the very true distinction between freedom and necessity and from the consideration of the different causes of each. For from the fact that God is said to be able or unable to do something, it can be inferred only contrary to all truth and piety that he is able or unable to do it by permission or prohibition of some superior lord, especially since it is plain that God is the supreme Lord of all things, bound to no one and subject to no one's guidance, and entirely the opposite [ἀντιθέτως]. God indeed cannot do certain things, but not because of some external hindrance, but because they are at odds with the perfection, truth and excellence of the divine nature, and are joined with manifest injustice, or natural vice, or some similar defect, and involve a contradiction either in God or in created things. Therefore our theologians ascribe the reason why God cannot dismiss sins unpunished not to a power of command or authority of some superior over the divine power, but to the excellence and perfection of the divine nature, by which it cannot happen that God should ever deny his justice or renounce the truth by failing to carry out the threatened penalty of death on a sinful man. As for the second point, namely those arguments by which those who hold that satisfaction for sins depends on the necessity of the divine nature confirm their doctrine, as far as it concerns this, the opponents have certainly not yet shown how God would necessarily punish that which he nonetheless pursues with natural and necessary hatred. (I will mention only one of their arguments, to avoid a long list.) But these things I leave to be explained more fully by others. To the proof of the first member of the minor premise of the principal syllogism I reply that both premises are false, and the inference too: first, because the forgiveness of our sins is wholly gratuitous with respect to us, and proceeds from the supreme and unspeakable mercy of God, who demanded satisfaction for our sins not from us but from Christ our Mediator, and gave him to us as surety out of grace, and imputes his satisfaction to us for righteousness. Second, because among those very wrongs which are in every transgression and offence of a neighbour against us, a distinction must be made. One kind is against God and his commands, and is properly called sin; the other is against man and his good and welfare, and is properly called injury or harm. The former is forgiven by God alone, while we are commanded to forgive the latter to our neighbour and to pardon it from the heart. This is not because God wishes any injury, or the lust and wantonness of harming by which one rages against a neighbour, to go unpunished and unavenged; rather, the Lord has reserved vengeance and retribution to himself, and does not wish sins to be punished except by those whom he has equipped with public power and authority. These matters ought to have been considered more carefully by the opponent before he built so weighty a matter upon them. The minor premise, moreover, is false insofar as it asserts that it is absurd that God does not do what he commands and enjoins upon us. As if God, who is the supreme Lord of all things and holds supreme dominion over all his creatures, were bound to render to men equal duties of obedience and worship, which he himself obliges men to render by right both of creation and of redemption! For what, I ask, would this be but thrusting God down from the majesty of his supreme and heavenly rule and from the dignity and authority of a kingly power beneath that of earthly and human rulers? Since all these things are absurd and impious, how vain and trifling the opponent's argument is becomes evident. As for the book against George Tradelius and the other written by Faustus Socinus on Jesus Christ the Saviour, since what is contained in them has been refuted by the most distinguished and learned men, Dr. David Pareus, Dr. Sibrandus Lubbertus and Dr. George Sarnovius, it would be superfluous to wish to repeat those points here. And so far we have demonstrated by the most evident arguments the truth of the orthodox doctrine concerning the sacrifice, merit and satisfaction of Christ, and have defended it against the opponent's objections and sophisms. May God, the author of every good, grant us grace so that, measuring the value of our sins by the greatness and worth of the price by which we have been redeemed, and renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, piously and justly in this present age.

units.la: CAPVT XXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVI.

units.la: In quo reliqua doctrinæ capita, quibus iustificationis nostræ coram Deo, modus & ratio, ab Aduersario explicatur, examinantur: & quæstiones illæ, An videlicet homo in hac vita Christum possit imitari? deinde: An homo in hac vita Christū perfectè imitari possit? seu: An homo in hac vita perfectam obedientiam præceptis Dei per Christum latis, præstare possit? denique: An illa obedientia, quæ præceptis Christi præstatur, seu imitatio illa Christi, homini ad iustitiam imputetur, sic vt homo per eam iustificetur? breuiter excutiuntur, veritas defenditur, falsitas refutatur.
units.tr: In which the remaining heads of doctrine, by which the Opponent explains the manner and method of our justification before God, are examined. The questions are briefly sifted: namely, whether a man in this life can imitate Christ; then: whether a man in this life can imitate Christ perfectly; or: whether a man in this life can render perfect obedience to the precepts of God given through Christ; and finally: whether that obedience which is rendered to the precepts of Christ, or that imitation of Christ, is imputed to a man for righteousness, so that he is justified by it. The truth is defended and the falsehood refuted.

units.la: Storrodius Institutionum suarum capite trigesimosexto, sectione quarta, postquam veram iustificationis nostri coram Deo causam aliquot argumentis impugnasset, pergit, & primò quænam sit nostra coram Deo iustitia, seu id propter quod Deo gratis sumus, ac remissionem peccatorum consequimur, exponit, ac dicit primò, ex sua sententia colligi non debere, quasi ad iustificationem nostri, & remissionem peccatorum nihil aliud, quàm decretum diuinum requireretur: quamuis enim ille nec satisfactionem istam, nec vllam aliam causam meritoriam, aut impulsiuam iustificationis nostræ, qua videlicet Deus ad nos iustificandum permotus & impulsus fuerit, extra Deum ipsum concedat: tamen aliquid in nobis quoque reperiri oportere, sine quo Deus nos iustificare non velit, nempe fidem in Filium ipsius Iesum Christum. Secundò: Quoniam verò hæc fides nihil aliud sit, quam fiducia in Christum & obedientia, vt antea demonstratum: ideò manifeste apparere, quod Deus hominem illum qui in peccatis perseuerat, non iustificet, hoc est, peccata ipsi non remittat, ac proinde perseuerantibus in peccatis omnem iustificationis ac remissionis peccatorum spem præclusam esse. Tertiò: Hanc sententiam non pugnare cum verbis Apostoli, quibus dicit, hominem fide iustificari absque operibus Legis: quoniam verborum illorum sensus non sit, quod Deus nulla plane opera à nobis iustificari desiderantibus requirat, (hoc enim falsum esse, ex eo manifestum fieri, quòd in Nouo Testamento illi tantùm saluari dicantur, qui præcepta Dei per Christum lata seruant,) sed quod Deus hominem, modò in Christum credat, iustificare velit, etiamsi legem perfectè non seruet: vnde Apostolus non simpliciter dicat absque operibus, sed absque operibus Legis, id est, talibus qualia Lex exigit, nimirum perfectis: sicut dictum: Maledictus qui non manserit in omnibus quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, vt faciat illa: Deut. 27. ver. 17. Gal. 3. ver. 10. Quandoquidè ex operibus iustificari volentes, tanquam ex debito, ac merito, Legem ita seruare oporteat, vt eam nullatenus transgrediantur: quum autem hoc à nemine præstetur, ideò etiam neminem ex operibus Legis iustificari posse. Quartò: Idcirco Deum ex magna sua misericordia, aliam viam ac rationem, beneficium illud iustificationis consequendi nobis monstrasse: nimirum fidem in Iesum Christum, hoc est, obedientiam, tiam, quam spe beatæ immortalitatis consequendæ, præceptis Christi præstamus, propter quam ille, qui præstat eam, etiamsi aliquando peccator & hostis Dei extiterit, Deo nihilominus gratus, & omnium peccatorum suorum veniam ac remissionem consequuturus sit.
units.tr: Storrodius, in the thirty-sixth chapter, fourth section, of his Institutes, after he had attacked the true cause of our justification before God with several arguments, goes on. First, he sets out what our righteousness before God is, that is, that on account of which we are freely accepted by God and obtain the forgiveness of sins. He says, first: It should not be inferred from his opinion that only the divine decree is required for our justification and the forgiveness of sins. For although he does not grant that satisfaction, or any other meritorious or impulsive cause of our justification outside God himself, by which God would be moved and impelled to justify us, nevertheless something must also be found in us, without which God is unwilling to justify us, namely faith in his Son Jesus Christ. Second: Since this faith is nothing other than trust in Christ and obedience, as was shown earlier, it is therefore clear that God does not justify the man who persists in sins, that is, does not remit his sins; and consequently, for those who persist in sins, all hope of justification and forgiveness of sins is shut off. Third: This opinion does not conflict with the words of the Apostle, in which he says that a man is justified by faith without the works of the Law. For the sense of those words is not that God requires no works at all from us who desire to be justified (for this is false, as is clear from the fact that in the New Testament only those are said to be saved who keep the precepts of God given through Christ), but that God is willing to justify a man who believes in Christ, even if he does not keep the Law perfectly. Hence the Apostle does not simply say "without works," but "without works of the Law," that is, without works of the kind the Law demands, namely perfect ones, as it is said: Cursed is he who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them: Deut. 27. v. 17; Gal. 3. v. 10. Since those who wish to be justified by works, as by debt and merit, must keep the Law in such a way that they do not transgress it at all; but since no one does this, therefore no one can be justified by the works of the Law. Fourth: Therefore God, in his great mercy, has shown us another way and method of obtaining that benefit of justification, namely faith in Jesus Christ, that is, the obedience which we render to the precepts of Christ in hope of attaining blessed immortality, on account of which he who renders it, even if at some time he has been a sinner and an enemy of God, will nevertheless be pleasing to God and will obtain pardon and remission of all his sins.

units.la: Resp. Ad primum: Neque nos affirmamus ad iustificationem, ac vitam æternam consequendam, nihil aliud nisi merum ac nudum Dei decretum requiri, sed insuper etiam gratuitam ipsius exequutionem, cum omnibus illis mediis, quibus iustificationis, ac vitæ æternæ participes reddi possumus, & sine quibus Deus nos neque iustificare, neq; saluare decreuit, necessariam esse dicimus. Inter quæ media etiam non extremum locum obtinet vera, viua, & saluifica fides in IesumChristū, testante Apostolo, 2. Thes. 2. v. 13. Nos autem debemus gratias agere Deo semper de vobis, fratres, dilecti à Domino, quod elegerit vos Deus ab initio ad salutem, per sanctificationem Spiritus, & fidem habitam veritati. Quid verò de satisfactione pro peccatis nostris per Christum præstita sentiendum sit, & quibus, ac quanti momenti, & ponderis rationibus, & argumentis Aduersarius illam impugnauerit, ex capite trigesimoquarto & trigesimoquinto, huius defensionis nostræ fiat iudicium.
units.tr: Reply. To the first: We do not affirm that for obtaining justification and eternal life nothing else is required but the bare and mere decree of God; we also say that his free execution is necessary, with all those means by which we can be made partakers of justification and eternal life, and without which God has decreed neither to justify nor to save us. Among these means, true, living and saving faith in Jesus Christ holds no small place, as the Apostle testifies, 2 Thess. 2. v. 13: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning to salvation, through the sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth. But what must be thought about the satisfaction made for our sins through Christ, and with what weight and force of reasons and arguments the Opponent has attacked it, will be judged from the thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth chapters of this our defence.
