units.la: Ad secundum: Antecedens falsum est, quo asseritur, fidem iustificantem nihil aliud esse, quàm obedientiam, quæ præceptis Dei, per Christum datis, præstatur, neque potuit Aduersarius illam sententiam suam, sufficientibus argumentis demonstrare, quemadmodum ex iis, quæ capite trigesimo, & trigesimoprimo, de fide iustificante disputauimus, liquido constat. Consequens verò, nimirum perseuerantes in peccatis suis, à Deo non iustificari quandiu tales sunt, imò ipsis, nisi resipiscant, gratiæ ac vitæ æternæ ianuam occlusam esse, vltrò concedimus, neque Dei gratiam promiscuè & sine discrimine omnibus propinandam censemus. Quum enim iustificemur per fidem illam quæ non mortua, sed viua, & cum vera resipiscentia, ac serio bonorum operum studio, coniuncta est: ideo à iustificationis & vitæ æternæ participatione hominem excludit, quicquid cum fide iustificante simul consistere nequit. Hominem autem qui nullo virtutum Christianarum studio accensus, voluptatibus & cupiditatib. carnis sese famulum ac mancipium præbet, atque in peccatorum luto securè se volutat, fide iustificante præditum esse, nemo, nisi qui veræ fidei naturam ignorat, dixerit.
units.tr: To the second: The antecedent is false, by which it is asserted that justifying faith is nothing other than the obedience rendered to the precepts of God given through Christ. Nor could the Opponent prove that opinion of his with sufficient arguments, as is clear from what we argued in the thirtieth and thirty-first chapters concerning justifying faith. The consequent, namely that those who persist in their sins are not justified by God as long as they are such, we readily concede; indeed, unless they repent, the door of grace and of eternal life is closed to them. Nor do we judge that the grace of God is to be offered indiscriminately and without distinction to all. For since we are justified by that faith which is not dead but living, and is joined with true repentance and with a earnest zeal for good works, therefore whatever cannot stand together with justifying faith excludes a man from participation in justification and eternal life. But that a man who is kindled by no zeal for Christian virtues, who gives himself as a slave and bondsman to the pleasures and lusts of the flesh, and wallows securely in the mire of sins, is endowed with justifying faith, no one will say except one who is ignorant of the nature of true faith.

units.la: Ad tertium : Deum nulla plane opera à nobis iustificari volenti- bus requirere,ambigue dicitur. Vel enim requiri, aut non requiri dicuntur opera ab iis qui iustificationis ac remissionis peccato- rum consequendæ studio ac desiderio ducûtur, vt materia & causa iustificationis , propter quam nimirum peccatorum remissionem consequamur: vel vt qualitas, vt sic dicam, fidelium, & veræ fidei fructus consequens, atque effectus indissolubili nexu , & vinculo cum illa coniunctus. Si posteriori modo, ac sensu , bona opera à iustificandis exigi dicat Aduersarius, tum allegatum testimonium Pauli sententiam illam non tantum non euertit, sed maximè stabilit, dum videlicet bonis operibus à veris iustificationis nostræ causis efficientibus, reiectis,causam illius in solam fidem transcribit. Sin vero priori sensu opera illa à nobis requiri statuat, tum doctrinam ac sententiam Samofatenianorum tantisper negabimus, donec illi solidioribus,quàm hactenus factum est, argumentis,fidem iustificantem, & refipiscentiam, ac bona opera vnum ac idem esse ostenderint,& hominem ex operibus, nomine videlicet operum proprie sumpto, coram Deo iustificari, ex ipsis Scripturæ sacræ verbis disertis,ac testimoniis demonstrauerint. Rationes illæ duæ quas subiungit Aduersarius,sententiam ipsius non confirmant:primam enim quantum concernit,ex eo quod in NouoTeftamento illi tantum saluari dicuntur,qui præceptis Dei per Christum datis obtemperant, minimè sequitur bona opera in censum causarum iustificationis efficientium , aut materiam eius constituentium referenda esse : tum quia iustificatio vitam æternam ordine naturæ & tempore antecedit, rei autem consequentis plures solent esse causæ, quàm antecedetis, ita vt ex eo quod bona opera vitæ æternæ causas efficientes esse detur, minimè tamen sequeretur eadem materiam aut causam iustificationis quoque existere: tum etiam,quia bona opera,ne vt ipsius quidem vitæ æternæ causæ efficientes, sed vt via, iter, ac medium illius consequendæ, atque vt fructus, & testimonia veræ fidei in Scripturis facriis recen- fentur, quemadmodum nostri Theologi, aduersus grauissimos Dei gratiæ inimicos, & propriæ iustitiæ ftupidiffimos patronos, Pontificios nimirum , passim demonftrarunt. Alteram verò rationem , qua Aducrfarius ipsius Apostoli, opera generatim omnia, à iustificationis causis excludentis, telum retundere conatur, quod attinet, quod videlicet Apostolus non simpliciter ex operibus,sed ex operibus Legis dixerit, ne illa quidem sententiæ ac doctrinæ ipsius patrocinari poterit, quum nullum opus ih se bonum sit, nisi quod Lex bonum iustúmque esse pronunciauerit,quandoquidem illa ipsa Lex Dei vnica omnium bonorum operum norma ®ula est, quemadmodum ex boni operis,& contrarii peccati forma,ac definitione solidè demonstratur.
units.tr: To the third: The statement that God requires no works at all from those who wish to be justified is ambiguous. For works are said to be required, or not required, from those who are led by zeal and desire for obtaining justification and remission of sins, either as the matter and cause of justification, on account of which we obtain remission of sins; or as the quality, so to speak, and the consequent fruit and effect of believers and of true faith, bound to it by an indissoluble bond and connection. If the Opponent says that good works are demanded of those to be justified in the latter manner and sense, then the testimony of Paul which he cites does not overturn that opinion at all, but rather greatly establishes it, since by setting aside good works as the true efficient causes of our justification, it transfers the cause of it to faith alone. But if he maintains that those works are required from us in the former sense, then we will deny the doctrine and opinion of the Samosatenians, until they show, with more solid arguments than has been done so far, that justifying faith, repentance and good works are one and the same, and until they demonstrate from the plain words and testimonies of Holy Scripture that a man is justified before God by works, taking the name "works" in its proper sense. The two reasons which the Opponent adds do not confirm his opinion. As to the first, namely that in the New Testament only those are said to be saved who obey the precepts of God given through Christ, it by no means follows that good works should be counted among the efficient causes of justification or among those constituting its matter: first, because justification precedes eternal life in the order of nature and in time, and a consequent thing usually has more causes than an antecedent one, so that even if it were granted that good works are efficient causes of eternal life, it would by no means follow that they are also the matter or cause of justification; second, because good works are not reckoned in Holy Scripture even as the efficient causes of eternal life, but as the way, path and means of obtaining it, and as the fruit and evidence of true faith, as our Theologians have shown everywhere against the most serious enemies of the grace of God and the most stupid defenders of their own righteousness, namely the Papists. As to the second reason, by which the Opponent tries to blunt the weapon of the Apostle, who excludes works in general from the causes of justification, namely that the Apostle did not say simply "by works" but "by works of the Law," this reason cannot support his opinion either. For no work is good in itself, unless it is what the Law has pronounced good and right, since that very Law of God is the only rule and standard of all good works, as is soundly demonstrated from the form and definition of a good work and of the contrary sin.

units.la: Ad quartum : Deum,quum propter carnis fragilitatem,& natiuam generis humani corruptionem , per obedientiam Legis perfectam,iustitiam consequi non possemus , ex ineffabili sua misericordia & gratia,aliam salutis ac iustitiæ consequendæ viam nobis patefecisse,ac mõstrasse,pia gratáque mente agnoscimus. Sed quis, quid,aut quænam illa via sit diserte docet Apostolus Rom. 8.verf. 3. Cùm Legis impotentia nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio missó, conformato carni peccato obnoxia,idque pro peccato,condemnauit peccatum in carne.Et Christus ipse,quum se viam,veritatem,ac vitam dicit,Ioh.14.verf.6. quatenus videlicet ille factus pro nobis peccatum: 2. Corint. 5.verf.21. & execratio. Gal.3.verf.13. Seipsum per Spiritum æternum obtulit Deo victimam & oblationem in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ.Heb. 9.verf.14. Ephes.5.verf.2. vt multorum peccata tolleret, Heb. 9.verf.27.Et seruare posset eos,qui per ipsum ad Deum accedunt. Heb. 7.verf.25. Vnde apparet,in quæ errorum dumeta suos deducat,quibus illam iustitiæ , ac remissionis peccatorum consequendæ, viam monstrat , quæ in bonis nostris operibus sita est , quibus ille fidem iustificantè definit,qua de re iam sæpius , vt & de toto iustificationis nostræ negotio, in antecedentibus, actum est,vbi,quidnā illud fit,propter quod Deo grati simus,& remissionem peccatorū adipiscamur,prolixè ostendimus,&quænam sit illa iustitia,per & propter quā iusti coram Deo constituimur , ex ipsis Scripturis S.demonstrauimus. Si verò aliqui doctrina illa de iustitiæ Christi imputatione, ad securitatem & petulantiam carnis abutuntur, hoc non ipsi doctrinæ, sed hominum malitiæ est imputandum, ac proinde Ostorrodius illud conuitium capite trigesimo sexto, sectione quinta, iniquissimè in veritatem sententiæ nostræ eiaculatur. Neque etiam locus ille quem ibidem citat, ex 1.Ioh.3. verf.7. Filioli nemo vos seducat,qui exercet iustitiam,iustus est,sicut ille iustus est, eandem doctrinam nostram euertit: quoniam Apostolus ibi non de causa, sed de testimonio , signo , ac declaratione iustificationis loquitur, & docet,non quo modo coram Deo iustificemur,sed quibus argumentis ac testimoniis, iustificatos nos esse, declaremus, nempe vitæ nouitate & bonis operibus, tanquam veris, viuæ,& iustificantis fidei fructibus. Atque hunc genuinum esse loci illius sensum, ex v. 10. vbi de iustificationis declaratione, & signis apertius agit: Per hoc manifesti sunt, inquiens, filij Dei, & filij Diaboli, quisquis non exercet iustitiam, non est ex Deo, & qui non diligit fratrem suum, liquido constat.
units.tr: To the fourth point: We gratefully and devoutly acknowledge that God, since we could not attain righteousness through perfect obedience to the Law, because of the frailty of the flesh and the inborn corruption of the human race, has, out of his ineffable mercy and grace, opened and shown us another way of obtaining salvation and righteousness. But what that way is, and what it is, the Apostle plainly teaches in Rom. 8.3: Since the Law was powerless in the flesh, God, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh. And Christ himself, when he calls himself the way, the truth, and the life (John 14.6), does so in that he was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5.21) and a curse (Gal. 3.13); he offered himself through the eternal Spirit to God as a victim and offering of a sweet-smelling savour (Heb. 9.14; Eph. 5.2), so as to take away the sins of many (Heb. 9.28), and to be able to save those who come to God through him (Heb. 7.25). From this it is clear into what thickets of error Ostorrodius leads his followers, when he shows them a way of obtaining righteousness and forgiveness of sins that lies in our good works, and when he defines the justifying faith by them. On this matter, as on the whole business of our justification, we have already spoken more than once in the preceding chapters: there we have shown at length what that is on account of which we are pleasing to God and obtain forgiveness of sins, and from the Holy Scriptures themselves we have demonstrated what that righteousness is, through and for which we are constituted righteous before God. If some people abuse that doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness to feed their security and the wantonness of the flesh, this must be imputed to human wickedness, not to the doctrine itself; and therefore Ostorrodius most unjustly hurls that reproach against the truth of our teaching in chapter thirty-six, section five. Nor does the passage he cites there, 1 John 3.7, Little children, let no one deceive you; he who does righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous, overthrow our doctrine. For the Apostle there is not speaking of the cause of justification but of its testimony, sign and declaration, and he teaches not how we are justified before God, but by what arguments and evidences we declare ourselves to be justified, namely by newness of life and good works, as true fruits of a living and justifying faith. That this is the genuine sense of that passage is quite clear from verse 10, where he treats of the declaration and signs of justification more openly: By this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whoever does not practise righteousness is not of God, nor is he who does not love his brother.

units.la: Deinde exponit Aduersarius, quousque se extendat illa obedientia, quam præceptis Christi præstare tenemur, & sine qua Deus hominem non vult iustificare? Seu: quid ab homine requiratur, vt iure de ipso dici possit, illum præceptis Christi obedire? Nos sententiam Aduersarii ad certas theses redigemus, deinde ad singulas respondebimus. Thesis prima est: Quemadmodum Deus Pater Filium suum in exemplum proposuit eorum omnium, quos ipse post hanc vitam nobis est largiturus: ita etiam eundem nobis dedit exemplum in hac vita imitandum, atque sequendum. Secunda: Hùc igitur contendendum, & in hoc elaborandum, atque incumbendum est, vt ipsi Christo quàm simillimi, & perfecti siamus, nec mandata Dei vlla ratione transgrediamur. Tertia: Si Deus hoc propositum ac studium perfectionis assequenda, à nobis non requireret, neutiquam tam perfectum virtutum exemplar nobis proposuisset: nec etiam dubitandum, quin per summam diligentiam, ac Dei gratiam, homo perfectus fieri possit. Quarta: Qui hunc scopum sibi non habet præfixum, nempe vt quotidie in iustitia, & sanctimonia proficiat, & sic seipsum superet, donec tandem perfectionem assequatur, ille Deo per Christum non vere obedit, quandoquidem vera imitationis natura in hoc consistit, nempe vt operam demus, quo tandem æquales siamus illi, quem imitamur. Quinta: Qui verò hunc eundem scopum sibi habet præfixum, etiamsi perfectionis metam non assequatur, Deo tamen vere obedire dicitur, quandoquidem vt quis dici possit, Christum reuera imitari, non necesse est, vt ipsum exaquet, & per omnia ipsi æqualis sit, sed hoc tantum, vt reuera iustus, & sanctus sit, quemadmodum Christus est.
units.tr: Next the opponent sets out how far that obedience extends which we are bound to render to the precepts of Christ, and without which God does not wish to justify a man? Or: what is required of a man, so that it may rightly be said of him that he obeys the precepts of Christ? We shall reduce the opponent's view to definite theses, and then answer each one. The first thesis is: Just as God the Father set his Son before us as the example of all those whom he is himself going to bestow upon us after this life, so also he has given us the same Son as an example to be imitated and followed in this life. The second: Therefore we must strive, labour and apply ourselves to this, that we become as much like Christ himself as possible, and perfect, and in no way transgress the commandments of God. The third: If God did not require of us this purpose and pursuit of perfection, he would never have set before us so perfect a pattern of the virtues; nor is there any doubt that through the greatest diligence and the grace of God a man can become perfect. The fourth: He who does not have this goal set before him, namely that he daily make progress in righteousness and holiness, and so surpass himself, until at last he attains perfection, does not truly obey God through Christ, since the true nature of imitation consists in this, that we take pains to become at last equal to him whom we imitate. The fifth: But he who has this same goal set before him, even if he does not reach the mark of perfection, is nevertheless said to obey God truly; for in order that one may be said to imitate Christ in fact, it is not necessary that he equal him and be in all things his equal, but only that he be really righteous and holy, as Christ is.

units.la: Resp. Ex hisce quinque thesibus facile videre est, quænam sit Aduersarii de proposita ab ipso quæstione sententia: quia verò propositam illam quæstionem ita explicet, vt nouas nobis lites & controuersias moueat: ideò vt perspicua, aperta,& solida sit, ad omnia, quæ quinque illis thesibus comprehenduntur, responsio nostra, quæstiones illas controuersias proponem is. eásque ita que ita excutiemus, vt inde clare elucescat, quid de singulis illis thesibus fit sentiendum. Quæstio igitur prima est: An homo, in hac vita, Christum possit imitari? Secunda : An homo, in hac vita Christum perfecte imitari possit? Seu : An homo in hac vita perfectam obedientiam præceptis Dei, per Christum latis, præstare possit? Tertia: An illa obedientia, quæ præceptis Christi præstatur, seu imitatio illa Christi, homini ad iustitiam imputetur, seu an homo per eam iustificetur? Quia vero illarum quæstionum subiectum propter duplicem hominis etiam post lapsum considerati statum, obscura ambiguitate inuolutum est, & de homine vel in statu corruptionis, & dominantis peccati, vel in statu gratiæ ac regenerationis intelligi potest: ideo ad singulas non simpliciter, sed distinctè nobis respondendum erit.
units.tr: Answer. From these five theses it is easy to see what the opponent's view is on the question he has proposed. But since he explains the proposed question in such a way as to stir up new quarrels and controversies for us, therefore, so that our answer may be clear, open and sound, we shall set out the questions that these five theses contain, and examine them in such a way that it becomes plain what is to be thought of each of these theses. The first question, then, is: Can a man in this life imitate Christ? The second: Can a man in this life imitate Christ perfectly? Or: Can a man in this life render perfect obedience to the precepts of God given through Christ? The third: Is that obedience which is rendered to the precepts of Christ, or that imitation of Christ, imputed to a man for righteousness, or is a man justified by it? But since the subject of these questions is wrapped in obscure ambiguity, on account of the twofold state of man, considered even after the fall, and can be understood of man either in the state of corruption and dominant sin or in the state of grace and regeneration, therefore we must answer each one not simply but with distinctions.

units.la: Quæstionem igitur primam quantum concernit, si illa de homine animali, ac non regenito, sed in natiuæ cæcitatis, ac dominantis peccati statu cōstituto intelligatur, tum negamus, hominem ciusmodi, Christum iustitia & sanctimonia vitæ, vlla ratione imitari posse. Cùm enim homo animalis, priusquam Spiritus sancti gratia imbuatur, nec intelligere res spirituales, nec velle ac perficere possit actiones sanctas ac Deo placentes, sed peccati iugo ac seruitute Sathanæ totus opprimatur, imò in peccatis & iniquitatibus penitus mortuus sit, nec aliud quicquam nisi peccare queat, adeo vt tota ipsius vita nihil aliud sit, quàm perpetuum quoddam peccatorum curriculū, priusquam Deus ipsi gratia sua illuxerit, quemadmodum capite vigesimosexto & vigesimoseptimo ex Scripturis sacris solidè demonstrauimus, ideo sanctimonia & integritate vitæ Christum imitari non potest. Si vero quæstio illa intelligatur de homine regenito, & in statu gratiæ & libertatis spiritualis constituto, tum dicimus, ipsum debere & posse Christum imitari, licèt propter humanam fragilitatē, & carnis reliquias, à iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ via ac tramite interdum exorbitet, & in illo imitationis cursu, modò leuius, modò grauius impingat, nec perfectionis illius, cuius laudibus & gloria Christus illustris est, metā, in hac vita, nunquam assequatur. Atque hoc sensu thesi secundę & quintę vtro adstipulamur, primam vero eatenus admittimus, quatenus videlicet Christum ita nobis in exemplum propositum esse statuit, vt tamen meritum & satisfactio Christi, cum reliquis functionibus, & actionibus sacerdotalibus, non excludatur. Quæstionem secundam quod attinet, ne hominem quidem renatum, atque per Spiritum Christi, ex illa seruitute ac dominio peccati liberatum, nedum animalem, & peccati seruum, Christum perfecte imitari, aut eam obedientiam præceptis diuinis præstare posse, vt lex nihil habeat, quod in vita, dictis, factis, & cogitationib. ipsius reprehendat, & ille operum suorum ac vitæ integritate seuero Dei iudicio respondere queat, grauissimis argumentis & rationibus adducti, affirmamus. Quicunque enim legem Dei perfecte implent, quemadmodum Christus illam exactissime impleuit, perfectámque obedientiam præstant, illi quoque sibi possunt arrogare ἀναμάρτητον, saltem ab illo tempore, quo Christum perfecte imitari, & legem perfecte implere inceperunt: quia ἀναμάρτητον, immaculatum ac penitus inculpatum esse, & Christum perfecte imitari, seu perfectam obedientiam lege requisitam præstare, æquipollent: Atqui nullus renatorum, ne sanctissimus quidem, & in quem tanta cadit perfectio virtutis, quanta in huius vitæ spatio in hominem cadere potest, ἀναμάρτητον sibi arrogare audet, 1. Reg. 8. v. 46. Non est homo qui non peccet. Eccles. 7. v. 21. Non est iustus in terra qui faciat bonum, & non peccet. Pro. 24. v. 16. Septies cadit iustus, & resurgit. 1. Ioh. 1. v. 8. Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas non est in nobis. Et omnes cum Dauide clamare coguntur: Ne intres Domine in iudicium cum seruo tuo, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens, Psalm 145. v. 2. Item: Si iniquitates observaueris Domine, Domine quis sustinebit? Psalm. 130. v. 3 Et cum tota Ecclesia: Remitte nobis debita nostra. Ergo nullus renatorum, ne sanctissimus quidem, Christum in hac vita perfecte imitari, aut partibus & gradibus omnibus perfectam, qualem lex requirit, obedientiam præstare potest. Deinde: Qui Christum in hac vita perfecte imitari, & imitando perfectionem virtutum ipsius æquci, ac proinde accuratissimam obedientiam lege requisitam præstare possunt, illi diligunt Deum ex toto corde suo, ex tota anima sua, & ex tota cogitatione sua, proximum autem sicut seipsos. Matt. 22. v. 37. 39. Atqui nullus homo in hac vita Deum diligit ex toto corde suo, ex tota anima sua, & tota cogitatione sua, quod ex Spiritus & innatæ concupiscentiæ lucta, qua caro aduersus spiritum, & spiritus aduersus carnem perpetuo concupiscit, vt non quæcunque volumus faciamus, Galat. 5. v. 17. apparet: Ergo nullus in hac vita Christum perfecte imitatur, & imitando perfectionem virtutum ipsius æquci, ac proinde neque acque accuratissimā illam, quæ à lege requiritur, obedientiam præstare potest.Tertiò, eadē veritas sententiæ nostræ etiam inde probatur, quod regeneratio nostri in hac vita nec momentanea est, nec perfecta: momentanea non est, quia non vno momento perficitur, sed per quotidiana incrementa indies prouehitur ac promouetur: perfecta non est ob concupiscentiæ originalis labem perpetuò etiam in ipsis renatis in hac vita remanentem, cuius vires, quandiu homo hoc mortale circumfert corpus, nūquam penitus extinguntur. Vtrunque inde demonstratur euidentissimè, tū quod Apostolus iubet fideles incumbere in studium renouationis mentis, vt Rom.12.v.2. Ne configuremini seculo isti, sed transformemini per renouationem mentis vestræ, ad hoc, vt probetis, quæ sit voluntas illa bona, accepta ac perfecta. 2.Cor. 4.v.16. Etiamsi externus homo noster corrumpitur, interuus tamen renouatur quotidie: Ephes.4.v.22.23.24. Si edocti fuistis deponere quod ad pristinam conuersationem attinet, veterem illum hominem, qui deceptricibus cupiditatibus corrumpitur, renouari verò spiritu mentis vestræ, & induere nouum illum hominem, qui secundum Deum conditus est, ad iustitiam, & sanctimoniam veram: tum etiam quia idem Apostolus Deum precatur, vt fidelium mentem renouet: Ephes.cap.1.vers.17.18. Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Pater illæ gloriæ det vobis Spiritum sapientiæ, ac reuelationis per agnitionem ipsius: illuminatis oculis mentis vestræ, vt sciatis, quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius in sanctis. Vnde iam necessariò sequitur duplicem esse in homine renato potentiam, & agendi principium internum, sanctitatis nimirum, & corruptionis primitias spiritus, ac noui hominis, & reliquias carnis, ac veteris hominis, ac proinde ipsum in hac vita perfectam obedientiam præstare non posse. Denique mirabilis esset illa in homine potentia, quam hactenus ex tot millesenis millibus nec vnus quidem in actum producere potuit. Atque hinc apparet, thesin tertiam falsam esse, quartam verò ex secunda sic corrigendam: Quod ille veram Deo obedientiam præstare non possit dici, qui non in hoc studio summo incumbit, & elaborat, vt vestigia virtutum & sanctimoniæ Christi, quantum fieri potest, sequatur, neve peccando, & leges diuinas transgrediendo, misericordem & benignum Deum nostrum offendat, & ad iram prouocet: qui verò &c. Quæstionem verò tertiam, & vltimam, quantum concernit, obedientiā operum, quocunque etiam sensu Aduersarii opera interpretētur, seu imitationem Christi, non esse materiā iustificationis scu,non esse id quod nobis ad iustitiam imputatur, ex iis, quæ capite trigesimosecundo & trigesimotertio, de iustificationis nostræ causis disseruimus, manifestum est: Quibus hac vice hoc tantummodò addo, quod ille quem Deus iustificat, in se consideratus est impius: Roman.capite quarto,veriu quinto & sexto, Ei qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides sua adjustitiam. Atqui ille qui facit iustitiam, ex hypothesi Aduersariorum, non impius, sed reuera iustus est: unde necessario sequitur, hominem quatenus præceptis diuinis obtemperat, iustificationis subiectum non esse, ac proinde bona nostra opera, materiam iustificationis falsò constitui, quippe quæ iustificatio nihil aliud est, quàm iustitia ad subiectum priuatiuum, & iustitia destitutum applicatio,iustitia autem omni destitutus nō est, qui Christum assiduè imitando,debitam obedientiam præceptis diuinis præstat,vel etiam præstare conatur.
units.tr: Taking the first question as far as it concerns the matter: if it is understood of the natural man, not regenerate but placed in the state of native blindness and dominant sin, then we deny that a man of this kind can in any way imitate Christ in righteousness and holiness of life. For since the natural man, before he is imbued with the grace of the Holy Spirit, can neither understand spiritual things nor will or perform holy actions pleasing to God, but is wholly oppressed under the yoke of sin and the slavery of Satan, and indeed is utterly dead in sins and iniquities, and can do nothing but sin, so that his whole life is nothing other than a continual course of sins before God shines his grace upon him, as we have solidly demonstrated from the sacred Scriptures in chapters twenty-six and twenty-seven, therefore he cannot imitate Christ in holiness and integrity of life. But if the question is understood of the regenerate man, placed in the state of grace and spiritual liberty, then we say that he ought to and can imitate Christ, although, on account of human frailty and the remnants of the flesh, he sometimes strays from the way and path of righteousness and holiness, and in that course of imitation stumbles now more lightly, now more heavily, and never attains in this life the goal of that perfection by whose praises and glory Christ is made illustrious. In this sense we agree with the second and fifth theses, but the first we admit only so far as it is stated that Christ has been set before us as an example in such a way that yet the merit and satisfaction of Christ, together with the remaining sacerdotal functions and actions, is not excluded. As to the second question, we affirm, on very weighty arguments and reasons, that not even the regenerate man, freed from that slavery and dominion of sin by the Spirit of Christ, far less the natural man and servant of sin, can perfectly imitate Christ, or render such obedience to the divine precepts that the law has nothing in his life, words, deeds and thoughts to reprove, and that he can answer with the integrity of his works and life before the severe judgment of God. For whoever perfectly fulfils the law of God, as Christ fulfilled it most exactly and renders perfect obedience, can also claim for himself ἀναμάρτητον (sinlessness), at least from the time when they began to imitate Christ perfectly and to fulfil the law perfectly; for to be ἀναμάρτητον, that is, spotless and wholly blameless, and to imitate Christ perfectly, or to render the perfect obedience required by the law, are equivalent. But no one of the regenerate, not even the most holy, and upon whom falls as great a perfection of virtue as can fall upon a man in the span of this life, dares to claim ἀναμάρτητον for himself: 1 Kings 8:46, "There is no man who does not sin." Eccles. 7:21, "There is not a just man upon earth who does good and does not sin." Prov. 24:16, "A just man falls seven times and rises again." 1 John 1:8, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." And all are compelled to cry out with David: "Enter not into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living man shall be justified," Psalm 143:2. Likewise: "If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" Psalm 130:3. And with the whole Church: "Forgive us our debts." Therefore no one of the regenerate, not even the most holy, can perfectly imitate Christ in this life, or render in all parts and degrees the perfect obedience that the law requires. Next: those who in this life can perfectly imitate Christ, and by imitating equal the perfection of his virtues, and accordingly render the most exact obedience required by the law, those love God with their whole heart, with their whole soul, and with their whole mind, and their neighbour as themselves, Matt. 22:37, 39. But no man in this life loves God with his whole heart, with his whole soul, and with his whole mind, as is evident from the struggle between the Spirit and innate concupiscence, by which "the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do whatever you wish," Gal. 5:17. Therefore no one in this life perfectly imitates Christ, and by imitating equals the perfection of his virtues, and accordingly cannot render that most exact obedience which the law requires. Thirdly, the same truth of our position is also proved from this: that our regeneration in this life is neither momentary nor perfect. It is not momentary, because it is not completed in one moment, but is advanced and promoted day by day through daily increases; it is not perfect, because of the stain of original concupiscence which remains continually in the regenerate themselves in this life, whose powers, as long as a man carries this mortal body, are never wholly extinguished. Both points are demonstrated most clearly from this: that the Apostle bids the faithful to devote themselves to the study of the renewal of the mind, Rom. 12:2, "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good, acceptable and perfect will." 2 Cor. 4:16, "Even if our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Eph. 4:22-24, "If you have been taught to put off, as concerns your former conversation, the old man who is corrupted by deceitful lusts, and to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and to put on the new man, who after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." Then also because the same Apostle prays that God would renew the mind of the faithful: Eph. 1:17-18, "May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your mind being enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling among the saints." Hence it necessarily follows that in the regenerate man there is a twofold power and internal principle of acting, namely the first-fruits of holiness of the spirit and of the new man, and the remnants of the flesh and of the old man; and therefore he cannot render perfect obedience in this life. Finally, that power would be a marvellous thing in a man, which hitherto, out of so many thousands of thousands, not one has been able to bring into act. From this it appears that the third thesis is false, and the fourth must be corrected from the second thus: "That he cannot be said to render true obedience to God who does not devote himself with the greatest zeal and labour to follow, as far as possible, the footsteps of the virtues and holiness of Christ, and who does not, by sinning and transgressing the divine laws, offend and provoke to anger our merciful and kind God; but he who etc." As to the third and last question, so far as it concerns the obedience of works, in whatever sense the Adversary may interpret the works, or the imitation of Christ, it is clear from what we set out in chapters thirty-two and thirty-three, on the causes of our justification, that it is not the matter of justification, nor that which is imputed to us for righteousness. To these points I add for now only this: that the one whom God justifies is, considered in himself, ungodly. Rom. 4:5, "To him who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness." But he who does righteousness, on the hypothesis of the Adversaries, is not ungodly but is truly just; whence it necessarily follows that man, insofar as he obeys the divine precepts, is not the subject of justification, and therefore our good works are falsely constituted as the matter of justification, since justification is nothing other than the application of righteousness to a subject who is privative, and destitute of righteousness; but he who by constantly imitating Christ renders, or even attempts to render, due obedience to the divine precepts, is not destitute of righteousness.

units.la: Atque ex illis thesibus suis infert Ostorrodius: Cauendum igitur esse, inquiens, ab errore tum Nouatianorum, & modernorum Perfectistarum,existimantium, illum verum Christianum non esse æstimandum, qui iustitia & sanctitate, Christo non plane sit æqualis: tum verò maxime ab illorum Euangelicorum, qui statuunt, hominis Christiani iustitiam & sanctimoniam in pio tantum sanctè pieque viuendi proposito, conatuque, & exiguo virtutum initio, consistere, nostrámque iustitiam & sanctimoniam, tantùm quantùm cælum à terra distat, à iustitia & sanctimonia Christi differre. Hanc verò sententiam & doctrinam plane falsam esse, ex illo Iohannis testimonio demonstrari posse, 1.epist. capite quarto, versu decimoseptimo: Per hoc expleta est charitas in nobis, vt fiduciam habeamus in die iudicii, quod qualis ille est, & nos sumus in hoc mundo. Ac proinde, ait, inter hosce duos errores mediam viam incundam esse, quæ sit, vt iustus & sanctus is censeatur,cuius operæ vt plurimum iusta & sancta sunt, etiamsi ille interdum non quidem studio,aut destinata malitia,sed ex humana imbecillitate aliquid designet, quod iustitia & sanctimonia non est consentaneum, quandoquidem infirmitas humana admodum magna sit, & perfectionem vix assequatur. Huius itaque fragilitatis Deum, addit, misertum, non voluisse stricto iure nobiscum agere, sed nobis per Christum non modò præteritorum peccatorum remissionem pollicitum esse, sed etiam velle nos tales æstimare, quasi ipsius mandata perpetuo obseruassemus, etiamsi interdum impingamus, modò vestigia Christi pro virili. virili sequamur, nostramque vitam, secundum normam praeceptorum ipsius instituamus, sic ut merito non secundum carnem, sed secundum Spiritum ambulare dici queamus. Hoc enim sufficere nobis ad hoc, ut extra damnationis periculum constituamur, aut illi non obnoxii simus, & ius illud legis in nobis impleatur, docente id Apostolo capite octano, Epistola ad Romanos.
units.tr: And from those theses of his Ostorrodius infers: "We must beware, therefore," he says, "of the error both of the Novatians and of the modern Perfectists, who think that a man is not to be reckoned a true Christian unless he is wholly equal to Christ in righteousness and holiness; and still more of the error of those Evangelicals who hold that the righteousness and holiness of a Christian consist only in a pious purpose and effort to live holily and piously, and in a small beginning of virtues, and that our righteousness and holiness differ from the righteousness and holiness of Christ as far as heaven is from earth. That this opinion and doctrine is plainly false can be shown from that testimony of John in the first Epistle, chapter 4, verse 17: 'By this is love made perfect in us, that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world.' And therefore," he says, "a middle way is to be taken between these two errors, namely that a man is to be judged righteous and holy whose works for the most part are just and holy, even if he sometimes, not from zeal or settled malice but from human weakness, does something that does not agree with righteousness and holiness, since human frailty is very great and scarcely attains perfection. God, having mercy on this frailty," he adds, "was not willing to deal with us by strict right, but has promised us through Christ not only the forgiveness of past sins, but also wishes us to be reckoned as if we had kept his commandments perpetually, even if we sometimes stumble, provided we follow the footsteps of Christ to the best of our power and order our life according to the rule of his precepts, so that we may rightly be said to walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For this is enough for us to be placed outside the danger of condemnation, or to be not liable to it, and for that demand of the law to be fulfilled in us, as the Apostle teaches in the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans."

units.la: <bl>Resp.</bl> Nouatianorum, ac Perfectistarum errorem grauissimum suis autoribus, ac patronis excusandum ac defendendum relinquo, alterum vero errorem, quem Oftorrodius, illis exprobrat, qui Euangelicam veritatem profitentur, quantum attinet, Aduersarius, aut ambiguitate ludit, aut à praesente quaestione aberrat, & sic crimen illud Ecclesiis nostris falso impingit. Iustitiam enim nostri distinguunt, in vniuersalem, ac particularem: iustitiam vniuersalem distinguunt, in iustitiam personę, aut nouae obedientiae: particularem in iustitiam causae, aut facti alicuius particularis. Si itaque Aduersarius loquatur de iustitia personae qua videlicet homo conueniitus vel coram tribunali seuerae iustitiae diuinae iustus in se, & ex debito, ac vitae aeternae praemio dignus censetur à Deo secundum doctrinam legis: vel coram tribunali gratię remissionem peccatorum, & vitam aeternam consequitur, secundum promissiones Euangelicas: tum verissimè negamus, Ecclesias Euangelicas, aut Doctores ipsarum, iustitiam illam qua videlicet per & propter quam iusti à Deo, ac vita aeterna digni pronuntiamur, in pio, sancte & iuste viuendi proposito, aut virtutum initio collocare, quum notum sit omnes orthodoxos, vnanimi consensu docere ac profiteri, iustitiam illam esse iustitiam Christi, nobis per fidem imputatam: quemadmodum ex harmonia confessionum, & catechismis nostris apparet. A iustitia vero Christi, & sanctitatis perfectione, virtutumque omnium splendore & excellentia, iustitiam nostram, inhaerentem videlicet, quàm longissimè abesse, à summa illa naturae humanae imbecillitate, ac infirmitate, & illa, quae inter perfectionem iustitiae, ac obedientiae, quam lex à nobis exigit, & virtutes nostras est, ἀσυμμετρία, deinde à carnis, & concupiscentiae originalis reliquiis, & regenerationis, ac renouationis natura, denique à grauissimis illis, hominum etiam sanctissimorum lapsibus, & peccatis, ad demonstrandam veritatem sententiae nostrae (de qua paulò ante quoque egimus). euidentissima argumenta desumuntur. Hanc vero doctrinam nostram locus ille ex 1. Ioh. 4. v. 17. allegatus, minime euertit aut impugnat, quum ille de imagine ac similitudine, qua videlicet Deum per gratiam Spiritus sancti nos renouantis & regenerantis, proximum syncero, & in fide iustificante ceu radice fundato animi affectu amando ac diligendo, referre debemus, agat, thesis vero nostra de æqualitate obedientiæ ac iustitiæ Christi & nostræ loquatur, quæ ex illa similitudine & imagine Dei in nobis instaurata, demonstrari minimè potest. Quemadmodum enim ipso Aduersario fatente, Christum vere imitari is dicitur, qui resipiscentiæ & virtutum Christianarum studio indesinenter ac serio incumbit, etiamsi æqualem perfectionem, Christi perfectioni non assequatur: ita etiam Deum, & Christum vera imagine & similitudine referre censendus est, qui relectis omnibus animi turbidis affectibus, crucifixa carne per virtutem mortis ac sepulturæ Christi, & abnegata impietate, ac mundanis cupiditatibus, non cōcupiscentiarum impetum, sed Spiritus diuini duclum sequi, omnes mundi illecebras contemnere & aspernari, mentemque & animum ab omni prauitate & intemperie auersum habere, ac sese cum omni modestia & sanctitate, Christo Domino, & Spiritui eius sancto, in obsequium dare, denique Christianam illam εὐσέβειαν pietate erga Deum, id est, puro ac syncero cius cultu, piáque nominis eius veneratione, recta inuocatione, & assidua verbi ipsius meditatione, atque iustitia, & omnibus charitatis officiis erga proximum testatam facere serio conatur, etiamsi propter carnis fragilitatem propositam perfectionis metam non assequatur: quum vera illa imitatio Christi, illa ipsa similitudo & imago Dei sit ad quā per Spiritum sanctum renouamur ac regeneramur, & quæ non tantum in iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ interno habitu consistit: sed virtutum Christianarum studio pietatis erga Deum, & charitatis erga proximum exercitio potissimum elucescit. Si vero Aduersarius de illa iustitiæ specie loquatur, quæ in vitæ sanctimonia integritate, ac nouitate consistit, tum omnia illa sunt ἀναστάσεως, quum ut iam monuimus, nullus nostrum illam iustitiam inhærentem, iustificationis nostræ coram Deo materiam constituat. Quod vero addit, nostros iustitiam illam in pio tantum iuste & sancte viuendi proposito conatúque, & exiguo virtutum initio collocare, falsum est, & falsò Ecclesiarum nostrarum Doctoribus impingitur, neque etiam sine iniuria sanctissimorum rum Dei hominum, quorum iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ, luculentissimum testimonium in Scripturis sacris, à Deo ipso perhibetur, idipsum affirmari potest. Sed quia Deus diuersa admodum mensura, nobis prout vult & fidem, & dona fidem consequentia, admetitur: ideo nostri inter iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ gradus, ad quos sancti in hac vita perue nientes, iustitiæ dotibus, ac splendore alii alios antecellunt, verissimè distinguunt, sic tamen, vt piū illud, & serium pie viuendi desiderium, verúmque ac syncerum Deo obediendi affectum, simulationi ac hypocrisi contrarium, suisque iam fructibus & effectis conspicuum, verae iustitiæ & sanctimoniæ titulo indigitandum esse doceant, etiamsi ad summum perfectionis gradum non peruenerit, quemadmodum etiam infans verissimè hominis nomine dignus censetur, qui omnia membra, ac partes hominis essentiam & naturam constituentes etiam in infantia habet, etiamsi perfectio staturæ & magnitudinis desit. Quæ omnia aut malitiosè Ostorrodius peruertit, aut imperitè confundit. De materia autem iustificationis, vt & de loco illo, ex capite octauo epistolæ ad Romanos, iam in antecedentibus aliquoties actum est. Atque sic locum illum de iustificatione hominis coram Deo, ad finem perduximus, Deus omnipotens ex ineffabili sua misericordia, largiatur nobis gratiam, vt magnitudinem beneficiorum ipsius agnoscentes ac celebrantes, debitæ gratitudinis officia serio præstemus, ipsi cum Filio, ac Spiritu sancto sit laus, honor, & gloria, in secula, Amen.
units.tr: Answer. I leave the error of the Novatians and the Perfectists, which is very grave, to be excused and defended by their own authors and patrons. As for the other error, which Ostorrodius charges against those who profess the Evangelical truth, the opponent either plays on an ambiguity or strays from the present question, and so falsely fastens that charge on our Churches. For we distinguish righteousness into universal and particular. Universal righteousness we distinguish into the righteousness of the person, or of new obedience; particular righteousness into the righteousness of a cause, or of some particular act. If the opponent therefore speaks of the righteousness of the person, by which a man is judged righteous, in himself and by right, and worthy of the reward of eternal life by God before the tribunal of strict divine justice according to the doctrine of the law, or before the tribunal of grace obtains forgiveness of sins and eternal life according to the Evangelical promises, then we most truly deny that the Evangelical Churches or their teachers place that righteousness, by which and on account of which we are pronounced righteous and worthy of God and eternal life, in a pious, holy and upright purpose of living, or in a beginning of virtues. For it is well known that all the orthodox teach and profess with one accord that this righteousness is the righteousness of Christ, imputed to us through faith, as appears from the harmony of the confessions and from our catechisms. And that our righteousness, namely inherent righteousness, is very far from the righteousness and perfection of holiness of Christ, from the splendour and excellence of all virtues, is shown by the most evident arguments: from that highest weakness and infirmity of human nature, from that disproportion [ἀσυμμετρία] which lies between the perfection of righteousness and obedience that the law demands of us and our virtues, then from the remnants of the flesh and original concupiscence, and from the nature of regeneration and renewal, and finally from those very grave lapses and sins even of the holiest men. These arguments are used to demonstrate the truth of our view, which I have also discussed a little earlier. That passage from 1 John 4:17, which the opponent cites, in no way overturns or attacks this doctrine of ours, since it speaks of the image and likeness, by which we ought to resemble God through the grace of the Holy Spirit who renews and regenerates us, namely the love and affection of the soul toward a neighbour that is sincere and rooted in justifying faith as in a root. Our thesis, however, speaks of the equality of the obedience and righteousness of Christ and of ours, which cannot be demonstrated from that likeness and image of God restored in us. For just as the opponent himself admits, he is said truly to imitate Christ who applies himself unceasingly and earnestly to repentance and to the pursuit of Christian virtues, even if he does not attain perfection equal to the perfection of Christ. So too he is to be regarded as bearing the true image and likeness of God and of Christ who, having cast off all turbulent affections of the mind, having crucified the flesh through the power of the death and burial of Christ, and having renounced impiety and worldly desires, follows not the impulse of concupiscence but the leading of the divine Spirit, despises and spurns all the allurements of the world, keeps mind and soul turned away from all wickedness and intemperance, and gives himself in all modesty and holiness to Christ the Lord and to his Holy Spirit in obedience; and who in the end earnestly strives to show forth that Christian piety [εὐσέβειαν], that is, toward God, in his pure and sincere worship, in pious reverence of his name, in right invocation and constant meditation on his Word, and in righteousness and in all the duties of charity toward his neighbour, even if on account of the frailty of the flesh he does not reach the goal of perfection set before him. For that true imitation of Christ, that very likeness and image of God, is that to which we are renewed and regenerated through the Holy Spirit, and it does not consist only in the inner habit of righteousness and holiness, but shines forth chiefly in the zeal for Christian virtues, in piety toward God and in the exercise of charity toward our neighbour. If, however, the opponent speaks of that species of righteousness which consists in the holiness and integrity and newness of life, then all those things are irrelevant [ἀναστάσεως], since, as we have already noted, none of us makes that inherent righteousness the matter of our justification before God. As for his further claim, that our people place that righteousness only in a pious purpose and effort to live justly and holily and in a small beginning of virtues, that is false, and it is falsely charged against the teachers of our Churches; nor can the same be asserted without injury to the holiest men of God, to whose righteousness and holiness God himself bears the most splendid testimony in the sacred Scriptures. But because God measures out to us, as he wills, both faith and the gifts that follow faith, in very different measure, our people rightly distinguish among the degrees of righteousness and holiness, to which the saints attain in this life, and some surpass others in the gifts and splendour of righteousness. Yet they teach that the pious and earnest desire to live piously, and the true and sincere affection to obey God, which is opposed to pretence and hypocrisy and is already visible in its own fruits and effects, is to be designated by the title of true righteousness and holiness, even if it has not reached the highest degree of perfection. Just as an infant is rightly considered a man, though he is not yet full grown, since he has all the members and parts that make up the essence and nature of a man even in infancy, even though he lacks the perfection of stature and size. Ostorrodius either maliciously distorts all these points or foolishly confuses them. The matter of justification, and also the passage from the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, has already been discussed several times in what precedes. Thus we have brought our treatment of this passage on the justification of man before God to its end. May almighty God, out of his ineffable mercy, grant us grace so that, acknowledging and celebrating the greatness of his benefits, we may seriously render the duties of due gratitude; to him, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be praise, honour and glory, for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXXVII. DE OFFICIO CHRISTI REGIO.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII. ON THE KINGLY OFFICE OF CHRIST.

units.la: In quo duæ illæ quæstiones controuersæ: Primò: An dignitas illa, & maiestas Regia Christi præcipua sit causa propter quam ille Saluator, & Deus noster, ac Dei Filius sit, &c. in sacris Scripturis appelletur? Deinde: An Sacerdotium Christi nihil aliud sit, quam regij muneris Christi, administratio, ac proinde non proprie, sed figurate intelligendum? breuiter explicantur, veritas defenditur, ac falsitas refutatur.
units.tr: Two controverted questions are at issue here. First: is that dignity and kingly majesty of Christ the principal reason why that Saviour and our God, the Son of God, is called so in the holy Scriptures? Second: is the priesthood of Christ nothing other than the administration of his kingly office, and so to be understood not properly but figuratively? These questions are briefly explained, the truth is defended, and the falsehood is refuted.

units.la: ACTENVS, quid de Libero hominis Arbitrio, eiusque viribus, de æterna Dei prædestinatione, item de Fide iustificante, denique de iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo & eius causis sentiendum, atque credendum sit, ex verbo Dei dilucidè ostendimus, & doctrinam orthodoxam aduersus Samosatenianorum errores & sophismata defendimus. Hisce autem capitibus subiicit Aduersarius Institutionum suarum capite trigesimooctauo, & trigesimonono, doctrinam ac disputationem de Sacramentis, Coena Domini videlicet, & Baptismo: verum quia omnia illa, quae vel ad explicationem illius rei, vel ad veritatis defensionem requiruntur, tam abundè passim à doctissimis Viris tractata, & exposita sunt, vt actum, quod dicitur agere, aut videatur, qui illis aliquid adiicere vellet: ideo illa duo capita lubens praetereo, & me ad caput quadragesimum, in quo de officio Christi Regio, & huius occasione, de Sacerdotio Christi agitur, confero. Et quia Regii illius officii definitionem iam supra capite vigesimotertio Defensionis nostrae tradidimus, atque ex Scripturis sacris demonstrauimus: ideo nihil restat, nisi vt ἀνακεφαλαιώσωμεν, & examen instituamus eorum, quae ab Aduersario hac de re docentur, ac proponuntur.
units.tr: Up to this point we have shown clearly from the Word of God what is to be felt and believed about man's free will and its powers, about the eternal predestination of God, likewise about justifying faith, and finally about the justification of sinful man before God and its causes, and we have defended the orthodox doctrine against the errors and sophisms of the Samosatenians. To these chapters the Adversary, in chapters thirty-eight and thirty-nine of his Institutes, adds a teaching and discussion about the sacraments, namely the Lord's Supper and Baptism. But since everything that is required either to explain those matters or to defend the truth has already been handled and set forth everywhere by very learned men, so that anyone who wished to add something to them would seem to be doing what has already been done, I gladly pass over those two chapters and turn to the fortieth chapter, in which the kingly office of Christ is treated and, on this occasion, the priesthood of Christ. And since we have already given the definition of that kingly office in chapter twenty-three of our Defence and demonstrated it from the holy Scriptures, nothing remains but to sum up (ἀνακεφαλαιώσωμεν) and to examine what the Adversary teaches and sets forth on this matter.

units.la: Tria itaque, praedicto capite tractat Oftorrodius.
units.tr: Osiorrodius treats three things in the said chapter.

units.la: Primò ostendit ac demonstrat primis sex sectionibus, idque aduersus Chiliastas, seu Millenarios, ac Cerinthianos, Christum iam reuera Regem, ac Dominum nostrum esse, & omni potestate in cælo, ac terra donatum, regnum suum possidere, & illud spirituali ac diuino modo gubernare & administrare.
units.tr: First, in the first six sections he shows and demonstrates, against the Chiliasts, or Millenarians, and the Cerinthians, that Christ is now in truth our King and Lord, has been given all power in heaven and on earth, possesses his kingdom, and governs and administers it in a spiritual and divine manner.

units.la: Secundo, probare conatur, dignitatem ac maiestatem illam Christiregiam praecipuam causam esse, ob quam Christus Seruator & Deus noster, ac Dei Filius sit, & in Scripturis sacris appelletur.
units.tr: Second, he tries to prove that that kingly dignity and majesty of Christ is the chief cause on account of which Christ is called the Saviour and our God, and the Son of God, in the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Tertiò, demonstrare vult, Sacerdotium Christi nihil aliud esse, quàm muneris ipsius Regij administrationem, & exequutionem, ac proinde non proprie, sed figuratè intelligendum.
units.tr: Third, he wishes to show that the priesthood of Christ is nothing other than the exercise and execution of his kingly office, and so is to be understood not properly but figuratively.

units.la: Et primum quidem tractationis ac disputationis huius caput quantum concernit, quum internos & Aduersarios, quod ad thesin ipsam attinet, nulla fit dissensio & controuersia, licet Ostorrodius in veritatis defensione interdum impingat, & à recto tramite aberret: ideo ad duarum sequentium thesium refutationem progrediemur.
units.tr: As far as the first part of this treatment and discussion is concerned, there is no disagreement or controversy between us and the Adversaries regarding the thesis itself, although Osiorrodius sometimes stumbles in defending the truth and wanders from the straight path. We will therefore proceed to refute the two following theses.

units.la: Secundum igitur disputationis caput, atque thesin quod attinet, quia tria diuersa praedicata in illa de subiecto enuntiantur, & quae diuersis argumentis tum ab Aduersario muniuntur, tum etiam à nobis refutantur: ideo singula praedicata cum suo subiecto seorsim disponemus, & de tribus illis quaestionibus sigillatim disputiciemus: Primò, An haec Regia Christi dignitas, & maiestas praecipua sit causa ob quam videlicet Christus Seruator noster appellatur? Secundò: An eadem illa dignitas, ac maiestas Regia praecipua sit causa propter quam Christus Deus sit, & in Scripturis sacris Deus vocetur? Tertiò: An eadem illa dignitas, ac maiestas Regia praecipua sit causa, cur Christus Dei Filius sit, & appelletur?
units.tr: Regarding the second part of the discussion and its thesis: since three different predicates are asserted in it of the subject, which the Adversary supports with various arguments and which we also refute, we will set out each predicate separately with its subject and discuss those three questions one by one: First, Is this kingly dignity and majesty of Christ the chief cause for which Christ is called our Saviour? Second: Is that same dignity and kingly majesty the chief cause why Christ is God and is called God in the holy Scriptures? Third: Is that same dignity and kingly majesty the chief cause why Christ is and is called the Son of God?

units.la: Ostorrodius omnes illas tres affirmat: nos contrà negamus. Et quoniam primam quaestionem, capite trigesimoquarto prolixè tractauimus, nec Aduersarius hoc loco argumentum vllum aliud ad stabiliendam, sententiam, ac doctrinam suam adducit: ideo nos illa omissa, ad duarum sequentium tractationem pergemus.
units.tr: Osiorrodius affirms all three; we on the contrary deny them. Since we have treated the first question at length in chapter thirty-four, and the Adversary in this place brings forward no other argument to establish his opinion and doctrine, we will set that question aside and proceed to the treatment of the two following.

units.la: Secundam igitur quantum concernit: Eandem ob causam, inquit Ostorrodius, Christus merito Deus noster, id est, diuinum gubernator haberi ac censeri debet. Nam si Iohannes ipsum propter munus eius Propheticum Deum appellauit, quemadmodum capite decimo demonstrauimus, tum multo magis propter regnum ipsius, quod plane diuinum est, Deus appellari ac haberi debet.
units.tr: As for the second question: for the same reason, says Osiorrodius, Christ ought rightly to be held and considered our God, that is, the divine governor. For if John called him God on account of his prophetic office, as we showed in chapter ten, then much more on account of his kingdom, which is plainly divine, he ought to be called and held God.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Si Christus, propter officium ipsius Propheticum, à Iohanne Deus appellatus est, tum multò magis propter regnum ipsius diui-num Deus appellari ac haberi debet:
units.tr: If Christ was called God by John on account of his prophetic office, then much more ought he to be called and held God on account of his divine kingdom:

units.la: Atqui prius verum, & capite decimo demonstratum est:
units.tr: But the former is true, and was demonstrated in chapter ten:

units.la: Ergo & posterius verum est.
units.tr: Therefore the latter is also true.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem esse falsam, quemadmodum ex defensio-nis nostræ capite vigesimotertio & decimoquarto, in quo omnia illa, quæ Osiorrodius Institutionum suarum capite decimo, ad af-sumptionem illam stabiliendam adduxit, prolixè refutauimus, ap-paret. Deinde totum argumentum à propositá quæstione aberra-re: siquidem non hoc probandum incumbit Aduersario, An Christus propter officium ipsius Regium Deus sit & appellari possit? Sed, An præcipua causa, quare videlicet Christus Dei nomine indigitetur, ab illa dignitate Regia desumatur? Seu: An officium Christi Regium præcipua sit causa, ob quam ille Deus sit & vocetur? quod Aduersarii argumentum nec probat, nec concludit, nos autem verissimè negamus, & negationem nostram grauissimis & firmissimis argumentis muniimus, quemadmodum ex capitibus antecedentibus manifestè liquet.
units.tr: Answer: the assumption is false, as is clear from chapters twenty-three and fourteen of our Defence, where we thoroughly refuted everything that Osiorrodius, in chapter ten of his Institutes, brought forward to establish that assumption. Further, the whole argument strays from the question proposed. For the Adversary's task is not to prove whether Christ can be God and be called so on account of his kingly office, but whether the chief reason why Christ is designated by the name of God is drawn from that kingly dignity; or: whether the kingly office of Christ is the chief reason why he is God and is called so. The Adversary's argument neither proves nor concludes this; we, however, most truly deny it, and we support our denial with the weightiest and firmest arguments, as is plain from the preceding chapters.

units.la: Quæstionem tertiam quantum attinet, dicit Osiorrodius, Christum propter hoc idem regnum, etiam Filium Dei appellari: Atque hoc ipsum duobus argumentis probare conatur. Primum est: quia nihil sit, quod Christum Deo magis similem reddat, quàm hoc ipsum regnum. Similitudinem enim illam, quæ est inter Deum & hominem, homines filios Dei efficere, neminem esse, inquit, qui ignoret. Attamen quod ad illam similitudinem, quæ videlicet inter Deum & Christum ratione dominij intercedit, attinet, sciendum esse, quòd etiam alij homines propter dominium ipsorum, quod tamen dominio Christi nullo modo æquiparari potest, filij Dei nominati sunt. Psal. 82. verf. 6. Ego dixi: Dii estis & filii excelsi omnes. Si igitur illi, inquit, propter exiguam illam imperij similitudinem, filij Dei dicti sunt, tum multò magis ipse Christus, propter regnum suum, Filius Dei appellari debet, quandoquidem ex vi illius regni, non secus, ac Deus ipse, Dominus est omnium, solo Deo excepto.
units.tr: As for the third question, Osiorrodius says that Christ is also called the Son of God on account of this same kingdom. He tries to prove this by two arguments. The first is: because there is nothing that makes Christ more like God than this very kingdom. For, he says, no one is ignorant that the likeness between God and man by which men are made sons of God is something real. But as to that likeness which exists between God and Christ by reason of lordship, it must be understood that other men too have been called sons of God on account of their lordship, which nevertheless cannot in any way be compared with the lordship of Christ. Psalm 82, verse 6: "I have said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." If therefore, he says, they were called sons of God on account of that slight likeness of rule, then much more Christ himself ought to be called the Son of God on account of his kingdom, since by the power of that kingdom, just as God himself, he is Lord of all, God alone excepted.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows:

units.la: Si nihil est quod Christum Deo magis similem reddat, quàm quod ille talis Rex est: tum sequitur, ipsum etiam propter Regiam illam dignitatem Filium Dei appellari: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If there is nothing that makes Christ more like God than that he is such a King, then it follows that he is called the Son of God also on account of that royal dignity. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Connexi probationes duæ sunt: prima:
units.tr: There are two proofs of the connection. The first is this:

units.la: Si illa similitudo quæ est inter Deum & homines, homines Dei filios efficit: tum si nihil est, quod Christum Deo magis similem reddat, quàm quod ille talis Rex est: sequitur ipsum etiam propter Regiam illam dignitatem Filium Dei appellari.
units.tr: If that likeness which exists between God and men makes men the sons of God, then, if there is nothing that makes Christ more like God than that he is such a King, it follows that he is called the Son of God also on account of that royal dignity.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Posterior est:
units.tr: The second proof is this:

units.la: Si alij etiam homines propter dominium ipsorum, quod tamen dominio Christi nullo modo æquiparari potest, filij Dei nominati sunt: tum, si nihil est, quod Christum Deo magis similem reddat, quam quod ille talis Rex est, & illa similitudo inter Deum & Christum, longè excellentior est similitudine illa, quæ inter Deum & homines intercedit: sequitur Christum propter Regiam illam dignitatem Filium Dei appellari:
units.tr: If other men too have been called sons of God on account of their dominion, which nevertheless can in no way be compared with the dominion of Christ, then, if there is nothing that makes Christ more like God than that he is such a King, and if that likeness between God and Christ far surpasses the likeness that exists between God and men, it follows that Christ is called the Son of God on account of that royal dignity.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. primò: Totum argumentum Aduersarii ἀπογεσδιόνυσον esse, & à scopo præfixo aberrare, quia non quæritur: An Christus propter potestatem ac dignitatem illam Regiam Filius Dei appelletur? Sed: an nulla alia grauior & potior causa sit, ob quam Christus Filius Dei nuncupetur, quam Regia ipsius potestas, & excellentia; quod falsum est, & tota illa Aduersarii argumentatione nec probatur, nec concluditur. Secundò, ipsum connexum syllogismi principalis esse falsum, quia nec essentiæ, nec virtutum, nec potestatis, aut dominii aliqua similitudo, sed ταυτότης, & ineffabilis illa ac æterna generatio, & essentiæ diuinæ communicatio, causa illa non præcipua tantùm, sed etiam sola & unica est, propter quam videlicet Christus, si diuinam eius naturam respicias, Filius Dei est, & in Scripturis sacris appellatur, quemadmodum capite nono aduersus Osiorrodium demonstrauimus: vbi etiam ostendimus, Christum etiam humanæ naturæ respectu non esse factum Filium ex non Filio, sed eo ipso momento, quo cœpit esse, etiam Filium Dei extitisse, cuius ἐνσάρκωσις ius proinde non ipsum statum exaltationis, sed naturæ ipsius Christi conditionem & sanctam ipsius conceptionem sequitur: quod vel solum sententiam Aduersarii euertit, quam duo subiuncti prosyllogismi probare non possunt. Primum enim quantum attinet, connexi consequentia plane falsa est, quû ὑοῦ Χριστοῦ Christi, & nostrae modus & ratio plane diuersa sit, ac proinde ab hac & modo eius, ad illam & modum, rationem atque causas illius nulla detur consequentia. Ius enim nostrum filiationis cum gratuitum plane sit, & per, ac propter Christum ex mera misericordia nobis concessum, Christi autem naturale, totam Angelorum excellentiam & conditionem superans, quomodo quaeso hoc ex modo, & ratione, atqz causis illius iudicabitur? qua de re iam praedicto capite nono prolixe egimus. Atque ex hac solutione apparet, connexum posterioris quoque prosyllogismi falsum esse. Nam si ὑοῦ Christi, & nostrae modus & ratio toto genere inter se differunt, vt differunt necessario, tum quamcunque rationem & causam ὑοῦ humanae afferat Oftorrodius, ab hac tamen ad illam, & modum, rationem, atque causam, vt sic dicam, formale & proximam illius, nunquam firmam ac legitimam nectet consequentiam. Quanto euidentius igitur falsitatis conuincetur idem connexum illud, postremum, quippe in quo non tantum res toto genere differentes confunduntur, sed insuper etiam genus ipsum praedicationis mutatur. Quum enim Christus Filius Dei proprius sit, & dicatur enuntiatione propria, Magistratus autem & Principes Psal.82.ver.6. filii excelsi appellentur, loquutione metaphorica, & improparia, metaphora videlicet à iure liberorum, quibus parétes principes partem aliquam iudiciariae potestatis concedunt & conferunt, desumpta, quis non videt Aduersarium ab hac filiationis ratione, & modo, ad ὑοῦ Christi modum, & causam imperitissime argumentari? Sed de illis omnibus in antecedentibus satis prolixe disputauimus.
units.tr: First, I reply: the whole argument of my opponent is beside the point [ἀπογεσδιόνυσον] and wanders from the stated aim. For the question is not, "Is Christ called the Son of God on account of that royal power and dignity?" but, "Is there no other weightier and stronger cause for which Christ is named the Son of God than his royal power and excellence?" This is false, and by his whole argument it is neither proved nor concluded. Second, the connection of the main syllogism is itself false, because no likeness of essence, of virtues, of power or of dominion is the cause; rather the identity [ταυτότης] and that ineffable and eternal generation and communication of the divine essence is the not only principal but also the sole and unique cause on account of which Christ, if you look at his divine nature, is the Son of God and is so called in the holy Scriptures, as we showed against Ostorodius in the ninth chapter. There we also showed that Christ did not become the Son from a non-Son even with respect to his human nature, but from the very moment he began to exist he was also the Son of God; and his incarnation [ἐνσάρκωσις] therefore follows not his state of exaltation but the nature and condition of Christ himself and his holy conception. This alone overturns my opponent's view, which the two subjoined prosyllogisms cannot prove. For first, as far as it concerns us, the consequence of the connection is plainly false, since the sonship [υἱοῦ] of Christ and ours differ entirely in mode and reason, and therefore from this mode of ours no consequence can be drawn to that mode, reason and cause of his. For our right of sonship is wholly a gift, granted to us through and for Christ out of pure mercy, whereas the sonship of Christ is natural and surpasses the whole excellence and condition of the angels. How, I ask, could it be judged from this mode, reason and cause? On this matter we have already discussed at length in the ninth chapter. And from this reply it is clear that the connection of the second prosyllogism is also false. For if the mode and reason of the sonship of Christ and of ours differ entirely in kind, as they necessarily do, then whatever reason and cause for human sonship Ostorodius may offer, he will never establish a firm and legitimate consequence from it to that mode, reason and, so to speak, formal and proximate cause of his. How much more clearly, then, is that last connection convicted of falsity, since in it not only things wholly different in kind are confused but the very kind of predication is changed as well. For Christ is the proper Son of God and is so called in a proper expression, whereas magistrates and princes are called "sons of the Most High" (Ps. 82:6) in a metaphorical and improper way, the metaphor being drawn from the right of children, to whom parents grant and confer some part of their judicial power. Who does not see how unskilfully my opponent argues from this manner and mode of sonship to the mode and cause of the sonship [υἱοῦ] of Christ? But we have disputed at sufficient length about all these things in what has gone before.

units.la: Argumentum secundum ad demonstrandâ eandem sententiam Samosatenianorum inde desumit Oftorrodius, quod Deus Christum Iesum, in Regem ac Dominum ordinauerit, Psal.2.v.6. Ego inungens Regem meum, praefeci Tziioni monti sanctitatis meę: Act.2.v.36. Certo sciat tota domus Israel, hunc esse factum à Deo Dominum, & Christum, hunc Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis. Christum autem per decretum seu statutum, & coronationem illam filium Dei factum, & à Deo genitum esse, & hanc ipsam coronationem nihil aliud esse, quâ quod Deus ipsum Filium suum effecerit, & genuerit: inde probare conatur: tum quod in eod. Psal.2.v.7. Christus sic loquens introducitur: Decretū enarraenarraturus sum, Iehoua dixit mihi, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te:tum quod Apoft. Paulus, Act.13. v.32.33. eadë illa verba Psalmi, de hac ipsa re exposuerit: Nos quoque inquiens, vobis euangelizauimus eam promissionem, quæ Patribus facta est, Deum expleuisse filiis illorum, id est, nobis, excitato Iesu: Vt etiam in Psalm.2. scriptum est, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Vbi animaduertendum esse, inquit Ostorrodius, perrefurrectionem Christi ex mortuis in illo loco, vt & in multis alijs, omnia illa, quæ resurrectionem cosequuta sunt, Christi immortalitatem videlicet, potestatem, regnum & similia intelligenda esse: tum denique quod Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos, c.5.v.5: eadem illa verba Dei, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, de sacerdotio Christi exposuerit, quod nihil aliud sit, quàm ipsius Regÿ munetis Christi administratio.
units.tr: The second argument by which Ostorodius derives the same view of the Samosatenes is that "God appointed Christ Jesus as King and Lord" (Ps. 2:6: "I have anointed my King upon my holy hill of Zion"; Acts 2:36: "Let all the house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ"). He tries to prove from this that Christ was made the Son of God and begotten of God by decree or ordinance and by that coronation, and that this coronation is nothing other than God making his own Son and begetting him. Then he adduces that in the same Psalm (2:7) Christ is introduced speaking thus: "I will declare the decree: Jehovah said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you." Next, he argues that the Apostle Paul (Acts 13:32–33) expounded those same words of the Psalm concerning this very matter: "We too," he says, "preach to you that promise which was made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to their children, that is, to us, by raising up Jesus; as it is also written in the second Psalm, You are my Son, today I have begotten you." "It is to be noted there," says Ostorodius, "that in that passage, as in many others, the resurrection of Christ from the dead means all those things which followed the resurrection, namely the immortality, power, kingdom and the like of Christ." Finally, he argues that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews (5:5) applied those same words of God, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you," to the priesthood of Christ, which is nothing other than the administration of the kingly office of Christ.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Si Deus Christum Iesum, Dominum ac Regem constituit: tum sequitur ipsum propter Regiam illam dignitatem, ac potestatem Filium Dei appellari:
units.tr: If God has appointed Christ Jesus Lord and King, then it follows that he is called the Son of God on account of that royal dignity and power.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Connexi probatio hæc est:
units.tr: The proof of the connection is this:

units.la: Si per decretum, ac statutum illud, quo Christus in Regem ordinatus & constitutus est, nihil aliud intelligitur quàm quod Deus ipsum Filium suum effecerit, ac genuerit: tum si Deus Christum Dominum ac Regem constituit, sequitur Christum propter Regiam illam dignitatem ac potestatem Filium Dei appellari:
units.tr: If by that decree and ordinance, by which Christ was ordained and appointed King, nothing else is understood than that God made and begot him as his own Son, then, if God appointed Christ Lord and King, it follows that Christ is called the Son of God on account of that royal dignity and power.

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Assumptionis huius Epilogismus talis est:
units.tr: The epilogism of this assumption runs as follows:

units.la: Si Christus in eodem illo Psalmo, in quo Deus decreto & statuto suo ipsum regem constituisse perhibetur, sic loquens introducitur: decretum enarraturus sum, Iehoua dixit mihi, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, Paulus autem Act. capite decimotertio, versu 32. 33. eadem illa verba Psalmi de Regno Christi, Autor vero Epistolæ ad Hebr. capite quinto, v.5. illa de Sacerdotio Christi, quod nihil aliud est, quàm officij Christi Regij administra-tio, exponunt: tum [sequitur per decretum & statutum illud, quo Christus in Regem ordinatus & constitutus est, hoc intelligendum esse, quod videlicet Deus ipsum Filium suum effecerit, ac genuerit:
units.tr: If in that same Psalm, in which God is said to have appointed him king by his decree and ordinance, Christ is introduced speaking thus: "I will declare the decree; Jehovah said to me, You are my Son, today I have begotten you"; and if Paul, in Acts 13, verses 32 and 33, explains those same words of the Psalm of Christ's kingdom, and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, in chapter 5, verse 5, explains them of Christ's priesthood, which is nothing other than the administration of Christ's royal office; then [it follows that by that decree and ordinance, by which Christ was ordained and appointed King, this must be understood: that God made and begot him as his own Son]:

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Resp. Primò: Etiam hanc totam argumentationem à scopo disputationis & quaestionis propositae aberrare, quandoquidem, vt antea monuimus, non de hac quæstione instituta est præsens disceptatio nostra: An videlicet Christus propter Regnum, & dominium suum Filius Dei appelletur? Sed: An Regia illa potestas & autoritas, præcipua sit causa, quare videlicet Christus in Scripturis sacris Filij Dei nomine indigitetur? quod falsum est, & tota illa Aduersarii argumentatione, nec probatur, nec concluditur. Falsum illud inquam est, quod ab Aduersario hic affirmatur, quia Christus ideò potissimum Dei Filius est, & in sacris Scripturis dicitur, quia videlicet ab æterno per eiusdem essentiæ diuinę communicationem, modo ineffabili, à Patre genitus, ac proinde eiusdem gloriæ, potentiæ, maiestatis, ac potestatis particeps, nobisq; viua Dei voce ac testimonio, missione & ordinatione in Saluatorem ac Redemptorem mirandis ac plane diuinis operibus, promissionibus, mandatis, resurrectione, & glorificatione, aliisque innumeris, & certissimis ac infallibilibus argumentis, atque documentis talis declaratus est, quemadmodum in antecedentibus demonstrauimus, ex quib. duo illa tantum reperimus argumenta, & in se alioquin firmissima, ipsa Aduersariorum nostrorum hypothesi, & confessione stabilimus.
units.tr: Reply. First: this whole argument also wanders from the aim of the dispute and the question proposed. For, as we said before, our present discussion is not concerned with this question: whether Christ is called the Son of God on account of his kingdom and lordship?
