But with this: whether that royal power and authority is the chief cause why Christ is designated by the name of Son of God in the holy Scriptures? This is false, and the whole of the opponent's argument neither proves nor concludes anything. I say this is false, which the opponent asserts here, because Christ is chiefly the Son of God and is so called in the holy Scriptures because, from eternity, by the communication of the divine essence in an ineffable manner, he was begotten of the Father, and therefore partakes of the same glory, power, majesty and authority. He was also declared such to us by the living voice and testimony of God, by his sending and appointment as Saviour and Redeemer, by wonderful and plainly divine works, promises, commands, resurrection and glorification, and by countless other, most certain and infallible arguments and proofs, as we have demonstrated in what came before. Of these, we have found and established two arguments in particular, which are in themselves most firm, and also established by our opponents' own hypothesis and confession.

units.la: Primum est:Si Christus propter Regnum illud œconomicum, mediatorium, & acquisitum, Filius Dei est, & appellatur, tū ille multò magis propter supremum illud, vniuersale, ac independens, & Deo naturale ac essentiale dominium & regnum Filius Dei est, & vocatur, quia etiam hoc posterius dominium, & quidem iure naturali, non autem ex dispensatione, & œconomia voluntaria ipsi competere, cap. 11. huius defensionis nostræ demonstrauimus: Atqui prius affirmat Oftorrodius: Ergò etiam posterius concedat necesse est. Vnde iam necessariò sequitur, longè grauiorem, & potiorem causam, atque rationem, illâ quam Aduersarius ab autoritate, & dignitate Regni Christi mediatorii desumit, quare videlicet Christus Filius Dei sit, & appelletur, reddi posse.
units.tr: The first is this: If Christ is and is called the Son of God on account of that economical, mediatorial and acquired kingdom, then he is much more the Son of God and is called so on account of that supreme, universal and independent lordship and kingdom, which belongs to God naturally and essentially; because this latter lordship also belongs to him by natural right, and not by dispensation and voluntary economy, as we demonstrated in chapter 11 of this our defence. But Ostorodius affirms the first; therefore he must also concede the second. From this it now follows necessarily that a far weightier and more powerful cause and reason can be given for why Christ is the Son of God and is so called, than the one the opponent derives from the authority and dignity of Christ's mediatorial kingdom, namely why Christ is the Son of God and is so called.

units.la: Secundum est: Qui ita filius Dei est, vt simul etiam sit verus atque æternus Deus, ille non ideo potissimum filius Dei est & appellatur, quia Deus ipsi tanquam mediatori omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra in tempore dedit, ipsúmque Regem ac Dominum constituit super omnia ipsi Ecclesiæ: sed ideo præcipuè, quia ab æterno à Patre genitus, ac proinde eiusdem cum ipso essentiæ, gloriæ ac maiestatis particeps est : Atqui Iesus Christus ita filius Dei est, vt simul etiam sit verus atque æternus Deus :Ergo Iesus Christus non ideo potissimum filius Dei est & appellatur, quia Deus ipsi tanquam mediatori omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra tempore certo dedit, ipsúmque Regem ac Dominum constituit super omnia ipsi Ecclesiæ : sed ideo præcipuè, quia ab æterno à Patre genitus, ac proinde eiusdem cum ipso essentiæ, gloriæ, ac maiestatis particeps est. Assumptionem sic demonstro: Qui Dei filius religioso cultu, & vera cum fiducia animi, non tantum iure inuocari potest, sed etiam ex iussu & mandato Dei à nobis inuocari debet, ille ita Dei filius est, vt simul etiam sit vnus ille, verus atque æternus Deus Israelis: Atqui Iesus Christus Dei filius religioso cultu, & vera cum fiducia animi non tatum iure inuocari potest, sed etiam ex iussu & mandato Dei à nobis inuocari debet: Ergo (nam vtramque præmissam suprà capite decimoquinto huius defensionis, ex Scripturis sacris, & ipsa Aduersariorum confessione demonstrauimus) Iesus Christus ita Dei filius est, vt simul etiam sit vnus ille, verus atque æternus Deus Israelis. Secundo: Hinc igitur apparet, connexum syllogismi principalis esse falsum: quum enim dignitas illa Regia Christi sit ex dispensatione & œconomia ipsi concessa, & communicata, cuius finis & principium in tempore, cum principio & consummatione Ecclesiæ coniunctum, adeóque ad statum Christi externum pertineat: ius autem illud Chrisi fit essentiale & naturale ipsi, & secundùm naturam diuinam ipsius, principio non originis quidem, sed temporis, & fine, secundùm humanam verò naturam non quidem principio nec temporis, nec originis, sed fine tamen careat: inde luculenter apparet, illam dignitatem & autoritatem Regiam, seu ordinationem illam qua Rex & Dominus est constitutus, causam existere non potuisse, quare videlicet Christus filius Dei sit, & nomine illo indigitetur. Ex hac ipsa autem ratione euidenter liquet, assumptionem prosyllogismi vnà cum epilogismi connexo falsam esse, quandoquidem Christus ab æterno secundum naturam suam diuinam, non ex libero voluntatis decreto, sed per ineffabilem essentiæ communicationem à Patre genitus, regnum autem ac dominium illud Mediatorium, ex libero Dei decreto, & dispensatione voluntaria, cōsequutus, & secundum naturam humanam, non factus ex non Filio, Filius, sed Filius natus est. Vnde iam porrò sequitur, illa verba Psalmi, Ego hodie genui te, ad ipsam exhibitionem Christi, adeóque ad genituraм illam quæ non κατ' ἀρχὴν, vt ita loquar, sed κατὰ φύσιν facta est, & in missione atque conseruatione in Prophetam, Regem, & Sacerdotem constitit, referenda esse, quo etiam Paulus in Apostolorum Actis, & Epistola ad Hebræos respexit, qua de re in antecedentibus à nobis est disputatum.
units.tr: The second is this: He who is the Son of God in such a way that he is at the same time true and eternal God, is not chiefly the Son of God and so called because God gave him, as Mediator, all power in heaven and on earth in time, and appointed him King and Lord over all things for the Church; but chiefly because from eternity he was begotten of the Father and therefore partakes of the same essence, glory and majesty as the Father. But Jesus Christ is the Son of God in such a way that he is at the same time true and eternal God; therefore Jesus Christ is not chiefly the Son of God and so called because God gave him, as Mediator, all power in heaven and on earth at a certain time, and appointed him King and Lord over all things for the Church; but chiefly because from eternity he was begotten of the Father and therefore partakes of the same essence, glory and majesty with him. I demonstrate the assumption thus: he who can rightly be invoked as the Son of God with religious worship and true confidence of mind, and who ought to be invoked by us by the command and order of God, is the Son of God in such a way that he is at the same time that one true and eternal God of Israel. But Jesus Christ, the Son of God, can rightly be invoked with religious worship and true confidence of mind, and ought to be invoked by us by the command and order of God; therefore (for we demonstrated both premises above, in chapter 15 of this defence, from the holy Scriptures and from our opponents' own confession) Jesus Christ is the Son of God in such a way that he is at the same time that one true and eternal God of Israel. Second: from this it therefore appears that the connection of the principal syllogism is false. For since that royal dignity of Christ is granted and communicated to him by dispensation and economy, and its beginning and end are bound up in time with the beginning and consummation of the Church, and so it pertains to Christ's external state; whereas that right is essential and natural to him, and according to his divine nature it has no beginning of origin, indeed, but of time, and no end; according to his human nature it has neither beginning of time nor of origin, yet it lacks an end. From this it clearly appears that that royal dignity and authority, or that ordination by which he was constituted King and Lord, could not be the cause why Christ is the Son of God and is designated by that name. And from this same reasoning it is plainly evident that the assumption of the prosyllogism, together with the connected epilogism, is false: since Christ, from eternity, according to his divine nature, was begotten of the Father not by a free decree of the will but by an ineffable communication of essence, while that mediatorial kingdom and lordship he obtained by a free decree of God and voluntary dispensation; and according to his human nature he was not made a Son from a non-Son, but was born a Son. Hence it further follows that those words of the Psalm, Today I have begotten you, must be referred to the very manifestation of Christ, and so to that generation which was made not κατ' ἀρχήν, as I may put it, but κατὰ φύσιν, and which consisted in his sending and preservation as Prophet, King and Priest; to which Paul also looked in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Epistle to the Hebrews, as we have discussed in what came before.

units.la: Venio ad tertium disputationis caput, quod est de Sacerdotio Christi, quod Aduersarius nihil aliud esse dicit, quam spiritualis regni ipsius, quatenus videlicet illud salutis, ac felicitatis nostræ curâ spectat, administratione, quæ figuratè Sacerdotium dicatur, vt hac ratione significetur, Christum, non tantum vt potentem Dominum, nobis fiduciam in ipsum collocantibus, in omnibus miserijs & calamitatibus nostris succurrere posse, sed etiam tanquam misericordem, & similiter in omnibus, absque peccato, tentatum, id præstare velle, quod ipsum sectione octaua prolixius exponit. Atque hanc ob causam, ait, Christum Sacerdotem nostrum appellari, non autem propterea, quod ille se in cruce obtulerit pro nobis: Hoc enim falsum esse, ex eo liquere, quod Christus tum demum postquam ex mortuis resurrexit & in cælum ingressus est, Sacerdos noster factus sit, quemadmodum sequentia loca id docent: Heb. 5. v. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. & cap. 6. v. 20. & cap. 7. v. 23. 24. 25. 26. & cap. 8. v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 6. & 10, v. 21.
units.tr: I come to the third head of the dispute, which concerns the priesthood of Christ, which the opponent says is nothing other than the administration of his spiritual kingdom, insofar as that kingdom looks to the care of our salvation and happiness, which is figuratively called a priesthood, so that by this means it is signified that Christ, not only as a powerful Lord, is able to help those who place their trust in him in all our miseries and calamities, but also, as merciful and tempted in all things like as we are, yet without sin, is willing to do this; which he sets out at greater length in the eighth section. And for this reason, he says, Christ is called our Priest, and not because he offered himself on the cross for us. For this is false, as is clear from the fact that Christ became our Priest only after he rose from the dead and entered heaven, as the following passages teach: Heb. 5. vv. 4–10; and ch. 6. v. 20; and ch. 7. vv. 23–26; and ch. 8. vv. 1–4, 6; and 10. v. 21.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs thus.

units.la: Si Christus tum demum Sacerdos noster factus est, postquam ex mortuis resurrexit, & in cælum ingressus est, tum non propter illam oblationem in cruce factam, sed propter Regni illius spiritualis administrationem Sacerdos noster appellatur:
units.tr: If Christ was made our Priest only then, after he had risen from the dead and entered into heaven, then he is called our Priest not on account of that offering made on the cross, but on account of the administration of that spiritual Kingdom;

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Ipsum autem Sacerdotium Christi figuratè de regni ipsius administratione intelligendum esse, duobus argumentis probare conatur:
units.tr: Ostorodius, however, tries to prove by two arguments that the priesthood itself of Christ is to be understood figuratively, of the administration of his kingdom.

units.la: Primum est: quia illius Sacerdotij Christi in Nouo Testamento, Epistola Epistola ad Hebræos excepta, raro fiat mentio: Secundum est: quia administrationis Regni illius Christi, & Sacerdotalis officij idem modus, ratioque, & effecta eadem, nempe continua cura, pro Ecclesiæ salute deprehendantur.
units.tr: The first is this: that mention of this priesthood of Christ is rarely made in the New Testament, except in the Epistle to the Hebrews. The second is this: that the same manner, reason and effects are found in the administration of Christ's kingdom as in the priestly office, namely continual care for the salvation of the Church.

units.la: Syllogismus primi argumenti talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism of the first argument runs thus:

units.la: Si Sacerdotij Christi in Novo Testamento, epistola ad Hebræos excepta, raro fit mentio, tum sequitur illud figurate de Regni ipsius administratione intelligendum esse:
units.tr: If mention of the priesthood of Christ is rarely made in the New Testament, except in the Epistle to the Hebrews, then it follows that it is to be understood figuratively, of the administration of his kingdom;

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Syllogismus posterioris argumenti talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism of the second argument runs thus:

units.la: Si Regni illius Christi, & Sacerdotalis officij ipsius eadem ratio, idemque modus, & effectus est: tum sequitur Sacerdotium Christi, & officij ipsius Regij administrationem, reipsa unum idemque esse:
units.tr: If the reason, manner and effect of Christ's kingdom and of his priestly office are the same, then it follows that the priesthood of Christ and the administration of his kingly office are in fact one and the same;

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Hisce duobus argumentis duplicem Osiorrodius subiungit prolepsin: prima est: illud, quod de purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per Christum facta in Epistola ad Hebræos scriptum est, nihil aliud esse, quam quod alibi in Novo Testamento dicitur, nempe ipsum Christum potestatem consequutum esse, nos a morte, quam peccatis nostris meriti sumus, liberandi, ipsumque perpetuo nostri curam gerere, nec permittere, ut nos tanquam peccatores omnis generis aerumnis & calamitatibus affligamur, sed ab illis omnibus nos tandem liberaturum, ac vitam aeternam nobis daturum esse. Secunda est: Quod, si quis obiiciat Christum non tantum nos a peccatis nostris purgare, verum etiam apud Deum pro nobis intercedere. Rom. 8. v. 34. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est, imo vero etiam qui excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiā postulat pro nobis. Hebr. 7. v. 25. Unde & servare prorsus potest eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, semper viuens, ut interpellet pro nobis: illamque interpellationem non ad Regium, sed ad sacerdotale Christi officium pertinere, ac proinde duo illa officia a se invicem distingui debere: respondendum esse, illam ipsam interpellationem Christi, aeque ac Sacerdotium ipsius figurate intelligendam esse: tum quia Christus necesse non habeat, ut ea ipsa quae se nobis daturum promisit, & iam quoque dat, orando, aut intercedendo revera a Deo Patre impetret, quandoquidem ille Dominus omnium sit constitutus: tum quia neque nos vera Christi intercessione indigeamus, quoniam Deus ipse nos diligat, ac proinde necesse non sit, vt Christus vere ac proprie pro vobis oret & intercedat, Ioh. 16. v. 26. 27. Non dico vobis me rogaturum Patre pro vobis: ipse enim Pater amat vos, quia vos me amastis, & credidistis me a Deo exiuisse. Ac proinde illam interpellationem nihil aliud esse, inquit, quam quod ille per potestatem & autoritatem a Deo acceptam, ex omni malo nos semper eripere velit, Christumque ideo potissimum pro nobis interpellare dici, vt illam potestatem non a seipso, sed a Deo tanquam donum habere intelligatur.
units.tr: To these two arguments Ostorodius adds a double prolepsis. The first is this: that what is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews about the cleansing of our sins through Christ is nothing other than what is said elsewhere in the New Testament, namely that Christ has obtained power to free us from the death which we have deserved by our sins, and that he constantly takes care of us and does not permit us, as sinners, to be afflicted with every kind of distress and calamity, but will at last free us from all these and give us eternal life. The second is this: "But if someone objects that Christ not only cleanses us from our sins but also intercedes for us with God," Rom. 8:34, "Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died, yea rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us." Heb. 7:25, "Wherefore he is able also to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for us"; "and that this intercession pertains not to the kingly but to the priestly office of Christ, and that therefore these two offices must be distinguished from each other": the answer is that this very intercession of Christ, just like his priesthood, is to be understood figuratively. For, first, because Christ has no need to obtain from God the Father, by praying or interceding, those things which he promised to give us and already in fact gives, since that Lord has been constituted Lord of all; and second, because we have no need of Christ's true intercession, since God himself loves us, and therefore it is not necessary that Christ truly and properly pray and intercede for us. John 16:26-27, "I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you; for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came out from God." Therefore, he says, that intercession is nothing other than that he, by the power and authority received from God, always wills to rescue us from every evil; and Christ is called to intercede for us chiefly so that it may be understood that he has this power not from himself but as a gift from God.

units.la: Syllogismus primae τεσλήψεως talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism of the first prolepsis runs thus:

units.la: Si per purgationem peccatorum nostrorum per Christum factam, nihil aliud intelligitur quam potestas nos a morte liberandi, & perpetua illa cura pro nobis: tum ex illa demonstrari non potest, Regni ac Sacerdotij Christi diuersos esse effectus, ac proinde illa duo officia tanquam diuersa inter se distingui debere:
units.tr: If by the cleansing of our sins made through Christ nothing else is understood than the power to free us from death and that constant care for us, then it cannot be shown from that that the kingly and priestly offices of Christ have different effects, and therefore these two offices must be distinguished from each other as different:

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Syllogismus secundae τεσλήψεως talis est:
units.tr: The syllogism of the second prolepsis runs thus:

units.la: Si illa intercessio seu interpellatio Christi figurate intelligenda est, tum ex ea demonstrari non potest, officiu Christi Regiam tanquam diuersum, ab officio sacerdotali distinguendum esse:
units.tr: If that intercession or interpellation of Christ is to be understood figuratively, then it cannot be shown from it that the kingly office of Christ must be distinguished as different from the priestly office:

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Assumptionis probatio prima haec est:
units.tr: The first proof of the assumption is this:

units.la: Si Christus vtpote rerum omnium Dominus constitutus, necesse non habet, vt eas res, quas nobis se daturum esse promisit, & iam reipsa dat, orando aut interpellando pro nobis apud Deum impetret: tum illa interpellatio non proprie, sed figurate intelligenda est:
units.tr: If Christ, as constituted Lord of all things, has no need to obtain by praying or interceding for us from God those things which he promised to give us and in fact already gives, then that intercession is to be understood not properly but figuratively:

units.la: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: But the first is true; therefore the second also.

units.la: Assumptionis probatio posterior haec est:
units.tr: The second proof of the assumption is this:

units.la: Si nos illa intercessione Christi nihil indigemus, vtpote quos Pater ipse diligit: diligit, tum sequitur illam interpellationem non proprie, sed figurate intelligendam esse: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If we need nothing from that intercession of Christ, since the Father himself loves us, then it follows that that intercession must be understood not properly but figuratively. But the first is true; therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Resp.Christum vere ac proprie Sacerdotem esse, ex promissionibus ac testimoniis Veteris Testamenti, & nomen Sacerdotis, & rem nomine significatam Messiae tribuentibus, ex collatione item dignitatis personae & sacerdotii, ex natura populi cui praepositus est Messias, & ex Noui Testamenti apertissimis testimoniis, & titulum Sacerdotis, & omnia ad munus sacerdotale pertinentia, de Christo praedicantibus, denique ex illis actionibus, quae nobis ad salutem non communicandam, aut promittendam tantum, sed etiam acquirendam, impetrandam & promerendam necessariae sunt, & ad exequendum munus mediatorium necessario requiruntur, Christoque quem non efficacia tantum, sed etiam merito, redemptorem ac saluatorem nostrum esse ostendimus, nec ut Prophetae, nec ut Regi, sed ut Sacerdoti ac summo Pontifici nostro, vere ac proprie competere possunt, in antecedentibus demonstrauimus. Unde iam necessario sequitur, functiones & actiones sacerdotales Christi, a functionibus ipsius & actionibus regalibus distinguendas, ac proinde falsum esse id, quod affirmat Ostorrodius, nempe Sacerdotium Christi nihil aliud esse, quam Regni ipsius administrationem, quae figurate Sacerdotium appelletur. Ad argumentum vero Aduersarii respondemus assumptionem esse falsam, neque allegatis illis ex epistola ad Hebraeos testimoniis demonstrari posse. Falsam esse syllogismi illius assumptione, inde solide euincitur: tum quod Christus non in coelo, sed in terra, nempe in ara crucis, animam suam in [illegible, ~3 letters], ac redemptionis pretium Deo obtulit, sanguinem suum pro nobis effudit, & sic morte ac passione sua peccata nostra in ipsum vt vadem ac sponsorem nostrum deriuata expiauit, & Deo pro ipsis satisfecit, sicuti in articulo de Iustificatione hominis coram Deo demonstrauimus, & ostendimus, Christum vere ac proprie peccata nostra morte & passione sua expiasse, Deoque persoluto vero redemptionis pretio, pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, nobisque amissam Dei Patris gratiam recuperasse, & sic vitam ac salutem aeternam nobis acquisiuisse: quae omnia Regio Christi officio, vel ipsis etiam Aduersariis suffragantibus, minime conuenire possunt: unde iam necessario sequitur, Sacerdotium Christi, & officii ipsius regii administrationem reipsa vnu ac idem esse non posse: tum quia ipsa Scriptura sacra, opus redemptionis in hac terra consummatum esse, Christúmque tum demum, postquam peccata nostra expiasset, ad Regiam illam dignitatem ac maiestatem evectum esse, testatur Iohan. 19. v. 30. Quum accepisset Iesus acetum, dixit, consummatum est, & inclinato capite tradidit spiritum: ex quibus verbis luculenter apparet, in morte & passione Christi, ac sanguinis ipsius effusione in cruce facta, totius salutis ac redemptionis nostrae complementum consistere. Hebr. 1. verf 3. Qui purgationem peccatorum nostrorum per se ipsum fecit, sedit ad dexteram maiestatis illius excelsis. Testimonia vero illa ex epistola ad Hebraeos allegata, quibus Aduersarius illam suam assumptionem stabilire conatur, quantum concernit, sciendum est, duplicem Christi oblationem nobis in Scriptura sacra proponi, unam quae in terra perfecta est, qua videlicet ille per Spiritum aeternum se ipsum in αἰῶνι, & victimam expiatoriam ac satisfactoriam pro peccatis nostris Deo in cruce obtulit: alteram qua ille purgatione peccatorum nostrorum facta seipsum ἀντιλυτρωτὴν, Redemptorem, ac Sponsorem nostrum, in coelis coram Deo praesentauit, & sanguine suo, quo aspersus est, se pro peccatis nostris Deo satisfecisse, & iniunctum ipsi redemptionis opus consummasse, declarauit. Atque de hac posteriore, non autem de priore illa oblatione, citata illa testimonia loquuntur, neque aliud quicquam, quantum ad praesentem disputationem attinet, inde concludi poterit, quàm talem nos oportuisse habere Pontificem, qui videlicet coeleste sacrarium ingrederetur, ibique reliquas Sacerdotii partes perageret, quod nos vltro concedimus, quum inde non sequatur. Christum, priusquam in coelum ingrederetur, revera Sacerdotem non fuisse. Ad argumenta vero illa duo, quibus probare conatur Aduersarius, Sacerdotium Christi, figurate de regni ipsius administratione intelligendum esse, quantum attinet, respondeo connexum syllogismi primi cum assumptione syllogismi vtriusque falsum esse. Etiamsi enim prius illud daretur Aduersario, nempe Sacerdotii Christi, in Nouo Testamento, epistola ad Hebraeos excepta, raro mentionem fieri, quibus tamen quasi mediis inde concludet Oftorrodius, illud vel figurate, vel de Regni Christi administratione intelligi debere? An existimat Aduersarius illud quod frequentius docetur in scripturis sacris, verius esse illis doctrinae capitibus, quorum tam frequens mentio in illis non fit, & quae in: sola epistola ad Hebræos fusius explicantur ? Apage. Illa ad sa-lutem scitu magis necessaria esse, quàm ista, forte probabit inde Ostorrodius: sed illa his veriora esse, nisi nefario ausu Spiritum sanctum mendacii insimulare, & diuinam illam epistolam ad Hebræos scriptam, diuina veritate, αξιοπιστια, autoritate, & dignitate exuere voluerit, non affirmabit. Quia vero officii Christi sacerdotalis veritas non in sola vocatione & nominis impositione consistit, sed potissimum in ipsa exequutione, actionibus atque functionibus, quæ ad expianda peccata nostra, & vitam ac salutem æternam nobis acquirendam & impetrandam requirebantur, idcò Christum reuera ac proprie Sacerdotem esse, non tantum ex illis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis, in quibus ille nomine isto Sacerdotis indigitatur, verùm etiam ex illis, in quibus ipsi actiones & functiones illæ tribuuntur, demonstratur, ac proinde assumptionem syllogismi primi falsam esse, ex illis argumentis, & scripturæ sacræ testimoniis, quibus Christum peccata nostra vere expiasse probauimus, manifeste apparet, ex quibus etiam constat, vim illam ac naturam Sacerdotii Christi, à munere Regio velut diuersam distinguendam esse, siquidem ille vt Sacerdos vitam, ac salutem æternam Ecclesiæ acquisiuit, & impetrauit, vt Rex autem communicat, de quibus omnibus in antecedentibus actum est, vnde iam sequitur, secundi quoque syllogismi assumptionem falsam esse, quam prima illa ἀντιλογίας aduersus argumentorum nostrorum tela, defendere non potest. Falsum enim esse, quod in minori propositione illius affirmat Ostorrodius, nempe per purgationem illam peccatorum nostrorum nihil aliud quam potestatem Christi, nos à morte liberandi, perpetuámque ipsius pro nobis curam denotari, vel ex eo tantùm liquet, quod expiatio peccatorum nostrorum resurrectionem Christi antecedit, & in cruce facta, atque cum sensu iræ diuinæ coniuncta est, quod de potestate, ac dignitate illa Regia, quam Christus velut obedientiæ suæ præstitæ præmium in cœlo confequutus est, affirmari non potest. Interpellationem verò, ac intercessionem Christi (quæ est altera functio, & actio muneris Christi Sacerdotalis, cuius capite trigesimoquarto mentionem fecimus) quantum concernit, etiam nos statuimus ac docemus, illam non proprie, sed metaphoricè intelligendam, neque carnale quicquam hic nobis de Christo imaginandum esse, quasi videlicet ille supplex genibus flexis ad pedes Patris prouolutus ac procumbens, & manibus expansis Patrem deprecaretur, & sic vitam ac salutem æternam, & remissionem peccatorum nobis ab ipso impetraret: Ac proinde Christum pro nobis interpellare ac intercedere dicimus vigore ac virtute sacrificii sui, quo peccata nostra expiauit, quatenus videlicet gloriosa corporis sui præsentatione, coram Patris conspectu, assiduè apparet cum morte & resurrectione sua, quæ vice sunt æternæ intercessionis, & viuæ orationis efficaciam habent. Ex quibus iam apparet assumptionem syllogismi secundæ θεωλήψεως veram quidem esse, nec duobus eius prosyllogismis quicquam contra nos concludi, sed per illam interpellationem ac intercessionem, ideo actionem aliquam Regiam intelligendam esse, quia videlicet illa non proprie, sed metaphoricè sit accipienda, tum probabit Aduersarius, quum omnia illa, quæcunque de Christo in scripturis sacris enuntiantur, sensu metaphorico aut improprio, de spiritualis regni ipsius administratione exponenda & explicanda esse demonstrauerit, quam prouinciam ipsi ornandam relinquo, & ad reliquorum duorum capitum examen progredior.
units.tr: Reply. That Christ is truly and properly a Priest is shown from the promises and testimonies of the Old Testament, which ascribe to the Messiah both the name of Priest and the reality signified by that name; also from the comparison of the dignity of the person with that of the priesthood, from the nature of the people over whom the Messiah was set, and from the most manifest testimonies of the New Testament, which speak of Christ with the title of Priest and attribute to him everything that pertains to the priestly office. Finally, it is shown from those actions which are necessary, not merely to communicate or promise salvation to us, but to acquire, obtain and merit it, and which are required for the performance of the mediatorial office. We have shown in what precedes that Christ is our Redeemer and Savior not merely in efficacy but also in merit, and that the titles belong truly and properly to him not as Prophet or as King but as our Priest and High Priest. From this it follows necessarily that the priestly functions and actions of Christ must be distinguished from his royal functions and actions. Therefore what Ostorrodius affirms, namely that the priesthood of Christ is nothing other than the administration of his kingdom itself, which is called a priesthood figuratively, is false. As for the adversary's argument, we answer that its assumption is false, and that it cannot be demonstrated from those testimonies of the Epistle to the Hebrews which he has cited. That the assumption of that syllogism is false is firmly proved: first, because Christ offered his soul in [illegible] and the price of redemption to God not in heaven but on earth, namely on the altar of the cross; he shed his blood for us, and so by his death and passion he expiated our sins, which were transferred to him as our surety and bondsman, and satisfied God on their behalf. As we have shown in the article on the justification of man before God, Christ truly and properly expiated our sins by his death and passion, and having paid God the true price of redemption, he satisfied for our sins and recovered for us the grace of God the Father that we had lost, and so acquired for us life and eternal salvation. None of these things can belong to the royal office of Christ, even if the adversaries themselves agree. From this it follows necessarily that the priesthood of Christ and the administration of his royal office cannot in fact be one and the same. Second, Holy Scripture itself testifies that the work of redemption was completed on this earth, and that Christ was raised to that royal dignity and majesty only after he had expiated our sins: John 19:30, When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished, and bowing his head he gave up the spirit. From these words it clearly appears that the completion of all our salvation and redemption consists in the death and passion of Christ and in the effusion of his blood on the cross. Hebrews 1:3, He, having made purification of our sins by himself, sat down at the right hand of the majesty on high. As for those testimonies from the Epistle to the Hebrews which the adversary cites in an effort to establish his assumption, it must be noted, so far as they concern the matter, that two offerings of Christ are set before us in Holy Scripture. One was completed on earth, in which he offered himself through the eternal Spirit [αἰῶνι] as a sacrifice of expiation and satisfaction for our sins to God on the cross. The other is that by which, having made purification of our sins, he presented himself in heaven before God as our Redeemer and surety, a ransom in our place [ἀντιλυτρωτὴν], and declared by his blood, with which he was sprinkled, that he had satisfied God for our sins and completed the work of redemption entrusted to him. Those cited testimonies speak of this latter offering, not of the former one, and so far as the present dispute is concerned nothing more can be concluded from them than that we ought to have such a High Priest, one who would enter the heavenly sanctuary and there perform the remaining parts of the priesthood. This we freely concede, since it does not follow that Christ was not truly a Priest before he entered heaven. As for the two arguments by which the adversary tries to prove that the priesthood of Christ must be understood figuratively, of the administration of his kingdom, I answer that the connection of the first syllogism with the assumption of the second is false. For even if the adversary were granted the premise that in the New Testament, apart from the Epistle to the Hebrews, the priesthood of Christ is rarely mentioned, from what intermediate step would Ostorrodius conclude that it must be understood either figuratively or of the administration of Christ's kingdom? Does the adversary think that what is taught more frequently in the Scriptures is truer than those heads of doctrine which are not so often mentioned there, and which are explained at greater length in the Epistle to the Hebrews alone? Away with the thought! Ostorrodius may perhaps argue that the former are more necessary for salvation to know than the latter; but he will not affirm that the former are truer than the latter, unless he wishes to accuse the Holy Spirit of lying with impious daring, and to strip that divine Epistle to the Hebrews of divine truth, authority, trustworthiness and dignity. But because the truth of Christ's priestly office does not consist merely in his calling and the bestowal of the name, but chiefly in the very execution, actions and functions which were required to expiate our sins and to acquire and obtain for us life and eternal salvation, Christ is shown to be truly and properly a Priest not only from those testimonies of Holy Scripture in which he is designated by the name of Priest, but also from those in which those actions and functions are attributed to him. Therefore the assumption of the first syllogism is false; this is manifest from the arguments and the testimonies of Holy Scripture by which we have proved that Christ truly expiated our sins. From these it is also clear that the power and nature of the priesthood of Christ must be distinguished as something different from his royal office, since as Priest he acquired and obtained life and eternal salvation for the Church, while as King he communicates them. All these matters have been dealt with in what precedes. From this it follows that the assumption of the second syllogism is also false, and the first counter-argument [ἀντιλογίας] cannot defend it against the weapons of our arguments. For that the minor premise of his argument, namely that by that purgation of our sins nothing else is signified than the power of Christ to free us from death and his perpetual care for us, is false, is clear from this alone: the expiation of our sins precedes the resurrection of Christ, was made on the cross, and was joined with a sense of divine wrath. This cannot be affirmed of that royal power and dignity which Christ obtained in heaven as the reward of his obedience. As for the intercession and mediation of Christ (which is the second function and action of his priestly office, and of which we spoke in chapter thirty-four), we too hold and teach that it is to be understood not properly but metaphorically. We must not imagine anything carnal here about Christ, as if he were kneeling as a suppliant, prostrate at the feet of the Father, begging the Father with outstretched hands, and so obtaining from him life and eternal salvation and the forgiveness of sins for us. Therefore we say that Christ intercedes and mediates for us by the power and virtue of his sacrifice, by which he expiated our sins, insofar as, by the glorious presentation of his body before the Father's sight, he continually appears with his death and resurrection, which take the place of eternal intercession and have the efficacy of living prayer. From these things it now appears that the assumption of the second syllogism is indeed true, and that nothing against us can be concluded from its two prosyllogisms. But that the intercession and mediation are therefore to be understood as some royal action, because they are not to be taken properly but metaphorically, the adversary will prove only when he has demonstrated that everything said of Christ in the Scriptures in a metaphorical or improper sense must be expounded and explained of the administration of his spiritual kingdom. I leave that task to him, and proceed to the examination of the remaining two heads.

units.la: CAPVT XXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII.

units.la: In quo tres illæ quæstiones: primò: Qualenam corpus post resurrectionem ex mortuis habuerit Christus, ac proinde qualia corpora etiam nos habituri simus? Secundò: An & quando Regnum Christi finem sit habiturum? Tertiò: Quisnam verborum illorum, quibus Melchisedec sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, nec initium dierum, nec vitæ finem habens, assimilatus Filio Dei, Sacerdos in æternum manere dicitur, sit sensus, excutiuntur, veritas explicatur ac defenditur, falsitas refutatur.
units.tr: In this chapter three questions are examined, the truth is explained and defended, and falsehood is refuted. First: what kind of body Christ had after his resurrection from the dead, and therefore what kind of bodies we too are to have? Second: whether and when the Kingdom of Christ will have an end? Third: what is the meaning of those words by which Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, is said to be made like the Son of God and to remain a priest for ever?

units.la: STORRODIVS Institutionum suarum capite quadragesimoprimo, duas illas quæstiones proponit & explicat: primò: Qualenam corpus habuerit Christus post resurrectionem ex mortuis, ac proinde, qualia nos quoque corpora post vniuersalem illam resurrectionem habituri simus? Secundò & incidenter: An, & quando Christi Regnum finem sit habiturum? cuius explicationi ille tertiam quoque inserit: Quis nempe verborum illorum, quibus Melchisedec sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, nec initium dierum, nec vitæ finem habens, assimilatus Filio Dei sacerdos in æternum manere dicitur, sit sensus? Quas ipsas quæstiones, etiam nos, quanta fieri poterit breuitate, & perspicuitate, excutiemus, & explicabimus.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in the forty-first chapter of his Institutes, proposes and explains two of these questions. First: What kind of body did Christ have after his resurrection from the dead, and therefore what kind of bodies shall we also have after that general resurrection? Second, and incidentally: Will the Kingdom of Christ ever have an end, and if so, when? To this explanation he adds a third: What is the meaning of those words by which Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, is said to be made like the Son of God and to remain a priest for ever? We too will examine and explain these same questions, as briefly and clearly as we can.

units.la: Et primam quidem quæstionem quantum concernit, in hoc inter nos & Aduersarios nostros conuenit, quatenus videlicet vtraque pars docet, Christum reuera ex mortuis resurrexisse, omnésq; credentes in Christum, suo tempore, virtute & beneficio resurrectionis ipsius, ad beatam immortalitatem, vitámque, gloriam, ac felicitatem æternam resurrecturos esse. Sed de hoc ambigitur ac disceptatur, qualenam corpus Christus post resurrectionem habuerit, ac proinde, qualia etiam sint futura corpora nostra, ipsius corpori gloriosò conformanda?
units.tr: So far as the first question is concerned, we agree with our opponents on this point: both sides teach that Christ truly rose from the dead, and that all who believe in Christ will rise, each in his own time, by the power and benefit of his resurrection, to blessed immortality, life, glory and eternal happiness. But the dispute is about what kind of body Christ had after his resurrection, and therefore what kind our own bodies will be, conformed to his glorious body.

units.la: Nos credimus, ac docemus, Christum post resurrectionē corpus quidem spirituale habuisse, sed κατὰ τι & secundum quid, ratione videlicet qualitatum nouarum, & excellentissimorum donorum, incorruptibilitatis nimirum, roboris, agilitatis, immortalitatis, splendore ac gloriæ cælestis, vitæque diuinæ & æternæ, quib. corpus Christi gloriosum per exaltationem donatum, atque instructum fuit, non autem simpliciter, & ratione substantiæ, ac partium eius, quæ proprietates suas essentiales retinuit, ac proinde definitione etiamnum à spiritu differt. Hæ autem ipsæ dotes, corpori Christi, per gloriosam exaltationem collatæ, licet maiores & perfectiores omnium creaturarum donis, adeoque non quidem contra, sed supra naturam, ac tantæ, & tam perfectæ sint, quantæ in creaturam cadere possunt: tamen proprias & essentiales humani corporis proprietates & qualitates nec tollunt, nec destruunt, sic vt corpus Christi, vtcunque glorificatum sit excellentissimè, tamen solidum, circumscriptum, visibile, palpabile, & alicubi situm, perpetuóque talé mansurum intelligatur. Non igitur μα- νυσίων aliquam, seu imitationem substantiæ cum Flaccianis, sed ἀλλοίωσιν tantum, id est, qualitatum alterationem, in statu gloriæ, cum scriptura sacra agnoscimus.
units.tr: We believe and teach that after the resurrection Christ had indeed a spiritual body, but in a certain respect and according to some quality [κατὰ τι], namely in respect of its new qualities and most excellent gifts: incorruptibility, strength, agility, immortality, the splendour and glory of heaven, and divine and eternal life. These gifts were bestowed upon and furnished to the glorified body of Christ through his exaltation. But it is not spiritual simply, or in respect of its substance and parts, which kept their essential properties, and so by definition still differ from spirit. These same endowments, bestowed on the body of Christ through his glorious exaltation, though greater and more perfect than the gifts of all creatures, and so not contrary to nature but above it, and as great and as perfect as a creature can receive, nevertheless do not remove or destroy the essential properties and qualities of a human body. So the body of Christ, however gloriously it has been exalted, is still to be understood as solid, circumscribed, visible, tangible, situated somewhere, and to remain such for ever. Therefore we acknowledge from Holy Scripture, not any change of substance [μεταουσίωσιν] or imitation of substance, as the Flacians hold, but only an alteration [ἀλλοίωσιν], that is, a change of qualities, in the state of glory.

units.la: Et quia ipso Paulo teste, Christus pro efficacitate, qua potest omnia subiicere sibi, transformabit corpus nostrum humile, vt conforme fiat corpori suo glorioso: ideo necessario inde sequitur, corpora nostra etiam secundum quid tantùm, videlicet ratione qualitatum & donorum, immortalitatis videlicet, potentiæ, gloriæ, ac vitæ diuinæ (quæ dotes & qualitates eædem futuræ sunt cum donis & qualitatibus Christi ratione speciei, sed gradibus, & excellentia hisce longè inferiores, quod ipsum discriminen inter caput & membra, inter eum qui glorificat, & eos qui glorificantur, euidenter docet) credentium corporibus conferendarum: non verò simpliciter, & ratione substantiæ, spiritualia futura, ac proinde eadem corpora nostra, quod ad substantiam attinet, resurrectura esse, sed spiritualibus quibusdam qualitatibus, quales nimirum in corpus cadere possunt, ornata, atque instructa. Atque licet huius sententiæ, ac doctrinæ nostræ veritas, pluribus argumentis ac rationibus demonstrari posset: nos tamen reliquis omissis, vnius enumeratione contenti erimus.
units.tr: And since, as Paul testifies, Christ, by the power whereby he is able to subject all things to himself, will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, it necessarily follows that the bodies of believers will receive, even in a certain respect only, that is, in respect of qualities and gifts (namely immortality, power, glory and divine life; these gifts and qualities will be the same in kind as those of Christ, but far inferior to his in degree and excellence, as the difference between head and members, between him who glorifies and those who are glorified, clearly teaches), and not that they will be spiritual simply, or in respect of substance. Hence it follows that our bodies, as far as substance is concerned, will rise as the same bodies, but adorned and furnished with certain spiritual qualities such as can belong to a body. Although the truth of this opinion and of our doctrine could be proved by many arguments and reasons, we shall be content with the mention of one, leaving the rest aside.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum igitur illud desumitur ex Lucæ capite vigesimoquarto, versu trigesimooctauo, trigesimonono, & quadragesimo: Tum dixit eis, Quid turbati estis? & quare disceptationes subeunt corda vestra? videte manus meas, & pedes meos, nam ego ipse sum: contrectate me, & videte, nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout me conspicitis habere: & quum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus, & pedes: & vers. 42. 43. tumederunt ei partem piscis assi, & aliquid ex fauo apiario, quæ accepit, & in eorum conspectu comedit. Iohan. 20. v. 20. Et quum hæc dixisset, ostendit eis manus ac latus suum: & vers. 25. Nisi videro in manibus eius vestigium clauorum, & immisero digitum meum vestigio clauorum, & immisero manum meam lateri eius, nequaquam credam: vers. 27. Dicit Iesus Thomæ, infer digitum tuum huc, & vide manus meas, & profer manum tuam, & immitte lateri meo, & ne esto incredulus, sed credens. Quibus in locis Christus etiam corporales discipulorum sensus testes adhibet, quibus se verum & palpabile, non autem spirituale & ἀσώματον aliquod corpus habere demonstret. monstret. Roman. 6. verf. 9. Qui sciamus Christum excitatum ex mortuis, non amplius mori, mortem, inquam, ei non amplius dominari: unde sic argumentamur: Nullum corpus ἀσώματον, & simpliciter, & ratione non tantum qualitatum, sed etiam substantiae, spirituale, carnem & ossa habet, & visu, tactuque ac sensibus externis percipi potest: Atqui corpus Christi, etiam postquam resurrexit, & immortale factum est, carnem & ossa habuit, & visu tactuque, ac sensibus externis percipi potuit, quemadmodum ex praedictis scripturae sacrae testimoniis liquet: Ergo corpus Christi postquam resurrexit, & immortale factum est, ἀσώματον, & simpliciter, ac non qualitatum tantū, sed etiam substantiae ratione spirituale non fuit.
units.tr: Our argument, then, is taken from Luke chapter twenty-four, verses thirty-eight, thirty-nine and forty: Then he said to them, Why are you troubled? And why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. And verses 42 and 43: They gave him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb, which he took and ate in their sight. John 20:20: And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Verse 25: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will by no means believe. Verse 27: Jesus says to Thomas, Put your finger here, and see my hands, and put forth your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing. In these passages Christ even calls on the bodily senses of the disciples as witnesses, to show that he has a true and tangible body, and not some spiritual and incorporeal [ἀσώματον] body. Romans 6:9: Knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more; death, I say, no longer has dominion over him. From this we argue as follows: No body that is incorporeal [ἀσώματον], spiritual simply and in respect of substance and not only of qualities, has flesh and bones, and can be perceived by sight, touch and the external senses. But the body of Christ, even after he rose and was made immortal, had flesh and bones, and could be perceived by sight, touch and the external senses, as is clear from the testimonies of Holy Scripture cited above. Therefore the body of Christ, after he rose and was made immortal, was not incorporeal [ἀσώματον], nor spiritual simply, nor spiritual in respect of substance and not merely of qualities.

units.la: Huic adde & illud, quod, etiamsi Aduersarii resurrectionem mortuorum amplectantur, ex sententia tamen illorum, qui corpora nostra post resurrectionem simpliciter spiritualia futura esse tuentur, necessario sequitur, nullam corporum resurrectionem expectandam, aut credendam esse. Quum enim substantia, & accidens, seu qualitates substantiae, totum ens, ac proinde etiam totum corpus hominis diuidant, ideo si corpora nostra nec quo ad substantiam, nec quo ad qualitates resurrectura sunt: necessario sequitur illa plane non esse resurrectura, quod est contra apertissima scripturae sacrae testimonia, in quibus resurrectio corporum nostrorum diserte asseritur ac docetur.
units.tr: Add to this that, even if our opponents accept the resurrection of the dead, yet on the view of those who maintain that our bodies after the resurrection will be spiritual simply, it necessarily follows that no resurrection of bodies is to be expected or believed. For since substance and accident, or the qualities of substance, make up the whole being, and therefore the whole body of man, if our bodies are to rise neither as to substance nor as to qualities, it necessarily follows that they will not rise at all. This is contrary to the most manifest testimonies of Holy Scripture, in which the resurrection of our bodies is plainly asserted and taught.

units.la: Ostorrodius contra capite praedicto docet ac statuit, Christum ab eo tempore, quo Deus ipsum Regem ac Dominum constituit, corpus spirituale ac caeleste, & proinde nec carnem nec sanguinem habuisse. Atque hanc suam sententiam inde probare conatur, quod corpus Christi ab eo tempore, quo ille a Patre glorificatus est, morti, corruptioni, aut mutationi, nullo modo fuit obnoxium.
units.tr: Ostorodius, in the chapter just mentioned, teaches and maintains against this: that Christ, from the time when God appointed him King and Lord, had a spiritual and heavenly body, and therefore had neither flesh nor blood. And he tries to prove this opinion from the fact that the body of Christ, from the time when he was glorified by the Father, was in no way subject to death, corruption or change.

units.la: Syllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The syllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Si corpus Christi, ab illo tempore, quo ille a Patre glorificatus est, morti, corruptioni, aut mutationi, nullo modo fuit obnoxium, tum sequitur, Christum ab eo tempore, quo Deus ipsum Regem ac Dominum constituit, corpus spirituale & caeleste, ac proinde nec carnem, nec sanguinem habuisse: Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If the body of Christ, from that time when he was glorified by the Father, was in no way subject to death, corruption, or change, then it follows that Christ, from the time when God constituted him King and Lord, had a spiritual and heavenly body, and therefore had neither flesh nor blood. But the first is true; therefore so is the second.

units.la: Assumptionem, cuius probationem primo loco ponit Aduersarius, inde demonstrare conatur: quod videlicet Christus rex sit spiritualis & caelestis, ita ut in mortem & inferos potestatem habeat, id est, suos a morte & inferis liberare possit, unde necessario sequatur, ipsum quoque in posterum non amplius moriturum esse: secus enim alios a morte eripere non posset, quum nemo id quod ipsemet non habet, aliis impertiri, aut dare queat.
units.tr: He tries to demonstrate the assumption, whose proof the Opponent puts first, in this way: namely that Christ is a spiritual and heavenly king, so that he holds power over death and hell, that is, he is able to free his own from death and hell. From this it necessarily follows that he himself will not die again in the future. For otherwise he could not snatch others from death, since no one can impart or give to others what he does not himself have.

units.la: Prosyllogismus talis est.
units.tr: The prosyllogism runs as follows.

units.la: Si Christus Rex spiritualis ac caelestis est, sic ut imperium in mortem ac inferos obtineat, hoc est, suos a morte & inferis liberare possit: tum necessario sequitur corpus Christi, ab illo tempore quo Pater ipsum glorificauit, morti, corruptioni, aut mutationi, nullo modo fuisse obnoxium. Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If Christ is a spiritual and heavenly King, such that he holds dominion over death and hell, that is, is able to free his own from death and hell, then it necessarily follows that the body of Christ, from the time when the Father glorified him, was in no way subject to death, corruption, or change. But the first is true; therefore so is the second.

units.la: Connexum vero syllogismi principalis inde probare conatur, quod Christus si carne & sanguine praeditus esset, non haberet corpus spirituale, ac proinde mortalis esset, quandoquidem caro, id est mortale, & interitui obnoxium est, quicquid ex carne est: Ioh.3. v.6. Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est. Es. 40. v.7. omnis caro gramen. 1.Pet.1. v.24. Omnis caro ut gramen, & omnis gloria hominis, ut flos graminis, exaruit gramen, & flos eius decidit: & ex eo, quod Apostolus Paulus 1.Cor.15. postquam de credentibus disseruisset, illos post resurrectionem non terrenos, sed spirituales, & caelestes futuros esse, v.50. concluserit, carnem & sanguinem non posse regni Dei hereditatem consequi.
units.tr: He tries to prove the connection of the main syllogism in this way: if Christ were endowed with flesh and blood, he would not have a spiritual body, and so would be mortal, since whatever is of the flesh is mortal, liable to perish: John 3:6, "That which is born of the flesh is flesh." Isaiah 40:7, "All flesh is grass." 1 Peter 1:24, "All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass: the grass withers and its flower falls." And from the fact that the Apostle Paul, after discussing believers, concluded in 1 Corinthians 15:50 that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, having said that after the resurrection they would be not earthly but spiritual and heavenly.

units.la: Prosyllogismus connexi illius talis est.
units.tr: The prosyllogism of this connection runs as follows.

units.la: Simorti & corruptioni obnoxium est, quicquid carnem & sanguinem habet: tum, si corpus Christi, ab eo tempore, quo ille a Patre glorificatus est, morti, corruptioni, aut mutationi nullo modo fuit obnoxium, sequitur, Christum ab eo tempore, quo Deus ipsum Regem ac Dominum constituit, corpus spirituale, ac caeleste, & proinde nec carnem nec sanguinem habuisse. Atqui prius verum est: Ergo & posterius
units.tr: Whatever has flesh and blood is subject to death and corruption. Then, if the body of Christ, from the time when the Father glorified him, was in no way subject to death, corruption, or change, it follows that Christ, from the time when God constituted him King and Lord, had a spiritual and heavenly body, and therefore had neither flesh nor blood. But the first is true; therefore so is the second.

units.la: Huic autem probationi subiicit Aduersarius prolepsin, ac dicit. per carnem & sanguinem in illo loco 1.Cor.15.v.50.non homines carnales, qui videlicet carnaliter affecti sint, sed carnalia corpora intelligenda esse: quandoquidem scopus & finis Apostoli non fit, vt demonstret, qualesnam homines ad salutem peruenturi sint, sed qualia nam corpora Christiani, tam illi, qui ex mortuis resurrecturi sunt, quam illi qui transmutabuntur, sint habituri: quemadmodum id ex disputationis serie, à verf. 35.vsque ad verf. 57.capitis illius, manifeste apparet.
units.tr: To this proof the Opponent adds a prolepsis, saying: by "flesh and blood" in that passage, 1 Corinthians 15:50, are not meant carnal men, that is, men carnally disposed, but carnal bodies. For the aim and purpose of the Apostle is not to show what kind of men will attain salvation, but what kind of bodies Christians will have, both those who will rise from the dead and those who will be changed. This is clear from the course of the argument in that chapter, from verse 35 to verse 57.

units.la: Resp. Assumptionem syllogismi principalis esse verissimam, ac proinde examine aut responsione non indigere: sed connexum sit ὁλως consideratum, esse falsum: & quia Aduersarius ex verissimo illo antecedente, duplex elicit & educit consequens, quorum prius æquiuocum, alterum vero falsum est, ideo quomodo illud prius seu antecedens, ad vtrumque consequens se habeat, & affectum sit, diligentius nobis erit disputiendum: Et prius quidem consequens, quod videlicet Christus corpus spirituale ac cæleste habeat, tollenda est æquiuocatio. Corpus enim aliquod, vti ex antecedentibus patet, spirituale ac cælestæ dicitur duobus modis, vel simpliciter ac ratione substantiæ & essentiæ, partiúmque, proprietatum & qualitatum omnium: vel κατὰ τι & secúdum quid, ratione videlicet qualitatum tantum & præstantissimorum donorum spiritualium, ac cælestium. Si Aduersarius corpus spirituale priore significatione accipiat, tū consequētia falsa est, nec subiúcto profyllogismo fulciri ac demonstrari potest, quemadmodum paulò post ostendemus. Sin vero illud accipiat significatione posteriore, tum prius illud consequens ex illo antecedente legitimè, ac necessaria cōsequentia decitur. Vnde iam patet, totam consequentiam respectu illius posterioris consequentis, quod duplici fulcro antecedente nimirum & substracto priori consequente nititur, falsam esse. Nam ex ipso antecedente, hoc posterius consequens, quod Christus nimirum carnem & sanguinem non habeat, deduci non pot st, quia ex eo, quod Christi corpus, à glorificationis tempore morti, corruptioni, & mutationi non fit obnoxium, nihil aliud sequitur quàm totum Christi corpus, ac proinde etiam essentiales, ac substantiales eius partes carnem & sanguinem, ab omni fragilitate, morte, passione, cunctisque etiam minimis infirmitatibus, omnibúsque illarum causis vindicatum esse, quæ infirmitates, vt ipsam substantiam, & essentiam corporis humani non constituebant, nec vt proprietates essentiales ipsam naturam ac definitionem corporis, sed vt qualitates accidentales statum & conditionem Christi sequebantur: ita ipsarum abolitio, ipsam quoque corporis substantiam tollere non potest. Neque etiā hoc idem in priori illo consequente, quicquam praesidii habet, quia ex illo nihil aliud conficitur, quā corpus Christi glorificationis beneficio, summa, eáque spirituali & cœlesti puritate, robore, agilitate, & claritate ornatum fulgere, quæ accidentia non totius substantiæ transmutationem & μετουσιωσιν, sed qualitatum tantum ἀλλοίωσιν & alterationem infert, sic vt inter corpus Christi in statu gloriæ, & statu infirmitatis ac humiliationis, non essentiale, sed accidentale tantum fit discrimen, & corpus illud glorificatum, à non glorificato nec numero, nec specie, nec genere, nec τῷ τὶ seu ὑποκειμένῳ, sed λόγῳ & qualitatibus accidentalibus differat, & vnum idemque corpus subiectum, tum infirmitatis, tum gloriæ sit agnoscendum. Sed ad examen syllogismi progredior, cuius assumptio sic vniuersaliter accepta, quum nomina carnis & sanguinis in scripturis sacris sint æquiuoca ac πολυσήμια, & variæ admodum significationis, vt cuiuis notum est, manifesta falsitate laborat, nec quatuor illis scripturæ sacræ testimoniis probatur. Nam primum locum ex Iohan. cap. 3. verf. 6. quantum concernit, nomine carnis non ipsam substantiam corpoream, qualis illa à Deo creata, sed hominem carnalem, morti & dominio peccati addictum, qui 1. Corinth. 2. verf. 14. homo ψυχικὸς, & 2. Corinth. 4. verf. 16. ὁ ἔξω ἄνθρωπος, & Ephes. 4. verf. 22. vetus homo appellatur, per metonymiam illam, qua nomina appellatiua pro adiectiuis vsurpantur, significari ex eo liquet manifestissimè, tum quòd non massa illa corporea, præsertim qualis illa à Deo creata est, verum totus homo, sed corruptus, & peccato inquinatus illius de qua agitur, regenerationis, ac παλιγγενεσίας obiectum est: tum etiam quòd carni illi tribuitur σάρξ... Roman. 8. verf. 6. & vss. Coloss. 2. ver. 18. quorum neutrum moli corporeæ potest competere: tum denique ex antithesi, spiritus videlicet nomine, quo non ipse animus hominis, sed totus homo spiritualis, & Spiritus sancti gratia Christo insitus, ac in ipso renouatus & regenitus denotatur, qui alibi, nempe 1. Cor. cap. 2. verf. 19. ἄνθρωπος πνευματικὸς, & 2. Corinth. 5. verf. 6. ἐν σῶμα ἀνθρωπος, & Ephes. 4. verf. 24. καινὸς ἄνθρωπος vocatur. Apud Esaiam verò capite 40. versu 6. qui locus ab Apostolo Petro 1. epist. capite 1. versu 24. allegatur voce carnis etiam synecdochicè totus homo, qualis ille post peccatum est, intelligitur, ac tum naturæ, quæ propter peccatum vanitati, corruptioni ac morti obnoxia est, imbecillitas,tum etiam vitæ humanæ fragilitas significatur, quia Propheta ibi hominem, & quicquid in ipso excellens & præclarum, ac laude dignum videtur naturaliter, vanitatis damnat, ipsámque adeo vitam hominis fragilem ac fluxam esse ostendit, quemadmodum Propheta Dauid illam, quod emarcida fit, & caduca, fœno comparat: Psalmo 103. versu decimoquinto & decimofexto, Hominis sicut herba sunt dies, sicut flos agri sic floret: quoniam ventus transfit in illum, & non est, nec agnoscit eum vltra locus eius. Hæc enim de ipsa natura hominis, qualis fuit in statu integritatis, & creationis splendore, nisi summam Deo opifici iniuriam inferre velimus, affirmare minimè possumus, vnde sequitur naturam humanam peccato inquinatam & corruptam, nomine carnis in illis locis significari. Carnis verò & sanguinis nomine 1.Cor.15.ver.50. lubens fateor & concedo, corpus humanum denotari, sed cum infirmitate & imbecillitate, peccato contracta, coniunctum, quemadmodum ipsa epexegefis, quam subiunxit Apostolus, neque posse inquiens corruptionem, naturæ incorrupta hæreditatem consequi (vbi, quod prius carnem & sanguinem vocauit, φθορὰ seu corruptionem nuncupat) diserte docet. Quia verò hæc corruptio qualitatem corporis tantummodò denotat, illa verò assumptio, vti & præsens, de qua disceptamus, quæstio de ipsa substantia intelligitur: ideo manifeste hinc appáret, prædictam assumptionem falsam esse, nec illis quatuor allegatis Scripturæ sacræ testimoniis confirmari, ipsúmque Aduersarium subiuncta illa prolepfi, suam confirmationem tueri non posse.
units.tr: Reply. The assumption of the main syllogism is most true, and so needs no examination or answer. But the connection, taken as a whole [ὅλως], is false. And since the Opponent from that most true antecedent draws out a double consequent, of which the first is equivocal and the second false, we shall have to discuss more carefully how that first consequent, or antecedent, relates to each of the consequents and is affected by them. As for the first consequent, namely that Christ has a spiritual and heavenly body, the equivocation must be removed. For a body, as is clear from what goes before, is called spiritual and heavenly in two ways: either simply [simpliciter], in respect of its substance and essence and all its parts, properties and qualities; or in a certain respect [κατὰ τι], that is, in respect of its qualities alone and its most excellent spiritual and heavenly gifts. If the Opponent takes "spiritual body" in the first sense, then the consequence is false, and it cannot be supported or demonstrated by the subjoined prosyllogism, as we shall show shortly. But if he takes it in the second sense, then that first consequent follows legitimately and by necessary consequence from that antecedent. From this it is now plain that the whole consequence, with respect to that second consequent, which rests on two supports, namely the antecedent and the rejected first consequent, is false. For from the antecedent itself this second consequent, that Christ does not have flesh and blood, cannot be deduced. For from the fact that the body of Christ was not subject to death, corruption, and change from the time of his glorification, nothing else follows except that the whole body of Christ, and therefore also its essential and substantial parts, flesh and blood, were freed from all frailty, death, suffering, and even all the smallest infirmities, and all their causes. These infirmities did not constitute the substance and essence of the human body, nor were they its essential properties that define its nature, but accidental qualities that followed the state and condition of Christ. So their abolition cannot take away the substance of the body itself. Nor does the first consequent give any help to this second one, since from it nothing else is inferred except that the body of Christ, by the benefit of glorification, shines adorned with the highest, and that spiritual and heavenly, purity, strength, agility and brightness. These accidents bring about not a change of the whole substance and transubstantiation [μετουσίωσις], but only an alteration [ἀλλοίωσις] of qualities, so that between the body of Christ in its state of glory and in its state of infirmity and humiliation there is only an accidental, not an essential, difference. The glorified body differs from the unglorified not in number, species, or genus, nor in the [τὸ τί] or subject [ὑποκείμενον], but in account [λόγῳ] and accidental qualities. One and the same body must be acknowledged as subject both to infirmity and to glory. But I proceed to the examination of the syllogism. Its assumption, taken universally in this way, suffers from manifest falsity, since the names of flesh and blood in the sacred Scriptures are equivocal and polysemous and of very varied meaning, as is known to everyone. Nor is it proved by those four testimonies of Scripture. For, as far as the first passage, John 3:6, is concerned, by the name of flesh is meant not the corporeal substance itself, as it was created by God, but the carnal man, given over to death and to the dominion of sin, who is called psychikos (natural) man in 1 Corinthians 2:14, "the outward man" in 2 Corinthians 4:16, and "the old man" in Ephesians 4:22. That this is so, by that metonymy in which abstract nouns are used for adjectives, is most clearly shown: first, because the object of regeneration and palingenesis is not that corporeal mass, especially as it was created by God, but the whole man, corrupted and polluted by sin, of whom the passage speaks; second, because the term sarx [σάρξ] is applied to that flesh in Romans 8:6 and following, and Colossians 2:18, neither of which can apply to corporeal mass; and finally from the antithesis with the name spirit, by which is denoted not the man's mind itself, but the whole spiritual man, engrafted into Christ by the grace of the Holy Spirit and renewed and regenerated in him, who elsewhere is called pneumatikos anthropos [ἄνθρωπος πνευματικός] in 1 Corinthians 2:15, "one flesh" [ἓν σῶμα] and "one man" in 2 Corinthians 5:6, and "new man" [καινὸς ἄνθρωπος] in Ephesians 4:24. In Isaiah 40:6, a passage which the Apostle Peter cites in 1 Peter 1:24, by the word flesh is understood, also by synecdoche, the whole man as he is after sin; and by it is signified both the weakness of a nature which, on account of sin, is subject to vanity, corruption and death, and also the frailty of human life. For the Prophet there condemns man, and whatever in him seems naturally excellent, distinguished, and worthy of praise, as vanity, and shows that human life itself is fragile and fleeting. In the same way the Prophet David compares it, in its withering and falling, to hay: Psalm 103:15-16, "As for man, his days are as grass; as a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more." For to affirm these things of the nature of man as it was in the state of integrity and the splendour of creation would be to do the Creator great injury, which we can by no means do. Hence it follows that in those passages the nature of man polluted and corrupted by sin is signified by the name flesh. But by the name of flesh and blood in 1 Corinthians 15:50 I gladly confess and concede that the human body is denoted, yet joined with the infirmity and weakness contracted through sin. This the Apostle clearly teaches by the explanation he appends, saying that "corruption cannot inherit incorruption," where he calls by the name phthora [φθορά], or corruption, what he had first called flesh and blood. But since this corruption denotes only a quality of the body, and that assumption, as also the present question which we are disputing, is understood of the substance itself, it therefore clearly appears that the aforesaid assumption is false, and is not confirmed by those four cited testimonies of Scripture, and that the Opponent, with the prolepsis he has added, cannot defend his confirmation.

units.la: Ex illis autem quæ Aduersarius hactenus de qualitate corporis Christi disseruit, iam fecundo loco infert, Si igitur, inquiens, Christus non terrenum & carnale, sed spirituale ac cœleste corpus habet: tum sequitur, etiam illos, qui in ipsum credunt, non terrena & carnalia, sed spiritualia ac cœlestia corpora habituros esse, quandoquidem teste Apostolo, Philip.capite tertio, versu vigesimofecundo: Christus, corpus nostrum humile corpori suo glorioso conformaturus est, & quemadmodum ipse Christus quatenus glorificatus est, ita etiam fideles, quatenus in ipsum credunt, originem suam ex cœlo traxerunt, quemadmodum Adamus, & homines alij, quatenus ab eo propagati sunt, ex terra orti sunt. Atque huc respexit Apostolus, quum 1.Cor.15 v.47. diceret: Primus homo e terra terrenus: Secundus homo Dominus, de coelo est. Sic enim verba illa distinguenda ac legenda sunt, quasi scriptum esset. Secundus homo, nempe Dominus, de coelo est, quemadmodum primus ex terra fuit, quemadmodum proxime precedentia verba, primus homo e terra terrenus, manifeste demonstrant. Hoc igitur vult Apostolus, quemadmodum homines quatenus ex Adamo sunt, qui corpore terreno praeditus fuit, corpora terrena habent: ita quatenus ex Christo sunt corpora spiritualia habet ut, quale & Christus habet, ac proinde mox subiungit Apostolus, & quemadmodum gestavimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus imaginem coelestis: nomen enim coelestis, ad hominis, non autem ad Domini vocem referendum est, quasi dictum esset hominis coelestis, non autem Domini coelestis. Quamvis enim Christus, Dominus sit, & nomine illo potissimum significetur: tamen in illo loco non quatenus Dominus, sed quatenus primus coelestis homo est, consideratur.
units.tr: From what the Opponent has so far argued about the quality of Christ's body, he now draws a second inference: "If, then, Christ has not an earthly and fleshly but a spiritual and heavenly body, it follows that those who believe in him will also have not earthly and fleshly but spiritual and heavenly bodies, since, as the Apostle witnesses in Philippians chapter 3, verse 21, Christ 'will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body'; and just as Christ himself, insofar as he has been glorified, has drawn his origin from heaven, so the faithful, insofar as they believe in him, have drawn their origin from heaven, just as Adam and other men, insofar as they have been propagated from him, have arisen from the earth." The Apostle had this in view when he said (1 Cor. 15:47): "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven." For the words must be divided and read as if it were written: "The second man, namely the Lord, is from heaven, just as the first was from the earth," as the immediately preceding words, "the first man is of the earth, earthy," make plain. The Apostle therefore means this: just as men, insofar as they are of Adam, who was endowed with an earthly body, have earthly bodies, so insofar as they are of Christ they have spiritual bodies, such as Christ himself has. Accordingly the Apostle immediately adds (verse 49): "And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly." For the word "heavenly" must be referred to man, not to the Lord, as if it had been said "the heavenly man," not "the heavenly Lord." For although Christ is Lord, and is principally signified by that name, yet in that passage he is considered not as Lord but as the first heavenly man.

units.la: Resp. Habituros esse fideles, & Christianos, post hanc vitam, & quidem virtute, & beneficio Christi, corpora spiritualia ac coelestia, non quidem ratione substantiae, sed novarum qualitatum respectu, quemadmodum ab Adamo corpora terrena, & morti fragilitati, & corruptioni obnoxia accepimus: iam in antecedentibus docuimus, & idem Apostolus etiam confirmat, qui in verbis ab Aduersario allegatis, non materiae, sed originis, dignitatis, qualitatum, & habituum comparationem instituit, Christumque & Adamum, tanquam duo capita ad hoc introducit, ut in illis originem & conditionem tum mortalitatis, imbecillitatis, & fragilitatis humanae, tum etiam glorificationis nostrae exprimat & offendat, omnes, quotquot carnali generatione ab Adamo descenderunt, parent is sui gestare imaginem, hoc est, terrenos esse, & morti atque corruptioni obnoxios: fideles vero, qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, aut viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt, ad glorificationem & beatam immortalitatem resurrecturos esse. Vt iam nihil referat, aut nostra interfit, sive verba illa vers. 47. cum Tertulliano, Ambrosio, & Hieronymo, sive etiam cum reliquis interpretibus, sive denique cum ipso Aduersario legamus ac distinguamus, nec etiam opus sit, ut ea, quae ab Oecolampadio fusius explicata sunt, operosius excutiamus.
units.tr: Answer: After this life the faithful and Christians will have spiritual and heavenly bodies, by the power and benefit of Christ, not indeed in respect of substance but in respect of new qualities, just as from Adam we received earthly bodies, subject to death, frailty and corruption. We have already taught this in what has gone before, and the same Apostle also confirms it: in the words the Opponent has cited, he draws a comparison not of matter but of origin, dignity, qualities and habits, and introduces Christ and Adam as two heads for this purpose, so that he might express and set forth in them both the origin and condition of human mortality, weakness and frailty, and also our glorification. All who have descended from Adam by carnal generation bear the image of their parent, that is, they are earthly and subject to death and corruption; but the faithful, who are born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of man, but of God, will rise to glory and blessed immortality. So it matters nothing to us whether we read and punctuate those words of verse 47 with Tertullian, Ambrose and Jerome, or with the other interpreters, or finally with the Opponent himself; nor is it necessary for us to examine at length what Oecolampadius has explained more fully.

units.la: Tertio refellere conatur duo argumenta, quibus illa consequentia quentia conuellitur,quod videlicet Christus ideo nec carnem,nec sanguinem, sed corpus simpliciter spirituale habeat, quia caro & sanguis, regni Dei hæreditatem consequi non posse dicantur : primum inde desumptum est, quod ex Scripturis sacris demonstratur, Christum post resurrectionem, carnem & sanguinem habuisse,& tamen corpore immortali præditū fuisse : unde iam sequitur, verba illa,quę ex 1. Corinth. 15. verf. 50. allegantur aliter,quàm ab Aduersario fit, explicanda esse. Secundum ex symbolo Apostolico depromptum est,in quo articulus ille,credo resurrectionem mortuorum,continetur. Ad primum respondet : primò,nondum demonstratū esse, quod corpus Christi,quod ille statim a resurrectione habuit, immortale fuerit. Quamuis enim Christus ita resurrexerit, ut nunquam amplius moriturus fuerit,inde tamen non sequi,ait, ipsum iam tum corpus immortale habuisse,aliud siquidem sit, non amplius mori,aliud vero mori non posse, ut videre sit in illis fidelibus, quos Christi aduentus viuos deprehendet, & qui non morituri, sed transmutādi,nec tamen corpora immortalia,sic ut non possint mori,habituri sint,priusquam transmutentur. Secundò, dicit, ex modo resurrectionis Christi, modum & rationem resurrectionis nostræ,æstimandam ac metiendam non esse, quandoquidem necessarium fuerit,ut Christus cum illis vulnerum vestigiis & cicatricibus resurgeret,quippe sine quibus, ij qui veritati resurrectionis ipsius testimonium perhibere debuerunt,ipsum cognituri non fuissent. Tertiò,neminem,inquit ,tam simplicem esse,qui non videat,eiusmodi vulnerum vestigia,in corpore immortali & glorificato remanere non posse. Ad secundum respondet,verba illa symboli non tanta pollere auctoritate, ut ipsis contra Scriptura sacra testimonia,fides haberi debeat( ut nihil dicat, quod illa ab articulo Credo in Spiritum sanctum ad finem vsque,proprie ad symbolum non pertineant, sed diu postquam illud compositum esset, ipsi adiuncta fuerint ) quandoquidem nondum demonstratum sit, Apostolos illud composuisse. Quanquam illa ipsa verba symboli consistere posse videantur,modò rectè intelligantur, nempe quatenus illis significatur,idipsum, quod aliquando caro fuit, resurrecturum esse,quemadmodum etiam Matt. 21. verf. 31. Meretrices & Publicani Pharisæis præituri dicuntur,quod tamen secundum literalem sensum falsum esset,quandoquidem tales regnum Dei non possidebunt, 1. Cor. 6. v. 9. ex quibus proinde Christus eos intellexit, qui aliquando tales fuerunt, non autem qui tales esse perseuerant. Kesp. Aliud esse actu ipso non mori,aliud mori non posse, vel pueri norunt, ac proinde non indiget distinctio illa probatione vlla,quamuis illa eorum, quos Christi aduentus viuos deprehen-det,exemplo nec illustretur nec confirmetur, quandoquidem su-bita & momentanea illa tranfmutatio ipsis mortis instar erit, & idem in ipsis, quod in nobis mors, effectura est,Christum vero ab eo ipso tempore, quo potenter & gloriose resurrexit, corpore immortali & incorruptibili indutum fuisse, demonstrari potest euidentissime.
