Nam si Christus post resurrectionem corpus gestauit mortale, & φθαρτὸν, tum necessario sequitur nostra quoque corpora etiam post resurrectionem mortalia & corruptibilia, non vero incorrupta, potentia, gloriosa, cœlestia,ac spiritualia,futura esse. Quum enim inter resurrectionem Christi, & resurrectionem credentium eam affectionem & relationem constituat Apostolus, qualis est inter causam propriam & effectum ipsius, sic vt posita vna ponatur & altera, negata vna, negetur & altera, & sic ab vna ad alteram affirmatiuam & negatiuam nectat consequentiam:1.Corint.capite decimo quinto, versu duodecimo. Quod si Christus praedicatur ex mortuis excitatus esse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos, non esse resurrectionem mortuorum? versu decimo tertio, Nam si resurrectio mortuorum non est, Christus quoque non est excitatus. ver. decimo sexto decimo septimo, & decimo octauo, Nam si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoque non est excitatus: quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra, adhuc estis in peccatis vestris, nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo perierunt: versu vigesimo & vigesimo primo. Nunc autem Christus excitatus est ex mortuis, & primitiae eorum qui obdormierunt, factus est: quia enim per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio mortuorum: ideo necessario sequitur, credentes virtute & efficacia resurrectionis Christi resurgere, & cõsequi quicquid resurrectionis beneficio in ipsos donorū & gloriae confertur, vnde etiam Apostolus,ipsum primitias eorum qui obdormierunt, appellat, eo quod vis resurrectionis Christi ad omnes diffundatur, quemadmodum in primitiis totius anni proventus consecrabatur, sic vt mortui eum sequantur, quemadmodum tota messis primitias sequebatur:quum igitur corpora nostra post resurrectionem futura sint immortalia, incorrupta, potentia, gloriosa & spiritualia.1.Cor.15.v.42.43.44. Seminatur corpus corruptioni obnoxium, excitatur incorruptum: seminatur ignominiosum, excitatur gloriosum: seminatur infirmum, excitatur potens: seminatur corpus animale, excitatur spirituale: ideo necessario sequitur ipsum etiam Christi corpus, ab ipso resurrectionis momento, gloriosum, spirituale, coeleste, & immortale fuisse, nec mori amplius potuisse. Hisce adde, quod, si corpus Christi post resurrectionem carne & sanguine praeditum, mortale adhuc fuit, & per aut post ascensum in coelos, plane spirituale factum, carneque & sanguine omni exutum est, necessario sequatur, nec numero nec specie idem corpus Christi excitatum ex mortuis, & in coelos euectum esse, quum sublatis rei alicuius substantia & qualitatibus, nihil quod ad rei essentiam & accidentia pertinet, remanere posset, ac proinde totum subiectum aboleatur, totumque compositum substantiale, in aliud nouum substantiale, nullo sensibili remanente, transmutatur. Quae omnia cum falsa sint, & omnis solatii ac spei nostrae fundamentum pervertant, sequitur ipsam quoque Aduersariorum sententiam, falsam atque erroneam esse. Quod vero Christus corpore vulnerum vestigiis & cicatricibus insignito, resurgere voluit, id non ad ipsum resurrectionis modum & rationem formalem, quae in reductae animae cum restituto corpore copulatione & vnione personali consistit, referendum, sed eius causa & ratio singularis haec reddenda est, quod videlicet Christus hisce argumentis ac testimoniis certos nos reddere voluerit, idem ipsum corpus suum crucifixum mortuum atque sepultum resurrexisse. Quinetiam illa ipsa vulnerum vestigia & cicatrices nullam corpori glorificato deformitatem, sed potius summam triumphanti victori atque haec pugnae suae insignia circumferenti, addunt dignitatem, immensamque eius erga nos, quorum causa tam dira pertulit ac passus est, commendant charitatem. Quanquam verisimile sit, Christum illas notas & stigmata illa nostri causa tantum ad tempus gestasse, & postmodum depositisse: Sed haec vt ipsam substantiam corporis, carnis ac sanguinis nec constituunt nec tollunt, sic etiam veritatem sententiae nostrae non euertunt. Spondeo vero, me tum fidem habiturum esse Aduersario, vbi certi aliquid ex apertis sacrae Scripturae testimoniis hac de re demonstrauerit. Symbolum vero fidei nostrae quantum concernit, illud non video nec eo sensu Apostolicum appellatur, quasi Apostoli praeter res, & sensus in eo comprehensos, stylum etiam ipsum, ordinem, atque verba sic disposuerint & conscripserint: sed quia illud ex doctrina & scriptis Apostolorum haustum summa religionis capita, quae in scriptis Apostolorum comprehenduntur, ac proponuntur complectitur, & cum doctrina ac confessione Apostolorum consentit. Neque enim illius symboli conscripti finis hic est, ut illud vnà cum Scriptura sacra, fidei nostrę collaterale sit fundamentum, sed ut professionis publicæ, & agnitionis veritatis extet compendium: vnde nihil refert, quo tempore articulus ille de resurrectione carnis, cæteris fuerit adiunctus, sufficit nobis illius veritatem ex Scripturis hauitam,& omnibus temporibus ab Ecclesiis orthodoxis agnitam fuisse, vnde glossema subiunctum suo autori relinquo.
units.tr: Third, he tries to refute two arguments by which that inference is overthrown: namely, that Christ therefore has not flesh and blood but simply a spiritual body, because flesh and blood are said not to be able to inherit the kingdom of God. The first argument is drawn from the fact, demonstrated from the holy Scriptures, that Christ after the resurrection had flesh and blood and yet was endowed with an immortal body; from which it follows that the words cited from 1 Corinthians 15:50 must be explained otherwise than the Opponent does. The second is taken from the Apostles' Creed, in which the article "I believe the resurrection of the dead" is contained. To the first he replies: first, that it has not yet been demonstrated that the body Christ had immediately after the resurrection was immortal. For although Christ rose in such a way that he was never again to die, it does not follow, he says, that he already then had an immortal body; for it is one thing not to die any more, and another thing not to be able to die, as can be seen in those faithful ones whom Christ's coming will find alive, and who are not going to die but to be changed, and yet will not have immortal bodies, such that they cannot die, until they are changed. Second, he says that the manner and mode of our resurrection is not to be estimated and measured by the manner of Christ's resurrection, since it was necessary for Christ to rise with the traces of his wounds and scars, without which those who were to bear witness to the truth of his resurrection would not have known him. Third, he says, no one is so simple as not to see that traces of such wounds cannot remain in a glorified and immortal body. To the second he replies that the words of the creed do not carry such authority that they must be believed against the testimonies of holy Scripture (to say nothing of the fact that those words, from the article "I believe in the Holy Spirit" to the end, properly do not belong to the creed, but were added to it long after it had been composed), since it has not been demonstrated that the Apostles composed it. Yet those very words of the creed may seem to stand, provided they are rightly understood, namely insofar as they signify that what was once flesh will rise again, just as also (Matt. 21:31) harlots and publicans are said to go before the Pharisees, which nevertheless, according to the literal sense, would be false, since such people will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:9); from which passages Christ therefore understood those who were once such, not those who persevere as such. Answer: That it is one thing not to die in actual fact, and another not to be able to die, even children know; and therefore that distinction needs no proof at all, although the example of those whom Christ's coming finds alive is neither illustrated nor confirmed by it, since that sudden and instantaneous change will be like death for them, and will effect in them what death does in us. But it can be demonstrated most evidently that Christ, from the very moment in which he rose powerfully and gloriously, was clothed in an immortal and incorruptible body. For if after the resurrection Christ bore a mortal and corruptible [φθαρτόν] body, then it necessarily follows that our bodies too, after the resurrection, will be mortal and corruptible, and not incorrupt, powerful, glorious, heavenly and spiritual. For since the Apostle establishes between the resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of believers the same relation as holds between a proper cause and its effect, so that when the one is posited the other is posited, and when the one is denied the other is denied, and thus connects by affirmative and negative consequence the one with the other: 1 Corinthians 15:12: "Now if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?"; verse 13: "For if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither is Christ raised"; verses 16, 17 and 18: "For if the dead are not raised, neither is Christ raised; and if Christ is not raised, your faith is vain, you are still in your sins; then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished"; verses 20 and 21: "But now Christ is raised from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; for since by man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead." Therefore it necessarily follows that believers rise by the virtue and efficacy of Christ's resurrection, and obtain whatever gifts and glory are conferred upon them by the benefit of that resurrection. Hence the Apostle also calls him the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, because the power of Christ's resurrection is spread to all, just as in the firstfruits the produce of the whole year was consecrated, so that the dead follow him just as the whole harvest followed the firstfruits. Since, then, our bodies after the resurrection will be immortal, incorruptible, powerful, glorious and spiritual (1 Cor. 15:42–44): "It is sown a body subject to corruption, it is raised incorruptible; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body" — therefore it necessarily follows that Christ's own body too was glorious, spiritual, heavenly and immortal from the very moment of the resurrection, and could not die any more. Add to this that if Christ's body after the resurrection was still mortal, endowed with flesh and blood, and afterwards, either after the ascension into heaven or during it, became altogether spiritual and was stripped of all flesh and blood, then it necessarily follows that the body of Christ raised from the dead and carried up into heaven was not the same either in number or in kind; since, when the substance and qualities of a thing are removed, nothing that pertains to the essence and accidents of the thing could remain, and thus the whole subject would be annihilated, and the whole substantial composite transformed into another new substance, with nothing sensible remaining. Since all these consequences are false and overturn the foundation of all our comfort and hope, it follows that the Opponent's own opinion is also false and erroneous. As for the fact that Christ willed to rise with a body marked by the traces of wounds and scars, this must not be referred to the very manner and formal mode of the resurrection, which consists in the personal union and joining of the restored soul with the restored body; rather its particular cause and reason must be given thus: namely, that Christ wished by these arguments and testimonies to make us certain that this same body of his, crucified, dead and buried, had risen. Moreover, those very traces of wounds and scars add no deformity to the glorified body, but rather give the highest dignity to the triumphant victor who carries these as the marks of his battle, and they commend his immense love towards us, for whose sake he endured and suffered so dreadful things. Although it is likely that Christ bore those marks and stigmata only for a time for our sake, and afterwards laid them aside, yet just as these do not constitute or remove the substance of the body, flesh and blood, so they do not overturn the truth of our position. I promise, however, that I will then give the Opponent credence, when he has demonstrated something certain on this matter from the plain testimonies of holy Scripture. As for the creed of our faith, as far as it concerns us, I do not see that it is called Apostolic in the sense that the Apostles, apart from the matters and senses contained in it, also arranged and wrote down the style itself, the order and the words; rather, it is called so because it has been drawn from the doctrine and writings of the Apostles, and embraces and sets forth the chief heads of religion which are contained and proposed in the writings of the Apostles, and agrees with the doctrine and confession of the Apostles. For the purpose of composing that creed was not that it should stand as a foundation alongside Holy Scripture for our faith, but that it should exist as a compendium of public profession and acknowledgment of the truth. Hence it matters little at what time that article "of the resurrection of the flesh" was added to the others; it is enough for us that its truth was drawn from the Scriptures and acknowledged by the orthodox Churches at all times. Whatever is added as a gloss I leave to its own author.

units.la: Quæstionem secundam, An & quando nimirum Christi regnum finem sit habiturum? quam Aduersarius ita tractat, ut illam functionem Christi regiam, & regni administrationem, cum Ecclesiæ confirmatione finem habituram esse, affirmet, quantum concernit: observandum est id, quod aliquoties iam inculcauimus, regnum ac dominium Christi duplex esse, vnum essentiale, supremum, vniuersale, & tribus personis diuinis commune, quod Christo vt Deo vero atque æterno conditione naturali, & iure creationis competit, quemadmodum capite vndecimo demonstrauimus: alterum vero temporarium, œconomicum, ac dispensatiuum, Filio ac Mediatori ex libera Patris voluntate impositum, ac dispensatione œconomica ab ipso susceptum. Illud æternum est, & principio ac fine caret: huius autem administrationem œconomicè sibi imperatam, & à se receptam ac procuratam, in manus Dei & Patris traditurus est, quum omnem principatum, omnémque potentque potentiam & dominatum abolecuerit, & sic Pater in Filio totam illam œconomiam salutis nostræ perfecerit: quemadmodum administrationis illius finem, & certam œconomici illius regni, quod Christus ad salutis nostræ complementum à Patre habuit, determinationem Paulus 1.Cor.15. ex Psal.110. luculenter confirmat ac demonstrat: & huius posterioris, non autem prioris Regni, de quo in antecedentibus egimus, finem, argumenta Aduersarii euincunt, quæ proinde animaduersione non indigent, licet ille suo more, etiam in ipsius veritatis explicatione interdum impingat, & argumenta infirma cum firmis coniungat.
units.tr: The second question, namely whether and when Christ's kingdom will have an end, which the Adversary treats in such a way as to affirm that "that royal function of Christ and the administration of the kingdom will come to an end together with the confirmation of the Church," must be noted, insofar as it concerns this point: as we have often insisted, the kingdom and dominion of Christ is twofold. One is essential, supreme and universal, common to the three divine persons, which belongs to Christ as true and eternal God by natural condition and by the right of creation, as we demonstrated in the eleventh chapter. The other is temporal, economical and dispensatory, imposed on the Son and Mediator by the free will of the Father, and taken up and carried out by him in economical dispensation. The former is eternal and has neither beginning nor end. The administration of the latter, which was economically laid upon him and which he received and carried out, he will hand over into the hands of God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality, every power and dominion, and so the Father will have brought to completion in the Son that whole economy of our salvation. Paul, in 1 Cor. 15, from Psalm 110, clearly confirms and demonstrates both the end of that administration and the fixed limit of that economical kingdom which Christ received from the Father for the completion of our salvation. And the arguments of the Adversary establish the end of this latter kingdom, not of the former kingdom of which we spoke in the preceding sections; these therefore need no comment, although he, after his manner, sometimes stumbles even in the explanation of the truth itself, and joins weak arguments to strong ones.

units.la: Quæstionem tertiam & vltimam, Quis nimirum verborum illorum, quibus Melchisedec Hebr.7. v.3. fine patre, fine matre, fine genere, nec initium dierum, nec vitæ finem habens, assimilatus Filio Dei, Sacerdos in perpetuum manere dicitur, genuinum sit sensus? Ostorrodius totum illum versum ad Sacerdotium Melchisedecia-num, & Christi refert, & hunc illorū verborum sensum essestatue-re videtur, quod quemadmodum Melchisedec sacerdotiū non ex generis sui priuilegio, sed singulari Dei gratia consequutus sit : nec quisquis e-tiam ipsi successisse legatur : sic etiam Christus nec antecessorem, nec suc-cessorem in illo munere habeat. Ac proinde audacter, imo impuden-ter nimis detestabilem dicit esse ruditatem & negligentiam summam illorum, qui verba illa ad essentiam Christi, quasi ille in cælo matrem nullam, & in terra patrem nullum haberet, interpretantur: quia hoc in Melchisedec locum habere non possit, qui tamen Filio Dei assimiletur. Nos vero contra verba illa partim ad personam, partim ad Sacer-dotium Melchisedeci & Christi referenda esse censemus. Ad per-sonam, quatenus videlicet vterque sine patre, sine matre, sine recen-sione generis, nec initium, nec finem vitæ habens introducitur. Quæ omnia de Melchisedec dicuntur, non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, & quatenus ille personæ Christi typus fuit : seu non quod il-le reuera talis fuerit, sed quod ipsum sacra Scriptura talem repræ-sentet, quæ nec patrem, nec matrem, nec genus, nec ortum aut obi-tum ipsius prodidit, sed illis omnibus διαφορας διαφορας dissimilatis, ip-sum ἀμήτωρ, ἀπάτωρ proposuit : vt videlicet hoc typo, Christum re-uera talem esse ostenderet. Hæc omnia autem de Christo verissi-mè, tanquam complemento antecedentis typi enunciantur. Quū enim ille secundum carnem, non naturali propagatione, quæ fit per interuentum viri, natus, sed sine patre ex Spiritu sancto, id est, operatione illius, conceptus, & ex muliere factus: secundum diui-nam naturam vero, æternus Dei Filius fit : ideo ille diuersarum naturarum respectu ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, verissimè appellatur. Quum ve-rò idem, Christus videlicet, verus atque æternus Deus sit, a patre, ab æterno, generatione inexplicabili genitus, quomodo quæso ipsi principium dierum, aut finis vitæ competeret, aut genealogiam i-psius quis describeret? Vnde manifestè apparet, illa verissimè de persona Melchisedec, & Christi, licet de illo typicè, de hoc verò li-teraliter, & Χριστος λογος διηγησις explicati : Quibus & hoc accedit, quod nemo ratione officii, sed ratione naturæ, patre, matre, & familia carere dicitur : neque sacerdotes vt sacerdotes, sed vt homines, pa-trem, matrē, & genus habere censentur, & quod Apostolus ipsum non principium & finem sacerdotij, sed principium & finem vitæ ha-bere negat. Neque hanc expositionem elumbis illa Aduersarii ratio, quod videlicet illa Melchisedeco, qui tamen Christo assimiletur, proprie competere nequeant. Quum enim ista omnia de Melchisedeco vt typo Christi enuncientur, qui Filio Dei assimilatus, id est, similis factus esse dicitur, non secundum substantiam, sed secundum rationem, & modum narrationis historicae: inde apparet,illa de Melchisedeco mystice, de Christo autem literaliter & vere enuntiari, quemadmodum analogia, & proportio typi ac veritatis id ipsum luculenter evincit ac demonstrat. Reliqua vero illius versus tertii verba ad officium sacerdotale Christi, in persona Melchisedeci adumbratum, recte referuntur, qui Saluator noster, ideo Sacerdos in perpetuum manere dicitur, quia ipsi nullus alius in officii illius dignitate, successurus est unquam, cui proinde sit laus & honor in secula.
units.tr: The third and last question, namely what is the genuine sense of those words by which Melchisedec, in Heb. 7:3, "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like to the Son of God, is said to remain a priest continually," is this: Ostorrodius refers the whole of that verse to the priesthood of Melchisedec and of Christ, and seems to lay down this sense of those words: that just as Melchisedec obtained the priesthood not by the privilege of his lineage but by the singular grace of God, and no one is read to have succeeded him, so also Christ has neither predecessor nor successor in that office. And so he boldly, indeed far too shamelessly, says that the ignorance and gross carelessness of those who interpret those words of the essence of Christ, as if he had no mother in heaven and no father on earth, is "detestable," because this cannot hold of Melchisedec, who nevertheless is made like to the Son of God. We, on the contrary, judge that those words are to be referred partly to the person, partly to the priesthood of Melchisedec and of Christ. To the person, insofar as each is introduced as "without father, without mother, without recorded lineage, having neither beginning nor end of life." All these things are said of Melchisedec not simply but in a certain respect, and insofar as he was a type of the person of Christ; or not because he was really such, but because holy Scripture represents him as such, since it has told neither his father, nor his mother, nor his lineage, nor his origin or death, but, having set all these aside as dissimilar, has presented him as "without mother, without father" [ἀμήτωρ, ἀπάτωρ], so that by this type it might show that Christ is really such. All these things, moreover, are stated most truly of Christ, as the fulfilment of the preceding type. For he, according to the flesh, was born not by natural propagation, which comes about through the agency of a man, but was conceived without a father from the Holy Spirit, that is, by his operation, and was made of a woman; while according to the divine nature he is the eternal Son of God. Therefore in respect of the diverse natures he is most truly called without father and without mother. But since the same Christ is true and eternal God, begotten from the Father from eternity by an inexplicable generation, how, I ask, could a beginning of days or an end of life belong to him, or who could describe his genealogy? Hence it is plain that those things are most truly said of the person of Melchisedec and of Christ, although of the former typically and of the latter literally, and are explained as "the word of Christ's teaching" [Χριστος λογος διηγησις]. To which is added this, that no one is said to lack father, mother and family by reason of office, but by reason of nature; nor are priests, as priests, but as men, considered to have a father, mother and lineage; and that the Apostle denies that he had "a beginning and end of priesthood," but says he had "a beginning and end of life." Nor does that feeble argument of the Adversary, that those things cannot properly belong to Melchisedec, who nevertheless is made like to Christ, overturn this exposition. For since all these things are said of Melchisedec as a type of Christ, who is said to have been made like the Son of God, that is, made similar, not in substance but in the manner and mode of historical narration, it follows that those things are said of Melchisedec mystically, but of Christ literally and truly, as the analogy and proportion of type and truth clearly prove and demonstrate. The remaining words of that third verse, however, are rightly referred to the priestly office of Christ, prefigured in the person of Melchisedec; and our Saviour is said to remain "a priest continually" for this reason, that no other will ever succeed him in the dignity of that office, to whom therefore be praise and honour for ever and ever.

units.la: Restaret adhuc Institutionum illarum caput quadragesimum primum, quod est de Ecclesia, examinandum: verum, quia Adversarius toto illo capite, grauissimos Pontificiorum & Anabaptistarum errores impugnat, ideo nostri instituti ac propositi non esse iudico, analysin aut examen eorum, quae ibi ab ipso disputantur, licet quaedam etiam a veritate aliena inferantur, instituere, ac proinde finem scribendi facio. Deus Opt. Max. pro ineffabili sua misericordia & gratia, veritatis caelestis luce, mentes nostras indies magis ac magis illuminet, Spiritus sui [Greek] nobis adaugeat, errantes in viam salutis & iustitiae reuocet, ac in vera ac salutari Christi agnitione confirmet, errorum ac sophismatum praestigias dissipet, nocentissima illa schismata & dissidia, omniaque illorum semina, ex Ecclesia extirpet, eamque benigne ac potenter protegat, ad nominis sui gloriam, & omnium electorum salutem. Amen.
units.tr: There remained, indeed, the fortieth-first chapter of those Institutes, which concerns the Church, to be examined; but since the Adversary in that whole chapter attacks the most grievous errors of the Papists and the Anabaptists, I judge that it is not part of my purpose and plan to set out an analysis or examination of those things which he disputes there, although some things foreign to the truth are also introduced; and accordingly I make an end of writing. May God, most good and great, by his ineffable mercy and grace, daily illuminate our minds more and more with the light of heavenly truth, increase in us his Spirit, recall those who wander into the way of salvation and righteousness, confirm them in the true and saving knowledge of Christ, dispel the deceptions of errors and sophisms, root out from the Church those most harmful schisms and dissensions and all their seeds, and graciously and mightily protect her, to the glory of his name and the salvation of all the elect. Amen.

Reliqua doctrina capita, quibus iustificationis nostrae coram Deo, modus & ratio ab Aduersario explicatur, examinantur: & quaestiones illae, An videlicet homo in hac vita Christum possit imitari? deinde: An homo in hac vita Christum perfecte imitari possit? seu: An homo in hac vita perfectam obedientiam praeceptis Dei per Christum latis praestare possit? denique: An illa obedientia quae praeceptis Christi praestatur: seu imitatio illa Christi, homini ad iustitiam imputetur, sic ut homo per eam iustificetur? breviter excutiuntur, veritas defenditur, falsitas refutatur 498
units.tr: 36. The remaining heads of doctrine by which the opponent explains the manner and method of our justification before God are examined; and those questions are briefly reviewed: whether man in this life can imitate Christ; then, whether man in this life can perfectly imitate Christ; or whether man in this life can render perfect obedience to the precepts of God given through Christ; and finally, whether that obedience which is rendered to the precepts of Christ, or that imitation of Christ, is imputed to man for righteousness, so that man is justified by it; the truth is defended and the falsehood refuted, page 498

units.la: 37. Duae illae quaestiones controversae: I. An dignitas illa & maiestas Regia Christi praecipua sit causa, propter quam ille Seruator & Deus noster, ac Dei Filius sit, & in sacris Scripturis appelletur? II. An Sacerdotium Christi nihil aliud sit quam Regij muneris Christi administratio, ac proinde non proprie, sed figurate intelligendum? breviter explicantur, veritas defenditur, ac falsitas refutatur 509. 510
units.tr: 37. Those two controverted questions: I. Whether that royal dignity and majesty of Christ is the chief cause on account of which he is our Saviour and God, and the Son of God, and is so called in the holy Scriptures? II. Whether the priesthood of Christ is nothing other than the exercise of his royal office, and therefore is to be understood not properly but figuratively? These are briefly explained, the truth is defended, and the falsehood refuted, pages 509, 510

units.la: 38. Tres illae quaestiones, I. Qualenam corpus post resurrectionem ex mortuis habuerit Christus, ac proinde qualia corpora etiam nos habituri simus? II. An & quando Regnum Christi finem sit habiturum? III. Quisnam verborum illorum, quibus Melchisedec sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, nec initium dierum, nec vitae finem habens, assimilatus Filio Dei, Sacerdos in aeternum manere dicitur, sit sensus: excutiuntur, veritas explicatur ac defenditur, falsitas refutatur. 524
units.tr: 38. Those three questions: I. What kind of body Christ had after his resurrection from the dead, and therefore what kind of bodies we too shall have? II. Whether and when the Kingdom of Christ will have an end? III. What is the sense of those words by which Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, and made like the Son of God, is said to remain a priest for ever? These are examined, the truth is explained and defended, and the falsehood refuted, page 524.

units.la: Quum huius operis author procul esset à nobis, & inter excudendum, multa occurrerent quæ nobis faciesserunt negotium, præsertim operarum incuriâ, factum est vt tum in citationibus locorum Scripturæ, tum in tota disputatione non pauca emendatione digna, quantum ad artem nostram, deprehenderentur. Hæc vt feras, vel corrigas, vehementer à te petimus, tantisperdum auctoris ipsius auxilio alteram editionem emendatiorem, Christo annuente moliemur. Nec enim quædam annotare, reliqua supprimere libet, quæ pro benignitate tua condonare, vel facilè tollere potes. Vale.
units.tr: Since the author of this work was far away from us, and while the book was being printed many problems arose that caused us difficulty, especially through the carelessness of the proofreaders, it happened that not a few things in the citations of Scripture passages, as well as throughout the discussion, were found to need correction, so far as our craft is concerned. We earnestly ask you to bear with these errors or to correct them. Meanwhile, with the author's own help, and with Christ's assent, we shall prepare a second edition that is more accurate. For we do not wish to note some things and leave out the rest; you can readily pardon or remove them, as you are kind. Farewell.
